But since he was mocked by everyone for his unsightly limp, and he understood himself to be unfit for handling political affairs, he grew weary of the military and political life to which he had hitherto been more than sufficiently devoted, and resolved to change the manner of his former life and take up another. It happened that there came into his hands the Legends, most full of lies, which people commonly call the Lives or Flowers of the Saints; for he was of such dull intellect that he could neither understand nor grasp higher things. Yet these he read most eagerly, as superstitious men do, and such religious fervour came over him as he read that he began to think of founding a new Order. So rightly did that man say: Despair makes a monk.

units.la: Vt autem persuaderent Iesuitæ hominibus, non casu aut fortuito cogitationes has in animo Loyolæ de novo instituendo Ordine ortas fuisse, fingunt, ut res in maiore admiratione & authoritate esset, B. Mariam Deiparam, portantem in ulnis puerulum Iesum, apparuisse Ignatio, eumq; ut in Filij Iesu honorem, Societatem sex seu Ordinem institueret, hortatam esse, simulque promisisse, sibi & Socijs indulgentissimam matrem, adiutricem & promotricem futuram.
units.tr: Now, to persuade people that these thoughts of founding a new Order arose in Loyola's mind not by chance or accident, the Jesuits make up a story, so that the matter might be held in greater admiration and authority: that the Blessed Virgin Mary, carrying the little child Jesus in her arms, appeared to Ignatius, and exhorted him to found the Society, or Order, in honour of her Son Jesus, and at the same time promised that she would be a most indulgent mother, helper and promoter to him and his companions.

units.la: Anno igitur aetatis suae 26. domo, patria ac propriis laribus relictis, ita se comparat Ignatius, tanquam ad Ducem Nagera seu Naiarae profecturus esset, reversus autem ad templum Deiparae virgini dedicatum, quod Montem ferratum vocant, concessit, ibique vestibus pretiosioribus exutus, laceras ac viles induit, in quibus rigidissimam aliquandiu vitam egit. Delituit etiam per tempus aliquod solitarius in specu quodam ad littus fluvii per campum Maurefanum decurrentis: ibique de asperiore vita incunda, & de peregrinatione Hierosolymitana secum ipse deliberans, viatorum & pauperis peregrini habitum tandem coemit, sparteos nimirum calceos, talarem e sacco tunicam, funemque pro balteo, tornatilem baculum, & in usum aquae cucurbitam. Vt igitur Minoresam accessit, cppidúmque hoc amictu ingressus est, ad publicum infimae plebis hospitium precario se contulit, ibique paupertatis & poenitentiae studio inter egentes ac sordidos vitam exorsus est. Ita quidem Matthaeus & Ribadeneira: quorum tamen hic alibi de eodem scribit, eum delectatum fuisse cultu corporis mundo, & alienum fuisse a sordibus. Hanc autem contradictionem Ignatiani tollere conantur distinguendo tempora: quo tamen ipsi praeclare arguunt hypocrisin Ignatij. Vir bonus semper fui similis est & esse debet, tum in aliis, tum in victu & cultu corporis. Ignatius igitur ut homines in suam naufam pelliceret, primum usus est vestitu sordido, post naufus id quod voluerat, abiecit laceram penulam, ut Monachus ille rete, quo se aliquandiu texerat, Pontificatum adeptus, quod decreuit, captum a se pisces, cui diu insidiatus esset.
units.tr: So in the twenty-sixth year of his age, having left his home, country and own hearth, Ignatius made ready as if he were about to set out for the Duke of Nájera or Nájera, and then, turning back to the temple dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, which they call Montserrat, he withdrew there, and, stripping off his more costly clothes, put on ragged and mean ones, in which for some time he lived a most rigid life. He also lay hidden for some time as a solitary in a certain cave by the bank of a river that runs through the Moorish plain; and there, deliberating with himself about a harsher way of life and about a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, he at last bought the dress of a traveller and a poor pilgrim: namely, sandals of esparto grass, a tunic of sackcloth down to the ankles, a rope for a belt, a turned staff, and a gourd for water. So when he came to Manresa and entered the town dressed in this way, he betook himself as a beggar to the public hostel of the lowest common people, and there began his life among the needy and squalid, in zeal for poverty and penance. Thus indeed Matthaeus and Ribadeneira report; but Ribadeneira writes elsewhere about the same man that he delighted in clean bodily dress and was far from squalor. The Ignatians try to remove this contradiction by distinguishing the times; yet by doing so they clearly expose the hypocrisy of Ignatius. A good man is and must always be the same, both in other things and in food and bodily dress. Ignatius, therefore, in order to lure men into his net, first used a squalid garb; afterwards, when he had what he wanted, he cast off the ragged cloak, like that monk who, having obtained the Papacy, cast aside the net with which he had covered himself for some time, deciding that the fish he had caught was the one he had long lain in wait for.

units.la: Victum quoque ostiatim emendicavit quotidie: totam hebdomadam, excepto die Dominico, ieiunavit, in ipso cibatu simplici pane contentus: humo nuda cubavit, auctoque supplicio singulis diebus ter se flagellis quam acerrime excedit: sacrificio quoque matutino, vesperarum item & Completorij officijs interfuit assidue. Vexatus autem diuturna & periculosa aegrotatione, demum ita convaluit, ut ex reliquijs morbi dolore stomachi cruciaretur, ob eamque causam calceos induit, & panni crassioris tunica cinerea, & capitis tegumento contra hyemem se munivit.
units.tr: He also begged for his food from door to door every day. For the whole week, except Sunday, he fasted, content with plain bread alone as his food. He slept on the bare ground, and, increasing his penance, he scourged himself three times a day with the utmost severity. He also attended the morning sacrifice of the Mass and the Vespers and Compline services without fail. Afterwards he was afflicted by a long and dangerous illness, and though he recovered at last, the pain in his stomach that remained from the sickness tormented him. For this reason he put on shoes and a coarse grey tunic, and protected his head with a covering against the winter.

units.la: In hac palaestra cum se ad tempus exercuisset, inde in pauperis peregrini habitu Hierosolymam proficisci constituit, Christi sepulchri adorandi & caeteralocaví fendi gratia. Hoc igitur mentis propositio sub initium anni 1523. Minoresa prosectus Barcinonem, indeque Romam, ac tandem Venetias pervenit. Venetijs in Cyprum insulam, ac deinde in Palaestinam vectus, demum Hierosolymam accessit, & loca illa, quae vocant sacra, invisit, ijsque locis usque adeo delectatus fuit, ut censitueret omnem aetatem suam reliquam illic consumere: quia vero multi eum ab hoc instituto dehortabantur, cum reliquis peregrinis naves ascendit, & in Hispaniam redijt.
units.tr: After he had trained himself in this school for a time, he resolved to set out for Jerusalem in the dress of a poor pilgrim, to worship at the sepulchre of Christ and to visit the other holy places. This purpose was formed at the beginning of the year 1523. He set out, and came first to Barcelona, then to Rome, and at last to Venice. From Venice he sailed to the island of Cyprus and then to Palestine, and at last he reached Jerusalem and visited the places that are called holy. He was so delighted with those places that he decided to spend the rest of his life there. But since many people advised him against this plan, he boarded a ship with the other pilgrims and returned to Spain.

units.la: Quia vero intelligebat ad eam vitae rationem, quam animo proposuerat, litterarum cognitionem, quarum hactenus nullam prorsus habuerat, imo ne scribere quidem norat, plurimum valere, animum ad eam rem appulit. Vt igitur Barcinonem revertit, anno Christi 1524. aetatis autem 33. repuerascere & elementarius fieri coepit. Tam autem obtusi & stupidi ingenij erat, ut rudimenta Grammaticae, verborum item ac nominum inflexiones vix edissere posset: ex quo fiebat, non solum ut nihil novi mandare memoriae posset, sed etiam ut si quid antea impressum esset, id ipsum confestim deleretur. Nihilominus tamen in Grammaticalibus praeceptis addiscendis strenue perrexit, & fructum mediocrem inde percepit, Communi plutumque ad graviora studia se contulit. Ibi artium curriculum inijt non admodum felici successu: nam praepropera festinatione, sine omni iudicio & delectu, nullo servato vel ordine vel discrimine disciplinae, multa & varia uno eodemque tempore adgressus est: in Logicis terminos, quos vocant, in Physicis Albertum, in Theologia Magistrum sententiarum, qui libri tum in Hispania praelegebantur, evolvere, & plures quotidie in Scholis audire coepit interpretes, quod tamen ei ad id, quod cupiebat assequi, maximo impedimento fuit: nam cum avide sequeretur omnia, nihil propemodum assequebatur: iuxta tritum proverbium, In omnibus aliquid, in toto nihil.
units.tr: Since he understood that for the way of life he had chosen he needed knowledge of letters, of which he had none at all until then, and indeed did not even know how to write, he set his mind to this with great effort. So when he returned to Barcelona, in the year of Christ 1524, at the age of thirty-three, he began to become a boy again and to learn the elements. His mind was so dull and slow that he could scarcely recite the rudiments of grammar or the inflections of verbs and nouns. As a result he could not commit anything new to memory, and whatever he had learned before was at once wiped out. Nevertheless he pressed on energetically in learning the precepts of grammar, and gained a moderate measure of progress from them. Then he turned, as is common, to more serious studies. There he began the course of the arts, but without any great success. In his headlong haste, without judgement or selection, and without keeping any order or distinction in his studies, he took up many different subjects at one and the same time. In logic he worked through the so-called terms, in physics Albertus, and in theology the Master of the Sentences, which books were then lectured on in Spain. He also began to hear several lecturers every day in the schools. Yet this was a very great hindrance to what he wished to achieve. For while he eagerly pursued everything, he achieved almost nothing, according to the well-worn proverb: In everything something, in the whole nothing.

units.la: Cum autem in vili suo habitu coopertus sacco, publice homines ad poenitentiam hortaretur, nulla accepta ab Episcopis concionandi licentia, nec eruditione sufficiente praeditus esset, bis in carcerem coniectus fuit, semel Compluti, deinde Salmanticae, quo Complluto relicto concesserat, & ab Inquisitoribus, de doctrina & novo quodam vitae genere suspectus, examinatus fuit.
units.tr: While he went about in his wretched garb, covered with sackcloth, exhorting people publicly to repentance, without having received a licence to preach from the bishops, and without having sufficient learning, he was twice thrown into prison: once at Complutum, and then at Salamanca, to which he had withdrawn after leaving Complutum. There he was examined by the Inquisitors, who suspected him of his teaching and of a new kind of way of life.

units.la: Interrogationes autem Inquisitorum, Ignatio in carcere propositae, hae fuerint.
units.tr: The questions the Inquisitors put to Ignatius in prison were these.

units.la: I. Utrum credat, sacram scripturam esse doctrinam imperfectam, mutilam, mancam, quae non contineat omnia, ad salutem, fidem, mores pie vivendi pertinentia. Affirmavit Ignatius. II. Utrum credat, defectum illum farciendum esse assumendo traditiones. Affirmavit Ignatius. III. Utrum credat, sacram scripturam in illis quae continet & proponit, esse veluti nasum cereum, non praebentem certam aliquam & immotam sententiam, sed quae in quamvis interpretationem flecti possit. Affirmavit Ignatius. IV. Utrum recte fiat, quod in universum Laici a lectione sacrarum literarum arceantur. Affirmavit Ignatius. V. Utrum lectio S. Scripturae non tantum non sit utilis, sed multis modis perniciosa. Affirmavit Ignatius. VI. Utrum credat, quod post susceptum Baptismum peccatum in renatis nullum remaneat, sive quod apertum sit, sive quod tegatur vel aperiatur. Affirmavit Ignatius. VII. Utrum credat, quod concupiscentia, quae reliqua est in renatis, etsi repugnet legi Dei, tamen non sit proprie, vere, in se vel ex se, & sua natura, peccatum. Affirmavit Iesuita. VIII. Utrum credat, falsum esse, quod peccatum sit, quicquid legi Dei repugnet. Affirmavit Ignatius. IX. Utrum graviùs peccent homines violantes Ecclesiae praecepta quam committentes ea, quae legi Dei repugnant. Affirmavit Iesuita. X. Utrum renati in hac vita possint suis operibus legis perfectionem consequi. Affirmavit Ignatius. XI. Utrum doctrina Evangelij proprie sit, Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Affirmavit Ignatius. XII. Utrum in rebus ad salutem pertinentibus, liberum arbitrium tantum valeat, ut nihil homo agere possit quicquam ipsomet non annuente, & ad divinae gratiae susceptionem non parato, & prompto. Affirmavit Ignatius. XIII. Utrum fides sit firmissima assensio non tantum eorum, quae in scriptura patefacta sunt, verum etiam illorum, quae sine scripto in manus tradita sunt. Affirmavit Iesuita. XIV. Utrum credat, quod justus ex fide vivens non habeat illud in Christo, sed ex operationibus suis. Affirmavit Ignatius. XV. Utrum credat, quod fides justificans illam formam seu vim non habeat ex Christo, quem apprehendit & posfidet, sed ex charitate. Affirmavit Ignatius. XVI. Utrum credat, justificationem nihil aliud esse quam justitiae acquisitionem, vel, si philosophice loquendum sit, motum ad justitiam. Affirmavit Ignatius. XVII. Utrum credat, quod misericordia Dei in Christo, in qua nostra salus consistit, haec sit, quod Deus recte operantibus, hoc est, legem implentibus vitam aeternam promiserit. Affirmavit Ignatius. XVIII. Utrum homo possit satis facere pro peccatis Deo, secundum mensuram proportionis, etiamsi offensio sit infinita & satisfactio nostra finita. Affirmavit Iesuita. XIX. Utrum Sancti invocandi sint, ut pro nobis apud Deum intercedant. Affirmavit Ignatius. XX. Utrum invocatio Sanctorum recipienda & concedenda, etiamsi nusquam de ea scriptura docet. Assirmavit. XXI. Utrum traditiones Ecclesiae, etsi ex scriptura probari non possunt, parem tamen authoritatem habeant, & eadem fide sint credenda, sicut illa, quae manifesta habent in scriptura, testimonia. Affirmavit Ignatius. XXII. Utrum recte adorentur imagines. Affirmavit Iesuita. XXIII. Utrum matrimonij doctrina impudicitiae januam aperiat, ac animis libidinis faces subministret. Affirmavit Ignatius. XXIV. Utrum eorum qui voverint qui voverint cælibatum, & se continere non possint, legitimæ nuptiæ appellandæ sint, an contra fornicatio, incestus, summum nefas ac adulterium? Affirmavit Ignatius. XXV. Utrum credat purgatorium? Affirmavit Iesuita. XXVI. Utrum credat, Pontificum Romanorum perpetuä successionem apertum indicium esse Catholicæ Ecclesiæ, & fidei Apostolicæ. Affirmavit Ignatius. XXVII. Utrum credat, penes Ecclesiam esse quasdam etiam in sacris literis expressa commutandi authoritatem, nonnulla instituendi parem facultatem, ideoque non minorem illi quàm expresso Dei verbo vindicandam esse authoritatem. Affirmavit Iesuita. XXVIII. Utrum credat, panem Cœnæ in verum Christi corpus transsubstantiari vi consecrationis. Affirmavit. XXIX. Utrum tota quantitas dimensiva corporis Christi sit in sacramento. Affirmavit Ignatius.
units.tr: (1) Whether he believes that Holy Scripture is an imperfect, mutilated and maimed teaching, which does not contain everything pertaining to salvation, faith, and the morals of living piously. Ignatius affirmed it. (2) Whether he believes that this defect is to be supplied by the assumption of traditions. Ignatius affirmed it. (3) Whether he believes that Holy Scripture, in the matters it contains and sets forth, is like a waxen nose, not offering any certain and fixed sense, but one that can be bent to any interpretation. Ignatius affirmed it. (4) Whether it is right that laymen in general should be kept from reading the Holy Scriptures. Ignatius affirmed it. (5) Whether the reading of Holy Scripture is not only not useful, but harmful in many ways. Ignatius affirmed it. (6) Whether he believes that after baptism no sin remains in the reborn, whether it is open or hidden, covered or uncovered. Ignatius affirmed it. (7) Whether he believes that the concupiscence which remains in the reborn, although it resists the law of God, is not properly, truly, in itself or of itself, and by its nature, sin. The Jesuit affirmed it. (8) Whether he believes it false that whatever resists the law of God is sin. Ignatius affirmed it. (9) Whether men sin more gravely by violating the precepts of the Church than by committing those things which resist the law of God. The Jesuit affirmed it. (10) Whether the reborn in this life can by their works attain the perfection of the law. Ignatius affirmed it. (11) Whether the teaching of the Gospel is properly: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Ignatius affirmed it. (12) Whether in matters pertaining to salvation free will has such power that a man can do nothing without his own consent, and without being prepared and ready to receive divine grace. Ignatius affirmed it. (13) Whether faith is the firmest assent not only to those things which are made known in Scripture, but also to those which have been handed down by word of mouth without writing. The Jesuit affirmed it. (14) Whether he believes that the righteous man who lives by faith does not have his life in Christ, but from his own works. Ignatius affirmed it. (15) Whether he believes that justifying faith does not have that form or power from Christ, whom it apprehends and possesses, but from charity. Ignatius affirmed it. (16) Whether he believes that justification is nothing other than the acquisition of righteousness, or, if one must speak philosophically, a motion towards righteousness. Ignatius affirmed it. (17) Whether he believes that the mercy of God in Christ, in which our salvation consists, is this: that God has promised eternal life to those who work rightly, that is, who fulfil the law. Ignatius affirmed it. (18) Whether man can make sufficient satisfaction to God for sins, according to the measure of proportion, even though the offence is infinite and our satisfaction finite. The Jesuit affirmed it. (19) Whether the saints are to be invoked, that they may intercede for us with God. Ignatius affirmed it. (20) Whether the invocation of the saints is to be accepted and allowed, even though Scripture nowhere teaches it. He affirmed it. (21) Whether the traditions of the Church, even though they cannot be proved from Scripture, nevertheless have equal authority and are to be believed with the same faith as those things which have clear testimonies in Scripture. Ignatius affirmed it. (22) Whether images are rightly adored. The Jesuit affirmed it. (23) Whether the doctrine of marriage opens the door to impurity and supplies the torches of lust to minds. Ignatius affirmed it. (24) Whether the marriages of those who have vowed celibacy, and who cannot contain themselves, are to be called lawful marriages, or on the contrary fornication, incest, the greatest wickedness and adultery? Ignatius affirmed it. (25) Whether he believes in purgatory. The Jesuit affirmed it. (26) Whether he believes that the perpetual succession of the Roman Pontiffs is a clear sign of the Catholic Church and of the apostolic faith. Ignatius affirmed it. (27) Whether he believes that the Church has an authority to change certain things even expressed in the sacred letters, and an equal power to institute some things, and therefore that this authority is to be claimed for her no less than for the express word of God. The Jesuit affirmed it. (28) Whether he believes that the bread of the Supper is transubstantiated into the true body of Christ by the power of consecration. He affirmed it. (29) Whether the whole dimensive quantity of the body of Christ is in the sacrament. Ignatius affirmed it.

units.la: Utrobique igitur, tam Compluti, quàm Salmanticæ, Pontificiæ doctrinæ addictissimus inventus, extra omnem noxam e custodia dimissus fuit.
units.tr: Therefore, since he was found most devoted to Papist doctrine both at Complutum and at Salamanca, he was released from custody, free of all blame.

units.la: Salmantica relicta Lutetiam Parisiorum se contulit sub initium anni 1528, ibi sese totum litteris dedit, ac tandem Magister artium creatus est.
units.tr: Having left Salamanca, he betook himself to Paris at the beginning of the year 1528, where he devoted himself wholly to letters, and at last was created Master of Arts.

units.la: Quia vero illic loci paupertatem sustabatur, stipem oftiatim colligebat, pueros gratis erudiebat, omnibus ultro, nulla petita mercede, sua obsequia, labores & studia offerebat, sicque aliquam apud populum rudem existimationem sibi comparavit: factum est, ut nonnulli studiosi, amore eius incensi, illi se socios & imitatores adiunxerint. Primus fuit Petrus Faber Allobrox, pago Villareto Gebennensis diœcesis humili loco natus, qui iam antea se in solitudines abdere, ibique radicibus herbarum vivere decreverat. Secundus fuit Franciscus Xaverius nobilis Cantaber, qui iam antea Ignatij hypocriticam vitam vehementer irrisit. Hos deinde imitati sunt Iacobus Laines Segutinus, Alfonsus Salmeron Toletanus, Græcis & Latinis literis mediocriter eruditus. Nicolaus Bobadilla Placentinus, Simon Rodericius Lusitanus, & post aliquanto Claudius Iaius Gebennensis, & Ioannes Coduncius Ebredunensis, Paschasiusque Broëtus Ambianensis, Fabri præcipue monitis permoti.
units.tr: Since he was in great poverty there, he begged alms from door to door, taught children for nothing, and offered all people, without asking any payment, his services, labour and study. In this way he won for himself some reputation among the unlearned people. It came about that several eager students, fired with love for him, joined themselves to him as companions and imitators. The first was Peter Faber, a Savoyard, born of humble parents in the village of Villaret in the diocese of Geneva, who had already decided to withdraw into solitude and live on the roots of herbs. The second was Francis Xavier, a noble Cantabrian, who had already mocked Ignatius's hypocritical way of life bitterly. After them came James Laynez of Segovia, Alfonso Salmerón of Toledo, moderately learned in Greek and Latin literature, Nicholas Bobadilla of Piacenza, Simon Rodrigues of Portugal, and a little later Claude Jay of Geneva, John Codure of Embrun, and Paschasius Broët of Amiens, moved chiefly by the admonitions of Faber.

units.la: Progressu temporis Imagines aliquot horum Patrum scitè ære expressas, & ad imitationem Symboli Apostolorum, unicuique symbolum additum est. Ex his picturis prima plena impietatis est, in qua visuntur nescio qui Principes vel Reges à sinistra parte, una cum Pontifice Romano à dextra & Cardinalibus, ac universo clero genibus flexis & manibus sublatis nescio quid adorare. Neque enim puto preces fundi ad literas in luce coruscæ cum crucis imaguncula effictas. Etsi autem infra scriptum est, In nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur cœlestium, terrestrium & infernorum: Mysterium tamen huius dicti non omnibus notum est. Hoc enim volunt dicere, Quòd Papa maior sit omni aliâ creatura, ac illius potestas se extendat ad cœlestia, terrestria ac infernalia, ut apud Antoninum Florentinum in Summa eius videre est. Unde etiam prope Papam ignis purgatorius conspicitur, in quo excoquuntur nescio qui miseri homines. Nam animas quis esse putet, cùm faciem, barba & ora intueatur? Ignatij symbolum est, Ad maiorem Dei gloriam: quo ipso indicatur, ab hoc milite Ordinem institutum & introductum, qui gloriam Dei ante à Lutheranis obscuratam illustret. Deum autem intellige non illum, quem adorant omnes fideles, sed Felini Deum, id est, Papam, qui possit secundum Decium & Gomesium facere omnia, quæ Deus facit. Symbolum Iacobi Laynesij est: Apprehendite disciplinam, à Iesuitis scilicet præscriptam. Franciscus Borgia usurpavit, A te quid volui super terram: nihil videlicet aliud voluit quàm superstitionum multarum confirmationem & idololatriæ horrendæ propagationem. Quartus Pater Euerhardus Mercurianus hoc sibi adscribi voluit, In nomine tuo salvum me fac. Si de Iesu solo loquuntur, sed
units.tr: As time went on, some images of these Fathers, neatly engraved in bronze, were produced, and, in imitation of the Apostles' Creed, a motto was added to each one. Of these pictures the first is wholly impious. In it one can see I know not what princes or kings on the left side, together with the Roman Pontiff on the right and the Cardinals, and the whole clergy, kneeling with hands raised, adoring I know not what. For I do not think prayers are poured out to a little image of the cross, figured in the light of the letters gleaming. Although it is written below, In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, the mystery of this saying is not known to everyone. For they mean by it that the Pope is greater than every other creature, and that his power extends to heavenly, earthly and infernal things, as may be seen in Antoninus of Florence in his Summa. Hence also near the Pope a purgatorial fire is seen, in which I know not what wretched men are being refined. For who would think these are souls, when he looks at their faces, beards and mouths? The motto of Ignatius is To the greater glory of God, by which it is indicated that this soldier founded and introduced the Order to vindicate the glory of God, which had previously been obscured by the Lutherans. But understand by God not the God whom all the faithful adore, but the God of Felinus, that is, the Pope, who can, according to Decius and Gomesius, do all the things that God does. The motto of James Laynez is Lay hold on discipline, that is, of course, the discipline prescribed by the Jesuits. Francis Borgia used What have I wanted on earth but you? Clearly he wanted nothing else than the confirmation of many superstitions and the spreading of horrible idolatry. The fourth Father, Everard Mercurian, wished this to be ascribed to himself: In your name save me. If they speak only of Jesus, but

units.la: In responsione Sim. Stenij ad Ap. 1. giā Gratiam pro vita Ignatij Loyolæ pag. 241. cris suis haereticus est: si Maria intelligit, Calvinianis idololatra est. Francisci Xaverij symbolum mirificum est, Satis est, Domine, satis est, deceptionum scilicet et hypocriseos, vel linctus ulcerum. Alfonsi Salmeronis est, Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua. Fortasse Pontificem Romanum compellat: nam eloquia Dei sordes sunt Iesuitis, eloquia autem Paparum non tantum faucibus, sed etiam stomachis melle dulciora sunt. Nicolai Bobadillae symbolum est, Non confundar in aeternum. Sed confunduntur magis magisque ob sua tetra facinora, dolos, fraudes et mendacia, &c.
units.tr: In the reply of Simon Stenius to the Apologia ... (p. 241 of his "Gratia pro vita Ignatii Loyolae") he is a heretic; if he means Mary, he is an idolater in the eyes of the Calvinists. The motto of Francis Xavier is remarkable: It is enough, Lord, it is enough, that is, of deceptions and hypocrisy, or of ointment for ulcers. That of Alfonso Salmerón is How sweet are your words to my throat. Perhaps he is addressing the Roman Pontiff, for the words of God are filth to the Jesuits, while the words of the Popes are sweeter than honey not only to the throat but also to the stomach. The motto of Nicholas Bobadilla is I shall not be put to shame for ever. But they are put to shame more and more because of their foul crimes, deceits, frauds and lies, etc.

units.la: Hos socios nactus Loyola, quod iam diu moliebatur et agitabat animo, ipsa aggredi primo quoque tempore statuit: videlicet, ut Hierosolymam, cum Papae venia, repeteret, gentesque Turcicas ad Pontificios errores converteret et am cum mortis periculo, et in eandem sententiam socios suos, superstitiosos homines, facile adduxit. Cum igitur singuli peccata sua confessi essent et Eucharistiam sumpsissent in aede suburbana, quae Mons martyrum dicitur, voto se obstrinxerunt, emensis Theologiae spatiis, mundo renunciare, et in paupertate perpetua vivere: ac nominatim ad constitutam diem, Hierosolymam propter infidelium conversionem navigare: hoc vero propositum si non succederet, Romam redirent, suamque operam Papae in convertendis haereticis offerrent. Votum hoc ediderunt in dicto templo Anno 1534. 18. Calend. Septemb.
units.tr: Having gained these companions, Loyola decided to undertake at the first opportunity what he had long been planning and turning over in his mind: namely, to return to Jerusalem with the Pope's permission and to convert the Turkish peoples to the Papist errors, even at the risk of death. He easily brought his companions, superstitious men, to the same opinion. When each of them had confessed his sins and received the Eucharist in a church in the suburbs called Mons Martyrum, they bound themselves by a vow, once their studies in theology were completed, to renounce the world and live in perpetual poverty, and to sail to Jerusalem for the conversion of unbelievers on a fixed day. If this plan did not succeed, they would return to Rome and offer their labour to the Pope for the conversion of heretics. They published this vow in the said church in the year 1534, on the 18th day before the Kalends of September.

units.la: Sub finem anni 1536. itineri se se accingunt, et Venetias proficisci statuunt. Viam igitur capessunt suo quisque baculo innixi pedites. Vestitus erat omnium ut peregrinorum et pauperum: pendebat e scapulis mantica ex corio, in qua Biblia et Breviarium allervabantur. Rosaria palam gestabant e collo suspensa. Hoc habitu ad tertium Idus Ianuarias anni 1537. Venetias pervenerunt: Ibi valetudinarijs seu nosocomiis inter se distributis, aegrotos et pauperes curarunt, Confessiones audiverunt, Eucharistiam ministrarunt, quibus id per Sacerdotium licebat. Imo ne vilissima quidem et servilia corporibus pauperum curandis defugerunt ministeria: strauerunt lectulos, everterunt sordes, purgarunt scaphia, cadavera mortuorum sepelierunt, interdiu noctuque omnibus praesto erant, et his officijs mirifice apud quoscunque Venetijs se se insinuarunt.
units.tr: Towards the end of the year 1536 they made ready for the journey and resolved to set out for Venice. So each of them, leaning on his staff, set out on foot. All were dressed like pilgrims and beggars. From their shoulders hung a leather wallet in which the Bibles and the Breviary were carried. They openly wore rosaries hanging from their necks. In this dress they came to Venice on the 11th day before the Ides of January, 1537. There they divided the hospitals among themselves, tended the sick and the poor, heard confessions, and administered the Eucharist to those to whom this was allowed by their priesthood. Indeed they did not shrink from even the most menial and servile tasks in caring for the bodies of the poor: they made beds, cleaned filth, emptied chamber pots, buried the bodies of the dead, and were at hand to all day and night; and by these services they wonderfully insinuated themselves with all sorts of people in Venice.

units.la: Interea etiam de profectione Hierosolymitana deliberantes, primo omnium Romam ire constituunt, et a Papa ius tum ad sacros, quos vocant, Ordines, titulo voluntariae paupertatis, tum ad mansionem Hierosolymitanam petere.
units.tr: Meanwhile, deliberating also about the journey to Jerusalem, they first of all resolved to go to Rome and to ask of the Pope, both the right to the so-called sacred orders under the title of voluntary poverty, and a house in Jerusalem.

units.la: Nugantur hic Iesuitae, Ignatio non procul ab urbe templum ingresso, Deum Patrem illi se se ostendisse, et Iesu filio suo baiulanti crucem, et crudelissimis affecto supplicijs, praesentem Ignatium socios commendasse: cumque ille, eos in fidem ac patrocinium recepisset, ad Ignatium dixisse: Ego vobis Romae propitius ero: atque hoc ipsum vel inprimis fuisse causae, ob quam Ignatius postea confirmatae societati nomen Iesu indiderit: de quo paulo post plura.
units.tr: Here the Jesuits talk nonsense: that when Ignatius entered a church not far from the city, God the Father appeared to him, and commended to Ignatius, who was present, his Son Jesus, who was carrying the cross and had been subjected to the cruellest punishments; and when he had received them into his faith and protection, he said to Ignatius: "I shall be gracious to you at Rome." And this very thing, above all, was the cause for which Ignatius afterwards gave the name of Jesus to the society when it was confirmed. About this I shall say more shortly.

units.la: Urbem ingressi a Petro Ortizio Hispano Caesaris Legato ad Paulum III. Papam introducuntur, ab eoque post pedum osculla, omnia quae volebant de sacerdotio, deque Hierosolymitana Provincia a Papa impetrarunt: obsequia etiam, quae Pontifici offerebant in Apostolicis functionibus, non aspernatus est, instructos insuper pecunia eos a se dimisit.
units.tr: Having entered the city, they were introduced by Peter Ortiz, a Spaniard and envoy of the Emperor, to Pope Paul III, and after kissing his feet they obtained from him everything they wished concerning the priesthood and the province of Jerusalem. He did not disdain the services they offered the Pontiff in apostolic functions, and besides he dismissed them, furnished with money.

units.la: Quia vero navigationis et peregrinationis Hierosolymitanae consilia in irritum ceciderant, subinde autem aliqui ad Loyolae institutum aggregarentur, aliqui etiam a Papa varias in urbes mitterentur, visum est eis, ut de stabilienda Societate primo quoque tempore inter se consulerent. In unum igitur congregati locum, quaesitum inter alia est, placeretne ad vota duo, paupertatis et castitatis, tertium quoque perpetuae obedientiae adiungere, et e suo numero aliquem eligere, qui ceteris ampla cum potestate praeesset: et omnes unanimiter censuerunt, deligendum unum esse, cui omnes in terris, tanquam Christo, parerent, cuius in verba iurarent, & cuius denique nutum ac voluntatem sibi instar divini oraculi ducerent: placuerunt haec omnibus ac paulo post Ignatium elegerunt, eumque Generalem Præpositum appellarunt: Additum adhæc in eodem Conventu, ut Societatis candidati, cum aliis experimentis, tum vero præcipue peregrinatione, & infirmis publici alicuius valetudinarii probarentur. In hoc quoque Conventu tribus communibus votis quartumquoque additum est, ut paulo infra indicabitur.
units.tr: But since their plans for a voyage and pilgrimage to Jerusalem had come to nothing, and since some men kept joining Loyola's institute while others were sent by the Pope to various cities, it seemed good to them to consult together as soon as possible about establishing the Society. Gathered together in one place, it was asked among other things whether they should add to the two vows of poverty and chastity a third, of perpetual obedience, and choose from their own number one who would preside over the rest with full authority. All unanimously agreed that one should be chosen, whom all on earth should obey as they would Christ, whose words they should swear to, and whose nod and will they should regard as a divine oracle. These proposals pleased everyone, and shortly afterwards they chose Ignatius and called him General Superior. It was further added at the same assembly that candidates for the Society should be tested, not only by other trials, but above all by pilgrimage and by service to the sick in some public hospital. At this same assembly a fourth common vow was added to the three, as will be indicated a little further on.

units.la: Hæc & alia plura tum quidem ab eis decreta sunt, & Ignatio mandatum, ut ea in summam redacta, Papæ Apostolicæ auctoritate sancienda atque approbanda proponeret: deinde ut eadem ipse postea fusius explicaret ordinaretque, & quam accommodatissimas ad Societatis vocationem & spiritum leges canonesque perscriberet.
units.tr: These and many other matters were then decreed by them, and Ignatius was commissioned to reduce them to a summary and propose them for ratification and approval by the apostolic authority of the Pope; then he himself was to explain and arrange them more fully afterwards, and to write out the laws and canons best suited to the calling and spirit of the Society.

units.la: Post decem annos, quibus Generalatum administravit Ignatius, sub specie & prætextu humilitatis & modestiae cuiusdam sese Generalatu suo omnino abdicare constituit. Sociis igitur Romam evocatis, cum in consilium convenissent, exposuit, se, qui vitia sua noffet, & initio invitum, atque adeo coactum, Societatis gubernacula recepisse, perque Christi sanguinem petere atque obtestari sese, ut sine ullo sui respectu communi utilitati consulant, & quam primum sibi sufficiant virum & animo & corpore firmiorem: Et ut hoc libere faciatis, inquit: Ego in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti depono Generalatum meum simpliciter & absolute, meque abdico hoc munere privoque: & omnibus animae meae viribus obsecro tu Professos, tum si quos Professi adhibere ad hanc deliberationem volent, ut huic meo tam iusto desiderio faveant, piamque oblationem libenter admittant. Cum autem quisque metueret, ne forte alius sibi praeferretur, ut ventum est ad suffragia, omnium consensus in eo retinendo exstitit, qui olim in eligendo fuerat, modo publicam rem ordinaret, & leges Ordini vel Societati praescriberet. Ignatius, ne minus dicto audiens videretur, precibus Sociorum non invitus cessit, & hoc onus in se recepit: & scripsit libellum Exercitiorum spiritualium, itemque librum decem in partes distributum, in quo leges dedit Societati, & formam gubernationis praescripsit.
units.tr: Ten years after Ignatius had administered the generalate, he resolved to renounce it entirely, under the appearance and pretext of a certain humility and modesty. He therefore summoned the companions to Rome, and when they had met in council he explained that he, who knew his own faults, had at first accepted the government of the Society unwillingly and under a kind of compulsion. He begged and besought them, by the blood of Christ, to consider the common good without any regard for himself, and to provide as soon as possible a man firmer in spirit and body. So that they might do this freely, he said: "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I lay down my generalate simply and absolutely, and I renounce and deprive myself of this office. With all the strength of my soul I beg you, the professed members, and any professed members whom you may wish to call into this deliberation, to favour my so just desire and gladly accept my pious offer." But because each man feared that someone else would be preferred to him, when it came to the vote the consensus of all was to keep in office the very man who had been chosen before, provided that he would order the public affairs and prescribe laws for the Order or Society. Ignatius, lest he seem less obedient to them, yielded not unwillingly to the prayers of his companions and took this burden upon himself. He wrote the little book of the Spiritual Exercises, and likewise a book divided into ten parts, in which he gave laws to the Society and prescribed the form of its government.

units.la: Cum haec scriberem, venit mihi in mentem Augusti Caesaris factum, cui praefens fraus ac dolus Ignatij Loyolae non absimilis videtur, si parva magnis comparare licet. Augustus enim bis terve de reddenda Republica Senatui Romano cogitavit, ut hoc pacto invidiam & suspicionem Monarchiae a se declinaret. Cumque in Senatu sententiam suam exposuisset, Rationarium Imperij tanquam illud restituturus, Consulibus tradidit. Senatoribus autem sive per simulationem, sive metu, vel etiam ex composito, ut Ignatiani Socij, reclamantibus, variasque rationes afferentibus, cur Reipublicae Monarchia praestaret, in principatu perseveravit, Deos quoque, ut Ignatius, hominesque testatus, intra decennium se omnem administrationem depositurum. Sed cum ea tempora elapsa essent, rursusque eiurare velle Imperium simularet, Senatus alios decem annos, quibus in eodem magistratu esset, decrevit: atque iterum alios decem annos, quibus mortuus est, prorogavit.
units.tr: As I write this, the deed of Augustus Caesar comes to mind, to which the present fraud and deceit of Ignatius Loyola seems not unlike, if small things may be compared with great. For Augustus twice or thrice considered handing the commonwealth back to the Roman Senate, so that in this way he might turn away from himself the odium and suspicion of monarchy. And when he had set out his view in the Senate, he handed the account-books of the empire to the consuls, as if he were about to restore it. The senators, however, either through pretence, or from fear, or even by prior agreement, like the Ignatian companions, objected and advanced various reasons why monarchy was better for the commonwealth. He persisted in the principate, calling on the gods and on men, as Ignatius did, to witness that within ten years he would lay down all administration. But when those years had passed, and he again pretended that he wished to renounce the empire, the Senate decreed him another ten years in the same office, and again another ten years, after which he died.

units.la: Sub idem tempus Papa Socios aliquot ab Ignatio postulavit quos hinc inde mitteret: Idque peregrinationis Apostolicae fuit exordium: de quo, capite de propagatione Ordinis Iesuitici, infra plura dicentur.
units.tr: About the same time the Pope asked Ignatius for some companions whom he might send hither and thither. This was the beginning of the apostolic journeys, of which more will be said below, in the chapter on the propagation of the Jesuit Order.

units.la: Interea cum Societas magis magisque cresceret, Ignatius, ut erat illi iam antea a Sociis iniunctum, totius instituti formulam, latius postea explicandam, ad certa capita breviter redegit. Deinde nactus opportunitatem, quod Papa Tiburfereceperat, eam formulam auctoritate Apostolica eidem Papae obtulit per Contarenum Cardinalem. Eam ubi perlegit Papa, non improbavit quidem: sed tamen ne minus inconsulte aliquid statuisse videretur, totum negotium tribus Cardinalibus delegavit. Hi etsi approbationem dissuaderent Pontifici, & potius numerum religionum minuendum, quam augendum censerent, pervicerunt tamen Societas: nam Papa Societatem approbavit 5. Non. Octob. anno 1540. hac tamen conditione, ut in universum non plures quam sexaginta numerarentur Socij. Triennio tamen post liberum reliquit Pontifex Paulus III. Ignatio & successoribus, quotquot vellent in Societatem adscisere.
units.tr: Meanwhile, as the Society grew larger and larger, Ignatius, as the companions had already earlier enjoined upon him, briefly reduced the outline of the whole institute to certain heads, to be explained later at greater length. Then, seizing an opportunity, he offered this outline with apostolic authority to the same Pope through Cardinal Contarini. When the Pope had read it through, he did not disapprove, but lest he seem to have decided the matter without sufficient deliberation, he delegated the whole business to three cardinals. Although these advised the Pope against approval, and thought that the number of religious orders should be reduced rather than increased, they nevertheless prevailed in favour of the Society. For Pope Paul III approved the Society on 3 October 1540, on this condition: that in all not more than sixty members be counted. Three years later, however, Pope Paul III left Ignatius and his successors free to admit into the Society as many as they wished.

units.la: Regimen quoque & curam foeminarum a Societate sua prorsus depulit Loyola. Cum enim Elisabetha Rosella Barcinonensis, quae eius prima literarum studia fovera, sese Romam ex Hispania contulisset, ut cum aliis feminis ad normam & praescriptum illius viveret, ille curam foeminarum suscipere sese posse negavit: Papam quoque adiit, ac petijt, ut non ab illis modo, sed ab omnibus in perpetuum foeminarum collegijs gubernandis immunem Societatem esse iubeat. Annuit Papa & Societati ab eiusmodi munere vacationem in perpetuum dedit, eaque postea trium Bullis testata & confirmata est.
units.tr: Loyola also entirely removed from his Society the government and care of women. When Elisabetha Rosella of Barcelona, who had fostered his first literary studies, had travelled from Spain to Rome to live with other women according to his rule and direction, he refused to take charge of women. He also went to the Pope and asked that the Society be ordered to be exempt in perpetuity not only from these but from the governing of all colleges of women. The Pope assented, and granted the Society exemption from such a duty in perpetuity. This was afterwards attested and confirmed by three Bulls.

units.la: Praeterea Praelaturis & aliis honoribus Ecclesiasticis in Societatem suam Loyola prorsus omnem aditum obstruere conatus est, sed frustra; ut suo loco indicabitur.
units.tr: Moreover, Loyola tried with all his might to block the Society's access to prelacies and other ecclesiastical honours, but in vain, as will be shown in its place.

units.la: Febri autem ardente correptus, ut intima urerentur eius praecordia, obiit Ignatius Iesuitarum Patriarcha, post Solis ortum prima, feria sexta, prid. Calend. Augusti, anno post Christum natum 1556, anno aetatis 65, suae conversionis 35, confirmatae vero Societatis 16, quo tempore iam tum ab ipso constitutae numerabantur Provinciae 12. & in iis varia Ordinis domicilia fere centum.
units.tr: Seized by a burning fever, so that his inmost parts were consumed, Ignatius, patriarch of the Jesuits, died after sunrise, at the first hour, on Friday, the day before the Kalends of August, in the year of Christ 1556, in the sixty-fifth year of his age, the thirty-fifth of his conversion, and the sixteenth since the Society was confirmed. At that time twelve provinces were already counted as founded by him, and in them about a hundred various houses of the Order.

units.la: Maffaeus, qui Ignatij Loyolae vitam descripsit, lib. 2. cap. 23. placide ipsum defunctum refert. At Hafenmullerus, qui aliquot annis & ipse Iesuita fuit, & in multis Iesuitarum Collegiis vixit, in fine Iesuiticae suae historiae sancte testatur, Turrianum Iesuitam saepe dixisse sibi, Ignatium in coena, prandio, Missa, in recreationibus etiam ita a daemonibus exagitatum, ut magna copia frigidissimum mortis sudorem fuderit. Bobadillam quoque Iesuitam saepe fallum, Loyolam saepius conquestum, se nunquam & nullibi a daemonibus tutum esse posse. Octavianum Iesuitam, Romae ministrum, seu Novitiorum Oeconomum, dixisse sibi, Sanctus erat pater noster Ignatius: sed circa agonem mortis ita premebatur, quasi febri correptus esset, & suspirans dixit: Multa bona contuli in Ecclesiam Romanam: multas nostrorum provincias, Collegia multa, domus, residentias & opes Societatis nostrae vidi: sed haec omnia me deserunt, & quo me vertam nescio. Turrianum insuper dixisse, ipsius comitem assiduum usque ad Missae aram fuisse daemonem: tandem vero cum tremore ipsum obiisse: mortuumque nigerrimo vultu conspectum fuisse, eundem affirmasse. Cum etiam, inquit Hafenmullerus, corpus ipsius ad templum, quod Cardinalis Farnesius extruxit, transferre vellent, testibus omnibus Iesuitarum professis, cadaveris eius ossa non sunt inventa, Iesuitis iam finitis gentibus; ea forsan per angelos translata esse.
units.tr: Maffei, who described the life of Ignatius Loyola, book 2, chapter 23, reports that he died peacefully. But Hafenmuller, who was himself a Jesuit for some years and lived in many Jesuit colleges, solemnly testifies at the end of his Jesuit history that the Jesuit Turrianus often told him that Ignatius was so harassed by demons at dinner, at supper, at Mass, and even during recreation, that he sweated a great quantity of icy death-sweat. Bobadilla, the Jesuit, also often said that he was sick, and Loyola complained even more often that he could never and nowhere be safe from demons. Octavianus, the Jesuit, minister at Rome, or steward of the novices, told him: "Our holy father Ignatius was indeed holy, but near the agony of death he was so oppressed, as if he had been seized by fever, that he sighed and said: I have conferred many good things on the Roman Church; I have seen many provinces of ours, many colleges, houses, residences and the wealth of our Society: but all these forsake me, and I do not know where to turn." Turrianus further said that the demon, Ignatius's constant companion, had been at the altar of the Mass; and at last he died trembling, and when he was dead he was seen with a very black face, as the same man affirmed. Also, says Hafenmuller, when they wished to transfer his body to the temple which Cardinal Farnese built, with all the professed Jesuits as witnesses, his bones could not be found. The Jesuits had by then been dispatched to the nations, and perhaps the bones had been carried away by angels.

units.la: Vt autem Ignatio suo, militi truculento & Ordinis Iesuitici Auctori, nec non doctrinae, dolis, impostturis & nefarijs facinoribus Iesuiticis maiorem auctoritatem conciliet, multa & quidem stupenda miracula ex Ribadeneira & Maffaeo recenset Gretserus in Responsione altera ad alteram Cl. V. Simonis Stenij Apologiam pro Scholijs suis ad Ignatij vitam, quae ordine ex Stenio cum notationibus eius adscribere placuit.
units.tr: In order to lend greater authority to Ignatius, his own cruel soldier and the author of the Jesuit Order, and likewise to their teaching, their deceits, impostures and nefarious crimes, Gretser, in his second reply to the second Apology of the learned Simon Stenius for his Scholia on the life of Ignatius, recounts in order, from Stenius with Stenius's annotations, many stupendous miracles drawn from Ribadeneira and Maffei. It has pleased me to set these down.

units.la: 1. Graviter aegrotanti sanctus Petrus apparens sanitatem reddit. (Frontispicium sane egregium, quippe idololatricum, huic ordini pulchre conveniens, quo nihil est pugnacius in idololatria asserenda & defendenda.
units.tr: 1. When he was gravely ill, St Peter appeared to him and restored his health. (A truly excellent frontispiece, and indeed idolatrous, admirably suited to this Order, than which nothing is more pugnacious in asserting and defending idolatry.)

units.la: 2. Septem diebus in perpetua Ecstasi perfisit. Saepe inter orandum a sensibus abstrahitur. strahitur. Cum autem sensus sint & interiores & exteriores, de utris loquatur Iefuita, indicare debebat. Nam si exteriores intelligit, facilis & expedita de somno coniectura est: si utrousque, miror vnde habeant hoc Iesuitæ, nisi forte stupidis suis discipulis persuasit Ignatius, se in tertium cœlum fuisse raptum.
units.tr: 2. For seven days he remained in perpetual ecstasy. He is often withdrawn from the senses during prayer. But since there are senses both inward and outward, the Jesuit ought to have indicated which he means. For if he means the outward senses, the conjecture about sleep is easy and plain; if he means both, I wonder where the Jesuits get this, unless perhaps Ignatius persuaded his stupid disciples that he had been caught up into the third heaven.

units.la: 3. Maximarum rerum scientia momento pene temporis diuinitus infunditur. Huic ne fidem derogem, exemplis Apostatarum adducor. Qui enim cum Lutherani essent, indulgentiarum nomen vix noverant, iam in sinum Romanæ Ecclesiæ recepti integra volumina de ipsdem magno labore descripta ediderunt. Ad quod sane argumentum necessitas credo eos impulit. Abnegatio enim veritatis copiosa veritatem indicet. Caeterum olim Anabaptistis vitio vertebatur, quod gloriarentur, copiam scientiæ sibi diuinitus conferri universis. Alia ratio Iesuitarum modo est. Pontificis privilegio quidvis & fingere & dicere illis licet.
units.tr: 3. The knowledge of the greatest things is poured into a man by divine means in almost a moment of time. Lest I seem to detract from this belief, I am led to it by the examples of apostates. For those who, while they were Lutherans, scarcely knew the name of indulgences, once received into the bosom of the Roman Church, published whole volumes on the same subjects, written with great labour. Necessity, I believe, indeed drove them to this argument. For a copious denial of the truth indicates the truth. Otherwise, the Anabaptists were formerly found fault with for boasting that a store of knowledge was conferred on them all by divine means. The Jesuits have a different method: by the Pope's privilege they are allowed both to invent and to say whatever they like.

units.la: 4. Aliquoties à terra sublimis miro splendore radiat.
units.tr: 4. Sometimes he rises from the earth and shines with wonderful splendour.

units.la: Ergo Iesuitæ nobis fingunt nova μετεωρα. Si enim Ignatius à terra miro splendore radiavit, inter μετεωρα eum referri posse quis neget? Præsertim cum neque ex planetis neque ex stellis fixis fuerit. Superavit autem Ignatius ipsum Mosen, cuius cutem faciei legimus radiasse & splenduisse, non tamen à terra sublimis. Etsi Hieronymus vertit cornutam fuisse Mosis faciem. Ac credo multo rectius faceren; pictores, si Ignatii si onti cornua appinxerint, quam Mosis. Huic miraculo adiungitur appendix. Matre cum puero Iesu adveniente castitatis dono ornatur. O sanctum hominem Ignatium, ad quem castitatis dono ornandum non simplex Mariæ descensus de cœlo requiritur, se etiam pueri Iesu apparitio matrem comitantis. Germaniæ me miseret, quæ cogitur magnis sumptibus alere eiusmodi θαυμαστοποιός.
units.tr: So the Jesuits invent new meteora [μετεωρα] for us. If Ignatius shone with wonderful brightness from the earth, who could deny that he may be counted among the meteora? Especially since he was neither a planet nor a fixed star. Yet Ignatius surpassed Moses himself, whose face we read gave off rays and shone, though not from the earth. Jerome, however, translated that Moses' face was horned. I think painters would do far better to paint horns on the face of Ignatius than on Moses. To this miracle is added an appendix: When the mother comes with the boy Jesus, he is adorned with the gift of chastity. O holy man Ignatius, to be adorned with the gift of chastity required not merely the descent of Mary from heaven, but also the appearance of the boy Jesus accompanying his mother! I pity Germany, which is forced to support at great expense such a wonder-worker [θαυμαστοποιός].

units.la: 5. Senator Venetus cœlesti iussu admonitus in publico cubantem (Ignatium) nostu conquirit, & in domum suam adduxit. Nomen Senatoris Veneti aveo scire, ut & modum cœlestis mandati.
units.tr: 5. A Venetian senator, warned by a heavenly command, seeks out Ignatius lying in the public street at night and brings him into his own house. I long to know the name of this Venetian senator, and also the manner of the heavenly command.

units.la: 6. Quendam, qui sepræ desperatione suspenderat, ad dolendum de peccatis suscitat. Ambiguè hæc dicuntur. Possit enim aliquis suspicari, suscitatum fuisse ab Ignatio mortuum, de quo Lutherani & Calviniani valde dubitant: alius fortasse hoc cogitabit, ab Ignatio fuisse interpellatum conatum suspedij, quod si Iesuitis miraculum est, scire velim, quo pacto ipsi definiant miraculum.
units.tr: 6. He raises up a man who had hanged himself in despair so that he grieves for his sins. These words are ambiguous. Someone might suspect that the man was raised from the dead by Ignatius, a point on which the Lutherans and Calvinists have serious doubts. Another person will perhaps think that Ignatius merely interrupted an attempt at suicide. If this is a miracle for the Jesuits, I should like to know how they define a miracle.

units.la: 7. Mulierem arido à multis annis brachio ipsius abluentem pannos sanat, alia Dæmonum spectra fugat. Quo in loco asserventur panni illi Ignatiani, non facile predent Iesuitæ ante Patris sui ἀποθέωσιν, hæc publicata proferentur in multorum salutem, & in Iesuitarum quæstum. De fugatis spectris rescerta. Ex Ribadeneira enim pridem cognovimus, & ex sequentibus intelligemus, solitum fuisse Ignatium baculo abigere dæmonem.
units.tr: 7. He heals a woman whose arm had been withered for many years, as she washes his cloths, and drives out other apparitions of demons. In what place those Ignatian cloths are kept, the Jesuits will not readily disclose before their father's deification [ἀποθέωσιν]; these things will be published when they bring salvation to many and profit to the Jesuits. As for the expelled spectres, I have read of them. From Ribadeneira we learned long ago, and from what follows we shall understand, that Ignatius was accustomed to drive out demons with a staff.

units.la: 8. Morbo caduco à multis annis laborantem suo contactu sanat.
units.tr: 8. He heals by his touch a man who for many years had suffered from epilepsy.

units.la: 9. Diuturnam à femina tabem precibus abigit. Felicem Italiam hoc medico, cuius contactus si tantum valuit, cur non ipsi claudicationem ademit? Idem dico de precibus.
units.tr: 9. By prayers he drives away a long-lasting wasting disease from a woman. Happy Italy, with such a physician! If his touch had such power, why did he not also take away a limp? I say the same of his prayers.

units.la: 10. Moribundos à morte revocat. Caute, neque enim audebat poneremortuos.
units.tr: 10. He recalls the dying from death. Cautiously done, for he did not dare to raise the dead.

units.la: 11. Multos energumenos à Dæmonibus, ægros ab incurabilibus morbis liberat. De primo nulli litem movemus, cogitantes de vi baculi Ignatiani: de altero viderint medici Itali.
units.tr: 11. He frees many possessed people from demons and the sick from incurable diseases. Concerning the first we raise no dispute, thinking of the power of the Ignatian staff. As for the second, let the Italian doctors look to it.

units.la: 12. Dum febri quotidiana laborans sæpe in campo concionatur, eius verba ultra trecentos passus distincte audiuntur. Vento nimirum seundo, hoc addi debebat. Sic enim ἴσα Ignatij πλεφιοντα facilius ad auditores advolare vel deferri potuerunt.
units.tr: 12. While suffering from a daily fever he often preaches in the open field, and his words are heard distinctly more than three hundred paces away. Obviously with a favourable wind; this ought to have been added. For in that way the winged words [πτερόεντα ἔπεα] of Ignatius could more easily fly or be carried to the hearers.

units.la: 13. Multa futura prædicit, multa occulta & absentia divinitus cognoscit. Πεσγῆα ἃ κα illa cur non divulgantur. Fortasse enim plures emptores invenirent, quam Astrologorum.
units.tr: 13. He foretells many future things and by divine power knows many hidden and absent things. Why are those predictions [προγνώσεις] not published? Perhaps they would find more buyers than those of the astrologers.

units.la: 14. Obscurum ejus agrotantis cubiculum divinus splendor illustrat. Additur (divinus) alias enim obscura illatis luminibus illustrari scimus.
units.tr: 14. A divine splendour lights up the dark room of the sick man. The word divine is added; for we know that dark places are otherwise lit up by introduced lights.

units.la: 15. A Deo Patre cum sociis commendatum Iesus in tutelam recipit. O beatos Iesuitas, hoc commendatore & tutore, utinam ascriptum fuisset, quibus verbis, quo gestu, quo habitu, quibus præsentibus, quibus audientibus, quo in loco, quo tempore hæc facta fuerint.
units.tr: 15. Jesus, commended to him by God the Father together with his companions, takes him into his protection. O blessed Jesuits, with such a commender and protector! I wish it had been written down with what words, with what gesture, in what dress, in whose presence, before whose hearing, in what place and at what time these things were done.

units.la: 16. Animam Beati Hozij luce clarissima circumfusam cælum intrantem videt. Præcedens miraculum si verum est, de præsente nemo dubitaverit. Cur enim non videat animam Hozij, qui DEVM Patrem vidit, quem nemo vidit unquam.
units.tr: 16. He sees the soul of the blessed Hozius, surrounded by the brightest light, entering heaven. If the preceding miracle is true, no one will doubt the present one. For why should he not see the soul of Hozius, when he saw God the Father, whom no one has ever seen?

units.la: 17. Iudæum obstinato animo Christiana sacra respuentem, tribus tantum verbis repente convertit. Fortasse ex Hebræorum Cabala desumpta fuerunt hæc verba, de quibus iudicent ipsi Iudæi, qui, ut puto, difficulter credent hoc, quod hic narratur factum fuisse.
units.tr: 17. He suddenly converts a Jew, who obstinately rejected the Christian sacred things, with only three words. Perhaps these words were taken from the Hebrew Cabala. The Jews themselves may judge this, though I think they will find it hard to believe what is related here as having happened.

units.la: 18. In S.S. Eucharistia IESVM aliquoties videt. Maffæus enim sic scribit lib. 1. cap. 8. in eius vita: Dum à Sacerdote de more salutaris hostia attollitur, vidit Ignatius illa specie Christum, Deum eundem, & hominem verissime contineri. Videmus & animo & oculis: de utro videndi modo loquatur, nos ignoramus. Potuit fieri, ut neutro viderit. Christum enim fide intuentur Christiani fideles, in quorum numero Ignatius idololatra non fuit; oculis non cernunt, nisi, ut Stephano, ceteri aperti fuerint. Idem dico de cœlesti Sanctorum choro.
units.tr: 18. In the Holy Eucharist he sometimes sees Jesus. For Maffei writes thus in book 1, chapter 8 of his life: While the saving host is lifted up by the priest, as is customary, Ignatius saw Christ, the same God and man, truly contained under that appearance. We see with the mind and with the eyes; which mode of seeing he means, we do not know. It may be that he saw in neither way. For faithful Christians behold Christ by faith, and Ignatius was not one of them, being an idolater. Nor do they perceive him with the eyes, unless, as with Stephen, the others' eyes are opened. I say the same of the heavenly choir of saints.

units.la: 19. Eius facies divino lumine splendens sæpe à diversis cernitur. Si splenduit, tam ab uno, quam à diversis cerni potuit, & quidem sæpe. In antecedente difficultas est. Sed si, ut est apud Livium, L. Martio equiti Romano flamma concionanti fusa e capite sine ipsius sensu, cum magno pavore circumstantium mirabilitum: fieri fortasse potuit, ut etiam in hoc Hispano equite nobili simile quid existerit.
units.tr: 19. His face, shining with divine light, is often seen by various people. If it shone, it could be seen by one person as well as by many, and indeed often. The difficulty lies in the preceding statement. But if, as Livy records, a flame poured out from the head of Lucius Martius, a Roman knight, while he was speaking, without his own awareness and to the great terror of the bystanders, then perhaps something similar could also have happened to this Spanish noble knight.

units.la: 20. Cœlestes sæpenumero voces, sacrificans audit. (Sacrificavit in terris, unde igitur noverat e cœlo istas voces esse? quasi vero princeps aeris ludificare Ignatium non potuerit vocibus aliquibus conformatis, quæ artolatriam & idololatriam, quibus Ignatium immersum videbat, confirmarent. Addit, multa de Sanctissimæ Trinitatis mysterio, Deo revelante, cognoscit. Hæc si communicasset cum suis Ignatius, felicius & minore, credo, cum labore refutarent Arianos in Polonia Iesuitæ.
units.tr: 20. He often hears heavenly voices while he sacrifices. (He sacrificed on earth; how then did he know that those voices came from heaven? As if the prince of the air could not deceive Ignatius with voices shaped to confirm the artolatry and idolatry in which he saw him steeped!) He adds that, by God's revelation, he came to know many things about the mystery of the most holy Trinity. If Ignatius had communicated these to his followers, I think the Jesuits in Poland would have refuted the Arians more successfully and with less labour.

units.la: 21. Orans, sacrificans, iter faciens, gravibus de rebus differens, Christum ac B. Virginem sæpissime videt. (De duplici modo videndi paulo ante monuimus. Neutrum in Ignatium cecidisse afferimus.)
units.tr: 21. Praying, sacrificing, travelling, discussing weighty matters, he most often sees Christ and the blessed Virgin. (We noted the twofold mode of seeing a little earlier. We maintain that neither fell to Ignatius.)

units.la: 22. Dæmonem ad tentandum venientem frequenter baculo per contemptum abigit. (Si Apostolum legisset Ignatius, alia se armatura instruxisset adversus tentationes Diaboli. Nam baculo puto, non magis abigitur, quam ture, vel aqua lustrali.)
units.tr: 22. When the devil comes to tempt him, he often drives him away with a staff, out of contempt. (If Ignatius had read the Apostle, he would have equipped himself with different armour against the temptations of the devil. For I think a staff drives away the devil no more than incense or holy water does.)

units.la: 23. Suæ splendore faciei graviter ægrotantem sanat, & cubiculum obscurum illustrat. (Plus hoc Pseudomiraculum tribuit Hispano militi, quam filio Dei Scriptura. Neque enim usquam legimus filium Dei sanasse ægrotantes splendore faciei. Atqui ... Quod idem de suo patre pronunciant satis impie Iesuitæ. Quid enim præter solem obscura illustrat?)
units.tr: 23. He heals a man gravely ill by the splendour of his face, and lights up a dark room. (This pseudo-miracle gives more to the Spanish soldier than Scripture gives to the Son of God. For nowhere do we read that the Son of God healed the sick by the splendour of his face. And yet... The Jesuits quite impiously pronounce the same of their father. For what, besides the sun, lights up dark places?)

units.la: 24. Dæmones sæpe Laureti apparentes post multa remedia frustra ab aliis suscepta, per Epistolam fugat. ( Apparet valde familiarem fuisse Diabolum Ignatio, cum quo etiam per Epistolam egerit. Notet hic lector novum genus sugandi daemones.)
units.tr: 24. Demons, often appearing at Loreto after many remedies had been tried in vain by others, he drives away by a letter. (The devil seems to have been very familiar with Ignatius, with whom he even dealt by letter. Let the reader note this new kind of driving away of demons.)

units.la: 25. Quidam incendium ei per iniuriam imprecatus, subito ipse incendio extinguitur. Duorum mortem ei intentantium, unus repente obrigescit: alter divina voce terretur. Multiplex hoc est miraculum. (Puerum aliquem incendio perire, fidem non superat. Sed repente obrigescere hominem, illud ad μεταμόρφωσιν Ovidianam relegandum. De divina voce etiam quaestio moveri possit a curiosis.)
units.tr: 25. A certain man, who had wished through injustice a fire upon him, is suddenly consumed by the fire himself. Of two men who threatened his death, one is suddenly stiffened, the other is terrified by a divine voice. This is a manifold miracle. (That some boy perished in a fire does not surpass belief. But that a man was suddenly stiffened, that is to be referred to the Ovidian metamorphosis [μεταμόρφωσιν]. Curious people might also raise a question about the divine voice.)

units.la: 26. Multis se post mortem saepe ostendit, & deinceps, quo obiit temporis momento magna collucens gloria apparet: (Diabolus, credo, assumpta specie Ignatij Iesuitis illudit interdum. Nam quod magna collucens gloria apparuerit eodem momento, quo obiit, suspicionem nobis non minuit, scientibus etiam Diabolum se posse transformare in angelum lucis.)
units.tr: 26. He often shows himself to many after death, and then, at the moment he died, appears shining with great glory. (The devil, I think, sometimes assumes the appearance of Ignatius and mocks the Jesuits. For the fact that he appeared shining with great glory at the very moment he died does not lessen our suspicion, since we know that the devil can also transform himself into an angel of light.)

units.la: 27. Corpus illius effossum multis luminibus fulget (appositis illis pro more a Iesuitis:) addit, Coelestis harmoniae concentus saepe audiuntur (ad sepulchrum, credo, Ignatij.) O stolidos nostros Germanos, qui Romae aliquad[iu] commorantes Symphoniam illam angelicam barbare aspernantur.
units.tr: 27. His body, dug up, shines with many lights (lamps placed there, as the Jesuits customarily do). He adds that heavenly harmonies are often heard (at the tomb of Ignatius, I suppose). O foolish Germans of ours, who, while staying some time at Rome, boorishly scorn that angelic symphony!

units.la: 28. Multas a partu, a vitae discrimine, multos a pestilentia & gravibus morbis, tentationibusque eripit. (Hac ratione numerum Divorum imminuent Iesuitae: Surrogabitur Rocho Ignatius, itemque Cosmae & Damiano ac Christophoro, imo etiam, quae in Papatu Iuncni Lucinae successerit.)
units.tr: 28. He rescues many from the pains of childbirth, from mortal danger, from plague and serious diseases, and from temptations. (In this way the Jesuits will diminish the number of the saints: Ignatius will be substituted for Roch, and likewise for Cosmas and Damian and Christopher, and indeed even for the goddess who, in Papal times, succeeded Lucina.)

units.la: 29. Daemoniacos liberat, caecis visum, surdis auditum, moribundis vitam & salutem reddit.
units.tr: 29. He frees the demoniacs, restores sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and life and health to the dying.

units.la: Has visiones & similia Miracula plura Iesuitae referunt, ut Ignatij sui doctrinam, institutA, Regulas & alias confirment, & pro veris, hominibus obtrudant. Unde vero, vel a quo illa habent? A Iesuitis, praesertim a Maffaeo & Ribadeneira, qui Vitam Ignatij conscripserunt. Maffaeus authorem nullum nominat: Ribadeneira dicit, se illa habere a quodam Vuilhelmo Confalvo, Confalvus autem ab Ignatio Loyola, qui ei annum fere ante suum obitum haec omnia communicarit. Nemo autem haec miracula vidit, nec iis interfuit: solus Ignatius narravit, Petrum, itemque Virginem Mariam sibi apparuisse: bis se a diabolo in visibili specie tetatum esse: se Sacro Sanctam Trinitatem in coelis: Christum etiam corporaliter in hostia, animam quoque Hostij in coelum ascendere vidisse. Deum insuper sibi monstrasse modo, quo universum mundum creavit: Iesum Christum denique promisisse, quod ei propitius esse velit Romae. Haec omnia solus Ignatius communicavit Confalvo. Quis autem Loyolae, homini superstitioso & idololatrae credat, praesertim in propria causa?
units.tr: The Jesuits report these visions and similar miracles in great number, in order to confirm the teaching, the institute, the Rules and the other things of Ignatius, and to press them on people as true. But where, or from whom, do they have them? From the Jesuits, above all from Maffeo and Ribadeneira, who wrote the Life of Ignatius. Maffeo names no author. Ribadeneira says that he had these things from a certain Wilhelm Gonzalez, and that Gonzalez had them from Ignatius of Loyola, who communicated all of this to him almost a year before his death. No one, however, saw these miracles or was present at them. Only Ignatius reported that Peter and also the Virgin Mary had appeared to him; that twice he had been assailed by the devil in visible form; that he had seen the Most Holy Trinity in the heavens; that he had seen Christ bodily in the host, and also the soul of the host ascending into heaven. Moreover, God had shown him the way in which he created the whole world, and finally Jesus Christ had promised that he would be favourable to him at Rome. Only Ignatius communicated all this to Gonzalez. But who would believe Loyola, a superstitious man and idolater, especially in his own cause?

units.la: Quaeritur etiam, si maxime talia miracula edidisset Ignatius, An propterea ea doctrina, institutA, &c. pro veris suscipienda sint, quae videmus multis & magnis miraculis comprobari? Iesuitae aiunt, nos negamus. Ratio negationis est, quod Deus propter peccata hominum permittit interdum etiam per falsos Doctores, perque malos & impios homines miracula edi, Exod.7. & a Paulo 2. Thess.
units.tr: It is also asked whether, even if Ignatius had performed such miracles, that teaching, institute and so on should for that reason be accepted as true, when we see that many things are confirmed by many great miracles. The Jesuits say yes; we deny it. The reason for our denial is that God, on account of the sins of men, sometimes permits miracles to be wrought even through false teachers and through wicked and impious men: Exod. 7; and Paul in 2 Thess.

units.la: 2. Antichristi adventus describitur secundum operationem Satanae, cum signis & prodigiis mendacibus. Unde Cyrillus quoque lib.7. cap.13. in Evang. Ioh. Miracula, inquit, nihil adijciunt sanctitatis homini, cum malis & reprobis id etiam competat, dicente Domino apud Matth.: Multi dicent mihi in die illa, Domine, &c. Ergo ut possimus vera miracula, quibus credendum, a falsis discernere, oportet definire quaenam sint miracula vera: externa scilicet quaedam opera & facta, in admiratione
units.tr: 2. The coming of Antichrist is described as according to the working of Satan, with lying signs and wonders. Hence Cyril also, book 7, chapter 13, on the Gospel of John, says: "Miracles," he says, "add nothing of holiness to a man, since they belong also to the evil and the reprobate," the Lord saying in Matthew: "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, etc." Therefore, so that we may distinguish the true miracles, which are to be believed, from the false, it is necessary to define what true miracles are: namely, certain external works and deeds, in admiration

units.la: Iudicium de miraculis Ignatij
units.tr: Judgement on the miracles of Ignatius

units.la: An doctrina, pro vera habenda sit quae miraculis comprobatur
units.tr: Whether a doctrine that is confirmed by miracles is to be held as true

units.la: Quae miracula vera sint, & quo modo a falsis distinguenda apud homines habita, & talia revera, qualia apparent divina virtute, & ad declarandam doctrinam fidei, vel promissionum divinarum, vel potentiae Dei veritatem & certitudinem, & ad Dei gloriam edita. Haec definitio ex causis collecta est, atque ex ea intelligi potest, quomodo vera miracula a falsis sint distinguenda. Vera habent Deum authorem; cuius vi atque virtute fiunt praeter naturae ordinem, nec ibi est aliqua impostura; in eum quoque finem eduntur, ut Deum rite colamus; eiusque verbo, missis erroribus, fidem habeamus. Falsorum author est Satanas; qui illa vel per seipsum, vel per impostores, tanquam organa edit, idque variis modis. Non igitur negamus, multa in Papatu fieri; quae pro miraculis habentur; cum nihil sint minus, sed impostura, doli & fraudes Menacherum, sacrificulorum & similium superstitiosorum hominum: de quibus Nicolaus Lyra in cap.14. Danielis etiam conqueritur, dicens: In Ecclesia Dei populus saepe decipitur a sacerdotibus fictis miraculis lucri causa. Huius generis plurima apud Gentes quoque accidisse legimus, ut est videre apud Eusebium lib.3. de vita Constantini: & lib.9. Ecclesiast. hist. cap.3. & alibi. Secundo concedimus multa in Papatu vere fieri, minime tamen pro veris miraculis habenda sunt, cum reliquae causae, quas in veris & proprie dictis miraculis spectari oportet, desiderentur, inprimisque cum abducant homines a Deo ad idola, & a veritate religionis ad superstitiones.
units.tr: What true miracles are, and how they are to be distinguished from false ones, are those held among men to be such as they really appear, wrought by divine power, and for declaring the teaching of the faith, or the divine promises, or the truth and certainty of God's power, and for the glory of God. This definition has been gathered from the causes, and from it it can be understood how true miracles are to be distinguished from false. True miracles have God as their author, by whose power and virtue they occur beyond the order of nature, and in them there is no imposture; they are also wrought to this end, that we may worship God duly and, putting away errors, have faith in his word. The author of false miracles is Satan, who works them either himself or through impostors as his instruments, and in various ways. We do not therefore deny that many things happen in the Papacy which are held to be miracles, though they are anything but, being rather the trickery, deceit and frauds of the Menachem-men, the little priests and similar superstitious men. Nicholas of Lyra also complains of these in his commentary on Daniel chapter 14, saying: "In the Church of God the people are often deceived by false priests with fictitious miracles for the sake of gain." We read that many things of this kind also happened among the Gentiles, as can be seen in Eusebius, book 3, On the Life of Constantine, and book 9 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 3, and elsewhere. Secondly, we concede that many things truly do happen in the Papacy, yet they are by no means to be held as true miracles, since the remaining causes which ought to be observed in true and properly so-called miracles are lacking, and especially since they lead men away from God to idols, and from the truth of religion to superstitions.

units.la: Tutissimum igitur semper fuerit, ex doctrinae veritate de miraculis iudicium facere, non de doctrina ex miraculis. Et hoc consilium Deus ipse Deut. 13. dedit nobis, & Chrysostomus in Oratione 5. adversus Iudaeos docet, miraculis credendum non esse adversus sacram Scripturam. In hanc sententiam Augustinus quoque contra Faustum Manichaeum lib.13. cap.4. scribit: Si faceretis maxime miracula, ea tamen ipsa in vobis caveremus per instruentem nos Dominum, & dicentem: Exurgent multi Pseudochristi & Pseudoprophetae, & facient signa & prodigia multa, ut fallant, si fieri potest, etiam electos, &c. Visque adeo nihil credi voluit adversus confirmatam Scripturarum authoritatem, quae fidem suam in rebus ipsis probat, &c.
units.tr: It will therefore always be safest to judge miracles by the truth of the doctrine, and not to judge the doctrine by miracles. God himself gave us this counsel in Deut. 13, and Chrysostom, in his fifth Oration against the Jews, teaches that miracles are not to be believed against the holy Scripture. To this effect Augustine also writes against Faustus the Manichaean, book 13, chapter 4: "Even if you were to perform the greatest miracles, we would still be on our guard against them, the Lord having instructed us and said: 'Many false Christs and false prophets will arise, and will do great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if it were possible, even the elect,' etc." And so much did he wish that nothing be believed against the confirmed authority of the Scriptures, which proves its faith by its own content, etc.

units.la: Nec illud omittendum videtur, quod in diligenti authorum lectione observavi, a nullo fide digno authore veteri eiusmodi falsa & mendacia signa, ad confirmandum cultum Deorum alienorum, variasque superstitiones, excogitata, referri, qualia post Gregorii Magni demum tempora, cum omnis generis superstitiones catervatim in Ecclesiam irruerent, & hodie a Iesuitis de suo Ignatio referuntur.
