And in book 2, letter 3: "There are not lacking," he says, "those who affirm that St Thomas the Apostle penetrated into China and converted a great number of its people to the faith of Christ. Before the Portuguese brought India under their rule, the Greek Church sent bishops there to care for the Christians spread by the work of St Thomas and his disciples. So when the Portuguese first began to take possession of India, one of the Greek bishops I have mentioned is reported to have declared that he had learned from other bishops whom he found in India that St Thomas, having entered the borders of China, had brought very many of the natives to Christ by spreading the Gospel." Thus he writes. John Lery also writes in his history of the voyage to Brazil that he had heard nothing of that island from anyone, but that the same Christ whom he himself announces was preached in that island in ancient times, and that the Brazilians had handed down from their ancestors that salvation was to be obtained from him, and that he had heard this from his own parents. He thinks, moreover, that this tradition came down from the Apostle Thomas, as if handed from hand to hand. So either Thomas or others snatch from the Jesuits both the name of Apostles and the glory of this conversion.

units.la: Quicquid sit, hoc cognomine Manetis hæresis ab inferis revocatur, à quo Manichæi orti sunt. Nam Manes Paracletum se, & duodecim suos discipulos Apostolos nominavit, eosq; in diversas provincias ad venenum suum hominibus instillandum dimisit. Reprehendit igitur non iniuriâ hoc tanquam superbissimum cognomen in Apotacticis Augustin. lib. 1. ad Quod vult Deum de Hæref. Apostolici, inquit, qui se isto nomine arroganter vocaverunt, eò quod in suam communionem non reciperent uxores conjugibus, & res proprias possidentes, etc. Quid dicturum fuisse putas sanctissimum virum, si eius tempore fuissent, qui se vel Apostolos, vel de Societate, vel etiam Socios Iesu, aut Iesuitas appellassent?
units.tr: Whatever the case, by this title the heresy of Manes is called back from the dead, the heresy from which the Manichaeans arose. For Manes called himself the Paraclete, and named his twelve disciples Apostles, and sent them into various provinces to instil his poison into men. Augustine therefore rightly rebukes this title as most arrogant, in his book On the Apostolic Tradition, book 1, against the Heresies: "The Apostolici," he says, "who arrogantly called themselves by this name because they did not admit into their communion wives with their husbands, and those who possessed their own property," and so on. What do you think that most holy man would have said, if in his time there had been those who called themselves Apostles, or of the Society, or even Companions of Jesus, or Jesuits?

units.la: Monachorum nomen horrent Iesuitæ, nec immeritò, non enim illis hoc tempore vere & proprie competit, licet Monachis annumeretur. Movaxós enim Græca vox, unde Monachus, significat hominem solitarium, qui solus vivit, & solitariæ vitæ genus elegit. Iesuitæ autem non in solitudinibus, nec extra hominum consortia vivunt, sed in mediis urbibus, in foro, in vicis, in compitis, in curiis Senatorum & Aulis Regum ac Principum versantur, in castris quoque & inter armatorum acies circumvolitant, denique in ipsa quoque gynæcea & penetralia mulierum usque penetrant: Ut non minus illis dici possit, quàm quod olim Hieronymus Paulino dixit: Si cupis esse quod diceris Monachus, id est, solus, quid facis in urbibus, quæ utique non sunt solorum habitacula, sed multorum. Et ad Rusticum in eandem sententiam ait: Quid desideramus urbium frequentiam, qui de singularitate censemur? his significare voluit, Monachum in urbibus commorantem, & inter homines viventem, nequaquam suo nomini respondere. Et Antonium Eremitam dixisse accepimus: Lethalem esse piscibus extra undas conversationem: neque minus Monachum in periculum cœlestis vitæ, & professionis sanctioris amittendæ venire, si nomini suo non satisfaciens, moras in urbibus trahat.
units.tr: The Jesuits shrink from the name of monks, and not undeservedly. For it does not properly and truly belong to them at this time, although they are counted among the monks. The Greek word monachos [μοναχός], from which "monk" comes, means a solitary man, one who lives alone and has chosen a solitary way of life. But the Jesuits do not live in deserts or apart from human company; they dwell in the midst of cities, in the marketplace, in the streets, at the crossroads, in the councils of senators and the courts of kings and princes; they also move about in camps and among the lines of armed men; and finally they even penetrate into women's apartments and their inner chambers. So what Jerome once said to Paulinus may be said no less to them: "If you wish to be what you are called, a monk, that is, a solitary, why do you live in cities, which are not the dwellings of solitaries but of many?" And to Rusticus he says to the same effect: "Why do we desire the crowds of cities, when we are reckoned by our solitude?" By this he meant that a monk who lives in cities and among men does not at all answer to his name. We are also told that Antony the Hermit said: "Living outside the water is deadly for fish; and likewise a monk who fails to satisfy his name and lingers in cities comes into danger of losing the heavenly life and the holier profession."

units.la: IESVITÆ SINT NE MONACHI, AN EPISCO- PI VEL SACERDOTES.
units.tr: Are the Jesuits Monks, or Bishops or Priests?

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Iesuitæ, ut diximus, ægre ferunt, se in idem album cum aliis Monachis referri: sic indignatur quoque Monachi, privilegia sua Iesuitis communicari, à quibus ceu maiorum gentiu Episcopis in infimum ordinem amandantur, nec enim in Tridentino Synodo, cum de prœdrialis inter partes controverteretur, assignatum sibi inter Monachos locum, suæ dignitati parem existimarunt. Itaque Iesuitas aiunt fluvialis cuiusdam avis esse similes, quæ indicto avium conventu piscem se profitebatur, indicto piscium concilio, avis se nomine tuebatur. Urgentur igitur ut depositâ tandem persona se Monachis aut Episcopis ascribant. Illi neutris se adiungunt, sed modo ad hos, modo ad illos divertunt, amborum, ut lubet, participes.
units.tr: As the Jesuits, as we have said, take it badly that they are listed on the same roll as the other monks, so the monks in turn are indignant that their privileges are shared with the Jesuits, whom they relegate to the lowest rank, as if the Jesuits were bishops of greater nations. For when the question of precedence was disputed at the Council of Trent, the Jesuits did not think that a place among the monks was equal to their dignity. So people say the Jesuits are like a certain river bird, which, when a gathering of birds was called, declared itself a fish, and when a council of fish was called, defended itself as a bird. Accordingly they are pressed to drop their disguise at last and enrol themselves either with the monks or with the bishops. But they join neither, and turn now to these, now to those, sharing in both as it suits them.

units.la: Manes suos disci pulos Apoft. Iosnominavit.
units.tr: Mani called his disciples Apostles.

units.la: Iesuitæ nolunt vocari Monachi. tipes. Nam cū Monachū solitudo iuvet & otiū, ipsi quoq; se a populo segregant, ne curarū terrenarū contagione afficiantur, sed in umbra soli perspaciosas porticus inambulantes cogitationibus suis indulgeant. E diverso, cum Episcopi munus actione cōtineatur, ipsi quoq; animi gratia ad populū declamant, sacramenta sua sanis, aegris, publice & privatim ingerentes. Sed quoniā languida nimis videbatur Monachorū conditio, si se toti meditationi dederent, aut odiosa, si rerum gerendarum satagerent: e diverso aerumnosum nimis & anxium Episcoporū munus esset: ideo medium quoddā & ad felicitatē propensius vivendi genus placuit, quod laboris civilioris & mediocritatis vicibus temperaretur. Itaq; id eatenus attingetes, quatenus commodum visum est, libera ad meditationem & otium sibi tempora reservarunt, ficq; rem gesserunt, ut inter Episcopos sesqui-monachi, inter monachos semiepiscopi, utrisq; merito suspecti habeantur. Adde quod non inertem navant operam erudiendis pueris, & ad suam rationem informandis, atq; inter has curas non pauca alia moliuntur. Vnde nonnimmerito Monachismo praxis adiungitur, id est, πολυπραγμοσύνη, cuius cum Monachismo fermentatura artem substituit Iesuiticam, medullamq; doctrinae Papae continet. Vt enim medulla alimentum est ultimum perfectissime elaboratum, ita haec ultima Monachorū natio una omnium reliquarum instar est, ipsiusq; doctrina subtilior quidam succus ex omnium antiquorum Monachorum regulis delibatus & expressus. Etenim Monachorum triplex est genus, ut item triplex animarum gradus, alij tantum vivunt ut frutices: alij vivunt & sentiunt ut bestiae: primi sensu carentes, secundi sensu & ratione simul: tertij ad humanitatem propius accedunt quidem, & ratiocinantur, sed non emendate. Tres hos gradus arte sua Iesuitae eximie complexi sunt, Nam vivunt ut primi, & vitam longe vitaliorem: sentiunt ut secundi, & sensu multo liberiore: ex secundis enim hi se aspectu formarum, hi segustu ciborum orbarunt: utramq; licetiam Iesuitae sibi indulserunt, ultimorumq; paralogismis correctis, ex ipsis quod utile visum est decerpserunt, sibi Monachos & Episcopos tanquam regulas Lesbias accommodaverunt. Differuntigitur Iesuitae a Monachis, nō magis quām species a genere: aut testudo exerto capite hinc inde praedam captans a testudine intra suam cochleam vicitanti.
units.tr: The Jesuits do not want to be called monks. For while solitude and leisure suit a monk, they too separate themselves from the people, so as not to be infected by the contagion of earthly cares, and stroll in the shade of very spacious colonnades, indulging their thoughts. On the other hand, since the office of a bishop consists in action, they too preach to the people for the sake of display, administering their sacraments publicly and privately to the healthy and the sick. But since the condition of the monks would seem too sluggish if they devoted themselves wholly to contemplation, and the office of bishops too troublesome and anxious if they were busy with affairs, a kind of middle way was chosen, one more inclined to happiness, which would be tempered by the alternation of more civil labour and moderation. So they engage in these things only as far as seems convenient, and they have reserved free times for meditation and leisure. And they have so conducted themselves that among bishops they are regarded as half-monks, and among monks as half-bishops, and so are rightly suspected by both. Add that they expend no idle effort in educating boys and shaping them to their own method, and amid these cares they undertake not a few other projects. Hence it is not without reason that busybodiness [πολυπραγμοσύνη] is joined to monasticism as a practice. The Jesuit art replaces the leaven of monasticism and contains the marrow of papal doctrine. For just as marrow is the ultimate and most perfectly worked nourishment, so this last race of monks is equal to all the others together, and its doctrine is a subtler juice drawn and pressed out from the rules of all the ancient monks. For there are three kinds of monks, just as there are three grades of souls. Some live only as plants do; some live and feel as beasts do; the first lack sensation, the second have sensation and reason together; the third come closer to humanity and do reason, but not properly. The Jesuits have skilfully embraced these three grades in their art. For they live as the first do, but with a far more vigorous life; they feel as the second do, but with much freer feeling. For the second group have deprived themselves, some of the sight of forms, others of the taste of foods; the Jesuits have allowed themselves both. Having corrected the paralogisms of the last group, they have plucked from them whatever seemed useful, and they have fitted monks and bishops to themselves like the Lesbian rule. The Jesuits therefore differ from the monks no more than a species differs from its genus, or a tortoise that thrusts out its head to snatch prey on every side differs from a tortoise living within its own shell.

units.la: Huius artis repertor & princeps est Loyola Hispanus, ut diximus, qui praeceptionibus omnibus, quae ad hanc artem pertinent collectis, turbam quandam hominum collegit, iureiurando que astrictam ex artis huius praescripto & formula vivere coegit. Is primum miles, mox perfosa tibia, belli pertaesus, ad scholas literarias, a scholis deinde ad peregrinandum se contulit, semper suum finem animo versans, quod erat cum dignitate otium. Quem finem licet multi Monachi viderent, eo tamen pertingere non poterant, quin monasticam desinerent, hoc est, e finibus suis in Episcopatum exilirent. Vnus Loyola ita callide circumspexit, ut neque ab eo fine aberrarit, neque finem suum transiliierit. Namque Episcopatu ad leve quoddam exercitij genus restricto, simulque Monachatu ex certis illis legibus relaxato, fecit ut intra Monachatum consistens Episcopalium commoditatum potitus fit, hinc oneris expers, illinc severioris disciplinae. Itaque sicut nonnullis authoribus nonnullarum artium inventionem acceptam ferimus, quod primi earum usum vagantem & dubium certis regulis circumscripserunt: ita Loyolam ars Iesuitica laudat authorem, e multis illa quidem Monachorum rivulis deducta, sed ab ipso Loyola ad summum adducta.
units.tr: The inventor and chief of this art is Loyola the Spaniard, as we have said. He gathered together all the precepts that pertain to this art, collected a crowd of men, and bound them by oath to live according to the prescription and formula of this art. He was first a soldier, but soon, with his shin pierced, grew weary of war and turned to literary schools, and from the schools he went on to wandering abroad, always keeping in view his end, which was leisure with dignity. Many monks saw this end, yet they could not reach it without abandoning monasticism, that is, without leaping out of their own bounds into the episcopate. Loyola alone looked around so cleverly that he neither strayed from that end nor overshot it. For, restricting the episcopate to a light kind of exercise, and at the same time relaxing monastic life from its strict laws, he made it so that, by remaining within monasticism, he gained the advantages of a bishop, free of its burden on the one hand, and of the stricter discipline on the other. Accordingly, just as some authors are credited with the invention of certain arts, because they first confined the wandering and uncertain practice of them within fixed rules, so the Jesuit art honours Loyola as its author: it was drawn from many streams of the monks, but brought to its height by Loyola himself.

units.la: Ostendam tamen breviter, quibus in rebus Iesuitae a reliquis Monachis differant maxime. Monachis ex testamento suorum, aut ab intestato legaticapio nulla erat, ideo neque querela de inofficioso competebat. Iesuitae vero id iuris sibi reservarunt, ut haereditates ad se devolutas nomine quisque privato adire, ac praetextione testamenta rumpere possent. Et quamvis dona grandia Monachi à caducis & moribundis hominibus aucuparentur, negari tamen non potest, quin id ipsum, vel accuratius, Iesuitæ præstent. Sed illud tamen interest, quòd non ad recitandas mane & vespere nænias se adstringunt, neque cadaveribus Divorum delubra funestant, sed quicquid id est quod donatur, putum purum sibi habere volunt. Reformârunt item eam Monachorum turpitudinem, qui mantica per vicos onusti stipem & annonam oftiatim mendicabant: In templis vero sicut in foro, vinum, polentas, ova gratis mercabantur. At Iesuitæ domi & foris nil nisi nitorem & lautitiam præ se ferunt. Suppresserunt præterea quasdam mei & tui appellationes, quæ iam inter Monachos gliscebant, magnámque incommodorum causam secum trahebant. Simul etiam ac rerum proprietates distinctæ esse coeperunt, deserta causa publica, ad suum commodum quisque collimavit. Unde si ab uno collegio in aliud commigrandum erat, colligendæ simul omnes erant Sarcinulæ, alioqui nuda omnia & inania reperturis. Iesuitæ soli reperêre modum, quo nihil possidentes omnia possideant: nam & depositis omnibus impedimentis securi passim ambulant, & quocunque gentium proficiscuntur, omnem supellectilem & corporis cultum inter suos opportunum nanciscuntur. Præterea informi quodam habitu Monachi incedentes, tetricum quiddam & inhumanum sapiut: hi nudis pedibus, hi feneftratis calceis, hi turbinato vertice & capucio, hi cucullâ vel nigrâ, vel albâ, vel cinericia, &c, aut contortis funibus horrendi. At Iesuitæ formam communem & usitatam tenent, ut se turbis hominum ultro citróque misceant, rumusculos impune captent, suumque vigilum & speculatorum, seu potius probitorum munus exequantur. Inde est quod ad extremas oras nullo pene sumptu abeunt, & gravissimas Papæiussu Legationes obeunt, quæ Cardinalibus antea demandari solebant. Tantum etiam inter Monachos & Iesuitas, quod ad habitus victusque formam attinet, interest, quantum inter veteres meretrices aulicas & recentiores illæ pulchritudinem suam in ieiuna quadam corporis exilitate constituebant, unde miserè genium suum affligebant: hæ vero veterem illam hæresim damnantes, corpus suum intus & in cute splendide curandum, neque quicquam in fraudem generis de demenso detrahendum censent.
units.tr: I shall nevertheless show briefly in what respects the Jesuits chiefly differ from the other monks. The monks could receive no legacies from the wills of their own people, nor from those who died intestate, so no complaint of an undutiful will could lie against them. The Jesuits, however, have reserved for themselves the right to take up inheritances that fall to them in a private capacity, and to break wills on that pretext. And although the monks used to hunt for large gifts from dying and failing men, it cannot be denied that the Jesuits do the same, or do it more carefully. But there is this difference: they do not bind themselves to chant prayers morning and evening, nor do they defile the shrines of the saints with corpses; whatever is given to them, they wish to hold as pure and clean for themselves. They also reformed that shameful practice of monks who went through the villages laden with wallets, begging grain and alms from door to door, while in the churches, as in the marketplace, they bought wine, porridge and eggs for nothing. But the Jesuits, at home and abroad, display nothing but neatness and elegance. Moreover, they have suppressed certain expressions of mine and yours, which were already spreading among the monks and bringing great trouble with them. As soon as the ownership of goods began to be separated, each man, abandoning the common cause, aimed at his own advantage; so if one had to move from one college to another, all the baggage had to be gathered together, or else they would find everything bare and empty. The Jesuits alone have found a way by which, possessing nothing, they possess everything: for, with all encumbrances laid aside, they walk about carefree, and wherever they travel among the nations they find among their own people every household goods and bodily comfort they need. Again, monks going about in unsightly dress seem gloomy and inhuman: some go barefoot, some in patched shoes, some with pointed hoods and cowls, black or white or ash-coloured, and so on, others frightening with knotted ropes. But the Jesuits keep a common and ordinary form of dress, so that they can mingle freely with crowds of men, catch little rumours with impunity, and perform the duty of watchmen and spies, or rather of informers. Hence it is that they go to the furthest shores at almost no expense, and undertake the most serious embassies at the command of the Pope, which were formerly entrusted to cardinals. There is as much difference between monks and Jesuits in dress and manner of living as there was between the old courtesans and the newer ones: the former placed their beauty in a meagre slenderness of body, by which they miserably afflicted their own nature; the latter, condemning that old heresy, think the body should be splendidly cared for both within and on the skin, and hold that nothing should be withdrawn from the natural measure to the detriment of their kind.

units.la: CAPUT III. DE HABITV ET VESTITV IE- SVITARVM.
units.tr: Chapter III. On the Habit and Dress of the Jesuits.

units.la: ABINITIO, cùm simularent peregrinationem Hierosolymitanam, Venetias proficiscebantur baculo innixi pedites: vestitus eorum omnium erat, ut peregrinorum pauperum: pendebat è scapulis mantica ex corio: Rosaria palàm gestabant de collo suspensa, ut supra quoque diximus. Sed audi quæso quantum hodie Ignatiani mutati sint ab illis. Nam cùm hinc inde peregrinantur, galeris utuntur seu pileis turritis: Baretam autem suam consecratam apud se nihilominus reservant: Et si Collegium vel domum Iesuiticam ingrediantur, pileo turrito remoto, Baretas, ut agnoscantur, recipiunt, quâ re nescio quam existimationem sibi creari putant. Hæ Baretæ quadrangulares, & in formam crucis ex pretiosa materia formatæ sunt: expendunt enim pro qualibet ut minimum coronatum. Perhibent Ioannem 6. Mifnenfem Episcopum viso Monacho, dicere solitum fuisse: Nullum animal audacius esse eo, quod è cucullo prosiliceret. Si quis nostra ætate assereret, Nullum animal impudentius esse eo, quod caput pileolo quadrato, seu quadricornuto, tegit, à vero opinor non aberraverit.
units.tr: At the beginning, when they pretended to be making a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, they set out for Venice on foot, leaning on staves. All of them dressed like poor pilgrims, with a leather wallet hanging from their shoulders. They openly wore rosaries hung from their necks, as we also said above. But please hear how much the Ignatians today have changed from those men. When they travel about here and there, they wear travelling hats or towered caps. Yet they keep their consecrated biretta at home all the same. And when they enter a college or Jesuit house, they take off the towered cap and put on the biretta, so that they may be recognised, and by this they think some esteem is created for them. These birettas are square and shaped like a cross, made of precious material; for they cost at least a crown each. It is reported that John VI, Bishop of Meissen, when he saw a monk, used to say: "No animal is more bold than that which springs out of a cowl." If someone in our own age were to assert that no animal is more shameless than the one that covers its head with a square or four-cornered cap, I think he would not be far from the truth.

units.la: Pro Cucullis, quod sanctissimum tamè hactenus Monachorum indumentum habitum fuit, utuntur pallijs philosophicis, hoc est, oblongis & quidem nigris. Sub his pallijs tuniculas habent, quas Solannas dicunt, ad plantam usq; pedis fere dependentes, quas Canabe holosericâ stringunt.
units.tr: Instead of the cowl, which has nevertheless always been the most holy garment of the monks, they wear philosophers' cloaks, that is, long ones, and indeed black. Under these cloaks they have little tunics, which they call soutanes, hanging almost down to the sole of the foot, and they fasten them with a cord of silk.

units.la: Sub tuniculis thoraces, caligas & tibialia gestant de optimo pannorum genere, quo etiam dum seculares erant, utebantur.
units.tr: Under the tunics they wear waistcoats, breeches and stockings of the best kind of cloth, which they also used when they were still laymen.

units.la: Calceos habent corrigijs constrictos.
units.tr: They have shoes fastened with straps.

units.la: Regula enim praecipit, habitum illorum conformem esse debere vestimentis, quibus Clerici & Sacerdotes utuntur: ne novo & peregrino habitu hominibus, quibus cum versantur & agunt, molestiam vel aversionem creent. Ideo in Regula additur. Paupertatem illorum non debere esse vestium immunditiâ, sordibus vel pannositate sordidatam: sed puram, mundam, elegantem & hominibus gratam.
units.tr: For the Rule commands that their habit should be like the clothing that clerics and priests use, so that they do not cause annoyance or aversion to the people among whom they live and work by a new and strange habit. Therefore the Rule adds that their poverty should not be stained by dirt, filth or shabbiness of clothing, but should be pure, clean, elegant and pleasing to men.

units.la: Cum igitur reliquorum Monachiorum incedant alij nudis pedibus, alij fenestratis calceis, alij turbinato vertice, alij cucullâ aut contortis funibus ipso aspectu horrendi, Iesuitæ soli formam communem tenuerunt, ut se turbis hominum ulro citroq; misceat, rumusculos impune capterint, suumq; vigilum & speculatorum munus solertius exequantur.
units.tr: So while the other monks go about, some barefoot, some in perforated shoes, some with shaven crowns, some in cowls or with twisted ropes, horrifying in their very appearance, the Jesuits alone have kept a common form of dress, so that they may mingle freely with crowds of people, come and go, gather little bits of news with impunity, and carry out their duty of watching and spying more skilfully.

units.la: His suis vestimentis spiritualem interpretationem affingunt. Pilei enim mysterium est signum crucis: significat etiam Trinitatis unitatem, & cum eadem Beatæ Virginis Mariæ coniunctionem. Eorum praeterea hoc volunt mysterium esse, ut quatuor cornua vel anguli quatuor mundi plagas designent; ad quas vel à Pontifice ipso, vel à suo Generali, etiam non accepto viatico, ablegantur. Tunicula interior Albam, quâ Iesum Herodes derisit, designat. Thoracem, caligas, calceos, cingulum vel zonam, fascias crurales ex Pauli epistola ad Ephesios 6. cap. interpretantur. Indusium volunt esse perpetuæ castitatis devotæ memoriam. Si etiam se induunt, vel vestibus exuunt, certas preculas recitant. Exempli gratia, si Calceos laudunt, dicunt: Domine non sum dignus, solvam corrigiam calceamenti tui. Si se constringunt: Cinge Domine femora mea castitatis cingulo, &c.
units.tr: To these garments they attach a spiritual interpretation. For the mystery of the towered cap is the sign of the cross; it also signifies the unity of the Trinity and the union of the Blessed Virgin Mary with it. They further want the mystery to be this: that the four horns or corners designate the four quarters of the world, to which they are sent, either by the Pope himself or by their General, even without taking provisions for the journey. The inner tunic signifies the white robe in which Herod mocked Jesus. They explain the breastplate, the breeches, the shoes, the girdle or sash, and the leg-bands from the sixth chapter of Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians. They want the undershirt to be a memorial of perpetual and devoted chastity. And if they put on or take off their garments, they recite certain little prayers. For example, if they praise their shoes, they say: "Lord, I am not worthy; I will loose the latchet of thy shoe." If they fasten themselves: "Gird my loins, Lord, with the girdle of chastity," and so on.

units.la: Hunc vero habitum, cum peregrinantur, interdum deponunt, & alium induunt, puta mercatorum, nobilium, opificum, &c. ut sic eo tutius inter Evangelicos latere, & omnia facilius expiscari & explorare possint.
units.tr: When they travel, they sometimes lay aside this habit and put on another, that of merchants, nobles, craftsmen and so on, so that they may hide more safely among the Evangelicals in this way, and may more easily fish out and examine everything.

units.la: Sed in quascunque tandem sese formas flexerint, sive cucullati, sive palliati vel quocunque alio habitu induti sint, unicus tamen salutis portus nobis omnibus est propositus, ad quem syncera & recta fide nisi quis collimet, quocunque tandem pallio, aut cucullâ, aut veste exornatus fuerit, naufragium patiatur oportet.
units.tr: But into whatever forms they have at last bent themselves, whether cowled or cloaked, or clothed in any other habit, there is nevertheless one harbour of salvation set before us all, and unless a man aims at it with sincere and right faith, however adorned he may be with cloak, or cowl, or garment, he must suffer shipwreck.

units.la: Quod si ab hoc illorum externo habitu oculos ad mores illorum & gestus externos aversas, ita sunt ad speciem humanitatis, pietatis omniumq; virtutum compositi, ut opinari possit aliquis, Ioannem Baptistam, in severo isto cultu non fuisse sanctiorem. Fingite enim, Lectores, vos iam videre ex Iesuitarum grege aliquem: hominem oculis videbitis humanissimum, si vultui: pientissimum & humilimum, si gestui creditis: caput elegantèr comptum & in unam partem habet inclinatum, ut videatur eius similis, qui nostri causa in cruce dependit: cruces etiam, dictas & sculptas in manibus habet. At enim vero gestuum hic apparatus nihil aliud est, nisi pellis ovina, & larva virtutum, ad decipiendos & fallendos homines comparata. Nec mentior, si dico, sub isto vestitu, gestu & habitu latere lupinum animum, imo antiquum serpentem, auctorem dissidiorum, turbarum, bellorum, caedium, atq; adeo omnium malorum, à quibus usquam Ecclesiæ & Reipubl. periculum esse potest.
units.tr: But if you turn your eyes away from their outward habit to their manners and outward gestures, they are so composed in appearance of humanity, piety and all virtues that someone might suppose John the Baptist was not holier in that severe dress. Imagine, readers, that you already see one of the Jesuit flock: you will see a most humane man if you judge by his face, a most pious and humble one if you trust his bearing; his head is neatly combed and inclined to one side, so that he may seem like one who hangs on the cross for our sake; he also has crosses, pictures and carvings in his hands. But indeed this display of gestures is nothing but a sheep's skin and a mask of virtues, prepared to deceive and beguile men. Nor am I lying if I say that under this dress, bearing and habit lies a wolfish mind, indeed the ancient serpent, the author of dissensions, disturbances, wars, slaughters, and therefore of all the evils from which there can ever be danger to the Church and the commonwealth.

units.la: REGVLÆ CAPVT IV. DE REGVLIS ET CONSTITVTIONI- BVS IESVITARVM.
units.tr: THE RULES, CHAPTER IV. CONCERNING THE RULES AND CONSTITUTIONS OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: SVMMARIVM EARVM CON- STITVTIONVM, QVAE AD SPIRI- TVALEM NOSTRORVM INSTITVTIO- nem pertinent, & ab omnibus obser- vandæ sunt.
units.tr: A SUMMARY OF THOSE CONSTITUTIONS WHICH PERTAIN TO THE SPIRITUAL INSTITUTION OF OUR PEOPLE AND ARE TO BE OBSERVED BY ALL.

units.la: QVAMVIS summa sapientia, & bonitas Dei Creatoris nostri ac Domini sit, quæ conseruatura est, gubernatura, atque promoturam in suo sanctoser-vitio hanc minimam Societatem Iesu, ut eam dignata est inchoare: ex parte vero nostra interna charitatis, & amoris illius lex, quam Sanctus Spiritus scribere, & in cordibus imprimere solet, potius quàm nullæ externæ Constitutiones, ad id adiuuta sit: Quia tamen suæ-uis dispositio diuinæ prouidentiæ suarum creaturarum cooperationem exigit, & quia Christi Domini nostri Vicarius ita statuit, & Sanctorum exempla, & ratio ipsa nos docet in Domino: necessarium esse arbitramur, Constitutiones conscribi, quæ juvent ad melius in via incepta diuini obsequij procedendum, juxta instituti nostri rationem.
units.tr: Although the highest wisdom and goodness of God our Creator and Lord will preserve, govern and advance in his holy service this smallest Society of Jesus, as he has deigned to begin it, and although on our part the inner law of charity and love, which the Holy Spirit is wont to write and imprint on hearts, has helped it more than any external constitutions could, nevertheless, since the disposition of his divine providence requires the cooperation of his creatures, and since the Vicar of Christ our Lord has so decreed, and the examples of the saints and reason itself teach us in the Lord, we judge it necessary that constitutions be drawn up which may help us to proceed more effectively on the way of divine service once begun, according to the manner of our institute.

units.la: 1. Finis huius Societatis est, non solum saluti & perfectioni propriarum animarum, cum diuina gratia vacare: sed cum eadem impense in salutem, & perfectionem proximo-rum incumbere.
units.tr: 1. The end of this Society is not only to devote itself, with divine grace, to the salvation and perfection of its own souls, but also to labour earnestly for the salvation and perfection of its neighbours.

units.la: 3. Nostra vocationis est, diuersa loca peragrare & vitam agere in quauis mundi plaga, ubi maius Dei obsequium, & animarum auxilium speratur.
units.tr: 3. Our vocation is to travel through diverse places and to live in any region of the world where a greater service of God and help of souls is hoped for.

units.la: 4. Ratio viuendi in exterioribus justas ob causas, majus Dei obsequium semper inuendo, communis est: nec ullas ordinarias pœnitentias, vel corporis afflictiones ex obligatione subeundas habet, sed illas assumere quiuis poterit, quas sibi videbuntur, cum approbatione Superioris, ad maiorem sui spiritus profectum conuenire, & quas propter eundem finem Superiores eis poterunt imponere.
units.tr: 4. The manner of living in external matters, for just causes and always seeking the greater service of God, is common to all. Nor are there any ordinary penances or bodily afflictions to be undertaken as an obligation. Anyone may take up those which seem to him suited to the greater progress of his spirit, with the approval of the Superior, and the Superiors may impose on them for the same end those which they think fit.

units.la: 5. Ipso initio sui in Societatem ingressus, debet quisque generalem totius vitæ consessionem apud aliquem Sacerdotem à superiore assignatum facere, & post eam sacratissimum Christi Domini nostri corpus sumere: & sic sexto quoque mense eodem modo genera-liter ab ultima inchoando confitebitur. Et omnes tam Professi quàm formati Coadjutores semel singulis annis parati esse debebunt ad confessionem generalem, quæ ab ultima generali inchoetur, ei, quem Superior sibi substituerit faciendam.
units.tr: 5. At the very beginning of entering the Society, each should make a general confession of his whole life to some priest assigned by the Superior, and after it receive the most sacred body of Christ our Lord. So every sixth month he will confess in the same way generally, beginning from the last. And all, both professed and formed coadjutors, must be ready once a year to make a general confession, beginning from the last general one, to the person whom the Superior has appointed.

units.la: 6. Vtantur quotidie omnes conscientiæ suæ examinatione consueta: Si sacerdotes non fuerint, confiteantur oportet, & sanctissimum Sacramentum Eucharistiæ sumant octavo quoque die: & unus omnium sit Confessarius à Superiore constitutus: quod si fieri non poterit, quisque certè suum stabilem habeat Confessarium, cui ipsius conscientia profundis aperta sit.
units.tr: 6. All should daily use the customary examination of conscience. If they are not priests, they must confess and receive the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist every eighth day. Let there be one confessor appointed for all by the Superior; but if this cannot be done, each should at least have his own fixed confessor, to whom his conscience is fully opened.

units.la: 7. Qui autem alij, quàm suo Confessario designato confiteretur, debet postmodum (quantum recordari poterit) eidem suo Confessario totam suam conscientiam aperire, ut nihil ignorando quod ad eam pertineat, melius in Domino possit eundem juuare.
units.tr: 7. Whoever confesses to someone other than his designated confessor must afterwards (as far as he can recall) open his whole conscience to that same confessor, so that, leaving nothing unknown that pertains to it, the confessor may better help him in the Lord.

units.la: 8. Vnusquisque eorum, qui Societatem ingrediuntur, consilium illud Christi sequendo, Qui dimiserit patrem, &c. existimet sibi patrem, matrem, fratres, & sorores, & quicquid in mundo habebat, relinquendum: imo sibi dictum existimet verbum illud: Qui non odit patrem, & matrem, insuper & animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Et ita curandum ei est, ut omnem carnis affectum erga sanguine junctos exuat, ac illum in spiritualem convertat, eósque diligat eo solùm amore, quem ordinata charitas exigit, ut qui ommdo mundo, ac proprio amori mortuus, Christo Domino nostro soli vivit, eumque locoparentum, fratrum, & rerum omnium habet.
units.tr: 8. Each of those who enter the Society, following the counsel of Christ, "He who leaves father, etc.", should consider that father, mother, brothers, sisters, and whatever he had in the world, must be left behind. Indeed, let him take to himself that word: "He who does not hate father and mother, and even his own soul, cannot be my disciple." And so he must take care to strip off every fleshly affection towards blood relations and turn it into a spiritual one, loving them with that love only which ordered charity demands; so that, dead to the whole world and to his own self-love, he lives for Christ our Lord alone, and has him in place of parents, brothers and all things.

units.la: 9. Ad maiorem in spiritu profectum, & praecipue ad maiorem submissionem, & humilitatem propriam, contentus esse quisque debet, ut omnes errores, & defectus ipsius, & res quaecunque, quae notata in eo, & observata fuerint, Superioribus per quem vis, qui extra confessionem eas acceperit, manifestentur.
units.tr: 9. For greater progress in the spirit, and especially for greater submission and humility of his own, each one ought to be content that all his errors and defects, and whatever things are noted and observed in him, be made known to the Superiors through whatever person has received them outside confession.

units.la: 10. Boni etiam omnes consulant, ab aliis corrigi, & ad aliorum correctionem juvare, ac manifestare sese invicem sint parati debito cum amore, & charitate, ad maiorem spiritus profectum: praesertim ubi a Superiore, qui illorum curam gerit, fuerit ita praescriptum, aut interrogatum ad maiorem Dei gloriam.
units.tr: 10. All good men should also be willing to be corrected by others, and to help in the correction of others, and to reveal themselves to one another with due love and charity, for greater progress of the spirit; especially where this has been prescribed by the Superior who has their care, or asked for the greater glory of God.

units.la: 11. Diligenter animadvertant oportet (magnificando summique momenti id esse ducendo in conspectu Creatoris ac Domini nostri, quantopere juvet, ac conferat ad vitae spiritualis profectum, omnino, & non ex parte abhorrere ab omnibus, quae mundus amat, & amplectitur, & admitti & concupiscere totis viribus quicquid Christus Dominus noster amavit, & amplexus est. Quemadmodum enim mundani homines, qui ea, quae mundi sunt, sequuntur, diligunt, & quaerunt magna cum diligentia, honores scilicet, famam, magni nominis existimationem in terra, sicut mundus eos docet: sic qui procedunt in spiritu, & contra ferio Christum Dominum nostrum sequuntur, amant, & ardenter exoptant, quae ijs omnino contraria sunt, indui nimirum eadem vestes, ac insignibus Domini sui pro ipsius amore, ac reverentia, adeo ut si fine offensione ulla divinae majestatis, & absque proximi peccato foret, vellent contumelias, falsa testimonia, & injurias pati, ac stulti haberi & existimari (nulla tamen ad id per eos data occasione) eo quod exoptant assimilari, ac imitari aliquo modo creatorem, ac Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, eius & vestibus & insignibus indui: quandoquidem illa ipse propter maiorem profectum nostrum spiritualem induit, nobisque exemplum dedit, ut in omnibus, quoad eius fieri poterit, divina gratia aspirante, eum imitari & sequi, cum vera sit via, quae ducit homines ad vitam, velimus.
units.tr: 11. They ought carefully to observe (magnifying this and counting it of the highest importance in the sight of our Creator and Lord) how greatly it helps and contributes to progress in spiritual life to abhor entirely, and not in part, all those things which the world loves and embraces, and to admit and desire with all their strength whatever Christ our Lord loved and embraced. For just as worldly men, who follow what belongs to the world, love and seek with great diligence honours, fame, and the esteem of a great name on earth, as the world teaches them, so those who advance in the spirit and follow Christ our Lord against the world love and eagerly desire what is wholly contrary to these: namely, to be clothed in the same garments and insignia of their Lord, out of love and reverence for him. So much so that, if there were no offence to the divine majesty and no sin against the neighbour, they would wish to suffer insults, false witness and injuries, and to be held and regarded as fools (no occasion for this being given by them), because they desire to be made like, and in some way to imitate, the Creator and our Lord Jesus Christ, and to be clothed in his garments and insignia. For he himself put these on for our greater spiritual progress, and gave us an example, that in all things, as far as it can be done, with divine grace inspiring, we should wish to imitate and follow him, since he is the true way that leads men to life.

units.la: 12. Ut melius ad hunc perfectionis gradum in spirituali vita tam preciosum perveniatur, majus, ac impensius studium cuiusque sit, quaerere in Domino majorem sui abnegationem, & continuam in rebus omnibus, quoad poterit, mortificationem.
units.tr: 12. So that this most precious degree of perfection in spiritual life may be reached more readily, each one should have a greater and more earnest zeal to seek in the Lord greater self-denial and continual mortification in all things, as far as he is able.

units.la: 13. In exercendis officiis abjectis, & humilibus, promptius ea suscipi convenit, a quibus sensus magis abhorrebit: si quidem injunctum fuerit, ut in eis se exerceat.
units.tr: 13. In performing lowly and humble offices, it is fitting to undertake more readily those which the senses most shrink from, if indeed it has been enjoined that he exercise himself in them.

units.la: 14. Ante vertere oportet tentationes, adhibitis earum contrariis, ut cum quis animadvertitur ad superbiam esse propensus, exerceri is debet in rebus abjectioribus, quae ad humiliandum ipsum utiles futurae videantur: & sic de aliis pravis animae propensionibus.
units.tr: 14. Temptations ought to be overcome beforehand by applying their contraries: so that when someone is seen to be prone to pride, he should be exercised in humbler tasks which seem likely to be useful for humbling him; and so with other evil propensities of the soul.

units.la: 15. Omnes constanti animo incumbamus, ut nihil perfectionis, quod divina gratia consequi possimus, in absoluta omnium Constitutionum observatione, nostrique instituti peculiari ratione adimplenda praetermittamus.
units.tr: 15. Let us all with steadfast mind strive not to omit any perfection which we can attain by divine grace, in the absolute observance of all the Constitutions and in fulfilling our institute in its particular manner.

units.la: 16. Omnes, qui se Societati addixerunt, in virtutum solidarum, ac perfectarum, & spiritualium rerum studium incumbant: ac in hujusmodi majus momentum, quam in doctrina, vel aliis donis naturalibus, & humanis constitutum esse ducant: Illa enim interiora sunt, ex quibus efficaciam ad exteriora permanare ad finem nobis propositum oportet.
units.tr: 16. All who have devoted themselves to the Society should apply themselves to the study of solid and perfect virtues and spiritual things, and they should hold these to be of greater moment than learning or other natural and human gifts. For those are inner things, from which efficacy must flow out to external things for the end proposed to us.

units.la: 17. Omnes rectam habere intentionem studeant non solum circa vitae suae statum, verum etiam circa res omnes particulares: id semper in eis sincere spectantes, ut serviant, & placeant divinae bonitati propter seipsam, & propter charitatem, & eximia beneficia, quibus praevenit nos, potius quam ob timorem poenarum, vel spem praemiorum (quam vis hinc etiam juvari debeant) & in omnibus quaerant Deum, exuentes se, quantum fieri potest, amore omnium creaturarum, ut affectum universum in ipsarum Creatorem conserant, eum in omnibus creaturis amando, & omnes in eo, juxta sanctissimam, ac divinam ipsius voluntatem.
units.tr: 17. All should take care to have a right intention, not only regarding the state of their life but also regarding all particular matters, always sincerely aiming at this: that they serve and please the divine goodness for its own sake, and out of charity and the outstanding benefits with which it has anticipated us, rather than out of fear of punishments or hope of rewards (although they ought to be helped by these also). In all things let them seek God, stripping themselves, as far as possible, of love for all creatures, so that they may direct their whole affection to the Creator of them, loving him in all creatures and all of them in him, according to his most holy and divine will.

units.la: REGVLÆ
units.tr: REGULÆ

units.la: 18. In conciónibus domesticis de iis crebrò tractent, quæ ad sui abnegationem, & in virtutibus professum, & omnimodam perfectionem attinent: ad ea se invicem exhortando, & præcipuè ad unionem & charitatem fraternam.
units.tr: 18. In domestic conferences let them often discuss those matters which pertain to self-denial, to advancement in virtue, and to perfection in every respect, exhorting one another to these things, and especially to unity and fraternal charity.

units.la: 19. Magnopere conferet, devote, quoad fieri poterit, ea munera obire, in quibus magis exercetur humilitas & charitas. Et in universum loquendo, quanto aliquis se arctiùs Deo adstrinxerit, & liberaliorem erga summam maiestatem se præstiterit, tanto eum in se liberaliorem etiam experietur, & ipse in dies magis idoneus erit ad gratias, & dona spiritualia uberiora recipienda.
units.tr: 19. It will greatly help, devoutly and as far as it can be done, to undertake those duties in which humility and charity are more exercised. And speaking generally, the more closely someone binds himself to God, and the more generously he shows himself toward the supreme Majesty, the more generous he will find God to be toward him, and day by day he himself will become more fit to receive graces and richer spiritual gifts.

units.la: 20. Postquam aliquis in corpus Societatis cooptatus fuerit in aliquo gradu, ad alium progredi curare non debet: sed in suo persici, & obsequio Dei, & gloriæ sese impendere.
units.tr: 20. Once someone has been admitted into the body of the Society in some rank, he ought not to strive to advance to another, but to devote himself to his own perfection, to the service of God, and to the glory of God.

units.la: 21. Omnes suum tempus rebus spiritualibus impendant, & devotioni quarendæ pro mensura gratiæ Dei ipsis communicatæ insistant.
units.tr: 21. Let all spend their time on spiritual things, and labour at devotion according to the measure of God's grace communicated to them.

units.la: 22. Ab illusionibus Dæmonis in suis spiritualibus exercitationibus cauent, & se contra omnes tentationes tueantur: simul rationes sciant, quæ adhiberi possint, ut eas superent: & ad veras, solidasq; virtutes consequendas insistant: sive plures adsint visitationes spirituales, sive pauciores: curent verò semper in via diuini seruitij progressum facere.
units.tr: 22. Let them beware of the illusions of the Devil in their spiritual exercises, and guard themselves against all temptations; at the same time let them know the means that can be employed to overcome them, and let them labour to attain true and solid virtues, whether there are many spiritual visitations or few; and let them always take care to make progress on the way of divine service.

units.la: 23. Paupertas, ut murus religionis firmus, diligenda, & in sua puritate conseruanda est, quantum diuina gratia aspirante fieri poterit.
units.tr: 23. Poverty, as the firm wall of the religious life, is to be cherished and preserved in its purity, as far as divine grace shall enable it.

units.la: 24. Diligant omnes paupertatem, ut matrem, & iuxta mensuram sanctæ discretionis suis temporibus eius effectus aliquos experiantur: nullaq; re tanquam propria utantur, parati sint ad mendicandum ostiatim, quando vel obedientiæ vel necessitas id exiget.
units.tr: 24. Let all love poverty as a mother, and in due measure, according to the discretion of holy prudence, let them experience some of its effects at their proper times; let them use nothing as their own, and be ready to beg from door to door whenever obedience or necessity demands it.

units.la: 25. Victus, vestitus, & lecti ratio erit ut pauperibus accommodata: & unusquisq; sibi persuadeat, quod quæ vilißima erunt ex iis, quæ domi sunt, ei tribuuntur propter ipsius maiorem abnegationem, & spiritualem profectum.
units.tr: 25. The manner of food, clothing and bedding shall be suited to the poor; and let each persuade himself that the cheapest of those things that are in the house are assigned to him for the sake of his greater self-denial and spiritual progress.

units.la: 26. Intelligant omnes, quod mutuo dare, vel accipere, vel dispensare quidquam de iis, quæ domi sunt, minimè possunt, nisi Superior conscius consensum præstiterit.
units.tr: 26. Let all understand that they can by no means lend, borrow, or distribute anything of those things that are in the house, unless the Superior, aware of it, has given consent.

units.la: 27. Omnes, qui sub obedientia sunt Societatis, meminerint se gratis dare debere quæ gratis acceperunt, nec postulando, nec admittendo stipendiu, vel eleemosynas ullas, quibus Missæ vel Confessiones, vel Prædicationes, vel quod vis aliud officium exijs, quæ Societas, iuxta nostrum institutum exercere potest, compensari videatur: ut sic maiori cum libertate possit, & proximorum ædificatione, in diuino seruitio procedere.
units.tr: 27. All who are under the obedience of the Society should remember that they ought to give freely what they have received freely, neither demanding nor accepting any stipend or alms by which Masses, Confessions, Preachings, or any other office that the Society can perform according to our institute, might seem to be compensated; so that they may proceed in the divine service with greater freedom and to the edification of their neighbours.

units.la: 28. Quæ ad votum castitatis pertinent, interpretatione non indigent, cum constet, quam sit perfectè obseruanda, nempe enitendo angelicam puritatem imitari, & corporis, & mentis nostræ munditia.
units.tr: 28. Matters pertaining to the vow of chastity need no interpretation, since it is well established how perfectly it is to be observed, namely by striving to imitate angelic purity, and the cleanness of both body and mind.

units.la: 29. Omnes diligentissimè curent portas sensuum suorum (oculorum præcipuè, aurium, & linguæ) ab omni inordinatione custodire, ac se in pace, & vera humilitate interna conseruare, & eam in silentio, cùm id obseruandum est, cùm autem loquendum in circumspectione, & ædificatione verborum, & modestia vultus, ac maturitate incessus, motuumque omnium, sine ullo impatientiæ, aut superbiæ signo exhibere: in omnibus procurando atque optando potiores partes aliis deferre, omnes in animo suo tanquam sibi superiores ducendo, & exterius honorem, ac reverentiam, quam exigit cuiusque status, cum simplicitate & moderatione religiosa exhibendo: atque ita fiat, ut se mutuo considerantes in devotione crescant, Deumque Dominum nostrum laudent, quem quisque in alio, ut in illius imagine, agnoscere studeat.
units.tr: 29. Let all most diligently take care to guard the doors of their senses (especially of the eyes, ears and tongue) against all disorder, and to keep themselves in peace and true inward humility; and let them show this in silence when silence is to be observed, but when speech is needed, in circumspection, edifying words, modesty of countenance, maturity of bearing and of all movements, without any sign of impatience or pride; always seeking and wishing to give the preferred place to others in all things, esteeming everyone in their mind as superior to themselves, and showing outwardly the honour and reverence that each person's status requires, with simplicity and religious moderation; and so let it come about that, considering one another, they grow in devotion and praise our Lord God, whom each should strive to recognise in another, as in his image.

units.la: 30. In refectione corporis curandum est, ut temperantia, modestia, & decentia interius, & exterius in omnibus obseruetur. Præmittatur benedictio, & sequatur actio gratiarum: quas omnes agere debent, cum ea, quæ par est, devotione, & reverentia. Et dum corpus edendo reficitur, sua etiam animæ refectio præbeatur.
units.tr: 30. In the refreshment of the body care must be taken that temperance, modesty and decorum are observed in everything, inwardly and outwardly. Let a blessing be said first, and let a thanksgiving follow, which all ought to offer with the devotion and reverence that is fitting. And while the body is refreshed by eating, let the soul also be given its own refreshment.

units.la: 31. Expedit in primis ad profectum, & valdè necessarium est, ut omnes perfectâ obedientiæ se dedant: superiorem (quicunque ille sit) loco Christi Domini nostri agnoscentes, & interna reverentia & amore eum prosequentes, nec solùm in executione externa eorum, quæ rum, quæ injungit integrè, prompte, fortiter, & cum humilitate debita, sine excusationibus, & obmurmurationibus obediant; licet difficilia, & secundum sensualitatem repugnantia jubeat, verumetiam conentur interius resignationem, & veram abnegationem propriæ voluntatis, & judicij habere, voluntatem, ac judicium suum cum eo, quod Superior vult & sentit, in omnibus rebus (ubi peccatum non cerneretur) omnino conformantes, propositá sibi voluntate, ac judicio Superioris pro regula suæ voluntatis, & judicij, quo exactius conformentur primæ; ac summæ regulæ omnis bonæ voluntatis, & iudicij, quæ est æterna bonitas, & sapientia.
units.tr: 31. It is most useful for progress, and very necessary, that all devote themselves to perfect obedience, acknowledging the superior (whoever he may be) in the place of Christ our Lord, and following him with inward reverence and love; and not only in the outward execution of those things he enjoins should they obey entirely, promptly, vigorously and with due humility, without excuses and murmuring, even if he commands difficult things and things repugnant to sensuality; but they should also strive to have inwardly resignation and true denial of their own will and judgment, conforming their will and judgment wholly to what the Superior wills and thinks in all matters (where no sin is discerned), setting before themselves the will and judgment of the Superior as the rule of their own will and judgment, so that they may be more exactly conformed to the first and highest rule of every good will and judgment, which is eternal goodness and wisdom.

units.la: 32. Liberam sui ipsorum, rerumq; suarum dispositionem omnes cum vera obedientia Superiori relinquant; nihil ei clausum, ne conscientiam quidem propriam tenendo, non repugnando, non contradicendo, nec ulla ratione iudicium proprium ipsius iudicio contrarium demonstrando: ut per unionem eiusdem sententiæ & voluntatis, atq; per debitam submissionem melius in divino obsequio conferventur, & progrediantur.
units.tr: 32. Let all leave the free disposition of themselves and their possessions to their Superior in true obedience; keeping nothing from him, not even their own conscience; not resisting, not contradicting, nor by any means showing their own judgment to be contrary to his judgment; so that through unity of opinion and will, and through due submission, they may be better preserved and advance in divine service.

units.la: 33. Omnes obedientiam plurimum observare, & in ea excellere studeant: nec solum in rebus obligatorijs, sed etiam in alijs: licet nihil aliud quàm signum voluntatis Superioris sine ullo expresso præcepto videretur. Versari autem debet ob oculos Deus creator ac Dominus noster, propter quem homini obedientia præstatur: & ut in spiritu amoris, & non cum perturbatione timoris procedatur, curandum est.
units.tr: 33. Let all strive to observe obedience greatly and to excel in it, not only in obligatory matters but also in others, even where nothing but a sign of the Superior's will appears, without any express command. God the Creator and our Lord, for whose sake obedience is rendered to man, ought to be kept before their eyes; and care must be taken that they proceed in a spirit of love and not with the disturbance of fear.

units.la: 34. Ad Superioris vocem perinde, ac si à Christo Domino egrederetur, quàm promptissimi simus, re quavis, atq; adeò litera à nobis inchoata, nec dum perfecta relicta.
units.tr: 34. Let us be most prompt at the voice of the Superior, just as if it came from Christ the Lord, leaving whatever matter, or even a letter begun by us, unfinished.

units.la: 35. Ad eum scopum vires omnes, ac intentionem in Domino convertamus, ut sancta obedientia tum in executione, tum in intellectu, sit in nobis semper omni ex parte perfecta cum magna celeritate, spirituali gaudio & perseverantia, quicquid nobis iniunctum fuerit obeundo, omnia justa esse nobis persuadendo, omnem sententiam, ac iudicium nostrum contrarium cæca quadam obedientia abnegando.
units.tr: 35. Let us turn all our powers and intention toward the Lord to this end: that holy obedience, both in execution and in understanding, may always be in us perfect in every respect, with great speed, spiritual joy and perseverance, performing whatever has been enjoined on us, persuading ourselves that all things commanded are just, and denying every opinion and judgment of our own that is contrary to it by a certain blind obedience.

units.la: 36. Quisq; sibi persuadeat, quod qui sub obedientia vivunt, se ferri, ac regi à divina providentia per Superiores suos, sinere debent perinde, ac si cadaver essent, quod quoquo versus ferri, & quacunq; ratione tractari se finit: vel similiter, atq; senus baculus, qui ubicunq;, & quacunq; in re velit eo uti, qui eum manu tenet, ei inservit.
units.tr: 36. Let each persuade himself that those who live under obedience ought to allow themselves to be carried and ruled by divine providence through their Superiors, just as if they were a corpse, which allows itself to be carried whithersoever and handled in whatever way; or like an old staff, which serves him who holds it in his hand, wherever and for whatever purpose he wishes to use it.

units.la: 37. Adimplere quisque debet quaevis pœnitentias, quæ propter defectus, & negligentiam suam, vel quidvis aliud fuerint iniunctæ. Pœnitentias verò huiusmodi prompta voluntate admittere deberet, cum vero emendationis, & spiritualis profectus desiderio, etiam si propter defectum non culpabilem iniungerentur.
units.tr: 37. Each one ought to perform whatever penances are imposed on him on account of his defects and negligence, or for any other reason. Indeed, he should accept such penances with a ready will, with a desire for amendment and spiritual progress, even if they were imposed for a fault that was not culpable.

units.la: 38. Cum aliquis ad ministeria culinæ obeunda ingreditur vel ad eum iuvandum, qui coquus est, eidem obedire cum magna humilitate, in rebus ad ipsius officium pertinentibus debet. Atque valde necessarium est, ut omnes non solum Superiori Societatis, vel Domus, sed etiam subordinatis officialibus, qui ex illo auctoritatem acceperunt, obediant: & affuescant non intueri, quis ille sit cui obediunt, sed potius quis ille, propter quem & cui in omnibus obediunt, qui est Christus Dominus.
units.tr: 38. When someone enters upon the duties of the kitchen, or to help the one who is the cook, he ought to obey him with great humility in those matters that pertain to his office. And it is very necessary that all obey not only the Superior of the Society or of the House, but also the subordinate officials who have received authority from him; and let them accustom themselves not to look at who that person is whom they obey, but rather at who it is for whose sake, and to whom, they obey in all things, namely Christ the Lord.

units.la: 39. Si aliquis ex ijs qui domi sunt, cuiquam scriberet, non nisi obtenta facultate, & literis ei ostensis, quem superior destinaverit, id faciat. Si ad eundem litera mitterentur, ei primo reddentur, qui à Superiore fuerit constitutus: qui eas lectas reddet, aut non reddet illi, ad quem sunt destinatæ, prout in Domino expedire ad maius ipsius bonum & Dei gloriam existimabit.
units.tr: 39. If any of those at home are to write to someone, they should do so only after obtaining permission and showing the letters to the superior whom he has appointed. If letters are sent to a member of the household, they shall first be given to the one whom the Superior has appointed. That person will read them and then either deliver them or withhold them from the addressee, as he judges best in the Lord for that person's greater good and for the glory of God.

units.la: 40. Quicunque hanc Societatem in Domino sequi volet, & in eadem ad maiorem Dei gloriam manere, sub sigillo confessionis, vel secreti, vel quacunque ratione ei placuerit, & ad maiorem ipsius consolationem fuerit, debet conscientiam suam magna cum humilitate, puritate, & charitate manifestare, rē nulla, qua Dominum universorum offenderit, celata, & totius anteactæ vitæ rationem integram, vel certè rerum maioris momenti Superiori, qui tum fuerit Societatis, vel cui ex Præpositis, vel aliis ex inferioribus ille iniunctus, prout magis convenire videretur, reddat: & sexto quoque mense rationem hanc sui. ab ultima, quam reddiderit, incipiendo quisque reddet. Sic etiam videtur, quod Coadiutores formati, & Professi singulis annis, vel crebrius, si Superiori videbitur, suæ conscientiæ rationem dicto modo eì reddant.
units.tr: 40. Whoever wishes to follow this Society in the Lord, and to remain in it for the greater glory of God, should disclose his conscience with great humility, purity and charity, under the seal of confession or of secrecy, or in whatever way seems good to him and most comforting to him. He must hide nothing by which he has offended the Lord of all, and he should give an account of his whole past life, or at least of matters of greater importance, to the Superior of the Society at the time, or to one of the Prepositi, or to another of the inferiors to whom he has been assigned, as seems most fitting. He should render this account of himself every sixth month, each beginning from the last one he rendered. It also seems right that the formed Coadjutors and the Professed should render an account of their conscience in the said manner to the Superior once a year, or more often if the Superior thinks fit.

units.la: 41. Nullam debent celare tentationem, quam Præfecto rerum spiritualium, vel Confessario, vel Superiori non aperiant: imò vero totam animam suam illis integrè manifestam esse, pergratum habeant; nec solùm defectus aperiant, sed etiam pœnitentias, vel mortificationes, & devotiones, ac virtutes omnes, voluntate pura optantes ab illis dirigi, sicubi à rectitudine deflecterent, nolentes suo proprio sensu duci, nisi conveniat cum iudicio illorum, quos Christi Domini nostri loco habent.
units.tr: 41. They must conceal no temptation that they do not reveal to the Prefect of spiritual affairs, the Confessor, or the Superior. Indeed, they should count it a great favour that their whole soul is fully open to them; and they should disclose not only their faults but also their penances, mortifications, devotions and all virtues, desiring with a pure will to be directed by them wherever they stray from the right path, and not wishing to be led by their own judgment, unless it agrees with the judgment of those whom they hold in the place of Christ our Lord.

units.la: 42. Idem sapiamus, idem, quoad eius fieri posset, dicamus omnes; iuxta Apostolum. Doctrina igitur differentes non admittantur, nec verbo in concionibus, vel lectionibus publicis, nec scriptis libris (qui quidem edi non poterunt in lucem sine approbatione, atque consensu Præpositi Generalis) Imò & iudiciorum de rebus agendis diversitas, quæ mater esse solet discordiæ, & inimica unionis voluntatum, quantum fieri potest, evitari debet. Unio verò, & conformitas mutua diligentissimè curanda est, nec quæ ei adversantur, permittenda: quo iuncti invicem fraternæ charitatis vinculo, melius & efficacius possint se divino obsequio, & auxilio proximorum impendere.
units.tr: 42. Let us all think the same and, as far as possible, say the same, according to the Apostle. Therefore those who differ in doctrine are not to be admitted, neither in word in sermons or public lectures, nor in written books (which indeed may not be published without the approval and consent of the Father General). Moreover, the diversity of opinions about matters to be done, which is usually the mother of discord and an enemy of the union of wills, should be avoided as far as possible. Union and mutual conformity should be most diligently cultivated, and nothing that opposes them should be permitted, so that, bound together by the bond of fraternal charity, they may be better and more effectively able to devote themselves to divine service and to the help of their neighbours.

units.la: 43. In Societate, nec fit, nec sentiatur animorum propensio ad partem alterutram factionis, quæ esset fortasse inter Principes, vel Dominos Christianos: sed fit potius quidam universalis amor, qui partes omnes (licet sibi invicem contrariæ sint) in Domino nostro amplectatur.
units.tr: 43. In the Society no inclination of minds to either side of a faction should arise or be felt, such as there may perhaps be among Christian princes or lords. Rather, a certain universal love should arise, which embraces all parties (although they may be opposed to one another) in our Lord.

units.la: 44. Omnes quamdiu corpore bene valent in spiritualibus, vel exterioribus rebus habeant, in quo occupentur, ne otium malorum omnium origo, quoad eius fieri possit, domi nostræ locum habeat.
units.tr: 44. As long as all are in good bodily health, they should have something to occupy them in spiritual or external matters, so that idleness, the origin of all evils, may, as far as possible, have no place in our house.

units.la: 45. Ut plenius possit Societas rebus spiritualibus iuxta suum institutum vacare, quoad eius fieri poterit, à negotijs secularibus abstineat: (qualia sunt testamentariorum, vel executorum, vel procuratorum rerum civilium, aut id genus officia) nec ea ullis precibus adducti obeunda suscipiant, vel in illis se occupari sinant.
units.tr: 45. So that the Society may be able to devote itself more fully to spiritual things according to its institute, it should, as far as possible, abstain from secular business (such as acting as executor or trustee of wills, or as agent in civil affairs, or offices of that kind). Nor should they undertake such duties at the request of anyone, nor allow themselves to be occupied with them.

units.la: 46. Ut nimia solicitudo in ijs, quæ ad corpus pertinent, reprehensibilis est: ita cura moderata tuendæ ad divinum obsequium valetudinis, ac virium corporis laude digna, & ab omnibus adhibenda est: & ea de causa cum animadverterint aliquid sibi nocere, vel aliquid aliud necessarium esse circa victum, vestitum, habitationem, officium, aut exercitationem, & sic de aliis rebus, admoneant omnes ea de re Superiorem, vel quem ad id Superior constituerit, duo interim observantes: Primum, ut antequam ad eum quid referant, se ad orandum recipiant, & post orationem si senserint rem deferendam ad Superiorem, id faciant: Alterum, ut cum verbo, aut scripto brevi (ne excidat memoria) Superiori rem expositam relinquant: & quicquid ille statuerit, optimum ducant; nec contendere, aut urgere per se, vel alium (sive concedatur quod petitur, sive non) peragant: quandoquidem sibi persuadere debent, id magis expedire ad divinum obsequium ac suum maius bonum, quod Superiori, re intellecta, in Domino visum fuerit.
units.tr: 46. Just as excessive anxiety about bodily matters is blameworthy, so a moderate care for maintaining health for the service of God, and a strength of body worthy of praise, should be shown by all. For this reason, when they notice that something is harming them, or that something else is needed concerning food, clothing, lodging, duties or exercise, and so on for other things, all should inform the Superior, or whoever the Superior has appointed for this, observing two points in the meantime. First, before they report anything to him, they should betake themselves to prayer, and after prayer, if they judge the matter should be referred to the Superior, they should do so. Second, they should leave the matter explained to him, by word or in brief writing (lest it slip from memory), and whatever he decides they should consider best; nor should they contend or press the matter, either themselves or through another, whether what is asked is granted or not, since they ought to be persuaded that what the Superior, once the matter is understood, judges fitting in the Lord is more conducive to divine service and to their own greater good.

units.la: 47. Ut non expedit tanto labore corporali quenquam onerari, ut spiritus obruatur, & corpus detrimentum patiatur: ita aliqua corporalis exercitatio, quæ utrumque iuvet, omnibus communiter convenit, etiam illis, qui mentalibus exercitijs debent insistere, quæ quidem externis interrumpi deberent, & non continuari, nec sine mensura discretionis assumi.
units.tr: 47. Just as it is not expedient to burden anyone with such great bodily labour that the spirit is overwhelmed and the body suffers harm, so some bodily exercise that helps both is suitable for all in common, including those who must devote themselves to mental exercises. These should indeed be interrupted by external activities rather than continued, and should not be undertaken without a measure of discretion.

units.la: 48. Corporis castigatio immoderata esse non debet, nec indiscreta in vigiliis, & abstinentijs, & alijs pœnitentijs externis, ac laboribus, quæ & nocumentum afferre, & maiora bona impedire solent. Ideo suo Confessario detegi ab unoquoque convenit, quidquid in hac parte faciat.
units.tr: 48. Immoderate chastisement of the body should not be practised, nor indiscreet use of vigils, abstinences and other external penances and labours, which are wont both to cause harm and to hinder greater goods. Therefore it is fitting that each person disclose to his Confessor whatever he does in this respect.

units.la: 49. AEgritudinis tempore non solum observare unusquisque obedientiam magna cum puritate debet: erga Superiores spirituales, ut ipsius animam regant: sed cum eadem humilitate erga medicos corporales, & infirmarios, ut corpus eius regant. 50. Qui
units.tr: 49. In time of sickness each one must observe obedience with great purity, not only towards the spiritual Superiors, who govern his soul, but also with the same humility towards the bodily physicians and infirmarians, who govern his body. 50. He who

units.la: 50. Qui aegrotat, humilitatem & patientiam suam praeferendo, non minorem aedificationem, dum morbo laborat, iis qui ipsum invisent, & cum eo versabuntur & agent, quam dum valebat corpore, ad maiorem Dei gloriam praestare curet, verbis piis, & ad aedificationem facientibus utendo, quae ostendant aegritudinem acceptari, ut donum de manu Creatoris, ac Domini nostri, quandoquidem non minus donum est, quam sanitas.
units.tr: 50. He who is sick, by putting forward his humility and patience, should take care that, while he suffers from illness, he gives no less edification to those who visit him and who associate and deal with him, than he gave when he was in health, for the greater glory of God, using pious words that build up others, which show that sickness is accepted as a gift from the hand of the Creator and our Lord, since it is no less a gift than health.

units.la: 51. Aliquoties singulis annis omnes a Superiore sibi poenitentias iniungi propter defectum observationis Regularum petant; ut haec cura indicium sit illius, quam de suo profectu spirituali in via Dei quisque habet.
units.tr: 51. Every so often, each year, all should ask the Superior to impose penances on them for their failure to observe the Rules, so that this care may be a sign of the concern each one has for his spiritual progress on the way of God.

units.la: 52. Omnes demum observationi Constitutionum studeant: ad quam eandem scire, saltem quae ad quemlibet pertinent, necesse est. Quare legere, vel audire eandem singulis mensibus oportebit.
units.tr: 52. Finally, all should strive to observe the Constitutions, for which it is necessary to know them, at least those parts that pertain to each person. Therefore it will be right to read or hear them every month.

units.la: REGVLAE COMMVNES.
units.tr: COMMON RULES.

units.la: SInguli praefinitum sibi tempus suae conscientiae bis quotidie examinandae, orationi, meditationi, lectionique impendant, cum omni diligentia in Domino.
units.tr: Each one is to set aside for himself a fixed time twice daily for examining his conscience, for prayer, meditation and reading, with all diligence in the Lord.

units.la: 2. Omnes quotidie sacro decenter intersint: & concionem, lectionemve sacram cum in templo nostro habebitur, audiant.
units.tr: 2. All are to attend Mass every day with becoming devotion, and to hear the sermon or sacred reading whenever it is given in our church.

units.la: 3. Singuli statuto die, & assignato sibi Confessario confiteantur, & non alteri sine Superioris facultate.
units.tr: 3. Each one is to confess on a set day to his assigned confessor, and not to another without the permission of the Superior.

units.la: 4. Omnes (qui Professi, aut formati Coadiutores non sunt) bis in anno sua vota renovabunt, praemissa confessione generali: quo tempore rationem suae conscientiae reddent, & quoties etiam Superiori visum fuerit, iuxta morem Societatis.
units.tr: 4. All (except the Professed and the formed Coadjutors) are to renew their vows twice a year, after a general confession; at that time they are to give an account of their conscience, and also as often as the Superior sees fit, according to the custom of the Society.

units.la: 5. In abstinentia sextae feriae, Societatis consuetudo servetur.
units.tr: 5. The Society's custom of abstaining on Friday is to be observed.

units.la: 6. Nullus mortificationem publice faciat, nec concionetur, nisi Superiore approbante.
units.tr: 6. No one is to perform public mortification or preach, unless the Superior approves.

units.la: 7. Nemo pecuniam apud se habeat: apud alium vero, nec pecuniam, nec quicquam aliud.
units.tr: 7. No one is to keep money on his own person; with another, however, he may keep neither money nor anything else.

units.la: 8. Libros nemo habeat sine facultate: in iis vero quibus uti licet, nec scribat quicquam, nec notam ullam imprimat.
units.tr: 8. No one is to keep books without permission; and of those which he is allowed to use, he is not to write anything or print any mark.

units.la: 9. Nemo rem ullam ex domo, vel ex alterius cubiculo sibi usurpet, aut ab externo, quovis modo sibi, aut alij accipiat, sine Superioris licentia.
units.tr: 9. No one is to take for himself anything from the house, or from another's room, nor is he to receive anything in any way from an outsider, either for himself or for another, without the licence of the Superior.

units.la: 10. Ad maiorem unionem eorum, qui in Societate vivunt, maiusque auxilium eorum, apud quos habitant, singuli addiscant eius regionis linguam, in qua resident, nisi forte ipsorum nativa illic esset utilior: salva tamen Latini sermonis lege in iis, qui literis dant operam.
units.tr: 10. To promote closer union among those who live in the Society, and greater help from those among whom they dwell, each is to learn the language of the region in which he resides, unless perhaps his native tongue would be more useful there; the rule of Latin speech is nevertheless to be kept for those who devote themselves to letters.

units.la: 11. Nullus ita cubiculum suum claudat, quin aperiri extrinsecus possit: aut arcam seu quicquam aliud habeat observatum absq; Superioris facultate.
units.tr: 11. No one is to lock his room so that it cannot be opened from outside, nor to keep a chest or anything else under lock without the Superior's permission.

units.la: 12. Apertae fenestrae nemo noctu dormiat, nec sine indusio, aut non cooperturs.
units.tr: 12. No one is to sleep at night with the window open, nor without an undershirt, nor without being covered.

units.la: 13. Nemo cubiculo egrediatur, nisi decenter vestitus.
units.tr: 13. No one is to leave his room unless decently dressed.

units.la: 14. Nemo eorum, qui ad domestica ministeria admittuntur, aut legere discat, aut scribere, aut si aliquid scit, plus literarum addiscat: nec quisquam eum doceat sine Praepositi Generalis facultate: sed satis ei erit sancta cum simplicitate, & humilitate Christo Domino nostro servire.
units.tr: 14. None of those who are admitted to domestic service is to learn to read or to write, or, if he already knows something, is to learn more letters; nor is anyone to teach him without the permission of the Father General. It will be enough for him to serve Christ our Lord with holy simplicity and humility.

units.la: 15. Signo campanae constitutis horis audito, omnes statim vel imperfecta litera relicta, ad id, ad quod vocantur, se conferant.
units.tr: 15. When the bell signals the appointed hours, all are immediately to go to whatever they are summoned to, leaving off even a letter half-written.

units.la: 16. Ut consulatur valetudini, nemo extra consueta tempora bibat, nec extra domum cibum sumat absque facultate Superioris.
units.tr: 16. To look after health, no one is to drink outside the usual times, nor take food outside the house without the Superior's permission.

units.la: 17. Qui male se habere praeter solitum senserit, id Infirmario, vel Praefecto sanitatis aut Superiori referat. Nemo vero medicinam ullam accipiat, aut medicum eligat, vel consulat, nisi approbante Superiore.
units.tr: 17. Whoever feels unwell beyond the usual, is to report it to the infirmarian, or the prefect of health, or the Superior. No one, however, is to take any medicine, choose a physician, or consult one, unless the Superior approves.

units.la: 18. Singuli etiam si Sacerdotes sint, cum primum surgunt, lectum operiant, eumque & reliqua componant hora consueta, & scopis cubiculum verrant, tertio saltem quoque die, exceptis iis, qui ob occupationes maioris momenti, aut valetudinis causa, iudicio Superioris sublevandi sunt.
units.tr: 18. Each one, even if he is a priest, as soon as he rises is to cover his bed and tidy the rest at the usual hour, and is to sweep his room at least every third day, except those who, on account of more important duties or for reasons of health, are to be relieved of this at the Superior's judgement.

units.la: 19. Mundities, quæ & ad valetudinem & ad ædificationem confert, omnibus curæ sit, tam circa seipsos quam circa alia omnia.
