Atq; ita, si non hominem externis oculis, sed Deum inspexeritis internis, haud sanè grave fuerit vobis voluntates vestras, atque judicia conformare ad eam regulam actionum vestrarum, quam ipsimet elegistis.
units.tr: Moreover, unless this obedience exists in judgment, it cannot happen that either the consent of the will or the execution is of the kind it ought to be. For nature has so ordered things that the powers of our soul, which are called appetitive, follow the apprehensive powers. Unless force is applied, the will, when judgment resists, will not be able to obey for long. But if anyone obeys for some period of time through that common apprehension, by which it is thought that one must obey even a command that is wrong, certainly such obedience cannot be stable and fixed. Thus perseverance fails, or at least the perfection of obedience, which consists in obeying promptly and eagerly. For there cannot be eagerness and diligence where minds and opinions are divided. The zeal and speed of carrying out also perish, when we hesitate whether it is expedient or not to do what we are commanded. That famous blind simplicity of obedience perishes, when we call into question among ourselves whether the command is rightly given or not, and perhaps even condemn the Superior for ordering things that are not so pleasing to us. Humility perishes, because although on one side we obey, on the other we prefer ourselves to the Superior. Fortitude perishes in difficult matters. Finally, to sum up, all the force and dignity of this virtue perish. In their place come grief, irritation, sluggishness, weariness, grumbling, excuses, and other vices, by no means slight, by which the reward and merit of obedience is utterly extinguished. So holy Bernard, speaking of those who bear with ill grace commands less agreeable to them, says: If you take it badly and endure these things, if you judge your prelate, if you murmur in your heart, then even if you carry out inwardly what is commanded, this is not the virtue of patience but a veil for malice. Since peace and tranquillity of mind are sought, certainly he will not enjoy them who has within himself the cause of disturbance and tumult, namely the disagreement of his own judgment with the obedience of the law. And for this reason, for the sake of preserving the concord which is the bond of every society, the Apostle urges so strongly that all should think and speak the same thing: namely, that by agreeing in both words and wills they may be mutually cherished and preserved. Now if the members and the head must have one and the same sense, it is easy to see which is more fitting, that the head should agree with the members, or the members with the head. From what has been said so far, it sufficiently appears how necessary obedience of judgment is. How pleasing it is to the Lord, and how perfect, is shown first by the fact that the most excellent and precious part of man is consecrated to the Lord through it; second, because the obedient man is a living holocaust, pleasing to the divine Majesty, since he retains nothing of himself at all; and finally, because the difficulty of this struggle is great. For the obedient man, for the sake of God, breaks himself and resists the natural inclination which is implanted in all men to embrace and follow their own opinion. From these things it follows that obedience, even if it seems properly to perfect the will, since it renders the will ready and prepared at the nod of the Superior, must nevertheless, as I said, also pertain to the understanding and lead it to think the very thing the Superior thinks. For in this way it will come, with all the strength of will and understanding combined, to swift and complete execution. I seem to hear you, dearest brothers, saying that you no longer doubt the necessity of this virtue, but that you very earnestly wish to know how you may attain its perfection. To this question I answer with holy Leo: nothing is difficult for the humble, and nothing harsh for the meek. Only let humility and meekness not be lacking to you. Certainly God's kindness will not be lacking to help you, so that you may be able to perform what you have promised, with a mind not only equable but also willing. Moreover, I set before you by name three things which greatly help to acquire obedience of judgment. The first is this: as I said at the beginning, do not look at the person of the Superior as a man subject to errors and miseries, but at Christ himself, who is supreme wisdom, immeasurable goodness, and infinite charity, who cannot be deceived and does not wish to deceive you. And since you are aware that for the love of God you have taken upon yourselves the yoke of obedience, so that by following the will of the Superior you might follow the divine will more surely, do not doubt that the most faithful charity of the Lord will continue to govern you henceforth through the ministry of those whom he has set over you, and lead you by right paths. Therefore receive the voice and commands of the Superior not as the voice of a man, but as the voice of Christ. For the Apostle, writing to the Colossians in this same sense, when he exhorts subjects to obey their superiors, says: Whatever you do, work at it heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; serve the Lord Christ. And holy Bernard says: Whether God or a man who is God's vicar delivers any command, it must certainly be obeyed with equal care and shown equal reverence, provided that man does not command what is contrary to God. So too, if you look upon God with inward eyes and not upon a man with outward eyes, it will hardly be burdensome for you to conform your wills and judgments to that rule of your actions which you yourselves have chosen.

units.la: Altera est ratio, ut quod Superior mandat, vel sentit, defendere semper apud animos vestros studiose nitamini, improbare autem nequaquam: atque ad eam ipsam rem proderit bene animatos; affectosque esse ad id omne, quod ipse jusserit: sic enim fiet, non solum ut sine molestia, sed etiam ut cum voluptate, laetitiaque pareatis; nam (ut est apud sanctum Leonem) non dura ibi necessitate servitur, ubi diligitur, quod jubetur.
units.tr: A second reason is this: strive earnestly always to defend in your minds whatever your Superior commands or thinks, and by no means to disapprove of it; and to this end it will be helpful to be well disposed and inclined toward everything he has ordered. For in this way you will obey not only without distress but even with delight and gladness; for (as St Leo says) that is no hard servitude where what is commanded is loved.

units.la: Postrema subjiciendi judicij ratio est cum facilior, tutiorque; tum etiam apud sanctos Patres in more posita: ut statuatis vobiscum ipsi, quicquid Superior praecipit, ipsum Dei praeceptum esse, & voluntatem: atque ut ad credenda, quae Catholica fides proponit, toto animo assensuque vestro statim incumbatis: sic ad ea facienda, quaecunque Superior dixerit, caeco quodam impetu voluntatis parendi cupida sine ulla prorsus disquisitione feramini. Sic egisse credendus est Abraham, filium Isaac immolare jussus: sic Novi Testamenti tempore aliqui e sanctis Patribus ijs, quos commemorat Cassianus; ut Joannes Abbas, qui quod erat ei imperatum, non reputabat utile ne esset, an inutile: ut cum aridum lignum tanto, ac tam diuturno labore per annum irrigavit: nec utrum fieri posset nec ne: ut cum conatus est tam ex animo ingens saxum solus dimovere loco, quod ne multi quidem simul homines impellere potuissent. Quod Obedientiae genus ipsis interdum miraculis divinitus comprobatum videmus. Nam (ut alios taceam, quos ipsi non ignoratis) Maurus, sancti Benedicti discipulus, mandato Superioris lacum ingressus, nec mersus est: alius quidam a Superiore jussus, leaenam ad se ducere, illam cepit, atque perduxit. Est igitur haec ratio subjiciendi proprij judicij, ac sine ulla quaestione sanciendi; & collaudandi apud se quodcunque Superior jusserit, non solum sanctis viris usitata, sed etiam perfectae Obedientiae studiosis imitanda omnibus in rebus, quae cum peccato manifesto conjuncta non sunt.
units.tr: The last reason for subordinating one's judgment is both easier and safer, and it is also established among the holy Fathers: you should resolve with yourselves that whatever the Superior commands is itself the precept and will of God; and just as you immediately apply your whole mind and assent to believing what the Catholic faith sets before you, so for doing whatever the Superior has said you should be carried along, eager to obey with a certain blind impulse of the will, without any examination at all. In this way we must believe Abraham acted, when he was ordered to sacrifice his son Isaac. In this way, in the time of the New Testament, some of the holy Fathers whom Cassian mentions acted: as Abbot John, who did not consider whether what had been commanded him was useful or useless, when he watered a dry piece of wood for a whole year with such great and long labour, nor whether it could be done or not; and when he alone tried to move from its place a huge stone which many men together could not have pushed. We see this kind of obedience sometimes confirmed by God through miracles. For (to say nothing of others, whom you yourselves know) Maurus, the disciple of St Benedict, entered a lake at a Superior's command and was not drowned; and another man, ordered by his Superior to lead a lioness to him, seized her and brought her. This, then, is the reason for subordinating one's own judgment and, without any questioning, approving and praising in oneself whatever the Superior has commanded: it is customary not only for holy men but is also to be imitated by those eager for perfect obedience, in all matters which are not joined with manifest sin.

units.la: Nec tamen idcirco vetamini, si quid forte vobis occurrat a Superioris sententia diversum, idque vobis (consulto suppliciter Domino) exponendum videatur, quominus id ad Superiorem referre possitis. Verum in hac re, ne vos amor vestri judiciumque decipiat, illa cautio est adhibenda, ut animo sitis, & ante, & post relationem aequissimo, non solum quod pertinet ad eam rem, de qua agitur, vel suscipiendam, vel deponendam: sed etiam ad approbandum, rectiusque putandum quicquid Superiori placuerit.
units.tr: Yet you are not for that reason forbidden, if something perhaps occurs to you that differs from the Superior's opinion, and this seems to you to be set forth (after humbly and deliberately seeking the Lord) so that you may refer it to the Superior. But in this matter, lest self-love and your own judgment deceive you, this caution must be observed: that you be entirely even-minded both before and after the report, not only with regard to the matter in question, whether it is to be undertaken or abandoned, but also toward approving and judging more rightly whatever has pleased the Superior.

units.la: Atque haec, quae de Obedientia diximus, aeque privatis erga proximos Superiores, sed atque Rectoribus Praepositisque localibus erga Provinciales, Provincialibus erga Generalem. Generali denique erga illum, quem Deus ipsi praefecit; nempe suum in terris Vicarium, observanda sunt: sic, ut & ordinum perfecta distinctio, ac proinde pax retineatur, & charitas, sine qua nec Societatis nostrae, nec alterius cuiuslibet sodalitij posset recta gubernatio conservari. Nimirum hoc modo providentia illa divina disponit omnia suaviter, infima per media: media per summa, suos ad fines cuncta perducens. Hinc illa videlicet in Angelorum unius Hierarchia ad aliam subordinata series: hinc & coelestium, & aliorum omnium, quae cientur, corporum certis locis, sedibus inter se apta connexio, quorum conversiones ac modus ab uno movente supremo gradatim omnes usque ad infimos rite proveniunt. Idem in terris, cum in omni civitate bonis institutis legibus, tum vero in Hierarchia Ecclesiastica cernitur, cuius omnia membra, & functiones ab uno generali CHRISTI Domini nostri Vicario derivantur, & quo accuratius haec dispositio, & collatio custoditur, eo rectior est, gubernatio, & melior: contra vero huius ordinis negligentia, quam gravia incommoda multis hominum Societatibus importentur, nemo non videt, atque idcirco in hac, cuius mihi nonnullam procurationem, ac curam Dominus tradidit; tam diligenter hanc virtutem exerceri, vigereque percupio, quasi in ea Societatis nostrae bonum, ac falsus universa confislat.
units.tr: What we have said about obedience applies equally to private persons toward their immediate Superiors, and to Rectors and local Prepositi toward the Provincials, and to Provincials toward the General; and finally it is to be observed toward him whom God has set over us, namely his Vicar on earth. Thus both the perfect distinction of the orders, and consequently peace, is preserved, and charity, without which the right governance of our Society, or of any other fellowship, cannot be maintained. Indeed, in this way that divine providence orders all things sweetly, the lowest through the middle, the middle through the highest, bringing all things to their ends. Hence in the hierarchy of the Angels there is that series subordinated one to another; hence too there is the fitting connection of the heavenly and all other bodies which are moved, each in its certain place and seat, whose revolutions and manner, proceeding from the one supreme mover, duly reach all the way down to the lowest. The same is seen on earth, both in every well-ordered state with good laws and especially in the ecclesiastical hierarchy, whose members and functions all derive from the one general Vicar of our Lord Christ; and the more carefully this arrangement and conferral is kept, the more upright and better is the governance. Conversely, everyone sees how grave the inconveniences are that befall many human societies from the neglect of this order. Therefore I earnestly desire that this virtue be practised and flourish with such diligence in this Society, over which the Lord has entrusted me with some charge and care, as if the good of our Society and its whole welfare depended upon it.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint, ut unde exorsa est, ibidem terminetur epistola: vos ego per Christum Dominum nostrum obtestor, qui se nobis non modo praeceptorem, sed etiam exemplar praebuit Obedientiae, ut ad eam virtutem toto pectore incumbatis, & gloriosa victoria appetentes, atque a vidi, vosmetipsos superare, id est, excelsiorem, & difficiliorem animi partem, voluntatem dico, atque judicium, expugnare, & subjicere studeatis: quo Dei Domini nostri inostri solida veraque cognitio, atque amor vestros ad se animos penitus trahat: totoque vitæ huius, & quasi peregrinationis curriculo usque eo gubernet, ac regat, dum nos demum aliosque complures, vestra opera exemploque adjutos ad ultimum & felicissimum finem, ninirum ad beatitudinem sempiternam perducat. Vestris ad Deum precibus me valde commendo. Roma vij. Calend. Aprilis, M. D. LIII.
units.tr: Since these things are so, let the letter end where it began. I entreat you through Christ our Lord, who has shown himself to us not only as teacher but also as the pattern of obedience, that you apply yourselves with your whole heart to this virtue, and, aiming at glorious victory, strive to overcome and subdue yourselves—that is, to conquer the higher and more difficult part of the soul, I mean the will and the judgment; so that a sure and true knowledge and love of God our Lord may draw your minds wholly to himself, and govern and direct them through the whole course of this life, as if of a pilgrimage, until at last, with your labour and example assisting many others, he brings us to the final and most happy end, namely everlasting blessedness. I most earnestly commend myself to your prayers to God. Rome, the 7th day before the Calends of April, 1553.

units.la: REGVLAS IESVITARVM NON EVVLGANDAS ESSE.
units.tr: The Jesuits' Rules Are Not to Be Published.

units.la: Esuitæ in suis REGVLIS mandant ac severè præcipiunt, ne quis eas cuiquam extraneorum concedat vel communicet, vel quidquam de illis vel scripto vel sicto aliis referat. Paulus III. quoque in Bulla Anno 1549. Iesuitis data, concessit Generali Ordinis, ut eas Regulas evulgantes seu in apertum producentes, vel illorum Vota revelantes, in quocunque habitu contigerit inveniri, possit ac debeat excommunicare; capere, incarcerare, & si opus sit, brachij secularis auxilio invocato, libere & licite invadere, captivos ducere, & pro arbitrio tractare. Voluit quoque; ut nulli Prælatorum liceat, Regulas & Constitutiones Iesuitarum, excepto Papa, sub censura sumere.
units.tr: The Jesuits in their RULES command and sternly order that no one is to grant or share them with any outsider, or report anything about them to others, whether in writing or orally. Paul III also, in the Bull given to the Jesuits in the year 1549, granted to the General of the Order that he may and ought to excommunicate, seize, imprison, and, if necessary, with the aid of the secular arm invoked, freely and lawfully attack, lead away captive, and treat at his pleasure whoever is found in any habit publishing these Rules or bringing them into the open, or revealing their vows. He also wished that none of the prelates be permitted to take up the Rules and Constitutions of the Jesuits under censure, except the Pope.

units.la: Quia enim Regulæ illorum nihil aliud sunt quam cento, rapsodia & fragmenta ex omnibus reliquorum Monachorum Regulis confuta; & nihil aliud docent & præcipiunt, quam traditiones humanas; superstitionis, hypocrisis, dolomaniæ & proprię s·ϑλοϑρησκείας opera; qualia sunt per omnes orbis terrarum plagas oberrare; homines Christianos ad Ethnicas superstitiones ac idolomanias revocare; habitu religiosum se declarare; Horas Canonicas & Rosaria recitare; Sanctos, vel opinione saltem tales, utpote à Papa canonizatos invocare; quotidie Missis adstare easque audire; perfectam obedientiam Superioribus præstare; Ecclesiæ Romanæ decreta, placita, statuta & præcepta inculcare; ad Papæ obedientiam omnes cogere; homines ad auricularem confessionem excitare; ieiunare; flagellis & ciliciis se ipsos excruciare; mundum & parentes spernari, &c. mirum certè non est, si ipsosmet pudet has aliasque superstitiones ac dolomanias in suis Regulis contineri & divulgari.
units.tr: For their Rules are nothing but a cento, a rhapsody and a patchwork of fragments drawn from the Rules of all the other monks, and they teach and prescribe nothing but human traditions, the works of superstition, hypocrisy, deceit and self-chosen worship: such as wandering through every corner of the world, calling Christians back to pagan superstitions and idolatries, declaring themselves religious by their habit, reciting the Canonical Hours and Rosaries, invoking the saints, or at least those thought to be such because canonized by the Pope, attending Masses daily and hearing them, rendering perfect obedience to their superiors, inculcating the decrees, opinions, statutes and precepts of the Roman Church, compelling all to obey the Pope, stirring up men to auricular confession, fasting, and tormenting themselves with whips and hair shirts, despising the world and parents, etc. It is certainly no wonder if they are ashamed that these and other superstitions and deceits are contained and divulged in their Rules.

units.la: Eodem modo non licebat apud Ethnicos quoque arcana, quæ in Sibyllinis libris continebantur, effutire & nota facere. Similiter Cereris Mysteria tam arcana esse debuerunt & secreta, ut vulgò proverbium iactaretur in secretos & taciltos Ἀτθικοὶ τὰ μυστήρια. Et Aristophanes in Nebulis ἀρρητα ἱερά, id est; non evulganda sacra nominat. Et Iustinus dixit: Mysteria Cereris nulla alia re magis quam silentio sacra fuisse. Ac Orpheum dixerunt aliqui; fulmine ictum concidisse; quod arcana hæc rudibus & profanis hominibus divulgasset. Aristoteles quoque lib.
units.tr: In the same way, among the pagans too it was not permitted to disclose and make known the secrets contained in the Sibylline books. Similarly, the Mysteries of Ceres had to be so hidden and secret that the proverb was commonly bandied about concerning those who were secret and silent: the Athenians have their mysteries [Ἀτθικοὶ τὰ μυστήρια]. And Aristophanes in the Clouds calls them unspeakable sacred things, that is, sacred things not to be published [ἀρρητα ἱερά]. And Justin said: the Mysteries of Ceres were sacred through nothing so much as silence. Some also said that Orpheus was struck down by a thunderbolt because he had divulged these secrets to rude and profane men.

units.la: 3. Ethic. narrat, Aeschilum poetam ad Areopagum in judicium vocatum fuisse, quod in suis poematis arcana Cereris edidisset. Alcibiadē etiam simili de causa ab Atheniensibus condemnatum & morti addictum fuisse historici prodiderunt.
units.tr: Aristotle also, in Book 3 of the Ethics, relates that the poet Aeschylus was called before the Areopagus for judgment because he had published the secrets of Ceres in his poems. Historians also record that Alcibiades, for a similar reason, was condemned by the Athenians and handed over to death.

units.la: Rectè autem Augustinus in Quæstionibus utriusque Testamenti ait: Nihil apud nos in tenebris vel occultè geritur. Omne enim quod honestum scitur, publicari non timetur. Illud autem quod turpe est & inhonestum, prohibente pudore non potest publicari. Quamobrem Paganı mysteria sua in tenebris celebrant, vel in eo prudentes. Erubescunt enim palam illudi: piacula enim, quæ illic vice legis aguntur, nolunt manifestare, &c.
units.tr: Augustine rightly says in his Questions on both Testaments: Nothing among us is done in darkness or in secret. For whatever is known to be honourable is not feared to be made public. But what is shameful and dishonourable cannot be made public, since modesty forbids it. Therefore the pagans celebrate their mysteries in darkness, and are wise in this, for they are ashamed to be mocked openly; they do not want to reveal the expiations which are performed there in place of the law, etc.

units.la: Cùmiraque Regulæ Iesuitarum hactenus ab orthodoxis comparari & legi non potuerint, singularí Dei beneficio factum est, ut Lugduni Galliæ typis Iacobi Rousin Superiorum permissu anno 1607. ab ipsis Iesuitis excusæ sint, non quidem ut in publicum ederentur; hoc enim singulari studio prohibitum est; sed uthoc compendio tyrannidis huius novæ Constitutiones Summariæ per Collegia Domusq; probationum, perque officia Provincialium, Præpositorum, Præsectorum, Rectorum, Examinatorum, Magistrorum, Novitiorum, aliorumq; Ministrorum distribuerentur, velut leges, quibus coeco quodam impetu voluntatis, sine ulla prorsus disquisitione, eos, qui sub obedientia vivere decreverunt, haud aliter ac seni baculum obtemperare oportet. Cumque hæ Regulæ ad manus meas pervenerint, eas in Christiani Lectoris gratiam integras adscripsimus.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the Rules of the Jesuits could hitherto not be obtained or read by the orthodox, it came about by a singular blessing of God that they were printed at Lyon in France, in the press of James Rousin, with the permission of the superiors, in the year 1607, by the Jesuits themselves. Not indeed that they should be published abroad, for this was forbidden with especial care; but that these Summary Constitutions of this new tyranny might be distributed through the colleges and houses of probation, and through the offices of the provincials, prefects, rectors, examiners, masters, novices and other ministers, as laws by which, with a certain blind impulse of the will and without any inquiry whatever, those who have decided to live under obedience ought to comply no otherwise than the old man with his staff. And since these Rules have come into my hands, I have appended them entire for the benefit of the Christian reader.

units.la: CAPVT V. VARIA DE IESVITICAE OE- CONOMIAE MEMBRIS, AD REGVLAE DECLARATIONEM PER- TINENTIA: Ac primò DE GENERALI PRÆPOSITO.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. VARIOUS MATTERS CONCERNING THE MEMBERS OF THE JESUIT ECONOMY, PERTAINING TO THE EXPLANATION OF THE RULE: and first concerning the General Superior.

units.la: CVm ab initio primi Patres & Socii Iesuitarum sine certis & propriis legibus, ac magistratibus vixissent, necesse esse iudicarunt, ut de stabilienda quam maxime Societate primo quoque tempore inter se consulerent. Vbi igitur eam ob causam convenissent, in secundo & tertio consessu de religione relatum est in primis, placeretne ad vota duo, Paupertatis & Castitatis suscepta, tertium quoque perpetuæ Obedientiæ adiungere, & e suo corpore unum eligere, qui cæteris amplissima cum potestate præesset? Omnium igitur in unum congruerunt sententiæ, quandoquidem Christum Magistrum sibi imitandum propositum, prorsus oportere ut ipsi quoque Christum effingerent. Hoc sic constituto, Ignatius suasit, talem deligendum sibi videri, cui omnes in terris tanquam Christo subiecti essent ac parerent, cuius in verba etiam iurarent, eiusque sibi nutum ac voluntatem instar divini cuiusdam oraculi ducerent. Quæsitum est etiam de huius ipsius potestate, utrum certo temporis spatio definitam, an vero perpetuam esse oporteret, perpetuam esse placuit Ignatio, ac cæteris omnibus, idque cum alias ob causas, tum vero ut negotia graviora, quæ ad conficiendum non modo plenæ libertatis, sed verum etiam longi temporis indigent, ex animi sui sententia ad exitum sine ulla trepidatione perducere posset.
units.tr: Since the first Fathers and companions of the Jesuits had at the beginning lived without fixed and proper laws or magistrates, they judged it necessary to consult together, at the first opportunity, about establishing the Society as firmly as possible. When they had met for this purpose, the first matter raised at the second and third sessions concerning religion was whether it pleased them to add to the two vows, of poverty and chastity, a third, of perpetual obedience, and to elect from their own body one man who would preside over the rest with the fullest power. All agreed, since they had set Christ before themselves as their Master to imitate, that they ought also to fashion themselves entirely after Christ. With this settled, Ignatius advised that they should choose a man to whom all on earth would be subject and obey as to Christ, whose words they would swear to follow, and whose nod and will they would regard as a kind of divine oracle. The question was also raised whether this man's power should be limited to a fixed span of time or should be perpetual. Ignatius and all the others were pleased that it should be perpetual, partly for other reasons, but chiefly so that he could bring to completion, by his own judgment and without any hesitation, the weightier business which requires not only full freedom but also a long period of time.

units.la: Cum igitur Generalis Præpositi (sic enim qui cunctis præesset appellare placuerat) tempus eligendi adesset, Ignatij Socij, qui quidem in Italia erant, per literas moniti, creandi Præpositi causa ad urbem accederent, sub initium Quadragesimæ anni 1541. Convenere omnes, uno Bobadilla excepto, ac omnium suffragijs Præpositus Generalis Ignatius declaratur, quo munere etiam functus est ad annum usque 1556. eo enim obijt Romæ Prid. Calend. Augusti ætatis anno 65.
units.tr: When therefore the time came to elect the General Superior (for so they had resolved to call the one who would preside over all), the companions of Ignatius who were in Italy were warned by letter and came to the city to create the Superior, at the beginning of Lent in the year 1541. All assembled, except Bobadilla alone, and by the votes of all Ignatius was declared General Superior. He held that office until the year 1556, for he died at Rome on 31 July, in the sixty-fifth year of his age.

units.la: In hoc munere constitutus, omnia Erasmi opera in Societate sua legi vetuit, quod singula hæretico veneno infecta putaret, & ne quis forte facetijs & eloquentia viri caperetur, Maffæo teste in eius vita.
units.tr: While he held this office, he forbade that any works of Erasmus be read in his Society, because he thought each of them was infected with heretical poison, and lest anyone be caught by the wit and eloquence of the man, as Maffei testifies in his life.

units.la: In Ignatij locum eligitur Iacobus Laynez, natione Hispanus, & Loyolæ in constituenda Societate inter primos socius & adiutor. Cardinalitiam dignitatem à Paulo IV. ei oblatam repudiavit. Mortuo vero Pontifice isto ac sede vagante, vacante, duodecim Cardinales in ipsum extra conclave Romae agentem, sua suffragia contulerunt, ut Pontifex eligeretur. Societatem octo annos cum dimidio rexit.
units.tr: In Ignatius's place was elected James Laynez, a Spaniard by birth, and among the first companions and helpers of Loyola in founding the Society. He refused the dignity of cardinal offered to him by Paul IV. When that Pope died and the see was vacant, twelve cardinals, while he was staying at Rome outside the conclave, gave their votes to him so that he might be chosen Pope. He governed the Society for eight and a half years.

units.la: Anno 1561. a Pio IV. cum Hippolyto Estensi Cardinale Legato in Galliam ad Colloquium inter Pontificios & orthodoxos a Rege & Proceribus regni de eligione institutum, mittitur. Ribadeneira in libro de Scriptoribus Iesuiticis mendacissime scribit, eum in publico totius Regni conventu Theodorum Bezam, Petrum Martyrem & alios a partibus Evangelicorum, maxima sententiarum & verborum gravitate repraesisse, frenavisse ac mutos reddidisse. Nam anc laudem ipsos quoque Pontificios, praeter Ribadeneiram, ei tribuere hactenus potuit. Habuit quidem orationem Italica lingua contra nostros, in qua inprimis Evangeliistarum in concepta forma consensum ursit; nimirum τοῦτο in verbis, Hoc est corpus meum: sed Beza solide illi respondit in vestigio, & errexisset, ni Espensius Sorbonista responsionem eius exceptionibus suis interrupisset, ut parte altera historiae nostrae Sacramentariae pag. 303 docuimus. Moritur anno D. 1565. die 19. Ianuarii aetat. LIII.
units.tr: In 1561 he was sent by Pius IV, together with Cardinal Hippolytus d'Este as legate, to France, to a colloquy between the Papists and the orthodox on religion, instituted by the King and the nobles of the realm. Ribadeneira, in his book on Jesuit writers, most mendaciously writes that before the public assembly of the whole kingdom he so overwhelmed, restrained and struck dumb Theodore Beza, Peter Martyr and others on the side of the Evangelicals, with the greatest weight of arguments and words. For even the Papists themselves, apart from Ribadeneira, have so far been unable to ascribe that praise to him. He indeed delivered a speech in the Italian tongue against our side, in which he especially urged the Evangelicals' agreement in the form of words, namely that [τοῦτο] "this" in the words This is my body. But Beza replied to him solidly on the spot, and would have prevailed, had not Espencé, the Sorbonnist, interrupted his reply with his own objections, as we showed on page 303 of the other part of our Sacramentarian history. He died in the year of our Lord 1565, on 19 January, in the fifty-third year of his age.

units.la: Successit huic Laynezio Franciscus Borgia Hispanus, patria Valentinus, spreto Gandiae Ducatu, ut Ribadeneira refert, & amplissimis honoribus, opibus, deliciis, clientelis & familiae suae ornamentis, Societatem hanc recens natam, & nondum satis cognitam, atque explicatam, ingressus est, anno D. 1547. Cardinalatum a Iulio III. sibi oblatum respuit. Eiusdem Societatis in Hispania Commissarius generalis fuit, Romae bis Vicarius: ac demum Praepositus generalis tertius, in quo munere septem annos & tres menses versatus est. Mortuus est anno Christi 1572. aetatis 62. Prid. Cal. Octob.
units.tr: Francis Borgia, a Spaniard, a native of Valencia, succeeded Laynez. As Ribadeneira reports, he spurned the Duchy of Gandia and the very ample honours, wealth, pleasures, clients and the ornaments of his family, and entered this Society, newly born and not yet well known or explained, in the year of our Lord 1547. He refused the cardinalate offered to him by Julius III. He was General Commissary of the Society in Spain, twice Vicar at Rome, and at last the third General Superior, in which office he spent seven years and three months. He died in the year of Christ 1572, in the sixty-second year of his age, on 30 September.

units.la: In eius locum eligitur Everardus Mercurianus quartus Iesuitarum Generalis, Leodius patria.
units.tr: In his place was elected Everard Mercurian, the fourth General of the Jesuits, a native of Liège.

units.la: Huic suffectus est Claudius Aquaviva, natione Italus, patria Neapolitanus, Ducis Atrii filius, & Pii V. cubicularius. Ducatum suum filio tradidit, & Iesuitis se mancipavit, quorum ordini maximas opes, & ut aliqui referunt, ultra 0. ducatorum millia contulit. Ea de causa Provincia Neapolitana primum gubernanda demandatur ei, ac postea etiam Romana. Demum in Comitiis, quae habita sunt Romae anno Domini 1581. die 19. Februarii Praepositus Generalis creatur. Eo die, quo electus erat, cubiculum ascendens, salutanti turbae omnis generis hominum, exosculandas manus, instar Papae, praebuit, ut habetur in annuis epistolis Iesuiticis anni 81. Moritur Romae 3. seu ultima die Ianuarii secunda hora noctis, stylo novo, vetere autem 21. eiusdem mensis, Anno 1615.
units.tr: Claudius Aquaviva succeeded him. He was an Italian by nation, a Neapolitan by country, son of the Duke of Atri, and a chamberlain of Pius V. He handed over his dukedom to his son and gave himself over to the Jesuits, to whose order he contributed very great wealth, and, as some report, more than 100 thousand ducats. For this reason he was first entrusted with governing the Neapolitan province and afterwards also the Roman. At last, in the assembly held at Rome in the year of our Lord 1581, on 19 February, he was created General Superior. On the day he was elected, climbing to his chamber, he offered his hands to be kissed, like a Pope, to a crowd of people of every kind who greeted him, as is recorded in the Jesuit annual letters of the year 1581. He died at Rome on the third, or last, day of January at the second hour of the night, by the new style; by the old style, on the 21st of the same month, in the year 1615.

units.la: Huic successit Marius vel Mutius Vitellesius. Paulo antequam expiraret Claudius Aquaviva, misit ad Papam nuncium, qui ei significaret, in electione successoris grave datum irifcandalum, propter duas contrarias in Societate factiones; quarum una Iustinianum quendam, altera Marium Vitellesium eligere omni studio tentatura fit: rogare igitur se vehementer Papam, ut authoritatem suam interponere dignetur. Papa, ut voto eius satisfaceret, Cardinalem Burgesium destinavit, qui electioni interesset, eamque authoritate sua moderaretur, ac, ut liximus, Vitellesius eligitur.
units.tr: Mutius Vitelleschi (some call him Marius) succeeded him. Shortly before he died, Claudius Aquaviva sent a messenger to the Pope to tell him that a grave scandal had arisen in the election of a successor, because of two opposing factions in the Society: one of them would strive with every effort to elect a certain Justinian, the other Marius Vitelleschi. He therefore urgently begged the Pope to deign to interpose his authority. The Pope, to satisfy his wish, appointed Cardinal Burghese to attend the election and moderate it by his authority; and, as we have said, Vitelleschi was elected.

units.la: Cum anno Domini 1558. post mortem Ignatii primum suum Conventum generalem Iesuitae celebrarent, Paulus IV. Papa Cardinalem Pacochum ad eos misit, qui suo nomine significaret eis, placere sibi, ut Generalis Praepositi potestas certo annorum numero definita, non perpetua sit, ne videlicet in tyrannidem verteretur, aut sese supra Papam efferret. Nihil tamen apud eos obtinere potuit, licet per Cardinalem Tranensem de eodem rursus eos moneret. Evenit igitur quod Papa metuebat. Nam Romae semper habitat, & per hanc fixam sedem Romanæ fedi & Consistorio quasi affigitur & implantatur; ibique suam iuxta Papæ sellam collocat: semper etiam a latere & secretis Pontificis sedet, ut inter se consilia communicent, nec alter sine altero quicquam in hæreticos machinetur.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 1558, after the death of Ignatius, when the Jesuits held their first general assembly, Pope Paul IV sent Cardinal Pacheco to them, to tell them in his name that it pleased him that the power of the General Superior should be limited to a fixed number of years and not be perpetual, lest, of course, it should turn into tyranny or raise him above the Pope. Yet he could obtain nothing from them, although through Cardinal Trani he warned them again about the same matter. So what the Pope feared came to pass. For the General always dwells at Rome, and through this fixed seat he is as it were fastened and planted to the Roman See and the Consistory; and there he places his own seat beside the Pope's chair. He always also sits at the Pope's side and in his private counsels, so that they may share their plans, and neither of them may plot anything against heretics without the other.

units.la: Potestatem igitur suam perpetuo retinet; quum Provincialium, Rectorum & aliorum plerumque triennis sit; ab eode tamen Generali interdum prorogari potest. Licet Paulus III. anno 1549. in Bulla decreverit, posse & debere Præpositum per personas ad id a Societate facultatem habetes, & ad id deputatas, in certis casibus amoveri, & alium ipsius loco, per easdem personas substitui.
units.tr: He therefore keeps his power perpetually, whereas that of the Provincials, Rectors and others is for the most part for three years; yet the same General may sometimes extend it. Although Paul III, in the year 1549, decreed in a bull that the Superior could and should be removed in certain cases by persons having the Society's authority for this and appointed to it, and that another should be substituted in his place by the same persons.

units.la: Ad eundem quicquid Iesuitæ per totum terrarum orbem faciunt, explorant, & resciscunt, ipsi diligenter singulis mensibus deferri curant. Is deinde omnia ac singula, Papæ refert: & tunc ab utroque, qui suam operam sedulo & gnaviter impenderint, honoribus augentur, & opibus ditantur, ut Annales ipsorum attestantur.
units.tr: Whatever the Jesuits do, discover and learn anywhere in the whole world, they take care to report diligently to him every month. He then refers all and each thing to the Pope; and then both of them, those who have zealously and eagerly applied their efforts, are enlarged with honours and enriched with wealth, as their Annals attest.

units.la: Officium quoque eius est, Iesuitarum potestatem secundum Ignatij Constitutiones in omnibus dirigere.
units.tr: It is also his office to direct the power of the Jesuits in all things according to the Constitutions of Ignatius.

units.la: Licet tamen illi etiam, ut Papæ, novas interdum condere leges, vel etiam veteres pro circumstantiarum varietate mutare & abrogare.
units.tr: Yet it is lawful for him too, as for the Pope, sometimes to make new laws, or also to change and abrogate old ones according to the variety of circumstances.

units.la: Licet ei bona ordinis sui vendere, oppignorare & abalienare, & nulli de ea ratione reddere tenetur.
units.tr: He is permitted to sell, pledge and alienate the goods of his order, and he is not bound to give anyone an account of it.

units.la: Parte 5. Constitut. c. 3. & parte 6. c. 1. vocatur Dei Legatus. Glossa part. 4. Constitut. c. 3. vocat eum Vicarium Christi. Montaignes c. 27. scribit; Cum vovent ei obedientiam, id ea de causa fit, quod in huius Societatis Republica Dei Vicarius est. Bullae quoque Pauli III. anno 1540. & Julij III. anno 1550. Iesuitis datae, hortantur eos, ut in Generali Christum velut præsentem magnos cant.
units.tr: In part 5, chapter 3, and part 6, chapter 1, of the Constitutions he is called the Legate of God. The Gloss on part 4, chapter 3, calls him the Vicar of Christ. Montaignes, chapter 27, writes: When they vow obedience to him, this is done for the reason that in the commonwealth of this Society he is the Vicar of God. The bulls also given to the Jesuits by Paul III in 1540 and by Julius III in 1550 urge them to esteem the General greatly, as though Christ were present in him.

units.la: Hinc fit, ut quicquid ordinat ac præcipit, id Iesuitæ tanquam oracula suscipiat; credant ac faciant, haud aliter quam si ipse Christus vel eius Vicarius esset. Sic enim Maffæus in vita Ignatij; Sine, inquit; controversia deligendus est (Generalis) cui omnes in terris, tanquam Christo parerent; cuius in verba iurarent; deniqque cuius sibi nutum ac voluntatem, instar cuiusdam divini oraculi ducerent.
units.tr: Hence it follows that they receive whatever he orders and commands as oracles; they believe and do it, no differently than if Christ himself or his Vicar were present. Thus Maffaeus in the Life of Ignatius: Without controversy he is to be chosen (the General), to whom all on earth should submit as to Christ; whose words they should swear to; and whose nod and will they should follow, as though it were some divine oracle.

units.la: Aliud etiam solent hodie Generalem eligere, qui in seculo Principem vitiu egerit; ut sic etiam in mundo potentes ad suam Societatem pertrahant, sibique apud supremos & infimos tanto maiorem authoritatem & potentiam comparent.
units.tr: Nowadays they also are accustomed to elect as General someone who has lived as a prince in the world, so that they may draw the powerful of the world into their Society too, and win for themselves far greater authority and power among both the highest and the lowest.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligitur, Generalem Iesuitarum Papæ cō rivalem, imo ad Pontificiam dignitatem evectum; adeoque alterum Ecclesiæ Romanæ caput esse.
units.tr: From all this it is understood that the General of the Jesuits is a rival of the Pope, indeed raised to the Papal dignity, and so is another head of the Roman Church.

units.la: Reliqua de gradibus seu generibus Iesuitarum ex Hafenmullero & Colloquio a sacræ Theologiæ Doctore & Professore, Paulo Florenio, cum Christiano Franken Philosophiæ Professore in Cæsareo Iesuitarū Gymnasio Viennæ, Anno 1578. 2 o. Ianuarij habito, in sequentibus referam.
units.tr: I will report the remaining matters concerning the grades or kinds of Jesuits in what follows, from Hafenmuller and from a colloquy held on 20 January 1578 at the Imperial Jesuit Gymnasium in Vienna, between Paul Florenius, Doctor and Professor of sacred theology, and Christian Franken, Professor of philosophy.

units.la: Quod autem Romæ est & præstat Generalis, id est & præstat in singulis regnis Provincialis. Primum Provincialem Ignatius Loyola Lusitaniæ præpositum fuit Simonem Roterigium; Hispaniæ Antonium Araozium Cantabrum; Italiæ Iacobum Lainem; Indiæ Franciscum Xaverium; Germaniæ Petrum Canisium; Galliæ Paschasium Broetium, aliisque deinde alios. Ac diligenter cavent Iesuitarum Patres, ne in Nationibus Provinciales unquam ex indigenis eligant, sed vel Hispanis vel Italis dignitates has conferant, aut saltem iis, qui ex Anglia, Gallia, &c. propter facinora aliqua profugerunt, & propter nimium Hispaniæ studium ex prædictis Nationibus proscripti sunt.
units.tr: But what the General is at Rome, the Provincial is also in each kingdom. The first Provincial whom Ignatius Loyola set over Portugal was Simon Rodriguez; over Spain, Antonio Araoz of Cantabria; over Italy, Jacob Lainez; over India, Francis Xavier; over Germany, Peter Canisius; over France, Paschasius Broet; and then others after them. The Jesuit Fathers take great care never to choose Provincials from among the natives of a nation, but confer these offices either on Spaniards or Italians, or at least on those who have fled from England, France and elsewhere on account of some crimes, and who have been banished from those nations because of their excessive zeal for Spain.

units.la: Vnufquifq; Provincialis ab ea Provincia, vel Regno potius, quod inspectio= ni vel curæ suæ commissum habet, denominatur. Eius officium est invisere Colle= gia, eorumq; supputare reditus & census, insuper annotare diligenter, quinam ex magnatibus liberos in Collegijs erudiri curent; & quot illorum sint numero: cum quotannis fiat accessio discipulorum, & amplificatio fortunarum & opum: cum qui sint & quot ex Lutheranismo conversi: si nulli aut etiam aliqua facta Pontificiæ religionis imminutio, aut iactura bonorum; exprobrat negligentiam & socordiam, mandatq; severiter, ut acceptum damnū relarciat. Quod si gesse= runt se egregie, multos converterunt, multū comparserunt & corraserunt; omni laude cumulat, & cœlo effert. Insuper sciscitatur; quænam sit vicinorum hæreti= corū de ipsis opinio: quænam consilia magnatum: quales habeant conventus: & quot: & ubi: quid decernant, quid volutent: Item, an hæreticorum Principes rebrius sint domi, an alibi: ad quosnā proficiscantur frequentius: quali quisq; it ingenio: quibus rebus ut plurimum delectetur: an cura aliqua suscipiat Rei= publicæ: an studio & amore aliquo teneatur religionis: an potius vino, veneri & venatui indulgeat: an potius habeat in aula Catholicos: quinam sint populares humores de suis Principibus: num Ecclesiæ adversariorū ferveant: nū pastores ecclesiarum sint viri docti & diligentes, an vero somnolenti & illiterati: num Theologica facultas in vicina Academia hæreticorū floreat: num crebriores habeant Theologi disputationes; & contra quos maximè: quos libros & de qua materia in lucem ediderint nuperrime: Ad hæc & alia si respondeant Regens & reliqui Patres appositè; mirificè prædicat industriam & vigilantiam: Sin minus, ofq; adeo rerum istarum nescios deprehendit, acerbè vituperat. Quid agitis, inquit, vos somnolenti & desides: cur perditum itis Romam Ecclesiam: quo modo ummo Pontifici hanc inertiam vestram probabitis: cur insinuatis vos agendis rebus: cur metuitis: cur non intrepide rem aggredimini? Dudum hæc gesta; dum perfecta oportuit. Videte vigilantiam hæreticorum incredibilem; & vos certitis. His & similibus verbis ipsos increpat, & exacuit. Tandem quærit de dis= ipulis, convictoribus, novitijs & reliquis, quot eorum sint numero; quanti cuiusque profectus: ad quod quisq; studium inclinet: num quis inter eos spinosior & scrupulosior: Talem enim a Theologico studio prorsus removendum existimat, ist scholasticis disputationibus probè exercitatum & opinione religionis imbu= um. Quærit præterea, num quem habeant in grege, qui pro amplificanda Ro= mana Ecclesia laudabili aliquo facinore se obstringere, & vitam deniq; profun= dere non dubitet, si quidem necessitas aliquando flagitare videatur: Ad extre= mum, omnia isthæc cōsignata Generali transmittit Romam, per quem immedia= te significantur Pontifici. Atq; sic per totum orbem Christianum nihil geritur aut consultatur, quod non per hos Imperij proditores Papæ innotescat. Per Provin= cialem etiam Iesuitæ ab uno Collegio in aliud transferuntur, idque fere trien= nio quolibet.
units.tr: Each Provincial is named from the province, or rather the kingdom, which has been committed to his oversight and care. His duty is to visit the colleges and to reckon up their revenues and incomes; moreover, to note carefully which of the magnates have their children educated in the colleges, and how many of them there are, since each year there is an increase of pupils and a growth of fortunes and wealth; and who and how many have been converted from Lutheranism; whether there has been no decline or loss of goods for the Papist religion. He reproaches negligence and sloth and orders them sternly to make good the loss suffered. But if they have acquitted themselves well, have converted many, and have gained and collected much, he heaps every praise upon them and raises them to heaven. He further inquires what the opinion of their heretical neighbours about them is; what the plans of the magnates are; what assemblies they hold, how many and where, what they decree and what they plan; likewise whether the heretical princes are more often at home or elsewhere, to whom they travel most frequently, what kind of disposition each has, what things he most delights in, whether he takes any care for the commonwealth, whether he is held by some zeal and love of religion, or rather indulges in wine, love and hunting, and whether he has Catholics at his court; what the popular moods are about their princes; whether the hatred of the Church's adversaries is boiling; whether the ministers of the churches are learned and diligent men or rather sleepy and unlettered; whether theology flourishes among the heretics in the nearby university; whether the theologians hold more frequent disputations, and against whom especially; which books and on what subject they have most recently published. If the Rector and the other Fathers answer these and other questions to the point, he wonderfully praises their industry and vigilance; but if not, and he finds them ignorant of these matters, he rebukes them bitterly. "What are you doing," he says, "you sleepy and idle men? Why do you allow the Church of Rome to be lost? How will you prove this idleness of yours to the Supreme Pontiff? Why do you make yourselves out to be busy with affairs? Why are you afraid? Why do you not tackle the matter fearlessly? These things should have been done long ago, and should now be finished. See the incredible vigilance of the heretics, and you are sluggish!" With such and similar words he scolds them and spurs them on. Finally he asks about the pupils, boarders, novices and the rest, how many of them there are and how great the progress of each; to which study each inclines; whether any among them is more fastidious and scrupulous. For he thinks such a man must be entirely removed from theological study, having been well trained in scholastic disputations and steeped in the opinion of the religion. He further asks whether they have anyone in the flock who does not hesitate to bind himself by some praiseworthy deed for the enlargement of the Roman Church, and even to pour out his life, if indeed necessity seems at some time to demand it. Lastly, he sends all these things, recorded, to the General at Rome, through whom they are reported directly to the Pope. And thus throughout the whole Christian world nothing is done or consulted that does not become known to the Pope through these traitors to the Empire. Through the Provincial the Jesuits are also moved from one college to another, and this is done almost every three years.

units.la: §. DE IESVITARVM ASSISTENTIBVS SEV INTIMIS PAPAE ET GENERALIS CON= SILIARIIS.
units.tr: §. Concerning the Assistants or Intimates of the Pope and the General of the Jesuits.

units.la: GEneralem proximè sequuntur primi Assistentes, quatuor numero. Hos o= portet Romæ residere, secretioribus Papæ & Generalis Societatis Iesuitı= æ deliberationibus assidere, ipsis assistere, & in rebus Romanam Ecclesiam co= ernentibus, atq; in perniciem Orthodoxorum facientibus, consilijs ac scriptis desse: hos propulsare, illis totis viribus propugnare. Et ut Generalem Papæ in omnibus, sic hos vicissim Generali ad amussim obedire oportet.
units.tr: Next after the General come the First Assistants, four in number. It is their duty to reside at Rome, to attend upon the more secret deliberations of the Pope and of the General of the Society of Jesus, to assist them, and to lend their counsels and writings in matters that concern the Roman Church, or that work to the destruction of the Orthodox; to repel these men and to defend those with all their strength. And just as the General must obey the Pope in all things, so these in turn must obey the General to the letter.

units.la: Vt autem quatuor illorum sunt, ita etiam officium eorum est in quatuor mundi plagis res Pontificias curare & promovere: & ad eos Provinciales, Visitatores, Rectores, Regentes ac Spirituales Præfecti, quæcunque in mundo Iesuitæ reliqui agunt, omnia ac singula scribunt. Oportet etiam illos non minus quam reliquos quarto etiam voto, absolutæ obedientiæ, Papæ obligatos esse, ne quid vel contra Papæ vel sui Generalis voluntatem decernere audeant. Si res magni momenti ipsis aliunde significantur, illas confestim Generali vel Secretario indicant, qui eas deinde ad Papam referunt, quo sic ipsorum opera ac studio consilia iniri possint de coercendis, impediendis, vel etiam opprimedis hæreticorum conatibus: ipsorum autem res magis magisque promoveantur, augeanturque.
units.tr: As there are four of them, so their office is to look after and advance papal affairs in the four quarters of the world; and to them the Provincials, Visitors, Rectors, Regents and Spiritual Prefects write everything and anything that the rest of the Jesuits do in the world. They too, no less than the others, are bound to the Pope by a fourth vow of absolute obedience, so that they dare decide nothing contrary to the will of the Pope or of their General. If matters of great moment are reported to them from elsewhere, they at once indicate them to the General or the Secretary, who then refer them to the Pope, so that by their work and zeal counsels may be taken for restraining, hindering, or even crushing the attempts of heretics; and their own affairs may be advanced and increased more and more.

units.la: Summa vero literarum, quas ex diversis mundi regnis & provinciis accipiunt, hæc plerunque est, Quis sit Regum ac Principum erga Papam & Ecclesiam Romanam, atque etiam Societatem eorum affectus, & quinam illos clementer excipiant. Hos mirifice commendant, qui autem Iesuitarum conatibus resistunt, tanquam capitales hostes Romanæ Ecclesiæ accusant.
units.tr: The substance of the letters which they receive from the various kingdoms and provinces of the world is usually this: what is the disposition of Kings and Princes towards the Pope and the Roman Church, and also towards their Society, and who receive them kindly. Those who favour them they commend wonderfully; but those who resist the efforts of the Jesuits they accuse as capital enemies of the Roman Church.

units.la: Vt autem de his Assistentes diligentius certiores facere queant, in omnia, Germanorum præcipue Principum consilia & acta accurate inquirunt, cunctaque, licet ex vanis falsisque rumoribus multa sæpe cognoscant, Romam perscribunt. Vtque facilius in rerum Germanicarum notitiam perveniant, sæpe mutato habitu, vel pedites vel equites Germaniæ aliarumque nationum provincias peragrant & proditorum more cuncta explorant. Exempla in promptu sunt.
units.tr: So that the Assistants may be better informed about these matters, they inquire carefully into all the counsels and acts of the Germans, especially of the Princes, and report everything to Rome; and although they often learn many things from empty and false rumours, they write them all down. And so that they may more easily come to know German affairs, they often, with changed dress, travel through the provinces of Germany and of other nations, on foot or on horseback, and spy out everything in the manner of traitors. Examples are at hand.

units.la: His cognitis, Assistentes eos in proposito suo confirmant, eosque, ut strenue sic pergant, hortantur, Papæ clementiam in illos prædicant, & eis plenarum indulgentiarum remittunt, quas illi Germanis aliisque nimis stupidis & credulis auro vendunt.
units.tr: Having learned these things, the Assistants confirm them in their purpose, urge them to press on vigorously, proclaim the Pope's clemency towards them, and grant them full indulgences, which those men sell for gold to the Germans and other peoples who are all too dull and credulous.

units.la: Assistentium quoque officium est, in tota Societate Visitatores, Inspectores, Rectores, Regentes, Concionatores, Spirituales Præfectos & Inquisitores ordinare, non tamen nisi cum consensu Generalis. Adhæc munera autem non promovent alios, quam quos norunt in Papatus idolomania induratos, & orthodoxorum capitales hostes esse.
units.tr: It is also the office of the Assistants to appoint, throughout the whole Society, Visitors, Inspectors, Rectors, Regents, Preachers, Spiritual Prefects and Inquisitors, yet not without the consent of the General. Moreover, they promote to these offices only those whom they know to be hardened in the idolatry of Papacy and to be capital enemies of the Orthodox.

units.la: 4. DE IESVITARVM PRO- FESSIS.
units.tr: 4. Concerning the Professed of the Jesuits.

units.la: Quartum Iesuitarum genus, Professi sunt: qui præter tria vota se insuper speciali quodam, quod votum Professionis vocant, Pontifici Romano obligant, eoque promittunt ac profitentur, se Papæ in omnibus absolutam obedientiam præstituros; neque unquam commissuros, quin in obedientia etiam præstanda, in rebus fidem & mores concernentibus, primi inveniantur, sic, ut etiam non petito viatico, licet ad ipsos Turcas occidendi mitterentur, sine ulla tamen intellectus, iudiciique repugnantia obedire velint: Hoc Ignatius omnino fieri voluit: & Paulus Tertius quoque in sua Bulla approbavit & confirmavit. Sic enim verba eius habent: Et quamvis Evangelio doceamur, & fide orthodoxa cognoscamus, ac firmiter profiteamur, omnes Christi fideles Romano Pontifici tanquam capiti ac IESV CHRISTI Vicario subesse: ad maiorem tamen nostræ Societatis humilitatem ac perfectam uniuscujusque mortificationem & voluntatum nostrarum abnegationem: summopere conducere judicavimus, singulos nos ultra illud commune vinculum, speciali voto astringi, itaut quicquid Moderni & alii Romani Pontifices, pro tempore existentes jusserint, ad profectum animarum & fidei propagationem pertinens, & ad quascunque provincias nos mittere voluerint, sine ulla ergi versatione aut excusatione illico quantum in nobis fuerit, exsequi teneamur. Sive miserit nos ad Turcas, sive ad quoscunq; alios infideles etiam in partibus, quas Indias vocant, existentes, sive ad quoscunq; haereticos, sive schismaticos, seu etiam ad quosvis fideles.
units.tr: The fourth kind of Jesuits are the Professed, who, beyond the three vows, bind themselves to the Roman Pontiff by a special vow, which they call the vow of Profession. By it they promise and profess that they will render absolute obedience to the Pope in all things; and they are never to hold back from being first in obedience, in matters concerning faith and morals, so that, even without asking for provisions for the journey, they are willing to obey even if they are sent to the Turks to be killed, and without any conflict of understanding or judgment. Ignatius wished this to be done without exception, and Paul III also approved and confirmed it in his Bull. For his words are these: "And although we are taught by the Gospel, and know by the orthodox faith, and firmly profess, that all the faithful of Christ are subject to the Roman Pontiff as to the head and to the Vicar of Jesus Christ; yet, for the greater humility of our Society and the perfect mortification of each one and the denial of our own wills, we have judged it very helpful that we should each be bound, beyond that common bond, by a special vow, so that whatever the present and future Roman Pontiffs shall command, pertaining to the progress of souls and the propagation of the faith, and whatever provinces they shall wish to send us to, we are bound to carry out at once, as far as lies in us, without any delay or excuse. Whether he sends us to the Turks, or to any other infidels, even those existing in the regions called the Indies, or to any heretics or schismatics, or even to any faithful."

units.la: Ad hoc votum Professorum non nisi beatissimos, & quorum industria in zizaniis Pontificijs dissipandis cognita & explorata est, admittunt. Antequam autem ad hoc votum accedant, totum triduum tenentur oftiatim victum quaerere, prima exercitia repetere, vota renovare, & omnia humilitatis officia, quaecunq; excogitare possunt, subire. Huius generis sunt, loca secreta expurgare, calceos lavare, aliorum pedes osculari, domum verrere, vasa eluere, coco ministrare, humi cubare, nudipedes incedere, sub mensa edere, cilicia induere, seipsos flagellare, peregrinari, sceleraque omnibus subijcere. Posthaec abiurare coguntur omnes haereses, & iurare, se operam omnem daturos, ut Romana religio floreat, Evangelica autem exstirpetur.
units.tr: Only the most blessed are admitted to this vow of the Professed, and those whose diligence in scattering the Papist tares is known and tested. Before they come to this vow, they are bound for three full days to beg their food from door to door, to repeat the first exercises, to renew their vows, and to undergo all the offices of humility that they can devise. Of this kind are: cleansing the privies, washing shoes, kissing the feet of others, sweeping the house, rinsing out the vessels, serving the cook, lying on the ground, walking barefoot, eating under the table, wearing hair shirts, scourging themselves, going on pilgrimage, and submitting to all as to sinners. After this they are compelled to abjure all heresies, and to swear that they will make every effort so that the Roman religion may flourish and the Evangelical religion be rooted out.

units.la: Horum Professorum Romae ultra ducentos aluntur, qui proprium, & quidem amplissimum habent Collegium, in eoq; laute splendideq; sumptibus Papae, Cardinalium & Episcoporum, quorum illorum utuntur consiliis & scriptis, sustentantur. Nihil proprij, nullos reditus, ut reliqui Iesuitae, possident.
units.tr: More than two hundred of these Professed are supported at Rome, who have their own, indeed a very spacious, college, and in it they are maintained lavishly and splendidly at the expense of the Pope, the Cardinals and the Bishops, whose counsels and writings they use. They possess nothing of their own and no revenues, unlike the rest of the Jesuits.

units.la: Distinguuntur etiam a reliquis Iesuitis in eo, quod sunt illorum quasi Episcopi, qui in caeteros inquirunt, ijsq; praeficiuntur. Ex horum numero enim, inprimis qui sunt Hispani vel Itali, Visitatores, Inquisitores, Rectores, Regentes & Spirituales Praefecti eliguntur: qui quod sint rerum Iesuiticarum & Papisticarum peritissimi, sibi subiectos egregie in palestra Pontificia exercere noverunt. Germanis non Germanum praeficiunt Rectorem, sed vel Italum, vel Hispanum: aut si nobilior ex Germanis constituitur, habet tamen Hispanum, qui eum observet, ne quid praeter morem Hispanicum agat.
units.tr: They are also distinguished from the other Jesuits in this, that they are, as it were, their bishops, who inspect the others and are set over them. For from their number, chiefly those who are Spanish or Italian, the Visitors, Inspectors, Rectors, Regents and Spiritual Prefects are chosen; who, because they are most skilled in Jesuit and Papist affairs, know how to train those subject to them splendidly in the Papal arena. They do not set a German over the Germans as Rector, but an Italian or a Spaniard; or if a German of higher birth is appointed, he still has a Spaniard to watch him, lest he do anything contrary to the Spanish custom.

units.la: Generali quoq; se totos devovent & obstringunt, abnegatione honorum, quod nimirum extra Societatem vel Cardinales vel Episcopi fieri nolint: Et tamen hoc ipso nomine fiunt Cardinales in Societate; ex quibus Generales, ipsorum Papae, eligantur: quibus tanquam cardinibus, tota Societas vertatur: qui habent existimationem doctrinae & sanctitatis. Sicq; vana ac stulta Societas dum ambitionem se fugere simulat, in ipsam ambitionem incurrit. Non secus ac vani illi Philosophi, qui ijs ipsis libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribebant, in ijs nomina inscribentes sua, inanem gloriam aucupabantur, ut sapienter de ijs Cicero libro 1. Tusculanarum Quaest. refert.
units.tr: They also devote and bind themselves wholly to the General, renouncing honours, namely that they are unwilling to become either Cardinals or Bishops outside the Society; and yet by this very name they become Cardinals within the Society, from whose number the Generals, the Pope's own men, are elected, on whom the whole Society turns as on hinges, and who have a reputation for learning and holiness. Thus this empty and foolish Society, while it pretends to flee ambition, falls into ambition itself. Just as those vain philosophers, who, while writing books on despising glory, inscribed their own names on those very books and hunted after empty glory, as Cicero wisely relates of them in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations.

units.la: 5. DE TRIVM VOTORVM PROFESSIS.
units.tr: 5. CONCERNING THE PROFESSION OF THE THREE VOWS.

units.la: Iesuitarum genus quintum, sunt trium tantum vulgariu, & cum reliquis Monachis communium Votorum Professi. Hi se Papae & suo Generali in hanc formam obligant ac devovent: Omnipotens sempiterne Deus: Ego licet undecunq; divino tuo conspectu indignissimus, fretus tamen pietate ac misericordia tua infinita, & impulsus tibi inserviendi desiderio: voveo coram sacratissima Virgine Maria, & curia tua coelesti universa, divinae majestati tuae, paupertatem, castitatem & obedientiam perpetuam in Societate Iesu, & promitto eandem Societatem me ingressurum, ut vitam in ea perpetuo degam, omnia intelligendo, juxta ipsius Societatis constitutiones. A tua ergo immensa bonitate & clementia per Iesu Christi sanguinem peto supplicitur, ut hoc holocaustum in odorem suavitatis admittere digneris, & ut largitus es ad hoc desiderandum & offerendum, sic etiam ad splendum gratiam uberiorem largiaris.
units.tr: The fifth class of Jesuits is that of the professed of the three vows only, which they share with the other monks. They bind and devote themselves to the Pope and to their General in this form: Almighty, eternal God: I, though most unworthy in Your divine sight wherever I may be, yet trusting in Your infinite goodness and mercy, and moved by a desire to serve You, vow before the most holy Virgin Mary and before Your whole heavenly court, to Your divine majesty, perpetual poverty, chastity and obedience in the Society of Jesus; and I promise that I will enter that Society, so as to live in it for ever, understanding all things according to the constitutions of the same Society. Therefore I beg and entreat of Your immense goodness and clemency, through the blood of Jesus Christ, that You deign to accept this holocaust for a sweet-smelling savour, and as You have granted me the desire to make and offer it, so also You would grant me a fuller grace to carry it out.

units.la: Haec est formula Iuramenti, quo Iesuitae non Deo, sed Societati suae, eiusq; servitio se totos mancipant. Ad haec autem vota facienda studiosi ac literati, bieniio probationis exacto, illiterati vero uno, vel dimidio absoluto, admittuntur.
units.tr: This is the form of the oath by which the Jesuits devote themselves wholly, not to God, but to their Society and its service. Students and men of letters are admitted to make these vows after a probation of two years completed, but the unlettered after one year or a half.

units.la: DE OECONOMIA ET REGIMINE
units.tr: On the Economy and Government

units.la: Trium hi votorum professi, sunt ijs proximi, qui ad quartum votum, quod professionis vocant, admittuntur: eosq; in hos sequentes articulos, quos Canones Professionis, cum ratione credendos, Iesuitæ vocant, iurare oportet.
units.tr: Those who have made the three vows are next in line for admission to the fourth vow, which they call the vow of profession. They must swear to the following articles, which the Jesuits call the Canons of the Profession, to be believed with their reasons.

units.la: 1. Ego N. N. credo & recipio quæcumque sacrum generale Concilium Tridentinum credit & recipit, etiamsi ea in Concilio non fuissent definita. Conveniunt enim illa, cum ijs, quæ in Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis continentur, verbi gratia Purgatorium esse, &c.
units.tr: 1. I, N. N., believe and accept whatever the holy General Council of Trent believes and accepts, even where those things were not defined in the Council. For those things agree with what is contained in the Gospel and Apostolic writings, for example that there is a Purgatory, etc.

units.la: 2. Prædictis vero Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis atq; alijs, quæ prædictum Concilium credi jubet: etiamsi ea in Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis non invenirentur, credo, propter auctoritatem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quæ insu Ecclesiastico prædicta scripta, & non scripta recipit.
units.tr: 2. As for the aforesaid Gospel and Apostolic writings, and the others which the said Council orders to be believed: even where those things are not found in the Gospel and Apostolic writings, I believe them on account of the authority of the Catholic Church, which by its ecclesiastical power receives the aforesaid written and unwritten books.

units.la: 3. Catholicam Ecclesiam credo esse eorum universitatem, qui Romanam Ecclesiam, ut omnium Ecclesiarum magistram ac matrem sequuntur, & Romanum Pontificem, Petri Apostolorum Principis successore, & Iesu Christi Domini nostri Vicarium esse agnoscunt.
units.tr: 3. I believe the Catholic Church to be the whole body of those who follow the Roman Church as the mistress and mother of all churches, and who acknowledge the Roman Pontiff to be the successor of Peter, prince of the Apostles, and the Vicar of Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: 4. Hanc ego esse Catholicam Ecclesiam, eiusdemque fidem verissimam esse credo, quia sanctorum Patrum Orientalium & Occidentalium, Australium & Aquilonarium ab Apostolis usque ad nos consentiens, & continua traditio, & ipsam esse Catholicam Ecclesiam, & eidem Ecclesiæ credendum esse docet.
units.tr: 4. I believe that this is the Catholic Church and that its faith is most true, because the consent and continuous tradition of the holy Fathers of East and West, of South and North, from the Apostles down to us, teaches both that it is the Catholic Church and that this Church is to be believed.

units.la: 5. Prædictæ autem sanctorum Patrum traditioni credo, qui eam doctrinam tradunt, quæ à sanctis Apostolis fuit prædicata, ut ipsa doctrinæ successio demonstrat.
units.tr: 5. I believe in the aforesaid tradition of the holy Fathers, who hand down that doctrine which was preached by the holy Apostles, as the succession of that doctrine itself demonstrates.

units.la: 6. Sanctis vero Apostolis ideo credo, quia illi à Domino nostro Iesu Christo, ut ex ipsius Domini verbis constat, ad docendas gentes missi sunt.
units.tr: 6. I believe the holy Apostles because they were sent by our Lord Jesus Christ to teach the nations, as is clear from the words of the Lord himself.

units.la: 7. Christo Domino nostro, & in alijs, & in eo etiam, quo se Deum esse testatus est, propterea credo, quia Deus illum misit lumen ad revelationem gentium.
units.tr: 7. I believe in Christ our Lord, both in other things and also in that in which he testified that he is God, because God sent him as a light for the revelation of the nations.

units.la: 8. Missum autem fuisse Christum Dominum nostrum à Deo Opt. Max. credo, quia illi omnia conveniunt, quæ S. Prophetæ de venturo Messia & à Deo mittendo prædixerunt.
units.tr: 8. I believe that Christ our Lord was sent by God the best and greatest, because all the things which the holy Prophets foretold about the coming Messiah and the one to be sent by God agree with him.

units.la: 9. Prophetis prædictis & alijs etiā & in eo etiam, quod Dei ipsis locutum per hibent, ideo credo, quia quæ de Christo Domino prædixerunt, non nisi per divinam revelationem prædici potuerunt, impleta jam esse video, quale illud est; Gentes fuisse in Christum crediturus.
units.tr: 9. I believe the aforesaid Prophets, and the others also, and in that too in which they say that they spoke by the word of God, because what they foretold about Christ the Lord could only have been foretold by divine revelation; and I see that it has now been fulfilled, such as that statement that the nations would believe in Christ.

units.la: 10. Prophetas prædixisse illa, quæ de Christo Domino sub eorum nomine prædicta leguntur ideo credo, quia non solum Christianus orbis, sed etiam ipsi hæretici, Mahumetani & Iudæi Christianorum inimici, eaedem fatentur eos prædixisse, quæ cum Gentium & Sibyllinis oraculis conveniunt.
units.tr: 10. I believe that the Prophets foretold those things which are read as having been foretold about Christ the Lord under their names, because not only the Christian world but also the heretics themselves, the Mahometans and the Jews, the enemies of the Christians, confess that they foretold these things, which agree with the oracles of the Gentiles and the Sibyls.

units.la: 11. Propter prædictas rationes magis credo, quam propter passiones martyrum, cum & Diabolus suos martyres habeat: aut propter miracula, nam & Antichristus facit miracula, falsa quidem illa, sed quæ vera esse videbuntur, aut propter quamvis aliam rationem.
units.tr: 11. On the aforesaid grounds I believe more than on account of the sufferings of the martyrs, since the Devil too has his martyrs; or on account of miracles, for Antichrist too works miracles, false indeed, but which will appear to be true; or on account of any other reason whatever.

units.la: 12. Communis ergo ratio credendi hodie ad Prophetarum oracula ultimo resolvitur, id est, ad divinam convenientiam Veteris Testamenti cum Novo, ut merito S. Petrus dixerit: Habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem.
units.tr: 12. So the common ground of belief today is finally resolved into the oracles of the Prophets, that is, into the divine agreement of the Old Testament with the New, as St. Peter rightly said: "We have a more sure prophetic word."

units.la: 13. Profiteor septem esse vere ac proprie Sacramenta novæ legis à Iesu Christo Domino nostro instituta, ad salutem generis humani: licet non omnia singulis necessaria, scilicet; Baptismum, Eucharistiam, Confirmationem, Pœnitentiam, extremam Unctionem, Ordinem & Matrimonium. Et horum omnium ceremonias rite venerandas & colendas esse.
units.tr: 13. I profess that there are seven true and proper Sacraments of the New Law, instituted by Jesus Christ our Lord for the salvation of mankind, though not all are necessary for each individual: namely Baptism, the Eucharist, Confirmation, Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders and Matrimony. And I profess that the ceremonies of all of these are to be duly reverenced and observed.

units.la: 14. Profiteor pariter in Missa offerri Deo, verum, proprium & propitiatorium sacrificium pro vivis & defunctis.
units.tr: 14. I likewise profess that in the Mass a true, proper and propitiatory sacrifice is offered to God for the living and the dead.

units.la: 15. Profiteor in sanctissimo Eucharistiæ Sacramento esse vere, realiter, substantialiter & transsubstantialiter, verum corpus & sanguinem, una cum anima & divinitate Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: 15. I profess that in the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist there is truly, really, substantially and transubstantially the true body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: 16. Profiteor fieri conversionem totius substantiæ panis in corpus, & totius substantiæ vini in sanguinem, quam conversionem Ecclesia Catholica Transsubstantiationem vocat.
units.tr: 16. I profess that there takes place a conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the blood, which conversion the Catholic Church calls Transubstantiation.

units.la: 17. Profiteor, sub altera tantum specie, totum atq; integrum Christum sumi, & Laicis sub una tantum specie porrigendum altaris Sacramentum. 18. Constanter teneo, sanctos una cum Christo regentes, orationes pro nobis Deo offerre, nos juvare, interdum visitare, scire, quae apud nos geruntur, opem ferre animabus purgatorij, & has regere, visitare & illuminare.
units.tr: 17. I profess that under one kind only the whole and entire Christ is received, and that the Sacrament of the altar is to be offered to the laity under one kind only. 18. I firmly hold that the saints who reign with Christ offer prayers to God for us, help us, sometimes visit us, know what is done among us, bring aid to the souls in Purgatory, and rule, visit and enlighten these.

units.la: 19. Constanter teneo Sanctorum reliquias esse venerandas.
units.tr: 19. I firmly hold that the relics of the saints are to be venerated.

units.la: 20. Firmiter affero, imagines Christi ac Deiparae semper Virginis, nec non aliorum Sanctorum, habendas & retinendas esse, atque illis debitum honorem & venerationem impertiendam.
units.tr: 20. I firmly affirm that the images of Christ and of the ever-Virgin Mother of God, as well as of the other saints, are to be had and kept, and that due honour and veneration are to be given to them.

units.la: 21. Indulgentiarum etiam potestatem a Christo in Ecclesia relictam fuisse, illarumque usum Christiano populo maximè salutarem affirmo. Ex qua, ceu ex Spirituali Ecclesiae thesauro, possint dari indulgentiae ex superabundantia operum Christi & sanctorum, quibus ipsi non indigent.
units.tr: 21. I also affirm that the power of indulgences was left by Christ in the Church, and that the use of them is most salutary for the Christian people. From this, as from the spiritual treasury of the Church, indulgences can be granted out of the superabundance of the works of Christ and the saints, of which they themselves have no need.

units.la: 23. Constanter teneo purgatorium esse, animas ibi detentas fidelium suffragijs juvari.
units.tr: 23. I firmly hold that there is a Purgatory, and that the souls detained there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful.

units.la: 24. Omnia & singula, quae de peccato Originali & de Justificatione in sacro sancta Tridentina Synodo definita & declarata sunt, complector & recipio.
units.tr: 24. I embrace and accept all and each of the things which have been defined and declared in the most holy Synod of Trent concerning Original Sin and Justification.

units.la: Quod si aliqui trium votorum professi ad altiora aspirèt, & sive in Doctores, sive in Magistros promoveri cupiant: vel si quidam ex Evangelicis idolomaniae papisticae se devovere voluerint, eos secundum Tridentinum Concilium in hunc modum iurare oportet, ut habetur ab initio Tridentini Concilij: Ego N. N. Apostolicas & Ecclesiasticas traditiones, reliquasque eiusdem Ecclesiae, observationes & constitutiones, firmissime admitto & complector. Item, sacram Scripturam, juxta eum sensum, quem tenuit, & tenet sancta mater Ecclesia, cujus est judicare de vero sensu & interpretatione sacrarum Scripturarum, admitto, nec eam unquam, nisi juxta unanimem consensum Patrum, accipiam, & interpretabor. Profiteor quoque, septem esse vere & proprie Sacramenta novae legis, a Iesu Christo Domino nostro instituta, atque ad salutem humani generis, licet non omnia singulis necessaria, scilicet Baptismum, Confirmationem, Eucharistiam, Poenitentiam, extremam Unctionem, Ordinem & Matrimonium, illaque gratiam conferre, & ex ijs Baptismum, Confirmationem & Ordine sine sacrilegio reiterari non posse. Receptos quoque & approbatos Ecclesiae ritus, in supra dictorum omnium Sacramentorum solemni administratione, recipio & admitto: omnia & singula, quae de peccato Originali & Justificatione in S.S. Tridentina Synodo definita & declarata fuerunt, amplector & recipio. Profiteor pariter in Missa offerri Deo verum, proprium ac propitiatorium sacrificium pro vivis ac defunctis.
