Atque interim tamen ausus es Galliæ Regem taxare, quòd cum protestantibus, Cæsarem verò, quòd cum Angliæ Rege coleret amicitiam. Annon turpissimum est, rependere totum ab astrologis & necromanticis? negari factum non potest: nam & honoribus illos & facultatibus atque donis amplificasti Cecium, Marcellum, Gauricum, Lusitanum, & alios. Quæ sane res impietatis te manifeste redarguit, & satis est gravis, quam ob rem à Pontificatu debeas removeri. Egregius, si Diis placet, Iesuitarum patronus.
units.tr: Certainly the Order of Jesuits is most worthy of such a confirmer and patron as Pope Paul III. Before his death an Italian pamphlet was published, with a preface addressed to Ascanio Colonna, which he had suppressed. In this pamphlet the author recounts various and truly monstrous crimes, and, calling him Antichrist, says: "Pope Innocent, you were cast into chains, most unjust prelate, on account of two murders and a parricide committed, your mother and a nephew of yours being removed by poison so that the whole inheritance might come to you; and then, when you were set free, you did not hesitate to seek the purple galero, and although you were three times rejected by the College, your own sister Giulia Farnese at last prevailed. When she threatened that from then on she would no longer grant you access to herself, Pope Alexander VI, fearing offence and her anger, chose you for the company of the Cardinals. Then you also poisoned your other sister, chaste according to the custom of your family. While you were Legate in the province of Ancona, under Pope Julius II, you shamefully ensnared a girl of that city, concealing who you were and passing yourself off as some nobleman from the legate's household, and you violated her. This crime the girl's cousin, the Cardinal of Ancona, a man of the city, threw in your face in the gravest words before Pope Clement, while he was a captive. Niccolò Querceus, finding you with Laura Farnese, your niece and his wife, struck you with a dagger, and the scar of that wound is still visible. About your daughter Costanza, with whom you had relations so often, what shall I say? For in order to enjoy her more freely you poisoned her husband Bosio Sforza, who, when he had noticed your wickedness, conceived incredible grief in his mind and was never afterwards seen to be cheerful. Moreover, in lust you far surpass Commodus and Heliogabalus, and this can be shown from your many bastards. Lot violated his daughters unknowingly and drunk; you, sober, have had intercourse not only with a niece but also with a sister and a daughter. Now what about the abomination which your wicked son Pietro Luigi committed against the Bishop of Fano? How foul and horrible a deed is it to tell! When Pope Clement was held captive in the mole of Hadrian, and you were sent as his envoy to the Emperor to recover his freedom, you would not set out until he granted the bishopric of Parma to your grandson Farnese, then a boy of ten years. Having done this, you nevertheless deceived him, and when you arrived at Genoa you pretended to be detained by illness. And what a trade in sacred goods you did not carry on as Cardinal? And after you became Pope, immortal God, how shamefully did you squander the revenues of the Roman Church? Are you not ashamed to have conferred the highest prefecture and office on your wicked son, with forty thousand gold pieces a year, and nearly as much on your grandson Ottavio? Not to mention what and how great goods you have lavished on all the women of your family and the Sanfiorian nieces. Later you will be heard bringing up the Turks, who already lie heavy on wretched Italy. Why do you do this, except to have some cause and occasion to plunder the people, who under you as Lord bear a most grievous and truly intolerable burden? You sold Modena and Reggio to the Duke of Ferrara; you alienated Parma and Piacenza, which the Roman Church had by no means acquired, a thing that Pope Clement was surely ashamed to do. To enrich your family and house you harassed others contrary to right and justice, and you made war on those who could not or would not bear that servitude; the people of Perugia teach this, among others, and so does Ascanio Colonna. He demands from his subjects every year, beyond the ordinary, three hundred thousand gold pieces as a subsidy, and from time to time imposes some new tax, now on salt, now on other goods; he now exacts tithes, now half of the fruits. That man ought rightly to be regarded as an enemy of Christian blood. A Turkish fleet, under you as Pope, sailed unharmed through the borders of the Roman Church, not long ago, when Barbarossa entered our sea. That secret commerce which you have with the barbarians cuts off your soul, so that you cannot wipe out in future the name of Turkish war. And yet at the same time you have dared to censure the King of France for his dealings with the Protestants, and the Emperor because he cultivates friendship with the King of England. Is it not most shameful to take everything from astrologers and necromancers? The deed cannot be denied: for you have enriched and honoured with offices, revenues and gifts Cecio, Marcello, Gaurico, Lusitano and others. This thing surely clearly convicts you of impiety, and it is grave enough that you should be removed from the Pontificate. An excellent patron of the Jesuits, if it pleases the gods!"

units.la: Iulius Tertius Pauli successor 12. Calend. Augusti. Anno 1550 ad instantiam Iesuitarum vota sua renovantium præcedentis Bullæ privilegia omnia confirmavit: & addidit insuper, omnes Episcopi curent, ut priora perpetuæ sint facultatis, eaq; inviolabiliter observent, nisi in omnipotentis Dei iram incurrere velint.
units.tr: Julius III, Paul's successor, on the twelfth day before the Calends of August in 1550, at the request of the Jesuits who were renewing their vows, confirmed all the privileges of the earlier bull. He added that all bishops should see to it that the earlier privileges remain in perpetual force and are observed inviolably, unless they wish to incur the wrath of Almighty God.

units.la: Cum etiam in Bulla Anni millesimi quingentesimi quadragesimi à Paulo Tertio prohibitum esset, ne aliis in locis ullis Collegia erigerent, quàm apud approbatas Universitates, Iulius in hac Bulla concessit Iesuitis ad instantiam eorum, ut ubicunque vellent ædificarent ea, & instituerent. Verba supplicationis eorum sic habent: Quia tamen domus, quas Dominus dederit ad operandum in vinea ipsius, & non ad Scholasticas Studia, destinandæ erunt, cum valdè opportunum fore alioqui videatur, ut ex juvenibus ad pietatem propensis, & ad literarum studia tractandis idoneis, operarij eidem vineæ Domini parentur, qui Societatis nostræ, etiam professæ, velut quoddam Seminarium existant, possit professa Societas, ad studiorum commoditatem, Scholarium habere Collegia, ubicunque ad ea construenda & dotanda, aliqui ex devotione movebuntur. Quæ simul ac constructa & dotata fuerint, non tamen ex bonis quorum collatio ad sedem Apostolicam pertinet, ex nunc authoritate Apostolica erigi supplicamus, ac pro erectis haberi. Quæ Collegia habere possint reditus, census, seu possessiones, usibus & necessitatibus studentium applicandas, retenta penes Præpositum, vel Societatem omnimodâ gubernatione, seu superintendentia super dicta Collegia, & prædictos studentes, quoad Rectorum seu Gubernatorum ac studentium electionem, & eorundem admissionem, emissionem, receptionem, exclusionem, statutorum ordinationem, & circa studentium, eruditionem, ædificationem, ac correctionem victus vestitusque, & aliarum rerum necessariarum eis ministrandarum modum, atq; aliam omnimodò gubernationem, regimen ac curam, ut namq; studentes dictis bonis abuti, neque Societas professa in proprios usus convertere possit, sed studentium necessitati subservire, &c.
units.tr: Since the bull of 1540 issued by Paul III had forbidden them to erect colleges anywhere except at approved universities, Julius, in this bull, granted the Jesuits, at their request, that they might build and found such colleges wherever they wished. The words of their petition run as follows: "Because, however, the houses which the Lord shall give for working in his vineyard, and not for scholastic studies, are to be set aside, although it would otherwise seem very useful that workers for the same vineyard of the Lord be prepared from young men inclined to piety and suited to the study of letters, who may serve as a kind of seminary of our Society, even of the professed, the professed Society may, for the convenience of study, have colleges for scholars, wherever some men are moved by devotion to build and endow them. As soon as these have been built and endowed, we beg that, not however from goods whose collation pertains to the Apostolic See, they be erected from now on by Apostolic authority and be regarded as erected. These colleges may have revenues, rents or possessions to be applied to the uses and needs of the students, the Provost or the Society retaining over the said colleges and the said students complete governance and superintendence, as to the election of rectors or governors and of the students, and their admission, dismissal, reception and exclusion, the drawing up of statutes, and, concerning the students, their instruction, their upbringing, and the correction of their food and clothing and the manner of supplying other necessary things, and all other governance, rule and care of every kind; so that the students may not abuse the said goods, nor may the professed Society turn them to its own uses, but serve the needs of the students, etc."

units.la: Idem Papa 2 2. die Octobris Anno 1552. Iesuitis nova, praeter Superiora, tribuit privilegia: videlicet, licere professis circa jejunia & cibos prohibitos dispensare: haereticos absolvere: horas vel officium Missae postponere: intra domorum & collegiorum suorum privatos parietes, suos, ad quoscunq; volunt, gradus promovere. Ne quis autem illos, ut qui publica non subierint examina, arguat, rideat & contemnat, praecipit Papa, ut tales graduati, qualificati & formati, quasi in publico id factum esset, in honore habeantur. Concedit etiam illis eadem privilegia, quae habent ij, qui legitime promoti sunt.
units.tr: On 22 October 1552 the same Pope granted the Jesuits new privileges, beyond those they already had, namely: that the professed may dispense with fasts and forbidden foods, absolve heretics, postpone the hours or the office of the Mass, and promote to degrees, within the private walls of their houses and colleges, whomever they wish. Lest anyone, on the ground that such men have not undergone public examinations, should accuse them, mock them or despise them, the Pope orders that such graduates, qualified and formed as if the thing had been done in public, be held in honour. He also grants them the same privileges as are enjoyed by those who have been lawfully promoted.

units.la: Digni sunt Iesuitae hoc quoque Pontifice Patrono & Confirmatore Ordinis sui. Is galerum suo more Pontificio, cuidam adolescenti, Innocentio nomine, dare constituit, nō modo nullis praedito virtutibus, sed pravis & obscoenis moribus a puero imbuto: quem ille in delitijs habuerat, dum esset Bononiae legatus. Romae rama erat, & libellis quoq; taxatum a Iove Ganymedem foveri. Cum ergo institutum suum de donando suo pileo Innocentio, deferret ad Senatum Cardinalium, & omnes resisterent, unus in primis diceret, Et quid obsecro B.P. vides in hoc adolescente, quem vis purpurae exornare splendore? Respondit Iulius, Et quid obsecro in me vidistis, quod Pontificia dignitate ornaretis? &c.
units.tr: The Jesuits have been worthy of this Pope too, as their patron and confirmer of their Order. In his usual papal manner he resolved to give a cardinal's hat to a certain young man named Innocent, who was not only endowed with no virtues but had been trained from boyhood in wicked and obscene habits, and whom he had kept as a darling when he was legate at Bologna. At Rome it was a common saying, and was even put into verse, that a Ganymede was being cherished by Jove. When, therefore, he brought his plan of giving his own cap to Innocent before the senate of cardinals, and all opposed it, one of them in particular said: "And what, I beg you, Holy Father, do you see in this young man, that you wish to adorn him with the splendour of the purple?" Julius replied: "And what, I beg you, did you see in me, that you should adorn me with the papal dignity?" etc.

units.la: Pius Quartus Aprili 13. Anno millesimo quingentesimo sexagesimo primo animadvertens Iesuitas in ipsius primatu defendendo sedulos, & ad omnia paratissimos esse: concedit illis potestatem aedificandi collegia ubicunq; velint. Et mandat ut in huiusmodi conatibus Parochi, Antistites & Episcopi Iesuitas adiuvent, inobedientes autem coerceant.
units.tr: Pius IV, on 13 April 1561, noticing that the Jesuits were zealous in defending his primacy and most ready for every task, granted them the power of building colleges wherever they wish. And he ordered that in such undertakings the parish priests, the prelates and the bishops should help the Jesuits, and restrain those who disobey.

units.la: Augusti decimo nono die eodem anno Iesuitas ab omnibus oneribus & gravaminibus tum Ecclesiae, tum Reipublicae eximit. Nam praecipit, ut & ipsi & Collegia & bona ipsorum in perpetua libertate, sine ullo juramento, excepto quo Papae devincti sunt, sine omni usura, foenore, censura, decimis, & exactionibus liberi relinquantur, tam ijs quae jam possident, quam quae in illorum usum futuris temporibus ventura sunt: tam in domibus & Collegijs, quam in civitatibus & Universitatibus. Nullum tributum, nullum censum, nullas decimas, de domibus, Collegijs & feudis solvant: sed sua ab omni solutione exempta & libera possideant. Secundo, non vult, ut Iesuitae, sicut reliqui qui Monachi, intra latibula sua se contineant, sed liberè ad omnes exeant, praeceptores & profess ores agant, & ubique etiam, ubicunque sperant se commoditatem habituros hominex ad Ecclesiam Romanam adducendi, Collegia & Scholas erigant. Contradicentes vult graviter puniri. Tertiò, tribuit illis facultatem ad gradus promovendi eos, praesertim pauperiores, quos publici Academiarum Professores admittere & promovere noluerint: vel etiam ditiores, quos interdum non eruditio, sed vita minus probata exludit: ita tamen, ut sumptus cedant in usum Doctorum publicorum, vel juribus Universitatum. Et tali ratione promotos, isdem privilegijs gaudere vult, quibus fruuntur qui publicè sunt promoti. Etiam hic Pontifex praedecessorum suorum vestigia sedulò sequutus est.
units.tr: On 19 August of the same year he freed the Jesuits from all burdens and grievances, both of the Church and of the commonwealth. For he ordered that they themselves, their colleges and their goods be left free in perpetual liberty, without any oath, except that by which they are bound to the Pope, without any usury, interest, censure, tithes or exactions, both those they now possess and those which shall come to their use in future times, in houses and colleges as well as in cities and universities. Let them pay no tax, no rent, no tithes, on houses, colleges or fiefs, but let them hold their possessions exempt and free from every payment. Secondly, he does not want the Jesuits, like the other monks, to keep themselves shut within their hiding places, but to go out freely to all, to act as teachers and professors, and everywhere, wherever they hope to have an opportunity of bringing men to the Roman Church, to erect colleges and schools. He wishes those who oppose them to be severely punished. Thirdly, he granted them the faculty of promoting to degrees those, especially the poorer, whom the public professors of the academies were unwilling to admit and promote, or even the wealthier, whom sometimes not learning but a less approved life shuts out; yet in such a way that the expenses go to the use of the public doctors or to the revenues of the universities. And he wishes those so promoted to enjoy the same privileges as those who have been promoted publicly. In this too this Pontiff diligently followed the footsteps of his predecessors.

units.la: Pius Quintus Anno 1565. 6. Calend. Februarij cum ex Iesuitarum relatione intelligeret, nonnullos cognita hac nova Sodalitate studijsque perspectis poenitentia ductos Societatem hanc reliquisse, & vitam politicam sectari: ut iis metum incuteret, & reliquos intra Societatis limites coarctaret, decreuit etiam, ut egredientes ex Societate, licentia Generalis vel Papae, si alium ordinem ingredi velint, in nullum alium quam in Carthusianorum recipiantur: Egredientes vero sine permissu Papae vel Generalis, si in Romana Ecclesia permaneant, excommunicentur:
units.tr: Pius V, in 1565, on the sixth day before the Calends of February, when from the report of the Jesuits he understood that some, having recognised this new fraternity and examined its studies, had been moved by repentance to leave the Society and to pursue a worldly life, in order to strike fear into them and to confine the rest within the limits of the Society, also decreed that those leaving the Society, if they wish to enter another order, may be received, with the permission of the General or the Pope, into no other than the Carthusians; but those leaving without the permission of the Pope or the General, if they remain in the Roman Church, are to be excommunicated.

units.la: Iulius 3. quis & qualis fuerit
units.tr: Julius III: who and what sort he was

units.la: Privilegia quae Pius 4. Iesuitis dedit
units.tr: The privileges which Pius IV gave to the Jesuits

units.la: Privilegia a Pio 5. Iesuitis data si transeant ad Ecclesiæ Romanæ hostes, quibuscunque possunt artibus & insidijs capiantur, incarcerentur, & secundum jus Pontificium cum ipsis procedatur: hoc est, ut vel ad vomitum redeant, vel comburantur.
units.tr: The privileges given by Pius V to the Jesuits: if they pass over to the enemies of the Roman Church, they are to be taken by whatever arts and snares can be devised, imprisoned, and dealt with according to Papal law; that is, either they return to their vomit or they are burned.

units.la: Tandem ne Iesuitæ aliorum etiam destituantur privilegijs, idem Papa concedit illis omnia privilegia, quæ sunt Ordinibus Mendicantibus concessa: ut sic ubicunque, quocunque venerint, sua habere possint diversoria, & socios invenire, qui illos in rerum Pontificiarum executione iuvent.
units.tr: Finally, so that the Jesuits may not be deprived of the privileges of others also, the same Pope granted them all the privileges that have been conceded to the Mendicant Orders, so that wherever and whenever they come they may have their own lodgings and find companions who may help them in carrying out Papal business.

units.la: Anno 1568. 3. Calend. Septemb. idem Papa omnia priora Iesuitarum privilegia repetendo confirmat, omnes eorum constitutiones probat, contractus concedit, & ab aliorum capitulis, poena & censura reddit immunes.
units.tr: In 1568, on the third day before the Kalends of September, the same Pope, repeating all the earlier privileges of the Jesuits, confirmed them, approved all their constitutions, granted them contracts, and made them immune from the chapters, penalties and censures of others.

units.la: Die decimo Martij Anno 1571. alia Bulla concedit Iesuitis facultatem liberè & publicè legendi, etiam ubi Universitates sunt. Vbicunque ergo ad Academias veniunt, etiam non vocati, cathedras & suggestum docendi causâ ascendunt. Permittit etiam studiosis quibusque, ut eiusmodi Professores adventitios audiant reclamantibus Ordinarijs: qui si nolint Iesuitarum auditores promovere, licet Iesuitis illos domi promovere. Et ne Universitatum Rectores pro iure suorum privilegiorum in Iesuitas & illorum discipulos procedant, & ceu illegitimos arceant, vult eos omnes excommunicari, qui vel impedire, vel molestare Iesuitas præsumunt. Verba Bullæ sunt hæc: Decernimus & declaramus quod præceptores huiusmodi Societatis, tam literarum humanarum, quam liberalium artium, Philosophiæ, Theologiæ, vel cuiusvis earum facultatum, in suis Collegijs, etiam in locis ubi Universitates exstiterint, suas lectiones, etiam publicas legere (dummodo per duas horas de mane, & per unam de fero, cum Lectoribus Universitatum non concurrant) libere & licitè possint: quodque quibuscunque scholasticis liceat in huiusmodi Collegijs, lectiones & alias scholasticas exercitationes frequentare, ac quicunque in eis, Philosophiæ vel Theologiæ fuerint auditores, in quavis Universitate, ad gradus admitti possint, & cursuum, quos in eis Collegijs fecerint, ratio habeatur. Ita ut si ipsi in examine sufficientes inventi fuerint, non minus, sed pariformiter, & absque ulla penitus differentia, quam si in Universitatibus præfatis studuissent, ad gradus quoscunque, tam Baccalaureatus, quam Licentiariæ & Doctoratus, admitti possint & debeant, eisque super præmissis licentiam & facultatem concedimus. Districtius inhibentes, Universitatum quarumcunque Rectoribus & alijs quibuscunque, sub excommunicationis maioris, alijsque arbitrio nostro, moderandis, infligendis & imponendis pœnis, ne Collegiorum huiusmodi Rectores & Scholares, in præmissis, quovis quæsito colore, molestare audeant, vel præsumant. Decernentes quoq; præsentes literas, nullo unquam tempore, de subreptionis vitio, aut intentionis nostræ, vel alio quopiam defectu notari, vel impugnari nullatenus posse, minusq; sub quibusvis similium, vel dissimilium gratiarum revocationibus, limitationibus, & alijs contrarijs dispositionibus comprehendi posse.
units.tr: On 10 March 1571 another bull granted the Jesuits the faculty of freely and publicly lecturing, even where universities exist. Wherever, therefore, they come to the academies, even uninvited, they mount the chairs and platforms to teach. It also permits any students whatever to attend such outside professors, the ordinaries objecting; and if the ordinaries are unwilling to promote the Jesuits' pupils, it is lawful for the Jesuits to promote them at home. And lest the rectors of the universities, in defence of the rights of their privileges, should proceed against the Jesuits and their pupils and keep them out as illegitimate, he wishes all who presume to hinder or harass the Jesuits to be excommunicated. The words of the bull are these: "We decree and declare that the teachers of this Society, both of the humane letters and of the liberal arts, of philosophy, theology, or of any of these faculties, may freely and lawfully read their lectures in their colleges, even in places where universities exist, even public lectures (provided they do not coincide with the lecturers of the universities, for two hours in the morning and one in the afternoon); and that to any scholars whatever it be lawful to attend lectures and other scholastic exercises in such colleges; and that whoever in them shall have been hearers of philosophy or theology may be admitted, in any university, to degrees, and account be taken of the courses they have completed in those colleges; so that if they are found sufficient in examination, they may and must be admitted to whatever degrees, both of bachelor, of licentiate and of doctor, not less, but in like manner and without any difference at all, than if they had studied in the aforesaid universities; and we grant them licence and faculty in the premises. We most strictly forbid the rectors of any universities whatever and all others, under the penalty of greater excommunication, and other penalties to be moderated, inflicted and imposed at our discretion, to dare or presume to harass the rectors and scholars of such colleges in the premises, under any pretext whatever. We also decree that the present letters can at no time be noted or impugned for the vice of surreption, or for any defect of our intention, or any other defect whatever, and still less be comprehended under any revocations, limitations and other contrary dispositions of similar or dissimilar graces."

units.la: Paulo post die 7. Iul. concedit illis omnia Mendicantium privilegia, licet ipsi propria Collegia habeant, & domos ubiq; ædificent. Alij Monachi peregrinantes Iesuitas hospitio excipere nolebant, illisq; occurrentibus dicebant: Nobis estis ditiores, Collegia habetis & ædes, ad eas divertite. At Iesuitæ impetrârunt à Pio V. ut Monachi ipsos diversari & pernoctare in suis cænobijs petentes recipere cogantur, nisi in Papæ indignationem incurrere & pœnas dare velint.
units.tr: Shortly afterwards, on 7 July, he granted them all the privileges of the Mendicant orders, although they had their own colleges and built houses everywhere. The other monks did not want to receive the Jesuits as guests when they travelled, and when they met them they said: "You are richer than we are; you have colleges and buildings; go and lodge there." But the Jesuits obtained from Pius V that monks who were asked should be compelled to receive them and let them lodge and spend the night in their monasteries, unless they wished to incur the Pope's displeasure and suffer punishment.

units.la: Gregorius XIII. sub initium Pontificatus Iesuitis dedit facultatem Confessores, Iudices & Advocatos assumendi in quibusvis causis. Illos autem iuvare renuentes excommunicari iubet: sic ut & sub Ecclesiæ Romanæ custodia, & civium seu populicorum tutela liberè, absque omni impedimento res Papæ exequi possint. Vult etiam, ut Archiepiscopi & reliqui Clerici Iesuitas laborantes vel periclitantes, cum potentia, tum opibus iuvent, neq; permittant, ut Iesuitæ vel impediantur, vel molestentur, vel expellantur, vel bonis suis cedere cogantur.
units.tr: Gregory XIII, at the beginning of his pontificate, gave the Jesuits the power to take on confessors, judges and advocates in any cases whatever. He ordered that those who refused to help them should be excommunicated, so that the Pope's affairs could be carried out freely, without any hindrance, both under the protection of the Roman Church and under the safeguard of citizens and subjects. He also wished the archbishops and the other clergy to support the Jesuits, whether they were struggling or in danger, both with their influence and with their resources, and not to allow the Jesuits to be hindered, troubled, expelled, or forced to give up their goods.

units.la: Idem Papa Anno 1573. Prid. Calen. Mart. concedit Iesuitis præ Clericis reliquis, ut suas horas Canonicas extra chorum, & ubi voluerint, recitare possint.
units.tr: In the year 1573, on 28 February, the same Pope granted the Jesuits, in preference to the rest of the clergy, the right to recite their canonical hours outside the choir and wherever they wished.

units.la: Permittit etiam illis, ut quandocunq; voluerint, vel ante, vel post vota suscepta Sacerdotales ordines suscipiant, modò sint idonei.
units.tr: He also allowed them, whenever they wished, either before or after taking their vows, to receive the priestly orders, provided they were suitable.

units.la: Anno 1575. Ianuarij octavo, prorsus novum illis concessit privilegium, quo eos Bibliothecarios Pontificios creavit, varias facultates illis tribuens circa librorum prohibitorum lectionem, emendationem, mutationem, interpretationem, abolitionem, expunctionem & concrematiónem.
units.tr: In the year 1575, on 8 January, he granted them an entirely new privilege, by which he appointed them papal librarians, giving them various powers over the reading, correction, alteration, interpretation, suppression, expunging and burning of prohibited books.

units.la: Sequenti mense Maio eiusdem Anni Gregorius hic favorem suum totum in suos Iesuitas infundens, tribuit & concessit illis omnibus facultatem omnium Ordinum & locorum privilegijs, more suo, utendi. Quocunque igitur perveniunt Iesuitæ in regno Pontificio, nemo tamen illis dicere audet: Quis vos vocavit? quid facitis? quare intra vestrorum Collegiorum parietes, ut Monachos decet, vos non continetis? Aut si quid tale audiunt, mox Papæ Bullas proferunt.
units.tr: In the following month of May of the same year, Gregory, pouring all his favour upon his Jesuits, granted them the right to use, in his usual manner, the privileges of all the Orders and places. Therefore, wherever the Jesuits arrive in the Pope's kingdom, no one dares to say to them: "Who called you? What are you doing? Why do you not keep yourselves within the walls of your colleges, as monks ought to?" Or, if they hear anything of the kind, they at once produce the Pope's Bulls.

units.la: Mense Iulio Anno 1576. die 16. eximit illos hic ipse Papa necessitate interessendi recibus, processionibus & funeratis associationibus.
units.tr: In the month of July of the year 1576, on the 16th day, this same Pope exempted them from the obligation of attending funerals, processions and funeral associations.

units.la: Aliorum Pontificum Rom. qui his successerunt privilegia, Iesuitis concessa, non minora vel leviora prioribus fuisse, sequentium annorum historia probat. Nihil autem sunt aliud quam exaltatio Iesuitarum Ordinis supra omnes Clericorum & Monachorum Ordines, ac licentia quodlibet agendi.
units.tr: The history of the following years proves that the privileges granted to the Jesuits by the other Roman Pontiffs who succeeded these were no less or lesser than the earlier ones. These privileges are nothing else than the exaltation of the Jesuit Order above all the orders of clergy and monks, and a licence to do whatever they please.

units.la: Mirum autem non immerito videri alicui posset, quo consilio, seu, ut verius dicam, qua astutia, post tot Monachorum examina, quibus totus mundus scatet, Thais Babylonica hunc novum foetum enixa sit, præsertim cum iam pridem in Lateranensi Concilio anno 1215. sub Innocentio Tertio, & in Lugdunensi anno 1273. sub Gregorio Decimo celebrato decretum fuerit, ne quis de cætero novam religionem instituat, ne nimia Religiosorum diversitas gravem in Ecclesia Dei offensionem inducat. Idemque censuerit etiam Petrus de Alliaco Cameracensis Cardinalis in suo libro de Reformat. Ecclesiæ Constantiensi Concilio oblato: similiter Armacanus & Guilielmus de sancto Amore sanctæ Theologiæ Doctor insignis quondam in Sorbona Parisiensi, quem Ioannes Gerson summis laudibus extulit. Et novissime novem selecti præstantissimi & doctissimi viri, quorum quatuor erant Cardinales, reliqui Archiepiscopi, Episcopi & Abbates, à Paulo Tertio Pontifice Romano Anno millesimo quingentesimo trigesimo octavo congregati & diris adiurati, ut absque ulla dissimulatione veritatem ederent, et consilium darent ad iudicandum & corrigendum abusus & medendum moris Ecclesiæ. Hi inter alios abusus corrigendos, censuerunt prohibendam esse additionem novorum Religiosorum etiam in conventualibus iam receptis ordinibus: Sed omnes qui tum nondum erant professi abigendos & expellendos: & multo minus novos conventus erigendos, etiam Ordinum vel Religionum approbatarum: & multo minus novas factitias Religiones admittendas. Sed quia intellexit homo ille peccati & filius perditionis, tempus illud adesse, quo Dominus ipsum Spiritu oris sui confectus sit: simulque vidit reliquorum Ordinum, quantumvis præpingues & crassos entres, non posse labascentem Rom. Ecclesiam fulcire: ut afflictis suis rebus malaire succurreret, novam hanc creaturam edidit, sollicitèque in regula cavit, ne oneretur multitudine ceremoniarum, sed curandum, ut literas discant, studia lingua cognoscant, & scripta veterum evolvant, quo erroribus & abusibus, ex verbo Dei toti iam mundo detectis, plausibilem aliquam saltem speciem orationis lenocinio induere, & nervos regni Pontificij conservare possent, ut si usus periclitans iam in tanta luce Evangelij regni istius, ita expostulaaret, ex hoc Ordine possint tanquam emissarij in omnem terram submitti propugnatores & patroni.
units.tr: It may seem to someone, and not without reason, a wonder what purpose, or, to speak more truly, what cunning, lay behind the Babylonian harlot bringing forth this new offspring, after so many examinations of monks, with which the whole world swarms. This is especially so since a decree had long before been issued at the Lateran Council in 1215 under Innocent III, and at the Council of Lyons in 1273 under Gregory X, that no one should from now on found a new religious order, lest the excessive diversity of religious orders cause serious offence in the Church of God. Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, held the same view in his book on the reform of the Church, presented to the Council of Constance; likewise Armachanus, and William of Saint-Amour, once an outstanding doctor of sacred theology at the Sorbonne in Paris, whom John Gerson praised with the highest commendation. And most recently, nine chosen, most distinguished and most learned men, four of whom were cardinals and the rest archbishops, bishops and abbots, were gathered by Pope Paul III in the year 1538 and solemnly bound by oath to set forth the truth without any concealment, and to give counsel for judging and correcting abuses and for healing the morals of the Church. Among the other abuses to be corrected, they judged that the addition of new religious, even to the conventual orders already accepted, should be forbidden; and that all who were not yet professed should be driven away and expelled; and, much more, that new convents should not be established, even of approved orders or religions; and much less that new made-up religions should be admitted. But because that man of sin and son of perdition understood that the time had come when the Lord would consume him with the breath of his mouth, and at the same time he saw that the other orders, however fat and gross their members, could not prop up the tottering Roman Church, he brought forth this new creature to come to the aid of his afflicted affairs with some remedy. He carefully provided in its rule that it should not be burdened with a multitude of ceremonies, but that its members should learn letters, know languages and study and unroll the writings of the ancients, so that, once the errors and abuses have been revealed to the whole world from the Word of God, they might at least be able to put on some plausible appearance of argument with the aid of rhetoric, and preserve the sinews of the papal kingdom; so that, if the cause should be in danger in such a great light of the Gospel of this kingdom, they might from this Order be sent out as emissaries into every land as champions and patrons.

units.la: Factum hoc in Germania praecipuè, in cuius perniciem hic Ordo potissimum institutus videtur. Quia enim in illa natione, ij quoque qui Pontifici iurati sunt, quíque magná mercede conductitiam linguam Romanæ Curiæ locárunt, nonnullos manifestos errores & nimium crassos abusus improbárunt, quaedam etiam timidius defenderunt, de quibusdam denique nimis modeste & mitius quàm status Pontificij regni ferat, loquuti sunt: ideirco sedulò curárunt in primordijs statim Ordinis huius, ut in teneris annis mox pueri ingenio pollentes in hunc ordinem cooptarentur, & Romam missi, ibi in medijs abominationibus educarentur instituerenturque: & postquam viderentur imis visceribus imbibisse abominationes, quæ Thaïs Babylonica calice suo propinavit, fatisque charactere bestiæ confirmati, tûc per Germaniam, tanquâ locustarum examina, dispergerentur, ut hoc artificio fortissima illa gens sub iugum Pontificiorum errorum reduceretur, & lux Evangelij ei eriperetur, aut certè obscuraretur, sicut sæpè factum legimus, ut agmina locustarum oculis hominum solemque luce mque eripuerint.
units.tr: This was done chiefly in Germany, for whose ruin this Order seems mainly to have been established. For in that nation even those who had sworn allegiance to the Pope, and who for a large wage had hired out their tongue to the Roman Curia, condemned some manifest errors and very gross abuses; some things they defended rather timidly, and about certain matters they spoke too modestly and mildly for the state of the papal kingdom to bear. Therefore, from the very beginnings of this Order, they took great care that boys of promising talent should be enlisted into it in their tender years, and sent to Rome, there to be brought up and trained amid the abominations; and when they seemed to have soaked up to the depths of their bowels the abominations which the Babylonian harlot had poured out to them from her cup, and were confirmed with the mark of the beast, then they were to be scattered through Germany like swarms of locusts, so that by this device that most valiant nation might be brought back under the yoke of Papist errors and the light of the Gospel might be snatched from it, or at least darkened, just as we read it has often happened, when swarms of locusts have snatched the eyes of men from the sun and the light of the moon.

units.la: Quæ igitur de Draconé magno & russo, eiúsque ministris Ioannes in Apocalypsi scribit, quæque Hilarius & Ignatius de iis referunt; Quod nimirum seducere & scandalizare soleant quidam pusillos in CHRISTVM credentes, bona omnia instar aranearum corrumpendo, officia patris sui diaboli perficiendo, zizania in agro DOMINI superseminando, quorum sermo sicut cancer serpat: Haec, inquam, in nullos quadrant aptius, quàm in hanc Iesuitarum sectam. Quum primùm enim pofi horrendos, diuturnos, Pontificios ac crassos errores tenebrasque plus quàm cimmerias, lux verbi Dei, immensâ ipsius bonitate illuxit mundo, statim Draco ille magnus foetum parturire coepit novissimum, qui & seculorum aliquot veternosos, turpissimos ac perniciosissimos, luce meridianâ manifestior res errores, claritate doctrinæ cœlestis, hoc nostro seculo ingenti Dei beneficio, immensáque bonitate detectos, palliare, verborum lenocinijs involvere, rhetoricisque coloribus pingere, maximè autem augustissimo titulo & prætextu Catholicæ Ecclesiæ coeperunt: nihilque adeo est tam crassum, tam putidum, tam impurum, tam insulsum atque impium in Pontificia lacuna, seu potius cloaca, quod novis istis, Sociis non optimè oleat, quod editorum ab ipsis librorum lectio certissimè docere potest.
units.tr: Therefore, whatever John writes in the Apocalypse about the great red dragon and his ministers, and whatever Hilary and Ignatius report about them, namely that they are wont to seduce and scandalise some little ones who believe in Christ, corrupting all good things like spiders, carrying out the works of their father the devil, sowing tares in the field of the Lord, and whose speech creeps like a cancer: all this, I say, fits no one more aptly than this sect of Jesuits. For when, after the dreadful, long-lasting, Papist and gross errors and darkness more than Cimmerian, the light of God's Word shone upon the world by his immense goodness, at once that great dragon began to bring forth his last offspring, which has begun, with the lures of words, with rhetorical colours and above all under the most august title and pretext of the Catholic Church, to cloak the old, most foul and most pernicious errors of several centuries, errors now more manifest than the midday light, uncovered in this our age by the clarity of heavenly doctrine, through God's great benefit and immense goodness. Nothing is so gross, so stinking, so impure, so insipid and so impious in the Papist pool, or rather sewer, that does not smell sweet to these new Companions; as the reading of the books they have published can most certainly teach.

units.la: Recte igitur Princeps quidam magni nominis comparavit Iesuitas chartis aleatorijs, quas maximi valoris postremas proferunt ponuntque lusores, ad vincendum adversarium (vulgo jum Stich) sic enim Pontifices ad extremum auxilium stultissimos illos emissarios in Germaniam ablegasse ad amissam sibi authoritatem recuperandam, & quæ superat confervandam.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, a certain prince of great name compared the Jesuits to those playing-cards which gamblers put down last, of the greatest value, to win against their opponent (commonly called the trump card). For in this way the Popes, as a last resort, sent those most foolish emissaries into Germany to recover the authority they had lost, and to preserve what remains of it.

units.la: Cùm igitur Pontificiæ Sedi iam ruenti humeros suos certatim supposuerint Iesuitæ, oportuit etiam Pontifices Romanos tam fidis satellitibus diligenter providere, ne quid detrimenti Secta illorum nova, aliis Monachorum Sectis supra modum exosa, caperet, sed incrementa haberet maxima. Vnde Gregorius XIII. Papa Iesuitarum Annales legens, ac opera considerans, quae hinc inde artibus Iesuitarum efficiuntur, dixisse fertur, Tot sunt mihi millia Clericorum; sed soli Iesuitæ omnes superant in stabiliendo Regno nostro. Digni ergo sunt quæ prae cæteris etiam foveantur.
units.tr: Since the Jesuits have eagerly put their shoulders under the Papal See as it was already collapsing, the Roman Pontiffs had to take careful care of such faithful henchmen, so that their new sect, hated beyond measure by the other orders of monks, would suffer no harm but would instead grow as greatly as possible. Hence Pope Gregory XIII, reading the Jesuits' annals and considering the work that is done here and there by the Jesuits' arts, is said to have remarked: "I have thousands of clergy, but the Jesuits alone surpass them all in establishing our kingdom. They therefore deserve to be cherished above the rest."

units.la: Vt etiam his privilegijs à Pontificibus Romanis ornati ad summum authoritatis gradum in Ecclesia Romana evecti Iesuitæ, gratos sese aliquo modo præberent, ipsi vicissim Pontificibus sese in omnibus subijciunt, ab eorum nutu pendent, omnia ipsorum facta & dicta pro oraculis habent, & eos tantùm non pro Deo colunt ac venerantur. Sic Iesuita Andreas, Romae in monte di Ca... ballo
units.tr: So that the Jesuits, adorned with these privileges from the Roman Pontiffs and raised to the highest level of authority in the Roman Church, might show themselves grateful in some way, they in turn submit themselves to the Pontiffs in everything. They depend on their nod, regard all their words and deeds as oracles, and honour and worship them almost as God. Thus the Jesuit Andreas, at Rome on the Monte di Cavallo, spoke as master of the Jesuit novices at St Andrew's:

units.la: Iesuitae factus ra-ad draconis. allò Iesuitarum neophytorum apud D. Andream moderator, dixit: Impossibile est eos à Deo in cœlis non diligi, quos summus eius in terris Vicarius, Pontifex Romanus diligit, per quem quasi scala quædam ad cœlorum gaudia ascenditur. Præterea in prima regula tradunt, Papæ Romani vocem non aliter ac sermonem Christi, audiendam esse. Hunc si habemus, aiebat Iesuita Pietro Lanspergæ in Catechismi Canisiani explicatione, quis contra nos erit? Cardinales, Episcopi, Canonici, nobis non modò resistere non audent: sed etiam in hoc multi illorum ordinati sunt, ut nos sua potentia & auctoritate juvent atque defendant: ut in Bulla secunda constitutum est. Quid? Quod achium seculare, volente Pontifice, omni postposita appellatione à nobis invocatum, rha capere, & nobis resistentes, si ita opus sit, tollere, proscribere & comburere debet? Quamobrem, dilecti fratres, aiebat, Pontificis amorem, parentum, amicorum, opum & itriæ dilectioni præferatis. Hoc enim facientes, & huius vitæ præmia, & æternæ lætitiæ gloriam consequemini. Ille enim est, qui nostram Societatem confirmavit, ditavit, navit, & hactenus conservavit. Et Ioannes Iesuita, Augustæ ædilis, aiebat: Caveamus dilectissimi, ne Pontificem Romanum offendamus, ab illius Majestate & ostrum esse & interesse dependent: hoc est, quicquid sumus & habemus, id omne & tum Papæ Romano acceptum ferendum est. Imo aiebat Turrianus: ipse est nostra anima, nos eius corpus. Et sicut corpus absque anima mortuum est: Ita etiam Societas absque Pontificis Romani clementia mortua est, planèque cadaverosa. Dicebat etiam Iesuita Gregorius Augustæ, quam diu inter Societatem nostram & Pontificem Romanum pax atque concordia fuerit conservata: tamdiu cathedra Petri, & sedes Apostolicæ erecta, nostræ vero sodalitates salve manebunt. Dissensione autem orta, utrane concidens, nosque omnes toti mundo ludibrio futuri sumus. Agnoscamus ergo, filii, Pontificem Romanum Patrem, & huic soli in omnibus, quæ vult obediamus. Eius enim est nobis imperare & facienda præscribere: nostrum vero est, non petita ratione, absque ulla tergiversatione, ut filios obedientes & Papæ dilectos decet obedire. Sic dixit Iesuita Bonaventura Ingolstadij Rector, apud Pythagoreos, pro argumenti & causæ ratione fuit ὡς ἐφα: quanto maiori obedientia nos faciamus, & sine ulla refragatione exequamur ea, quæ in mandatis à Pontifice Romano accipimus. Illi est dicere hoc fiat: nostrum vero est agnoscere illud ὡς ἐφα & ut votis nos cogi nostris, addere, Amen. Alij dicunt sodalibus suis: Est sane magnum, esse in gratia eiusdem Comitis: maius in Principis & Cæsaris: at maximum est vivere sub gratia, favore, pace & indulgentia Romani Pontificis, pro sua Sanctitate & Majestate nos omnibus ornare & beare intendentis. Qui quanta nobis bona tribuerit, partim ex Residentiis, omnibus, collegiis, feudis, reditibus, partim etiam ex Epistolis & Bullis notum est. Atque sic quidem Mutuum mulscabunt, ut est in proverbio, videlicet, Pontifices Romani & Iesuitæ.
units.tr: "It is impossible that those whom the Roman Pontiff, his supreme Vicar on earth, loves should not be loved by God in heaven, since through him, as by a kind of ladder, one ascends to the joys of heaven. Moreover, in the first rule they teach that the voice of the Roman Pope is to be heard no differently than the word of Christ. If we have him," said the Jesuit Pietro Lanspergius in his explanation of the Canisian Catechism, "who will be against us? Cardinals, bishops and canons not only do not dare to resist us, but many of them have been ordained for this very purpose, to help and defend us with their power and authority, as is laid down in the second Bull. What more? The secular arm, when the Pontiff wills it, must seize without any appeal to us, and must remove, proscribe and burn those who resist us, if need be. Wherefore, beloved brothers," he said, "prefer love of the Pontiff to love of parents, friends, wealth and fatherland. For by doing so you will obtain both the rewards of this life and the glory of eternal joy. For it is he who confirmed, enriched, adorned and hitherto preserved our Society." And the Jesuit John, architect at Augsburg, said: "Let us take care, most beloved, not to offend the Roman Pontiff; all that we are and all that we have depends on his Majesty and is owed to him. Whatever we are and have must be credited to the Roman Pope." Indeed Turrianus said: "He is our soul, we are his body. Just as a body without a soul is dead, so the Society without the clemency of the Roman Pontiff is dead and utterly like a corpse." The Jesuit Gregory also said at Augsburg: "As long as peace and harmony are kept between our Society and the Roman Pontiff, the chair of Peter and the Apostolic See will stand, and our fraternities will remain safe. But if a dispute arises, and one of them falls, we will all become a laughingstock for the whole world. Let us therefore acknowledge, sons, the Roman Pontiff as Father, and obey him alone in all things that he wishes. For it is his to command us and prescribe what is to be done; ours is to obey without asking for reasons and without any evasion, as obedient sons beloved of the Pope ought to obey." Thus the Jesuit Bonaventura, rector at Ingolstadt, spoke in the manner of the Pythagoreans, [ὡς ἔφα], as the matter and the reason of the case required: "The more obediently we act, and carry out without any objection what we receive as commands from the Roman Pontiff, the better. It is for him to say 'let this be done'; it is for us to acknowledge that 'so he said' [ὡς ἔφα], and to add 'Amen', as we are compelled by our vows." Others say to their companions: "It is indeed a great thing to be in the favour of a count, greater to be in that of a prince or emperor; but the greatest thing is to live under the grace, favour, peace and indulgence of the Roman Pontiff, who intends to adorn and bless us with all things for the sake of his Holiness and Majesty." How many good things he has bestowed upon us, partly in residences, colleges, estates and revenues, and partly in letters and bulls, is well known. And so indeed they will flatter one another, as the proverb has it: the Roman Pontiffs and the Jesuits.

units.la: CAPVT VIII. EXAMEN REGVLARVM DE VOTIS IESVITA- RVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. EXAMINATION OF THE JESUITS' RULES CONCERNING THEIR VOWS.

units.la: De Voto Paupertatis.
units.tr: On the Vow of Poverty.

units.la: In Iesuiticarum Constitutionum Summario trium tantum votorum, quæ Simplicia vocant mentio fit, nempe, Paupertatis, Obedientiæ & Continentiæ, & qualia ea velint esse indicatur. De Paupertatis Voto sic habet Constitutio 23. Paupertas, ut murus religionis firmus, diligenda, & in sua puritate conseruanda est, quantum diuina gratia aspirante fieri potuerit.
units.tr: The Summary of the Jesuit Constitutions mentions only three so-called simple vows, namely poverty, obedience and continence, and indicates what they are meant to be. Constitution 23 says of the vow of poverty: "Poverty, as the firm wall of the religious life, is to be loved and preserved in its purity, as far as divine grace, breathing upon us, may allow."

units.la: Constitutio 24. Diligant omnes paupertatem, ut matrem, & juxta mensuram sanctae discretionis suis temporibus eius effectus aliquos experiantur: nullaque re tanquam propria utantur, paratique sint ad mendicandum ostiatim, quando vel obedientia, vel necessitas id exigeat.
units.tr: Constitution 24: "Let all love poverty as a mother, and let them experience some of its effects at the proper times, within the measure of holy discretion. Let them use nothing as their own, and be ready to beg from door to door whenever obedience or necessity requires it."

units.la: Const. 25. Victus, vestitus, & lecti ratio erit ut pauperibus accommodata: & unusquisque sibi persuadeat, quod quae vilissima erunt ex ijs, quae domi sunt, ei tribuentur propter ipsius maiorem abnegationem & spiritualem profectum.
units.tr: Constitution 25: "The manner of food, clothing and bedding shall be suited to the poor; and each one shall persuade himself that the cheapest of the things that are kept at home shall be assigned to him, for the sake of his greater self-denial and spiritual progress."

units.la: Const. 26. Intelligant omnes quod mutuo dare, vel accipere, vel dispensare quidquam de ijs, quae domi sunt, minime possunt, nisi Superior conscius consensum praestiterit.
units.tr: Constitution 26: "Let all understand that they may by no means lend or borrow, or dispense anything of what is kept at home, unless the Superior, being aware of it, has given his consent."

units.la: In his Constitutionib. multa & speciosa de paupertate sua gloriatur Iesuitae, cum tamen nulla, sed eius loco potius Croesi opes reperiantur. Ideo recte Constit. 23. habet: Paupertatem eos diligere oportere, QVANTVM diuina gratia aspirante fieri poterit: id est, religiosa paupertate sua mundi opes corradant; interea autem ita se gerant, ut pauperes coram mundo videantur. Et ob hanc famam comparandam, Novitij eorum saepe ostiatim mendicare coguntur: ipsi etiam Patres ad diuites mittere & eleemosynas, sed opimas, petere solent. Recte etiam Regula 15. matrem suam vocant Paupertatem. Est enim illis indulgentissima mater, a qua tenerrime, mollissime, lautissime, delicatissime & splendidissime foventur, nutriuntur & aluntur. Addunt, ut interim eum amorem mensura & conformitate sanctae discretionis metiantur. Ea discretio & moderatio est, ne quis honestatem & gravitatem religiosam nimio Paupertatis studio, inedia corpus affligendo, vel nimis sordide se vestiendo contemptam reddat, sed sancta discretione & conformitate sic moderetur, ut Paupertas illorum, ut sequens regula habet, fit pura & munda, ne aliquod fastidium vel taedium & nauseam aliis praebeat. Volunt etiam, ut certis temporibus effectus aliquos Paupertatis experiantur. Hoc vero in Collegijs & aedibus eorum non fit, in quibus rerum omnium copiam & abundantiam habent. Hypocritice tamen paupertatis huius experimenta quaedam edunt. Quando enim Socij mensae accubuerunt, & splendide epulantur, progreditur in medium illorum Iesuita aliquis, & indutus centone, calceis perforatis, pileo dilacerato & seminudus. Is, ut grave paupertatis Iesuiticae iugum experiatur, patinam & lagunculam ligneam manibus tenet, & a Patribus, reliquisque Socijs cibum potumque emendicat: quibus acceptis, post ianuam sedet & cibum capit. Est hic voti huius primus effectus.
units.tr: In these Constitutions the Jesuits boast much and fine things about their poverty, though no poverty is to be found there, but rather the wealth of Croesus. Therefore Constitution 23 rightly says that they must love poverty AS FAR AS divine grace, breathing upon them, may allow: that is, they may amass the riches of the world under the name of religious poverty, while meanwhile they conduct themselves so as to appear poor in the eyes of the world. And in order to obtain this reputation, their novices are often compelled to beg from door to door; the Fathers themselves are accustomed to send to the rich and ask for alms, but generous ones. The Rule 15 also rightly calls Poverty their mother. For she is to them a most indulgent mother, by whom they are cherished, nourished and fed most tenderly, softly, sumptuously, daintily and splendidly. They add that they must measure this love by the measure and conformity of holy discretion. This discretion and moderation means that no one should make his religious decency and dignity contemptible through excessive zeal for poverty, by afflicting the body with hunger or by dressing too meanly; rather, by holy discretion and conformity, poverty is so tempered that, as the following rule has it, their poverty is pure and clean, so as not to offer others any disgust, weariness or nausea. They also wish that at certain times they should experience some effects of poverty. But this does not happen in their colleges and houses, where they have an abundance and plenty of everything. Yet they put on some hypocritical displays of this poverty. For when the members have sat down at table and are feasting splendidly, a certain Jesuit comes forward into their midst, dressed in a patched cloak, with perforated shoes, a torn cap, and half-naked. So that he may experience the heavy yoke of Jesuit poverty, he holds a dish and a wooden flask in his hands and begs food and drink from the Fathers and the other members; having received them, he sits behind the door and eats. This is the first effect of this vow.

units.la: Sed ne extra quidem collegia sua paupertatem aliquam experiuntur. Nam primis probationis annis absolutis, aliquos ad experiendam paupertatem Iesuiticam Rector ad unius mensis spacium cum literis commendatitijs emittit. Ii ab Abbatibus, Prioribus & Episcopis liberaliter recipiuntur & tractantur lautissime: ut in istis emissionibus vel peregrinationibus ne unum quidem paupertatis actum experiantur.
units.tr: But they do not experience any poverty even outside their colleges. For when the first years of probation are over, the Rector sends some of them out, with letters of recommendation, to experience Jesuit poverty for the space of one month. They are received liberally by abbots, priors and bishops and entertained most lavishly, so that on these journeys or pilgrimages they do not experience even one act of poverty.

units.la: Additur in eadem regula, ne re aliqua tanquam propria utantur. Hinc crebrae rerum omnium mutationes, non solum vestium, sed etiam cubiliū, musaeorum & similium. Praecipitur etiam, ut omnes parati sint ad mendicandum ostiatim, quando vel obedientia; vel necessitas id postulaverit. Necessitas autem haec illis tantum incumbit, qui votum professionis suscipere volunt. Hi enim triduum ostiatim vitum quaerere coguntur: ut sic probati inventi & in omnibus mortificati, sese dignae gerere possint. Obedientia autem tunc illos iubet ostiatim mendicare, quando hominibus nimis divites facti videntur, ut hoc modo falsum id esse probent & revera pauperes habeantur.
units.tr: It is added in the same rule that they must use nothing as their own. Hence the frequent changes of all things, not only of clothes, but also of bedding, books and the like. It is also enjoined that all should be ready to beg from door to door whenever obedience or necessity demands it. This necessity, however, presses only on those who wish to take the vow of profession. For these are compelled to seek their living from door to door for three days, so that, having been tested and found mortified in all things, they may show themselves worthy. Obedience, on the other hand, orders them to beg from door to door when they seem too rich in men's eyes, so that by this means they may prove that this is false and may be regarded as truly poor.

units.la: Praeterea Regula 26. ipsis iniungit, ut etiam victus, vestitus, & lecti ratio sit tanquam nquam pauperibus accommodata: & unusquisq; sibi persuadeat, quod quae vilissima sint eijs, quae domi habentur sibi tribuenda sint. Contrarium autem fieri ipsi negare nequeunt. Lecti enim ipsis sunt partim Matarazza, ut vocant; quae sunt lana molli floccis subtilibus, partim mollibus plumis repleta. Quilibet proprium lectum habet, quem ipse sibi sternit, qui etiam, ne forte nudus conspiciatur, velo circumcirca cingitur. Et ne quid desit, vel situ pereat, proprium habent lectorum inspectorem: qui si quos in illis curandis negligentiores, vel sordidos & impuros deprehendit, eos Rectori indicat, qui deinde illis circa prandii & coenae tempus poenitentias imponit: quales sunt, lectos non bene adornatos circumportare, in medium refectorii deponere, & ab Inspectore vel Visitatore discere, quomodo ro more Societatis suum lectum recte adornare debeat. Singulis diebus Sabbathi, vesperi ad illorum lectos, indusiorum & lodicum custos, cuilibet mundatum indusium, duo strophiola & vittam ponit: decima autem quarta, lavis die lodices. Si autem sudavit, semper nova & pura recipit indusia ac lodices mundas: & haec quidem omnia quam mundissima & tenerrima; quae pauertas Iesuitica est in cubilibus.
units.tr: Furthermore, Rule 26 enjoins on them that the manner of food, clothing and bedding should be suited to the poor, and that each one should persuade himself that the cheapest of the things kept at home should be assigned to him. Yet they cannot deny that the opposite happens. Their beds are partly the so-called materasses, which are stuffed with soft wool in fine flocks, and partly filled with soft feathers. Each has his own bed, which he makes up himself, and which is surrounded by a curtain on every side, lest he be seen naked. And so that nothing may be lacking or spoil through neglect, they have their own bed-inspector, who, if he finds any who are negligent or dirty and foul in caring for them, reports them to the Rector; the Rector then imposes penances on them at the time of lunch and supper, such as carrying badly made beds around, laying them down in the middle of the refectory, and learning from the Inspector or Visitor how to make up their bed properly in the manner of the Society. Every Saturday evening the keeper of the linen and blankets places beside each one's bed a cleaned shirt, two bands and a strip of cloth; on the fourteenth day, that is, on washing day, the blankets. If anyone has sweated, he always receives new and clean shirts and clean blankets. And all these things are as clean and as delicate as possible: such is Jesuit poverty in the bedrooms.

units.la: Quod ad vestitum attinet, Emptor iuxta Regulam, non vilia vel mediocria, sed optima & pretiosa quaeque emit, quod haec diutius quam illa usui esse & durare possint.
units.tr: As for clothing, the buyer, according to the Rule, does not buy cheap or middling things but the best and most costly of everything, because these can be of use and last longer than those.

units.la: Sequitur in Regula; Quilibet persuadeat sibi semper data iri viliora. Vt igitur hac Ignatio regulam illis praescriptam, in tanta rerum copia servare possint, in dispensatione vestimentorum & aliarum rerum, iumentorum & ijs qui Sacerdotes non sunt, viliora solent distribuere: ut sic etiam paupertatis quendam gustum percipiant.
units.tr: The Rule continues: "Let each one persuade himself that always cheaper things will be given to him." So that they may keep the rule prescribed to them by Ignatius amid such abundance of goods, in distributing clothing and other things, beasts of burden, and to those who are not priests, they are accustomed to give out the cheaper ones, so that in this way they too may taste a certain flavour of poverty.

units.la: Haec autem omnia facere iubentur, ad maiorem sui mortificationem & ad profectum spiritualem. Qui igitur quam diligentissime regulas observat, eum etiam virtutum Societatis prae caeteris habere dicunt: qui profectus illorum spiritualis est. Mortificatio eorum est, in omnibus sensibus repugnantia & naturae contraria appetere: in omnibus rebus mortificationem, in nulla voluptatem, affectum vel appetitum quaerere aut sequi.
units.tr: They are commanded to do all these things for the greater mortification of themselves and for spiritual progress. Therefore they say that whoever observes the rules most diligently is held to possess the virtues of the Society above others, and this is their spiritual progress. Their mortification consists in seeking, in all the senses, what is contrary to and opposed to nature; in every matter, mortification; in nothing, pleasure, affection or appetite to be sought or followed.

units.la: Item, omnes quidquam mutuo dare, vel accipere, vel dispensare de ijs, quae domi sunt, nisi Superior conscius consensum praestiterit, ut habet regula 26. Habent quidem res omnes communes, inferioribus tamen non licet aliquid sibi ipsis sponte, neque Superioris licentia sumere, neque alteri dare, neque res domus sine Rectoris permissu disponere, vel dispensare. Et hac ratione absque Superioris quidem licentia pauperes sunt, mihilque proprii possident, in Rectoris tamen opulentia, quae egere non sinit, omnia habent.
units.tr: Likewise, Rule 26 says that "all may lend or borrow nothing, or dispense anything of what is kept at home, unless the Superior, being aware, has given his consent." They indeed hold all things in common, yet it is not permitted to the inferiors to take anything for themselves of their own accord, nor with the Superior's leave, nor to give it to another, nor to dispose of or dispense the goods of the house without the Rector's permission. And in this way, without the Superior's permission, they are poor and possess nothing of their own; yet in the Rector's wealth, which does not allow them to be in need, they have everything.

units.la: Quae denique ratio Iesuiticae paupertatis sit, satis declarant maximae & tantum non Croesi opes quas possident. Vel unius enim Claudius Aquaviva, olim Princeps & Papae Cubicularius, non ita pridem vero Generalis, adeoque ix & caput Iesuitarum, tradito filio Ducatu, multas opes, & ut Hafenmuller testatur pag. 29. se ex multis audivisse; ultra 50. millia ducatorum Societati intulit.
units.tr: Finally, the nature of Jesuit poverty is sufficiently shown by the enormous riches they possess, almost the wealth of Croesus. For Claudius Aquaviva alone, formerly a prince and chamberlain of the Pope, and recently General, and thus the head of the Jesuits, after handing over his duchy to his son, brought into the Society, as Hafenmuller attests on page 29, from what he heard from many people, more than 50,000 ducats.

units.la: Idem declarant amplissimi, quos habent reditus. Author historiae Iesuitarum, id dicam, inquit, de illorum paupertate? Certe quod per Italiam & Germaniam expertum, sic Iesuitas opibus & divitiis, domibus & Collegiis, hortis & fundis, proventibus & reditibus, multos Comites, adeoque nonnullos Principes superare. Sunt qui G. Baderum Suitam, & in Bavaria eorum Provincialem, his verbis gloriantem audiverunt: Vostra inopia Episcoporum & aliorum copia ita crevit, ut Comites & Barones adaequare possimus.
units.tr: Their very ample revenues show the same thing. The author of the history of the Jesuits says: "Shall I speak of their poverty? Certainly, what has been seen through Italy and Germany is that the Jesuits surpass many counts, and indeed some princes, in resources and wealth, in houses and colleges, in gardens and estates, in income and revenues." There are those who heard G. Bader, a Swiss and Provincial of theirs in Bavaria, boasting in these words: "Through our poverty, the wealth of bishops and others has grown so much that we can rival counts and barons."

units.la: Anno 1616. Iesuitae magnificentissimum & tantum non regium convivium instituerunt Viennae in honorem Legati Turcici, ad Imperatorem Romanum pacis concilianda causa missi.
units.tr: In the year 1616 the Jesuits held a most magnificent and almost royal banquet at Vienna, in honour of the Turkish Legate, who had been sent to the Roman Emperor to arrange peace.

units.la: DE OECONOMIA ET REGIMINE
units.tr: CONCERNING THE ECONOMY AND GOVERNMENT

units.la: Augustæ Vindelicorum, quod Hafenmullerus refert, se ex Gregorio Roaudivisse, Fuggerorum opibus, civitatis iura & privilegia emerunt. Iactant etiam, se hodie vigesies centies aureorum millia quotannis ex vectigalibus Collegiorum suorum percipere. Huic summæ adde quod provenit ex fraudibus & impostuiris Iesuitarum, & intelliges rationem esse maximam. Quid autem fiet si ad centum adhuc annos Ordo hic duraverit?
units.tr: At Augsburg, as Hafenmüller reports, the Jesuits bought the rights and privileges of the city with the wealth of the Fuggers, having (he says) heard it from Gregory Roaud. They also boast that today they receive two thousand times one hundred thousand gold pieces a year from the revenues of their colleges. Add to this sum what comes from the frauds and impostures of the Jesuits, and you will understand that the reckoning is very great. What, then, will happen if this Order endures for another hundred years?

units.la: Quid vero adhæc Hieronymus ad Principiam? Frustra profecto, inquit, eius lingua prædicat paupertatem, & docet eleemosynas, qui nisi divitijs tumet, vilius opertu pallio pugnat contra eas vestium sericarum.
units.tr: And what does Jerome add to this, in his letter to Principia? "Surely in vain," he says, "does her tongue preach poverty and teach almsgiving, when she, who swells with riches, fights against the silk garments more cheaply than with an opened cloak."

units.la: Sunt igitur pauperes sine defectu. Et recte Nobilis quidam non procul à Landsperga arcem habens, dixit: Si mendicare vellet, quod cum Iesuitis vellet mendicare. Illos enim non obulum unum vel alterum, sed mille coronatos plerumque una vice à Principibus asportare, ut Hafenmullerus cap. 6. refert.
units.tr: There are therefore paupers without end. And a certain nobleman, who had a castle not far from Landsberg, spoke rightly: if he wished to beg, he would wish to beg with the Jesuits. For they carry off from princes not a single obol or two, but often a thousand crowns at one time, as Hafenmüller reports in chapter 6.

units.la: DE VOTO OBEDIENTIAE IESVITARVM.
units.tr: On the Vow of Obedience of the Jesuits

units.la: Habent quidem Iesuitæ hoc secundum obedientiæ votum cum reliquis Monachis commune. Ignatius autem Loyola hoc voto sectatores suos omnes Monachos & Clericos superare voluit. Sic enim in Epistola ad Lusitaniæ Patres fere scribit: Ab aliis religiosis Ordinibus facilius patiamur superari in jejunijs, vigilijs, & cætera vitæ cultus asperitate, quam suo quique ritu ac disciplina sanctè suscipiunt: vera quidem, ac perfecta obedientia, abdicationeque voluntatis atque iudicij maxime velim esse conspicuos, quicunque in hac Societate Deo deserviunt, eiusque Societatis veram germanamque sobolem hac quasi nota distingui, qui nunquam intueantur personam ipsam, cui obediunt, sed in ea Christum, cuius causa obediunt. Siquidem Superiori nec si prudentia, bonitate, cæterisque quibuslibet donis ornatus, instructusque sit propterea obtemperandum est, sed ob id solum, quod vices gerat Dei: nec contrà sive consilio, aut prudentia minus valeat, quidquam idcirco de Obedientia remittendum, quatenus ille Superior est, quandoquidem illius personam refert, cuius sapientia falli non potest.
units.tr: The Jesuits do indeed have this second vow of obedience in common with the other monks. But Ignatius Loyola wanted his followers to surpass all monks and clergy in this vow. He writes roughly this in his letter to the Fathers in Portugal: "We would more readily suffer ourselves to be outdone by other religious orders in fasting, vigils and the harshness of their way of life than in the way each of them devoutly embraces its own rule and discipline. I would particularly wish that those who serve God in this Society be conspicuous for true and perfect obedience, and for the renunciation of will and judgment, and that the true and genuine offspring of this Society be marked by this sign: that they never look at the person they obey, but see in him Christ, for whose sake they obey. For a Superior is to be obeyed not because he is adorned with prudence, goodness or any other gifts, or is equipped with them, but for this alone: that he stands in the place of God. Nor, on the other hand, should anything be conceded from obedience because the Superior is less able in counsel or prudence, since he represents the person of him whose wisdom cannot be deceived."

units.la: Quocirca sedulo vos in eam curam atque exercitationem incumbere cupio, ut Christum Dominum in Superiore quolibet agnoscere studeatis, in eoque divinæ Majestati reverentiam atque obedientiam summa cum religione præstare.
units.tr: Therefore I wish you to apply yourselves diligently to this care and exercise, so that you strive to recognise Christ the Lord in any Superior whatever, and in him render reverence and obedience to the divine Majesty with the utmost devotion.

units.la: Iam vero illud etiam in animis vestris penitus infidere vehementer cupio, infirmam & valde imperfectam esse primam illam Obedientiæ formam, quæ mandata duntaxat operaque exequitur, nec virtutis nomine dignam, nisi ad alterum gradum ascendat, qui voluntatem Superioris suam efficit, & cum ea ita concordet, ut non solum in effectu executio appareat, verum etiam in affectu consensio sicque idem velit uterque, idem nolit. Quocirca voluntatem vestras, quoad eius fieri potest, omnino deponite, libertatem Conditori vestro, quam vobis ipsemet elargitus est, in eius ministris libere tradite ac dicate.
units.tr: Now indeed I very earnestly wish this also to sink deeply into your minds: that the first form of obedience, which only carries out commands and works and does not deserve the name of virtue unless it rises to the second degree, is weak and very imperfect. That second degree makes the Superior's will its own and agrees with it in such a way that not only the execution appears outwardly but there is also agreement in feeling, so that each wills the same and refuses the same. Therefore, as far as it is possible, lay down your own wills entirely, and freely surrender and dedicate to the ministers of your Creator the liberty which he himself has bestowed upon you.

units.la: Itaque diligenter illud etiam cavendum est, ne Superioris ullo unquam tempore voluntatem ad vestram detorqueri nitamini: id enim esset non vestram divinam conformare, sed divinam vestræ voluntatis normam regere velle, eiusdem divinæ sapientiæ ordinem invertentes. Sane quam magnus est error eorum, quos amor sui obcæcavit, obedientes existimare sese, cum Superiorem ad id, quod ipsimet volunt, aliquâ ratione pertraxerint.
units.tr: Accordingly, care must also be taken, with diligence, that you never strive to bend the Superior's will to your own at any time. For that would not be conforming your will to the divine will, but wanting to rule the divine will by the standard of your own, thereby inverting the order of that same divine wisdom. Indeed, how great is the error of those whom self-love has blinded, who think themselves obedient when they have by some means drawn the Superior to what they themselves wish.

units.la: Qui vero se totum penitus immolare vult Deo, præter voluntatem, Intelligentia quoque qui tertius & summus est gradus Obedientiæ, offerat necesse est, ut non solum idem velit, sed etiam ut idem sentiat, quod Superior, eiusque iudicio subiiciat suum, quoad potest devota voluntas Intelligentiam inflectere.
units.tr: But he who wishes to sacrifice himself wholly and entirely to God must offer, besides the will, also the understanding, which is the third and highest degree of obedience; so that he not only wills the same as the Superior but also thinks the same, and subjects his own judgment to the Superior's, bending his understanding as far as a devoted will can.

units.la: Et paulo post: Tria vobis nominatim propono, quæ ad obedientiæ iudicij comparandum multum ultum juvant. Primum illud est, ut quemadmodum interdixi, non intueamini in persona superioris hominē obnoxium erroribus atque miseriis; sed Christum ipsum, qui est sapientia summa, bonitas immensa, charitas infinita, qui nec decipi potest, nec vult vos ipsos decipere. Et quoniam conscij vobismet estis, vos Dei amore jugum obedientiæ subijisse, ut in Superioris voluntate sequenda, voluntatem divinam sequeremini; nolite dubitare, quin pertut fidelissima Domini charitas, eorum ministerio, quos Deus vobis præfecit, vos deinceps ubernare, & rectis itineribus ducer. Itaque Superioris vocem ac jussa non secus ac Christi vocem excipite, &c.
units.tr: And a little later: "I set before you by name three things which greatly help in acquiring obedience of judgment. The first is that, as I have forbidden, you do not look in the person of the Superior at a man subject to errors and miseries, but at Christ himself, who is supreme wisdom, immense goodness and infinite charity, who can neither be deceived nor wish to deceive you. And since you are conscious that for love of God you have submitted to the yoke of obedience, so that in following the Superior's will you follow the divine will, do not doubt that the most faithful charity of the Lord will guide you and lead you on right paths through the ministry of those whom God has set over you. Therefore receive the Superior's voice and commands no differently than the voice of Christ, etc."

units.la: Item: Altera est ratio, ut quod Superior mandat, defendere semper apud animos veros studiosè nitamini, improbare autem nequaquam: atq; ad eam ipsam rem proderit bene animatos, affectos ad id omne, quod ipse jusserit, &c.
units.tr: Likewise: "The second reason is that you should always strive earnestly to defend in your minds what the Superior commands, and by no means disapprove of it; and to this same end it will help to have minds well disposed and inclined toward everything he has ordered, etc."

units.la: Paulo post: Postrema subijciendi judicij ratio est cum facilior tutiorque, tum etiam apud sanctos Patres in more posita: ut statuatis vobis cum ipsi, quidquid Superior accipit, ipsius Dei præceptum esse & voluntatem; atque ut ad credenda, quæ Catholica des proponit, toto animo assensuque vestro statim incumbitis, sic ad ea facienda, quæcunque Superior dixerit, cæco quodam impetu voluntatis parendi cupida sine ulla prorsus difiditione feramini.
units.tr: A little later: "The last reason for submitting one's judgment is both easier and safer, and is also customary among the holy Fathers: that you should hold within yourselves that whatever the Superior prescribes is the command and will of God himself; and just as you apply yourselves with your whole mind and assent to believing what the Catholic Church proposes, so you should be carried, with a certain blind impulse of a will eager to obey, without any hesitation at all, to doing whatever the Superior has said."

units.la: Et in fine: Hæc, quæ de Obedientia diximus, atque privatis erga proximos Superiores, atque Rectoribus, Præpositisque localibus erga Provinciales; Provincialibus erga Generalem, Generali denique erga illum, quem Deus ipsi præfecit, nempe, suum in terris vicarium) Papam Romanum) &c.
units.tr: And at the end: "These things which we have said about obedience, both toward the local Superiors and Rectors, and the Provosts toward the Provincials, the Provincials toward the General, and finally toward him whom God has set over him, namely (his vicar on earth, the Roman Pope), etc."

units.la: In Summario quoq; Constitutionum Ignatianarum, in quas Iesuitas omnes tenrare oportet, Constitut. 31. sic præcipitur: Expedit imprimis ad perfectam, & valde necessarium est, ut omnes perfectæ obedientiæ se dedant. Superiorem, quicumque fuerit, loco Christi Domini Nostri agnoscentes, & interna reverentia & amore eum prosequentes, nec solum in executione externa eorum, quæ injungit integrè, promptè, fortiter & cum humilitate debita, sine excusationibus & obmurmurationibus obediant, licet difficile sit, & secundum sensualitatem repugnantia jubeat, verùm etiam conentur interius resignationem, & veram abnegationem propriæ voluntatis & judicij habere, voluntatem & judicium suum cum eo, quod Superior vult, & sentit, in omnibus rebus, ubi peccatum non cernetur, omninò conformantes, propositâ sibi voluntate ac judicio Superioris pro regula & voluntatis & judicij, quò exactius conformentur primæ ac summæ regulæ omnis bonæ voluntatis & judicij, quæ est æterna bonitas & sapientia.
units.tr: Also in the Summary of the Ignatian Constitutions, which all Jesuits must observe, Constitution 31 commands as follows: "It is especially fitting, indeed highly necessary for perfect obedience, that all give themselves to perfect obedience, recognising whichever Superior they have in the place of our Lord Christ, and following him with inward reverence and love; and that they obey him not only in the external execution of what he enjoins, wholly, promptly, bravely and with due humility, without excuses or grumbling, even if it is difficult and enjoins things opposed to the senses, but also that they strive inwardly to have resignation and true abnegation of their own will and judgment, conforming their will and judgment wholly to what the Superior wills and thinks, in all matters where no sin is discerned, setting the will and judgment of the Superior before them as the rule of their will and judgment, so that they may be more exactly conformed to the first and highest rule of all good will and judgment, which is eternal goodness and wisdom."

units.la: Et Constitut. 32. Liberam sui ipsorum, rerumque suarum dispositionem omnes cum tota obedientia Superiori relinquant, nihil ei clausum, ne conscientiam quidem propriam tenendo, non repugnando, non contradicendo, nec ulla ratione judicium proprium, ipsius judicio contrarium demonstrando: ut per unionem eiusdem sententiæ, & voluntatis, atq; per perfectam submissionem melius in divino obsequio conferventur & progrediantur.
units.tr: And Constitution 32: "All should leave to the Superior the free disposal of themselves and of their goods, keeping nothing from him, not even their own conscience; not resisting, not contradicting, nor in any way showing their own judgment to be contrary to his, so that by the unity of the same opinion and will, and through perfect submission, they may be better preserved and advance in the divine service."

units.la: 33.
