Omnes obedientiam plurimum observare & in ea excellere studeant; nec solum in iis obligatoriis, sed etiam in aliis; licet nihil aliud quam signum voluntatis Superioris, nulloque expressoque præcepto videretur. Versari autem debet ob oculos Deus creator, ac Dominus noster, propter quem homini obedientia præstatur: & ut in spiritu amoris & non cum perturbatione timoris procedatur, curandum est.
units.tr: Constitution 33: "All should strive to observe obedience most diligently and to excel in it, not only in those things which are obligatory, but also in others, even when it seems nothing other than a sign of the Superior's will and no express command is given. God the creator and our Lord, for whose sake obedience is rendered to man, ought to be kept before the eyes; and care must be taken that one proceeds in a spirit of love and not with the disturbance of fear."

units.la: 34. Ad Superioris vocem perinde, ac si à Christo Domino egrederetur, quam promptissimi simus, re quavis, atq; adeo litera à nobis inchoata, nec dum perfecta relicta.
units.tr: Constitution 34: "We should be most prompt at the voice of the Superior as if it came from Christ the Lord, leaving aside any task begun by us, even a single letter, not yet finished."

units.la: 35. Ad eumscopum vires omnes, ac intentionem in Domino convertamus, ut sancta obedientia, tum in executione, tum in voluntate, tum in intellectu fit vobis semper exnii parte perfecta; cum magna celeritate, spirituali gaudio & perseverantia, quicquid vobis injunctum fuerit, obeundo; omnia justa esse vobis persuadendo; omne sententiam ac judicium vestrum cæcâ quadam obedientia abnegando: & id quidem in omnibus, quæ à Superiore imponuntur; ubi definiri non possit, aliquod peccati genus intercederet. Et sibi quisquè persuadeat, qui sub obedientia vivunt, se ferri ac regiâ divinâ providentiâ; quod ser Superiores suos vivere debent perinde ac si cadaver essent, quod quoquo versus se vergi; & quacunq; ratione tractari se sinit: vel similiter atq; sensus baculus, qui ubicunq;, & quacunq; in re velit eo uti, qui eum in manu tenet, ei inseruit.
units.tr: Constitution 35: "Let us turn all our powers and intention to the same goal in the Lord, so that holy obedience, in execution, in will and in understanding, may always be perfect in every respect for you; obeying with great speed, spiritual joy and perseverance whatever is enjoined upon you; persuading yourselves that all things are just; renouncing your own opinion and judgment by a certain blind obedience; and this in all things which are imposed by the Superior, where no kind of sin could be defined as intervening. And let each who lives under obedience persuade himself that he is carried along and ruled by divine providence through his Superiors, and that he ought to live toward his Superiors as if he were a corpse, which lets itself be turned in any direction and handled in any way; or like an old man's staff, which is put into the hand of whoever holds it, to be used wherever and for whatever purpose he wishes."

units.la: Ex his omnibus intelligit Lector, judicasse quidem Ignatium, imò præcepisse, sic obediendum Superiori, ut inferiores eius mandata ac jussa hilariter, prompte, velociter, libenter & integrè exequantur opere & facto, hanc tamen primam obedientiæ formam imperfectam esse: ideò requirit secundo loco ab inferiore, ut Superioris voluntatem suam faciat, seu potius exuat, & eam quæ à Superiore exposita sit ei, induat. Tertiò vult, ut obedientia suorum subditorum comprehendat non solum executionem, ut imperata quis faciat, & voluntatem, ut libenter id faciat, sed etiam intelligentiam, & judicium, ut quæcunque Superior mandat ac sentit, eadem inferiori & recta, & vera, & iusta & æqua esse videantur. Obedientia ergo, quam Ignatius à suisIesuitis requirit, non solum in externa mandatorum executione, sed etiam in propria voluntatis, judicii & intellectus abnegatione & omnimoda resignatione, cum omni devotione & reverentia, haud aliter quàm si ipsi Christo obedirent, consistit.
units.tr: From all of this the reader understands that Ignatius did judge, indeed did prescribe, that a superior should be obeyed in such a way that inferiors carry out his commands and orders cheerfully, promptly, swiftly, willingly and wholly, in deed and in act. He held, however, that this first form of obedience is imperfect. For that reason he requires in the second place that the inferior make the superior's will his own, or rather strip off his own will and put on the will set before him by the superior. Thirdly, he wills that the obedience of his subjects should embrace not only the execution of what is commanded and the will to do it gladly, but also understanding and judgement, so that whatever the superior commands and thinks may seem to the inferior right, true, just and equitable. The obedience, then, which Ignatius requires of his Jesuits consists not only in the outward execution of commands but also in the renunciation of one's own will, judgement and intellect and in complete surrender, with all devotion and reverence, just as if they were obeying Christ himself.

units.la: Qualem autem in suis obedientiam esse velit Ignatius, atque etiam ab ipsis exigat, Hafenmüllerus ridiculis aliquot exemplis capite sexto declarat, quorum aliqua in Lectoris gratiam adscribam. Si Rector uni dicat, se illum ad mastationem ducturum & immolaturum, ceu agnus sine murmure sequatur, ac ut Isaac non solum ligna, sed etiam, si opus sit, ferrum offerat: Sicuti Bobadilla, qui unus ex primis Ignatij Loyolæ socijs fuit, Romæ ad Hafenmüllerum, in monte di Caballo dixit Anno millesimo quingentesimo octogesimo tertio, 1. Augusti: Si jussu & mandato à Superiori mittitur, voluntate, judicio, & intellectu nutum Rectoris, ceu cæcum manuum, ac tastum ducentis, sequatur. Si duris afficitur pœnitentijs: à patribus reprehenditur; à fratribus contemnitur, & pedibus etiam petitur; imò si omnes in eum exspuent, suamque libidinem, ut Iesuita ait Bonaventura, adimplere in eo conentur, instar cadaveris, sese habeat, ac si plane esset mortuus. Si Superior ipsi ausert omnia quæ habet, eumque omnibus bonis spoliat: vestes ipsi adimit pretiosas, ac loco earum tenuissimas reddit, se ut statua gerat, quæ patitur se in quemvis transferri locum, & quovis habitu indui: Si contemnitur: si reprehenditur: si in locum, qui ipsi non placet, mittitur: si quæ non vult audit: si cibi insipidi & ingrati apponuntur: atq; instar stulti huc illuc trahitur: sit ut statua neq; ullum de se det impatientiæ & indignationis signum.
units.tr: What kind of obedience Ignatius wishes his men to show, and actually demands of them, Hafenmüller sets out in the sixth chapter with some ridiculous examples, some of which I will add for the reader's benefit. If the Rector tells one man that he will lead him to the slaughter and sacrifice him, he should follow like a lamb without complaint, and, like Isaac, offer not only the wood but also, if need be, the knife. So Bobadilla, one of the first companions of Ignatius of Loyola, said at Rome to Hafenmüller on the Monte di Caballo in the year 1583, on 1 August: "If he is sent by the command and order of the superior, he should follow the nod of the Rector with his will, judgement and intellect, like a blind man led by the hand. If he is subjected to harsh penances, he is rebuked by the fathers, despised by the brothers, and even kicked; indeed, if they all spit on him and try to satisfy their lust upon him, as the Jesuit Bonaventura says, he should behave like a corpse, as if he were quite dead." If the superior takes away everything he has and strips him of all his goods, takes from him his costly clothes and gives him in their place the meanest, he should bear himself like a statue, which allows itself to be moved to any place and dressed in any garb. If he is despised, if he is rebuked, if he is sent to a place that does not please him, if he hears things he does not want to hear, if tasteless and unpleasant food is set before him, and he is dragged hither and thither like a fool, he should be like a statue and show no sign of impatience or indignation.

units.la: Apud sanctum Andream in monte di Caballo Romæ, Octavianus Pater Novitio, cum expiarentur, dixit: Vade & in hoc stercore te volyтa, sicque domum perge. Novitius vere Suita se in cœno huc illuc versat, sicque Epicuri de grege porcus domum redit, cunctis eum videntibus risum exhibens. Quem, ut Rector vidit, eum quidastum esset interrogat, & re cognitâ, ait: Vade ad Sartorem, teq; novis vestimentis indui cura. Hoc enim promeruit obedientiæ tuæ virtus.
units.tr: At St Andrew's on the Monte di Caballo in Rome, when the novices were being purified, Octavianus the Father said to a novice: "Go and roll yourself in this dung, and then go home." The novice, a true Jesuit, wallowed here and there in the filth, and so, like the pig from Epicurus' herd, returned home, provoking laughter in all who saw him. When the Rector saw him, he asked what had happened to him, and when he learned the reason, said: "Go to the tailor and see that you are dressed in new clothes. For the virtue of your obedience has earned this."

units.la: Lādspergæ Christoph. Zieglerus Novitio tradit rapas & arbores teneras, s ait: Vade infere eas terræ, radicibus sursum erectis; ramis autem in terræ profundum deмepsis. Frater vadit, sed ut natura postulat, radices terræ, ramos aëri mandat. Huius pœnitentia erat dicere: non quæ Natura, vel strata ratio jubent: sed Superioris mandata executienda sunt: ac in refectorio plantulas ac rapas ter circumportari.
units.tr: At Landsberg, Christoph Ziegler handed a novice some turnips and young trees and said: "Go and plant them in the earth, roots upward and branches down into the depths of the ground." The brother went, but, as nature requires, he gave the roots to the earth and the branches to the air. His penance was to say that what nature or sound reason dictates must not be done, but the commands of the superior must be carried out; and to carry the little plants and turnips around the refectory three times.

units.la: Quidam frater Veronæ laborabat imbecillitate stomachi. Cui Medicus ordinavit, ut Zingiber mane comederet, vesperi vero unguento, quod ei exhibuerat, ventre circa umbilicum inungeret. Minister vero suspicans Fratrē illum stomachi infirmitatem simulare, modo ut jejunij temporibus, carnis eius ipsi concederetur, infirmait: Non Medico, sed mihi vovisti obedientiam. Hoc ergo unguentum comede, & te hozingibere unge, usq; dū sanguis effluxerit. Frater obtemperat. Minister vero eius obedienti-mirum nirum in modum Rectori commendat, qui etiam deinde novitio non solum carnes vitulinas, sed capones & gallinas dandas praecipit.
units.tr: A certain brother at Verona was suffering from weakness of the stomach. The doctor ordered him to eat ginger in the morning, and in the evening to rub into his belly around the navel the ointment he had prescribed. But the minister, suspecting that the brother was pretending the stomach ailment so that meat might be allowed him in the times of fasting, said: "You vowed obedience not to the doctor but to me. So eat this ointment and rub yourself with ginger until the blood flows." The brother obeyed. The minister commended this obedience of his in the highest terms to the Rector, who then also ordered that the novice be given not only veal but capons and hens.

units.la: Vt autem Novitij Iesuitæ rectius, quænam sit illorum obedientia, intelligere possint, iis in musæis & cubilibus ob oculos huiusmodi imagines ponunt. Est in medio picturæ puer, qui dorsum incurvat, quo humeris impositam fert tabem, cui inscriptum est: Fortiter. Portat deinde Cythuram, quâ volunt obedire debere eum hilariter. A dextra illius assurgit catulus: ut obediat velociter. Pectus gerit apertum, ut obediat toto corde, propria voluntate abiecta: vel certè Superiori tota tradita. Os tenet clausum, ut obediat sine murmure. Baiulat res viles & abiectas, ut obediat etiam in rebus sensibus repugnantibus. Pedibus fert ocreas, ut obediat constanter. Ambabus manibus vasa tenet, ut obediat sincere seu integrè. Aures habet obseratas, ut obediat in iis, quæ ipsi auditu jucunda non sunt. Caput inclinat, ut obediat humiliter.
units.tr: So that the Jesuit novices may better understand what their obedience is, they place before their eyes pictures of this kind in their studies and bedrooms. In the middle of the picture is a boy who bends his back, so that he carries on his shoulders a load, on which is written: Fortiter. Then he carries a lyre, by which they wish him to show that he must obey hilariter. Beside his right side a puppy stands up, to show that he should obey velociter. He bears his breast open, so that he may obey toto corde, his own will cast aside, or certainly wholly surrendered to the superior. He keeps his mouth shut, so that he may obey sine murmure. He carries base and worthless things, so that he may obey even in rebus sensibus repugnantibus. With his feet he bears greaves, so that he may obey constanter. With both hands he holds vessels, so that he may obey sincere or integrè. He has his ears closed, so that he may obey in those things quæ ipsi auditu jucunda non sunt. He bows his head, so that he may obey humiliter.

units.la: Si quis autem contra has obedientiæ Iesuiticæ formulas, & conditiones peccat, huic pro qualitate delicti poena iniungitur, quæ ipsis pœnitentia dicitur. Vergratiâ: Minister mandat Novitio, quem putat esse superbum, ut abeat, & locum secretum (refero illorum pœnitentias, uti eas faciunt, mihi igitur venia detur, si quæ minus modesta videntur: Nolo enim Iesuitarum vel verba vel facta mutare, sed res illorum, quales sunt, veré demonstrare) aut caligas decrepitum excrementis repletas, aut matulas, aut etiam alia vasa immunda expurget. Novitius sentiens istas res sensui suo repugnare, se excusat, murmurat, aut etiam operam suam denegat. Huius pœnitentia est coram Fratribus, vel prandij, vel cœnæ tempore suam profiteri culpam. Reverendi Patres, dilecti Fratres (dicit in genua proiectus) dico vobis meam culpam, quod hodie inobediens fui, neque cloacas vel caligas quorundam expurgavi: quare mihi data est pœnitentia: Primum ut in refectorio circumeam, vobisque demonstrem, quomodo me non excusaverim, & rebellem declararim. Tunc horrendum videns, vocéque utens stentoria, pedibus quatiens, ait: Nolo hoc facere: non veni ut cloacas expurgem. Quid ad me Magister? quid aliorum calligæ? expurgent illi, qui cæno as replerunt humano. His dictis in refectorij medio consistit, & secum habet caligas lavandas, usque dum cæteri cibum sumpserint, & tenetur abire & iussa exsequi.
units.tr: If anyone sins against these formulas and conditions of Jesuit obedience, a penance is imposed on him, proportionate to the kind of offence, which they call pœnitentia. For example: the minister orders a novice, whom he thinks proud, to go away and clean out a secret place (I report their penances as they perform them, so let me be pardoned if some seem less than modest; for I do not wish to alter the words or deeds of the Jesuits, but to show truly what their things are like), or to clean out boots filled with excrement, or chamber pots, or other filthy vessels. The novice, feeling that these things go against his senses, makes excuses, grumbles, or even refuses to do the work. His penance is to confess his fault before the brothers at dinner or supper, saying: "Reverend Fathers, dear brothers," on his knees, "I tell you my fault: that today I was disobedient and did not clean out the latrines or the boots of certain men; therefore I have been given a penance. First, that I go round the refectory and show you how I made no excuse and declared myself rebellious." Then, looking dreadful, with a stentorian voice and stamping his feet, he says: "I do not want to do this; I did not come to clean out latrines. What is it to me, Master? What are the boots of others to me? Let those clean them who have filled them with human filth." Having said this, he stands in the middle of the refectory with the boots to be washed in his hands, until the others have taken their food, and he is bound to go away and carry out the orders given.

units.la: De hac Obedientia Iesuitica sic à quodam Iesuita Ordinis desertore scriptum est: Porrò ad perpetuò occultandam, conservandam & augendam superstitionem & idolatriam, bestia hæc catulus suus intellectum, si quem habent, ipsumque sensum ligat, dum nonet & mandat ferio, ut ea, quæ Superior jubet, cum obedientia perficiant, quæque ipse iacit, cæco iudicio pertranseant, non considerantes, an bonum vel utile sit, necne, quod præcipitur; quandoquidem omnis eiusmodi cogitatio meritum tollit & valorem obedientiæ.
units.tr: Of this Jesuit obedience, a certain Jesuit who deserted the Order has written as follows: "Moreover, in order to hide forever, preserve and increase superstition and idolatry, this beast binds the understanding of its puppy, if they have any, and the very sense itself, while it seriously admonishes and orders them to carry out with obedience whatever the superior commands, and to pass through with blind judgement whatever he does, not considering whether what is enjoined is good or useful, since every such thought takes away the merit and worth of obedience."

units.la: Quâ quidem in re Societas Canonistas imitatur pernitiosissimos Pontificis adulatores. Hi enim orbi Christiano quondam persuaserunt, Romanum Pontificem tantæ esse dignitatis & authoritatis, ut, etiamsi ille totum mundum perderet, nemo tamen ex ipso dicolici huius facti vel possit, vel quæ rere rationem deberet. Sic prorsus, imò multò peius, quos Societas alumnos instituit, cùm docet, quæcunque Superior iubet, quæque ipse facit, non solum iudicanda non esse, multò verò minus reprehendenda, sed etiam tamquam bona & sancta, ut Patriarchæ Ignatij verbis utar, præsupponenda: Quo nimirum omnis tandem ultitia, idololatria & superstitio Sanctitatis nomen obtineat.
units.tr: In this matter the Society imitates the most pernicious flatterers of the Pope. For these men once persuaded the Christian world that the Roman Pontiff is of such dignity and authority that, even if he were to destroy the whole world, no one could or should ask him for a reason for this act. Just so, or rather much worse, does the Society train the pupils it educates, when it teaches that whatever the superior commands and whatever he himself does must not only not be judged, much less be censured, but must be presupposed as good and holy, to use the words of the Patriarch Ignatius. Thus, of course, every wickedness, idolatry and superstition may at last obtain the name of holiness.

units.la: Hanc quidem obedientiam voventes promittunt Superioribus suis imprimisque Romano Pontifici: Politico verò Magistratui sibi à Deo ordinato sunt nobedientissimi, ut ex sequentibus manifestum fiet.
units.tr: They promise this obedience by vow to their Superiors, and above all to the Roman Pontiff; but towards the civil magistrate, who is ordained by God, they are most disobedient, as will become clear from what follows.

units.la: Excipit quidem Loyola, in omnibus rebus obediendum Superiori, VBI NON COGNOSCITVR PECCATVM, hoc est, ea, quæ sine peccato commitli possunt.
units.tr: Loyola does indeed make one exception: that in all things one must obey the Superior, WHERE NO SIN IS RECOGNISED, that is, in those things which can be done without sin.

units.la: Novitij, ut obediant doceantur.
units.tr: Novices are taught to obey.

units.la: Poena delinquentium.
units.tr: The punishment of offenders.

units.la: Ex literis cuiusdam de obedientia Iesuitica.
units.tr: From a letter concerning Jesuit obedience.

units.la: Exceptiones Loyolæ de obedientia Iesuitica. mittinequeunt. Si quis autem examinet illius Regulā & scripta perpendat, mox intelliget, Iesuitas nihil aliud, quam vel hypocrisin, vel idololatriam, superstitiones & similia Dei legibus & pietati contraria, praecipere, facere, & aliis, ut similiter faciant auctores, & fautores esse; ac propterea in iis Superiori minime obedire deberent, vel iuxta ipsius Loyolae exceptionem.
units.tr: The exceptions of Loyola concerning Jesuit obedience cannot be sustained. But if anyone examines their rule and weighs their writings, he will soon understand that the Jesuits enjoin, perform, and act as authors and supporters, for others to do likewise, nothing other than hypocrisy or idolatry, superstitions and similar things contrary to the laws of God and to piety; and therefore in such matters they ought in no way to obey their Superior, even according to Loyola's own exception.

units.la: Deinde praecedentia & sequentia hanc exceptionē liquidō ostendunt, cognitionem & probationem mandatorum illis ademptam: dum simpliciter statuunt, quicquid sibi praecipiatur id iustum esse; dumque aperte fatentur, se caecā suā obedientia iudicium suum abnegare, & similes esse vel cadaveri, vel baculo senis, qui ubicunque, & quacunque in re eo uti velit, qui eum in manu tenet, ipsi inseruit. Laelius, ut legitur apud Ciceronē, narrat, C. Blossium Cumanum tanti Tiberium Gracchum fecisse, ut quicquid ille vellet, sibi faciendu putaret, Cumq; Laelius quaereret: etiamne, si te in Capitolium faces ferre vellet? Nunquam, inquit, voluisset id quidem: sed si voluisset, paruissem. Amicitiae Blosianae per quam similis est Iesuitica obedientia. Nam si Pontifex Rom. vel eorum Generalis vel Reges interficere iusserit, morem gerent. Sed ut nefaria vox est Blosii, sic detestabilis haec est parendi servitus, cum externa impietate coniuncta.
units.tr: Furthermore, what goes before and what follows make this exception plain: they deprive the Jesuits of the knowledge and judgement of commands, while they simply lay down that whatever is commanded them is just; and while they openly confess that by their blind obedience they renounce their own judgement, and become like a corpse or the staff of an old man, which the one who holds it in his hand uses wherever and for whatever purpose he wishes. Laelius, as we read in Cicero, relates that Gaius Blossius of Cumae was so devoted to Tiberius Gracchus that he thought he must do whatever he wished; and when Laelius asked him, "Would you even, if he wished you to carry torches to the Capitol?" "He would never have wished that," he said; "but if he had wished it, I would have obeyed." Jesuit obedience is very much like the friendship of Blossius. For if the Roman Pontiff, or their General, or kings, order them to kill, they will comply. But just as the words of Blossius are wicked, so this slavish obedience is detestable, joined as it is with outward impiety.

units.la: Atque hoc modo Iesuitae a Patribus suis stulte persuasi, Caecam obedientiam, sic enim illi vocant, Rom. Pontifici, suisque Praepositis, sancte promittere: hoc est, nullam rationem, quantumvis evidentem, contra id, quod semel animo imbiberunt, admissuros se iurare cogitur: Atque ita clausis oculis & animis obfirmatis contra veritatem, & suo & aliorum maximo malo, luctantur.
units.tr: In this way the Jesuits, foolishly persuaded by their Fathers, solemnly promise to the Roman Pontiff and to their Superiors what they call "blind obedience"; that is, they are compelled to swear that they will admit no reason, however evident, against whatever they have once drunk in with their minds. And so, with eyes closed and minds made obstinate, they struggle against the truth, to their own greatest harm and that of others.

units.la: DE VOTO CONTINENTIAE PERPE- TUAE IESVITARVM.
units.tr: On the Jesuits' Vow of Perpetual Continence

units.la: DE hoc voto Regula 28. sic habet: Quae ad votum castitatis pertinent, interpretatione non indigent, cum constet, quam sit perfecte observanda, nempe enitendo angelicam puritatem imitari, & corporis & mentis nostrae munditia. Ex his patet, non sufficere Loyolae eam esse puritatem, quae in hac vita in hominem cadere potest: sed exigere Angelicam. Requirit igitur maiora viribus humanis & impossibilia suis discipulis imponit.
units.tr: Rule 28 concerning this vow says: "What pertains to the vow of chastity needs no interpretation, since it is clear how perfectly it is to be observed, namely by striving to imitate angelic purity and the cleanness of both body and mind." From this it is plain that Loyola did not think it enough that this purity should be the kind that can befall a human being in this life; he demands angelic purity. He therefore requires things beyond human strength and imposes impossibilities on his disciples.

units.la: Regulam etiam habent Iesuitae, Ne permittant, ut foemina aliqua ipsorum vel domus, vel Collegia ingrediatur. Si autem quaedam ingressa fit Ianitoris incuria, mox pulverem eijciant, ne illius tactu inquinentur. Aliam item: Ut ambulantes per plateas oculos a foeminis avertant. Si qua foemina ad januas illorum pulsset, porta ipsi non aperiatur: sed per cancellos Ianitor eam audiat, & paucis absolvat: non in Collegium illam intromittat: Si autem petat Confessarium, ad templum remittatur, & Confessarius averso vultu & sella ab ipsa diversa, per cancellos confessionem eius excipiat: neque solus ad audiendum eius confessionem descendat, sed a longe stet Socius, qui quidem illos non audire, sed tamen videre possit, Ne quid aliud quam confessionem tractent. Tantae enim sunt puritatis & castitatis, ut etiam in templo publico Iesuita non audit sibi & suae carni confidere, ut solus foeminae confessionem excipiat.
units.tr: The Jesuits also have a rule: that they must not allow any woman to enter their houses or colleges. If a woman has entered through the porter's carelessness, they are to sweep out the dust at once, lest they be defiled by her touch. Another rule reads: "When walking through the streets, they are to turn their eyes away from women. If any woman knocks at their doors, the door is not to be opened to her; the porter is to hear her through the grating and dismiss her briefly, and he is not to admit her into the college. If she asks for a confessor, she is to be sent back to the church, and the confessor, with his face turned away and his chair placed apart from hers, is to receive her confession through the grating. Nor is he to go down alone to hear her confession, but a companion should stand at a distance, who may not hear but can see, so that they treat of nothing other than confession." For so great is their purity and chastity that a Jesuit does not trust himself and his flesh to hear a woman's confession alone, even in a public church.

units.la: Commendant quidem Patres Iesuitarum discipulos suos ob insigne castitatis & continentiae donum: iactantes, habere se iuvenes & adolescentes formā, vultu & robore praestantes, tantae tamen continentiae esse; ut ne igniculum quidem carnis in ipsis per confessionem animadvertere possint: Vocantes etiam suos Angelos terrestres, qui Dei gratia ceu cultro, omnem carnis fomitem praefciderint, ut iuratam facile possint praestare continentiam. Si quis autem Iesuitis larvam hypocriticam detrahat, eos in corde longe aliud sentire, quam e, quam quod verbis loquuntur videbit: contrarium etiam testantur cives & rustici, totúsque adeo mundus, quemadmodum Hasenmüllerus aliquot exemplis capite sexto declarat.
units.tr: The Fathers of the Jesuits indeed commend their disciples for the remarkable gift of chastity and continence. They boast that their young men and adolescents excel in looks, bearing and strength, and yet are of such continence that, through confession, they can notice not even a spark of the flesh in them. They even call them their earthly angels, who, by God's grace, have cut away every fuel of the flesh as with a knife, so that they can easily keep the vow of continence they have sworn. But if anyone strips the Jesuits of their hypocritical mask, he will see that in their hearts they think quite otherwise than they say in words. Citizens and country folk testify to the contrary, and indeed the whole world does, as Hasenmüller shows with several examples in chapter six.

units.la: DE QVARTO IESVITARVM VOTO, QVO SE PONTIFICI ROMANO PECVLIARI- TER MANCIPANT ET OB- STRINGVNT.
units.tr: On the Fourth Vow of the Jesuits, by which they especially bind and oblige themselves to the Roman Pontiff

units.la: Vartum Iesuitarum Votum Professorum est: hoc est, illorum, qui iam in omnibus Iesuitarum institutis probati, perfecti inventi sunt, & Pontificiâ cyclopædiam absolverunt: exindeq; Patres vocantur. Ignatius Loyola enim Generalis illorum factus, primos illos 10. Patres, quos supra nominavimus, atq; adeo tiâ illos sequetes, coegit non solû sese triû simplicium votorû vinculo obligare: sed etiam sese totos corpore & anima, in rebus fidei & morum, speciali-ter Papæ evovere, & eius se servitio sub sui damnatione mancipare, si vel in minimo vel maximo religionis ac fidei articulo, à Pontificis Rom. placitis & decretis deficerent, vel aliud quàm ille sentirent: vel diversum ab eius canonibus statuerent. Vt igitur reliqui Iesuitæ omnes, qui non sunt Professi, ab arbitrio Generalis hærent, ita omnes eorum Professi, ac ipse quoq; Generalis, à Pontificis Romani nutu dependent, iurantq;, se in omnibus ipsi obsequium præstituros, quaecunq; in illos præsumat vel statuat, atq; etiam ad quascunq; fidelium & infidelium terras Papæ ipsos mittere placuisset, eò sine ulla tergiversatione atq; adeo sine ulla nô modò mercede, sed ne viatici quidé petitione ituros: ideoq; etiâ Missionis votû appellatur. Et hoc speciali vel extraordinario voto à reliquis omnibus Monachis & Clericis differunt: qua de causa etiam Papa eos, ceu pupillam oculi sui custodit, ut corpus suum tuetur, alit, nutrit, auget & ditat, nec non extraordinariis privilegiis, liberalissimè donat, magno cum totius Cleri Romani damno ac detrimento. Hi sunt Pontificis Romani molosi & canes venatici, quos robustus ille venator Antichristus, ad indagandos Evangelicos & verè fideles emittit, ut eos capiat, dilaniet ac devoret. Hi sunt, qui instar proditorum & exploratorum totam Germaniam perreptant, ut Germanos sub iugum Pontificium redigant; cùm eo toti sunt, ut Germania in pristinum statum reducatur. Hi sunt, qui Germanorum iuratos hostes in perniciem eorum instigant & incitant: qui manus Pontificum Romanorum ad sanguinem innocentum effundendum armant: quorum aures his clamoribus opplent, Ecclesiam Romanam & Apostolicam semel interituram, nisi Germanorum Principum nomen & ditiones deleantur & exstirpentur: qui prodigiosis medacijs Evangelicos & orthodoxos coram Principibus Pontisicijs prægravant, eos seditionum, rebellionum, conspirationum & aliorum malorum insimulant, & in odium Principum adducunt: à quibus sanguinolentæ conspirationes & coniurationes non tantum contra Germanos, sed contra omnes orthodoxos in cunctis provinciis fabricantur, ut in titulo de doctrina Iesuitarum prolixè indicabitur.
units.tr: The fourth vow of the Jesuits is the vow of the Professed: that is, of those who, having been tested in all the Jesuit institutes and found perfect, have completed their Papist encyclopaedia, and are therefore called Fathers. For Ignatius Loyola, having become their General, compelled those first ten Fathers whom we named above, and those who followed them, not only to bind themselves by the bond of the three simple vows, but also to dedicate themselves wholly, body and soul, in matters of faith and morals, especially to the Pope, and to submit themselves to his service under pain of damnation, if in the smallest or greatest article of religion and faith they should deviate from the decrees and decisions of the Roman Pontiff, or think otherwise than he thinks, or make rules different from his canons. Just as all the other Jesuits who are not Professed cling to the will of the General, so all their Professed, and the General himself, depend on the nod of the Roman Pontiff. They swear that they will render him obedience in all things, whatever he may demand or decree of them, and that wherever the Pope may wish to send them, to any lands of the faithful or the unfaithful, they will go without any hesitation, and without asking for any pay, or even for travelling money. Therefore it is also called the vow of Missions. In this special or extraordinary vow they differ from all the other monks and clergy; for this reason the Pope guards them as the apple of his eye, protects, feeds, nourishes, increases and enriches them, and bestows on them extraordinary privileges with great generosity, to the great loss and detriment of the whole Roman clergy. These are the mastiffs and hunting dogs of the Roman Pontiff, whom that strong hunter, Antichrist, sends out to track down the Evangelicals and the truly faithful, so that he may seize, tear to pieces and devour them. These are the men who, like traitors and spies, creep through the whole of Germany, to bring the Germans under the Papal yoke; they labour entirely to bring Germany back to its former state. These are the men who stir up and incite the sworn enemies of the Germans to their destruction; who arm the hands of the Roman Pontiffs to shed innocent blood; whose ears they fill with these cries: that the Roman and Apostolic Church will perish once and for all unless the name and dominions of the German princes are destroyed and uprooted; who, with monstrous lies, weigh down the Evangelicals and the orthodox before the Papist princes, accuse them of sedition, rebellion, conspiracy and other evils, and bring them into hatred with the princes. From these men bloody plots and conspiracies are fabricated, not only against the Germans but against all the orthodox in every province, as will be shown at length under the title on the doctrine of the Jesuits.

units.la: Formula autem quarti huius voti, quam decem primi huius Societatis Patres cum suo Ignatio Loyola Paulo III. Papæ obtulerunt, quamq; Papa Iulius III. revivit & confirmavit, ita ad verbum habet: Quicunque in Societate nostra, quam ipsi nomine insigniri cupimus, vult sub crucis vexillo Deo militare, & soli Domino atque Romano Pontifici, eius in terris Vicario, servire, post solemne perpetuæ castitatis votum, proponat sibi in animo, se partem esse Societatis, ad hoc potissimum institutæ, ut ad profectum animarum in vita, & doctrina Christiana, ad fidei propagationem, per publicas prædicationes & verbi Dei ministerium, spiritualia exercitia, & charitatis opera, & nominatim per puerorum ac rudium in Christianismo institutionem, ac Christi fidelium in confessionibus audiendis, spiritualem consolationem præcipuè intendat: curetque primò Deum, deinde huius summi instituti rationem, quæ via quædam est ad illum, semper ante oculos habere, & finem hunc sibi à Deo propositum totis viribus assequi. Unusquisque tamen secundum gratiam, sibi à Spiritu Sancto subministratam, ut vocationis suæ proprium gradum; ne quis forte zelo utatur, sed non secundum scientiam. Cuius proprij cuiusque gradus, judicium & officium, discretio ac distributio tota fit in manu Præpositi seu Prælati, per nos eligendi, ut congruus ordo servetur, in omnibus bene instituta communitate necessarius. Qui quidem Præpositus, de consilio Sociorum, constitutiones ad constructionem huius propositi, nostro fini conducentes, in consilio, condendi auctoritatem habeat: maiori suffragiorum parte, semper statuendi jus habente. Consilium vero statuatur esse in rebus quidem gravibus, ac perpetuis, maior pars totius Societatis, quæ à Præposito commodè vocari potuit: In levioribus autem & temporaneis, omnes illi, quos in loco, ubi Præpositus noster residebit, præsentes esse contigerit. Iubendi autem jus totum, penes Præpositum erit.
units.tr: The formula of this fourth vow, which the ten first Fathers of this Society, with their Ignatius Loyola, offered to Pope Paul III, and which Pope Julius III revived and confirmed, reads word for word as follows: Whoever in our Society, which we wish to be named by this name, desires to serve God under the banner of the cross, and to serve the Lord alone and the Roman Pontiff, his Vicar on earth, after the solemn vow of perpetual chastity, let him resolve in his mind that he is a part of the Society, instituted chiefly for this purpose: that he should above all aim at the progress of souls in the Christian life and doctrine, at the propagation of the faith, through public preaching and the ministry of the Word of God, spiritual exercises, works of charity, and especially through the instruction of children and the unlearned in Christianity, and the hearing of confessions of the faithful, giving spiritual consolation. And let him take care to keep always before his eyes, first God, and then the plan of this highest institute, which is a certain way to Him, and to pursue with all his strength the end which God has set before him. Yet each one, according to the grace given him by the Holy Spirit, should observe the proper degree of his calling, lest anyone perhaps use zeal without knowledge. The judgment, office, discernment and distribution of each one's proper degree rests entirely in the hand of the Provost or Prelate, to be chosen by us, so that a fitting order may be kept, which is necessary in every well-ordered community. This Provost, with the counsel of the Fellows, shall have authority to make, in council, constitutions suited to the building up of this purpose and to our end, always holding the right of enacting them by the greater part of the votes. The council, moreover, shall be understood to consist, in weighty and lasting matters, of the greater part of the whole Society, which can conveniently be summoned by the Provost; but in lighter and temporary matters, of all those who happen to be present in the place where our Provost resides. The whole right of command, however, shall rest with the Provost.

units.la: Sciant omnes Socij, & non solum in primis professionis suæ foribus; sed quoad vixerint, quotidie animo volvant: Hanc Societatem universam, & singulos, sub Sanctissimi Domini nostræ Papæ, & aliorum Romanorum Pontificum succedentium eius fideli obedientia Deo militare. Et quamvis Evangelio doceamur, & fide orthodoxa cognoscamus, ac firmiter profiteamur, omnes Christi fideles Romano Pontifici; tanquam capiti, ac IESV CHRISTI Vicario subesse: ad maiorem tamen nostræ Societatis humilitatem, ac persectam uniuscuiusque mortificationem, & voluntatum nostrarum abnegationem, summopere conducere judicavimus, singulos nos, ultra illud commune vinculum Speciali voto astringi: itaut quicunque Modernus alijq; Romani Pontifices, pro tempore existentes, jusserint, ad profectum animarum & fidei propagationem pertinens, & ad quascunque provincias nos mittere voluerit, sine ulla tergiversatione, aut excusatione, illico, quantum in nobis fuerit, exequi teneamur: sive miserit nos ad Turcas, sive ad quoscunque alios infideles, etiam in partibus, quas Indias vocant, existentes; sive ad quoscunque hæreticos, sive schismaticos, seu etiam ad quosvis fideles.
units.tr: Let all the Fellows know, and not only at the threshold of their profession, but as long as they live let them turn it over in their minds every day, that this whole Society, and each of its members, serves God under the faithful obedience of our Most Holy Lord the Pope and of the other Roman Pontiffs who succeed him. And although we are taught by the Gospel, and know by the orthodox faith, and firmly profess, that all the faithful of Christ are subject to the Roman Pontiff as to the head and as to the Vicar of Jesus Christ, nevertheless, for the greater humility of our Society, and for the perfect mortification of each one and the denial of our own wills, we have judged it very helpful that we should be bound, each of us, by a special vow in addition to that common bond, so that whatever the present Pope and the other Roman Pontiffs in their time shall command, pertaining to the progress of souls and the propagation of the faith, and whatever provinces they wish to send us to, we are bound to carry out at once, as far as lies in us, without any hesitation or excuse; whether he sends us to the Turks, or to any other unbelievers, even those in the regions called the Indies; or to any heretics or schismatics; or even to any of the faithful.

units.la: Quamobrem, qui ad nos accessuri sunt, antequam huic oneri humeros supponant; diu multumque meditentur; an tantum pecuniæ spiritualis in bonis habeant; ut turrim hanc juxta consilium Dominicum, possint consummare, hoc est, an Spiritus Sanctus; qui illos impellit, tantum illis gratiæ polliceatur; ut huius vocationis pondus, illo adjuvante, sefeluturos sperent. Et postquam, Domino inspirante; huic IESV CHRISTI militiæ, nomen dederint, diu noctuque succincti lumbos, & ad tam grandis debiti solutionem, prompti esse debebunt. Ne quæ autem possint esse inter nos Missionum ac Provinciarum huiusmodi aut ambitio vel detractatio: profiteantur singuli; se nihil quam directe aut indirecte de huiusmodi missionibus, quidquam cum Romano Pontifice curaturos: sed omnem hanc curam Deo & Pontifici ipsi, tanquam eius Vicario, & Societatis Præposito dimissuros. Quidem Præpositus, sicut cæteri, etiam profiteatur, se nihil de suimetipsius missione, in alterutram partem, nisi de Societatis consilio, cum dicto Pontifice esse curaturum. Voveant singuli se in omnibus, quæ ad regulæ huius nostræ observationem faciunt, obedientes foré Societatis Præposito. Ille autem jubeat ea, quæ ad consecutionem propositi sibi à Deo, & à Societate, finis, cognoverit esse opportuna. In prælatione autem sua, benignitatis ac mansuetudinis, Charitatisque Christi, Petri, Pauliqueque formulæ semper sit memor, & tam ipse, quam consilium ad normam hanc assiduè spectent: & nominatim commendatam habeant institutionem puerorum, ac rudium in Christiana doctrina, decem Præceptorum, atque aliorum similium rudimentorum: quæcunque secundum circumstantias personarum, locorum ac temporum illis congrua videbuntur. Est enim maximè necessarium circa providentiam huius rei, diligenter Præpositum, & consilium invigilare: cum & in proximis ædificium fidei, sine fundamento non possit consurgere; & in nostris periculum fit, ne ut quisque erit. rit Doctior, ita provinciam hanc, tanquam primo aspectu minus speciosam, forsitan detreare, conetur: cum tamen revera nulla sit fructuosior, vel proximis ad aedificationem, vel aliis ad charitatis & humilitatis officia simul exercenda. Subditi vero tum propter inentes Ordinis utilitates, tum propter nunquam satis laudatum humilitatis assiduum exercitium, Praepositο in omnibus ad institutum Societatis pertinentibus parere semper tenentur, & in illo Christum, veluti praesentem agnoscant, & quantum decet, venerentur. Cum autem experti fuerimus, jucundiorem, puriorem & ad proximi aedificationem aptiorem esse vitam, ab omni avaritiae contagione quam remotissimam, & Evangelicae paupertati quam milimam: cumque sciamus, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, servus suis regnum Dei solum inquirentibus, necessaria ad victum & vestitum esse subministraturum, voveant singuli & universi, perpetuam paupertatem, declarantes quod non solum privatim, sed nec etiam communiter possint pro Societatis sustentatione, aut usu, ad bona aliqua stabilia, ut ad proventus seu introitus aliquos, jus aliquod civile acquirere, sed sint contenti usu rerum, sibi donatarum, ad necessaria sibi comparanda, recipere. Possint tamen habere in Universitatibus Collegium, seu Collegia habentia reditus, census seu possessiones, sibus & necessariis studentium applicandas, retenta penes Praepositum & Societatem omnimoda gubernatione, seu Superintendentia, supra dicta Collegia, & praedictos studentes, quoad gubernatoris, seu gubernatorum ac studentium electionem, ac eorundem admissionem, emissionem, receptionem, exclusionem, statutorum ordinationem, circa studentium instructionem, eruditionem, aedificationem ac correctionem, victus vestitusque eis administrandi modum, atque etiam omnimodam gubernationem, regimen & curam. Sic tamen ut neque Studentes, dictis bonis abuti, neque Societas in proprios usus convertere possit, sed studentium necessitati subvenire. Qui quidem, post cognitum in spiritu & literis eorum profectum, & post sufficientem probationem, in Societatem nostram admitti possunt. Socij omnes, quicunque in sacris fuerint, quamvis beneficia Ecclesiastica, aut eorum reditus non habeant: teneantur tamen singuli privatim ac particulariter, & communiter, ad dicendum officium, & secundum Ecclesiae ritum.
units.tr: Therefore, those who are about to come to us, before they put their shoulders to this burden, should meditate long and hard whether they have so much spiritual wealth that they can complete this tower, according to the counsel of the Lord; that is, whether the Holy Spirit, who impels them, promises them such grace that they hope, with his help, not to fail under the weight of this calling. And after they have given their name, by the inspiration of the Lord, to this militia of Jesus Christ, they must be girded about the loins night and day, and be ready to pay so great a debt. Lest there be any ambition or detraction among us concerning such missions and provinces, let each one profess that he will not take any step, directly or indirectly, with the Roman Pontiff concerning such missions, but will leave all this care to God and to the Pontiff himself, as his Vicar, and to the Provost of the Society. Let the Provost himself, like the others, also profess that he will take no care, in either direction, about his own mission, except by the counsel of the Society, with the said Pontiff. Let each one vow that in all things which pertain to the observance of this our rule, he will be obedient to the Provost of the Society. Let him command those things which he shall judge fitting for attaining the purpose set before him by God and by the Society. In his governance, let him always be mindful of the formula of kindness, gentleness and the charity of Christ, Peter and Paul, and let both he and the council always keep this norm in view; and especially let them have commended to them the instruction of children and of the unlearned in Christian doctrine, the Ten Commandments, and other similar rudiments, in whatever ways shall seem fitting according to the circumstances of persons, places and times. For it is most necessary, in providing for this matter, that the Provost and the council watch diligently; since among the neighbours the edifice of faith cannot rise without a foundation, and among our own members there is a danger that each, as he is more learned, may try to disparage this work as seemingly less distinguished at first sight; yet in truth there is no work more fruitful, either for building up our neighbours or for practising charity and humility together. The subjects, moreover, both on account of the manifold advantages of the Order and on account of the ever-to-be-praised constant exercise of humility, are always bound to obey the Provost in all matters pertaining to the institute of the Society, and to recognise and reverence Christ in him as if present, as far as is fitting. Since we have found that life is more pleasant, purer, and better suited to the building up of our neighbour when it is as far as possible free from every contagion of avarice and as close as possible to Evangelical poverty; and since we know that our Lord Jesus Christ will supply the necessities of food and clothing to his servants who seek only the kingdom of God, let each and all vow perpetual poverty, declaring that they may not acquire, either privately or in common, for the support or use of the Society, any civil right to stable goods, or to any incomes or revenues, but that they will be content with the use of things given to them, receiving them for procuring what is necessary for themselves. They may, however, have in the Universities a College, or Colleges, possessing revenues, rents or possessions to be applied to the food and needs of the students, the Provost and the Society retaining complete government and superintendence over the said Colleges and the said students, as to the choice of the governor or governors and of the students, their admission, dismissal, reception, exclusion, the ordering of statutes, the instruction, education, and formation and correction of the students, the manner of providing them with food and clothing, and also all manner of government, direction and care. Yet in such a way that the students may not abuse the said goods, nor the Society be able to turn them to its own uses, but only to relieve the needs of the students. These students, indeed, after their progress in spirit and letters has been recognised, and after sufficient testing, may be admitted into our Society. All the Fellows who are in holy orders, although they may not hold ecclesiastical benefices or their revenues, are nevertheless each bound, privately and individually, and together, to recite the office according to the rite of the Church.

units.la: Haec sunt, quae sub praefati Domini nostri Pauli, & Sedis Apostolicae beneplacito de nostra professione, typo quodam explicare potuimus. Quod nunc fecimus, ut summatim sumptione hac informaremus tum illos, qui nos de nostro vitae instituto interrogant: tum etiam posteros nostros, si quos, Deo volente, imitatores unquam habebimus huius vitae. Quam cum multas magnasque habere difficultates fuerimus experti, opportunum judicavimus etiam statuere, ne quis in hac Societate recipiatur, nisi diu ac diligentissime fuerit probatus cum prudens in Christo, & vel doctrina, seu vitae Christianae puritate apparuerit conspicuus: tunc demum admittatur ad Iesu Christi militiam, qui tenuibus coeptis nostris favere dignetur, ad gloriam Dei Patris, cui soli semper decus & honor in secula. Amen.
units.tr: These are the things which, under the approval of the aforesaid lord Paul and of the Apostolic See, we have been able to set forth in outline concerning our profession. We have now done this so that, by this brief account, we might inform both those who question us about our way of life, and also our descendants, should God will that we ever have imitators of this life. Since we have found it to have many and great difficulties, we have judged it expedient also to lay down that no one is to be received into this Society unless he has been tested for a long time and most diligently, and has appeared conspicuous, prudent in Christ, and eminent either in learning or in the purity of his Christian life. Only then is he to be admitted to the warfare of Jesus Christ, who may deign to favour our humble beginnings, to the glory of God the Father, to whom alone be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: Hanc formulam, ceu pium, sanctum ac spiritualem profectum, Apostolica auctoritate, ex certa scientia approbavit, confirmavit & benedixit, ac perpetuae firmitatis munimine roboravit: ac sub sanctae Sedis Apostolicae protectione suscepit Paulus Tertius Anno Domini 1540. Quinto Calend. Octob. Pontificatus sui anno sexto.
units.tr: This formula, as a pious, holy and spiritual undertaking, was approved, confirmed and blessed by Apostolic authority, from certain knowledge, and strengthened with the bulwark of perpetual firmness; and it was taken under the protection of the holy Apostolic See by Paul the Third, in the year of the Lord 1540, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth year of his pontificate.

units.la: Iesuitae igitur hac in parte non dissimiles sunt L. Flacco: ut enim, Cicerone teste, legem ille iniquissimam de Sulla tulit, ut omnia quaecunque ille fecisset & dixisset, rata essent: sic Iesuitae nulla pietatis, nulla aequitatis, nulla iuris ratione habita, id & approbandum & exequendum esse ducunt, quod a Pontifice Rom. vel a Generali suo mandatum & iniunctum ipsis fuerit. At vero se homini alicui, praesertim Antichristo, sic obligare, ut omnia eius iussa accuratius observes, quam ipsius Dei mandata, & quidem ita, ut te comparet quasi corpus mortuum, sic enim loquuntur Iesuitae, aut nervis alienis mobile lignum, id partim superstitiosi est hominis, partim trunci & stipitis.
units.tr: In this respect, therefore, the Jesuits are not unlike Lucius Flaccus: for, as Cicero bears witness, he proposed a most unjust law concerning Sulla, that everything he had done or said should be valid. So the Jesuits, with no regard for piety, equity or the reason of law, think that whatever has been commanded and enjoined upon them by the Roman Pontiff or by their General must be both approved and carried out. But to bind oneself to any man, especially to Antichrist, so that one obeys his orders more carefully than God's own commands, and indeed so that one makes oneself like a dead body (for so the Jesuits speak), or a wooden thing moved by another's strings, this belongs partly to a superstitious man and partly to a block and a stump.

units.la: CAPVT IX. NOTAE ET ANIMADVER- SIONES AD REGVLAS IE- SVITICAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. NOTES AND REMARKS ON THE JESUIT RULES.

units.la: HAS autem suas Regulas & Constitutiones Ignatij Loyolæ Hispani militis Dei verbo & Christi Evangelio longissime præferunt. Si quis enim in legem Dei peccat, vel concionesΩ sacras negligit, nihil is delinquere videtur Iesuitis, aut peccatum eius veniale est: sin vero peccat in Iesuitarum Regulas, hic ex illorum sententia mortale crimen committit. Hinc Iesuita Sacerdos, inquit Hasenmullerus, pag. 115. nomine Henricus, alumnorum Scholasticorum Principis Bavariæ in Albertino contubernio Ingolstadij, Regens & Oeconomus, Anno 1584. in septimana sancta, quæ ultima dicitur jejunij, die Veneris suis discipulis dixit: Per hoc sacrum jejunij tempus libenter audivistis historiam Passionis Christi ex quatuor Evangelistis: fecistis multas pænitentias, vigilijs, jejunijs, orationibus, peregrinationibus, cilicijs, ferulis & flagellis, quibus vos Christo conformastis, eius passionem adimpleveritis, & propectatis vestris satisfecistis: sed dico vobis, nihil ista omnia vobis proderunt, si non juxta præscriptum nostri Superioris cras omnes & singuli peccata vestra confessi fueritis, & Sacramentum more Catholico sub una specie sumpseritis. Quia hæc sancta mandat Ecclesia Romana, quam in omnibus audire debemus. Libenter audire concliones multas, & libenter ac sæpius legere sacram Scripturam, id profecto non est signum boni Catholici, sed potius hæretici, qui sei istis rebus, ceu simianuce delectant. Verus autem Catholicus non multum delectatur concionibus, quæ cito ceu ventus transeunt, neque lectione capitur Scripturæ, si quidem ea mortua est litera, quam non intelligit: sed unica eius voluptas est multas audire Missas & sæpius conspiceri. Hæc qui negligit & contemnit, gravius peccat, quam qui in omni vita sua nullam unquam concionem audivit, nec Biblia vidit. Cum autem exhortationem finivisset, eumque (mihi enim inquit Hasenmullerus familiariter notus erat) interrogassem, unde ista probaret: Respondit breviter: Audi, inquit, sancta mater Ecclesia Romana sic statuit, cui si non simpliciter obedieris, bonus Catholicus non eris. Addidit præterea, Ecclesia Romana, non verbum, verbum, aut Scripturam Scripturam, ut vos facitis Lutherani hæretici, sed Missam & Confessionem inculcat. Hanc ergo audiamus: quia hæc est magistra: est viva Dei litera: ipsa Lex: illa autem est litera mortua, nihil contra Ecclesiæ Romanæ authoritatem decernens, ut nec filia contra matrem, nec servus vel discipulus contra dominum & magistrum suum.
units.tr: The Jesuits place these Rules and Constitutions of Ignatius Loyola, the Spanish soldier, far above the Word of God and the Gospel of Christ. For if anyone sins against the law of God or neglects the sacred sermons, the Jesuits seem to think he has done no wrong, or that his sin is venial; but if he sins against the Jesuit Rules, he commits, by their judgment, a mortal crime. Hence the Jesuit priest Henricus, by name, Regent and Steward of the students at the Albertine college at Ingolstadt, the Prince of Bavaria's scholars' seminary, in the year 1584, in Holy Week, which is called the last week of the fast, on Friday said to his pupils, as Hasenmüller reports on page 115: "During this holy time of fasting you have gladly heard the history of Christ's Passion from the four Evangelists. You have done many penances, vigils, fasts, prayers, pilgrimages, hair shirts, rods and scourges, by which you have conformed yourselves to Christ, fulfilled his passion, and satisfied for your sins. But I tell you, all these things will profit you nothing unless, tomorrow, all and each of you confess your sins according to the directions of our Superior and receive the sacrament in the Catholic manner, under one kind. For the Roman Church, which we must obey in all things, commands these holy things. To listen gladly to many sermons, and to read Holy Scripture gladly and often, is certainly not a sign of a good Catholic but rather of a heretic, who delight in these things as monkeys do in nuts. The true Catholic does not take much delight in sermons, which pass away quickly like the wind, nor is he captivated by reading Scripture, since it is a dead letter which he does not understand; his only pleasure is to hear many Masses and to be seen there often. Whoever neglects and despises these things sins more gravely than one who in all his life has never heard a sermon nor seen a Bible." When he had finished this exhortation, I asked him (for Hasenmüller was well known to me) on what authority he based these claims. He answered briefly: "Listen: holy mother the Roman Church has so decided, and if you do not obey her without qualification, you will not be a good Catholic." He added moreover: "The Roman Church does not press upon us the word, word, or the Scripture, scripture, as you Lutheran heretics do, but the Mass and Confession. Let us therefore hear her, for she is the teacher; she is the living letter of God, the very law. But the Scripture is a dead letter, deciding nothing against the authority of the Roman Church, just as a daughter may not act against her mother, nor a servant or pupil against his master and teacher."

units.la: Interea quoque, quæ in Regulis Iesuiticis notanda occurrunt, duo videntur esse non contemnenda: Prius est de religionis, seu potius superstitionis suæ propagatione: Alterum institutiuti sui spectat oeconomiam, seu administrationis ordinem, utrumque ad certi cuiusdam & latentis instituti, cuius in his Regulis sæpissime mentionem faciunt, promotionem tendere, omnes, qui scripta illorum cum operibus conferent, facile intelligent.
units.tr: Meanwhile, two matters that call for notice in the Jesuit Rules seem not to be negligible: the first concerns the propagation of their religion, or rather superstition; the second concerns the economy of their institute, or the order of its administration. Both tend toward the advancement of a certain hidden purpose, which these Rules mention very often; anyone who compares their writings with their deeds will readily understand this.

units.la: Verum ne quis ea, quæ in illis Regulis proponuntur, tanquam levia, aut non talis momenti esse temere iudicet, ut ijsdem refutandis & debellandis plurium animos & operas, ijs occupare necesse sit, tantum hoc ab eodem expetitur, ut potestatem, quam illi in potentissimos orbis terrarum Reges, Principes & Respub. artibus hisce usurpärunt, aspiciat, & in domos professas, Collegia, domos probationum, seminaria & residentias, Oratoria (quæ non templa, sed regiæ sunt, sirpeljectilibus aureis, argenteis, sericis aliisque supra fastum Babylonicum ornamentis dicata, maximisque reddititibus dotata, oculos intendat: confestim videbit, illorum dit, illorum zelū non ullius Regis aut Principis territorio circumscribi, sed eos ordini suo universum orbis globum ad occupandum, & libidini subiugandum, non ad veritatem propagandam proposuisse, itaque sub Titul. primo in Summario Constitutionum, versiculo 3. ita scribitur: Nostrae vocationis est diversa loca peragrare & vitam agere in quavis mundi plaga, ubi majus Dei obsequium & animarum auxilium sperat ur. Sic enim sonus eorum Romā exivit in universum mundum, per totam Italiam, Siciliam, Sardiniam, Hispaniam, Africam, Indiam, Orientalem, Occidentalem, in Praesiliam Mexicanam, in ipsas insulas, in Galliam, in Belgium, Germaniam superiorem & inferiorem, Austriam, Poloniam aliasque quaevis regiones citra ullum Territorium aut iurisdictionum respectum, etiam in coelum more Gigantum manus impuras extensuri, nisi gladio oris sui altissimus illos decurtaret. Quod non iniuria se facere ducunt, cum Generalem suum loco Christi, qui sine ulla termini praefinitione in coelis & in terra Dominus est, obedientia caeca colendum & honorandum esse statuant. Adeo ut etiam liberos invitis parentibus plagiarii illi abducant, ad quod cum blasphemia impuri illi Christi doctrina abutuntur, ut videre est d. tit. verf. 88, ubi notanda & examinanda est illa quaestio cum improbos illos ambitio & avaritia usque ad extremos orbis fines pro superstitione, imo tyrannide Romana propaganda impellant; Quid veris Christianis incumbat ad Regnum Dei per universum mundum propagandum & an ulla terminorum circumscriptio illos ab officio charitatis Christianae impedire debeat: Item an seminaria pietatis, apud vicinos propagandae fidei, & fatis diligenter ab orthodoxis excultā, item annon horum defectus non solū conservationi, sed & propagationi Regni Christi, id est, verae pietati & unioni Christianae, item annon horum vigilantia & prudentia quorundam Evangelicorum negligentiae & officiantiae merito exprobari posit.
units.tr: But lest anyone rashly judge that the things proposed in those Rules are trivial, or of no such importance that it is necessary for many minds and labours to be occupied in refuting and overthrowing them, let him look at this one thing: the power which they have seized by these arts over the most powerful kings, princes and commonwealths of the world; let him look at their professed houses, colleges, houses of probation, seminaries and residences, and their oratories (which are not churches but royal palaces, dedicated with silken hangings, gold and silver ornaments and other finery beyond Babylonian pomp, and endowed with very great revenues). He will at once see that their zeal is not confined within the territory of any king or prince, but that they have proposed to their order the whole globe of the earth to be occupied and subjected to their lust, not to the propagation of truth. Thus under title one of the Summary of the Constitutions, verse 3, it is written: "It is our calling to roam through diverse places and to live in whatever part of the world where greater service to God and help for souls may be hoped for." For in this way their sound went forth from Rome into the whole world: through all Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Spain, Africa, East India, West India, New Spain, the islands themselves, France, Belgium, Upper and Lower Germany, Austria, Poland, and other regions of every kind, without any regard for territory or jurisdiction; they would even stretch out their impure hands to heaven, like giants, unless the Most High cut them short with the sword of his mouth. They do not think they do wrong in this, since they hold that their General must be obeyed and honoured with blind obedience in the place of Christ, who is Lord in heaven and on earth without any fixed limit. So much so that these kidnappers even carry off children against the will of their parents; and in this matter those impure men abuse the doctrine of Christ with blasphemy, as may be seen in the same title, verse 88. Here must be noted and examined that question: how far ambition and avarice have driven those wicked men to propagate their superstition, indeed Roman tyranny, to the furthest ends of the earth; what is incumbent on true Christians for propagating the kingdom of God throughout the world; and whether any boundary of territories ought to hinder them from the duty of Christian charity. Likewise: whether seminaries of piety among neighbouring peoples for the propagation of the faith, cultivated with sufficient diligence by the orthodox, are of use; likewise, whether the defects of these do not only harm the preservation but also the propagation of the kingdom of Christ, that is, of true piety and Christian unity; and whether the vigilance and prudence of these men may not rightly be cast in the teeth of certain Evangelicals for their negligence and sloth.

units.la: Secundo inter alios, versiculus 3 i. cum quibusdam sequentibus de obedientia diligenter examinandus esse videtur, quia in illis Iesuitae, ut fidissimi Antichristi ministri, se supra Deum, eiusque verbum & ipsam denique aequitatem naturalem extollunt, statuentes quemcunque Superiorem Christi loco agnoscendum & reverendum esse, & voluntatem ac iudicium furum, cum eo quod Superior vult & sentit in omnibus, ubi peccatum non cernitur omnino confortmandum, &c. non repugnando, non contradicendo, nec ulla ratione iudicium proprium ipsius iudicio contrarium demonstrando, sed sinere se debere per Superiores suos ac si cadaver essent, baculūsque senis, ita se illorum nutu & voluntate regi.
units.tr: Second, among the others, verse 31 with some of the following verses concerning obedience seems to require careful examination. In these the Jesuits, as the most faithful ministers of Antichrist, exalt themselves above God, his Word, and finally natural equity itself, laying down that whatever Superior is to be acknowledged and revered in the place of Christ, and that one's own will and judgment must be conformed to the will and judgment of the Superior in all things where no sin is evident at all, and so on; that one must not resist, nor contradict, nor by any reason demonstrate one's own judgment to be contrary to his, but must allow himself to be governed by his Superiors as if he were a corpse, or like an old man's staff, moved at their nod and will.

units.la: In quo primum observandum est, & si in ibi verbis quemcunque superiorem, &c. utatur, non ideo eos loqui de Christiana & legitima obedientia Regibus & Principibus, qui Vicarii Christi in hoc mundo sunt a subditis debita: sed de ea, quam per suos sectarios suis Superioribus praestandam esse volunt, eum supra Deum, supra Reges & Principes extollendo, imo eosdem, licet unctos Dei, pedibus calcando iugulum eorum, si usus sectae suae requirat, perfectae suae obedientiae ministros & discipulos praescindendo. Praecepta scelerati hominis, aeternis divinae & incorruptibilis sapientiae mandatis praeferendo, sic ut his repugnantes, dummodo illis pareant, pro perfectae obedientiae filiis habeant, qui veri Dei mandatis obediunt, & humanis traditionibus repugnant, eos pro rebellibus & seditiosis prosciscunt, imo ipsos Reges & Principes ob non servata superioris sui mandata, Regnis, Principatibus & subditis, ipso iure excidisse, subditos ab omni obedientia respecta legitimorum suorum magistratuum solutos esse.
units.tr: In this, first, it must be observed that although they use the words "whatever Superior," and so on, they are not thereby speaking of the Christian and lawful obedience owed by subjects to kings and princes, who are the Vicars of Christ in this world. They mean rather that obedience which they wish to be rendered by their followers to their own Superiors, exalting these above God and above kings and princes; indeed trampling on the kings and princes themselves, though anointed of God, under foot and cutting their throats, if the practice of their sect requires it, and casting off those who are ministers and disciples of their perfect obedience. They prefer the precepts of a wicked man to the eternal commands of divine and incorruptible wisdom, so that those who oppose these, provided they obey the Jesuits, they count as sons of perfect obedience; while those who obey the commands of the true God and oppose human traditions they proclaim as rebels and seditious men. Indeed, they declare that kings and princes themselves, because they have not kept the commands of their Superior, have by law forfeited their realms, principalities and subjects, and that subjects are released from all obedience to their lawful magistrates.

units.la: An non hanc obedientiam, perfectam scilicet, Regibus liberis (si enim qui oculo abominationum inebriati sunt difficile haec intelligunt) aliter, quam hactenus fuit, suisque coloribus depingendam & commendandam esse sanae doctrinae. næ sectatores iudicaverint, exemplis perfectæ illius Iesuiticæ obedientiæ in lu-
units.tr: Ought not this obedience, namely the perfect kind, to be depicted and commended to free kings in a different way from hitherto, and with its own colours, by the sound teaching of the wise? (For those who are drunk with the cup of abominations find these things hard to understand.) Let the examples of that perfect Jesuit obedience be brought to light, so that the disgrace of that great harlot becomes known to all, and that son of perdition is at last destroyed by the help and counsel of all, according to the command of God's zealots.

units.la: cem prolatis, ut scorti illius magni probrum omnibus innotescat, & filius ille perditionis tandem omnium ope & consilio destruatur, secundum Dei zelotis mandatum.
units.tr: ...to light, so that the shame of that great harlot becomes known to all, and that son of perdition is at last destroyed by the help and counsel of everyone, according to the command of God's zealots.

units.la: In cap.I. quo Regulæ communes traduntur, verf.30. observatione dignum est, quo præcipitur, ut aliæ de aliis nationibus bene sentiant, & nemo bella vel contentiones inter Christianos Principes in colloquium inducat; hic Iesuitarum qui præcipuæ omnium factionum, seditionum, bellorum, rebellionúmq; & scelerum faces sunt, artes & machinationes ab omnibus veritatis amatoribus sublægendæ, communicandæ & velut in tabella exhibendæ, ut Reges & Principes sibi ab illa Leonum Romanensium colluvie queant ocius & priusquam cum illis pereant, vigilantius caveant.
units.tr: In chapter I, where the common rules are set out, verse 30 deserves notice. It orders that people think well of other nations, and that no one bring wars or quarrels among Christian princes into conversation. Yet the Jesuits, who are the chief torches of all factions, seditions, wars, rebellions and crimes, must have their arts and machinations exposed by all lovers of truth, passed on and displayed as on a placard, so that kings and princes may learn to beware of that brood of Roman lions more quickly and more watchfully, before they perish along with them.

units.la: Monopoliorum Iesuiticorum industria cap.4. de Admittendis verf.33. ostenditur, quibus perfectius delineandis, non inutile videtur posse impendi studium.
units.tr: The industry of the Jesuit monopolies is shown in chapter 4, on admitting (candidates), verse 33. It seems that some effort might not be useless in describing these more fully.

units.la: Cum verba sint notæ rerum, neque hæ sine illis recte intelligi possint, semper ab omnibus commendatum fuit, ut qui res perfecte cognoscere vellent, verborum proprietatibus prius operam darent, Iesuitæ more suo in cap.8. literarum studiis verf.51. non ante Hebraicæ linguæ studium iuventuti permittunt, quam cum in Theologiæ facultate mediocriter eruditi sint, ut nimirum adversus veritatis salutarem cognitionem quæ per exactam linguæ sanctæ scientiam ex verbo Dei perfecte hauriri potest, sophisticæ Theologiæ antidoto prius præmuniri possint. Ita veritatis simplicem viam cavillationibus suis obstruunt.
units.tr: Since words are the signs of things, and things cannot be rightly understood without them, it has always been recommended by everyone that those who wish to know things thoroughly should first attend to the proper meanings of words. The Jesuits, in their usual way, in chapter 8 on literary studies, verse 51, do not allow young men to study Hebrew until they are moderately learned in theology, so that they may first be fortified against the saving knowledge of truth (which can be drawn perfectly from the Word of God through an exact knowledge of the holy tongue) by the antidote of sophistical theology. In this way they block the simple path of truth with their cavils.

units.la: Quæ ipsorum prævaricatio clarius ostenditur ex versu sequente, ubi summi Philosophi scripta commentariis orthodoxorum illustrata, non aliter a sophistis suis legi volunt, nisi quatenus Theologiæ scholasticæ subservire possint.
units.tr: Their prevarication is shown more clearly in the following verse, where they want the writings of the greatest philosophers, illustrated by the commentaries of the orthodox, to be read by their sophists only insofar as they can serve scholastic theology.

units.la: Quod 54. versu eodem capite traditur, notatu & observatione dignissimum esse videtur, ad unionem (quâ res parvæ crescunt) inter Socios conservandam, videlicet, ut ingeniorum licentia in opinionibus novis, vel introducendis vel sectandis, omnibus modis certa aliqua lege coerceatur, hac enim facile veritas & Reipublicæ tranquillitas perturbantur, & intervertuntur. Quod si eadem opera Theologiæ Scholasticæ Professoribus præcepissent, ut veritatem utriusque Testamenti omnibus novis opinionibus, quibus pseudo Christiani illam infecerunt, diligenti veritatis perscrutatione, repurgarent, syncerius illi agerent.
units.tr: What is laid down in verse 54 of the same chapter seems most worthy of notice and observation. To keep unity among the members (by which small things grow), namely that the licence of minds in introducing or pursuing new opinions be restrained in every way by some fixed rule, is ordered. For by this means truth and the tranquillity of the commonwealth are easily disturbed and overturned. But if at the same time they had instructed the professors of scholastic theology to cleanse the truth of both Testaments of all the new opinions with which pseudo-Christians have infected it, by a diligent search for the truth, they would have acted more sincerely.

units.la: Versiculo sequente 56. præcipitur ut diligens adhibeatur cura ne desint operarij, qui confessionibus audiendis sint idonei, utq; ad id casibus conscientiæ operam dent, haud dubie in eum finem ut conscientiarum tortores eo crudelius piorum mentes excruciare & ad varia pœnitentiarum genera carnifices adigere possint, hic confessionum Iesuiticarum artes & fines detegendi.
units.tr: In the next verse, 56, it is ordered that diligent care be taken that there be no lack of workers suited to hearing confessions, and that they devote effort to cases of conscience. Doubtless the purpose is that these torturers of consciences may torment the minds of the pious all the more cruelly and drive their executioners to various kinds of penances. Here the arts and aims of Jesuit confessions are to be exposed.

units.la: Inter alia & id notari potest, quod capite 1. verf. 8. de officio Rectoris traditur, quod etsi severissimæ sint leges obedientiæ, non tamen Rectorem, authoritate sibi ad eam tuendam concessa ubiq; & semper uti debere, quod appellant in virtute obedientiæ iubere, ne scilicet non obediendo authoritas vilescat: Nec Romani quoque nisi ex gravissima causa imperio utendum esse censebant, utilius esse rati, ut res agantur authoritate suadendi magis, quam iubendi potestate.
units.tr: Among other things it may be noted that chapter 1, verse 8, on the office of the Rector, lays down that although the laws of obedience are most severe, the Rector should not use the authority granted him to uphold them everywhere and always, which they call "ordering in the virtue of obedience," lest authority become cheap through disobedience. Nor did the Romans themselves think that power should be used except for a very serious cause, judging it more useful that things be done by the authority of persuasion rather than by the power of command.

units.la: Quod conscientiæ rationem a suis Rectorem exigere volunt, cap.3. verf.22. Tit. Regulæ Rectoris, eo iniustius videtur, quod Deus ipse sibi [illegible, ~8 letters] reservavit, ita in cœleste regnum involantes, non contenti terreno; sicuti & id absurdissimum videtur, quod eodem cap. verf.26. cum sequentibus de pœnitentiarum generibus additur. Quid autem rationem conscientiæ reddere appellitent, icent, id in instructione ad reddendam conscientiæ rationem iuxta morem Societatis docetur, his verbis: Totam, inquit, animam suam integrè manifestam faciat nullam rem celando, quæ Dominum universorum offenderit.
units.tr: That they want the Rector to demand an account of conscience from his subjects (chapter 3, verse 22, the title "Rules of the Rector") seems the more unjust, since God himself has reserved this to himself. Thus they fly into the heavenly kingdom, not content with the earthly. Likewise what is added in the same chapter, verse 26, with the following verses, on kinds of penances, seems most absurd. What they mean by "rendering an account of conscience" is taught in the instruction on rendering an account of conscience according to the custom of the Society, in these words: Let him, he says, make his whole soul fully manifest, concealing nothing which has offended the Lord of all.

units.la: Arcani sui tegendi & alieni revelandi ratio ostenditur versu trigesimo quin- to eiusdem capit. ubi literas in Collegio ad exteros vel ab exteris ad Collegiaos scriptas, diligenter Rectori legendas committit, quo etiam referenda reula tertia Ianitoris, quâ præcipitur, ut literæ omnes & schedulæ, quæ domestis mittuntur, Superiori tradantur, ita ut nei ad quos mittuntur, intelligant eas se acceptas.
units.tr: The method of hiding their own secrets and revealing those of others is shown in verse 35 of the same chapter, where he commits to the Rector, to be read carefully, the letters written in the college to outsiders, or from outsiders to members of the college. To this also refers the third rule of the porter, which orders that all letters and notes sent to members of the household be handed to the superior, so that those to whom they are sent know that they have been received.

units.la: Improbum atq; impudentiæ plenum est, quod in opinionum diver sitatibus, theologiæ Professores ad constitutiones suas, nō autem ad sacras literas remitunt: unde etiam ex duobus alterum verum esse necesse est, ut nimirum sacras lieras nō habeant pro norma veritatis, vel institutum suum non ad Regnum Dei, ed Antichristi Tyrannidem promovendam tendat.
units.tr: It is shameless and full of impudence that, in differences of opinion, the professors of theology refer us to their constitutions, and not to the sacred letters. Hence of two things one must be true: either they do not hold the sacred letters as the norm of truth, or their institute does not aim at advancing the kingdom of God but the tyranny of Antichrist.

units.la: Mirum est quod capit. 6. eiusdem tituli vers. 64. præcipitur, de deposito pecuniæ nullo recipiendo, nisi forte nimis sibi durum fore putent, reddere quod mel acceperint.
units.tr: It is strange that chapter 6 of the same title, verse 64, orders that no deposit of money be received, unless perhaps they think it too hard for themselves to return what they have received.

units.la: In examine recipiendorum, quod de quinque impedimentis essentialibus ribitur, nimirum quod inprimis ita sint interrogandi, ut ea impedimenta se quæ à Societate excludunt, qui recipi se volunt, non intelligant, ne veum occultandi occasionem accipiant, in eo certè illorum ingeniị dexteritas manifestatur.
units.tr: In the examination of candidates, what is said about the five essential impediments, namely that they are first to be questioned in such a way that those who wish to be received do not understand the impediments which exclude them from the Society, so that they do not get an opportunity of concealing them, certainly shows the dexterity of their minds.
