units.tr: In 1576, on 16 February, Pope Gregory also granted the Jesuits the faculty to practise medicine and surgery, with the exception of cauterising. He ordered that no physician or surgeon should hinder them. The greed of the Jesuits extorted this privilege, so that they would not be forced either to pay the usual fees to ordinary physicians when they themselves were ill, or rather, so that they would not have to reveal their shameful diseases to other people. For this reason they keep their own physicians, barbers and apothecaries, so that they can make a profit everywhere and in every business.

units.la: Eodem Anno Julij die 16. eximit Iesuitas necessitate interessendi processioibus & funeratis assoeiationibus. Et tamen Iesuitarum est animadvertere tam a clerum, quàm in plebem, ut rite & more Romano recte, devote, reverenter, rnate & decenter omnia peragantur: secus facientes Episcopis produnt, qui inde pro sua, ut loquuntur, taxa, eos puniunt. Datum est autem hoc eis privilegium, non propterea solum, ne a concionibus, lectionibus & confessionius avocarentur, sed inprimis ne in processionibus postremos eos esse oporret ob nuperum suum ortum & originem. Indultum vero hoc est ipsis contra Tridentinum Concilium, quod Seff. 25. cap. 17. decrevit, ut tam Clerici seculaes, quàm regulares, quicunque etiam Monachi ad Processiones publicas vocati accedere compellantur, his tantùm exceptis, qui strictiore clausura peretuo vivunt.
units.tr: In the same year, on 16 July, he exempted the Jesuits from the obligation to attend processions and funeral associations. Yet it is the duty of the Jesuits to set an example to the clergy and the common people, so that everything is done properly and in the Roman manner: rightly, devoutly, reverently, orderly and decently. Those who act otherwise they betray to the bishops, who then punish them according to their so-called tax. This privilege was granted to them not only so that they would not be called away from sermons, lectures and confessions, but above all so that they would not have to walk at the back of processions because of their recent origin and beginnings. This indulgence was given to them in defiance of the Council of Trent, which decreed in Session 25, chapter 17, that secular clergy and regular clergy alike, including monks, when summoned to public processions, must be compelled to attend, except only those who live forever in stricter enclosure.

units.la: Sed quid multis Notis & animadversionibus opus est? Eustochius Belius Episcopus Parisiensis sententiam rogatus, uno verbo omnia dixit: neme, Multa in privilegijs his Sodalibus à Paulo III. Papa concessis, inesse, quæ cum jure ommuni pugnent, ac Episcoporum, Curibnum & Universitatum authoritati & potestati rejudicent.
units.tr: But why do we need many notes and comments? Eustachius Bellius, Bishop of Paris, when asked for his opinion, said everything in one word: namely, that many things are contained in the privileges granted to this Society by Pope Paul III, which conflict with the common law and diminish the authority and power of bishops, curates and universities.

units.la: DE MAGNA IESVITARVM MACHINA QVAE CONFESSIO DICITVR, ET IN REGVLA CVM PRIMIS INSTITVITVR, EXIGITVR AC PRAECIPITVR.
units.tr: ON THE GREAT ENGINE OF THE JESUITS CALLED CONFESSION, WHICH IS FIRST SET UP IN THEIR RULE, DEMANDED AND PUSHED FORWARD.

units.la: NVllam arcem Philippus Macedonum Rex inexpugnabilem censebat, in quam asinus onustus auro introire posset: nullam ego itidem arcem tuam esse puto, ad quam Confessionis machina à Iesuitis admoveri possit. A Iesuiis inquam veteranis, qui soli eius tractandae rationem norunt, deque modis ius machinae ad quosvis muros applicandae bis in hebdomada disputare solent.
units.tr: Philip, King of Macedon, thought no fortress impregnable into which a donkey laden with gold could enter. I likewise think there is no fortress of yours against which the engine of Confession can be brought up by the Jesuits. I mean the veteran Jesuits, who alone know how to handle it, and who are accustomed to debate twice a week the methods of bringing the engine to bear on any walls at all.

units.la: Hac enim, cum nudo & aperto Marte petere videantur, cuniculos agunt, murofq; surdis ictibus suffodiunt, quibus vigiles quantumvis auritos & oculatos fallant. Arces autem caducas & ruinosas potissimum appetere solent, veteres fœneratores, meretrices obsoletas, nuper nuptas puellas; tenera ingenia; & quidquid facile everti potest, in quo multas utilitates cum voluptate coiunctas habent. Quid enim æque voluptas est curiosis præsertim hominibus, ac rerum occultissimarum veritatem elicere, quam ne supplicijs quidem iudices summi extorquerent? quid autem dulcius, quam a fœneratoribus, & id genus aliis, una opera emungere, quod ipsi multo labore hinc inde corraserunt? Itaq; si cuiusque labes tam liberter audiunt, eas non tam oderunt, quam ex acroamate utilitate cum voluptate quærunt. Cur enim si quis diu de peculatu, aut aliis malis artibus locupletatus est, ad eum potissimum machinam admovere laborant? Cur non in pauperibus æque vitiorum ansas præcidere studient? certe more eorum faciunt, qui latrones vestigant, non tam iustitiæ studio, quam ut eos excutiant raptoque potiantur; aut quorundam Principum, qui Præfectos provinciarum, sicut hirundines sanguine suorum subditorum satiari sinunt, ut cum plenos viderint & turgidos in ius vocent, id est, in torcular, ac semel illum omnem sanguinem exprimant, quem honeste ipsi a populo fugere non potuissent.
units.tr: For although they seem to attack with open and naked force, they in fact dig mines and undermine walls with silent blows, so that they may deceive guards however sharp of ear and eye. They are accustomed to aim chiefly at feeble and crumbling strongholds: aged usurers, faded courtesans, young brides recently married, tender minds, and anything that can easily be overthrown. In these they find many advantages joined with pleasure. For what is more pleasant, especially to curious men, than to draw out the truth of the most hidden matters, which not even the most powerful judges could extort by torture? And what is sweeter than to squeeze money from usurers and men of that kind in one operation, money which they themselves have scraped together with great labour from here and there? So if they listen so gladly to each man's failings, they do not hate them so much as seek from the hearing both profit and pleasure. For why, if someone has long grown rich by embezzlement or other evil arts, do they labour above all to bring the engine against him? Why do they not also take care to cut off the handles of vice in the poor? They certainly act like those who hunt down robbers, not so much from zeal for justice as to shake them out and seize their plunder; or like certain princes who let provincial governors be gorged with the blood of their subjects, as swallows are, and then, when they see them full and swollen, summon them to judgement, that is, to the winepress, and squeeze out all that blood which they themselves could not honourably have taken from the people.

units.la: Quo autem arcana eruant, mirum quam astute machinam suam admoliantur. Negantiu primis arcana confessionis a se revelari posse, quæ enim sibi clanculum aperiuntur, ea non homini, sed Deo aperiri; nec si revelarentur, sibi fidem ullam utpote indignis omni fide testibus adhibitum iri. Sed sane hic, si ut quam alibi, locum habet Italicum proverbium: Qui ha fatto la legge, ha fatto l'ingamo. Nam si quicquam Sociis revelare cupiunt eorum, quæ clanculum audita sunt, rogant confitentem, ut eadem ipsas res extra confessionem sibi enarrare velit. Quod cum ingenue confitens negare non possit, locum & horam accipit, qua ipsos adeat, atque adeo eos omni animæ scrupulo liberet, si quid earum rerum deinceps aperire cupiant. Confessionem autem dilucidam & resupinam esse debere probant, non insicita narratiunculæ. Quendam cum peccata confiteretur, totidem ex ore serpentes eiectare visum esse narrant: ad extremum, cum grave quoddam flagitium fateri erubesceret, maiorem quendam serpentem, identidem caput exerentem, apparuisse, eumque cum foras prorumpere non potuisset, reliquos minores ad se intro revocasse. His miraculis meticulosas mentes percellunt, ut quicquid fraudis & pernicie intus latet, totum in Iesuitarum sinum effundant. Præcipue cum solenniores festivitates appetunt, in quibus de more maiorum in machinam quisque se invitare solet. Hic ergo immanium usurarum, hic expilatæ hæreditatis se accusat, hic subiectum testamentum aut alia fraude quæsitam pecuniam confitetur: Iesuitæ instar Crocodilorum, qui homini, quem devoraturi sunt, collachrymantur, mœstitiam vultu simulant, premunt alto corde lætitiam. Itaque cum restitutione opus esse dicant, benigni interpretes, legis rigorem ita temperant, ut simul iis qui damnum acceperunt, simul raptoris famæ & existimationi consulant. Cum enim sine dedecore res palam iis reddi nequeat, quibus erepta, aut interversa est, ipsi vice restitutionis aliud ἀντάξιον comminiscuntur. Constituunt se Procuratores, aut sequestros omnium qui læsi sunt, ideo hoc aut illo nomine res restitutas usurpare non verentur. Hoc si quis indigne factum autumat, rem non recta reputat via, nam vice earum rerum indulgentias se repensuros pollicentur; quæ non solum præsentibus prosint, sed & natis natorum, & qui nascentur ab illis: χρύσεα χαλκείων σιδηρέων τομβοια ἐντεαβόιαν.
units.tr: Yet how cleverly they bring up their machine to dig out secrets! They claim first that the secrets of confession cannot be revealed by them, since what is secretly disclosed to them is disclosed not to man but to God; and that even if such things were revealed, no faith would be given to them, as witnesses unworthy of any trust. But truly, if ever, the Italian proverb applies here: He who made the law has made the trick. For if they wish to reveal to their Fellows anything of what they have heard in secret, they ask the penitent to tell the same things to them outside confession. When the penitent, being honest, cannot refuse, they take a time and place at which he may visit them, and so free him from every scruple of conscience should they later wish to disclose any such matter. They prove that confession ought to be clear and open, not hidden, with a little tale: they say that when a certain man was confessing his sins, as many serpents seemed to come out of his mouth; and at last, when he blushed to admit some grave crime, a larger serpent appeared, thrusting its head out again and again, and when it could not burst forth, it called the smaller ones back inside it. By such marvels they strike terror into timid minds, so that whatever fraud and ruin lies hidden within is poured out into the bosom of the Jesuits. This happens especially when they seek the more solemn festivals, on which, after the custom of their forefathers, each person is accustomed to invite himself to the engine. Here one accuses himself of monstrous usuries, another of a plundered inheritance, another confesses money gained by a forged will or some other fraud. The Jesuits, like crocodiles, who weep with tears over the man they are about to devour, feign sorrow in their faces and hide joy deep in their hearts. So when they say that restitution is needed, they, as kindly interpreters, soften the rigour of the law in such a way that they look after both those who have suffered loss and the good name and reputation of the thief. For since a thing cannot be openly restored without dishonour to those from whom it was taken or diverted, they devise in place of restitution some other [ἀντάξιον] equivalent. They make themselves procurators or trustees of all who have been injured, and so they do not scruple to use the restored goods under this or that name. If anyone complains that this is done unworthily, he judges the matter by the wrong road; for in place of those goods they promise indulgences, which will benefit not only the present but also the children of their children and those yet to be born: [χρύσεα χαλκείων σιδηρέων τομβοια ἐντεαβόιαν] gold for bronze, bronze for iron, as in Homer.

units.la: Hæc utilitas aliam adiunctam habet; nam pervestigādis omnibus quas vo- cantant circumstantijs, crimine ab uno discunt omnes crimīnis participes, quos ftri-ũ to nexu deinceps obnoxios tenent, eorumq; capiti semper & cervicibus impeet. Huius tamen inventi laudem non est quod sibi arrogent, aut Alexandrum Abonoticheitam, cognomento Ⳑευσϐαμινν, de quo Lucianus librum conscripsit, ude sua privent. Is enim cum Prophetam ageret, ac se omnium petitionibus spôsurum profiteretur, libellos offerentium manu subsignatos perlegebat, in uibus si quod grave in Rempub. flagitium conceptum reperisset, eos penes se -tinebat, ut homines sibi male conscij silentium suum muneribus redimerent. ed haec attigisse sat sit.
units.tr: This method has another advantage attached to it. By investigating all the circumstances, as they call them, they learn from one crime all the partners in the crime, whom they then keep bound in a tight knot and always hang over their heads and necks. Yet they should not claim credit for this invention, nor should they deprive Alexander of Abonoteichos, surnamed [Ψευδομάντις] the False Prophet, about whom Lucian wrote a book, of his own glory. For he, while playing the prophet and professing to answer all petitions, read through the notes handed to him by those who offered them, sealed with their hands; and if he found in them any grave crime against the commonwealth, he kept them in his own possession, so that men conscious of guilt might buy his silence with gifts. But enough has been said on these matters.

units.la: Nunc venio ad alteram huius machinae partem, quae voluptas est. Nemo morat quam dulce malum sit curiositas, & quam quisque affectuum suorum i alienis comparatione delectetur. Solet enim hominum vanitas ad antea actae vicommemorationem gestire, magnamque voluptatem cogitatione usurpare. nde fama vulgatus est mos veteris cuiusdam aulicae, Iesuitis veteranis non cognitae (ac ne miretur Iesuitae eam me sibi cognitam afferere, ea ipsa est cui Masiae Clemens VII. eius gratia captus, tantum indulgentiarum indulsit, si transferfum per os corollam suam duceret, quantum aliis singillatim ad quemq; gloulum salutationem angelicam recitantibus) quae magna aviditate hodie ab adentatoribus sciscitari, perindeque audire solet, quid quisq; nequissimum in vigesserit: Ita veterani, tum quod alienarum actionum narratione in suarum cordationem inijciuntur: tum quod praesentium narratione titillantur, mira gacitate odorantur omnia, interrogationibus anxijs omnia pertentant, in ones animi caulas se penetrant, praesertim si tenerum aliquod ingenium nacti nt, unde aliquid insolens, aut delicatum eos pupugerit. Nec enim simplimalefactorum historia contenti sunt, sed eosdem habitus, vultus, accentus sibi praesentari volunt: unde aliquando accidit, ut quaedam foeminae, ad honestam paulo propensiores, lachrymis & pudore suffusae, putidas Iesuitarum inrrogatiunculas abruperint.
units.tr: Now I come to the second part of this engine, which is pleasure. Nobody is unaware how sweet an evil curiosity is, and how each man delights in comparing his own passions with those of others. For human vanity is wont to rejoice in recalling what it has done in the past, and to enjoy great pleasure in the thought of it. Hence the well-known custom of an old courtly practice, unknown to the veteran Jesuits (and let no Jesuit be surprised that I claim to know it; it is the very practice for whose sake Clement VII, at Massa, was so moved that he granted so many indulgences to anyone who drew his rosary across his mouth as are granted to those who recite the Angelic Salutation over each bead one by one), which nowadays the tempters are accustomed to inquire into with great eagerness, and so to hear what each has done most wickedly. Thus the veterans, both because they are drawn into the reckoning of other men's actions in order to pride themselves on their own, and because they are tickled by the narration of present deeds, sniff out everything with a strange eagerness, probe everything with anxious questions, and penetrate the hidden corners of the mind, especially if they have found some tender disposition from which some unusual or delicate matter has pricked them. For they are not content with a bare account of wrongdoing, but want the same postures, faces and tones presented to them. Hence it sometimes happens that certain women, somewhat too inclined to what is honourable, suffused with tears and shame, have broken off the foul little questions of the Jesuits.

units.la: Mirabitur aliquis tantam mali scientiam in tam sanctis pectoribus habitare, iaeretque forsan, unde illa tandem haustaa sunt? Atqui sciat Iesuitas, ea quae Cajetano & Soto Hispano hac de re scripta sunt, non paucis additamentis cumulatae sunt. Si quid enim turpis, vafrive paulo ingeniosius excogitatum, aut tumve est, continuo in arcanas tabulas refertur, in usum Patrum Societas Iesu, qui hanc artem supra modum excoluerunt. Quemadmodum enim in fundendo auro, si quid iusto ponderi deest, addito scrupulo impletur pondus gitimum: sic in expendenda gravitate vel levitate peccatorum, momenta circumstantiarum ita examinant, ut una detracta, vel addita, facile cognoscant, peccatum sit mortale, vel immortale, statimq; pronunciant, ut bonus ille Hirion ex odore corporum, Voila qui sent le diable: Voila qui sent le diablotin.
units.tr: Someone may wonder that such great knowledge of evil dwells in such holy breasts, and perhaps ask where it was finally drawn from. Yet let the Jesuits know that what Cajetan and the Spaniard Soto have written on this matter has been heaped up with no small additions. For if anything shameful or somewhat cunning has been devised or practised, it is at once entered into their secret tables, for the use of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, who have cultivated this art beyond measure. For just as, in refining gold, if something is lacking in the proper weight, the lawful weight is made up by adding a small grain, so in weighing the gravity or lightness of sins, they examine the weights of the circumstances so exactly that by taking away or adding one, they easily see whether a sin is mortal or venial, and at once pronounce, like that good Hirion who judged by the smell of bodies: "There! It smells of the devil! There! It smells of the little devil!"

units.la: Praeterea doctrinam quandam de casibus reservatis conscripserunt, quarum lutio extra ordinem olim ab Episcopis, interdum a Cardinalibus, atque adeo abso Pontifice petenda erat. Nunc penes Iesuitas tota est, magno id quidem suo sorum merito: nam cum Venetijs primum confessoriam artem agerent, ubi nc Petrus Carrapha famae Sanctitatis serviebat, ad eum tanquam ad oracum confitentes amandabant, si quid τῶν ἁλυτῶν incideret. Qui a Iesuitis clancumonitus libros promptos, inibiq; apertos habebat, ubi de quaestione sermo at, ut cum consulentes adventarent, divinitus id accidisse videretur: quo artiio & Prophetae suspicionem tulit, gradumq; sibi ad Pontificiam dignitatem fecit. uius deinde compos factus, cum beneficij tanti recordaretur, Iesuitas hac omnitente facultate remuneravit.
units.tr: Moreover, they have written a certain doctrine concerning reserved cases, the absolution of which was formerly to be sought outside the ordinary course, from bishops, sometimes from cardinals, and indeed from the Pope himself. Now the whole matter is in the hands of the Jesuits, and they have earned this for their own great benefit. For when they first practised the art of the confessional at Venice, where Pietro Carafa then served the reputation of holiness, they sent penitents to him as to an oracle, if any [ἁλυτῶν] unsolvable case arose. He had books prepared and open, secretly sent to him by the Jesuits, in which the matter in question was discussed, so that when those who consulted him arrived, it would seem that the answer had come by divine inspiration. By this trick he won a reputation for prophecy too, and made for himself a step to the papal dignity. Afterwards, when he had attained it and remembered so great a favour, he rewarded the Jesuits with all his power.

units.la: Superest, referre ratione eius machinae ad versandos iuvenum animos adhiben- e. Laudant Iesuitae mirislaudib. eas consc ientias, quae frenum libenter admittunt; ac fe ultro citroq; versari patiuntur. Quibus laudib; gustatis ambitiosæ metes iuvenū certatim fe dedunt in machinâ verlandas. Huius ambitionis fpecimē aliquod referre nō pigebit. In humilioribꝫ clafsib; interdū, tentandi causa provocat Ludimagister, fi quis amore in Deū, Deiparámve virgíne verbera pati velit, continuò videas innumeros hinc inde discipulos, dissolutis caligis, nudas oftetare nates: Magistru aut succinctaiñ lævam tunicā, ab extremo ad extremū cursitare, & nūc hās, nunc illas aspergere natēs. Vide quid possit ambitio. Itaq; quasi quiddā valde serium gererent, sua omnia Iesuitis enuntiant, casus, insomnia, cogitationes, lætitiàs, iras, impetus, quicquid otiū, ignorātia & iuvetus suggerere potest. Iesuitæ singulis malis suas medelas adhibent, suaꝙ pietatis admíniscula subministrant, cruces ligneas, imaguncúlas, cotollas versatiles, agnos benedictos, libellósque mirificos, quibus religionis suæ facie fucis & pigmentis exornat. Vbi quis ita diu machinā versatus est, ut iam vertigine correptus videatur, sicut res in sublimi suspensæ factili momento huc illuc impelluntur, ad se quantum potis est trahunt, interdum & pertrahunt. Perraró enim hæc alea fallit, præsertim si methodice fiat.
units.tr: There remains the matter of explaining how this machine is applied to turning young men's minds. The Jesuits praise with extravagant praise those consciences that willingly accept the bridle and let themselves be turned back and forth. Once their ambitious minds have tasted this praise, the young men rush to give themselves over to being turned in the machine. I will not hesitate to give one example of this ambition. In the lower classes, the schoolmaster sometimes tests them by challenging anyone who is willing to bear blows for love of God and the Virgin Mother. You would at once see countless pupils on every side, their breeches undone, showing their bare buttocks, while the master, his left tunic girded up, runs from one end of the line to the other, now striking these buttocks, now those. See what ambition can do. And so, as though they were engaged in something very serious, they report everything to the Jesuits: accidents, dreams, thoughts, joys, angers, impulses, whatever idleness, ignorance and youth can suggest. The Jesuits apply their remedies to each evil and supply their little aids to piety: wooden crosses, little images, versatile cottas, blessed lambs and wonderful little books, with which they adorn the face of their religion with paints and cosmetics. When someone has been turned in the machine for so long that he seems already seized by dizziness, he is like things suspended on high, which are pushed this way and that at the slightest moment. They draw him to themselves as far as they can and sometimes pull him in altogether. This dice-game very rarely fails, especially if it is played methodically.

units.la: Est autem methodus huiusmodi. Vbi sæpiùs eam facilitate animi, seu solum ferax, in quo semina iactastatim radices agunt, laudibus, omnibus muneribusq; prosequuti sunt, aliū gradum superare aggrediuntur. Eam ætate esse aiunt, quæ ad aliquod certum vivendi genus se debeat comparare, quæ difficillima cogitatio fit. Itaq; Herculē in trivio constituunt, cui virtus hinc, voluptas illinc aurem vellicet; hæc agmine venerū & lepōrū circumsepta: illa maligna fronte supercilioq; venerāda: hæc in viam initio plana invitans, sed quæ ad extremū dumis horreat: illa viam angustam commonstrans, sed quæ paulatim se explicet, ac in magnificum dignitate otiū. Hortantur itaq; iuvenē, ut quantum fieri potest, cogitet & quidquid in mentem venerit, ad ipsos renūtiet. Iuvenis, sive quod ita videatur, sive gratificandi causa refert, tædere se societatis hominum, ac incessisse sibi cupiditatem, totum se deorum altaribus consecrandi. Afflatum numinis Iesuitæ venerantur, inibiq; paululum subsistentes, multiplices ad otium feretes vias ostendunt, hinc fratrum Cordigerorum, & Benedictorum Sodalitates: hinc Capucinorum, Carmelitarum, Carthusianorum angelicos greges, quibus tamen singulis sua adhærent vitia. Cordigeri petulantes sunt & vagi: Benedictini Simoniaci toti, beneficijs emundis & vendundis occupati. Carmelitæ, iuriūm ligurītores, tanquā ex Apitij schola coqui. Carthusiani fætidum quiddam, & porcīnum oleū animamq; sibi pro sale data putant. Capucini toti ulmei sunt, habituq; cum caco daemonijs imaginibus pene gemino. Videor audire illos versus.
units.tr: The method is of this kind. When they have won over the young man's mind, or soil that is fertile enough for seeds thrown into it to take root at once, with frequent praise and every kind of favour, they set about bringing him up to the next step. They say that this is the age that must prepare itself for some definite way of life, and that this is the most difficult thought of all. So they set Hercules at the crossroads, with virtue pulling at his ear from one side and pleasure from the other: the one surrounded by a band of Venuses and Graces, the other revered for her grim brow and frown; the one inviting him onto a road that is smooth at first but at the end bristles with brambles; the other pointing out a narrow way, which gradually opens out and leads to a leisure magnificent in dignity. They therefore urge the young man to think as much as he can and to report to them whatever comes into his mind. The young man, whether because it seems so to him or to please them, reports that he is weary of human company and has been seized by a desire to devote himself wholly to the altars of the gods. The Jesuits venerate this inspiration of the divinity, and pausing there a little, they show him many paths leading to leisure: here the sodalities of the Cordeliers and the Benedictines; here the angelic flocks of Capuchins, Carmelites and Carthusians, each of which, however, has its own vices clinging to it. The Cordeliers are wanton and wandering. The Benedictines are wholly Simoniacal, busy buying and selling benefices. The Carmelites, lickers of the courts, are like cooks from the school of Apicius. The Carthusians think they have something fetid and piggish about them, and that their soul is given in place of salt. The Capuchins are all wooden-headed, and their habit is almost twin to the images of evil demons. I seem to hear those verses:

units.la: Hinc Numidæ infrani cingunt, & inhospita syrtis:
units.tr: Here the unbridled Numidians surround them, and the inhospitable Syrtis;

units.la: Hinc regio deserta siti, lateq; furentes Barcæi.
units.tr: here a region deserted by thirst, and the far-raging Barcaeans.

units.la: Sola superest diči Iesu Societas, quæ una omniū perfectiones, severitatem, amanitate, disciplinam, laxitate, opes, paupertate, usum & abusum simul complexa est. Quid ni ergo huic subscribat iuvenis? Hortantur tamen denuō, ut se deosq; cosulat, ad id quod optimū maximumq; erit eligendum. Procumbit humi iuvenis ante ora Deum, & eorum numina, quantum potest, obtorto collo deprecatur. Ir ediditad machinam plenus imaginibus, sibiq; cum in omnes partes animum ci cumegisset, unicam Iesuiticam arrisisse profitetur. Hic Iesuitæ lætitia suam dissimulantes, agnis benedictis granifq; diris oneratum, ad preculas amandant. Ito rum magno stridore deos summos, medios, infimos adorat: semperq; magis m gifq; vitæ Iesuiticæ desiderio inflammatur. Vbi ignem hunc languidum Iesuitæ mis medullis conceptum exarsisse vident, ad veteranos veteratores mittunt, cu quibus negotiū nunc, olim otium, transigendum est, apud quos quantum grat valent, tantum se in gratiam iuvenis enixum iri pollicentur. Quasi operostu quiddam, votisq; magnis exorandum fit, Iesuitam conscribi. Audiunt iuven supplic upplicationem veterani, compolito ad severitatem vultu, seseque aiunt à tam multis urgeri, ut sanctæ societatis venter eos iam capere non possit: se tamen estimonio suorum fretos de pietate iuvenis, eum in numerum suorum allectuos: his actis pessimum it iuvenis sub gurgite vasto.
units.tr: Only the Society of Jesus remains, which alone has combined all the perfections of the others: severity with kindliness, discipline with laxity, wealth with poverty, use and abuse at once. Why then should the young man not sign up with it? Yet they urge him again to consult himself and the gods, so as to choose what will be best and greatest. The young man falls prostrate on the ground before God's face and their deities, and, as far as he can, begs with twisted neck. He goes into the machine full of images, and having turned his mind in every direction, he professes that only the Jesuit one has pleased him. Here the Jesuits, hiding their joy, send him off to his little prayers, burdened with blessed lambs and grievous curses. With loud noise he adores the highest, middle and lowest gods, and he is ever more and more inflamed with desire for Jesuit life. When the Jesuits see this languid fire kindled in his innermost marrow now blazing up, they send him to the old veteran deceivers, with whom business must now be transacted, though once it was leisure, and they promise that he will be brought forth into their favour as far as their influence avails. As though something laborious and to be obtained by great prayers, his enrolment as a Jesuit is carried through. The veterans hear the young man's supplication with a severe face composed, and say that they are pressed by so many applicants that the belly of the holy Society can no longer hold them; yet, relying on the testimony of their own people as to the young man's piety, they admit him to the number of their own. With these things done, the unhappy youth goes down beneath the vast whirlpool.

units.la: DE CARCERIBVS IESVITARVM, ET POENIS EORVM QVI IN ILLORVM ORDINE PRAEFRACTARII SVNT.
units.tr: Concerning the prisons of the Jesuits, and the punishments of those in their order who are stubborn.

units.la: SI quis, ut interdum evenit, præfractior est, ac paulò duriore cervice renititur, eum in Trophonij antrum conjiciunt, ut in exercitiorum spiritualium maore, tanquam æs, æruginem contrahat, ac viru contracto sibi ipsi contemnenus evadat. Includunt hominem maligno quodam in gurgustio, ad respiranum quidem satis apto, ad ambulandum autem neq; spatij satis, neque lucis haenti. Ibi totas tres hebdomadas eo more patrū, sub pellibus rite excubat, quanumq; potest maximè vaticinatur: nulli ad eum aditus patet, præterquam Patri spiritali, qui semel bisve in die eum ad machinam admovet: ac deinde breves hartulas, in quibus sententiæ sunt, devorandas obtrudit, quas bene nec-ne cooxerit, ex responsis eius ita cognoscit, ut medici ex excrementorum aspectu ruditate stomachi conjicere solent. Huius pastus amaror, licet initio nauseam ariat, assuetudine tamen ita mitēscit, ut meliorem succum & sanguinem in se onvertat. Sic nonnullis ægris evenisse scio, ut post crebras potiones à mediis propinatas, immutato tandem gustu iis delectari coeperint, neq; meliorum ibiorum dulcedinem desiderârint. Sunt autem illæ sententiæ pietatis Iesuiticæ uasi apices, quibus nil nisi cavum & eximium continetur.
units.tr: If anyone, as sometimes happens, is more obstinate and resists with a somewhat harder neck, they throw him into the cave of Trophonius, so that in the exercise of spiritual discipline he may gather rust like bronze and, once the rust is gathered, may emerge despising himself. They shut the man up in a certain wretched hole, fit enough for breathing but with neither room enough to walk nor light enough to see. There he lies for three whole weeks, in the manner of the Fathers, sleeping on skins, and prophesies as well as he can. No one has access to him except his spiritual father, who brings him up to the machine once or twice a day; then he thrusts upon him short scraps of paper containing maxims, to be swallowed down. Whether he has digested them well or not, the father judges from the man's answers, just as doctors are wont to judge the state of the stomach from the look of the excrement. The bitterness of this food, although at first it stirs nausea, becomes so mild by habit that it turns into better juice and blood. I know that this happened to some sick men: after frequent draughts prescribed by the physicians, their taste at last changed, they began to delight in it, and no longer desired the sweetness of better foods. Now these maxims of Jesuit piety are, as it were, the letters of an alphabet, containing nothing but what is hollow and empty.

units.la: Quis, verbi gratia, religiosorum ordo de Deo superisq; fit optimè meritus: trum maiora sint Francisci Cordigeri, an Loyolæ Iesuitæ facinora.
units.tr: Who, for example, has deserved better of God and the heavenly powers, the order of the Franciscan friars or the deeds of Loyola the Jesuit: which are greater?

units.la: An melius fit vigilando somniare, an somniando ea intuerí quæ vigilantes ident.
units.tr: Is it better to dream while awake, or to see in dreams the things that the waking see?

units.la: In quot dies homo ex sacra hostia cum nonnullo alterius panis & vini admisiculo vitam producere possit.
units.tr: For how many days can a man live on the sacred host, with some small addition of other bread and wine?

units.la: An sacra hostia recepta dormiendo idem operetur atque vigilando.
units.tr: Whether the sacred host received while asleep works the same as when received awake.

units.la: An Bellerophon somniis vel alis volaverit.
units.tr: Whether Bellerophon flew with dreams or with wings.

units.la: An non mirabile fit instrumentum à Iesuitis repertum, quo quis per inane olans suum etiam in multos dies commeatum deferre possit.
units.tr: Is it not a wonderful instrument, discovered by the Jesuits, by which a man flying through the void can carry his own provisions even for many days?

units.la: De quibus omnibus nisi aliquid satis cavum somniaverit, demensum ei minuunt, ut facilius commercium cū insomniis habere possit. Sed quia non omnes a cum umbris & spectris familiaritate gaudent, interdum fit, ut nonnulli, post uatuor aut quinq; dies, ringi secū incipiant ac fenestram quærere, unde se præipites dare queant. Ex inanitate enim cerebri, ex somniorum imaginibus, ex pæotribæ monitis, variumin modum afficiuntur; ut ad delirium prope & amenam adigantur. Exacto mysteriorum tempore emittitur in lucè iuvenis vivus, idensq;, somnians: non caput, non pes, non mens satis officium suum facit. Olim Ieraclitus vigilantibus unū communem mūdum esse dicebat, sopitos in suum uemq; discedere: at qui ex hoc antro redeunt, ne vigilantes quidem communium aliis mundo fruuntur: novos enim mundos novasq; formas, Tragælaphos, shimæras, Hippocentauros loquuntur. Sane in eorum vultu gestuq; contemlando non parum voluptatis inest. Hic se totum circumspicit, ac quocunq; caut agit corporis sui figuram in aere suspensam intuetur: hic se testaceum facst se credit, metuq; ne allidatur obvios quosq; vitat: hic hominum insomnium se idere autumat, secumq; dissolvere nequit an somnians vigilet, an vero vigians vaticinetur. Vno enim tempore fulgura, tonitrua, Iesuitarum, & Cacodæmonum voces audire videtur.
units.tr: If he has not dreamed something sufficiently empty about all these things, they cut down his rations, so that he may more easily have intercourse with dreams. But since not all are on friendly terms with shades and phantoms, it sometimes happens that some, after four or five days, begin to rave to themselves and look for a window from which they may throw themselves headlong. For from the emptiness of the brain, from the images of dreams, and from the admonitions of the tormentors, they are affected in various ways, so that they are driven almost to delirium and madness. When the time of the mysteries is over, the young man is brought out into the light alive, yet dreaming: neither head, nor foot, nor mind performs its office satisfactorily. Heraclitus once said that the waking share one common world, while the sleeping each turn away into their own; but those who return from this cave do not even enjoy the common world when awake: they speak of new worlds and new forms, goat-stags, chimaeras, and centaurs. Indeed, there is no small pleasure to be had in contemplating their faces and gestures. Here one looks all around himself, and wherever he goes he sees the figure of his own body hanging in the air; here one believes himself to be made of earthenware and, fearing he will be dashed to pieces, avoids whomever he meets; here another declares that he is a dream of men and cannot tell whether he is dreaming while awake or prophesying while dreaming. For at one and the same time he seems to hear the lightnings, thunders, and the voices of the Jesuits and of the evil demons.

units.la: DE OECONOMIA ET REGIMINE DE REGIMINE ET REPVPLICA IESVI[?] TARVM, EORVMQVE SOCIETATIS EXCELLEN- TIA, EX EPISTOLA ITALICA.
units.tr: ON THE ECONOMY AND GOVERNMENT, ON THE GOVERNMENT AND COMMONWEALTH OF THE JESUITS, AND THE EXCELLENCE OF THEIR SOCIETY, FROM AN ITALIAN LETTER.

units.la: Anno 1609. in lucem editum est exemplar literarum Barifonij Iesuitæ ad Venetum adolescentem 21. Aprìl. Anno 1608. qui relictâ Societate hac ad suos redierat; Bononiæ datarum, in quibus Regimen & Respublica Iesuitarum, cum Ordinis illorum excellentia & perfectione ita exacte depinguntur & oculis contemplanda subjiciuntur, ut totius illorum Ordinis ideam, seu formam & speciem quandam perfectam inde quisquis mente sua concipere queat. Et quia Iesuitarum artibus factum est, ut non omnium manibus teratur, præcipua inde in Lectoris gratiam adscribam.
units.tr: In 1609 there was published a copy of a letter from the Jesuit Barifonius to a young Venetian, dated at Bologna on 21 April 1608, written to a man who had left this Society and returned to his family. In it the government and commonwealth of the Jesuits, together with the excellence and perfection of their Order, are so exactly portrayed and laid out for the eye to contemplate that anyone can form in his mind from it an idea, or a certain perfect form and picture, of the whole Order. And because, through the Jesuits' craft, the letter has not come into everyone's hands, I shall set down its principal passages here for the reader's benefit.

units.la: In Societatis nostræ Ordine, inquit auctor literarum illarum, in promptu & parato reperiuntur ea, quæ in hac vita animo generoso necessaria esse queunt; & quæ vel in sæculari & mundana vita, vel etiam apud ullam aliam Religionem sive Ordinem nunquam quis assequi poterit. Nec vero auferunt illud Religiosi nomen & Clausuræ quenquam deterreat. Tantum enim abest ut quidquam inde damni metuendum sit, ut plus etiam lucri, quam nulli hominum e qualibet Civitate, aut etiam alia congregatione civili possit contingere, hinc sperare licet. Religiosus enim si universim consideres, præter quam quod sacrorum ministeriorum exercitio occupatur, re profecto quovis pretiosissimo thesauro venerabiliori, absque labore vivit, cultus & honoratus ab omnibus, tam in ceremonijs publicis, quam privatis, sublevatus in necessitatibus, a personalibus factionibus, & militia exemptus, a quovis onere & exactione immunis, ad duellum sive singulare certamen non adstrictus, & multis denique falsis ac popularibus opinionib. minime obnoxius. Similiter & clausuræ illæ non ita se habent, ut ipsimet Religiosi sub his veluti conclusi teneantur, sed ut aliorum bona in iis adserventur, atque ut ipsi haud magna cum molestia, Dei laudes commemorando vita magis libera & securâ fruamur.
units.tr: In our Society's Order, says the author of that letter, there are ready to hand and prepared those things which can be necessary in this life for a noble spirit, and which no one could ever attain in secular and worldly life, or indeed in any other religious community or order. Nor let the name of religious, or the cloister, deter anyone. For so far is anything of harm to be feared from this that one may hope for more gain than anyone in any city, or in any other civil association, could obtain. For if you consider a religious in general terms, apart from the fact that he is occupied with the exercise of sacred ministries, he lives, without labour, with a treasure more precious than any gem, honoured and esteemed by all, both in public and in private ceremonies, relieved in his needs, exempt from private factions and from military service, free from every burden and levy, not bound to duel or single combat, and, in short, very little exposed to the many false and popular opinions. Likewise, those enclosures are not such that the religious themselves are held as if shut up within them, but rather that the goods of others are kept safe in them, and that we may enjoy a life more free and secure, praising God without any great trouble.

units.la: Deinde si ad particularia pervenerits, tum vero longe meliorem conditionem hanc nostram invenies; quandoquidem Societates nostræ Clausuris isiusmodi, uti & alio extraordinario vinculo disciplinæ, vigiliarum, & jejuniorum, quæ certe homines & stupidos faciunt, & conversationi, tum negotijs ad proximi salutem necessarijs, minus reddunt idoneos, nequaquam sunt obligatæ: sicuti antiquæ illæ Religiones sive Ordines omnes, nullæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ usui existentes, eius generis apparentibus, & in oculos occurrentibus operibus necessum habent. At nos à Choro, à Processionibus, ab Exequijs liberi & immunes, veluti simplices Sacerdotes sæculari quadam libertate gaudentes, omnes operationes nostras ad ea studia dirigimus, quæ homines circumspectos & admirandos reddere, atque insuper etiam sanctam Sedem Romanam valde exaltare, & magis magisque illustrare queant; quamobrem etiam digni ab ea sumus judicati, ut quemadmodum veteribus illis Religionum Ordinibus, propter exiguam, quam habent, Sedis ipsius evehendæ aptitudinem, quotidie privilegia & indulta auferuntur, ita nobis e contra veluti utilissimis eius Ministris singulis fere horis ea dilatentur & augeantur.
units.tr: Next, if you come to particulars, you will find our condition far better; for our Societies are not bound by such enclosures, nor by the other extraordinary bonds of discipline, of vigils and fasts, which certainly make men dull and render them less fit for conversation and for the business necessary for the salvation of our neighbour. Those ancient religious orders, all of them, which are of no use to the Roman Church, must perforce engage in works of that kind, which are visible and conspicuous. But we, free and exempt from the choir, from processions, and from funerals, rejoicing in a certain secular liberty like simple priests, direct all our operations to those pursuits which can make men thoughtful and admirable, and moreover greatly exalt and make ever more illustrious the Holy See of Rome. For this reason we have also been judged worthy by it: just as privileges and indults are taken away every day from those old orders of religion, on account of the small aptitude they have for advancing that See, so to us, on the contrary, as its most useful ministers, these are extended and increased almost every hour.

units.la: Quæ sigillatim ita considerata, præterquam quod certum aliquem reddere possunt facilitatis Institutorum nostrorum, præcipue etiam cognoscendam exhibere queunt Superioritatem illam, qua Congregatio nostra omnibus alijs Ordinibus præeminet. Idque non absque gravissima ratione: quoniam isti in extremis fundati, domi apud se non admodum sunt durabiles, foris autem etiam animis periculosi. Monachi namque maiorum Ordinum solâ divitijs cumulandis operam dantes, servi evaserunt peccati & mundi: & ob id etiam exosi redditi, quotidie Epicedijs precationibusque incumbunt, officium hoc suum ea tantum parte impendentes, quæ redditibus ex alieno statu hauriendis, ad sublevandam Prælatorum & Curiæ Romanæ necessitatem commoda esse queat & utilis. Medicantes deinde pro ter affectatam paupertatem suam contempti, quamcunque etiam minutissimam eleemosynam
units.tr: These things, considered one by one in this way, can not only make clear the ease of our Institutes, but can also show in particular that superiority by which our Congregation surpasses all other Orders. Nor is this without a most serious reason: for those orders, founded on extremes, are not very durable at home among themselves, and abroad they are even dangerous to minds. For the monks of the greater orders, devoting their effort solely to piling up riches, have become slaves of sin and of the world; and for this reason they have also become hateful, and daily busy themselves with funeral dirges and prayers, devoting this their office only to that part which can be of use in drawing revenues from another's estate, to relieve the needs of the prelates and of the Roman Curia. Then the mendicant friars, despised on account of their affected poverty, go about with any collection, however very small an alms, or even beg at the villages; and at the request of any most abject little woman they celebrate the most holy sacrifices of the Mass at the cheapest price, in the porticoes of houses and in the huts of private persons, and distribute the divine mysteries by communicating them, mixing themselves with the world and defiling themselves with its errors. Hence an pressing occasion has arisen for reformation, and, if that should not succeed, for thinking about the total destruction of that Order. But our Society, which is a well-instituted commonwealth, placed in moderation by the prudence and sagacity of our Fathers, does not puff itself up above monastic opulence, and yet does not for that reason sink to the lowest beggary; it takes part only in the one or other thing, only as far as the worship of God requires, and always keeps before itself this aim with a certain salvation of souls, how it may deserve the weightier and most important benefits to the Roman Catholic faith. Hence it will be pleasing to the Pontiffs, observed by Princes, cultivated by the people, a rival of the sun's circle, glorious with its sons in all parts of learning, and blessed in heaven.

units.la: synar[?] ynam collectum circumeunt, vel ad pagos usque mendicando; & ad postulationem cuiusue etiam abiectissimæ mulierculæ in ipsis ædium Epistylijs, & privatorum casis sanctissima Missarum sacrificia vilissimo pretio celebrant, divinaque mysteria communicando distribuunt, seculo sese immiscentes, atque ijs sese inquinantes erroribus; unde urgens nata est occasio de Reformatione, & si illa non successerit, de universali Ordinis illius destructione cogitandi. At nostra Societas, quæ bene instituta Respub. est, prudentia & sagacitate Patrum nostrorum, in mediocritate constituta, super Monachicam opulentiam sese non effert, & nec tamen ideo ad infimam mendicitatem deflectit, sed tantum ab una atq; altera, tantum ad Dei Cultum opus est, participans, cum certa animæ salute hunc sibi finem semper abet proprofitu, quomodo Romani Catholicæ fidei graviora, & maximi momenti beneficia ossit promereri. Unde Pontificibus grata, à Principibus observata, & à populo culta, atq; circuli solaris æmula, cum filijs suis in omnibus literarum partib. gloriosa erit, in cælo beata.
units.tr: synar[?] from which collections are gathered; they go about the streets, or even beg as far as the villages; and at the request of any most abject little woman they celebrate the most holy sacrifices of the Mass in the very porticoes of houses and in the huts of private persons for a most cheap price, distributing the divine mysteries by communicating them, mixing with the world and staining themselves with its errors; hence an urgent occasion has arisen for reformation, and, if that should not succeed, for thinking about the universal destruction of that Order. But our Society, which is a well-ordered commonwealth, placed in a mean by the prudence and sagacity of our Fathers, does not lift itself up above monastic wealth, and yet does not for that reason sink to the lowest mendicancy; it shares only in one or another thing, only as far as the worship of God requires, and always has this aim before itself with a certain assurance of the soul's salvation, how it may deserve the heavier and most important benefits to the Roman Catholic faith. Hence it will be pleasing to the Pontiffs, observed by Princes, cultivated by the people, a rival of the sun's circle, glorious with its sons in all parts of learning, and blessed in heaven.

units.la: Hinc nascuntur invidæ illæ voces, à depressis æmulis nostris contra mores & exemplaem doctrinæ nostram effectæ, quæ auribus multorum insusurratæ haud dubie in causa sunt, quod Societatem nostram immani odio prosequuntur. Incusant nos primum Superbia, quod SOCIORVM titulum usurpemus, & aliorum hominum Ordines vix Servorum nomine lignemur. Quasi quisquam sit, qui sincero animo judicans non intelligat, Nos divina providentia in normam & correctionem aliorum electos esse, ideoque justum, dilectam hanc congregationem eius, insigni & speciosò aliquo vocabulo à tot Monachorum & Fraternitatum inutilibus fetus distingui. Præterea & hoc reprehendunt, quod recusemus cilicijs vestiri, aut cibis pasci rusticis: sed illudentes, dicunt, nos vestib. uti ex lana tenuissima, & utem tegere candidissimo linteo, nutritos optimis & delicatissimis cibis, qui vel in urbe, vel territorijs vicinis reperiatur. Insuper nolle nos in pagis habitare, aut sub tectis humilib. sed cum Patribus nostris, varias mundi partes peragrantib. omnis commoditas & venustas excogitata sit, possidere nos dicunt in omnib. regnis & provincijs Christianissimi, meliores & præstatiores situs atq; palatia, quàm alibi haberi queant, non quidem in villis aut castellis cassas fundantes, sed in urbibus primarijs, & ijs rebus abundantibus, quæ generi humano possint sufficere: Sed neq; sic Ædes illas acceptari, nisi prius & reditus, & habitationes pro Patrum & Coadjutorum temporalium numero ibi fuerint præparatæ. Non animad vertunt aut affectibus corrupti obtrectatores, id quod de vestimentis, cibis & habitationibus dicunt, ad summam laudem Societatis totius, & Patris Ignatij primi Institutoris nostri vergere; qui ut omnium hominum sapientissimus vestes incultas, cilicia & cibos agrestes, quæ mira corporis afflictiones sunt, ipsum etiam spiritum affligere & debilitare intelligens, usu illarum rerum nobis interdixit, & voluit de ijs vestibus & alimentis nobis esse prospectum, quæ ei conveniant, qui ad exaltationem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Romanæ, mentem in studijs, linguam verò, ad sanctorum Apostolorum exemplum, in persuasionibus publicis & privatis exercet. Habitationes verò quod attinet, quis non videt, ad decus & ornamentum sanctæ Religionis sive Ordinis hoc fieri? idq; ita aut fiat necessum esse: si quidem in his fovenda sunt feminaria eorum hominum, quibus Ecclesia & tota Christianitas regatur? Quantum postea ad doctrinam, quum maledici isti ad vera dogmata sustinenda inhabiles sint, ne impotentes dicam, ad operas & labores Societatis nostræ exæquandos, eo fatigantur, ut in Dei gratiam & voluntatem omnia reponentes, vanum esse demonstrent grande illud meritum nostrum: Ideoq; Pelagianos nos vocant & Epicuri discipulos; propterea quod ex assertione nunquam satis laudata Molinæ dicamus, Deum nolle physice moveri animos hominum, sed in æterna quiete sua expectare, ut suâ gratiâ ad hoc destinati, cum merito bonorum operum, ipsimet per se paradisum acquirant. Cæci non vident, Deum in divinitate sua immobilem, & immediate, & variis modis gloriam suam amplificare: & nobis in hunc finem deorsum à Majestate illa concessum esse, Regnum ipsius propagare, & mediantibus Regulis nostris, librisq; spiritualibus, hominum animos persuasionis vi, quam nobis largitur, movere, & facilem ad cælum viam reddere cunctis fidelibus, qui exuti omni politica curiositate, nostris duntaxat præceptis salutiferis obedierint. Et quod mains aut certius bonitatis & integritatis doctrinæ
units.tr: Hence arise those envious voices, made by our depressed rivals against our manners, example and doctrine, which, whispered into the ears of many, undoubtedly are the cause why they pursue our Society with monstrous hatred. First they accuse us of pride, because we take the title of Companions, and scarcely brand the other orders of men with the name of Servants. As if there were anyone who, judging with a sincere mind, did not understand that we have been chosen by divine providence as the rule and correction of others, and that therefore this beloved congregation of His is rightly distinguished by a remarkable and splendid name from the useless brood of so many monks and fraternities. Besides, they also find fault with this, that we refuse to clothe ourselves in hair-shirts or to feed on rustic foods; but, mocking, they say that we use garments of the finest wool, cover ourselves with the whitest linen, and are nourished with the best and most delicate foods that can be found in the city or the neighbouring territories. Moreover, they say that we are unwilling to live in villages or under humble roofs, but that, while our Fathers travel through various parts of the world, where every convenience and charm has been devised, we possess in all the kingdoms and provinces of the most Christian monarchs the finest and most distinguished sites and palaces that can be had elsewhere; not indeed founding empty houses in farmhouses or castles, but in the chief cities, and in places abounding in those things which can suffice for the human race. But not even so are those buildings accepted, unless first both revenues and dwellings have been prepared there in proportion to the number of Fathers and temporal coadjutors. The slanderers, corrupted by their passions, do not notice that what they say about clothing, food and dwellings tends to the highest praise of the whole Society, and of Father Ignatius, our first founder; who, as the wisest of all men, understanding that rough garments, hair-shirts and rustic foods, which are a wonderful affliction of the body, also afflict and weaken the spirit itself, forbade us the use of those things, and wished that we be provided with those clothes and foods which suit one who exercises his mind in studies for the exaltation of the Catholic Roman Church, and his tongue, after the example of the holy Apostles, in public and private persuasions. As for dwellings, who does not see that this is done for the honour and ornament of the holy Religion or Order? And that it must be so done, since in these are fostered the seminaries of those men by whom the Church and all Christendom are governed? As for doctrine, since those slanderers are unfit to uphold true dogmas, not to say impotent, to match the works and labours of our Society they toil so hard, that, placing everything in the grace and will of God, they show that our great merit is vain: therefore they call us Pelagians and disciples of Epicurus, because we say, from the never sufficiently praised assertion of Molina, that God does not wish the minds of men to be moved physically, but waits in His eternal rest, so that men destined by His grace, with the merit of good works, may acquire paradise for themselves by themselves. The blind do not see that God, immobile in His divinity, amplifies His glory immediately and in various ways; and that to us, for this end, it has been granted from that Majesty on high to propagate His Kingdom, and by means of our Rules and spiritual books to move the minds of men by the power of persuasion which He bestows on us, and to make the way to heaven easy for all the faithful who, stripped of all political curiosity, have obeyed only our salutary precepts. And the world can desire no surer sign of the goodness and integrity of our doctrine than that the public errors of the greatest universities, and singularly of the royal city of Paris, have been corrected through us.

units.la: nostræ mundus signum desiderare potest, si publici errores maximarum universitatum, singulariter vero Regiæ urbis Parisiorum per nos fuerunt correcti. Ibi enim, paucis quibusdam seniorum literatorum exceptis, reliqui omnes Moderni & iuniores Doctores facile doctrinæ nostræ accesserunt, non amplius scribentes, Rom. Pontificum errores quantum vis exorbitantes, à Concilijs posse corrigi; aut vero defendentes, licitum esse Gallorum Regi liberā administrationem rerum Ecclesiasticarum impedire, & si quæ aliæ eius regni Maximæ sunt, sive Regulæ alicuius momenti aut ponderis. Etsi enim ob multas rationes, & scripturarum allegationes ab antiquissimis & celeberrimis Doctoribus approbatas, itaque vanos multorum labores inexpugnabile id existimabatur, constat tamen, à nostris idipsum Patrib. iam esse evictū: dico illam tantopere decantatam Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ libertatē; quæ expugnatā, & veluti monstro à novis illis (ut ita dicā) Theologiæ Herculibus sepulto, liberum omnino à quovis impedimento in omnibus. Principatib. rursum evasit absolutū S. Sedis Rom. dominium. Nonne eius rei indubitata quoque fide facit, cum videtur, quomodo apud nos cōtra hæreticā pravitatē omnes scientiæ divinæ & humanæ floreat? & quod hic viri insignes, & Magistri in omni disciplina celeberrimi reperiantur? à quib. absqué vlla pecuniæ spe (quæ sibi siquidem alij habent propositū) maior & melior pars iuuentutis Christianæ instituitur: & quidem in dedecus & confusione male affectorū, & suum salte commodū inde quærentiū pædagogulorū, qui cessantib. commoditatib. & emolumentis illis, quibus quā primum Patres nostri apparuerunt, destituti fuère, variis imposturis curarunt laudabiles operationes nostras inquinare, in vulgus spargentes, ad Scholarū eruditionem nos utilitate & voluptate moveri, non vero charitate, aut proximi amore. Idq; inde liquere, quod ad divites & formosos duntaxat animum applicemus, de alijs vero parum simus soliciti, utrum maiores progressus faciant, quam qui ad apparentiam illam confervandam, quā cognatos & parentes eorum perpetuō nobis veluti mancipatos habeamus, sint necessarij.
units.tr: Our order can point to no surer sign of the goodness and soundness of our teaching than this: the public errors of the greatest universities, and especially of the royal city of Paris, have been corrected through us. There, with a few older men of letters excepted, all the rest of the modern and younger teachers have readily come over to our doctrine. They no longer write that the errors of the Roman pontiffs, however extravagant, can be corrected by councils, nor do they defend that it is lawful for the King of France to hinder the free administration of ecclesiastical affairs, or any other of the maxims of that kingdom that carry weight or importance. For although, on many grounds and on scriptural arguments approved by the most ancient and celebrated teachers, that liberty of the Gallican Church was held to be impregnable despite the vain labours of many, it is nonetheless certain that our Fathers have already overcome it. I mean that liberty so much trumpeted, which, once stormed and, as it were, buried by those new Herculeses of theology (if I may so call them), has left the absolute dominion of the Holy See of Rome free from every hindrance among the princes. Does not the fact that here, against heretical depravity, every science, divine and human, flourishes, give indubitable assurance of this too? Are not here found distinguished men and teachers most renowned in every branch of learning, by whom the greater and better part of Christian youth is trained without any hope of money, which others indeed make their aim? And this is done to the shame and confusion of ill-disposed men, and of those tutors who seek their own advantage from it. Deprived of those profits and rewards with which our Fathers first appeared, they have tried by various slanders to stain our praiseworthy labours, spreading abroad that we are moved to the teaching of schools by profit and pleasure, not by charity or love of our neighbour. And this, they say, is clear from the fact that we attend only to the rich and handsome, and care little about others, whether they make greater progress; that is, unless such people are needed to keep up the appearance by which we always hold their kinsfolk and parents as if they were bound to us.

units.la: Hoc amplius subjungunt obtrectatores, Nos sub religionis sanctissimæ prætextu in tenneros animos subditorum aut civium, scholas nostras, contemptūs & inobedientiæ feminā adversus naturales eorum Principes spargere, persuadentes eis, quod illi folūmodo Principi, quem nos veluti Monarcham omnium constituimus, credendum & obediendum sit. Et cum eiusmodi quidem diabolicis inventionibus ausi fuerunt hoc agere, ut schole nostræ proħiberentur. Sicuti in nobili quadam Italiæ civitate hoc illis succéssit, extremo cum damnatum illius, tum aliarum civitatum liberorum nobilium & primariorum, qui studiorum causa ad eam convenerant. Quibus calumnijs, à linguis lucripetis, sive suum speētantibus commodum professis, prolixè quidē responderi, posset: sed præstat eas, secundum regulas nostras logicales silentio præterire. Hoc tamen dico, fortunæ bona necessaria esse ei, qui literis animum est applicaturus, & pulchritudinem verum vivacitatis spiritus, & ingenij bonitatis signum esse atq; indicium. Vnde si iis, qui eiusmodi dotibus sunt præditi, incumbimus, faciemus hoc tanquam in subjectis aptis ad disciplinam natis; non autem voluptatis ergo aut facultatu comparadarum gratiā. Deniq;, cum videre licet, Scholas nostras undiq; velab ipsis etiam Principum filijs, tanto cum concursu, solitis illis præceptoribus repudiatis, appeti, hinc infallibilis sequitur conclusio, quemadmodū Nos & existentiā & reputatione omnes aliós Ordines superamus, ita etiam doctrinas è Domibus & Collegijs nostris prodeuntes, reliquas itidem omnes, sive D. Thomæ, sive Scoti sint, & pietate, & dogmatū soliditate exce- dere. Quo etiam fit, ut quod alijs prohibitum est, nobis liceat, libros nempe & scripta tenere atq; perlegere: ex quibus quandoq; ob publicum bonum, impiorum hæreticorum nomine sublato, & celebris cuiusdam Patris nostri in vicem eius substituto, in publicum ea rursus emittamus. Ideoq; hac ætate in Collegijs & Scholis nostris non amplius auditur Aristoteles & Cicero, monstrosa gentilitatis monumenta, sed cathedræ auctoribus longè illustrioribus Doctoribus ornatæ cernuntur; & in universum solis ibi Alvari, Toleti, Molinæ, atque alij Societatis nostræ Theologi leguntur.
units.tr: Our detractors add further that under the pretext of most holy religion we spread among the tender minds of subjects or citizens, through our schools, contempt and disobedience towards their natural princes, persuading them that only that prince whom we set up as the monarch of all should be trusted and obeyed. With such diabolical inventions they have dared to work toward having our schools banned, as in a certain noble city of Italy they succeeded in doing, to the great loss both of that city and of the other cities whose noble and leading young men had gathered there for study. These calumnies, spoken by greedy tongues that look to their own advantage, could be answered at length; but it is better to pass them over in silence, according to our logical rules. Yet this I say: good fortune is necessary for one who is going to apply his mind to letters, and beauty is the true sign and mark of a lively spirit and a good mind. So if we devote ourselves to those endowed with such gifts, we do so as to subjects fit and born for discipline, not for the sake of pleasure or of gaining wealth. Finally, since we can see that our schools are sought from every quarter, even by the sons of princes themselves, with such a crowd, the solid tutors being rejected, the following conclusion infallibly follows: just as we surpass all other orders in numbers and reputation, so also the doctrines that issue from our houses and colleges surpass all the rest, whether they belong to St Thomas or to Scotus, in piety and soundness of doctrine. Hence it also comes about that what is forbidden to others is permitted to us: namely, to keep and to read through books and writings, from which, sometimes for the public good, when the name of impious heretics has been removed and that of some famous Father of ours put in its place, we send them forth again into public. And so in this age in our colleges and schools Aristotle and Cicero, monstrous monuments of paganism, are no longer heard; instead, chairs adorned by teachers far more illustrious are seen, and on the whole only Alvarez, Toledo, Molina and the other theologians of our Society are read there.

units.la: Possunt etiam nostri Socij facile invenire viam & modum, quo ad honores & gradus summos evehantur. Acpotuerunt scientiarū nostrarum facilitate, & mediante vivacitate ingeniorum, aut praedicando, aut docendo celebres evadere: ex quorum uno atq; altero maximam utilitatem, & non exiguam existimationem referunt: quandoquidem à viris, à mulieribus, à populo & magnatibus ipsis coluntur atq; sublevantur: nec quicquam ipsis in mentem veniet, quod non ilico, quàm primum fuerit rescitum, promissuri ipsis sint & donaturi. Ipsis privatorum ædes apertæ erunt: cum ijs de maximis reb. civitatis cosultabitur: eos secreto suorum quilibet faciet participes: & quado animum ad hoc applicuerint, extrinseca illa pietatis umbra simplicis multitudinis opinionem attrahendo, pro arbitrio ex Magistris aut radicatoribus, non quidem specietenus, sed reipsa Imperatores & Monarchæ fiunt: & non solum sibi ipsis commodu & honores conciliabunt, verum etiam gloria ita auctí Societates nostras illustriores & ditiores reddere poterunt: sicut multis Patrib. in Polonia, Transylvania, Lusitania, Bavaria, Hispania, atq; aliis in locis usu venit: imò in ipsis etiam Indijs maxima Societatis nostræ Monarchia erecta & plantata est. Qui exactam informationem, horum quæ scribo, curiosius apprehenderet, deprehensurus esset, Provincias Ferdinando Archiducis subiectas supremâ inspectione Societatis nostræ regi, & vel inde felices esse, quòd omnia Patrum consiliis gerantur, sive de dignitate & magistratibus conferendis, sive de belli et armim apparatu tractetur. In Bavaria quoq; omnia Patrum nostrorum prudentia gubernantur. Trasylvania à solo administrata fuit Carigtio, qui curavit, ut Imperatoris manui potestati ea subij ceretur. Nonne Galliam & Regem ipsum Pater Cotton in præsentia gubernat? Et in Polonia, non obstante paucorum satis Christianorum tergiversatione, ex sanctitatis nostræ spiritu atq; instinctu vivit. In Hispania, Lusitania, Belgio, Italia & Sicilia, cui ignotæ sunt divitiæ & authoritas, quâ polle.nus? Sed quid de Patre Perronio dicâ? qui Romæ agens, plus auctoritatis habet in Anglia quâ Rex ipse: nec Comes ibi est, Marchio, aut Prælatus Catholicus, quin pro Superintendente aut gubernatore conscientiæ suæ aliquem ex Societate nostra habeat. Ac ut summatim dicam, Generalis noster, sicuti manifestum est omnibus, Romam regit & Pontificatum.
units.tr: Our members can also easily find a way and means by which they may be raised to the highest honours and degrees. By the ease of our sciences, and through the lively wit of their minds, they have been able to become famous either in preaching or in teaching. From one or another of them we derive very great usefulness and no small esteem, since they are honoured and supported by men, by women, by the common people, and even by the great. Nor will anything come into their minds that they will not promise and give to them as soon as it is known. Private houses will be open to them; with them the greatest affairs of the state will be discussed; each of the great will make them partners in his secrets; and when they have set their mind to it, drawing the common crowd's opinion by the outward shadow of piety, they become, not in name but in fact, emperors and monarchs, chosen from among teachers or advisers as they please. They will not only win for themselves advantage and honours, but also, so enlarged by glory, will be able to make our Societies more illustrious and richer, as has happened to many of our Fathers in Poland, Transylvania, Portugal, Bavaria, Spain and other places. Indeed, in the Indies themselves a very great monarchy of our Society has been raised up and planted. Anyone who more curiously sought an exact account of what I write would discover that the Provinces subject to the Archduke Ferdinand are governed under the supreme oversight of our Society, and are fortunate for this alone, that everything is done by the counsels of our Fathers, whether the bestowing of dignities and magistracies is being discussed or the preparation of war and arms. In Bavaria too, everything is governed by the prudence of our Fathers. Transylvania was administered by Carigtius alone, who saw to it that the power was brought under the hand of the Emperor. Does not Father Coton at present govern France and the King himself? And in Poland, despite the evasions of a few Christians, it lives by the spirit and impulse of our holiness. In Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Italy and Sicily, where riches and authority are unknown to us, what power do we not have? But what shall I say of Father Perron? He, while acting at Rome, has more authority in England than the King himself; nor is there a count, marquis or Catholic prelate there who does not have one of our Society as superintendent or governor of his conscience. And, to sum up, our General, as is manifest to all, rules Rome and the Papacy.

units.la: Nos etiam certo obedientiæ voto sanctæ Sedi obstricti tenemur, ut scilicet non petito iudicio eò nos conferamus, quocunq; etiam locorum ab ea destinati fuerimus. Inde nos ipsius sedis ministri facti, & gravissimorum secretorum eius conscij, id, quod in commodum nostrum dit, Pontificibus persuademus: Omnes, qui ad functiones aut Præluturas aspirant, necessitate obstringentes, ut ad intercessionem nostram confugiant. Atq; hoc Pontificio ministerio insigniti, & excitatâ in hos totius mundi opinione, in civitates, Regna, & ipsorum Principum corda penetramus. Ita fit, ut cum hi dominium super vitam & bona subditorum teneant, Nos possessionem voluntatis cum Principum, tum subditorum occupemus.
units.tr: We are also bound by a firm vow of obedience to the Holy See, so that we do not, without being asked for judgment, betake ourselves to whatever places we are sent to by it. Thus, having become ministers of that very See and privy to its most weighty secrets, we persuade the Pontiffs of what is to our advantage, binding all who aspire to offices or prelacies by necessity to take refuge in our intercession. And so, marked with this papal ministry, and with the opinion of the whole world roused on our behalf, we penetrate cities, kingdoms and the hearts of their princes themselves. So it comes about that, while these hold dominion over the lives and goods of their subjects, we seize possession of the will of princes and subjects alike.

units.la: Et quemadmodum sanctâ fides, ubi ubi innotuerat, maximos faciebat progressus: ita & ubicunq; agimus, sub nomine Iesu, insensibiliter, tale obsequium acquirimus, ut posteà in Principum potestate non sit inde nos depellere. Cui rei fidem facere potest amplissimum & tentissimum Galliæ Regnum suis illis turbis novissimis. Quapropter arbitri sæpenumerò intentionum non tantum inter Principem & Principem, verum etiam inter Dominos & vasallos constituti, pro lubitu nostro & bellum & pacem mundo adportamus: non absq; evidenti prætensione, quòd sanctæ illius Sedis possessio, in Patribus aliquando nostris casura, succedive posteâ perpetuari queat. Quod cum evenerit, tam insigne capiet incrementum omnia Religio, ut spes sit, brevi videri posse ex Principatibus Christianis & mundo universo factum esse unum ovile & unum Pastorem.
units.tr: And just as holy faith, wherever it became known, made the greatest progress, so also wherever we act, under the name of Jesus, we gain such compliance without being noticed that afterwards it is not in the power of princes to drive us out from there. The very wide and extensive kingdom of France, with its recent troubles, can bear witness to this. Therefore, appointed as arbiters of intentions not only between prince and prince but also between lords and vassals, we bring both war and peace upon the world at our pleasure, not without the evident pretext that the possession of that holy See, which may fall to our successors at some time, can be perpetuated in succession. When this happens, all religion will take such remarkable increase that there is hope that, before long, it may be seen that from the Christian principalities and the whole world one fold and one Shepherd has been made.

units.la: Nec vero propter votum illud veluti ligati tenemur, aut quidquam imminuitur libertas aut præeminentia nostra: quinimò ob concitatum in nos omnium timorem & existimationem non dubitamus quandoq; pro maiori securitate, etiam adversus ipsos Pontifices, ex redionis zelo, calamos & linguam stringere: singulariter verò, si interesse, vel emolumentum Magnatum quorundam, quorum in nos beneficia constant, interveniat. Econtra negatum est, qui adversus Nos, auctoritatem Pontificiam regentes, quidquam proferre ausit. Astris enim oppugnatus pro haeretico & schismatico ab omnibus habebitur: sicut cæli gratiâ etiam sacrosanctos & inviolabiles nos conservemus.
units.tr: Nor indeed are we bound as though tied by that vow, nor is our liberty or pre-eminence diminished by it; rather, on account of the fear and esteem for us that has been stirred up in everyone, we do not hesitate, at times, for greater security, to sharpen our pens and tongues even against the Pontiffs themselves, out of zeal for the cause; and especially if the interest or advantage of certain great men, by whom benefits to us are secured, is involved. On the other hand, whoever dares to put forward anything against us, while ruling the papal authority, is forbidden. For he will be regarded by all as a heretic and a schismatic if he is attacked; just as, by the grace of heaven, we keep ourselves sacrosanct and inviolable.

units.la: De Oeconomia et Regimine
units.tr: Of Economy and Government

units.la: Quod si forsan animus alicui non fuerit, gravioribus Mundi negocijs se immiscere, aut Principum sectando familiaritatem, incertam subire fortunā, arbitrij sui erit in quaDomo aut Collegio sibi quàm maximè placuerit, felicissimā frui quiete, & in Ecclesijs sermocinādo, pietatem in hominum timidorum, & mulierculārum devotarum pectoribus fovere: quod ipsum maiore quoq; honorem & comodum ei coparabit. Nam si eos, qui peccata sua illi confitentur, recensione rerum terribiliū, & miraculorū à Patrib. nostris ad hoc collectorum, in officio, ut à peccatis abstineant, continuerit, tum de facultatib. & personis eorum disponet, in honorem Dei, quomodocunq; ipsi placuerit.
units.tr: But if perhaps someone has no inclination to meddle in the weightier affairs of the world, or to seek the favour of princes and undergo their uncertain fortune, it will be left to his own judgment to enjoy the most happy quiet in whatever house or college pleases him best, and, by preaching in the churches, to cherish piety in the breasts of timid men and devout little women. This will also bring him greater honour and profit. For if he keeps those who confess their sins to him in the duty of abstaining from sin, by recounting terrible things and miracles collected for this purpose by our Fathers, then he may dispose of their goods and persons in whatever way pleases him, for the honour of God.

units.la: Ac tametsi sanctus hic zelus ex malitiosa interpretatione finistrè accipiatur, & pastim spargatur, Nos eandē rem diversimodè huic atq; illi referentes, discordia & lites differnare inter maritū & uxorem, patrē & liberos, fratres & cognatos; atq; hac ratione ad trucinā confiliorū nostrorū suspectos habentes privatos, Civitates, & integra Regna, dominiū Nos & absolutam tyrannidem in quoslibet usurpare: omninò tamen actiones illæ reprehendi nequaquam possunt, cum omne id ad animarum salutem fit directum, Nosq; in hoc conformes reddamur verbo Evangelico, quod habet: Non veni mittere pacem, sed gladium. Venì enim separare hominem adversus patrem suum, & filiam adversus matrem suam. Unde pro errore habendum non est, loqui aut tractare contradictoria, & cognatorum ac civium animos disjungere, dummodo id totum ad utilitatem cedat Ecclesiæ, & sanctæ Sedis; in cuius servitio & magnitudine vera pietas summaq; Religio consistit.
units.tr: Although this holy zeal is taken amiss through malicious interpretation and rumours are spread about it, we, by reporting the same matter in different ways to this person and that, sow discord and quarrels between husband and wife, father and children, brothers and kinsmen. In this way, holding private individuals under suspicion of our cruel designs, we usurp dominion and absolute tyranny over whoever we like, over cities and whole kingdoms. Yet those actions can by no means be reproved, since all of it is directed to the salvation of souls, and in this we are made conformable to the word of the Gospel, which says: "I came not to send peace but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother." Hence it should not be considered an error to speak or act in contradictory ways and to divide the minds of kinsmen and fellow citizens, provided that all of it turns to the advantage of the Church and the holy See, in whose service and greatness true piety and the highest religion consist.

units.la: Et ut scrupulos aliquot, qui ex vulgi obmurmurationibus mentib. aliquorum iniecti esse possent, illis eximā, advertere eos volo, quod cum primarij Domini, & nobilissimæ civitatum matronæ, ex devotione sua ad Ecclesias nostras concurrant, tum invidi bonum in malum detorquentes, id singulari artificio nostro fieri dicant, & hac illac disseminent, quod in Confessionibus audiendis difficiles quidem plebeijs atq; pauperibus nos exhibeamus, eosq; à nobis fugemus, in absolutionibus rigidi, in reprehensionibus asperi, & in poenitentia iniungenda intolerabiles. Adversus divites autem, & mulieres viduas, aut coniugatas aliter procedentes, parvulā aut nullā indictā poenitentiā, saepe etiam absq; auriculari confessione, solâ schedulâ consignatorum errorum inspectâ, gravissima eis peccata remittamus, exigendo à quolibet poenitente generalem confessionem, licet à Deo non mandatam, haud minus tamen animarum salutì necessariam, ut naturalibus poenitentium inclinationibus detectis, peccata eorum conformiter iustificare, atq; his rebus uti eis ac frui permittere liceat, quas a Religiosi nunquam concesserint.
units.tr: And so that I may remove some scruples which might have been put into the minds of some by the murmurings of the common people, I wish them to note this: when the chief lords and the noblest matrons of the cities flock to our churches out of their devotion, then our envious rivals turn the good into evil and say, and spread here and there, that we show ourselves, by a singular artifice of ours, difficult in hearing confessions to the common folk and the poor, and flee from them; that we are harsh in absolutions, rough in rebukes, and intolerable in imposing penance. But toward the rich and toward women, whether widowed or married, who approach us in a different way, we impose little or no penance, often even without auricular confession, merely by inspecting a little schedule of the errors they have written down, and we remit their most grievous sins.
