We demand from every penitent a general confession, although not commanded by God, yet no less necessary for the salvation of souls, so that, once the natural inclinations of the penitents have been uncovered, we may accordingly absolve their sins, and permit them to use and enjoy those things which the Religious never allowed. [The rivals say this.]

units.la: Magnam verò illam patientiam, quam imbecillis mulierum animis à scrupulis & superstitionibus, quibus naturaliter subiecta sunt, expurgandis sustinemus, malevolis malitiosè interpretantes, Nos cum illis ajunt, longis & frequentibus solere uti alloquijs, quibus ita mediantibus, quicquid desiderauerimus modò, ab ipsis obtineamus, & silentio earum sanctissimis Sacramentis confirmato, illis nos spirituali matrimonio devinciamus, in id incumbentes, ut ubiq; velut examina Vrsularum, Clericatarum, Diaconissarum appareant: quibus etiam in casu magnæ cuiusdam necessitatis ut sanctissima Sacramenta administrare possint, concedamus, idonea ad hoc inventa à nobis repræsentatione, per quam licitum illis fit, loco hostiæ apprehendenda, toreuma quoddam consecratum, & ad formam Agni Dei effigiatum Sororibus in conventiculis suis osculandum porrigere: quo ipso eas vinculis hisce nostris invicem coniunctas teneamus, & sanctæ Sedi in casu politicæ resistentiæ strictissimè obligatas, in tantum, ut hæc earum devotio secreto habeatur, atque ipsos etiam maritos, parentes, liberos & alios conjunctos latere at. Id quod summa utilitate, emergente non itapridem occasione, usurpatum quidem fuit, tandem tamen aliqua ex parte in lucem prorupit ob penetrantem æmulorum nostrorum sagacitatem, & simplicem devotarum istarum animularum confidentiam, a oraculis consiliorum nostrorum longè disitarum, & necessario fragilitatis suæ fulcro pri Vatarum. Cæteroquin, ubicunq;, etiam cōmorentur, non est quod metuamus, ne actiones nostræ unam propalentur: siquidem, cum Magnatibus duntaxat commercium habeamus, à quibus, præter quotidiana honoraria, omne publicum secretum cognoscimus. Ita fit, ut vel proprium honor ipsis os occludat: contrario plane modo, quàm aliis Religiosis usu venire solet: qui ne discrimine cum quolibet conversantes, absq; sanctis hisce artificijs difficulter possint fragilitatem suam occultare. Verum etiam hæ nebulæ facile dissipari queunt: quoniam & as, & omnes alias operationes nostras cum mysterio peragimus: quandoquidem in pauperem plebeculam non ea cadit peccatorum qualitas, aut gravitas casuum, ad quorum resolutionem opus sit singulari & exacto intellectu, aut discursus profunditate: sed delicta illa vulgares quidam errores sunt & consueti; quibus cum à quovis Fraterculo satisfieri possit, ingratum sane divinæ majestati fuerit, si elaboratæ operæ nostræ in his inutiliter consumerentur. Et quamvis confitentibus nobis, asperos nos atque severos exhibeamus; tamen hoc non ad repellendos eos fit, sed ut ordinariorum sive consuetorum peccatorum persi à gravioribus abstineant. Id quod divitibus non usu venit, qui ob facultatum & negotiorum publicorum, in quibus versantur, tractationem, multis scrupulis & dubitationib. periculosis sunt suppositi: ideoque in magnam animarum ipsorum utilitatem vergit, si à viris doctis & sapientibus, prout sunt Patres nostri, examinentur & corrigantur. Qua de causa libenter eos ad Ecclesias nostras recipimus & leniter tractamus, ne ad desperationem adigantur, sed potius, ut ex opibus illis, quæ ipsis peccandi causam præbuerunt, largas eleemosynas domibus & Ecclesiis nostris facientes, & cœlum lucrantes, à via, quæ eos ad infernum ducturæ erat, declinent. Sic & adversus fœminas, propter sexus fragilitatem mire & absque rigore procedimus: & quò facilius eas ad divinorum præceptorum obedientiam perducamus, res quasdam parvi momenti ijs permitti solent, dummodo id quod est est cognoscentes, tanquam creaturæ Dei, debitas ei gratias reddant. Sed neque ab viris aut illis confessionem generalem exigimus, ut appetitui eorum obsecundemus, sed potius, ut pravi illi affectus, & mala inclinationes naturæ detegantur; quibus postea um discretione, & quidem suam cuilibet singulatim medicinam applicamus; non vero ut veteres illi Religiosi, omnibus confusim peccatoribus idem remedium adhibemus. Modus profecto salutaris, & à Deo, ad exaltationem fidei suæ, nobis revelatus: cum quo detectis etiam animis resolutis & fortibus, multoties eos, mediante Camera Meditationum nostrarum (quarum secreta revelare non est licitum) ad internecionem hæreticorum & inobedientium inimicorum sanctæ Sedis Romanæ confultò exstimulavimus; & quidem non privatorum tantum, verum etiam magnorum Principum & Regum; heroicis ijs factis boni illius Ahodi, de quo in sacra Scriptura legitur, figuram repræsentantes, & immortali cum laude congregationis nostræ, sedes Paradisi Sanctis atque Martyribus complentes. Cuirei testimonio esse queunt multæ effigies, quæ variis typis pæneis passim videntur impressæ.
units.tr: But that great patience which we show in cleansing the weak minds of women of the scruples and superstitions to which they are naturally subject, they maliciously twist, saying that we, as they claim, are accustomed to use long and frequent addresses, by means of which, whatever we desire, we then obtain from them; and that, with their silence confirmed by the most holy Sacraments, we bind them to us by a spiritual marriage, labouring so that everywhere, like swarms of Ursulines, Clericatae and Deaconesses, they appear. To them too, in case of some great necessity, we grant that they may administer the most holy Sacraments, having devised for this purpose a suitable representation by which it is permitted to them, instead of taking hold of the host, to hold out to their Sisters in their little conventicles to kiss a consecrated little image, shaped like the Lamb of God. By this very means we keep them bound to us by these ties, and strictly obliged to the holy See in case of political resistance, to such a degree that this devotion of theirs is kept secret, and is hidden even from their husbands, parents, children, and other relatives. This was indeed used to great advantage when an occasion arose not long ago, yet at last it broke out to some extent into the light, through the penetrating shrewdness of our rivals and the simple trust of those devout little souls, who are far removed from the oracles of our counsels and are left to the support of their own frailty. Otherwise, wherever they may dwell, there is no reason for us to fear that our actions will be made public, since we have dealings only with the great, from whom, besides daily honours, we learn every public secret. Thus it comes about that their very honour shuts their mouths, in the plain opposite of what usually happens to other Religious, who, to avoid mixing with anyone at risk, can scarcely hide their frailty without these holy devices. Indeed, even these clouds can easily be dispelled, since we carry out both confession and all our other operations in secret. For the poor common folk do not have such a quality of sins, or such gravity of cases, as need a singular and exact understanding, or depth of reasoning, for their resolution; those offences are rather certain common and customary errors, which can be atoned for by any little Brother, and it would surely be displeasing to the divine majesty if our elaborate labour were wasted uselessly on these. And although we show ourselves harsh and severe to those who confess to us, yet this is not done to repel them, but so that they may abstain from the graver sins by means of the ordinary or customary ones. This does not happen to the rich, who, because of the management of their property and public business in which they are engaged, are subject to many dangerous scruples and doubts; so it tends greatly to the benefit of their souls if they are examined and corrected by learned and wise men, such as our Fathers are. For this reason we willingly receive them into our churches and treat them gently, lest they be driven to despair, but rather, so that by making generous almsgiving to our houses and churches from those riches which provided them with a cause of sinning, they may gain heaven and turn aside from the road that was going to lead them to hell. Thus we also proceed toward women with wonderful gentleness and without severity, on account of the frailty of their sex; and so that we may more easily bring them to obedience to the divine precepts, certain matters of little importance are usually allowed to them, provided that they recognise what is, as creatures of God, and render due thanks to him. But neither do we demand a general confession from men or from them, so that we may yield to their appetites; rather, so that those perverse affections and evil inclinations of nature may be uncovered, to each of which, afterwards, with discretion, we apply its own remedy one by one. We do not, as those old Religious did, apply the same remedy indiscriminately to all sinners. This is surely a salutary method, revealed to us by God for the exaltation of our faith; by means of which, once the resolute and brave spirits have been uncovered, we have often, through our Chamber of Meditations (whose secrets it is not lawful to reveal), deliberately stirred them up to the destruction of heretics and of disobedient enemies of the Roman holy See, and not only of private persons but even of great Princes and Kings, representing by those heroic deeds the figure of that good Ehud, of whom we read in Holy Scripture, and, to the immortal praise of our Society, filling the seats of Paradise with Saints and Martyrs. Many images bear witness to this, which are seen printed here and there in various almost-pictorial types.

units.la: Et sane quilibet commemoratorum virorum atque mulierum de sanctissimis Sacramentis non alibi, quàm in nostris Ecclesijs debebat participare & confessionem exercere: ibi præter facultatem & privilegia, quibus à quavis culpa quilibet expiari potest, à summis Pontificibus concessa, facile habituri essent modum animas suas salvandi: modum nquam, à nobis inventum, qui in propria solummodo voluntatis privatione, & in hoc consistit, ut absque laboriosa requisitione alterius, sequatur quis eius præcepta, qui propter ipsum studijs insudat & defatigatur: id quod Patres hi spirituales faciunt. Et quidem omnne peccandi periculum hoc modo tollitur, non visi aut cognito ab alijs Religiosis, qui in veteri illa simplicitate educati, dum pænitentes suos in libertate relinquunt, parum semper profecerunt, atque etiam nunc proficient.
units.tr: And indeed each of the men and women mentioned ought to have received the most holy Sacraments and made confession nowhere but in our churches. There, besides the faculty and privileges, by which anyone may be cleansed of any fault, granted by the highest Pontiffs, they would easily have the means of saving their souls: a means invented by us, which consists solely in the surrender of one's own will, and in this, that without laborious inquiry of another, one follows the precepts of him who toils and wearies himself for that very purpose. This is what those spiritual Fathers do. And indeed every danger of sinning is removed in this way, a thing not seen or known by other Religious, who, brought up in that old simplicity, while they leave their penitents in liberty, have always made little progress, and still do make little progress.

units.la: Ac licet à Politicis, atque alijs mundi huius sapientibus hæc nostra doctrina hæresis dicatur, non tamen hoc illorum dicterium in ullam considerationem trahendum est; cum videamus illam ab Episcopis, Cardinalibus, & omnibus Pontificibus approbatam esse. Et ut concludam, quod plus, quam nulla res alia eos relevat, qui Ecclesias nostras frequentantes sanctam istam obedientiam amplectuntur; id vero est, quod participes fiunt innumerabilium meritorum, quae divina Majestas sufficientia esse indicat, non solum ad tollendum delicta jam praeterita, sed ad cancellandum, vel annihilandum ea, quae in posterum committi possent, & ad redimendum quamcunque animam, quae ad purgatorium fuerat condemnata.
units.tr: Although the Politicians and others wise in this world call our doctrine heresy, their taunt should not be taken into any account, since we see it approved by Bishops, Cardinals and all the Popes. To conclude: nothing benefits those who attend our churches and embrace this holy obedience more than this, that they become sharers in the countless merits which the divine Majesty judges sufficient not only to remove sins already committed, but to cancel or annul those that might be committed in future, and to redeem any soul that has been condemned to purgatory.

units.la: Nolim vero aliquem vereri, ne commemorata commoda & honores settaturus, in difficultatem aliquam offendat: quandoquidem viae, quae in Societate nostra ad eos ducunt, ita tritae, & tanta cum prudentia accommodatae sunt, ut quilibet absque vacillatione ulla eorum obtinendorum atque fruendorum spem habere possit. Ibi enim assidue de Verbis & Rebus tractatur: & quicquid vel publicum vel privatum ad aures nostras pervenerit, de eo consultatur: nec quisquam ulli rei unquam adhibetur, nisi examinata prius natura eius, & perpenso talento eius a Patre Generali (qui omnibus exploratis signa & notas exquisitas distinctas habet) aptus ad eam perficiendam deprehendatur. Admonitio postea illius, quod hoc vel illo die dignum consideratione occurrit, detegitur id ei familiaribus colloquiis nostris, aut per confessionem nobis devotorum. De eo nam conferentes inter nos, & literas a Collegio ad Collegium scriptas, ei quod sequuturum est, aut sequi poterat, anticipando femper obviamus, in quemcunque casum praparati. Eiusmodi considerationibus aut collationibus, quibus nullum dubium remanet indecisum, Seniores & sapientissimi, quos habemus, Rectores assistunt, qui in qua vis materia quam maxime versati definiunt, quomodo viris & mulieribus, viduis aut maritatis, obsequium & beneficentia erga Collegia, & particulatim etiam erga nos ipsos debeat persuaderi, quomodo itidem paradisi iter ingrediendum fit, ac qua ratione Principum gratia quis insinuetur, quibus medijs voluntas eorum capetur, & quibus in possessionem animi & opinionis populorum perveniatur.
units.tr: I would not want anyone to fear that, in seeking the advantages and honours mentioned, he will meet some difficulty. The paths that lead to them in our Society are so well trodden and so prudently arranged that anyone may hope to obtain and enjoy them without any hesitation. For there, words and things are constantly discussed: whatever comes to our ears, whether public or private, is deliberated upon, and no one is ever assigned to any task until his nature has been examined and his talent weighed by the Father General, who has the exact signs and marks of everyone he has tested, and until he is found fit to carry it out. Afterwards, the matter that occurs on this or that day as worthy of consideration is revealed to him, either in our familiar conversations or through confession by those devoted to us. Conferring together about it, and about letters written from college to college, we always anticipate what will or may follow, prepared for every case. Senior and very wise Rectors, whom we have, attend these deliberations and conferences, in which no doubt is left undecided. Those who are most experienced in any subject define how men and women, widows or married, ought to be persuaded to show obedience and generosity towards the colleges and, in particular, towards ourselves; likewise how the way to paradise is to be entered; by what means someone may be introduced into the favour of princes; by what means their will may be captured; and by what means one may gain possession of the minds and opinion of the people.

units.la: Laborent sane in hoc inimici nostri coelestis voluntatis ignari, & obloquantur, Nos hisce regulis & rationibus damnum privatorum Domibus & Principatibus huius mundi adferre. Alij quidem, dum afferunt, Nos re[illegible, ~3 letters] orribilium commemoratione, quas simplicioribus pro concione in templis, & domi animam jam exhalaturis ingerimus, nosmetipsos & Collegia nostra ditantes, debita haereditate liberos & parentes eorum spoliari. Alij vero, quod simulata quadam servitute Principes Christiani ad instantiam Ecclesiasticae Majestatis, fidei nostrae se committentes, imprudentibus consilijs quandoque eos redigantur, ut & statum & vitam perdant. Singularem vero pietatem illam, quae pro auctoritate sanctae Sedis dilatanda exercetur, improbi illi Politici traditionum & rebellionum a nobis perpetratarum nomine denigrantes, mundo exosam reddere fatigentur sane, affirmantes scilicet, praedicationes, & divitiarum atque laudum praemia, ad haereticos exstirpandos a nobis inventa, proditorios esse modos adversus Principes, & voces adulatrices, quibus veluti sanctitatis & Martyriorum involucro quoda parricidia obtegamus. Exclament, sed falso, Nos per has ipsas destructionum vias, contra veram Iesu fidem, Iesuitarum nomen mereri, per quas Scipio Carthaginensium Imperium evertens, Africani nomen consecutus fit. Caeterum re tota prout decet, considerata liquet, pro peccato istud nequaquam haberi posse, sed veram demum pietatem esse, quae in Catholica Romana Ecclesia commodum, animarumque ei devotarum servitium resultat. Inprimis enim non inconveniens est, ut pater propria salutis gratia filium, & cognatus cognatum haereditate privet, eo quod ex Evangelica doctrina quilibet animae suae magis, quam patri, matri, aut liberis fit obligatus. Atque ita opus quoque erit meritorium, si subditi eius Principis, qui de juris dictione sua, & comodo subditorum magis, quam animae salute solicitus, Pontificijs praeceptis obedire recusat, fidelitatis juramento exsolvantur, sijsdem significetur, quadoquidem ipsi met se regere nequeant, ut alij Principi Catholico, qui quidem obsequens sit, aut Romano Pontifici confoederatus, adhaereant. Ac si propter inobedientis illius principis potentiam & robur ad eiusmodi apertas declarationes perveniri non poterit: tum legibus Canonicis & sanctissimi [illegible, ~20 letters]tissimis Decretalibus minimè erit contrarium, occultè eum, peccatorum absolutio-
units.tr: Surely our enemies, who are ignorant of God's heavenly will, labour at this and complain that we use these rules and methods to bring harm to private households and to the princes of this world. Some of them argue that we enrich ourselves and our colleges by recounting horrible things in sermons in the churches, and at home to simple people who are about to breathe their last, and that thus children and parents are robbed of their rightful inheritance. Others say that Christian princes, committing themselves to our faith under a pretended servitude at the urging of ecclesiastical majesty, are sometimes led by imprudent counsels to lose both their state and their lives. Those wicked politicians, blackening that remarkable piety which is practised to extend the authority of the holy See with the charge of treasons and rebellions committed by us, labour hard to make it hateful to the world. They assert, of course, that the preaching, the rewards of riches and praise which we have devised for rooting out heretics, are treacherous methods against princes, and flattering words by which we cover parricides under a kind of cloak of holiness and martyrdom. They cry out, but falsely, that through these very paths of destruction we earn the name of Jesuits against the true faith of Jesus, just as Scipio, overthrowing the empire of the Carthaginians, obtained the name of Africanus. Yet when the whole matter is considered as it deserves, it is clear that this can by no means be held to be a sin, but is rather true piety, which results in the advantage of the Roman Catholic Church and in the service of the souls devoted to her. For first, it is not unfitting that a father should deprive his son, or a kinsman his kinsman, of an inheritance for the sake of his own salvation, since by evangelical doctrine each person is bound more to his own soul than to father, mother or children. And so it will also be a meritorious work if the subjects of that prince, who, anxious for his own jurisdiction and the advantage of his subjects rather than for their soul's salvation, refuses to obey Papal commands, are released from the oath of allegiance, and it is made known to them that, since they cannot govern themselves, they should attach themselves to another Catholic prince who is obedient to, or allied with, the Roman Pontiff. And if, on account of the power and strength of that disobedient prince, such open declarations cannot be made, then it is by no means contrary to the Canon laws and the most holy Decretals that he be secretly removed from life,

units.la: ne aut premio interfectoribus proposito, vita tollere: afferente idipsum etiam doctissi-
units.tr: by the absolution of sins, or by a reward offered to the killers

units.la: mo historico nostro Ioanne Mariana in quodam tractatu suo ad magnum Hispaniae Re-gem; ubi venena, & horum compositiones, tanquam tutissima media proponens, conclu-
units.tr: as our historian Juan de Mariana also affirms, in a certain treatise of his addressed to the great King of Spain; where, proposing poisons and their preparations as the safest means, he concludes

units.la: dit, in eum finem ipsa venena ita praeparata, cuilibet bono Catholico semper in promptuesse debere. Atque in Sacro Sanctis Bibliis exemplo Ieroboami & aliorum legitur, quàmgraviter Reges & populi dilecti à Sacerdotibus & Prophetis, propter inobedientiamafflicti fuerint. Quin imò maximam in populi utilitatem cessurum esset, si pestifero semine Politicorum sublato, & temporali dominio cum spirituali conjuncto, solummodò ànobis Ecclesiasticis regerentur & gubernarentur: sic enim maiori cum pietate forent tractati. Atque hic mentis conceptus à Patribus nostris ubique locorum praedicatus, non minùs quam articulus fidei debuerat observari; quandoquidem alij quidem flectunt, nos autem pro salute eorum semper vigilamus. Atque hoc est prudentissimum Regimen, & Respub. Societatis nostrae, nunquam à Philosopho aliquo tam perfectè descripta, sed à celeberrimo illo Ignatio Loyola miraculosè fundata.
units.tr: that poisons prepared in such a way ought always to be ready to hand for any good Catholic for that very purpose. And in the Holy Scriptures we read, in the example of Jeroboam and others, how grievously kings and beloved peoples were afflicted by priests and prophets because of disobedience. Indeed, it would turn to the greatest advantage of the people if, with the pestilent seed of the politicians removed and temporal dominion joined to spiritual, they were ruled and governed by us ecclesiastics alone; for thus they would be treated with greater piety. And this notion, preached everywhere by our Fathers, ought to have been observed no less than an article of faith, since others indeed bend, while we always watch over their salvation. And this is the most prudent government and commonwealth of our Society, never so perfectly described by any philosopher, but miraculously founded by that most famous man Ignatius Loyola.

units.la: FINIS LIBRI PRIMI.
units.tr: END OF THE FIRST BOOK.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE ET INCREMENTIS OR- DINIS IESVITIC- I. Liber Secundus. CAPVT I.
units.tr: On the Propagation and Growth of the Jesuit Order. Book Two, Chapter 1.

units.la: IESVITAE, serpentum in morem, initio terrae pulverem effitabant, & summa inopia adacti solum solo identidem vertere cogebantur. Romae enim ut excepti fuerint primo, supra indicavimus.
units.tr: The Jesuits, like serpents, at first crept along the dust of the earth, and, driven by extreme poverty, were constantly compelled to turn over one piece of ground after another. For, as we have shown above, they were first received at Rome.

units.la: Irrepsere autem primum in gratiam hominum, eosque in suam admirationem pertraxerunt diligentia & solicitudine sua in aegrorum morbis curandis, vulneribus obligandis, & molesta, gravi ac putida sanie abstergenda.
units.tr: They first crept into the favour of men, and drew people to their own admiration by their diligence and care in treating the sicknesses of the sick, binding up wounds, and cleansing away foul, grievous and putrid matter.

units.la: Secundo, auscultandis confessionibus, unde miserè victum suum excerpebant.
units.tr: Second, by hearing confessions, from which they miserably scraped together their living.

units.la: Mox ubi paululum firmitatis accessit, pueros sine mercede docendos & erudiendos susceperunt: quo artificio non vulgarem vulgi favorem emeruere, criminandis praesertim aliis doctoribus, quorum doctrina venalis esset, & scholae nulli sine mercede paterent; ac interdum etiam doctrina peregrina personarent. Incredibile dictu est, quantum haec criminatio valuerit. Inprimis, ut facile est in magna piscium multitudine rete suum implere; sic etiam in hac iuvenum frequentia Iesuitis facile fuit continuo aliquos institutis suis implicare. Ea etenim est aetas hodie, quae blanditiis simul & doctrinae admiratione permovetur, & propediem ad operam navandam praesto esse potest. Ac reliquorum quidem Monachorum in hoc a Iesuitis emendatus est error, qui pusiones vix dum e cunabulis egressos ad se admiserunt, totosque quindecim aut viginti annos nutrierunt, antequam ad praxin eos admovere possent. Hoc sagaces & solertes animadvertentes Iesuitae, suos in eo aetatis flexu intercipiunt, qui iam ad adultam vergit.
units.tr: Soon, when a little strength had come to them, they undertook to teach and train boys without payment. By this device they won no small popularity with the common people, chiefly by slandering other teachers, whose teaching was for sale, and whose schools were open to no one without payment; and sometimes they even disparaged foreign learning. It is incredible to say how much this slander availed. Chiefly, just as it is easy to fill one's net in a great multitude of fish, so in this crowd of young people it was easy for the Jesuits to entangle some of them at once in their institutes. For this is the age of today, which is moved both by flattery and by admiration for learning, and which can soon be ready to be put to work. And indeed the error of the other monks has been corrected by the Jesuits in this respect: they admitted to themselves boys scarcely out of the cradle, and nourished them for fifteen or twenty whole years before they could bring them into practice. The Jesuits, being shrewd and skilful, noticed this and seize their people at that turning point of age which is already drawing towards adulthood.

units.la: Firmato autem & communito a Pontificibus Romanis Iesuitarum Ordine ac vitae instituto, per omnes se Italiae urbes Iesuitae spargebant, & mox ubicumque in ea regione collegia eis aedificabantur. Inprimis autem Romae sedes suas fixerunt, superstitionum & errorum omnium matre seu officina. Tria enim ibi collegia exstruxerunt Iesuitae, unum pro se, alterum pro Anglis, tertium pro Germanis. Nam Ioannes Moronius & Episcopus Praenestinus, qui in Tridentina Synodo legatus fuit Pontificis & Synodi praeses, consilium communicavit cum Ignatio, quanto usui esse posset Ecclesiae Pontificiae, si Romae amplissimum Collegium exstrueretur, in quo maxima Germanorum multitudo in bonis literis & religione, sumptibus Pontificis institueretur, ut tandem in patriam redeuntes, col, collapsam & conculcatam Pontificiam religionem ibi instaurare aliquâ ex re possent. Opus igitur illud aggressi sunt Iesuitae anno Domini 1553. ex: ucto tali Collegio Romae non procul à suorum Collegio. Adolescentes vero ermanos, narrant Payva Andradius & Surius, in illud Collegium assumi, ut cooptentur tandem in ordinem Iesuiticum, sed Iesuitas tantum alendi illos, moderandi & instituendi curam gerere, & ad hunc laborem suscipiendum, illum Germaniae salutis desiderio fuisse incitatos, ut per istos emissarios Germaniam ad gremium, vel si hoc nimium est, ad oscula pedum Romani Pontificis ulatim reduceretur.
units.tr: Then, once the Order of the Jesuits and their way of life had been established and fortified by the Roman Pontiffs, the Jesuits spread through all the cities of Italy, and soon colleges were built for them wherever in that region. But above all they fixed their seats at Rome, the mother and workshop of all superstitions and errors. For the Jesuits built three colleges there: one for themselves, another for the English, and a third for the Germans. For John Morone and the Bishop of Palestrina, who was the Pontiff's legate at the Council of Trent and president of the Council, communicated a plan with Ignatius: how greatly it might serve the Papal Church if a very large College were built at Rome, in which a great multitude of Germans would be instructed in good letters and religion at the Pontiff's expense, so that, returning at last to their homeland, they might in some way be able to restore there the fallen and trampled Papist religion. The Jesuits therefore undertook that work in the year of the Lord 1553, and the College was built not far from the College of their own people. Payva Andrada and Surius relate that the young Germans are taken into that College so that they may eventually be enrolled in the Jesuit order; but that the Jesuits have only the care of feeding, governing and instructing them, and that these men were stirred to undertake this labour by a desire for the salvation of Germany, so that through these emissaries Germany might be led back, at once, to the bosom, or if this is too much, to the kissing of the feet of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Mirum autem videri nemini debet, Italos tanto animorum & corporum impetu hoc novum sodalitium iam olim excepisse, & adhuc hodie fovere ac in stupore admirari. Nam, ut omnia fere sua ipsorum monumenta testantur, semper fuerunt & etiamnum hodie sunt, ex naturali quadam ad hypocrisim imitatione, ad Deorum multitudinem colendam, & ad omnes, quantumvis profanas atque horrendas superstitiones recipiendas, prae caeteris fere omnibus tionibus propensiores. Ex quo fornicationis poculo permulta in Christianam religionem transfuderunt, eamque fere totam veneno mortifero infecerunt, quo huc maxima pars orbis Christiani, suavitate, dulcedine, antiquitate & pulchritudine ipsius illecta deceptaque inebriatur validissime.
units.tr: Nor should it seem strange to anyone that the Italians have long since received this new fraternity with such impetus of minds and bodies, and still today cherish it and admire it with wonder. For, as nearly all their own monuments attest, they always were, and even today still are, more inclined than almost all other nations, by a certain natural imitation of hypocrisy, to worship a multitude of gods and to receive all superstitions, however profane and horrible. From this cup of fornication they have poured very many things into the Christian religion, and have almost wholly infected it with deadly poison, so that the greatest part of the Christian world, enticed and deceived by its sweetness, charm, antiquity and beauty, is most strongly intoxicated.

units.la: Ex Italia recta in Hispanias Iesuitae suas duxerunt colonias. Erat enim rca initium confirmationis huius Ordinis Romae Petrus Mazcarenhas, à Iohanne Tertio, Lusitaniae Rege ad Pontificem Orator, qui multum cum Pontifice egit, ut ex viris illis, quorum tunc adhuc pauci numero erant, duos in Lusitaniam mitteret: quo tandem impetrato, profecti sunt illuc Franciscus Xavier, Simon Roderícus anno Christi 1541, ubi à Rege totoque populo, sicut & a in reliqua Hispania humanissime excepti, & ubivis locorum in ea gente certa in Collegia eis exstructa fuerunt, nec ullo in loco hodie maiori cum studio foventur. Nam vulgo in Hispania & Lusitania Apostoli & Apostolici viri etiamnum odie nuncupantur.
units.tr: From Italy the Jesuits led their colonies straight into Spain. For at the beginning of the confirmation of this Order at Rome there was Pedro Mascarenhas, ambassador of John III, King of Portugal, to the Pontiff, who dealt much with the Pontiff so that he would send two of those men, who were then still few in number, into Portugal. When this was at last obtained, Francis Xavier and Simon Rodriguez set out there in the year of Christ 1541, where they were received most kindly by the King and the whole people, as also in the rest of Spain, and in every place in that nation colleges were built for them, nor is the Order fostered with greater zeal in any place today. For commonly in Spain and Portugal they are still called Apostles and apostolic men today.

units.la: Neque mirum: nam gentis huius homines plus quam fervilliter in Romaa religione nascuntur, educantur, instituuntur & confirmantur, nec alibi fere bsequentiores & ferventiores filios habet Romana Ecclesia. Tanta enim apud eos fit de fide & religione Romana Inquisitio, tamque arcta, ne inde avolet, servata tenetur custodia, ut nisi ipsi filij ad parètes suos, haeresefos damnatos, exurendos, allatis propria ex domo lignis, carnificem adiuvent, ipsique propemodum parentum carnifices exi stant, haeretici fere ab omnibus iudicentur, eodemque ligni supplicio censeantur. Ex quo certe necesse est Hispanos superstitiosos exsadere, actusque religionis externos multiplicare, & vel mortuos fidem Romanam spirare: ne si minus multa religionis suae signa dederint, suspecti extemplo de fide reddantur, & in tertiam ac quartam usque generationem crudelissime exruciati puniantur. Accedit huic, quod ab antiquis temporibus Marani, seu infideles nuncupati sunt Hispani, quippe à quibus prognati fuerunt. Ut igitur hanc calumniam à se depellant, in excessu peccant, & Iesuitis, tanquam Romanae Ecclesiae columnis, immensos honores exhibent & privilegia dant Hispani per universum suum regnum, imo aliquibus in locis magistratibus ipsis parere & obedire praecipiunt.
units.tr: This is no wonder: for the men of this nation are born, brought up, instructed and confirmed in the Roman religion more than slavishly, and the Roman Church has scarcely any more obedient and fervent sons elsewhere. For there is such an Inquisition about the faith and the Roman religion among them, and so strict a watch is kept lest anyone escape from it, that unless the sons themselves, bringing wood from their own house, help the executioner to burn their parents condemned for heresy, and almost become the executioners of their parents, the heretics are judged by nearly everyone and are reckoned worthy of the same death by fire. From this it is certainly necessary that the Spaniards be superstitious, multiply the external acts of religion, and even when dead breathe the Roman faith; lest, if they gave fewer signs of their religion, they should at once be suspected in the faith and be most cruelly tormented and punished down to the third and fourth generation. To this is added that from ancient times the Spaniards have been called Marranos, or unbelievers, since they were descended from them. So, in order to ward off this calumny from themselves, they sin in excess, and the Spaniards pay immense honours to the Jesuits, as to pillars of the Roman Church, and grant them privileges throughout their whole kingdom; indeed, in some places they command that the magistrates themselves obey and submit to them.

units.la: Ioannes Silicews tamen Archiepiscopus Toletanus in Hispania Iesuitarum acerrimus infestator fuit. Complutii in sua dioecesi Collegium ipsis repente exstructum, ita aegre ferebat, ut de Iesuitis à sua ditione pellendis, toto animo dies noctesque cogitaret. Quotquot è suo clero Iesuitis favere nollet, eos iuris in Ecclesia Toletana dicundi potestate privat: vetat etiam in Ecclesia Complu-
units.tr: Yet John Silíceo, Archbishop of Toledo, was the most bitter enemy of the Jesuits in Spain. When a College was suddenly built for them at Alcalá in his diocese, he took it so ill that day and night he thought with his whole mind about driving the Jesuits from his jurisdiction. Whichever of his clergy were unwilling to favour the Jesuits, he deprived of the power of exercising jurisdiction in the Church of Toledo; he also forbade anyone in the Church of Complu-

units.la: P tensi omnino quemquam à Iesuitis Ecclesiæ Sacramenta sumere. Quæ res in tota Hispania plurimorum animos vehementer commovit, ut qui existimarent, tantum Antistitem non sine gravi aliqua certáque ratione ita de Iesuitis statuisse.
units.tr: tense to receive the Sacraments at all from the Jesuits. This matter greatly stirred the minds of very many throughout Spain, so that they thought the bishop had not decided thus about the Jesuits without some grave and certain reason.

units.la: DE IESVITARVM ADVENTU, IN- CREMENTIS AC PROPAGATIONE IN GALLIA.
units.tr: On the Coming, Growth and Spread of the Jesuits in France.

units.la: IN Gallia vero non eadem facilitate, quâ ab Italis & Hispanis, Iesuitæ fuerunt cepti sunt. Cùm enim Episcopus Claromontanus Guilelmus de Prato eos Lutetiæ primùm, exiguo quidem numero, in Claromontium, quod ibi est Collegium, præ nimio erga illos favore, introduxisset, Anno Christi 1550. & moriens testamento ultra 60000. aureorum legâsset, eâ lege, ut Billonij & Mauriaci in Avernis Schola instituta iuventuti erudiendæ incuberent: ante Loyolæ morte Broetus in Gallia commendatione Caroli Lotharingi Cardinalis, cuius & nomen diplomati appositum est, ab Henrico II. impetraverat, ut iuxta Pontificium diploma Societas hæc in Gallia reciperetur, & Sodalibus ex eleemosynis ædes & Scholam Lutetiæ, non etiam in aliis urbibus construere, ibique iuxta normam Ordinis vivere liceret. Haud diu post supplicater à Parlamento conten-derunt, ut & in Regno hoc tolerarentur, & Societas hæc sub specie tám religiosi Ordinis, quàm Collegij tandem approbaretur. A Gallo-Francis vero tum quidem repulsam tulerunt.
units.tr: In France, however, the Jesuits did not find the easy welcome they had met with among the Italians and Spaniards. When Guillaume de Prato, Bishop of Clermont, first brought them to Paris and then, out of excessive favour toward them, introduced a small number of them into Clermont, where they set up a college, in the year of Christ 1550, and when he died he left them more than 60,000 gold pieces in his will, on the condition that they devote themselves to teaching youth through a school to be founded at Billom and Mauriac in Auvergne, then before Loyola's death Broët had obtained from Henry II, through the recommendation of Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, whose name was also appended to the document, that according to the papal diploma this Society should be received in France, and that the members might build a house and school from alms in Paris (but not in other cities) and live there according to the rule of the Order. Soon afterwards they petitioned the Parlement that they might be tolerated in this kingdom, and that this Society might at last be approved under the appearance both of a religious Order and of a college. But at that time they met with a rebuff from the Gallican French.

units.la: Post quatuor nihilominus annos, iterum ut admitterentur, supplicarunt. Cùm autem diploma, cuius paulo ante meminimus, in Curia lectum esset, 3. Non. Sextil. & id Procurator regius Noe Bruslardus vehementer oppugnaret, Parlamentum decrevit, ut regium ac Pontificium diploma, Episcopo Parisiensi, necnon Theologorum Parisiensium Collegio, hoc est, Sorbonæ communicaretur, quibus auditis de tota re decerneretur. Sorbona Anno 1554. Decemb. 1. multis in medium adductis rationibus firmissimis, evidentissimisque, hanc Iesuitarum petitionem omnibus modis aversata est, & vehementer impugnavit ac reiecit. Decretum autem hoc & sententia Sorbonæ de verbo ad verbum sic habet.
units.tr: Nevertheless, four years later they petitioned again to be admitted. When the diploma mentioned a little earlier was read in court on 3 August, and the royal procurator Noël Brulard strongly opposed it, the Parlement decreed that the royal and papal diplomas should be communicated to the Bishop of Paris and also to the college of the Parisian theologians, that is, to the Sorbonne, so that once their views had been heard, a decision might be made on the whole matter. On 1 December 1554 the Sorbonne, bringing forward many very firm and very evident arguments, rejected this petition of the Jesuits in every way, opposed it vigorously and refused it. The decree and judgement of the Sorbonne read word for word as follows.

units.la: Anno Domini 1554. die 1. Decemb. sacratissima Theologia Parisiensis, post Missam de Spiritu Sancto, in æde sacra Collegij Sorbonæ, ex more celebrata, jam quarto in eodé Collegio per juramentu congregata est, ad determinandum de duobus diplomatibus, quæ duo sanctissimi Dni Summi Pontifices Paulus 3. & Iulius 3. his qui Societatis Iesu nomine insignirí cupiunt, concessisse dicuntur. Quæ quidem diplomata, Senatus, seu Curia Parlamenti Parisiensis dictæ facultati visitanda & examinanda, misso ad rem Hostiario, comiserat. Antequam verò ipsa Theologiæ facultas, tanta de re, tantiq; ponderis tractare incipiat, omnes & singuli Magistri Nostri, palam atq; aperto ore professi sunt, nihil se adversus Summorum Pontificum authoritatem & potestatem, aut decernere, aut moliri, aut etiâ cogitare velle. Imò verò omnes & singuli, ut obedientiæ filij, ipsum Summum Pontificem, ut summum & universalem Christi Iesu Vicarium, & universalem Ecclesiæ Pastorem, cui plenitudo potestatis à Christo data sit, cui omnes utriusq; sexus obedire, cuius decreta venerari, & prosusquè tueri & observare teneantur, ut semper agnoverunt & confessi sunt, ita nunc quoque sincere, fideliter & libenter agnoscunt & confitentur. Sed quoniam omnes, præsertim verò Theologos, paratos esse oportet ad satisfactionem omni poscenti de his quæ ad fidem, mores, & ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ pertinent, dicta facultas, poscenti, mandanti & exigenti Curiæ prædictæ satisfaciendum duxit. Itaq; utriusq; Diplomatis omnibus frequenter lectis articulis, repetitis, & intellectis, & pro rei magnitudine per multos dies, menses & horas, pro more prius diligentissimè discussis & examinatis, tum demùm unanimi consensu, sed summa cum reverentia & humilitate, rem integrâ correctioni Sedis Apostolicæ relinquentes, ita censuit. Hæc nova Societas, insolitam nominis Iesu appellationem sibi vendicans, tam linter, & sine delectu quoslibet personas, quantum libet facinorosas, illegitimas & infames admittens, nullam à Sacerdotibus secularibus habens differentiam in habitu exteriore, in tonsura, in horis canonicis privatim dicendis, aut publice in templo decantandis, clausuris & silentio, in delectu ciborum & dierum, in jejuniis & aliis variis ceremoniis, quibus status Religionum distinguuntur & conservantur, tam multis, tamque variis privilegiis, indultis & libertatibus donata, præsertim in administratione Sacramenti Pœnitentiæ & Eucharistiæ, idque sine discrimine locorum, aut personarum, officio etiam prædicandi, legendi & docendi in præjudicium Ordinariorum, & Hierarchici Ordinis, in præjudicium quoque aliarum Religionum, imò etiam Principum & Dominorum temporalium, contra privilegia Universitatum, denique in magnum populi gravamen, Religionis Monasticæ honestatem violare videtur, studiosum, pium, & necessarium, virtutum, abstinentiarum & austeritatis enervat exercitium; imò occasionem dat liberè apostatandi ab aliis Religionibus, debitam Ordinariis obedientiam & subjectionem subtrahit, Dominos tam temporales quam Ecclesiasticos suis juribus injuste privat, perturbationem in utraque politia, multas in populo querelas, multas lites, dissidia, contentiones, æmulationes, rebelliones, variaque schismata inducit. Itaque his omnibus aliis diligenter examinatis & perpensis, HAEC SOCIETAS videtur in negotio periculosa, pacis Ecclesiasticæ perturbativa, Monasticæ religionis everfiva, & magis ad destructionem, quàm ad ædificationem. Interfuerunt huic Conventui Maillarus, Demochares, Perionius, & Ori Inquisitor fidei, &c. Procuratores fuerunt Benedictus Decanus & Courselles Subdecanus Theologiæ facultatis Parisiis; emque Faber Syndiac & Noe Brulardus; non Petrus Ramus & Mercerus, et Iesuitæ mentiuntur.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1554, on 1 December, the most sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris, after the Mass of the Holy Spirit had been celebrated in the sacred church of the Sorbonne college as is customary, and now gathered under oath for the fourth time in the same college, met to decide upon two diplomas which the two most holy Lords, the Supreme Pontiffs Paul III and Julius III, are said to have granted to those who wish to be known by the name of the Society of Jesus. The Senate, or Parlement of Paris, had committed these diplomas, by sending a usher for the purpose, to be visited and examined by the said Faculty. Before the Faculty of Theology itself begins to treat of so great a matter, of such weight, all and each of our Masters declared openly and with unveiled mouth that they wished to decree, attempt or even think nothing against the authority and power of the Supreme Pontiffs. Indeed, all and each, as obedient sons, have always acknowledged and confessed, and now likewise sincerely, faithfully and gladly acknowledge and confess, the Supreme Pontiff himself as the highest and universal Vicar of Jesus Christ and the universal Pastor of the Church, to whom plenary power has been given by Christ, and to whom all of either sex are bound to submit, whose decrees they are bound to venerate, and to uphold and observe most faithfully. But since all, and especially the theologians, ought to be ready to give satisfaction to anyone who asks about those things which pertain to faith, morals and the edification of the Church, the said Faculty judged that it ought to satisfy the aforesaid Court when it asked, commanded and required this. Therefore, when all the articles of both diplomas had been frequently read, repeated and understood, and had been discussed and examined most diligently, as is customary, over many days, months and hours, according to the weight of the matter, at last by unanimous consent, yet with the greatest reverence and humility, leaving the whole matter intact to the correction of the Apostolic See, it judged as follows. This new Society, claiming for itself the unusual appellation of the name of Jesus, admits indiscriminately to its membership any persons whatever, however criminal, illegitimate and infamous; it has no difference from secular priests in outward dress, in the tonsure, in the canonical hours to be said privately or sung publicly in the church, in enclosure and silence, in the choice of foods and days, in fasts and other various ceremonies by which the state of religious orders is distinguished and preserved; it has been endowed with so many and so various privileges, indults and liberties, especially in the administration of the sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist, and this without regard to places or persons, and also with the office of preaching, reading and teaching, to the prejudice of the ordinaries and the hierarchical order, to the prejudice also of other religious orders, and even of princes and temporal lords, against the privileges of universities, and finally to the great burden of the people. It seems to violate the honour of the monastic religion, and it weakens the studious, pious and necessary practice of virtues, abstinences and austerity; indeed it gives occasion to apostatise freely from other religious orders, it withdraws the due obedience and subjection owed to the ordinaries, it unjustly deprives both temporal and ecclesiastical lords of their rights, and it brings disturbance into both polities, many complaints among the people, many lawsuits, dissensions, contentions, rivalries, rebellions and various schisms. Therefore, having carefully examined and weighed all these other matters, THIS SOCIETY seems dangerous in its undertaking, disruptive of ecclesiastical peace, subversive of monastic religion, and more conducive to destruction than to edification. Maillard, Demochares, Périon, and the Inquisitor of the faith of Ory, etc., took part in this assembly. The procurators were Benedict, Dean, and Courselles, Sub-dean of the Faculty of Theology at Paris; and Le Fèvre, syndic, and Noël Brulard; not Peter Ramus and Mercier, as the Jesuits falsely claim.

units.la: Sic iudicavit hoc tempore Sorbonianum Collegium de Iesuitis, hodie vero non parum illis favet. Artibus enim suis in illud Collegium paulatim intrusunt Theologos, qui in eorum Collegiis literis operam dederunt, & nunc res Iesuitarum vehementer ibi promovent.
units.tr: Thus the Sorbonne college judged the Jesuits at that time; today, however, it favours them not a little. For by their arts they have gradually infiltrated that college with theologians who studied at their colleges, and now they vigorously promote the Jesuits' cause there.

units.la: Iesuitæ vero hanc Sorbonæ censuram per Hispanicam Inquisitionem annihilari & abrogari curarunt. De quo Ribadeneira lib. 4. cap. 11. sic scribit: Porrò in Hispania, quod Sorbonense decretum esset contra sanctam Sedis Apostolicæ authoritatem, à qua religio nostra confirmata & probata est, fidei quæsitores illud tanquam falsum, quod pias aures offenderet, suo decreto legi prohibuerunt.
units.tr: The Jesuits, however, took care that this censure of the Sorbonne should be annulled and abrogated by the Spanish Inquisition. Concerning this, Ribadeneira writes as follows in book 4, chapter 11: "Moreover, in Spain, since the Sorbonne decree was against the holy authority of the Apostolic See, by which our religion has been confirmed and approved, the inquisitors of the faith forbade it to be read, as false and offensive to pious ears, by their own decree."

units.la: In Gallia autem hac Theologorum Parisiensium sententia territis Sodalibus, tum tempori obsecundandum ducerent, & novi Ordinis invidiam tempore mitigatum iri sperarent Iesuitæ, altum ea de re silentium fuit, usque ad Francisci Galliarum Regis tempora, sub quo potentibus rerum Guisianis, qui impensiuscùlo novo Sodalitio favebant, Iesuitæ intermissum negotium persequuntur; & ante omnia iuxta S. C. Eustochius Bellaius Parisiensis Episcopus sententiam quam ille scriptis mandavit. In ea Societatem Iesuiticam, ut novos ordines, summè periculosam, & his temporibus admotus potius concitandos, quàm Ecclesiæ concordiam farciendam, institutam asserit: Inprimis Iesuitarum nomen, ut arrogantiæ plenum, improbat; quippe cum ita solis sibi tribuant, quod Ecclesiæ Catholicæ competit, quæ propriè fidelium congregatio dici potest, cuius caput est CHRISTVS; illi verò cùm hoc nomen sibi sumunt solis, & hoc dicere videri, solos se Ecclesiam constituere: tum multa in privilegiis ei à Paulo Tertio concessis inesse dicit, quæ iuri communi repugnent, Episcoporum, Curionum & Universitatum auctoritati ac potestati præiudicent, ac proinde consultius esse, ut quando ad Turcorum & infidelium instructionem & verbi Dei apud illos populos promulgationem a Pontifice auctorati sunt, in locis, qui ijs vicini sunt, domicilia his Sodalibus assignentur, uti olim in Christiano limite Rhodiensis equites excubare iussi sunt.
units.tr: In France, however, when the Sodalists were frightened by the judgement of the Parisian theologians, the Jesuits thought they must yield to the times, and hoped that the odium against the new Order would be softened with time; so there was a deep silence on this matter until the reign of Francis, King of the French. Under him, when the affairs of the Guises were in power, who favoured the new Sodality more zealously, the Jesuits pursued the abandoned business again. And above all, in accordance with the S. C., Eustochius Bellaius, Bishop of Paris, set out in writing his judgement on it. In it he asserts that the Jesuit Society, as a new order, is most dangerous and was established in these times, which were stirred up rather than calmed, to disturb the concord of the Church rather than to repair it. First of all, he disapproves of the name Jesuits as full of arrogance, since in this way they claim for themselves alone what belongs to the Catholic Church, which can properly be called the congregation of the faithful, whose head is Christ; and by taking this name for themselves alone they seem to say that they alone constitute the Church. Then he says that many things in the privileges granted to them by Paul III are contrary to common law and prejudicial to the authority and power of bishops, parish priests and universities; and therefore it would be more advisable, since they have been authorised by the Pontiff to instruct the Turks and infidels and to publish the Word of God among those peoples, that dwellings be assigned to these Sodalists in places near them, just as the Knights of Rhodes were once ordered to keep watch on the Christian frontier.

units.la: His sententiis a Rege in Consistorio expensis, instigante Cardinali Lotaringo, diplomate dato 7. Calend. Maij Anni millesimi quingentesimi sexagesimi primi Curiæ mandatur, ut nulla habita Theologorum Parisiensium & Episcopi ipsius intercessionis ratione, tam Pontificia quam Regia diplomata in Societatis gratiam facta promulget.
units.tr: Having weighed these opinions in the Consistory, and at the urging of Cardinal of Lorraine, the King by a diploma dated 7 Calends of May 1561 ordered the Court to publish both the Papal and the royal diplomas granted in favour of the Society, without any regard to the intercession of the Parisian theologians or of the bishop himself.

units.la: Et quanquam Sodales porrecto Senatui libello supplici se iuri communi subiicerent, & iuribus ac privilegiis contra illud a Pontificib. concessis, & Episcoporum, Collegiorum, Curionum, Universitatum auctoritati, Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ & pactionum inter Reges ac Pontifices initarum iuri præiudicantibus renuntiare se testarentur, nihilominus Senatus 8. Calend. Mart. decreto facto negotium omne ad Concilium universale, aut Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ conventum remittit, ut ab eo novus ordo approbaretur.
units.tr: Although the members of the Society presented a supplicating petition to the Senate, submitting themselves to common law and declaring that they renounced the privileges granted by the Popes against it, and those rights that prejudiced the authority of bishops, colleges, parish priests and universities, the Gallican Church, and the agreements made between kings and popes, the Senate nevertheless, by a decree of 8 Calends of March, referred the whole matter to a universal council or to a meeting of the Gallican Church, so that a new order might be approved by it.

units.la: Tandem cum posisiaci iussu Regis Præsules de religionis negotio magno numero convenirent Francisco Turnonio Cardinali Lugdunensi Archiepiscopo Præside, 7. Calend. Octob. referente Bellaio Episcopo Parisiensi, & pluribus conditionibus appositis, conventus iuxta potestatem ei a Curia factam, causa cognita novam Societatem admisit & approbavit, sub Societatis & Scholæ nomine, non etiam Ordinis recenter instituti, hoc est, tanquam Collegium solum modo quoddam, non autem novum religionis institutum vel ordinem, astutissimo Cardinalis Turnonij instinctu: expresså insuper hac conditione, ut aliud quam Societatis IESV, aut Iesuitarum nomen assumant, in ipsosque Socios Episcopo in sua diœcesi, ut in alios Sacerdotes, iurisdictio salva maneat, utque nihil agere possint in Episcoporum, Collegiorum, Curionum, Universitatum, aut aliorum Ordinum præiudicium, illorumve iurisdictionem & functionem, sed iuxta iuris communis præscriptum regantur, privilegiisque ei contrariis renunciare teneantur. Insuper additum est, nisi pareant, aut in posterum nova a Pontificibus privilegia obtineant, ut adprobatio præsenti decreto facta iam nunc revocata intelligatur.
units.tr: At last, when by the King's command a large number of prelates met at Poissy on the question of religion, with Francis Tournon, Cardinal and Archbishop of Lyons, presiding, and on the report of Bellièvre, Bishop of Paris, on 7 Calends of October, the assembly, with several conditions attached and within the power granted it by the Court, after hearing the case, admitted and approved the new Society under the name of Society and School, not of a newly founded Order. That is, it was approved as a mere kind of college, not as a new religious institute or order, by the very crafty instigation of Cardinal Tournon. It was expressly made a condition that they should assume no name other than the Society of Jesus or Jesuits; that the bishop's jurisdiction in his diocese over the members themselves, as over other priests, should remain intact; and that they should do nothing to the prejudice of bishops, colleges, parish priests, universities or other orders, or of their jurisdiction and functions, but be governed according to the prescription of common law and be bound to renounce privileges contrary to it. It was further added that, unless they complied, or obtained fresh privileges from the Popes in future, the approval granted by this present decree was to be understood as already revoked.

units.la: Quid Iesuitæ? nulli istarum conditionum instiluerunt, multoque minus appellationem istam Ordinis sui intermiserunt: imo cum primum hoc decretum impetrassent, ludum Lutetiæ aperiunt, & portæ Collegii sui inscripserunt, COLLEGIVM DE SOCIETATE NOMINIS IESV.
units.tr: What did the Jesuits do? They accepted none of these conditions, and much less did they give up that title of their Order. On the contrary, as soon as they had obtained this decree, they opened a school at Paris and inscribed over the gate of their college: COLLEGE OF THE SOCIETY OF THE NAME OF JESUS.

units.la: Cum igitur universa Parisiensis Academia eorum libertatem audaciam que effrenem interpellaret, rursus res ad Senatum devoluta est. Antequam autem res in Senatu agitaretur, ab Academia consultus Carolus Molinæus, Franciæ & Germaniæ Iurisperitus celeberrimus, & in supremo Parisiorum Senatu Advocatus, An Iesuitæ, sic enim eos vocavit, in regno Franciæ & Universitate Parisiensi sint admittendi? consultatione scriptis mandata, quæ postea etiam publicata est, responderat, Non solum id non esse e Republica, sed contra Rempublicam & utilitatem communem Franciæ Regni, præsertim Universitatis Parisiensis, quæ omnium Academiarum primaria sit; his adductis rationibus.
units.tr: Since the whole Parisian Academy protested against their liberty and unbridled audacity, the matter was again referred to the Senate. Before it was debated there, the Academy consulted Charles Molinaeus, the most celebrated jurist of France and Germany and an advocate in the supreme Senate of Paris, on the question: Are the Jesuits (for so he called them) to be admitted into the kingdom of France and the University of Paris? In a written opinion, afterwards published, he replied that this was not only not in the interest of the commonwealth but contrary to the commonwealth and the common good of the kingdom of France, especially of the University of Paris, which is the chief of all academies. He gave the following reasons.

units.la: 1. Primùm, inquit, Iesuitæ illi novam Religionem instituunt contra antiquos Canones etiam Conciliares: quibus veticum est, novam ullam Religionem erigere; sed receptos & approbatos conventus subire: alioquin non esset finis novarum sectarum & adinventionum, ad expilationem populi Christiani, turbationem & confusionem ordinis Ecclesiastici, qui certis in statis suis finibus contineri debet. Ut est text. in cap. ult. de Religiosis domibus. Quod xs. Quod desumptum est de Concilio Generali sub Innocentio Tertio Romæ habito Anno 1215.
units.tr: (1) First, he says, those Jesuits are setting up a new religion contrary to the ancient canons, even the conciliar ones, which forbid the erection of any new religion and require men to submit to communities already received and approved. Otherwise there would be no end to new sects and inventions, to the plundering of the Christian people, and to the disturbance and confusion of the ecclesiastical order, which ought to be kept within its fixed limits. See the text in the last chapter, de Religiosis domibus. This is taken from the General Council held at Rome under Innocent III in the year 1215.

units.la: 2. Secundò, & nominatim, hoc est contra arresta supremi Parisiorum Senatus: quinus præfati Iefuistæ jam non semel repulsi sunt, non solùm ut ignoti, sed etiam ut peregrini: imò etiam ut incapaces totius & juris & tituli collegialis, huiusmodi sectæ & Religione factitia à tanto Senatu rejectâ.
units.tr: (2) Second, and specifically, it is contrary to the decrees of the supreme Senate of Paris. The said Jesuits have already been rejected more than once, not only as unknown but also as foreigners, and indeed as wholly incapable of any right or title of a college, since a sect and a factitious religion of this kind has been rejected by so great a Senate.

units.la: 3. Tertiò, contra solennè Concilium & conclusionem longâ & maturâ deliberatione factam Nicææ mense Julio, Anno sesquimillesimo trigesimo octavo, à novem sectis præstantissimis & doctissimis viris. Quorum quatuor erant Cardinales, reliqui Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Abbates, à Paulo Tertio Pontifice Romano congregati & diis adjurati, ut absque ulla dissimulatione veritatem edicerent, & consilium darent ad judicandum & corrigendum abusus, & medendum morbis Ecclesiæ: Qui inter alios abusus corrigendos, censuerunt perhibendam esse admissionem novorum religiosorum, etiam in Conventualibus jam receptis ordinibus: Sed omnes, qui tum nondum erant professi, abigendos & expellendos; & multò minus novos Conventus erigendos etiam ordinum vel Religionum approbatarum: multò minus novas factitias Religiones admittendas. Idem ante eos censuit Petrus de Alliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis in suo libro de Reformat. Ecclesiæ, edito in concilio Constantiensi, considerat. Idem ante eos censuerunt Archiepiscopus Armacanus & Gulielmus de Sancto Amore, sacræ Theologiæ doctor insignis quondam in Schola Sorbonæ huius Academiæ & Scholæ.
units.tr: (3) Third, it is contrary to the solemn council and conclusion reached after long and mature deliberation at Nice in July 1538 by nine most distinguished and learned men, four of whom were cardinals and the rest archbishops, bishops and abbots, gathered by Pope Paul III and bound by oath in God's name to declare the truth without any dissimulation and to give counsel for judging and correcting abuses and for healing the diseases of the Church. Among the other abuses to be corrected, they judged that the admission of new religious should be curbed, even into orders already received in convents, and that all who were not yet professed should be driven out and expelled. Much less should new convents be erected, even of approved orders or religions, and much less should new factitious religions be admitted. Before them, Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, had given the same opinion in his book on the reform of the Church, published at the Council of Constance, in the chapter considerations. The Archbishop of Armagh and William of Saint-Amour, a distinguished doctor of sacred theology once in the Sorbonne school of this Academy, had likewise held this view before them.

units.la: 4. Quartò, contra bonum publicum totius regni nimis jamdudum multitudine Conventuum gratari, ut res ipsa clamat. Quòd si nova hæc secta ad novum unum Conventum exigendum admissa fuerit, mox per totum regnum serpet non solum sumptu & ontere populi, sed etiam Ecclesiarum regni detrimento & gravamine luculento. Cuius rei recens extat exemplum, quòd à leviori principio nondum septuaginta annis ortum habuit: Anachoreta ille Franciscus à Paula, qui sub ortum Ludovici Undecimi venit in agrum Turonensem, ubi cum sex jugera terræ emisset, obiit: famuli eius petulio magistri non contenti, quanam arte intra viginti annos tam multa nova suæ Misericordiæ sectæ monasteria ample dotata in Gallijs ædificarunt? Iefuistæ isti ut maius & augustius sese habere principium gloriantur, ita maiores spiritus colligunt, & maiora sese brevis factuROS sperant & jastant. Principijs igitur potissimum obstandum.
units.tr: (4) Fourth, it is contrary to the public good of the whole kingdom, which has long been burdened by the multitude of convents, as the matter itself cries out. For if this new sect is admitted to found a single new convent, it will soon creep through the whole kingdom, to the expense and burden of the people and to the great detriment and clear grievance of the churches of the realm. A recent example of this exists. It arose from a slight beginning less than seventy years ago: the anchorite Francis of Paola, who came under Louis XI into the territory of Tours, where, after buying six acres of land, he died. His servants, not content with their master's impudence, by what arts within twenty years built so many new monasteries of his sect of Mercy, amply endowed, throughout France? These Jesuits boast that they have a greater and more august beginning, and so they gather greater spirits and hope and boast that they will soon achieve greater things. Therefore one must resist chiefly at the beginnings.

units.la: 5. Quintò, non solum tam est contra commoda publica, sed etiam vergit in maximum periculum Regni, nempe detegendorum & revelandorum passim secretorum exteris. Multos enim non solum commorantes, sed etiam identidem communicantes alliciunt & alunt Italos & Hispanos, & quosvis exteros: Nimis opportunares exploratoribus secretis Regni revelandis; quod ut suspectum & periculosum, omni animadversione & prohibitione dignum censuerunt antiquæ & politicæ leges. leg. omne delictum. Exploratores. Pandect. de re militari. leg. mercatores. C. de commerc. & mercator. Adeò ut hac ratione etiam rite electi Episcopi repelli possint, ut post Innocentium, in cap. cum superis tradunt. Ibi Panorm. col. 3. Fel. col. 4. extra. de appellat. Innocentius, in cap. quod sicut. & ibi Parnorm. extra. de Electione. & in cap. cum terra. eod. tit. Domin. de sancto Geminiani. in cap. in novo, col. ult. 21. distinct. Zangelin. in extravagant. execrabilis, in verb. diversorum Regnorum, sub tit. de prabend. Quanto fortius excludi possunt novi Monachi?
units.tr: (5) Fifth, it is not only contrary to public advantage but also tends to the greatest danger to the kingdom, namely the disclosure and revelation of secrets to foreigners everywhere. For they attract and nourish not only Italians and Spaniards who live among us, but also, through constant communication, any foreigners at all, and they are far too convenient for spies to reveal the secrets of the kingdom. Ancient and political laws regarded this as suspect and dangerous and judged it worthy of every penalty and prohibition: Digest, law omne delictum; Exploratores, Pandect. de re militari; law mercatores, C. de commerc. et mercator. So much so that on this reasoning even duly elected bishops can be rejected, as after Innocent the authors teach on chap. cum superis: there Panorm. col. 3, Fel. col. 4, extra de appellat.; Innocent on chap. quod sicut, and there Panorm., extra de Electione; and on chap. cum terra, same title; Domin. de sancto Geminiano on chap. in novo, col. last, distinct. 21; Zanchinus on extravagant execrabilis, in verb. diversorum regnorum, under the title de praebendis. How much more strongly, then, can new monks be excluded?

units.la: 6. Sextò, istud est contra jus publicum, quo novorum Collegiorum erectio prohibetur. Et in summa omne Collegium illicitum est, nisi specialiter approbatum appareat. lib. 1. leg. Collegia. ff. In summa. Pand. de coll. illic.
units.tr: (6) Sixth, it is contrary to public law, by which the erection of new colleges is forbidden. In short, every college is illicit unless it is clearly shown to be specially approved: Book 1, law Collegia, Digest; In summa, Pand. de coll. illic.

units.la: Porrò Collegium illicitum usurpans non minori pœna tenetur, quàm tenentur hi, qui hominibus armatis loca publica vel templa occupant. leg. 2. Pandect. de colleg. illic.
units.tr: Moreover, one who usurps an illicit college is liable to no lesser penalty than those who occupy public places or temples with armed men: law 2, Pandects, de colleg. illic.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: Concerning the Propagation

units.la: Et Collegium non specialiter approbatum, nec passivam quidem Testamenti factio- nem habet l. Collegium. C. de hæred. instituend. Non obstat l. C. de Sacrosanctis Ecclesia, quia loquitur de publico & ordinario ministerio Ecclesiæ, seu Collegio Catholico, sive Romæ sive alibi per universalem Ecclesiam Christianam, cui ante Constantinum non licebat aliquid legare, nec Ecclesiam Christianam hæredem institnere; quod cum Lucina matrona fecisset, Maxentius, qui tum ante adventum Constantini Romæ rerum potiebatur, eam relegavit: teste Platina in Marcello. Quod Constantinus de visto Maxentio factus Imperator correxit d.l. 1. ad populum lata, quæ non est facta nisi in favorem Ecclesiarum Christianarum, & ministerij ordinarij. In Ecclesia nulla erant cœnobia; nulla Collegia nisi Episcoporum & Parochorum, qui in locum Apostolorum & discipulorum Christi successerunt, quod nullo modo dici potest de cœnobijs seu monasterijs institutis, quæ manent sub Regula prohibitiva, & sub genere collegiorum illicitorum, nisi de speciali approbatione appareat. leg. 1. & 3. Pandest. de colleg. illicit. Et sic nullo modo includi possunt nec contineri sub gratia & promissione, dict. leg. 1. quæ adhuc propter abusum clericorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ, facultatibus morientium insidiantium, revocata fuit per Valentinianum, & Valentem Imperatores tempore B. Hieronymi, qui eam legem laudat, propter sordidam & insatiabilem avaritiam clericorum & Monachorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ: quam avaritiam valde deplorat & detestatur in epist. 2. ad Nepot. tom. 1. Epistolarum suarum: qui si viveret, non minus deploraret & execraretur sordidum quastum & avaritiam dictorum Iesuistarum, qui preces suas & suffragia venditant: Non enim alium habent reditum: & tamen nec manibus operari volunt: ut exemplo Beati Pauli jubet sanctus Augustinus in libro suo de opere Monachorum: Nec se aliis antiquis approbatis Conventibus submittere, ut sacri canones jubent. can. ult. de religios. domibus. Sed sibi solis novum regnum erigere, idque stipe simplicium, quod vetat & maledicit Christus, Matth. 23.
units.tr: Nor does a college that has not been specially approved have the capacity to be a beneficiary under a will (l. Collegium, C. de hæred. instituend.). The law C. de Sacrosanctis Ecclesiis does not stand in the way, because it speaks of the public and ordinary ministry of the Church, or of the Catholic college, whether at Rome or elsewhere throughout the universal Christian Church. Before Constantine it was not lawful for that body to bequeath anything, nor to institute the Christian Church as heir. When the matron Lucina had done this, Maxentius, who then held power at Rome before Constantine arrived, revoked the gift; so Platina reports in his life of Marcellus. Constantine, having become emperor after defeating Maxentius, corrected this in the law (d.l. 1, ad populum lata), which was made only in favour of the Christian churches and the ordinary ministry. In the Church there were no monasteries at first; there were no colleges except those of the bishops and parish priests, who succeeded the apostles and the disciples of Christ. This cannot in any way be said of monasteries or cloisters founded later, which remain under a prohibitive rule and fall under the category of illicit colleges, unless a special approval is shown (leg. 1 and 3, Pandect. de colleg. illicit.). Therefore they cannot in any way be included or contained under the grace and promise of that law (dict. leg. 1). That law was itself revoked, because of the abuse of the clergy of the Roman Church, who lay in wait for the property of the dying. It was revoked by the emperors Valentinian and Valens in the time of St. Jerome, who praises that law, on account of the filthy and insatiable greed of the clergy and monks of the Roman Church. Jerome deplores and detests that greed greatly in his second letter to Nepotianus, in the first volume of his letters. If he were alive, he would not deplore and execrate less the sordid gain and the greed of the said Jesuits, who peddle their prayers and their suffrages, for they have no other income; and yet they will not work with their hands, as St. Augustine bids them follow the example of St. Paul in his book on the work of monks. Nor will they submit themselves to other ancient approved convents, as the sacred canons bid (can. ult. de religios. domibus). Instead they seek to raise a new kingdom for themselves alone, and this from the alms of simple people, which Christ forbids and curses (Matth. 23.).

units.la: 7. Septimo, quod in medio ipsius Academiæ, sine eius permissione, de facto construant novam Ecclesiam, novum Collegium, novos lectores & novas lectiones: Nec volunt eidem Academiæ subijci, sed novum Collegij & exercitij caput erigere. Quod nonsolum monstrosum est, sed seditiosum, & contra jus publicum. l. 1. ff. huius studij, Pand. de Institut. & Iur.
units.tr: 7. Seventh, they construct a new church and a new college, with new lecturers and new lectures, de facto, in the very midst of this Academy and without its permission. Nor do they wish to be subject to the same Academy; they set up a new head for their college and their practice. This is not only monstrous but seditious, and contrary to public law (l. 1, ff. huius studij, Pand. de Institut. et Iur.).

units.la: 8. Octavo, Academia Parisiensis abundat multis congruis & approbatis Collegijs, & ab antiquo fundatis, etiam plus quam sufficientibus; imo quædam superflua sunt: Et sic multo minus admitti & tolerari debet Collegium novum Iesuistarum.
units.tr: 8. Eighth, the Academy of Paris already has many suitable and approved colleges, founded long ago, more than enough; indeed some are superfluous. Therefore a new college of the Jesuits ought much less to be admitted and tolerated.

units.la: 9. Nono, sine auctoritate Episcopi, & approbatione doctorum Theologiæ concionantur, & novum suum Catechismum quasdam superstitiones continentem, plebi & etiam mulieribus, omnibus promiscue obtrudunt, ut de industria sese ingerere videantur ad dandum occasionem infringendi pacificationis edicta: quare nihil perniciosius esset, & periculum irreparabile secum trahit.
units.tr: 9. Ninth, they preach without the authority of the bishop and without the approval of the doctors of theology, and they thrust upon the common people, and even upon women, indiscriminately, their new catechism, which contains certain superstitions. They seem to thrust themselves forward on purpose, so as to give occasion for breaking the edicts of the peace. Therefore nothing could be more pernicious, and it brings with it an irreparable danger.

units.la: Quibus confideratis, Procurator generalis eiusdem almæ Universitatis Parisiensis justam causam habet, & pro debito officij debet præfatis Iesuistis novum opus nunciare, eosque ut ab indebitis illis novitatibus desistant per legitimos tramites compellere. Et ita censeo ego Carolus Molinæus Franciæ & Germaniæ IC. & in supremo Parisiorum Senatu antiquus Advocatus.
units.tr: Having considered these things, the Procurator General of the same nourishing University of Paris has a just cause, and by the duty of his office he ought to bring a formal objection against the said Jesuits, and to compel them by lawful means to desist from those improper novelties. Thus I, Charles Molinaeus, jurist of France and Germany and long-serving advocate in the supreme Senate of Paris, give my opinion.

units.la: Secundum hæc igitur & alia similia causa ista in frequenti Senatu acriter agitata est. Pro Sodalib. Petrus Versorius magni nominis Patronus laudata multorum origine, quam supra memoravimus, & institutione, peroravit. Stephanus Pascasius vel Pasquierius contra pro Academia Parisiensi disseruit, & sectam eam ambitiosam & fucatæ religionis plena appellans, in Hispania natā, Lutetiæ adultam, Venetijs exercitatam, Romæ initio exagitatam, postremò receptam, & privilegijs immodicis & á iure communi exorbitantibus donatam, postea in Gallia Theologorum Parisiensium sententia damnatam, itemque á Parisiensi Episcopo
units.tr: In accordance with these and similar arguments, this case was hotly debated in a full session of the Senate. Peter Versorius, a patron of great repute, spoke for the Companions; he praised their origin, which we mentioned above, and their foundation. Stephen Pasquier, or Pasquierius, argued on the other side on behalf of the Academy of Paris. He called the Society an ambitious sect full of feigned religion, born in Spain, grown up at Paris, practised at Venice, first harassed at Rome, finally received, and endowed with excessive privileges that depart from the common law. He said that it was later condemned in France by the judgement of the theologians of Paris, and likewise rejected by the bishop of Paris.

units.la: Stephanus Pasquierius de Iesuitis iudicium ifcopo reiectam fuisse dixit; nunc vero gratuitæ puerorum institutionis spe• ie grassari, & inde familías captatis testamentis exhaurire, inde iuventutem pecie religionis corrumpere, & fascinatis per superstitiones puerorum inge• ijs iam nunc seditiones & defectiones in regni perniciem aliquando eruptu• as moliri. Tum inter plura eorum vota illud exágitat, quo Præposito suo, quem anquam Deum præfentem in terris venerari fe dicant, obedientiam, quam ɛcam appellent per omnia & in omnibus polliceantur. Deinde in ambitiosum orum nomen invehitur, quod cum sectarij alij ante ducentos annos ufurpâf• ent, ab Ecclesia reiecti, & iusto Dei iudicio ac flagello omnino dissipati pe• ierint. Hoc nomine nihil aliud agi, quam ut inter eiusdem religionis Professo• es scissura constituatur, & Iesuitæ alij sint, alij Christiani. Quod vero adeo fe rga Pontificem obsequentes præbeant, eo magis suspectos eos Gallis esse de• ere, qui Pontificem quidem tanquam caput & Principem Ecclesiæ agnoscant, ed ita, ut sanctis decretis & œcumenicis Concilijs tanquam inferior parere te• neatur: nihil adversus regnum ac Reges pronunciare, aut contra Curiæ placi• a, aut in præiudicium Episcoporum intra eorum fines decernere valeant: tum• ubijcit, novis Sectarijs istis semel admissis, totidem hostes intra regni vi• cera ali, qui si contingat, ut excandescente perversa bile in Gallos arma ver• ant Pontifices, Regi nominiq; Gallico bellum indicturi sint. Postremo versa d Senatores oratione, Vos, inquit, qui nunc Iesuitas toleratis, aliquando ipsi, edsero c edulitatem vestram accusabitis, cum connivcntia vestra effectum videbitis, ut orum astu, dolis, superstitione, dissimulatione, praestigijs ac malis artibus publica tranquillitas, non solum in hoc regno, sed etiam per universum orbem Christianum mpe• iclitetur.
units.tr: Pasquier said that the Jesuits were now spreading under the appearance of free instruction of boys, and from this they drained families through legacies; from this they corrupted the youth under the guise of religion, and, having bewitched the minds of children through superstitions, they were at last preparing seditions and rebellions for the ruin of the kingdom. He then criticised among their many vows the one by which they promise obedience, in all things and without exception, to their Provost, whom they say they venerate as God present on earth. Next he inveighed against the ambitious name they use, which other sectaries had used two hundred years earlier, and who, having been rejected by the Church and entirely scattered by the just judgement and scourge of God, had perished.
