By this name, he said, nothing else was being done than that a split should be created among the professors of the same religion, so that some would be Jesuits and others Christians. As for the fact that they show themselves so obsequious to the Pope, he said that this made them all the more suspected by the French, who acknowledge the Pope indeed as head and prince of the Church, but in such a way that he is bound to obey holy decrees and the ecumenical councils as an inferior; and who can pronounce nothing against the kingdom and the kings, nor decree anything within their borders contrary to the pleasure of the court or to the prejudice of the bishops. He added that once these new sectaries were admitted, as many enemies would be nourished within the vitals of the kingdom; and if it should happen that the Pontiffs, with their perverse bile inflamed, turned their arms against the French, they would declare war on the King and on the French name. Finally, turning to the senators, he said: You who now tolerate the Jesuits will one day yourselves accuse your own leniency, when you see that, by your connivance, the public tranquillity, not only in this kingdom but throughout the whole Christian world, has been brought to ruin by their cunning, deceit, superstition, dissimulation, trickery and wicked arts.

units.la: Post eum replicavit Verforius; ac demum Baptista Menilius Cognitoris Regij partes sustinens, qui increpita initio Patronorum utrinque acerbitate, postquam de novis Ordinibus & periculo in eorum admissione non solum quantum ad religionem; sed etiam quantum ad civilem administrationem multa dixit: tandem contra Iesuitas peroravit, qui, utpote voto obligati, in Scholae Parisiensis corpus ad iuventutem erudiendam nullo modo cooptandi essent, & Senatu petijt, videret in quam rem Claromontani Episcopi legatum converti posset, aut deberet, ut memoria testatoris & voluntas alio genere conserva• etur. Causa hæc biduum integrum agitata est. Senatus sive futuri securus, sive odio Protestantium, quibus debellandis isti homines nati credebantur, de hoc negotio amplius deliberandum censuit, libertate interim Sodalibus ludum aperiendi & iuventutis erudiendæ concessa. Hoc Non. April. decretum, Anno 1565.
units.tr: After him Versorius replied again; and at last Baptista Menilius, who took on the role of the King's prosecutor, spoke. He first rebuked the bitterness of the patrons on both sides, and then said much about the new orders and the danger in admitting them, not only as regards religion but also as regards civil administration. Finally he spoke against the Jesuits, arguing that, being bound by vows, they could in no way be co-opted into the body of the Parisian school for the education of youth. He asked the Senate to consider to what purpose the legacy of the Bishop of Clermont might be or ought to be turned, so that the memory and will of the testator might be preserved in some other way. The case was debated for two full days. The Senate, either confident of the future or out of hatred for the Protestants, whom these men were thought to have been born to overthrow, decided that this business should be considered further; meanwhile the Companions were granted liberty to open a school and to teach the youth. This decree was issued on the 5th of April, in the year 1565.

units.la: Hac igitur occasione Societas ista paulatim in Gallia augetur & firmatur, & non tantum communis populi, sed Principum sanguinis & Regum ipsorum gratiam ac favorem sensim adipiscuntur, qui magnifica Collegia eis in diversis, & quidem primarijs Vrbibus ædificarunt atq; liberaliter dotarunt. Mansit nihilominus alta mente repositum conceptum, non solum Sorboniftarum, sed etiam totius Vniversitatis & studij Parisiensis in Iesuitas odium, ita ut occulte semper inter hos & illos fuerint æmulationes & contentiones: frementibus nimirum in eos Academiæ Profesforibus, quod seorsum & extra ordinem privatum habeant sodalitium; quod in hunc usq; diem decreta Vniversitatis derecent, Rectori non sint audientes, sed suis duntaxat Præfectis privatim mo• em gerant; quod castoris instar dubij sint ordinis, omnium plumas furentur, non una Sparta sint contenti, pastoribus suas oves surripiant, privatis sacrifi• ijs quoslibet suscipiant & absolvant, cæterorum exuvijs dites sint, & nescio quo hamo ex nobiliori qualibet familia adolescentes incautos expiscentur, suis quoq; fascinationibus bello durante omnem pubem pcftfe traxerint, obliti & euriente Lutetia, frequenti in Schola docuerint, & foli Vniversitatem fecerint, quae olim tot mulæis frequentibus & vix turbas auditorum capientibus floruerit.
units.tr: On this occasion the Society gradually grew and became established in France, and it gained not only the favour of the common people but also that of princes of the blood and of the kings themselves, who built magnificent colleges for them in various cities, and indeed in the chief cities, and endowed them generously. Nevertheless, the hatred against the Jesuits remained deeply fixed in the mind, not only of the Sorbonnists but of the whole University and the study of Paris; so that secret rivalries and contentions always existed between these and those. The professors of the Academy were incensed against them, because they keep a separate society outside the ordinary order, which to this day disregards the decrees of the University, does not obey the Rector, and conducts itself privately under its own prefects alone. They are like the beaver of doubtful order, they steal the feathers of all, they are not content with one Sparta, they snatch their sheep from the pastors, they take on and absolve private penitents, they grow rich on the spoils of others, and with some hook or other they fish for unwary young men from every noble family. By their enchantments they have drawn the whole youth into the plague during the war, forgetting that Paris was in ruin and teaching in a crowded school, so that they alone made up the University, which once flourished with so many scholars and hardly held the crowds of its audience.

units.la: Quum autem paulò ante deditam Henrico 4. Lutetiam consilia Iesuitarum in Gallia rursus concrisare acin deterius ferri, vicissim autem omnia in bonum Regis & universi Regni quietum ac tranquillum statum inclinare paulatim inciperent; Generalis eorum Aquaviva, ut impendenti malo aliquo modo occurreret ac praeveniret, Provinciales, Rectores, ac praecipuos seu Seniores ordinis universi Patres omnes Anno 1593. Romā ad generale Congregationem evocavit, ubi tum, occasione siferente, quo tempori nempe se accommodarent, in Novembri Decretum tale condiderunt: Vt ab omni specie mali abstineatur, & querelis, etiam ex falsis suspicionibus provenientibus, praecipitur omnibus in virtute sancta obedientia, & sub poena inhabilitatis ad quaevis officia & dignitates seu praelationes vocis quam activa quam passiva privationes, ne quispiam PVBLICIS ET SECVLARIVM PRINCIPVM NEGOCIIS ulla ratione se immiscere, nec etiam quantumvis per quos cunque requisitus aut rogatus, eiusmodi res tractandi curam suscipere audeat vel praesumat. Idq; serio commendatur superioribus, ne permittant socios ijs rebus ullo modo implicari, & si quos ad ea propensos animadverterent, eos loco mutandos quamprimum commutent, si alicubi sit occasio vel periculum se eiusmodi implicationibus irretiendi.
units.tr: When Paris had recently surrendered to Henry IV, and the Jesuits' schemes in France had begun to turn for the worse while everything was gradually inclining toward the good of the King and the peaceful, tranquil state of the whole kingdom, their General, Aquaviva, in order to meet and forestall the threatening evil in some way, summoned to Rome in 1593 all the Provincials, Rectors, and the chief men or seniors of the Order, for a general Congregation. There, taking the occasion and seeking to suit the times, they framed in November a decree to this effect: That every appearance of evil be avoided, and that complaints, even those arising from false suspicions, be prevented, all are commanded in holy obedience, and under penalty of being disabled from all offices, dignities, or preferments, both active and passive voice, that no one presume to involve himself in the PUBLIC AFFAIRS AND BUSINESS OF SECULAR PRINCES in any way, nor dare or presume to take up the care of handling such matters, even if he is asked or requested by anyone whatsoever. Superiors are also earnestly charged not to allow members to be entangled in these matters in any way, and if they notice any inclined to them, they are to transfer them to another place as soon as possible, wherever there is an occasion or danger of being ensnared in such entanglements.

units.la: Iesuitas autem in istiusce Decreti promulgatione non ferio egisse; sedhoc minimibus ita saltem imponere oculos & perstringere voluisse, ne videlicet, minus ipsis sideretur; vel inde liquet; quod eorum Superiores istud nunquam observarunt; quin potius ubicunq; & quandocunq; vel paululum relaxatio adeptos esse se putarunt, antiquos dolos & astutias reassumere, & iuxta praesentem rerum conditionem sua consilia moderari neutiquam intermiserunt: quum tamen Decretum istud allegatum & iurata illa coeca obedientia diversum plane requireret; nisi si aliud in recessu reconditum id habuisset, & ipsimet eiusdem sensum melius intellexissent. Remita se habere inde quoque manifestum est, quod Comoletus Iesuita in concione quadam super caput Iudic. Lutetiae habita, post excitatos de Henrici 111. Galliarum Regis occasu plausus ingentes & evectionem istius Parricidae Iacobitae vel supra Sanctos omnes, in hanc erupit exclamationem: Ahodum nos oportet aliquem habere; sive Monachus sit, seu miles, sive cerdo denique seu subulcus; Perinde enim est; saltem ut Ahodum quempiam habeamus. Hoc videlicet unicum adhuc restat; tum quidem omnia nostra probe componemus, & ad optatum denique finem perducemus. Idem Commoletus postea quoque in Regem Henricum 4. similiter debacchatus est, & ad perduellionem, seditiones, tumultus ac bella civilia subditos concitavit. Unde quidam sic de eo: Concio, Romani dicta est furiosa Tribuni Quae rapit ad caedem seditione suos. In Cathedra stantem, rabida cum voce boares Commole te populus vidit & obstupuit Qui Regis cadem, Regni qui funera suades, Qui varios motus hic & ubique cies, Cujus in ore frequens furor est patriaeq; ruina, Haec est Iesita concio sacra pij, Cum tua parturiat civiles lingua procellas, O Iesita Dei sancte Tribuna vale.
units.tr: Yet the Jesuits did not act in earnest in promulgating this decree; they wanted only, at least, to dazzle the eyes of the simple and blind them, so that it would seem less to them. This is clear from the fact that their Superiors never observed it. Indeed, wherever and whenever they thought that even a little relaxation had been obtained, they never ceased to resume their old tricks and cunning and to shape their plans to the present state of affairs. And yet that decree and that blind obedience they had sworn to required something quite different, unless it had some other meaning hidden away in reserve, and they themselves understood its sense better. That they were of the same mind is also plain from the fact that the Jesuit Commolet, in a sermon he delivered at Paris on the chapter of Judges, after great applause had been raised over the death of Henry III, King of France, and the exaltation of that parricide, the Jacobite, above all the saints, burst out in this exclamation: We must have some Ehud, whether he be a monk, or a soldier, or a cobbler, or finally a swineherd; for it makes no difference, so long as we have some Ehud. This alone remains: then indeed we shall arrange all our affairs well and at last bring them to the desired end. The same Commolet afterwards raged in the same way against King Henry IV, and stirred up his subjects to treason, sedition, tumults and civil wars. Hence someone wrote of him: "A sermon, such as the furious tribune of Rome once delivered, which drives his followers to slaughter by sedition. Standing in the pulpit, Commolet, with a raging voice, the people saw you bellow and were stunned. You who urge the murder of the King and the deaths of the kingdom, you who stir up various upheavals here and everywhere, whose mouth is ever full of fury and the ruin of the fatherland: this is the Jesuit sermon, the holy sermon of a pious man. While your tongue brings forth civil storms, farewell, O holy Jesuit tribune of God."

units.la: Ita quoq; postea Anno 1597. Iesuita Richardus Walfodt Eduardo Squi-red venenum
units.tr: So too afterwards, in the year 1597, the Jesuit Richard Walfodt gave Edward Squire poison

units.la: Decretum Iesuitarum.
units.tr: The Jesuits' decree.

units.la: Iesuitae decreto suo non satisfaciunt. o venenum præbuit, quo Principem suam legitimam Angliæ Reginam interceret & exstingueret. Ita Iesuitæ quoque Duacenses Anno seq. 1598. victo quendam Hyprensem Petrum Panneum induxerunt, ut illustrissimum illum belli ducem Mauritium Nassovium interimere cogitarit. An autem hoc PRINCIPVM SÆCVLARIVM NEGOCIIS NVLLA RATIONE SE IMMISCERE, & literalis istius Decreti sensus ita observetur, Iesuitis quidem ad prendendum, omnibus autem præiudicijs nondum occupatis hominibus alijs judicandum relinquitur.
units.tr: The Jesuits do not keep their decree. He provided poison with which to kill and destroy their lawful Queen of England, their Prince. So too the Jesuits of Douai, in the following year, 1598, persuaded a certain Petrus Panneus of Ypres, a man already won over, to plan to kill that most illustrious commander Maurice of Nassau. Whether this decree, that they should not in any way involve themselves in the business of secular princes, and whether the literal sense of this decree is observed in this way, is left for the Jesuits to decide, and for other men not yet occupied with any prejudices to judge.

units.la: Lutetia vero Regi an. 1594. restituta, ac bello civili sedato, cum apud omnes, præsertim Academicos, constaret, Iesuitas perduellionis, seditionū, tumultuum omnium turbarum præteritarum in Gallia primariam causam fuisse, ac suis ibunitrijs concionibus, tamquam facibus, civile bellum magis magisque accensse; Vniversitas Parisiensis Ioanni Pasferacio, Regio Eloquentiæ Professori fertissimo iniunxit, ut Iesuitarum expulsionem authoritate quoque sua provideret. Is igitur præfatiunculam in Disputationem de Ridiculis, quæ est apud Ciceronem lib. 2. de Oratore, gravissime in Iesuitas, suppresso tamen illorum nomine, invectus est, & illorum eiectionem ex Regno vehementer suasit: Lu-tetia, inquit, & expiāda nunc est Academia, Musis iterum dedicanda, diligenti cultione adhibita, ne amplius earum templa & ceremonia contaminentur. Idut recte fiat que ordine, abigenda sunt inprimis obscœnæ volucres (Iesuitæ) quæ rapinis, contactu omnia fœdant immundo. Decolor est illis vultus, deterrima ventris Proluvies, uncaq; manus, & pallida semper Orafame: ——— Non agnoscitis volucres, agnoscite sine plumis bipedes. Cur va quibus pullam subnectit fibula vestem.
units.tr: But when Paris was restored to the King in 1594 and the civil war was quieted, and it was clear to everyone, especially to the scholars, that the Jesuits had been the chief cause of treason, sedition, and all the disorders of the past troubles in France, and that by their seditious sermons, like torches, they had kindled the civil war more and more, the University of Paris charged Jean Passerat, the royal professor of eloquence and a most learned man, to provide, by his own authority also, for the expulsion of the Jesuits. He therefore, in a little preface to a disputation on jokes, which is found in Cicero, De Oratore, book 2, attacked the Jesuits very severely, though without naming them, and strongly urged their expulsion from the kingdom. "Paris," he said, "must now be purified, and the University dedicated again to the Muses, with careful cultivation applied, so that their temples and rites are no longer defiled. So that this may be done rightly and in order, the foul birds (the Jesuits) must be driven out first, who befoul everything with their plundering and their filthy touch. Their face is discoloured, their belly the most wretched of excrement, their hands hooked, and their hunger ever pale: ——— You do not recognise them, birds; recognise them as two-footed creatures without feathers, who fasten a black robe with a clasp."

units.la: Has harpyias nisi Senatus, & amplissimi ornatissimi viri, quibus Academiæ Scholaq; egia instaurandæ tradita est provincia, fugarint & exterminarint, ut pinnati Aquilonis filij infabulis, frustra littoralibus Diis vota nuncupabitis: rursus ad eos scopulos, quos nuper est fermè adflicta, navis nostra referetur. Ne quicquam in excolendo Murum fundo sudabimus: ne quicquam lolium, carduos, lappas & tribulos exstirpabimus, si ex agro nostro hæc filix radicitus evellitur.
units.tr: Unless the Senate, and the most distinguished and honourable men to whom the task of restoring the Academy and the School has been entrusted, drive off and banish these harpies, like the winged sons of the North Wind in the fables, you will vainly offer vows to the gods of the shore, and our ship will be carried back again to those rocks on which it has just been nearly wrecked. We shall sweat in vain in tilling the field if we do not root out the darnel, the thistles, the burdock, and the caltrops from our field, if this fern is not torn out by the roots.

units.la: Meminisse debemus, quonam pacto profugi homines, nec minus vagi quam Schytæ, va gratuita doctrinæ professione vulgo commendati, huc irrepserint; quibus artibus, hiantes locupletum fortunis, divites orbos, vel celibes, deliros senes, superstitiosas mulierculas, & adolescentulos imperitos deceperint, & velut Circeo poculo, repente immutarint: ut religionis specie, quam inexplebili avaritia, sunt fraudibus obtendunt, æquum Troianum paulatim introduxerint: ut semper in insidijs manserint, & in speculis steterunt: proditionis occasionem expectantes: ut ea oblata, machinam suam continuo aperuerint, armatisq; hostibus hanc urbem, & totam Galliam omni genere calamitatum replerint.
units.tr: We ought to remember in what manner these men, fugitives and no less wandering than the Scythians, crept in here, recommended to the public by a pretended profession of free teaching. By what arts, gaping for the wealth of the rich, they deceived childless rich men, widowers, foolish old men, superstitious women, and inexperienced young men, and as if by a Circean cup suddenly transformed them. Under the guise of religion, which they hide behind their insatiable greed, they gradually introduced a Trojan horse. They have always remained in ambush and stood on watch, awaiting an opportunity of betrayal; and when it was offered, they at once opened their machine, and with armed enemies they filled this city and all of France with every kind of calamity.

units.la: Ne vero insidias & paratam pestem cavereimus, nec ve impendentia prospicientibus pradicentibus cordatis viris crederemus, obstiterunt Corœbi quidam & calegontes, ut plures in Ilio nostro quam Laocoontes fuerunt. Et hos adhuc in Sinu habemus Si-renes? Quid hos, malum, fovemus? aut quid hi sciunt? Nisi unCta de vorare patrimonia.
units.tr: Lest we should guard against their snares and the plague prepared against us, and lest we should believe the wise men who foresaw the coming dangers and foretold them, certain Corœbi and Calegontes stood in the way, as there were more Laocoöns in our Troy than one. And do we still keep these Sirens in our bosom? Why, for heaven's sake, do we cherish them? Or what do they know? Nothing but to devour patrimonies.

units.la: At Gratis docent. Muta literulam, rem acu retigeris: Gratis nocent, eoq; maiandi ajore infortunio, quod gratuito sunt mali: quamquam vix istuc tibi persuadebit, qui is bene noverit. Testes honestissimæ amplissimaq; familiæ, quarum sanguinem pro levi ocendi opella, & exiguo Minervali, isti hirundines ex orbuerunt. Testis immanis eorum census, qui cum Regum & summorum Pontificum opibus certat. Praeclara liberalitas, repudiare drachmam, & talentum extorquere. Mirum genus benignitatis, pro stipe menstrua immensae pecuniae legata, opimas quoque captare & rapere haereditates. Institutio puerorum his aucupibus est illix, pendebunt pulchre qui ab ea transfenna turdi lumbricum petent. Gratuita doctrina illis est pro hamo, vel potius pro reti-iaculo, qua callidi piscatores cuncta convertunt cum pulvisculo. Stolidi parentes, qui suos ijs credunt liberos, eadem opera columbas accipitribus, pullos milvis, & oves committent lupis. Sed quid tandem isti per aureum funem de caelo delapsi magistri discipulis suis tradunt? nihil sapere, ritus Hispanos, odium legum institutiq; patrij, & ut prisci utar verbis, imbelliam, imbalnitiam, impolitiam, imparentiam, meramq; cum Lavernae sacris barbariem, quam consulto huc invexerunt, opinor, ut eam soli docerent. Interim delitescunt in vepretis nostris, nicedulae, quae rem civium arrodunt; nobis cum impune versantur speculatores & exploratores Philippi, & ejus tyrannidis acerrimi satellites.
units.tr: But they teach for nothing! Change a single letter and you touch the matter with a needle: they harm for nothing, and so their misfortune is greater, because they are harmful for free. Yet hardly anyone who knew them well would be persuaded of that. Witnesses are the most honourable and distinguished families, whose blood those swallows have drained for a small service of education and a meagre tuition fee. Witness their immense wealth, which vies with the riches of kings and the highest Pontiffs. A splendid liberality: to refuse a drachma and to extort a talent! A strange kind of kindness: to gather immense sums as a monthly alms, and to snatch up rich inheritances as well. The instruction of boys is a lure for these fowlers; thrushes will hang prettily from it who seek a worm from that baited trap. Free teaching is for them a hook, or rather a net and a drag-net, by which crafty fishermen turn everything into dust. Foolish parents who entrust their children to them will at the same time be committing doves to hawks, chicks to kites, and sheep to wolves. But what, pray, do these masters who have descended from heaven on a golden chain hand on to their pupils? Nothing but to be wise in Spanish fashion, a hatred of the laws and of the institutions of our country, and, to use an old phrase, unwarlikeness, unpolish, unfilial conduct, and sheer barbarism with the rites of Laverna, which they have brought in here on purpose, I suppose, so that they alone might teach it. Meanwhile there lie hidden in our thickets the little weasels who gnaw at the property of the citizens; with impunity among us move the spies and informers of Philip, and the sharpest henchmen of his tyranny.

units.la: Atqui discuntur apud eos boni pudicitiae mores. Sane tristes, cum aspicias frugi censeas, nec tamen fifibulam gestant, sunt Hippolyti: nec si bonos authores evirant, ideo boni placent, Gallis praesertim, quibus natura sunt invisi Deliaci. Magna laus est scilicet, ac palmarium facinus, ex hirco caprum, ex ariete vervecem, & ex verre majalem facere. Atque utinam fabri Patribus eorum, quā parte opus fuit, perpetuam impostuissent fibulam: rectā hic non depravarent ingenia, dum curva corrigere videntur, nec suos edocerent artem mentiendi & dolos, quos appellant industrios. Quid autem aliud praeciperent vulpeculae, si schola aperirent? Sic amant verum hi Chamelae ontes, polypi ac stellionis. Huiusmodi doctrinam & hos mores illis non invidemus: sibi habeant, abeantq; simul cum strigibus ἀχυπόρους ἐπιν ὑπας, & inde revertantur unde malum pedem huc attulerunt. Iam pridem vasa collegerunt, profectionis signum datur: quid morantur amplius? Academia nostra certe, quae longum periculosumq; morbum eorum contagione contraxit, nisi hoc levetur vomitu, vix unquam convalesceret, &c. Hucusque Pasferacius.
units.tr: Yet good moral conduct in chastity is learned among them. Indeed they look grave, and when you see them you would judge them sober, yet they do not wear the clasp; they are Hippolytuses. Nor, if they castrate good authors, are the authors therefore pleasing, especially to the French, to whom the Delians are hateful by nature. It is certainly a great boast and a masterpiece of deed to turn a billy-goat into a goat, a ram into a wether, and a boar into a young hog. Would that the craftsmen had fastened a permanent clasp on their Fathers where it was needed! Then they would not corrupt straight minds while seeming to correct crooked ones, nor teach their own pupils the art of lying and the tricks they call clever. What else would the little foxes teach if they opened a school? So these chameleons, octopuses and lizards love the truth. We do not envy them this doctrine and these morals: let them keep them for themselves, and let them go away together with the owls [ἀχυπόρους ἐπιν ὑπας], and return whence they brought their bad foot here. Long since they have packed their baggage; the signal for departure has been given. Why do they linger any longer? Our university, at least, which has caught a long and dangerous disease from their contagion, would hardly ever recover unless it were relieved by this vomiting, etc. Thus far Pasquier.

units.la: Boucerétus artium Doctor, opportunitatem quoque inde nactus, institit Universitati, ut Iesuitae in ius vocarentur & e regno Franciae prorsus ejicerentur. Universitas igitur huiusmodi rescriptum Boucereto dedit: Anno Dom. 1594, die Lunae 18. Mensis Aprilis convocata Universitas omnium Ordinum huiusce inclyti studij Parisiensis, apud eandem S. Mathurini pro supplicatione peragenda ab Academia ad aedem Sanctae Capellae Regalis Palatij Parisiensis, ad reddendas gratias Deo altissimo, pro reductione felici huiusce almae Urbis, prosperitate, & felicissimo successu Christianissimi & invictissimi Domini nostri Henrici IV. Regis Francorum & Navarrae, conservatione dictae urbis, sub ditione & protectione dicti Domini nostri Regis, & pro quampluribus aliis rebus ad Academiam spectantibus, atque super supplicatione facta a D. & M. Laurentio Boucerer, artium Doctore, de injus vocandis Iesuitis, ut omnino ejiciantur. Dicta Universitas debite (ut moris est) hora solita convocata, ex consensu unanimi omnium Doctorum & Magistrorum, singularum quatuor facultatum, quatuor Procuratorum nationum, nemine repugnante censuit & determinavit, esse annuendum supplicationi dicti D. Boucereti, ideoque in iudicium & jus rite & convenienter Iesuitas vocandos, ut ejiciantur omnino. Eandem ob rem censuit Universitas ex singulis ordinibus nominandos aliquot selectos viros, qui ea diligenter curent, quae ad litem contra Iesuitas movendam pertinent. Unde facultas Theologorum nominavit D. Magistrum Adrianum d' Amboise, summum Regiae Navarrae moderatorem, & alium Doctorem, quem dictus D.d' Amboise voluerit eligere. Facultas Decretorum quae acta sunt approbavit; & quia unicus tantum Doctor, nomine Dominus David Son aderat; promisit se nominaturum aliquem alium ex suis Doctoribus. Facultas autem Medicorum ordinavit D. & M. Iacobum Caufinotum. Postremo facultas artium nominavit dictum Mag. Laurentium Boucerctum, & D. Georgium Critonium. Sicque statutum fuit unanimiter, & conclusum nemine reclamante, per D. Iacobum d' Amboise Academiae Rectorem, totamque Academiam anno & die praefatis, quod rescriptum subsignatum fuit
units.tr: Laurent Boucher, Master of Arts, seizing the opportunity too, pressed the University to have the Jesuits summoned to court and utterly expelled from the kingdom of France. The University therefore gave Boucher this written decree. In the year of the Lord 1594, on Monday, 18 April, the University of all the faculties of this famous Parisian school was convened at St Mathurin, for a procession from the Academy to the chapel of the Royal Palace of Paris, to give thanks to God Most High for the happy recovery of this kindly city, for the prosperity and most fortunate success of our most Christian and invincible lord, Henry IV, King of the French and of Navarre, for the preservation of the said city under the rule and protection of our said lord the King, and for many other matters belonging to the Academy; and concerning the petition made by Master Laurent Boucher, Doctor of Arts, that the Jesuits be summoned to judgment and utterly expelled. The said University, duly convened at the customary hour, as is the rule, by the unanimous consent of all the Doctors and Masters of each of the four faculties and of the four procurators of the nations, with no one dissenting, judged and determined that the petition of the said Master Boucher should be granted, and that the Jesuits should therefore be rightly and properly summoned to judgment and law, to be utterly expelled. For the same reason the University decided that several selected men should be nominated from each order, who would diligently attend to those things that pertain to bringing the suit against the Jesuits. Accordingly the faculty of Theology nominated Master Adrian d'Amboise, chief warden of the Royal College of Navarre, and another Doctor whom the said d'Amboise would choose. The faculty of Decrees approved what was done; and since only one Doctor, named Master David Son, was present, it promised to nominate another of its Doctors. The faculty of Medicine appointed Master James Caufinot. Finally the faculty of Arts nominated the said Master Laurent Boucher and Doctor Georges Critonius. And thus it was resolved unanimously and concluded, with no one objecting, by Master James d'Amboise, Rector of the Academy, and the whole Academy, on the aforesaid year and day; and the decree was signed.

units.la: Rescriptus Universitatis Parisien. de ejiciendis Iesuitis. VVAL, & a latere visum nos Rectore Iacobum d'Amboise, sigillo rubriceri munitum. avebant tempora postulatis Academiae, & recordatio malorum recentium in bel‐ ci vili a Iesuitis excitatorum vel silenti Rectori & Vniversitati patrocinabatur.
units.tr: Decree of the University of Paris concerning the expulsion of the Jesuits. Seen and approved by us, Rector James d'Amboise, and sealed with red wax. The times favoured the demands of the Academy, and the memory of the recent evils stirred up by the Jesuits in the civil wars spoke in support of the Rector and the University, though they kept silent.

units.la: Ad hanc igitur litem Iesuitis intendendam, designati, postquam consilia in r se contulisset, libellum supplicem Parlamento Parisiensi exhibuerunt, cu‐jus haec fere summa est. Submisse supplicant Rector, Decani & facultates, nationum curatores, suffragatores, & studiosi Academiae Parisiensis, dicentes se jam pridem con‐ci ejus esse apud Curiam, de ingenti confusione, quam in Academia peperit nova quaedam ex Hispania & locis finitimis oriunda, ambitiosum titulum Societatis nominis Iesu ascisens, quae semper, sed his potissimum postremis civilibus bellis sese factiosam, & utricem Hispanicae conjurationis exhibuit, ad statum nostri eversionem, non in hac urbe Parisiensi tantum, sed in omnibus aliis regni locis. Quod quidem a primo ipsorum adventu profectum fuerat a praedictis supplicatoribus, & praesertim decreto facultatis Theologiae, quod tunc temporis interpositum fuit, quoniam haec seta introducta videbatur ad dinem Ecclesiae tum politicum, tum Hierarchicum & inprimis Academiae subverten‐ m, abnuens Rectori obsequium, atque adeo Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, Curionibus & aliis Ecclesiae superioribus. Effluxerunt autem anni triginta, ex quo suffragatores praedicti Societatis nomen Iesu sibi arrogantes cum in hac urbe tantum, & non in aliis regni oppidis suum effudissent, libellos supplices obtulerunt, postulates in Academiam nostram ifci: Quae causa cum primum propositu fuisset ad futuri confessus disceptationem rejecta, & statutum, ut res in eodem statu relinquerentur, quod erat prohibere, quo minus Iesuitae quicquam in illius sententia praejudicium aggrederetur. Cui tamen non satisfecerunt, quod gravius fuit, funestis suis consiliis res politicas perturbantes ministros et explo‐ratores se in Galliam gesserunt, ut Hispani commoda promoverent, sicut omnibus manifestum fuit. Haec causa ad futuros concessus relata, non amplius in judicium venit, necutrin‐que actiones excerptae fuerunt, ac proinde penitus concidit. His ergo rite examinatis, Do‐mini, placeat vobis, decreto vestro, hanc sectam, non solum ex Academia, sed ex universa ancia solo eliminare, & sic ex jure & aequo statuetis. Signatum Le Royer, & a latere Amboise Academiae Rector.
units.tr: To press this suit against the Jesuits, the men designated, after they had conferred their plans together, presented a supplicatory petition to the Parliament of Paris, the substance of which is roughly this. The Rector, Deans and faculties, the curators of the nations, the supporters and the students of the Paris Academy humbly beg, saying that they have for some time been bringing before the Court the great confusion that a certain new society, arising from Spain and the neighbouring places, has caused in the Academy. Assuming the ambitious title of the Society of the Name of Jesus, it has always shown itself factious, and especially in these latest civil wars, a bellows of the Spanish conspiracy for the overthrow of the state, not only in this city of Paris but in all the other places of the kingdom. This had indeed been begun from the very first arrival of these men by the aforesaid petitioners, and especially by a decree of the faculty of Theology, which was then issued, since this sect was seen to have been introduced to subvert the discipline of the Church, both political and hierarchical, and above all the Academy, refusing obedience to the Rector and so to the Archbishops, Bishops, parish priests and other superiors of the Church. Thirty years have now passed since the aforesaid supporters, arrogating to themselves the name of the Society of Jesus, when they had poured it out in this city alone and not in the other towns of the kingdom, presented petitions demanding entry into our Academy. When this cause was first laid before the assembly, it was rejected for future debate, and it was decided that matters should be left in the same state, which had the effect of preventing the Jesuits from being harmed in their own cause. They did not, however, comply with this; and what was more serious, by their baneful counsels disturbing political affairs, they conducted themselves in France as ministers and spies, so that they might advance the interests of the Spaniards, as is clear to everyone. This cause, having been referred to a future assembly, no longer came to judgment, and neither side's actions were examined, and so it has entirely lapsed. Therefore, gentlemen, once these matters have been duly examined, may it please you by your decree to expel this sect, not only from the Academy but from the whole soil of the realm, and so decide according to right and equity. Signed, Le Royer; and on the side, d'Amboise, Rector of the Academy.

units.la: Si vero Patres Ignatianae Societatis tam graviter essent accusati, & tam ca‐es haberet inimicos, non destitere tame se opponere, neque hoc solum: sed in actionibus publicis, privatisque confessionibus multa in praesentem Galliae sta‐tum, in Principes Regni, in Regem ipsum tam defunctum, quam praesentem eriis forte, quam prudenter locuti sunt. Quare potentum in se indigna‐ nem magis provocarunt, ignemque (ut aiunt) gladio foderunt: Hinc in suspicio‐ne seditionis concitandae venerunt. Sed & ex confessione cuiusdam Barrierij, elodunì ob tentatum in Regem parricidium extremo supplicio affecti, cri‐minis laesae Maiestatis rei sunt habiti.
units.tr: But even if the Fathers of the Ignatian Society were accused so grievously, and had such powerful enemies, they did not cease to oppose them, and not only that: in public acts and private confessions they spoke about the present state of France, the princes of the realm and the King himself, both the dead and the living, with much imprudence. Thus they provoked the anger of the powerful against themselves, and, as they say, fed the fire with a sword. Hence they came under suspicion of stirring up sedition. Moreover, from the confession of a certain Barrière, who was executed with the utmost punishment for an attempted parricide against the King, they were held to be guilty of the crime of treason.

units.la: Quae omnia multorum animos ab illis abalienarunt; adeo, ut tandem Cu‐ Parisiensi 7. die Iulij an. 1594. eis diem dixerit, eosque in ius vocaverit, ut publi‐ causam dicerent, seseque defenderent. Iesuitae, post varias tergiversationes, ac volas hinc inde conquisitas excusationes, per Advocatum suum Claudium tretum, a Parlamento petierunt, ut causa sua, non uti solitum alias esset, pa‐lam, sed occlusis ianuis secreto tractaretur: isto cum praetextu, quod pro Apo‐stolis suae ratione seu conditione, adeoque necessitate ipsa, non possent aliter, nisi ut multos, qui Regis ministri admodum fidi velint haberi, perstringerent, et non parum offenderet. Quod ipsis, ut ut longe aliud spectantibus, permis‐sum tamen atque concessum fuit. Decretum igitur est ut processus iuris clausis fo‐ribus instituatur. Designati sunt Advocati Academiae M. Antonius Arnaldi; Parisiensis urbis, qui se Academiae iunxerant, Ludovicus; Dolleus; Societatis M. Claudius Duretus; Procuratoris Generalis suae Maiestatis, Dom. Seguirrus. Societatis defensiones uti & aliorum accusationes videre nobis non conti‐ gitimus M. Antonij Arnaldi accusatio nuper ad manus nostras pervenit, cuius haec fere praecipua capita sunt.
units.tr: All these things alienated the minds of many from them, so much so that at last the Parliament of Paris, on 7 July 1594, set them a day and summoned them to court, that they might publicly plead their case and defend themselves. The Jesuits, after various evasions and excuses sought out on all sides, through their advocate Claude Tretus, asked Parliament that their cause should not be heard openly, as had been the custom in other cases, but be conducted in secret with the doors closed. Their pretext was that, because of their position and condition as Apostles, and the necessity itself, they could not otherwise do this without offending many who wished to be considered most faithful ministers of the King. This was permitted and granted to them, although they were aiming at something quite different. Therefore it was decreed that the legal process should be conducted with the doors closed. The advocates were designated: for the Academy, Master Antoine Arnauld, who had joined the Academy, and Louis Dolle, of the city of Paris; for the Society, Master Claude Duret; for the Procurator General of His Majesty, Dom Seguier. We have not been able to see the defences of the Society nor the accusations of the others; the accusation of Master Antoine Arnauld has recently come into our hands, and its main heads are roughly these.

units.la: Iesuitas ad summas opes pervenisse : In Italia & Hispania Comitatus & Baronias possidere, ad Cardinalatum evectos, & post Pontifices Romanos futuros. In Hispania novem aut decem millia esse; Collegia ibidem habere ducenta viginti octo, possidere plusquam viginti centena aureorum millia, &c.
units.tr: That the Jesuits have risen to very great wealth: that in Italy and Spain they possess counties and baronies, that they have been raised to the cardinalate and will be Roman Pontiffs afterwards. That in Spain there are nine or ten thousand of them; that they have two hundred and twenty-eight colleges there and possess more than two thousand hundred thousand gold pieces, etc.

units.la: 2. Primarium eorum votum est, per omnia, & in omnibus obedire suo Generali, aut procuratori, qui semper est Hispanus, aut Hispaniae Regi subjectus. Qui si dixerit; Abi & interfice Regem Franciae, eundum esset.
units.tr: 2. Their chief vow is to obey their General, or the procurator, who is always a Spaniard, or subject to the King of Spain, in all things and through all things. If he should say: Go and kill the King of France, they would have to go.

units.la: 3. Societas haec primum probata est in Hispanijs. Videtur nata ad Imperium Hispanicum promovendum, vocant Regem Philippum maximam potentiam, murum & antemurale Domus Dei, orant pro Rege Philippo, &c. Pro Rege autem Franciae non orant.
units.tr: 3. This Society was first approved in the Spanish realms. It seems to have been born to advance the Spanish empire: they call King Philip the greatest power, the wall and bulwark of the House of God, they pray for King Philip, etc. But they do not pray for the King of France.

units.la: 4. Docent Pontificium jus esse ex communicandi Reges Franciae, subditos ab eorum obedientia solvendi. Cuius contrarium offendere conatur.
units.tr: 4. They teach that it is the right of the Papacy to excommunicate the Kings of France and to release their subjects from obedience to them. They try to pass off the contrary as an offence.

units.la: 5. Patriarcha eorum Ignatius Lajola Castilanus, capitaneus unius peditum vexilli in oppugnatione Pampilonae militavit: ibique ab obsessis in crure vulneratus, incredibiles sensit dolores. Quare vouit perpetuum se & capitalem Franciae fore hostem, & quidem infiniorem, quam Hannibal Romanorum. Eum sectantur omnes eius filij. Naturam, ait, prudenter agere, ut animalia ferociora & noxiora minus sint fecunda. At Iesuitas 60. qui primum hanc Societatem instituerunt, ita brevissimo spatio multiplicatos, ut decem millia inventa sint, quae Societatis institutum profiterentur. Commemorat deinde quam parvi initijs favore Cardinalis Turonensis, et Lotharingij ad magnam amplitudinem pervenerint.
units.tr: 5. Their patriarch Ignatius Loyola, a Castilian, served as captain of one company of foot in the siege of Pamplona, where, wounded in the leg by the besieged, he suffered incredible pains. Therefore he vowed that he would be a perpetual and chief enemy of France, and indeed a more implacable one than Hannibal was of the Romans. All his sons follow him. Nature, he says, acts wisely in making the fiercer and more harmful animals less fertile. But the sixty Jesuits who first instituted this Society were so multiplied in a very short space that ten thousand were found who professed the Society's rule. He then recounts how, from small beginnings, with the favour of the Cardinal of Tours and of Lorraine, they came to great eminence.

units.la: 6. Coniurationes plusquam Catilinarias in eorum Collegijs, in platea S. Antonij, & S. Iacobi a Legatis Hispanicis Mendoza, Daguillonio, Diego, Varra, Taxi, Feri et aliis fabricatas, Nobiles quosdam absolvere noluerunt, nisi iuramento, quo Regi defuncto erant devincti, renunciarent, seditiosis suis concionibus multas urbes & oppida perderunt. Cum duobus Cardinalibus Legatis Francicis consilia contulerunt; urbem Parisiensem Philippo Regi Hispaniarum tradere voluerunt; Regi Philippo statum Regni perscripserunt. Eorum dictum esse, Unus Deus, unus Papa, unus Rex Christianismi, magnus Rex Catholicus & universalis. Omnia eorum acta & dicta, omnes eorum cogitationes spectare, ut Regem Hispaniarum Europae Monarcham constituant. Parricidae fuerunt Maiestatis Regiae, ut ex confessione Barrierij, Meloduni extremo supplicio interfectus omnibus est notissimum. Nam etsi propositum male successerit; maluissent tamen patratorem inepti facinoris esse rei. In publicis concionibus laudarunt factum Iacobi Clementi Henrici Regis III. interfectoris. Docent, licere omnes Principes Regni, a Pontifice excommunicatos interficere, &c.
units.tr: 6. In their colleges, in the square of St Anthony and St James, they fabricated conspiracies more than Catilinarian, with the Spanish envoys Mendoza, Daguillon, Diego, Varra, Taxis, Ferreri and others; some noblemen they would not absolve unless they renounced the oath by which they had been bound to the dead King; by their seditious sermons they have ruined many cities and towns. They took counsel with two Cardinal legates of France; they wanted to hand the city of Paris over to Philip, King of Spain; they set out the state of the realm to King Philip in writing. Their saying was: one God, one Pope, one King of Christendom, the great Catholic and universal King. All their acts and words, all their thoughts, aim to make the King of Spain the monarch of Europe. They were parricides of the royal majesty, as is most widely known from the confession of Barrière, who was put to death with the utmost punishment at Melun. For although the plan turned out badly, they would nevertheless have preferred the perpetrator of that foolish crime to be the accused. In public sermons they praised the deed of Jacques Clément, the slayer of King Henry III. They teach that all princes of the realm excommunicated by the Pope may be killed, etc.

units.la: 7. In suis statutis articulum habent; Absq. anno probationis se recipere eos, qui se offerunt ad faciendum votum suum; post quod, etsi simplex sit, hi qui votum fecerunt, irrevocabiliter suo Generali obligantur. Generalis autem votum illud reddere potest irritum quandocunque illi placuerit, etiam post 25. aut 30. annos. In quam constitutionem Magister Antonius magno orationis fervore invehitur.
units.tr: 7. In their statutes they have an article: that those who offer themselves to make their vow are received without a year of probation; after which, although the vow is simple, those who have made it are bound irrevocably to their General. The General, moreover, can render that vow void whenever it pleases him, even after twenty-five or thirty years. Master Antoine Arnauld inveighs against this constitution with great fervour of speech.

units.la: 8. Iesuitae authores sunt mortis Regis Lusitaniae Sebastiani. Per Iesuitas Hispanus Regno Lusitaniae potitus est: Iesuitis impulsoribus in Insulis Terceris 28. Barones, & 5. nobiles Franci uno die, in una cataafa sunt capite multati; infiniti milites suspensi, 500. etiam Franciscani, aliique Monachi strangulati.
units.tr: 8. The Jesuits are the authors of the death of Sebastian, King of Portugal. Through the Jesuits the Spaniard gained possession of the kingdom of Portugal. At the instigation of the Jesuits, on the Azores, twenty-eight barons and five French noblemen were beheaded on one day, in one execution; countless soldiers were hanged, and five hundred, including Franciscans and other monks, were strangled.

units.la: 9. Iesuitae sunt ministri Regis Hispaniarum: testatur hoc favor, benevolentia & liberalitas, qua illos prosequitur.
units.tr: 9. The Jesuits are ministers of the King of Spain: the favour, goodwill and liberality with which he courts them bear witness to this.

units.la: 10. Iesuitae sunt Cardinales, ut postea fiant Pontifices. Toletanus enim Cardinalis est, qui Duci Nivernensi tam superbum responsum reddidit.
units.tr: 10. The Jesuits are cardinals, so that afterwards they may become Popes. For the Toledan is a cardinal, the one who gave the Duke of Nevers such a haughty answer.

units.la: 11. Iesuitae ante 38. annos, cum locum in Gallia peterent, tam a Curia, quam a Sociis bona sunt rejecti. Et quia nec seculares sunt, nec Religiosi, etiam cum confirmatione Societatis peterent, a Cardinalibus repulsi sunt.
units.tr: 11. Thirty-eight years ago, when the Jesuits sought a place in France, they were rejected by the Court as well as by the other societies. And because they are neither secular nor regular clergy, even when they sought confirmation of their Society, they were repulsed by the cardinals.

units.la: 12. Etsi Iesuitæ edicto Regio non comprehendantur; comprehenduntur tamen Edicto 4. Aprilis, anni 1594. quia sacrosfoederi nolunt renunciare, & Regi juramentum fidelitatis præstare.
units.tr: 12. Although the Jesuits are not included in the royal edict, they are nevertheless included in the edict of 4 April 1594, because they will not renounce the sacred covenant and render the oath of allegiance to the King.

units.la: 13. Salvis Iesuitis, salva non potest esse Parisiensis Academia.
units.tr: 13. If the Jesuits are safe, the Parisian Academy cannot be safe.

units.la: Inhis omnibus tacitæ simul objectioni occurrit: Iesuitæ instituunt & docent juventutem. Respondet, imò docent, sed Reges suos jugulare & occidere, seditiones movere, tyrannidem Hispanicam stabilire: Qui filios suos Iesuitis tradunt instituendos, et filijs & bonis suis periclitantur. Ab adolescentibus magnum minerval pro institutione accipiunt. Tyrannus Hispaniæ seminavit Iesuitas per Galliam, ut teneris Gallorum animis amorem sui nominis & dominationis inserant.
units.tr: In all these things he also meets an objection unspoken at the same time: the Jesuits instruct and teach the youth. He replies: indeed they teach, but to cut the throats and slay their own kings, to stir up sedition, to establish Spanish tyranny. Those who hand their sons over to the Jesuits to be educated expose their sons and their goods to danger. From the young they take a large fee for instruction. The tyrant of Spain has sown the Jesuits through France, so that they may implant in the tender minds of the French a love of his name and dominion.

units.la: Deinde, quia Societas maximè se tueri videtur Concilio Anni 64. ea quæ pro Iesuitis facere videntur quoq; refutat.
units.tr: Then, since the Society seems chiefly to be protected by the Council of the year 1564, he also refutes what seems to be done in favour of the Jesuits.

units.la: Vocat illos non sine gravi causa Hispanorum corycæos, homines sceleratissimos, ruentis manibus, immani avaritia, nocentissimos ac superbissimos, quibus fides, decus, ietas, honesta atq; inhonesta omnia quæstui sint: ad excogitandum acutissimos, ad audendum impudentissimos, ad efficiendum acerrimos.
units.tr: He calls them, not without serious cause, the Corycians of Spain: most wicked men, with rash hands, of monstrous avarice, most harmful and most arrogant, for whom faith, honour, piety, and everything honourable and dishonourable are matters of gain; most keen to devise, most shameless to dare, most fierce to accomplish.

units.la: Occurrit etiam illis, qui dicunt; Si eiciamus Iesuitas, quid dicent Romæ? dicingue, ait, inter ipsos dicentes, Hispani dicent; Qui Iesuitas Francia expulerunt omnes sunt Hæretici. Alij vero qui Romæ & in Italia sunt, & Hispaniam non viderunt, dicent; egregium esse factum, quo Franci significant, se libertatem amare, in libertate velle manere, & inimicos esse juratos omnium Hispanorum.
units.tr: He also meets those who say: If we drive out the Jesuits, what will they say at Rome? Among themselves, he says, they will say: the Spanish will say that those who expelled the Jesuits from France are all heretics. But others, who are at Rome and in Italy and have never seen Spain, will say that the deed was splendid, by which the French show that they love liberty, wish to remain in liberty, and are sworn enemies of all Spaniards.

units.la: Si Iesuitæ tam perniciosi sint Franciæ, cur tanta miracula fecere in India? Hic omnem tyrannidem Hispanorum, quam miro verborum ornatu amplificat, solis Iesuitis adscribit.
units.tr: If the Jesuits are so pernicious to France, why did they work such great miracles in India? Here he ascribes to the Jesuits alone all the tyranny of the Spaniards, which he magnifies with a remarkable ornament of words.

units.la: Respondet quoque illis, qui dicunt; Si tam scelerati sint Iesuitæ, cur non condemnantur & occiduntur? & respondet, occidi quidem posse, ut Fratres olim, qui Humiliati dicebantur, & ut Templarij, sed non expedire.
units.tr: He also replies to those who say: If the Jesuits are so wicked, why are they not condemned and killed? And he replies that they could indeed be killed, as the Brethren once were who were called Humiliati, and as the Templars were, but that it is not expedient.

units.la: Denique occurrit his qui dicunt; Non omnes Iesuitæ esse externos & advenas. Fatetur quidem multos esse indigenas, natione, at quia mente peregrini sunt, inter ingenas non esse numerandos. Ego, inquit, potius cives credam qui in extrema Scythia nati, bene de Gallia cogitant, quam qui Lutetiæ geniti & educati, locum, libertatem, gloriam, in qua nati sunt, per summum scelus perdere velint & conentur.
units.tr: Finally he meets those who say: not all Jesuits are foreigners and strangers. He concedes indeed that many are natives by birth, but because in mind they are foreigners, they are not to be counted among natives. I, he says, would rather believe citizens who were born in the furthest Scythia and think well of France to be citizens, than those who were born and brought up at Paris, and who wish and try, by the greatest wickedness, to lose the place, the liberty and the glory in which they were born.

units.la: Pervicerunt tamen hoc adhuc tempore Iesuitæ, tum privatis flagitatioibus, tum Principum summorum-que procerum suffragijs; ut lis mota suspenderetur, adeoq; veteraseceret. Carolus Borbonius Cardinalis procellæ huic, qua obicem, sese opposuit, dato supplici libello ad hos qui actioni huic destinati erant, cum gravissimè decumberet; adiecto in calce propria manu, si per valetudinem liceret, vox peragereret, quod tremula manu exarat calamus. Ludovicus Gonzaga Dux Nivernensis, supplici itidem libello, non solum rogat in Nivernensi oppido & Ambarris suis; musæum Iesuitarum sartum salvumq; reinquì, sed etiam ob collegarum aliquot dementiam non esse vindicandum in universos. Claromontanus Episcopus similiter intercessit.
units.tr: Yet the Jesuits, even at this time, prevailed, both by private solicitations and by the votes of the highest princes and nobles, so that the lawsuit begun was suspended and so grew old. Cardinal Charles de Bourbon set himself against this storm, which was an obstacle, by presenting a humble petition to those who had been appointed to this business, although he was very gravely ill; he added at the foot, in his own hand, what the quill traces with a trembling hand, if his health permitted him to say it aloud. Ludovico Gonzaga, Duke of Nevers, likewise in a humble petition, asks not only that the Jesuit college in the town of Nevers and in his own Ambert be kept intact and safe, but also that on account of the madness of some of their colleagues it should not be avenged upon all of them. The Bishop of Clermont likewise interceded.

units.la: Nonâ quoque die Iulij Anno 1594. supplicem libellum obtulerunt Iesuitæ facultati Theologicæ Parisiensi, in quo exposuerunt, superioribus mensibus Rectorem, tam suo, quam omnium facultatum nomine, à suprema Parlamenti Curia petijsse, ut ipsi cum universa Societate, ex toto Galliæ regno pelerentur: Se autem non credere, sacratissimam facultatem huic petitioni assensum præbuisse: petere igitur, quatenus placeret dictæ facultati, declaratione aliqua testificari, eam huius petitionis & litis intentæ, nullo modo participe esse. Facultas igitur dicta in hunc modum decrevit; Se quidem censere Iesuitas redigendos & recensendos in ordinem & disciplinam Universitatis, non autem Regno Galliæ expellendos esse. Et hoc quidem decreto Societatem hanc non simpliciter approbavit facultas Theologica; sed quatenus Universitatis decretis & statutis sese subiiciat.
units.tr: On the ninth day of July in the year 1594 the Jesuits also presented a humble petition to the Theological Faculty of Paris, in which they set out that in the preceding months the Rector, in his own name and in the name of all the faculties, had sought from the supreme Court of Parliament that they, together with the whole Society, be driven from the entire kingdom of France; that they, however, did not believe the most sacred faculty had given assent to this petition; they therefore asked that, so far as it pleased the said faculty, it should attest by some declaration that it was in no way party to this petition or to the suit brought. The said faculty therefore decreed in this manner: That it judges the Jesuits should be brought back and reckoned into the order and discipline of the University, not expelled from the kingdom of France. And by this decree the Theological Faculty did not simply approve this Society, but only so far as it submits itself to the decrees and statutes of the University.

units.la: Finita autem hac postrema actione forensi, scriptum Apologeticum ediderunt Iesuitæ, in quo probare conantur, Rectorem & Academicos non esse ferendos, cum sua non interfit, sed publicæ cognitionis ac Triumvirorum fiscalium, in quorum potestate publica sit censura & animadversio. Decretum Mathurineum Sorbonica definitione convulsum his verbis: Censere prædictos Patres Societatis Iesu redigendos esse in ordinem & disciplinam Universitatis, regno autem Gallico nullo modo expellendos. Facultatem artium decreto fidem abrogasse, syngrapha trium Procuratorum nationalium, Decanum Profess. Iuris Pontificii, Medicinæque Syndicum, non de expellendis, sed tantum in ordinem cogendis cogitasse; Rectorem pene unum Decreti esse conditorem. Ex quadraginta circiter Pastoribus urbanis, quatuor esse duntaxat qui controversiæ nomen dederint, Episcopo & Decano infscijs: non licuisse autem paucis Universorum nomine in foro causam dicere. Sodalitium Iesuitarum in Tridentina Synodo Pontificijs relatum; Pauli 3. Iulij 2. Pij 4. & 5. Gregorij 13. & 14. & à Clero Gallicano in Poissiaceno consessu ab Henrico 2. Francisco 2. Carolo 9. Henrico 3. atque à supremis Curijs approbatum & receptum. Senatum Parisiensem non semel pias largitiones & legata sibi facta addixisse. Cameram rationalium computorum immunitati Collegiorum suorum calculum adiecisse; Non esse quod Rector ipse & commilitones Academici conquerantur, si quidem parati sint iurare in verba & decreta Academiæ, Regi Henrico 4. summam fidem & intimum obsequium pollicentes, colere & observare pro suo legitimo Principe, qui à Ludovico 9. indigete ortum duxerit, quem ordo sanguinis & cognationis, ac patriæ leges ad avitum imperium acciverint. Publica & universali clementia Regis, & rerum præteritarum condonatione non esse excludendos, qui cum cæteris dictorum & factorum consortium habuerint, ut publicis delictis gratia aliquandos; si sua domestica facta citra livorem excutiantur, minus fuisse populares, tribunitios & rerum bellicarum gnaros, cum nec fœderationi publicæ, quam Unionem vocant, nomen dederint, ut ab Ecclesiasticis pro caecitate illorum temporum factum sit: non galeam, non arma induisse: non in publica lustratione nedum Ecclesiasticorum, sed religiosorum armatorum conspicuos, aut irridendos potius fuisse; non externo auro aut stipendijs venalem fidem habuisse: non cæteribus illicitis aut cruentis consilijs interfuisse; peccasse quidem exemplo & cum cæteris publicam insaniam insanivisse: in posterum non esse metuendum ab illis, ut rebus aulicis & politicis se immiscerent, quandoquidem sui fodolitij privatis legibus in nova congregatione Romæ recensitis Novembri 1593. Cautum vetitumque sit distringere, ut ab omni rerum secularium tractatione, & Principum negotiis abstineant. Si regno facessere cogantur æmulorum invidia, non leve damnum bono publico illatum iri, cum pij elargitores conditoresque sui Collegij Claromontani, legatorum indictionibus anniversarijsque parentalibus priventur. Ex primarijs patricijsque viris non paucos, emissis regno Iesuitis, qui hoc institutum professi sint, liberis agnatisque caritatis: pubem Christianam, ac præcipue egentes, quorum minervalibus persolvendis res angusta domi impar sit, non levem jacturam facturos: qui subsunt ferulæ Iesuitarum, magno compendio temporis & sumptus, plurimum proficere, præcipue in disciplinis placitisque Philosophorum, in quibus citra invidiam, sui Professores primas teneant.
units.tr: After this last court action, the Jesuits published an Apologetic writing, in which they try to prove that the Rector and the Academics had no right to act, since the matter did not concern them but the public inquiry and the three fiscal Triumvirs, in whose power the public censure and punishment lie. They say the Mathurin decree was overturned by the Sorbonne's definition, which reads in these words: "We judge that the aforesaid Fathers of the Society of Jesus are to be brought back into the order and discipline of the University, but are in no way to be expelled from the kingdom of France." They claim that the Faculty of Arts had annulled the decree by a agreement signed by three national Procurators, the Dean of the Professors of Canon Law and the Syndic of Medicine, who had thought not of expelling them but only of bringing them into line; and that the Rector was almost the sole author of the decree. Of about forty city ministers, only four had given their names to the dispute, the Bishop and the Dean being unaware of it; and it was not permitted for a few men to plead a case in court in the name of all. The Jesuit fraternity had been listed among the Papists at the Council of Trent; Popes Paul III, Julius II, Pius IV and V, and Gregory XIII and XIV had approved it, and the Gallican clergy at the assembly of Poissy had approved and received it under Henry II, Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III, as had the supreme courts. The Parisian Senate had more than once assigned to itself pious gifts and bequests made to it. The Chamber of Accounts had added its reckoning to the immunities of their colleges. The Rector himself and his fellow Academics had no reason to complain, since they were ready to swear to the words and decrees of the Academy, promising to King Henry IV the highest loyalty and the deepest obedience, and to honour and obey him as their lawful prince, who traced his descent from Louis IX, whom the order of blood and kinship and the laws of the country had summoned to the ancestral throne. They said that by the public and universal clemency of the King, and the pardon of past events, those who had shared in the words and deeds of the others should not be shut out, just as some are pardoned for public offences. If their own domestic acts were examined without malice, they had been less rash, less given to the tribunes and less skilled in warfare than was thought; since they had not even given their names to the public league which they call the Union, as the churchmen wrongly claimed because of the blindness of those times. They had not put on helmets or arms; in the public review they were conspicuous not as armed men, let alone churchmen, but rather as men to be laughed at. They had not sold their loyalty for foreign gold or pay; they had not taken part in other unlawful or bloody plots. They had sinned, indeed, by example and had gone mad together with the others in the public madness; but for the future there was no need to fear that they would meddle in court or political affairs, since by the private rules of their fraternity, reviewed in a new congregation at Rome in November 1593, it was laid down and forbidden that they should abstain from all secular business and the affairs of princes. If they were forced to leave the kingdom through the envy of their rivals, no slight loss would be inflicted on the public good, since the pious benefactors and founders of their College of Clermont would be deprived of the bequests and annual memorial gifts. Not a few of the leading and patrician men, if the Jesuits were sent out of the kingdom, would lose their children and kinsmen who had professed this institute, out of love; the Christian youth, and especially the needy, whose small household means could hardly pay the tuition fees, would suffer no slight loss; while those who are under the rod of the Jesuits gain much in a short time and at small cost, especially in the disciplines and doctrines of the philosophers, in which, without envy, their teachers hold the first place.

units.la: Hæc vel non dissimilia Apologeticus ille scriptor multo latius explicuit, ac probra forensia sigillatim diluere conatus est. Quatuor autem potissimum, præter superiora illis obijciebantur. Primo quod Pontifici Rom. nimium addicti sint; secundo, quod à Gallis degeneres, Hispanicos mores induerint; tertio, quod uód irrequieti sint & tribunitij in vulgo: quarto, quód Regum Principumq; carij sint.
units.tr: The Apologist explained these or similar points at much greater length, and tried to refute the court's charges point by point. Four main charges, besides those mentioned above, were brought against them: (1) that they were too devoted to the Roman Pope; (2) that, being degenerate Frenchmen, they had adopted Spanish manners; (3) that they were restless and given to stirring up the common people; (4) that they were creatures of kings and princes.

units.la: Ad primum respondit Apologeticus, Iesuitas una cum caeteris Ecclesiæ ascendis Christianis, Pontificem Rom. ut vicarium Christi in navicula Petri gubernatorem, caput Ecclesiæ agnovisse. Hæc elogia & obsequia non esse privata neq; recentia suitarum, sed orbis universi, qui Christo regeneratus sit. Papam nunquam rerum temporalium moderatorem, clientelari obsequio & vasallorum more agnovisse, qui in Principum Regumq; ditiones & imperia jus summum distringere, & ea ad nutum variare posse. Falsò collegæ suo Bellarmino tribui, quòd in ea fuerit sententia lib. 5. c. 9. de Rom. Pontifice. Affirmasse quidem eum, Papam in Exarchatu, Bononia, Spoleto, Aemilia, Ravenna, caeterisq; Pontificijs ditionibus summum esse Principem, jus habere vitæ et necis, denique agere quod Reges omnes in regnis suis. Tribus votis tantum alligari: quarum habere aliud certo modo circa missiones duntaxat; hoc est, si Pontifex cuiperiam extubernalibus, ut ad juvandam rem Christianam ad Indos, Peruvianos, Lestrigonas profectionem imperaverit. Quarto illo voto ad obeundam illam provinciam, & duriorem, jubeatur, alligari, votum illud ut a probro vindicetur, eius hanc esse conceptis verbis formulam: Insuper promitto summo Pontifici specialem obedientiam circa missiones. Votum hoc quartum non tam Ignatianum, quam commune cum universis presbyteris esse, qui in initiantur, apud suos praesules hoc sacramento se alligant: Promittis mihi & successoribus meis reverentiam & obedientiam? promitto.
units.tr: To the first, the Apologist replied that the Jesuits, together with the other Christians of the Church, acknowledged the Roman Pontiff as the vicar of Christ, the governor of Peter's little ship, and the head of the Church. These honours and acts of obedience were not private or recent in the Jesuits, but belonged to the whole world, which has been regenerated in Christ. The Pope had never acknowledged himself as the ruler of temporal affairs, with the servile obedience of a client and the manner of vassals, who could claim the supreme right over the dominions and empires of princes and kings, and change them at his nod. Their colleague Bellarmine was wrongly credited with holding that opinion in book 5, chapter 9, on the Roman Pontiff. He had indeed affirmed that the Pope, in the Exarchate, Bologna, Spoleto, Emilia, Ravenna and the other papal dominions, is the supreme prince, has the right of life and death, and may in short do what all kings do in their kingdoms. But he is bound by only three vows, and of these one has a special application to missions alone; that is, if the Pope should order any member of the society to go to the Indians, the Peruvians or the Laestrygonians to help the Christian cause. As for the fourth vow, to undertake that province, which is harder, when he is ordered to do so, the vow is to be cleared of reproach; its formula, in these words, is: "Moreover I promise the Supreme Pontiff special obedience in regard to missions." This fourth vow is not so much Ignatian as common to all priests who are ordained; by this sacrament they bind themselves to their superiors, saying: "Do you promise me and my successors reverence and obedience? I promise."

units.la: Secundo, quòd Celtiberi sint, pugnantia illis exprobrari: nam si, ut primo capite insinuantur, Pontificis Rom. clientes sint, eiq; serviliter addicti, non posse fieri, ut Hispano vivant, cum dominium sit impatiens consortis: Pontificem & Hispaniæ Reges esse plenaeque in saeculariabus admodum divisos & discrepantes, ita ut invicem armis decernant. Non caelo & solo Hispanico natos; tota Gallia nullum habere Hispanum commilitonem: cum religione neutiquam exuisse patrios mores, non illam ademisse ingenium & manuetudinem Gallicam: non esse hoc opprobrium tribuendum optimo instituto, ut quasi Cireo poculo in aliam gentem transformati & efferati sint; vel vultu ipso testari patriam, non adusta & fusca cute referre Africanos. Concordes esse votis & ritibus vivendi, sed ingenio & natura; cum Stoica fide veritate Hispanorum multum discrepantes. Non solum indigenis esse quotquot Galliam incolant Iesuitæ, sed non paucos esse qui genitilitate & conatione proxima Patres Conscriptos attingant. Mirari se plurimum, quòd pro exploratoribus, institoribus, emissariis, ambaesque Hispanorum traducantur; cum, si in eam noxiam inciderint, patriam, parentesque, & amicos hac proditione venderent. Ab Hispano aurum, non stipendia meruisse, ut plurimi, qui in Lutetiana egestate, auro Indico fidem venalem habuerint. Angustias annonae cum caeteris anxie tolerasse; in eadem navi cisse, quod lex nautica & Rhodia de jactu cogit, quod argumento sit ut plurimum, nusquam se Regi Hispanorum devovisse; cum prece, pretio, Comitijsque publicis, regnum Galliæ affectaret & ambiret, illum ad eos non scripsisse, ut ad plurimos, quorum interceptae literae nomina & syngraphas prodidere. Cum vero anno superiori popularii infamia; Austæ seu Infanti Hispanicae & Ernesto Archiduci (quasi lilia hastae & auctionibus ac luris licitanti subjacerent) deferendum regnum publicaretur, Iesuitas tam in solens prositum ut portentum, privatim verbo & facto exhorruisse. Non esse vero simile, fodalitium suum D. Ludovici memoriæ tum ob summum inter Coelites suum principatum; tum ob senioris Borbonij Cardinalis sui gentilis summa beneficia addictissimum; Juis nepotibus avita lilia eriperentur & Francico solo avulsa in alienam gentem coalescerent, proraffe. Cunabula Ignatij Loyolæ institutoris sui, à maledictis male intellecta, cum ille non Hispanus, sed Astur & Cantaber fuerit, adeoq; Navarraeus: & si jura sinerent Henrici 4. & proavorum indigena & subditus erat. Sed fuerit Hispanus, tamen Dominicus Calpuritanus, merecq; Hispanus; Franciscus Assisias, atq; Italus fuit; nihilominus tolerantur
units.tr: Second, they are reproached with being Spaniards (Celtiberians), which is inconsistent with the charges. For if, as was hinted in the first charge, they are clients of the Roman Pontiff and slavishly devoted to him, they cannot be Spanish in spirit, since lordship does not tolerate a partner; and the Pope and the kings of Spain are often, in worldly matters, so divided and at odds that they settle their disputes by arms. They were not born under a Spanish sky or on Spanish soil; the whole of France has no Spanish fellow-soldier. They had by no means put off their native customs with their religion, nor had religion taken away their French nature and gentleness; and it is not fair to cast this reproach on an excellent institute, as if they had been turned into another nation and made wild, as if by Circe's cup; or as if their very face did not bear witness to their country, or their scorched and dark skin did not show them to be Africans. They agree with the Spaniards in their vows and in their manner of life, but not in their disposition and nature; in their faith, which is Stoic, and in truth they differ greatly from the Spaniards. The Jesuits are not only natives of France, all who live in France, but there are not a few among them who by birth and close relationship touch the Conscript Fathers. He marvelled greatly that they were taken for spies, traders, emissaries and ambassadors of the Spaniards; for if they had fallen into such a crime, they would by this treachery sell their country, their parents and their friends. They had received gold, not pay, from the Spaniard, as many did who, in their poverty at Paris, had sold their loyalty for Indian gold. They had endured the shortage of food anxiously with the others; they had been in the same ship, which the nautical and Rhodian law of jettison requires; and this is, for the most part, a proof that they never devoted themselves to the King of Spain. For while by prayer, bribery and public assemblies they aimed at and sought the kingdom of France, they did not write to him, as many did, whose intercepted letters and bonds revealed their names. But when, in the year before, amid public infamy, the kingdom was announced to be handed over to the Infanta of Spain, or Ernest the Archduke (as if the lilies were on the spear and subject to auction and bidding), the Jesuits, so unaccustomed to such a betrayal, shrank from it in private, by word and deed, as from a monstrous thing. It is not likely that their fraternity, mindful of St Louis, would have pushed for the lilies of their ancestors to be torn away from his descendants and carried off from French soil to join a foreign nation, both because of his supreme rule among the heavenly citizens and because of the great favours of his kinsman, the elder Cardinal of Bourbon. The birthplace of Ignatius of Loyola, their founder, was misread by the slanderers; for he was not a Spaniard but an Asturian and Cantabrian, and therefore a Navarrese; and, if the laws permitted, he was a native and subject of Henry IV and of his forefathers. But even if he had been a Spaniard, Dominic was of Calahorra and a Spaniard, and Francis was of Assisi and an Italian; nevertheless they are tolerated.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: DE PROPAGATIONE

units.la: in Gallia. Nec Ignatij institutum in Hispania, sed in Regina Gallia Lutetia, primordia duxit, qui cum sibi acciris decem artium magistris, lucro animarum & juventutis institutioni devovit. Qui objiciant, non nisi Hispanum creari Generalem inter Iesuitas, vel hoc uno rerum gestarum et recentium profiteri imperitiam, cum Claudius de Aquaviva, ex Parthenopaeorum Principum familia ortus, hoc nunc munere perfungatur, cujus gentilibus Hispanus infensissimus fuerit, quod partes Gallicas Andegauorumque Ducum adversus Aragonios sequuti sint: qui eum ante cesserit, fuisse Trajectensem Belga-Germanum. Similiter loco figmenti habendum, quod illis exprobratur, adversus Antoninum Lusitaniae Regem pro Philippo steterisse. Et qua Genua ad oram Ligusticam historia excusa dicitur, Genevae potius excusam fuisse, nec pro germana, sed ab aemulis conficta habenda. Matthaeum illum, qui ad Regem Hispaniae, a Sexdecim vulgo nominatis personatus tabellarius scriptas literas deferebat, ut exprobatur, non fuisse Iesuitam, sed ex Mendi cantium familia & quidem Hispanum. Iesuitas non Gallos iuvenes in Hispanos commutare, sed caveresolum, ne haeretica pravitate imbuantur.
units.tr: in France. Nor did Ignatius's institute take its beginnings in Spain, but in the royal city of Paris, where he, having gathered ten masters of the arts to himself, devoted himself to the winning of souls and the instruction of youth. Those who object that only a Spaniard can be made General among the Jesuits show their ignorance of past and recent events by this one point alone, since Claudio Acquaviva, sprung from the family of the princes of Naples, now holds that office. His kinsmen, they say, were most hated by the Spaniard, because they followed the French party and the Dukes of Anjou against the Aragonese. His predecessor, they say, was a Belgian-German from Maastricht. In the same way, what is thrown in their faces, that they took Philip's side against Antonio, King of Portugal, must be counted as a fiction. And the history said to have been printed at Genoa on the Ligurian coast was rather printed at Geneva, and is to be regarded not as genuine but as fabricated by their rivals. That Matthew who, disguised as a courier, carried written letters to the King of Spain for the men commonly called the Sixteen, as is alleged, was not a Jesuit but of the Mendoza family, and indeed a Spaniard. The Jesuits do not change young Frenchmen into Spaniards; they take care only that they not be imbued with heretical depravity.

units.la: Quod ad tertium objectum attinet, Iesuitas seditiosos & vulgi concitatores esse; ab hoc scelere se alienissimos esse. In Italia, Hispania, Germania, Belgio & Sarmatia a plurimis annis scholas & sodalitia habuisse, nec apud gentes illas de eorum moribus ullum rusticum & vicanum conquestum; scholis & concionibus occupatos, longe a tumultu & intemperiis vulgi, in Musaeis quietos vixisse.
units.tr: As for the third objection, that the Jesuits are seditious and stir up the common people, they are most remote from this crime. In Italy, Spain, Germany, Belgium and Poland they have for many years kept schools and sodalities, and among those peoples no rustic or villager has complained of their morals. Occupied with schools and sermons, far from the tumult and disorders of the crowd, they lived quietly in the retreats of the Muses.

units.la: Quartum similiter negat, nempe, Iesuitas esse Regum ac Principum sicarios. Vara-dum enim Regia caedis sicario Barierio non solum non suasorem fuisse, sed cum aperto & dementi urgiretur, hominem ablegasse: fiducia insontis animi, post ingressum Regis Lutetiae, manssisse Varadum, donec certior factus, tanti criminis labe aspergi, atque hinc in discrimen vocari, livori delatorum se subduxisset, nec illum tam conscientiae celeris, quam quod intellexisset, maluisse Regem eum alibi esse, quam Lutetiae, ut voto morem gereret discessisse. In suo sodalitio pro Regibus & Principibus preces & vota quotidiana indiscriminatim fieri, sed privatim enixe & effuse pro iis, in quorum finibus incolatum habeat. Eundem Augerium, sui Ordinis olim tota Gallia notissimum, in sua Christiana Parenesi; pro incolumitate Regum Galliae privatas preces scripsisse. Ribadanairam Hispanum pro Hispano Rege id ipsum fecisse, id Gallia Iesuitis vitio verti iniquum esse: nec in liturgia aliisque precationibus vocem illam ab ullo mortalium exauditam, Oremus pro Rege nostro Philippo, sed hoc ab aliis fictum esse. Haec quidem ille, sed protestatio contraria est facto, ut infra Cap. de Iesuitarum nefariis facinoribus, prodinitionibus, &c. videbitur.
units.tr: Fourthly, they likewise deny that the Jesuits are assassins of kings and princes. Varadus, they say, was not only not an instigator of the royal murder by the assassin Barrière, but when Barrière pressed him with open and mad urgings, he sent the man away. Trusting in the innocence of his mind, Varadus remained at Paris after the King entered the city, until he learned more certainly that he was being stained with the taint of so great a crime and was being called into danger. Then he withdrew from the malice of the informers. Nor did he leave so much from a quick conscience as because he understood that the King would rather he were elsewhere than at Paris, so he departed to gratify that wish. In their sodality, prayers and daily vows are made for kings and princes indiscriminately, but privately, earnestly and fervently for those in whose realm one has one's residence. Auger, the same man once very well known throughout France in his Order, wrote in his Christian Exhortation private prayers for the safety of the Kings of France. Ribadeneira, a Spaniard, did the same for the Spanish King, and it is unjust, they say, for France to charge this against the Jesuits. Nor has that phrase, "Let us pray for our King Philip," ever been heard from any mortal in the liturgy or in other prayers; this, they say, was invented by others. So he says, but his protestation is contrary to the deed, as will be seen below in the chapter on the Jesuits' nefarious crimes, betrayals, and so on.
