units.la: Non possumus etiam omittere, quin singulares Majestati vestræ, ut Academiæ huius isereri velit, preces exhibeamus. Reges vestri Antecessores hoc optimæ vestræ civitati Parisiensi ornamentum relinquere voluerunt: at nunc intra paucos dies bona eius pars desetur: Fieri non potest, quin si quantam huius urbis partem videatis incultam, & à tam multis familijs, Bibliopolis & alijs, qui à literarum studijs victum quæritare solebant, nunc ad stipem redacti, relictam; idq; ad gratificandum tantum novorum Doctorum paro cuidam numero; qui sanè studere, legere, docere, & publico bono servire cum cæteris, nullum corpus singulare, ex ordine & religione novâ compositum, facere debebant.
units.tr: We cannot also refrain from offering special prayers to your Majesty, that you will be pleased to show favour to this Academy. Your predecessor kings wished to leave this ornament to your most excellent city of Paris, but now, within a few days, its better part is being deserted. It cannot be that, if you see how much of this city lies neglected and is abandoned by so many families, booksellers and others who used to earn their living from the study of letters, now reduced to begging, and all this merely to gratify a small number of new teachers, you will not be moved. These men ought indeed to study, read, teach and serve the public good along with the rest; they ought not to form a separate body, composed of a new order and religion.

units.la: Cimus sanè quòd Universitas reformatione opus habeat; verum hæc per ipsius ruinam eri non debet: quæ evitari non potest: non quidem ob horum, qui in hac sunt Societate, sentiam, sed propter Collegiorum, quæ in diversis sententijs permittetis, multitudinem; uæ ubi eam commoditatem ad manum habuerint, liberos suos in hanc urbem non amplius ittent: quod vos facile magni præjudicij esse judicabitis, quia facile est videre; quòd, ui hic educantur, sese à teneris ad Reges, & summi Imperij insignia suspicienda & anoscenda assuefaciant, illi verò qui in parvis oppidis educabuntur; eandem educatioem non recipient, neque similem affectum habebunt. Et sic Academia hæc, alias florensima, penitus evertetur, constitutis decem; aut duodecim Collegijs eorum, quorum Soetas semper suspecta, & institutio juventutis periculosissima erit.
units.tr: We know indeed that the University needs reform, but this ought not to come through its ruin, which cannot be avoided. It is not because of those who belong to this Society that this would happen, but on account of the multitude of colleges which you will permit in various places. When those who have such colleges at hand find this convenience, they will no longer send their children to this city. You will easily judge this to be a great prejudice, since it is plain to see that, when children are educated here, they grow accustomed from tender years to revere and recognise kings and the insignia of supreme authority; but those who are educated in small towns will not receive the same education and will not have a similar affection. And so this Academy, otherwise most flourishing, will be utterly overthrown once ten or twelve of those colleges, whose Society has always been suspect and whose instruction of youth will be most dangerous, are established.

units.la: Hæ sunt humilimæ obtestationes, rationesque summariæ, quæ nos à literarum pulicatione hactenus abstinuerunt, metuentes, ne justè nobis vitio verteretur, quòd niis leviter ad earum approbationem descendissemus. Humilimè supplicamus, ut eas in meliorem partem accipiatis, eamque nobis gratiam faciatis, ut si nobis aliquid manↄveritis, quod nobis videatur salvâ conscientiâ executioni mandari non debere, id on inobedientiæ nostræ, sed muneris nostri officio adscribatis. Quandoquidem existiamus, vos illam non velle, nisi in quantum ea justa, & æqua est, & intellestis ratioibus, propter quas illa talis declarari non possit, non graviter laturos quod obedientia vobis praestita non sit. E contrario, quando admonebimini, ut promissum aliquod praestetis, illius Monarchae responsum dare velitis, qui cum rogaretur, ut promissum suum verbis Regijs factum impleret, respondit, se id velle praestare, si justum esset, & verbum non ultrius obligare.
units.tr: These are the most humble entreaties and summary reasons which have hitherto kept us from publishing our writing, fearing that we might justly be blamed for having too readily given our approval to them. We humbly beg you to take them in good part, and to grant us this favour: that if you should command us to do anything which seems to us not to be carried out with a clear conscience, you will ascribe it not to our disobedience but to the duty of our office. For we believe that you do not wish this except insofar as it is just and fair, and that when you understand the reasons why it cannot be declared in such a way, you will not take it hard that obedience has not been rendered to you. On the other hand, when you are reminded to perform some promise, you may wish to give the answer of that Monarch who, when he was asked to fulfil his promise made in royal words, replied that he was willing to do so if it were just, and that his word did not bind him any further.

units.la: Domine, Rex es, & quidem Rex magnus, qui melius judicas id, quod justum est, quam omnes vestri subditi Verba vestra ipsa justitia sunt. Verum si nos vobis supplices esse possimus, vosque permissuri sitis, ut vobis cum omni humilitate offendamus: dicemus, quod Antecessores vestri illo semper Parlamenta honore dignati sint, quo Imperatores senatum: nimirum, ut causas Justitiae ipsorum consilio moderarentur: & quamvis absoluta potestate uti potuissent, illam nihilominus ob hunc respectum depositerunt, ac voluntates civilitatis Legum accommodaverunt.
units.tr: Sire, you are King, and indeed a great King, who judge better what is just than all your subjects; your own words are justice itself. Yet if we may be permitted to approach you as suppliants, and if you will allow us to offer our submission with all humility, we shall say that your predecessors always honoured the Parlements with that dignity with which the emperors honoured the Senate: namely, that they might moderate the cases of justice by their counsel; and although they could have used absolute power, they nevertheless laid it aside for this reason, and adapted their wills to the sense of the laws of civil society.

units.la: Pergite hac erga nos uti gratia, & conservate autoritatem illam, quam Antecessores vestri Curiae vestrae Parlamenti concesserunt, quae re ipsa non ipsius, sed vestra est, quia non aliunde, quam a vobis dependet: & quamvis illa eam perderet, ignoscite quaesumus nobis, dicentibus, quod ja&tura non in ipsam, sed in vos cessura sit. Deum totis corde & affectu precabimur, ut dies vestros in omni potestate & felicitate amplificet, Reginam, & D. Delphinum tam vobis quam subditis vestris conservet, & hanc nobis gratiam largiatur, ut omni felicitate humilimisque servitiis nostris demonstrare possimus, quod nullam majorem corporis animiqe felicitatem optemus, quam ut a vobis habeamur pro ijs, qui sumus humilimi videlicet, obedientissimi & fidelissimi vestri subditi & ministri.
units.tr: Continue to show us this favour, and preserve that authority which your predecessors granted to your Parlement, which in truth belongs not to itself but to you, since it depends on no one else than you; and even if it should lose it, we beg you to pardon us for saying that the loss would fall not upon it, but upon you. We shall pray to God with all our heart and affection that He may increase your days in all power and happiness, preserve the Queen and the Dauphin for you and for your subjects, and grant us this favour: that by all happiness and humble service we may show that we desire no greater felicity of body and soul than to be held by you as those who are your most humble, most obedient and most faithful subjects and servants.

units.la: ORATIO EXHORTATORIA AD REGEM CHRISTIANISSIMUM DE IESVITIS IN REGNO GALLIAE NON RECIPIENDIS.
units.tr: ORATION EXHORTING THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING NOT TO RECEIVE THE JESUITS INTO THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE.

units.la: AB hoc etiam proposito Gallo-Franci quidam alij seu patriae vere amantes omnibus modis Regem avertere conati sunt. Excusa est anno 1603, ingenua Oratio Galli cuiusdam, de eo quod tum postulatum & in deliberationem adductum fuit; nempe, ut Iesuitae restituantur in Regno Galliae; in qua multis rationibus & argumentis gravissimis & firmissimis hoc Regi dissuadet. Hanc orationem integram huc adscribam, in Lectoris gratiam, ad cuius manus forte illa non pervenit, ut omnes tam Pontificij, quam Reformati inde excerpant ac mutuentur, sibi quod ex usu fiet, & quod sapientis esse aiunt, ex aliorum infortunio ac damno praecaveamus nostrum. Et hic quidem Orator, quisquis sit, tanto apud Oes dignior esse debet, in iis quae ad profligandam Iesuiticam monstra promit armis, quanto minus favet Lutheranis & Calvinianis, ab utrisque enim partibus se alienissimum esse profitetur, & quanto est <bl>xa3wlix</bl>, se disq; Romanae observantior, quatenus non Hispanizat.
units.tr: Some other Frenchmen, who truly loved their country, also tried in every way to turn the King from this plan. In 1603 there was published a frank speech by a certain Frenchman about what was then demanded and put up for deliberation, namely that the Jesuits be restored in the kingdom of France. In it he dissuades the King from this with many reasons and very weighty and firm arguments. I shall set down the whole oration here for the reader's benefit, in case it has not come into his hands, so that all, Papists as well as Reformed, may draw from it and make use of it, and so that we may guard ourselves, as is good practice and as the wise say, against the misfortune and loss of others. This orator, whoever he is, ought to be all the more esteemed by everyone for the weapons he offers against the Jesuit monsters, since he favours the Lutherans and Calvinists the less. For he declares himself most alien to both parties, and he is more observant of himself and of the Roman side, inasmuch as he does not play the Spaniard.

units.la: In hac autem oratione PRIMO respondet ad ea, quae huic salutari consilio obstare videri potuissent: ac Verum quidem est, inquit, o Rex, posse te plurimum Iesuitarum restitutione magna Catholicorum parti in regno tuo satisfacere, qui eos ducunt utiles ad novas opiniones, quae in causa religionis exstiterunt, convellendas; te, eadem opera Cardinales non paucos tibi obstrictos rurum, qui eorum causae multis nominibus studeant: vel eo maxime, quod magnos labores sufferunt ad fidem Catholicam, & potestatem Pontificiae sanctitatis in orbe terrarum propagandam. Homines sunt assiduos, diligentes, studiosi, animosi, quibus multum Sedes illa debet: venerunt in tempora rerum difficultatibus admodum circumfluentia.
units.tr: In this oration he FIRST answers the objections that might seem to stand in the way of this wholesome counsel. "It is true, O King," he says, "that by restoring the Jesuits you can greatly satisfy the Catholic party in your kingdom, which regards them as useful for overturning the new opinions that have arisen in the cause of religion. By the same token you would oblige to yourself not a few Cardinals, who strive for their cause in many ways, not least because they undergo great labours for the Catholic faith and for spreading the power of the Papal holiness throughout the world. They are assiduous, diligent, studious and spirited men, to whom that See owes much. They have come into times that abound in great difficulties."

units.la: Haec sunt, o Rex, maximae & praecipuae causae, quae te possunt in illorum partem commovere. Nam quod de juventutis institutione dicitur, id magni fieri non debet: quia revera omnib. expensis, plus damni literis, quam utilitatis attulerunt. Ratione breviter explicabo. Antequam venissent in Gallam, praestantia quaeque ingenia, & adolescentes ingenui literis
units.tr: "These, O King, are the greatest and chief reasons that could move you to their side. For what is said about the education of the young ought not to count for much, because in truth, all expenses considered, they have brought more harm than benefit to learning. I shall explain the reason briefly.

units.la: {a} Restitutio Iesuitarum huic consilio obstare videtur.
units.tr: {a} The restoration of the Jesuits seems to stand in the way of this counsel.

units.la: {b} Iesuitae plus damni literis, quam utilitatis afferunt. teris opera dabant in Parisiensi Academia: ubi semper ad viginti aut triginta studiosorum millia Gallorum exterorumque. Haec tanta multitudo attrahebat eò doctissimos viros, & celeberrimos Europae viros, sive eminendi animo, sive utilitatis capiendae. Lectio- um publicorum loca à Rege Francisco I. instituta captabantur ambitiose, retinebantur: & lumina literarum summa toto ante decennio quàm essent vacua: In unica Gymnasij Caeracensis aula meliores doctioresque lectiones, uno mense habebantur, quàm toto anno postea a tota Academia, comprehensis quoque Iesuitis, fuerunt habitae. Hi artem invenerunt sese stabiliendi paulatim in optimis quibusque civitatibus regni; atque hoc facto obstruxerunt ontes; unde tanta illa studiosorum multitudo profluebat, eademque maximum bonum alterum terverterunt ad juventutem perveniens studentem Parisijs: Magna enim juventus exolebatur, & sermone Gallico, & moribus & studio erga Remp. totam, quàm postea exculta erit, ex quo subsitit in provinciarum suarum finibus.
units.tr: {b} The Jesuits bring more harm than benefit to learning. Before they came to France, the most outstanding minds and the noble young men devoted themselves to learning at the University of Paris, where there were always some twenty or thirty thousand students, French and foreign. This great crowd drew to it the most learned men and the most celebrated men of Europe, whether from a desire for distinction or to gain some advantage. The chairs of public lectures founded by King Francis I were eagerly sought and held on to, and the lights of literature were at their brightest for the whole decade before they became vacant. In the single hall of the Caen college, better and more learned lectures were given in one month than were given by the whole University in the entire year afterwards, even counting the Jesuits. The Jesuits found the way of gradually establishing themselves in all the best cities of the kingdom, and by this means they blocked the channels from which that great multitude of students had flowed. The same thing that had been the greatest good for the youth coming to study in Paris they turned to another purpose. For a great youth was formed in Paris, in the French language, in manners, and in devotion to the whole commonwealth, which it has not been since, now that it has been confined within the borders of its provinces."

units.la: Accedit altera ratio, qua Patavina Academia observavit, cum anno cIↄ.Ↄxcl. apud Remp. Venetam de iis quaereretur, quando fuit interdictum, ne alijs quàm sibi ipsis legerent, aut sive instituerent: nempe quod, prout Theologiae incubunt maximè, non alios fere singulis classibus exceptà primà, praeficiunt quàm juvenes, qui potius discunt ipsi quàm alios doceant: adeò ut pueri, qui in doctiorum juvenum cura ad annum usque decimum quintum aut sextum committi sunt, non fiant unquam magni admodum. Paucos certe videmus de numero eorum, qui in congressibus eminent. Demonstravit res ipsa luculentissimè anno clɔlɔ. xciiii. Cum eos libello supplice pulsavit Parisiensis Academia. Nam de suo numero investigarunt aptum aliquem Advocatum, qui causam ipsorum ageret: quae res aliquo pacto ea adiuvisset. Multos quidem à se institutos, & omnis aetatis invenerunt, qui vero graui causa instituendae essent idonei, invenerunt neminem. Quapropter ad optimum quidem patronum congere eos oportuit, si quid unquam ab eis quicquam didicissent. In contemplatione quidem agis, quàm in studio & actione informant suos. Inter medicos, quae facultas est plenissima scientiae, pauci sunt qui praeluceant defchola ipsorum. Literis humanioribus & arcanis linguarum minus dant adhuc operam: Vera certe professio ipsorum est Theologia: hic illis theaurus, hic Marathò, in quo versantur plurimum: ideoque ingenia excitata, & acumine alio praedita deligunt tempestive: qui in manus ipsorum venerunt, effugiunt raro: diversarum gentium turba miscella est, juvant, & studia inter se conferunt. Necesse est deniq; fatentur omnes, illos disputationibus huius scientiae, aliarum reginae, excellere.
units.tr: "There is also another reason, which the Academy of Padua observed when, in the year 1606, it was asked of the Venetian Republic about them, when it was forbidden that they teach or instruct anyone but themselves. The reason was that, since they devote themselves above all to theology, they put in charge of nearly every class, except the first, none but young men who learn for themselves more than they teach others. As a result, boys who are committed to the care of these more learned young men until their fifteenth or sixteenth year never become very great. Certainly we see few of their number who stand out in public debate. The matter itself was demonstrated most clearly in 1594, when the Parisian Academy pressed them with a humble petition. For they searched among their own number for some suitable advocate to plead their cause, and this might somehow have helped them. They found many men of every age whom they had themselves taught, but of those who were fit to be entrusted with serious business they found no one. Hence, if they had ever learned anything from anyone, they ought to have chosen a very good advocate from among them. They form their own people more in contemplation than in study and action. Among physicians, a profession very full of learning, few are there who shine out in their school. They devote less effort still to the humane letters and the secret arts of languages. Their true profession is theology: that is their treasure, that is their Marathon, in which they are chiefly engaged. Therefore they choose in good time the minds that have been stirred and endowed with some other keenness. Those who have fallen into their hands rarely escape. The crowd of various nations is mixed together; they help one another and compare their studies. Finally, everyone must admit that in the disputations of this science, the queen of the others, they excel."

units.la: Quum arcana linguarum ab eis tenerinego, non continuò inveniri apud eos nego viros mediocri literarum humaniorum scientiâ tinctos: sed hoc est quod volo, non esse quaerendos numero ipsorum viros aequales quatuor illis Galliae luminibus, literarum Regibus, qui ales agnoscuntur, & censentur in universo mundo, quorum tres adhuc sunt superstites, & quartus adhuc vivit optimâ sui parte.
units.tr: "Although I do not deny that the secrets of languages are not immediately found among them, nor that there are men tinctured with a moderate knowledge of the humane letters among them, this is what I want to say: the men among them are not to be sought who equal those four lights of France, the kings of letters, who are acknowledged and reckoned as such throughout the whole world. Of these, three are still surviving, and the fourth is still living in his better part."

units.la: Omnes Iesuitae, quotquot exstiterunt, vix unquam digni sint, qui unius de quatuor illis discipuli mereantur dici: atque hoc confido agnituros quicunque ex ipsis aliquid habent scientiae. Hoc unum responsuri sunt, se nô dedisse operam huic studio, praecipuumque suum studium esse Theologia: & verum est. Tenendum illud praeterea, quicunque in numero sunt ipsorum aliqua scientia insignes, eos non amplius informationi juventutis incumbere. Statim enim ad Theologiae studium conferunt, ubi maximorum, qui inter ipsos fuerunt labore adjuti, scribendum veniunt: neque infitiandum est, commodare illis admodum defensioni nostrae religionis Catholicae contra nostrorum adversariorum scripta. Quorum in tanto numero unus & item alter, si forte inventus est dictione bona, stilo audace, motibus excelsis, dispositione commoda, & elegantibus mille acuminibus.
units.tr: "All the Jesuits who have ever existed are scarcely worthy to be called the disciple of one of those four. And I trust that all of them who have any learning will acknowledge this. They will answer only this, that they did not devote themselves to this study, and that their chief study is theology. And that is true. One must further keep in mind that whoever among them is distinguished by some learning does not go on to devote himself to the instruction of the young. For at once they turn to the study of theology, where they are drawn into writing with the help of the greatest men among them. Nor must it be denied that they are of great service to the defence of our Catholic religion against the writings of our adversaries. Among so many of them, one or another, if he happens to be found with a good style, a bold pen, lofty movements, a suitable arrangement and a thousand elegant turns of wit."

units.la: Deniq;, si quid judicare possum, libelli supplices, quos exhibuerunt Majestati Tuae, duo ut scripta insignia, in quibus ea omnia quae summi artis magistri docuerunt, accurate deprehenduntur observata. Causa quidem certe ipsorum defendi melius non poterat. Atque quidem magno labore illorum in studio Theologiae irritatos fuisse eos, qui religionis reformatae dicuntur, dubium esse non potest: Verumtamen neque hoc quoque negari potest, mul-
units.tr: "Finally, if I can judge anything, their humble petitions, which they presented to Your Majesty, are two outstanding writings, in which all the things that the masters of the highest art have taught are carefully observed. Certainly their cause could not have been defended better. And indeed there can be no doubt that those who are called the Reformed were stirred up by their great labour in the study of theology. Yet neither can this be denied: many"

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: On the Propagation

units.la: taastionib. multa doctrinæ illorum inesse, quæ odium ipsis Catholicorum summorum crea‑verint, qui nihilo ipsis in religionis studio inferiores sunt. Dicam de uno tàtum, capite ipso‑ rum, quia iniquum est tanti Principis abuti audientia: Sed hoc professo dignum, si ullum est, quia in hoc rei summa agitur. Interdum apud Sorbonistas, ô Rex, coperti sunt, sed pauci & raro, qui se patientes decipi eorum pigmentis, qui Romæ scripta ediderunt de potestate cla‑vium, auderent affirmare penes Pontifices esse, ut Reges excomunicent, & à jurejurando a fide data absolvant subditos: Sed propositiones istæ illico, tanquâ Schismaticæ tum à cor‑ pore Sorbonæ fuerunt damnatæ, conjunctâ Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ totius auctoritate, tũ Arre‑stis Parlamenti tui: qui duo maximi clypei exstiterunt, quibus maiores tui aduersus omne impetus, quos tentabant hostes, fuerunt defensi.
units.tr: ...in their many publications there is much in their teaching that has made the greatest Catholics hostile to them, though these men are in no way inferior to them in the study of religion. I shall speak of only one point, their chief one, since it is unfair to abuse the hearing of so great a Prince. Yet this point, if any, is worthy of your attention, because the whole matter turns on it. At times among the Sorbonists, O King, there have been some who, though concealed, and few and rarely, dared to assert, while pretending to be deceived by the trickery of those who published writings at Rome on the power of the keys, that the Popes hold the power to excommunicate kings and to absolve subjects from their oath and from the faith they have pledged. But these propositions were at once condemned as schismatic, both by the body of the Sorbonne, with the full authority of the Gallican Church joined to it, and by the Decrees of your Parliament. These two were the greatest shields by which your ancestors were defended against every assault that their enemies attempted.

units.la: Sunt sæpe, ut & nunc est, optimi Pontifices, proclives studiis in Galliam, maximorum me‑ ritorum recordatione, quibus S. Sedes, ô Rex, coronæ tuæ obstricta est: sed etiam nonnunquam eliguntur alij, qui in partes Hispanicas, & tibi aduersas inclinant planè.
units.tr: Often, as is the case now, the best Popes are inclined to favour France, mindful of the greatest services by which the Holy See, O King, is bound to your crown. But sometimes others are chosen who clearly lean toward the Spanish side and are opposed to you.

units.la: Si quando contingit istud malum, si crederent Galli posse Regem suum excommuni‑ cari legitimè, seque à jurejurando & fide data absolvi, professo gravissimum Regibus nostris foret periculum, ne spoliarentur dignitate suâ, & revera nullum imperium nisi pre‑ carium obtinerent, id est, omninò pendens ex bona vel mala gratia illius, quem D. Cardinales elegissent: quorum numero semper insunt multi, qui maxima beneficia in ditio‑ ne Mediolanensi, regno Neapolitano, atq; adeo in ipsa Hispania obtinent. Hic nõ amplius Rex futurus esset, sed Prorex, nomine Rex, Vicarius generalis, vel τοποτηρητὴς re & ve‑ ritate: cuiusmodi Reges illi erant, quibus Romani dabant & tollebant sceptra arbitratu suo. Propterea quotquot in hoc regno, ex quo Christianum factum est, vixerunt, Pro‑ positionem istam exploserunt, velut omnium (si insideret animis populi) periculosissimam, & summè aduersantem verbo Dei, qui dixit, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, Ioh. 18. Quem in locum August. tract. 115. Audite Iudæi & Gentes; audi præputium; audite omnia regna terrena: non impedio dominationem vestram in hoc mundo. Et apud S. Lucam cap. 12. ait quidam de turba: Magister, dic fratri meo, ut dividat mecum hæreditatem. At ille dixit ei, ô homo, quis me constituit judicem, aut divisorem super vos? Qua de re D. Bern‑ hard. lib. 1. de consideratione: Non monstrabunt, puto, qui hoc dicent, ubi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum sederit judex hominũ, aut divisor terminorum, aut distributor terrarum. Stetisse deniq; legõ Apostolos judicandos, sed disse judicantes non lego. Erit illud, non fuit.
units.tr: If that evil should ever happen, and if the French believed that their King could be lawfully excommunicated and that they could be absolved from their oath and their pledged faith, there would be the gravest danger for our kings, lest they be stripped of their dignity and in truth hold no power except a precarious one, that is, one wholly dependent on the good or ill favour of whoever the Lord Cardinals had chosen. Among these Cardinals there are always many who hold the greatest benefices in the Duchy of Milan, the Kingdom of Naples, and indeed in Spain itself. Such a king would no longer be king but viceroy: king in name, a vicar general, or a locum tenens [τοποτηρητής] in fact and truth. Such were the kings to whom the Romans gave and took away the sceptre at their pleasure. For this reason, all who have lived in this kingdom since it became Christian have rejected that proposition as the most dangerous of all, if it were to take root in the minds of the people, and as wholly opposed to the Word of God, who said, My kingdom is not of this world (John 18). On this text Augustine, in tractate 115, says: "Hear, Jews and Gentiles; hear, uncircumcised; hear, all earthly kingdoms: I do not hinder your dominion in this world." And in Luke 12 someone from the crowd says, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." But he said to him, "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" On this matter Bernard, in the first book On Consideration: "They will not show, I think, those who say this, where any of the Apostles ever sat as judge of men, or as divider of boundaries, or as distributor of lands. I read that the Apostles stood to be judged, but I do not read that they sat as judges. That will be a case of 'it was not.'"

units.la: Ex quibus indubitatis rationib. & aliis innumeris, quas brevitatis causa omitto, Sor‑ bona & unà cum ea Gallicana Ecclesia tota semper definivit, schismaticam illam pro‑ positionem esse, quòd Papa habeat potestatem excommunicandi Reges nostros, aut institu‑ endi quisquam in majestatem Christianissimam ipsorum. Ideoq; Ioannes Tanquerellus anno cIↄ.lxxi. Arresto Parlamenti fuit condemnatus in solennem professionem honorariæ pœnitentiæ, & ut à Rege veniam de eo posceret, quod suis thesibus propositionem istam suis‑set ausus inferere, quamvis exposuisset eam à se tantùm disputandi gratia perscriptam es‑ se: & parùm abfuit, quin adjudicaretur morti. Commodè accidit, quod Rex undecim tan‑ tummodo annorum esset, si annum egisset Rex decimum quartum, nunquam tale supplicium mortis effugisset.
units.tr: From these indubitable reasons, and from countless others which I omit for the sake of brevity, the Sorbonne, and with it the whole Gallican Church, has always determined that the proposition that the Pope has power to excommunicate our kings, or to set anyone over the most Christian majesty of theirs, is schismatic. Therefore John Tanquerel, in the year 1571, was condemned by a Decree of Parliament to a solemn public act of honorary repentance, and to ask the King's pardon for having dared to put forward that proposition in his theses, although he had explained that he had written it down only for the sake of disputation. He narrowly escaped being sentenced to death. It was fortunate that the King was then only eleven years old; had the King been fourteen, he would never have escaped such a deadly punishment.

units.la: Quod dixi Propositionem istam semper à Sorbona fuisse damnatam, id volo intelligi ad illud demũ usque tempus, quo Patres isti Iesuitæ complureis studiosos instituissent lectionibus suis assiduis Theologiæ. Etenim anno millesimo quingentesimo octogesimo nono, quum excommunicatio in defunctum Regem piæ memoriæ fuit allata, & in Sorbona quæsitum est, utrum potestatem istam haberet Pontifex: continuò Doctores antiqui, Faber Syndi‑ cus, Camusus, Chabotus, Faber Curio S. Pauli, Chavagnacus, omnesq; alij vetustiores, & bonâ notâ fortiter restiterunt; sed bene prospectum erat huic choragio: omnes enim juve‑nes qui apud Iesuitas Theologiæ studuerant, Boucherus, Pichenatus, Varades, Semel‑ la, Cullius, Aubourius, & alij innumerabiles vicerunt pluribus suffragijs contra ver‑bum Dei, omniaque axiomata Galliæ. Quinetiam hanc Iesuitarum sententiam esse quòd uod Papa Reges excommunicare possit, populareis a juramento fidei absolvere, & sceptra, coronas, dignitatemque eis adimere, bona fide negari non potest. Nam cum Parisiensis Academia periculosum illud dogma eis objecisset, tantum ab eo negando abfuerunt, ut contra suis defensionibus communi totius Societatis judicio editis commodo suo, anno 1.1.xcv. quarum inscriptio est: Veritas defensa contra actionem Antonij Arnaldi pag. 0. utantur his ipsis verbis: Non erat cur probares, Reges esse, aut esse oportere dominos laicos temporales in regnis suis: cum Papa, ut dixi, nihil arroget sibi in isto imperio summo, ut corrigat tanquam pater, atque adeo TANQVAM IVDEX, eos qui pernitiosi Ecclesiae futuri essent. Tum enim id non solum potest, sed etiam debet se ostendere SVPERIOREM ILLIS bono ipsorum & publico. Exceptio haec stomachum tibi commovet, facit ut ingaris; sed oportet haurias & de catero fatearis tibi nec rationem esse, nec conscientiam. Nam primum id Principibus est utile, qui continentur persaepe, aut ad officium retrahuntur potius REI TEMPORALIS METV, quae semper illis est cordi, licet improbis, quam rei spiritualis: cujus tantum non habent curam, nisi habeant & bonam conscientiam, quod non semper accidit. Idcirco Deus Regibus Israelis minabatur potius se AMOTVRUM TEMPORALE REGNVM, nisi observarent legem, quam eos privaturum aeterna vita: ATQVE HOC IPSVM IN PRIMVM REGEM EXERCVIT; CVI SCEPTRVM ABSTVLIT.
units.tr: When I said that this proposition had always been condemned by the Sorbonne, I wish it to be understood only up to that very time when those Jesuit Fathers, by their constant lectures in theology, had instructed many students. For in the year 1589, when excommunication was pronounced against the late King, of pious memory, and it was asked in the Sorbonne whether the Pope held that power, at once the older Doctors, Faber the Syndic, Camus, Chabot, Faber Curio of St Paul's, Chavagnac, and all the other more senior men of good repute, resisted strongly. But this performance had been well arranged in advance: for all the young men who had studied theology among the Jesuits, Boucher, Pichenat, Varades, Semelle, Cullius, Aubourius, and countless others, prevailed by large majorities against the Word of God and all the axioms of France. Indeed, that this is the Jesuits' view, that the Pope can excommunicate kings, absolve subjects from their oath of allegiance, and strip them of their sceptres, crowns and dignity, cannot in good faith be denied. For when the Parisian Academy had charged them with this dangerous doctrine, they were so far from denying it that, in their own defences, published in 1595 with the common judgment of the whole Society, and entitled "Truth defended against the action of Antoine Arnauld," p. 0, they used these very words: "There was no reason for you to prove that kings are, or ought to be, the temporal lay lords in their kingdoms, since the Pope, as I have said, claims nothing for himself in that supreme empire except to correct, as a father and thus AS A JUDGE, those who would become harmful to the Church. For then he can show himself not only able but bound to be SUPERIOR TO THEM for their own good and the public good." This objection stirs your bile and makes you angry; but you must swallow it and, for the rest, confess that you have neither reason nor conscience. For first, this is useful to princes, who are often restrained, or called back to their duty, rather by fear of temporal affairs, which are always dear to them, however wicked they are, than by fear of spiritual affairs, for which they have no concern unless they also have a good conscience, which does not always happen. Thus God threatened the kings of Israel that he would rather take away their temporal kingdom, if they did not keep the law, than deprive them of eternal life; AND THIS VERY THING HE FIRST EXERCISED ON THE FIRST KING, FROM WHOM HE TOOK AWAY THE SCEPTRE.

units.la: Quia vero animadvertunt, o Rex, omnia axiomata Ecclesiae Gallicanae, & Arresta Parlamenti tui pericidosa isti doctrinae adversari, quam instillant paulatim mentibus populi, ab hac peste olim maximopere abhorrentis, eo tandem venire cogatur audacia, ut historias Regum nostrorum, quas adferimus, dicant exempla rebellionum esse, his ipsis verbis: adeo desipis & adeo improbus Gallus es, ut velis producere exempla REBELLIONIS e historiis Galliae, obscurantia splendorem Regum nostrorum, & matris communis nostrae, &c. Et post duas fere paginas: In Rege, inquiunt, sive virtus, sive vitium, magna omnia: qui si potentiam suam ad malefaciendum occupet, nulla nisi magna potentia inhibere potest. Ac propterea videmus gladium in persona multorum Regum, in multis regnis usque usurpatum, quod si non semper fuit utile exercitium ejus, semper tamen utile potuit esse: SIQVIDEM SVBIECTI BENE FVISSENT DISPOSITI. Nihil unquam scritum evidentius: nihil unquam in orbe terrarum existit, quod magis pugnet cum verbo Dei, hoc enim praecipit gratias agi Deo, si bonos Reges misericordia nobis; sin malos; vult etiam laudemus, eumque credamus facere bono nostro, ut minus hunc mundum diligamus, eoque alacriter discedamus de mundo.
units.tr: But since, O King, they perceive that all the axioms of the Gallican Church and the Decrees of your Parliament are opposed to that dangerous doctrine, which they gradually instil into the minds of the people, a doctrine from which the people once shrank in great horror, their audacity is at last driven to such a point that they say the histories of our kings, which we cite, are examples of rebellion, in these very words: "You are so foolish and so wicked a Frenchman that you wish to bring forward examples of REBELLION from the histories of France, obscuring the splendour of our kings and of our common mother, etc." And nearly two pages later: "In a King, they say, whether virtue or vice, all things are great; and if he uses his power to do evil, nothing but great power can restrain him. And therefore we see the sword used in the person of many kings, in many kingdoms, and used so long; for if its use has not always been profitable, it could always have been so, PROVIDED THE SUBJECTS HAD BEEN WELL DISPOSED." Nothing more evident was ever written; nothing ever existed in the whole world that fights more against the Word of God. For that Word commands us to give thanks to God if he gives us good kings, and, if bad, wills that we also praise him, and believe that he does it for our good, so that we may love this world less and depart from the world more eagerly.

units.la: Deus solus statuit Reges, idemque solus potest amovere, & cum videtur, eos retinere, claves quas dedit S. Petro, & S. Patrib. successoribus ipsius, ad regnum coelorum duntaxat pertinent, ad regnum terrae nullo modo. Ille ipse omnipotens, cum hic in terris ageret, non instituit tastigare Reges, non coronas eorum effringere; sed contra vita ipsius fuit quidam spectus humilitatis liber. Nec alia arma dedit Apostolis ad stabiliendam legem suam: dixit: Reges nationum dominantur ipsis, & qui auctoritate in eas valent, dicuntur benefici. Sed non ita erit vobis. Noluit Deus ut S. Petrus, successoresve illius S. Patres nostri plus agerentur ipso: neque vero hoc fecerunt qui successerunt primi. Si alii contra hoc venerint, butantur hic potestate sua, nec sunt audiendi. Hoc semper Gallicana Ecclesia iudicavit, eos excommunicavit, qui contra affirmarunt, velut inhumanae et infelicissimae doctrinae auctores: quae per impietatem volens homines pios efficere, mundum (ut ita dicamus) parit innumerabilem caedium, incendiorum, raptuum feminarum virginumque, & desolationum per urbes provinciasque totas. Abyssus abyssorum est, abominationum Oceanus: hoc ad extremum usque exerti fumus: et tamen Iesuitae magis magisque obfirmant se: quibus si credimus, poterunt Romanae bullae spoliare omnes Reges terrae, EISQVE TEMPORALE DOMINIVM ET SCEPTRVM EXCVTERE. Atque his quoque conveniunt ea, quae D. Bellarm. Iesuita, nunc Cardinalis scribit de hoc argumento: Quantum ad personas, inquit, non potest Papa, ut Papa, ordinarie temporales Principes deponere, etiam justa de causa, eo modo quo deponit Episcopos, id est, tanquam ordinarii
units.tr: God alone sets up kings, and he alone can remove them, and when he seems to let them keep their thrones, the keys he gave to St Peter, and to the Fathers who succeeded him, pertain only to the kingdom of heaven and in no way to the kingdom of earth. That almighty one himself, while he was living on earth, did not appoint that kings should be humbled or their crowns broken; on the contrary, his own life was a free pattern of humility. Nor did he give the apostles any other weapons for establishing his law. He said: "The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so with you." God did not want St Peter, or his successors, or our holy Fathers, to do more than he himself did, and indeed those who succeeded them first did not do so either. If others have come forward against this, they misuse their power here, and they are not to be listened to. The Gallican Church has always judged this, and has excommunicated those who have asserted the contrary, as authors of an inhuman and most unhappy doctrine, which, while it wishes by impiety to make men pious, gives birth (so to speak) to countless slaughters, fires, rapes of women and virgins, and devastation through whole cities and provinces. It is an abyss of abysses, an ocean of abominations; we have been exercised on this point to the very end, and yet the Jesuits harden themselves more and more. If we believe them, Roman bulls can strip all kings of the earth and wrest from them temporal dominion and the sceptre. The writings of D. Bellarmine, the Jesuit, now a Cardinal, on this subject agree with these views too, when he writes: "As far as persons are concerned, the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily depose temporal princes, even for a just cause, in the way that he deposes bishops, that is, as ordinary..."

units.la: {v} Contra Apol. Lib. 1. ... Edit. Ann. 1. 4
units.tr: Against the Apology, Book 1 ... Edition of the year 1 ... 4

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: ON PROPAGATION

units.la: & tamen potest mutare regna, & VNI AVFERRE, atque ALTERI CONFERRE, tanquam summus Princeps spiritualis, si id necessarium sit ad animarum salutem, ut probarimus. Id probaturus cap.8. adfert instituta violenta, quaeque ex diametro pugnantia cum verbo Dei, & quae historia omnes exsecrantur: quorum serie docemur stabilimentum Mahumetani illius Imperij maxime ex bellis intestinis, et furiosis Christianorum inter se provenisse, quae usurpationes ipsae pepererunt, fecerunt, ut Europa ab Ortu et Occasu pariter suorum ipsius liberorum sanguine innataret. Optime S. Ambrosius se temperavit, ne vel de attingendo sceptro, corona, & temporali dominio cogitaret, deque subdito ullo liberando a iurisiurandi fide: nec vero potuisset, nisi directe venire contra Dei mandata voluisset. Acri solum admonitione usus est, ut culpae gravissimae notitia ac sensu Imperatorem afficeret.
units.tr: Yet he can change kingdoms, and take them away from one and confer them on another, as supreme spiritual Prince, if this is necessary for the salvation of souls, as we have proved. Intending to prove this in chapter 8, he brings forward violent institutions, which are diametrically opposed to the word of God and which all history execrates. From their sequence we learn that the establishment of that Mahometan empire arose chiefly from the internal and frenzied wars of Christians among themselves, which these usurpations themselves produced and caused, so that Europe floated in the blood of its own children from east and west alike. Saint Ambrose very wisely restrained himself, so that he did not even think of laying hands on the sceptre, the crown and temporal lordship, or of freeing any subject from the bond of an oath. Nor indeed could he have done so unless he had wished to act directly against God's commands. He used only a mild admonition, so that he might impress upon the emperor the knowledge and sense of his most grievous fault.

units.la: Id etiam valde observandum, quod idem Bellarm. atque Iesuitae in suis Defensionibus sustinent, & confirmare nituntur famosam illam Extravagantem communem, Vnam sanctam, de maioritate, & obedientia, quam semper damnavit Gallia. Nam si Papa fallitur, si errat, si plus instituit quam ex officio debeat; hac tamen Extravagante homines tenentur obsequi; Deus, qui solus eum judicare potest. Itaque licet Papa plane injustissime fulminata iaculare tur in Regem, prout factum vidimus anno CIↃ I↑LXXXXIX: contra defunctum Regem nostrum summe Catholicum, nemo tamen ex Iesuitarum doctrina de causa potest cognoscere, omnibus interdicta est cognitio, & Deo soli reservata. Interea vero oportet Rex ante ora & oculos subditorum omnium; etiam per ipsos, dignitate & corona sua spoliatur, & succedat in locum ipsius quemcunque suprema illa potestas voluerit statuere, ut habent illa Bellarmi verba; MVTARE REGNA ET VNI AVFERRE, atque ALTERI CONFERRE: quae eadem sunt Tanquerelli verba; regno & dignitatibus privare potest, celebri Arresto condemnata. Etsi nondum eo audacia venerat Tanquerellus, ut diceret dare posse uni Papam; quod alteri ademisset.
units.tr: It is also to be carefully noted that Bellarmine and the Jesuits in their Defences maintain, and strive to confirm, that famous common Extravagant, Unam Sanctam, concerning the greater authority and obedience, which France has always condemned. For if the Pope is deceived, if he errs, if he imposes more than his office requires, men are nonetheless bound to obey this Extravagant, since God alone can judge him. Therefore, although the Pope most unjustly hurls his thunderbolts at a King, as we saw done in the year 1589 against our late most Catholic King, yet no one may, according to the doctrine of the Jesuits, take cognizance of the cause; cognizance is forbidden to all and reserved to God alone. Meanwhile the King is stripped of his dignity and crown before the eyes and faces of all his subjects, even by their own hands, and whoever that supreme power decides to appoint succeeds him, as Bellarmine's words have it: TO CHANGE KINGDOMS AND TO TAKE AWAY FROM ONE, AND TO CONFER ON ANOTHER. These are the same words as those of Tanquerellus: he can deprive of kingdom and dignities, as condemned by a famous Arrest. Yet Tanquerellus had not yet reached such boldness as to say that the Pope can give to one what he has taken from another.

units.la: Idem Iesuita Bellarm. procedit ulterius: affirmat enim disertis verbis: Omnes Ecclesiasticos regni tui non amplius tibi subjectos esse. Quae sententia tamen directe adversatur verbo expresso Dei & thesibus Ecclesiae Gallicanae, quam caeteris illa, quod dixi-mus. Audet tamen tueri istud & S. Pauli verba cavillis puris tentat evertere: Omnis anima subjecta sit potestatibus superioribus: non enim potestas est nisi a Deo, & potestates supereminentes sunt a Deo ordinatae: ideo qui resistit potestati, resistit ordinationi Dei. Et postea: Quapropter oportet subjectos esse non solum ad vitandam iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Nam eadem de causa pendite tributa illis, quia administri sunt Dei, in hoc se occupantes. Quem in locum S. Ioannes Chrysostomus observavit haec verba non solum laicis imperari, sed etiam clericis, religiosis, ipsisque adeo Apostolis. Vult etiam idem Bellarm. haec S. Petri verba eludere: Itaque estote subditi omni humano ordini propter Deum, sive Regi, ut eminentiori, sive Gubernatoribus, ut missis ab eo. Et inter caetera idem Bellarminus, Tempore illo, inquit, valde erat necessarium moneri Christianos diligenter, ut obsequerentur Regibus, ne impediretur fidei praedicatio. Hoc pacto efficeretur religio nostra religio circulatorium Cybeles; religio vulpinantium: qui primum quidem dicerent, Regnum nostrum non est de hoc mundo, non omnes aeque Ecclesiastici a calij Regibus Praesidibusque obedimus: postea vero quum loco superiores sunt, & in auctoritatem ostentatam pedem, tum demum sermone contrario plane utererentur, idque arrogarent sibi, quod Deus ille omnipotens sibi soli in Reges Israelis & alios omnes reservavit. Haec bona fide vera doctrina Iesuitarum est, haec technae illorum, haec via quam insistunt, ut se in honores intrudant. Sed longe aliter se habet religio Christiana: quae semper loquitur ingenue, vere, sine fraude, sine fuco & fallaciis: nec subditum quemquam a vertit a suo Principe, aut ei eripit, ut doctrina Iesuitarum facit. Nam haec demum conclusio ipsa est eius dem Bellarmini, pag. 271. tractatus illius de Exemptionibus; Sed dices, Principibus fieret injuria, si contra voluntatem ipsorum privarentur iure, quod habuerunt in clericos, antequam clericatum adepti essent. Respondeo: Nullam fieri injuriam eis, quia nemini injuriam facit,
units.tr: The same Jesuit Bellarmine goes further, for he affirms in plain words that all the ecclesiastics of your kingdom are no longer subject to you. Yet this opinion directly contradicts the express word of God and the theses of the Gallican Church, more than the other things we have mentioned. Yet he dares to defend it, and he tries to overturn the words of St Paul with empty quibbles: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; for there is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained of God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God." And afterwards: "Wherefore you must needs be subject, not only for wrath but also for conscience' sake. For for this same reason pay tribute also, for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing." On this place St John Chrysostom observed that these words are enjoined not only on laymen but also on the clergy, the religious, and even the Apostles themselves. Bellarmine also wishes to evade these words of St Peter: "Submit yourselves therefore to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king, as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him." Among other things, the same Bellarmine says: "At that time it was very necessary to warn Christians carefully to obey kings, lest the preaching of the faith be hindered." In this way our religion would become the religion of Cybele's wandering priests, a religion of foxes. These would at first indeed say, "Our kingdom is not of this world," and that we ecclesiastics do not all equally obey other kings and governors; but afterwards, when they are superior in rank and have set foot in ostentatious authority, they would then speak quite the contrary, and claim for themselves what that almighty God reserved for himself alone over the kings of Israel and all others. This, in good faith, is the true doctrine of the Jesuits; this is their craft, and this is the way they pursue in order to thrust themselves into honours. But the Christian religion is far otherwise: it always speaks ingenuously, truly, without fraud, without paint and deceit. Nor does it turn any subject away from his Prince or snatch him from him, as the doctrine of the Jesuits does. For this is indeed the very conclusion of the same Bellarmine, p. 271 of his treatise on Exemptions: "But you will say, it would be an injury to princes if they were deprived, against their will, of the right they had over clergy before they were admitted to the clerical state. I reply: no injury is done to them, because he does no injury who uses his own right."

units.la: Bellarm. 1. cent. 1. lib. 5. p. 7. Iesuitae p. 4. Vent. de exempt. edit. Tract. de exempt. cler. edito anno 1595, Tu altero de immunitatis.
units.tr: Bellarm. 1. cent. 1. lib. 5. p. 7. Iesuitae p. 4. Vent. de exempt. ed. Tract. de exempt. cler., published in the year 1595, and the second, on immunity.

units.la: Rom. 3. facit, qui jure suo utitur. Is autem utitur jure suo, qui statum eligit, quem sibi convenientiorem judicat. QVAMVIS PER ACCIDENS SEPARATVR, PRINCIPEM RIVARI SVOIVRE. Hoc non est aginari, non tergiversari, non circuitione uti: hic acisè dicit Majestati Tuae uno verbo, quot in Gallia sunt Ecclesiastici, tot esse subditos Pontificis. Quinetiam pag. 255. his verbis utitur: Papa exemit omnes Ecclesiasticos a subjectione Principum suorum secularium: ex quo sequitur, non esse illos Principes sui emos in eo quod ad personas Ecclesiasticas attinet, &c. sic, ut aperte dicam, alterum imperium in tuo, o Rex, constituitur, alterum regnum in tuo. Itaque ut doctrinam istam prorsus Christianae fidei adversatur plane, eodem in loco argumentatione utitur a simili, inde esse dicens, ac si Rex aliquis partem regni sui alteri subjici ceret, atque hoc pacto juxta belli, justóve alio quocunque titulo partem imperii sui amitteret. Et verissimum est quod idem dicit, stabilimentum istius propositionis principibus plus creare periculi, quam si agno vincantur praelio, aut amplam provinciam amiserint. Nam in visceribus delitescit malum, & ij qui jam sunt perditi, alios persaepe adducunt eo secretis suis confessionis, ut ipsam Monarchiam, in qua nati sunt, subruant. Quod si interdum magistratus susceperunt agnoscere, ut vi dicunt fieri, vela contrahi oportere, sed ex eo non valere consequentiam: quod diligenter opus est observari.
units.tr: Rom. 3. he does no injury who uses his own right. He uses his own right who chooses the state he judges more convenient for himself. ALTHOUGH BY CHANCE IT IS SEPARATED, THE PRINCE IS DEPRIVED OF HIS RIGHT. This is not beating about the bush, not shifting or evading, not using circumlocution; here he tells Your Majesty plainly, in one word, that as many ecclesiastics as there are in France, so many are subjects of the Pontiff. Moreover, on p. 255 he uses these words: "The Pope has exempted all ecclesiastics from subjection to their secular princes; from which it follows that those princes are not theirs in what concerns ecclesiastical persons, etc." Thus, to speak openly, another empire is established within your realm, O King, another kingdom within yours. Accordingly, since this doctrine is wholly opposed to the Christian faith, he uses in the same place an argument from likeness, saying it is as if some king were to subject part of his kingdom to another and so, by war or by some other title, lost part of his empire. And it is most true, as he himself says, that the establishment of this proposition creates more danger for princes than if they were conquered in a battle or lost a large province. For the evil lies hidden in the vitals, and those who are already lost often lead others, through their secret confessions, to overthrow that very monarchy in which they were born. But if at times magistrates have undertaken to acknowledge, as they say happens, that sails must be furled under compulsion, it does not follow from this that the consequence holds; this must be carefully observed.

units.la: Amplius dicunt, Edictis Regum, etsi nihil est quod Scripturae canonibusque & sanctis decretis adversetur, tamen non obligari Ecclesiasticos nisi ad directionem, non ad coactionem. Haec propria ipsorum verba pag. 269. quod idem afferunt post eapag. 271. cum ajunt, ericos non esse amplius temporali Principi subjectos, hunc illos amittere: prout id revera contra controversiam est, eum non amplius subjectum esse, qui non amplius ad obsequium leg. cogi potest. Ista haereses olim fuerant radicitus, o Rex, e Gallia tua exstirpatae? Sed ce venerunt artifices, qui eas magna copia femina verunt denuo, & nova quadam arte irraginis tractatui de indulgentiis hunc tractatum inferciverunt, intrusseruntque in sententes alias nequa observari possent.
units.tr: Furthermore, they say that royal edicts, although there is nothing in them contrary to Scripture, the canons and the holy decrees, do not bind ecclesiastics except to direction, not to compulsion. These are their own words, on p. 269; and they set down the same thing after that passage, on p. 271, when they say that clergy are no longer subject to the temporal prince and that he has lost them. Yet it is indeed beyond dispute that one is no longer subject if he can no longer be compelled to obedience by law. Were these heresies once uprooted from your France, O King? But artificers have come, who have revived them in great numbers, and by some new art have stuffed this treatise into a treatise on indulgences, and inserted it among other sentences so that it could not be noticed.

units.la: Ex ista autem Propositione, Ecclesiasticos non esse amplius subjectos, admirabile naturam consectarium, posse illos intentare in Regem suum citra laesae Majestatis crimen. Atque haec consequentia diserte verbis habetur in Aphorismis Confessorum, quos Iesuita Manuel Sa composuit, in voce Clericus. Ait enim; Clerici rebellio in Regem non est crimen laesae Majestatis, quia non est subditus Regi. Et in voce, Princeps, demonstrat advertentius quantum Dei verbo adversentur: quo praecipitur ferri Principes malos instantes majorum suorum throno, velut manu illius datos. Sic enim illi: Rex potest, inquit, per Rempubl. privari ob tyrannidem, & si non faciat officium suum, & quum est causa iqua justa: & eligi alius a majori parte populi. Quidam tamen solum tyrannidem causam putant.
units.tr: From that proposition, that ecclesiastics are no longer subject, they draw a remarkable consequence: that they may bring charges against their own king without the crime of treason. This consequence is stated in express words in the Aphorisms of the Confessors, which the Jesuit Manuel Sa composed, under the word Clericus. For he says: "A cleric's rebellion against the King is not the crime of treason, because he is not a subject of the King." And under the word Princeps he shows more clearly how much they oppose the word of God, by which it is commanded that evil princes be pressed hard upon the throne of their ancestors, as if given into his hand. For he says: "The King can be deprived by the commonwealth on account of tyranny, and if he does not perform his duty, and when there is a just cause, and another be chosen by the greater part of the people. Some, however, think tyranny alone is the cause."

units.la: Inprimis certae malitiae est, quod rem tam gravem haerere in incerto finiunt. Deus novit, arte faciant, ut pro ratione optati consiliorum suorum modo hoc, modo illud sentire fiant.
units.tr: First, it is clearly a matter of deliberate malice that they leave a thing of such gravity in doubt. God knows they do this on purpose, so that, as their aims require, people are made to think now this and now that.

units.la: Secunda, quid magis cum fide Christiana pugnat, quam si libertatem tribueris populo judicandi de bona & mala principis sui administratione, eique persuaseris, posse eum conscientia integra & secundum Deum aut eicere, aut trucidare Principem. Veruntamen haec utione aut lege, ut ita pars major censeat: quae conditio apprinie est necessaria. Nam si rentem istam opinionem pars minor defenderet, periclitaretur de vita: magna autem cura esset, si perderentur homines BENE DISPOSITI ad Iesuitarum doctrinam, id ad eijciendum Dominum & Principem suum, excitatis in tyrannum clamoribus, ex credit ate ipsius. Idcirco in calce illius libri Inquisitor Antuerpianus, Pardo Anno Dó. Ió. xcvii. pronunciat eum magnam utilitatem allaturum. Cognovit Dominus, utrum us utilitatis allaturum esse Domino suo censuerit, quam promovendo dissipationem retui, quod tum flamma & ferro oppugnabat. Idem Iesuitae in suis illis Aphorismis Confessorum, quos indesinenter obtrudunt animo populi, in voce TYRANNVS: addunt ista: Tyrannice gubernans juste acquisitum dominium non potest spoliari sine publico judicio: lu-
units.tr: Second, what could be more contrary to the Christian faith than to grant the people freedom to judge the good and bad administration of their prince, and to persuade them that they may, with a clear conscience and according to God, either expel or slay the prince? Yet this is to be done only under this condition or law: that the greater part so judge. This condition is above all necessary. For if the smaller part were to hold that opinion, its members would be in danger of their lives. But it would be a great concern if men well disposed to the doctrine of the Jesuits were lost, men who, once roused by cries against the tyrant, would expel their Lord and Prince on the strength of their belief in it. Hence at the end of that book the Antwerp Inquisitor, Pardo, in the year of our Lord 1597, declares that it will bring great benefit. The Lord knows whether he thought it would be of benefit to his own lord, since it promotes the overthrow of the commonwealth, which he was then attacking with fire and sword. The same Jesuits, in their Aphorisms for Confessors, which they unceasingly press upon the minds of the people, add these words under the heading TYRANT: "One who governs tyrannically cannot be stripped of lawfully acquired dominion without public judgment; but by that same sentence anyone may become the executor."

units.la: Ed. Antverp. vel Colon. 1. Pet. 2. tá vero sententiá potest quisque fieri executor: potest autem deponi à populo, etiam qui ju-ravit et obedientiam perpetuam, si monitus non vult corrigi.
units.tr: Ed. Antverp. vel Colon. 1. Pet. 2. Yet anyone may be deposed by the people, even one who has sworn perpetual obedience, if, when warned, he will not correct himself.

units.la: Utrum autem hæc doctrina tota ad te, ô Rex, pertineat maximè, judicare tuum est. Non tam attingit simul reliquam terram totam, quàm te & posteritatem tuam: Gallia est tua hæreditas, quam à Deo solo obtines, & justo gladio tuo. Si decies mille annos staret mundus: & tantundem tua posteritas (ut sperari à nobis convenit) ex ratione est ut semper in Gallos imperium teneat: ac non Pontifices, qui interdum hostes tuæ familiæ possunt existere, possint Gallum unicum ab solvere à jurejurando fidelitatis, quo posteris tuis tenebuntur. Quod si thesis ista in nostros animos illabantur, coronam suam posteritas tua, ô Rex, geret, sceptrumque tenebit, tantisper dum sanctæ sedi videbitur, ac non diutius.
units.tr: Whether this whole doctrine concerns you, O King, above all, is for you to judge. It touches not so much the whole rest of the world as you and your posterity. France is your inheritance, which you hold from God alone and by your just sword. Even if the world should stand for ten thousand years, and your posterity likewise (as we ought to hope), it is reasonable that they should always hold rule over the French. But the Popes, who may at times become enemies of your family, may not release a single Frenchman from the oath of fidelity by which they are bound to your descendants. But if this thesis should steal into our minds, your posterity, O King, will wear the crown and hold the sceptre only for as long as it pleases the holy see, and no longer.

units.la: Ab hac propositione prima dependet altera, super cujus argumento video tam multa ultrò citróque scripta, sed nemo rem acu tetigit. Dicunt quidam: Jesuitas auctores esse, ut Reges occidantur: hoc falsum: nam contra eos ministrant, idque non raro ex animo. Sed hæc rei distinctio: Credunt, si quos excommunicavit Papa, eos amplius non esse Reges, sed tyrannos. Audivisti quid illi in vocem TYRANNVS pronuncient. Plane si de prima illa propositione convenit, secunda est consectaria. Nam si potest Papa manum injicere in sceptrum Regum, & dominium temporale ipsorum, ut Jesuitae asserunt, ex eo procul dubio constat, si quem Regem fulmine petit Pontifex privatum eum reddi, privatum permanere, Regem non esse amplius: quod si velit & perfiet regnare, tyrannum esse. Quisquis in propositionem primam consenserit, necessario ad secundam hanc compelletur. Itaque liber scriptus propria manu Ioannis Guignarti Jesuitæ, quem in pleno Parlamento agnovit Camerii duabus una congregatis, habuit ambas istas Propositiones contumeliosè scriptas. Nam inter alia exstabat scriptum: Sævum Neronem ab uno Clemente occisum esse, & monachum simulatum manu veri monachi confectum: FACTVM HEROICVM A IACOBO CLEMENTE PATRATVM VELVT S. SPIRITVS DONVM, HOC NOMINE A THEOLOGIS NOSTRIS APPELLATVM, juste per defunctum Priorem Jacobitarum Bourgoing Confessorem & Martyrem laudatum esse. Coroniam Galliæ in alteram familiam quàm Borboniam transferri debere & posse: Cum Bearnensis, QVAMVIS AD FIDEM CATHOLICAM CONVERSO, lenius actum iri, quàm fit promeritus, si detur ipsi corona Monachalis in conventu aliquo bene reformato, ut illic poeniten-tiam agat, de tot malis quæ apportavit Galliæ, & gratias agat Deo, quod ipsi gratiam contulerit sui ante obitum agnoscendi. SI ABSQVE BELLO DEPONI NON POTEST, GERATVR BELLVM: SI BELLVM GERI NON POTEST, MORS PARETVR IPSI. Protocollum Majestas tua potest consulere: res lectu digna est.
units.tr: From this first proposition depends a second, on which I see that so much has been written back and forth, yet no one has touched the point precisely. Some say that the Jesuits are the authors of the killing of kings. That is false, for they work against such things, and often from sincere conviction. But here is the distinction: they believe that if the Pope has excommunicated any ruler, he is no longer a king but a tyrant. You have heard what they proclaim under the heading TYRANT. Clearly, if one agrees with that first proposition, the second follows as a consequence. For if the Pope can lay hands on the sceptre of kings and on their temporal dominion, as the Jesuits assert, it undoubtedly follows that if the Pope strikes a king with his thunderbolt, that king is made a private man, remains a private man, and is no longer a king; and if he wishes to go on reigning, he is a tyrant. Whoever assents to the first proposition will necessarily be driven to this second. So a book written in the own hand of Jean Guignard, a Jesuit, which was acknowledged in full Parliament at Chambéry (or Camerino?) when the chambers were assembled together, contained both these propositions set out in insulting terms. For among other things there stood written: that the savage Nero was slain by one Clement alone, and that a monk, feigned, was done away with by the hand of a true monk; that this heroic deed, performed by James Clement, is called by our theologians a gift of the Holy Spirit, and that the late prior of the Jacobins, Bourgoing, rightly praised him as a confessor and martyr. That the crown of France ought and can be transferred to another family than the Bourbon. That, although Béarnais has been converted to the Catholic faith, it would go more gently with him than he has deserved if he were given a monastic crown in some well-reformed convent, there to do penance for the many evils he has brought upon France, and to give thanks to God that He granted him the grace to recognise his sin before his death. IF HE CANNOT BE DEPOSED WITHOUT WAR, LET WAR BE WAGED; IF WAR CANNOT BE WAGED, LET DEATH BE PREPARED FOR HIM. Your Majesty may consult the record; the matter is worth reading.

units.la: Præterea Ambrosius Varades Parisiis fuit Gymnasiarchus Collegii Iesuitici per ipsos electus, tanquam unus ex optimis in Ordine ipsorum, & adhuc inter ipsos eundem honorem, quem ante obtinet. Verumtamen si placebit Majestati Tuæ mandare, ut acta Bareriæ ad se afferantur, comperies illum fuisse Varadem, qui post menses à felici conversione tua, suasit ipsi, ut cultrum suum bipennem inderet in ventrem tuum, datoque Eucharistiæ Sacramento eum obligavit, confirmans per Deum viventem nil ab eo posse fieri magis meritorium, fore ut ipsum Angeli in Paradisum exportarent. Si id non est verum, purgare se fe Varadem oportuit: latitavit dies aliquot in hac urbe, quum ingrederetur Majestas tua, & veste mutata abijt, Romamque profectus est, ubi fruitur admodum magnis honoribus. Non est difficile inficiari voce, sed facta validiora sunt, & sermonis mendacia redarguunt. Varades perpetrato isto horrendo & exsecrabili scelere vinctus per Iesuitas ipsos adduceretur, ut justo supplicio alijs exemplo esset, si eadem sententia non insideret mentibus ipsorum.
units.tr: Moreover, Ambrose Varades was at Paris the Gymnasiarch of the Jesuit college, chosen by them as one of the best in their Order, and he still holds among them the same honour he held before. Nevertheless, if it pleases Your Majesty to order that the proceedings at Bar be brought before you, you will find that it was this Varades who, some months after your happy conversion, persuaded him to drive his two-edged knife into your belly; and, having given him the sacrament of the Eucharist, he bound him by swearing by the living God that nothing he could do would be more meritorious, and that the angels would surely carry him into Paradise. If this is not true, Varades ought to have cleared himself. He lay hidden for some days in this city while Your Majesty was entering it, then changed his clothes and left, and went off to Rome, where he enjoys very great honours. It is not difficult to deny a thing by word, but deeds are stronger and expose the lies of speech. After committing this horrible and accursed crime, Varades would have been seized by the Jesuits themselves and brought to justice, as an example to others, if the same opinion did not dwell in their minds.

units.la: Nunc vero ubi tam fides hominem istum, & supra quàm unquam ab istis honore affici; adeoque tam audaces esse illos, ut eum inter viros maximos ordinis sui referant, omnino sequitur, eos voto, voluntate, studio per Varadem Gymnasiarcham suum, velut organon appositissimum, animavisse Bareriam, nec particulare istud, sed generale parricidium esset. um esse. Nititur enim profecto maxima propositione illorum, a cujus exsecutione & effectu plus sibi spondent ipsi laudis, quàm ex alia re ulla, ut post dicturi sumus. Et ubi nam quaesso, adhuc locant Varadem istum inter praecipua societatis suae columina? habetur locus pag. 265. Defensae veritatis ipsorum (ut ipsi quidem obtendunt) post annum excusae, quàm Varades aufugerat.
units.tr: But now, since they so openly favour this man, and honour him beyond anything they have ever shown, and are so bold as to count him among the greatest men of their order, it altogether follows that by their vow, will and zeal they have animated Barrière through Varades their Gymnasiarch, as a most suitable instrument; and this was not a particular murder but a general parricide. ...rests indeed on their greatest proposition, from whose execution and effect they promise themselves more praise than from any other matter, as we shall say later. And where, I ask, do they still place this Varades among the chief pillars of their society? There is a passage at page 265 of their Defence of the Truth (as they call it), published a year after Varades had fled.

units.la: Quid enim multi (inquiunt) & MAGNI VIRI hujus societatis pertulerunt? Quis nescit (ut de Gallia nostra dicamus) contumelias ibi intortas, & calumnias enunciatas contra Ioan. Maldonatum, Emundum, Augerium, CLAUDIVM Matthaeum, Iacobum Tyrium, & nunc etiam contra Annibalem Codretum, Iacobum Commoletum, Bernardum Roilletum, Ambrosium Varradem? Atque hic observatu dignum est, hos scilicet esse magnos martyres, & multa perpessos. Tam propria, tam Christiana est haec appellatio, quàm illa quaestionis habitae Parisijs anno 1564. Nam terribilem persecutionem illam vocant, incredibiliter hac voce abutentes. Magis vero proprium fuerit si furiosa funestaque bella, quae in toto hoc regno Iesuitae excitarunt, persecutionem bonorum omnium Gallorum appellaverint.
units.tr: For what, they say, have so many and GREAT MEN of this society suffered? Who does not know (to speak of our France) the insults heaped up there and the calumnies uttered against John Maldonatus, Emond, Auger, Claude Matthieu, James Tyrius, and now also against Annibal Codret, James Commolet, Bernard Roillet, Ambrose Varradès? And it is worth observing here that these are, of course, great martyrs who have endured many things. This term is as proper and Christian as that question raised at Paris in 1564. For they call that a terrible persecution, abusing the word incredibly. It would rather be more fitting to call the furious and deadly wars which the Jesuits have stirred up throughout this whole kingdom a persecution of all good Frenchmen.

units.la: Quod si Iesuitarum discipulus fuisset Barreria, educatus & institutus in doctrina ipsorum, Varadem vix accusavisset: nam eos credunt esse damnatos, qui judicibus auctores suasoresque facinorum istorum indicaverint. Atque haec tertia jam propositio est ex prima illa & secunda consequens. Nam si potest Reges excommunicare Papa, & bonum est factum ac meritorium si quis post vibratum Papale fulmen eos occiderit; continuo sequitur, martyrium ferri potius constanter oportere, quàm in causa esse, cur ij tradantur morti, qui iter ad vitam aeternam obstenderint. Hae propositiones catena quadam inter se devinctae & pari procedunt passu.
units.tr: But if Barrière had been a pupil of the Jesuits, brought up and trained in their doctrine, he would scarcely have accused Varades; for they believe that those are damned who have pointed out to the judges the authors and instigators of such deeds. And this third proposition follows from that first and second. For if the Pope can excommunicate kings, and it is a good and meritorious act if anyone slays them after the Papal thunderbolt has been hurled, it follows at once that one ought rather to suffer martyrdom constantly than be the cause of those being handed over to death who have pointed out the way to eternal life. These propositions, linked together as by a chain, advance with equal step.

units.la: Quapropter etiam Chastellus noluit accusare nominatim Iesuitarum quenquam; cum praesumpta fiducia faciendi bene, ut ipse exposuit, statuisset cultro jugulum suum petere. Credidisset enim ex eo argumento se damnationem sibi accersere, si indicasset eum, qui iter Paradisi ipsi ostenderat, prout depravatum erat judicium illius. Veruntamen ut Deus ille protector regum eruit veritatem ex ore illorum, qui eam celatam maximè & dissimulatam volunt, ecce affero ipsissima verba ex actis interrogatoriis vel quaestionibus Chastelli, quorum protocollum Majestas tua potest consulere, & quorum aliorum veritatem D. Praesides aut Consiliarij amplius triginta confirmabunt, ijque mille modis digniores fide, quàm sit dignum fide quicquid istius rei in sua ipsorum causa partes ve afferre possunt. Quaesitum, ubi Theologiam istam non vam didicerit, respondit, ex Philosophia. Rogatus utrum Philosophiae studuerit in Iesuitarum collegio: respondit studuisse, idque sub patre Guereto, qui sum ad annos duos cum dimidio sit versatus. Rogatus, annon fuerit in conclavi Meditationum, quo graviores peccatores intromittebant Iesuitae, ubi spectarent figuras multiformes Diabolorum complurium horrendas, specie revocandi eos in meliorem vitam, ut commoverent animos ipsorum, & monitis eiusmodi adpatrandum grande aliquod facinus, exitarent. Rogatus quis persuaserit ipsi, ut Regem occideret: Respondit, multis se in locis audivisse, hanc propositionem verissimam haberi oportere, quòd Regem liceat occidere, et qui affirmabant, TYRANNVM eum appellasse. Rogatus, annon sermones de occidendo Rege apud Iesuitas essent ordinarij? Respondit se audivisse dicentes, licere Regem occidere, extra Ecclesiam esse, nec ei obsequendum esse, eúmve habendum pro Rege, donec à Papa fuerit approbatus. Interrogatus iterum in magna Camera D. praesidibus & Consiliarijs ejus atq; Turnellis congregatis, eadem responsa dedit: expressè vero propositit & defendit thesin istam, quòd Reges liceat occidere, etiam Regem nunc regnantem, ut qui in Ecclesia non sit, prout ajebat, quia non est à Papa approbatus.
units.tr: Therefore Chastel also refused to accuse any Jesuit by name. With a presumptuous confidence that he was doing good, as he himself explained, he had resolved to turn the knife on his own throat. He believed that by that reasoning he would bring damnation upon himself if he named the man who had shown him the way to Paradise, given how depraved his judgment was. Yet God, the protector of kings, drew the truth from the mouths of those who most wish it hidden and concealed. Here, then, are the very words from the record of Chastel's interrogation, which Your Majesty may consult in the protocol, and whose truth the lord presidents and more than thirty councillors will confirm. These men are a thousand times more worthy of trust than anything the parties in their own cause can allege on this matter. He was asked where he had learned that theology, which was so unsound. He answered, from philosophy. Asked whether he had studied philosophy in the Jesuit college, he said he had, under Father Guéret, with whom he had spent about two and a half years. Asked whether he had been in the room of meditations, into which the Jesuits brought more serious sinners, where they viewed the many horrible, multiform figures of devils, supposedly to call them back to a better life, but really to stir their minds and, by such admonitions, to incite them to some great deed, he answered as follows. He was asked who had persuaded him to kill the King. He answered that he had heard in many places that it was a most true proposition that it is lawful to kill the King, and that those who affirmed this called him a TYRANT. Asked whether sermons about killing the King were regular among the Jesuits, he answered that he had heard them say that it was lawful to kill the King, that he was outside the Church, that he was not to be obeyed, and that he was not to be regarded as king until he had been approved by the Pope. Questioned again in the great chamber, with the lord presidents and councillors and the Turnelles assembled, he gave the same answers. He expressly put forward and defended the thesis that it is lawful to kill the Kings, even the King now reigning, since he is not in the Church, as he said, because he has not been approved by the Pope.

units.la: Quisquis libellos supplices leget, quos tibi, ô Rex, obtulerunt Iesuitae, statuet, illos non fuisse à Chastello accusatos: adeo negant audacter veritatem. Ego vero haud scio, an trium gravior accusatio inveniri possit, aut quod gravius excogitari crimen, quàm quo tenellos adhuc juventutis animos tam furibunda doctrina fascinent, quâ ad trucidandum Principem suum feruntur praecipites.
units.tr: Whoever reads the humble petitions which the Jesuits have offered you, O King, will conclude that Chastel did not accuse them at all, so boldly do they deny the truth. As for me, I do not know whether a graver charge can be found, or a more serious crime imagined, than that by which they bewitch the still tender minds of the young with such a frenzied doctrine, and so drive them headlong to murder their own prince.

units.la: Huic persimile est, quod legimus de confessione Guillelmi Paryfatta ante excessum ipsius, se Benedicti Palmij Iesuitae suasu adductū esse, ut de caede ista cogitaret: quam rem cum Sacrificio quodam, cui nomen Vates, communicavisse: hunc vero dissuasisse, dicendo ipsum damnatum fore: ideoque se Confessionis ergo ad Annibalem Codretum Iesuitam abiisse, qui ex necessitate esse dixerit, ut ille Vates esset haereticus: Quoniam vera Ecclesia nimirum dubitat Reges à Papa excommunicatos, Tyrannos esse, acproinde occidendos. Itaque Commentator libri, qui inscribitur summa Constitutionū, alias, septimi Decretalium pag. trecentesimā octavā, postquam Iesuitas supra modum laudibus extulisset (ut bonis rebus vera doribus instructi sunt) tandem ut laudum cumulo exornet eos, pronunciat de eis: Tyrannos aggrediuntur, lolium ab agro Dominico evellunt.
units.tr: Similar to this is what we read in the confession of William Parry before his death: that he had been led, at the persuasion of the Jesuit Benedict Palmio, to think about that murder. He had shared the matter with a certain priest named Vates, but Vates had dissuaded him, saying that he would be damned. Therefore Parry went for confession to the Jesuit Annibal Codretus, who said it was necessary that Vates be a heretic, since the true Church doubts that kings excommunicated by the Pope are tyrants and therefore to be killed. So too the commentator of the book entitled Summa Constitutionum, or otherwise the seventh book of the Decretals, page 308, after praising the Jesuits beyond measure (as men truly endowed with good gifts), finally, to crown their praises, pronounces of them: "They attack tyrants; they pull up the darnel from the Lord's field."

units.la: Poterit Majestas tua librum istum in manus sumere: facile sermonem istum Latinum intelliget: audivi quum difficilius rem exponeret. Significatur denique his verbis, optimè illos & animosissimè novisse lolium ex arvo Domini evellere, eosque tollere quos Roma excommunicaverit: hoc certo certius, omnes quacunque tandem religione sint, tyrannos vocant.
units.tr: Your Majesty may take this book into your hands; you will easily understand this Latin sentence. I heard it explained with some difficulty. The meaning of these words, in short, is that they know most excellently and most boldly how to pluck up the darnel from the Lord's field, and to remove those whom Rome has excommunicated. And, more certainly than certain, all of them, of whatever religion they may be, they call tyrants.
