units.la: Enimvero Rex defunctus nunquam alius fuit quàm summè Catholicus: id noverunt omnes, & quàm bene esset de Ecclesia meritus multis nominibus. Atqui simul Roma excommunicatus est, simul pater Commoletus, pater Bernhardus (quos suis defensionibus ante prolatis in coelum evehunt) & universè omnes alij Iesuitae nunquam post illud tempus eum ad mortem usque alio nomine donaverunt, quàm tyranni, Holophernis, Moab, Neronis, quae omnia belle cum definitione tyranni, quàm supra adduxi, consentiunt.
units.tr: Indeed the late King was never anything other than most fully Catholic. Everyone knows this, and how well he deserved of the Church in many respects. Yet at the very time Rome excommunicated him, Father Commolet and Father Bernard (whom they exalt to heaven in their earlier defences) and all the other Jesuits never again, until his death, called him by any name but tyrant, like Holofernes, Moab, or Nero. All of these fit well with the definition of a tyrant which I cited above.

units.la: Die natali Christi anno MDLXXXI. tua Majestas erat Catholica: & tamen ille ipse Commoletus in aede S. Bartholomaei dicebat, Ahod nobis opus est, sive monachus, sive mendicus, sive pastor, nihil refert: sed Ahod nobis opus est. Postea vero ubi cognovit quaestionem de eo haberi, sibi consuluit fugâ.
units.tr: On Christmas Day in the year 1581, Your Majesty was Catholic. And yet that same Commolet said in the church of St Bartholomew: "We need an Ehud, whether a monk, a beggar or a minister; it makes no difference, but we need an Ehud." Afterwards, when he learned that an inquiry was being made about him, he took counsel for his own safety and fled.

units.la: Hoc negari magis non potest, quàm factum Varadis: etsi hoc valere quarunt, dicentes Barreriam quidem ipsi exposuisse consilium suum: hunc vero illi respondisse, Non posse fieri, cum sit Presbyter, ipsi de re consilium dare.
units.tr: This cannot be denied any more than the deed of Varade can be. Though they try to make it count for little, saying that Barrière indeed explained his plan to him, but that Varade answered that it could not be done, since he was a presbyter and could not give counsel on such a matter.

units.la: Sed demus sanè, hoc unum esto: quid hoc revera aliud est dicere, quàm illud? tuum erat facere, ac non amplius communicare: plus praestat, & effare minus.
units.tr: But let us grant, for the sake of argument, this one thing. What does it really amount to, other than saying that? It was his to do, and not to share the plan any further. He does more, and says less.

units.la: Veruntamen si Majestas tua Acta de morte Barreriae adferri ad se curarerit, Val. radem ipsum Iesuitarum Gymnasiarcham hortatum esse, hominem accendisse, & S. Sacramento altaris obstrinxisse, ut manum promptè alacriterque inijceret. Et certè nunquam majore periculo, dum vixit, versata est Majestas tua: Novit Dominus quae miracula de tua morte confinxissent, cum de morte defuncti Regis tam affabre fecerint, monumentum eius superbè insultantes, litteris in omnes partes orbis terrarum datis, quas etiam Roma ad majorem ostentationem excudi curaverunt.
units.tr: But if Your Majesty has taken care to have the Acts concerning the death of Barrière brought to you, you will find that the same Varade, the Jesuits' head of the college, urged the man on, inflamed him, and bound him by the sacrament of the altar to lay hands on the King promptly and eagerly. And certainly Your Majesty was never, while he lived, in greater danger. The Lord knows what miracles they would have invented about your death, since they fashioned such skilful tales about the death of the late King, insolently mocking his memorial, and sent letters to every part of the world, which they even had Rome print for greater display.

units.la: Haec inter solennes litteras & annales ipsorum relata sunt pag. 35. quarum haec verba sunt: quo die nos Regis edicto Burdegalâ pellebamur, eo die Rex ipse, qui edixerat, vitâ depulsus est. Ab eo compingebamur ad S. Macarij, ut simul opprimeremur omnes (sive hoc suspicio, sive fama tulit) nisi antea oppressus ille unus fuisset. Hoc porrò nunciatum cum esset, afflixit animos adversariorum. Nunquam gravior incessit animum meum admiratio, quàm quum partem istam litterarum, quas perscripserunt, legerem. Eteniam quis unquam putavisset homines Religiosos, adeoque Christianos fore, qui furorem tantum, & inimicitias ferreas atque irreconciliabiles etiam post mortem ostenderent. Naturam docet inimicorum nostrorum miserari, quum eos videmus humi prostratos; non posse amplius nobis inimici esse, qui non sunt amplius. At subditum pedibus proterere venter heri fui, domini fui, Regis fui, & primi in Christiano orbe Regum, atque de eo paeana canere c vero crimen, & omnem barbariem, omnem inhumanitatem, omnemq; saevitiam exfurans, quae unquam in mentem possit cadere.
units.tr: These things are related in their solemn letters and annals, page 35, whose words are these: "On the day we were driven out of Bordeaux by the King's edict, on that very day the King who issued it was removed from life. From there we were pressed on to St Macarius, so that we should all be crushed together (whether it was suspicion or rumour that reported this), unless that one man had been crushed first. When this was announced, it afflicted the spirits of our adversaries. Never did greater wonder come over my mind than when I read that part of the letters which they wrote. For who would ever have thought that religious men, and so Christians, would display such fury, such iron and irreconcilable enmity, even after death? Nature teaches us to pity our enemies when we see them stretched on the ground; he who is no more cannot be our enemy any longer. But to trample under foot one who was yesterday my master, my lord, my King, and the first of the kings in the Christian world, and to sing a paean over him, raging with a true crime, and with every barbarity, every inhumanity, every savagery that could ever come into the mind."

units.la: Ac ist am quidem contumeliam non sensit miser ille Princeps: neque vero tam est illata si, quam tuae Majestati, o Rex, & iis omnibus, qui gerunt Francorum nomen.
units.tr: Indeed that unhappy prince did not feel this insult. Nor was it aimed so much at him as at Your Majesty, O King, and at all who bear the name of the French.

units.la: Verum sensit gravissime venenum Ligae conspiratorum ve, sibi a Iesuita Claudio Mataeo praeparatum, qui sub finem anni 1588. in Italia obiit ex laboribus molestiis, quae indefinter fecerat in Hispaniam, Italiam, Helvetiam, Germaniam, Belgium, ut extremam ruinam adderet, confringeret atque confirmaret maximam illam atque horrendam conspirationem, quae in defunctum Regem, totamq; Borboniam familiam fuerat inita. Vidit Majestas tua, quid super hac re Iesuita Guignartus scripserit, Coronam Galliae posse & debere familia alteram, quam in Borboniam transportari. Et quicunque noverunt arcana conspirationis istius, aperte clamunt: Patres Iesuitas fuisse germanos istius conspirationis auctores: hos reos esse, & omni jure teneri mortis eorum, qui in profundissimam istam abyssum corruerunt. En tibi per brevem historiam, quae rem confirmabit luculentissime. Nomen est consilium Sedecim virorum ex literis interceptis, quibus urbem Parisiorum dederunt Regi Hispaniae. Et ubi homines isti praesidem sanguinarij consilij sui quaesiverunt? Id Iesuitas accesserunt reliqua, qui patrem Odonem Pichenatum rei praefecerunt. Hoc suis sensionibus agnoscunt Lutetiae excusis: sed ideo factum praedicant, ut lenirent Sedecimvirorum impetum. Non desunt qui responderent, oleum camino addi, quum Iesuita in turbam seditiosorum immittitur: Ego vero aliter sentio, istos Sedecim viros freno ac non caloribus opus habuisse, nec aliam viam extitisse, qua celeratum consilium ipsorum daretur effectum, quam si violentior ipsorum impetus sisteretur. Et quis, obsecro, non videat consentientiam istorum Sedecim carnificum admirabilem (nam aliter vocari non possunt, cum illum praesidem illum Parlamenti, qui Lutetiae restabat, suspenderint) quis, inquam, non videat admirabilem istorum Sedecim cum Iesuitica Societate convenientiam, quando unum potius de numero illorum sibi depositerunt Praesidem, quam alterum Ecclesiasticum, icunque quemquam.
units.tr: But he felt most grievously the poison prepared for him by the Jesuit Claude Matthieu, who was in the League of conspirators. Matthieu died in Italy toward the end of 1588, worn out by the labours and troubles he had undertaken without rest in Spain, Italy, Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, in order to bring about the final ruin, and to break and confirm that huge and horrible conspiracy which had been entered into against the late King and the whole Bourbon family. Your Majesty has seen what the Jesuit Guignard wrote on this matter, that the Crown of France could and should be transferred from the Bourbon family to another. And all who know the secrets of this conspiracy openly cry out that the Jesuit fathers were the chief authors of it, that they are guilty, and that by every right they are bound to the death of those who fell into that deepest abyss. Here, in brief, is a history which will confirm the matter most clearly. It is called the council of the Sixteen, from letters intercepted, by which they gave the city of Paris to the King of Spain. And where did these men seek the president of their bloody council? They approached the other Jesuits, who appointed Father Odo Pigenat to the task. They acknowledge this in their own writings printed at Paris, but they declare it was done so as to soften the assault of the Sixteen. There are not lacking those who answer that oil is added to the fire when a Jesuit is sent among a crowd of seditious men. I think otherwise: those Sixteen needed a bridle, not heat, and there was no other way for their wicked design to be carried into effect than if their more violent impetus were checked. And who, I ask, does not see the remarkable agreement of these sixteen executioners (for they cannot be called anything else, since they hanged that president of the Parlement who remained at Paris) with the Jesuit Society? Who, I say, does not see that remarkable agreement, since they chose as their president one of their own number rather than any churchman at all?

units.la: Tum inde ab ineunte anno 1585. Iesuitarum domos Lutetiae & alibi passim, stativa esse perpetua omnibus, quibus res Hispanicas curabant promoveri: litterarum fasces eodem tos, apertos, distributos esse: consilia ordinarie cum Legato Mendoza & successoribus suis Parisijs, cumq; alijs gestoribus & procuratoribus negotiorum Regis Philippi in ponitoribus quibusq; civitatibus, ubicunq; erant, communicasse; Res nota est atq; notoria. Hoc quis melius novit, quam Majestas tua?
units.tr: From the beginning of the year 1585, the houses of the Jesuits at Paris and elsewhere were, everywhere, a permanent base for all who looked after Spanish interests. Bundles of letters were open and circulated to all, and they shared their plans regularly with the legate Mendoza and his successors at Paris, and with the other agents and managers of King Philip's affairs in the provinces and in whatever cities they were. The matter is well known and notorious. Who knows this better than Your Majesty?

units.la: Ajunt quidem illi, te, o Rex, tam arcto vinculo cum Rege Hispaniae constrictum esse, ut videtur hoc dicto magis, quam ladatur ipsorum causa. Nam Majestate tuam nemini tam videre, quam ijs, qui ex animo Hispanum diligunt.
units.tr: They say, indeed, O King, that you are bound to the King of Spain by so close a tie that this saying seems to do more harm than good to their cause. For nothing seems so pleasing to Your Majesty as to those who love the Spaniard from the heart.

units.la: Hoc nunc forte obtendi posset: At mihi quidem certe permirum videbatur, istos homines, quo tempore maxime nostrum fervebat bellum cum Philippo Rege, his verbis uti: Nam tempore Caroli IX. nunquam de Hispanis sermo, nisi in parte optima habebatur: sed haeretici non odio gentis (nam Anglos & Germanos eis plus odio oportet esse, qui graviore injuria Galliam, quam alia gens ulla affecerint) sed magis religionis odio eos efficere exosos duerunt causa pratextara regni. Videntur profecto mihi plus studium suum erga Hispanos eo tempore retexisse, quo Gallorum millia aliquot in Picardiae finibus trucidabant.
units.tr: Someone might now put this forward as an objection. But it seemed to me quite remarkable that these men, at the very time when our war with King Philip was at its height, should use such words. For in the time of Charles IX the Spanish were never spoken of except in the best light. The heretics, however, did not make them hated from hatred of the nation (for the English and the Germans ought to hate them more, since they have done France a greater injury than any other people), but from hatred of religion, and they used the pretext of the kingdom's cause to make them odious. Indeed, they seem to me to have revealed their partiality for the Spanish more clearly at the time when they were slaughtering some thousands of Frenchmen on the borders of Picardy.

units.la: Non decet viros bonos usquam adeo traduci communi studio & voto regula sua, ut oblivi-scantur natales suos, & ab aliquo sensu doloris ex miseriis patriae suae conceptis abstineant: praesertim cum illi ipsi essent Catholici, quos omni aetate & sexu, maximo numero & sine ulla misericordia jugulabant. Duri videtur plane & feri animi esse, si hoc de ijs pronuntietur, qui eodem tempore in Gallorum, & quidem Catholicorum sanguine mersabant sese. Si majores colunt, honorant & reverentur Hispani; si majoribus bonis officijsq; Iesuitas patres efficiunt: si eos vocant Apostolos, ut scribunt ipsi: tamen non convenit, ut de ijs tempore bello perinde sermonem habeas ac pacis.
units.tr: Good men should not be so led by a common zeal and wish for their own rule that they forget their birth and refrain from any feeling of grief at the miseries conceived for their country, especially when those same men were Catholics, whom they butchered in great numbers, of every age and sex, and without any mercy. It is plainly the mark of a hard and savage spirit to say this of men who at the same time were steeping themselves in the blood of the French, and indeed of Catholics. If the Spanish cultivate, honour and revere their ancestors, and if the Jesuit fathers make themselves worthy of good offices and of their own kind, and if they call themselves Apostles, as they write, nevertheless it is not fitting to speak of them in war in the same way as one would in peace.

units.la: Pap. 1f9. Def. verit. ed. craf. etp. 119. mm. ed.
units.tr: Pap. 1f9. Def. verit. ed. craf. etp. 119. mm. ed.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: On the Propagation

units.la: Supplice libello, quem post exhibuerunt Majestati tuæ, in hoc argumentum liberius ex-currerunt: & majori cum ratione, his verbis; Quod nos criminabantur Hispanos esse, fabrefacta fuit in fabrica temporis criminatio, cui vires addebat opportunitas temporum ac occasionis respectu solum, id est, cum Gallia & Hispania bellum inter se miscerent: tunc nomen erat odiosum, suspectum, ingratum nomen: nunc vero ubi Christianiss. Majestas tua nodum firmavit sanctæ pacis cum Rege Catholico, ubi Gallus frater est Hispano, & Hispanus Gallo, antiquata est hæc criminatio, intempestiva, à ratione omni aliena.
units.tr: In the humble little book which they afterwards presented to Your Majesty, they ran on more freely about this subject, and with greater reason, in these words: "The accusation that we were Spaniards was manufactured in the workshop of the times, and it gained strength only from the opportunity of the moment, namely when France and Spain were waging war against each other. Then the name was hateful, suspect and unwelcome. But now that Your Most Christian Majesty has tied the knot of holy peace with the Catholic King, so that the Frenchman is brother to the Spaniard and the Spaniard to the Frenchman, this accusation has become obsolete, untimely, and foreign to all reason."

units.la: Id tamen apud te, ô Rex, fatear necesse est, ut taceam jamq; plus nobis de hac re constare, homines istos videri mihi hac bella sua oratione prodere, quàm mirifice Regi Hispaniæ obstrictifint. Vehementer cupiunt omnes tibi suspiciones eximere, et in id laborant accurato plane artificio: id tamen optime novimus, in eo maxime ab eis operam fumi, nolle ut videantur subditi tui alios ipsos esse, quàm servos studiosissimos Philippi Regis, quia hoc rebus suis valde judicant commodare. Cum autem ista compato cum Arresto Inquisitionis, quo antiquatum est decretum Sorbonæ contra ipsos datum 1564. ut quidem gloriantur ipsi, & cum prima institutione ipsorum per capitaneum Hispanum facta, postremo cum istis verbis, quæ extant in vita Ignatij, pag. 169. Debemus etiam atq; etiam orare Deum noctes & dies, ut servet quàm diutissime in omni sanitate & prosperitate Philippum Regem Catholicum, qui hereditaria et excellenti pietate ac devotione sua, prudentia singulari, vigilantia incredibili, & potentia ad infinitum majore quàm unquam fuerit in mundo ullius regis, est propugnaculo ad defensionem religionis Catholicæ.
units.tr: Yet, O King, I must confess this much to you, and I say nothing of how much more is known to us about this matter: these men seem to me, by this very speech of theirs, to betray how wonderfully they are bound to the King of Spain. They are eager to remove every suspicion from you, and they labour at it with a very careful art. Yet we know full well that in this they chiefly take pains, that your subjects should not appear to be anything other than the most devoted servants of King Philip, because they judge this to be very useful for their own affairs. When I compare these claims with the decree of the Inquisition, by which the decree of the Sorbonne issued against them in 1564 has been annulled (as they themselves boast), and with their original founding through a Spanish captain, and finally with these words, which stand in the Life of Ignatius, page 169: "We ought also, again and again, to pray God day and night that He may preserve for as long as possible, in all health and prosperity, Philip the Catholic King, who by his hereditary and excellent piety and devotion, his singular prudence, his incredible vigilance, and his power, far greater than that of any king ever in the world, is a bulwark for the defence of the Catholic religion."

units.la: Quam rem non solum armis juvet præstat, quæ semper fuerunt invicta, sed etiam opera magni illius Senatus Inquisitionis, qui vigilat continenter pro religione Catholica. Quum ista simul omnia compare, hoc ego apud te, ô Rex, profitear necesse est, si quo infortunio bellum tibi oriretur, in metu fore mi pergravi, ne isti homines clanculum omnibus modis præstarent operas iniquissimas. Nec tamen alio tempore otiosi jacent: Semper enim doctrinæ illius suæ quam destrinximus ante, curant propagationem, in qua se plurimum laboravisse, & valde jamq; provexisse anno 1589. ostenderunt. Nam si contra Henricum II. Regem talis prolata fuisset ex communicatio, ne minimam quidem Regni urbem commovere tantillum potuisset: patrum vero Iesuitarum opera & labore quasi triginta annorum exitum filio illius attulit, qui illam perinde ut antecessores sui ludum fuisset factaurus. Rem stupendam, ne copias quidem ducentes mille hominum fuisse tantum effecturas contra defunctum Regem, quantum ducentorum Iesuitarum manus, disponendo subditos illius, id est, animos eorum ita abalienando, ut ex templo incendium ab eis exarserit, cum prius Gallia magnus quidam Oceanus esset, in quo simul cadebat, simul exstinguebatur hoc fulgur.
units.tr: This is a matter which he assists not only with arms, which have always been unconquered, but also by the work of that great Senate of the Inquisition, which watches continually for the Catholic religion. When I put all these things together, O King, I must declare to you that if some misfortune should bring war upon you, I would be greatly afraid that these men would secretly lend every means of most wicked service. Nor do they lie idle at other times. For they always take care to propagate that doctrine of theirs which we have described above, and in the year 1589 they showed that they had laboured hard at it and had made great progress. For if such an excommunication had been published against King Henry II, it could scarcely have stirred the smallest city of the kingdom. But by the work and labour of the Jesuit fathers, over some thirty years, it brought about the end of his son, who would have made the kingdom a plaything just as his predecessors had done. A remarkable thing: the armies of a hundred thousand men would not have achieved as much against the dead king as the band of two hundred Jesuits did, by arranging his subjects, that is, by so alienating their minds that a fire broke out at once among them. Before this, France was a great ocean, in which the spark was extinguished as soon as it fell.

units.la: Ac tantisper quidem dum bene Majest. tuæ & tuis convenerint cum Pontificib. magnum doctrinæ istius effectus non est proditurus. Quod semper bene fit conventurum, sperare oportet, sed futura incerta sunt. Quapropter recte fit, quod de pacis tempore diligenter finibus tuis prospicis. Vix autem fieri potest, ut ter ex ordine sanctæ sedi prospiciatur, ne in manus hominum veniat partium Hispanicarum studiosi: adeo magno sunt numero inter D. Cardinales. Tum vero ingenue dico, ô Rex, & sine assentatione, Corona tua sceptrumq; tuum & regnum ab hac voce unica penderet, si plures in subditorum tuorum numero doctrinam Iesuitarum quàm adversam colerent. Si doctrina ipsorum obtineret, nullus futurus esses: sin esset infirmior, retineres quidem Dominium tuum, sed plane sanguine exitioq; multorum ex subditis bonorum, malorum promiscue conjunctum.
units.tr: For the time being, while things go well between Your Majesty and your people and the Pontiffs, the great effect of that doctrine is not going to show itself. One must hope that this will always go well, but the future is uncertain. Therefore it is right that you take careful thought, in time of peace, for the borders of your realm. Yet it can hardly happen that three times in succession the Holy See is provided with a man who is not a partisan of Spanish interests, so great are their numbers among the Lord Cardinals. Then indeed I say it frankly, O King, and without flattery: your crown, your sceptre and your kingdom would hang on this single word, if more of your subjects cultivated the doctrine of the Jesuits than opposed it. If their doctrine prevailed, you would be no one at all; but if it were weaker, you would indeed keep your dominion, yet it would be mixed, without distinction, with the blood and ruin of many good subjects.

units.la: Hic etiam cogitare oportet Majest. tua, istud ex communicationis caput longè nunc nobis esse periculosius, quàm quû ditiones in Italia et copias haberemus. Hac etenim via poteramus Papæ adjumento esse, si qua forte vis eum cogeret, ut noceret nobis. Hodierno autem die unus Prorex Neapolitanus cum factiosis Hispanienfibus in urbe Roma jugulum premit sanctorum patrum, qui ter obsessi, ter capti essent antequam dimidium iter emensi essemus in subsidium ipsorum. Ut illud taceam, quod nunquam Roma vixit, nisi ex tritico Siciliæ, sui granarij.
units.tr: Here Your Majesty must also consider that this head of excommunication is now far more dangerous to us than when we had domains and forces in Italy. For in that way we could be of help to the Pope, if some force should perhaps compel him to harm us. But today a single Neapolitan viceroy, together with the factious Spaniards in the city of Rome, has the holy fathers by the throat, who, having been besieged and captured three times, would have been captured before we had gone half the journey to their aid. Not to mention that Rome has never lived except on the wheat of Sicily, its granary.

units.la: Accedit ad hæc omnia, unum hoc observatu dignu, quod videntes Iesuita quantu periculi c doctrina Principibus afferat, astutè ab ea retegenda cavent, quum se insinuant pri-um ditionibusque illabuntur: quum autem in loco bene radicati sunt, tum eam paulatim influere, quasi de manu in manum per populum, hauriendo isti veneno plus facis à natura idoneum. Quid enim suavius in multorum ingenijs, quàm ab ea subjectione absolvi, obstringuntur suis natalibus? Non sum nescius bonos viros tenere scitum illud dictum Philosophi, Regi suo obsequi veram magnamque libertatem esse: nos & naturâ & civium jure doceri atque obligari, ut serviamus honoremusque Principem, cujus sub imperio Solem primum lucemque vidimus: neminem hominem in orbe terrarum liberare nos ab eo obsequio posse, quo nos ipsi obstrinxit Deus. Sed sicubi mens una est composita, quae in ea opinione sit, comperias ternos qui diversum sentiunt.
units.tr: All this brings with it one thing worth noting: the Jesuits, seeing how much danger their doctrine brings to princes, take cunning care to conceal it when they first insinuate themselves and slip into a realm. But once they are well rooted in a place, then they let it flow in gradually, as if from hand to hand through the people, drawing from it a poison all the more suited to human nature. For what is more pleasant to many minds than to be freed from that subjection by which they are bound through their birth? I am not unaware that good men hold that saying of the Philosopher, that to obey one's king is true and great liberty. But we are taught and bound by nature and by the right of citizens to serve and honour the prince under whose rule we first saw the sun and the light; no man in the whole world can free us from that obedience to which God Himself has bound us. But wherever you find one mind settled in that opinion, you will find three who think otherwise.

units.la: Tum vero pessime habet quod dacissimi quique, & ad licentiam projectissimi in hoc praecipitium ruunt plurimum, paucique fere ijdem orum mobilium hominum & axitiosorum manus multitudine aliorum super exsistit. Quid? nonne hoc experti sumus? Est omnino mihi persuasum, cum Lutetiae perunt isti Tyrannum dicere defunctum Regem, ut qui à Papa excommunicatus esset, nque exterminari oportere, duplò plures fuisse, qui contra judicarent, & qui Regem sluissent videre in Lupara tranquillè regnantem, duodecimque seditiosos pendentes de tibulo: sed respiciebat alter in alterum animus, non vis deerat: quemadmodum continsæpè, ut mercatores decem à tribus prædonibus ex improviso invadentibus spolientur. ut regiam insistunt viam, sequeque in obsequio naturæ continent, dormiunt de nocte: diem in negotijs singularibus occupant. At ex contrario qui rebus novis student, & eversioni publicæ, hi de nocte coeunt, conspirant, inque dies confirmant sese, nihil aliud satagunt, vint ex occultis pensitationibus, & alios tandem inopinanteis opprimunt: qui primus in navigium ruit, primas tenet.
units.tr: Moreover, it is very bad that the most reckless and those most abandoned to licence rush most eagerly into this precipice, and that there are scarcely any of these same restless and troublesome men, few in number, who stand above the multitude of others. What? Have we not experienced this ourselves? I am completely persuaded that when those men said in Paris that the dead king was a tyrant, since he had been excommunicated by the Pope and ought to be driven out, there were twice as many who thought otherwise, and who wished to see the king reigning peacefully in the Louvre, and twelve seditious men hanging from the gallows. But one mind looked to another, and there was no lack of force: just as it often happens that ten merchants are plundered unexpectedly by three robbers. The robbers keep to the king's highway, and keep themselves within the obedience of nature, and sleep at night, and occupy the day with their private affairs. But on the contrary, those who are eager for revolution and public overthrow meet by night, conspire, and strengthen one another day by day; they busy themselves with nothing else than secret plotting, and at last they crush others who suspect nothing. Whoever first rushes into the ship holds the first place.

units.la: Cum itaque Iesuitæ constanter periculosas istas propositiones teneant, & in mundo semiit, ut ante fuit demonstratum: equidem non possum quin profitear, ô Rex, videri mihi peulum impendens à doctrinâ istius propagatione, si bene examinabitur: longè gravius esomnibus rationum momentis, quæ in contrarium appendi possunt.
units.tr: Since, then, the Jesuits constantly hold these dangerous propositions, and spread them through the world, as was shown before, I cannot but declare, O King, that if it is examined carefully, the danger hanging over us from the spread of this doctrine seems to me far more serious than all the weight of the arguments that can be set on the other side.

units.la: Nam quod ad confutandas opiniones novas in religionis causa, verè possumus adfirre, quemadmodum primis illis quinquaginta annis fuerunt Lutheri & Calvini errores erbè propositi, prædicati atque promulgati: Sic inde à viginti quinque, & quasi triginta an-, eos jam magnificè, potenterque, & vivâ voce & scriptis esse convulsos, & infinitâ qun profunditate scientiæ superari in hoc tempore, quit quid alij unquam attulerunt: adeò ut ipsi opinionum istarum auctores revertantur in hanc lucem, eos putem fore à suo errore cessuros, quum magna illa argumenta sua, quorum præsidio tantopere considebant, desa animad verterent. Itaque primores videmus & acutissimos eorum redire quotidie in ecclesiæ gremium: quæ in re opinor, animi nostri debent plurimum acquiescere. Felices en conversiones istæ non fiunt equuleis, non tormentis, non terroribus mortis, ut Inquisitio et Hispanica, (cui unà cum Castellanis armis, Iesuitæ ut ceptam fecerunt religionis Calica conservationem, ut ante demonstravimus) sed gladio S. Spiritus æterno, verbo, ad docent nostri Doctores, Pastoresque & boni Episcopi, qui in causa doctrinæ nihilo iniores Iesuitis patribus videntur esse, quam vis interdum optimis & validissimis arguntis eorum utantur. Ita enim censeo, tam diligenter à nobis colligi eorum libros in conversis capitibus religionis oportere, quàm eos procul abijci quibus dissentiatur doctriilla, quam supra attigimus.
units.tr: For as to refuting new opinions in the cause of religion, we can truly bring forward that, just as in the first fifty years the errors of Luther and Calvin were freely proposed, preached and published, so for some twenty-five or about thirty years they have now been shaken, both by living voice and by writings, and are overcome at this time with an infinite depth of learning, such as others never brought. So much so that I think the very authors of those opinions are returning to this light, and will cease from their error, when they see that those great arguments of theirs, on which they relied so heavily, have failed them. Thus we see daily their leading and most acute men returning to the bosom of the Church; in this matter, I think, our minds ought to be greatly content. Those happy conversions are not brought about by the rack, by torments, or by terrors of death, as the Inquisition and the Spanish methods are (with which, together with the Castilian arms, the Jesuits have undertaken, as we showed before, to preserve the Catholic religion), but by the eternal sword of the Holy Spirit, the Word. Our teachers, pastors and good bishops, who seem in the cause of doctrine to be in no way inferior to the Jesuit fathers, bring this about, although sometimes they use the most excellent and strongest arguments. For I think that the books of those who dissent from that doctrine which we touched on above ought to be gathered up by us as diligently in the matter of the converted heads of religion as they ought to be cast far away.

units.la: Neque verò hoc celaturus sum, etsi nonnunquam patres Iesuitæ conversionibus quoque fueit adjumento, eos tamen non æquè mihi in hac re fortunatos videri, ut sunt Episcopi & Pastores nostri. Austerior illorum ratio, à natura Gallorum alienior, homines prima fronreddit attonitos: adeò sæpè cum exteris agunt, & ita sese exemplo primi auctoris sui genHispani conformarunt, ut vultu, gestu, actione saltem plerisque ipsorum grandiorem præsperit atem ferant.
units.tr: I will not conceal this either: although the Jesuit fathers have sometimes also been of help in conversions, they do not seem to me to have been as fortunate in this matter as our bishops and ministers have been. Their harsher method, more alien to the French temperament, strikes people at first sight with astonishment. They so often deal with foreigners, and have so conformed themselves to the Spanish cast of their first founder, that most of them show at least in face, gesture and manner a more lofty bearing.

units.la: Ita est tamen, accommodari nos oportet ad rationem ægri, & de medicis non ingratis
units.tr: Even so, we ought to adapt ourselves to the condition of the sick, and [we should speak] of physicians who are not ungrateful.

units.la: Axitiosi dicun-tur factiosi, teste Festo.
units.tr: Those called "axitiosi" are said, as Festus attests, to be factious.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: On the Propagation

units.la: prospici: si quis eum recte curari volet: Is nullo pacto Gallus Iesuita est. Tam furenter ma[illegible, ~3 letters]ximas contumelias blasphemiasque in Regem defunctum intonuerunt, ut adhuc animus horreat. Inest Gallis nescio quae naturalis in amore sui Principis inclinatio, quae justam pariter nauseam horroremque, uti sermones ita favos de suis Regibus audiunt pronunciari. Curavi illis aliquando dici (nam diligebam eos forte supra quam debuerim) aegre mihi esse, quod eos viderem tam infestos mortuo; videri mihi officia, quae miser ille Princeps erga Ecclesiam ac sanguinem et vitam usque toties totque praeliis et tot obsidionibus fecerat, saltem mereri ut aliquid memoriae ipsius condonetur. Responderunt quidam ex intimis, apud quem rem exposueram, speciosum quidem esse illius dictum: sed tempus ita flagitare, nunc demum religionem Catholicam stabiliri in Gallia, aut nunquam oportere. Satis his intellexi, quid sibi velint: ipsis nempe certum et deliberatum esse, ut exosam redderent populo monarchiam, quae tam diu vixerunt, curarentque mutari Dominum, extinctaque Borboniorum stirpe. Vt itaque vidi praesidia Hispanica et Neapolitana post ingressam Lutetiam; tum verum principium esse duxi, quo responsum illud suum effectum redderent. Et ne quid apud te, o Rex, dissimulem, exordium hoc putabam esse Tragoediae, atque esse, nunquam regressura Parisios Majestatem tuam, et tandem minora oppida majoribus et potentioribus esse concessura.
units.tr: Look: whoever wishes him to be rightly cared for is in no way a French Jesuit. They thundered such furious abuse and blasphemies against the late King that my spirit still shudders. The French have I know not what natural inclination in their love for their Prince, which makes them equally right to be nauseated and horrified when they hear such things said of their Kings as they hear them spoken. I once told them (for perhaps I loved them more than I ought) that it grieved me to see them so hostile to the dead man; it seemed to me that the services which that unhappy Prince had rendered to the Church, and the blood and life he had spent so often and in so many battles and sieges, deserved at least that something be forgiven to his memory. Some of the intimate ones, to whom I had laid out the matter, replied that his remark was indeed fine, but that the times demanded otherwise: now at last the Catholic religion must be established in France, or never. From this I understood well enough what they meant: namely, that they were certain and resolved to make the monarchy, which had lasted so long, hateful to the people, and to bring about a change of lord, with the Bourbon line extinguished. So when I saw the Spanish and Neapolitan garrisons after they had entered Paris, I judged this to be the true beginning by which their reply would be made effective. And, that I may conceal nothing from you, O King, I thought this was the prelude of a tragedy, and that Your Majesty would never return to Paris, and that at last you would concede the smaller towns to the greater and more powerful ones.

units.la: SECUNDO, ad rem ipsam accedit Orator noster, et Necesse est, inquit, ut de tribus his capitibus unum aliquod statuatur: ut aut Iesuitis fiat satis ex animi ipsorum sententia; aut iubeantur Arresto obsequi, quod exilium omnibus ex regno imperat; aut denique eo loco res, quo nunc sunt, sinantur esse.
units.tr: SECONDLY, our orator comes to the matter itself and says: "It is necessary that one of these three courses be decided upon: either that the Jesuits be satisfied according to their own wishes; or that they be ordered to obey the Arrêt, which commands exile for them from the kingdom; or finally that things be left in the state they are now."

units.la: Initium faciam ab ultimo, quia maxime prima fronte videtur planfibile; et tamen hoc ipsum re, et veritate est, quod minimum habet speciei, cum id omnino constet; Iesuitas aut ubique restitui, aut ubique ad parendum cogi oportere. Ista segmentata opera turpia sunt, periculosa sunt, attingunt existimationem, auctoritatem tuam. Si justum et utile est eos retinere, cives oportet maneant, ac non exules: sin minus, oportet exeant, non exemplum rebellionis praebeant pervicacia sua, ut adhuc fecerunt diutius aequo. Breve solum ex membrana ad semunciam mittebat Lacedaemonij: et momento eodem necesse erat mandatum exsequi. Id omnino est necessarium ut tam Burdegala et Tholosa pareatur Majestati tuae, quam Lutetiae aut ad Bellaquaeum fonte. Sunt tibi illic fervi et bono numero: quod Regis et Domini auctoritate jusseris, id efficietur, ne dubita. Quod si Iesuitae tibi non sunt utiles, ne altius radices in provinciis duabus illis agere sinas. Arbor quam hoc anno potes unica manu convellere, anno altero nonnisi ambabus manibus eradicabitur: ligone et securi opus est in anno tertio. Suspectam nobis oportet esse istam vicinitatem Hispaniae: semper accusati fuerunt Hispanienses partium: id omnibus suis actionibus confirmarunt, quo antiquior fuit de illis querimonia, eo verior fuisse, eoque justiores. Ex regno catero exacti sunt: ecce autem praemuniunt et circumvallunt sese in duabus provinciis, conterminis Hispaniae, qui ex Hispania venerunt. Quod nam hoc humilitatis exemplum est atque obsequii? Si locus ullus est ubi confirmantes eos sejungi minime oportet, id profecto est in regione regni limitanea, remota a nostro Sole ad Madritanum propius accedente. Ibi videntur Hispaniae eos humeris sustinere: ibi se videntur jam quoque obvallare contra Majest. tuam, et palam dicere: Tu nos Lutetia et aliis locis ejecisti, sed breviores tibi lacerti sunt, quam ut hos propellas ulterius. Hoc vero est indignissimum. Quid sibi nonnulli velint, qui se Scabinos praedicat, prius eorum discipuli, et nunc veneno ipsorum imbuti, equidem nescio qui tam ferociter pro illis dimicant. Hi illi tamen oportet sentiant, se aeque tibi, o Rex, debere obsequium, quam debet tenuissimus Lutetiae incola. Nimia hic est arrogantia, nimis obfirmata rebellio. Hactenus sprevetunt illi orbitate tua, ut olim ajebat quidam: cura nunc, ut sentiant, se tibi et toti posteritati tuae perpetuo semper debere obsequium: nemo tam celsus futurus est, qui non contremiscat. Nunquam in filio excidit injuriarum, quae patri facta sunt, recordatio. Igitur aut Iesuitae parere necesse est; aut irrita fiant Arresta tua. Atque hoc est maximum deliberationis argumentum. Ex priore illo gaudebunt multi, o Rex, de posteriori multi. De me autem, non arbitror te a Majestate tua oportere, quid sit his aut illis placiturum, quam quid justum sit, quid utile. Non potes de hac re, ita statuere, quin voluptatem ex ea multi dolore. olorem percipiant multi. Semel tamen oportet statui, non semper in incerto fluitare. Et quæ meliores, obsecro, anchoræ eligantur, quàm utilitatis & justitiæ, quæ honestum commestitur.
units.tr: I will begin with the last, because at first sight it seems most plausible; yet in fact and truth it has the least appearance of being so, since it is quite certain that the Jesuits must either be restored everywhere or be compelled everywhere to obey. Such half-measures are shameful, dangerous, and damage your reputation and authority. If it is just and useful to keep them, they ought to remain as citizens and not as exiles; if not, they ought to leave, and their obstinacy should not set an example of rebellion, as it has done for far too long already. The Lacedaemonians sent a short letter on a membrane no wider than half an ounce, and the command had to be carried out at once. It is entirely necessary that Bordeaux and Toulouse obey Your Majesty just as much as Paris or Bellaquaeum by its fountain. You have servants there in good number: whatever you order by the authority of King and Lord will be done, do not doubt it. But if the Jesuits are not useful to you, do not allow them to put down deeper roots in those two provinces. A tree that you can uproot with one hand this year will in the second year be eradicated only with both hands, and in the third year you will need a mattock and an axe. We must regard that neighbourhood to Spain with suspicion: the Spaniards have always been accused of partisanship, and by all their actions they have confirmed it, so that the older the complaint against them, the truer it has been found and the more justified. They have been expelled from the rest of the kingdom, and yet look, they fortify and surround themselves in two provinces bordering Spain, and they came from Spain. What example of humility and obedience is this? If there is any place where those who support them should by no means be separated, it is surely in the border region of the kingdom, far from our Sun, drawing nearer to Madrid. There Spain seems to bear them on her shoulders; there they seem already to wall themselves in against Your Majesty, and to say openly: "You drove us out of Paris and other places, but your arms are too short to push us further away." This is truly most unworthy. What some men want, who call themselves Scabins, formerly their disciples and now steeped in their poison, I do not know, but they fight so fiercely for them. Yet these men ought to understand that they owe you, O King, as much obedience as the humblest inhabitant of Paris. Here arrogance is excessive and rebellion too hardened. Hitherto they have scorned your bereavement, as someone once said of old; now take care that they feel they owe you and your whole posterity perpetual obedience: no one will be so high that he does not tremble. A son never forgets the injuries done to his father. Therefore either the Jesuits must obey, or your Arrêts must be annulled. And this is the greatest matter for deliberation. Many will rejoice at the former, O King, and many at the latter. As for me, I do not think Your Majesty should consider what will please these or those, but what is just and what is useful. You cannot decide this matter in such a way that many will not take pleasure in it and many feel pain. Still, a decision must be made once and not wander forever in uncertainty. And what better anchors, I beg you, could be chosen than usefulness and justice, which together make up what is honourable?

units.la: Quod ad justitiam, manibus Regum eam commisit Deus. Antecessores tui, ô Rex, inde ab omni antiquitate eam fidei Parlamenti illius tui, quod Parium vocabant, permiserunt, & prout abundaverunt negotia, insuper alia Parlamenta ad septenarium usque numerum statuerunt. Sed Parlamenti Parium semper obtinuit hæc prærogativa atque auctoritas (ut æquum fuit ac necessarium) quòd ea decidit quæ spectant Universitatem regni. Hic ordo magnus viris est confertissimus in omni argumentorum genere versatissimis: qui omnium maximè in cognoscendis causis capitalibus atq; judicandis solent excellere. Iam si qui sunt in orbe terrarum, qui summum judicium industriamque ad cognitionem usarum afferant, hi professo sunt: itaq; nunquam quisquam est accusatus insons, qui hos bi judices præ aliis omnibus non postulaverit. Hoc novit Majestas tua.
units.tr: As for justice, God has committed it into the hands of kings. Your predecessors, O King, from the earliest times entrusted it to that Parlement of yours which they called the Parlement of the Peers, and as business grew they established other Parlements, up to the number of seven. But the Parlement of the Peers always held this prerogative and authority (as was fitting and necessary), that it decides the matters which concern the whole kingdom. This body is made up of great men, most practised in every kind of argument, who above all are accustomed to excel in examining capital cases and judging them. Now if there are any in the world who bring the highest judgement and diligence to the knowledge of causes, these are they; and so no innocent man has ever been accused who has not asked for these judges before all others. Your Majesty knows this.

units.la: Non est autem novum quod querimoniæ contra Iesuitas ad Parlamentum hoc delatæ sunt. Nam inde ab anno 1564. decem advocatos unico Actu audiverunt, qui litem eis intenderunt: quorum is, qui orationem communem habuit, vir bonus, & qui tam studiosus fuit Domini sui, quàm qui maximè (rem miram stupendamq; narro) prædixit omnes actiones atque instituta, quæ in istis hominibus postea comperimus.
units.tr: It is not new that complaints against the Jesuits have been brought before this Parlement. For from the year 1564 they heard ten advocates in a single sitting, who brought suit against them; and of these, he who delivered the general speech was a good man, as zealous for his lord as anyone (I relate a strange and wonderful thing), and he foretold all the actions and institutions which we afterwards discovered in those men.

units.la: Quum ea omnia videmus contigisse, quæ ille præviderat: primum casum Academiæ, quam ad paucitatem studiosorum ter mille adegerunt, pro eo quod tricies mille in ea viverent prius, ut principio diximus: deinde, se subducentes paulatim subditos ab eo obsequio, quod suo Principi debent, et ad Polum alterum spectantes: hic omnes demum fremere (nam suitæ jam stabiliverant potentiam suam, & facti erant aliis formidabiles) omnes musitare, & voce submissa dicere, Hoc reste nobis Messinius Advocatus Regius fuerat vatinatus: nec ipsi fidem habere visum est, nec Sorbona; quæ prævnonebat eodem tempore Societatem istam esse ad destruendum, non ad ædificandum natam; importaturam turbas, & temporalibus principibus maximum damnum allaturam. Hæc ipsa verba sunt Decreti illius, quæ ex authentico exemplari eius (si exhiberi jußeris) recognoscet Majestas tua.
units.tr: When we see that all those things have happened which he had foreseen: first the fall of the Academy, which they reduced to a small number of students, three thousand, whereas thirty thousand had lived in it before, as we said at the beginning; then, gradually withdrawing their subjects from that obedience which they owe to their Prince, and looking toward the other pole; at last everyone murmurs (for the Jesuits had by now established their power and become formidable to others), everyone mutters and says in a low voice: "Messinius, the King's advocate, had truly prophesied this to us." Nor did it seem right to believe him, nor the Sorbonne, which at the same time foretold that this Society was born to destroy, not to build up; that it would bring in disturbances and cause the greatest harm to temporal princes. These are the very words of that decree, which Your Majesty will recognise from its authentic copy, if you order it to be produced.

units.la: At ubi ante ora & oculos omnium ordo politicus eversus est, habenæ obsequii resectæ, Magistratus in vincula rapti, etiam excarnificati quidam, furibundus populus ad exemplum leonum liberè vagantium in bonos sæviens; tum Iesuitæ patres plebem, belluâ istam nimantes, & hinc Commoletus, inde Bernardus Oceanum blasphemiarum in Regem suum, Dominum suum evomentes. Contrà verò efferentes Hispaniæ Regem, & Panegyricis rationibus eum celebrantes, quem maximum orbis terrarum Monarcham pingebant, potentiorem Romanis ipsis, et ampliore dominatu, nunquàm se ab illo desertum iri, se illi esse charismos, tantùm bono esse animo & recognoscere vires suas oportere, nunquam sibi auxilium viris, pecunia, comeatu esse defuturum: tum demum bonos omnes, qui radicatum in animo dhuc lilij florem gestabant, pœnituit vehementissimè fidem Cassandris istis minimè habuisse: At ferò sapiebant Phryges.
units.tr: But when the political order was overturned before the eyes of everyone, the reins of obedience were cut, magistrates were dragged off into chains, some were even torn limb from limb, and the frenzied populace, like lions roaming free, raged against good men. Then the Jesuit fathers stirred up the common people, that beast: here Commoletus, there Bernardus, pouring out an ocean of blasphemies against their King, their own Lord. On the other side, they extolled the King of Spain and celebrated him with panegyric arguments, portraying him as the greatest monarch on earth, more powerful than the Romans themselves and with wider dominion. He would never desert them; they were his favourites [χαρίσματα]; they had only to take heart and recognise their own strength; help in men, money and supplies would never be lacking to them. Then at last all the good men who still bore the lily flower fixed in their hearts repented bitterly of having put no faith in those Cassandras. But the Phrygians grew wise too late.

units.la: Quum urbem Parisiorum Majestas tua, ô Rex, in obsequium suum revocasset, omnes pro certo habuerunt, te eodem momento infidos à poculis istis ejectūru, qui bonam pottuli tui parte suo veneno infecerant, & qui tam aperte conjurati hostilia omnia in defunctum Regem & in Te exercuerant: sed prudentissimè visum est Majest. tuæ rem manibus eorum tradere, qui juri dicundo præsunt. Academia, quæ multis de causis ruinam particularem suam Iesuitis ratione maximâ imputabat, ut de causa generali taceam; mense Maio anno 1594. libellum supplicem obtulit Parlamento tuo: Idem fecerunt Curiones & Parochi urbis: causa fuit agitata, sed occlusis foribus; quæ res Iesuitis maximè commodavit. Iam pleraque crimina, quæ objecta fuerunt ipsis, testari potuissent multi, qui foribus uertis circumstetissent; & nova crimina fuissent prolata, dum causa illa compluribus diebus ageretur. Supervenit istus ille, quem Deus avertit à tuis faucibus, teque dentibus tuis bvallavit. Nemo dubitavit, à quibus auctoribus præsertim ubi innotuit, alumnum lesuitarum esse, qui se ex illis ajebat didicisse, Regem adhuc extra Ecclesiam esse, Occidendum esse, ut in pleno Parlamenti consessu testatus est. Extremum illud atque infelix institutum non aliunde poterat exsistere, quàm ab istis saevis ferocibus & propositionibus, quas antea diximus. Haec cogitata non crescunt naturaliter praecipue in animis Gallorum, qui procul absunt ab Africa, & qui monstra prius non viderant, quàm Iesuitae ad nos ingressi essent. Nostrum solum non fert haec venena ex se: necesse est ut ab alio dicantur fata.
units.tr: When Your Majesty, O King, had restored the city of Paris to its obedience, everyone was certain that you would at that very moment cast out of your cups those who had infected a good part of your people with their poison, and who, so openly conspiring, had directed every hostile act against the late King and against you. But it seemed most prudent to Your Majesty to hand the matter over to those who preside over the administration of justice. The University, which for many reasons, not to mention the general cause, rightly blamed the Jesuits for its own particular ruin, in May 1594 presented a petition to your Parlement. The curates and parish priests of the city did the same. The case was argued, but with the doors shut, and this greatly favoured the Jesuits. Many people who had stood around with the doors open could have testified to most of the crimes charged against them, and new crimes would have come to light while the case was pleaded over many days. Then came that man whom God turned away from your throat, and who wounded you with his teeth. No one doubted by whose instigation he had acted, especially once it became known that he was a pupil of the Jesuits, who declared that he had learned from them that the King, still outside the Church, ought to be killed, as he testified in full session of Parliament. That final and unhappy deed could have arisen from nothing but these savage, fierce teachings and propositions which we mentioned before. Such thoughts do not naturally grow in the minds of the French, who are far from Africa and had not seen such monsters before the Jesuits came among us. Our soil does not produce these poisons of itself; it is necessary that the fatal words be spoken by another.

units.la: Quamobrem itur in Collegium ipsorum: invenitur inter alia narratio patris Guignardi, manu ejus tota, quae succum medullamque totius furiosae, cruentae, & horrendae istius doctrinae continebat, omnia convenientia cum iis, quae praevisa fuerant inde ab anno 1564. & quae recens fuerant praenunciata, licet non haberetur fides. Cognitio itaque in- stituitur plene atque solenniter, convocatis duabus Camerls seu Collegijs Parlamenti manum suam Guignardus agnovit: Chastellus omnibus dominis audientibus dicit, hunc Ordinarium Iesuitarum sermonem esse, Regem adhuc extra Ecclesiam esse, licet Catholicum, quia perduret adhuc excommunicatio, eumque tolli oportere e medio. Haec plane consona cum Guignardi scripto: Si non potest componi fine bello, geratur bellum: si bellum geri non potest, occidatur. His omnibus cognitis, quid potui lenius Parlamentum tuum, ô Rex, statuere, quàm ut judicaret secundum libellum supplicem Academiae? Cum Deus ipse quadam specie miraculi judex in hac causa esse voluerit revelans funditus, & tamen sine incommodo, idipsum quod toties dictum, repetitum fuerat contra Societatem istam; & cui ne certa haberetur fides, artes eorum, multita verba et hypocrisis impedimentum semper attulerat, ne cito ab eis expediremur.
units.tr: Therefore they went to the Jesuits' college. Among other things they found a narrative written entirely in the hand of Father Guignard, which contained the juice and marrow of that whole furious, bloody and horrible doctrine, agreeing in every respect with what had been foreseen since 1564 and what had recently been foretold, though it was not believed. An inquiry was therefore set in motion fully and solemnly, with the two Chambers or Colleges of Parliament convened, and Guignard acknowledged his own handwriting. Châtel, with all the judges listening, said that this was the ordinary language of the Jesuits: that the King, though Catholic, is still outside the Church because the excommunication continues, and that he must be removed from the midst. This agrees exactly with Guignard's writing: "If it cannot be settled without war, let war be waged; if war cannot be waged, let him be killed." With all these things known, what could your Parliament, O King, have decided more leniently than to judge in accordance with the Academy's petition? God himself, in a kind of miracle, chose to be the judge in this case, revealing everything to the bottom, and yet without harm to you; the very thing that had so often been said and repeated against this Society. Lest any firm trust be placed in it, their arts, their many words and their hypocrisy had always stood in the way, so that we might not be quickly rid of them.

units.la: Post maximam igitur cognitionem causae, Parlamentu Parisiense tuum Arrestum suum pronunciat, quo jubentur exsulare ex toto regno tuo, omnibusque tuis subditis interdicitur. Ne liberos suos ablegent peregre in collegia ipsorum: quae quidem vere cautio est maxima, & sine cujus observatione vix dimidium fructum ex eo perceptura est Majestas tua. Semper enim daturi sunt operam diligentissime, ut periculosas istas propositiones doceant adolescentes, qui amandabuntur ad se, & obstringent eorum conscientias, ut eaedem alijs inculcent.
units.tr: After the fullest possible examination of the case, your Parisian Parlement pronounced its decree, by which they are ordered to go into exile from your whole kingdom, and all your subjects are forbidden to send their children abroad to their colleges. This is indeed the greatest safeguard, and without its observance Your Majesty will hardly reap half the benefit from it. For they will always take the greatest pains to teach these dangerous propositions to the young whom they summon to themselves, and they will bind the consciences of their pupils so that the same doctrines may be passed on to others.

units.la: Dicitur quidem tibi, Rex Christianissime; non posse id exsequutioni mandari; parentes non posse impediri, quo minus extra hoc Regnum liberos ad Iesuitas ablegent informandos: Sed nihil est in orbe terrarum facilius. Statuatur solum in eos, qui primo contra hoc Arrestum venerint multa coronatorum millenum, cujus dimidium ad delatorem pertineat: ergo toties duplicetur, quoties reus contra Arrestum fecerit: ne unus quidem postea compariturus est. Itane ergo haec res videtur factu difficilis, ut etiam merito impossibilis dicatur esse?
units.tr: It is said to you, most Christian King, that this cannot be carried into effect, and that parents cannot be prevented from sending their children abroad to the Jesuits to be instructed. But nothing in the world is easier. Let a fine of many thousands of crowns be fixed against those who first act against this decree, half of it going to the informer; then let it be doubled each time the offender acts against the decree, and not one will afterwards appear. Does this matter then seem so difficult that it may rightly be called impossible?

units.la: Altero Arresto Guignardus fuit adjudicatus morti: horror blasphemiarum, quibus defunctum Regem dominum suum subditus petiverat, furensque doctrina illius adversan vita tua, non sinebant ei servari vitam sine pergravi tuo periculo.
units.tr: By a second decree Guignard was condemned to death. The horror of the blasphemies with which this subject had assailed his lord the late King, and the raging doctrine by which he opposed your life, did not allow him to be spared without grave danger to you.

units.la: Atque haec Arresta adeo justa & necessaria comperta sunt, ut in alijs omnibus Iuris dicis conventibus sine mora effecta data sint, si a Tholosano & Burdegalensi discesseris.
units.tr: And these decrees were found so just and necessary that, if you exclude Toulouse and Bordeaux, they were carried out without delay in all the other courts.

units.la: De Tholosa, nihil mirum: Nam adhuc erant abalienati ab obsequio Majestatis tuae quo mense demum Aprili anno 1596. reducti sunt. Burdegalae autem degebant multi sumi Catholici, sed Hispanorum & Iesuitarum (qui Hispanorum tibicines sunt atque erimata) hostes infensissimi, qui summis votis expetebant, ut ex Aquitania sua parter ex truderentur, ut ex alijs regni partibus ejecti sunt. Sed Iesuitae illico, ubi de sententia contra se lata cognovissent, factionem magnam & potentem excitarunt, per intimos congresiones suos in duabus Civitatibus Aginni; & Vesunna Petracoriorum, ubi tum adhuc calebant cineres perduellis hujus incendij. Sic intercessiones perscribi curaverunt, adeo miras, adeo horredas, ut nihil possit excogitari hujusmodi: sed non est ignotus Iesuitarum calamus. Nam ut summatim dicam, Parlamenta omnia, quae ipsis exilium imperaverunt, tum & Majest. ad istud edictum pertractaverunt, erant haeretica. Haec ipsa sunt illorum verba
units.tr: As for Toulouse, nothing is surprising: they were still estranged from the obedience of Your Majesty and were only brought back in April 1596. But many honest Catholics lived in Bordeaux, yet there were also the bitterest enemies of the Spanish and the Jesuits (who are the Spaniards' flatterers and their pillars), who most earnestly desired that the Jesuits be expelled from their part of Aquitaine, as they had been expelled from other parts of the kingdom. But the Jesuits, as soon as they learned of the sentence passed against them, stirred up a great and powerful faction through their intimate meetings in the two cities of Agen and Périgueux, where the embers of this incendiary fire still glowed. They took care to have petitions drawn up of such strange and horrible content that nothing of the kind could be imagined; but the pen of the Jesuits is no stranger to us. To put it briefly, all the parlements which had ordered their exile, and also those which dealt with Your Majesty's edict on this matter, were heretical. These are their very words.

units.la: Religio elig. Catholicę, Apostolicę, atq; Rom. inimici Maiest. tuâ imbuerunt faisis iminib. ut eos ipsi regnoq; ipsius exosos, & suspectos redderet. Ite: sine aliafor ia & modo processus, & causæ cognitione minimū in consilium missa, exilio eos ultaverūt. An vero unquâ Parlamentū Galliæ, tantâ iniquitate, medacio, & sycophâa laceratū ab ullo fuit, atq; proculcatū? Sed ne hoc quidé fuit illis satis: procedunt longius, untur minis, affirmantes supplicib. libellis suis, res novas Remp. invasuras, non posse ista utatione sine alteratione & rebus novis exist ere. Si ætate Francisci I. Regis, non libellus pplex hujusmodi (nā quis cogitare fuisset ausus?) sed scriptum ullū ad hos sermones vel ntillum accedens prodijsset, capite suo fuisset luituru, quisquis illud offerre præsumpsisset. Enimvero ista præsumptio, insolentia ista, ista σκώμματα voces, istæ contumeliæ mantes ab illis, discipulisq; ipsorum, qui veneno ipsorum infecti sunt, (est autem hoc, Principes, mandata, Senatumq; ipsorum contemni oportere) gravissimè offenderunt viros tuos, Rex; quibus iderat constitutum, ut eos cogerent in Majest. tua obsequium, nec controversi mandata tua paterentur. Vicit tamen multitudo urbiu, quæ tamen adhuc rebellabat, holofæ subsidio fultæ: facitq; ut consiliū de tolerando malo caperetur. Videbant oes rabiem roremq; inimicorum tuorum, qui gladium adhuc strictum gestabant contra te, perstare diu n posse: omnia ipsos deficere, post itaq; breviter facile effectum iri. Hanc exsecutionem riæ cogitationes, varij casus adhuc retardarunt. Habes narrationem bonâ fide, ò Rex, sine fuco, quomodo res illæ gestæ sunt, expositam: quid judicatum & decretum contra Iesuitas, quid effectum ex parte, quid non.
units.tr: "The religion of the elect, Catholic, Apostolic and Roman, enemies of Your Majesty, imbued with false suspicions so that they might make them hateful and suspect to the King and his realm. Thus, without any formal process or manner of trial, with scarcely any examination of the case, sent to council, they punished them with exile. Was the Parlement of France ever torn and trampled upon by such iniquity, lies and sycophancy? But even this was not enough for them: they go further, they threaten, affirming in their supplicating libels that they will bring new things upon the Commonwealth, that such an agitation cannot occur without upheaval and revolution. If in the time of King Francis I not a supplicating libel of this kind (for who would have dared to think of it?) but any writing approaching these speeches had come out, whoever presumed to offer it would have paid with his head. Indeed that presumption, that insolence, those scoffings [σκώμματα], those insults thrown out by them and their disciples, who are infected with their poison (and the principle is this: princes' commands and their senates must be despised), have gravely offended your magistrates, O King, to whom it had been entrusted to compel them to your obedience and not to suffer those who oppose your commands. Yet the multitude of the cities, which still rebelled, was overcome, supported by the aid of the Holy League; and it came about that a plan was adopted to tolerate the evil. All saw that the rage and foaming of your enemies, who still held the sword drawn against you, could not last long: everything would fail them, and so the thing would soon be easily done. This execution was delayed by various other considerations and chances. You have, O King, in good faith and without disguise, the account of how these things were done: what was judged and decreed against the Jesuits, what has been carried out in part and what has not."

units.la: Iam vero non ignorat Majest. tua, vim Reip. in conservatione & exequutione Arrestorum placitorumq; consistere, quæ summæ Curiæ statuerint. Quoties de tuis lauefactandis itur, sæpè multumq; deliberari necesse est: Opus est gravissimum, cuius multa sunt conseq; ria. Arresta hæc nomen tuum in fronte gerunt, ac infringi non possunt, quin læsa datur Majestas Regum; quorum judicia ab omni retractatione & mutatione convenit esse alienissimā. Adde, quod in illo consessu, ò Rex, è duabus Cameris adunato, ne unus quidem nominari potest, qui summus non sit Catholicus, & omnis adversæ suspicionis expers. Anni jam septimus agitur, quum Iesuitæ vitam scrutantur illorum: an unquam res ullæ vitæ, cuius nomine eæ res criminari possent? Quorsum igitur occentari ista, Oderunt nos, in opinionem sequuntur novam? hoc quidem verum est: sed quis cum illo cætu? quid consessu illo potuerunt? non magis profecto, audeo dicere: quam in consistorio Romanæ magis.
units.tr: Now Your Majesty surely knows that the strength of the Republic consists in the preservation and execution of the decrees that the supreme Court has laid down. Whenever something is proposed that might weaken your decisions, it is necessary to deliberate often and at length. The matter is most grave, and it has many consequences. These decrees bear your name on their face, and they cannot be infringed without injury to the majesty of kings, whose judgments ought to be wholly free from any retraction or alteration. Add to this that in that assembly, O King, made up of two Chambers, not even one man can be named who is not a most upright Catholic and free from every hostile suspicion. Now it is the seventh year since the Jesuits have been under scrutiny, and was there ever any act of their lives for which they could be accused? Why, then, do they make this clamour, "They hate us," and follow a new opinion? This, indeed, is true; but who sat in that gathering, and what could they do in that assembly? I dare say, certainly no more than in the consistory at Rome.

units.la: Feruntamen insistant, & ajunt Parlamento se fuisse odio. Quamobrem quæso? Anideo ad Turonibus non fuerint? Hæc vero cur illi dicerent, cum maxima pars confessus Cu- e pedem Lutetiâ non movit? An ergo quod Iesuitæ summi sunt Catholici? multo mi- s: Nam domini illi, qui sunt in consessu Curiæ, magis Catholici sunt quam illi, & sine lahæresos. Qua igitur causa male in vos fuissent animo? nihil sane adductur esset, quod l minimam speciem habere posset, nisi forte dixeritis: Oderant nos, quia fueramus causa tot malorum, quæ obtigerant Galliæ. At ego vobis respondeo, nullo jure hac tionem odii in censum venire posse. Si Catilina fuisset comprehensus, an ergo Romæ dices non fuisset inuenturus? Certè: & tamen omnes Magistratus optimique cives odii facem illam patriæ oderant. Novum igitur Parlamentum Parium instituendum et damnandis seditiosis, & ijs, qui factiones exteras adjuvant. Atque hic tibi, ò Rex, unam breviter suggero, quam agnoscent Iesuitas, aut si tui omnes subditi amavissent ut Iesuitæ isti, non jam tot elegantes libelli supplices ad te afferrentur, nunquam Lupami illam Regiam ingressus esses. Anisti hoc negaturi sunt? si negent, annon tua tamen Lajestas mecum sentiet?
units.tr: Yet they persist and say that they were hated by the Parlement. Why, I ask? Was it because they were not at Tours? But why would they say this, when the greater part of the Court's assembly did not stir a foot from Paris? Was it then because the Jesuits are the most upright Catholics? Far more so are those gentlemen who sit in the Court's assembly, and they are free from every taint of heresy. What reason, then, could there have been for them to have ill will against you? Surely nothing would be brought forward that could have even the faintest appearance of truth, unless perhaps you say: "They hated us, because we had been the cause of so many evils that befell France." But I answer you that no right reasoning can bring such hatred into account. If Catiline had been arrested, would you say he would not have been found at Rome? Certainly; and yet all the magistrates and the best citizens hated that torch of their country. A new Parlement of Peers must therefore be established for the condemnation of seditious men and of those who aid foreign factions. And here, O King, I briefly offer you one point which the Jesuits will recognise; for if all your subjects had loved you as these Jesuits did, not so many elegant supplicating pamphlets would now be brought to you, and you would never have entered that royal Louvre. Will they deny this? If they deny it, will not Your Majesty nevertheless agree with me?

units.la: Postremò aut, ubi non habent, quod lustitiam Arresti huius labefactet, eò prorumpunt, dicat: Sinos Castellus accusavit, si rei sumus, cur nō afficiebamur supplicio ultimo? Hic ò respondeo: metiri homines istos alienum animum ex suo. Cum enim uento eorum consilio præfuerint, qui innumera capita tradiderunt morti, ut tyrannidem suam horrore confirmarent, iudicant homines isti se acerbiorem poenam fuisse meritos. Cur ergo non sunt adiudicati morti? quia non Chasteliani, non Iesuitae fuerunt ipsorum Iudices, qui in Terceris Insulis cervices praescindi viginti octo proceribus, & nobilibus quinquaginta duobus Gal-lis uno die in tabulato eodem curaverunt, & quingentos Franciscanos aliosque religiosos suspendi, qui Conciones secundum Lusitaniae Regem habuerunt. Saevitiā istam odimus Galli: in clementiam semper inclinamus, modo ne in humana sit. Tot homines si morti fuissent traditi, crudele fuisset factum: sin e diverso ferrentur ii, qui tot barbaricis maleficiis causam attulerunt, nec rebus aliis incubant, haec altera fuisset gravissima crudelitas. Quid igitur facto fuit opus ut damnarentur exilio. Admodum scitum est illud apud Tacitum: Si, Patres conscripti, unum id spectamus, quae immania sunt istorum hominum scelera, non laqueus ipsos suffecerit; sed viam novi, qua nos clementiae simul ac severitatis non paeniteat: jubeamus eos exire regno.
units.tr: Finally, when they have nothing with which to shake the justice of this decree, they break out and say: "If we were guilty, why were we not punished with the ultimate penalty, as Châtel was?" Here, O, I answer: these men measure others by their own mind. For since they were the authors of the counsel of those who delivered countless heads to death so as to confirm their tyranny by terror, these men judge that they deserved a harsher punishment. Why, then, were they not sentenced to death? Because the judges of these men were not Châtel and not the Jesuits, who in the Terceira Islands had twenty-eight nobles beheaded and fifty-two French gentlemen executed on one scaffold in a single day, and who had five hundred Franciscans and other religious men hanged, men who had preached according to the will of the King of Portugal. We French hate such cruelty; we always lean towards clemency, provided it is not inhuman. If so many men had been handed over to death, the deed would have been cruel; but if, on the other hand, those who had caused so many barbaric crimes were carried off, and did not persist in other matters, this would have been the other, most grievous cruelty. What, then, had to be done, but that they be condemned to exile? That saying of Tacitus is most apt: If, Conscript Fathers, we looked only to how monstrous the crimes of these men are, a noose would suffice for them; but let us find a new way by which we need not regret either clemency or severity: let us order them to leave the kingdom.

units.la: Et ipsi quoque Iesuitae ut se telis destitutos vident, quae in hoc Arrestum adeo utile et necessarium Galliae iaculentur, dicere non dubitant, (vide quousque rabie & furore suo traducantur) non esse amplius Parlamentum Parisiense Parisiis. Ubi ergo quaeso, nunc est maximum illud Parisiense Parlamentum, quod in pretio est & admiratione omnibus Gallis, omnibus exteris? An forte est Madriti? Eon vultis provocare a Rege & Parlamento ipsius? Placetne ut ibidem cum Paeane triumphali magnum illud Arrestum fiat irritum, prout ibidem fieri curavistis decreto Sorbonae, quod anno 1564. fuerat editum? Vide per DEVM immortalem, oro, vide, o Rex, hominum impudentiam, fastum, superbiam, qui audent in Gallia dicere, Parlamentum Parium Galliae non esse amplius in Gallia, non amplius Parisiense Parlamentum esse Parisiis. Sed cur ab iis parci supremae Curiae petimus, cum reges bipennibus cultris occidi curent, & suborneant emissarios?
units.tr: And the Jesuits themselves, when they see that they are deprived of the weapons with which they might hurl against this decree, which is so useful and necessary for France, do not hesitate to say (see how far they are carried away by their rage and fury) that the Parlement of Paris is no longer at Paris. Where, then, I ask, is now that greatest Parlement of Paris, which is held in high esteem and admiration by all the French, and by all foreigners? Is it perhaps at Madrid? Do you wish to appeal from it to the King and Parlement of Spain? Do you want that great decree to be annulled there, with a triumphal paean, just as you took care to have it done there with the decree of the Sorbonne, which had been issued in 1564? Look, I beg you, by the immortal God, look, O King, at the impudence, the pride and the arrogance of these men, who dare to say in France that the Parlement of Peers is no longer in France, that the Parlement of Paris is no longer at Paris. But why do we spare these men of the supreme Court, when they arrange for kings to be killed with axes and knives, and suborn emissaries?

units.la: Iustum igitur est, o Rex, iustissimum procurari, ut mandetur exsequutioni Arrestum Parlamenti tui: Iustitia ipsa est. Non aberrat, qui hoc iter insisti-ter ab omnibus tuis maioribus tritum, qui magis studuerunt, laboraverunt, ut iudicatum fieret Parlamenti sui quam aliud quidpiam. Nam abs hoc suisset, quomodo confirmari potuissent fore, ut liberi fui, quos nonnunquam in cunis, etiam in matrum utero relinquebant, tot magnis post se populis imperarent sine his viribus Iustitiae suae, fulcimento sceptri sui, columnis coronae suae & stabilimento successionis suae.
units.tr: It is therefore just, O King, most just, that the decree of your Parlement be carried into execution; it is justice itself. He does not go astray who keeps to this path, trodden by all your ancestors, who took more pains and laboured more that the judgment of their Parlement should be carried out than anything else. For without this, how could it have been secured that your children, whom they sometimes left in their cradles, or even in their mothers' wombs, would rule so many great peoples after them, without the strength of this justice, the support of their sceptre, the pillars of their crown and the foundation of their succession?

units.la: Quicunque autor est tibi, o Rex, ut commoveas Arresta de gravissima causa Regis in Parlamento tuo pronunciata, nunquam istius plagae gravitatem, consequentiam, adjunctaque omnia expendit satis. Nihil deinceps tibi in orbe certum futurum esset, si quando imminueres, si infirmares, si denique labefactares amplitudinem tuam amplissimam, maximumque tuum propugnaculum contra omnes rebelliones subditorum eorum, & contra omnium extraneorum instituta.
units.tr: Whoever advises you, O King, to shake the decrees pronounced in your Parlement on this most serious matter of the King, has not weighed sufficiently the gravity of this wound, its consequences, and all the circumstances attending it. Nothing would thenceforth be certain for you in the world, if at any time you were to diminish, weaken, or finally undermine your very ample dignity and your greatest bulwark against all rebellions of your subjects, and against the designs of all foreigners.

units.la: Atqui haec de jure: ad utilitatem veniamus. Quis tam hebes est, o Rex, qui non videat hoc ipsum Arrestum in magna felicitatis parte ponendum esse, quam Deus in te contulit. Si parricidam unum spatio novem mensium in plantario suo, in suo illo seminario nati sunt, quam multos septennio adepti essent? Plurimum refert utrum conficias centum pasus, an octingenta passuum millia. Dum otium datur cogitandi, dum indormiscendi, aversa saepe subit cogitatio: unico solum bono momento operis est, & horae insunt diei viginti quatuor, quod vulgo dici solet. Sed cum eodem aestu, eadem rabie, eodem furoris impetu qui ex illo infernali cubiculo Meditationum prodit, horae momento potest latera sua tegere hic alea gravis est, o Rex, hic periculum evidentissimum. Non est in diversoriis com-municandum, non adferuntur Lugduno monita (nosti quid dicam) non lingua differens, nec vestes varia. Nulla ex parte monita; nam signa imagines que adferri possunt: simul con-
units.tr: But these things concern right; let us come to utility. Who is so dull, O King, as not to see that this very decree must be counted among the great blessings of happiness which God has bestowed upon you? If they had brought forth a single parricide in their nursery, in their own seminary, over a space of nine months, how many would they have reared in seven years? It makes a great difference whether you traverse a hundred paces or eight hundred thousand. While there is time for thinking, while there is time for dozing, a distracted thought often comes; but it is worth acting in a single good moment, and the hours of the day are twenty-four, as is commonly said. But with the same heat, the same rage, the same onset of fury that comes forth from that infernal chamber of meditations, in the moment of an hour a man can cover his flanks; here, O King, the risk is grave, here the danger is most evident. It is not to be communicated in inns, nor are warnings brought from Lyon (you know what I mean), nor a different tongue, nor varied dress. No warnings on any side; for signs and images that can be brought forward are at once in agreement.

units.la: {a} Anno itatum, simul factum. An dubitat quispiam, quò nobis propior, eò formidabiliorem esse silentiam?
units.tr: No sooner said than done. Does anyone doubt that silence becomes more formidable the nearer it comes to us?

units.la: Ad alia descendamus: videamus ex actionibus ipsorum, quanam spes nobis ab ipsis hominib. in posterum ostendatur. Quanquam æquum est ante omnia, ô Rex, concedi illis postulatum suum: nempe, ne persequaris vindictam cansarum Navarreni Regis, Aureliaensis Ducis. Iustissima postulatio. Quicquid Iesuitæ mandato defuncti Regis commiserunt contra Majestatem tuam, non debet ipsis obesse; Amplius affirmabo, ipsis prodesse debet. Domino suo servierunt, tum eis non fuisti Dominus. Sed neque de ea re unquam tantum verbum fuit cum illis communicatum. Monstra mea fingunt, quæ oppugnent, quod solemne: hoc nunquam eis objectum est, nec speciem ullam in Parlamento tuo habuisset. Illa irrationem venerunt, diversa omnia: Nam inter res alias innumeras observatum fuit, quo fe modo erga regem defunctum gesserint. Huic se bene fideliterque, dum opus est, servierunt in adversis rebus, etiamsi contra germanum ipsius filium (si quem habuisset) homines ipsi ministrassent, mererentur laudem.
