Rex vero defunctus non fuit Rex Navarræ, non Dux aliquis Aurelianensis: Rex fuit Galliæ. Non adjiciam illud gratius, Regem fuisse erga ipsos beneficum, favisse ipsis per omnia; ignoravisse scelesta omnia cinora, quæ machinabantur in ipsum, nam quum dixi Regem fuisse Galliæ, dixi omnia. Erat Dominus illorum, illi natalibus subditi illius: huic serviendum fuit, quacunque esset (an vero unquam exstitit melior?) fecerúntne isti? utrum fideliter servierunt, an prodiderunt ipsum nequissime? Hic Rhodus, hic saltus, hic palæstra. Non cet hic excurrere, non campos patentes quærere, non plausibiles communes locos, ut oftentint eloquentiam suam: ad hunc nodum, ad caput istud redeundum. Audite Domini Iesuitæ; non loquor de Aureliaensi Duce, non de Navarreno Rege; mihi vobiscum de Rege vestro sermo est. An huic domino, bono huic Domino, inquam, bono regi, qui vos intifecerat, servi vi'stis? qui tam fuerat gratiosus vobis, tam ad assentationem blandus? Ultra rogo, non sunt responsuri, cavebunt diligentissime. Quid huc prolaturi sunt, quò dementiatur Majest. tua? Alium testem eorum non desidero, quæ Rex defunctus de ipsis pronunciabat. Nunquam Princeps ullus tot effudit querimonias, et justas querimonias subditorum suorum proditionibus. Ac propterea Rex ille mitis, benignus, facilis, cilior æquo præ aliis omnibus subditis, curavit istos Burdegala exturbari, quo certissimo argumento docemur, istos summopere et quasi ad infinitum læsisse Regem suum atque lendisse. Et quis hæc in dubium vocare possit? an ergo usque adeò hic peregrinamur, nondum teneamus eum scripta legisse, et certò comperisse, hos veros Ligæ et conirationis auctores esse? qui omnes æquo magnos ac parvos eloquentia sua fascinaverunt, qui iam conspirationem confirmaverint agitaverintque adversus Rempublicam, ut velis remisque contenderint, ut Romæ Majestas regia excommunicatione feriretur, procuraverint ut istud tonitru Galliam percelleret, postquam hanc scelestam fidem subtus infudissent, Regem excommunicari potuisse, non amplius esse Regem, sed tyrannum, et ipsos a jure jurando fidei absolutos esse? Et quis nostrum adeò malitiosus, ut dlit istud cernere, si Iacobus Clemens non fuisset veneno isto Iesuitice doctrinæ imbutus, cogitaturum quidem fuisse unquam de hero suo, domino suo, suoque Rege trucidando? Nonne abominanda ista perfuasio firmè infixa et in animo ipsius radicata fecit, ut cultum in ventrem unctí domini impelleret? nonne hæc brachium firmavit, itemque irari jussit; credenti se hoc facto Heroico (sic nominabat Guignardus) a-olatum in Paradisum esse? Verum committit eadem, lapisne vel telum, an is qui imiferit? Quis, inquam, adeò malitiosus, aut rerum nostrarum imperitus est, ut sciat, quàm Iesuitæ primum in hoc regno posuerunt pedem, omnes Gallorum amos tam procul abfuisse ab istis hæresibus (nam alio nomine qui vocentur, potestne la existere periculosior?) ut inter decies centena hominum millia non fuisset unis inventus, qui tantum scelus vel cogitatione voluisset attingere? contra vero ajores nostri pertuderunt montes ipsos, Italiamque transmiserunt, ut abirent enim comprehensuri, qui Regem floris Liliacei excommunicare tentaverat, hominemque audacem ad honorariam multam & poenitentiam publicam impulerunt, qui scintillam aliquam incendij immiserat. Ante denique quàm isti homines advenissent, nihil tam ab istis sceleratissimis propositionibus, quàm Gallorum animus abhorruit.
units.tr: Let us turn to other matters: let us see from their actions what hope they hold out to us for the future. Yet it is only fair, O King, that before all else their plea be granted: namely, that you not pursue vengeance for the causes of the King of Navarre and the Duke of Orléans. It is a most just plea. Whatever the Jesuits committed against your Majesty at the command of the late King ought not to harm them; I will go further and say it ought to benefit them. They served their lord, and you were not their lord then. Yet this matter was never even raised with them. They invent monsters to attack, as is customary: this charge was never brought against them, nor would it have had any semblance in your Parliament. Those accusations come from irrelevance and are wholly beside the point. Among countless other matters, it has been observed how they conducted themselves toward the late king. If they had served him well and faithfully while there was need, in adverse circumstances, and even if they had served against his own brother (had he had one), they would deserve praise. But the late king was not King of Navarre, nor some Duke of Orléans: he was King of France. I will not add the more welcome point that the king was kind to them and favoured them in every way, that he was ignorant of all the wicked plots being devised against him; for when I say he was King of France, I have said everything. He was their lord, and they were his subjects by birth. To him they owed service, whoever he was (and was there ever a better one?). Did they do so? Did they serve him faithfully, or did they betray him most wickedly? Here is Rhodes, here is the leap, here is the arena. I need not run off elsewhere, nor seek open fields or plausible commonplaces to display their eloquence: we must return to this knot, this main point. Hear me, Jesuit gentlemen. I am not speaking of the Duke of Orléans or the King of Navarre; my discourse is with you, concerning your own King. Did you serve this lord, this good lord, I say, this good king, who had made you what you are, who was so gracious to you, so lavish in flattery? I ask further, and they will not answer; they will take the greatest care. What will they bring forward here, where your Majesty is being driven out of its mind? I need no other witness to what the late king said of them. No prince ever poured out more complaints, and just complaints, at the treacheries of his subjects. And so that gentle, kindly, easy-going king, more indulgent than was right toward all his other subjects, saw to it that these men were driven out of Bordeaux. By this most certain argument we are taught that they had greatly and almost infinitely wronged and offended their king. And who could call this in doubt? Are we then so foreign here that we have not yet read his writings and found out for certain that these men are the true authors of the League and the conspiracy? They who with their eloquence have bewitched all alike, great and small; who had already stirred up and promoted conspiracy against the commonwealth, striving with all sails and oars so that the royal majesty might be struck by excommunication at Rome; who arranged that this thunderbolt should fall upon France, after they had secretly poured in this wicked doctrine that the king could be excommunicated, no longer be king but a tyrant, and that they themselves were absolved from their oath of allegiance. And which of us is so malicious as to deny that, if James Clement had not been steeped in this poison of Jesuit doctrine, he would never have thought of slaying his master, his lord and his king? Did this abominable persuasion, firmly fixed and rooted in his mind, not drive the knife into the belly of the anointed lord? Did it not strengthen his arm and bid him strike, believing that by this heroic deed (so Guignard named it) he would be carried off into Paradise? But does the guilt belong to the stone or the weapon, or to the one who threw it? Who, I say, is so malicious, or so ignorant of our affairs, as not to know that when the Jesuits first set foot in this kingdom, the minds of all the French were so far removed from these heresies (for what else should they be called, or what could be more dangerous?) that among a thousand times a hundred thousand men not one was found who would have wished even to think of so great a crime? On the contrary, our ancestors broke through the mountains themselves and crossed into Italy to seize the man who had tried to excommunicate the King of the Lilies, and they drove that bold man into an honourable fine and public penance, he who had cast some spark of fire. Finally, before these men arrived, nothing was so abhorrent to the French spirit as these most wicked propositions.

units.la: Dicitur Iacobi Clementis Apologiam Boucherus probavisse. Res facile facilis. Novit Boucherus nunquam se Lutetiam reversurum esse; lata in Guignardum sententia est, illius gubernatio; Spondent sibi quotidie Iesuitae, se eò regressuros esse: facit amici officium, cum probat Apologiam: certior illis amicus nunquam fuit, neque conjunctior. Neque verò studuit Theologiae, quàm illius praeceptoribus. Haec tota facit Academia. Sed nisi reficiamus istas: folia aperiamus illi infausto libro, infausta Apologia, spectemus fundamenta principiaque illius. An alia sunt fundamenta eius, quàm posse excommunicari Regem eiusque subditos à jurejurando fidei praestito liberari? Quid dicunt aliud, quid proclamant Iesuitae libris suis omnibus, quos ante contulimus? Pergamus longius. Quid aliud ista concludit Apologia, quà Ahodem quaeri, inveniri Ahodem oportere? Unde hoc didicit, nisi ex Commoleto & Guignardo, qui scripsit: Si non potest deponi sine bello, geratur bellum; si bellum geri non poterit, occidatur? Et ante: Factum heroicum à Iacobo Clemente patratum, & donum Spiritus Sancti vocatum hoc nomine à nostris Theologis, iuste laudandum est. Observemus istas voces, nostris Theologis. Quinam sunt isti Theologi? Sanctissime Augustinus & Bernardus & alij illi boni & docti Patres? nequaquam: contrarium plane ostendimus: hi sunt isti reverendi Patres Iesuitae, ab illis quàm diversissimi. Apostoli sunt, sunt de Societate Iesu; at illi quos modo nominabam, nihil quàm servi illius erant abjectissimi, indigni qui corrigiam solverent calceamentorum eius. Tandem vero Pater ille Guignardus, qui thesES istas calamo ferreo imbuto Regum nostrorum sanguine perscripserat, defletur ab illis p.266. Defensionis ipsorum, tanquam si jācturam fuissent passi gravissimam. Quid magis canina rabie, magis furiosum in ista latronum parricidarum, Apologia?
units.tr: It is said that Boucher approved James Clement's Apology. The matter is easily explained. Boucher knows he will never return to Paris; sentence has been passed against Guignard, and his conduct is under scrutiny. The Jesuits daily promise him that they will return there, so he does a friend's service by approving the Apology: he has never had a more trustworthy or closer friend. Nor has he devoted himself to theology more than to its teachers. This whole thing is the work of the Academy. But unless we unfold these leaves, let us open that ill-omened book and that ill-omened Apology, and look at its foundations and principles. Are its foundations anything other than that the king can be excommunicated and his subjects freed from the oath of fidelity they have sworn? What else do the Jesuits say, what else do they proclaim in all their books, which we have already compared? Let us go further. What else does this Apology conclude, namely that Ahod must be sought and Ahod must be found? Where did he learn this, if not from Commolet and Guignard, who wrote: "If he cannot be deposed without war, let war be waged; if war cannot be waged, let him be killed"? And earlier: "The heroic deed performed by James Clement, and called by our Theologians by this name, a gift of the Holy Spirit, is rightly to be praised." Let us note those words, "our Theologians." Who are these Theologians? Are they the most holy Augustine and Bernard and those other good and learned Fathers? By no means: we have plainly shown the contrary. These are those reverend Jesuit Fathers, most unlike those men. They are apostles, they are of the Society of Jesus; but those whom I have just named were nothing but the most abject servants of Christ, unworthy to loose the thong of his sandals. And finally, that Father Guignard, who had written out these theses with an iron pen, steeped in the blood of our kings, is bewailed by them in the defence of the Apology, p. 266, as if they had suffered the greatest loss. What is more furious, with a dog's rage, than this Apology of thieves and parricides?

units.la: Hic autem subit animum quaerere, si non probarent Iesuitae istam Apologiam, eâdem Duaci palam vendi, ut fit, permitterent? paterentúrne ibi hanc narrationem postulare? Etsi non sum auctor cuiquam, ut occidat Regem Hispaniae. Mori malim, quàm auctor esse. Contrà enim affero, quisquis intentat in vitam ullius Regis, eum procul dubio damnatum esse: Nam sic intentatur in DEVM, à quo institutus est.
units.tr: But here the question comes to mind: if the Jesuits did not approve of that Apology, would they permit it to be openly sold at Douai, as it is, and would they allow the demand for it to be made there? I am not the author of any plan to kill the King of Spain. I would rather die than be its author. For I maintain that whoever plots against the life of any king is undoubtedly damned, since such a plot is directed against God, by whom the king was set up.

units.la: Sane Iesuitae non possunt impedimento esse, quin illa Apologia Duaci vendatur palam & circumferatur in diversoria, ut venditantur Gallis. Miseri scilicet Religiosi illi nihil auctoritatis obtinent in ijs oppidis, quae domui Austriacae parent, nullo pretio sunt. Mirum est quod dicam, sed tamen verissimum. Noverunt omnes quàm sit homini Gallo difficile ut ingrediatur in artem Mediolani: Sabaudi speciem oportet induat, & maximo periculo si compertus fuerit, compareant Iesuitae omnes, qui adhuc in Aquitania & linguâ Occitana supersunt, eò ingressuri; & unus Pater Iesuita, Mediolani agens, ditat se eos pro Iesuitis agnoscere; sine morâ sternetur pons, magnae aperientur portae. Adeò baphium Iesuiticum omnes colores exsuperat. Enimvero qui nam sunt homines in orbe terrarum, qui melius sint de Castelanis meriti, quàm qui Societatis istius? quid ad exaltationem & amplificationem imperij illorum tantum operâ contulit? Nam huic Lusitaniam debent, ut narrat ipsorum historia. Sed unde, obsecro, tantum Iesuitarum in Hispanum studium? duae animadverto causas. Prior est ab ortu ipsorum Hispanico, quo tanquam de manu in manum accepto, in hoc ardente spiritu, aluntur, augescunt, educantur. Posterior est, quod propositionem hanc ipsi persuadent sibi, non posse Ottomanicum imperium everti nisi ab eo, qui Monarcha sit totius orbis Christiani: & postquam huc illuc oculos in omnes partes circumduxerunt, nihil à se videri putant adeo potens, adeo opulentum, adeo magnis ditionibus imperans, quàm domum Austriacam, quae tenet imperium, partem Germaniarum & Belgij, amplius dimidium Italiae, Hispanias omnes, & ab ortu & occasu Indias: ut tacea illi persuasum esse, solu Hispania Regem sufficere, qui totam Christianitatem efficiat Catholicam.
units.tr: Certainly the Jesuits cannot prevent that Apology from being openly sold at Douai and carried about in the inns, as it is sold to the French. Those wretched religious men, it seems, have no authority in those towns which obey the House of Austria; they count for nothing there. What I am about to say is strange, yet most true. Everyone knows how hard it is for a Frenchman to enter the citadel of Milan: he must put on the appearance of a Savoyard, and at the greatest risk if he is discovered. Yet if all the Jesuits who still remain in Aquitaine and in the Occitan tongue were to go there, and if a single Jesuit Father acting in Milan were to declare that they were to be recognised as Jesuits, the bridge would be laid down without delay and the great gates thrown open. So far does the Jesuit cloak surpass all colours. Indeed, what men in the world have deserved better of the Castilians than those of that Society? What have they contributed to the exaltation and enlargement of that empire with such effort? For to them, as their own history tells, Portugal is owed. But whence, I beg you, comes such great zeal of the Jesuits for the Spanish cause? I notice two causes. The first is their Spanish origin, which, handed on from hand to hand, is nourished, grows and is brought up in this burning spirit. The second is that they persuade themselves of this proposition: the Ottoman empire cannot be overthrown except by him who is the monarch of the whole Christian world. And after they have turned their eyes in every direction, they think nothing is seen to be so powerful, so wealthy, ruling over such great dominions, as the House of Austria, which holds the empire, part of Germany and the Low Countries, more than half of Italy, all the Spains, and the Indies from east to west. So they have evidently persuaded themselves that the King of Spain alone is enough to make all Christendom Catholic.

units.la: Nemo autem est in orbe terrarum, qui melius noverit quàm Majestas tua, quousque ràntur consilia domus Austriacae, & quàm parum id sibi spondeat, quòd Iesuitae exoptant res fratres aut affines te circumstant; à Bajona Caletum usque Geryon est: sed modo rsilium arcanum ipsorum, & quicunque suis muficitationibus conciliant eis gratiam apud os subditos, ex regno tuo exeant, non est quòd labores: Geryon fuit Rex Hispaniae, sed allum Herculem nactus est. Scit Majestas tua fabulam illam equi Trojani, non alia causa fuisse inventam, quàm ut doceamur, quinquaginta hostes ignotos unà nocte in Republica effecturos ea, quae aperti hostes quinquagies mille non possint toto decennio: Indivit etiam aliquos fere existere, qui istos latentes inimicos retegant, sed eis fidem multos bere nolle. Haec profectò nobis adhuc contigerunt: nihil enim de Iesuitis ac consiliis rum dictum est, quod non evenerit: nihil de Iesuitis dictum, quod nisi post illum obtinuit fidem.
units.tr: No one in the world knows better than Your Majesty how far the designs of the House of Austria reach, and how little that house can promise itself from them. The Jesuits long for these things; your kinsmen and allies surround you. From Bayonne to Calais is Geryon's land, but if their secret plots, and whoever wins the favour of your subjects by their flattery, leave your kingdom, there is no need to worry. Geryon was king of Spain, but he met another Hercules. Your Majesty knows the fable of the Trojan horse. It was invented for no other reason than to teach us that fifty unknown enemies could accomplish in one night in a commonwealth what open enemies with fifty thousand men could not accomplish in ten years. Some of these hidden enemies, I suppose, are being exposed, but many are unwilling to believe them. These things have indeed happened to us already. Nothing has been said of the Jesuits and their plans that has not come to pass, and nothing has been said of them that has not gained credit afterwards.

units.la: Ut autem in gratiam redeant, duo exponunt nobis, se magno numero esse, & se ofia magna Principibus quibusdam praestitisse. Primum illud, multitudinem adduci, non deo cuiusbono, nisi forte, ut nobis incutiant metum. Equidem valdè ab eis metuo, dum regno iunt: foris vero non sunt venturi ad Bajonam obsidendam, modò ne Burdegalà à quibus separemur. Persuadere studeant fortasse nobis, suam illam magnam propagationem benedictionis Dei argumentum esse. Haec conclusio & periculosissima est & pestifera: non enim post multos adhuc annos Arsacidas vel parricidas confortes suos numero aturi sunt: ut de Arrianis, Albigensibus, Iudaeis & Mahumetanis taceam. Hoc argumentum Lutheranì frequentarunt, Iesuitae frequentaverunt: nunc vero abuti eo in suam volunt; non bene conveniunt ista.
units.tr: To win back our favour, they set out two points: that they are great in number, and that they have done great services for certain princes. As to the first, the multitude is brought forward for no good purpose, unless perhaps to frighten us. Indeed I am very much afraid of them while they remain in the kingdom; but outside it they will not come to besiege Bayonne, provided they do not come to separate us from Bordeaux. They may perhaps want to persuade us that their great spread is a sign of God's blessing. This conclusion is both most dangerous and pestilent. For after many more years they will not count among their fellows Arsacids or parricides, not to mention Arians, Albigensians, Jews and Mahometans. The Lutherans used this argument, and the Jesuits have used it too. Now they wish to turn it to their own advantage, but these things do not fit well together.

units.la: Quod de suis officijs praedicant, quae Principibus nonnullis praestiterunt, nunquam vitavimus, quia homines sunt capaces, atque ad illa idonei. Sed in mundo quid periculosius ingenio studente malefacere? Quorsum tot jactationes illius ingenij & sufficientiae suae, nemo dixit eos stolidos & barbaros esse. Officia quidem illa, opinor, praestiti sunt: sed ijs qui virgulâ divinâ quadam nec Papam inimicum unquam habuerint, causam cum domo Austriaca ullam disceptandam: quisquis vel de obolo cum illa litiget, si fidat istis hominibus, deiciatur tandem aliquando, sive cito sive tarde: hoc illi permissum esto.
units.tr: As to what they boast of, the services they rendered to certain princes, we have never denied it, since they are men who are capable and fit for such things. But what in the world is more dangerous than a clever mind bent on doing harm? Why so much boasting of that cleverness and their own competence? No one has called them dull or barbarous. I suppose they did render those services, but to men who, by some divine twist, never had the Pope as an enemy, and had no cause to dispute with the house of Austria. Whoever goes to law with that house, even over a penny, if he trusts such men, will at some time be cast down, sooner or later. Let them have that permission.

units.la: Si placebit Majestati tuae curare, ut praelegantur orationes, quas nobiles Poloni quin in Comitijs habuerunt; videbit seditionum civilium & bellorum Iliadem, quae inter Christianos vastarum regionum illarum, quae à Septentrione ad Ortum pertinent, Iesuitae soli exaruerunt: qui plurium illic praeliorum fuerunt auctores, quae per quingentos integros annos fuerunt olim commissa. Non est huius rei ignara Majest. tua, si volet meminisse. Quanquam habemus opus ullis exteris historijs; qui alijs suppeditamus ipsi exemplorum satis est. Oerelae nostrae, & justae metus causae minus haberent veritatis.
units.tr: If it pleases Your Majesty to have read aloud the speeches which the Polish nobles delivered in their Diets, you will see an Iliad of civil sedition and wars. The Jesuits alone have kindled these among Christians in those vast regions that stretch from the north to the east. They were the authors of many battles, which were fought there over five hundred full years. Your Majesty is not ignorant of this, if you care to remember. Yet we need no foreign histories; we ourselves supply enough examples. Our complaints and our just cause for fear would have less truth if we did not.

units.la: Sed annon eas potius duplicaturi sumus, si attenderimus regulas, & bullas ipsorum cave, ut jurèt se obsequuturos suo generali per omnia & in omnibus, ut Christo praesenti? Responsum est, si Deus ipse aliquid nobis mandaret suo ipsius ore, nonne faciendum esset? licet cum Abrahamo de occidendo filio Isaaco ageretur? Quis ergo non videat, si quis miser educatus in disciplina propositionum istarum de excommunicatione Regum, includatur in illo Meditationum conventi, & alter Varades mandatum à Generali adferat; quum Princeps, cuius agitur caedes, satur in proximo: quis, inquam, non videat miserum illum, qui credit se damnatum fore animam suam perditurum, nisi obsequatur Generali suo, rem in momento aggressurum esse?
units.tr: But shall we not rather double these fears, if we consider their rules and bulls, in which they swear to obey their General in all things and in every matter, as if Christ were present? It has been answered: if God himself commanded us something with his own mouth, would it not have to be done? Even when Abraham was ordered to kill his son Isaac? Who then does not see that if some wretch, brought up in the discipline of these propositions about the excommunication of kings, is shut up in that gathering of meditation, and another Varades brings him a mandate from the General, while the prince whose murder is at stake is nearby, the wretch, who believes he will lose his soul unless he obeys his General, will undertake the deed in an instant? Who, I say, does not see this?

units.la: Esto autem; decem, viginti, triginta renuant: unus tamen inveniatur necesse est, qui nos rymis & aerumnis cumulet. Equidem non possum, o Rex, cum animo meo comminisci, modo ij qui importunius causam hanc agere apud tuam Majest. volent, eò delabatur, ut non ponant id ante oculos, quod jam viderunt; nec reputent se suosque posteros in tota illa probro aeterno fore, si infortunium alterum accideret. Eos itaque rogatos volo, tent diligenter ac recordentur, nihil facilius abscondi quàm scelaratum consilium, nec posse quenquam penetrare in animum atq; cogitata hominum, nisi Deum solum. Cur ergo tam periculosam aleam ineundam putant?
units.tr: Granted, ten, twenty or thirty refuse: yet one must surely be found who will load us with ruin and misery. Indeed, O King, I cannot bring myself to imagine that those who want to press this cause more insistently before Your Majesty will fall so far as not to keep before their eyes what they have already seen, nor to consider that they and their posterity will be held in eternal disgrace if a second disaster should befall us. I therefore want them asked to consider carefully and to remember that nothing is easier to conceal than a wicked plan, and that no one can penetrate the mind and thoughts of men except God alone. Why then do they think such a dangerous gamble must be undertaken?

units.la: Quod si qui obfirmatiores in sua sententia futuri sunt (etsi non putem) cogita, placet, ô Rex, non esse illos cultrum Iesuiticum expertos ore; non irruisse in eos Barreriam; posse vades eorum esse innumerabiles subditos, sicubi Iesuitis opus habuerint: fort adhuc nonnullos esse, qui statuant æquo diutius Galliam bellis civilibus vacaturam esse, nisi hæ turbæ, hæ faces revertantur. Quisquis attendit ad consilia sua: quisque suis consulit negotijs. Tua Majestatis est, ô Rex, ut imperium hoc tuum posterorumque tuorum confirmes adversus omnia turbinum, procellarum, fulminumq; genera.
units.tr: But if some are more obstinate in their opinion (though I do not think they are), consider, I beg you, O King, that they have not yet felt the Jesuit knife at their throats; that Barrière has not fallen upon them; that they may have innumerable subjects as sureties, wherever they have need of the Jesuits. Perhaps there are still some who judge that France will be free of civil wars for no longer than a while, unless these disturbances and these firebrands return. Let each man attend to his own counsel; let each look after his own affairs. It is for Your Majesty, O King, to confirm this your empire, and that of your posterity, against every kind of whirlwind, storm and thunderbolt.

units.la: At Papa, inquiunt, postulat, cupit, vult: an hoc illi tam bene multis nominibus merito recusaturus es? Respondeo, multis modis. Primum namque sanctissimus Pater ea probaturus est; qui persuadere cupiunt Majest. tuæ rem damnosissimam; idque hac specie, quod interpellaverit Majestatem tuam, qui de ea optime sit meritus. Hic enim audi quid dicat vetus author: Nihil beneficijs periculosius, si nos servitute obligent, ut faciamus id, quod perniciosum nobis iudicabimus. Et alter elegantius: Si homini bene merito postulationem rem fecero, quæ mihi valde sit damnosa, non solum perit gratia, sed etiam iusta mihi superesset occasio querimoniæ. Rex profestò Galliin conditionem miseram delapsus est, si alia via meritum non potest agnoscere, atque compensare, quam turbando regnum suum incendio. Secundò, nego plane hoc desiderari à Sanctitate ipsius: magis diligit Galliam. Novit se de hac vita discessurum esse: hanc vero Societatem perpetuam in subrogationem. Hæc cum nos invadet, non poterit ille amplius succurrere. Ajebat quidam Philosophus: Vt noris si quis quid velit, oportet idem posse nolle. Quis autem hoc nescit, non posse Papam Iesuitis recusare, quin subscribat omnibus literis, quas illi poposcerint? Quid D. Cardinales dicturi essent; studentes Regi Hispaniæ, quorum parti annuam pensitationem pendit? nonne acerbe & supra modum quererentur, deseri in suis difficultatibus homines, qui tot labores ad sanctæ Sedis amplificationem tulerunt? Cogitur ergo sanctitas illius optatis eorum subscribere: voluntas autem coacta, ne voluntas quidem dicenda est. Progrediar longius: Si Papa tuperet Valentiæ ad Comitatum Avenionensem adijci, an propterea fieret? certè nequaquam: Quod ad fundam rei spectat regnumque universum, id nonne plures est, quam Valentia decem? Quarto, hoc quidem ego dixeram, Arrestis Parlamenti irritas fieri bullas, quæ veniunt contra libertates & theses Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ, aut contra Edicta statutaque nostrorum Regum aut contra Arresta Parlamentorum eius, id vero nunquam dixeram voluntate Papa Galliæ posse Arresta subrui. Quid ergo hic opus facto? Rem facilem. Oportet sanc- titatem eius de rationibus præcipuis informari, cur omnino sit necesse mandari exsequutioni Arresta Parlamenti. Inter eas autem hæc observatione digna, quæ nondum adducta sunt: in aliis quidem cœtibus & communitatibus quibusdam homines compertos esse, qui furenter gesserint contra officium Regi debitum, nec Iesuitis in re ulla cesserint. Pariter cerunt illis: si quis altâ contendit voce, alter pulmonem rupit clamoribus. Hoc illi accerate annotant hodierno die, & tamquam oratores magni personant mirificè: exstant scriptis eorum supplicibusque libellis de hac re narrationes integræ, quarum summa hæc red- dit: Si multum mali attulimus, alij Religiosi eadem ferme vestigia sequuti sunt. Sed nodicunt quod est rei caput; ab hoc cavent, hoc præterereunt silentio. Quid autem? Quod inlijs cœtibus, si qui animi perturbatione partibus Hispani studuerunt, alij tamen non derant eiusdem ordinis, qui ex dignitate servirent, Turonibus, Cadomi, Redonibus, Andabus, Catalauni, & in aliis civitatibus paucis insignibus, quæ in obsequio nostri Regis disancti perstiterunt. Hi boni viri, vere Christiani, vere Catholici, ac religiosi refellebant, destruebantque in suis cathedris veritatis ac non mendacij, consolationis, ac non scandaperversam defectionis doctrinam, quam Iesuitæ & discipuli ipsorum in civitatibus rebelibus indefinienter prædicabant. Apud Iesuitas vero omnes, mirum, permirum, ne unum quidem inventum esse, qui uno lucius s itet u dico, ne unu quidem inventu esse, qui inde ab anno 89. ad annum usq; 94. vocem prolucerit, qua patriae suae, Principi suo comodaret: summis fuerunt in laudib. alienae, & in levando metu dominationis illius. Quae cum ita sint, quid amplius adduci possit? Quis neget conspirationem generalem, maximam, horrendam, furiosamq; exstitisse? Nunc vero quum male cecidit, miseros esse nos & plenos stultoris arbitrantur, si adhuc spe- rent, se apud nos servatum iri, ut alia occasione, melius provisis rebus, non omneis cum republica pessumdent.
units.tr: But, they say, the Pope demands, desires and wills it: will you therefore refuse him, though he has deserved so well of you in many ways? I reply, in many ways. For first, the most holy Father would approve these things; those who wish to persuade Your Majesty of a most damaging thing do so under this pretext, that he has interceded with Your Majesty, who has deserved so well of him. Listen to what an old author says: nothing is more dangerous than benefits, if they bind us in servitude so that we do what we judge to be harmful to us. And another says more elegantly: if I make a request of a man who has deserved well of me, which would be very damaging to me, not only does the favour perish, but a just occasion of complaint would remain for me. The King of France has indeed fallen into a wretched condition if he cannot acknowledge and repay merit in any other way than by setting his kingdom ablaze. Secondly, I flatly deny that this is wished by His Holiness; he loves France more. He knows that he will depart from this life, but this Society is perpetual, as his successor. When it attacks us, he will no longer be able to help. A certain philosopher said: so that you may know whether someone wishes something, you must see that he could also be unwilling. Who does not know that the Pope cannot refuse the Jesuits, but must sign every letter they demand? What would the lords Cardinals say, those who favour the King of Spain, and to whose party he pays an annual pension? Would they not complain bitterly and beyond measure that men who bore so many labours for the enlargement of the Holy See are deserted in their difficulties? So His Holiness is forced to subscribe to their wishes; but a forced will should not even be called a will. I shall go further: if the Pope wished Valence to be added to the County of Avignon, would it happen for that reason? Certainly not. As for the whole matter and the entire kingdom, is that not more than ten Valences? Fourthly, I had indeed said this: that the bulls which come against the liberties and theses of the Gallican Church, or against the edicts and statutes of our kings, or against the decrees of Parliament, are made void by the decrees of Parliament. But I never said that the decrees of France could be overturned by the Pope's will. What then is needed here? An easy matter. His Holiness must be informed of the principal reasons why the decree of Parliament must absolutely be carried out. Among these, one worth noting, not yet adduced, is this: in other bodies and communities, men have been found who acted furiously against the duty owed to the King, and yielded to the Jesuits in nothing. Likewise they yield to them: if someone shouts loudly, another bursts his lungs with clamour. These men today note such things with care, and like great orators they bellow wonderfully. Written accounts and supplicating pamphlets about this matter exist, whose summary is this: "If we have done much harm, other religious orders have followed nearly the same footsteps." But they pass over the heart of the matter; they take care to avoid this and keep silent about it. Well then? In other bodies, if some, through a disturbance of mind, favoured the Spanish party, yet others of the same order were not lacking who served with dignity at Tours, Caen, Rennes, Andelys, Châlons, and in a few other notable cities, and who stood firm in obedience to our King. These good men, truly Christian, truly Catholic and religious, refuted and destroyed from their chairs the perverse doctrine of defection, which the Jesuits and their disciples preached without restraint in the rebel cities: a doctrine of truth and not of falsehood, of consolation and not of scandal. Yet among all the Jesuits, astonishing, most astonishing, not even one can be found who raised a voice for his country or his prince, from the year 1589 to the year 1594. They were highest in praise of foreigners, and in easing the fear of that dominion. Since this is so, what more can be adduced? Who would deny that a general conspiracy, the greatest, horrible and furious, has existed? Now that it has turned out badly, they think we are wretched and full of folly if they still hope to be kept by us, so that on another occasion, with things better provided for, they do not ruin everything together with the commonwealth.

units.la: Ac duo quidem, o Rex, adducuntur, ut tibi omnis recordatio istius rei & sensus eximarum unum est, homines istos valde mutatos esse: non eos jam esse, quos ante videris, qui te motis tam multis infestaverint: alterum quod ostenditur est, etiamsi illis animus esset nocendi laeseft. tuae, non tamen posse.
units.tr: Two things, O King, are brought forward so that all memory and sense of this matter may be taken from you: first, that these men have changed greatly and are no longer the men you saw before, who stirred up so many disturbances to harass you; second, it is shown that even if they had the will to harm you, they could not.

units.la: De priore, ostendatur in oculis tuis Decretu magnum ab ipsis factum: Ne se deinceps egotiis status, sive regnorum rerum publicarum sit, eis publici inficiant. Age, diem Decreti illius faciamus videamus. Dicunt factum esse anno 93. Quid ergo? jamne oblitus es, o Rex, istos homines ab eo tempore caedem tuam procurasse? Quaenam haec Decreti executio est? An ignoraveris generalem exceptionem in statutis suis omnibus (nisi si quid est pro religionis bono) exceptionem ad omnia, quae velit aliquis, prorogandam? Veruntamen si placet cognoscere, quaero constituerint, ne se porro negotiis ad statum pertinentib. immiscean t, & quanti statum ciant Reip. legenda solum sunt nobis defensiones ipsorum, quas veritatis defensae nomine liderunt pag. 229. ubi utuntur his verbis: Sed status ille quaenam creaturae est? vieamus in os illum, ne Iesuitae negotia illius ineant, neque indignationem coum experiantur, qui propugnant ipsum, & sunt aemuli ipsius. Item pag. 231. Exndant itaque boni isti Catholici, quid dicant, cum eos accusant, quod se negotiis quo pluribus occupent: & ipsi viderint, ne perdant statum, dum tam parvam ae fidei rationem habent: & ne terrenam requiem procurando, tu eam non reiperent, tum illam, quae in coelis est, amittant. Potestne superbius & arrogantius monstrari hanc ipsius voluntatem esse, ut pergant diligentius quam fecerint unquam perre & subvertere statu, quem se non vivere negant? atq; hoc quide cum ratione dicunt: nunquam imo illorum alia insedit cogitatio, quam ut res omnes publicas subvertant, Magistratuum contemptum, motum subditorum excitent: prout se conjuratos eorum hoes declarant esse, qui sunt amantes pacis. Et illud plurimum observatu dignum, quod in dem p. 229. ut odium populi concilient iis, qui tuum statum, o Rex, tuam coroam, tuum sceptrum colunt, novam vocem Gallicam fabrefecerunt, ut Estatiens, Staales appellaret. Durantibus procellis ipsorum, nos Politicos appellabant: hac voce jam non audent uti, exolevit; cuderunt alteram; hae perpetuae illorum artes.
units.tr: Concerning the first point, let the great Decree that they made be set before your eyes: that they will henceforth not meddle in the affairs of any state, whether of kingdoms or commonwealths. Come, let us examine the date of that Decree. They say it was made in the year 1593. Well then? Have you forgotten, O King, that from that time these men have plotted your murder? What sort of execution of the Decree is this? Or are you unaware that all their statutes contain a general exception (unless something is for the good of religion), an exception to be extended to whatever anyone wishes? Still, if you care to know, I ask what they resolved, namely that they would no longer involve themselves in affairs pertaining to the state, and how much they stir up the commonwealth. We need only read their own defences, which they published under the name of the Defence of Truth, p. 229, where they use these words: "But what sort of creature is that state? Let us look it in the face, lest the Jesuits engage in its affairs, and lest they experience the indignation of those who defend it and are its rivals." Likewise on p. 231: "Let those good Catholics, then, say what they mean when they accuse them of occupying themselves with too many affairs. Let them see to it that they do not lose the state while they have so little regard for faith, and that by seeking earthly rest they do not obtain it and at the same time lose that which is in heaven. Can this will of theirs be shown to be more proud and arrogant, namely that they should go on more diligently than ever to overthrow and subvert the state, which they deny they are living under?" And they say this with good reason, for no other thought has ever settled in their minds than to overturn all public affairs, to stir up contempt for magistrates and unrest among subjects, as they show themselves to be conspirators against those who love peace. And it is most worthy of notice that on p. 229, in order to win the hatred of the people against those who cultivate your state, your crown and your sceptre, O King, they coined a new French word, calling them Estatiens and Staales, whereas during their storms they used to call them Politicos. They no longer dare use this word; it has fallen out of use, so they have coined another. These are their constant arts.

units.la: Vides igitur, o Rex, quam pelle Iesuitae suum illud Decretum exequantur: atq; hoc tame untur propugnaculo, ut labefactent omnia, quae Majestati tuae exponuntur. Sed quis quam fando audivit, eiusmodi promissionibus, eiusmodi decretis haberi fidem? Tandem facio, quam si Piratae mercatoribus ostenderent, se in consessu generali statuisse, ne amplius exerceant piraticam, nec praedentur amplius, se liberam eis copiam facere secum vigandi. Hoc pueris facile persuaserint. Et quis tam imperitus administrationis mun- , qui nesciat, Iesuitas nunc ad omnia tam admovere manum, & amplius, quam unquam cerint? Quid longe abeamus? Proximi vicini nostri sub tyrannide ipsorum gemunt, & unum cogitant, qua via se fe ab illis expediant. Sed ut ad institutum sermonem redeam, Iesuitae ad nos revertissent, quis eorum observator esset, sive autigrapheus? quis de onibus nuncijs faucibus q; subeuntibus in domos & per domos ipsorum cognosceret? de armis consiliis quae haberentur? de iis quae adferrentur judiciis? Quis non illos momento ideat in eandem libertatem, qua anno octogesimo octavo usi sunt, venturos esse? Amplius hoc dico; etiamsi artes illorum contra dignitatem tuam, o Rex, compertae essent, quis pus, deinceps eas indicaturus esset Magistratui? quis sibi non metueret ab anni 89. redin-
units.tr: You see, then, O King, by what pretext the Jesuits carry out that Decree, and yet they use it as a bulwark so that they may undermine everything that is set before your Majesty. But who has ever heard of placing faith in promises of this kind, in decrees of this kind? It is as if pirates were to show merchants that they had resolved in a general assembly no longer to practise piracy or plunder, and that they gave them free licence to sail with them. This would easily persuade children. And who is so inexperienced in the business of government as not to know that the Jesuits now lay their hands on everything, and more than ever before? But why go far away? Our nearest neighbours groan under their tyranny and think of only one thing: by what way they may free themselves from them. But to return to my subject: if the Jesuits were to return to us, who would be their observer or informer? Who would learn of the messages that go in and out, of the men who enter houses and pass through their houses, of the arms and plans that are being made, of the judgments that are brought forward? Who does not see that in a moment they would return to the same liberty they enjoyed in the year 1588? I say this further: even if their arts against your dignity, O King, were discovered, who would then be willing to report them to the magistrate? Who would not fear, from the year 1589 onward, that ...

units.la: Notae Iesuit.
units.tr: Notes of the Jesuits.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: On the Propagation

units.la: tegratione, ne quando iterum superbam ipsorum tyrannidem subeat, praesertim si ex tam solenni exilio reversos viderit. Cernentes itaque patroni illorum, aegrius tibi, o Rex, persuaderi posse, nunquam Iesuitae voluntatem pravam deposuerunt; ad caput alterum transfiliunt, non eis adfore potestatem malefaciendi tibi. Atque ut ad hanc fidem melius adducant Majestatem tuam in libellis supplicibus suis exultat Iesuitarum oratio, victorias tuas efferentium, et sermones quosque Panegyricos in vernaculum nostrum sermonem convertentium. Homines a natura amant audire, quum narratur ipsorum felicitas, o Rex, amplitudo, firmitas status et dignitatis suae posterumque suorum laudibus ipsorum conjuncta. Gaudeo equidem, cum video homines aeque tui amantes ac vitae suae, ex animo studiosos tui in caelum usque arma tua, triumphos tuos provehere. Hoc meretur virtus, hoc pabulum, hoc elementum ipsius, haec pulcherrima ipsius compensatio. Sed caveamus, o Rex, obsecro, caveamus ab inimicorum nostrorum laudibus. Annotaverunt veteres, magos argutissimos laudando fascinasse. Caveamus, o Rex, ab istis Sirenibus, quae adeo suaviter auribus adblandiuntur, ut soporent nautas, et gravatos somno lacerent. Quum tam speciosa verba audis, o Rex, in ore ipsorum, annon recordaris, os tuum ab uno de seminario isto vulneratum? cum tot flores audis eloquentiae, nonne tibi in mentem venit, Gymnasiarcham eorum Barreriae animum accendisse hoc flumine eloquentiae? Non male observaverunt illi, o Rex, in suo libello supplice, non dico clementiam (quae semper est laudabilis judicii conjuncta, alioqui virtus esse definit.) sed bonitate stolidam Iulij Caesaris ab illo Principe Romanae eloquentiae evectam esse, et quinquaginta duobus proelijs, quae ille gesserat, ante positam: Sed non perducunt ad finem historiam: nempe, sic eum obstupefecisse sui sermonis elegantia, ut suos capitales hostes revocaverit, lateribusque suis adesse curaverit; qui paulo post eis stilis confecerunt, quae neque Mars, neque Bellona, neque multa centena armatorum millia potuerant offendere. Patere fucum sic tibi fieri, non magis tibi parcituri sunt. Ac tum aequum triumphum canent, ut Orator ille, qui postclamabat: Pauci manu percusserunt Caesarem, sed omnes animo occiderunt. Scio te respondsurum, maximum illum Imperatorem fuisse usurpatorem: at ego vicissim respondeo, unicam membranam Romanam ex Iesuitarum doctrina posse efficere, ut tyrannus habearis: quam doctrinam profitentur, et jactant hoc adhuc tempore; neque deinceps negaturi sunt, nisi Generalis ipsorum, subjectus Hispano, ut alij quatuor omnes exstiterunt, prius dispensatione indulserit, ad cautelam, dissimulandi doctrinam suam, ut pedem reponant in Galliam. Sed hoc verbum aegre pronunciaturi sunt; Non posse Papam excommunicare et fulmine ferire pro auctoritate Reges, et subditos religione iurisiurandi et datae fidei exsolvere. Quo modo scripta ipsorum omnia conciliaturus esset? Haec mutationes novae in ipsos crimina novaeque probationes essent. Ad institutum redeamus.
units.tr: ...lest they ever again rise up to their proud tyranny, especially if he sees them return from so solemn an exile. Therefore their patrons, seeing that it is harder to persuade you, O King, that the Jesuits have never put aside their wicked will, leap to another point: that they will not have the power to do you harm. And so that they may bring Your Majesty to this belief more effectively, the Jesuits in their supplicatory pamphlets exult, extolling your victories and rendering into our vernacular all the panegyrics they can. Men by nature love to hear of their own good fortune, O King: the greatness, firmness and standing of their position, and the praises of their posterity joined to them. I am indeed glad when I see men who love you as much as their own lives, and who zealously devote themselves to you, raising your arms and your triumphs up to heaven. Virtue deserves this, this is its food, this is its element, this is its most beautiful reward. But let us be on our guard, O King, I beg you, let us be on our guard against the praises of our enemies. The ancients noted that magicians bewitched by praising. Let us be on our guard, O King, against those Sirens, who caress the ears so sweetly that they lull sailors to sleep and then tear them apart while they are weighed down with sleep. When you hear such fine words from their mouths, O King, do you not recall your own face wounded by one man from that seminary? When you hear so many flowers of eloquence, does it not come to mind that their Gymnasiarch Barrière fired his spirit with this river of eloquence? Those men, O King, observed not badly in their supplicatory pamphlet, not that clemency (which is always joined with sound judgement, otherwise it ceases to be a virtue), but that the goodness of Julius Caesar, which was foolish, was praised by that prince of Roman eloquence and set before his fifty-two battles that he had fought. But they do not carry the story to its end: namely, that he was so astonished by the elegance of his speech that he recalled his chief enemies and saw to it that they stood by his side, who shortly afterwards with their pens accomplished what neither Mars, nor Bellona, nor many hundreds of thousands of armed men had been able to inflict. Suffer yourself to be so deceived; they will spare you no more. And then they will sing a triumph fitting for them, as that orator did who cried out afterwards: a few struck Caesar with their hands, but all of them killed him in spirit. I know you will reply that that greatest of commanders was a usurper. But I answer in turn that a single Roman parchment, from the teaching of the Jesuits, can make you be regarded as a tyrant. This is the teaching they profess and boast of even at this time; nor will they deny it hereafter, unless their General, subject to the Spaniard, as all four of the others have been, first grants a dispensation, as a precaution, for concealing their doctrine, so that they may set foot in France. But they will be reluctant to pronounce this statement: that the Pope cannot, by his authority, excommunicate and strike kings with lightning, and release subjects from the obligation of an oath and of a given faith. How would they manage to reconcile all their writings? These would be new changes, new accusations and new proofs against them. Let us return to our purpose.

units.la: Hoc ergo tibi dicitur, o Rex; quam optime constabilitus es, admodum metueris, valde de eis terrori, tremunt omnia sub pedibus tuis, quid Iesuitae possent in te efficere? Speciosa verba, et eo speciosiora, quod maxima ex parte vera: quo bene nobis est, et illis male. Sed in primis te oportet, o Rex, id advertere, eos, qui tantopere magnificant potestatem tuam, se adhuc in duabus provinciis regni tui, contra auctoritatem tuam, contra edictum tuum, contra Arresta tua tutatos esse. Non sum nescius, eos ex pauculis annis speciem aliquam dilationis exorasse: at eam non semper habuerunt. Praeterea meminerit, si placet, o Rex, in mense Majo anni 84. fuisse optime constitutum defunctum Regem in haereditatem fratrum, patris, avi; et tamen post annos quatuor eum a Iesuitis Lupara extrusum esse. A Iesuitis dico: nam alij brachia fuerunt, et pedes solum: hi fuerunt illud ipsum corpus quod regebat scapham. Haec quis melius noverit, quam Majestas tua?
units.tr: Therefore this is said to you, O King: however securely you are established, you are greatly fearful, and in great terror of them; all things tremble under your feet. What can the Jesuits do to you? Fine words, and all the finer because for the most part true: how well it goes for us, and how badly for them. But above all, O King, you must take note that those who so greatly magnify your power have still been sheltered in two provinces of your realm, against your authority, against your edict, against your decrees. I am not unaware that in the last few years they have obtained some appearance of delay; but they have not always had it. Moreover, let Your Majesty, if you please, O King, remember that in the month of May of the year 84 it was most firmly settled that the late King would succeed to the inheritance of his brothers, father and grandfather; and yet after four years he was driven out of Lupara by the Jesuits. I say by the Jesuits: for the others were only arms and feet; these were that very body which steered the boat. Who would know this better than Your Majesty?

units.la: Ut tamen libere dicam, o Rex, quod sentio, nec amplificatis justis metus causis, nec imminutis (hoc posterius foret longe periculosius: Optimum pharmacum in causis statuas et Reipubl. est diffidentia: saepe usa est Majestas tua et bene fuit) ut igitur dicam tibi, quod sentio, non arbitror dum superstes futurus es, (faxit Deus, ut sis superstes quinquaginta adhuc dhuc annos & amplius) Iesuitas aperte scenam suam acturos esse. Veruntamen pro certo abeo, in hac re mihi assensuram Majestatem tuam, neque in tua esse, neque in tuorum Parlamentorum manu, impedire, quin leniter & sensim animus subditorum tuorum infundant opinionem suam de causa excommunicationis, viribus illius, in locis omnibus, ubi uturi sunt.
units.tr: But, to speak freely, O King, what I think: neither have the grounds for fear been magnified, nor diminished (the latter would be far more dangerous: the best remedy for the state of affairs and the Commonwealth is distrust; Your Majesty has often used it, and well). So, to tell you what I think: I do not believe that, while you are still alive (may God grant that you survive for another fifty years and more), the Jesuits will openly act out their drama. Yet I am certain that Your Majesty will agree with me in this, and that it is not in your power, nor in that of your Parlements, to prevent them from gently and gradually infusing into the minds of your subjects their opinion about the cause of excommunication and its force, in all the places where they are going to live.

units.la: Ecce igitur malum, non parvum, non mediocre, sed magnum, maximum; & quod gravius malum potest existere, quam si tibi forte ante quadriennium eripiantur amplius decies centena subditorum millia? o lucem periculosissimam! hoc, inquam, malum est, quod te superstite, te Rege accidet, ut ut diligentiam summam, providentiam maximam hic adhibueris, non poteris impedire. Memento dictum.
units.tr: Behold, then, an evil, not small, not moderate, but great, very great; and what more serious evil can there be than that, perhaps four years ago, more than a million of your subjects were snatched from you? O most dangerous light! This, I say, is the evil which will happen while you live, while you are King, and which, however great your diligence and your highest foresight here, you will not be able to prevent. Remember what I have said.

units.la: Quod regulae, restrictiones, & modificationes tibi proponuntur, falleris. Et quae possunt esse regulae elegantes esse? Videamus, agedum, ea sit in consilium mittamus. Quid, an Iesuitae eminem deinceps alloquuturi sunt? nemine usuri? quis ergo usus illorum futurus est? nonne uentute informaturi sunt? Hic vero solus eorum praetextus est, qui patrocinatur illis; etsi vera literas supra quae ex parte dimidia exstinxerunt, quas magnus Rex Francisus Muaru pater in Galliam revocaverat (cessante aut causa in regno universo, cessabit malum) Ergo juventute sub ferula sua habituri sunt: & qua via hic nos putamus impedire posse, neam imbuant illis periculosis omnibus documentis, quae ante diximus.
units.tr: You are mistaken that rules, restrictions and modifications are being proposed to you. And what elegant rules could there be? Let us look, come now, and let us send them to be considered. What? Will the Jesuits henceforth address no one? Will they use no one? What use, then, will they be? Will they not, surely, instruct the young? Here indeed is their only pretext, the one which defends them; although the true letters, which King Francis, the great father of Muaru, had recalled to France, have largely extinguished them in part (once the cause ceases throughout the whole kingdom, the evil will cease). So they will have the young under their rod; and by what means we think we can prevent them from imbuing the young with all those dangerous teachings which we have mentioned before.

units.la: Sed fingamus eis non esse Collegia: omnes certe veteres ipsorum fratres, sentinam urbium non impedies, quin revisant ipsos. Et novit Deus, quam admirabilia effecta novias in Gallia assequatur? Deus novit, quae tubae, qui praecursores, qui jam adventarint? Deus novit, quam fortiter cantaturi triumphos, & signa reposituri sint! Certe non mandabis ocludi eorum januas, ne quis invisat: an potest ulla hora praetextus pietatis homines ipsos decere? Tum quam importune instabunt (reputet Majestas tua) qui in regno & extra regnum atrocinantur ipsis, ut haec omnes regulae, omnes restrictiones amoveantur; quas proponunt in hoc tempore, ut janua eis aperta sit? Illi ipsi, qui nunc proponunt eas, primum omnium acturi sunt, ut expungantur, & ubique restituatur Iesuitis locus. Hoc ipsum est, quod illis in aurem insufflurant: Hoc tantum accipite, in hoc tantum esse, minuamus Arrestum istud, caetera vobis ne sunto curae. Quot inter veteres illis praesentib. futuri sunt, quib. absenibus sunt tam multi? Tum vero Majestati tuae non est amplius magnum illum clypeum habiura, Arrestu Parlamenti sui, quod esse oportet inviolabile. An ulla in mundo potest tibi julior suppetere excusatio contra ista omnia importune dicta? Hic Clypeus ubi effractus fuerit, quid tum poterit afferri, ut impediatur, ne pedem ubi ponant, sicut anno 88. nisi istud, esse periculorum artifices? Deum immortalem! quid est, cur istud non dicas hoc ipso tempore? Est adhuc tibi eorum memoria recens, quae noverunt facere: si oblitus es, per fenestram respice: vix in ullo regni tui loco futurus es, quin ex eo videas innumera domuum rudera, quas corruperunt igne; orphanos infinitos, quos ad pauperitatem redegerunt. Et hoc tibi non afficit animum? Afficit, scio; nam tibi melior est animus. At interfectores ipsorum te jugulo tenent: an tibi lacerti desunt?
units.tr: But let us suppose they have no colleges: certainly you will not prevent all their old brethren, the sewer of the cities, from revisiting them. And God knows what admirable results they will achieve in France once they have arrived again! God knows what trumpets, what forerunners, have already come! God knows how loudly they will sing their triumphs and how they will raise their standards! Surely you will not order their doors to be shut so that no one may visit them: can the pretext of piety ever befit such men? Then how importunately will those (let Your Majesty consider) who plead their cause within the kingdom and outside it press that all these rules and all these restrictions, which they propose at this time, be removed, so that the door may be open to them! Those very men who now propose them will be the first to act for their erasure, and for the restoration of the Jesuits' place everywhere. This is precisely what they whisper into the ear: "Accept only this much; in this matter only, let us weaken that decree; you need have no other concern." How many of the old ones will be among those present, and how many are there who are absent? Then Your Majesty will no longer have that great shield, the decree of your Parlement, which ought to be inviolable. Can anything in the world offer you a more just excuse against all these things said unseasonably? Where this shield has been broken, what then can be offered as a reason why they should not set foot wherever they please, as in the year 88, except that they are artificers of dangers? Immortal God! Why is it that you do not say this at this very time? Their memory of what they know how to do is still fresh to you: if you have forgotten, look out of the window: you will scarcely be in any place in your kingdom from which you do not see countless ruins of houses which they have destroyed with fire, and countless orphans whom they have reduced to poverty. And does this not move your mind? It does, I know; for your mind is better than that. But their murderers hold you by the throat: or do you lack arms?

units.la: Centesimam forte mali partem, o Rex, habes, quod illi te vivo & videnti allaturi sunt. Si chartam hanc meam in aliquem conclavis tui angulum conjeceris, postea vero imprudens aliquando casu in eam inciderit, me vera dixisse judicabis.
units.tr: Perhaps you have only a hundredth part of the evil, O King, which they are going to bring upon you while you live and look on. If you throw this paper of mine into some corner of your room and then one day, by chance and unawares, someone comes across it, you will judge that I have spoken the truth.

units.la: Sed esto, demus, eos nec mutire, nec spirare ausuros, dum videbunt asperitatem tuum: nonne prudentia magnorum Principum tenetur ulterius penetrare & prospicere propter vitam suam; praecipue si adsunt liberi? Dum corpora nostra bene habent, o Rex, non sentimus plurima incommoda, quae invadente morbo solent existere: Ita, cum valetudo magnorum regnorum accidentibus perturbatur, quae Deo placet immittere, excitantur non pauci homines pravi, quorum stante felicitate nullus sensus exstiterat. Haec sunt tempora, hae occasiones, quas Iesuitae observant statarij, nec unquam sinunt effugere. Si primo impetu loquuntur, non obtinent, altero vires ingeminant, itemque tertio. Vincunt in omnibus pervicaces.
units.tr: But grant, let us suppose, that they will neither mutter nor dare to breathe while they see your severity. Would not the prudence of great princes still be bound to look further and to foresee for the sake of their own life, especially if children are present? While our bodies are in good health, O King, we do not feel the many discomforts that usually arise when disease attacks. So too, when the health of great kingdoms is disturbed by the accidents which God is pleased to send, not a few wicked men are stirred up, whose existence was not felt at all while prosperity lasted. These are the times, these the opportunities, which the Jesuits watch for as their regular practice, and never allow to slip away. If they speak at the first onset and do not prevail, they renew their strength at the second, and likewise at the third. They conquer in all things by their obstinacy.

units.la: Non semper idem vigor inest, idem ad resistendum animus. Quis morbus recidivo gra-
units.tr: The same vigour is not always present, nor the same spirit for resisting. What disease, returning again and again...

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: On the Spread

units.la: vior? cuius minor est commiseratio, si quâ nostrâ culpâ factum est: præsertim ubi causa malì bene animad versa est, & nobis cura non fuit, ut bene ab eo caveremus. Fecit Deus, ut sim falsus vates: sed prospicio animo tandem hoc regnum operâ Iesuitarum in cineres abiturum. Id semel vidimus per illos conflagrasse tam horribili incendio, ut inde ab Asia ipsa videretur: inventus est Rex magnus, plenus virium, plenus experientiæ, non capiens somnum, nisi quum vellet, ferreus ad labores, ad pugnas chalybeus, qui hoc impetu extinxit malum. At non semper magnos illos Principes, & florente ætate largitur Deus. Ecquis nō videt, quum huius regni prima nox incubuerit, hoc incendium male extinctum gravius quam ante unquam redarsurum, & liberos nostros perditurum? vos deploro, ô miseri mei liberi: nam mihi quidem hunc metum adimit ætas caduca & canities mea.
units.tr: a more serious relapse? Our pity for it is the less if it came about through our own fault, especially where the cause of the disease has been well observed and we took no care to guard against it. God grant that I be a false prophet, but I foresee in my mind that this kingdom will at last go up in ashes through the work of the Jesuits. We have seen it once before, when they set it ablaze with such a terrible fire that it seemed to have come from Asia itself. A great King was found, full of strength and full of experience, who did not need sleep unless he wished it, iron for labours and steel for battles, and who put out that evil with a single onslaught. But God does not always grant such great Princes, nor Princes in their prime. Who does not see that now that the first night of this kingdom has fallen, this fire, badly put out, will flare up again more fiercely than ever and destroy our children? I lament you, my unhappy children. As for me, my failing age and white hair at least take this fear away.

units.la: Animad verto aliquem tibi, ô Rex, in aurem dicturum: Regie quidem tecum agitur scripto & speciem magnam habent quæ exponuntur tibi: sed capere animo non possum, quomodo Iesuitæ officia tibi non multa essent delaturi, si ita esset doctrina illorum, ut modo audivimus. Fortasse etiam, ô Rex, qui hoc tibi dicit, idem credit, agitque bona fide: quemadmodum plerique eorum, qui causam illam agunt apud te, sunt ignari veritatis, quam modo coram te protuli. Quam illi si tenerent, non minore studio rogarent, ut Arrestorum tuorum executionem mandes, quàm importuni sunt hodierno die ut infringas ea. Iam ergo rei declarationem ex veritate affero. Quum tibi Iesuitæ, ô Rex, magnos illos supplices libellos exhibuerunt, adeo phaleratos, adeo splendidos, adeo mellitos, convenierat tum optime tibi cum Patre sanctissimo: quæ ratio igitur fuisset impedimento illis, ne tibi sponderent ossicia sua? quid aliud fuissent dicturi? an gloriaturi adhuc fuissent se tibi hostes conjuratos & capitales esse? Hæccine Lutetiam via?
units.tr: I notice that someone will whisper to you, O King: "The matter is indeed put before you in writing, and what is set out to you has a great appearance. But I cannot bring myself to believe that the Jesuits would not have promised you many services, if their teaching were what we have just heard. Perhaps, O King, the person who says this also believes it and acts in good faith, just as most of those who plead their cause before you are ignorant of the truth that I have now set forth before you. If they held it, they would ask with no less zeal that you order the execution of your decrees, than they now insist, unreasonably, that you overturn them." Now, then, I will set out the true account of the matter. When the Jesuits, O King, presented you with those great supplicatory pamphlets, so ornate, so splendid, so honeyed, and when it was all arranged so well with the most holy Father, what would have prevented them from pledging their duties to you? What else would they have said? Would they still have boasted that they were your sworn and mortal enemies? Is this the way to Paris?

units.la: Sed an observâsti, ô Rex, quam vis libelli isti supplices circumfluant longitudine supra modum, tamen eos non protulisse, neque attigisse hoc caput quæstionis, hunc nodum controversiæ, hunc doctrinæ scopulum periculosissimum? videlicet, Nonne credant, docearntque, posse Papam excommunicare Reges, & manum inficere coronis ipsorum? quæ certa basis & fundamentum est cædium omnium, quæ perpetrata in Europa aut intentata sunt, & fons calamitatum omnium, quas perpessi sumus, ex quo scelestissima hæc doctrina tam audacter fuit seminata. Huc, boni Oratores, huc vos venire oportet; non autem narrationes pertexere de obsequio, quod à natura subditi suo Regi debent. Rem magnam scilicet: quid? nonne semper instructi estis exceptione vestra? quâ tandem? nimirum ista: Modo ne Reges sint excommunicati à Papa, qui potest omnes subditos à religione iurisiurandi & datæ fidei absolvere. Hoc demum est rei caput. Præcisè nobis respondete, & nihil circuitione utimini: Utrum verum est, vobis hanc exceptionem præsto esse ad manum, an vero esse calumniam? Sed quid ego consumo tempus in roganda super hac re ipsorum sententia? En libros illorum, plenos istius argumenti: hoc unum clamant, hoc unum intonant. Ex quo alio fonte profluxit malum, quod tulimus? fumusne expertes sensus? Quis ergo fecit, ut excommunicatio contra defunctum Regem anno millesimo quingentesimo octogesimo nono in Gallia obtineret? quæ profectò abs-que Iesuitis fuisset, non valuisset amplius quam illa anni 1591. Turonibus, ubi non erant nigræ animæ Iesuitæ, & ab extraneis redeptæ. Nonne videmus, tantum abesse, ut doctrinam iflam negaverint, ut contra gloriati de ea sint, etiam post exilium suum, ut principio demonstravi? An vero ita imperitos eos putamus esse, ut supplicibus suis libellis in has cassesruant? Professo non bene versavissent suam Rhetoricam, quæ silentio præterire eas objectiones jubet, ad quas nō datur responsio. Ad has Lector accurate non semper attendit, traduntur oblivioni: modo respondeatur ad id, quod prope abesse videtur, sufficit. An unquam melius sua ars oratori cessit, quà Iesuitis ista? Quis certiorem fecit Majest. tua, eos silentio præterire magnum hoc quæstionis caput? An quisquam expositum tibi, Iesuitas parcos in dicendo esse? Gallicè non loqui? nunc assentari, quando bene cum Papa agitur? At illi cavent sibi diligentissimè ab eo dicendo, quod dicturi essent, si Deus nos usque adeo affligeret, sanctissimo hoc Patre recepto adfe. dse, Roma aliquem nobis daret Bonifacio VIII. Benedictum III. Iulium II. qui excommunicationem ad nos transmitteret alijs consimilem, quarum fulmina vibraverunt contra reges nostros is Christianissimos, summe Catholicos, & primos orbis Christiani Reges, ex litteris illorum, ex omnibus actionib. & ex tot praedicationibus illorum, o Rex, agnovimus, si des ipsis haberetur, illos tali occasione data, te aut successorem tuum effecturos Regem a subditis, dominium ab haereditate nudum, privatum hominem, particularem, maledictum, execrabilem, miserum, errabundum, deniq; eiusmodi, qualem te & defunctum Regem sperarverat eum iri, & reipsa fuisset effecturi, si omnes Catholici Galliae fuissent boni Iesuitae: quemadmodum plane consilia dantur ad hoc efficiendum, istorum hominum revotatione: ut doceant, certam hanc fidem mentibus infigant juventutis, & Te & totam posteritatem tuam in perpetuum unica Bulla ex throno S. Ludovici exturbari posse.
units.tr: But have you observed, O King, that although these supplicatory pamphlets overflow beyond measure in length, they have neither mentioned nor touched upon this chief point of the question, this knot of the controversy, this most dangerous rock of their doctrine? Namely, do they not believe and teach that the Pope can excommunicate Kings and stain their crowns with his hand? This is the sure basis and foundation of all the murders that have been committed or attempted in Europe, and the source of all the calamities we have suffered since this most wicked doctrine was so boldly sown. Here, good orators, here you ought to come, and not to spin out narratives about the obedience that subjects owe by nature to their King. A great matter indeed! But what? Have you not always been prepared with your exception? And what is it, pray? Surely this: "Provided only that Kings are not excommunicated by the Pope, who can absolve all subjects from the bond of an oath and of a given pledge." This at last is the heart of the matter. Answer me plainly, and do not use circumlocution: is it true that you have this exception ready to hand, or is it rather a slander? But why do I waste time asking their opinion on this matter? Look at their books, full of this argument: this alone they cry out, this alone they thunder. From what other source has the evil we have endured flowed? Are you devoid of sense? Who then brought it about that the excommunication against the late King held force in France in the year 1589? Surely it would have had no more effect than that of 1591 at Tours, where there were no Jesuits of black soul, and which was bought back by foreigners, had it not been for the Jesuits. Do we not see that they are so far from denying this doctrine that they boast of it, even after their exile, as I showed at the beginning? Or do we think they are so unskilled that they would fall into these snares in their supplicatory pamphlets? Surely they would not have practised their rhetoric well, which bids one pass over in silence those objections to which no answer can be given. The reader does not always attend carefully to these points; they are consigned to oblivion, provided that a reply is made to what seems almost irrelevant. Has art ever served an orator better than this has served the Jesuits? Who has informed Your Majesty that they pass over in silence this great chief point of the question? Or has anyone set it before you that the Jesuits are sparing in speech? That they do not speak French? That they now flatter, now that matters go well with the Pope? Yet they take the greatest care to avoid saying what they would say if God so afflicted us that, with this most holy Father received among us, Rome gave us some Boniface VIII, Benedict III, or Julius II, who would send to us an excommunication like those which they have hurled against our Kings, the most Christian, most Catholic, and foremost Kings of the Christian world. From their letters, from all their acts and from all their preachings, O King, we have learned that if they were given the opportunity, on such an occasion they would make you, or your successor, a King stripped of subjects, a lordship bereft of inheritance, a private, partial, cursed, execrable, wretched, wandering man, in short, of the kind that they had hoped you and the late King would become, and that they would indeed make you so if all the Catholics of France were good Jesuits. Plainly, counsels are being given to bring this about by the rebellion of these men: that they should teach, implant this certain belief in the minds of the young, and that you and your whole posterity could be cast down forever by a single Bull from the throne of St Louis.

units.la: Sed quid rationibus opus est, cum exempla suppetant, quae Te attingunt proxime? Accipe, o Rex, notitiam historiarum multarum: audivi Te historias narrantem, quas norabant multi, qui polyhistores sibi videbantur. Quod si nunquam forte nisi unicam dicisses, ea haec futura esset: narrabo tamen paucis, quia necesse est eam Tibi e memoria excidisse. Anno millesimo quingentesimo duodecimo agebatur annus vigesimus nonus, cum Catharina Regina frueretur Navarrae regno, quod ipsi obtigerat excessu Francisci huius fratris, ex successione quam plurimorum antecessorum Regum. Anni octodecim erant, ex quo cum Ioanne Albretano marito suo coronata fuerat Pompelone: Deus filium unum dederat cum filiabus tribus: regnum eorum opibus & potentia adeo floreret, ut semper Castellanos & Aragonios feliciter cederet. Iusta pace cum illis utebatur, mmoq; & antiquo sedere cum regno Galliae, Regi nostro Ludovico 12. magno Regi, magno uci quam dilectissimi: denique, non videbatur fore, ut ipsa tota Europa de aggrediendis vel cogitare praesumeret. Papa tamen percitus Gallorum odio, in hos Reges vibravit excommunicationem suam, subditos eorum a religione juris jurandi, & data fidei liberavit, regnumque eorum exposuit praedae, primo cuivis occupaturo: qui stilus est ordinarius. Eadem Bulla in Regem quoque nostrum vibratur fulmen, ut jam ante factum. Quid autem accidit? a Gallis ne unus quidem nutavit unquam: contra vero (atque hic rari possis, o Rex, indolem bonam nostram & naturale studium erga Reges, antequam staviffemus doctrinam illam Iesuiticam: quae res evidentius commonstrabit, plagam recto tuo per illos impositam) contra, inquam, majores omnes nostri, nemine excepto, genas vireis animi contulerunt, ut servirent Regi, frendente Iulio, qui odio in ipsum arbat; & amorem suum in Principem suum adeo amplificaverunt, ut vix crederent columem nisi viderent, Patrem suum, Servatorem suum, Regem optimum appellant: Denique permansit illi ex eo tempore inditum nomen Patris populi, & in aeternum rmanfurum est.
units.tr: But why do we need arguments, when examples lie ready which touch you most nearly? Hear, O King, the account of many histories. I have heard you telling histories which many who thought themselves learned in many fields knew. But if perhaps you had told only one, it would be this one, and yet I shall relate it briefly, because it must have slipped from your memory. In the year 1512, the twenty-ninth year was running when Catherine, the Queen, enjoyed the kingdom of Navarre, which had fallen to her on the death of her brother Francis, by succession from so many of her ancestors. It was eighteen years since she had been crowned at Pamplona with her husband John of Albret. God had given them one son and three daughters. Their kingdom flourished so much in wealth and power that it always gave way happily to the Castilians and the Aragonese. It kept a just peace with them and had an ancient alliance with the kingdom of France, with our King Louis XII, the great King, the great and most beloved. In short, it did not seem that all Europe would dare even to think of attacking it. Yet the Pope, stirred by hatred of the French, hurled his excommunication against these Kings, freed their subjects from the obligation of an oath and of a given pledge, and exposed their kingdom as prey to whoever first seized it, as is the usual practice. The same Bull hurled its thunderbolt at our King too, as had been done before. And what happened? Not one of the French ever wavered; on the contrary, all our forefathers, no one excepted, bent their knees with all the strength of their spirit to serve the King, while Julius raged and burned with hatred against him. They so increased their love for their Prince that they scarcely believed him safe unless they saw him, and they called him their Father, their Saviour, their best King. In short, from that time the name of Father of the people has remained attached to him, and it will remain forever.

units.la: Ex contrario autem quid Navarreno Regi accidit? Rex & Regina Tutelam omnes convocarunt: placuit, eis servitium praestari vel ad mortem usque, non obstante apa excommunicatorio fulmine. Ecce autem repente seditiosi homines exstiterunt, turbatores, atque obærati, rerum novarum studiosi, qui nunquam parce velum religionis ducunt rebus suis, qui soli hominum (fi fides habebitur) sunt plane Catholici: isti in polo caeperunt disseminare illam ipsam doctrinam, quam ante expositam, quamq; postea Iesuitarum opera fatam in Gallia vidimus. Quid itaque factum est in Navarreno regno? Seditiosi isti alios omnes effecerunt veterno sos, destitutos manibus pedibusq; hos religione, osseditioforum interminantium metu: adeo ut abavius & abavia tua, o Rex, in medio bditorum suorum sine subditis comperti sint, & sine milite per medias acies. Nunquam nique defectio proditioque exstitit adeo foeda, & pudenda, & miserabilis, qua illi coacti nt trahentes quaternos liberos, ex quorum uno genus ducis, o Rex, fugā se in Galliam ripere, efficiente membranā unā Rom. spatio unius horulae, quod tota Arragonia & Calla tota mille annis non fuisset effectura. Cum regnum amittitur, post trium aut quatuor aliorum insignium jacturam, quae res innumeris alijs accidit, id sal tem aliquid confclationis habet: sed ubi Rex se regno expulsum videt, nemine subditorum contra stringente gladium, religionis praetextu; hoc vero indignationes omnes, omnes desolationes, & omnes calamitates superat, quae apud homines excogitari possunt.
units.tr: On the other hand, what happened to the King of Navarre? The King and Queen called all their people together to defend them, and it was agreed that they should be served even unto death, notwithstanding the excommunicating thunderbolt of the pope. But suddenly seditious men appeared, troublemakers and debtors, lovers of revolution, who never count the veil of religion too dear to use for their own affairs, who alone of all men (if their word is to be believed) are truly Catholic. These men began to spread in the pulpits that very doctrine which we saw set out before, and which we later saw spread in France through the work of the Jesuits. What then was done in the kingdom of Navarre? These seditious men made all the others sluggish, stripping them of hands and feet, some by religion, others by fear of threatening rebels, so that your great-grandfather and great-grandmother, O King, were found in the midst of their subjects without subjects, and without soldiers amid the battle lines. Never was there a defection and betrayal so foul, shameful and wretched, by which they were forced to drag their four children, one of whom is the stock of the king, O King, and flee into France.
