A single bull from Rome achieved in the space of an hour what all Aragon and Castile could not have achieved in a thousand years. When a kingdom is lost, after the loss of three or four other notable things, as happens to countless others, there is at least some consolation in it; but when a king sees himself driven from his kingdom, with no subject drawing the sword against him, on the pretext of religion, this surpasses all indignities, all desolations and all calamities that can be imagined among men.

units.la: Sequente anno Rex noster juslo dolore percitus, quod Regem Reginamque sua occasione uideret exules regno, collectis copiis transmittit Pyrenaeos saltus, & recta Pompelone petiit: quam adeo graviter pressit, ut ab Insula Villerijs & Cannaeo signa muris imponerentur oppidi; sed ita fortiter est propugnata, ut re infecta oportuerit discedere. Post annos 8. rogatu Henrici Albretani Navarrae Regis, alterum exercitum submisit Rex Francisus, qui Popelone recepit; sed mox iterum amissa est. In hoc bello Ignatius Loyola viru se praestitit, & unus ex ducib. signorum Hispanicorum fuit: sed rem ita gessit pretio unius pedis, & altero pede infirmior est factus ex vulnere. Hic Dux, auctor, & Pater Iesuitarum est. Nunc vide, Rex, an non discipuli vestigia magistri sui secuti sunt? nonne ardens suum studium erga Castellanum imperium, & extremum odium contra Galliam scite aluerunt?
units.tr: In the following year our King, stirred by just grief that he saw the King and Queen exiled from their kingdom on his account, gathered troops, crossed the Pyrenean passes and made straight for Pamplona. He pressed it so hard that Villeroy and Cannaeus, from the island, planted their standards on the town walls; but it was so bravely defended that they had to withdraw with the business undone. Eight years later, at the request of Henry of Albret, King of Navarre, King Francis sent a second army, which retook Pamplona; but it was soon lost again. In this war Ignatius Loyola showed himself a man and was one of the commanders of the Spanish standards, but he acquitted himself at the cost of one foot, and was made weaker in the other from his wound. This commander is the author and Father of the Jesuits. Now see, O King, whether his disciples have not followed the footsteps of their master! Have they not skilfully nourished their ardent zeal for the Castilian empire and their utter hatred of France?

units.la: Admodum fundator eorum juvit, ut Navarreni perstarent sub Castellano jugo, discipuli vero alea unius praelij exposuerunt Galliarum libertatem. Unius dico nam unum praelium non poteramus perdere, quin te perderemus, o Rex, qui nunquam aliud perfugium habere quam ad signa florum lilij voluistis: te autem perdito, ecquis non videt manifuram fuisse Galliam, sicut & Navarram servam, captivamque sub Castellano jugo ad remos & vincula? Quid amplius? auctor istorum fuit unus ex Ducibus praesidij Hispanici Pompelone: discipuli vero, Lutetiae per triennium praesidium Castellanum loca verunt, atque defenderunt. Veruntamen haec omnia nihil sunt ad illud, quod jam sum dicturus. Loyolae istius discipuli acri judicio praevidentes, Regis illius Reginaeque tam miserè exturbatorum ex haereditate nepote Castellanis olim terrori fore, fecerunt quicquid in mentem conjurati simorum, ac summe capitalium hostium venire potest, ut hanc sobolem perderent: quumque eam invito furore suo in thronum S. Ludovici evectam animad verterent, & metum & conatus suos contra ipsum regnumque ipsius ingeminaverunt, idem venenum in populum illius copiose effundentes, quod olim regnum Navarrae perdiderat, & quod nunquam in Galliam, nisi per istos subtiles & audaces pharmaceutas poterat importari. Nihil horum fugere haredem illum Catharinae Reginae potuit; & tamen nescio qua influentia, nescio quod infortunium aeque Gallis ac Navarrenis fatale atque inevitabile mox persuaserit, ut eosdem Loyolae discipulos retineat in regno, ex quo solenniter justi sunt per Parlamenta ipsius exulare. Quis rem tam inauditam unquam creditur esse, postquam leonina pelle pugnatum est tam diu, nunc eum se vulpina decipiendum exponere? At non invenitur Iulius Secundus in omni tempore. Certe; at nec semper exstant quae amittantur regna. Non opus est tot Iulijs: unico opus est, si modo Gallos tam bene Dispositos, quam Navarrenos invenerit. Ponderā, Rex, etiam atque etiam quod mox sum dicturus. Excommunicatio Sixti Lutetiam, Lugdunum, Tholosam, Massiliam, Ambianum, Narbonem, Aurelianum, Biturigas, Nannetas, Trecas, Divionem in defectionem adduxit, & alia innumerata. Quid de Iesuitis dicas? nonne strenui sunt milites, homines industrii? si tantum spatio triginta annorum progressi sunt, quid deinceps fuissent facturi, postquam tot conscientias commoverunt & tot juvenes docuerunt, qui ad honores in diem assurgebant? Cur in consessibus senes fermè omnes probi Galli, juvenes fermè omnes inimici tui comperti sunt? Cur toties filium plane adversante patris judicio vidimus, nisi quia senes lac Iesuiticum minimè suxerint?
units.tr: Their founder greatly helped to keep the Navarrese under the Castilian yoke, while his disciples staked the liberty of France on the hazard of a single battle. I say a single battle, for we could not lose one battle without losing you as well, O King, who have never wished to have any refuge other than under the standards of the lily. And with you lost, who does not see that France would have been, like Navarre, enslaved and held captive under the Castilian yoke, condemned to the oars and the chains? What more? The founder of these men was one of the commanders of the Spanish garrison at Pamplona; but the disciples, for three years at Paris, installed and defended a Castilian garrison. Yet all these things are nothing compared with what I am about to say. The disciples of that Loyola, foreseeing with keen judgment that the nephew of that King and Queen, so wretchedly driven out, would one day be a terror to the Castilians, did whatever the most sworn and deadly enemies could devise to destroy this offspring. And when they saw him raised, against their raging will, to the throne of St Louis, they redoubled their fear and their efforts against him and his kingdom, pouring out in abundance upon his people the same poison that had once destroyed the kingdom of Navarre, and which could never have been imported into France except through these subtle and bold apothecaries. That heir of Queen Catherine could not escape any of this; and yet, by I know not what influence or what misfortune, fatal and inevitable alike to French and Navarrese, he was soon persuaded to keep in his kingdom the same disciples of Loyola, whom his parlements had solemnly judged must be exiled. Who would believe such an unheard-of thing: that, after fighting so long in the lion's skin, he now exposes himself to be deceived in the fox's? "But a Julius II is not to be found at all times." Certainly; but neither are there always kingdoms to be lost. There is no need of so many Julii: one is enough, provided he finds the French as well disposed as the Navarrese were. Weigh, O King, again and again, what I am about to say. The excommunication of Sixtus brought Paris, Lyons, Toulouse, Marseille, Amiens, Narbonne, Orléans, Bourges, Nantes, Troyes, Dijon and countless others into revolt. What do you say of the Jesuits? Are they not vigorous soldiers and industrious men? If in a space of only thirty years they have advanced so far, what would they have done afterwards, once they had stirred so many consciences and taught so many young men who were rising daily to honours? Why are almost all the old men in the councils honest Frenchmen, and almost all the young men found to be your enemies? Why have we so often seen a son openly opposed to his father's judgment, unless it is because the old men did not suck the Jesuit milk?

units.la: Sed placetne, o Rex, cognoscere audaciam istorum, qua gloriantur magnum istud & horrendum vulnus animis subditorum tuorum a se fuisse illatum, quod singulis diebus augent, scabiit, atque amplificant? Oportet eas solum voces in animum revocari, quas ante transscripsi ex Defensionibus ipsorum. Ac propterea, inquiunt, videmus gladium in personam multorum Regum in multis regnis fuisse usurpatum: quod si non semper fuit utile exercitium eius, semper tamen utile potuit esse. Siquidem subiecti bene fuissent dispositi: Nonne hi perspicue clamant? Olim non fuerunt Galli bene dispositi ad deferendos Reges, cum primum intonaret excommunicatio, sed contra potius studium suum erga eos ingeminaverunt: Nos vero triginta annis adeo bonam magnamque eorum partem disposueramus, ut paim abfuerit, quin victoriam fimus assequuti. Quod si artibus nostris, & tam variis hinc de commendationibus nos adhuc ibidem tutari possumus, tam bene disponemus Gallorum animos, ut plenum triumphum canamus altero impetu. Enimvero plurimum fueris, o Rex, in posteritate meritus, si eam miserè subjeceris ejus arbitrio, qui primus insidens sanctae partes Hispanicas coluit; eos homines reflituendo, qui eo audaciae superbiaeq; devenerunt, ut schismaticam hanc doctrinam ferant, deque ea glorientur, eam alta voce proclament, locisq; omnibus promoveant. Sic opus accelerabitur. Et quorsum, o Rex, tot blanditiae, quibus infantem in cunis excipis, si eodem tempore structores intromittas, potentes arces in Gallia exstructuros, ut ad prima tubae significationem subditi eius tam attoniti efficiantur, tam dispositi quam anno 1512. fuerunt Navarreni? Annon id tibi satis est, hac doctrina ipsi Pompelonem ereptam esse, nisi & Lutetiam per eam ereptam sit?
units.tr: But do you wish, O King, to learn the audacity of these men, by which they boast that they have inflicted that great and dreadful wound on the minds of your subjects, a wound they increase, fester and enlarge every day? One need only recall the words I copied out earlier from their Defences. "And therefore," they say, "we see the sword having been wielded against the persons of many kings in many kingdoms; and if its use has not always been profitable, it could always have been profitable, provided the subjects had been well disposed." Do they not cry out plainly? "Formerly the French were not well disposed to abandon their kings when excommunication first thundered; rather they redoubled their zeal for them. But we, in thirty years, have so disposed a good and large part of them that it was but a little short of our obtaining victory. If by our arts, and by such various commendations from here, we can still keep ourselves safe there, we shall dispose the minds of the French so well that we shall sing full triumph at a second assault." Indeed, O King, you will have deserved very much of posterity if you subject that unhappy nation to the will of him who, sitting in the holy seat, first cultivated Spanish interests, by restoring those men who have come to such audacity and pride that they bear this schismatic doctrine, glory in it, proclaim it aloud and promote it in every place. Thus the work will be hastened. And to what end, O King, are all those flatteries with which you receive the infant in the cradle, if at the same time you admit the builders who will erect powerful citadels in France, so that at the first sound of the trumpet your subjects may be as stunned, and as ready to fall, as the Navarrese were in 1512? Is it not enough for you that Pamplona itself was snatched away by this doctrine, unless Paris is snatched away by it too?

units.la: Offerunt quidem tibi Iesuitae supplicibus tuis libellis sponsores, qui tibi & tuis omnem annum praestituri sunt. Sed inauditum mihi adhuc fuerat, o Rex, in causis regni fidei justies dari. Etenim apud quos judices poterunt citari, si quis ejectus, errans, vagabundus it per orbem terrarum? Rem tamen oportet accommodari. Acquiescamus ergo cautionibus, modo sint idoneae: alioquin frustra est.
units.tr: Indeed the Jesuits offer you, in their humble petitions, sureties who will undertake for you and yours every year. But it has hitherto been unheard of to me, O King, that sureties be given in matters of the kingdom's faith. For before what judges could they be summoned, if someone expelled, wandering and vagabond goes about the whole world? Still, the matter must be adjusted. Let us then accept the securities, provided they are adequate; otherwise it is in vain.

units.la: Videamus, quaenam futurae sint. Apud tuos subditos, o Rex, nemo futurus est opulentus satis: nam ejus bona ne millesima quidem pars istius summae futura sunt, de qua est plus caveri. Apud exteros quem idoneum offerant, ut caveat de Regno Galliae? Video quid fit, o Rex, fideijussor, quem tibi daturi sunt, cavens de fide, de studio ipsorum in servitium tuum, est Rex Hispaniae, qui corpus suum pro corpore ipsorum pignori dedicavit est. Hic tam opulentus est, tam multarum ditionum Dominus, tam amat Galliam: ut eum renuas?
units.tr: Let us see what they will be. Among your own subjects, O King, no one will be rich enough, for his goods would not amount to even the thousandth part of the sum that is to be guaranteed here. Among foreigners, whom will they offer as a suitable guarantor for the Kingdom of France? I see, O King, what is happening: the surety they are going to give you, vouching for their faith and their zeal in your service, is the King of Spain, who has pledged his own body for theirs. He is so rich, lord of so many dominions, and loves France so much. Will you refuse him?

units.la: Atqui haec quidem de cautionibus, bene est: transeamus ad cetera. Quid fiet illa columna, Rex, quae ante Curiam hanc tua praefert notam in marmore posteris nostris illius studii, quo magnus ille populus universus flagrat erga suum bonum Regem, suum magnum Regem, liberatorem suum, qui eodem anno e cervicibus ipsius jugum Hispanorum exemerat? Columna magis honorata, magis gloriosa, quam illae Trajani & Antonini cum annis ut antes, & immortalitati consecratae?
units.tr: But enough of sureties; let us pass to the rest. What will become of that column, O King, which stands before this Court and bears your mark in marble for our posterity, a monument to the zeal with which that great people burns for its good King, its great King, its liberator, who in the same year had lifted the yoke of the Spaniards from their necks? A column more honoured and more glorious than those of Trajan and Antoninus, which, though consecrated to immortality, have crumbled with the years.

units.la: Eamne adhuc stare fines, si contra omnino feceris, quam tu ipse Arresto sanxisti, quod ibi incisum est? Quid dicturi sunt, qui contra videbunt, quam legent? hiccine magnus ille Senatus Galliae? sunt quidem sculpta in marmore Arresta ejus, sed revera contemptui sunt, et proteruntur pedibus.
units.tr: Will these limits still stand if you act wholly against what you yourself decreed at Arrest, which is carved there? What will those say who see the opposite and read it? Is this the great Senate of France? Their Arrests are indeed carved in marble, but in truth they are held in contempt and trampled underfoot.

units.la: Rem profecto pudoris plenam. Quid ergo faciamus? eundum jam jam, & columna everterenda? Quid? evertenda? Extaretne in mundo quis quam adeo infortunatus, ut tibi abominandum istud consilium vellet suggerere, ut tu ipse, o Rex, maximarum & amplissimarum victoriarum tuarum tropaea subruas? tuam memoriam metu & pusillanimitate itane foedes? ut quemadmodum primum ex strenuis Regibus nostris annotemus eum, qui effregit jugum Romani imperii, sub quo miserae Galliae tot annos languerant; sic te e diverso in perpetuum historia annotet fuisse primum, qui fractus ad mandatum Romae, ipse tuas laurus avulseris, marcidaveris palmas tuas, monumentaq; miserè dejeceris rerum tuarum fortiter gestarum, & beneficiorum tuorum erga regnum tuum & Lutetiam tuam, domicilium magni hujus Imperii, gloriam Europae, & mundi miraculum?
units.tr: This is a matter truly full of shame. What then shall we do? Must we go at once and have the column overthrown? What? Overthrown? Is there anyone in the world so unfortunate as to wish to suggest to you this abominable counsel, that you yourself, O King, should tear down the trophies of your greatest and most splendid victories? Would you so foully disfigure your memory through fear and pusillanimity? Just as we record first among our valiant Kings him who broke the yoke of the Roman empire, under which wretched Gaul had languished for so many years, so history, on the contrary, would record for ever that you were the first who, broken at Rome's command, tore away your own laurels, withered your palms, and miserably cast down the monuments of your bravely accomplished deeds and of your benefits to your kingdom and to your Paris, the home of this great empire, the glory of Europe and the wonder of the world.

units.la: Proh, quid amplius Generalis Iesuitarum optare posset? si magna acies Hispanica deducta a suis & suorum fede cimvirorum reliquis universa per muri labem ingrederetur Lutetiam, nonne initium ab effractione istius columnae facturi essent? Galliamne pati, o Rex, te Rege, te mandante maximam turpitudinem, facinusq; maximum quod ab insolentia Caesellana unquam subire posset?
units.tr: Alas, what more could the General of the Jesuits wish for? If a great Spanish army, led by his own men and by the loyal support of their fellow-conspirators, were to enter all together through a breach in the wall into Paris, would they not begin by breaking down that column? Would you, O King, while you are King and by your command, allow France to suffer the greatest disgrace and the greatest crime that any insolence of the Caesellani could ever inflict?

units.la: Si postridie felicis illius conversionis tuae, o Rex, in fanum Dionysii advenisset Angelus e caelo, qui tibi Lutetiam ostendens dixisset, Iesuitae praesidium Hispanicum, quod in magna illa urbe locaverunt, & quod in ea continent habendo conciones apud populum in gratia illius, hi soli impediunt ingressum tuum, desiderant te in ea omnes boni, ingredie-
units.tr: If on the day after that happy conversion of yours, O King, an angel had come down from heaven to the church of St Denis, showing you Paris and saying: "The Jesuits have placed a Spanish garrison in that great city, and by preaching sermons to the people in its favour, they alone hinder your entry; all good men long for you there; go in..."

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: ON THE PROPAGATION

units.la: ris tamen istis sceleratis invitis, et brevi; Post novem menses dabunt operam, ut trucidefris, sed non poterunt efficere: magnus ille Deus superne avertet illum, facietque ut confiteantur parricida nefariam Iesuitarum doctrinam & quotidianos eorum sermones contra te habitos, ipsum perduxisse, & impulliffe in cædem tuam: Dabit etiam Deus ut ista declaratio insuper scriptis & propria manu ipsorum comprobetur: Itaque omnes in exilium mittentur: tu vero septimo post anno restitues eos ad eversionem regni tui, & desolationem familiæ tuæ: fi (inquam) Angelus è cœlo hæc tibi prædixisset, o Rex, fuissesne pro vero habituros sermonem illum? Minime gentium pro culdubio: adeo postremum hoc caput à tua voluntate pendens tibi visum fuisset alienum. Vide tamen, fi placet, vide quam prope abfueris à perficiendo hoc malo, tam citò oblitus mali, quo affecerunt te, & quotidie possunt afficere homines isti, qui antiquos Reges nostros Rebelles vocant, quod sua diademata, coronas suas ad primum strepitum excommunicationum contra ipsos emissarum in solum non afflixerint; & qui furiosæ istius doctrinæ confessarium istud innumeris de populo persuaserunt, Regem defunctum nostrum Tyrannum & Rebellem extitisse: quæ res profecto ei cruentam mortem attulit.
units.tr: ...enter, though these wretches are unwilling, and soon. Within nine months they will take pains to have you slain, but they will not be able to do it. That great God above will turn them aside and bring it about that the parricide confesses that the Jesuits' impious teaching, and the daily sermons they delivered against you, led him on and drove him to your slaughter. God will also grant that this declaration is confirmed in writing and in their own hand. Thus they will all be sent into exile, and you, seven years afterwards, will restore them to the overthrow of your kingdom and the ruin of your family. If, I say, an angel from heaven had foretold these things to you, O King, would you have taken that account for true? Certainly not; this last point, which depends on your own will, would have seemed to you altogether alien. Yet see, if you please, see how near you came to bringing this evil about, so quickly have you forgotten the evil they have done to you, and which these men, who call our former kings rebels because they did not lose their diadems and crowns at the first noise of the excommunications issued against them, can do to you every day. These men have persuaded countless people of the common folk to hold to the confession of that mad doctrine, that our late king was a tyrant and a rebel, and this indeed brought him a bloody death.

units.la: Non ponis tibi, o Rex, ante oculos imaginem excelsam, pallentem, cogitabundam, tristem magni illius Principis, optimi tui fratris; ut erat quum affectus vulnere & sanguine madens, paternum studium testabatur tibi ad extremum usque halitum, amplexando te in media sua acie, tota madente lachrymis, & ultionem spirante?
units.tr: Do you not set before your eyes, O King, the lofty, pale, pensive and sorrowful image of that great prince, your best father, as he was when, wounded and dripping with blood, he bore witness to his paternal care for you to his last breath, embracing you in the midst of his battle line, all wet with tears and breathing vengeance?

units.la: In superis agit, beatus est, mortuus pro libertate patriæ, pro liberis ex captivitate liberandis: contemplatur actiones tuas. Quid? irrita facere te Arresta Parlamenti fui, facta contra parricidas ipsius, qui ipsum viventem cultro maftari curaverunt, mortuumque suis pugionibus confoderunt, proclamnando in universa Europa: Eodem die, quo nos Burdegalæ jubebat eijci, vita depulsus est: Ajunt, eum mandavisse ut ad S. Macarij compingeremur omnes ibidem jugulandi, nisi jugulatus fuisset prius? Non est unicus Iesuita, o Rex, corpus Iesuitarum est, Iesuitæ omnes, qui suis literis, annalibus; folennibusque in univerfa Europa decantant hunc triumphum. Europa autem? imo in universo terrarum orbe in suis coloniis, ubi nunc crudelia effecta suarum propositionum periculi plenarum offtentant, ubi tropæum statuunt cruentum induftum nostri defuncti Regis; superba, inquam, spolia primi in mundo Regis, quasi de cœlo tacti tonitrubus, quæ in Galliam vibrari curaverunt, ubi ante adventum ipsorum nullis unquam viribus extiterant.
units.tr: He acts among the blessed in heaven; he is happy, having died for the liberty of his country and for freeing his children from captivity; he looks upon your actions. What? Would you make void the decree of the Parlement, issued against his murderers, who had him stabbed with a knife while he was alive and finished him off with their daggers when he was dead, and who proclaimed throughout Europe: "On the same day that he ordered us to be expelled from Bordeaux, he was driven from life." They say he had ordered that we should all be shut up at St. Macarius to be butchered there, unless he himself had first been butchered? It is not a single Jesuit, O King; it is the whole body of Jesuits, all of whom proclaim this triumph throughout Europe in their letters, annals and festivals. Europe? Indeed, throughout the whole world, in their colonies, where they now display the cruel results of their dangerous propositions, where they set up a bloodied trophy of our late king. These are proud spoils, I say, of the first king in the world, as if he had been struck from heaven by thunderbolts, which they arranged to be hurled into France, where, before their arrival, they had never prevailed by any force.

units.la: An ergo placeret, o Rex, consolationem, quæ restat nobis eripere, & solam notam, & monimentum solum, quod nepotes nostri de cæde Regis defuncti, & Domini nostri defuncti habituri sunt?
units.tr: Would it then please you, O King, to snatch away from us the consolation that remains to us, and the only mark and the sole memorial which our descendants are to have of the slaughter of our late king and lord?

units.la: O miser Domine mi! o miser Princeps Domine mi! Si nihil aliud potui, hos saltem extremos fletus, has ultimas lacrymas humillimi fervi tui & fidelissimi subjecti habeas: forte etiam suspiria comitabuntur decies centies mille Gallorum me legentium, fi non hac ætate, at certe posterioribus. Cur enim singultus mei, cur mei gemitus non durarent tantum, quantum boni Galli in terra duraturi sunt?
units.tr: O my wretched Lord! O my wretched Prince and Lord! If I can do nothing else, at least accept these last tears, these final weepings of your most humble servant and most faithful subject. Perhaps sighs will also accompany them from a hundred thousand Frenchmen who read me, if not in this age, then certainly in later ones. For why should my sobs and my groans last no longer than the good Frenchmen on earth are going to last?

units.la: Si majores nostri, o Rex, venenatam istam ex communicationis doctrinam, & de potestate Regnorum transferendorum hausissent, magna hæc successio non fuisset ad te usque ventura; olim tuis majoribus avulsa effet. Exilium Iesuitarum est sceleratæ istius doctrinæ exitium: exitium vero doctrinæ istius, vita est & gloria & splendor regalis familiæ tuæ. Si qui contra apud te dixerint, eam videre humi prostratam cupiunt. Rem tenes: quod fi tenens non medicaberis, subruis ipse fundamenta regni tui, quæ tuum est confirmare.
units.tr: If our ancestors, O King, had imbibed this poisonous doctrine of excommunication and of the power to transfer kingdoms, this great succession would never have come down to you; it would long ago have been torn from your forebears. The exile of the Jesuits is the destruction of that wicked doctrine, and the destruction of that doctrine is the life, the glory and the splendour of your royal family. If anyone has said otherwise to you, they wish to see it lying prostrate on the ground. You hold the matter in your hands; if, holding it, you do not apply the remedy, you yourself will undermine the foundations of your kingdom, which it is your task to strengthen.

units.la: Magnanimus & generosus Regis animus non solum in bello spectatur, in principijs ferææ aciei accendens nobilitatem suam, fultus multiplicibus undequaque plumis, ut fit hoftibus conspicuus, proritans audaciam illorum & lanceárum silvam, quam mox fulmineo impetu protriturus est: sed magis adhuc elucet, o Rex, in magnis gravibusque negotijs regni consilio tractandis. Ibi prudentia opus est emicet: sed exterminandus omnis motus diffidendi, omnis creandæ molestiæ formido: hæc te indigna est, indigna Rege Gallia, etiamfi non effet id, quod es, Rex Gallia legem aliunde, quam à Deo non patitur. Vide, o Rex, quid id justum; vide, quid tibi, posteris tuis, & regno tuo utile: aliud ne spectes.
units.tr: A magnanimous and noble spirit in a king is seen not only in war, when he kindles his nobility at the head of the wild battle line, adorned with plumes on every side so that he is conspicuous to the enemy, provoking their boldness and the forest of lances which he will soon crush with a lightning rush. It shines even more, O King, in the handling of great and weighty affairs in the council of the realm. There prudence must shine forth; but every motion of distrust must be banished, every fear of stirring up trouble. This is unworthy of you, unworthy of a King of France, even if you were not what you are, since the King of France suffers no law from anyone but God. See, O King, what is just; see what is useful for you, your descendants and your kingdom. Do not look at anything else.

units.la: Ius est, ô Rex, ut Arresta Parlamenti tui, Parlamenti Galliae, mandentur executioni in Gallia: hic maxime regni tui vires. Quis ergo tibi auctor est, ô Rex; ut brachium externum ipse praecidas tibi? revera, mentitis nominibus Rex Philippus est, qui spirat, qui inflat, qui molitur. Frater tuus est, novi, sed consiliis periculosis utitur. Junius est, ambitiosus est, magnus est: scit Reginae Catharinae haereditatem à se detineri, hoc vermè arrosum fuisse animum patris ad morte decumbentis. Dum vixit, assentatus ipse sibi, fretus Iulij potestate: quum vero sensus ejus quod sibi coram magno domino, ram magno Iudice mox comparendum esset, horrorem attulit; tum inquisitionis illius tentationes, blanditiae Iesuitarum illius non potuerunt ipsum contra conscientiam ipsam, intra conscientiam suam defendere: necesse habuit loqui, necesse testari, & istam perturbationem, istam facem, ista tormenta dispositione testamentaria allevare. Verum tantum abest, ut hoc testamentum filius velit exequi, ut contra infinita, incredibilia consilia agitet: à Gallia inhibet cursum illius. Quam foret ipsi commodum, si haberet semper in visceribus magni hujus regni homines certos, promptos, acres, fortesque, exequendis omnibus optatis ipsius, quovis periculo? Quam commodum, si semper haberet exploratores adeo pervigiles, adeo audaces, adeo peritos dissimulandi arcani, ut quisquis sive Gallus, sive extraneus regnum conspiraturus, nunquam dubitet eos appellare? In aliis conventibus fieri potest, unus pro altero per errorem accedatur, proditio veniat. Sic fecit Barreria: si institutum in Iesuiticum solum retexisset, erat de te omnino actum. Quid unquam commiserunt similes Templarij in Gallia? Humiliati in Italia? Franciscani conventuales in Hispania? Finita quidem est potestas Regum, fateor: sed ita, si conjunctam habet prudentiam, virtutem in Principem principum. Quum magna culpa commissa est, admodum est difficile, plerumque possibile ut curetur. Quis putas, ô Rex, deinceps sit cogitaturus de consilio ullo contra os agitando, quam vis in regnum tuum, in caput tuum machinentur? quis porro actor esse velit? quis testis? quis judex? Exiliunt principio homines, ô Rex, qui improbis obsistunt: ibi se desertos vident, ubi domos suas à serpentibus circumclusas vident, qui aliquando umpentes liberos suos voraturi sunt, eo fit ut desperent omnes, eo animus abjicitur: tandem vero paulatim quisque flectitur, se quisque accommodat: ô vocem Regibus periculosissimam! Defunctus Rex in vivis esset, haberet quod diceret super hac re: hoc uno defectu eo devenit, quo tandem deductus est. Ex ejus exemplo, ô Rex, utilitate cape, etiam ex finitimorum exemplo: observa, unquam mne Carol. V. aut filius ejus, magni illi politici, in publica regni ipsa, infirmari siverunt aut percelli administros suos. Observa, an unquam homines admittunt, qui in suspicione apud se vocari possent. Etiamsi Majestas tua nihil spectaret amplius, in prima Iesuitarum institutione, ortu, progressum, locum, unde veniunt, eos tibi abominanda esse oporteret. Postquam vero horrenda effecta expertus es, quibus graviora hostes maneri optare nequeant: & ab ista exitiali & periculosa secta magno Arresto liberatus: quâ die parricidas tuos in regno tuo restituas, seditionem in populo tuo, factiones in provinciis, quae plus tranquillitatis ab exilio Iesuitarum, quam prius totos annos 30. experta sunt? Non vult tentari Deus: jam te bis, ô Rex, à cultro illorum vindicavit, circumdedit te tot bonis Praelatis Doctoribusque, tot doctis atque devotis Religiosis omnium ordinum plenitate, doctrina, obsequio, studio erga Majestatem tuam, millies aptioribus ad exaltanda nomen religione, nostra Catholica, quam sint homines isti imbuti hac exitiali haeresi, cujus fundamentum unum est, potestas mutandi regna, ad medii huic, & tradendi illi. Cur sperat ipse gratiam, quam tibi fecit divina bonitas, te è sepulchro, ex ulnis mortis educendo? ortis per eos optatae, appetitae, conjuratae, qui Galliam eodem feretro cum duobus suis tremis Regibus elatam sepultamque volunt? Non metuis, ô Rex, ne offendas eum, qui adationi vult esse providentiam suam, & sibi gratias haberi de bonitate & protectione? An tibi in dubium venit praesedisse ipsum magno illi consensu, magno Parlamento ius orbis terrarum augustissimo, consilia ineunti de rebus ad vitam sui Principis, & conservationem Regni pertinentibus? Quid? Hoc Arrestum à te infirmari? Et qui scis, ô rex, an illud fit in causa cur adhuc vivas? qui scis an Deus hoc uti voluerit ad te in vita servandum? hoc uti propugnaculo adversus impetus illorum? potesne pervestigare judicia & arcana ejus? an nescis magnas abyssos esse?
units.tr: It is right, O King, that the decrees of your Parlement, the Parlement of France, be carried out in France; here lies the greatest strength of your kingdom. Who, then, is the adviser who persuades you, O King, to cut off your own external arm? In truth, under false names it is King Philip who breathes, who inflates, who schemes. He is your brother, I know, but he uses dangerous counsels. Junius is ambitious and great; he knows that the inheritance of Queen Catherine is kept from him by himself, and this worm gnawed at the mind of your father as he lay dying. While he lived, he flattered himself, relying on the power of Julius; but when the thought that he must soon appear before the great Lord and the great Judge brought him horror, then the temptations of that inquisition and the blandishments of those Jesuits could not defend him against his own conscience. He had to speak, he had to bear witness, and to relieve that disturbance, that torch, those torments, he resorted to a testamentary disposition. But so far is the son from wishing to carry out this testament that he pursues countless, incredible plans, and holds its course back from France. How advantageous it would be for him if he always had in the heart of this great kingdom men who were reliable, ready, keen and brave, to carry out all his wishes at any risk! How advantageous if he always had spies so watchful, so bold, so skilled at concealing secrets, that whoever, whether a Frenchman or a foreigner, was about to conspire against the realm would never hesitate to approach them! In other gatherings it can happen that by mistake one man is approached in place of another, and betrayal comes. So it was with Barreria; if he had revealed the plot against the Jesuit institute alone, it would have been all over for you. What ever did the Templars in France, or the Humiliati in Italy, or the Conventual Franciscans in Spain, commit that was similar? The power of kings is indeed limited, I admit, but only so; if it has prudence joined to it, a virtue in the Prince of princes. When a great fault has been committed, it is very difficult, though usually possible, to cure it. Who do you think, O King, will henceforth dare to propose any plan against those who plot against your kingdom and your person? Who would wish to be the agent? Who the witness? Who the judge? At first, O King, those men who oppose the wicked are driven into exile; there they see themselves abandoned, and they see their houses surrounded by serpents, which will one day break in and devour their children. So everyone despairs, and so the spirit is cast down; finally, however, each gradually bends, each accommodates himself. O most dangerous voice to kings! If the late King were alive, he would have something to say about this matter; by this one failing he came to the point to which he was at last led. From his example, O King, take profit, and from the example of your neighbours too. Observe whether Charles V or his son, those great statesmen, ever allowed their ministers to be weakened or struck down in the public affairs of the realm. Observe whether they ever admitted men who could be called suspect in their eyes. Even if your Majesty considered nothing further, the first institution of the Jesuits, their origin, their progress, and the place from which they come, ought to make them abominable to you. But since you have experienced their horrible deeds, such as enemies could not wish worse, and have been freed by the great Arrest from this deadly and dangerous sect, on what day will you restore your murderers to your kingdom? Will you restore sedition among your people and factions in the provinces, which, since the Jesuits' exile, have enjoyed more tranquillity than in all the thirty years before? God does not wish to be tested. Twice already, O King, he has rescued you from their knife; he has surrounded you with so many good prelates and teachers, so many learned and devoted religious of every order, full of learning, obedience and zeal for your Majesty, a thousand times better suited to exalting the name of religion, our Catholic religion, than these men, who are steeped in this deadly heresy, whose one foundation is the power of changing kingdoms, to take from one and hand to another. Why should he hope for the grace which divine goodness has shown you, in drawing you out of the tomb and from the arms of death, by means of those who desire, seek and conspire, and who want France carried out on the same bier, and buried together with her two trembling kings? Do you not fear, O King, lest you offend him who wishes his providence to be acknowledged, and who wishes thanks to be given to him for his goodness and protection? Or do you doubt that he presided over that great and most august agreement of the Parlement of the whole world, which deliberated on matters pertaining to the life of its prince and the preservation of the realm? What? Will you weaken this Arrest? And how do you know, O King, whether it is the cause of your still being alive? How do you know whether God has willed to use it to keep you alive, as a bulwark against their assaults? Can you search out his judgments and his secrets? Or do you not know that the abysses are great?

units.la: Deus ille Optimus Maximus, qui e coelo novit figmenta, hypocrisin, venenum, quod in pectore Jesuitae fovent: Deus ille maximus, qui non vult cnnsilium perpetuum, essentiale, inventis ipsorum radicatum, de evertenda gloria corona hujus atque monarchia: det tibi gratiam, o Rex, ut bene ab amicis Jesuitarum discernas amicos Alexandri: & exsequutionum jubendo magni illius Arresti tui, probes toti Christiano orbi, te aeque tibi bene prudenterque cavere posse a tectis, animis, cuniculisque tectis tuorum hostium, ac fortiter magnoque animo frangere, dissipare, & perdere copias, & vires apertas ipsorum, &c.
units.tr: May that most good and greatest God, who knows from heaven the fictions, hypocrisy and poison that the Jesuits nurse in their breasts, and who does not wish the lasting, essential plan of their inventions, rooted in the overthrow of this crown's glory and monarchy, to succeed, grant you the grace, O King, to distinguish well the friends of Jesuits from the friends of Alexander. And in ordering the execution of your great Arrest, may you prove to the whole Christian world that you can wisely and prudently guard yourself against the hidden snares, minds and covered tunnels of your enemies, and that you can with courage and a great spirit break, scatter and destroy their open forces and strength, etc.

units.la: Accidit autem opportune pro Jesuitis, ut Anno Christi, 1603. Rex ex Mediomatricibus revertens, per Virodunum iter faceret. Tunc enim ab Academicis Jesuitis rogatur, ut interdicto decreti Parisiensis, qui in Virodunensi literario versarentur, eximantur, quod ditionis Gallicae non sit Virodunum. Rex Arresto non comprehendi respondet, ea tamen lege, ut qui in Pontamusina Schola literis dant operam Virodunum redeant, in Galliam reversionis dat fiduciam, si in posterum sint fidi clientes, Regem illis fore propitium.
units.tr: It happened, opportunely for the Jesuits, that in the year of Christ 1603 the King, returning from the Mediomatrici, was travelling through Verdun. The Jesuits who taught at the academy there then asked that, since Verdun is not under French jurisdiction, those studying at the Verdun college be exempted from the interdict of the Parisian decree. The King replied that they were not caught by the Arrest, on the condition that those who studied letters at the school of Pont-à-Mousson should return to Verdun. He gave them confidence of returning to France: if in future they proved faithful clients, the King would be favourable to them.

units.la: Ut haec secunda aura illis affulsit, deliberatum a Virodunensibus & Pontamusinis Jesuitis de Rege adeundo & alloquendo. Hebdomada igitur magna ante Pascha, Ignatius, Armandus, Castellerius, Broffardus & Turrius a foda litio misi opportune adsunt feria S. in Coena Domini. Rex de more & mystico ritu maiorum, pauperum pedes abluit, detergit & exosculatur, cuilibet cum regali epulo 13. nummis argenteis attributis.
units.tr: As soon as this second breeze blew upon them, the Jesuits of Verdun and Pont-à-Mousson resolved to approach and address the King. So in the great week before Easter, Ignatius, Armandus, Castellerius, Broffardus and Turrius, sent from ..., arrived opportunely on the holy day of the Lord's Supper. The King, according to the custom and mystic rite of his ancestors, washed, wiped and kissed the feet of the poor, giving each of them 13 silver coins together with the royal meal.

units.la: Post prandium, Varanneo Jesuitis ad regium colloquium aditum facienti, Ignatius in haec verba loquutus esse dicitur. Cum primum avito regno, numinis stupendis auspiciis, potiri, Rex Christianissime, tibi caelitus tributum, summas in te virtutes, quibus Reges & Principes omnes, qui antecessere, longe superas, agnovimus, ac potissimum regiae Celsitudinis tesseram & summum ornamentum, maximam virtutum Clementiam, qua perduellium gravissimas offensas condonasti, eademque in nos quoque aequaliter usurum confidimus. Sed o saecularium rerum spes lubricae, in primordiis regni, cum omnium nostrorum sodalium vota & obsequia in te conspirarent, feralis casus & nullo non praecognitus contigit, quo veluti ingenti turbine perculsi, a te non solum alienati, sed extorres facti sumus: quocunque tamen terrarum sparsi fuimus, nec in te Principem nostrum, nec in patriam ingenium, amorem & debitum obsequium, nec spem tuae manifestudinis exuimus, quamvis congerie omnium scelerum malevoli nos apud te cumulaverint, hac una spe securi, nostram innocentiam, aliquando discussis nebulis famae insultantium, tibi exploratam fore confidimus, rati nostrarum arumnarum tempus esse medelam. Fiducia illa tuae clementiae antea obscurior, ut hunc regni angulum tuo aspectu illuminati, liquidius affulsit, & ad tua genua advolvere cogit, rogamus ne mora tuae gratiae beneficium diutius protrahas, cum nobis nihil sit acerbius, quam illa excludi, finibusque patriis semotos, quibus alienas & peregrinas gentes juvamus, non posse ingenio & industria natalem Galliam prosequi. Heu, nimis exploratum nobis est, apud te longe alios quam simus, insimulatos habitosque fuisse, hoc est omnium flagitiorum colluvie contaminatissimos, regni & omnibus Ordinibus exitiales: gentem nostram ut novam & nova molientem, Gallicanae Ecclesiae adversam, denique quaecunque deterrima livor & impietas comminisci potuere, in nos omnibus diris & devotionibus congestum. Sed sodalitia nostra non semel a provis Regibus Galliae, & Curia placitis probata sunt, ut quae longe antea a Pontificibus max. Christianae Reip. salutaria sancita sint; ex quibus tanquam ex instructissima officina, adversus bacchantes haereses tela promi possint. Privatae constitutiones contubernii nostri, quaecunque nobis falso tribuuntur, ut divinis praeceptis & mutuae dilectioni proflua discentanea distincte prohibent. Quod si vera sunt quibus falso inquinamur, nostra Societas non [illegible, ~20 letters]is non solùm ad salutem animarum esse non potest, sed ad præsentissimum exitium. At [illegible, ~10 letters]uis credat, ingenio & rerum scitu dignissimarum scientiâ pollentes homines, ultrò se in societatem nostram dedere, quæ, ut caussantur malevoli, omnium facinorum sententia & vorago: num verò proximum est qui salutem quærunt, in eum non appellere portum, in quo per tot scelera certum sit animæ naufragium. At inquiunt, nos penitissimo obsequio generali nostro devinctissimos, eaque cathena votorum, ut ei in omnibus & per omnia mus audientes.
units.tr: After dinner, when Varanneus had gained the Jesuits access to a royal audience, Ignatius is said to have spoken in these words: "When you first came into possession of your ancestral kingdom, under stupendous auspices of the divine power, most Christian King, sent to you from heaven, we recognised in you the highest virtues, which far surpass all the kings and princes who went before you, and above all the badge and highest ornament of royal majesty, the greatest clemency of virtue, by which you pardoned the gravest offences of traitors; and we trust that you will use the same clemency towards us equally. But, O hopes of worldly affairs, how slippery you are! At the beginning of your reign, when the wishes and obedience of all our companions were united in you, a deadly event occurred, foreseen by nobody, by which, as if struck by a huge whirlwind, we were not only estranged from you but made exiles. Wherever we have been scattered across the lands, however, we have not lost our loyalty, our love and our due obedience towards you, our Prince, nor towards our country, nor our hope of your clemency. Although malicious men have heaped upon us before you a heap of every crime, we trust that, secure in this one hope, our innocence will at last be made clear to you once the clouds of rumour that insult us are dispersed; for we think the time for our remedy has come for our troubles. That trust in your clemency, which was formerly rather obscure, has now shone out more clearly, now that this corner of your kingdom is lit by your sight, and it compels us to throw ourselves at your knees. We ask that you not delay the benefit of your grace any longer, since nothing is more bitter to us than to be shut out from it, and, removed from our native land, we cannot serve our native France with our talent and industry, though we help foreign and alien peoples. Alas, it is only too well known to us that before you we have been accused and considered to be far other than we are: that is, most polluted by a heap of every crime, destructive of the kingdom and of all its orders, a people who are new and plot new things, hostile to the Gallican Church; in short, with every foul accusation that envy and impiety could devise heaped upon us. But our fellowships have more than once been approved by the wise kings of France and by the decisions of the Court, since they were long ago sanctioned by the supreme Pontiffs as salutary to the Christian commonwealth; from them, as from a well-stocked workshop, weapons may be brought forth against raging heresies. The private constitutions of our society, whatever is falsely attributed to us, clearly forbid, as contrary to divine precepts and mutual love, the things which are said. But if the things with which we are falsely stained were true, our Society would not only be unable to serve the salvation of souls, but would be for the most immediate destruction. Yet men of learning and of the most worthy knowledge of things voluntarily give themselves over to our society, which, as the malicious claim, is the sentence and whirlpool of every crime. Surely those who seek salvation do not make for the nearest harbour, in which by so many crimes the shipwreck of the soul is certain? But they say that we are bound by the deepest general obedience, and by that chain of vows, so that we obey him in all things and through all things."

units.la: Non abnuimus, nos ut membra capiti nostro penitissimè obsequi, sed [illegible, ~8 letters]egibus, magistratibus & politico regimini minùs esse obsequentes non prohibemur, quin ipso adigimur & Apostolico præcepto, quo devijs & minùs recte dominus subditos ob[illegible, ~3 letters]mperare necesse est. Adijciunt, venari nos et inescare ad sodalitium nostrum ex patriis similijs selectissimos adolescentes, ut his accitis hereditatis suæ ad nos fiat accessio.
units.tr: We do not deny that we obey our head most deeply, as members do, but we are not forbidden to be less obedient to kings, magistrates and the civil government; indeed we are compelled to this by the apostolic precept, by which it is necessary that the rulers of subjects who go astray or do not rule rightly be obeyed. They add that we hunt and lure the most select young men from their native families into our fellowship, so that, these being summoned, an accession of inheritance may come to us.

units.la: Qui [illegible, ~3 letters]c de nobis fabulantur, minùs recte & accuratè privatas nostras leges noverunt, quæ verissimè distinguunt, ne quemlibet ulla arte ad institutum nostrum pellicriamus, divino iramini cætera relinquentes: abundè munus nostrum implevisse credimus, si juvenes re[illegible, ~2 letters]è & probè in Scholis nostris doceantur: Vel exemplis hoc liquet, in Gallia nos non esse heredipetas, cùm ex nulla gente instituti nostri Professores sint quàm Galli; Lutetianum, quod in urbe regia ita proclamatur ab invidis fuisse opulentum, coacervatis Claromontani Episcopi & præsidum S. Andreæ & Hannequini pijs largitionibus, vix tria millia librarum annui reditûs adæquat. Quid tantillum illud ad tot Professorum in omnibus scientiis centurias? Ne magno Regi in tot publicis negotijs longior Oratio tædio aut [illegible, ~2 letters]mno sit, uno verbo tuam illam nulli negatam clementiam deprecamur, nos, qui tui indi[illegible, ~2 letters]næ sumus, Hispanis, Italis et Germanis, cæterarumque gentium commilitonibus nostris, ga te inofficiosiores esse nolumus, nec eam tibi non præstare fiduciam, vel cum præsenti itæ discrimine, quàm illi Regibus Principibusque gentilitijs præstant. Sacra tempora, ipsi Christi, quæ nunc colitur, lugubris recordatio, nobis æqua postulantibus patrocinari [illegible, ~2 letters]dentur; sanguis ab eo in ara crucis pro noxijs mortalibus ultrò effusus, ad indulgen[ illegible, ~2 letters]um nobis concitat. Tantâ gratiâ indignos nos fatemur, sed concessum indultumque velis [illegible, ~2 letters] e Christo, in cujus nomine magis de ejus gratia, quàm de meritis nostris confidentes, no[illegible, ~2 letters]ra hæc postulata facimus.
units.tr: Those who talk such nonsense about us know our private laws less accurately and carefully. Those laws very truly forbid us to entice anyone into our institute by any art, leaving the rest to divine providence. We believe we have fully performed our office if the young men are taught well and properly in our schools. This is clear from examples: that in France we are not fortune-hunters, since our professors are drawn from no nation more than from the French. The Lutetian college, which in the royal city is proclaimed by our envious critics to be wealthy, is scarcely equal to three thousand pounds of annual income, even with the pious gifts of the Bishop of Clermont and of the presidents of Saint-André and Hannequin added together. What is that tiny sum against so many hundreds of professors in all the sciences? That the great King may not be wearied by a longer speech amid so many public affairs, in a single word we beg for that clemency which is denied to no one. We, who are your subjects, wish not to be less dutiful towards you than the Spaniards, Italians and Germans, our fellow soldiers, and the other nations; nor do we want to deny you that trust, even in the present danger, which they show to their native kings and princes. The holy season, and the sad memory of Christ himself whom we now honour, let them plead for us, as we ask fair things; the blood which he freely poured out on the altar of the cross for guilty mortals moves us to ask for pardon. We confess that we are unworthy of so great a grace, but if you are willing to grant this indulgence, we make these requests, trusting in the name of Christ more in his grace than in our merits.

units.la: Postquam dicendi finem fecit Ignatius, Rex pauca hæc respondit; Nihilâ Se[ illegible, ~2 letters]itu Parisiensi incogitato in Iesuitas pronunciatum esse, nullo etiam se in eos ferri odio, [illegible, ~2 letters]dum in aliquem mortalium; jubet verbis enunciata scripto exarata sibi tradi. Habe[illegible, ~2 letters]ant illi codicillum recitatæ orationis in promptu, quem ut Rex accepit, Vil[illegible, ~2 letters]regio tradit, præcepitque Ignatianis, ut in aula solennia Paschæ peragerent.
units.tr: When Ignatius had made an end of speaking, the King replied briefly with these few words: that nothing had been pronounced against the Jesuits by the Parisian decree without consideration, and that he himself was moved by no hatred against them, or against any mortal. He ordered that what had been spoken be handed to him in writing. They had a little codicil of the speech they had recited at hand; as soon as the King received it, he handed it to Villeroy, and he ordered the Ignatians to celebrate the solemnities of Easter at court.

units.la: Postridie Dominicæ Resurrectionis admissis in lararium, non levis be[illegible, ~2 letters]evolentiæ specimen dedit, palám testatus, toto regno esse reduces non solùm [illegible, ~2 letters]cupere, sed eorum opera etiam uti velle. Ignatio dat in mandatis, ut Lutetiæ [illegible, ~2 letters]um Cotoneo ad se veniat.
units.tr: On the day after the Lord's Resurrection, admitted into the chapel, the King gave no small proof of his goodwill, openly declaring that he wished not only for the return of the exiles to the whole kingdom, but also wished to make use of their services. He gave Ignatius instructions to come to him at Paris together with Cotoneus.

units.la: Paulò post cùm Rex & Regina per Lotharingiam iter faciunt ac Nan[illegible, ~2 letters]i divertunt, sororem Principes que Lotharingos invisuri, Iesuitæ Regiæ pollî[illegible, ~2 letters]rationis memores, cunctatione non amplius opus esse arbitrantur, dum enim [illegible, ~2 letters]calescit ferrum tundendum, ut vulgò dicitur, Regem adeunt, rogant, urgent [illegible, ~2 letters]er se & alios: Fronto Ducæus & Richomus apologeticis libellis de obiectis [illegible, ~2 letters] iminibus sodalitium suum excusant purgantque, quàm sint regno necessarij [illegible, ~2 letters]d iuventutis Christianæ educationem, stirpitusque eradicandas hæreses præ[illegible, ~2 letters]icant.
units.tr: Shortly afterwards, when the King and Queen made their journey through Lorraine and lodged at Nancy, the Jesuits, mindful of the King's political shrewdness and of the Lorraine princes whom the king's sister was to visit, judged that there was no longer any need for delay. For while the iron is hot, as the common saying goes, it must be struck; so they approached the King, asking and urging on their own behalf and on behalf of others. Fronton Ducaeus and Richôme, in apologetic pamphlets, excused and defended their society against the objections raised against it, and showed how necessary they were to the kingdom for the education of Christian youth and for rooting out heresies utterly.

units.la: Pontificio legato deprecatore utuntur, nec ille parûm negotium matura[ illegible, ~2 letters]it, æmulorumque molitiones irritas fecit. Clementis quoque Pontificis Rom[ illegible, ~2 letters]tercessio, cui Rex nihil unquam negatum esse voluit, Iesuitarum caussam ve[illegible, ~2 letters]ementer promovit.
units.tr: They used a Papist legate as intercessor, and he, who was no little involved in the business, brought it to a timely conclusion and rendered the rivals' schemes void. The intercession of Pope Clement also, to whom the King wished nothing ever to be refused, powerfully advanced the cause of the Jesuits.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: ON THE PROPAGATION

units.la: Postliminio reversuris in Galliam plurimi obluctantur, dicentes, vim Arreito & pyramidi fieri: illis regno & urbe receptis, exitiq; monimentum altissimo vertice fastigiatum & literatum funditus destruendum diruendumq;: standum esse rebus iudicatis: nihil in eos incogitanter, invide & malevole decretum: obsisco everso Senatus Consultum labi & corruere: infirmatione rerum iudicatarum regna convelli: Senatum Parisiensem caeteris qui sunt in Gallia praestare, cum ille olim unus esset, a quo universum regnum ius acciperet, atque hanc gloriam sibi privatim vindicasse, ut sit Parium Franciae Senatus: isto ariete non solum pyramidem illam, flagitiorum proscriptionis tabellariam, sed totam Parlamenti machinam concuti: a longe plura adversus Frontonem, Richomum & Iesuitas omnes obsciebantur Regi.
units.tr: Many object to the Jesuits returning to France by right of postliminy. They say that violence would be done to the Arrêt and to the pyramid: once the Jesuits were restored to kingdom and city, the monument of their expulsion, crowned with its lofty summit and inscribed, would have to be utterly torn down and demolished, and the rulings already made must stand. Nothing had been decreed against them carelessly, spitefully or with ill will. If the decree of the Senate were overturned, it would collapse and fall, and the kingdoms would be shaken by the invalidating of judgments already rendered. The Parisian Senate, they said, surpasses all the others in France, since it was once the only body from which the whole kingdom received its law; and it has claimed this glory for itself alone, so that it is the Senate of the peers of France. By this battering ram, they argued, not only that pyramid, the register of the crimes of proscription, but the whole machinery of the Parlement would be shaken. Far more was being cried out to the King against Fronto, Richeome and all the Jesuits.

units.la: Nihilominus Rex, ut sibi uni redditum suum in Galliam deberent Ignatiani, edixit, ut Tholosae, Auxis, apud Garites, Ruthenos, Burdegalae, Petrogorij, Ratiasci, Turnoni, Albenati & Bitteris, ubi antea precario agebant, perpetuo & quiete illis esse liceret: Divione praeterea & Lugduni antiquas sedes repetere, & novas Flexiae instituere, vel in regia natalitia, in qua Rex conceptus acnatus est.
units.tr: Nevertheless the King, so that the Ignatians should owe their return to France to him alone, issued an edict that they might be allowed to live peacefully and permanently in Toulouse, Auch, among the people of Gaures, Rodez, Bordeaux, Périgueux, Riasc, Tournon, Albenas and Béziers, where they had previously lived on sufferance. In addition they might return to their old seats at Dijon and Lyon, and found new ones at La Flèche, or at the royal birthplace where the King was conceived and born.

units.la: Admissi sunt autem & recepti in Galliam non simpliciter, sed sequentibus conditionibus. Primo, Ne ulla Collegia in Civitatibus Regni, aut Provinciis Regi subiectis, sine expressa Regis permissione instituant, sub poena amissionis omnium privilegiorum, & beneficij huius, ex mera Regis gratia ipsis concessi.
units.tr: The Jesuits were admitted and received into France, however, not simply but on the following conditions. First, that they should not set up any colleges in the cities of the kingdom, or in provinces subject to the King, without the express permission of the King, under penalty of losing all privileges and this favour, granted to them by the King's sheer grace.

units.la: Secundo, ut omnes Iesuitae in Gallia natione Galli sint, nec quemquam externorum, seu alterius nationis in Collegia sua admittant aut recipiant, sine Regis peculiari permissu; peregrinis si qui iam inter ipsos inveniantur, omnibus a se dimissis. Avenionensem tamen & Vencienfem Comitatum verbo externorum vel peregrinorum non comprehendi.
units.tr: Second, that all Jesuits in France should be French by nation, and that they should not admit or receive into their colleges anyone who is a foreigner or of another nation, without the King's special permission; and that any foreigners already found among them should be dismissed. The county of Avignon and the Venaissin, however, is not included under the word foreigners or aliens.

units.la: Tertio, ut semper aliquem habeant natione Gallum, qui Regi a sacris concionibus esse, & de omnibus negotijs rationem totius Societatis nomine ipsi reddere possit.
units.tr: Third, that they should always keep someone of French nation who may be the King's preacher at court and who can render account to him of all affairs in the name of the whole Society.

units.la: Quarto, ut omnes iam admissi, vel in posterum forsan admittendi, purum praestent iusiurandum, eoq; se obstringant, nihil se moliturös, quod in perniciem Regis, vel Regni salutisq; publicae vergere possit: cuius iurisiurandi formulam iuridici Praetores ad Cancellarium mittant: qui iusiurandum detrectaverint, regno protinus extorres sint.
units.tr: Fourth, that all who have been admitted, or who may in future be admitted, should take a pure oath and bind themselves by it to attempt nothing that could tend to the ruin of the King or the public welfare of the kingdom. The judicial praetors are to send the formula of this oath to the Chancellor. Whoever refuses the oath is to be banished from the kingdom at once.

units.la: Quinto, ne quid bonorum immobilium, sive emptionis, sive dationis nomine, ad se transferant, nec ab illis etiam accipiant, qui transitum ad Societatem suam faciant, sed haeredibus legitimis id omne relinquant.
units.tr: Fifth, that they should not transfer to themselves any immovable goods, whether by purchase or by gift, nor accept them from those who pass over to their Society, but leave all of it to lawful heirs.

units.la: Sexto, ut legibus statutisq; Regni, sicut reliqui omnes clerici, libenter se subiiciant.
units.tr: Sixth, that they should willingly submit to the laws and statutes of the kingdom, like all other clergy.

units.la: Septimo, ne quid vel Ecclesiasticorum vel Politicorum negotiorum suscipiant tractentq;, in praeiudicium Episcoporum, Capitulorum & Academiarum Regni, sed ordinariis constitutionibus per omnia se conformes gerant.
units.tr: Seventh, that they should not take up or handle any affairs, ecclesiastical or political, to the prejudice of the bishops, the chapters and the universities of the kingdom, but should conduct themselves in every respect in conformity with the ordinary constitutions.

units.la: Octavo, ut nulla Sacramenta, & nec poenitentiae quidem, aliis quam suis Ordinis hominibus administrent, sine permissu Archiepiscoporum & Curiarum, quibus singuli subiecti sint.
units.tr: Eighth, that they should administer no sacraments, not even that of repentance, to anyone except men of their own Order, without the permission of the archbishops and the courts to which each of them is subject.

units.la: Nono, ut habeant unde vivere & sustentare se possint, non permissum ipsis solum est a Rege, uti frui redditibus, quorum ante haec tempora participes fuerunt, sine ullo impedimento, sed & de proventu annuo 1000. coronatorum ac 20. annos in urbe Parisiensi, ipsis liberalissime prospectum est, literis super hac re scriptis & Sigillo regio munitis. cestituti suis penatibus Ignatiani ludisq; literariis, in praescriptis urbibus, sensim se effundunt, incq; dies vires maiores acquirunt. Avarici Biturigum etiam, Rothomagi, Ambiani, Rhodonibus antiqua Collegia repetunt, ac tum illa, tum Aedilium Decurionumq; intercessione nova condenda impetrant. Lutetiae vero media Academia, non Scholam Claromontanam, in qua docere non fuit permissum, sed sacrarium et secessum seniorum Ludovici indigetis titulo insignitum, Borbonij senioris Cardinalis sumptibus conditum, repetunt.
units.tr: Ninth, so that they should have the means to live and to support themselves: the King has not only permitted them to use and enjoy, without any hindrance, the revenues of which they were partakers before these times, but has also most generously provided them with an annual income of 1,000 crowns for twenty years in the city of Paris, by letters written on this matter and sealed with the royal seal. Restored to their household gods, the Ignatians and their schools are gradually spreading out in the aforesaid cities, and daily they gain greater strength. The Jesuits of Bourges, Rouen, Amiens and Rennes also seek back their old colleges, and by the intercession of both the town councillors and the aldermen they obtain permission to found new ones. At Paris, indeed, they seek back the middle Academy, not the Clermont School, where they were not permitted to teach, but a shrine and retreat for the elders, bearing the title of Louis the Saint and founded at the expense of the elder Cardinal de Bourbon.

units.la: Quia vero pyramis, in memoriam Iesuitarum ejectionis ex Gallia, eiusq; inscriptio Iesuitas singulariter mordebat, ideo ex singulari Regis clementia et gratia in Galliam iterum admissi et recepti, quiescere noluerunt, donec everterent onem huius columnae sive pyramidis a Rege impetrarent. Hac igitur destructa, libellus quidam lingua Gallica prodiit, in quo per insignem prosopopoeiam columna ipsa metaloquens introducitur: Comprime os tuum Perverse, ut lapides loquantur, attendite vero vos ex Gallis meliores quicunque, cum alii aures ad audiendum non habeant. Sum quod non eram antea, Pyramis nempe seu lapis mutus, vos ad audiendum excitans, et columna auditu sensibusq; aliis destituta, quos vobis jam excitare conabor. Loquor jam, non existens amplius, et cum adhuc essem, loquente me nemo audijt: Debonitate et gratia plus conqueror, quam de saevitia et crudelitate, ut ijsdem medijs everter iterum quibus disjecta sum, et in memoriam hominum excitem id, quod de terra delatum est, per justitiam elevata ego, per misericordiam destructa et in nihilum redacta sum; misericordiam autem dico intempestivam, cum aeque misericordiae adversum sit omnibus noscere, quam gratiam declarare nemini. Per parricidam prognata ego, eadem ratione, qua bonae ex malis moribus leges natae sunt, surrexi, ictus cultri, in faciem maximae conspicui in hoc orbe Regis, delatus, me in maxime conspicuam hujus orbis faciem statuit, sed videte quaeso rerum humanarum fluxibilitatem: Ego quae aliquot perdurare et numerare debeam secula, vix lustrum vidi unicum: Quid posteros dicturos existimem, cum viderint me fundatoribus meis superesse non valuisse? Quis non mirabitur oblivionem tam cito traditum esse, quod in monumentum perpetuae recordationis excitatum erat? Et quis rebus mundanis fidei aliquid habebit in posterum, cum et firmissima consilia, mutationibus subjecta deprehendantur? quod marmor quaeso tam solidum reperietur, ut tempori non cedat? quae consilia tam firma sint, ut robur mihi perpetuum conferant? cui credat gypsypio, tantam inesse vim ut vel exigua ejus particula, tot lapides marmoreos demoliri et dissipare queat? Vix equidem habetenus Cottonij sive Gosypij virtus omnibus innotuit. Verum dicite mihi quaeso vos, qui Cottonij sectamini Societatem, et Iesuitarum vobis nomen vendicatis, quando Galliae regno tanta officia exhibuistis, ut tantam promererigratiam potuissetis? Condemnati haud ita pridem fuistis, rectene an secus, dicite: si minus recte, iniquequidem vobis cum actum est, cum in exilium ejiceremini: At si recte, sententia equidem semel pronunciata, quomodo mutata est? injuria prosecto nobis nulla facta est, quid enim ad hoc promerendum, unquam a vobis intermissum fuit? Certe non juventutem solum corrumpere, sed et adultiores aduniversalem aliquam sedionem inflammare cordi vobis et curae semper fuit, quod quidem usque adeo notum et manifestum omnibus est, ut nullo ullius Cottonianae eloquentiae colore et fuco obliterari obfuscari possit: Quod igitur reverti in Galliam estis, misericordiae Regis unice acceptum referre debetis, qui vel propriae salutis immemor, vos in Majestatis suae perniciem ex exilio revocavit, sed redire tamen absque peculiari facinore religio vobis fuit, nec aulam ingredi regiam, quam per interitus mei porta voluistis. Verum enimvero quid vulgo praedicari audio, Galliae Iesuitas Regno prodesse? Certe, ut opinor, propter nova hujus sectae religionem. Sed quid? propius ne ad Catholicam religionem accedunt quam Sorbonistae, a quibus haereticorum sunt adscripti numero? Ad offensionem equidem potius quam ad aedificationem eos comparatos dixerim: At informandis puerorum ingenijs aptiores sunt quam tot Collegium per universam Galliam Rectores. Quid audio? praestantiores ne ex illorum Collegijs
units.tr: Because the pyramid, erected in memory of the expulsion of the Jesuits from France, and its inscription bit the Jesuits especially hard, therefore, having been admitted and received again into France by the singular clemency and grace of the King, they were unwilling to rest until they obtained from the King the overthrow of this column or pyramid. So, when it had been destroyed, a certain little book appeared in the French language, in which the column itself is introduced speaking, by a remarkable prosopopoeia: Restrain your mouth, perverse one, so that the stones may speak; but you, the best of the French, pay attention, since others have no ears for hearing. I am what I was not before, namely a pyramid or mute stone, rousing you to hear, and a column deprived of hearing and of the other senses, whom I shall now try to rouse for you. I now speak, though I no longer exist, and while I was still standing no one heard me speak. I complain more of kindness and grace than of cruelty and savagery, that I should be overthrown again by the same means by which I was cast down, and that what was brought down from the earth should be brought back to the memory of men. I was raised up by justice and destroyed and reduced to nothing by mercy; but I call it untimely mercy, since it is equally contrary to mercy to acknowledge everyone as to declare grace to no one. Born of a parricide, I rose in the same way that good laws are born out of bad morals. Struck by the blade of a knife, aimed at the face of the King most conspicuous in this world, I was set up in the most conspicuous face of this world. But consider, I beg you, the fickleness of human affairs: I, who ought to have lasted and endured for many ages, have scarcely seen a single lustrum. What do I suppose posterity will say, when they see that I was not able to outlive my founders? Who will not marvel that a thing set up as a monument of perpetual remembrance was so quickly handed over to oblivion? And who will henceforth have any trust in worldly affairs, when even the firmest counsels are found subject to change? What marble, I ask, will be found so solid that it does not yield to time? What counsels are so firm that they can give me perpetual strength? Who would believe that there is such power in gypsum that even a tiny particle of it can pull down and scatter so many marble stones? Hitherto indeed the power of Cotton or Gosyp has scarcely become known to everyone. But tell me, I beg you, you who follow the sect of Cotton and claim for yourselves the name of Jesuits: what services have you rendered to the kingdom of France, that you could have earned so great a grace? Not long ago you were condemned. Tell me whether that was rightly done or not. If not rightly, then indeed you were treated unjustly when you were cast into exile; but if rightly, once a sentence has been pronounced, how has it been changed? Surely no injury has been done to us, for what has ever been left undone by you to earn this? Certainly to corrupt not only the young but also the adults, and to kindle some universal sedition, has always been dear to your heart and your care, which is so well known and manifest to all that it cannot be obscured or disguised by any colour or varnish of Cottonian eloquence. Since you have returned to France, you ought to ascribe this solely to the mercy of the King, who, forgetful even of his own safety, recalled you from exile to his own ruin and that of his majesty. Yet you did not scruple to return without some special crime, and you did not want to enter the royal court except by the gate of my destruction. But indeed, what do I hear being proclaimed among the common people, that the Jesuits of France benefit the kingdom? Surely, as I think, on account of the new religion of this sect. But what? Do they come closer to the Catholic religion than the Sorbonnists, by whom they have been enrolled among the number of heretics? I would say they are fitted rather for giving offence than for edification. Yet they are more suitable for training the minds of boys than so many rectors of colleges throughout all France. What do I hear? Are the more distinguished ones not from their colleges...

units.la: Iesuitarum propagatio in Gallia.
units.tr: The propagation of the Jesuits in France.

units.la: Pyramis in memoriam ejectionis Iesuitarum erecta destrueitur.
units.tr: A pyramid erected in memory of the expulsion of the Jesuits is demolished.

units.la: Prosopopoeia pyramidis. quàm ex alijs Gallię Academijs prodiere viri? At numquid non corruptores juventutis declarati sunt? Cur ergò in me demolienda vires suas exercuerunt? At prudentia sua Regi plusquàm Consiliarij aulici profuere? Credo: Verùm nunquid non injuria ipsi fata, cum in exilium mitterentur? si non, quis enim hoc dixerit, quid igitur in Gallia vobis negotij est? Carere utique vestra opera Galli facile omnes possunt, quod ipsum fatis etiam superque ex finibus vos suis eijcientes declararunt, sed impudentiam vide: verum esse quod dico, nolentes credere, necessariò in Gallię sese regno adesse oportere toti persuasum esse mundo expetunt. Quæ quæso impudentia est, si hæc non est, velle Gallis, præter & contra voluntatem eorum admisceri, & per posticum reverti ubi per antica eos eiecerint? Sed quid? Annon hoc merita vestra regno declarata effecerunt? Annon hinc probitatis vestræ argumentum egregium peti potest? Sunt equidem vel ex ipsa prognati, iniquitate aliqui, qui probi habentur, contra verò qui vitam suam Dei Regisque ministeriis postponere non dubitarunt, improbi existimantur. Qui sint illi quæritis? belli motuumque variorum tempore, Deorum accensebantur numero: At pace jam compositâ, pro idolis iterum habentur, regebant tum temporis communem populum contra Regem eum inflammando, jam Regem ipsum adversus populum armando moderantur. Age male egerunt, & puniti sunt. Quid Prodest autem odiosa hæc repetere & renovare? præstaret equidem Lysandrum cum prolixo suo sermone sepultum esse; At non indignum videri columnis Gallicis, subverti sese ab Hispanicis columnis putatis? Quamvis enim pœnitere aliquem nunquam debeat eorum quæ bene fortiterque gessit, videtur tamen melius esse, mali aliquid interdum perpetrasse, si melior reproborum quàm piorum conditio esse debeat. Quid Iesuitæ? quoties quæso & scriptis & viva voce, licere subditis Regem suum interficere professi sunt? nihilominus tamen Regem quasi devinctum sibi deducunt, seducentque indies magis magisque, si verbis ipsorum aures patentes diutius habuerit. Non quiescunt enim Iesuitæ, & petulantia eorum modum non habet, cujus rei vel egomet testis sum, cujus eversionem donec impetrarent, quiescere nulla ratione poterant. Reversi sunt itaque Iesuitæ in Galliam, non ut ab exilio revocati religiosi, sed ut triumphantes quasi de potentissimo orbis hujus Rege, quem lenocinijs suis demoliri et subvertere coegerunt, quod perpetuum laudis suæ monumentum non itapridem statuerat. Insolentiam hic vide & superbiam! recusabant redire in Galliam, nisi Galliæ Rex prius statuas magnanimitatis suæ monumenta demolitus esset. Cæsar olim Pompeio superesse ejus statuas voluit, suas uti stabiliret rectius; At vos superati & proscripti, jamque ex mera gratia iterum restituti, reditu vestro plus abutimini, quàm si libertate regni superessetis victores & superiores fuissetis. Quis enim credat, si Gallis Regno ejectis omnibus, Hispanos introducere vobis licuisset, amplius aliquid audere vos potuisse, quàm condemnationis & sententiæ in vos latæ monumentum tollere? Sed usque adeò nihil hac ratione profecisse vos, persuasum vobis habeatis velim, ut pro desolata & eversa Pyramide una, quæ constrici non nisi uno in loco poterat, aliquot hominum millia excitaverit, qui per universum orbem prædicent et palam profiteantur, juste vos & legitimè distinctis aliquot judicijs, Gallicæ juventutis corruptores, pacis tranquillitatisque publicæ turbatores, Regis proditores, & patriæ vestræ desolatores, declaratos pronunciatosque fuisse, &c.
units.tr: Prosopopoeia of the pyramid. Which men have come forth from the other academies of France? But were they not declared corrupters of youth? Why, then, did they exert their strength in demolishing me? Did their wisdom serve the King more than the courtly counsellors? I believe so. But were they not justly punished when they were sent into exile? If not, who would say so? What business, then, do you have in France? All Frenchmen can certainly do without your work, as the fates, and more than the fates, declared when they cast you out of their borders. But see the impudence: unwilling to believe that what I say is true, you seek to persuade the whole world that you must necessarily be present in the kingdom of France. What impudence, I ask, is this, if it is not this: to wish to mix yourselves in among the French, beyond and against their will, and to slip back in through the back door when they have thrown you out through the front? But what? Have your merits not made you known to the kingdom? Can an outstanding proof of your integrity not be drawn from this? Indeed, some men who are held to be upright are born of this very iniquity; on the other hand, those who did not hesitate to put their own lives second to the service of God and King are thought wicked. Who are they, you ask? In times of war and various uprisings they were counted among the gods; but now that peace is restored they are again regarded as idols. At that time they stirred up the common people against the King; now they govern the King himself by arming him against the people. Well, they acted badly, and they were punished. But what good is it to repeat and renew these hateful things? It would indeed be better for Lysander to be buried along with his long speech. But do you think it unworthy of the pillars of France to be overturned by the pillars of Spain? For although a man should never regret what he has done well and bravely, it seems nonetheless better to have committed some wrong at times, if the condition of the reprobate ought to be better than that of the pious. And the Jesuits? How often, I ask, have they professed, both in writing and by word of mouth, that subjects may lawfully kill their king? Nevertheless they lead the King along as if he were bound to them, and they seduce him more and more each day, if he has kept his ears open too long to their words. For the Jesuits do not rest, and their wantonness knows no bounds; of this I am myself a witness. Until they obtained his overthrow, they could by no means be quiet. So the Jesuits returned to France, not as religious men recalled from exile, but as conquerors, as if they had triumphed over the most powerful king of this world, whom by their enticements they forced to tear down and destroy the monument of his own glory, which he had set up not long before. See the insolence and pride here! They refused to return to France unless the King of France first had the monuments of his magnanimity demolished. Caesar once wished Pompey's statues to survive, so that he might establish his own more securely; but you, defeated and proscribed, and now restored by pure favour, abuse your return more than if you had survived as victors and superiors through the liberty of the kingdom.
