Junij, Schultes / Schöpffen vnd etliche alte Officirer auß der Gemeine/ im Bischofflichen Saal versamlet/ da geschlossen worden/ daß man ein sonderbare rechtfertigung wider Matthieu le Sot anstellen solte/ vnd jhn vorgericht/ deß übermüts halben/ den er vnbesinnter weise getrieben/ vorzumen/ vnd dieweil er sich auff den Herren Präsidenten verließ/ vnnd an vielen orten/ ehe er diesen handel angefangen/ gesagt hatte/ der selb würde jhn wol wissen zu redden worten: so bedachte die versamlung sehr weißlich/ daß man zum Herren Präsidenten gehen vnd jhn verständigen solte/ was geschlossen worden/ mit bitt/ daß er vermög deß ansehens/ welches er wegen seiner tugenden vnnd getrewen diensten den einwohnern zu Tropen hette/ solches vnwesen/ das sich in der Statt erregt hette/ stillen/ vnd die zertrente gemüter zu einer guten vnd rechtschaffnen einigkeit anleiten helffen wolte. Zu diesem end hat sich der Schultes Herr Pithou mit sechs Schöpffen vnd etlichen andern Officireren der Stätt zum Herren Präsidenten verfüget/ die zeigten ihm an/ auß was vrsächen sie zu jhm kommen/ vnd übergaben jhm schrifftlich/ was Matthieu le Sot für frefelhafftige stück begangen. Als der Schultes Herr Pithou außgeredt/ antworte der Herr Präsident/ wann er den Matthieu le Sot wurde gehört haben/ so wolte er sehen/ was der sachen zu thün were/ das recht stünde nem jeden offen: vnd damit er zuerkennen gebe/ wie übel er zu frieden/ daß man die Jesuiten nit einnemen wolte/ sagt er ferns/ daß derer in Tropen zehen tausent weiber/ die jhrer begerten/ vnd weren nur fünffzehen oder sechzehen Libertiner darwider/ denen zutruß sie gleichwol hinein kommen solten: daß wann er zu hofe were gewesen / er denen das maul wol wurde gestopfft haben / die dahin im namen der Statt gezogen weren/ er wolte/ daß es ihm einen schoppen seines bluts gekostet hette, daß er daselbst gewesen were/ die lesterungen / die man der Königin vorbracht hette, abzulcinen. Das übrige/ daß der Præsident geantwortet/ haben wir in diesem bericht nit melden wollen/ damit wir dem Leser durch erzehlung der schmehwort/ die er gegen dem Schultessen vnd Schöpffen gleichsam zur höflichen danckfagung/ daß sie ihm die ehr gethan vnd zu ihm in sein hauß kommen waren/ herauß gestossen hat/ keinen verdruß machen. Pater Cotton, als er auf bestimpte zeit zu Troyen ankommen / hat er mitwochen den 29. Junij auff S. Peters tag im Thumb geprediget / vnnd widerumb folgenden Sontags den 3. Julij in S. Magdalens kirche. Die gegenwart dieses Patris hat denen/ die gleich wie Matthes le Sot geartet vnd gesinnet waren / einen solchen müth gemacht/ daß ihrer viel nit vngeneigt gewesen/ zun waaffen zugreiffen/ vnd einen lermen anzufangen. Viel fromme vnd ehrliche leut vnder den einwohnern/ als sie gesehen/ daß grosse gefahr wegen einer aufrühr in der Statt vorhanden/ seufzeten sich selbs/ vñ kundten sich nit enthalten/ diesen proceß deß Bischoffs vnd deß Præsidenten zu schelten/ daß sie/ die zum friden helffen solten/ vneinigkeit vnnd aufrühr anstifften/ damit sie durch eine empörung vnd anflauf den Jesuiten zu ihrer einkommung die bahn machen könten.
units.tr: Several others of Sot's kind followed this notary and, thinking that everything was permitted to them, especially since Father Cotton was about to come to Troyes, began to mock and slander the deputies who had gone to Fontainebleau, and they spread about in particular what Sot had said publicly. One man, whose name is passed over here, outdid all the others, saying that they would have to take up arms to bring the Jesuits in; he knew well which side they would have to take up. So that this evil might be checked in time, and the mischief that might arise from such furious proceedings be prevented, the mayor, the aldermen and some of the older officials of the community met in the bishop's hall on the very same day, the 27th of June. They resolved to institute a special prosecution against Matthieu le Sot, and to summon him to answer for the insolence he had recklessly displayed; and since he relied on the president and had said in many places, before he began this business, that the president would know how to deal with his words, the assembly wisely judged that they should go to the president and inform him of what had been resolved, asking that, by virtue of the authority he enjoyed among the inhabitants of Troyes on account of his virtues and faithful services, he would help quell the disturbance that had arisen in the town and guide the divided minds towards a good and righteous unity. To this end the mayor, Master Pithou, went to the president with six aldermen and several other officials of the town. They told him why they had come and handed him in writing the outrageous acts Matthieu le Sot had committed. When the mayor Pithou had finished speaking, the president replied that once he had heard Matthieu le Sot he would see what was to be done in the matter, and that the law was open to everyone. And to show how ill he was pleased that the Jesuits were not to be admitted, he went on to say that there were ten thousand women in Troyes who wanted them, and only fifteen or sixteen libertines against them, whose opposition they would nevertheless have to overcome and come in anyway; that if he had been at court, he would have stopped the mouths of those who had gone there in the name of the town; and that he would have considered it well worth a pint of his own blood to have been there to refute the slanders that had been brought before the Queen. What else the president replied we have not wished to report in this account, so as not to trouble the reader with the abusive words he let fly against the mayor and aldermen, as if by way of courteous thanks for their having done him the honour of coming to his house. Father Cotton, when he arrived in Troyes at the appointed time, preached in the cathedral on Wednesday, the 29th of June, the feast of Saint Peter, and again the following Sunday, the 3rd of July, in the church of Saint Magdalen. The presence of this Father stirred up those who were of the same disposition and mind as Matthieu le Sot to such a pitch that many were not unwilling to take up arms and begin an uproar. Many pious and honest folk among the inhabitants, seeing that there was great danger of a riot in the town, sighed to themselves and could not refrain from rebuking this process of the bishop and the president: that they, who ought to help keep the peace, were stirring up discord and sedition, so that through a rising and tumult they might clear the way for the Jesuits to enter.

units.la: Damit nun die Statt vor aufrühr vnd lermen/ dessen man sich zubesorgen hatte/ versichert wurde/ haben Schulteß vnd Schöpffen ir zuflucht zu Herren Praslain Gubernatoren in Champagnien genoffen/ welcher sich als bald dahin begeben/ vnnd durch seine gegenwart vnd fürsichtigkeit alles wider gestillet vnnd in rühe gebracht, wie auß dem inhalt nachfolgenden schreibens/ so die Königin an in/ auf seinen beericht/ wegen seiner reiß nach Troyen/ abgehn laffen/ zu vernemen.
units.tr: So that the town would be secured against revolt and the uproar that was feared, the sheriff and aldermen sought refuge with Lord Praslain, governor of Champagne. He went there at once and, by his presence and prudence, calmed everything and restored order, as may be seen from the following letter, which the Queen sent him in reply to his report on his journey to Troyes.

units.la: Herr Praslain, nach dem wir vernommen/ auß was vrsachen ir euch gen Troyen begeben/ vnd welchen fleiß ihr angewendet/ dem vnwesen/ daß daselbst wegen der spaltung vnd verbitterung/ die ir vnder den einwohnern befunden/ hette entstehen mögen/ zu begegnen/ wie ist daß solches glücklich verrichtet: habt wir euch durch diß schreiben wissend machen wollen/ daß ihr daran dem König meinem sohn vnd mir einen sehr angenemen dienst bewiesen habt/ welcher nicht weniger vns zu sonderlichem gefallen/ als der Statt zur rühe gereichet. Wir hatten vns vorgenommen/ dem Bischoff vnd Præsidenten durch euch befehlen zu lassen/ daß sie etwas bescheidener/ als bißher/ sich erzeigen/ vnd ihren eyfer mäßigen solten/ vnnd euch schreiben an ihnen deßhalben zu senden: aber dieweil Pater Cotton vns höchlich versprochen hat/ daß sie sich künftig wol vnd nach vnserm willen verhalten werden/ vnnd daß es vnvon nöten/ daß wir jnen schreiben/ haben wir es anstehen lassen: jedoch haben wir darfür gehalten/ es könte nichts schaden/ daß ir jnen auf fürfallende gelegenheit zu verstehen gebet/ was vnsere meinung sey/ vñ was zu iren ehren vñ verrichtung ires ampts/ wie auch zu erhaltung friedens vnd einigkeit in gemelter Statt diene/ welche ir euch allzeit trewlich befohlen sein lassen wollet: Dann wir entschloffen sein/ auff alle zu tragende fäll/ vñ mit namen in diesem gegenwirtigen/ dahin fürnemlich zuschen vnd zutrachten/ daß friede erhalten werde/ vnd war vnsere meinung nit/ dit Jesuiten gen Troyen anderst/ dann auf das bitten vñ anhalten/ so vns im namen der einwohner daselbste geschehe/ einzuführe/ wie wir auch vns solches zuthun nit in den sin nemen wollen/ daß so fern sie es begerē. Gedachter Pater Cotton hat vns gleicher massen berichtet/ daß der Notarius, genandt le Sot, welcher etlicher ärgerliche vñ auffrärischen reden halben beschuldiget worden/ durch etliche/ die ihm übel wolten/ darzu gebracht worden/ vnd solches mehr auß zorn vnd unbedächtsamkeit/ als auß bösem willen gethan/ vnd daß er deßwegen mit keiner straf zu belegen sey/ weil man ohne dazu nichts wider in fürnemen könte/ man greiffe dann auch andere an/ die mehr sind/ dann er/ vnd die die fürnembste ämpter bedienen/ auf welche er sich berüffen/ daß n snen darzu were bestelt worden: vber diß/ daß er auch dergleichen reden für brin- n kønte/ die sein gegentheil solte haben lauffen lassen: also daß wann man also ese sachen wolte rüttlen/ein newe vnruhe/ärger als die vorige/die jhr gestillet/ daraus entstehen möchte/ vnd darumb daß es besser were/ solche entstandene vneinigkeit endlich aufzuheben vnd zu tilgen/ mit bitt/ solches euch also zubefehlen: darin wir gleich wol auß vrsachen/ die jr selber ermessen könnt/ nit haben willfaren wollen/ vnder vns erbotten/ euch alles das jenige/ was er vns vorbtracht/ zuzuschreibe/ damit als dem der gegenwertige zustand in der Statt/ die gelegenheit der sachen/ vñ wie sich mit einem vnd dem andern in der warheit verhelt/ was auch darauf erfolgen möchte/ am besten bekannt ist/ solches bedencket/ vñ darinn verfahret/ wie jr erkennen erdet/ daß es die Iustitia vnd deß Königs meines sohns vñ mehr gemeldter einwohr wolfart erheischet. Diß hab ich euch also zuschreiben wollen/ vnd könnet dem Kø-glichen Anwald von vnsert wegen vermelden/ daß wir einen sonderlichen genün haben an der bescheidenheit vñ gütẽ anstalt/ dessen er sich in dieser sache/ ewiem ugnus nach/ wie auch sonsten/ gebrauchet: Ins gleichem wollet dem Schultessen sagt/ daß wir vns seine trew vñ fleiß/ die er in dieser sache erwiesen/ gnedigist gefaln lassen: vnd ist diß vnser ernstliches vermanen an sie/ daß sie also fortfahren/ vns ol vñ trewlich zu dienen/ wie wir daß nit zweiffen/ daß sie thün werden: euch hiemit tlicher protection empfelend. Geben zu Pariß den 14. Iulij 1611. Vnd war die vn- rschriffi/ Maria, vnd besser drunden/ Pothier.
units.tr: Lord Praslain, since we have heard for what reasons you went to Troyes, what diligence you applied to meet the disorder that might have arisen there from the division and bitterness among the inhabitants, and how happily it has been accomplished, we wished to inform you by this letter that you have thereby done a very welcome service to the King my son and to me, one which pleases us no less than it brings peace to the town. We had resolved to have you command the Bishop and the President to conduct themselves somewhat more moderately than hitherto and to moderate their zeal, and to write to you to send them to us for this purpose. But since Father Cotton has solemnly promised us that they will henceforth behave well and according to our will, and since it is unnecessary for us to write to them, we have let the matter rest. Nevertheless we thought it could do no harm if you let them understand, when an occasion arises, what our opinion is, and what serves their honour and the discharge of their office, as well as the preservation of peace and unity in the said town, which you will always faithfully take to heart. For we are resolved to look, in all cases to come and especially in the present one, chiefly to this: that peace be maintained. Our intention was not to introduce the Jesuits into Troyes except upon the petition and entreaty made to us in the name of the inhabitants there, and we do not intend to do so even if they should desire it. The said Father Cotton has likewise informed us that the notary called le Sot, who was accused of certain scandalous and seditious words, was prompted to them by some who wished him ill, and that he did it more from anger and thoughtlessness than from ill will; and that therefore he is not to be punished, since nothing could be undertaken against him unless others were also seized, who are more numerous than he and who hold the chief offices, on whom he calls, saying that they had been appointed to him; and moreover that he could also bring forward similar words which his opponent had allowed to pass. So if these matters were stirred up, a new disturbance worse than the former, which has been quieted, might arise; and therefore it would be better finally to remove and extinguish the dissension that has arisen. We ask that you so command it. In this we, for reasons you can yourself judge, did not wish to comply; but we have agreed among ourselves to write to you everything he has put before us, so that you, who know best the present state of the town, the circumstances of the affair, how matters truly stand with each party, and what might follow, may consider it and proceed as you see that justice and the welfare of the King my son and of the said inhabitants require. I wished to write this to you. You may tell the King's advocate on our behalf that we have a particular liking for the moderation and good management he has shown in this affair, as also otherwise. Likewise you may tell the sheriff that we graciously accept the loyalty and diligence he has shown in this affair, and this is our earnest exhortation to him to continue thus, serving us faithfully, as we do not doubt he will. Herewith I commend you to their protection. Given at Paris, 14 July 1611. It was signed Maria, and below it Pothier.

units.la: Dieser Brieff ist ins Stattbüch eingeschrieben worden/ vnd beweiset der selbe klärh/ erstlich/ daß die Iesuiten shnen kein gewissen machen/ rottirungen vnd spaltunn o zürichten vñ zuerhalten/ wanns zu jrer Societet nutzen dienet. Zum andern ß Pater Cotton an seiner kunst vnd wolredenheit nichts erwinden lassen/ die pratin/ die der Bischoff vnd Præsident zu Troyen getrieben/ die Iesuiten daselbst einfüh-en/ bey der Königin zu verstrichen vnd bedecken. Zum dritten/ daß er sich zu ei-m advocaten für den aufrühr̈er Matthes le Sot gebrauchen lassen/ vnd sich vndernden/ den vnglimpff seines verbrechens auf die zu schieben/ die er seinen Gegenil nennet/ vnd die in dem/ daß er jnen aufrechnen wollen/ allerdings vnschuldig u: Diß ist gewiß vnd vnlaugbar/ daß Matthes le Sot nichts/ dann auß trieb vñ be-l deß Præsidenten geredt hat: inmassen le Sot selbs bey vielen fürnemen ansehn-hen leuten sich verlauten lassen/ vnd hats sein weib gutwillich vor dem Herzen de aslin gestanden/ da sie im zu füß gefallen/ vnnd für iren mann gebetten/ hernach t sie es vor Gericht / wie jederman weißt / bekandt. Wie nun der Præsident ƀ Matthieu le Sot ein schändliche vnd verweißliche thåt begangen/ jener/ daß er diebestelt/ dieser/ daß er sich bestellen lassen/ schmächliche/ vñ denen/ die auch nur ein nckleın Christlicher liebe in sich haben/ übel anstehende reden außzuspeẏngen: also es nit weniger dem Pater Cotton eine grosse vneħr / daß er also vnverschampter iß die Königin hinder das liecht fühzen/ vnd die vnschuldige beschuldigen wollen/ mit er die schuldigen entschuldigte.
units.tr: This letter was entered in the town book, and it plainly proves, first, that the Jesuits make no scruple about creating and maintaining factions and divisions when it serves their Society's interest. Second, that Father Cotton left nothing undone, by his art and eloquence, to smooth over and conceal before the Queen the practices by which the Bishop and the President of Troyes had worked to introduce the Jesuits there. Third, that he let himself be used as advocate for the rioter Matthes le Sot, and undertook to shift the blame for his offence onto those whom he calls his opponents, who were entirely innocent of what he wished to charge them with. This is certain and undeniable: Matthes le Sot said nothing except at the instigation and urging of the President. Le Sot himself let it be heard among many prominent men, and his wife, willingly, fell at the feet of Lord Praslain, begging for her husband, and afterwards confessed it before the court, as everyone knows. Just as the President committed a shameful and reprehensible act in hiring le Sot, and le Sot in letting himself be hired, to utter disgraceful words, which ill become anyone who has even a little Christian love in him, so it is no less a disgrace to Father Cotton that he so shamelessly wished to lead the Queen into the dark, accusing the innocent while excusing the guilty.

units.la: Der Schultes vnd die Schöpffen haben den Bischoff manchmal besücht vñ ansprochen/ damit er zu dem/ was recht vnd billich ist/ verstehen wolte/ vnd in gebetn/ daß das jenig/ so den 3. Iunij in voller versamlung wegen Abraham Drouots, r zu jrer Schulen vorgeschlagen/ beschlossen worde/ möchte ins werck gerichtet wern: aber er hats gänzlich abgeschlagen: als er dessen wider durch schrifften ersuchte rden/ hat er den 12. Iulij 1611. Diese schrifftliche antwort geben/ die Königin hette behlen/ mit der sachen einzustehen/ vñ daß er jre fernere resolution erwarten thete: inittels hette er wegen deß obersten Schulampts vorsehung gethan. Man hat nachals bey jm angehalten/ er wolle mit Abraham Drouot vbereinkommen: mit dem hang/ wann ers nit thûn wurde/ so wurde man nichts desto weniger in der sache rfahren. Darauf laßt er den Drouot welcher ein Priester vñ Baccalaureus Theologie ist/ zu sich kommen/ vnd drówet jm (in gegenwart Iacob Nivelle) daß er shn nicht der bann thún wolle/ wañ er den dienst im Collegio anneme. Dronot antwortet/ man habe sich vor solchem ban nit viel zuforchten. Nivelle wolt für den Bischoff reden/ vnd sagt: Etiam injusta excommunicatio pertimescenda. Dronot gab zur antwort/ man kö ute durch das appelliren wider solche straffen wol rath finden. Der Bischoff protestirt hingegen/ daß man jm schon das Parlament auferlegen solte/ jhn zu absolviren/ so wolte ers doch nit thún/ er aber Drovot könte diesem allen wol zuvor kommen/ wann er sich schriftlich verobligiren wolle/ auß dem Collegio zuweichen/ wann die Königin die Jesuiter wurde in Troyen einführen wollen. Der Schultheß vnd Schöpffen/ als sie dieser practicken überdrüssig worden/ lassen endtlich den Dronot die bestallung auf das oberste Schülampt/ deren sie sich den 12. Julij mit einander verglichen/ vnderschreiben/ wie auß diesem instrument zusehen.
units.tr: The sheriff and aldermen have often visited and addressed the Bishop, so that he would come to what is right and fair, and asked that what had been resolved in full assembly on 3 June concerning Abraham Drouot for their school should be put into effect. But he flatly refused. When they petitioned him again in writing, he gave this written answer on 12 July 1611: the Queen had commanded him to leave the matter in abeyance and to await her further decision; meanwhile he had made provision for the chief school office. Afterwards they pressed him to come to terms with Abraham Drouot, with the warning that otherwise the matter would nonetheless proceed. Thereupon he summoned Drouot, a priest and bachelor of theology, and threatened him, in the presence of Jacob Nivelle, that he would put him under the ban if he accepted the post at the college. Drouot replied that one need not fear such a ban much. Nivelle wished to speak for the Bishop and said: "Even an unjust excommunication is to be feared." Drouot answered that one could find a remedy against such punishments by appeal. The Bishop, for his part, protested that even if the Parlement should order him to absolve Drouot, he would not do so; but Drouot could forestall all this if he bound himself in writing to withdraw from the college should the Queen wish to introduce the Jesuits into Troyes. The sheriff and aldermen, at last weary of these machinations, had Drouot sign the appointment to the chief school office, on which they had agreed among themselves on 12 July, as may be seen from this instrument.

units.la: Im Jahr 1611. Donnerstags den 13. Julij umb vier vhren nach mittag haben wir endsbenante Königliche Notarij zu Troyen vns in den Bischofflichen Saal daselbsten verfüget/ da obgemelte Herr Schultheß vnd Schöpffen in vnserm beysein zugegen gewesen/ vnnd hat Herr Schulteß in aller namen Abraham Dronot persönlichen angeredt/ vnd von jhm begert/ daß er obigen Contract mit jhnen gegenwirtiglich vnderschreiben wolte/ vnd ist jhme Drovot solcher Contract von dem ehgenen gedachter Notarien in gegenwart deß andern als bald vorgelesen worden/ demnach solcher zu vnderschidlichen malen mit jhme Drovot also getroffen/ wie noch gestriges tages bemelte Tartier vnd Gombaults Schöpffen im namen vnd von wegen der andern allen zu jhm Drovot abgeordnet worden/ von jhm zuvernemen/ ob er seiner gethaner zusag nachkommen/ vnnd mehr besagten Contract ratificiren wolte. Welches bemeldter Drovot verwilligt. Nach welchem Herr Schultheß vnnd Schöpffen sampt ermeldten Räthen deß Schöpffenampts auf jetz besagten gestrigen tags vmb sechs vhren nach mittag ins Collegium gangen/ mit viel ermeltem Drovot zu reden/ welcher durch mehr gedachten Herren Schultheß befragt worden/ ober folgen den tags gegen mittag gemeldten Contract ratificiren wolte/ vnnd hat der Drovot geantwortet/ er wolte nit vnderlassen/ sich morgen/ wie obgemeldt/ in der Schöpffen Rathkammer einzustellen/ mehrbesagten Contract in gegenwart deß Herren Schultesseen vnd Schöpffen zu ratificiren. Darauf sich ermelter Drovot willig vnnd bereit zu sein erklärt/ gedachten Contract zu vnderschreiben/ wolte aber zuvor dem Ehrwürdigen Herren Bischoff eine schrifft wider geben/ welche er Bischoff jhme zu handen gestelt/ vnd daßer fast wüntsche/ daß sich gedachter Herr Bischoff mit gemelten Herren Schulteß vnnd Schöpffen vergleichen möchte/ damit jhme Drovot vom Bischoffen kein eintrag vnd verhindernuß im Collegio widerfahre/ dieweil gedachter Bischoff jhn in bann zuthún gedrówet/ welchen bann er nit aufheben wolte/ wanns schon das Parlament gebieten solte: begere demnach/ daß jhm eine Copey besagten Contracts gegeben werde/ die selbe in seinem Rath einzuliefern: vnnd das er außerhalb deß verbots vnd gedrówten banns vom Bischoff vrbietig were/ gedachten Contract zu vnderschreiben. Signatum Bourgeois vnd Trafel.
units.tr: In the year 1611, on Thursday, the 13th of July, at four o'clock in the afternoon, we, the undersigned royal notaries of Troyes, betook ourselves to the episcopal hall there, where the aforementioned mayor and aldermen were present in our presence. The mayor, speaking on behalf of them all, addressed Abraham Dronot in person and asked him to sign the above contract with them then and there. The contract was read aloud to Dronot at once by one of the said notaries, in the presence of the other. Such an agreement had been reached with Dronot on several occasions, as on the previous day the aforementioned Tartier and Gombault, aldermen, had been sent to him in the name and on behalf of all the others, to learn from him whether he would keep his promise and ratify the said contract. Dronot agreed to this. Thereafter the mayor and aldermen, together with the named councillors of the aldermen's office, went to the college at six o'clock in the afternoon of the said previous day to speak with Dronot, and the mayor asked him whether he would ratify the said contract on the following day, around noon. Dronot replied that he would not fail to present himself the next morning, as stated above, in the aldermen's council chamber, in the presence of the mayor and aldermen, to ratify the said contract. Dronot then declared himself willing and ready to sign the contract, but first wished to hand a written statement to the reverend lord bishop. The bishop had given it to him, and Dronot earnestly wishes that the said lord bishop might come to an agreement with the mayor and aldermen, so that Dronot might suffer no hindrance or obstruction from the bishop in the college, since the bishop has threatened to excommunicate him, a ban which he would not lift even if the Parlement itself commanded it. He therefore asks that a copy of the said contract be given to him, to deliver to his council, and that he is ready to sign the contract, outside the prohibition and the threatened ban of the bishop. Signed: Bourgeois and Trafel.

units.la: Auß diesem bericht kan ein vnparteyischer Leser leichtlich ermessen/ was der Jesuiten zweck vnd fürhaben sey/ vnd wie jhre heimliche vnd listige practicken gegen dem Franckreich gefährlich vnd beforglich seyen.
units.tr: From this report an impartial reader can easily judge what the aims and designs of the Jesuits are, and how dangerous and alarming their secret and crafty machinations against France are.

units.la: ACTIO MARTILIERI ADVERSVS IESVITAS IN PARLAMENTO PARISI- ENSI, ANNO 1611.
units.tr: ACTIO MARTILIERI ADVERSVS IESVITAS IN PARLAMENTO PARISIENSI, ANNO 1611.

units.la: ANno 1610. & 1611. tractata est rursus, & ut multis videbatur, prorsus finita, controversia, quae diu agitata fuit inter Iesuitas & Academiam Parisiensem. Cum enim Martilierus Academiae Advocatus in Parlamento statui controversiae inter Iesuitas & Academiam, Annimirum potestatem haberent Iesuitae artes quaslibet liberales in Collegio suo publice profitendi, dilucide admonuim explicasset, & iniquitate, turpitudine, flagitiis erroribus ꝯ tam vitae & morum, quam doctrinae ipsorum commemoratis, Academiae non solum, sed & universae Reip. detrimento eos esse maximo, certis immotis ꝯ argumentis ita commoveret, ut Regum eos parricidas esse, dubium amplius nemini videretur; Et ideo Advocatus Iesuitarum tam frigide ad argumenta ista die postero respondere, ut appareret facile, argutias eorum ad obfuscandum clarissimum veritatem: Solem momenti afferre nihil amplius posse, Seruinus statim, Advocatus eius, facto, a matris Hircani & Aristobuli, qui ex regia Maccabeorum stirpe erant, historia dicendi initio, Eam, inquit, Pharisaeorum & Scribarum, in vita morum, innocentia omnium in se oculos converterant, astutia, eo tande miseriam perductam fuisse, ut praeter nomen & titulum Reginae, (potestate et imperio omni ad Pharaos delato) nihil amplius retinuerit. Porro autem ex antiquorum Patrum & Doctorum Ecclesiae scriptis Monasticam, Eremiticam & in universum omnem Ecclesiasticam vitam, solitudini, humilitati, studiis, castitati, dilectioni, simplicitati, supertati, bonisque temporalibus & favori Principum contemnendis totam detestam esse oportere ostendens, longe hanc Iesuiticam ab ea alienam esse, utpote quae bonis aliorum per insidias & dolo malo occupandis inhiaret, & doctrinam in forma, quam in materia pessimam profiteretur, argumentis & exemplis veterum tam dilucide comprobavit, ut ne hisce quidem contra, qui adfuerat Iesuitarum primores, potuerint, sed & defendere suam volentes causam, omnimferisui exposuerint.
units.tr: In the years 1610 and 1611 the controversy that had long been waged between the Jesuits and the University of Paris was argued again, and it seemed to many to be entirely settled. Martilierus, advocate of the University, set out before the Parlement the question whether the Jesuits had the right to teach any of the liberal arts publicly in their college. He explained the matter clearly, and by unshakeable and cogent arguments he recalled their injustice, baseness, crimes and errors, both in life and morals and in doctrine, and showed how greatly they harmed the University and the whole commonwealth. He moved his hearers so far that hardly anyone any longer doubted that they were murderers of kings. The advocate of the Jesuits therefore answered these arguments the next day so feebly that it was easy to see that their subtleties were meant only to obscure the plainest truth, and that they could add no further weight. Then Servinus, their advocate, at the beginning of his speech, recounted the history of the mother of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, who were of the royal stock of the Maccabees. "That sect of the Pharisees and Scribes," he said, "had turned all eyes upon itself by the innocence of its morals and by its cunning, and had at last brought things to such a wretched state that the queen retained nothing beyond the name and title of queen, all power and authority having been transferred to the Pharisees." Furthermore, drawing on the writings of the ancient Fathers and teachers of the Church, Martilierus showed that monastic, hermit and, in general, all ecclesiastical life ought to be marked by solitude, humility, study, chastity, love, simplicity, despising superstition, worldly goods and the favour of princes. He showed that the Jesuit life was far removed from this, since it lusted after the goods of others, seizing them by plots and evil deceit, and he proved from the arguments and examples of the ancients, so clearly that not even the leading Jesuits present could answer them, that the doctrine they professed was bad in its substance as well as in its form. Wishing to defend their cause, they laid themselves open at almost every point.

units.la: ACTIO PETRI HARDIVILLERII PARI- SINAE ACADEMIAE RECTORIS PRO ACADEMIA ADVERSVS Presbyteros & Scholasticos Collegij Claromontani Iesuitas, habita in Senatu Parisiensi Anno 1611. die 22. Decemb.
units.tr: ACTION OF PETER HARDIVILLIER, RECTOR OF THE PARIS ACADEMY, ON BEHALF OF THE ACADEMY AGAINST THE PRIESTS AND SCHOLASTICS OF THE CLERMONT COLLEGE JESUITS, delivered in the Parisian Senate on 22 December 1611.

units.la: ACtionem a Martiliero pro Academia Parisiensi adversus Iesuitas suscepta, breviter modo enarravimus. Eam, uti commodius finiretur, Petrus Hardivilerius Academiae Rector, promovendam talem in modum sumpsit: Ecce, inquit, Academiarum omnium Princeps & Regina, Regum Christianissima proles, ad sacrum dignitatis vestrae, Iudices, tribunal prodit, non jam amplitudine venerabilis, non nati pulchritudine speciabilis, non vegeto illo succique eno corpore, non uberibus lacteo quodam iuvuχiας fonte manantibus, non flammeis illis flagrantibus oculis, quibus omnium gentium animos, divinis incendebat ardoribus, sed ida, marens, abiecta, in situ & squalore vitam trahens, miseriae & conditionis suae pudosuffusa, in vobis suae sortis et fortunae praesidium quaerens, vos enim madetibus oculis intuetur, quorum salutari manu nisi e caeno & sordibus extrahatur, non est quod aliud in rerum acerbitate doloris levimentum quaerat, quam ut saltem novissimas ejus voces Senatus audiat, & ipsa in vestro sinu innocentem, & Gallici candoris perpetuo reti-
units.tr: We have only briefly described the action brought by Martillier on behalf of the Paris Academy against the Jesuits. So that it might be brought to a more convenient end, Peter Hardivilliers, Rector of the Academy, pressed it in the following manner: Behold, he said, the Prince and Queen of all academies, the most Christian offspring of kings, comes before the sacred tribunal of your dignity, judges. She comes not now venerable in her size, not admired for the beauty of her birth, not with that vigorous and juicy body, not with breasts flowing with a milky fount of youth, not with those flaming, blazing eyes by which she once kindled the minds of all nations with divine ardour; but sad, cast down, dragging out her life in neglect and filth, overwhelmed with shame at her misery and condition, seeking in you the protection of her lot and fortune. For she looks upon you with tearful eyes. Unless she is drawn out of the mire and filth by your saving hand, she has nothing else to seek as a relief from the bitterness of her sorrow, except that the Senate would at least hear her last words, and that she be kept, innocent, in your bosom and in the perpetual net of Gallic candour

units.la: ꝶ 3
units.tr: [Signature mark] 3

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE
units.tr: ON THE PROPAGATION

units.la: nentem animam exhalet. Tametsi autem in Academia datus sit patronus, qui undique oculatus, animos Gallorum facile per avia, praeruptasque et anfractus Iesuitica Societatis ducere possit, se tamen affirmat, sic ad dicendum venire, ut pietatis potius quam defensionis, querela quam eloquentia, doloris quam ingenij partes a se susceptas quisque intelligat, quamvis interim non diffiteatur, eo adactu esse se importunitate adversariorum, qui toties moniti, ut captis desisterent, toties objurgati, ut ambitioni suae modum facerent, toties ab aris focisque Academiae depulsi, sese quin in alienajura et praedia irrumperent, continere nunquam potuerunt. Inter alia autem nefaria ipsorum scelera, illud certe indignum maxime et prorsus non ferendum esse, quod jam non per se et emissarios suos, sed per ipsos Parlamenti judices, Academiae tutores, Academicis periculum inferre conentur, et quos hactenus occulte consilijs dolisque extinguere non potuerunt, eos judicum sententijs et judiciorum religione oppressuros se arbitrentur. Quia autem inter cateras postulationis suae causas Academiae vastitate et confusione, nimiamque juvenilis aetatis licentia, veluti quosdam Academici corporis morbos objecerint, quibus curandis nec jussa Regiae Majestatis, nec pondus autoritatis Parlamenti par fit, sed sola eorum societas, caelitus in eu fine scilicet demissa, probaturum se dicit, tam Reverendorum patrum obsequiosas ad morbos eiusmodi tollendos manus haud quaquam requiri. Principio igitur conflare laboranti Academiae medicos eos adhibendos minime esse, quibus cuiuslibet alterius Societatis innatus contemptus sit, quorum consilijs et artibus ingens morborum cumulus Galliam occupavit, qui ut importuni haeredipetae circumstent, et morte nondum complorata, funeris arbitria petant, quin imo qui ut corvi praeda inhiantes, non nisi injecta in os offa recedere solent. Sanctissimos et regulares fuari tenacissimos patres, Academicis nihil tale cogitantibus. Vulnus cruentum et lethale superiori tempore inflixisse, eam enim belloru civiliu procellis jactata, ex communi naufragio vix emersisse, cum sagacissimi patres animadverterint, convulsos ejus nervos, fractasque vires, non sine peculiari regiae munificentiae affluxu reparari posse, Regi igitur eos adijisse supplicesque petijisse, ut parvulum istum gregem suum aliqua dulcedinis guttula respergeret, esse sibi animum, non tam nomine quam re, affectu et studio vere Gallicanum, et ad Regiae Majestatis obsequium omnino praesente: unica prae caeteris florib. sibi lilia cordi esse, omnes suos conatus cogitationesque ad commune Reip. bonum direetas esse. Litteras esse ornamentum Reip. praesidium imperij, Solem et oculum regni; non debere igitur solam Lutetiam frui litterarum benefitio et juventutis instituendae bono gaudere, sed diffundendum illud esse per varios ac multiplices regni totius tractus, civitates, provincias. Regem igitur opt. et magnificentissimum: clementiae sua mollioribus ulnis eos excepisse, suo sinu et pectore fovisse, et tum Flexia per tum in alijs regni partibus per subditos suos stipendijs amplissimis ditasse. Illis autem velut armis instructos, et nomine regio veluti numine tactos, Academiam inermem et omnii praesidio destitutam deinde aggressos esse, suumque illud adeo quaestuosum GRATIS perfonado, juventutem ab Academia abduxisse, ut mirum non fit, illum jam vitae literariae fontem exsiccari praecisis undiquaque venis et ductibus quibus sanguine et spiritu accipiebat. Falsa nunc quidem exspectatione sua Iesuitas, factum enim esse, ut totum laborantis Academiae corpus, circumfusis eorum gregibus obsessum, vires suas, Academicis cor morientes, undaque parentis doctrina puriore reficientibus, collegerit, et corvos hiantes aluerit. Hoc autem animadvertentes Claromontanos patres, ad alias artes extemplo confugisse, et a Rege diploma seu rescriptum obtinuisse, quo in ipso Academia Parisiensis gymnasio publice scholas aperiendi facultas eis concessa fuit, juventute igitur instituere coepisse non per se, sed alios quosdam magistellos, vel aliunde accitos, vel quasi fungos noctu in vacuo spacio e facunditate foli Claremontani prorumpentes. Nihil mirum igitur si Academia exhauista pene viribus non gemere tantum et lugere sua forte, sed contra vim fraudem exclamare et Deum hominumque fidem implorare cogatur. Ad clamorem autem ipsos patres, qui ejus vitae insidias fecerant, accurrere jam et petere, ut Academicorum sinu excipiantur, non quidem dominos fundi, sed ut colonos, imo ut servulos humiles familiam Academicam cooptari volentes, suaves illas quidem et melle illitas voces effundere, sed quas si quis sapit, ipso felle reperiat amariores. Panem eos sinistra manu porrigere... lapidem dextrâ abscondere. Academicos quidem optare, ut non modò velut socios eos mittere, sed etiam velut fratres completi, & ut Patres venerari liceret, sed campum um magnos montes habere & fieri id non possʃ, multas urbes, quas ad nutum suum n regant Iesuitæ, multas provincias, quas possideant, multas Academias, quæ in suis ulta cineribus jaceant, & ex quarum ruinis rerum suarum insanas substructiones erexeut, testari satis & vincere. Eas enim tacitis & occultis motibus Academiâ Parisiensem nere, ut suo periculo sapiat, & instantia sibi pericula non modò caute prudenterq; præviat, sed etiam fortiter & gloriosè depellat, offendentes, societatis Iesuitica similem esse vel ni Aquilarū, quæ sensim eas res atterunt, cū quib. inclusæ & recondita sunt; vel fluviis, i infulas completi, ijsq; adblandiri videntur, eas tamen cominuunt & perdunt. Non esse te necesse, ut in externa aliarū Academiarum discriminā inquirant, earūq; voces & mota desiderent, jamintus esse periculum, æstuare jam morbum in præcordijs, & ipsos Acamiæ hostes prætextu pharmacorum, eius venas meliori sanguine exhausstas, venenatis otericorum dogmatum poculis inficere, atq; dum gratis ambrosiam suam suumq; nectar, lestes scil. illas dapes Academicis languentibus apponere seja stant, Academiam suffore, linguam ei præscindere, ne loqui, oculos eruere, ne eorum fraudes possit intueri, julum petere, ipsum caput aggredi, & Sorbonam ipsam tentare atque lacessere. Speciosum cietatis Iesu nomen, & boni publici pondus ac momentum in eorum verbis sonare, sed ripsos jam licere subditis jugū excutere, licere Senatusconsultis & Regijs etiā rescriptis illudere, imperita multitudinis oculos eludere, licere veteres Academias pervertere, ere de patribus miracula comminisci, licere passim martyres conscribere, licere Sornica decreta non habere ludibrio tantum, sed contumelijs prosequi, licere denique omnia sundare, ut tandem sola Iesuitarum secta totum orbem dogmatum suorum facibus inndens, omnes etiam vitiorum spinas, vepres & noxios deterioris doctrinæ succcos exu- t. Quod Osorius quondam dixit, inclinante & in senium vergente mūdo nascituram nōcujusdam & cæteris inusitati nominis Societatem, quæ tumidis magisterijs silentium imsitura sit, & ad cuius, ut ad solis exortum, cæteri hominum jure sociatorum cætus, qua- si inora, & spurio quodam lumine lucentia sidera mortalium oculis eripiantur; Id Iesuis per universum pene orbem Christianum jam assecutos se gloriari, & certe prædaora quæque ac melioris notæ ingenia, suis undiquaque sedibus eos expulisse; passim umpentes nascentis industriæ gemmas velut pestilenti quodam turbine asflatas adhusisse; nem literatis, quâ emergere ac se proferre possent, viam præclusisse, unam adhuc restare cademiam Parisiensem, ad quam velut ad portū confugerent virtutis & eruditionis suæ ecimina editurì. Hanc quia scopulum esse videant Iesuitæ in quem irruentes frangantur, circo ad eius interitum omnes adhibere machinas statuisse, jamq; in maximi beneficii loco ponere, si specie Societatis cum Academicis ineunde, & salutis eorum conferendā noine, omnes eorum labores, vigilias & conatus, omnibus invidiæ turbinibus exponant, si lcademiam ab limen Claromontana domus, ut vile mendicabulum prostare, et alumnorum iorum præmia ab eorum Gazophylacio turpiter expectare cogant, atq; ut Societatis istius dus, fabulæ, ludibrium toto orbe habeatur, faciant. Academicos quidem stare procinctu, non dolis, non ambitu, non versutijs, sed ingenio, doctrina, industria, virtute & animi candore cum reverendis istis Patribus certaturos, velle igitur, ut proferant Iesuitice Societatis lumina & Gigantes illi, qui volumina voluminibus, ut montes ontibus imponendo, cælum sapientiæ scandere se putant, & Deos Academiæ tutelares de lio suo deturbare, sed optare tamen, ut Iesuitæ nudā cum nudis Academicis decernant, hoc enim si fiat, sperare se futurum, ut res tota, omnibus jucundum, utilem Reipublicæ, li- ris salutarem exitum sortiatur. Caeterum non doctrinæ saltem & eruditionis ratio- em; sed ipsius etiam Reip. salutem, & Gallicani Imperij dignitatē, quin imo Regis Chriianissimi securitatem postulare, ut Gallicana juventutis informatio solius Academiæ dei & Academicorum sedulitati permittatur, atque demandetur. Macenatem olim Auustum monuisse, ut ijs erudienda juventus traderetur, qui Imperium Romanum impensi damarent, Gallorum igitur adolescentum institutionem non posse cuiquam tutius, quam Academicis Parisiensibus commendari, qui eodem quo tota Gallia spiritu vivant, & propterea Academiae vitam servari unicè expetant, ut ipsi in ea velut in specula ad Regia Majestatis decus & securitatem pervigiles excubent, & Reipubl. Gallicanae amorem tenellis adolescentium ingenijs, Christianis pietatem erga Deum, subditis fidem erga Reges, civibus commune boni publici desiderium inferant. Regem piissimum & suorum amantissimum, priusquam atroci & cruento vulnere à nefario parricida confossus ad coelum migraret, de Academiae sua dignitate revocandaserio cogitasse, necfatis esse duxisse, si fidissima Majestatis suae filia viveret, nisi etiam splendide & regie viveret. Hanc igitur tanti Regis filiam stare jam in conspectu judicum, eosque per sacros illius manes obsecrare, ne labores, conatus, gloriam suam cum Iesuitis partiri cogatur. Non ea laborum suorum praemia rependi sibi Academiam postulare, quae ingentes familiarum amplissimos reditus adaequent, non quaerere eam Baronias, Comitatus, Abbatias, non captare hereditates, non arcana quadam arte munerum copiam passim ex omnium manibus & loculis elicere, sed tantum supplicitèr & demisse petere, ne in hoc squalore deferatur, neque in hoc miserarum caeno hactenus depressa opprimatur. Iesuitae quidem cur finibus Academicis se contineant, cur tantus eos Gallicanae juventutis educandae pruritus agitet, cur ovis Gallicis tam pertinaciter incubent, causam non esse aliam, quam ut Gallorum loco Milvios aut vultures excludant. Haec enim nisi ipsis mens esset, futurum certe, ut Academiam non tam assiduè impeterent, non eius fores tam proterve arietarent. At vero Academia totius in judices aequissimos eorumque dignitatem defixum aspectum esse, eosque eo sibi a- quiores magisque propitios fore confidere, quo adversariorum ambitus plus gratiae & favoris apud plerosque videatur obtinuisse. Non opibus eam contendere, quae exhausta sint, non dignitate, quae jam pridem jaceat, non amplitudine, quae indignissime conteratur, sed precibus, lachrymis, squalore & miseria, per Deum enim immortalem eam obtestari, per Henrici Magni, suavissimi patriae parentis pios ac propitios manes, per ultimas eius voluntates, per Christianissimi Regis, & Reginae Matris optimae ac Serenissimae securitatem, per Galliae totius incolumitatem, per decus & amorem patriae, per liberos eorum quorum praesertim res agitur, per eos ipsos & nominis eorum immortalitate, ut eripiant tandem aliquando literas ex profanis istis manibus, easque suae parenti & Academiarum Regina, vel potius suam eis parentem restituant, neque diutius purissimum ac verè Christalinum oculi Gallicani humorem, admixtis exotericae doctrinae sordibus turbari permittant, considerantes nempe, satius esse, ut ad Senatus Parisiensis nomen & recordationem totius deinceps gestiens prosiliat Academia, eique aeternum victuros gloriae lauros decerpat, quàm ut novus, & Gallicano praesertim genio initiatus religiosorum hominum coetus e finibus monasticae professionis exiliens, cum omnium pene Ordinum querela, cum totius Galliae periculo, cum certissima Musarum politiorum ruina, ubique jactet & proclamet, ipsis judicibus, societatem suam in Academicos irrupisse, Academiam & literas meliores ipsorum judicum sententia concidisse, & tertium istum Gallicani lilij apicem, judiciumque spiritu persculsum emarcuisse.
units.tr: ...breathing out its soul. Although an advocate has been given to the University, one who, keen-eyed on every side, can lead the minds of the French easily through the pathless, steep and winding ways of the Jesuit Society, he nevertheless declares that he comes to speak in such a way that each man may understand that the part he has taken up is that of piety rather than defence, of complaint rather than eloquence, of grief rather than talent. Yet he does not deny meanwhile that he has been driven to this course by the importunity of the adversaries, who, though often warned to desist from their seizures, often rebuked to set a limit to their ambition, and often thrust away from the altars and hearths of the University, have never been able to restrain themselves from breaking into the rights and properties of others. Among their other wicked crimes, the most unworthy and utterly intolerable is this: they are now trying to bring danger upon the members of the University not through themselves and their emissaries, but through the judges of Parliament themselves, the guardians of the University, and they think that those whom they have not until now been able to destroy secretly by plots and tricks they will overwhelm by the sentences of judges and the authority of the courts. Since, among their other grounds for the petition, they have objected to the University the devastation and confusion, and the excessive licence of youthful age, as certain diseases of the academic body, which the commands of the Royal Majesty and the weight of the authority of Parliament are not equal to curing, but only their society, sent down from heaven for that very purpose, will prove able to cure them, he says that the obliging hands of such Reverend Fathers are by no means required for removing diseases of this kind. First, then, the physicians are by no means to be called in to treat the suffering University who have that innate contempt for any other society, by whose counsels and arts a huge heap of diseases has taken possession of France; who, like importunate fortune-hunters, stand about, and, before death has been lamented, seek the management of the funeral; nay rather, who, like ravens gaping for prey, are wont to retire only when a morsel has been thrown into their mouths. The most holy and regular Fathers, most tenacious of their own, while the Academics think of nothing of the kind, have inflicted a bloody and deadly wound in former times. For, tossed by the storms of civil wars, the University had barely emerged from the common shipwreck, and since the most shrewd Fathers have noticed that its convulsed nerves and broken strength can be restored only by a special outpouring of royal bounty, they therefore went to the King and humbly asked that he would sprinkle that little flock of theirs with some drop of sweetness. They say they have a spirit truly French, not so much in name as in fact, in affection and zeal, and altogether present to the service of the Royal Majesty; that among all flowers the lily alone is dear to them; that all their efforts and thoughts are directed to the common good of the Commonwealth. Letters, they say, are the ornament of the Commonwealth, the defence of the realm, the sun and eye of the kingdom; therefore the city of Paris alone should not enjoy the benefit of letters and rejoice in the good of educating youth, but that benefit ought to be spread abroad through the various and manifold regions, cities and provinces of the whole kingdom. Thus the most excellent and magnificent King received them with the gentler arms of his clemency, cherished them in his bosom and heart, and then enriched them with the most ample stipends, in Flèche and in other parts of the kingdom, through his subjects. Then, armed as it were with those weapons, and touched by the royal name as by a divine power, they afterwards attacked the unarmed University, destitute of all protection, and, while they gave away gratis that so profitable business of theirs, drew the youth away from the University, so that it is no wonder that the fountain of literary life has now dried up, its veins and channels on every side cut off by which it had received blood and spirit. Now, indeed, the Jesuits are disappointed in their expectation, for it has come about that the whole body of the suffering University, besieged by their flocks thrown around it, has gathered its strength, which was failing as its heart died, and is reviving it with the purer doctrine of its parent, and has nourished the gaping ravens. The Fathers of Clermont, noticing this, at once fled to other arts, and obtained from the King a diploma or rescript by which the power of opening public schools in the very gymnasium of the Paris Academy was granted to them. Thus they began to instruct youth, not in person, but through certain little masters, some summoned from elsewhere, or like mushrooms bursting out by night in an empty space from the fertility of the Clermont soil. Nothing is surprising, then, if the University, drained almost of its strength, is compelled not only to groan and lament its fate, but to cry out against violence and fraud and to implore the faith of God and men. At that outcry the very Fathers who had laid snares for its life now come running and ask to be received into the bosom of the Academics, wishing to be enrolled as the family of the Academy, not as masters of an estate but as tenants, nay rather as humble servants; they pour out sweet voices smeared with honey, which, if anyone has sense, he will find more bitter than gall itself. They offer bread with the left hand and hide a stone in the right. The Academics indeed wish that they would send themselves not only as companions but as brothers, and that it were allowed to venerate them as Fathers; but that they have mountains of ground and this cannot be done, the many cities which the Jesuits govern at their nod, the many provinces which they hold, the many Academies which lie in their own ashes, and from whose ruins they have erected their mad structures of wealth, sufficiently attest and prove. For they, with silent and secret movements, are trying to ensnare the Paris Academy, so that it may be wise at its own peril, and not only cautiously and prudently anticipate the dangers threatening it, but also bravely and gloriously drive them off. They, offending, seem to be like the Society of Jesus, or like eagles which gradually wear away the things with which they are enclosed and hidden; or like rivers which, filling up islands, seem to flatter them, yet break them up and destroy them. There is no need for them to inquire into the external dangers of the other Academies, and to desire their voices and movements; the danger is already within, the disease already seething in the vitals, and the very enemies of the Academy, under the pretext of medicines, infect its veins, drained of better blood, with poisoned cups of corrupt doctrines; and while they are setting before the languishing Academics their freely offered ambrosia and nectar, those pestilent dainties, they stand ready to suffocate the Academy, to cut out its tongue lest it speak, to tear out its eyes lest it see their frauds, to strike at its foot, to attack its very head, and to try and provoke the Sorbonne itself. The name of the Society of Jesus sounds splendid in their words, and the weight and importance of the public good, but that now it is allowed for them to shake off the yoke from subjects, to mock the decrees of the Senate and even the royal rescripts, to deceive the eyes of the ignorant crowd, to overturn ancient Academies, to invent miracles about their Fathers, to write martyrdoms everywhere, to hold the decrees of the Sorbonne not merely in mockery but to pursue them with insults; in short, that all things may be overturned, so that at last the Jesuit sect alone, flooding the whole world with the torches of its doctrines, may shake out all the thorns of vices, brambles and noxious juices of worse teaching. What Osorius once said, that as the world leaned toward old age, there would be born a society of some unusual name, which with its swollen teachings would impose silence, and before whose rising, as before the rising of the sun, the other assemblies of men united by the law of humanity would be snatched from mortal eyes like stars shining with a feeble and spurious light, the Jesuits boast that they have now achieved this throughout almost the whole Christian world. And certainly they have expelled from their seats on every side the choicest booty and talents of better repute; everywhere, breathing out upon them, they have blasted the gems of budding industry, as if blown by some pestilential whirlwind; they have blocked the path by which men of letters could emerge and make themselves known. One Academy alone, they say, remains, the Paris Academy, to which, as to a harbour, the young may flee to publish the fruits of their virtue and learning. Because the Jesuits see this as a rock on which they will be broken if they rush against it, they have resolved to bring all their machines to bear on its destruction, and now they reckon it as the greatest benefit, if, under the appearance of the Society and in the name of uniting with the Academics and promoting their welfare, they expose all their labours, vigils and efforts to every whirlwind of envy, if they force the Academy to beg at the threshold of the Clermont house like a cheap beggar, and shamefully to wait for the rewards of its students from their treasury, and so make this Society a laughingstock and a fable throughout the world. The Academics, indeed, stand ready for battle; they will contend with those reverend Fathers not by tricks, not by ambition, not by cunning, but by talent, learning, industry, virtue and candour of mind. They wish, therefore, that the lights of the Jesuit Society and those giants, who think that by piling books upon books, as mountains upon mountains, they can climb to the heavens of wisdom, and who think they can cast down from its throne the guardian gods of the Academy, should come forward; yet they hope that the Jesuits will contend naked against the naked Academics, for if this were done, they hope the whole affair would have an outcome pleasing to all, useful to the Commonwealth and wholesome to letters. Moreover, they demand not only the reasoning of learning and erudition, but the safety of the Commonwealth itself, the dignity of the Gallic Empire, and indeed the security of the Most Christian King, that the instruction of French youth be entrusted and committed to the Academy alone and to the diligence of the Academics. They say that Augustus once advised Maecenas that youth should be handed over for education to those who were loudly denouncing the Roman Empire; therefore the training of French young men cannot be commended to anyone more safely than to the Paris Academics, who live with the same spirit as all of France, and who for that reason seek only that the life of the Academy be preserved, so that they may keep watch in it as on a lookout, vigilant for the honour and security of the Royal Majesty, and may instil love of the French Commonwealth into the tender minds of young men, piety towards God into Christians, loyalty towards kings into subjects, and the common desire for the public good into citizens. They say that the most pious King, who cherished his own people most lovingly, before he was pierced by a fierce and bloody wound from the wicked parricide and went to heaven, had thought of recalling the University to its dignity, and had judged it not enough that his most faithful daughter should live, unless she lived also in splendour and royal state. This daughter of so great a King, they say, now stands in the sight of the judges, and begs them by his sacred shade not to force her to share her labours, efforts and glory with the Jesuits. The Academy does not ask that the rewards of its labours be paid to it in such a way as to equal the huge revenues of great families; it does not seek baronies, counties or abbacies, does not catch at inheritances, does not by some secret art draw the abundance of gifts from everyone's hands and purses; it only asks humbly and meekly that it not be left in this squalor, nor be crushed any longer in this mire of wretchedness in which it has hitherto been held down. As for the Jesuits, why they keep within the bounds of the Academy, why so great an itch to educate French youth stirs them, why they sit so stubbornly upon French eggs, the reason is none other than that they may hatch out kites or vultures in place of Frenchmen. For if this were not their intention, they would certainly not assail the Academy so constantly, nor batter its doors so shamelessly. But the Academy has fixed its gaze on the judges, all of them most fair, and on their dignity; it trusts that they will be all the more favourable and well-disposed to it, the more the ambition of its adversaries seems to have gained favour and grace with most people. It does not contend with wealth, for that is exhausted; nor with dignity, which has long lain prostrate; nor with greatness, which is being most shamefully trampled; but with prayers, tears, squalor and misery. For it calls upon the immortal God, by the pious and gracious shades of Henry the Great, the sweetest father of the country, by his last wishes, by the security of the most Christian King and of the most excellent and most serene Queen Mother, by the safety of all France, by the honour and love of the fatherland, by the children of those whose cause above all is being treated, and by the immortality of their names, to snatch at last the letters from these profane hands and restore them to their parent, and to restore to it its own parent, and no longer to permit the most pure and truly crystalline humour of the French eye to be troubled, its purity mixed with the filth of exoteric doctrine. For they consider it better that the Academy, eager to leap forth henceforth into the name and remembrance of the Parisian Senate, should pluck laurels of glory that will live forever, than that a new company of religious men, initiated especially into the French spirit, should leap out from the bounds of monastic profession, with the complaint of almost all the Orders, with the danger of all France, with the most certain ruin of the more refined Muses, and should boast and proclaim everywhere to the judges themselves that their society has burst in upon the Academics, that the Academy and better letters have fallen by the sentence of the judges themselves, and that this third peak of the Gallic lily, and its judgment, struck through with spirit, has withered away.

units.la: Excusa est haec Actio iuxta exemplar Parisiis apud Ioannem Petit-pas, via Iacobaea sub scuto Venetiarum excusum, Anno 1612.
units.tr: This Action has been printed according to the copy printed at Paris by Jean Petit-Pas, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the sign of the Shield of Venice, in the year 1612.

units.la: ARRE
units.tr: ARREST

units.la: ARRESTVM CVRIAE PARLAMENTI: PRIMARIA, RERVM CAPITALIVM ET EDICTI Classibus convocatis 22. Decemb. 1611. LATVM In causa Sacerdotum, et Scholasticorum Colle- gii Claromontani qui se Iesuitas vocant, Diplomatis Regis 20. Augusti 1610. comprobationem postulantium, quo omne scientiarum artiumque genus, in Collegio Claromontano, iuxta Edicti Septemb. 1603. & aliarum constitutionum normam, publice docendi, potestas concedatur: ET Rectoris, Syndicorum ac Decanorum Vniversitatis, Intercedentium Editioni Diplomatis, ac libello supplice oblato 2. Decemb. 1611. petentium, ut ex lege Edicti Restitutionis Iesuitarum, & Decreti quo il- lud comprobatum est, ab omni Scholastico munere arceantur: nullo, ex personarum qualitate, praejudicio suborituro. Cui inseruntur ex D. Ludovici Servini Advocati fisci Regii, Actione, excerpta summa capita. EX ACTIS CVRIAE PARLAMENTI:
units.tr: ARREST OF THE PARLIAMENT: THE PRINCIPAL ARREST CONCERNING CAPITAL MATTERS AND THE EDICT, PRONOUNCED WITH THE CLASSES CONVENED, 22 DECEMBER 1611. In the case of the priests and scholastics of the College of Clermont, who call themselves Jesuits, petitioning for the confirmation of the King's letters patent of 20 August 1610, by which the power of publicly teaching every kind of science and art in the College of Clermont is granted, according to the norm of the Edict of September 1603 and of other constitutions; and of the Rector, Syndics and Deans of the University, who oppose the registration of the letters patent and, by a supplicating petition presented on 2 December 1611, ask that they be excluded from every scholastic office under the law of the Edict of Restitution of the Jesuits and the decree by which that edict was confirmed, without prejudice arising from the quality of the persons. To this are added the principal heads excerpted from the Action of Lord Louis Servin, Advocate of the King's Fisc. FROM THE ACTS OF THE PARLIAMENT:

units.la: Mane. PRIMARIO PRAESIDE, ARRESTVM pronunciante.
units.tr: Morning. THE FIRST PRESIDENT PRONOUNCING THE ARREST.

units.la: Ontroversia, ultro citroque copiose disceptata, hinc, inter Sacerdotes & Scholasticos Collegii Claromontani, qui se Iesuitas vocat, Diplomatis Regis 20. Augusti 1610. dati Impetratores, & quod decreto Curiae comprobari, petunt, quo omne scientiarum artiumque genus, in Collegio Claromontano, iuxta Edicti Septemb. 1603. & aliarum constitutionum, declarationumque norma, publice docendi potestas conceditur, quaeque defensorum quoque vices sunt: inde, inter Rectorem, Membra & Decanos Vniversitatis Parisiensis, intercedentes comprobationi Diplomatis, ac supplice libello 2. Decemb. 1611. oblato, postulantes, ut, iuxta legem Edicti, quo restituti sunt Iesuitae, prohibitio, ab omni munere & exercitio scholastico, arceantur: nullo ex personarum qualitate praejudicio suborituro.
units.tr: The controversy, debated at length on both sides, arises from the priests and scholastics of the College of Clermont, who call themselves Jesuits, who seek the confirmation by decree of the Court of the King's letters patent of 20 August 1610, by which the power of publicly teaching every kind of science and art in the College of Clermont is granted according to the norm of the Edict of September 1603 and of other constitutions and declarations, and who also act as their own defenders. On the other side, the Rector, members and Deans of the University of Paris, opposing the confirmation of the letters patent and asking by a supplicating petition presented on 2 December 1611 that, under the law of the Edict by which the Jesuits were restored, they be kept back from every scholastic office and practice, without prejudice arising from the quality of the persons.

units.la: Quumque iam in quartum usque diem, Maiore, Criminali & Edicti Classibus convocatis, Montholonius, Diplomatis Impetratorum nomine & Marteau, interceptorum partes sustinens, auditi sint: atque ea causa perorata somni intentionis clausula, illi Diploma comprobari petant, & hi vero recusent, supplice libello intercedant, cumque Rector quoque, & ex Impetratoribus nonnulli, verba fecerint. Quin etiam cum Cognitoris Regii nomine SERVIVS egerit, cuius orationis haec fuere capita: se iam, 17. mensis huius, cum in eius causae, inter Sacerdotes & Scholasticos Collegii Claromontani petitores,
units.tr: When the hearing had already continued for four days, with the Grand Chamber, the Criminal Chamber and the Chamber of Edicts convened, Montholon, speaking on behalf of the applicants for the letters patent, and Marteau, sustaining the part of the opponents, were heard; the case having been concluded with the closing clause of intention, they ask that the letters be confirmed, while the others refuse and oppose by supplicating petition; and the Rector also spoke, as did some of the applicants. Moreover, Servin spoke in the name of the King's Commissioner, whose speech contained these heads: that on the 17th of this month, when in the case between the priests and scholastics of the College of Clermont as petitioners...

units.la: { } Sacerdotes ut rescriptum Regium, 20. Augusti, 1610. Senatusconsulto comprobaretur, & inter Rectorem, Decanum Facultatum, Nationum procuratores, & alia Membra Universitatis, reluctantes & ex occasione Petitores, disceptandae nomen recitaretur: altercationibus, antequam Advocati causam agerent, occurrente, ea protulisse tum quae hodie quoq; referenda videantur. Nempe, pro muneris ratione, ut suarum est partium, ad gloriam Dei, Ecclesiae bonum spectare, ac Regiam, vitam, salutem, securitatem, & Reipublicae totius tranquillitatem fartam tectam tueri, se adhortationibus utrosque, Actores & Defensores, verbis sanctis Pauli commonefecisse, ut pacis, quoad fieri posset, & concordiae mutuae rationes inirent.
units.tr: ...the priests asked that the royal rescript of 20 August 1610 be confirmed by a decree of the Senate, and while the Rector, the Dean of the Faculties, the procurators of the Nations and other members of the University, reluctant, and the petitioners on this occasion, had the name of the debate read out, and altercations arose before the advocates pleaded the case, he had then put forward things which seem to deserve mention today as well. Namely, that, according to the nature of his office, as belongs to his part, looking to the glory of God and the good of the Church, and to guard the King's life, person, safety and security, and the tranquillity of the whole Commonwealth, he had admonished both the plaintiffs and the defenders, in the holy words of Paul, that they should take steps towards peace and mutual concord, as far as this could be done.

units.la: Ac propterea, Actoribus dixit, eos beneficium ab Henrico Magno, gloriosae memoriae, impetratum, grata mente iugiter recolere debere, qui cum unusquisque fidelissimorum & longo rerum usu prudentissimorum Ministrorum consiliis, ab illorum revocatione deterreretur, nihilominus, id beneficij largiri constituisset, hac spe ex promissionibus ipsorum concepta, inductus, fore videlicet, ut Indulgentiae & Clementiae Principali, officiis & obsequiis, Regiae Maiestati praestitis, gratiam aliquam referrent: eo etiam maxime, quod nullius rei, praeterquam reditus, gratiam postularent, nec alium sibi finem propositum esse significarent, nedum, ut ea, quae hodie efflagitant, expetituri viderentur.
units.tr: And therefore, he said to the plaintiffs, they ought always to recall with a grateful mind the favour obtained from Henry the Great, of glorious memory; who, although he was deterred from granting it by the counsel of each of his most faithful ministers, and of those most prudent through long experience of affairs, nevertheless resolved to bestow that favour, induced by the hope conceived from their promises, namely that they would make some return of gratitude to the royal Majesty for the indulgence and clemency of the Prince, by the services and obedience rendered; the more so because they sought no favour of anything except revenue, and signified that they had no other end proposed to themselves, much less that they would seem to aim at what they now demand urgently.

units.la: Addidit quoque, perpenderent secum ipsi an aequum esset, statim a Magni Regis obitu, illud postulare, quod ipsemet, nequaquam iis concedendum esse censuisset, & quod dum in vivis erat, urgere nequaquam essent ausi. Haec saltem lex, si pertinaciter petitioni insisterent, ipsis praescribebatur, ut sese prisci Universitatis Parisiensis Decretis, & Theologicae Facultati, in hisce quatuor capitibus, potissimum subiicerent.
units.tr: He added also that they should weigh with themselves whether it was fair to demand at once, after the death of the Great King, that which he himself had judged should by no means be conceded to them, and which, while he was alive, they had not dared to press. This, at least, was the law prescribed to them, if they persisted obstinately in their petition: that they should submit themselves, above all, to the decrees of the ancient University of Paris and to the Theological Faculty, in these four heads.

units.la: Primo, quo Regum salute & securitati consulatur, quos saepenumero iam impetitos, iterato parricidio, nefarie e vivis sublatos, scelestissimorum parricidarum manu vidimus, qui falso & detestabili Religionis obtentu, ac impura, temeraria-que doctrina, nuper causa, quam ex libris & scholis ipsorum Impetratorum hauserant, ut ex Regorum confessionibus & Curiae Arrestis, apparuit actis fuere: Petitores, tam detestandis opinionibus renunciant, nec tantum scriptoribus suae societatis, qui eas tradiderunt, non assentiantur, sed etiam scriptis editis, juxta verbum Dei, in Veteri & Novo Testamento comprehensum, illas oppugnent.
units.tr: First, that the safety and security of Kings be provided for, whom, attacked many times already, we have seen removed from life by the hand of most wicked parricides, by a second parricide, who, under a false and detestable pretext of religion, and by an impure and rash doctrine, which they had drawn from the books and schools of the applicants themselves, as appeared from the confessions of the kings and the arrest of the Court, carried out their crimes. The petitioners must renounce such detestable opinions, and not only not assent to the writers of their society who handed them down, but also, by published writings, according to the word of God contained in the Old and New Testaments, oppose them.

units.la: Dicant doceant, scribant ubique, nefas esse cuiquam, sive peregrinus, sive naturalis Regis subditus audiat, in Capita vitamque sacratissimas Majestatis Regum & Principum moliri, quantumlibet speciosum auctoritatis, vel spiritualis, vel temporalis nomine praetendatur, quaecunque praetexatur causa, etiam ubi de moribus & religione agitur; sanctè pollicentur & subscriptione sua confirment ac recipiant, pateface-turos se, quotquot intelligent, aut sentient, tam horrenda consilia agitare, nec unquam iis adstipulaturos dogmatis, quibus malesana perditorum hominum ingenia, directe vel indirecte, tanquam fulcro, admachinationes adversus Unctorum Dei capita, struendas, niterentur.
units.tr: Let them say, teach and write everywhere that it is unlawful for anyone, whether a foreigner or a natural subject of the King, to hear, or to plan against the head and most sacred life of the Majesty of Kings and Princes, however specious the name of authority, whether spiritual or temporal, under which it is put forward, whatever cause is pretended, even where morals and religion are at issue. Let them solemnly promise, and confirm by their signature and accept, that they will disclose to the magistrates all who understand or perceive that they are plotting such horrible counsels, and that they will never assent to those doctrines on which the mad minds of desperate men lean, directly or indirectly, as on a prop, for devising plots against the heads of God's anointed.

units.la: Secundo, Diplomatis Impetratores profiteantur, praedicent, doceant, inter ceteras potestates summas a Deo constitutas, Francorum Regem Christianissimum, in Temporalibus solo Deo minorem, non aliud in Terris supra se, praeter Dei numen agnoscere, cuius beneficio, absoluto in subditos dominii jure, potiatur: nec spiritualibus potestatibus, pietatis licet colore praetento; & promovendae vel defendendae Religionis specie, fas esse Temporalium Regum ac Principum jura usurpare, magis, quam Regibus, auctoritatis Regiae titulo, spiritualis auctoritatis, apicem invadere, quapropter in se recipiant, nunquam se hoc in argumento distinctionibus, nuper a quibusdam Doctoribus excogitatis, docendo usuros, quae hic vocabulis expressa fuerunt: Directe aut indirecte, per se aut per accidens.
units.tr: Second, let the applicants for the letters profess and preach and teach that, among other supreme powers ordained by God, the Most Christian King of the French, in temporal matters inferior only to God, acknowledges no other power on earth above himself except the divine majesty, by whose benefit he holds sway, with the right of dominion over his subjects absolutely granted; and that it is not lawful, under the colour of piety pretended, or under the appearance of promoting or defending religion, to usurp the rights of temporal Kings and Princes, nor, under the title of royal authority, to invade the summit of spiritual authority more than the Kings themselves. Therefore let them undertake never to use, in this matter, those distinctions lately devised by certain doctors, which have been expressed here in these words: directly or indirectly, per se or per accidens.

units.la: Agnoscam Agnoscant ingenuè, Scholasticis subtilitatibus, non res, sed verba tantùm mutari, quò Ecclesia, immensa quædam et nullis cohibita finibus potestas, omnibus imperiis & Rebuspublicis sæcularibus gravis et damnosa constituatur, & spiritualis potestas in temporale imperium transferat, juris & regiminis Regij Majestate, sacerdotalibus infulis tributa. Connivere inviolabili inviolatoque, nec problematico, axiomate afferant, penes authoritatem & potestatem nullius esse, Abdicatione, suspensione, ac Regni privatione, Reges, eorum dominos occupanti, vel depredanti expositâ multare.
units.tr: Let them frankly acknowledge that by scholastic subtleties not the thing but only the words are changed, so that the Church, a kind of immense power bounded by no limits, is established as burdensome and harmful to all empires and civil commonwealths, and that spiritual power is transferred into temporal empire, the right and royal majesty of kingship being assigned to the sacerdotal mitres. Let them not connive at, nor propose as a questionable axiom, the inviolable and unviolated principle that, Kings having no authority or power over their subjects, those who seize or plunder them may be punished by deposition, suspension, and deprivation of the kingdom.

units.la: Tertio, doceant, profiteantur scribantque: Omnes Regis subditos, tam Ecclesiastiquam seculares, ad eam, erga Regem, obedientiam teneri, quam Dominus noster Iesus Christus, humanam indutus naturam, Imperatoribus & Magistratibus, nascens, monstravit, quemadmodum hac lege sancivit: Reddite Cæsaris, quæ Cæsari, Deo quæ Dei, atque eam etiam ob causam, Regnum suum negavit esse mundanum, alioqui sibi defuturos satellites, qui arma expedirent.
units.tr: Third, let them teach, profess and write that all the King's subjects, both ecclesiastical and lay, are bound to that obedience towards the King which our Lord Jesus Christ, clothed in human nature, showed when he was born, towards the emperors and magistrates, and which he sanctioned by this law: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's"; and that for this reason also he declared that his kingdom was not of this world, otherwise, he said, there would be attendants who would take up arms for him.

units.la: Atque ista verba, ut & Pauli Rom. 13. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subiecta esto, quæ sunt non tantum præcepti alicuius, declarationis, aut exempli ad impus observandi vim obtinere, quando videlicet Christiani, Temporali potestate (ut ipsit quidam ex ipsorum societate Coryphæus) carebant, Infidelibus subjecti: fidelitatem in verbum omnes & in æternum, cuiusque fuerint ordinis Ecclesiastici et Laici, obligaretur nexu arctissimo adstringi.
units.tr: And these words, as also the words of Paul in Romans 13, "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers," are not merely of the force of some precept, declaration, or example to be observed by the faithful, since, namely, Christians, when they lacked temporal power (as one of their own society, their chief, has said), were subject to infidels; all, of whatever ecclesiastical or lay order, are bound by a most tight bond of fidelity, to be observed in word and for ever.

units.la: Ac proinde, ad huius legis amussim, vivendum esse, asseverent, quam Apostoli, & eos imitati vere Christiani, religiose observarunt, qui non modo tum, cum pauci veritatem Christianam ampleterentur, sed etiam, cum in amplissimum numerum excrevissent, Dominuli, Cæsaribus & Regibus, vel Hæreticis & Infidelibus, in temporalibus, fideliter fuerunt.
units.tr: Accordingly, they assert that one must live by the rule of this law, which the Apostles and those true Christians who imitated them observed faithfully, and that they were faithful to the Lord's kings and emperors, to Caesars and Kings, or to heretics and infidels, in temporal matters, not only when only a few embraced the Christian truth, but also when they had grown to a very great number.

units.la: Quapropter Diplomatis Impetratores, fide caveant, se dictis & doctrinâ professuros: ullam potestatem, qualiscunque tandem sit, nec ipsam etiam Ecclesiam, vel in Concilio congregatam, ut alia quapiam ratione, jure ullo præditam esse, quo subditos, à Fidelitatis juramento absolvere, & obedientiæ, ad quam jure divino, naturali, & humano, exhibendam tenentur, vincula, ullo pacto laxare valeat.
units.tr: Therefore the petitioners for the letters patent must solemnly pledge that they will profess, in word and in teaching, that no power of whatever kind, not even the Church itself, whether gathered in council or endowed with any other right in any way, can loosen the bonds by which subjects are released from the oath of fidelity and are held to render obedience, which they owe by divine, natural and human law.

units.la: Quarto, quod ad πολιτείαν Ecclesiasticam attinet, ad regis authoritatem, & Regni es tutandas, Diplomatis Impetratores, ore & scripto, tueantur libertates & jura Ecclesiæ, in cujus sinu viwunt, Gallicana: nec quicquam dicant, scribant, proponantve quorundam Decretorum, quæ in Francia nec probata, nec admissa sunt, prætextu novo quod illis adversetur.
units.tr: Fourth, as regards the ecclesiastical polity, the petitioners for the letters patent shall, by word and writing, defend the authority of the King and the rights of the kingdom, and likewise the liberties and rights of the Church in whose bosom they live, the Gallican liberties. They shall not say, write or put forward anything from certain decrees which have been neither approved nor admitted in France, on the pretext that some new thing is opposed to them.

units.la: Ac proinde, deinceps sese scripturos recipiant, & curaturos, ut à Generali & Provincialibus adprobentur, quæ sunt adversus suæ societatis homines conscripturi, qui libris suis, dogmata contraria, quatuor hisce capitibus posuerunt.
