units.tr: Accordingly, they shall undertake to write henceforth, and to see to it, that whatever is to be written against the men of their society who in their books have set out doctrines contrary to these four heads is approved by the General and the provincials.

units.la: In summa, Prisci Universitatis Parisiensis, ac Facultatis Theologicæ Decreta, ac Institutis stent per omnia.
units.tr: In sum, the decrees and institutions of the ancient University of Paris and of its Theological Faculty shall stand in every respect.

units.la: Quibus capitibus, donec plane satisfecerint, & indubitatis nixunt, sinceri animi, sunt fecerint, cancellis Editi Restitutionis, sese continent, atque postquam ita cavent, libera demum, arbitratu Curiæ, juris reddendi potestas esto, in iis, quæ nunc indulgent sibi postulant.
units.tr: Until they have fully satisfied these heads, and have done so on undoubted grounds of a sincere mind, they are to keep within the limits of the Edict of Restitution. Only after they have given such assurances shall the power of administering justice be left free, at the discretion of the Court, in those matters which they now claim for themselves.

units.la: Hæc, is qui verba facit, sæpenumero testatur, se Petitorum sociis significasse; hæc eadem complures clarissimi Viri, dignitate senatoria, in hac Curia, illustres intellexerunt, cum in hos sermones inciderent.
units.tr: The speaker often testifies that he had signified this to the companions of the petitioners; and several most distinguished men of senatorial rank in this Court have understood the same things when they fell into these discussions.

units.la: Quin etiam Patri Frontoni, & alteri sodali, pridie quam causa disceptarentur, ista proponebat, coram Amplissimæ Dignitatis Viro, pietate, doctrina, erga Ecclesiam, Regem, Regnumque fide & studiis conspicuo, in Curia suprema, Præside: qui suâ quoque authoritate & suffragio eosdem excitat, ut candidè & ingenuè, præscriptis sanctionibus in Senatu recitatis, subs scriberet, & eas fine ulla elufionis vel æquivocationis stropha, approbarent. A
units.tr: Indeed, on the day before the case was argued, he set these things before Father Fronton and another companion, in the presence of a man of the highest dignity, presiding in the Supreme Court, conspicuous for piety, learning, and his faithful zeal for the Church, the King and the kingdom. This man, by his own authority and vote, also urged them to subscribe frankly and ingenuously to the prescribed sanctions, read out in the Senate, and to approve them without any trick of evasion or equivocation.

units.la: quæ cùm Regis Advocatus, sibi certum quid responderi peteret, excepit Fro[?] to, Quantumvis ipse atque alij foci, qui Parifiis degunt, ita sentirent (nam fi[?] privatim ab hac sententia alienum non esse animum, utpote qui in Politicis arbitrarentur temporibus & locis, ubi vivitur, seruiendum esse) non tamen integrum sibi esse, pra[?] cifa declaratione uti, nisi ante, hac de re cum socijs, qui in hac urbe sunt, conse[?] ret: imo existimare fe, re communicata, constituturum, ad hasce propositiones nisi prius Generalis Præpositi, cuius sententia expectanda erat, animo explo[?] rato, expedite & tuto responderi non posse.
units.tr: When the King's Advocate asked for some definite answer, Fronton replied that however much he himself and the others who live in Paris might think so (for privately he was not averse to this opinion, since they judged that in political matters one must serve the times and places in which one lives), it was nevertheless not in his power to make a precise declaration unless he first consulted on the matter with the companions who are in this city. Indeed, he thought that once the matter had been shared, they would decide that these propositions could not be answered readily and safely unless first the mind of the General Provost, whose opinion had to be awaited, had been explored.

units.la: Quæ Rectori, & ijs, qui eum comitabantur, cum fuissent significata, re[?] fponderunt, sibi verba Frontonis probari non posse, captiosa & æquivocatio[?] nibus obnoxia, præsertim cum diceret, In politicis seruiendum esse tempor[?] bus & locis, ubi vivitur. Adde quod, cum effet in confesso, Postulantium fc[?] cietatem, in omnibus, & per omnia, à Generali suo pendere, qui maiore quar[?] cæteri Generales solent, potestate in sibi subditos religiosos potiretur, atq; ex[?] tra Regnum Gallia commoraretur, nullam rationem, ad fidem ipsis habendar[?] aperiri, tum etiam, quod Iesuitæ omnibus alijs ferre leges, à nullo vero accipe[?] re consueverint.
units.tr: When these things were reported to the Rector and to those who accompanied him, they replied that they could not approve Fronton's words, being captious and open to equivocation, especially since he said, "In political matters one must serve the times and places in which one lives." Add that, since it is admitted that the petitioners' society depends in everything and through everything on its General, who holds greater power over the religious subject to him than other Generals usually do, and who lives outside the kingdom of France, no reason has been offered for giving them credit. Also, the Jesuits are accustomed to lay down laws for all others, but to receive them from no one.

units.la: Prætere a, Iesuitas istius iustæ diffidentiæ causas ubique suis actionibus [?] inftitutis dedisse, ubicunque pedem fixerunt, affectato, tam in clericos, quar[?] in Laicos dominio: Quibus accedit, quod omnibus hic unicus fcopus, norm[?] instar ob oculos est, ut cuncta ad societatis, etiam ex aliorum damno, uti[?] tem, atque amplificationem dirigantur. Quod dogmata priscis legibus Regi[?] & Regni Constitutionibus contraria tuentur; Quod fi contingat aliquem e[?] societate exitiale scriptum edere, neque societatis coetus, nec ex ea quispiam[?] illud palam improbat, aut ad veritatis defensionem fe accingit. Addidit Rec[?] privatim, sibi complures esse rationes exponendas adversus petitorum peftul[?] tionem, quas Curiæ cognitioni, tam suo, quam Advocati ore subiecturus e[?] set, quod is qui Regis nomine verba facit, tum ut omnem culpam, coram De[?] & Hominibus, à fe derivaret, tum ut discordiæ fomitem, unde scandala & dif[?] dia, in Ecclesia & Republica, effent exoritura, extinguéret, ex fui muneris ra[?] tione, referendum esse duxit: Quocirca obnixe rogat Senatum, ut in meliore[?] partem, quæ proponuntur, interpretari dignetur, quo pacto omnes æquos re[?] rum æstimatores à privatis affectibus immunes, quique Religionis causam [?] Factionis malum non vertunt fano mentis iudicio, quæ dicta sunt, admitte[?] decet: hoc etiam addens, fi ulterius æstus contentionis feratur, ea quæ desid[?] rantur, & utrobique reprehendenda sunt, pro temporis & iuris ratione, prot[?] animadversionis officium requiret, significaturum esse.
units.tr: Moreover, the Jesuits have everywhere given just cause for such distrust, by their actions and their institutes, wherever they have fixed their foot, aiming at dominion over clergy and laity alike. To this is added that for them all there is one aim constantly before their eyes: that everything be directed to the advantage and enlargement of the society, even to the loss of others. They defend doctrines contrary to the ancient laws and to the constitutions of the King and kingdom. And if it happens that someone from the society publishes a pernicious writing, neither the society's assembly nor anyone from it openly disapproves it, or sets himself to defend the truth. The Rector added privately that many reasons were to be set forth against the petitioners' request, which he would lay before the Court's consideration by his own mouth as well as that of the Advocate. He thought it his duty, by reason of his office, to say this: both so that he might transfer all blame before God and men, and so that he might put out the spark of discord from which scandals and divisions would arise in the Church and the Republic. Therefore he earnestly asks the Senate to deign to interpret in the better part what is proposed, so that all fair judges of affairs, free from private passions, and who do not turn the cause of religion into the evil of faction, may with sound judgment admit what has been said. He adds also that if the heat of the contention goes further, then, for those things which are lacking and reprehensible on both sides, the office of punishment, according to the time and the law, will require him to signify it.

units.la: Enimvero, cùm in tertium usque diem, controversia utrinque agitata su[?] rit, ea iam refert, quæ in instrumentis, & copijs cautæ iudicialibus facerdotu[?] ac Scholasticorum Collegij Claromontani, qui fe Iesuitas vocant, observavi[?] excerpsit, collegitque, præter ea loca quæ à Montholonio, & à Martillerio sub[?] notata sunt: quæ partim ad ordinis eorum institutum, partim ad vitæ genus & Doctrinæ rationem spectant: quæ tria capita sunt excutienda, ut agnoscatur[?] utrum instituendæ iuventuti apti, & an eorum institutio utilis & salutaris[?] futura fit.
units.tr: Indeed, since the controversy was debated on both sides up to the third day, he now sets out what he has excerpted and gathered from the records and copies of the judicial cautions of the priests and scholastics of the Clermont College, who call themselves Jesuits, which he observed, apart from the passages noted by Montholon and by Marillac. These concern partly the institute of their order, partly their way of life and method of teaching. These three heads are to be examined, so that it may be recognized whether they are fit to instruct youth, and whether their instruction will be useful and wholesome.

units.la: Ac primum, quod ad Institutum ipsorum Clericorum, qui fe regulares[?] Religiosos appellant, nuncupantq;, liquet, eos non tam lege, quàm privilegi[?] gaudere. Hanc ob causam Ignatij Loyolæ Fundatoris scopum, vitam, & vitæ ra[?] tionem, à Ribadeneira & Maffæo conscriptam, expendit, atque constitutiones[?] & earum varias explicationes, Romæ excusas; bullas, quas à Pontificibus nu[?] mero 3[?] ero 37. impetraverunt; privilegia, & immunitates, quas subinde, vivæ vocis, ut quuntur, oraculo, elicuerunt: Congregationum Iesuiticarum canones & Generalium Epistolas, sedulò notavit & consideravit.
units.tr: And first, as to the institute of the clerics themselves, who call and name themselves regular religious, it is clear that they enjoy not so much law as privilege. For this reason he has carefully examined and considered the aim of the founder Ignatius of Loyola, and his life and way of life, as written by Ribadeneira and Maffei; the constitutions and their various explanations printed at Rome; the thirty-seven bulls which they obtained from the Popes; the privileges and immunities which they have since drawn, as they say, from the living voice of the oracle; and the canons of the Jesuit congregations and the letters of the Generals.

units.la: Quod verò ad ipsorum actiones & res gestas pertinet, retulit, se, ex Actis, (sicum tulit occasio, observatis) eorum, quæ ab eo tempore, quo sunt admissi, Gallia contigerunt, repetere. Quid de ipsis Eustatius Bellæus Episcopus Parisiensis 3. Augusti, 1554. iudicârit: quid declaraverit & decreverit Theologica facultas, in Sorbonæ Collegium eodem anno convocata; quæ postea Posfiaci ista, ubi suum dissimulabant institutum: quæ post ipsi fecerint: quid ad officium docendi, gratis, oblata, Academia exceperit; quid ea de re censuerit Turnerus. Expendisse quoque se, Actiones anno 1564. habitas, & præsertim, Actionem iniustam Mesnilij Advocati Fisci Regij, & quid causa Consilio permissa, à Curia creturn fuerit.
units.tr: As for their actions and deeds, he reports that he will recount, from the Acts (as occasion offered), what has happened in France since the time they were admitted. He sets out what Eustatius Bellæus, Bishop of Paris, judged of them on 3 August 1554; what the Theologica facultas, convened that same year in the Sorbonne College, declared and decreed; what they did afterwards at Poissy, where they concealed their institute; and what they did after that. He notes what the Academia received when they offered to teach free of charge, and what Turnerus thought of that matter. He also weighed the proceedings held in 1564, and especially the unjust action of Mesnil, Advocate of the King's Fisc, and what the Court decided when the case was committed to counsel.

units.la: Item ea retulit, quæ in Italia, Hispania, Germania, Polonia, Moscovia, Anglia, & Republ. Veneta, societatis causa, evenerint, ea etiam, quæ sodales anno 77. fecerint, & Actiones Potestati, quanta in Directorio Inquisitionis; ubi loca tavit, excuso Romæ, 1585. describitur, consentaneas; indicavit: unde colligi r, eos Inquisitionis arcanæ officio defungi.
units.tr: Likewise he recounts what happened in Italy, Spain, Germany, Poland, Muscovy, England and the Venetian Republic on account of the society, and also what the companions did in the year 77. He points out that the actions described are consistent with the power set out in the Directorio Inquisitionis, printed at Rome in 1585, where the passages are listed; from this he gathers that they discharge the secret office of the Inquisition.

units.la: Item diligenter collegit ea, quæ in sanctiori Regis consistorio, in Curia, an & post actionem, in Castellum parricidam, eorum discipulum, institutam, ac derunt. Ea, quæ secretis Annalibus annorum 1594. & 95. comprehenduntur, iorum exemplar Neapoli excusum, anno 1604. sub manu fit. Deinde idé Regius Advocatus, eorumdem usurpationes & molitiones ex Brevium, postquam fllíminij iure donati sunt, quod notandum, & contra positas edicto conditiones, impetratorum, excerptis attendit:
units.tr: Likewise he diligently gathered what was done in the more sacred consistory of the King, in the Court, both before and after the attack on Castel, the parricide, their former pupil. What is contained in the secret Annalibus for the years 1594 and 1595, of which a copy printed at Naples in 1604 is at hand, he has also noted. Then the same Royal Advocate, from the Brevium, examined their usurpations and machinations after they had been granted the right of the thunderbolt, and set against them the conditions of the edict, drawn from the petitioners' own impetrations, which deserve to be noted.

units.la: Item, quæ Regi, ab Harlæo, Senatus Principe, cuius Exempla, Virtutis ei nt præcepta, oratione fuerunt exposita:
units.tr: Likewise, what was said to the King by Harlay, Prince of the Senate, whose examples were set out in his speech as precepts of virtue:

units.la: Et, quibus illi Rex Magnus, Clementissimus, Invictissimus & Prudentissimus respondit verbis, quæ certum voluntatis Regiæ propositum exprimerent, certâ spe obsequiorum, quæ spondebant Diplomatis Imperatores, subum.
units.tr: And the replies with which the Great King, most clement, most invincible and most prudent, answered in words that expressed a fixed purpose of royal will, with a sure hope of the obedience which the Diploma's promoters had pledged:

units.la: Præterea, quæ ab ipsis facta, tanquam fidei, optimo Regi datæ, adversantia arguuntur, & quid ad hæc argumenta illi regerant, sedulò attendit.
units.tr: Further, what they had done, though given in good faith to the best of Kings, is shown to be contrary to it, and what they answered to these arguments, he carefully considered.

units.la: Deniq; alia commemoravit, quibus apparet, quid subinde ad captandam etiam, & authoritatem comparandam factitarint, quibus artibus domatim gentur, & ad exploranda arcana, & bona corradenda irrepant, ac negotijs o ibus sese conscientiarum obtentu intrudant.
units.tr: Finally, he recalled other matters, from which it appears what they habitually did in order to win favour and build up authority, by what arts they worm their way into households, and creep in to discover secrets and gather in property, and intrude into affairs under the pretext of conscience.

units.la: Doctrinam deniq; quod attinet: quæ in operibus Bellarmini, potissimum in actatu, De potestate Romani Pontificis in Temporalibus, notavit, quæ in Gregorij Lentiniani, Vasquez, Turriani, Tholosani, Suarez, Molinæ, Ribadeneirae, in libro, titulus Princeps Christianus, Kelleri, Andreæ Eudæmono Ioannis, Iosephi Crefli Angli, sub Philopatri nomine, Leonhardi Lessij, S. Heisij, Gretseri, Azorii, & ariana libris animadvertit. Item, quæ in Amphitheatro Honoris, excuso anno 06. nomine Clari Bonarscij, cuius proprium nomen Carolus Scribanius, ante Antverpiani Collegij Rectoris, de quibus is ipse, qui loquitur, defunctum egem Henricum Magnum monuerat, ut vitæ prospiceret, parricidiis & sicas, à Scriptore illo expositæ, in locis, quæ Regi ipsi, teste Illustrissimo quodam ro, fidelissimo ipsius Regis, iam à multis annis, Ministro, præelegit: teste oque ipso Patre Cottone, qui tum dixit, eum librum, nequaquam à suae sociatis hominibus emanasse, sed Genevæ, ad conflandum Iesuitis odium, fictum, ab Haereticis fuisse: qui tamen, postea, longe aliter, quid sentiret, ex-pressit, laudato Scribanij opere, & distributis multis illius exemplaribus: atque etiam, Claro admodum viro, Religioni Catholicae, non minus, quam Regno Francico addicto, cum hunc exhibuisset librum, eum stylo laudato, commendavit, tanquam iuventuti, Latinis literis imbuendae, adprime utilem, etiamsi verba, quibus ille utitur, simillima sint, imo ipsissima illa, quae novissimus parricida, cum super execrabili parricidio, in caede Regis patrato, interrogaretur, usurpare solebat. Quae advocatus, sine horrore referre nequit, de tam horribili libro loquens, quem Catalogo librorum suorum inscriptum, tanquam ab Authore laudato, profectum, Societas comprobavit. Idem, Aphorismorum Emmanuelis Sa, & aliorum Casuistarum mentionem fecit, qui Ethicam & Politicam Christianam, funditus evertunt. Item axiomatum Iohannis de las Salas, & librorum Sanchez, ex quibus excerpta quaedam sparsa sunt, quae supprimi, non imprimi decuit, ob horrendas, & flagitiosas, turpissimasque differentiones, quibus scatent. Retulit etiam de Richeomi Apologia, & aliis libris, quibus Richeomus & Cotto, aliique sodales, ad causae suae defensionem ediderunt. Necnon, de libro, cui titulus, Defensio Veritatis pro Religione Catholica, in Iesuitarum causa, oppositā Actioni Antonij Arnaldi, & de variis Responsis ad libellum, qui Anticotonus inscriptus: Declaratoriis literis eiusdem Cottonis ad Reginam, Rerum in Regno Administrationi praefectam, statim ab ipso Regis obitu: de quibus etiam Montholonius in contradictionibus adversus Martilleriurn. Quibus in libris, etsi multa speciosis, pietatem & aequitatem redolentibus verbis, fucata legantur: attamen veritatis & lucis obiectu, ruunt eorum dicta, quantumvis coloribus quaesitis adornata: & quae ad excusationem eorum proferuntur, crimen augent, & eiusdem culpae, cum ijs, quos tuentur, participes demonstrant. Scilicet, errorum levi nomine designantur, quae demulcentis novis & exotericis dogmatibus, ab eis in Ethica, Politica, Oeconomica, Ecclesiastica & Republica conduntur & propugnantur axiomata, quibus palam est, eos ad excidium potestatum, a Deo constitutarum, Iustitiae omnis everssionem, ipsius etiam Hierarchiae ὑπουργίας, Ecclesiae Catholicae & Apostolicae Romanae, & ordinum Religiosorum Clericorum Regularium veterum, ruinam, grassari, adversus quos Iesuitae subinde, multa tentarunt: atque ad Academiarum imminutionem, spectare; quum Doctoratus gradum praeter morem, examinis publici lege violata, conferre non dubitent.
units.tr: As for doctrine: he noted what is found in the works of Bellarmine, chiefly in the treatise On the Power of the Roman Pontiff in Temporal Matters; in Gregory of Lentinum, Vasquez, Turrianus, Tolosanus, Suárez, Molina, Ribadeneira, in the book entitled The Christian Prince; in Keller, Andreas Eudaemon-Joannes, Joseph Creswell the Englishman under the name Philopater, Leonard Lessius, S. Heisius, Gretser, Azor, and in similar books. He likewise noted what is in the Amphitheatre of Honour, published in 1606 under the name Clarus Bonarscius, whose real name is Carolus Scribanius, formerly Rector of the Antwerp College. Concerning this book, the speaker himself had warned the late King Henry the Great to look to his life, because of the parricides and daggers set out by that writer in places which he (as a certain most illustrious man, most faithful minister of the King for many years, attests) had chosen for the King himself. Father Cotton also attests this, who at that time said that the book had by no means come from his fellow Jesuits, but had been fabricated in Geneva by heretics to stir up hatred against the Jesuits. Yet he afterwards expressed a quite different opinion, praising Scribanius' work and distributing many copies of it. Indeed, when he had presented this book to a certain very distinguished man, devoted to the Catholic religion and no less to the French kingdom, he commended it warmly as especially useful for training youth in Latin letters, even though the words he uses are very like, indeed the very ones, which the last parricide used to employ when questioned about the execrable murder of the King. The advocate cannot relate this without horror, speaking of so horrible a book, which the Society approved by listing it in its catalogue of books, as coming from a praised author. He likewise mentioned the Aphorisms of Emmanuel Sá and other casuists, who utterly subvert Christian ethics and politics. Also the axioms of John de las Salas and the books of Sánchez, from which certain scattered excerpts were made, which ought to have been suppressed rather than printed, on account of the horrible, shameful and most foul propositions with which they abound. He also reported on Richeome's Apology and other books which Richeome, Cotton and other companions published in defence of their cause. And likewise on the book entitled Defence of the Truth for the Catholic Religion, in the cause of the Jesuits, written against the Action of Antoine Arnauld; and on the various Responses to the pamphlet entitled Anti-Cotton; and on the Declaratory letters of the same Cotton to the Queen, who had charge of the administration of the kingdom immediately after the King's death, concerning which Monthelon also wrote in his replies against Martellier. In these books, although much is read that is painted over in specious words smelling of piety and fairness, yet when the light of truth is brought to bear, their statements collapse, however carefully they are adorned with borrowed colours. And what is put forward in their excuse increases the crime and shows them to be sharers in the same guilt as those whom they defend. Namely, errors are called by a mild name, while with new and exoteric dogmas that flatter the ear they establish and champion, in ethics, politics, economics, ecclesiastical and civil affairs, maxims by which it is plain that they aim at the overthrow of powers ordained by God, the destruction of all justice, even of the ministry of the hierarchy itself, of the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, and the ruin of the old orders of regular clergy, against whom the Jesuits have repeatedly attempted much. These maxims also tend to the diminishing of the universities, since they do not hesitate, contrary to custom and violating the law of public examination, to confer the degree of doctor.

units.la: Rogavit quoque Curiam Advocatus, ut ex libro inscripto, Manuale Sodalitatis, praelegi locum notatum pateretur, & Rectori, ut praelegeret, traditum: ut liqueat, qua ratione iuventutem ad periuria, in iudiciis & coram Magistratu, erudiant.
units.tr: The advocate also asked the Court to allow a passage marked in the book entitled Manual of the Sodality to be read out, and handed it to the Rector to read, so that it might be clear by what method they train youth in perjury in courts and before the magistrate.

units.la: Denique, loco a Rectore loco, in Manuali, notato, alia multa capita recensuit, in quae Censura Facultatis Theologicae, stylum suum strinxit: & ea, quae tribus concionibus continebantur, Hispanico idiomate, ann. 1609, & 1610, in hunc modum Ignatij Fundatoris conscriptis, quas in Gallicum sermonem translatas Franciscus Solerius Iesuita, qui librum, quo ea, quae notata fuerunt, non sine blasphemia in Deum, iniuriain Theologos, illius Censores, asserere & tueri non est veritas, morat, & retulit.
units.tr: Finally, from a passage marked in the Manual, he recited many other heads, against which the Censure of the Theological Faculty directed its pen. He also reported those things contained in three sermons, written in Spanish in the years 1609 and 1610 by the founder Ignatius, which Francis Solerius, a Jesuit, had translated into French; and he related that the book in which the things noted occur defends them, and that to assert and defend these things, not without blasphemy against God and injury to the theologians who were its censors, is not truth.

units.la: Tandem ad Vniversitatis causam accedens monuit in Doctoribus & Magistris nonnullis, quaedam desiderari, qui omittenda committant, & committenda negligant. At, si supinitate, & legum ac decretorum, in Curia comprobatorum, aspernatione, peccatum fit, unde iusta nata fit querimoniae causa, quod non est inficiandum: Curia, ut par est, prospicere dignetur, quod aliorum, quae Petitorum opera fieri posse claret. Quibus, illud Basilij, aliorumque Sanctorum Patrum verbis, Regulas Ascetica Religiosis Regularibus praescribentibus, obijci merito potest, illos rem sua Profesione indignam, sibi inutilem, neque Reipublicae proficuam postulare, nec ulla ratione, exemplo ve laudabili, nec doctrina, quae in Parisiensi Schola frequentata est, siue Theologia, quae Scholastica appellatur, siue Politiva, Moralis ac Politica, potissimum ob quatuor capita propositæ, attendatur, siue denique humanioris literarum ratio sit habenda, quarum studijs paucos admodum, idoneos Doctores expedire & sufficere queant.
units.tr: Turning at last to the cause of the University, he observed that some doctors and masters are lacking in certain respects, who commit what ought to be omitted and neglect what ought to be done. But if the fault lies in sloth, and in contempt of laws and decrees approved by the Court, from which a just ground of complaint has arisen (which cannot be denied), the Court is asked, as is fitting, to provide that the other things which, it is clear, can be done by the work of the petitioners, be done. To the petitioners the words of Basil and of other holy Fathers, who prescribe ascetic rules to regular religious, may fairly be objected: that they demand what is unworthy of their profession, useless to themselves, and not profitable to the commonwealth. Nor, for any reason, are they to be considered by laudable example, or by the doctrine that is taught in the Parisian schools, whether scholastic theology, or positive theology, or moral and political teaching, chiefly on account of the four heads proposed; nor finally is the method of humane letters to be considered, for in these studies they can scarcely supply and furnish even a few suitable teachers.

units.la: Quocirca solemni clausula, ut Regis saluti, securitati, ut Ecclesiæ bono, regni & totius Reipublicæ tranquillitati, ut honori & perennitati literarum & disciplinarum, consulatur. Intercessioni Parisiensis Vniversitatis calculum suum Regius Aduocatus adjicit. Quod si, causa, ad Consilium, a Curia, reiecta, libros scripta, unde recitata quaedam fuerant, (quaeque sibi adesse praesto, dictorum cupletissimum perhibitura testimonium, Aduocatus Regius profitetur) Cura examinanda esse decernat; postulat, ut Diplomatis Impetratores, a quavis actione Scholastica, ad iuventutis, aliorumque in hac urbe institutionem, lege arceantur, donec in Curia aliter constitutum fuerit, poenæ, quae videbitur, irrogatione sancienda.
units.tr: Wherefore, by the solemn formula, provision is asked for the safety and security of the King, for the good of the Church, for the tranquillity of the kingdom and of the whole commonwealth, and for the honour and lasting good of letters and learning. The King's Advocate adds his own voice to the intercession of the University of Paris. But if the Court, having referred the cause to the Council, decides that the books from which certain passages were recited must be examined with care (the King's Advocate declares that these are at hand and will bear most abundant witness to what was said), he asks that the petitioners of the Diploma be barred by law from all scholastic activity, from the education of youth and others in this city, until the Court decides otherwise, and that a penalty be imposed as seems fit.

units.la: Curia, causam, de prolati Diplomatis editione, in Consilium mittendam esse pronunciavit.
units.tr: The Court pronounced that the cause concerning the publication of the Diploma presented is to be sent to the Council.

units.la: Litigatorum Causidicos, Actiones suas intra stidui emendare, & si quae videatur sublia causae futura, argumenta & contradictiones addere, judicio intra praescriptum tempus indicto, proferre jubet. Decernit, ut Provincialis, & e societate, quotquot eu intra septa uriae secuti sunt, imprasentiarum, subscriptione, rata habeat lege, cui se Provincialis subscribit, Doctrinae nimirum Sorbonicae consentiendi, in iis praesertim capitibus, quae ad S. Regem Majestatem eorum salutem & authoritatem, fartam tectam tuendam, ac libertatum alli canarum, ab omni aevo, in hoc Regno observatarum, conservationem, faciunt.
units.tr: It orders the advocates of the litigants to amend their pleadings within eight days, and, if any further arguments and objections seem likely to arise in the cause, to bring them forward within the time prescribed by the Court. It decrees that the Provincial, and all of the Society who have followed him within the enclosure of the Court, shall for the present ratify by subscription the law to which the Provincial subscribes, namely, to agree with the doctrine of the Sorbonne, especially on those heads which concern the safety and authority of the King and the firm protection of his person, and the preservation of the liberties of the Gallican Church observed in this kingdom from of old.

units.la: Vt ijs omnibus perspectis, ac Regio Cognitori communicatis, & Arresto, Curiae de causa filio permittenda, annexis, ex jure decretu fiat. Interea, praeter ea, quae Diplomate Restitutionis & Senatus consulto, quo illud comprobatum est; ferebantur, adjuventute erudienm, aut sua aut aliorum opera, quidquam conari, moliri ve, quacunque tandem id ratione fiat retitores prohibentur, & illis omnibus prorsus potestas, scholastica munia obeundi, interdicitur; ac denunciatur, ni pareant, futurum, ut ipso quo fruuntur, postliminij beneficio multentur: litis impendijs exceptis. Actum in Curia Parlamenti 22. Decemb. 1611.
units.tr: When all these things have been examined and communicated to the royal commissioner, and the Court's decree concerning the cause, to be permitted, has been annexed, a decision is to be made according to law. Meanwhile, apart from those things which were carried by the Diploma of Restitution and the decree of the Senate by which it was approved, the teachers are forbidden to attempt or undertake anything in the education of youth, by their own work or that of others, by whatever means this is done; and all power of performing scholastic duties is wholly forbidden them. It is announced that, if they do not obey, they will be punished by the forfeiture of the right of return which they enjoy, besides the costs of the suit. Done in the Court of Parliament, 22 December 1611.

units.la: Signat. DV TILLET.
units.tr: Signed: DU TILLET.

units.la: EXCERPTVM EX ORATIONE D. IOANNIS DISSIENII RECTORIS VNIVERSITATIS PARISIEN- SIS AD REGEM.
units.tr: EXCERPT FROM THE SPEECH OF MR JOHN DISSIENIUS, RECTOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF PARIS, TO THE KING.

units.la: Tsi vero Iesuitae tam gravi Decreto fuissent abstinere ab omni docendi genere & scholastico munere in urbe Parisiensi, non tamen cessarunt & paruerunt irrequieti homines, sed anno millesimo sexcentesimo decimo octavo, rursus apud Regem instituerunt, & obtinere conati sunt, ut ipsis publice docendi potestas ibidem concedatur. Rector autem Academiae gravi Oratione intercessit ram Rege, in qua inter alia sic inquit: Serenissime Rex, hac causa est, cur Majestati vestrae Academia Parisiensis hodie humilime supplicat, quod maximo periculo rursus posita est: nempe hoc ipso tempore, quo Iesuitae iterum nervos suos omnes intendunt, ut arissiis stabilire & confirmare sese possint. Quum enim jam oppressenint corpus integrum ordinis politici & secularis in omnibus partibus Majestatis vestrae Regni, excepto Cord[...] solo, quod vivit & respirat adhuc in Universitate Parisiensi, illud nunc operam dant, [...] semel stabiliti si fuerint, quàm primùm eam potestati suae subijciant, quemadmodum in o[...] omnibus aliis locis, quae semel occupârunt, fecerunt: Si autem in Regno M. V. Societas non restet ulla alia quae doceat juventutem, quàm Iesuitica, facilè inde apparet, magnam il[...]lam & celebrem Universitatem oppressum & suffocatum iri. Consideres obsecramus M[...] T. quot & quanta officia venerabile corpus illud Ecclesiae & Statui tuo semper praestitit; quomodo populos instruxerit Pastoribus, Episcopatus Praelatis, supremas Curia[...] Consiliarijs & Praesidentibus, Concilium Regium Cancellarijs, Custodibus Sigillorum, Magistris Supplicationum, Consiliarijs & Secretarijs publicis, qui innocentiam Ecclesiae puritatem linguarum, integritatem bonarum literarum, & immunitates atque libertates Galliae, contra omnes eos qui illas opprimere conabantur, propugnârit. Breviter, quae forte semper frenum extiterit, inhibendae violentiae, doctrinarum novarum, peregrinarum[...] & tum Ecclesiae, tum Reip. praejudicabilium. Ecce igitur perditam nunc eo modo grandem[...] istam Universitatem. Quod equidem non sine notabili detrimento huius & illius, hoc ejus Ecclesiae & Status Tui accidere poterit. Ne permitte igitur, ô Rex Magne, ut pulcher i[...] & locuples flosculus Coronae Galliae ita Tuo tempore defloresçat & cadat. Ne permitte ut dicatur, hanc magnam & celebrem Universitatem, quae ânongentis annis successive omnibus Regibus nostris antecessoribus, tanquam pars summè necessaria & essentialis Ecclesiae & Status, conservata fuit, pereat sub Regno Ludovici XIII.
units.tr: Although the Jesuits had been forbidden by so grave a decree to engage in any kind of teaching or scholastic office in the city of Paris, restless men did not stop; in the year 1618 they again approached the King and tried to obtain that the public right to teach be granted to them there. The Rector of the University, however, opposed them before the King in a grave speech, in which among other things he spoke as follows: Most Serene King, this is why the Parisian Academy today humbly begs Your Majesty, since it has again been placed in the greatest danger; namely, at this very time, when the Jesuits are once more straining every nerve to establish and confirm themselves as firmly as possible. For although they have already overpowered the whole body of the political and secular order in all parts of Your Majesty's kingdom, except the Cord[...] alone, which still lives and breathes in the University of Paris, they are now working, once they have established themselves there, to bring it as soon as possible under their own power, just as they have done in all the other places they have ever occupied. If, then, no other society is left in Your Majesty's kingdom to teach the youth except the Jesuit one, it is easy to see that that great and famous University will be crushed and suffocated. We beg you to consider, Most Serene King, how many and how great services that venerable body has always rendered to the Church and to your State: how it has furnished the people with ministers, the bishoprics with prelates, the supreme courts with counsellors and presidents, the Royal Council with chancellors, keepers of the seals, masters of requests, and public counsellors and secretaries; who have defended the innocence of the Church, the purity of languages, the integrity of good letters, and the immunities and liberties of France against all who tried to oppress them. In short, it has always been the bridle that restrains violence and novel and foreign doctrines, harmful both to the Church and to the Commonwealth. Behold, then, that great University is now ruined in this way; which indeed cannot happen without notable loss to this one, to that Church and to your State. Do not permit, therefore, O Great King, that this beautiful and rich little flower of the Crown of France should wither and fall in your time. Do not permit it to be said that this great and famous University, which has been preserved for nine hundred years in succession by all our predecessor kings as a part most necessary and essential to the Church and State, should perish under the reign of Louis XIII.

units.la: Hac Serenissime Rex, humillima est petitio, quâ Majestati V. hodie supplicat Universitas Parisiensis, ut cum Cereum recipiat de manu nostra M. V. accipiat simul arrabonem fidelitatis, pignus obedientiae suae, & protestationem integerrimam, quod vel in propriam ruinam jurare parata sit potius, quàm fallere votum, quod M. T. fecit, feerga illam quàm optimè affectam, subjectissimam & humillimam ancillam fore.
units.tr: This, Most Serene King, is the most humble petition which the University of Paris today makes to Your Majesty: that, as you receive this wax taper from our hand, you may at the same time accept a pledge of its loyalty, a token of its obedience, and a most sincere assurance that it is ready to swear, even to its own ruin, rather than break its vow to be, in all things, a most devoted, most subject and most humble handmaid to you.

units.la: Rex facie plena hilaritatis & benevolentiae respondit: Gratias vobis ago, pro vestra bona voluntate: Vos itidem de mea certi estote, & quod gratam habeam vestram supplicationem.
units.tr: The King replied with a face full of cheerfulness and goodwill: I thank you for your good will. Be assured of my own goodwill too, and that I take your petition in good part.

units.la: Ex impressso Lugduni apud Ioannem Celerier exemplari Gallico Latinam linguam verso anno 1618, cum permissione.
units.tr: From the printed copy issued at Lyon by John Celerier, a French copy translated into Latin in the year 1618, with permission.

units.la: Quid fiet? Rex, sic merentibus peccatis hominum, paulo post, praeter novum Collegiorum extructionem, in ipsa Parisiensi urbe Iesuitis potestatem fecit ad omnium prope invidiam exposito, ut in Collegio suo omnes disciplinas etiam Philosophicas & Theologicas, liberè deinceps ac publicè profiteri possent.
units.tr: What then happened? The King, as the sins of men deserved, shortly afterwards, besides building new colleges, granted the Jesuits, to the envy of almost everyone, the power in the city of Paris itself to teach freely and publicly in their college all the disciplines, including philosophy and theology.

units.la: IESVITIS IN REGNVM NAVARRAE PER[...]
units.tr: THE JESUITS' ENTRY INTO THE KINGDOM OF NAVARRE PER[...]

units.la: MISSVS INCOLATVS.
units.tr: ADMITTED AS RESIDENTS.

units.la: IGnatiani coërceri vno regno non ferebant: sed ut Gallico, sic etiam Navarreo & tota Asturia religionis suae ibi instaurandae & propagandae causa postulabant anno 1608, unâ hac ratione, non esse differentiae causas, cur uno regno potius quàm altero, quod uni Domino gentilitium sit & hæreditarium, fovtantur. Obstabant contra Asturiorum acerrimae postulationes, qui Ignatianos vehementer oderant ob irrequieta ingenia. Rex autem anno 1599, dum Blœsis ageret articulum Edictalis sanctionis, pro regno Navarreo & Asturia, magistratui & indi[...] nis cavent ibus de sua religione annuerat, ne Iesuitae in hos fines accedere[...] ne quid novi importarent, quo publica quies turbaretur. Nihilominus Episcopis gentilitiis contrariu depositentibus, mutavit Rex sententiam suam, decretque, ut aequè ac caeteri Ordines liberè & promiscuè admitterentur; abrogat contra[...] ntraria sanctione: Quinimó professus est, sibi in animo esse illuc transmittere fuitas, qui Episcopis socias manus adhibeant, & Romanam religionem reiciebant, Parisiensis autem Curia cæterique Ordines implacabiliter edictum tulerunt. Nam præcæteris mortalibus Ignatianum hoc genus cane & anguem peius oderunt, & longè à finibus suis propulsârunt, repertosque antea Sinones & exploratores morte affecerunt; ut refert Botoreus in magno Anciæ consilio Advocatus lib.15. Comment. pag.493.
units.tr: The Ignatians could not bear to be confined to one kingdom, so in 1608 they sought to plant and spread their religion in Navarre and all of Asturia as well as in France. Their argument was simply that there was no reason why they should be favoured in one kingdom rather than another, since both belonged by hereditary right to the same lord. Against this stood the fierce complaints of the Asturians, who hated the Ignatians intensely for their restless dispositions. In 1599, while the article of the Edict of Blois was being drafted, the king had agreed, for the kingdom of Navarre and Asturia, to the magistrates' guarantees about their religion, so that the Jesuits would not enter these territories or bring in anything new that might disturb public peace. Nevertheless, when the hereditary bishops testified to the contrary, the king changed his mind and decreed that the Jesuits should be admitted freely and on the same terms as the other orders. He abrogated the contrary sanction. Indeed, he declared that he intended to send there Jesuits who would lend their hands to the bishops and who rejected the Roman religion. But the Parisian Parlement and the other orders passed a relentless decree against it. For above all other mortals they hate this Ignatian breed worse than dogs and snakes, and they have driven them far from their borders, putting to death any Sinons and spies they had found there earlier, as Botoreus reports, Advocate in the great council of Ancia, in book 15 of his Commentaries, page 493.

units.la: CAPUT II. DE IESVITARVM IN AN- GLIAM, POLONIAM, TRANSILVA- NIAM, BAVARIAM, &c. ADVENTV.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. CONCERNING THE ARRIVAL OF THE JESUITS IN ENGLAND, POLAND, TRANSYLVANIA, BAVARIA, ETC.

units.la: IESVITARVM IN ANGLIAM ADVENTVS.
units.tr: THE ARRIVAL OF THE JESUITS IN ENGLAND.

units.la: ANno Domini 1580. Robertus Parsonius & Edmundus Campianus Iesuitæ primi Angliam ingressi sunt, & mirificis ac fraudulentis artibus ud clericos & laicos sese insinuârunt. Nolebant primò sacramenta administrare sine licentia Sacerdotum: pollicebantur laicis, se nihil nisi spiritualia traturos: paupertatem & humilitatem summam simulabant, & causam Pontificium plurimùm se promoturos sanctissimè promittebant, quo factum est, summa cum humanitate ab illis exciperentur etiam. Mox autem, cùm pedes paulò arctius fixerunt, insolentissimi, pro more suo, & prorsus intolerabiles facti sunt. Reginæ Elisabethæ, & Regi Iacobo per suos conductitios indecenter struxerunt insidias, eosque vel de Regno deturbare, vel vita privare nati sunt: nec cessârunt seditionibus, detractionibus artificiosissimè omnes, isque ullo discrimine, sive clericos, sive laicos, impetere, quos metuebant imdituros, ne pervenirent ad metam, ad quam collimabant: ut Lector intelligat infra, ex capite de illorum nefariis facinoribus, &c. in Anglia, & inprimis ex enedictinorum Anglorum literis ad Clementem 8. Pontificem Rom. missis.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1580, Robert Parsons and Edmund Campion, Jesuits, were the first to enter England, and by wonderful and deceitful arts they insinuated themselves among the clergy and the laity. At first they were unwilling to administer the sacraments without the permission of the priests. They promised the laity that they would deal only in spiritual matters. They feigned the utmost poverty and humility, and solemnly promised that they would greatly advance the cause of the Papists. As a result, they were received even with the greatest kindness by those people. Soon, however, when they had planted their feet a little more firmly, they became very insolent, as is their custom, and utterly intolerable. They shamelessly laid snares for Queen Elizabeth and King James through their hired agents, and they were born to drive them from the kingdom or deprive them of life. Nor did they cease from sedition and slander, attacking with the greatest cunning all, without distinction, whether clergy or laity, whom they feared would hinder them from reaching the goal at which they aimed. The reader will understand this further below, in the chapter on their wicked crimes, etc., in England, and especially from the letters of the English Benedictines sent to Clement VIII, the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: IESVITAE IN POLONIAM VENIVNT.
units.tr: THE JESUITS COME TO POLAND.

units.la: HAud diu etiam ante Stephanum Battorium Iesuitæ Poloniam ingressi sunt: in nulla autem, vel parva admodum gratia apud proceres Regni itió fuerunt. Stephano autem Rege creato, cùm familiam Bathoreorum in Transilvania, & forte etiam in Polonia firmare vellet, putaret autem, ut necoribus in Europa illustres affinitates conciliaret, Romani Pontificis sibi authoritate & favore opus esse, Iesuitas, quos Pontifices impensè amare sciebat, in Polonia amplecti cœpit, & Rigam 4. Id. Mart. cùm venisset anno 1582. Gotthardi Velingi Syndici urbis & Ioannis Taftij operâ templum Iesuitis à Senatu Iacobum impetravit, licet intercederet Gotthardus Curlandiæ Dux, & fidem Regis oppidani appellarent, qui nihil in religionis negotio se innovaturum reiosè promiserat. Verùm ad sedandam eorum querelam primarium urbis implum vicisim oppidanis concessit. Rex Stephanus quoque fratri suo Christophoro auctor fuit, ut idem in Transilvania, quantumvis reclamantibus subditis facitaret. Infausti autem huius consilij is tandem eventus fuit, ut Familia la, quam hac ratione extollere & ornare volebant, quæque tum aliquot gene-
units.tr: Not long before Stephen Báthory, the Jesuits entered Poland, but they were received with little or no favour by the nobles of the kingdom. When Stephen was made king, he wished to strengthen the Báthory family in Transylvania and perhaps also in Poland, and he thought that, in order to secure illustrious marriage alliances in Europe, he needed the authority and favour of the Roman Pontiff. So he began to embrace the Jesuits in Poland, whom he knew the Pontiffs loved dearly. When he came to Riga on 12 March 1582, through the efforts of Gotthard Velingus, syndic of the city, and Johann Taft, he obtained from the Senate a church for the Jesuits, although Gotthard, Duke of Courland, interceded and the townspeople appealed to the king's promise, for he had solemnly pledged that he would introduce no innovation in matters of religion. Yet, to calm their complaint, he in turn granted the chief church of the city to the townspeople. King Stephen also advised his brother Christopher to do the same in Transylvania, although the subjects protested. The outcome of this unfortunate plan was that the family, which they wished to raise up and adorn in this way, and which at that time flourished with several most noble young men, became entangled in inextricable difficulties through the unhappy folly of these same Jesuits, and in these it nearly perished utterly.

units.la: Iesuitæ in Anglia venerunt. rofissimis iuvenibus florebat, per eorundem Iesuitarū infelicem panurgiam, inextricabilibus difficultatibus implicaretur, in quibus funditus fere periit.
units.tr: The Jesuits come to England. The family, which flourished with several most noble young men, was entangled, through the unhappy folly of these same Jesuits, in inextricable difficulties, in which it nearly perished utterly.

units.la: DE PROPAGATIONE IESVITARVM IN BAVARIA.
units.tr: ON THE PROPAGATION OF THE JESUITS IN BAVARIA.

units.la: VIvebat adhuc Ignatius Loyola, quum sub Paulo IV. Papa Bavariæ Dux Albertus omnino decrevisset, ut Societas hæc Collegium Ingolstadii haberet. Huc illum inter alia excitabat quoque Regis Romanorum Ferdinandi exemplum, qui simile Collegium Viennæ nō ita pridem erexerat. Cum itaque Ignatius votis Bavari annuisset, aliquot Societatis huius viri ex Italia missi Ingolstadium pervenerunt, primoque Societatis huius in Bavaria initium dederunt anno Christi millesimo quingentesimo quinquagesimo sexto. Domicilium illis in veteri, ut vocant, Collegio assignatum fuit ad annum usque 1576, quando ad ædes ampliores & commodiores, quæ novæ adhærent Bibliothecæ gymnasii commigrarunt. Voluit enim Princeps, ut & Professorum & Studiosorum huius Societatis numerus ibi augeretur, qui & pædagogio & Convictorum externorum domicilio gubernando præessent, suamque darent operam novis parochiis instituendis; quorum velut seminarium idem Princeps erexit, illorumque curam concredidit. Hinc porro in proventib. annuis facta est accessio, ut circa sexaginta & septuaginta, partim Theologi, partim Philosophi, & variarum artium ac linguarum Professores; partim Scholastici, & administri ex hac Societate Ingolstadii beneficio Principis alerentur.
units.tr: Ignatius Loyola was still alive when, under Pope Paul IV, Duke Albert of Bavaria fully resolved that this Society should have a college at Ingolstadt. The example of King Ferdinand of the Romans, who had not long before founded a similar college at Vienna, also urged him towards this. Ignatius therefore assented to the Duke's wishes, and some men of this Society, sent from Italy, arrived at Ingolstadt. They first made a beginning of this Society in Bavaria in the year of Christ 1556. Their residence was assigned to them in the old, as it is called, college until the year 1576, when they moved to the larger and more convenient buildings that adjoin the new library of the gymnasium. For the Prince wished the number both of the professors and of the students of this Society to be increased there, so that they might take charge of governing the seminary and the house for outside boarders, and might devote their labour to founding new parishes; the same Prince established these as a kind of seminary for them and entrusted their care to them. From then on, an addition was made to the annual revenues, so that some sixty or seventy men, partly theologians, partly philosophers and professors of various arts and languages, and partly scholastics and assistants of this Society, were maintained at Ingolstadt by the Prince's bounty.

units.la: Anno Domini 1559, Albertus Bavariæ Princeps Iesuitarum Collegio Monachiensi initium dedit. Locus Collegii delectus est a principe Monasterium Augustinianorum; qui, cum pauci adessent, facile pasituri videbantur, ut pars horum ipsorum in usum novi huius Collegii converteretur, & illic schola & domus exstrueretur. Cives autem Monachienses male ab initio erga Iesuitas affecti fuerunt; & probra ingentia illis objecerunt.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1559, Albert, Prince of Bavaria, gave a beginning to the Jesuit college at Munich. The site of the college was chosen by the Prince: the monastery of the Augustinians, which, since there were few of them, seemed easily likely to be dispensed with, so that part of it might be converted to the use of this new college and a school and residence be built there. The citizens of Munich, however, were ill disposed towards the Jesuits from the beginning, and heaped huge reproaches upon them.

units.la: Cum etiam Comes Swuickardus de Helffenstein Præfectum Landspergensi ageret; a Principe Alberto petiit locum, montem scilicet arci Landspergensi vicinum, in quo sibi liceret proprium Iesuitarum domicilium exstruere, in gratiam Novitiorum sive Tyronum, ad hoc vitæ genus adspirantium, qui tyrocinii sui tempus ibi absolverent & probaretur. Sic igitur domus illa ædificata est, primum quidem, dicto Comite sumptus suppeditante, & aliis deinde amicis opitulantibus, ut fabrica integra duobus aut tribus annis absolveretur. In eam domum traducti sunt Novitii anno 1578, quum antea in Monachiensi Collegio incommode viverent & versarentur.
units.tr: When Count Schweikhard of Helfenstein was also governor of Landsberg, he asked Prince Albert for a site, namely a hill near the castle of Landsberg, on which he might be permitted to build a separate house for the Jesuits, for the sake of the novices or trainees who aspired to this way of life, so that they might complete and test their period of training there. And so that house was built, at first at the expense of the said Count, and then with other friends lending their help, so that the whole building was finished in two or three years. The novices were transferred into that house in the year 1578, since before this they had lived and been housed uncomfortably in the Munich college.

units.la: Ex Italia autem, Hispania, Gallia, Anglia, Polonia, Germania & aliis Regnis ac Provinciis Christiani orbis, de quibus hactenus diximus, penetrarunt etiam in Turciam, Moscoviam, Persiam; imo in Indiarum quoque regna remotissima, in quibus olim vix hominis Europæi vestigium conspectum fuit, ut mox referemus.
units.tr: Moreover, from Italy, Spain, France, England, Poland, Germany and the other kingdoms and provinces of the Christian world of which we have hitherto spoken, they also penetrated into Turkey, Muscovy and Persia; indeed, even into the most remote kingdoms of the Indies, where once scarcely a trace of a European man had been seen, as we shall shortly relate.

units.la: CONSILIVM DE NON RECIPIENDIS IESVITIS IN VALESIAM HELVETIORVM PROVINCIAM.
units.tr: CONSIDERATION ON NOT ADMITTING THE JESUITS INTO THE SWISS PROVINCE OF VALESIA.

units.la: ANno Christi 1610. Iesuitæ in Vualesia Helvetiorum nidificare, & sedes suas figere tentarunt. Quidam autem eius Provinciæ Primarius & patriæ amans receptionem illorum gravissimis rationibus sequentibus dissuasit, & impedivit.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1610 the Jesuits tried to nest in Valesia, a province of the Swiss, and to settle there. A leading man of that province, who loved his country, dissuaded and prevented their admission on the following very serious grounds.

units.la: I. Principio, cum in Concilio Generali, quod sub Innocentio III. Papa Anno 1215. Romae habitum fuit, expresse fuerit decretum, ne ullus praeterea novus institueretur ordo, & Iesuitarum ordo contra Concilij illius Generalis prohibitionem fuerit institutus: Senatus Valesiani est dispicere, non solum utrum utiliter, sed etiam an salva conscientia Ordinem hunc novum, contra Concilij Generalis decretum, recipere possint, cum pendente controversia: An Papa sit supra Concilium, nihil sit innovandum, & credibilius sit, Concilium esse supra Papam, quam hunc supra illud.
units.tr: I. First, the Fourth Lateran Council, held at Rome under Pope Innocent III in the year 1215, expressly decreed that no new religious order should be founded thereafter. The Jesuit order was founded in defiance of that general council's prohibition. The senate of Valesia must therefore examine not only whether it would be useful to admit this new order, but also whether they can do so with a clear conscience, contrary to the decree of a general council. While the controversy stands, namely whether the Pope is above the Council, nothing should be newly introduced; and it is more credible that the Council is above the Pope than that the Pope is above the Council.

units.la: II. Cum ad huius sustentationem Ordinis maxima requirantur sumptus: Domusque ipsorum Palatijs Principum sint similes: delicatissima quaeque comedant, bibantque: pannis vestiantur pretiosissimis: plurima ad se rapiant bona, integraque Dominia: suppelleclili utantur sumptuosissima, maximos altri, arbentique corrodant thesauros (ut quandoque Principibus sint ditiores) nec alium illae omnia, quam ab ijs, inter quos habitant, & commorantur, conquiri possint: Valesianorum vero is sit status & conditio, ut non suis tantum rebus indigeant ipsi: sed etiam aliorum annona carere nullo modo possint: illorum prudentiae deliberandum permittitur, an consultum fuerit, huiusmodi sumptuosos admittere hospites, qui per Pompas & luxum deglutirent ea, quibus ipsa Regio ad suam suorumque vitam parce sustentandam indiget, cum, si quae superesse possent, sanctius in pauperes, aliosque usus converti deberent.
units.tr: II. The upkeep of this order requires very great expenses. Their houses are like princely palaces; they eat and drink the most delicate foods; they dress in the most costly cloths; they seize many goods and whole estates; they use the most sumptuous furnishings and gnaw away the greatest treasures of altar and silver, so that they are sometimes richer than princes. All these things can be obtained only from those among whom they live and stay. Yet the Valesians are in such a state and condition that they not only lack their own resources but can in no way do without the supplies of others. Let their prudence decide whether it is wise to admit such costly guests, who by pomp and luxury would swallow up what the country itself needs to sustain the lives of itself and its people frugally. And if anything were left over, it ought to be turned more rightly to the poor and to other uses.

units.la: III. Cum captatoriae vivorum, aut defunctorum voluntates iure civili & canonico sint prohibitae, huicque Ordini mos sit, eos, a quibus ampla haereditas exspectanda patrimonia, sibi adiungere, ad opes divitiasque sibi in terris accumulandas: laudatissimae Valesianorum provinciae est, accurate sum evolvere, An Harpyas hasce, cum Rei publicae & privatae incommodo, admittere, hocque modo legitimos haeredes suis privari haereditatibus, peregrinos vero illis ditari, permittere, eosque, quibus illae maturae debentur, refuo frustrari velit. Iniquissimum profecto videtur futurum, ut peregrinus Iesuita civium & legitimorum haeredum adipisceretur patrimonium, cum icisim cives, vel legitimi, ne obulum quidem a Iesuitis unquam haberent expectandum.
units.tr: III. Wills made to catch the living or the dead are forbidden by civil and canon law, and it is the custom of this order to attach to itself those from whom a large inheritance is to be expected, so as to heap up wealth and riches on earth for itself. It is for the most praiseworthy province of Valesia to examine carefully whether it wishes to admit these Harpies to the loss of the commonwealth and of private persons, and in this way allow the lawful heirs to be deprived of their inheritances, and strangers to be enriched by them, and those to whom the ripe estates are rightly due to be cheated of their gain. It would surely seem most unjust that a foreign Jesuit should obtain the patrimony of citizens and lawful heirs, when in turn citizens or lawful heirs could never expect so much as a penny from the Jesuits.

units.la: IV. Cum insuper Hispaniae Rex, ante omnes alios Reges & Principes Pontificios, ad absolutam in subditos dominationem contendat, & Iesuitae undem pro summo Patrono & Benefactore agnoscant: cui etiam, ob summa beneficia ei accepta arctissime se obstrictos fatentur, ac propterea commodo quoque ipsius ubique locorum pro virili inservire studeant: rectissime hic facturi dentur Ordines Valesiani, si perpendant, an Iesuitarum principia (qualia sint, Unus Deus, Unus Papa, & Unus Rex, nempe Rex Hispaniarum, &c.) lebus suae Reipub. conveniant: An vero eiusmodi Presbyteris affectione Hispanicis, per institutiones Scholasticas, praedicationes, confessiones auriculares, & alias clandestinas artes, Hispanicam, vel peregrinam tyrannidem in Vuasia stabilire, utiliter permittendum putent.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, since the King of Spain strives for absolute dominion over his subjects more than all other Popish kings and princes, and since the Jesuits acknowledge him as their chief patron and benefactor, to whom they confess themselves bound very closely for his great kindnesses, and therefore strive to serve his advantage wherever they are, the Valesian orders would surely act most rightly if they weighed whether the principles of the Jesuits (which are: one God, one Pope, and one King, namely the King of Spain, etc.) agree with the affairs of their own commonwealth. Or whether they think it useful to permit such men, devoted to Spain, to establish in Valesia a Spanish or foreign tyranny by means of schools, sermons, auricular confessions, and other secret arts.

units.la: V. Cum praeterea Valesianorum laudabilis status ab omni antiquitate ber & Democraticus sit, & fuerit, Iesuitae autem nullam aliam Reipub. formam, quam tyrannicam unius Dominatoris potestatem approbent: (Richeoius enim Provincialis Iesuitarum in Aquitania nomine universae Societatis expostulatione Apologetica cap. 29. circa principium, popularem Democraticum statu furiosum appellat:) fortissimo prudentissimoque Valesiano populo diligenter expendendum relinquitur, an tales in Rempub. Hospites admittere scientes, volentesque debeant, qui cum Reipub. statum, quo nunc laborant, dabiliter fruuntur, velut Furiosum, improbant, & eversum cupiunt, & Hispanicam Tyrannidem in illius vicem introducere satagunt.
units.tr: V. Furthermore, since the praiseworthy condition of the Valesians has from all antiquity been and still is free and democratic, while the Jesuits approve no form of commonwealth but the tyrannical power of a single lord (for Richeome, the Jesuit provincial in Aquitaine, in the name of the whole Society, in his Apologetic Expostulation, chapter 29, near the beginning, calls the popular democratic state furious), it is left for the most brave and prudent people of Valesia to consider carefully whether they ought to admit into their commonwealth such guests, knowing and willing that they are such. These men, while they quietly enjoy the state in which the commonwealth now labours, condemn it as furious, desire its overthrow, and strive to introduce a Spanish tyranny in its place.

units.la: VI. Adhaec cum Iesuitae non solum Evangelicos, velut haereticos, sed & Pontificios moderatos, qui Evangelicis favent, aut cum illis foedera contrahunt, velut haereticorum fautores, & auxiliatores, hostili & mortali odio persequantur; Vualesianorum laudatissimo statui expedit, quam diligentissime expendere, an talium hospitium, aut hostium admissione & inclytam Venetorum Rempub. quae illos eiecit, & Helvetios Evangelicos, qui illos nunquam receperunt offendere, quam eorundem amicitiam per illorum repulsionem, conservare malint.
units.tr: VI. Again, since the Jesuits pursue with hostile and deadly hatred not only the Evangelicals, as heretics, but also the moderate Papists who favour the Evangelicals or make alliances with them, as supporters and helpers of heretics, it is most fitting for the most praiseworthy state of the Valesians to weigh very carefully whether they would rather preserve the friendship of the famous Venetian commonwealth, which expelled the Jesuits, and of the Evangelical Swiss, who never received them, by refusing them, or offend these by admitting such hospitality or such enemies.

units.la: VII. Praeterea cum eiusmodi in Vualesia status sit, ut Catholici, Evangelici que in una degant domo, familia que, & frater, affinis, cognatus, imo pater & filius, diversae sint confessionis; & apud Iesuitas constitutissimum sit, nullam aeliam Religionem pati, quam Inquisitionem Hispanicam, sic ut Evangelicos, ubicunque possunt, tribulent, persequantur & expellant; Vualesiani sapientissimi facile dijudicare possunt, an non ex illorum hominum recepta doctrina (qui ne Regibus quidem Evangelicis eorundemque fautoribus parcunt) Pater in filium & contra in se invicem illis parricidis instigantibus, irritabuntur, ex amicis inimici reddentur, et Provinciae seditionibus ac tumultibus propter Religionis diversitatem replebitur; miserrimaque quam Deus avertat, non solum rerum omnium perturbatio, sed & horrenda sanguinis effusio consequetur.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, since the state of Valesia is such that Catholics and Evangelicals live in one house; and a family, a brother, a relative by marriage, a kinsman, indeed a father and a son, are of different confessions; and since it is firmly settled among the Jesuits to tolerate no religion but the Spanish Inquisition, so that they harass, persecute and drive out the Evangelicals wherever they can, the most wise Valesians can easily judge whether, from the doctrine of these men (who spare not even Evangelical kings or their supporters), father and son, and conversely brother against brother, will be stirred up by those murderers, friends will become enemies, and the province will be filled with seditions and tumults because of the diversity of religion. And, which God forbid, there will follow not only the disturbance of all things but also a dreadful effusion of blood.

units.la: VIII. Deinde, cum nihil Reipub. Christianae & liberae salutarius atque utilius sit, quam civium liberos intelligentia, sapientia & vera pietate imbui, ad veram Deo legitimam patriae, & naturalem Parentibus, omnibusque debitam obedientiam praestandam: Iesuitae vero teneros liberorum animos, caecas obedientia imbuant, & intellectu, ratione & iudicio privent, eosdemque a parentibus velut plagiarii abducant, & in legitimos Magistratus ad omnia susque deque ferenda, arment: Prudentissimis Vualesianae Reipub. Administris diligenter considerandum est, an iustius impietatis & inobedientiae Doctores salva patria potestate, salva legitima sua authoritate, & vera erga Deum pietate, in Vualesia admittere debeant.
units.tr: VIII. Next, since nothing is more salutary and useful to a Christian and free commonwealth than that the children of citizens be imbued with understanding, wisdom and true piety, so that they may render true obedience to God, to their country and to their lawful magistrates, and the natural obedience owed to parents and to all; but the Jesuits imbue the tender minds of children with blind obedience, deprive them of understanding, reason and judgment, lead them away from their parents as if they were kidnappers, and arm them against lawful magistrates to bear everything recklessly: the most prudent administrators of the Valesian commonwealth must carefully consider whether they ought to admit into Valesia teachers of impiety and disobedience, when the paternal authority, their own lawful authority, and true piety towards God would remain intact.

units.la: IX. Adhaec, cum nihil ita sit sacrum atque religiosum, quod Iesuitae, citra ullam reverentiam in privatum suum luxum convertere non studeant, licet a maioribus in pios usus destinatum sit: Reverendus Vualesiae Episcopus, totus que clerus, etiam mature secum perpendere debent, num eiusmodi Corycaeos, Sacrilegos, Harpyias & Induperatores, sibi ipsis adiungere utiliter possint; cum certum sit, ubi hoc avium genus semel ibi nidificaverit, ad eorum cantum & fistulationem ipsis fore saltandum: dum alios Romam excurrere cogent, alios canonicatu & praebendis suis privabunt: alios haereseos insimulabunt, Episcopus summatim & clerici sibi accidisse brevi experientur, id quod proverbium habet: Turdus ipse sibi malum.
units.tr: IX. Again, since nothing is so sacred and religious that the Jesuits do not strive to turn it, without any reverence, to their private luxury, even if it has been set aside by our ancestors for pious uses, the reverend Bishop of Valesia and the whole clergy ought to weigh well beforehand whether they can usefully attach to themselves such Corycaeans, sacrilegious men, Harpies and Usurpers. For it is certain that once this kind of bird has nested there, the others will have to dance to its song and piping: while they force some to run off to Rome, they will deprive others of their canonries and prebends, and they will accuse others of heresy. The Bishop and the clergy will soon learn by experience what has happened to them, as the proverb has it: The thrush is its own undoing.

units.la: X. Vualesianis Abbatibus ac religiosis quoque qui opulenta & pinguia sua Monasteria possident, aeque mature considerandum videtur, An Dominos Iesuitas brevi vel successores vel bonorum suorum participes habere velint. Quod enim vultur mihi uo: id Iesuita est Monacho.
units.tr: X. For the Valesian abbots and religious men as well, who possess their rich and fat monasteries, it seems equally necessary to consider in good time whether they wish to have the lord Jesuits soon as their successors or as sharers in their goods. What the vulture is to me, the Jesuit is to the monk.

units.la: XI. Item, cum nihil certius sit, quam quod vera omnium Rerumpublicarum tranquillitas a legitima omnium subditorum erga Magistratum politicum cum obedientia dependeat, omnisque Respub. poenis & praemiis contineatur, Iesuitae autem eiusmodi Domini sint, qui nulli Magistratui politico, imo nec ipsis Episcopis subditi esse velint: ac si forte scelus a iquo Magistratumve commisisse deprehendantur, nec per Magistratus, nec per Episcopi propriam po[illegible, ~3 letters]testaten[illegible, ~3 letters] statem se puniri debere, aut posse dicant: Laudabili Vualefianorum Provinciæ considerandum relinquitur, ab huiusmodi liberos Dominos & Exlegês, salvâ Repub. salvaq; authoritate sibi à Deo concessa apud se admittere deeant.
units.tr: XI. Likewise, since nothing is more certain than that the true tranquillity of all commonwealths depends on the lawful obedience of all subjects towards the civil magistrate, and that every commonwealth is held together by penalties and rewards; but the Jesuits are such lords that they are unwilling to be subject to any civil magistrate, nor even to the bishops themselves, and if they should happen to be caught committing some crime against a magistrate, they say that they ought not, and cannot, be punished either by the magistrate or by the bishop by his own power: it is left for the praiseworthy province of Valesia to consider whether they ought to admit such free lords and lawbreakers among themselves, when the commonwealth and the authority granted to it by God would remain intact.

units.la: XII. Item, cum nulla Respub. citra censum, Decimas & cætera tributa diu consistere possit, & Iesuitæ semet non solum Iurisdictioni & oneribus omnibus ciuilibus & publicis eximant, sed etiam optimos fundos, agros & domos quorum omnium nomine possessores ciuiles censum, contributiones, cæteraq; omnia onera præstant:) sibi comparent, eorumq; coemptione & acquisitione ærarium publicum depauperent, atque non solum Reipub. enervent, sed etiam cæterorum ciuium bona & patrimonia intolerabilibus oneribus grauent, unde plerunque maximæ Reipub. perturbationes, atque adeo eversiones oriri solent: Vualefianus Senatus diligenter expendat, an eiusmodi Fuios in Repub. admittere consultum fuerit: cum iniquissimum sit, regionis & bonorum temporalium commodis uti, frui, & ab oneribus temporalibus, publicis & communibus liberum esse.
units.tr: XII. Likewise, since no commonwealth can long survive without revenue, tithes and other taxes, and since the Jesuits not only exempt themselves from all civil jurisdiction and public burdens, but also acquire for themselves the best estates, fields and houses (for the owners of which, as citizens, pay the census, contributions and all other charges), and by buying and acquiring these impoverish the public treasury, weaken the commonwealth, and burden the goods and property of the other citizens with intolerable charges, from which very great disturbances of the commonwealth, and indeed its overthrow, usually arise: let the Senate of Valais weigh carefully whether it has been advisable to admit such men into the commonwealth, since it is most unjust that they should enjoy the advantages of the region and of temporal goods, while being free from temporal, public and common burdens.

units.la: XIII. Item, cum ad supra dictas omnes causas gravissimas etiam accessat hæreseos crimen, & Iesuitæ ab ipsis etiam Catholicis hæreseos accusentur uti aperte convincitur ex libro illo, qui Catechismus, sive exacta vitæ, dostrinæq; Iesuitarum demonstratio, inscribitur); & nullum crimen ipsa hæresi Catholicis magis exosum sit: Senatus, Populusq; Vualefianus exacte perpendat, An ex Reipub. & Ecclesiæ usu fuerit, utriusq; eversores in Repub. tolerare.
units.tr: XIII. Likewise, to all the most serious causes mentioned above there is added the crime of heresy, and the Jesuits are accused of heresy even by Catholics themselves, as is plainly shown by that book which is entitled Catechism, or a demonstration of the exact life and doctrine of the Jesuits; and since no crime is more hateful to Catholics than heresy itself, let the Senate and People of Valais weigh carefully whether it is in keeping with the practice of the commonwealth and the Church to tolerate in the commonwealth the subverters of both.

units.la: XIV. Cum denique unumquenque Iesuitam Votum cæcæ obedientiæ facere oporteat, quo iurat & pollicetur, se quodcunq; suus ipsi superior iusserit, factutrum, quæcunque etiam mandaverit, iusta esse censurtum & contrarium suum iudicium sententiamq; per cœcam, ut verba constitutionis ipsorum sonant, obedientiam abnegaturum: an eiusmodi cœcitatis Doctores & Seductores in visceribus Reipub. tolerare utile sit, quivis de populo facile iudicaverit; Cum recenti experientia compertum sit, quod ex illiusmodi cœcæ obedientiæ præceptis maledicta filiorum in parentes, inobedientia, turbulenta ciuium & subditorum in Magistratus, Principes & Reges Rebellio; quid s infanda in sacras Regum & Principum personas parricidia, suprema omnium Regnorum & Rerumpub. mala proveniant.
units.tr: XIV. Finally, since every Jesuit must take a vow of blind obedience, by which he swears and promises that he will do whatever his superior orders, and judges whatever he commands to be just, and will renounce his own contrary judgement and opinion through blind obedience (as the words of their constitution have it), anyone among the people will easily judge whether it is useful to tolerate in the vitals of the commonwealth teachers and seducers of such blindness. For recent experience has shown that from precepts of this blind obedience there arise curses of sons against parents, disobedience, turbulent rebellion of citizens and subjects against magistrates, princes and kings, and, worst of all, the unspeakable murders of the sacred persons of kings and princes, the greatest evils of all kingdoms and commonwealths.

units.la: His aliisq; rationibus Vualefiani adducti sunt, quod Iesuitas Seduni, quæ est metropolis suæ provinciæ, & sedes cathedralis, hactenus recipere noluerunt.
units.tr: The men of Valais, moved by these and other reasons, have hitherto been unwilling to admit the Jesuits to Sion, which is the metropolis of their province and the seat of the cathedral.

units.la: CAPVT III. DE INGRESSV IESVITARVM IN INDIAM, EORVMQVE IN INDIIS PROPAGATIONE, PROFECTV ET MIRACVLIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. ON THE ENTRY OF THE JESUITS INTO INDIA, THEIR SPREAD IN THE INDIES, THEIR DEPARTURE AND THEIR MIRACLES.

units.la: PEtrus Matzarenius, ut supra indicavimus, qui pro Lufitaniæ Rege Ioanne legati munere fungebatur, petiit à Papa Regis sui nomine, ut ex decem Ignatij Loiolæ sociis aliquot promulgandi Evangelij causâ in Indiam mitterentur, cuius provinciæ ab Idolorum cultu ad Romanam fidem traducendæ Rex magno desiderio tenebatur. Misi igitur sunt ex illis duo, nec enim plures concessit Loiola, cuius arbitrio totam rem Papa permiserat, Franciscus Xaverius Navariensis, & Simon Rodericus Lufitanus Vlyssiponensis, Anno Domini 1540. Tum Francisco Xaverio India destinata, Simon autem Rodericus in
units.tr: Peter Mascarenhas, as we indicated above, who was acting as envoy on behalf of King John of Portugal, asked the Pope in the king's name that some of the ten companions of Ignatius of Loyola be sent to India to preach the Gospel. The king was eager to turn that province from the worship of idols to the Roman faith. Two of them were sent, since Loyola, to whose judgment the Pope had left the whole matter, would allow no more: Francis Xavier of Navarre and Simon Rodrigues of Lisbon, in the year of the Lord 1540. Francis Xavier was assigned to India, but Simon Rodrigues was kept back in Portugal. Since other men were already joining Loyola, he was to take charge of their college in the Academy of Coimbra, which was to serve as a seminary, supplying men who would afterwards be sent to India as reinforcements. The king assigned to that college annual revenues sufficient to support a hundred members, a number that was later doubled, together with funds for their education.

units.la: Lusitania retentus fuit, ut quoniam ad Loiolam alij plures se iam adiungere co{?} perant, instituendo in Conimbricensi Academia ipsorum Collegio praeessét quod velut seminarium foret eorum, qui deinceps in Indiam supplementi causa mitterentur. Ei Collegio Rex Vectigalium annuorum quod satis esset ad Socios centum alendos, qui tamen numerus postea duplicatus est, literisque erudiendis, attribuit.
units.tr: Rodericus was kept back in Lusitania, so that, since several others were already joining Loyola, he might preside over their college at the Academy of Coimbra, which was to serve as a seminary for those who would afterwards be sent to India as reinforcements. The King assigned to that college annual revenues sufficient to support a hundred Fellows, a number later doubled, and also for the teaching of letters.

units.la: Xaverius autem Anno 1541. cum Indiae Praefecto Martino Alphonso Sosa Vlysipone discessit; itineris comitem secum duxit e Societate Italum nomine Paulum. In Indiam pervenerunt Maio mense Anno 1542. ac Goam tandem appulerunt. Ibi cum aliquot mensés versatus esset, in eam oram discessit quae vulgo Comorini caput, seu Promontorium dicitur, ab urbe Goa passuum sexcenta millia. Ea gens quondam a D. Thoma Apostolo ad Christum conversa; sed quae iam Christiani praeter nudum nomen haberet nihil. Inde vero in alia regna ac provincias se contulit, ut in eius vita prolixe indicatur.
units.tr: Xavier, however, left Lisbon in 1541 with Martín Alfonso de Sousa, the Prefect of India; he took with him as his companion on the journey an Italian of the Society named Paul. They reached India in May 1542 and at length landed at Goa. After spending some months there, he moved on to that coast which is commonly called the Cape of Comorin, or Promontory, six hundred thousand paces from the city of Goa. That people had once been converted to Christ by the Apostle St Thomas, but now had nothing of Christianity beyond the bare name. From there he went on to other kingdoms and provinces, as is set out at length in his life.

units.la: DE MIRACVLIS A IESVITIS IN INDIA EDITIS.
units.tr: Concerning the miracles performed by the Jesuits in India.

units.la: HVnc Xaverium alij quam plurimi sequentibus annis subsequuti sunt periculosis navigationibus, & novas has insulas suis superstitionibus imbuerunt: ubi etiam multa eos edidisse, & adhuc quotidie edere miracula ex lapidicis ac Indicis illorum referunt ac gloriantur literis. Astutiores in hoc quoque quam reliqui Monachi, qui multa miracula ab se suisque edita gloriati sunt olim inter eos quibuscum habitarunt atque vixerunt, in quibus facile fraus & imposture deprehendi potuit, quum scirent illi, aut nihil unquam simile quid acciderit, aut fraude aliqua ac dolo ea perpetrata fuisse. Iesuitae igitur apud nos in Europa commorantes multa spargunt de suorum miraculis apud Indos & Antipodas editis, ne falsitas cognosci possit. Quis enim ad haec cognoscenda explorandaque eo usque excurreret aut penetraret?
units.tr: Many others followed Xavier in the years after him, making dangerous voyages, and they imbued these new islands with their superstitions.
