They report and boast in their letters that they performed many miracles there, and that they still perform them every day, through the stonemasons and Indians of those lands. In this they are more cunning than the other monks, who once boasted of many miracles performed by themselves and their companions among the people with whom they lived. In those cases fraud and imposture could easily be detected, since the people knew either that nothing of the kind had ever happened, or that the events had been brought about by some trickery and deceit. So the Jesuits who live among us in Europe spread many reports of miracles performed by their men among the Indians and the Antipodes, so that the falsehood cannot be recognised. For who would travel so far, or penetrate so deeply, to investigate and test these claims?

units.la: Bellarminus enim lib. 4. de Eccles. milit. c. 14. Hoc nostro, inquit, seculo clarui in India omni genere miraculorum B. P. Franciscus Xaverius Societatis Iesu Presbyter. Ibidem: Veritas, inquit, miraculorum Xaverij constat ex Indicis literis, quas ij, qui cum Xaverio versabantur, huc miserunt, etc. Acosta de Procur. Ind. sal. lib. 2. c. 10. In hunc, inquit, oculos coniiciamus, virum Apostolicae vitae, cuius tot & tam magna signa referuntur per plurimos eosque idoneos testes, ut vix de alio, exceptis Apostolis, plura & maiora legantur. Ozorius Iesuita tom. 4. Concion. Conc. de obitu. Hic, inquit, Xaverius eratnovi mundi Apostolus, innumera patravit miracula, daemones ejecit, caecos illuminavit, &c.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 4 of On the Military Church, chapter 14, says: "In our own age, the blessed Father Francis Xavier, a priest of the Society of Jesus, shone in India with every kind of miracle." In the same place: "The truth of Xavier's miracles," he says, "is established by the Indian letters which those who were with Xavier sent here," and so on. Acosta, On the Procuring of the Salvation of the Indians, book 2, chapter 10: "Let us fix our eyes on this man of apostolic life, of whom so many and such great signs are reported, attested by so many and such suitable witnesses, that scarcely any other man, apart from the Apostles, is said to have had more and greater ones." The Jesuit Ozorius, in volume 4 of his sermons, On the Death: "Here," he says, "Xavier was the Apostle of the new world. He performed countless miracles, cast out demons, gave sight to the blind," and so on.

units.la: Horatius Turselinus Iesuita, qui vitam Xaverij conscripsit lib. 6. c. 1. refert eum futura praedixisse, intimos sensus cordium novisse, caecos, claudos, mutos, surdos, leprosos & incurabiles morbos quam plurimos sanasse, recitatione saltem nuda super eos articulorum Fidei & Evangelij. Lib. 2. c. 7. narrat, eum uno tempore septem mortuos excitasse & pristinae vitae restituisse; inter quos fuerit Ethnica puella, quae cum primum surrexisset, Xaverium agnoverit, patriqué suo dixerit, Ecce hic est ille, qui animam meam ex inferno eripuit & liberavit. Refert praeterea rem hactenus inauditam, quod multas Indiae gentes etiam per Vicarios suos, qui fere nullam fidei Christianae cognitionem habuerint, converterit: multos & sanarit attactu solum sui Pater noster, ut vocant. Quod etiam dum Meliopori fuerit ex opulento cive loci illius multos daemones eiecerit per puerum tantum, impositione lignae Crucis & lectione Evangelij, daemonibus vehementer indignantibus, quod per puerum, & quidem Neophytum pelerentur. rentur. Idem Turselinus lib. 5. c. 4. & 12. aliquot miracula commemorat, quae post mortem etiam ediderit.
units.tr: Horatio Turselinus, the Jesuit who wrote the life of Xavier, book 6, chapter 1, reports that he foretold the future, knew the innermost thoughts of hearts, and healed very many blind, lame, dumb, deaf, leprous and incurably sick people, merely by reciting the articles of the faith and the Gospel over them. In book 2, chapter 7, he relates that on one occasion he raised seven dead people and restored them to their former life. Among them was a heathen girl who, as soon as she rose, recognised Xavier and said to her father: "Behold, this is he who snatched my soul from hell and set it free." He also records a thing unheard of until now: that he converted many nations of India, even through his vicars, who had hardly any knowledge of the Christian faith, and that he healed many by the mere touch of his so-called Our Father. And when he was at Meliapor, he is said to have cast out many demons from a wealthy citizen of that place by a boy alone, through laying on a wooden cross and reading the Gospel, the demons loudly protesting that they were being driven out by a boy, and indeed a neophyte. The same Turselinus, in book 5, chapters 4 and 12, mentions several miracles which Xavier is said to have performed even after his death.

units.la: De Aqua benedicta etiam multa miracula eius virtute in India patrata magnifice praedicat in Epistola Duartes a Sylva, quod nempe ea aegrotorum corpora, non alio medicamento curentur: eodem quoque Alexipharmaco multos pristinae valetudini restitutos, & alios morbos complures in India pulsos, a daemonibus liberatos Consalvus Ferdinandus testatur libro 3. Epistolarum.
units.tr: Duarte da Silva, in his letter, magnificently proclaims the many miracles performed in India by the power of holy water, namely that sick bodies are healed by no other medicine. Gonsalvo Fernandez attests in book 3 of his Letters that many have also been restored to health by this same antidote, and that several other diseases have been driven out in India and people freed from demons.

units.la: Aloisius Froes in Epistola de rebus Iapponicis miraculum, seu potius fabulam narrat mirabilem de multiplicatione Agnorum Dei. Allatam fuisse imitpyxidulam cerearum Agni coelestis imaginum, quas Pap. Rom. consecrarit, eas a quadam anu & aliis expetitas esse tanta aviditate, ut ceram in parvulas minutissimas secare coacti fuerint, quae tamen una mille quingentis aginta suffecerint, quas omnes vel argentea, vel aenea, vel stannea theca inclusas, cum nomine Iesu spinea corona circumdato, & cum tribus ad imam crucem clavis incisis religiose conservarint.
units.tr: In his letter on Japanese affairs, Aloisius Froes relates a wonderful miracle, or rather a fable, about the multiplication of the Agnus Dei. He says that a little box of wax images of the heavenly Lamb, which the Roman Pope had consecrated, was brought over, and that an old woman and others desired them with such eagerness that they were forced to cut the wax into tiny pieces; yet a single piece, it seems, sufficed for one thousand five hundred and sixty people. All of them, enclosed in silver, bronze or tin cases, with the name of Jesus surrounded by a crown of thorns and three nails cut beneath the foot of the cross, they kept with devotion.

units.la: Iis autem miraculis omnibus fides dubia, vel prorsus nulla haberi debet. Franciscus enim de Victoria Regius Professor in Salmanticensi Academia lect. 5. prop. 5. Non satis, inquit, mihi liquet, an barbaris Indis fides Christiana ita obvia proposita fuerit et annunciata, ut teneamur credere sub novo peccato. Nam miracula et signa NVLLA AVDIO, nec exempla vitae adeo religiosa, imo contra multa scandala et impietates: unde videtur, quod religio Christiana non fit ijs satis commode et pie dedicata, ut illi teneantur acquiescere. Acosta rerum Indicarum testis oculatissimus et fide dignissimus, libro de procur. Ind. sal. 6. c. 4. Quae est, inquit, praedicatio fira? quae fiducia? signa quidem non edimus. Et cap. 12. Nos prodigia, quibus Evangelicas voces confirmemus, nulla producimus. Et cap. 17. Neque vero est opus. Bonis operibus ita lucere coram hominibus, ut videntes glorificent Patrem, qui est in coelis, est opium ad persuadendum miraculum potentissimum.
units.tr: Yet no faith should be placed in any of these miracles, or rather none at all. For Francis de Victoria, royal professor at the Academy of Salamanca, lecture 5, proposition 5, says: "It is not sufficiently clear to me whether the Christian faith was so readily and so plainly proposed and announced to the barbarous Indians that we are bound to believe it under pain of a new sin. For I hear of no miracles or signs at all, nor of a life so religious as to be an example; on the contrary, many scandals and impieties. Whence it seems that the Christian religion has not been commended to them in a manner sufficiently fitting and pious for them to be obliged to assent." Acosta, a most careful and most trustworthy witness of Indian affairs, in his book On the Procuring of the Salvation of the Indians, book 6, chapter 4: "What kind of preaching is firm? What confidence? Indeed we do not work signs." And chapter 12: "We produce no prodigies by which to confirm the words of the Gospel." And chapter 17: "Nor is there any need. To shine so before men by good works that they see and glorify the Father who is in heaven is the most powerful means of persuading men, not a miracle."

units.la: Mirum etiam est, si tot tamen splendida fuerint Iesuitarum, imprimis aliorum miracula, ut vir tantus testimonium nullum fide dignum acceperit, praesertim de Indorum iure ex professo docte accurateque disputans. Secundo, non solum Iesuitis, sed etiam aliis sunt ad manum hodie ipsius etiam Xaverii rebus Indicis literae, mirabiliorum quorundam plenissimae, miraculorum item Apostolicorum inanissimae. Nicolaus Pimenta Provincialis Indiae Ontalis visitator epist. ad Claud. Aquaviuam pag. 6. Infidelis quidam, scribit, calumniator catechumenii recens conversum irridens, latere in caput adacto humi statim ostemitur, percussor nullus offendi potuit: itaque non dubitatum est divinam vindictam esse. Rursus pag. 119. Alium maledicum calumniatorem vita Patris Heriquez, qui a averio missus erat, Deus hoc probro castigavit, ut quoties eloqui vellet magna lingua ore exerta, ita praepediretur, ut intelligi non posset. Pag. 27. ibid. Navem in flumine turbido, alii nostrum; eramus numero 12; natandi periti, periculum evadere: ego fundum prolabor, nescio quomodo emergo, et capite super undas elato, video me a famulo Paulo ad ripam pertrahi. Ibidem pag. 77. Nos febri correptos Deus sanitati restituit, nullo remedio hominis freti, praeter sibi potionem, et vena incisionem.
units.tr: It is also strange that, if the Jesuits and especially others had so many splendid miracles, so great a man as Acosta should have received no trustworthy testimony, particularly when he disputes learnedly and accurately about the rights of the Indians as his special subject. Second, not only the Jesuits but also others today have at hand the letters on Indian affairs of Xavier himself, full of certain marvels but utterly empty of apostolic miracles. Nicolas Pimenta, Provincial and visitor of East India, in his letter to Claudius Aquaviva, page 6: "A certain unbelieving slanderer, mocking a newly converted catechumen, was struck to the ground at once when a stone was driven into his head; no one could be found who had struck him, so there was no doubt that it was divine vengeance." Again, page 119: "God punished another evil-speaking slanderer, the man sent by Xavier, with this disgrace: whenever he wished to speak, his tongue thrust out of his mouth so that he was hindered and could not be understood." Page 27 of the same: "A boat in a turbid river capsized; we were twelve in number, all skilled swimmers, and escaped the danger. I sank to the bottom, somehow rose again, and with my head raised above the waves I saw myself being dragged to the bank by my servant Paul." On the same page 77: "When we were seized with fever, God restored us to health, relying on no human remedy except a drink for him and the opening of a vein."

units.la: Nullum horum omnium est miraculum Apostolicum, quo eiiciebant daemones, sanabant mutos, caecos, &c.
units.tr: None of all these is an apostolic miracle, by which they cast out demons, healed the dumb, the blind, and so on.

units.la: Inquies, hoc modestiae Iesuitarum argumentum fuisse, non impotentiae. Sed haec tergiversatio, ut ex ipso Xaverio probari potest. Is enim libro 1. rebus Indicis epist. 3. ad Societatem Romae, In hac, inquit, Insula rem vidi incredibile, et ante hoc tempus inauditam. Caprum vidi lactefuo parvos alentem: hae des ubenim, quod prope genitalia unicum habet, tantum lactis reddebat quotidie, quantum scutella capere possit. Ego ipse rem perspexi his oculis, neq; enim aliter ut crederē, adduci potuissem &c. Si Xaverius hoc naturæ miraculū tam diligenter investigavit & in nostrum orbem scripsit, certè si quæ ipse miracula edidisset, nequaquam silentio præterirët. Nec est hæc modestia appellada in Xaverio et aliis: alioquin Apostoli in modestiæ accusandi forent. Deiis enim Lucas 14. c. scribit: Transeuntes Apostoli retulerunt quanta per eos fecisset Dominus. Actor. 15. Enunciantes quanta per se fecisset Deus. Ferus in hac loca: Apostoli, inquit, exponunt Spiritus sancti virtutem, ut à multis pro collata in Gentes gratia, gratiæ dicerentur Deo, & mutua fide confirmarentur. [illegible, ~10 letters] commendant, sed Dei opera ut Christus præcepit daemoniaco, Marc. 5. David etiam Psal. 104. dicit, Narrate omnia mirabilia ejus.
units.tr: You will say that this was a mark of the Jesuits' modesty, not of their inability. But this evasion can be proved from Xavier himself. For in book 1 of his Indian affairs, letter 3, to the Society at Rome, he says: "On this island I saw a thing incredible and unheard of until this time. I saw a goat feeding small kids from her udder, for she, having a single teat near her genitals, gave out daily as much milk as a bowl could hold. I myself saw the thing with these eyes, for I could not otherwise have been brought to believe it," and so on. If Xavier investigated this wonder of nature so diligently and wrote it down for our world, certainly he would by no means have passed over in silence any miracles he himself had performed. Nor should this be called modesty in Xavier and the others; otherwise the Apostles would have to be accused of modesty. For Luke writes of them in chapter 14: "The Apostles, passing through, reported how much the Lord had done through them." Acts 15: "Declaring how much God had done through them." Ferus, on these passages: "The Apostles," he says, "set out the power of the Holy Spirit, so that by many, on account of the grace given to the Gentiles, they might give thanks to God and be mutually strengthened in faith." [illegible, about ten letters] "they commend, but the works of God," as Christ commanded the demoniac, Mark 5. David also says in Psalm 104: "Tell of all his wonderful works."

units.la: Præterea, si necessarium fuit Iesuitis aliquod in conversione Indorum miraculum; tum illud, quod per se est ad alienigenas nationes maximè necessarium, videlicet variarum, & præsertim Indicarum linguarum donum. Atque hoc præsidio Iesuitæ omnes destituti sunt. Ergo etc. Consequentia maioris probatur. Ferus in hæc verba Actor. 2. Et apparuerunt eis dispertitæ linguæ, &c. Necessarium, inquit, erat novis illis Ecclesiis adificatoribus linguis varijs loqui, ut ab omnibus intelligerentur. Ob eam causam restituit Apostolis Deus omnium linguarum exactam notitiam, quà opus habuerant ad Evangelij negotium expediendum.
units.tr: Moreover, if the Jesuits needed some miracle in converting the Indians, the one most necessary for converting foreign nations would be the gift of many tongues, especially the Indian languages. The Jesuits lack this aid entirely. Therefore etc. The major premise is proved from Ferus, on these words of Acts 2: And there appeared to them divided tongues, etc. "It was necessary," he says, "for those who were to build the new churches to speak in various tongues, so that they might be understood by all. For this reason God restored to the Apostles an exact knowledge of all languages, which they needed to carry out the work of the Gospel."

units.la: IMPEDIMENTA CONVERSIONIS INDORUM AD RELIGIONEM CHRISTIANAM.
units.tr: IMPEDIMENTS TO THE CONVERSION OF THE INDIANS TO THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.

units.la: A Costa Iesuita de exiguo profectu Indorum in Christiana religione, et modo conversionis ad fidem, sic porrò scribit lib. 4. de Procurand. Ind. salut. cap. 3. Accusant, inquit, nostri Indorum tarditatem, ad capienda mysteria fidei, fructus in ijs edocendis tempus teri; denique post annos jam quadraginta, ab Evangelij ingressu in tam immensa turba, vix quemquam qui Symboli duo capita intelligat, quid Christus sit, quid vita æterna, quid Eucharistia, vel crasse agnoscat, reperiri: pecudes potius habendos quàm homines. Verum, qui ista jactant, respondeant mihi, quà diligentia ipsi erudiantur. Recitant illis bis terve in hebdomada Symbolum & preces, idque Hispanico idiomate: jam denique Hispanica hæc discere, quorum nessyllabam quidem intelligunt; & pro nuntiant ridicule. Vulgaris tamen & tritus doctrinæ tradendæ ipsè est modus; ubi exquisitius res agitur: Sacerdos Sermone Indico compositā quādam in Catechismi formam recitat, cum tamen ille lingua Indica prorsus est infans: quod si peritus sit; quod rarum est, tamen mysteria fidei neque explanat, neque vero satis novit: quis vero unquam Catechumenus ratione auditorum exegit? Denique perinde Indis doctrina traditur, atque cum Medicus stipis colligendæ causa, precationes aut versus aliqui cantillantur; qui illud tantum speitant, ut dicendo ipsi ad finem usque perveniant carminis: utrum vero auditores vel attendant vel delectentur, pecunia jam accepta, non admodum curant. Tota igitur catechizandi ratio umbratilis & ludicra similis. Hæc omnia Iesuita. Hæc legenti subit illud apud A. Gellium (quod in Iesuitas Catechistas & eorum Catechumenos Indos præclarè convenit) cum unus loquitur, quod alius non intelligit, mille esse, ac si alter hircum mulgeat, alter cribrum supponat.
units.tr: The Jesuit Acosta, on the meagre progress of the Indians in the Christian religion and the manner of their conversion to the faith, writes as follows in book 4 of De procuranda Indorum salute, chapter 3: They accuse our people of the slowness of the Indians in grasping the mysteries of the faith, and say that time is wasted in teaching them with little fruit. Yet after forty years since the entry of the Gospel into so vast a multitude, scarcely anyone can be found who understands the two articles of the Creed, or who grasps even roughly what Christ is, what eternal life is, or what the Eucharist is. They should be regarded as cattle rather than as men. But let those who make these complaints answer me: with what diligence are they themselves instructed? They recite the Creed and the prayers to them twice or three times a week, and that in the Spanish language. Then they are made to learn these Spanish things, of which they understand not a single syllable, and they pronounce them ridiculously. The common and familiar method of teaching doctrine is this: where the matter is treated more carefully, the priest recites in the Indian language some composition in the form of a catechism, though the listeners are utterly infants in that language. Even if the priest is skilled, which is rare, he neither explains the mysteries of the faith nor knows them well enough. And who has ever required a catechumen to be considered in light of his hearers? In short, doctrine is handed to the Indians just as when a physician, to collect alms, has some prayers or verses sung; they aim only at getting through the song to its end, and whether the hearers pay attention or are pleased, they do not much care, once the money is already received. The whole manner of catechizing is therefore shadowy and childish. So far the Jesuit. Reading this, one recalls what Aulus Gellius says (and it agrees admirably with the Jesuit catechists and their Indian catechumens): when one speaks what the other does not understand, it is as if one milked a he-goat while the other held a sieve underneath.

units.la: Rursus idem ibid. c. 4. Vere quidam, inquit, nostrorum scripsit Pater, Non vidi ri sibi ad Indorum horum animos penetrasse Evangelium, sed ad speciem tantum receptum. Negari enim non posse, quin si intimis sensibus radices egisset, copiosos manifestosque fructus ejus cerneremus. Quid enim potentius verbo Dei? quid ad immutandos homines efficacius? Mihi sanè monstrisimile semper est visum, inquit idem Iesuita ibid. lib. 5. c. 3. inter tot millia Indorum Christiano nomine donatorum, tam esse rarum qui Christū agnoscat, ut quod Ephesij olim de Spiritu S. Paulo responderunt, possint hi de Christo melius usurpare. rpare. (Neq an sit Christus audivimus. Haec ille. Hoc est Indos convertere, hoc asinos in mulos: par enim est in utrisque bruta ignorantia.
units.tr: Again, the same author in the same book, chapter 4: Truly, one of our fathers has written that he did not see that the Gospel had penetrated the minds of these Indians, but that it had been received only in appearance. For it cannot be denied that, if it had taken root in their inmost feelings, we would see its abundant and manifest fruits. For what is more powerful than the Word of God? What is more effective in changing men? Indeed, it has always seemed to me like a monstrous thing, says the same Jesuit in book 5, chapter 3, that among so many thousands of Indians given the Christian name, it is so rare to find one who acknowledges Christ, that they might rightly use of Christ what the Ephesians once answered about the Holy Spirit when Paul asked them (Acts 19:2), that they have not so much as heard whether there is a Christ. That is what he says. This is what it means to convert Indians: to turn asses into mules, for the brute ignorance is equal in both.

units.la: De eodem Andreas Vega opusc. de Fide & Operibus q. 3. Quidam, inquit, nostro tempore, habentes zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam, Indos ad Baptismum vocantes, indiscriminatim admiserunt nulla facta inquisitione de vita & moribus, imo nulla, vel pene nulla, iis tradita doctrina, de vita & moribus necessario servandis: sed hoc contenti, quod propositis fidei articulis, credere se respondeant, velle baptizari. Revoca eos ab hoc errore debuit illud Christi, Nolite sanctum dare canibus.
units.tr: On the same subject, Andreas Vega, in his little work On Faith and Works, question 3: Some people in our time, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, have called the Indians to baptism and admitted them indiscriminately, without any inquiry into their life and morals, and indeed with no, or almost no, teaching given them about the life and morals they must necessarily keep. They were content with this only: that, when the articles of faith were proposed, the Indians answered that they believed and wished to be baptized. The saying of Christ should have called them back from this error: Do not give what is holy to the dogs. (Matt. 7:6)

units.la: Acosta rursus lib. 1. de procur. Indorum salute c. 2. Notitia quaedam, inquit, testes Indis offertur, ut vel facile repudietur, vel ita recipiatur, ut no perniciosius deseratur. Id ita? Simulatoriam sanctitatis speciem praeferunt, non colunt Deum serio, nec credunt adjustitia. Et lib. 6. c. 3. testatur, ab Hispanis & Iesuitis multos Indos contra ipsorum voluntatem baptizari.
units.tr: Acosta again, book 1 of De procuranda Indorum salute, chapter 2: Some knowledge is offered to the Indians as witnesses, so that it is either easily rejected or so received that it is abandoned no less dangerously. Is this so? They put on a pretended outward show of holiness; they do not worship God in earnest, nor do they believe rightly. And in book 6, chapter 3, he testifies that many Indians were baptized by the Spaniards and Jesuits against their own will.

units.la: Idem lib. 4. c. 4. Expende, inquit, omnia subtiliter, invenies tam tenuis et inopis messis apud Indos potissimam caulam in eo esse, quod divinis & occultis quidem, sed justis consiliis, antiquis Gentibus praedicatores fuerint praedicatione sua digni, cum nostri tam sint rari, indigni, ut longe plus evertant & dissipent, quam aedificent atque plantent. Et lib. 1. c. 8. Equidem certum sum, si Evangelii introitus in has regiones is extitisset, quem Evangelii conditor maxime docuit, non alios istius progressus futuros fuisse, quam quos in primis & Apostolica Ecclesia legimus, &c. Et lib. 4. c. 5. Recte & prudenter scripsit Polus um Indicarum prudens indagator, tribus de causis tam multo tempore tam modicum movisse Evangelium. Primum, quod exempla prava nostrorum hominum fidem praedicationi Evangelicae derogarint: deinde, quod in cognoscendis exstirpandisque erroribus, sustitiosisque opinionibus nullam praedicatores operam collocarunt, &c. Ibidem capit. 11. quot ita misere corruere? ut merito ululare debeat abies, cum viderit altiss. & nobilissimos cedros Libani cecidisse. Ib. c. 15. Praeclare ageretur cum rebus Indorum, si Sacerdotes ea saltem modestia esset, ut non solutioris vitae licentiam quaererent, &c. Lib. 1. Soplurimum Indorum conversionem retardare pessimi exempli mores. Lib. 3. c. 8. Non ex causa mercatores negotiantur, vel judices praesident, vel Sacerdotes plerique Evangelizant, quam spe argenti & auri: argentum & aurum sibi subducit ex oculis, omnis civilis & sacerdotalis concursus brevi evanescit, & quo charitas non invitavit animarum, auri saltem cupiditas inescavit: & quemadmodum olim incredulitas Israelis fuit gentium, ita Christianorum avaritia Indorum vocatio facta est.
units.tr: The same author, book 4, chapter 4: Weigh everything carefully, and you will find that the chief reason for so thin and poor a harvest among the Indians lies in this: that the ancient Gentiles had preachers worthy of their preaching, by divine and hidden, but just, counsels, whereas ours are so rare and unworthy that they overthrow and scatter far more than they build up and plant. And book 1, chapter 8: Indeed I am certain that if the entrance of the Gospel into these regions had been of the kind that the Author of the Gospel chiefly taught, there would have been no other progress of it than what we read of in the first and apostolic Church, etc. And book 4, chapter 5: The prudent investigator of Indian affairs, Polus, has written rightly and wisely that the Gospel has moved so little over so long a time, for three reasons. First, because the wicked examples of our men have diminished faith in the evangelical preaching; second, because the preachers have made no effort to recognize and root out errors and superstitious opinions, etc. In the same place, chapter 11: How many have fallen so wretchedly? So that the fir ought rightly to wail, when it has seen the tallest and noblest cedars of Lebanon fall. In chapter 15: Affairs of the Indians would go on splendidly if the priests had at least such moderation that they did not seek a licence for a looser life, etc. Book 1: The very wicked example of manners greatly delays the conversion of the Indians. Book 3, chapter 8: Merchants do business, judges preside, and most priests evangelize for no other reason than the hope of silver and gold. Silver and gold withdraw themselves from sight, all civil and priestly zeal soon vanishes, and if the love of souls has not drawn them, the mere greed of gold has enticed them. And just as once the unbelief of Israel became the calling of the Gentiles, so the avarice of Christians has become the calling of the Indians.

units.la: Haec & multa alia acerbe dolenterque Iesuita Acosta queritur: ex quibus inligimus, ficta, vana & frivola esse omnia, quae Iesuitae referunt ac gloriantur de rerum morum Regnorum, Provinciarum, & multorum millium Indorum ad fidem Christianam conversione.
units.tr: These and many other things the Jesuit Acosta complains of bitterly and sorrowfully. From them we infer that everything the Jesuits report and boast of, concerning the conversion to the Christian faith of the customs, kingdoms, provinces and many thousands of Indians, is fictitious, empty and frivolous.

units.la: Assumptione Iesuitae concedunt. Pimenta Iesuita in Epist. p. 14. Nostra, inquit, societatis pater Franciscus Corsius scribit ad suos: Totus, inquit, sum in Persico idiomate addiscendo. Idem p. 80. Quod autem ad conversionem attinet, vitio meo, utpote idiomate ignaro, inquit pater Fernandus, parum effectum est. Acosta lib. 1. de procur. Ind. ut. c. 2. Ferunt, inquit, olim septuaginta linguas confusum fuisse genus mortalium: at diseptingentis, & eo amplius, inter se discrepant linguis. Lib. 4. c. 8. Qua ex repraedido verbo Dei impedimenta nobis gravia fiunt. Ibid. c. 9. Neq igitur immerito nostrae societatis sudator Ignatius Indicae linguae lectiones publicas praecepit: sunt enim perquam necessaria illa praesidia, ut facultas pareatur verbi divini in Gentibus annunciandi. Lib. 5. Quid quod confessiones saepe ita faciunt, ut neque Indus intelligat Sacerdotem, neque inligatur ipse quid dicat. Ipse Xaverius quoque lib. 3. Epist. 5. Si, inquit, nos linguam Iaponicam, non dubito, quin plurimi fierent Christiani. Faxit Deus ut eam brevi addiscamus: tum demum aliquam Christianae rei nav abimus operam: nam nunc quidem ex eos tamquam mutae statuae versamur: multa enim illi de nobis & dicunt, & agitant, ad nos obmutescimus, patrii ipsorum sermonis ignari in praesentia in linguae hujus percipiendis elementis repueraescimus. Aa
units.tr: The Jesuits concede the minor premise. Pimenta, a Jesuit, in his letter, p. 14: Our father of the society, Francis Corsius, writes to his own people: I am wholly occupied in learning the Persian language. The same, p. 80: As for conversion, through my own fault, since I am ignorant of the language, says Father Fernandus, little has been achieved. Acosta, book 1 of De procuranda Indorum salute, chapter 2: They say that the human race was once confused by seventy languages, but there are more than seven hundred, and even more, that differ from one another. Book 4, chapter 8: Because of this, grave obstacles arise for us in preaching the Word of God. Ibid., chapter 9: Not without reason, therefore, did Ignatius, the sweat-soaked founder of our society, order public lessons in the Indian language, for those aids are exceedingly necessary so that the opportunity may be obtained of announcing the divine Word among the Gentiles. Book 5: What of the fact that confessions often are so made that the Indian does not understand the priest, nor does the priest himself know what he is saying? Xavier himself also, book 3, letter 5: If we knew the Japanese language, I do not doubt that very many would become Christians. May God grant that we learn it soon; only then shall we at last be doing some useful work for the Christian cause. For now we stand before them like dumb statues. They say and do many things about us, and we are silent before them; ignorant of their native speech, we are like children in the presence of them, learning the rudiments of this language.

units.la: Ex hoc Catalogo (anno 1608. à Petro Ribadeneira in lucem edito) Regnorum, Provinciarum & urbium in quibus habitant Iesuitæ, Collegiorum item ac domorum, quæ in unaquaque Provincia sunt, propagationem & incrementa Iesuitici Ordinis, spacio 75. annorum, Lector colligere poterit.
units.tr: From this catalogue, published in 1608 by Pedro de Ribadeneira, the reader can gather the spread and growth of the Jesuit order over a space of 75 years: the kingdoms, provinces and cities in which Jesuits live, and likewise the colleges and houses in each province.

units.la: Et de hac quidem sua propagatione & incrementis multum gloriari solent Iesuitæ. Inprimis de Aquaviva Generali suo referunt, quod iactarit plures se evioriq; spacio, milites in castra cogere posse, quam quilibet Rex Christianus. Et tempore interdicti Veneti, cum iam undique certum Papæ immineret periculum, spopondisse idem Pontifici Paulo V. dicitur, quadraginta hominum millia in subsidium: ea lege tamen, ut quicunque in prælio obirent, in Martyrum numerum referrentur.
units.tr: The Jesuits are wont to boast much of this spread and growth. Above all they report that their General, Aquaviva, once boasted that he could muster more soldiers into the field, and in a shorter time, than any Christian king. And at the time of the Venetian interdict, when danger already threatened the Pope on every side, he is said to have promised Pope Paul V forty thousand men in aid, on the condition that whoever fell in battle should be counted among the martyrs.

units.la: Non cogitant autem boni isti Socij quod vulgò dicitur, Malam herbam cito scere. Et recte quidam magni nominis Princeps dixisse videtur, Iesuitas similes esse pediculis istis, quos, à parte corporis, quam maxime infestare solent, inguinales vocamus, quorum vel ex uno, ibi primum insidente, brevi innumera propagatur ac scaturit multitudo.
units.tr: But those good Jesuits do not reflect on the common saying, "A bad herb grows quickly." And a prince of great name seems to have rightly said that Jesuits are like those lice which we call groin lice, which infest that part of the body above all; from one louse, first settling there, a countless multitude soon spreads and swarms.

units.la: Similia autem vel etiam Maiora sensit incrementa Franciscanorum seu Minoritarum Secta. Ab anno enim Domini 1211. ad annum usque 1380. spacio nimirum 179. annorum, per orbem Christianum coenobia huius Sodalitatis plus 1500. ut instituta. Franciscus Antracinus in ijs Commentarijs, quos ad Sabellicum dir, testatur, difficile sibi videri locorum numerum posse ab ullo inveniri: multo difficilius initiatorum, qui tunc temporis fuerint ad 60. millia numero. Sabellicus autem refert Ennead. 9. lib. 9. & 6. sua ætate Minoritarum 90. millia fuisse; sæpe quoque se audivisse, Magistrum universi Ordinis, polliceri quanquam aurum Pio Pontifici expeditionem in Turcas paranti ex Minoritarum familia 30000. bellatorum, qui bellica munia gnauiter obire possent, nihil sacrorum cultu interpellato. Sabellici quoque tempore, hoc est, circa annos Christi 1494. Augustinensium Eremitarum Ordinis coenobia quorundam quidem ratio inire potest, circiter 2000. Virginum autem 300. fuerunt. Carmelitarum Monasteria 50. Prædicatorum 4143.
units.tr: The Franciscans, or Minorite sect, saw similar or even greater growth. From the year of the Lord 1211 to 1380, a space of 179 years, more than 1,500 monasteries of this brotherhood were founded throughout the Christian world. Francesco Antracino, in the commentaries he addressed to Sabellicus, testifies that he thought it hard to find anyone who could count the places, and much harder to count the initiates, who at that time numbered about 60,000. Sabellicus, however, reports (Ennead. 9. lib. 9. & 6.) that in his own age there were 90,000 Minorites. He also often heard that the Master of the whole Order promised Pope Pius, who was preparing an expedition against the Turks, 30,000 men from the Minorite family, fit to perform military duties vigorously, and that without any interruption of worship. Also in Sabellicus' time, that is around the year of Christ 1494, the monasteries of the Order of Augustinian Hermits can be reckoned at roughly 2,000; the convents of virgins were 300. Carmelite monasteries numbered 50, and those of the Preachers 4,143.

units.la: Hæc autem multitudo scarabæorum, bruchorum, locustarum, vermium & iscarum prædicta est à Spiritu sancto in Apocal. Ioan. 9. cap.
units.tr: This multitude of beetles, caterpillars, locusts, worms and fishes was foretold by the Holy Spirit in Apocal. Ioan. 9. cap.

units.la: Et recte monuit Laurentius Iustinianus Venetus Patriarcha, cum sub Mendicantibus Monachis numerus Coenobiorum in immensum crescieret, Rigiditatem vitæ, & Monasticum vigorem diutius non posse consistere; Raram enim esse perfectionem, ut refert Bernardus Iustinianus in eius vita. Quid dicturus fuisset si hodie viveret?
units.tr: Lorenzo Giustiniani, Venetian Patriarch, rightly observed that when the number of monasteries under the Mendicant monks grew beyond measure, the strictness of their life and their monastic vigour could not endure for long, since perfection is rare, as Bernardo Giustiniani reports in his life. What would he have said had he lived today?

units.la: CAPVT V. DE COLLEGIIS IESVITARVM, EORVM QVE MAGNIFICIS STRVCTVRIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. CONCERNING THE COLLEGES OF THE JESUITS AND THEIR MAGNIFICENT BUILDINGS.

units.la: Quod autem ad Collegia Iesuitarum attinet, quorum Catalogum paulo ante adscripsimus, illa Regum ac Principum Arces ac Palatia æquare vi[?] dentur. Gregorius XIII. Iesuitarum Annales legens, & intelligens opera qui[?] hinc inde illorum artibus efficiantur, Romæ contra Senatus decreta, Iesuitis tam attribuit insulam, in qua domos destruxerunt, viduas ac orphanos expulerunt; quod etiam Augustæ, Ingolstadii & multis aliis in locis fecerunt; ibiq; amplissimum, magnificentissimumq; Collegium exstruxerunt, ad cuius ædificationem, ut Iesuitæ Hafenmullero retulerunt, pag. 25. auri tonnas 25. prædictus Papa donavit. In eo Collegio 500. Iesuitas ex omnibus totius mundi partibus collectos alii voluit, qui in Pontificia idolomania instructi, tandem adversus Evangelicos in Germania aliisq; Regnis & Provinciis, emitti possent.
units.tr: As for the Jesuit colleges, whose catalogue I listed a little earlier, they seem to rival the citadels and palaces of kings and princes. Gregory XIII, reading the Jesuits' annals and understanding by what arts they carried out their projects, granted them, at Rome and against the decrees of the Senate, an island on which they pulled down houses and drove out widows and orphans. They did the same at Augsburg, Ingolstadt and many other places, and there they built a very large and magnificent college. Toward its construction, as the Jesuits reported to Hafenmuller (p. 25), the aforesaid Pope gave 25 tons of gold. In this college he wished 500 Jesuits, gathered from every part of the world, to be trained in Papist idolatry and then sent out against the Evangelicals in Germany and in other kingdoms and provinces.

units.la: De magnificentissima structura Collegii Iesuitarum Monachii in Bavaria, quæ Gallice scripsit Philippus Marnixius, sic quidam in Germanicam linguam translulit: Wer solte andere Gebäw zeugen können, die zuvergleichen weren dem oberauß prächtigen, welches der gütte Catholische Fürst vnnd Herr zu Bayeren, ían der Statt München auffgebauwen hat: dessen Gibel hoch erhaben, vnnd mit vielen stattlichen Bildern von Erz vnd Marmelstein gezieret ist, trotz zubieten allen den köstlichen Pallästen, die inn ganz Europa seynd, will geschweigen, daß es innwendig glitzert vnnd glantzet von lauterem Golde, Silber, Helffenbein, Chrystall vnd Edelgesteinen, wie ein Bäpstliche Crone. Vnnd damit dieses Werck inn allem vollkommen sey, vnnd ihm nichts mangele, so hat es zu einem jeden Altar sein Geräth, als Casulen, sampt seinem schönen Meßgewandt, Chorröcken, Alben, Gürtel, Stollen vnd andere rüstung etc.
units.tr: Concerning the most magnificent structure of the Jesuit college at Munich in Bavaria, Philippe de Marnix wrote in French, and someone translated it into German thus: "Who could point to other buildings that could be compared with the very splendid one which the good Catholic Prince and Lord of Bavaria has erected in the city of Munich? Its gable rises high and is adorned with many stately images of bronze and marble, and it defies all the costly palaces that are in all of Europe, not to mention that inside it glitters and gleams with pure gold, silver, ivory, crystal and precious stones, like a papal crown. And so that this work may be perfect in every way and lack nothing, each altar has its own furnishings: chasubles together with their fine vestments, surplices, albs, girdles, stoles and other equipment, etc."

units.la: Posnaniæ in Polonia, non Collegium pro docentibus & discentibus, sed arcem munitissimam summis præsidiis Iesuitæ ædificarunt. Regis Palatium Pe[?] snaniense, nulla parte cum hac Iesuitarum arce & propugnaculo conferendum est, ut refert Eques quidam Polonus in Oratione sua, quam in frequentiprocerum Regni illius conventu habuit. Eodem authore, Iaroslaviæ etiam, & Lublini, aliisq; in civitatibus Poloniæ eiusdem munitionis, firmamenti tantorum præsidiorum extructæ arces videntur, ut non scholasticos docere, aut mulierum peccata cognoscere, sed bellum gerere proxima quaque occasione velle videantur.
units.tr: At Posen in Poland, the Jesuits have built not a college for teachers and pupils but a most strongly fortified citadel with the greatest garrisons. The royal palace at Posen is in no way to be compared with this Jesuit citadel and bulwark, as a certain Polish knight reports in his speech which he gave before a crowded assembly of the nobles of that kingdom. On the same authority, citadels of the same fortification, built to hold such strong garrisons, are also to be seen at Jaroslau and Lublin and in other cities of Poland. They seem designed not to teach schoolboys or to hear the sins of women, but to wage war at the first opportunity.

units.la: De his Collegiis Costerus quoque in literis ex Belgio Romam missis, & interceptis, sic scribit: Quotquot nos in Germania Collegia habemus, tot nunc Rex noster (Hispanus) inibi Castella habet. Eaq; ad promovendam Ecclesiæ Romanæ Monarchiam & magnitudinem tendere, Petrus Ribadeneira Iesuita Hispanus apertissime testatur, cum apertis verbis Collegia & Seminaria Iesuitarum esse arces Hæreticorum exitia, & Apostolicæ Sedis propugnacula, in Catalogo illustrium Script. Societatis Iesu.
units.tr: Costerus also writes about these colleges in letters sent from Belgium to Rome and intercepted: "Every college that we have in Germany, our King (of Spain) now has as a castle there." That these colleges aim at advancing the monarchy and greatness of the Church of Rome, the Spanish Jesuit Pedro de Ribadeneira openly attests, when in his Catalogue of the Illustrious Writers of the Society of Jesus he plainly calls the colleges and seminaries of the Jesuits the citadels and bulwarks of the Apostolic See, and the ruin of heretics.

units.la: Non iniuria quoque Iesuitarum Collegia Armamentaria, seu receptacula & repositoria omnis generis armorum & instrumentorum bellicorum dixeris. In direptione Pragensis urbis in Bohemia repertæ sunt in Iesuitarum Collegio quingentæ bombardæ, thoraces ferrei pro centenis aliquot militibus
units.tr: Not unjustly, too, one might call the Jesuit colleges arsenals, or storehouses and repositories of every kind of weapon and war equipment. When the city of Prague in Bohemia was sacked, five hundred cannon, iron breastplates for some hundred soldiers,

units.la: {y} Iesuitarum Collegia sunt Armamentaria. itibus,& hastæ,aliaq; arma quàm plurima, tormentariq; etiam pulveris ma& vis, multaq; alia ad irruptionem illam promovendâ & Evangelicos oppri& ndos:Idcoq; numerum quoq; præsidiariorum ab Evangelicis in Collegium ad collocatorum auxerunt, quòd vererentur, hæc instrumenta omnia bellica ó ibi recòdita fuisse, ut Passavienses milites per pontem in Collegium, quod nti proximum est, inermes, velut Missæ audiendi gratia, excurrerent, ibiq; cultati, donec tempus commodum offerretur, velut ex equo Troiano ad por& n pontis, ipsumq; potem occupandum, ac deinceps Evangelicos opprimen & s, egrederentur.
units.tr: Jesuit colleges are arsenals: pikes, very many other weapons, and also gunpowder and large stores of ammunition, and much else to further that assault and to crush the Evangelicals. For this reason they also increased the number of garrison troops that were placed in the college by the Evangelicals, because they feared that all these military instruments had been stored there, so that soldiers of Passau, who would go out unarmed over the bridge into the college next to it, as if to attend Mass, would be armed there, and wait until a suitable time offered, and then come out like the men from the Trojan horse, to seize the gate of the bridge and the bridge itself, and afterwards crush the Evangelicals.

units.la: Hanc ob causam etiam in commodissimis urbium omnium locis, ad milites depellendos, vel excipiendos, si velint urbem aliquam oppugnare, Collegia ædificant.
units.tr: For this reason too they build colleges in the most convenient places of all cities, to repel soldiers, or to receive them if they wish to attack some city.

units.la: Exhis denique Collegijs hodie vigesies centies aureorum millia quotannis pro stigalibus percipere Iesuitæ dicuntur, licet pro mendicantibus haberi velint. Christus Iesus autem, cuius Socij isti videri volunt, locum non habuit, in quo caput reponeret, in capis, in mõtibus & piscatorum tuguriolis versari potius voluit, quàm in urbibus, aut propugnaculis & palatijs Regum ac Principum.
units.tr: Finally, from these colleges the Jesuits are said to draw every year two million gold pieces in revenues, although they wish to be regarded as mendicants. Yet Christ Jesus, whose companions these men wish to appear, had no place where he might lay his head. He preferred to dwell in boats, on mountains and in the little huts of fishermen, rather than in cities, or in the strongholds and palaces of kings and princes.

units.la: IESVITAE QVOS ET QVALES POTISSIMVM IVVE- nes in hac sua Collegia, suamq; Societatem illiciant.
units.tr: WHAT KIND OF YOUNG MEN, AND ESPECIALLY WHICH, THE JESUITS ATTRACT TO THEIR COLLEGES AND THEIR SOCIETY.

units.la: Eliquorum Ordines Monachorum pusiones vix dum e cunabulis egressos ad se admittunt, totosq; 15. aut 20. annos nutriunt, antequam ad praxim admoveri ssint. Hoc solerter animadvertentes Iesuitæ, ad alliciendos ex locis diversis quàm primos, expeditiorem accommodatiorem q;, ut gloriatur, viam repererunt, quà ra paucos annos ad fastigium Sapientiæ iuventutem ducere possunt. Nam Cavogocerto, cuius ingenij, cuius iudicij, cuius prudentiæ & experientiæ, cuius ofectus in literis sit, cuius complexionis naturalis, ad quæ Societatis ministe talentum habeat adolescens quisq;, inscribunt: ut nempe tanto facilius a pa& tribus liberos in eo ætatis flexu, qui iam ad adultam vergit; tatoq; observent uratius singulos, ne in nassa sua semel adductos, avolare citra negotiu sinat.
units.tr: Some orders of monks do not admit boys who have scarcely left the cradle, and they keep them for a full fifteen or twenty years before they are put to practice. The Jesuits, noticing this carefully, found a quicker and more convenient way, as they boast, of drawing the first youths from various places, so that in a few years they can lead young men to the summit of learning. For they record with precision each young man's talent, his intellect, his judgement, his prudence and experience, his progress in letters, his natural temperament, and for what service of the Society he is suited. The purpose is, of course, that they may more easily win children from their parents at that age which is just turning to adulthood, and watch each one more carefully, so that once they are drawn into their net they cannot slip away without difficulty.

units.la: QVIBVS ARTIBVS AC DOLIS IESVITAE IN COL- legijs suis maximas opes acquirant.
units.tr: By What Arts and Tricks the Jesuits Acquire Very Great Wealth in Their Colleges.

units.la: Ictu impossibile est quibus artibus, dolis, imposturis ac fraudibus Iesuitæ in his Collegijs suis ingentes divitias, & tantum non Croesi opes per fas & fas corraserint. Ex plurimis pauca saltem referam. Non solum ex Magnan ærarijs, sed ex ipsis etiam discipulorum bonis dici non potest quantum escant; siquidem in Examine suo generali cap. 4. Novitios suos obligant, ut nia bona sua temporalia distribuant, ac disponant de his, quæ ipsis obvenire possint, iuxta propriam devotionem, neglectis parentibus & consanguineis; unde miro quodam astu, tanquam pauperes, bona illorum facillime ad se rapiunt & pertrahunt.
units.tr: It is impossible to say by what arts, tricks, impostures and frauds the Jesuits have, in these their Colleges, scraped together enormous riches, and almost the wealth of Croesus, by right and by wrong alike. I will report only a few out of very many. It cannot be said how much they seize not only from the College treasuries but also from the very goods of their pupils. For in their General Examen, chapter 4, they oblige their novices to distribute all their temporal goods, and to dispose of whatever may fall to them, according to their own devotion, with parents and kinsfolk set aside; hence, with a wondrous craft, as if they were poor men, they very easily snatch up and draw those people's goods to themselves.

units.la: FINIS LIBRI SECVNDI.
units.tr: END OF THE SECOND BOOK.

units.la: DE VARIIS FACINORIBVS DO- LIS AC IMPOSTVRIS ET SANG- VINARIIS CONSILIIS IESVI- TARVM. Liber Tertius.
units.tr: ON THE VARIOUS CRIMES, DECEITS AND IMPOSTURES, AND THE BLOODY SCHEMES OF THE JESUITS. Book Three.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: DOC Libro ea referam Iesuitarum facinora, ex quibus interdum intelliget Lector, ab ultima hominum memoria nullo unquam tempore inter mortales, tot inhumanae crudelitatis facinora, ut sunt parricidia, veneficia, periuria, caedes, proditiones, tumultus, bella, &c. intra tam breve tempus audita & enumerata esse, quod ab exortu & origine saltem Iesuitarum prius ... vatim & publice perpetrata, vel saltem attentata fuerunt; hoc quidem sub zeli religiosi & Catholici praetextu: iubentibus etiam, vel quod peius est, approbantibus & dilaudantibus ijs, qui omne in his terris religionis magisterium sibi vendicant.
units.tr: In this book I shall relate the Jesuits' crimes, from which the reader may sometimes see that, since the earliest memory of man, no age among mortals has heard or recorded so many deeds of inhuman cruelty, such as parricides, poisonings, perjuries, murders, betrayals, uprisings, and wars, within so short a time. These were carried out or at least attempted openly and publicly from the very beginning and origin of the Jesuits, under the pretext of religious and Catholic zeal, and at the command, or, worse still, with the approval and praise, of those who claim for themselves the whole teaching authority of religion on earth.

units.la: IESVITAS OMNIVM FERE TVRBA- RVM, SEDITIONVM, BELLORVM, &c. IN EV- ROPA AVTHORES ESSE.
units.tr: THAT THE JESUITS ARE ALMOST ALL THE AUTHORS OF THE TUMULTS, SEDITIONS, WARS, ETC. IN EUROPE.

units.la: PRaetextus Iesuitarum actionum omnium est, Ecclesiae Catholicae Romanae reparatio & propugnatio; errantiumque & seductorum, ut ipsi quiloquuntur, conversio. Sub hoc pluteo cubiculos suos promovent. Scopus autem ad quem collimant & respiciunt, est Dominatus & tyrannidis Pontificis cum Romanorum in his terris restitutio; atque idolomaniae & superstitionum omnium plantatio in ijs Provinciis & regionibus, in quibus iamprídem evulsae & eradicatae sunt. Media autem, quibus id quod semel male coeperunt, impugnent & evincere conantur, sunt, periuria publica, ad quae Reges & Principes inducunt, vis conscientiis illata, fraudulentae & insidiosae pacificationes, Iurium corruptela, Innocentiae oppressio, &c. Haec, inquam, hodie sunt, per quae Iesuitae immanem tyrannidem & crudelitatem Antichristi Romani defendere & restituere, collapsum Ecclesiae Papisticae statum reparare, Concilium Tridentinum exequi, & haereses exstirpare conantur. Ex harum vero rerum tam contentiosa praxi, qualem hodie in Europa praecipue animadvertimus, nihil secundum naturae cursum aliud, quam bella, & quidem perniciosissima & calamitosa bella, caedes, parricidia, seditiones, tumultus, &c. exoriri possunt. Vnde non immerito Iesuitae omnium turbarum ac motuum in Europa hodie praecipui authores vulgo dicantur & habeantur.
units.tr: The pretext of all the Jesuits' actions is the restoration and defence of the Roman Catholic Church, and the conversion of those who err and are led astray, as they themselves put it. Under this shield they advance their designs. The goal at which they aim and look is the restoration of the lordship and tyranny of the Pontiff and of the Romanists in these lands, and the planting of idolatry and every superstition in those provinces and regions from which they were long ago uprooted and eradicated. The means by which they try to press on and carry through what they have once begun badly are public perjuries, to which they induce kings and princes; violence done to consciences; fraudulent and treacherous pacifications; the corruption of laws; the oppression of the innocent; and so on. These, I say, are the things by which today the Jesuits seek to defend and restore the monstrous tyranny and cruelty of the Roman Antichrist, to repair the collapsed state of the Papist Church, to enforce the Council of Trent, and to root out heresies. Yet from the practice of such contentious affairs, which we see especially today in Europe, nothing else can arise in the ordinary course of nature but wars, and indeed most pernicious and calamitous wars, murders, parricides, seditions, tumults, and so on. Hence the Jesuits are not undeservedly called and regarded, commonly, as the chief authors of all the disturbances and movements in Europe today.

units.la: Notum est omnibus, plerarumque Europæarum nationum internam pacem in illis Constitutionibus & pactis consistere, quibus ex præsentium temporum usu cautum est, Ne religionis nomine ulli vis inferatur, quocunque modo. Iam vero ne illud quidem obscurum est, Spiritus hos, seu Iesuitas, omnes suas res ubique locorum intendere, ut repagulum hoc, quo se in suo proposito & ninijs astutissimis impedíri sentiunt, difficultum & disípatum removeant. Ideoque Iesuitæ huiusmodi Constitutiones, in Gallia, Germania, Polonia, Vngaria, tot fœderum, pactorum, iuramentorumque Sacramentis, sanctitas, publice detestantur, easque, tamquam novum Atheismi, sive, ut alicubi luntur, Politicismi genus, pro sceleratis coniurationibus, Scythica barbaque con federatione, diabolique Politici blasphemo invento haberi volunt, nó contendunt, pacem Religionis inter Ordines Germanici Imperij concentam, uti per vim extortam, non esse obligatoriam, utpote ad tempus tantum concessam, nempe ad publicationem Concilij Tridentini, ideoque dilationem, moratoriam & tolerantiam fuisse. Et Paulus Vvindeck in deliberat. de rei. exstirpandis pagina quadringentesima decima quarta hæc scribit: Quod nunquam Catholici cum Sectarijs transegerunt, eo fine fecerunt, ut interea reliquis gotijs expediti, postea unum hoc bellum contra Sectarios administrarent, omnemque molem in ipsos converterent. Sin vero alicubi eo impudentiæ non audent progredi, illud saltem agunt, ut religionis pacem calumniosis & malitiosis suis interpretationibus & restrictionibus suggillent, incisisque nervis eius subditi illius fructu spolient. Opinor ne ipsas quidem inferni furias ad turbandum ropæ statu aliquid præsentius, perniciosius & efficacius excogitare potuisse. Ö harum Ranarum coaxatus hic assiduus ad aures Regum ac Principum perpetuo reverberat & obtundit, Subditis bona conscientia tantam licentiam non concedi: Religionis libertatem nihil aliud esse quam manifestam Malatis diminutionem cum maximo opprobrio coniunctam. Tunc, inquiunt, vivis & flores, non potes vel audeas retractare quæ Antecedunt, Parens, ius, &c. vel imprudens malevolè persuasus, vel etiam vi & armis coactus indulsit. Annon eodem iure Imperator, Rex, Princeps es, quo illi fuerunt? Ferrum est, ut demortui memoria plus apud Subditos valeat, quam præsentis, quæ regnantis persona? Annon vides, Eos, qui pericula tibi obiectant, quæ rebatam religionis pacem sequantur, tibi non tam consulere, quam aperte inimici? Diaboli hæc tentamenta sunt, per quæ generosis tuis cogitatis & conatibus remoram studet inficere. Mulierculârum hic, non magnanimorum incipium metus est: illi iuventutem tuam spernunt, fronte igitur severiore us est, ut sentiant te virum esse, animumque tam excelsis natalibus parem gerere. Possem alicui videri satis confidenter hæc me scribere, non aliter, quam is Iesuitarum ad Principes monitis interfuissem: sed ipsimet has consiliorum rationes in publicis scriptis suis nequaquam dissimulant, ex quibus cad verbum fere descripsimus.
units.tr: It is known to all that the internal peace of most European nations rests on those constitutions and treaties by which, in the custom of our times, it has been provided that no force of any kind be inflicted in the name of religion. Now it is no secret either that these spirits, that is, the Jesuits, direct all their efforts everywhere to remove this barrier, by which they feel themselves hindered in their most cunning plans, so that it may be cast down and scattered. Therefore the Jesuits publicly denounce such constitutions in France, Germany, Poland and Hungary, calling the sanctity of so many leagues, treaties and oaths a sacrament, and they want them regarded as a new kind of atheism, or, as in some places they are called, a kind of politicism, as wicked conspiracies, a Scythian and barbarous confederation, and a blasphemous invention of the political devil. They contend that the peace of religion agreed among the estates of the German Empire, being extorted by force, is not binding, since it was granted only for a time, namely until the publication of the Council of Trent, and was therefore only a postponement, a moratorium and a toleration. And Paul Windeck, in his book on the extirpation of heresy, page four hundred and fourteen, writes this: What Catholics never concluded with the sectaries, they did with this aim, that, once free of other matters in the meantime, they might afterwards wage this one war against the sectaries and turn the whole weight upon them. But if in some places they do not dare to go so far in their shamelessness, they at least strive to disparage the peace of religion by their slanderous and malicious interpretations and restrictions, and, having cut its sinews, to rob the subjects of its fruit. I think that not even the Furies of hell could have devised anything more effective and destructive for disturbing the state of Europe. The constant croaking of these frogs echoes and drones ceaselessly in the ears of kings and princes: that subjects cannot in good conscience be granted such freedom; that liberty of religion is nothing but a manifest diminution of majesty, joined with the greatest disgrace. "Since," they say, "you are alive and flourishing, you cannot or dare not revoke what your ancestors, parents and rights, and so on, or some ill-advised man, or one compelled by force and arms, granted. Are you not an emperor, king, or prince by the same right as they were? Is it the case that the memory of a dead man counts for more with your subjects than the person of the reigning prince? Do you not see that those who set before you the dangers that follow from the restored peace of religion are less concerned for your good than openly hostile to you? These are the devil's temptations, by which he seeks to taint your noble thoughts and efforts with a hindrance. Fear is the beginning of little women, not of great-souled men: they despise your youth, so put on a sterner countenance, so that they may feel you are a man and bear a spirit equal to such a noble birth." I might seem to some to write these things with too much confidence, as if I had been present at the Jesuits' counsels to the princes; but they themselves, in their public writings, by no means conceal these reasons of their plans, from which I have copied almost word for word.

units.la: Scire etiam debet Lector, hæc ipsa instigationis calcaria assidue illis incipibus adhiberi, quorum calor iuvenilis & incauta imperitia arietum instar ictui expositi sunt. Apud superstitiosos vero & cunctantiores etiam adiiciuntur: Eos, qui hanc religionis libertatem Subditis concesserint, in talem concessionem consenserint, in Purgatorio gravissimas peccatorum poenas luere. Item, Non Tartaros, non Turcas veros & natiivos Reipublicæ Christianæ hostes esse, sed hæreticos, quicunque nimirum contra ecclesiam Romanam insurgant: In his ergo opprimendis veram & Catholico Principe dignam laudem quaeri. Item, Cavendum esse, si Princeps bell[?] Turcico implicetur, ne rebelles haeretici cristas attollant, magistratuisque in[?] vito probrosam pacem extorqueant. Curandum vero, ut Germani cum ho[?] barbaro hoste ad animi usque deliquium colluctentur: ut praefracti illi haeret[?] tici suo tandem malo discant, quorsum deveniant, qui a Sedis Apostolicae ob[?] dientia recedunt. Si qui vero adhuc a turbarum periculo abhorrent, illis neg[?] gotij facilitas ob oculos ponitur; Severiore tantum vultu opus esse: uniu[s?] alterius clamatoris supplicio rem posse confici, quorum conspecto cruore r[?] liquae turbae animos fractum iri, &c. Interea Principem animam suam ab infe[?] rio liberaturum.
units.tr: The reader should also know that these very goads of incitement are constantly applied to those headstrong youths whose youthful heat and rash inexperience make them exposed to blows like rams. But among the superstitious and more hesitant they are also added: that those who have granted this liberty of religion to their subjects, or consented to such a concession, will pay in Purgatory the most grievous penalties for their sins. Likewise: that the Tartars and the Turks are not the true and native enemies of the Christian commonwealth, but the heretics, namely all who rise up against the Roman Church; and that in crushing these a true praise worthy of a Catholic prince is to be sought. Likewise: that care must be taken, if the prince is entangled in war with the Turk, lest the rebel heretics raise their crests and extort from the magistrates a shameful peace against their will. Rather, it must be arranged that the Germans wrestle with that barbarous enemy to the point of fainting of spirit, so that those stubborn heretics may at last learn to their cost where those end up who depart from obedience to the Apostolic See. If some still shrink from the danger of disturbance, the ease of the business is set before their eyes: there is need only of a sterner look; the matter can be finished by the punishment of one or two shouters, and at the sight of their blood the minds of the rest of the crowd will be broken, and so on. Meanwhile the prince will be saving his own soul from hell.

units.la: AVLAS REGVM AC PRINCIPVM OCCV- PANT ET INFESTANTIES SVITÆ.
units.tr: The Jesuits Occupy and Harass the Courts of Kings and Princes.

units.la: EST etiam hoc inter nefaria facinora & artes Sinonicas Iesuitarum referen[?] dum, quod in Aulas Regum ac Principum, quin etiam in ipsa Gynaec[?] sese impudenter intrudunt adeo, ut in hac sublunari regione, citius vacuum posse[?] dari, quam paulo celebriorem Aulam, quam phalanx Iesuitica non tota[?] possideat, dummodo aditus eo illis vel per angustam aliquam rimulam patea[?] & ab illis Aulis, ubi pestis haec nondum potuit habere locum, vix ullis prae[?] diis, ullaveue arte arceri possunt. Quin etiam Relationes & Epistolae Indicae[?] stantur, eos, quam primum in aridam ascenduntque, recta in Aulas & ad Reg[?] tendere, ut hos primos in potestatem suam redigant, & per eosdem deinceps[?] subiectos populos infestent. Quod si etiam vera sunt, quae isti narrant, in h[?] sui officij parte singularem quendam fortunae afflatum experti sunt, ut ad R[?] ges non solum aditus eis patuerit, sed etiam ab ipsdem multoties expetiti su[?] Narrationibus tamen istis parum tuto fidem adhibendam prudentes omn[?] existimant, ut qui norint, eas in Hispania refingi, & ita edi, ut illas ab haere[?] cis Europaeis, ex Ecclesiae Romanae commodo legi volunt. Alias constat, e[?] ad Reges illos Indicos percellendos Regis Hispaniae authoritate & terrore[?] plurimum uti.
units.tr: It must also be counted among the nefarious deeds and Sinon-like arts of the Jesuits that they shamelessly thrust themselves into the courts of kings and princes, and even into the women's quarters, so that in this sublunary region one could sooner find an empty place than a rather notable court which the Jesuit phalanx does not wholly possess, provided they have any access to it, even through some narrow crack. Courts where this plague has not yet been able to gain a foothold can scarcely be kept out by any precautions or any art. Indeed, Indian relations and letters are reported to say that the Jesuits, as soon as they set foot on dry land, hasten straight to the courts and to the kings, so as first to bring these under their power and, through them, to harass the peoples subject to them. But even if what they relate is true, they have experienced a singular gust of fortune in this part of their office, so that not only did access to kings lie open to them, but they were often sought out by those same kings. Yet prudent men think these narratives are not to be trusted safely, since they know that they are concocted in Spain and published in such a way that those in Europe want them read for the advantage of the Roman Church. Otherwise it is established that, to overthrow those Indian kings, they make very great use of the authority and terror of the King of Spain.

units.la: Vt ut autem se res habeat, illud tamen certissimum est, eos in istis etiam[?] remotissimis Orbis locis, secundum officij requisitum, recta Aulas appete[?] Vbi hoc etiam compertum est, Spiritus istos, quam primum hunc navig[?] tionis suae portum tenent, protinus omnia Regum, Principumque Solari[?] Palatia, Dicasteria, Gynaecea, penitioresque Aularum recessus perrepere, scr[?] tari & replere, ut hac vermiculatione omnia conclavia scateant.
units.tr: However that may be, it is nonetheless most certain that, even in those most remote regions of the world, they make straight for the courts, as their office requires. Here it has also been ascertained that these spirits, as soon as they reach this harbour of their voyage, at once creep through all the palaces of kings and princes, their offices, women's quarters and the innermost recesses of the courts, spying, writing and filling them, so that all the chambers swarm with this worm-like crawling.

units.la: Non autem hoc tam illis vitio vertitur, quod Regibus & Principib[?] operam suam in Aulis navant, postquam utique tam splendidis & opimis[?] lorum beneficijs fruuntur, quamvis hoc etiam citra illas larvas, quibus utu[?] tur, non minus commode facere possent: Sed quod ibidem se saepius hon[?] cati ingerunt, omnia ad se rapiunt, deque rebus ad Respublicam spectan[?] bus non est Reipublicae usu & commodo, sed ad illius arbitrium, a quo in Ap[?] calypsi Ioannis vel per Os Draconis, vel per os Bestiae emitti dicuntur,[?] quo ipso nullum se vel Regis Principisve, vel subditorum periculum impe[?] ri patiuntur.
units.tr: Yet this is not so much held against them, that they serve kings and princes in the courts, since they enjoy such splendid and rich benefits; although they could do this just as well without the masks they use. Rather, it is that they thrust themselves in there more often, uninvited, and seize everything for themselves; and in matters that concern the commonwealth they act not for the use and advantage of the state but at the will of him from whom, in the Apocalypse of John, they are said to be sent forth, either from the mouth of the Dragon or from the mouth of the Beast. By this very means they allow no peril to be incurred by the king or prince, or by the subjects.

units.la: Huic spirituali imperio illae praecipue Europae nationes obnoxiae sunt h[?] die, quae illius olim sub florente Papatu omnium impatientissimae fuerunt. I[?] Hispania omnes fatentur, istum robustissimum pollicem hoc tempore totu[?] l Iesuitarum nutum circumagi. Ferunt quidem, Iesuitas hoc tempore peius ibere, duriusq; coherceri, quam in ulla alia Europæ natione. Id si maxime verum sit, per illud tamen parum illis decedit, cum reliqui tanto liberius domi­entur. Hoc autem imperiosa ista natio ante annos ducentos, quando in multa gna adhuc divisa erat, tam patienter nunquam tulisset. Eadem dicitur esse oloniæ ratio in oppositio Europæ angulo, in qua Iesuitæ tam licenter domi­ari dicuntur, ut ipsis etiam Catholicissimis iam graves, adeoq; intolerabiles se perhibeantur. Sunt qui testantur, se legisse literas non ita dudum Legati iufdam, qui in Aula illa adhuc versetur, in quibus de Iesuitarum insolentia iratu digna scripta fuerint. Inter alia vero & hoc: Præsentium tumultuum, ibus regnum illud turbari perhibetur, causam in ipsos, & in ipsorum artes publice inferri. Hocipsum vero masculæ hæc natio olim suum pudendum dedecus in­terpretata fuisset.
units.tr: Above all, those nations of Europe are today subject to this spiritual dominion which, under the flourishing Papacy, were the most impatient of all. Everyone admits that in Spain that most robust thumb is now turned entirely at the nod of the Jesuits. They say indeed that the Jesuits there rule more harshly and are restrained more strictly than in any other nation of Europe. Even if this were most true, it does them little harm, since the rest are far freer at home. This proud nation, two hundred years ago, when it was still divided into many kingdoms, would never have endured it so patiently. The same situation is said to hold in the opposite corner of Europe, where the Jesuits are said to dominate at home so freely that they are reported to be already burdensome and even intolerable to the most Catholic. There are those who testify that they have lately read letters of a certain Legate who still remains at that court, in which the Jesuits' insolence was written about in a manner worthy of anger. Among other things, there was also this: "The present tumults by which that kingdom is said to be troubled are publicly laid to the charge of the Jesuits and their arts." That manly nation, had it once been so, would have interpreted this as its own shameful disgrace.

units.la: Rationem vero cur tam densi in Aulis volitent Iesuitæ, tantaq; impudent& shy;ase ingerant atque intrudant, Robertus Turnerus Anglus, qui Romæ ali­quandiu vixit inter Iesuitas, postea vero Ingolstadij Eloquentiæ Professor institutus fuit, in suis Epistolis indicat, quæ anno 1584. Ingolstadij editæ sint. Nam Epist. 19. quam ad Ioannem Bervitium scribit, inter alia hæc habet: QVARE cum Magistratus esse non possim, volui, quemadmodum omnibus locis, sic Augustæ in Comitijs maxime esse curiosus, Addit, VOLVI irrepere, volui rumpere in intimas Aulas Principum, volui videre omnia, ut adjustitiæ normam præ­sare exigerem. Pergit; Quâ mea vel curiositatis diligentia, vel diligentiæ curiositas conquisivi materiam Satyræ acrem voluptatis mellitam, utriusque uberem. Rursus, ix tæperam obire Principum Aulas, cum videam Hæreticorum illum Mundum admi­strari à Stultis. In Catholicis Aulis inveni Vitellios, Furios, Camillos, Senecas, qui onte, verbo, fide tuerentur locum. Item: In aliis extra paucos, viros Principes illos & eos putato, lustra, popinas, officinas malarum artium, fœdarum libidinum, fraudum, in& shy;niarum, &c. Ex his Turneri verbis liquet, cur Iesuitæ in Principum Aulas se intrudant, & quid ibidem agant.
units.tr: The reason why the Jesuits flit so thickly about the courts, and thrust and force themselves in so shamelessly, is indicated by Robert Turner, an Englishman who lived for some time in Rome among the Jesuits and was afterwards appointed Professor of Eloquence at Ingolstadt, in his Letters published at Ingolstadt in 1584. For in Letter 19, which he writes to John Bervitius, he has among other things this: "Wherefore, since I cannot be a magistrate, I wished, as in all places, so especially at Augsburg during the Diet, to be most inquisitive." He adds: "I WISHED to creep in, I wished to break into the innermost courts of princes, I wished to see everything, so that I might hold up the rule of justice and demand it." He goes on: "By the diligence of my curiosity, or the curiosity of my diligence, I have gathered material for a sharp satire, sweet with pleasure and abundant in both." Again: "I am wont to go round the courts of princes, since I see that world of heretics administered by fools. In Catholic courts I found Vitelliuses, Furiuses, Camilluses, Senecas, who by mouth, word and faith held their ground." Likewise: "In the others, apart from a few, think of those princes and them as brothels, dens, workshops of wicked arts, foul lusts, frauds, injuries, and so on." From these words of Turner it is clear why the Jesuits intrude into the courts of princes, and what they do there.

units.la: Tam quoque astuti, vigilantes, audaces, laboriosi, tantaq; denique agendi & decendi facultate prædití in Aulis ita obversantur, ut soli omnia possint, soli eos possideant & ita obsideant, ut nec veritas verbi Dei, nec vel aurula aliqua itæ ipsis inimica sit, eo penetrare possit.
units.tr: Being so cunning, vigilant, bold and industrious, and endowed with such a faculty for acting and speaking, they so dwell in the courts that they alone can do everything, alone possess them, and so beset them that neither the truth of God's Word nor any breath of air hostile to them can penetrate there.

units.la: Student etiam & adulantur eis non ij duntaxat, qui religionis & doctrinæ omine eos colunt, sed illi vel maxime, qui Aularum quadras sectantur, Romæq; præbendas & dignitates, vel pro se, vel pro liberis cognatisve venantur. Hi cum norint, unius alicuius Iesuitæ commendationem plus sibi profuturam, quam potentissimi Monarchæ intercessionem, in omnibus eis assentantur, cu­iditatibusq; illorum promptissime subserviunt.
units.tr: Those who worship them for the sake of religion and doctrine court and flatter them, but especially those who haunt the antechambers of the courts and hunt at Rome for prebends and dignities, either for themselves or for their children and relatives. Since they know that the recommendation of a single Jesuit will profit them more than the intercession of the most powerful monarch, they assent to them in everything and most readily serve their desires.

units.la: Nemo præterea Regum & Principum mentes, earumq; arcana tam exacte explorare & nosse potest, quam hipsi illorum ut plurimum Confessarij. Quæ confessio, illa præsertim, qua totius vitæ cursus explicatur, omnes regiarum entium recessus illis referat. Quæ confessionis species Pontificum Rom. con& shy;ijs plus vere confert, quam Hispaniarum Regi tot auri milliones, quos in e& shy;ssarios suos profundere dicitur. Vt mirum non sit, moderniam Ducem Venearum se intra hos quindecim annos ipsis nunquam examinandum exhibuisse. Veneti enim tam religiosi nunquam fuerunt, nec erunt, ut Reipub. suæ arcana acrificulorum fidei committant.
units.tr: Moreover, no one can explore and know the minds and secrets of kings and princes as exactly as their confessors mostly do. This confession, especially that by which the whole course of a life is laid out, opens to them all the recesses of royal minds. This kind of confession serves the plans of the Roman Pontiffs more truly than the many millions of gold which the King of Spain is said to pour out on his agents. So it is no wonder that the present Doge of Venice has not allowed himself to be examined by them these fifteen years. For the Venetians were never, and never will be, so religious as to entrust the secrets of their commonwealth to the faith of little sacrificers.

units.la: His de causis Aulæ Europeæ à Iesuitis gravius hodie infestantur & affligun­tur, quam Pharaonis olim à Ranis Ægyptiacis.
units.tr: For these reasons the courts of Europe are today harassed and afflicted more grievously by the Jesuits than Pharaoh's were of old by the frogs of Egypt.

units.la: Iesuitæ arcana Principum mentes explorant.
units.tr: The Jesuits explore the minds of princes.

units.la: Venetorum prudentia.
units.tr: The prudence of the Venetians.

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS IESVITAS PAPAE EXPLORATORES ESSE.
units.tr: ON THE WICKED DEEDS BY WHICH THE JESUITS ARE SPIES OF THE POPE.

units.la: HOc ipsorum etiam Iesuitarum legibus, constitutionibus, & scriptis probari facile potest; cum illa satis multis, ijsque ad hoc probandum indubitatis argumentis abundent. Nostrae vocationis est, inquiunt, vitam agere in quavis mundi plaga, per varia loca discurrere, & in quibusdam continentur residere, & literarum ultro citroque mittarum inter inferiores & superiores frequenti commercio, crebro alios de aliis certiores faciatis, de iis, quae variis ex locis ad aedificationem, & eorum quae geruntur, cognitionem adferatis. Haec sua esse Iesuitae non diffitebuntur.
units.tr: This can easily be proved from the laws, constitutions and writings of the Jesuits themselves, since these abound with many arguments, and certain ones, for proving it. It is our calling, they say, to live in any part of the world, to roam through various places, to remain in some places, and by frequent exchange of letters sent back and forth between inferiors and superiors, to keep one another informed, reporting from various places what serves for edification and for knowledge of what is going on. The Jesuits will not deny that these are their own rules.

units.la: His addE hanc ipsorum Regulam: Cum provinciales scribent Generali, curabunt, ut Statum Domorum & Collegiorum, ac totius Provinciae bene explicent, & supplebunt, si quid intellexerint; quod superiores minus declaraverint. Et in universum itidem scribere debent, ut GENERALIS omnium Personarum ac Provinciarum Statum quo ad ejus fieri possit, ante oculos habeat. Haec non minus quam priora Iesuitae pro sui agnoscent.
units.tr: To this add their rule: When the provincials write to the General, they shall take care to explain fully the state of the houses and colleges and of the whole province, and they shall supply whatever they have understood that the superiors have not made clear. Likewise, in general, they ought to write so that the General may have before his eyes, as far as possible, the state of all persons and provinces. The Jesuits will acknowledge this no less than the preceding rules as their own.

units.la: In hunc finem Iesuitae Cancellariam Regni Bohemiae solis suis Discipulis repleverunt, ut est videre in Gravaminibus Ordinum Evangelicorum Bohemiae Anno 1609. exhibitis.
units.tr: To this end the Jesuits filled the Chancery of the Kingdom of Bohemia with their own disciples alone, as can be seen in the grievances of the Evangelical Estates of Bohemia presented in the year 1609.

units.la: Sic etiam Iesuitae Gallici in Regni & Regiae Domus officia nullos, nisi suae disciplinae nutritos summittere nituntur.
units.tr: Likewise the French Jesuits strive to place in the offices of the kingdom and of the royal household no one except those raised in their own discipline.

units.la: Ob hanc causam etiam fraudibus suis effecerunt, ut subinde Regiorum domesticorum, vel praecipuorum ministrorum 24. liberi in novo Flesiaco Collegio Iesuiticis praeceptis imbuantur; & ex illis singulis annis sex Regijs muneribus praeficiantur, aliis sex in eorum locum ob eandem causam summittentes; & sic hisce cuniculis intra paucos annos Iesuitae totum illud regnum sub Papae & suam tyrannidem adigent, & per suos discipulos, & pro sua libidine cuncta administrabunt.
units.tr: For this reason, too, they have by their tricks arranged that, from time to time, twenty-four children of royal household officers or of the chief ministers are trained in Jesuit precepts at the new College of La Flèche; and each year six of these are placed in royal offices, while six others are sent in their place for the same purpose. And so, by these mines, within a few years the Jesuits will bring that whole kingdom under the tyranny of the Pope and of themselves, and will administer everything through their own disciples and at their own pleasure.
