units.la: Neminem igitur in dubium vocaturum existimo, hoc esse secreta Imperatorum, Regum & Principum explorare, & Curiae Romanae nuntiare ac prodere: ac nec Iesuitas quidem, nisi intellectu & iudicio privatos, & per caecam Antichristi obedientiam penitus excaecatos, et impudentes cavillatores agere velint, hoc negare posse arbitror. Nam definitoribus Iurisperitis et Pontificiis Canonistis, de poenit. Dist. 6. Can. Sacerdos de poenit. & remiss. C. Omnis Cardinalis in Clem. 1. Quia de Statu Monach. explorator is est, qui secreta alicuius Principis explorat ac alteri prodit & revelat, uti qui mittunt literas vel nuncios ad hostes. Iuxta Bartolum quoque in l. ult. D. ad legem Iuliam Maiest. Proditor etiam is est, qui scit, & non revelat, qualis Garnetus Iesuita fuit in Britannia. Vere ergo Pontifici suo, vel Regibus Christianis Proditores fiunt. L. Quisquis Cod. ad legem Iuliam Maiest. Etiam illi in Proditorum numero habentur, qui simulantes & secreto Principi damnum afferunt. Proditores & illi dicuntur. L. Omne delictum. exploratores. D. de re milit. qui cum aliquo amicitiam simulantes, hostibus consilia produnt, quod Graeci παραφρυκτωρ proverbialiter dicebant, quodque in omnes eos quadrat, qui hostis publicis rebus plus studeant quam Principis sui commodis; vel amicorum consilia corrumpunt, quo illis noceant, vel ea suadent, per quae fortunas omnes & opes amicorum fundit us everant. Hanc artem Iesuitae optime callent.
units.tr: I therefore think that no one who is in doubt will hold that it is to spy out the secrets of emperors, kings and princes, and to report and betray them to the Roman Curia; nor do I think that the Jesuits themselves, unless they wish to be men without understanding or judgment, blinded completely by the blind obedience of Antichrist and shameless jesters, can deny it. For according to the jurists who define these matters, and the Papist canonists (De poenitentia, Dist. 6, Can. Sacerdos; De poenitentia et remissione, C. Omnis Cardinalis; Clem. 1, Quia de Statu Monachorum), a spy is one who spies out the secrets of some prince and passes them on and reveals them to another, as do those who send letters or messengers to enemies. Also according to Bartolus, in l. ult. D. ad legem Iuliam Maiestatis, he is a traitor who knows and does not reveal, as the Jesuit Garnet was in Britain. Therefore they truly become traitors to their Pope or to Christian kings (L. Quisquis, Cod. ad legem Iuliam Maiestatis). Those are also counted among traitors who, pretending friendship, do harm to a prince in secret; they too are called traitors (L. Omne delictum). Spies (D. de re militari) are those who, while feigning friendship with someone, betray his plans to enemies; the Greeks proverbially called such a man a "paraphryktor" [παραφρυκτωρ]. This applies to all who care more for the public affairs of an enemy than for the advantage of their own prince, or who corrupt the counsels of friends in order to harm them, or who advise things by which they overturn utterly the fortunes and resources of their friends. The Jesuits are very skilled in this art.

units.la: Quod etiam famae & honori Regum & Principum Pontificiorum, imo & benefactorum suorum ingratissimi detrahant, Henrici 4. Galliarum Regis probat exemplum. Is enim, cum vix parricidales manus evasisset, iure & iudicio idicio legitimo Regnis suis in aeternum Iesuitas proscripserat; eos tamen, t deincepsá venefi cijs & ficis eorum tutus esset, incredibili clementiâ in primum statum restituit. In cuius beneficij compensationem, illi praecipua honos dignitate eum exspoliârunt; sicut id apud varios Scriptores, maximè verò ùud Richeomium Iesuitam evidentissimè videre licet. Hunc Augustissimum rincipem, postquam lenocinijs veneficiorum& sicarum suarum terrore ı retia venatoris Romani compulerunt, ipsecq; eos maioribus beneficijs & rærogativis cumulavit, quàm ab ullo Regum in universo terrarum orbe hacenus factum est, ad perpetua in turpissimae Iesuiticae ingratitudinis memoriâ, eum antiquissimo iure & honore denudârunt, nimirum Ecclesiae primonitura, quam ipsi raptam vel fraude subductam Hispaniarum Regi tribuerunt, eum quasi natu primum, in Expostulat. Apologet. c. 17. & 19. & Filium Ecclesiae quasi natu maximum per totum terrarum orbem proclamantes. Haec sit nere de Iesuitarum Facinoribus & studijs.
units.tr: That they also slander the reputation and honour of their own Papist kings and princes, and even of their most ungrateful benefactors, is proved by the example of Henry IV, King of France. For when he had barely escaped parricidal hands, he had by right and by lawful judgment banished the Jesuits from his kingdoms forever; yet when he was safe from their poisons and daggers, he restored them to their former state with incredible clemency. In return for this kindness, they stripped him of the highest honour and dignity, as may be seen most clearly in various writers, and especially in the Jesuit Richeome. After they had drawn this most august prince, by the enticements of their poisons and the terror of their daggers, into the nets of the Roman hunter, and after he had heaped greater benefits and prerogatives upon them than any king in the whole world has ever done, they, to mark their most shameful Jesuit ingratitude for all time, stripped him of his most ancient right and honour, namely the birthright of the Church. They had seized this by theft or taken it by fraud and given it to the King of Spain, calling him as firstborn, in the Expostulatio and Apologia, chapters 17 and 19, and proclaiming him as the eldest Son of the Church throughout the whole world. Let this suffice concerning the wicked deeds and pursuits of the Jesuits.

units.la: CAPVT II. RES GESTAE IESVITARVM IN LVSITANIA, &c.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. THE DEEDS OF THE JESUITS IN PORTUGAL, &c.

units.la: Vnc etiam in specie ex multis pauca referam: ac primo quidem, quid in Hispania ac Lusitania patrârint.
units.tr: Now I shall relate a few instances, selected from many, concerning the particular cases: and first, what they have accomplished in Spain and Portugal.

units.la: ANno 1578. Iesuitae Sebastiano Lusitaniae Regi vltimo, funestam expeditioin Africanam cum manifesta vitae iactura suscepta, suaserunt, classicum sciet canendo, ut Regnum Portugalliae, opima annui reditus recompensatioad Regem Hispaniarum devolverent. Chron. Belg. t. 1. p. 287.
units.tr: In 1578 the Jesuits persuaded Sebastian, the last King of Portugal, to undertake a disastrous expedition to Africa, at the manifest risk of his life, by sounding the trumpet call. They urged him to hand over the kingdom of Portugal to the King of Spain in return for a rich annual income. Chron. Belg. vol. 1, p. 287.

units.la: Necspes fefellit eos. Nam Sebastiano Rege cum filio, & tota fere nobilitate a Mauris in prelio occiso, statim Philippus Hispaniarum Rex Lusitaniae reum invadere & occupare duobus potentissimis exercitibus terrâ marique ad collectis, in animum induxit. Cum autem minime ignoraret, quam sinistri mores de se passim non solùm in Lusitania, sed etiam per totam Italiam spargerentur, aliquid famae dandum ratus, familiari sibi dissimulatione; quasi post eros apparatus poenitentiae locus esset, totum negotium ad conscientiae norm examinari voluit, quippe inde à Pontifice Rom. solicitabatur, ut rem conversam arbitrio suo committeret: inde opinione hominum praegravari se ætiebat, quasi vi alienum regnum invaderet, calcatâ iuris ratione, cui se infirores subiecerunt, atque adeo oppressâ regni, quod ambiebat, libertate, cuius dines in eare ius suum eripi sibi conquerebantur; & alioquin iurisiurandi igione teneri se dicebant, quo minus dictis & imperio ipsius audientes eset. Quibus difficultatibus ut citra difficultatem se expediret, rem Iesuitis & ancifcanis in Complutensi Academia, discutiendâ tradidit, & quaesivit ab iis, um sibi de iure suo in regno Portugalliae successione per mortem Henrici dea certò constaret, conscientiâ obligaretur, alicui se tribunali submittere, quod regnum adiudicaret, & in eius possessionem ipsum mitteret. Deinde si Porgallïae regno recusante eum in Regem admittere; antequam in iure cum aliis mpetitoribus re disceptata contrario iudicio obtinuerit, propriâ authoritate mi possessione sumptis contra resistentes armis apprehendere posset: hoc posito od, nullo scrupulo se teneri sentiat; & quia Gubernatores ac caeteri Lusita- : Ordines iurisiurandi religione prohiberi se dicebant, quo minus eum in egem admitteret, qui non in intre regni haeres declaratus esset, maximè reclamantibus competitoribus, qui se iuris authoritati offerebant. Quaesivit etiam, praetensum iusiurandum excusationis loco, quo Regem legitimum non reerent, accipi deberet. Adhæc Iesuitæ acerrimi Hispanicæ potentiæ propugnatores & Franciscani prorsus vero Philippi congruentia responderunt, & nullo eum conscientiæ vinculo obligari affirmarunt, ad subjiciendū se alterius iurisdictioni aut arbitrio, quippe cum propria authoritate regnū sibi adiudicare & possessione eius adipisci posset. Nullas in eo esse Pontificis partes, cum res nihil admistum habeat, cuius respectu sacri fori debeat intercedere authoritas: neque vero quicquam causæ esse, cur se Ordinum Lusitaniæ iudicio summittat: nam electis semel Regibus, iis & in eos, eorumque successores omne ius translatum intelligi, ut penes ipsos omnis sit iurisdictio, nec ab aliis iudicari possint. Quando igitur constet, Philippum verum ac legitimum regni hæredem esse, & hoc verum esse, nullius alterius tribunalis, præterquam proprii sui, iurisdictionem subire debere, delegatis autem illis vndecim viris ius nullum esse de causa tanta cognoscendi, nam a se non habere iurisdictionem, verum a Rege mandata; eamque ut ipso superstite valuerit, una cum extincto expirasse; neque enim iurisdictionem Regum post mortem prorogari posse. Denique quantum ad tertium caput, sic statuerunt, nulla iurisiurandi religione teneri Lusitanos, quo minus Philippum Regem admitterent, cum ex supra dictis constet, neminem esse velle dignitate, vel potentia in hac causa Philippo superiorem, qui de ea posset cognoscere. Atque hanc Iesuitarum sive sententiam, sive censuram approbavit Philippus, & ad arma conclamare iussit.
units.tr: Nor did their hope deceive them. When Sebastian had been killed in battle by the Moors, together with his son and almost the entire nobility, Philip, King of Spain, at once resolved to invade and seize the kingdom of Portugal, having gathered two very powerful armies by land and sea. Since he was not unaware how wicked the reports about him were, spreading everywhere not only in Portugal but throughout Italy, he thought he must give some concession to his reputation. With his usual pretence, as if there were still room for repentance after such great preparations, he wished the whole affair to be examined by the standard of conscience. For he was being pressed by the Roman Pontiff to leave the matter, now overturned, to his judgement. Otherwise he complained that he would be burdened in the opinion of men, as if he were invading another kingdom by force, trampling on the principles of right, to which they had subjected themselves, and so crushing the freedom of the kingdom he was seeking, whose inhabitants complained that their right was being snatched from them. Besides, they said they were bound by the obligation of an oath not to obey his commands and orders. To extricate himself from these difficulties without difficulty, he handed the matter over to the Jesuits and the Franciscans at the Academy of Alcalá for discussion, and asked them whether, if it was certain by right that he was the successor to the kingdom of Portugal on the death of Henry, he was bound in conscience to submit himself to some tribunal which would adjudge the kingdom to him and put him into possession of it. Then, if the kingdom of Portugal refused to admit him as King, could he, before his right had been contested with the other claimants and a contrary judgement obtained, take possession on his own authority and seize it by force of arms against those who resisted? Assuming this, he felt he was under no scruple. And since the governors and the other orders of Portugal said they were prevented by the religion of their oath from admitting as King one who had not been declared heir in a proper trial of the kingdom, especially as the rival claimants, who offered themselves to the authority of the law, were protesting, he also asked whether the alleged oath should be accepted as an excuse for not recognising the lawful King. The Jesuits, the fiercest champions of Spanish power, and the Franciscans, entirely in agreement with Philip's wishes, replied and affirmed that he was bound by no tie of conscience to submit himself to the jurisdiction or judgement of another, since he could by his own authority adjudge the kingdom to himself and obtain its possession. In this matter, they said, the Pontiff had no part, since the affair contained nothing over which the authority of the sacred court ought to intervene. Nor was there any reason why he should submit himself to the judgement of the Portuguese Orders, for once Kings have been chosen, all right is understood to have been transferred to them and to their successors, so that all jurisdiction rests with them and they cannot be judged by others. Therefore, since it is established that Philip is the true and lawful heir of the kingdom, and since this is true, he ought to submit himself to the jurisdiction of no tribunal other than his own. As for those eleven men delegated to the task, they had no right to examine so great a cause, for they did not hold their jurisdiction from themselves but from the King's commission; and that jurisdiction, while the King was alive, had been valid, but with his death it had expired together with him, for the jurisdiction of Kings cannot be extended beyond their death. Finally, as to the third point, they ruled that the Portuguese were bound by no religion of oath not to admit Philip as King, since it is clear from what has been said above that in this cause there is no one of greater dignity or power than Philip who could pass judgement on it. Philip approved this opinion, or rather censure, of the Jesuits, and ordered them to shout to arms.

units.la: Bello hoc inter Hispanos & Lusitanos fervente, Azorae insulae ad Lusitaniam pertinentes in fide Ordinum Regni permanserunt; Iesuitæ autem in urbe illarum, quæ Tertia nuncupatur, & situ ac fertilitate cæteris longe superiore habitantes, eam Hispanis prodere tentarunt: excitato igitur magno tumultu plebs ultra modum contra eos commota est, cum alii in iure sistendos tanquam patriæ proditores, alii sine mora, tanquam perduelles & Hispanis addictos, una cum Collegio incendendos dicerent.
units.tr: While this war between the Spanish and the Portuguese was raging, the Azores, islands belonging to Portugal, remained loyal to the Orders of the kingdom. The Jesuits, however, who lived in the city of those islands called Terceira, which far surpasses the others in position and fertility, attempted to betray it to the Spanish. A great tumult therefore arose, and the common people were stirred up beyond measure against them: some said they should be brought before the law as traitors to their country, others that they should be burned at once, together with their college, as enemies of the state and partisans of the Spanish.

units.la: CAPVT III. RES GESTAE IESVITA- RVM IN GALLIA.
units.tr: CAPVT III. RES GESTAE IESVITARVM IN GALLIA.

units.la: Ioannam Albretanam Navarræ Reginam viduam Evangelicorum reformatorum in Gallia patronam, venenatis chirotecis, quas unguentarius Regis Italus Lutetiæ, Iesuitarum instinctu ei dederat infectam, & repentino morbo correptam, necarunt anno 1572. vide historiam Gallic. tom. 4. pag. 19. & Belgic. tom. 1. p. 126.
units.tr: In 1572 they killed Joan of Albret, queen of Navarre and widow, the patron of the reformed Evangelicals in France. She had been given poisoned gloves by a perfumer of the King, an Italian, at Paris, at the instigation of the Jesuits, and was seized by a sudden illness. See the history of France, vol. 4, p. 19, and the Belgic history, vol. 1, p. 126.

units.la: DE LIGA SEV CONSPIRATIONE IN GALLIA A GVISIIS EXCITATA, ET A IESVITIS A- DVERSVS HENRICVM III. REGEM, REGIAMQUE FAMILIAM PROMOTA.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE LEAGUE OR CONSPIRACY IN FRANCE STIRRED UP BY THE GUISES AND PROMOTED BY THE JESUITS AGAINST KING HENRY III AND THE ROYAL FAMILY.

units.la: Postquam Lotharingica Guisiorum familia in Gallia sub Francisco I. Henrico II. & huiusce liberis Galliarum Regibus alacriter & admodum strenue se gessisset, & egregiis aliquot facinoribus exhibitis (in quibus unique Metensis urbis adversus Imperatorem Carolum V. propugnatio ac conservatio, tum expugnatum & Anglis ereptum Caletum inprimis eminent) Francisci fortitudinem ac fidelitatem probasset, eoque magnam apud omneis authoritatem & existimationem adsequuta fuisset; non exiguam inde spem adipiscendi tandem ipsius Regni, & regno tum potientem Vualesiorum familiam extinguendi.
units.tr: After the Lorraine family of Guise had conducted itself eagerly and very vigorously in France under Francis I, Henry II and Henry's children, the kings of France, and had displayed several outstanding exploits (among which the defence and preservation of the city of Metz against the Emperor Charles V, and the capture of Calais and its recovery from the English, stand out especially), it had proved the courage and loyalty of Francis and had thereby won great authority and esteem with everyone. From this it conceived no small hope of one day overthrowing the Valois family, which then held the kingdom, and of seizing the kingdom itself.

units.la: {y} marginal reference notes as above. inde deturbandi concepit. Quae spes haud parum aucta tum fuit, quum Franciscus II. Mariam Stuardam Scotiae Reginam matrimonio sibi iungeret, cuius equidem cognati proximiores & avunculi, Claudius ille Dux Guisi-us & Carolus Lotharingiae Cardinalis, omnibus etiam Regij sanguinis Principibus antepositi, suprema-que regni munera adepti, summum omnino ac eminentissimum apud Regem illum iuniorem, adfinitatis ist usce gratia, locum tinuerunt; & universum ita regnum, sub praetextu nominis regij, pro lubitu, sine cuius quam etiam renisu, absolute tantum non administrarunt. Inprimis item ipsis admodum profuit, quod praecipua tum Regiae domus capita, videlicet Rex Navarraeus & Condaeus Princeps, quorum alioquin ex recepta aliorum consuetudine munus hoc fuisset, ut proximum apud Regem obtinerent locum, reformatam Religionem amplexi fuissent, eamque publice prositeri coepissent. Unde Guisiani quidem istos usque quaque premendi & tanquam non opprimendi, tum non Catholicae solum Romanae Ecclesiae adsectas Galliam, sed & Regem ipsum adeoque Pontificem una cum Hispaniarum Regibus sibi devinciendi; Eoque futurae potestatis suae structuram cum extremo perniciei suorum Adversariorum interitu magis magisque tum fundandi solide, tum admodum quoque dilatandi splendidam arripuerunt occasionem. Quem iam in finem suam iam antea Genealogiam per Archiadiaconum quendam Lubensem (Toub) confici typisque publice divulgari curarunt: auctoritate cuius hominum animis paulatim occupatis persuadere conari sunt, a familia & stirpe Caroli Magni se oriundos esse, nec iniquum eo fore, si Franciae regnum, ab Hugone Capeto Maioribus olim suis iniusta vi ademptum eiusque heredis ita retentum, postliminio quasi iam denuo reciperent. Vt paulo quidem post apud advocatum quendam Parlamenti Parisiensis, David adpellatum, post quam is una cum eiusdem Civitatis Episcopo Romanum confecisset, eiusmodi sunt repertae literae, ex quibus abunde patuit, eiusce gratia haec iam tum Romae in Consistorio agitatum & tractatum, adeoque conclusum fuisset: nimirum ad exstirpationem Haereticorum in Gallia necessarium omnino esse, ut Capeti successores tanquam minus idonei removeantur; Posteaque autem Caroli illius Magni Regiae dignitati restituantur: quibus adiuncta est etiam delineatio seu designatio mediorum eatenus accommodate adhibendorum; prout ea postmodum usurpata & a Ligistis coniuratis in praxin etiam publicam deducta fuisse constat. Etsi vero consultationes & instructiones istae Regi non solum innotuerint, sed & Anno 1576. publice typis editae fuerint; pro figmentis tamen Hugonorum potius, quam pro narratis veris tum fuerunt habitae: Navarraeus autem & Condaeus necnon alij Religionis eiusdem socij pro seditiosis & adversariis tam Regis quam ipsius quoque Regni, quod adfectent utique, & turbarum calamitatum in Gallia sic omnium auctores exististant, iudicati sunt; ut econtra Guisiani fidelissimi Regis ministri ac servitores, adeoque fulcra quasi ac propugnacula Religionis simul ac Reipublicae constanter habiti fuere: donec tandem ipse Rex Henricus III. maximo cum damno, sed & interitu suo toti Mundo patefecit, quodnam utriusque partis institutum fuerit ac consilium; & uterque illis amicus fuerit aut hostis, defensor aut oppressor Regis & sui Regni universi. Liga vero seu Ligistarum illa coniuratio tum adversus Regem praemeditatum coepit, quum Anno 1577. postremā cum Hugonotis seu Reformatis gravissimae ac inissent; exinde res quae belli magis quam politicas & ad regimen adprobus spectantes alias fere nihil curaret: sed quieti se dederet, helluationi saltationib. que indulgeret, ac subditos interim crebris, adeoque continuis exactionibus emungeret. Ist haec enim eius socordia non alienam praebuit occasionem apud univer-
units.tr: {y} marginal reference notes as above. This hope was greatly increased when Francis II married Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots. Her nearest kinsmen and uncles, Duke Claude of Guise and Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, were placed above all the princes of royal blood, were given the highest offices of the realm, and held the highest and most eminent place with that young king because of this kinship. They administered the whole kingdom in the name of the king as they pleased, and almost without any consultation or opposition from him. It also greatly benefited them that the leading heads of the royal house, namely the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, who by the custom of others would have held the next place to the king, had embraced the reformed religion and had begun to profess it openly. Hence the Guises seized the splendid opportunity to press these men constantly and to crush them, as if they were not to be crushed; and to bind to themselves not only France, which adhered to the Catholic Roman Church, but also the king himself, and through him the Pontiff, together with the Kings of Spain. With the utter ruin of their adversaries, they seized the opportunity to build more and more solidly, and to widen greatly, the structure of their future power. To this end they had earlier arranged for a genealogy of their family to be compiled by a certain archdeacon of Lube (Toub) and published in print. On the authority of this, they tried gradually to persuade men's minds that they were descended from the family and line of Charles the Great, and that it would not be unjust, if the kingdom of France, which had once been unjustly taken from their ancestors by Hugh Capet and kept by his heirs, were now recovered as if by right of return. Soon afterwards, letters were found with an advocate of the Parisian Parlement named David, after he had drawn up a Roman document together with the bishop of the same city. These letters made it abundantly clear that this matter had already been discussed and debated in consistory at Rome, and finally decided: namely, that for the extirpation of heretics in France it was absolutely necessary that the successors of Capet be removed as unfit, and that afterwards the dignity of the royal crown be restored to that Charles the Great. To this was added an outline or designation of the means to be applied appropriately to this end, as it is known that these means were afterwards used and carried into public practice by the conspiring Leaguers. Although these consultations and instructions were not only made known to the king but were also published in print in 1576, they were then regarded as the fictions of the Huguenots rather than as true accounts. Navarre and Condé, and the other associates of the same religion, were judged to be seditious and enemies both of the king and of the kingdom itself, which they were said to aim at, and to be the originators of the disturbances and calamities in France. On the other hand, the Guises were constantly regarded as the most faithful ministers and servants of the king, and as the supports and bulwarks, as it were, both of religion and of the commonwealth. Until at last King Henry III himself, to his great loss and indeed to his own destruction, revealed to the whole world what the aim and purpose of each party had been, and who had been friend or enemy to each, defender or oppressor of the king and of his whole kingdom. The League, or that conspiracy of the Leaguers, began to be planned against the king in earnest when, in 1577, the most grievous peace was concluded with the Huguenots or Reformed; from then on the king, caring for almost nothing beyond war and political and administrative matters, gave himself over to quiet, to revelry and dancing, and meanwhile squeezed his subjects with frequent and continual exactions. For this sloth of his offered no small occasion for bringing the whole people into contempt and hatred of him, and especially for stirring up those who, out of a perverse zeal for the Catholic religion, feared that perhaps, if King Henry III died without children, Navarre, who had turned from the religion and was excommunicated by the Pope, would succeed in this very peaceful state of affairs.

units.la: Liga ex Guisiana occasione usque progressus. sum populum in contemtum & odium eum adducendi, maximeq; concitandos eos, qui ex præpositero quodam Catholicæ Religionis zelo metuebant, ne, quando forsan absq; prole Rex ille Henricus III. decederet, ipsi Navarræus de versæ Religionis & à Pontifice excommunicatus Rex in isto cum primis tran quilio rerum statu succeederet. Quapropter ut istí malo præveniretur, de Lig seu conspiratione quadam tractari clandestinè cœptum fuit; cuius benesici Romana quidem conservari, diversa autem ab ea Religio fundítus exstirpar tum exactiones etiam ac tributa nimia cum gravaminibus aliis ufquequaqu tolli vel mitigari saltem, & in contemtus divini numinis atque tyrannidis locur pietas ac iustitia denuò subrogari possit. Primus qui negocio huic se facilei præbuit, civis quida Parisien s fuit, nomine Rochus Blondus, insignis æmulatc aut æstimator tum Misse tum Guisiæ quoq; familiæ. Is ergo cum choragis, pra terca tribus alijs; Ioanne videlicet Prævosto Pastore ad S. Severinum, Iohann Baschero Pastore ad S. Benedict. & Matthæo Lanoyo Canonico Sossontin (Soissons) quibus initio statim adeoq; ante alios omneis suum proposuer consilium, & de eo quotidie cum ipsis contulerat ac multa præterea consultara ita prudenter, ita consideratè ac caute rem adgressi sunt, atque suffragio concr ditorum quorundam et adprime correspondentium amicorum, tam intra qua extra Parisiorū Lutetiam, in universo Galliæ regno ac præcipuis eius civitat bus sub iuraro capite seu Duce Guisio aliisq; Lotharingicæ familiæ Princip bus, tantam ad se clarum & adhærentium turbam nacti fuerunt, ut sceptra tu tenens Rex Henricus III. manifesta vi priùs adobrutus, & ex arce Regi Louure ipsaque Metropoli Lutetia exturbatus fuerit; quam callidorum istarum consiliorum ac conspirationis certam aliquam cognitionem habuerit; u ut Parisijs semper præsto fuerit; & de Liga seu confœderatione ista tali mus tationes nonnullas perceperit. At enim eius socordia, tum vero consœderat rum industria, iuxta contemtum ac odium illud populare; quod in Concion bus suis Sacrificuli, cumprimis autem Iesuitæ adversus ipsum mirè excitaban ut paulò post indicabitur, ita invalescebant, ut supradicti Ligæ 4. auctores ut cum aliis paulatim iis accedentibus in proposito suo per quam exigua obstacula, vicissim autem undiquaque promotiones & adminicula sane quàm efficac senserint. Ad promotionem autem istius validiorem ex sedecim Tribubus u bis, Parisiorum certus civium numerus eo deputabatur, quo in unaquaq; Tr buum istarum quæcunque tandem fierent, exactè tum observarent, tum con derarent ulterius; & probe demum ordinarent ac disponerent. Istos ergo tale Sedecimviros appellarunt, aut respectu iam memoratarum sedecim Tribuur in quas omnis Parisiorum civitas est distributa; aut quod ex iis omnibus Sed cim forte fuerint omnium importunissimi, adeo ut præcipua negocia iuxta p testatem ac directorium sibimet accersiverint. Vt ut autem fit, universus equ dem populus Parisiensis in sua coram Legato Pontificio Caietano propositi ne Sedecim istos, ut præsides ac tribunos plebis, nominatim allegavit; utpot La Bruiere, Cruce, Bufsi le Clere, Commissarium Loufchard, La Monier Senault, Commissarū Barot; Advocatum Drouard, Aluequin, Emonnot, Ia lier, Messier, Capitaneum Passart, Oudineau; Anroux & Morin: Loco tam istius Anroux aliquì Tellierum & pro Senaultio Amelinium ponunt; quan vis discrimen inter eos nec adeo magnum appareat. Quanta vero fuerit Arch ligistarum istorum auctoritas simulatq; potestas exinde liquet inter alia; quo statim post Regis è Lutetia fugam, quæ facta est 12. Maij die Anni 1588. unà cu capite suo Duce Guisio rem eò deduxerunt; ut Parisiensi civitati, per vota beramq; plebis electionem, novi darentur Officiarij; & omnes à Regis sta partibus habiti dimitterentur. Isti cum Guisio sæpe iam memorato, necnon o ficiari
units.tr: Liga ex Guisiana occasione usque progressus. Therefore, to forestall this evil, a certain League or conspiracy began to be discussed secretly. Its purpose was that the Roman religion should be preserved, a different religion utterly rooted out, the excessive exactions and taxes, with other burdens, be removed or at least softened in every way, and piety and justice be restored in place of contempt of the divine majesty and tyranny. The first who lent himself readily to this business was a certain citizen of Paris named Roch Blondel, a notable admirer, or rather esteemer, both of the Mass and of the Guise family. He, with the chief leaders, and three others besides, namely John Prévost, minister at St Severin, John Bachier, minister at St Benedict, and Matthew Lanoy, canon of Soissons, to whom at the very start, and before all others, he laid out his plan and conferred with them about it daily, and much more besides, undertook the matter so prudently, so considerately and cautiously, that by the support of certain trusted and closely connected friends, both within and outside Paris, in the whole kingdom of France and its principal cities, under oath to the head, Duke de Guise, and to the other princes of the Lorraine family, they gained such a great crowd of people attached to them that King Henry III, who held the sceptre, was first openly overpowered by force and driven out of the Louvre citadel and out of the capital city of Paris. Although he had some certain knowledge of these cunning counsels and of the conspiracy, and had heard some rumours about this League or confederacy, he did not remain in Paris. But his sloth, and the diligence of the confederates, together with the popular contempt and hatred which the priests in their sermons, and especially the Jesuits, stirred up against him wonderfully (as will be shown shortly), grew so strong that the four authors of the League mentioned above, with others gradually joining them, found very little obstacle to their purpose, but on the other hand found very effective help and advancement on every side. To promote this more strongly, a definite number of Parisian citizens was assigned from each of the sixteen wards of the city, whose task was to observe carefully and consider further whatever happened in each ward, and finally to arrange and dispose matters properly. These men they called the Sixteen, either with reference to the sixteen wards into which the whole city of Paris was divided, or because among them all there were perhaps sixteen most troublesome men, so that they took the chief business into their own hands by their own power and direction. However that may be, the whole Parisian populace, in its complaint before the papal legate Cajetan, named these Sixteen by name as its presidents and tribunes of the people: namely La Bruyère, Cruce, Bussi le Clerc, the commissary Louchard, La Morlière, Senault, the commissary Barot, the advocate Drouard, Aluequin, Emonnot, Jalier, Messier, the captain Passart, Oudineau, Anroux and Morin. Instead of this Anroux, some put Tellier, and for Senault, Amelin; though the difference between them does not appear to be very great. But how great the authority and power of these Leaguers was, appears among other things from this: immediately after the king's flight from Paris, which took place on 12 May 1588, they, together with their leader the Duke de Guise, brought matters to such a point that new officials were given to the city of Paris by votes and the free choice of the people, and all who were regarded as on the king's side were dismissed. These men, with the Guise already often mentioned, and with those new officials, daily consulted about the common state and about all the members of the Holy League; and these alone, after that famous murder of Guise, committed at Blois on 23 December of the same year, opposed the king and maintained the city of Paris in its rebellion...

units.la: Ligæ Sedecimviri arijs illis novis, quotidie consultabant de communi statu, & omnibus S. Ligæ essarijs: isti soli Parisiensem civitatem post Guisiocidium illud famosum, dei iusdem anni die 23. Decemb. Blæsis perpetratum est, adversus Regem obarunt, & in rebellione sua conservarunt, tum Aumalium quoq; Ducem, inentia Maynij, Gubernatorem constituerunt: isti consilium illud magnum seu lamentum etiam integrum anno 1589. Ianuarij die 16. e consessu pleno fuslunt, & per plateas publicas in arcis propugnaculum captivum abduxerunt: leniq; non adquieverunt prius, quam ad instantem improbamq; sollicitationem suam generalis omnium Ligistarum Conventus, sub nomine Comitiorum, itueretur, haberetur, & de novo Regis electione in eo tractaretur. Interea vele pace aut inducijs cum Rege ullis ne audire quidem sustinuerunt, quin egren potius de futuro felicissimo statu, & de auxilio inprimis Hispanico, spe poo fecerunt: ut & inter alia literas Regi Hispaniarum per Iesuitam quendam Matthæum curandas destinarunt; quæ tamen prope Lugdunum interceptæ, gnatæ, atq; Regi quam primum in originali, ut loquuntur, transmissæ fuet. In istis die 2. Novemb. anno 1591. datis hæc inprimis habentur talia: Catholi- V. Majest. hoc sanctè possumus affirmare, omnium Catholicorum vota eò directa esse, ath. V. Majestas sceptrum huius Regni tenere nobis q; dominari possit; quemadmodum uidem, ut Patri nostro, nos ex animo subij cimus: aut ex natis ut ea suis salte aliquem destinet. Sin autem alium forte quempiam nobis præstituere cogitet, de Genero sibi proat aliquo; quem nos utiq; reverentia & obedientia debita adeoq; extrema subjectione, egem nostrum lubentes volentes excipiemus, &c.
units.tr: The Sixteen of the League, those new officials, met every day about the common state of affairs and about all the agents of the Holy League. After the famous murder of Guise, committed at Blois on 23 December of that same year, they alone opposed the king on behalf of the city of Paris and kept it in their rebellion. They also appointed the Duke of Aumale, and Mayenne, as governor. On 16 January 1589 they dragged that great council, or lamentation, out of the full assembly, and led it away as a captive through the public squares to the bastion of the citadel. They did not rest until their restless and wicked urging brought about a general assembly of all the Leaguers, under the name of an Estates-General, to be held there and to debate a new election of king. Meanwhile they would not even listen to peace or truces with the king, but rather placed their hopes in a most happy future state and, above all, in Spanish aid. Among other things they sent a letter to the King of Spain, to be delivered through a certain Jesuit named Matthew. It was intercepted near Lyons, copied, and sent to the king as soon as possible in the original, as they say. In it, dated 2 November 1591, the following points stand out: "We can solemnly affirm that the wishes of all Catholics are directed to this end, that Your Majesty may hold and rule the sceptre of this kingdom; just as we submit ourselves to you from the heart, as to our father, so we would do to one of your sons, or to whomever you might appoint from your own. But if you should think of setting over us some other man, a son-in-law of your choosing, we will receive him gladly and willingly as our king, with due reverence and obedience and utmost submission, etc."

units.la: Coniurationis autem Ligistarum scopus & propositum erat, Regem Henm de solio regni deturbare, in claustrum vel coenobium aliquod detrudere, Henricum Guisium illi in regno surrogare. Hinc cum Henrici III. Regis sym- um Parisiis valuis Regis inscriptum esset;
units.tr: The aim and purpose of the League's conspiracy was to cast King Henry III from the throne of the kingdom, to thrust him into some cloister or monastery, and to set Henry Guise in his place. Hence, when a motto of King Henry III had been inscribed on the doors of the Louvre at Paris,

units.la: Qui dedit ante duas, trinam dabit ille coronam:
units.tr: He who gave two crowns before will give a third;

units.la: ita Cottonus ijsdem valuis huic symbolo subscribi curavit.
units.tr: Cotton had the same doors inscribed with the following verse beneath that motto:

units.la: Qui dedit ante duas, unam abstulit, altera natat, Tertia tonsoris mox facienda manu.
units.tr: He who gave two before took one away, the other floats; a third is soon to be made by the barber's hand.

units.la: Promoverunt & confirmarunt hanc Ligam, seu potius seditionem & rebellionem adversus Henricum 3. Vehementer admodum Iesuitæ Parisiis, aliisq; in urbibus. Quum Liga anno 1585. magnas vires acquireret & magis magisq; emergeret, Ieæ potestate sua audiendi confessiones & absolvendi quoscunq;, ad concitann cuiuscunq; status homines adversus legitimum suum magistratum, ita sunt ut nullum absolvere dignarentur, qui ad proposita eatenus Interrogatoria, delem Regis subditum ac ministrum obsequentem esse, profiteri aulus suisInterea vero numerus eorum, qui confitebantur ipsis, adeo crescebat & adebatur, ut anno 1587. in annuis illis Romæ impressis Epistolis ad Generalem m Claudium Aquavivam de Collegio suo Parisiensi Claromontano sic scriint: Confessiones audita, & quidem universæ vitæ quam plurimæ. Hæc est enim communis omnium opinio, tum deniq; factis fieri eorum conscientiæ, quum apud nos conitur: ideoq; nonnulli triginta milliarium confecerunt viam, ut à nobis audirentur. Etus anno 1589. Totius vitæ confessiones audita sunt trecentæ.
units.tr: The Jesuits at Paris, and in other cities as well, greatly promoted and strengthened this League, or rather this sedition and rebellion against Henry III. When the League gained great strength in 1585 and rose more and more, the Jesuits, using their power to hear confessions and to absolve whomever they pleased, stirred men of every rank to take up arms against their lawful magistrate. They refused to absolve anyone who did not, in answer to their set questions, profess that he would no longer be a loyal subject and obedient servant of the king. Meanwhile the number of those who confessed to them grew and increased so much that in the annual letters printed at Rome in 1587, sent to the General Claudius Aquaviva from their College of Clermont at Paris, they wrote as follows: "Confessions are heard, and indeed of the whole of life, very many. For this is the common opinion of all, that their consciences are then made clean when they confess to us; and therefore some have travelled a journey of thirty miles to be heard by us." And in 1589 three hundred confessions of the whole of life were heard.

units.la: Quicunq; igitur iuramenta Regi præstita & debita exinde obsequia sepo-suet, eoq; perfidiosi facti fuerant, & quos à peccatulis, ut loquebatur, isti Pastoac Sacerdotes alij non ita leviter aut temere volebant absolvere; si ad Iesuitas nt, quibus erant usquequaq; acceptissimi, et indulgentissima non tantum abitionem, sed & amplissimam promissionem æternæ retributionis inde conuebantur; modo in rebellione ista sua & perfidia fortiter perstiterent, gnavique pergerent. Unde passim in absolutionibus suis hunc modum observa-
units.tr: Whoever, therefore, had broken the oaths given to the king and the obedience owed on that account, and had thereby become faithless, and whom those Jesuits and other priests and ministers, as they put it, did not wish to absolve from their little sins lightly or rashly, if they came to the Jesuits, to whom they were most welcome and most indulgent, they were not only absolved but also promised the greatest reward of eternal recompense, provided they held firm in their rebellion and faithlessness and persisted in vigour. Hence in their absolutions they commonly observed this procedure: that all were required to swear upon the Gospels inserted in their breviaries.

units.la: C ¢ runt, ut nimirum ad inserta Breviarijs suis Evangelia iurare tenerentur omnes. Quod nec cum tempóris regnantem adhuc Regem Henricum 3. nec si forte sic deceret, successorem eius Navarraeum pro legitimo vellent agnoscere Domino, quod a multis, appendicem eam haud admittentibus, eoque sine absolutione c[?] missis, constanter confirmatum postea & contestatum fuisse author Notarum a[?] veram Orationem ad Regem Christianissimum, ne Iesuitae restituantur in regnum Galliae pag. 112. & 113. refert. Vix certe quidquam magis admiratione dignius accidit, quam quod Liga seu conspiratio illa ab exiguis sane primordijs ta exigui temporis spacio ad tantum fastigium evecta, tantusque, non personarum solum sed urbium quoque, & provinciarum integrarum adversus regnantem tum, [?] & residentem ibidem Regem, numerus concitatus ac conspiratione facta exa[?] matus fuit: & quidem in Gallia, cuius Regni incolas naturae quidam instinctus [?] Regum suorum venerationem, prae aliis nationibus Europaeis impellere cre[?] tur. Sed effecerunt hoc Iesuitae, ut dictum est, disponendo, sic enim ipsimet l[?] quuntur, illorum animos, quos non tam suis illis militaribus concionibus, qua[?] audiendarum confessionum artificio sic corruperant.
units.tr: They did this so that they would not acknowledge as their lawful lord King Henry III, who was still reigning at that time, nor, if it should happen to be fitting, his successor, the Navarrese. Many refused to accept this appendix, and so were sent away without absolution. That this was afterwards constantly affirmed and attested, the author of the Notes on the True Speech to the Most Christian King, that the Jesuits should not be restored to the kingdom of France, reports at pages 112 and 113. Certainly nothing more worthy of wonder could have happened than that this League, or conspiracy, raised from such small beginnings to such a height in so short a time, and that so great a number, not only of persons but of cities and whole provinces, was stirred up against the king who then reigned and resided there, and was brought to a conspiracy. This happened in France, whose inhabitants a certain natural instinct is thought to drive, more than other European nations, to venerate their kings. But the Jesuits brought this about, as has been said, by their manoeuvring; for so they themselves put it, they corrupted the minds of those whom they had so corrupted, not so much by their militant sermons as by the artifice of hearing confessions.

units.la: Non tamen sanguinolenta Iesuitarum consilia & manus illorum Rex effugere potuit. Na anno Domini 1589. Iacob. Clementem Senefem, Dominicanum Monachum, homine vili & servili ingenio, criminum ignobilium reum, ob furta & pessimos m[?] res iam ante Coenobiarcharum iudicio damnatum, Iesuitae claustro avellit, & var[?] daemonum praestigijs illudentes ei, tandem corruperunt, eiq; Regis caede mandat[?] Cum autem ab illis contenderetur ut securitate praestarent, & nisi ea data se non exit[?] ... respondentur illi, turpe esse monacho reditur vitae parcere; pergeret igit[?] audacter, politicorum omnium, praesertim nobiliorum in carcerem coniectoru[?] condemnatione obsidem illi dantes, si patrato facinore atrocius in eum anim[?] verteretur. His promissis persuadetur & vincitur monachus. Circumveniatur e[?] alio commento hominis egregii fallendi artificis & capitis pollutissimi, qui lite[?] mentitas & falsas ad Regem a viro gratissimo perferendas Dominicano trad[?] cui ut facilior aditus ad Regem essent, haec insusurrant Guisii & Iesuitae. Rex, [?] quiunt, & Regis familiares signa & manum eius requirent: est enim Regi charissimus, [?] metuendae custodiae: has tuferens literas late excipieris ab omnibus: pergas ita[?], & cre[?] tibi & omnibus qui tyrannos occiderunt, & patriam fervarunt, certum esse in coelo ac d[?] situm locum, ubi beati aevo sempiterno fruantur. Iisdem verbis impulsus ad Regis ca[?] proficiscitur. Eo cum venisset, ductus est ad Procuratorem generalem, qui dix[?] Se habere varias literas, inter alias etiam Harlaei Parlamenti praesidis, ad Re[?] deferedas; aliaque arcana quaedam, quae literis credi non potuerint, & tamen scire R[?] gem vel maxime necessaria esse. Erat autem Harlaeus hic Regi & fidelis & amic[?] ideoque Lutetiae captivus. Procurator haec ad Regem defert. Rex Procuratori m[?] dat, ut ea nocte monachum in suo hospitio excipiat, & humaniter habeat usq[?] posterum diem. Postridie Rex Iacobum ad se vocat, & in coclave, remotis ali[?] ducit. Tum praefert monachus varias literas, quas Rex cum avide legisset, int[?] rogat, habeat ne plures: habere se plures ait, & fingens se eas quaerere, cultr[?] promit, & capulo tenus in vetrem Regis adegit, adactumque in vulnere reliqu[?] Rex vulnus sentiens, cultrum confestim dilatando vulnus eduxit, & monach[?] circa guttur gravissime vulneravit, vimque sibi inferri clamavit. Accurrunt c[?] mestici, atque inter alios Nobilis quidam Bastidaeus, qui & ante 7. menses cum[?] Iijs 44. Guilium interfecisse dicitur. Hic educto gladio monachum adortus e[?] eique lethale vulnus inflixit; accurrit alius, & bipenne aliud superaddidit. M[?] riens tandem parricida Deo gratias egit, quod tam mite & facile genus mor[?] sibi defiinaffet: se multo atrocius & gravius expectasse. Mortuum fenestra e[?] ciunt, & haud multo post carnifici quatuor equis dilacerandum, ac igni comb[?] rendum tradunt.
units.tr: Yet the king could not escape the bloody counsels and hands of the Jesuits. For in the year of the Lord 1589 the Jesuits drew Jacques Clément, a Dominican monk, a base and servile man of ignoble crimes, who had earlier been condemned by the judgement of his prior for thefts and wicked deeds, away from his cloister. Deceiving him with the tricks of demons, they at last corrupted him and ordered him to murder the king. When he demanded from them that they guarantee his safety, and said he would not go unless it was given, they answered him that it was shameful for a monk to spare his life; he should go on boldly, and they offered as hostages for him the condemnation of all the political men, especially the nobles, cast into prison, should the matter turn more savagely against him after the deed was done. Persuaded and won over by these promises, the monk was taken in. He was then surrounded by another contrivance of a skilled and outstanding deceiver and most polluted head, who handed the Dominican false and lying letters to be carried to the king by a most agreeable man. So that he might have easier access to the king, Guise and the Jesuits whispered these instructions: "The king and his household will demand the signs and the hand of the king; for he is most dear to the king, and fears no guard. Bear these letters and you will be welcomed by all. Go on thus, and believe that a certain place in heaven is prepared for you and for all who have slain tyrants and saved the fatherland, where they enjoy blessedness in eternal time." Impelled by these words, he set out for the king's camp. When he had arrived there he was led to the attorney-general, and said that he had various letters to be delivered to the king, among them one from Harlay, president of the Parlement, and certain other secrets which could not be entrusted to letters, yet which the king would most need to know. Harlay was, however, both faithful and friendly to the king, and was therefore a captive at Paris. The attorney-general reported this to the king. The king ordered the attorney to receive the monk in his lodging that night and treat him kindly until the next day. On the following day the king summoned Jacques to him and led him into a private chamber, the others being removed. Then the monk produced various letters, which the king eagerly read, and asked whether he had more. He said he had more, and, pretending to search for them, drew a knife and drove it up to the hilt into the king's belly, and left it stuck in the wound. The king, feeling the wound, at once pulled out the knife, widening the wound as he did so, and gravely wounded the monk about the throat, crying out that violence was being done to him. Attendants ran up, and among the others a certain nobleman, Bastide, who is said to have killed Guise with his men seven months earlier. He drew his sword, attacked the monk, and dealt him a mortal blow; another ran up and added a further blow with an axe. Dying at last, the parricide gave thanks to God that he had been given so mild and easy a kind of death; he had expected something much more savage and severe. They threw the dead man out of the window, and not long afterwards handed him over to the executioner to be torn apart by four horses and burned in the fire.

units.la: Henricus III. Galliae R. anno hoc 1589 occiditur. Hoc parricidium & nefandum facinus Sixtus V. Papa unicè approbavit, & olixa Oratione in Consistorio Cardinalium laudavit. Quòd Monachus, inquit alter, religioni devotus infelicem Galliarum Regem in medio exercitus interfecit, rarum, insigne & memorabile est facinus. Et subiunxit: facinus hoc non sine Dei Opt. Max. particulari providentia & dispositione, Spiritus sancti suggestione designatum, facinusque maius quàm illud S. Iudith, quae Holofernum è medio iustulit. Neque hoc dissicetur Harminus: Quid, inquit, in ea (oratione Sixti) reperies, nisi laudes & admirationem Sapientiae & Providentiae Dei?
units.tr: Henry III, King of France, was murdered in the year 1589. Pope Sixtus V alone approved this parricide and vile crime, and praised it in a long oration in the consistory of Cardinals. "That a monk devoted to religion," he said, "has killed the unhappy King of the French in the midst of his army, is a rare, notable and memorable deed." He added: "This deed was marked out not without the particular providence and disposition of God Almighty, and the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and it is a greater deed than that of St Judith, who removed Holofernes from the midst." Harminus does not dispute this either: "What," he says, "will you find in that oration of Sixtus but praises and admiration of the wisdom and providence of God?"

units.la: Commendat etiam ac laudat id ipsum parricidium Ioan. Mariana Hispanus Iesuita in lib. de Rege & Regis institutione. Excusat quidem Marianae commendationem facinoris huius Pelletierius sic inquiens: Mirum videri non debere, si homo Hispanus in media Hispania, quo tempore bellum Hispani cum Gallis gerebat, de rebus Gallicis paulo acerbius scripserit. Sed haec excusatio indigna est thromine Christiano, & contraria Iesuitarum institutis. Nam in Reg. comitum, ff. 3 o. haec lex habetur: Caveat omnes ab illo affectu, quo alii de aliis nationib. finitime sentire, ac loqui solet: quin potius bene sentiant, & peculiari affectu diversas à sua natione, prosequantur in Domino.
units.tr: Juan de Mariana, the Spanish Jesuit, also commends and praises this same parricide in his book on the King and the education of a king. Pelletier does try to excuse Mariana's praise of the deed, writing: "It should not seem strange if a Spaniard, in the heart of Spain, at a time when the Spaniards were waging war with the French, wrote rather harshly about French affairs." But this excuse is unworthy of a Christian mind and contrary to the rules of the Jesuits. For in the Rules of the Companions, the thirtieth section, this law is found: "Let everyone beware of that feeling by which people are wont to think and speak ill of other neighbouring nations; rather let them think well, and with a special affection in the Lord love those nations that differ from their own."

units.la: Cum etiam in ultimis Galliae tumultibus et bellorum saevissimis motibus, ntum Tyardaeum Episcopum Cabillonensem, eruditionis ac pietatis singularis, Iesuitae in suam factionem & conspirationem contra Regem Henricum III. attrahere non possent, utpote pacis & tranquillitatis Regni cupidissimum, poli furiosum odium & invidiam in caput eius modis omnibus concitare studuerunt. Est Collegium Divionense Iesuitarum, quod Episcopi huius non exiguis beneficiis adauctum fuit: erat enim bonae partis fundi illius clientelaris Patronus, nisione iuris sui liberalis: quamobrem libello etiam Graecis, Latinis & Gallicis versibus atque oratione soluta scripto, & ipsi dicato, cum amplissimo laudum praedicatione, habuerunt gratiam, & fidem dederunt. Sed quod in conspirationem Iesuitarum & parricidium Regis consentire nollet, quidam Carolus, Iesuitas Collegii istius ascriptus, linguam suam & calamum, superiorum tinctu, vehementer contra illum acuit, quamvis ab eo nusquam, nec re, nec verbis laesus fuerit, aut lacessitus, unde in ipsum ansam invehendi arripere deerit. Contra hunc igitur Praesulem, ob dictam causam, saepissime, non solum familiaribus colloquiis, sed etiam publicis in concionibus, atque editis quoque libellis, debacchatus est: ac inter alia iactitavit impudenter publice & privatim, quadraginta quatuor haereses in tribus foliolis Homiliarum eius in orationem omnium exprompsisse. Has igitur aliasque multas criminationes, maledicta convitia diluere & à se depellere coactus est Episcopus, ut claritudinem nominis, & famae suae obscurationem liberaret. Id autem brevi quidem, sed accurato ipto sic praestitit, ut primum ipsum Carolum in specie, deinde totam Iesuitarum sectam depingat fideliter, eorumque studia, fraudes, conatus, &c. diligenter regat, & ad oculum demonstret.
units.tr: Also, in the last tumults of France and the most savage movements of war, the Jesuits could not draw Tyard, Bishop of Chalon, a man of singular learning and piety, into their faction and conspiracy against King Henry III, since he most desired peace and the tranquillity of the realm. So they set themselves in every way to stir up a furious hatred and envy against him. There is a Jesuit college at Dijon, which had been greatly enlarged by the generous benefactions of this bishop; for he was the patron of a good part of that founding and, by the generosity of his own right, a patron of its clients. Therefore they publicly gave thanks and pledged their loyalty to him in a little book written in Greek, Latin and French verse and in prose, dedicated to him, with the highest praise. But because he refused to consent to the Jesuits' conspiracy and the murder of the King, a certain Charles, enrolled in that college among the Jesuits, sharpened his tongue and pen very fiercely against him, dipped in the dye of his superiors, although the bishop had never injured him in deed or word, nor provoked him, so that he lacked no occasion to attack him. Therefore against this prelate, for the reason stated, he raged very often, not only in private conversations but also in public sermons and in printed pamphlets too. Among other things he boasted shamelessly, publicly and privately, that he had extracted forty-four heresies from three little sheets of the bishop's homilies, to the astonishment of all. The bishop was thus compelled to refute and ward off these and many other accusations, insults and slanders, so as to free his name from disgrace and his reputation from obscurity. He did this briefly, but with such accuracy that he first faithfully portrays Charles himself in particular, and then the whole sect of the Jesuits, and carefully sets out and shows plainly to the eye their pursuits, frauds, attempts and so on.

units.la: Ac primo quidem quod ad Carolum ipsum attinet, dicit, eum pios, tanquam haereticâ labe aspersos accusare, haereticorum vero dogmata aut nunquam, tremissius languidiusve confutare: in Cathedra pro lachrymis, risum effundere, latissimumque elicere à popello, cuius auribus nugas dissimulinet, & sacrae Scripturae locos plurimos detorquens incautum vulgus à veritate longe abducere et infatuare: Illustrissimorum Principum claram nobilemque memoriam, verbis loquacitate obliterare tentare: viros probos traducere: pium Regum iustissimum, pie mortuum, & impiissime trucidatum, inexpiabilem esse, quae apud inferos indeprecabilem poenam subire, clamitare. Ex vilissima vulgi plebis faece, vanos balatrones, impuros apostatas, rapaces rapinatores, latrones scelleratos, crudeles homicidas, capitales furciferos, iterum atque iterum minaci sacratarum legũ sanctione seruatos, horrendumq; & abominandũ Regis Henrici parricidium nefarium collaudare, ut merito honores improba fatuitas propudijs ist.s suis effundat & affingat. Ex oratione Dominica piũ scilicet Ithum Theologum, petitionem hanc: FIAT VOLVNTAS TVA, evellendam esse publice asseruisse, illudq; DE REMITTENDO DEBITORIBVS NOSTRIS obliterandum censuisse. Ad bellum, neces, crudelitatem, rebellionem caeteraq; impietatis scelera, populum cocitare: atq; nihil aliud quam Arma, Arma, in suggestu suggerere, & ad ravim usq; clamitare. Pios antistites, quia ab hi criminibus animum, linguam & manus arceant; quia sine fuco aut fallacijs vocib. & scriptis, Regibus pietatem, populo obedientiam, partium benevolam concil. liationem, pacem Reipub. Christianae, poenitentiam & resipiscentiam haereticis & ijs qui in errore sunt, ad veram viam reditum, veniam adhuc viventibus & requiem aeternam resolutis corporum vinculis, postulent & efflictim precentur, quia illis, qui mutuis inimicitijs, atq; vulneribus, sese confodiunt, in amicitiam coeant, & foedera iungant, suadeant, haereticos vocare: Haereticos declarare eos qui cum Ligae sanctae, ut vocant, inimicis & adversarijs, vel inter foederatos non ascriptis, pacem, aut concordiam ineundam esse dixerint: perinde ac si Apostolorum Symbolo, aut Nicaeno insuendus esset hic nondum auditus Fidei articulus; Credo sanctam Ligam seu unionem Hispanicae factionis, & conjurationis in Henricum Tertium Francorum & Polonorum Regem, eiusque consanguineos atque successores, nullusque Christiani dignus cognomine, cuius fides hoc novo Sacramento non rogata: & parum pij Apostoli, & Orthodoxi Patres, sanctique Ecclesiae Doctores antiqui, qui fuerint, qui in Reges & Imperatores etiam idololatras & haereticos, penes quos summa temporibus rerum erat summa, nunquam coniuraverunt, aut conjuratis seditiones concitantibus adhaeserunt.
units.tr: First, as regards Charles himself, the bishop says that he accuses the pious of being stained with the taint of heresy, but never or only feebly and half-heartedly refutes the doctrines of the heretics; that from the pulpit he pours out laughter instead of tears, and draws the greatest applause from the common crowd, whose ears he tickles with trifles; that by twisting many passages of Holy Scripture he leads the unwary multitude far from the truth and befuddles it; that he tries with his loquacious words to blot out the bright and noble memory of most illustrious princes; that he slanders upright men; that he cries out that the most just and pious King, piously dead and most impiously butchered, is unatoned for and must undergo an irremissible punishment in hell. He calls out from the vilest dregs of the common rabble: vain buffoons, impure apostates, rapacious robbers, wicked brigands, cruel murderers, capital gallows-birds, who have been kept again and again under the threatening sanction of the sacred laws; and he praises the horrible and abominable wicked parricide of King Henry, so that shameless folly may pour out and invent for him, as it deserves, its own disgraces. He had publicly asserted that the petition from the Lord's Prayer, "Thy will be done," ought to be torn out, and that "Forgive us our debts" ought to be erased, as the pious Jesuit Theologian Ithus had decided. From the pulpit he stirs up the people to war, slaughter, cruelty, rebellion and the other crimes of impiety, and does nothing but cry "Arms, arms!" until he is hoarse. He asks and earnestly begs that pious bishops, because they keep their mind, tongue and hands from these crimes, and because with words and writings free of paint or deceit they urge piety on kings, obedience on the people, a kindly reconciliation between the parties, peace in the Christian commonwealth, repentance and amendment for heretics and those who are in error, a return to the true way, pardon for the living and eternal rest for those whose bodies are released from their bonds, are to be called heretics. He declares heretics those who have said that peace or concord must be made with the enemies and opponents of the so-called Holy League, or with those not enrolled among its confederates, just as if this article of faith, not yet heard of, ought to be added to the Apostles' Creed or to the Nicene: "I believe in the holy League, or union, of the Spanish faction and conspiracy against Henry III, King of the French and Poles, and his kinsmen and successors." And no one is worthy of the name of Christian whose faith has not been asked about this new sacrament; and the Apostles, Orthodox Fathers and ancient holy teachers of the Church, whoever they were, who had supreme power in temporal affairs, never conspired against kings and emperors, even idolatrous and heretical ones, nor joined those who conspired and stirred up sedition.

units.la: Et paulo post paginam quadragesimam hunc ipsum Iesuitam in suis Demegorijs & declamationibus coram populo in hunc modum rudere solere & clamitare, dicit: Quotquot ejus scelestissimi scelerati, nomina vestra sacra nostrae Militiae conscribite: nostrarum partium contrarios, pro haereticis habete, e medio tollite, trucidate: pecua eorum abigite & expilate: supellectilem omnem diripite, in quos vestros usus convertite: hortos defragate: vinetorum topiaria deformate: virid. arborum arbores usque ad radicem resecate: domos funditus evertite: omnimodis ... vitia defacite: omnem eorum memoriam delete: sciantque dum exulant a nobis, ... sanctae nostrae Ligae & unionis adversarij, se omnia sua, non ad reditum, sed direptionem atq; incendijs reliquisse, illucq; aquâ & igne interdictum esse: quin diris devoveamus, & ni ... ferro gladio flammeo, atque formidabili, ab ipso paradyso expulsos, arceamus, & eius ad ... cum claudentes, eos ab ingressione propulsemus. Non enim Deum ipsum posse, & si vel miserocordiae suae fructus illis elargiri, & delictorum gratiam facere, fide mea obsidere ... credere jubeo. State ergo animis Phratores & Sodales, atque ad tantum facinus suscipiendum, Mafti viribus est: hoc certe in me recipio, vos extemplo puros, ab omni labe purgatos, februatos, elutos, emaculatos, noxae exemptos, omnisq; venialis Donativi, etiam ... cularium veniarum, meritissimos participes futuros. Monstrum autem prodigium ... esse iudicandus est quicunque credit, Deum homicidijs & rapinis gaudere: ... eos qui ferro & flamma populabundi, domos, praedia, supellectilia omne genus pecorum, vitas civium, incolarum, colonorum, omnia denique sacra & profana ad exitium & vastitatem vocant, rore suae misericordiae aspergere.
units.tr: And a little after page forty he says that this same Jesuit, in his harangues and declamations before the people, was wont to bellow and cry out in this manner: "All you who are most wicked criminals, enrol your names in our sacred army. Regard the opponents of our party as heretics, remove them from the midst, slaughter them; drive off and plunder their flocks; seize all their household goods and turn them to your own use; lay waste their gardens; deface the trellised vines; cut down the green trees right to the root; overthrow their houses from the foundations; wipe out their vices in every way; blot out all memory of them. Let the opponents of our holy League and union know that, while they are in exile from us, they have left all they own not for return but for plunder and fire, and that they are banned there by water and fire; indeed we shall curse them with dire curses, and unless ... with the iron sword, the flaming and the terrible, we shall drive them out from paradise itself and keep them away, shutting the gates against their entry. For I bid you believe, on my faith, that God himself cannot grant them any fruit of his mercy or pardon their offences ... State firm, therefore, brothers and comrades, and for undertaking such a crime be strong: this I certainly take upon myself, that you will straightway be future partakers, pure, cleansed of every stain, washed, purged, freed from guilt, of every venial pardon, even ... of the indulgences of the cloister. He is to be judged a monster and a portent who believes that God delights in murders and robberies ... Those who, ravaging with iron and flame, call for the destruction and devastation of houses, estates, household goods of every kind, the lives of citizens, inhabitants and farmers, and finally all things sacred and profane, are not to be sprinkled with the dew of his mercy."

units.la: Quod autem ad universam sectam Iesuitarum attinet, Cavete, inquit, Galo-Franci ab ipsis, qui cum domesticis vestris ingeniose familiaritatem ineunt, ut vobis insidias tendant: famulitia vestra lenocinio verborum suavitudine fictitia pietatis infecta, occultissima quaeq; illis aperiunt & recludunt. In domibus enim vestris Coryceas habent... ent, à quibus obstrusa omnia expiscatur, nihilque arcanum, nihil clausum, & nihil in nulijs vestris occultum, quod illis non prodatur. Ordinarias & inusitatas istorum per nos viduarum curjitationes, & frequentes ad aurem secretiores collocutiones suspectas bete: ansam enim malitiosis præbent, dubias conscientias & anxias decipiendi: hac cie confessionis simpliciores, à versutis expiatorijs auscultatoribus facile deluduntur.
units.tr: As for the whole sect of the Jesuits, he says: "Beware of them, Gallo-French, who cunningly strike up familiarity with your household servants so that they may lay snares for you. Your servants, tainted by the enticement of words and the sweetness of a feigned piety, open and unlock to them all your most hidden affairs. For in your houses they have spies, by whom they pry into everything concealed, and nothing secret, nothing closed, and nothing hidden in your affairs is withheld from them. Be suspicious of their unusual and unaccustomed frequent visits to your widows, and of their more private whispered conversations at the ear, for these give the malicious an opening to deceive doubtful and anxious consciences. In this way the simpler sort are easily deluded in confession by crafty confessors."

units.la: Nova vero Sancti, scilicet, pneumatici, quibusdam interrogationum formulis, circa scrutationem peccatorum differentias, obscæna & impudica quædam anquirunt, quæ sinu utriusque sexus interrogati (cuius auribus inauditæ turpidines & lascivia instillantur) rubore & interrogantis inhonesti appetitus titillatione, vix ullis verbis, acne vix quidem, enunciari possunt. Nova exempla quorum rumor quidam subortus est prætereo: vetus autem historia de Diacono & Matrona nota est. Attamen istud non possum silentio prætereundum esse ab ijs, quorum animus vultu, & flagitia parietibus teguntur: quam vis obstructio non ita sit obducta, ut à vigilanti oribus oculis perspici non possit. Quis vero illum inter vos sagacior, qui quæ sint quorundam ipsius Ordinis ingenia nesciat? Periosa eorum suasione Gallia, tot & tantis quodam fæcunda virtutibus, fit omnis pietatis politiæ sterilis: eorum perfidiosa & impudenti fallacia, facillimi & moderati nostrorum hominum mores, in barbaram crudelitatem; vera religio in fictitium & perfunctorium Dei cultum, aut in ceremoniam imposituræ fuco illitam; amicitia mutua & concordia fratrum & concivium, in infelicissimum odium demutantur: utque plebem suam fallunt, malorum omnium opinioni, populariter subscribunt: pios vero Catholicos, contumelijs infestantur, & in eos popelli furorem concitant: sanguinis Christianorum miserè entes rivos, siccis oculis, etiam gestientes, aspectant: bellum, esse viam Dei, ex Mahumetis doctrina, impiè prædicant amplas domos, & insanas substructiones auro undique publicis & privatis thesauris æruscato atque corraso, ædificant: & Chameuriarum molles culcitras incubant: nullis auditoribus sine lucrosissimo minervali, classium es patefacunt: perpetuum vero bonis & facultatibus omnium inhiant, adoptiones Testamentarias ab omnibus expetunt & expectant. Etenim Quale solet sylvis brumali frigore, Viscum Fronde virere nova, quod non sua seminat arbos.
units.tr: "But the new 'holy spirits,' by certain formulas of questioning concerning the investigation of sins and the differences between them, inquire into obscene and shameless matters, which are whispered into the bosom of persons of either sex who are questioned, into whose ears unheard-of filth and lewdness are dripped, and which can scarcely be expressed in any words at all, for the shame of the one questioned and the arousing of the questioner's dishonourable appetite. I pass over the new examples, of which a certain rumour has arisen; the old story of the deacon and the matron is well known. Yet this I cannot pass over in silence, since it concerns men whose minds are shown in their faces and whose crimes are hidden by walls, although the covering is not so thick that it cannot be seen through by eyes that are watchful. Who among you is more shrewd, who does not know the talents of some men of that Order? By their pernicious persuasion, Gaul, so fruitful of so many great virtues, becomes barren of all piety and good government; by their treacherous and shameless deceit, the most gentle and moderate manners of our people are changed into barbarous cruelty; true religion is turned into a fictitious and perfunctory worship of God, or into a ceremony daubed with the paint of pretence; mutual friendship and the concord of brothers and fellow citizens are turned into most unhappy hatred. And while they deceive their own common people, they go along with the opinion of all evils as popular; they harass the pious Catholics with insults and stir up the rage of the populace against them. They look on, dry-eyed, even eager, at the wretched streams of Christian blood; they impiously preach that war is the way of God, drawing this from the doctrine of Mahomet; they build vast houses and insane foundations, scraped and hoarded with gold from public and private treasuries on every side, and they lie on soft cushions of Chamuriae (fine stuffs). They sell the opening of the classes to no hearers without the most profitable school fees. Indeed they gape perpetually after the goods and property of all, and they seek and wait for testamentary adoptions from everyone. For as the mistletoe is wont to grow green with new leaves in the woods in the winter cold, which it does not sow from its own tree" (Aeneid 6).

units.la: ale est hoc hominum genus. Nam cum suam sedem non habeant, in aliena vivunt: Vitæ merus sunt: vescata sunt eorum verba, viscatus oris habitus & vultus: gestus motusque poris viscatus: viscata maxime, fictitia, superbaque humilitas: viscatum est ambitiosum iorum fastidium: avaraque divitiarum aspernatio & aversatio viscata est. Quid plura? sunt viscidi. Vestra certè nimis stolida erit facilitas, nisi hæc fallaciosum errore corrigitis. Siccine tam magnum vestro dispendio fiet illis compendium? Siccine tam diu vinulis orum sermonibus vos ludificari patiemini? Ergo sanctæ religionis velo, decipulæ, impiees, & omnis generis scelera contegantur? Ergo nefariæ, infandæ, ab Angelis desertoriæ prodita, & à Deo interdicta, vetitaque artes, sacris liturgijs immiscentur?
units.tr: "Such is this race of men. For since they have no seat of their own, they live in other people's; they are mere parasites of life. Their words are sticky as birdlime, and the look and bearing of their mouth are birdlime; their gestures and movements are birdlime; their humility, feigned and proud, is wholly birdlime; the ambitious disdain of their own pride is birdlime, and their greedy scorn and aversion for riches is birdlime too. What more? They are sticky. Your own simplicity will surely be too foolish unless you correct these deceitful errors. Shall they gain so great an advantage at your expense? Shall you allow yourselves to be mocked for so long by their smooth and sly speeches? Shall crimes of every kind be hidden under the veil of holy religion, the snares and impieties? Shall arts that are unlawful, unspeakable, betrayed by angels as deserters and forbidden by God, be mixed into the sacred liturgies?"

units.la: Etmox pag. 48. Apage, inquit, istos hypocriticos religionis simulatores, & pates dealbatos. Sunt e schola & pulvere rhetorculi declamatores, sefepro sacris conciotoribus venditantes, qui concionibus seditiose concitatis accommodatiores sunt quam tranquillis moderatisque sermonibus: quique loco Evangelicæ lectionis, signa dabant miibus, & pro divinis hymnis Classicum, hormum, seu Orthium bellicosum Minervæ ov: neq; Deo, militaris insaniæ sedatori, litant: sed sanguinei torrentis præcipitatori, pplicant: ut fratres parrici danece commoriantur, civilibusque dissensionibus totius orbis iter collidatur. Præcipuè vero, vicales & personatas aliquando, atque larvatas lustrationes, conceptivasque & stativas supplicationes, diurnas, nocturnas, inducunt; decernunt, atque nudi pedalia populo denunciant, ut Regni Galliæ Christianissimi & nobilissimi, antiquissimæ leges, Regius magistratus & suprema dignitas abrogentur & aboleanr: ut omnis Politia & Oeconomia religionis Christianæ, à tam multis retro sæculis, ad hristi, Apostolorum, & omnium Orthodoxorum regulam observabiles, ab animis simplicium convellantur & evellantur; totaq; Gallica Respubl. per summam juris divini & humani injuriam, evertatur.
units.tr: "And soon, on page 48: 'Away,' he says, 'with those hypocritical simulators of religion, whitewashed tombs. They are rhetorical declaimers from the school and the dust of the lecture hall, who hawk themselves as sacred preachers, and who, for seditiously stirred-up sermons, are more suited than to calm and moderate discourses. In place of the Gospel reading they give signals to the soldiers, and in place of divine hymns they sound the war-trumpet, the battle-cry of Minerva. They offer no sacrifice to God, the calmer of martial madness, but to the one who hurls men headlong into a bloody torrent; they pray that brothers may die together by parricide, and that the path of the whole world may be dashed by civil dissensions. Above all, they introduce processions now and then through the villages and in masks and disguises, and they decree and proclaim to the people, barefoot, supplications that are arranged in advance and fixed in place, by day and by night, so that the most ancient laws of the most Christian and most noble Kingdom of France, the royal magistracy and the supreme dignity, may be repealed and abolished; so that every polity and economy of the Christian religion, which for so many centuries past has been observed according to the rule of Christ, the Apostles and all the Orthodox, may be torn and plucked from the minds of simple people; and so that the whole Gallic commonwealth may be overturned by the greatest injury to divine and human law.'"

units.la: DE PARRICIDIO IN HENRICVM IV REGEM GALLIAE INSTINCTV IESVITARVM TEN- TATO, ANNO CHRISTI 1593.
units.tr: ON THE PARRICIDE ATTEMPTED AGAINST KING HENRY IV OF FRANCE AT THE INSTIGATION OF THE JESUITS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1593.

units.la: à PETRO BARRIERIO.
units.tr: by PETER BARRIERE.

units.la: CVm Rex Henricus 16. die Augusti Melodunum oppidum cum suo comitatu, Fontaine Bleau profecturus, ingrederetur, illo ipso die Rex ab igne to quodam Italo nobili Ludovico Brancaleono praemonitus fuit, quod stratic ta quidam Lugduno secutus eum fuerit interficiendi Regis causa: eiusque statura simul & proportio, sed & membrorum omnium, adeoque barbae, necnc vestimentorum ratio ita ab eo descripta fuit, ut exinde statim cognitus, & inc sequenti die Meloduni comprehensus, inque carcerem coniectus fuerit. In vinculis de nomine rogatus, Petrum Barriere se vocari dicit, & patria Aurelia nensem esse. Confessionis eius summa haec erat tandem, nam ab initio variis mulis elabi conabatur: se iam pridem, Rege adhuc aliam religionem profite te, secum cogitasse, quomodo ipsum interficere & vita privare posset. Cum autem Rex postea Catholicam Romanam religionem amplexus esset, apud Cla ricos nonnullos, nempe Carmelitam, Iacobitam, Capucinum & Iesuitam in trar situ Lugduni scisciratum se esse, An bona cum conscientia Regem interim re posset? qui respondissent, id neutiquam licere. Vbi vero Lutetiam postmodum venisset, & patori ad S. Andreae Aubrio detexisset suum propositum, a eo quidem laudatum id fuisse; sed tamen ad ipsum fontem, id est, ad Rectorem Collegij Societatis Iesu cui Varada nomen erat, se fuisse ab eo abla gatum. Istum autem dixisse, Propositum esse sacrosanctum, monuisseque praesenti saltem ut esset animo, confiteretur, & aures aliorum admonitionibu dehortationibusque occluderet, ac linguam contineret: si caperetur, aut capi plecteretur, se eam ob causam Martyrij coronam in coelo consecuturum. Id cumque Varadam, cum se confitentem audivisset, se adiurasse, ut hoc coeptum persequeretur, & Galliam a Rege Navarraeo, quem Tyrannum appellavisset, liberaret. Postea in cellam se ab eo introductum fuisse, & benedictio nem accepisse. Postero die se confessum esse alteri Iesuitae, sed mentionem istiu sui propositi nullam fecisse, sicque corpus Domini in illo Iesuitarum Collegi percepisse. Praeterea vero cogitationes suas adhuc alij patefecisse Iesuitae, qui & ipse tanquam pias & meritorias eas adprobaverit. Post haec demum emisse cultrum apud eum in carcere repertum, qui alterâ saltem ex parte, prope manc brium, sicut mensales plerumque solent esse, satis spissus fuit; deinceps autem utrinque acutus, & ad extremum rotundiori ad sicae formam, mucrone exactis tus, quo Regem interimere cogitaverit.
units.tr: When King Henry was entering the town of Melun with his retinue on 16 August, on his way to Fontainebleau, he was warned that same day by a certain Italian nobleman, Ludovico Brancaleone, that a man who had followed him from Lyon had come to kill the King. The man's height and build, all his limbs, and likewise the cut of his beard and his clothing, were described so exactly that he was at once recognised and seized at Melun the following day and thrown into prison. In chains, when asked his name, he said he was called Pierre Barrière and was a native of Orléans. The sum of his confession, in the end (for at first he tried to slip away with various lies), was this: some time ago, while the King was still professing another religion, he had thought about how he might kill him and deprive him of life.
