But when the King afterwards embraced the Roman Catholic religion, he had asked several clerics at Lyon, namely a Carmelite, a Jacobite, a Capuchin and a Jesuit, whether he could in good conscience kill the King in the meantime. They answered that this was by no means permitted. When he later came to Paris and disclosed his purpose to the priest at Saint-André-des-Arts, that man praised it; but he sent him on to the very source, that is, to the Rector of the College of the Society of Jesus, whose name was Varada. That man said the purpose was sacrosanct, and advised him at least to keep it in mind, to confess it, to close his ears to the admonitions and dissuasions of others, and to restrain his tongue: if he were caught, or were punished for being caught, he would for that reason win the crown of martyrdom in heaven. When Varada heard him confess this, he urged him to pursue the undertaking and to free France from the King of Navarre, whom he called a tyrant. Afterwards he was led by him into a cell and received a blessing. The next day he made confession to another Jesuit, but made no mention of this purpose, and so received the body of the Lord in that Jesuit college. Moreover, he had revealed his thoughts to other Jesuits as well, who approved them as pious and meritorious. After this he finally bought the knife that was found with him in prison. It was fairly thick on one side, near the back, as table knives usually are; on the other side it was sharp, and at the end it was rounded into the shape of a scimitar and tipped with a point, and with it he had intended to kill the King.

units.la: Huic confessioni firmiter institit, in eaque constanter usque ad mortem perseveravit: imo cum dextra eius igne iam absumpta, tum brachia quoque & crura confracta essent, in rota tandem eandem summatim repetijt, & denuò confirmavit; quibus haec insuper addidit, duos nigros Clericos (Iesuitas intelligens) eodem propositio Lugduno profectos esse, quibus ille palmam praeripere voluerit.
units.tr: He firmly stood by this confession and persisted in it constantly until death. Indeed, when his right hand had already been burned away and his arms and legs broken, he repeated the same account briefly on the wheel and confirmed it again. To this he added that two black clerics (meaning Jesuits) had set out from Lyon on the same purpose, and that he wished to snatch the palm from them.

units.la: Sumptum est de Barriério supplicium 1. Augusti. Die vero 19. qui erat Dominicus, Pater Comoletus Iesuita Parisiensis in Epilogo concionis suae monuerat & adhortatus fuerat Auditores, ut paululum adhuc obduraret & quietius esset animis, siquidem brevi miraculum à Deo magnum ipsos esse percepturos atque oculis suis visuros isuros. Interea vero sibi non aliter persuaderent, quam quasi iam tum istud iisum evenisset. Quae suggestio quidem & exhortatio cum praemissa narratione on male convenit, sed in eo tamen, quod Deus destinaverat, omnino falsa fuit. Lectionem huius parricidij facit auctor Orationis ingenuae acverae ad Regem Christianissimum perscripta, de eo quod postulabatur, ut Iesuitae restituantur Regno Galliae pag. 63. & 64. Item & Author Notarum in eandem Orationem 132. & 133. Meminit eiusdem author Catechismi Iesuitici pag. 462. cap. 6. l.
units.tr: Barrière was executed on 1 August. On the 19th, which was a Sunday, Father Comolet, a Jesuit of Paris, had in the epilogue of his sermon warned and exhorted his hearers to hold on a little longer and to be calmer in mind, since they would shortly perceive and see with their own eyes some great miracle from God. Meanwhile they were to persuade themselves of nothing other than that this had already happened. This suggestion and exhortation agreed not badly with the preceding narrative, but in what God had decreed it was altogether false. The author of the Ingenuous and True Oration, written to the most Christian King about what was demanded, namely that the Jesuits be restored to the Kingdom of France, gives an account of this parricide at pp. 63 and 64. Likewise the author of the Notes on the same Oration, at pp. 132 and 133. The author of the Jesuit Catechism also mentions it, at p. 462, chap. 6.

units.la: DE ALIO PARRICIDIO IN REGEM GALLIAE HENRICVM IIII, INSTINCTV IESVITARVM TENTA- TO A IOHANNE CASTELLO.
units.tr: ON THE OTHER PARRICIDE AGAINST KING HENRY IV OF FRANCE, ATTEMPTED AT THE INSTIGATION OF THE JESUITS BY JOHN CASTEL.

units.la: VBi finem etiam anni 1594. parricidium in Regem Franciae & Navarrae Henricum quartum tentatum fuit a Iohanne quodam Castellio, de quo exit adhuc literae Regis in hanc sententiam scriptae. Charissimi & dilectissimi ex his intelligetis infortunium quod mihi paratum fuerat, & quomodo Dei misericordia me ab mirabiliter liberavit. Altera hora, nec amplius effluxerat, post reditum meum ex expetione e Picardia, & adhuc ocreatus eram, ac circumstabant mihi Sobrini mei, Principes Conti, & Comites Suessiones & sancti Pauli, cum triginta aut quadraginta praecipuorum magnatum & nobilium huius aulae. Cum nobiles a Ragni & Motigni, qui me adhuc salutaverant, exciperem, adolescens quidam vocatus Iohannes Castel, corpore brevis, ate annorum octodecim aut novemdecim, qui cum turba in aulam irrepserat a nullo fere observatus, subito irrupit, ut me cultro, quem manu gestabat, transfigeret, sed ictus, quia corpus nitebam, ut praedictos nobiles salutandi causa inclinatos, sublevarem, in faciem tantum, ad labij superioris latus dextrum illatus fuit, & cum vulnere dentem unum fregit. Rursus ille subito comprehensus fuit, & cum aliquantulum prima fronte factum abnuisset, tandem nulla vi cogente id fassus est. Nihil tamen adhuc extorquere potuimus, praequam ipsum, in Collegio Iesuitarum triennio educatum fuisse. Quod prius occurrit, endum fuit, ut pro tanto & peculiari in me beneficio, Deo gratias redderemus, qui me ab homicidio tutatus esset. Quapropter subito, Te Deum laudamus, in omnibus urtemplis cantatum fuit, cives quoque ignes, signa laetitiae in omnibus compitis excitunt. Vulnus Dei beneficio tam leve est, ut propterea in lectum maturius ituri non simus, speramus nos opportunitatem non praetermissuros, cujus causa reditum nostrum accelerimus, ut scilicet festum & ceremonias Ordinis S. Spiritus celebraremus. Diutius autem exspectare nolui, quin vos de his certiores facere, ne vos reliquique fideles mei, nuncio unde citius percepto in sollicitudinem inciderit, imprimis vero, ut publice Deo gratias dere jubeatis, & precib. petatis, ut me ab eiusmodi parricidijs, sub sancta clientela semtueri velit. Ad quae cum hostes nostri tam saepius confugiant, manifeste perfidam & leratam suam mentem declarant, & se a divino favore deserros animadvertentes, perim exsecranda consilia ampleduntur, quia a Deo, ut speramus, in ipsorum ruinam contentur, &c.
units.tr: Towards the end of the year 1594 too, a parricide against Henry IV, King of France and Navarre, was attempted by a certain John Castel, and a letter of the King written to this effect still survives: "Most dear and beloved, from this letter you will understand the misfortune that had been prepared for me, and how by God's mercy he has marvellously delivered me. Not even an hour had passed since my return from the expedition from Picardy, and I was still in my riding boots, when my cousins the Princes of Conti and the Counts of Soissons and Saint-Pol, with thirty or forty of the chief magnates and nobles of this court, were standing around me. While I was receiving the nobles of Ragny and Montigny, who had greeted me, a young man called John Castel, short of stature and about eighteen or nineteen years of age, who had crept into the hall with the crowd and was hardly noticed by anyone, suddenly rushed at me to pierce me with a knife he held in his hand. But the blow, because I was bending down to raise up the aforesaid nobles who had bowed to greet me, struck only my face, at the right side of the upper lip, and with the wound it broke one tooth. He was at once seized again, and although at first he denied having done it, he finally confessed without any compulsion. Nevertheless we could extract nothing more from him, except that he had been educated for three years in the Jesuits' college. The first thing that comes to mind is that we must give thanks to God for so great and special a benefit to me, who has protected me from homicide. Therefore at once the Te Deum laudamus was sung in all the churches; the citizens too light fires and raise signs of joy at every crossroads. The wound, by God's benefit, is so slight that we shall not go to bed any the earlier for it; we hope not to let slip the opportunity for which we hastened our return, namely to celebrate the feast and ceremonies of the Order of the Holy Spirit. I did not want to wait any longer before informing you of these things, lest you and my other loyal subjects, having heard the news from elsewhere, fall into anxiety; and above all, so that you may order public thanks to be given to God and pray that he will wish to keep me under his holy protection from parricides of this kind. Since our enemies so often take refuge in such crimes, they plainly declare their faithless and wicked minds; and, perceiving themselves deserted by divine favour, they embrace accursed plans, which, as we hope, are turned by God to their own ruin, etc."

units.la: Ut literae hae Regis melius ac plenius intelligantur, praesertim quod ad consionem parricidae de impulsore huius facinoris attinet, res ita se habet. Laeso ege & parricida comprehenso, primum negare scelus summum, sed dum acrius getur, non aegre confessus est. Rex dimitti iubet condonata venia: sed ubi inlexit Iesuitarum alumnum fuisse, exclamavit, NVNC oportuit illos ore meo (hoc inens) reos peragi. Reus igitur a Lugolio rerum capitalium in aulae comitatu aesitore rogatus, quo oestro percitus tantum facinus nedum cogitare, sed maexequi tentasse, respondit, iam dudum hoc sibi animo conceptum immotumesse, dolere infectum, et filiceret rursus aggressurum, ratus id religioni ducere, iam pridem mente volvisse nefas, ac subripuisse cultrum ante prandium, cum in musaeo abdidisset, cum Patre & familiaribus pransu esse. Rogatus de tu in quorum scholis disciplinas didicisset, respondet, apud Ignatian. triennio in studijs exacto, ante aliquot dies, à Patre Petro Caftelæo ad Guererum Iefuitam deductum, ut ex animo scrupulum eximeret, quo propter summa flagitia de Dei misericordia dissidebat, in mentem sibi venisse, aliquo non vulgari facinore teterrimas noxas sibi expiandas esse, non semel cogitasse de Rege necando, patri detecta cogitatione, ab eo valde obiurgatum.
units.tr: So that this letter of the King may be understood better and more fully, especially as regards the parricide's account of the instigator of this crime, the matter stands thus. When the wounded King and the seized parricide were brought together, he at first denied the great crime, but when he was pressed more sharply, he confessed without difficulty. The King ordered him to be dismissed, with pardon granted; but when he admitted that he had been a pupil of the Jesuits, he cried out: "Now it is necessary that they be made guilty through my mouth." The accused, therefore, was asked by Lugolius, magistrate of capital cases in the court's retinue, what impulse had driven him not only to conceive but to attempt so great a crime. He answered that he had long had this intention in mind, that he grieved it had not been carried out, and that he would attack again, judging this to be a religious duty; that he had long turned the wickedness over in his mind, and had stolen a knife before dinner, when he hid it in the study, while the Father and the household were at dinner. Asked in whose schools he had learned his subjects, he replied that after three years of study among the Ignatians, some days earlier he had been taken by Father Peter Castel to the Jesuit Guéret, so that he might remove from his mind the scruple by which, on account of his very great sins, he doubted God's mercy; and it had come into his mind that his most loathsome offences were to be expiated by some uncommon crime. He had more than once thought of killing the King. When the thought was disclosed to his father, he was severely rebuked by him.

units.la: Habita ad hunc modum quæstione alta nocte, tota vrbe vndequaque accitis Centurionibus, Iesuitæ omnes dantur custodiæ, & vix ab illis vulgus temperavit, sed collocatis præsidiis foris intusque, in crastinam lucem a cæde & direptione servantur. Postridie Gueretus & Guignardus Iesuitæ ergastulis includuntur, cæteri in D. Ludovici, suo musæo & veteranorum secessu custodiuntur.
units.tr: Once the questioning had been carried out in the dead of night, with centurions summoned from every part of the city, all the Jesuits were placed under guard, and scarcely could the crowd be held back from them. But with guards posted outside and inside, they were kept safe from slaughter and plunder until the next morning. The following day the Jesuits Guéret and Guignard were shut up in prisons; the rest were kept under guard in the house of St Louis, in their museum and in the veterans' retreat.

units.la: In Palatinum carcerem deductus parricida, repetita quæstione, eademque ultro confessus est. Rogatus quale ingens hoc facinus, quo noxas suas deleri rebatur? Respondit, Regis cædem fuisse, quem iugulo appeteremens manus destinaverit, ictu inaniter adacto in dentes, quibus retusus fuisset, cuius ea sibi feralis insideret cogitatio, cum Antichristo devotum esse inferorum cruciatibus, ex duobus malis levius sibi eligendum duxisse, ut qui mallet damnari ut quatuor, quàm ut octo. Rogatus, unde hæc nova dogmata hausisset? Respondit, ex placitis Philosophorum, quæ sub ferula Guereti plus biennii didicisset. Rogatus, num sæpius admissus fuisset in Iesuitarum lararium meditationum, in quo spectra & larvæ dæmonum, cruciatus inferorum variaque portenta, quæ ad perterrendos animos scelestorum picta ostenduntur, ut terriculamentis horribili formidine concepta pœnarum, ad frugem probatam viris suam ignaviam, ipsa effera redeant? Respondit, ad huiusmodi pictos inferos sæpe deductum. Rogatus, quo magistro vel suasore didicisse Regem occidendum? Respondit, sparsim apud multos audivisse eandem illi permitti, quod eum Tyrannum nuncuparent. Rogatus, num crebris sermonibus apud Iesuitas hoc propositum usurparetur, fas esse Regem occidere? Respondit, audisse sæpissime, licere hoc facinus, quod extra Ecclesiam esset, et anathemate percussus, nec ideo regio titulo aut obsequio dignandum, donec Pontifice Romano coetui Christianorum atque aris restitueretur.
units.tr: The parricide was taken to the Palace prison, and when he was questioned again he confessed the same things of his own accord. Asked what this great crime was by which he thought his sins would be wiped away, he answered that it was the killing of the King, whose throat he had aimed at with his hand, the blow having been struck in vain against the teeth, by which it was blunted. This fatal thought had taken hold of him, that, devoted to the torments of hell as an Antichrist, he had judged it better to choose the lesser of two evils, as one who would rather be damned as four than as eight. Asked where he had drawn these new doctrines from, he answered from the opinions of the philosophers, which he had learned under Guéret's rod for more than two years. Asked whether he had often been admitted to the Jesuits' lecture room of meditations, in which the ghosts and masks of demons, the torments of hell and various portents are painted and shown to terrify the minds of the wicked, so that, by terrifying images of punishment conceived in horrible dread, their own cowardice may return, fierce, to a fruit that men have tested, he answered that he had often been led to such painted hells. Asked from which master or persuader he had learned that the King ought to be killed, he answered that he had heard here and there from many people that the same was permitted, since they called him a tyrant. Asked whether the proposition that it is lawful to kill a king was often put forward in frequent talks among the Jesuits, he answered that he had very often heard that this crime was lawful, since the King was outside the Church and struck by anathema, and therefore not to be honoured with royal title or obedience, until he should be restored by the Roman Pontiff to the fellowship and altars of Christians.

units.la: In hunc igitur Caftellium ob tentatum hoc parricidium, & Iesuitas impufores, huiusmodi sententia criminalis lata est. Cum in consessu magnæ Camerae, quæ & Tournelle dicitur, visus, auditusque sit processus criminalis, inceptus quidem à rerum capitalium Prætore palatij Regis, & tandem definitus ad petitionem Procuratoris generalis Regij, accusatoris Ioannis Caftellij, Parisiensis studiosi, qui studij fui cursum in Collegio Claremontio absolvit, nunc captivi in carceribus Palatij, ob detestandum & execrabile parricidium in Regem tentatum: auditis etiam interrogationibus, examinationibus & confessionibus dicti Ioannis Caftellij: Examinato insuper in eadem Curia eodem Caftellio super idem parricidium; & audito Ioanne Gueret, presbytero congregationis Societatis Iesu, in eodem habitante Collegio, atque olim dicti Ioannis Caftellij præceptore, auditis denique Petro Caftellio, & Dionysia Hazarda patre & matre Ioannis: Cum discusso Procuratoris generalis conclusione, omnibusque præcedentibus consideratis, clarævit, & declarat dictum Ioannem Caftellium teneri, & convictum esse criminis læsæ Majestatis, tam divinæ, quàm humanæ; ob sceleratum & detestabile parricidium in Regem tentatum. Pro cuius criminis expiatione & supplicio Curia condemnavit & condenat prædictum Ioannem pœnâ subsequente: Initio stabit ante valvas primarias Ecclesiæ Parisiensis nudus, sola tectus interula, & cereamque ardentem duarum librarum manu tenebit, procidensque in genua confitebitur, & dicet, se turpiter & proditorie inhumanum abominabile hoc parricidium committere voluisse, Regemque cultro in vultu vulnerasse, dicetque, se falsis & damnandis instructionibus & persuasionibus huc inductum esse, ut ciret sibi permissum, Reges interficere, & Henricum IV. modò regnantem, non esse membrum Ecclesiæ, priusquam à Pontifice maximo approbatus fuerit: Factum hoc in se detestatur, Deum, Regem, & justitiam orabit, ut sibi ignoscant. His factis curru obscæno detrahetur ad locum, cui nomen Greve, ibi forcipibus ignitis, seu candentibus ejus brachia & femora vellicabuntur, & lacerabuntur: dextera verò, in qua cultrum tenebit, quo factum perpetravit, amputabitur. Tandem quatuor equis alligatum corpus in totidem partes dirpetur: partes in ignem conijcientur, & in cinerem convertentur: cineres autem in ventum projecti, dispergentur. Declaravit eadem Curia, & declarat, omnia ejus bona Fisco regio esse subjignanda. Antequam hæc executio fiet dictus Joannes Castellius ordinariis extraordinariisque quæstionibus subijcietur, ut sciatur, qui ejus fuere complices, & ut inrogetur de aliis quibusdam hinc dependentibus. Prohibuit & prohibet omnibus hominibus, cujuscunque sint qualitatis & conditionis, sub pœna criminis læsæ Majestatis, ne publicè, vel privatim dicat, aut sustineat hujusmodi propositum, quasi id quod Curia decrevit, & judicat, sit scandalosum, seditiosum, Dei verbo contrarium, & tanquam haereticum in sanctis decretis condemnatum.
units.tr: Against this Castel, for the attempted parricide, and against the Jesuits as instigators, a criminal sentence of the following kind was therefore pronounced. In the assembly of the Great Chamber, which is also called the Tournelle, the criminal process was heard and examined. It was begun by the praetor of capital cases of the King's palace, and finally concluded at the petition of the King's Procurator General, acting as accuser of John Castel, a Parisian student who had completed his course of study at the College of Clermont, now held captive in the prisons of the Palace, for the detestable and execrable parricide attempted against the King. The interrogations, examinations and confessions of the said John Castel were also heard; Castel was examined in the same court about the same parricide; John Guéret, priest of the congregation of the Society of Jesus, who lived in the same college and had formerly been the teacher of the said John Castel, was heard; and finally Peter Castel and Denise Hazard, the father and mother of John, were heard. When the Procurator General's conclusion had been discussed and all that had gone before had been considered, it was made clear and is declared that the said John Castel is bound by, and convicted of, the crime of high treason, both against divine and against human majesty, for the wicked and detestable parricide attempted against the King. For the expiation of this crime and for his punishment, the Court condemned and condemns the aforesaid John to the following penalty: first he shall stand before the main doors of the church of Paris, naked, covered only by a shirt, holding a burning wax candle of two pounds in his hand, and, falling on his knees, he shall confess that he wickedly and treacherously wished to commit this inhuman and abominable parricide, and wounded the King with a knife in the face; he shall say that he was led to this by false and damnable instructions and persuasions, namely that it was permitted to him to kill kings, and that Henry IV, now reigning, is not a member of the Church until he has been approved by the supreme Pontiff. He shall detest this deed, and pray God, the King and justice to forgive him. When these things are done, he shall be dragged on a shameful cart to the place called Grève, and there his arms and thighs shall be torn with red-hot or glowing pincers and lacerated; his right hand, in which he held the knife with which he committed the deed, shall be cut off. Finally his body, tied to four horses, shall be torn into as many parts; the parts shall be thrown into the fire and turned to ash, and the ashes cast into the wind and scattered. The same Court declared, and declares, that all his goods are to be confiscated to the royal treasury. Before this execution takes place, the said John Castel shall be subjected to ordinary and extraordinary questioning, so that it may be known who his accomplices were, and so that charges may be brought concerning certain other matters dependent on this. It forbids and prohibits all men, of whatever quality and condition, under penalty of the crime of high treason, to say or maintain such a proposition publicly or privately, as if what the Court has decreed and judged were scandalous, seditious, contrary to the word of God, and condemned as heretical in the holy decrees.

units.la: Constituit insuper, ut omnes Sacerdotes Collegij Clermontij, & omnes alij prædictæ societati addicti, tanquam corruptores juventutis, perturbatores publicæ tranquillitatis, hostes Regis & Regni, infra tres dies post promulgationem hujus edicti, Lutetiâ, & aliis locis, ubi sua tenent collegia, discedant, & infra quindecim subsequentes dies toto Regno exeant. Quod nisi fecerint, & post præscriptum tempus usquam inventi suerint, tanquam læsæ Majestatis rei punientur. Illorum autem mobilia & immobilia bona retentur in alia pia opera, & distributis eorum fiet, secundum arbitrium & decretum Curiæ. Interdicit etiam omnibus Regis subditis, ne filios suos etiam extra Regnum in dictas societatis Collegia mittant, ut ibidem instituantur: si quis contravenerit, eadem læsæ Majestatis pœnâ tenebitur. Hactenus sententia Curiæ: post quam divulgatam, Joannes Castellius eadem die, quæ erat dies Iovis Decemb. 29. Anni 1594. vinctus publicum producitur, & secundum præscriptum mandati, seu sententiæ, mortem rapitur.
units.tr: Furthermore, the decree orders that all the priests of the College of Clermont, and all others attached to the said society, be treated as corruptors of youth, disturbers of public peace, and enemies of the King and the kingdom. Within three days after the publication of this edict they are to leave Paris and the other places where they keep their colleges, and within fifteen days following they are to leave the whole kingdom. If they do not do so, and are found anywhere after the appointed time, they will be punished as guilty of high treason. Their movable and immovable goods are to be seized and applied to other pious works, and their distribution is to be made according to the judgment and decree of the Court. It also forbids all the King's subjects to send their sons, even outside the kingdom, to the colleges of the said society to be educated there; whoever contravenes will be liable to the same penalty for high treason. So far the sentence of the Court. After it was published, John Castel, on the same day, which was Thursday, 29 December 1594, was brought out in chains in public and, according to the terms of the mandate or sentence, was seized and put to death.

units.la: Etsi vero sicut plerique sententiam in temerarium Joannis Castellij factum non imobarent, Iesuitis tamen eorumque patronis vehementer displicebat. Unde publicè scriptum Duaci excusum prodijt, quo huius sententiæ absurditas et iniustitiam ostendere conantur. Ait enim author, ex ipsius sententiæ contextu posse considerari, eam conditam & compositam ad mentem hæreticorum nostri sæculi non alio fine, quam ut Societatem Iesu reddant suspectam & exosam; ut quid enim in tio necessarium erat, tam diversis verbis exprimere; Studiosus, qui litteris operam dedit Collegio Iesuitarum? Et in ipsa sententia; Studiosi, qui studij sui cursum in Collegio Tremontio, nisi ut hoc modo loquendi Patres Societatis traducantur; quibus si eorum cipuli postea in crimen aliquod incidant; non major calumnia imponi debebat, quam Academiæ Parisiensi, aut alicui ejus membro, aut ipsis Sorbonistis, quod Calvinus, quod alij plures ibidem studuerunt. Secundo notant, non sine causa exprimi; Oa Præceptoris dicti Joannis Castellij, de quo nihil aliud dicitur. Neque enim fuisse Castellio authorem hujus parricidij, neque conscium scelerís fuisse exprimunt. Ideoque iminens esse, & non alia causa infertum, nisi ut Iesuitas in suspicionem trahant, ijsque ompopulare continent. Neque enim carere suspicione putant, quod in sententia Castelli jubetur dicere, Sefalsis & damnandis perfuasionibus inductum, ut crederet, sibi persum Reges interficere: & Henricum IV. modò regnantem, non esse membrum Ecclesiæ priusquam à Pontifice Maximo approbatus fuerit, etc. Iubetur quidem hæc dicere, sed additur: quod dixit antea, ut confessus est. Quis enim dubitet, quin iflorum Subornatorum & instructorum, si qui fuissent, nomina etiam exprimerentur? Quod cum non fiat, sufficio est, id non alio fine factu, quam ut Iesuitas calumnientur, quasi isti huiusmodi falsas, crandasque instructiones suggessierint. Neque verisimile esse; Castellium hoc anno in
units.tr: Although, indeed, like most people, they did not disapprove of the sentence passed on the rash deed of John Castel, the Jesuits and their patrons were nonetheless strongly displeased by it. Hence a public writing was printed at Douai, in which they try to show the absurdity and injustice of this sentence. For the author says that from the very wording of the sentence it can be seen that it was composed and drawn up according to the mind of the heretics of our age, with no other aim than to make the Society of Jesus suspect and hateful. For why was it necessary to express in such different words: "a student who has devoted himself to letters at the College of the Jesuits"? And in the sentence itself: "students who pursued their course of study at the College of Tremont", unless it was to slander the Fathers of the Society in this way; and if their pupils afterwards fell into some crime, no greater calumny ought to be laid on them than on the Parisian Academy, or any of its members, or the Sorbonnists themselves, because Calvin and many others studied there. Secondly, they note that it was not without reason that mention was made of the teacher of the said John Castel, about whom nothing else is said. For they do not state that Castel was the author of this parricide, nor that he was an accomplice in the crime. Therefore, they say, this was an insinuation, introduced for no other reason than to bring the Jesuits under suspicion and to stir up popular hatred against them. Nor do they think it free of suspicion that in Castel's sentence he is ordered to say that, induced by false and damnable persuasions, he believed it lawful for himself to kill kings, and that Henry IV, now reigning, is not a member of the Church until he has been approved by the Supreme Pontiff, and so on. He is indeed ordered to say these things, but it is added: "as he had said before, as he confessed." For who would doubt that the names of those who had suborned and instructed him, if there were any, would also have been stated? Since this is not done, it is enough to say that it was done for no other purpose than to slander the Jesuits, as if they had suggested such false and damnable instructions. Nor is it likely that Castel, in this year...

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: ON THE WICKED DEEDS

units.la: Artibus & Philosophia Magistrum promotum, tam stupido ingenio, inconsideratoque animo fuisse, ut ei persuaderi posset, Reges simpliciter licere interficere: cum omnium Catholicorum sententia sit plane contraria, qui jubent quam maxime Reges venerari. Credibile quidem esse Castellium dicere & defendere voluisse, probatos Doctores scribere & docere; Licitum esse occidere, non omnes Reges, sed eos tantum, qui tyranni sunt, & invasores; hos licitum esse interficere non tantum authoritate publica, sed etiam cujuscunque privata, praesertim ubi deest modus & via ad superiorem potestatem recurrendi, exempl
units.tr: That a man promoted to Master of Arts and Philosophy could have been so dull of wit and so thoughtless of mind as to be persuaded that kings may simply be killed is wholly contrary to the opinion of all Catholics, who most strongly urge that kings be honoured. It is credible that Castellus wished to say and defend that learned Doctors write and teach that it is lawful to kill, not all kings, but only those who are tyrants and usurpers; and that these may lawfully be killed not only by public authority but also by any private person, especially where there is no means or way of appealing to a higher power, example

units.la: Aiod Iud. 3. Caietan. 22. q. 64. a. 3. secundum Thomam 2. Sent. dist. 44. q. 2. a. 2. & Opus de Regim. Princ. lib. 1. cap. 1. Cajetan. Sylvest. Fumus in Summis verbo Tyrannus docent & probare nituntur. Quod autem in Concilio Constantiensi Sess. 15. prohibetur; ...
units.tr: Aiod Iud. 3. Caietan. 22. q. 64. a. 3. according to Thomas 2. Sent. dist. 44. q. 2. a. 2. and the Opus de Regim. Princ. lib. 1. cap. 1. Cajetan, Sylvester and Fumus in the Summa, under the word Tyrannus, teach and strive to prove this. But what is forbidden in the Council of Constance, Sess. 15; ...

units.la: Edidit etiam in lucem Iesuita Franciscus Verona Constantinus Apologiam pro Iohanne Castello Parisiensi, contra Edictum Parlamenti, & supplicium de eo ob parricidium sumptum. Apologiae summa est, Non obstante decreto Concilii Constantiensis, privatis & publicis personis licitum esse, Reges & Principes haereticos & tyrannidis damnatos occidere. In specie vero probat Iacobi Clementis parricidium in Henricum III. Galliae & Poloniae Regem perpetratum, quasi contra hostem publicum & juridice condemnatum. zfis perpetratum, quàm hostili impetu hodierno, quo ad oppressionem Religionis est prosus, mactando Sacerdotes, profanando Sacramenta, repudiando censuras, & favendo haereticis. Quibus de causis totum se privatum reddidit, & subjectum utrique juri, tam civili, quàm Canonico. Actio igitur Clementis neutiquam illicita fuit, quippe perpetrata contra hostem publicum, & condemnatum juridicè, in quem omnis obligatio reverentiae attributa debiti sublata fuit. De Henrico 4. sic scribit, Qui diligenter perpendit, excommunicatum, haereticum, relapsum, profanatorem rerum sacrarum, declaratum hostem publicum, rejiciendum Religionis, ab omni jure perveniendi ad regnum excludi; ac propterea tyrannum esse, non Regem; usurpatorem, non naturalem Dominum; criminis reum, non legitimum Principem; Is sane, nisi insanus sit, & destitutus omni humano sensu, & amore in Deum, Ecclesiam & Patriam, aliter sentire & dicere non potest, quàm facinus Castelli generosum, cum virtute coniunctum & heroicum, comparandum cum magnis, & summâ laude dignis factis, quorum antiqua, sacra & profana historia monumenta meminerunt: Unicum fuerit, quod improbare possit; nempe, quòd Castellus ipsum non penitus è medio sustulit.
units.tr: The Jesuit Francis Verona of Constance also brought into the light an Apology for John Castellus of Paris, against the Edict of Parliament and the punishment imposed on him for parricide. The sum of the Apology is that, notwithstanding the decree of the Council of Constance, it is lawful for private and public persons to kill kings and princes who are heretics and condemned as tyrants. In particular it defends the parricide committed against Henry III, King of France and Poland, as if against a public enemy and one lawfully condemned. ...committed, with a hostile assault such as that of today, by which religion is wholly overthrown: by slaughtering priests, profaning the sacraments, rejecting censures, and favouring heretics. For these reasons he made himself wholly a private person, and subject to both laws, civil and canon. The act of Clement was therefore in no way unlawful, since it was committed against a public enemy and one lawfully condemned, from whom every obligation of reverence due had been removed. Concerning Henry IV he writes thus: whoever weighs this carefully will see that one who is excommunicate, a heretic, a relapsed person, a profaner of sacred things, declared a public enemy, to be rejected from religion, is excluded from every right of coming to the kingdom; and therefore he is a tyrant, not a king; a usurper, not the natural lord; a guilty criminal, not a lawful prince. Such a man, unless he is mad and utterly destitute of human feeling and of love towards God, the Church and the fatherland, cannot think or say otherwise than that the deed of Castellus was noble, joined with virtue and heroic, to be compared with great deeds worthy of the highest praise, of which the ancient records of sacred and profane history make mention. There is only one thing he could find fault with: namely, that Castellus did not wholly remove him from the midst.

units.la: Deinde parte 2. cap. 2. dicit, Castellum non in animo habuisse interficere Regem, sed annum & haereticum excommunicatum. Nam licet ille Regem se dicat, Regis tyrannum se gerat, & ex Regum Galliae sanguine pronatum iactitet, atque etiam Rex is agnosci & honorari velit; cum tamen revera amplius talem non esse, quum a fide, non virtutum, non meritorum denique Regum Galliae sit haeres. Et quidem ob impietatem & haeresim suam ab Ecclesia & Statibus sit exsus, Regem omnino eum non posse esse, nisi de facto: de iure vero nequaquam: Quod ipsum tyrannis vocari solet.
units.tr: Then in part 2, chapter 2, he says that Castellus had no intention of killing the king, but an excommunicate and heretical man. For although that man calls himself king, behaves as a tyrant of the king, and boasts that he is descended from the blood of the kings of France, and even wishes to be recognised and honoured as king; yet in truth he is no longer such, since he is heir to the kings of France not in virtue, merits, or finally in faith. And indeed, on account of his impiety and heresy he has been cast out by the Church and the Estates, so that he can be king only in fact, and never in right. This is what is commonly called tyranny.

units.la: Cap. 4. dicit, Henricum Borbonium Regem appellari non posse, licet ad Catholico Religionem conversus sit, nam ipsum hoc fuco in alium finem non uti, quàm ut in ordine irrumpat, ad rabiem suam illic exercendi liberius.
units.tr: In chapter 4 he says that Henry of Bourbon cannot be called king, although he has been converted to the Catholic religion; for he uses this disguise for no other purpose than to break into the order and there to exercise his rage more freely.

units.la: Cap. 8. dicit, Henricum 4. si maximè ab excommunicatione absolutus esset à Papa, tamen illum Regem fore de jure, sed tantùm de facto.
units.tr: In chapter 8 he says that Henry IV, even if he were absolved from excommunication by the Pope, would nonetheless not be king by right, but only in fact.

units.la: Cap. 9. Illum Regem non dici etiam posse ex jure successionis.
units.tr: In chapter 9 he says that he cannot be called king even by right of succession.

units.la: Cap. 11. probare conatur, Haereticos & relapsos, e quorum numero etiam sit Henricus Borbonius, jure divino & humano interficipossè.
units.tr: In chapter 11 he tries to prove that heretics and relapsed persons, among whom is Henry of Bourbon, may be killed by divine and human law.

units.la: Cap. 12. 13. & 14. dicit, Haereticos & tyrannos, multoque magis qui haeretici et tyranni simul sint, ut Henricus 4. tolli posse etiam ab hominib. privatis, si aliter fieri nequeat.
units.tr: In chapters 12, 13 and 14 he says that heretics and tyrants, and much more those who are both heretics and tyrants at once, such as Henry IV, may be removed even by private persons, if this cannot otherwise be done.

units.la: Cap. 15. recenset multas utilitates, quae Regnum Galliae ex hoc facto Castelli accederent, si istius successisset.
units.tr: In chapter 15 he lists the many advantages that would accrue to the kingdom of France from this deed of Castellus, had it succeeded.

units.la: Parte 3. quoque cap. 1. probare vult. factum & conatum Castelli heroicum esse.
units.tr: In part 3, chapter 1, he also seeks to prove that the deed and attempt of Castellus was heroic.

units.la: Cap. 8. 9. 10. ad coelum usque extollit Castelli constantiam inter quaestiones ac tormenta, in perferendo supplicio: O Constantiam, inquit, plus quam puerilem, & perpetuâ omnium saeculorum futurorum memoriâ dignam. Prae hac nemo amplius mirabitur constantiam volae, punientis manum, quae erraverat.
units.tr: In chapters 8, 9 and 10 he raises Castellus's constancy to the skies, amid the questions and torments, in enduring punishment: "O constancy," he says, "more than childish, and worthy of perpetual memory in all the ages to come! Before this no one will any longer marvel at the constancy of the hand that is punished for having erred."

units.la: Parte 4. cap. 1. ostendere vult, Decreti Parlamenti contra Castellum facti & progati vitia & absurditates.
units.tr: In part 4, chapter 1, he wishes to show the faults and absurdities of the decree of Parliament made and published against Castellus.

units.la: Parte quintâ totâ, probare conatur, multa vitia & absurditates inesse Decreti Parlamenti, contra Iesuitas & universum eorum Ordinem facto.
units.tr: In the whole of the fifth part he tries to prove that many faults and absurdities lie in the decree of Parliament made against the Jesuits and their whole Order.

units.la: Cum igitur in hac Apologia doceatur, permissum esse etiâ hominib. privatis, furtiliter invadere et necare, ceu tyrannos, Reges et Principes, qui ad Pontificum voluntate, imò privatorum etiâ hominum iudiciū atque nutum, se totos non informant, ideoque etiam authoris huius Apologiae parricidia Henricorum tertii & quarti Regum Galliae, aliorumque publice defenderet: Iesuitae autè vererentur, ne commemorata Apologia cum detestabili sua doctrina, ipsos nimis invisos detestabiles Regib. et Principib. redderet, quia nõ aditu tantū suo et cõgressu
units.tr: Since therefore this Apology teaches that it is permitted even to private persons to invade and kill by stealth, as tyrants, kings and princes who do not wholly shape themselves to the will of the Popes, or rather to the judgment and nod of private persons; and therefore this author of the Apology publicly defends the parricides of Henry III and Henry IV, kings of France, and others; the Jesuits, however, are afraid that the aforesaid Apology, together with their detestable doctrine, would make them too hated and detestable to kings and princes, because not only by their approach and company...

units.la: {*} Apologia Veri ne supprimitur, sed recudatur. ut in quos machinæ illorum potissimum diriguntur, ipsos esse præclusuri, sed omnibus etiam regnis suis & Rebuspub. exterminaturi, sicut etiam antea eos Templarij exterminati sunt: ideo hanc suam Apologiam suppresserunt & sepelierunt: non quòd ipsos puderet aut pœniteret, sceleratissima sua parricidia, adeo impudenter defendisse ac propugnasse; sed tantum, ne horror, quem Reges & Principes iustissime inde concipere poterant, aditu ad Curias & Consilia sua ipsos prohiberet. Quis enim inter homines ratione præditos adeo vilis & abiectus est, ut spiritus tam fallaces ac scelestos accedere ad se patiatur? Ideo vero hanc Apologiam recudi curarunt, ut totus mundus sciat & comperta habeat Iesuitarum fraudes, dolos, impostituras, technas, consilia & conatus adversus Reges & Principes; ac in universum omnes illos, qui se tyrannidi Pontificis Romani subijcere nolunt.
units.tr: {*} The Apology of Verona is not suppressed but reprinted, so that those against whom their machinations are chiefly directed would be shut out by them, and would be driven out of all their kingdoms and commonwealths, just as the Templars were once driven out; therefore they have suppressed and buried this their Apology. Not that they are ashamed or repent of having so shamelessly defended and championed their most wicked parricides; but only so that the horror which kings and princes could most justly conceive from it should not keep them from access to their courts and councils. For who among men endowed with reason is so vile and abject as to allow such deceitful and wicked spirits to approach him? They have indeed taken care to have this Apology reprinted so that the whole world may know and have proven before it the frauds, deceits, impostures, tricks, plans and attempts of the Jesuits against kings and princes; and in general against all those who refuse to submit themselves to the tyranny of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: RELATA A CONSILIARIIS CVRIAE PAR- LAMENTI DELEGATIS AD INFORMANDVM ET INQ- VIRENDVM SVPER ILLIS, QVÆ IN COLLEGIO CLAREMONTANO IESVITÆ AGEBANT & DOCEBANT: VBI PRIMO DE IOHANNE GVIGNARDO IESVITA.
units.tr: Reported by the counsellors of the Parliament's court, deputed to inform themselves and inquire concerning those things which the Jesuits were doing and teaching in the Claremont College; where, first, concerning John Guignard, a Jesuit.

units.la: POst sumptum de Iohanne Castello supplicium, quidam Dominorum à Parlamento deputatorum, cum se in Collegium Claremontanum, ubi Iesuitæ erant, contulissent, & multas chartas scriptas deprehendissent, invenerunt inter alia duos libros, scriptos manu Iohannis Guignardi Presbyteri de Societate Iesu, qui etiam in illo Collegio Socius erat. Erant isti libelli famosi, quos illi post Edictum Amnestiæ & abolitionis generalis, per dictum Dominum Regem rebellibus suis subditis Parisiensibus, postquam Deo placuisset eosdem sub suam potestatem reducere, clementissime promulgatum, composuerat & servaverat; in quibus libellis ille non solum calumniis contra honorem defuncti Regis Henrici III. & contra successorem eius usus erat; verum etiam propositiones, plurimis salsissimis & seditiosissimis medijs refertas, conscripserat ad probandum, quòd parricidium in Rege antecessore patratum licitum suisset, perfuasionibus etiam seu inductionibus ad Regem ipsius successorem tradendum, in terminis sequentibus additis.
units.tr: After the execution of John Castel, some of the lords deputed by the Parliament went to the Claremont College, where the Jesuits were. Finding many written papers there, they discovered among other things two books written by the hand of John Guignard, a priest of the Society of Jesus, who was also a fellow of that college. These were infamous libels, which he had composed and kept after the Edict of Amnesty and general pardon, most graciously published by the said Lord King to his rebellious Parisian subjects, once it had pleased God to bring them back under his power. In these books he had not only used slanders against the honour of the late King Henry III and against his successor; he had also written out propositions, stuffed with the most foul and seditious means, to prove that the parricide committed against the former king was lawful, and also with persuasions or inducements to betray the king his successor, in the following terms added.

units.la: Nam primò, inquit: Si Anno 1572. die S. Bartholomæi venam Basilisci (sic Regem Navarrenum appellat) præcidissemus, e febri in pestem non incidissemus, quod iam comperimus. Sed quicquid delirant Reges pleCtuntur Achiui; sanguini parcendo, Galliam in ignem & sanguinem conjecerunt, & in caput reciderunt mala.
units.tr: For first, he says: If on the year 1572, on the day of St Bartholomew, we had cut the vein of the Basilisk (so he calls the King of Navarre), we would not have fallen from fever into plague, as we have now found out. But whatever kings rave about, the Achaeans suffer; by sparing blood they have cast France into fire and blood, and the evils have fallen back upon their own head.

units.la: 2. Quòd crudelis Nero per Clementem occisus, & Monachus hypocrita per manum veri Monachi è medio sublatus sit.
units.tr: 2. That the cruel Nero was killed by Clement, and that the hypocritical monk was removed from the midst by the hand of a true monk.

units.la: 3. Evocabimus nos Neronem aut Sardanapalum Gallicum, Vulpem Bearnensem, Leonem Lusitanicum, Lupam Anglicam, Gryphum Suecicum, & porcum Saxonicum?
units.tr: 3. Shall we summon a Gallic Nero or Sardanapalus, the Bearnese fox, the Lusitanian lion, the English she-wolf, the Swedish griffin, and the Saxon pig?

units.la: 4. Putasne pulchrum fuisse videre tres illos Reges, si modò Reges nominandi sunt, tyrannum defunctum, Bearnensem, & qui se Monarcham prætendebat, Antonium?
units.tr: 4. Do you think it was a fine thing to see those three kings, if they are to be called kings at all: the dead tyrant, the Bearnese, and Antony, who claimed to be monarch?

units.la: 5. Quod pulcherrimum Anagramma, quod unquam super nomine defuncti Tyranni repertum fuisset, hoc esset, quo impurus Herodes appellaretur.
units.tr: 5. What a splendid anagram it would have been, if one had ever been found on the name of the dead tyrant, namely that by which he would be called the impure Herod.

units.la: 6. Quod facinus illud Heroicum per Iacobum Clementem patratum, tanquam dum Spiritus sancti, hoc nomine à Iesuitis appellatum, per defunctum Iacobitarum primorem, Burgoinium, Confessorem & Martyrem, propter plurimas rationes tam Lutetiæ quod ego ipse, inquit Guignardus, meis auribus tum cum Iuditham suam explicaret, audivi, quam coram egregio illo Parlamento Turonensi, iure laudatum fit: id quod dictum Burgoinium, quod plus fit, sanguine suo contestatus sit, et morte propria confirmaverit, ne oporteret. rterefidem adhibereijs, quæ ab inimicis dicerentur, quòd nimirum ipse ultimùm suis facinus illud tanquam detestandum, improbaverit.
units.tr: 6. That heroic deed performed by James Clement, as if by the Holy Spirit, called by this name by the Jesuits, through the late chief of the Jacobins, Burgoing, confessor and martyr, for very many reasons, as I myself, says Guignard, heard with my own ears at Paris when he was explaining his Judith, and which that distinguished Parliament of Tours rightly praised; the more so since the said Burgoing confirmed it with his blood and by his own death, so that one ought not to give credence to those things which were said by his enemies, namely that he himself at the last had disapproved of that deed as detestable.

units.la: 7. Quòd Diadema Gallicum in aliam quam Borbonicam familiam transferri posse & debeat.
units.tr: 7. That the French crown can and should be transferred to a family other than the Bourbon.

units.la: 8. Quòd Bearnensis, licet ad fidem Catholicam reversus, mitius tamen, quàm meritus sit, tractaretur, si corona Monachalis in Cœnobio quodam benè reformato ipsi daretur, ut ibi de tantis malis Galliæ illatis pœnitentiam ageret, & Deo pro ea gratia, quòd eius mortem suam ipsum recognovisset, gratus esset.
units.tr: 8. That the Bearnese, although returned to the Catholic faith, has nevertheless been treated more gently than he deserved, if a monastic crown were given to him in some well-reformed monastery, so that there he might do penance for the great evils brought upon France, and be thankful to God for this grace, that he had recognised his own death in it.

units.la: 9. Si sine bello deponi non possit, bellum ipsi inferendum: si bellum inferri non possit, si mortua, clàm e medio tollatur.
units.tr: 9. If he cannot be deposed without war, war must be waged against him; if war cannot be waged, if he dies, he should be secretly removed from the midst.

units.la: Ex hisce propositionibus verissimè evincitur, Arrestum Parlamenti contra Iohannem Castellum parricidam declaratum, Iesuitarum quoque proscriptionem & e Regno eiectionem, continens, iustissimè factum esse, & iudicium rè divinum nominari posse: quum ex scriptis Guignardi Iesuitæ intelligatur, quàm pestifera & perniciosa sit huius generis hominum doctrina, & ad eam finem tendat.
units.tr: From these propositions it is most truly proved that the decree of the Parliament, declaring John Castel a parricide and containing also the proscription and expulsion of the Jesuits from the kingdom, was most justly done, and may be called a judgement of God itself, since from the writings of the Jesuit Guignard it is understood how pestilent and pernicious is the teaching of this kind of men, and to what end it tends.

units.la: Parlamentum cùm hæc scripta vidisset, auctorçq; eorum Guignardus de ipsi oblatis interrogatus, à se composita & suâ manu scripta agnovisset & confessus esset, Arrestum; quod sequitur, declaravit.
units.tr: When the Parliament had seen these writings, and Guignard, its author, having been questioned about the things put before him, had acknowledged and confessed that he had composed them and written them in his own hand, it declared the decree which follows.

units.la: ARRESTVM EX REGISTRIS PARLAMENTI, ET POENA CAPITALIS IOHANNIS GVIGNARDI IESVITAE.
units.tr: THE DECREE FROM THE REGISTERS OF THE PARLIAMENT, AND THE CAPITAL SENTENCE AGAINST JOHN GUIGNARD, JESUIT.

units.la: Ilso per Curiam magnæ Cameræ & Turricula Consiliarijs congregatis processu criminali per aliquem ejus Consiliarium formato, ad petitionem Procuratoris Generalis Regis, contra Iohannem Guignardum presbyterum, Collegij Claromontani in hac urbe Parisiensi Rectorem, in carceribus custodiarum Pallatij captivum, propterea quòd multi libri ab ipso compositi & ipsius manu scripti apud eum inventi fuere, qui inter cætera rudelissimi & immanissimi parricidij in Rege antecessore commissi, approbationem, ad præsentem etiam Regem occidendum inductiones & persuasiones continebant: Interrogatorijs & confessionibus dicti Guignardi, libris istis, quos composuerat & suâ manu scripserat, ipsi præsentatis, & ab eo agnitis, Conclusionibus Procuratoris Regis Generalis, dicto Guignardo coram Parlamento super criminibus ipsi objectis, & in istis libris contentis, audito & interrogato, & omnibus consideratis: Decretum est, quòd Parlamentum declaravit & declaret, istum Guignardum criminis læsæ Majestatis reum & convictum, quòd distos libros composuit & suâ manu scripsit, qui plurimas salsissimas et seditiosissimas regulas continent, quibus probare conatur, parricidium in Rege Antecessorem commissum licitum fuisse, et etiam præsentem Regem Henricum quartum occidere permissum esse. Ad cujus sceleris expiationem damnavit & damnat dictum Guignardum, ut coram principalem Ecclesiæ Parisiensis portam, ac ibi in genibus subsidens, facemque cereum ardentem duarum librarum in manu tenens, dicat & declaret, quòd scelerarè, & nefarie, & contra veritatem scripserit, Regem Antecessorem per Iacobum Clementem interfectum fuisse, & Regem nunc regnantem, nisi in bello occumbat, è medio tolli oportere. Horum autem se pœnitere, & gratiam à Deo, à Rege & à justitia precari. Hisce ductus & rapiatur in forum Grevarium, & ad palum, qui ad hanc rem ibi erit, suspendatur & stranguletur, & postea corpus mortuum per ignem, qui sub palo exabitur, in cineres redigatur. Declaravit etiam & declarat, ut omnia ejus bona fisco addicantur. Pronunciatum dictò Iohanni Guignardo, & executioni mandatum 7. mensis Ianuarij Anni 1595.
units.tr: Having met in the Great Chamber and the Tournelle, the councillors of the Court, after a criminal process had been drawn up by one of their number at the petition of the King's Procurator General, against John Guignard, priest, Rector of the College of Clermont in this city of Paris, held captive in the prisons of the Palace, on the ground that many books composed by him and written in his own hand were found in his possession, which, among other things concerning the most cruel and monstrous parricide committed against the late King, contained approval of that deed and inducements and persuasions to kill the present King also; and after the interrogations and confessions of the said Guignard, the books which he had composed and written in his own hand being presented to him and acknowledged by him, and after the conclusions of the King's Procurator General, the said Guignard having been heard and questioned before the Parliament on the crimes laid against him and contained in these books, and all things having been weighed: it is decreed that the Parliament has declared and does declare that this Guignard is guilty and convicted of the crime of high treason, in that he composed the said books and wrote them in his own hand; these books contain very many scandalous and seditious maxims, by which he attempts to prove that the parricide committed against the late King was lawful, and that it is also permitted to kill the present King, Henry IV. In expiation of this crime it has condemned and does condemn the said Guignard to go before the main gate of the Church of Paris, and there, kneeling, holding a burning wax torch of two pounds in his hand, to say and declare that he wrote wickedly, nefariously and against the truth, that the late King was killed by Jacques Clément, and that the King now reigning ought to be removed from the midst, unless he falls in war; and to declare that he repents of these things and begs grace from God, from the King and from justice. Having been drawn from there to the Place de Grève, he is to be hanged and strangled on the gibbet which will be set up there for this purpose, and afterwards his dead body is to be reduced to ashes by the fire which will be lit beneath the gibbet. It has also declared and does declare that all his goods are to be forfeited to the treasury. Pronounced to John Guignard and ordered to be executed on the 7th day of January, in the year 1595.

units.la: Dd
units.tr: Dd

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS DE IOHANNE GVERETO IESVITA.
units.tr: Concerning the Nefarious Crimes of John Gueret, Jesuit.

units.la: Eodem die instituto & peracto processu contra Iohannem Gueretum parti Ecidæ Præceptore, & Petrum Castellum Patrem, & matrem, & sorores, præsertim contra unam ex illis, quæ cum intellexisset, fratrem suum esse captum & ipsa in carcerem duceretur, Iesuitas dicto fratri suo consilium aliquod malum dedisse exclamaverat: Istis, Guereto, Petro Castello, uxore, & filiabus eius, & ipsorum servis, & ancillis, similiter & Curali D. Petri de Assisijs audtis, Arrestum sequens declaratum est.
units.tr: On the same day, proceedings were begun and completed against John Gueret, tutor to the party Ecida, and against Peter Castel the father, the mother and the sisters, especially against one of the sisters. When she learned that her brother had been arrested and that she herself was being led off to prison, she cried out that the Jesuits had given her brother some wicked advice. Having also heard the curate of St Peter de Assisiis, the court issued the following decree against Gueret, Peter Castel, his wife and daughters, and their menservants and maidservants.

units.la: EXTRACTVM EX REGISTRIS PARLA- MENTI PARISIENSIS.
units.tr: Extract from the Registers of the Parliament of Paris.

units.la: Visoà Parlamento, magnæ Camerâ, & Turriculæ Consiliarijs congregatis Procecriminali per præfectum prætorio Regio formato, & postea informationibus prodictis, ad instantiam procuratoris Generalis Regis petitoris & accusatoris contra Iohannem Gueretum Presbyterum, de congregatione & Societate nominis Iesu se denominatem, in Collegio Claremontano habitantem, & antehac Iohannis Castelli, non ita pridem per Arrestum dicti Parlamenti, morte affecti, Præceptorem; Petrum Castellum mercatorem pannarium, civem Parisiensem; Dionysiam Hazardam ipsius uxorem, parentes dicti Iohannis Castelli; Iohan. Comitem & Catharinam Castellam ejus uxorem; Magdalenam Castellam dicti Petri Castelli & Dionysiæ Hazardæ filiam, Antoninum Villierium, Petrum Russellium Thurinum, & Ludovicum Camum; ipsorum servos & ancillas; Magistrum Claudium Allemantum Presbyterum, Clericum in dicta parochia; & Magistrum Lucam Morinum Presbyterum in illa ordinarium, in carcere custodiarum Parisiensium captivos, interrogationibus, confessionibus, & denegationibus dictorum Captivorum dicto Iohanni Castello cum patre suo Petro Castello composito, inquisitione contra Petrum Castellum instituta, testibus in illa auditis cum ipso composito processu criminali Iohannis Castelli, propter execrandum & detestandum parricidium in Regem tentatum, & processu verbali executionis Arresti contra dictum Iohannem Castellum 29. proximi Decembris die declarati, conclusionibus procuratoris Generalis Regis, dictis Guereto, Petro Castello & Hazardæ super criminibus ipsis objectis, & in dicto processu contentis coram Parlamento auditis & interrogatis: Aliis interrogationibus & denegationibus per dictos Guerettu & Petrum Castellum in quæstione per instantiam Parlamenti ipsis exhibita factis omnibus consideratis: Decretum est quod dictum Parlamentum ipsis propter crimina in illo processu demonstrata, relegavit & relegat extra Regnum Franciæ dictos Guerettu, Petrum Castellum Gueretum quidem in perpetuum, & dicti Castelli ad tempus & spatium novem annorum, extra urbem & sub urbia Parisiensia in perpetuum. Indixit etiam illis, ut hanc suam relegationem observent, pœnâ suspensionis & strangulationis, sine ulla alia judicii forma in eos statuta. Declaravit & declarat, ut omnia & singula dicti Guereti bona infiscum Regium mittantur; & damnavit ac damnat dictum Petrum Castellum, ut Regi pro multa bis mille coronatos solvat, qui ad panes captivis in custodijs Palatij emendos & comparandos adplicentur & impendantur: nec ille e carceribus liberetur, priusquam dictam summam plenissime solverit, nec tempus relegationis nisi ista soluta incipiat. Statuit dictum Parlamentum, ut domus illa, in qua Petrus Castellus habitavit, deijiciatur, destruatur & planitus exscindatur, & locus ille seu area loci publicus annumeretur, ne in posterum quisquam ibi ædificare possit: quo in loco ad perpetuam hujus sceleratissimi et execrandi parricidij in Regem tentati memoriam, alta columna e lapide cæsostructa ponatur et erigatur, affixâ simul tabulâ, in qua causa dictæ demolitionis & erectæ columnæ scribantur, quâ ea pecuniâ fiet, quæ ex demolitione domus proveniet. Et quantum ad dictos Hazardam, Comitem, Catharinam & Magdalenam Castellam, Villierium, Roffelium, Thurinum, Camum, Allemantum, Bernardum & Morinum attinet, statuit dictum Parlamentum, ut carceres ipsis aperiantur. Pronunciatum dictis Hazardæ, Comiti, Catharinæ & Magdalenæ Castellis, Villierio, Roffelio, Thurino, C ,Allemanto, Bernardo & Morino 7. die Jan. & dictis Guereto & Petro Castello 10. e dicti mensis anno 1595.
units.tr: Having seen the proceedings of the Parliament, the councillors of the Grand Chamber and of the Tournelle being assembled, the criminal preliminary inquiry drawn up by the Provost of the Royal Court, and afterwards the informations laid before it, at the instance of the King's Procurator General, petitioner and accuser, against John Guéret, priest, who calls himself of the congregation and Society of the name of Jesus, living in the Collège de Clermont, and formerly tutor of John Castel, lately put to death by an Arrest of the said Parliament; Peter Castel, cloth merchant, citizen of Paris; Denise Hazard, his wife, parents of the said John Castel; John Comte and Catherine Castel, his wife; Magdalen Castel, daughter of the said Peter Castel and Denise Hazard; Antoine Villiers, Peter Rousselle of Turin, and Louis Cam; their male and female servants; Master Claude Allemant, priest, clerk in the said parish; and Master Luke Morin, priest, ordinary in that parish, held captive in the prisons of the Paris custody; the interrogations, confessions and denials of the said prisoners; the charge against John Castel, composed with his father Peter Castel; the inquiry instituted against Peter Castel; the witnesses heard in it; the criminal proceedings against John Castel, composed together with this process, on account of the execrable and detestable parricide attempted against the King; and the verbal record of the execution of the Arrest against the said John Castel, declared on the 29th day of last December; the submissions of the King's Procurator General; and the said Guéret, Peter Castel and Hazard having been heard and questioned in Parliament on the crimes laid against them and contained in the said process; the other interrogations and denials made by the said Guéret and Peter Castel in the examination put to them at the instance of Parliament, all having been considered: it is decreed that the said Parliament, on account of the crimes shown in that process, has banished and does banish from the Kingdom of France the said Guéret, and Peter Castel, Guéret indeed for ever, and the said Castel for a term of nine years, and for ever from the city and suburbs of Paris. It has also ordered them to observe this their banishment, under penalty of hanging and strangling, without any other form of judgement laid down against them. It has declared and does declare that all and each of the goods of the said Guéret are to be sent to the royal treasury; and it has condemned and does condemn the said Peter Castel to pay the King a fine of two thousand crowns, which are to be applied and spent on buying and providing bread for the prisoners in the Palace gaols; nor is he to be freed from prison until he has paid that sum in full, nor is the term of his banishment to begin unless this is paid. The Parliament orders that the house in which Peter Castel lived be pulled down, demolished and levelled to the ground, and that the site or plot be counted as public ground, so that no one may ever build there again; and that on that spot, in perpetual memory of this most wicked and execrable parricide attempted against the King, a tall column of cut stone be set up and erected, with a tablet fixed to it on which the reason for the said demolition and the erection of the column are to be written, and by what money it is to be done, which shall come from the proceeds of the demolition of the house. And as far as the said Hazard, Comte, Catherine and Magdalen Castel, Villiers, Rousselle, Turin, Cam, Allemant, Bernard and Morin are concerned, the Parliament orders that their prison doors be opened. It was pronounced to the said Hazard, Comte, Catherine and Magdalen Castel, Villiers, Rousselle, Turin, Cam, Allemant, Bernard and Morin on the 7th day of January, and to the said Guéret and Peter Castel on the 10th day of that month, in the year 1595.

units.la: Ex hoc processu videre est, quód Parlamentum in inquisitione & iudicio omnia ea adhibuerit, quae in bona, integra & sancta iustitia requiri possunt, in omnibus formis in processibus criminalibus consuetis, sic ut Arresta hoc modo decreta opus non habeant ut per quascunque rationes alias defendantur. Tamen Franciscus Verona Constantinus in sua Apologia pro Ioanne Castelparte 5. cap. 8. 9. & 10. utrumque, Gueretum & Guignardum, eorumque seditionefaria & parricidalia facta conatur defendere, & iustissima Parlamenti deeta, & supplicia de iis sumpta summae iniustitiae accusat, imo crudelitatem & crilegium appellat, quod in personis ipsorum commissum sit.
units.tr: From this process it can be seen that the Parliament, in its inquiry and judgement, employed everything that can be required in good, whole and holy justice, observing all the forms customary in criminal proceedings, so that Arrests decreed in this manner need no further defence on any other grounds. Yet Francis Verona of Constance, in his Apology for John Castel, part 5, chapters 8, 9 and 10, tries to defend both Guéret and Guignard, and their seditious and parricidal deeds, and accuses the most just decrees of Parliament and the punishments taken from them of the greatest injustice; indeed he calls it cruelty and sacrilege, committed against their persons.

units.la: DE ALIIS IESVITIS.
units.tr: Concerning Other Jesuits.

units.la: Plurima praeterea in Iesuitarum Collegio Parisiis Anagrammata contra Regem inventa sunt: quae non absimilia iis, quae apud Iohannem Castelum perta, et in scriptis Iohannis Guignardi inventa sunt; sicut & quaedam temer per Grammaticos dictata, quorum Argumentum de morte constanter suffenda, & Tyrannis invadendis erat. Praeterea cognitum est, quod Magistri Colgij Claremontani, Scholasticis suis, ne pro Rege precarentur, urbe Parisiensi b potestatem Maiestatis suae redacta, praeceperint, & eos qui ad Missam eius ent, excommunicatos esse dixerint.
units.tr: Moreover, many anagrams were found in the Jesuits' College at Paris directed against the King. They were not unlike those found among the papers of Jean Castel and of Jean Guignard. Likewise some verses were composed by the grammar masters, whose theme was the steadfast endurance of death and the invasion of tyrants. Furthermore, it became known that the masters of the Clermont College told their scholars not to pray for the King, and that, once the authority of His Majesty had been restored in the city of Paris, they ordered that those who attended his Mass should be excommunicated.

units.la: DE ALEXANDRO HAIO IESVI. TA, EIVSQVE POENA.
units.tr: ON ALEXANDER HAIUS THE JESUIT, AND HIS PUNISHMENT.

units.la: Inquisitiones insuper institutae fuerunt contra Alexandrum Haium Iesuitam, natione Scotum, qui publice docuerat, Oportere dissimulare, & Regi ad tem- per simulationem obedire, hisce verbis saepissime usus, Iesuita est omnis homo: hoc temporibus se accommodare novit, unde fan der mantel hencken nach dem der indgehet. Praeterea accusabatur hic Iesuita, quod saepe dixisset, Se velle, si Rex ud illorum Collegium praeteriret, ut ipse e fenestra in eum decideret, et collum ejus franret. His de causis Quaestione capitali contra eum instituta, & compertum, quod quaedam eius dicteria ante reductionem Parisiensium edita fuissent, mitis aliquanto quam Guignardus tractatus fuit, ut ex sequenti Arresto apparet, uod sic habet.
units.tr: Inquiries were also set on foot against Alexander Haius, a Jesuit by nationality a Scot, who had taught publicly that one ought to dissemble and, for a time, feign obedience to the King. He very often used these words: "Every man is a Jesuit; he knows how to accommodate himself to the times, so hang your cloak according to the wind that blows." This Jesuit was further accused of having often said that, if the King passed by their College, he would himself drop from a window onto him and break his neck. For these reasons a capital inquiry was instituted against him. It was found that some of his sayings had been published before the recapture of Paris, and he was treated somewhat more leniently than Guignard, as appears from the following decree, which reads thus.

units.la: EXTRACTVM EX REGISTRIS PARLAMENTI.
units.tr: EXTRACT FROM THE REGISTERS OF THE PARLIAMENT.

units.la: Visfo à Parlamento magnae Curiae & Turriculae consiliarijs congregatis, processu criminali formato & juxta consuetudinem instructo, ad postulationem Procuratoris Generalis Regis petitoris, contra Alexandrum Hajum Presbyterum, de congregatione & Societate nominis Iesu se dicentem, in carceribus custodiarum Palatij captiu- um, inquisitionibus, interrogationibus & testium compositionibus, Conclusionibus Procuratoris Regij Generalis, dicto Alexandro Hajo, super criminibus ipsi impositis & in dicto processu contentis, coram Parlamento interrogato & audito, & omnibus consideratis: Decretum est, quo dictum Parlamentum, propter crimina in dicto processu demonstrata, dictum Hajum e regno Gallico in perpetuum relegavit & relegat, ipsi injungens, ut Relegationem suam observet, poena suspensionis & strangulationis sine ulla alia judicij forma indicta. Pronunciatum dicto Hajo ad portulam dictorum carcerum propterea alligato, decimo die Januarij Anno 1595.
units.tr: Having seen the process, criminal in form and drawn up according to custom, brought by the Procurator General of the King as petitioner against Alexander Hajus, priest, calling himself of the congregation and Society of the name of Jesus, held captive in the prisons of the Palace, together with the examinations, interrogations and depositions of witnesses, and the conclusions of the King's Procurator General against the said Alexander Hajus concerning the crimes laid against him and contained in the said process; the said Alexander having been questioned and heard before Parliament, and all things having been considered: it has been decreed that the said Parliament, on account of the crimes demonstrated in the said process, has banished and does banish the said Hajus from the kingdom of France forever, enjoining him to observe his banishment, under penalty of hanging and strangulation, without any other form of judicial sentence. Pronounced to the said Hajus, who was bound at the gate of the said prisons, on the tenth day of January, in the year 1595.

units.la: DE ALIIS INQVISITIONIBVS, ET CRIMI- NIBVS IESVITARVM IN GALLIA.
units.tr: Concerning Other Inquiries and the Crimes of the Jesuits in France.

units.la: Er alias quoque inquisitiones cognitum est, quod quidam Iesuitæ, cum ijs quæreretur, quare in Gallia manerent, cum soli Papæ obedientia & fidelitatem iurarint, responderint, votum suum per hanc immorationem in Regni non violari, quoniam Breve a Pontifice accepissent, quod ipsis tempori obseq. permitteret.
units.tr: Furthermore, through other inquiries it became known that certain Jesuits, when they were asked why they remained in France, since they had sworn obedience and fidelity to the Pope alone, replied that their vow was not violated by this stay in the kingdom, because they had received a brief from the Pontiff which permitted them to yield to the circumstances of the time.

units.la: Per Inquisitiones præterea Biturigibus transmissas, & 7. Ianuarij habita compertum est, quendam, cui Francisco Iacobo nomen est, Iesuitarum in dice urbe scholarem ascisle, quod Regem occidere vellet, nisi eum iam mortuum & ab alio quodam occisum existimaret.
units.tr: Through inquiries also sent to Bourges and concluded on 7 January, it was discovered that a certain man named Francis James, a scholar of the Jesuits in that city, had conceived the intention of killing the King, unless he judged him already dead and killed by someone else.

units.la: Compertum insuper fuit, a Iesuitis multos pueros, qui eos parentibus suis rapuerant, seductos fuisse, ut in longinquas regiones secum abirent.
units.tr: It was further discovered that many boys, whom the Jesuits had snatched away from their parents, had been seduced so that they would go away with them to distant regions.

units.la: DE IOHANNE BELO IESVITA. RVM DISCIPVLO.
units.tr: Concerning John Bel, a Disciple of the Jesuits.

units.la: In primis præceptus institutus est contra quendam Iohannem Belum scho-larem, qui non ita pridem literis in Collegio Claremontano operam dederat, quod Franciscum Veroneum scholarem Pictavien-sem, literis operam dantem, contra Patris M. Pregentis Veronei in Parlamento Procuratoris voluntate seducere conatus esset, ut Iesuitas, contra inhibitionem per Arrestum Parl. intenti factas, extra Regnum Galliæ sequeretur.
units.tr: First, a charge was brought against a certain scholar, John Bel, who not long before had studied letters in the College of Clermont, because he had tried to lure Francis Veron, a scholar of Poitiers who was also studying letters, against the wishes of Master Pregent Veron, the Procurator in Parliament, so that he would follow the Jesuits outside the kingdom of France, despite the prohibition issued by the decree of Parliament.

units.la: Præterea idem Belus accusatus fuit, quod plurimas lectiones & compositiones in Societate Iesuitarum dictatas, & ab ipso, cum in eorum Collegio esset, exceptas, reservâsset, & apud se custodivisset, in quibus plurima præcepta damnata de Regibus occidendis, & approbatio ac laudatio execrandi illius parricidii in defunctum Regem designati continerentur, ut ex Arresto sequeti manifestum est.
units.tr: In addition, the same Bel was accused of having kept and stored away for himself very many lectures and compositions dictated in the Society of Jesuits, which he had taken down while he was in their college, and in which very many condemned precepts concerning the killing of kings were contained, together with the approval and praise of that execrable parricide against the late King, as is clear from the following decree.

units.la: EXTRACTVM EX REGISTRIS PARLAMENTI
units.tr: EXTRACT FROM THE REGISTERS OF PARLIAMENT

units.la: Visto a Parlamento processu criminali, per quendam ejus Consiliarium, cui hoc negotium commissum fuit, facto & formato, ad postulationem Procuratoris Generalis Regis petitoris, contra Iohannem Belum Scholarem, qui non ita pridem in hac urbe in Collegio Claremontano operam dedit literis, in carceribus custodiarum Palatij captivum, in interrogationibus super certis literis, & aliis scriptis, quæ a se scripta agnovit, ipsi facta, in conclusionibus procuratoris Generalis Regis, dicto Iohanne Belo coram Parlamento super criminibus ipsi impositis auditis & interrogatis, & omnibus consideratis: Decretum est, quod Parlamentum, propter crimina in dicto processu demonstrata, dictum Iohannem Belum damnavit & damnat, ut amendam faciat honorabilem in magna ejus Camera, in dicibus pro tribunali sedentibus, caput & pedes nudus, & induso tantum indutus, facem duorum pondo ardentem in manu tenens, & ibi in genibus subsidens dicat & declaret, quod temerarie & malo consilio Franciscum Veronem Scholarem in Academia Pictavien-si literis operam navantem, pellicere & seducere voluerit, ut supra dictos Presbyteros, Scholares Collegij Claromontani & alios illorum Societatis, contra inhibitionem Parlamenti, extra Regni limites sequeretur. Et præterea, quod imprudenter servarit & custodierit multas lectiones & compositiones per quosdam dictæ Societatis dictatas, et ab ipso exceptas, et propria manu in dicto Collegio Clarem. scriptas, multas doctrinas damnabiles contra Regib. trucidandis, & approbatione & laudatione detestandi & nefarij parricidij in Regie Antecessore Henrico 3. comisisti, cotinentes. Horum vero se pœnitere, et gratiam ac condonationem a Deo, a Rege et a Iustitia precari. Hisce peractis eū in perpetuū e Regno Galliæ relegavit. {Text at the top of the page, continuing from the previous division, set full width:} gavit & relegat, ipsi injungens, ut hanc Relegationem observet, poena suspensionis & excommunicationis, si deprehendatur, sine ulla alia judicij forma, inflicta Declaravit & declarat, ut omnia ipsius bona in fiscum Regium redigantur, ex quibus inprimis centum coronati ad reparationes necessarias custodiarum Palatij sumantur et impendantur. Decretum in Parlamento 21. Martij, & pronunciatum dicto Belo, & executioni mandatum in signa Camera dicti Parlamenti 10. die Aprilis. Anno 1595.
units.tr: Having seen the criminal process, drawn up and framed by one of its Counsellors to whom this business was committed, brought at the request of the King's Attorney General, the petitioner, against John Belus, a scholar who not long ago studied letters in this city at the Clermont College; he being held a prisoner in the prisons of the Palace; in the examinations concerning certain letters and other writings, which he acknowledged as written by himself and which were put to him; in the conclusions of the King's Attorney General; the said John Belus having been heard and questioned before Parliament on the crimes laid against him; and all things having been considered: It is decreed that Parliament, on account of the crimes shown in the said process, has condemned and condemns the said John Belus to make an honourable amends in the great Chamber of the same, before the judges sitting on the bench, bareheaded and barefoot, clothed only in a shirt, holding in his hand a torch of two pounds burning; and there, kneeling down, he shall say and declare that he rashly and with evil intent sought to entice and seduce Francis Veron, a scholar studying letters at the Academy of Poitiers, to follow the above-named priests, scholars of the Clermont College, and others of their Society, against the prohibition of Parliament, beyond the limits of the kingdom. And further, that he imprudently kept and preserved many lectures and compositions dictated by certain men of the said Society, taken down by himself and written in his own hand at the said College of Clermont, containing many damnable doctrines concerning the killing of kings, and the approval and praise of the detestable and nefarious parricide committed on the late King Henry III, his predecessor. Of these things he repents, and begs grace and pardon from God, the King and Justice. These things having been done, he has relegated and relegates him for ever from the Kingdom of France, enjoining on him that he observe this banishment, under penalty of suspension and excommunication if he is found, without any other form of judicial procedure being applied. It is declared and ordered that all his goods be brought into the royal treasury, from which first one hundred crowns shall be taken and spent on the necessary repairs of the prisons of the Palace. Decreed in Parliament on 21 March, and pronounced to the said Belus, and ordered to be carried out in the great Chamber of the said Parliament on 10 April, in the year 1595.

units.la: DE PARRICIDIO IN HENRICO IIII. GALLIA- RUM REGE PATRATO A FRANCISCO RAVAILLACO.
units.tr: On the parricide committed on Henry IV, King of France and Navarre, by François Ravaillac.

units.la: Cum Henricus 4. Galliae & Navarrae Rex, ingenti exercitu collecto, expeditionem extra regnum suum in Luliacensem Ducatum decrevisset, & vermortalitatis suae periculorumque multorum recordatus, quid Deus in festa illet nescire, Reginam coniugem suam regni gubernatricem inaugurare, Filium vero suum natu maximum futurum Regem declarare statuit. Indictis igitur Comitijs, & convocatis ad solennitatem illam Regni proceribus, cum tem is inaugurationi constitutum adesset, Rex 4.
