Martij veteris, vel 14. novi Calendarij, die, horam circiter quintam vespertinam, ascensō curru, ut & arcus triumphales, aliaque ad solennitatem illam facta praeparamenta perlustraret, & mariam deinde domum pro more suo ingrederetur, hinc inde per vicos & areas urbis Parisiorum vectus est.
units.tr: When Henry IV, King of France and Navarre, had gathered a great army and resolved on an expedition beyond his kingdom into the Duchy of Jülich, he remembered his mortality and the many dangers he had faced, and, not knowing what God had decreed for him, he determined to have his wife, the Queen, inaugurated as regent of the kingdom and to declare his eldest son the future King. Accordingly, the Estates were summoned and the nobles of the realm called together for that solemnity. When the appointed time for the inauguration had come, on 4 March, old calendar, or 14 March, new calendar, at about five in the evening, the King got into his carriage to inspect the triumphal arches and the other preparations made for the solemnity. He then intended to return home as was his custom, and was driven hither and thither through the streets and squares of the city of Paris.

units.la: Accidit autem, ut cum ad plateam Ferroneriam quam vocant, Rex in curru, Monbansonio & Espernonio Ducibus assidens, columnam advenientem contemplaretur, & impedimentum quoddam ab occursu alterius cuiusdam currus, forte fortuna ei obiceretur, Sicarius quidam ex turba currum subito invadit, & venenato ad eam rem peculiariter parato cultro utrinque acuto, Regem, sinistro pectore, sub quintam costam, ubi cordis domicilium est, geminato ictu percussit, tanta velocitate ut ipsum citius latrocinium, quam latro agnitus erit, & tam lethaliter vulneravit, ut sermo eum statim & vires defecerint. Dum igitur ei assidentes, & comitatus qui erat reliquus tam atroci & subito facto stupefacti, ad arcem statim properare aurigam iusserunt, ubi Rex animam exhalavit & mortuus est, nihilque praeter assiduas utriusque religionis hominum lamentationes & querelas auditum est.
units.tr: It happened that, when the King, seated in the carriage with the Dukes of Monbazon and d'Épernon, was looking at a column approaching at the Place de la Ferronnerie, as they call it, and a hindrance caused by another carriage coming the other way happened to block his path, a certain assassin from the crowd suddenly attacked the carriage. With a knife sharpened on both edges and specially prepared for the purpose, he struck the King twice in the left side of the chest, under the fifth rib, where the heart has its seat. He did it so quickly that the robbery was over before the robber was recognised, and he wounded him so mortally that speech and strength failed him at once. While those sitting beside him and the rest of the escort, stunned by so savage and sudden a deed, ordered the coachman to hurry at once to the palace, the King breathed his last and died. Nothing was heard but the constant lamentations and complaints of men of both religions.

units.la: Quod ad sicarium ipsum seu auctorem huius tam atrocis parricidii attinet, peracto facinore comprehensus statim & in carcerem coniectus est. Reperta sunt apud ipsum frustula quaedam panis consecrati & hostiolae, quas vocant, seu hostiae non fermentati rotundi, quorum in Missa Pontificia, & aliis in S. Coena usus est, itemque schedulae quaedam variis characteribus & litteris insignitae, in quibus ipse spem omnem positam habuerat. Interrogatus deinde & quaestioni subiectus, aliud nihil respondit, quam nomen sibi Franciscō Ravillaco esse, qui natione Gallus & quidem ex urbe Angoulesmia oriundus, ante annos aliquot ... men suum Franciscanorum mendicantium Ordini dedisset, & Monachus factus fuisset. Caeterum ad facinus hoc perpetrandum, peculiaribus quibusdam revelationibus & visionibus incitatum & impulsum, a praeterito Paschatis festo occasionem Regis interficiendi quinquies, nequicquam captasse, Laetari vero, quod tandem ex voto res successerit, nec de corpore suo sollicitum esse, licere roceribus quod velint de eo statuere. Sic igitur, eodem quo anno 1589. primo Augusti die, Regis huius antecessor, mortis genere, Henricus hic eius nominis quartus a Monacho interemptus, occubuit. Cum igitur extorqueri ex eo nihil amplius posset, lata in eum sententia, die 27. Martij, horam circiter pomeridiana... nam tertiam interulā albā indutum, & facem ardentem manibus tenentem, in templum S. Mariae currucarnifices, ut Deum ibi, Regemq; & iustitiae admi-ftros sive iudices veniam precaretur, quamvis diabolica eius lingua ad maledi-cta magis quam ad preces prona esset, duxerunt. Inde in aream Greve dictam pontemq; cum ob causam ibi excitatum, cum eo adstentes carnifices, manu eius primo, licam tenentem, cubito tenus admoto igne combusserunt, & in cinerem redegerunt, deinde forcipibus candentibus in utroque femore, brachio, pectore, reçq; convulsum, fervente oleo & liquefacto plumbo perfuderunt, praeterea infuso in ventrem eius plumbo & oleo eum excruciarunt, matre eius ad interfectionem usq; denudata, ob oculos ei posita, et stipatoribus uterum eum sua causa maledictum exquisitissimisq; iam cruciatibus destinatum esse, si forte ad agnitionem & detestationem perpetrati a se facinoris, commoveretur, nequicquam acclamantibus. Tandem cum nullum poenitentiae signum ederet, sed atroci & minaci vultu, nisi perpetratum facinus esset, etiam-num id se perpetraturum diceret, totum corpus quatuor equis in frusta raptatum & discerptum est, populo frusta illa per plateas raptante, & diris maledictionibusq; infinitis funus tam infandum prosequente, donec igni obiecta frusta omnia a carnifice in cinerem redacta sunt.
units.tr: As for the assassin himself, the author of this atrocious parricide, he was seized straight after the crime and thrown into prison. On him were found some fragments of consecrated bread and small round wafers, called hosts, of unleavened bread, which are used in the Papists' Mass and by others in the Lord's Supper; also some slips of paper marked with various characters and letters, in which he had placed all his hope. Questioned and put to torture afterwards, he answered nothing except that his name was François Ravaillac, a Frenchman born in the city of Angoulême, who some years earlier had given his name to the order of Franciscan mendicant friars and had become a monk. Moreover, he said he had been incited and driven to commit this deed by certain peculiar revelations and visions; that since the feast of Easter just past he had five times sought in vain an opportunity to kill the King; but that he rejoiced the thing had at last turned out as he wished, and that he was not anxious about his own body, and the magistrates might decide about him whatever they wished. Thus, on 1 August 1589, the predecessor of this king, Henry III, had died in the same manner, killed by a monk; and now this Henry, the fourth of that name, had perished. Since nothing more could be extracted from him, sentence was passed against him on 27 March, at about the afternoon hour. Clothed in a white linen shirt and holding a burning torch in his hands, he was led by the executioners to the church of St Mary, that he might there beg pardon of God, of the King and of the ministers of justice or judges; although his devilish tongue was more prone to curses than to prayers. From there they took him to the square called Grève and to the bridge, where a scaffold had been erected for this purpose. There the executioners, with him standing by, first burned the hand which had held the knife, applying fire up to the elbow, and reduced it to ashes. Then they tore at both thighs, arms and breast with red-hot pincers, and, as he writhed, poured boiling oil and molten lead over him. Besides this, they tortured him by pouring molten lead and oil into his belly. His mother was stripped naked up to the killing and placed before his eyes, and the bystanders cried out that the womb which bore him was cursed on his account and destined for the most exquisite tortures, if perhaps he might be moved to acknowledge and detest the crime he had committed; but in vain. At last, since he showed no sign of repentance, but with a fierce and threatening look said that, had the deed not already been done, he would still do it, his whole body was torn and dismembered by four horses, the crowd dragging the pieces through the streets and pursuing so unspeakable a funeral with countless dreadful curses, until all the pieces were thrown into the fire by the executioner and reduced to ashes.

units.la: Huius autem infandi facinoris reos fuisse Iesuitas, plurimis indiciis & coniecturis probat ac demonstrat author Refutationis literarum Cottonis Iesuitae ad Reginam viduam, in quibus hanc suspicionem a fui ordinis Socijs amovere & depellere conatur.
units.tr: That the Jesuits were guilty of this unspeakable crime is proved and demonstrated with very many indications and conjectures by the author of the Refutation of the letters of Cotton the Jesuit to the widowed Queen, in which he tries to remove and drive away this suspicion from the members of his own order.

units.la: Primo dicit, Hispanum quendam, quum primum Lutetiam Parisiorum venisset, in amicitiam & familiaritatem Cottonis Iesuitae se insinuasse, cui etiam instituta sua patefecerit. Cottonem Hispanum ad Regem duxisse, eumq; Regiae Maiestati vehementer commendasse. Post horas aliquot Regem a Dn. Forceo Gubernatore in Bearnia literas accepisse, ex quibus cognoverit, Hispanum quendam, cuius staturam, capillos & reliquum corporis habitum adscripsisset, Barcellone in Galliam proficisci statuisse, Regemq; veneno vel aliis artibus e medio tollere: ex his Regem intellexisse, Hispanum hunc illum ipsum esse, quem Iesuita Cotton ad se deduxerit. Cottonem igitur ad se vocasse, literas Forcei ei ostendisse, & legendi copiam fecisse: Iesuitam respondisse, vana, salsa & ficta haec omnia esse, Regemq; hortatum esse ne eis fidem habeat: Regem contra monuisse eum, hunc Hispanum iterum sibi sistat; cui respondisset, se deprehensum illum ad Regem reducturum; paulo post autem reversum ei significasse, se Hispanum istum investigare nusquam potuisse, ut qui iam rursus urbe excesserit, & fuga elapsus sit. &c. Quis hinc non intelligat, Cottonem iam tum conscium fuisse propositi huius Hispani, ab eo monitum, ut fuga ocyus elabatur, ne uterq; in maximum periculum veniat?
units.tr: First, he says that a certain Spaniard, when he first came to Lutetia of the Parisians, insinuated himself into the friendship and familiarity of the Jesuit Cotton, to whom he also revealed his plans. Cotton brought the Spaniard to the King and commended him very warmly to His Royal Majesty. A few hours later the King received a letter from Lord Force, governor in Béarn, from which he learned that a certain Spaniard, whose stature, hair and other bodily appearance Force had described, had resolved to set out from Barcelona for France and to remove the King by poison or other arts. From this the King understood that this Spaniard was the very man whom the Jesuit Cotton had brought to him. So he summoned Cotton, showed him Force's letter and gave him leave to read it. The Jesuit replied that all this was empty, false and made up, and urged the King not to believe it. The King, on the other hand, warned him to produce this Spaniard before him again. Cotton answered that he would bring the man back to the King once he was found. A little later he returned and reported that he could nowhere find this Spaniard, who had already left the city again and escaped by flight, etc. Who would not infer from this that Cotton already at that time knew of this Spaniard's plan, and had warned him to escape by flight as quickly as possible, so that neither of them would come into the greatest danger?

units.la: Secundo author Anticottoni scribit, post mortem Henrici III. cum iam declaratus esset Rex Henricus 4. Parisijs aliud nihil auditum esse, quam Iesuitarum seditiosos clamores, & huiusmodi conciones, in quibus auditores suos ad parricidium Henrici IIII. subinde hortarentur. Inter caeteros Commoletum Iesuitam saepe inter declamandum in haec verba erupisse: Alio Ehudo opus habemus, si fit, five Monachus is fit, five miles: hoc solum necessarium, ut Ehudum habeamus. Hordy quoq; Iesuitam, institoris supra pontem Nostrae Damae habitantis filium, in templo S. Severini publice pro concione dixisse: Hic quidem mos est Regum, ut intergentes thesauros ad sui amplitudinem & aliorum terrorem colligant, at rusticulum unum ad Regem suppriment dum sufficere. Huic concioni interfuisse dicit Anticotton, & haec verba audivisse Dn. le Grand. & Dn. de la Vau Consiliarios regios. Gontierum etiam Iesuitam dixisse, Recte bene fastum iri, si Rex interficeretur.
units.tr: Second, the author of the Anti-Cotton writes that after the death of Henry III, when Henry IV had already been proclaimed King at Paris, nothing was heard but the seditious clamours of the Jesuits and sermons of this kind, in which they repeatedly urged their hearers to the parricide of Henry IV. Among the rest, the Jesuit Commolet often burst out in these words while preaching: We need another Ehud, whether he be a monk or a soldier: this alone is necessary, that we have an Ehud. The Jesuit Hordy also, son of a shopkeeper living on the Pont Notre-Dame, publicly preached in the church of St Severin: Indeed it is the custom of kings to gather great treasures for their own greatness and the terror of others; but one little peasant is enough to dispose of the King. The Anti-Cotton says that he himself was present at this sermon and heard these words, as did Messieurs le Grand and de la Vau, royal councillors. He also says that the Jesuit Gontier said: It would turn out well and rightly if the King were killed.

units.la: Tertia Tertio refert Anticottonus, Bruxellis & Pragæ, ubi Iesuitæ dominatur, paucos dies ante cædem Regis, rumorem sparsum fuisse de obitu eius. Argentierum tiá Troiæ literas accepisse Pragâ à filiorû fuorû præceptore, in quibus inter alia scriptum fuerit, Iesuitam quendam sibi paulò ante parricidium hoc indicâsse, Regem mortuum esse; nec Delphinû, sed Regem Hispaniæ, Galliæ Regem creatum iri. Dixisse etiâ prætorem Poictiers, qui Iesuitarû familiarissimus fuerit, & quibus filiû suû erudiendû tradiderit, in ludo pilæ, Rex nostER hodierno die aut mortuus, aut graviter vulneratus est.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Anti-Cotton reports that at Brussels and Prague, where the Jesuits hold sway, a rumour of the King's death had spread a few days before the slaying. Argentier at Troyes received a letter from Prague, from the tutor of his sons, in which, among other things, it was written that a certain Jesuit had told him shortly before this parricide that the King was dead, and that not the Dauphin but the King of Spain would be made King of France. The provost of Poitiers also, who was a very close friend of the Jesuits and to whom he had entrusted his son for education, said while playing tennis: "Our King has either died or been gravely wounded today."

units.la: Quarto testatur, crastino die, post perpetratum hoc parricidium, cum aula regia, totaq; Lutetia in summo mœrore & luctu versarentur, animadversum fuisse, solos Iesuitas ridere & hilari vultu in arce regia, quâ Louure vocat, obambulâsse: oes etiâ Monachorû ordines, uno Iesuitarum excepto, ad exequias funeris regij cohonestandas convenisse, solos Iesuitas, licet longè plura & maiora beneficia, quàm reliqui Ordines omnes à Rege acceperint, in funeris comitatu non apparuisse, quod multis bonis suspicione non leuem movit. Didicerut sæpe hanc artem boni isti Socij, si Dijs placet, à Tiberio & Iulia, qui, quû Germani veneno suffulti fuissent, publicè in luctu comparere noluerunt, ne populus animadvertat eorum luctum & dolorem tantùmmodò simulatum esse.
units.tr: Fourthly, he testifies that on the day after this parricide was committed, while the royal court and all of Paris were in the deepest grief and mourning, it was noticed that only the Jesuits were laughing and walking about with cheerful faces in the royal citadel, which they call the Louvre. He also says that all the orders of monks, except one Jesuit, gathered to honour the king's funeral rites, but only the Jesuits, although they had received far more and greater benefits from the king than all the other orders, did not appear in the funeral procession, which gave rise to no small suspicion in many good men. These good fellows, so help me God, have often learned this trick from Tiberius and Julia, who, when their kinsman had been carried off by poison, refused to appear publicly in mourning, lest the people notice that their grief and sorrow were only pretended.

units.la: Exhis omnibus apparet, atrocissimi huius parricidij à Ravilliaco commissi, iniuratores & impulsores vel saltem consciós fuisse Iesuitas, nec hoc solû Gallia, sed Germania, aliæq; nationes constanter credidêrunt. Certè consciós & approbatores eius fuisse Iesuitas, ex modo adductis indicijs, exeplis & coniecturis quivis facile intelligere poterit. Nihil interest aut inter fuisse & approbatore facti, Cicerone este in Antonium. Vel si hoc quoq; non sit, saltem inter alia doctrinam Iesuitarum parricida iste secutus est. Nã Mariana Hispanus Iesuita in lib. de Institut. Regis efferdit, Litere subito Regem suû tyrannum occidere. Docet etiam alij Iesuitæ, ut inã indicaritur, Hæreticos & fautores eorum, potissimum vero relapsos, tum divino, tum humano jure morti addictos, ab hominibus privatis, si quidè aliter fieri nequeat, occidi posse, sicut apparet ex cap. 8. & seqq. part. 2. Apologiæ Francisci de Verona Constantiniprolohanè Castello. Et ipsemet Ravilliacus, cùm in tortura interrogaretur, quibus hoc haberet, confessus est, se audivisse sæpius in concionibus Iesuitarum id cere hoc. Cui etiâ cum Rávillíaco aliquid negotij fuit, quiq; eû probè exploavit, facilè deprehendere potuit, cùm in omnibus religionis capitibus prorsus udem, in hac vero quæstione, Num liceat privato homini, cùm, quem ipse pro tyranno habeat, occidere? quàm diligentissimè imbutum & institutum fuisse, & omnia Iesuitarum effugia & distinctiones plus satis cognitas habuisse.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear that the instigators and promoters of this most atrocious parricide committed by Ravaillac, or at least his accomplices, were the Jesuits; and not only France but Germany and other nations have consistently believed this. That the Jesuits were accomplices in and approvers of it, anyone can easily understand from the evidence, examples and conjectures just cited. It makes no difference whether one was an accomplice or an approver of the deed, as Cicero says against Antony. Or even if this is not so, at least this parricide followed the Jesuits' doctrine among other things. For the Spanish Jesuit Mariana, in his book on the institution of the king, writes that if a king becomes a tyrant, he may be suddenly killed. Other Jesuits also teach, as is shown elsewhere, that heretics and their supporters, especially relapsed ones, who are condemned to death by both divine and human law, may be killed by private persons if this cannot otherwise be done; as appears from chapter 8 and following of part 2 of the Apology of Francis of Verona, by Constantine Lohanè Castello. And Ravaillac himself, when questioned under torture as to where he had got this idea, confessed that he had often heard it preached in the sermons of the Jesuits. Also, anyone who had dealings with Ravaillac and examined him closely could easily discover that he had been thoroughly steeped and instructed in exactly the same teaching on all the heads of religion, and in this question in particular, whether a private man may lawfully kill one whom he himself holds to be a tyrant, and that he knew all the Jesuits' evasions and distinctions only too well.

units.la: CAPVT IV. DE CONIVRATIONIBVS, TVR- BIS, SEDITIONIBVS, PARRICIDIIS à IESVITIS IN ANGLIA EXCITATIS, ALIISQVE HORRENDIS ET INAVDITIS AB IISDEM IBIDEM PERPE- TRATIS FACINORIBVS.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. CONCERNING THE CONSPIRACIES, TUMULTS, SEDITIONS AND PARRICIDES STIRRED UP IN ENGLAND BY THE JESUITS, AND THE OTHER HORRIBLE AND UNHEARD-OF CRIMES PERPETRATED THERE BY THE SAME MEN.

units.la: Duuardus Coke Eques Auratus, Attornatus Regius in Anglia in Accusatione Henrici Garneti Iesuitarũ in Anglia Superioris, publicè coram iudicibus testatus, à primo Iesuitarũ in Angliam ingressu, adhuc usq; die, nunquã quadriennium integrũ effluxisse, in quo non coniurationes, turbas, proditiones, parricidia, seditiones in perniciẽ Regni totius machinati sint & excitârint Iesuitæ. Imò non solùm in Angliæ regno, sed etiam in aliis regionibus commorantes Iesuitas, vel ipsos varia ac proditoria in ipsfe adversus regnum illud, eiusq; legitimum magistratum consilia, vel alios ut id facerent hortatos esse, & in proposito anguinolento ac parricidiali vehementer confirmasse. Et veritatem illum dixisse, ex sequentibus etiam exemplis manifestissimum fiet.
units.tr: Edward Coke, Knight, the King's Attorney in England, in the prosecution of Henry Garnet, Jesuit in England, declared publicly before the judges that, from the first entry of the Jesuits into England up to the present day, there has never been a full four-year period in which the Jesuits have not plotted and stirred up conspiracies, disturbances, betrayals, murders and seditions for the ruin of the whole kingdom. Indeed, not only the Jesuits living in the kingdom of England, but also those residing in other countries, have either themselves devised various treacherous plans against that kingdom and its lawful government, or have urged others to do so, and have strongly confirmed them in their bloody and murderous purpose. And that he spoke the truth will become most evident from the following examples as well.

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: Of the Nefarious Crimes

units.la: Guilielmus Parrius Iurisconsultus tenuiori quidem loco seu fortuna natus, sed ingenio tamen exquisito praeditus, eoque non parum arrogans & elatus, postquam in Anglia, quae ipsi patria fuit, non adeo probe rem curasset familiarem, quin omnia potius sua, sed & coniugis suae bona foede dilapidasset, ac insuper etiam nobilem quendam in ipsiusmet habitaculo perimere conatus fuisset, in Galliam anno 1582. ac deinceps in Italiam profectus est. Venetiis igitur existens notitiam ac familiaritatem haud vulgarem cum P. Benedicto Palmio contraxit, cuius etiam suasu & auctoritate Reginam Angliae, Principem Patriae suae legitimam, e medio tollere, & huic uti succederet Scotiae Regina, viam itaque inere propositum: quo in proposito a Iesuitis Lugdunensibus, cum isthac transfret, valide confirmatus fuit. Parisiis demum inter Anglos istos e Patria fugitivos nobiles offendit quendam nomine Thomam Merganum, qui pollicebatur ipsi praeterea, se statim, ubi propositum istud in Anglia suum illic produxisset et in actum, effecturum esse, ut ex Scotia copiae mitterentur eo non exiguae, quibus regnum illud Reginae Scotiae adsereretur. Etsi vero Anglicani quidam sacrificuli, nominatim autem Vuatelius quidam, istud propositum nequaquam adprobarunt, quinimo publice tantum non refutarunt ac damnarunt; confirmavit tamen ipsum in hoc ac corroboravit Parisiis Iesuita Pater Hannibal Codretò, cui animi sui sensum ac propositum in confessione prius aperuerat; eumque deinceps ad communionem una cum aliis, secundum istorum morem & consuetudinem usurpandam adhortatus fuit, & instanter ipsi persuasit, istum Vuatelium, & quicunque tandem a proposito tam pio vellent eum avertere perversos haereticos esse. Ita demum in Angliam Parrius ille, & ad ipsam quidem Reginam in Februario anni 1585. se contulit, eique devarijs non minus callidis quam callidis, eoque valde periculosis transfugarum ex Anglia adversus Regiam ipsius Maiestatem consilijs multa memoravit, & quod ipsemet eorum se tantumnon participem reddiderit, offendit; quod tamen aliud in finem factum haud quaquam fuerit, quam ut eo certius indicium Maiestati Reginae praebere, sicque ipsam fideliter praemonere posset. Quia vero partim erant venenata ista indicia, partim vero ipsi Reginae non prorsus ignota; factum est ut in re aliquis ipsi plus quoque fidei tribueret, sicque in aula secum eum detineret, & a secretioretm tractationem seu communicationem interdum admitteret. Quo facto porro, ut in venatione quadam damarum apud Reginam ille solus aliquandiu versaretur in sylva, cum a ministris suis semota longius, sub arbore nonnihil requievisset, descendisset ab equo: ubi bis eum incessit libido perimendi ipsam, quo tamen nefario scelere tum fiduciae erga se Reginae tam insignis consideratione retractus fuit. Verum alio post tempore, quum iuxta Reginam in horto regiae arcis Vuidthalia Londini ad Tamesim idem a coena obambularet, & de navicula ad fugam perpetrato facinore capessendam adcommoda sibi iam prospexisset, atque vesperitinas solummodo tenebras aliquantum profundiores expectaturus esset, praeter expectationem eius evenit, ut Regina maturius a Palatium & conclave suum inde se reciperet, eo quod sequenti die venam incidendam curatura esset; cuius etiam gratia Parrium ipsum gratiose admodum & adridenti similis tum fuit affata, dixitque: Tantum sanguinis sibi non iri demtum aut minutum, quantum multi forsan exoptarent. Postquam igitur & haec ipsi fuit elapsa occasio, putavit tandem alio sibi ad exsequendum suum propositum opus esse nonnullo: ideoque rem omnem nobili cuidam Edmundo Nevilsio, quem ex multis ultro citroque habitis & collatis sermonibus ac circumstantiis, item aliis ab ea alienum esse persuasum habebat, aperuit & concredidit; & eidem porro offendit, qua ratione tum caedem illam perpetrare, tum vero naviculae beneficio fugae uga difabi, & sic ambo semet usquequaque salvare, & ab omni denique periculo liberare possent. Is autem etsi varie cogitationibus aliquandiu fluctuarit, & distractus hinc inde fuerit, horrendam tamen ac detestandam immanitatem aimo suo neutiquam probare potuit, quin universam isthanc rationem Reginae andem exhibere, sicque de periculo ipsam praemonere constituit: quod in Feruario demum anno millesimo quingentesimo octuagesimo quarto cordate praetitit: unde consequuta fuit amborum captivitas, in qua commemorata iam omnia assi sunt. In prima nec dum violenta causae cognitione Parrius nullius plane onspirationis adversus Reginam faciae conscium se volebat agnoscere, quod i-si vel maxime postea nocuit. Haec enim intempestiva eius negatio, tum spontanea vicissim confessio, Nevillii contestatio, & ipsiusmet reperta scripta & inicia multa effecerunt, utin publico damnatus iudicio, primo quidem suspensus, deinde vero statim a laqueo praefecatus, & dissectus, adeoque exenteratus erit, quo nimirum intestina eius ipsomet adhuc vivente & vidente concremanter; quae tandem omnia decollatio insecuta fuit, & corporis denique differatio & in quatuor partes distractio.
units.tr: William Parry, a jurist of humble rank and fortune but of keen intellect, and for that reason not a little arrogant and self-important, did not manage his affairs in England, his native country, so honestly. Instead he squandered his own goods and those of his wife shamefully, and he moreover tried to kill a certain nobleman in his own house. In 1582 he went to France and then, after that, to Italy. Staying at Venice, he formed a not inconsiderable acquaintance and friendship with Father Benedetto Palmio. At his urging and with his authority, Parry resolved to remove from the world the Queen of England, the lawful prince of his country, so that the Queen of Scots might succeed her. He set out on this course, and when he crossed over, he was firmly confirmed in this purpose by the Jesuits of Lyons. At last, at Paris, among those English nobles who had fled from their country, he met a certain Thomas Morgan, who further promised him that, as soon as he had brought this plan into effect in England, he would ensure that no small forces were sent from Scotland to secure that kingdom for the Queen of Scots. Although certain English priests, and especially one Watson, by no means approved of this plan, and indeed publicly all but refuted and condemned it, Father Hannibal Codretto, a Jesuit at Paris, confirmed and strengthened him in it. Parry had first disclosed to him the feeling and purpose of his mind in confession. Codretto then urged him to take communion, in the manner and custom of those men, along with others, and he earnestly persuaded him that Watson, and whoever else tried to turn him from so pious a purpose, were perverse heretics. So Parry at last came into England, and in February 1585 he presented himself to the Queen herself. To her he related many things about the plans of the fugitives from England against Her Majesty, plans that were various, no less cunning than dangerous. He also gave the impression that he had almost become a participant in them himself. Yet this was done for no other end than to give Her Majesty a more certain indication and so faithfully forewarn her. But since these disclosures were partly poisonous, and partly not entirely unknown to the Queen, it came about that some trust was placed in him, and she kept him at court and at times admitted him to more secret dealings. After this, once, while hunting does in the park, he was alone for a while in the wood, having gone some distance from the Queen's attendants. He had rested under a tree and dismounted from his horse. Twice a desire to kill her assailed him, but he was held back from that wicked crime by consideration of the Queen's so remarkable trust in him. Later, however, when he was walking near the Queen in the garden of the royal citadel at Whitehall by the Thames, having come from supper, and had already arranged a boat for escape after committing the deed, and was waiting only for the evening shadows to deepen somewhat, it happened beyond his expectation that the Queen withdrew earlier to her palace and chamber, because the next day she was to have a vein opened for treatment. She addressed Parry very graciously, as if smiling, and said that not as much blood would be drawn from her as many perhaps wished. When this opportunity had also slipped away, he thought he needed some other occasion to carry out his purpose. So he disclosed the whole matter to a certain nobleman, Edmund Neville, whom he was convinced, from many conversations and circumstances weighed back and forth, and from other evidence, was not averse to it. He set out for him the way in which they could both commit the murder and then escape by boat, and so save themselves wholly and free themselves from every danger. Neville, though he wavered for a time in various thoughts and was pulled this way and that, could not bring himself to approve in his mind such a horrible and detestable atrocity. He resolved instead to reveal the whole plan to the Queen and so warn her of the danger. He did this in February in the year 1584 [sic, 1585], and the result was the arrest of both men, in which all the things mentioned have now been set forth. At the first, not yet forcible, examination of the case, Parry wished to declare that he was aware of no conspiracy at all against the Queen's person, and this later did him great harm. For this ill-timed denial, then his voluntary confession in turn, Neville's testimony, and the many papers and signs of his own that were found, brought it about that he was condemned in public judgment: first hanged, then at once taken down from the noose while still alive, and disembowelled, so that his entrails were burned while he was still living and watching. All this was followed by beheading, and finally the division of the body and its quartering into four parts.

units.la: Executio autem haec facta est secundo Maii anno 1584. ad quam se tunica Parrii ex holosericeo Damascemo confecta indutus, & segmentato, nec non amyato, exindeque admodum extenso & erecto focali, pro temporis illius vestienti ratione, exornatus ita compositus erat, actu recta ad nuptias pergere vellet: cut & a carnifice postularet non est veritus, ut in diffibulatione seu restrictione etium illius focalis rationem habere vellet, ne forte attritum aut conquassaum petisset mandaretur.
units.tr: This execution was carried out on the second of May, 1585. Parry was dressed in a tunic of Damascene silk, with slashed and wide sleeves, and with a ruff that was then very large and stiff in the fashion of the time. He was arranged so neatly that he seemed about to go straight to a wedding. He was not ashamed to ask the executioner to take care, when unbuttoning or loosening that ruff, that it should not be rubbed or crushed.

units.la: Anno 1588. ingens exercitus ex Hispania in Angliam traiicere, regnumque illud recuperare & Hispaniarum Regi subjicere conatur, quem etiam benedictione sua apa dignatus est, & Invicta classis nomine insignivit, constabat enim 158. navibus commeatu, omnique genere armorum bellicorum instructissima erat. Regina ut Angliae auxilio Dei omnipotentis & subditorum suorum virtute hanc classem fiecit, pugnantibus pro ea igni, mari, scopulis, ventis & procellis, & ex 158. navibus vix 40. in portum pervenerunt. Huius Classis praevii & praenuntii Iesuitae citurfuiffe in Actis Garnetti pag. 76. qui ante biennium in Angliam traiecerant, ut coniurationes, proditiones & turbas contra Reginam concitarent.
units.tr: In 1588 a huge army was attempted to be carried from Spain into England, to recover that kingdom and subject it to the King of Spain. The Pope also honoured this with his blessing and named it the Invincible Armada. For it consisted of 158 ships, and it was very well equipped with provisions and every kind of military weapon. But by the help of Almighty God and the courage of her subjects, the Queen defeated this fleet, since fire, sea, rocks, winds and storms fought for England. Of the 158 ships, scarcely forty reached port. That the Jesuits were the forerunners and heralds of this fleet is clear from the Acts of Garnet, p. 76, who had crossed into England two years earlier in order to stir up conspiracies, betrayals and disturbances against the Queen.

units.la: Cum igitur aperto Marte infeliciter a parte Hispaniarum Regis debellatum esset anno 88. mox alia tentarunt via rem aggredi Iesuitae. Nam anno 1592. traiecit in Angliam Patricius seu Patakius Cullen, instigantibus eum Guilielmo Stanley, quite aurato, Hugone Owen, Iacobo Fraunces, & Holte Iesuita, cuius cosilio in Reginae caede armatus, in eum finem peccatorum remissionem & Eucharistia ab eo percepit. Persuasit etiam illi, parricidium hoc non tam per leges licere, quam divinum avore deinceps: subiecitque Iacobus iste, vilis lotricis filius, qui a multis iam annis una cum Cullen & aliis Reginae exitium machinatus fuit, Respublica Anglicana fundata constat, & constabit, ut nisi tollatur Domicella illa Elizabetha, totius Acheonis furiae eam convellere & labefactare nequaquam possint.
units.tr: Therefore, after the King of Spain's side had been unsuccessfully defeated in open war in 1588, the Jesuits soon tried to attack the matter by another route. For in 1592 Patrick, or Patacius, Cullen crossed into England, urged on by William Stanley, a knight, Hugh Owen, James Fraunces, and Holt, a Jesuit. With his counsel he armed himself for the Queen's murder, and from him he received remission of sins and the Eucharist for that purpose. This James, the son of a vile laundress, who for many years already had plotted the Queen's destruction together with Cullen and others, also persuaded him that this parricide was permitted not so much by the laws as by divine approval. He added that the English commonwealth is founded, and will remain so, on the principle that unless that Lady Elizabeth is removed, all the Furies of Acheron cannot overturn and undermine it.

units.la: Proditionem istius Cullen comitatus est liber, cui nomen Philopater, in huiusmodi patrocinium, a Crefvello Iesuita, qui tunc in Hispania agebat, conscriptus.
units.tr: Cullen's treason was accompanied by a book entitled Philopater, written in defence of it by Creswell, a Jesuit who was then active in Spain.

units.la: Vicesimo anno Reginae Elisabethae Campianus Iesuita, magna comitante eum caterva eius farinae hominum, in Angliam venit eo consilio, ut rudem plebecu-lam Papistis adiungeret, & Pij V. Papae Bullae exsecutionem promoveret, qua Ecclesias eius ex Ecclesiae gremio eliminata & regno exuta fuit, omnesque, qui ei debitam obedientiam praestarent diris devoti: Unde in Boreali parte Angliae bellio, ingensque tumultus concitatus est.
units.tr: In the twentieth year of Queen Elizabeth, Campian the Jesuit came into England with a large band of men of the same stamp. His aim was to win the common rabble to the Papists and to advance the execution of the bull of Pope Pius V, by which she was cast out of the bosom of the Church and stripped of her kingdom, and by which all who rendered her due obedience were devoted to curses. Hence war and great tumult were stirred up in the northern part of England.

units.la: De hoc proposito Thuanus lib. 74. pag. 8. sic fere scribit. Angliae Regina Elizabetha de sicariis & parricidis admonita, homines fidos misit Durocortorum Remorum, ubi Se-
units.tr: On this undertaking Thuanus, book 74, page 8, writes roughly as follows. Queen Elizabeth of England, warned about assassins and parricides, sent trusted men to Reims, where

units.la: Parricida Executio minarium Anglorum erat. Hi exploratores ob religionem patria aut pulsos, aut sponte exules simulantes, arcana sociorum rimabantur, & Reginam postea secretorum consiliorum certiorem faciebant, & nomina conjuratorum ac sociorum edebant. Miserat & Romam alios, ubi maioris moli consilia contra ipsam coquebantur. Eorum delatione captus Everardus Hansius Sacerdos Prid. Calend. Sextil. jam capite luerat. Ijsdem indicibus cognitum esset, Edmundum Campianum Londinensem, Radulfum, Schuervinum & Alexandrum Briantum, qui Iesuitico Sodalitio nomen dederant, a Thoma Golduello Asaphensi Episcopo, quijam octogenarius Româ obiit in Galliam venerat, persuasos diversis itineribus in Britanniam clam appulisse, misi qui latentes vestigarent. Prodenti Georgio Elioto, capitur Campianus; socij alio atque alio loco; eculeoque torti, postremo a duodecim viris ad mortem, tanquam perduelles damnati, & Calend. Decemb. anno 1581. summo supplicio affecti sunt. Iis crimini datum fuit, quod in transmarinis regionibus pestem & perniciem Reginae machinati essent, de ipsa regno sedibusque exturbanda cogitassent, populi & quorundam e nobilitate fidem solicitassent: ac producti sunt contra eos testes Georgius Eliotus, Crodocus, Sledanus, Mondaus, Hillaeus, qui de conjuratione eadem faciebant: nam sibi compertum dicebant, conjuratis constitutum esse, ut 50. deletis armata vestibus tegentes impetu facto Reginam, & cum ea Dudlaeum Lecestriae Comitem, magnum Thesaurarium, & Valsingamum Secretarium interficerent, captata occasione cum illa animi gratia regni partem aliquam videret: tum facinore perpetrato primarius quidam vir, cuius nomen non edebatur, exclamaret, Vivat Regina Maria. Addebant consilia illa Burocortori & Romae agitata fuisse. Damnati ergo ad Patibulum, ut conjurationis & consiliorum socij, sic eundem vitae exitum habuerunt.
units.tr: Parricida. The aim of the English threats was execution. These spies, pretending to be exiles who had been driven from their country on account of religion or had gone into exile of their own accord, searched out the secrets of their associates. Afterwards they informed the Queen of the secret counsels and gave her the names of the conspirators and their allies. They had also sent others to Rome, where plans of greater scale against her were being hatched. Through their information Everard Hanse, a priest, had already paid for it with his life on 31 July. By the same informers it was learned that Edmund Campian of London, Ralph Sherwin and Alexander Bryant, who had enrolled in the Jesuit fellowship, had been persuaded by Thomas Goldwell, Bishop of St Asaph, who was already eighty years old and later died at Rome, to come to France and had secretly landed in Britain by different routes. I sent men to track them down while they lay hidden. Campian was captured through the betrayal of George Eliot; his associates were taken at one place and another. After being tortured on the rack, they were finally condemned to death as traitors by twelve men and on 1 December 1581 suffered the extreme penalty. They were charged with having plotted in foreign lands the ruin and destruction of the Queen, with having considered driving her from the kingdom and from her seat, and with having tried to seduce the people and some of the nobility. Witnesses were produced against them: George Eliot, Crodock, Sledan, Mondy and Hill, who testified about the same conspiracy. For they said it had been settled among the conspirators that fifty chosen men, concealing weapons under their clothes, would make an attack and kill the Queen, together with Dudley, Earl of Leicester, the Lord Treasurer, and Walsingham, the Secretary, seizing the opportunity when she was enjoying the sight of some part of the kingdom. Then, once the deed was done, some leading man, whose name was not given out, would cry, "Long live Queen Mary." They added that these plans had been discussed at Reims and at Rome. Condemned to the gallows as partners in the conspiracy and its plans, they met that end of life.

units.la: Anno 1594. in Angliam appulerunt Wuilliam & Yorke, in Reginae caedem accincti: & ad hoc tam detestandum facinus in se suscipiendum suasu & adhortationibus Iesuitae Holte & aliorum eius gregis: & ut id alacrius perpetrarent Wuilliam, Yorke, alijque Iesuitae Eucharistiam ab Holte acceperunt. Huic autem proditioni librum adiunxerunt, a Iesuita Perfonio, qui Romae Rectoris munere fungebatur, compositum, de Titulis, Dolemani nomine fucatum exfigmentis, mendaciis & contumeliis totum confusum & consarcinatum.
units.tr: In 1594 William and York landed in England, girded for the murder of the Queen. To undertake this most detestable crime they were moved by the persuasion and exhortation of the Jesuit Holt and others of his flock. So that they might carry it out more eagerly, William, York and other Jesuits received the Eucharist from Holt. To this treachery they added a book, written by the Jesuit Parsons, who was then acting as Rector at Rome, on the Titles, disguised under Dolman's name, wholly jumbled together and patched up from fictions, lies and insults.

units.la: Anno 1597. Iesuita Richardus Vualpot, qui ab aliis Vualsode appellatur, ex Hispania in Angliam traiecit, ut rem ferro dolisque toties tentatam, alio modo perficeret. Nam Anglum Eduardum Squirre veneno instruxit, quod Reginae Angliae & Essexio Comiti non edendum aut bibendum praeberet, sed quo sellam tantum Reginae inungeret, ut ex eius contactu uterq; moreretur. Ab hoc Iesuita, post venia peccatis concessam, Sacramento adactus est Squirreus, ut negotium exequatur, idq; silentio supprimat. Memoriale Ligae Tom. 4. pag. 15. & seqq.
units.tr: In 1597 the Jesuit Richard Walpole, whom others call Walsode, crossed over from Spain to England, to accomplish by another means a thing so often attempted with steel and trickery. For he equipped the Englishman Edward Squire with poison, to be given to the Queen of England and the Earl of Essex, not to eat or drink, but with which he was merely to anoint the Queen's chair, so that both would die on touching it. After this Jesuit had granted him pardon for his sins, Squire was bound by oath to carry out the business and keep it silent.

units.la: Has coniurationes & proditiones omnes authores ipsi sponte & libere confessi sunt, propria uniuscuiusque manu exaratas, quod Attornatus Regius in Anglia tabulis obsignatis in Accusatione adversus H. Garnetum Iesuitam, demonstrari posse affirmat pag. 72.
units.tr: The authors themselves freely and voluntarily confessed all these conspiracies and treasons, each having written them out in his own hand. The King's Attorney in England affirms that these can be shown in sealed documents in the Accusation against H. Garnet the Jesuit, p. 72.

units.la: Anno 1601, quum artes proditoriae in Anglia deficerent, viribus iterum aggrediendam statuerunt. Nam mense Decembri Henricus Garnetus Iesuitarum in Anglia Superior, Robertus item Tesmondus Iesuita, Robertus Catesby, vir ingenio subacto & versuto, profunda perfidia, cum Francisco Treshamo & aliis, Anglorum Romanae-Catholicorum nomine & causa, Thomam Vuinterum in Hispaniam ablegarunt, illiq; Garnetus literas commendatitias Crefuuello Iesuitae, in Hispania tum agenti, perferendas dedit. Vuinter Tesmond, alias Greneeteay Iesuita, & unus ex coniuratis, comite sese adiungit.
units.tr: In 1601, when treacherous arts failed in England, they resolved to attack again by force. For in December Henry Garnet, Superior of the Jesuits in England, Robert Tesmond the Jesuit, and Robert Catesby, a man of disciplined and crafty wit and deep perfidy, together with Francis Tresham and others, in the name and cause of the English Roman Catholics, sent Thomas Winter into Spain, and Garnet gave him letters of recommendation to be delivered to Creswell the Jesuit, then active in Spain. Winter was joined as companion by Tesmond, alias Greenway, a Jesuit and one of the conspirators.

units.la: Legationis summa, Vuintero inprimis demandata, haec erat, apud Hispaniarum Regem Anglorum Romanae-Catholicorum nomine instaret, ut Rex exercitum in Angliam transmitteret, cui Romanae-Catholici in Anglia copias suas adiungerent. fungere, fidelemq; illi operam navare velint. Praeterea cum Hispaniarū Rege geret, ut pensiones annuas nonnullis Romane-Catholicis Anglis, & Maiestati us devotis, assignaret. Necnon eidē Regi significaret, plures in Anglia esse nobiles & virōs militares, rerum praesentium status pertæsos, quorum inopiam blevādo facile in suas partes pertraheret. Cūq; maxima difficultas hucusq; ex uorū trāsvectione intervenerit, quotiescunq; de Anglia invadenda deliberatū et, Romane-Catholicorū Anglorum nomine certò Hispaniarum Regi protterent, quòd in omnes occasiones 1500. vel etiam 2000. equos instructos, qui si militarent, educturi sint.
units.tr: The sum of the embassy, entrusted chiefly to Winter, was this: that in the name of the English Roman Catholics he should press the King of Spain to send an army into England, to which the Roman Catholics in England would add their forces and render faithful service. Besides, he was to deal with the King of Spain to assign annual pensions to some English Roman Catholics devoted to his Majesty. He should also tell the same King that there were many nobles and military men in England weary of the present state of affairs, whose need he could easily relieve and so draw them to his side. And since the greatest difficulty hitherto had arisen in transporting horses, whenever it was resolved to invade England, they should assure the King of Spain in the name of the English Roman Catholics that on every occasion they would produce 1,500 or even 2,000 fully equipped horses, which would serve if needed.

units.la: Haec mandata cum a Iesuitis & aliis coniurationis sociis Thomas Vuinter accepisset, & una cum Tesmundo in Hispania appulisset, Crefuuello Iesuita interuncio Petru Francesfam secundum Secretarium convenit, eiq; rem totam comunicavit, ut etiā Duci Lermaeo, qui asseveravit, hunc nuncium Hispaniarū Regi atissimum fore, seq; ad hoc negotiū promovendum nequaquam defuturum.
units.tr: When Thomas Winter had received these instructions from the Jesuits and the other associates of the conspiracy, and had landed in Spain together with Tesmond, Creswell the Jesuit, acting as intermediary, met Pedro de Franqueza, the second Secretary, and communicated the whole matter to him, as also to the Duke of Lerma. The Duke assured them that this message would be most welcome to the King of Spain, and that he himself would by no means fail to promote this business.

units.la: De loco in quo Hispanorum copiae exponerentur ut Angliam invaderent, inc in modum convenit. Si maiores essent, instructaeq; Spinolae triremibus, antium & Effexiae, opportunissimae; Sin autem minores essent copiae & Anglom subsidio considerent, Milfordum in Vuallia portum commodissimum fore.
units.tr: As to the place where the Spanish forces should land to invade England, they agreed as follows. If the forces were larger and equipped with Spinola's triremes, Antium and Essex would be most suitable. But if the forces were smaller and were to be supported by English help, Milford in Wales would be the most convenient port.

units.la: Rex Hispaniarum, qui Angliae Reginae iam ante infensissimus erat, legatione nc clementer audivit, & Angliae Romane-Catholicos no minus qua suos Catholicos sibi curae esse respondit. Sed ad plenius responsum Vuinterus aulam Reg illa aestate comitari iubetur; demūq; Comes Mirandae illi significavit, Regi oooo. aureos expensurum, quorum altera pars eodem anno, altera vere subsquete persolveretur; simulq; postulavit, ne Angli Romane-Catholici fide salrent, vere enim proximo ineunte Regium exercitum in Angliam traiecturum.
units.tr: The King of Spain, who was already most hostile to the Queen of England, listened to the embassy kindly and replied that the English Roman Catholics were no less a concern to him than his own Catholics. For a fuller answer Winter was ordered to accompany the court that summer. Finally the Count of Miranda told him that the King would spend four thousand gold crowns, one half of which would be paid that same year and the other half in the following spring. At the same time he demanded that the English Roman Catholics not lose faith, for in the early spring the royal army would cross over into England.

units.la: Postremo Regis nomine Vuinterum rogavit, ut se per literas quam primū certorem faceret, si interiecto tempore Elizabetha Regina moreretur. Thomas Vuinter spe plenius & tumidus mense Novembri in Angliam rediit, remq; tota prodicationis sociis, Garneto Iesuitae, Roberto Catesby & Francisco 'i remo explicavit.
units.tr: Finally, in the King's name, he asked Winter to inform him by letter as soon as possible whether Queen Elizabeth died in the meantime. Thomas Winter, full of hope and puffed up, returned to England in November and explained the whole business of the betrayal to his fellow conspirators, Garnet the Jesuit, Robert Catesby and Francis Tresham.

units.la: Hanc proditionem Pontifex Rom. Sanctissimus scil. ille, Vicarius item Christi Petri successor, vehementer promovere conatus est, duabus Bullis, ut vocant, ias Garneto misit, unam ad Clerum, ad populum alteram. Prioris titulus erat, dilectis filijs Archipresbytero & reliquo Clero Anglicano: Posterioris, Dilectis filijs, principibus, & Nobilibus Catholicis salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Summa haec ex. Post obitum Elizabethae sive naturalem, sive violentā, quicunq; jus regni sibi arrogant, quantumcunq; propinquitate sanguinis niterentur, nisi eiusmodi essent, qui fidem Catholicam non modo tolerarent, sed omni ope & studio promoverent, & more maiorum jurerando se idprasituros susciperent, ad Angliae sceptrum tenendum non reciperentur. Hae ullae Papales Vuinteri in Hispaniā traiectum sequutae sunt, quo tempore, vel aulo post traiiciedus fuit in Angliam exercitus, qui eam expugnaret. Et omnia haec tum fieri oportuit, quandocunq; contingeret miseram illam foeminam (sic Filio isti erditionis Reginam Elizabetham nominare placuit) ex hac vita excedere. Bullae autem hae, cum ex Catesbeio postea intellexisset Garnetus Iacobum iam public Regem Angliae declaratum, adeoq; Rempub. constabilitam esse, illico sunt, ipse affirmavit Garnetus, in ignem coniectae.
units.tr: The Roman Pontiff, that most holy man, the Vicar of Christ and successor of Peter, strove vehemently to promote this betrayal. He sent two bulls, as they are called, to Garnet, one to the clergy and the other to the people. The title of the former was: To our beloved sons the Archpriest and the rest of the English clergy. The latter read: To our beloved sons, the princes and noble Catholics, greeting and apostolic blessing. The substance of these was this: after the death of Elizabeth, whether natural or violent, whoever claimed the right to the kingdom, however closely they were related by blood, should not be admitted to hold the sceptre of England unless they were men who not only tolerated the Catholic faith but promoted it with all their power and zeal, and undertook to swear that they would do so, as their ancestors had. Several papal letters of this kind followed Winter's crossing to Spain, at which time, either then or shortly afterwards, an army was to be sent to England to conquer it. All these things were to be done whenever it should happen that that wretched woman (so it pleased this son of perdition to call Queen Elizabeth) departed this life. But these bulls, when Garnet afterwards learned from Catesby that James had already been publicly declared King of England and the state firmly established, were, as Garnet himself affirmed, immediately thrown into the fire.

units.la: Regina cum intelligeret, & reipsa expetiretur, se indesinenter Iesuitarum & aliorum Clericorum in Regno suo opera, instinctu & adhortationibus clandestinis ad necem peti, ut sibi totiq; Regno consuleret, omnes Iesuitas ac Sacerdotes edicto publico intra certum temporis spatium exire sub gravi poena praecipit. Id de verbo ad verbum sic habet.
units.tr: The Queen, understanding that she was being sought after in fact, and that she was incessantly being sought for death by the work, instigation and secret exhortations of the Jesuits and other clergy in her kingdom, commands by a public edict that all Jesuits and priests leave within a certain space of time, under heavy penalty, in order to provide for herself and for her whole kingdom. It stands thus word for word.

units.la: SERENISSIMAE PRINCIPIS ELISABETHAE, ANGLIAE, FRANCIAE, HI- BERNIAE, REGINAE INVICTISSIMAE, FIDEI APOSTOLICAE DEFENSATRICIS, EDICTVM Contra Iesuitas & Sacerdotes seculares, Anno Domini 1602. die 15. Novembris. EX ANGLICO SERMONE IN LATINVM CONVERSVM.
units.tr: THE EDICT OF THE MOST SERENE PRINCESS ELIZABETH, QUEEN OF ENGLAND, FRANCE AND IRELAND, MOST INVINCIBLE QUEEN, DEFENDER OF THE APOSTOLIC FAITH, Against the Jesuits and Secular Priests, in the year of our Lord 1602, on the 15th day of November. TRANSLATED INTO LATIN FROM THE ENGLISH.

units.la: Cum benevolentia ea, quâ cuiusvis ordinis subditos nostros complexi sumus, quamquam in intimo pectore penitus infixam esse sensimus, nos ab extrema earum legum executione, quæ sancitæ fuerunt Comitiorum Regni nostri decretis ad religionem orthodoxam propugnandam, & seductores omnes, (præsertim ab exteris ad nos advolantes) & illos, qui eiusmodi subsidium præbent, propulsandos, magis aliquandiu abstraxit, quàm vel status nostri salus ferre, vel Principum aliorum (à quibus una religionis professio semper culta & observata est) exempla, legitimè approbare possint: Idcirco in spem maximam devenimus, fore, ut Sacerdotes illi Pontificij, qui externa auctoritate permoti, in hoc Regnum ingressi sunt, quo populum à verâ religionis, adeoque fidelis erga nos subiectionis studio abducerent, vellent tandem, (præsertim jam antea experti legum nostrarum severitatem) vel experientia clementiæ nostræ adducti, vel judicij sui normâ edocti, à pristina sua improbitate avocari: nec irritare animum nostrum denuò, & extremum illis supplicium infligendum incendere. Etenim postquam nos tantæ tamque miseræ seductionis illorum miseriti, tantâ illos cum lenitate tractavimus: illi contra clementiæ nostræ penitus obliti, nostrum regnique nostri interitum machinati sunt. Nemo enim non novit, Regem Hispaniæ regnum Hiberniæ nostrum nuper perquam maliriosè invasisse, & Don Giovan (qui in illo exercitu summus Dux & Imperator constitutus erat) diploma illud à Sede Romana aeceptum audacter animoseque promulgâsse: cuius auctoritate scilicet nobis regno abdicati atque detrusis, eius Dominus Rex renunciatus est. Huius vero sui tam inauspicati & infelicis molimnis, Iesuitæ cum Socijs suis sæcularibus Sacerdotibus, suasores & velut buccinatores extitisse, vel ipsi Hispani in maximas tum redactí angustias, non modò liberè dixerunt, verùm etiam queribundi multoties doleriter deplorârunt. Regem enim Hispaniæ in eam mentem adduxerunt, ut vires nostras crederet tam angustas, tamque prorsus abjectas, partes verò suas tantas, tamque undiq; corroboratas fuisse, ut victoriam ipsam sibi spoponderet certissimâ polliceretur. Deinde futuræ istorum erga nos obedientiæ integræ, ipsem omnem nobis penitus esse sublatam, non dubitavimus, quin fere maximæ parti Europæ, vel ex ipsorum scriptis recens editis & divulgatis jam satis constiterit: nimirum, eos ad hostium nostrorum laudem prædicandam & amplificandam, subditos verò nostros in partes adversarias pertrahendas, denique ad interitum statûs nostri perpetuum machinandum, consensu maximo, vel intra regnum nostrum nequiter & malitiosè conspirâsse. Quid enim? Sacerdotes plerique omnes novæ subordinationi, à Pontifice sibi imperatæ, sese penitus addixerunt, seque totos consilijs Iesuitarum (qui homines Regis Hispaniæ partibus semper devotissimi, à subiectione nostra prorsus abhorruerunt) regendos tradiderunt: Hinc factum esse arbitramur, quòd utriusque sectæ homines timore erga Deum æternum, erga nostram Principem legitimam obsequio, denique erga matrem suam germanam, Regnum nostrum pietate
units.tr: Although we have felt that the goodwill with which we have embraced our subjects of every rank is deeply fixed in our inmost heart, we have held back for some time from the full execution of those laws, enacted by the decrees of the Parliament of our realm to defend the orthodox religion and to drive away all seducers (especially those flying to us from abroad) and those who give aid to such men. Neither the safety of our state nor the examples of other princes (among whom the one profession of religion has always been cultivated and observed) can rightly approve this delay any longer. We have therefore come to the greatest hope that those Papist priests who, moved by foreign authority, have entered this kingdom to draw the people away from the true religion and so from faithful submission to us, will at last wish, either led by the experience of our clemency (especially since they have already tasted the severity of our laws) or taught by the rule of their own judgement, to be called back from their former wickedness, and will not provoke our mind again or kindle the extreme punishment to be inflicted on them. For after we had pitied their so great and so wretched seduction and had treated them with such gentleness, they, on the contrary, utterly forgetful of our clemency, have plotted the ruin of ourselves and of our realm. For no one does not know that the King of Spain recently invaded our kingdom of Ireland most wickedly, and that Don Juan (who was made chief leader and commander of that army) boldly and spiritedly published that bull received from the Roman See, by whose authority we were of course cast out and deprived of our kingdom, and its lord the King was proclaimed in our place. Indeed, that the Jesuits, together with their companions the secular priests, were the advisers and, as it were, the trumpeters of this so ill-omened and unhappy undertaking, the Spaniards themselves, when they were reduced to the greatest straits, have not only said freely but have also many times lamented with complaints and bitter grief. For they brought the King of Spain to the mind that our forces were so weak and so utterly cast down, and their own so great and so strengthened on every side, that he promised himself victory and was assured of it as most certain. Then, that their future complete obedience to us would be wholly taken away, we have not doubted; this is already clear enough to almost the greatest part of Europe from their recently published and circulated writings. Namely, they have with the greatest unanimity wickedly and maliciously conspired, even within our realm, to extol and magnify our enemies, to draw our subjects into the opposing party, and finally to plot the perpetual ruin of our state. For what? Most of the priests have wholly devoted themselves to the new subordination imposed on them by the Pontiff, and have handed themselves over entirely to be guided by the counsels of the Jesuits, who, men always most devoted to the party of the King of Spain, have utterly shrunk from subjection to us. Hence we judge it has come about that men of both sects, having cast off fear of the eternal God, obedience to our lawful Princess, and finally piety towards their true mother, our kingdom,

units.la: Iesuitæ non solùm Papæ sed etiam Regi Hispaniarum devinctissimi sunt. Iesuitæ rebellionum et factionum fautores. etate excussa atq; abjecta, conjunctissimis animis nunc (si tamen magis potuerint) magis infracti & perniciosi, quàm anteà unquam evaserint. Eò namque perversitatis atque immobilitatis proruperunt, ut subditis nostris jam pene persuaserint, arma eos contra nos sumere debere, & copias suas cum hoste quovis conjungere, quem Papa sub prætextu stituendæ religionis Romanæ, ad Regnum nostrum subjugandum miserit. Præterea tam projecta & profligata eorum arrogantia, ut non sint veriti in omnibus regni negotiis immiscere, & verbis ac scriptis suis, de Regno & Corona nostra pro animi sui libidine lam decernere. Et si quis forte ex iis, ceu moderatoris ingenii, conscientiæ suæ duƈtu armotus, Gubernationis nostræ æquabilitatem cœperit agnoscere, hic dignus inprimis ilvifus est, quem hostili odio prosequantur. Quinetiam ne hoc hominum genus improbom temporis diuturnitate possit extingui, quoddam quasi juventutis monopolium exerant, summæ indolis juvenes aucupantes & ad exteras scholas transmittentes, quo nostrarum familiarum ipsorum inficiantur veneno; & rebellionis sax atque progeniem nobis invisimæ perpetuo alatur. Porrò ex acerrimis & acerbissimis dissidiis, quæ non itapridem inter Iesuitas, illisque adhærentes Sacerdotes seculares, cum aliis quoque secularibus præsteris intercesserunt, rationes offensionum, quas utriusque sectæ homines, contra nos nonumquè Regnum conceperunt, diversæ emerserunt: nimirum, Iesuitas omnes cum suis conjuratis presbyteris secularibus, eò cogitationes suas omnes contulisse: ut principes exteros non modò ad occupandum regnum nostrum, verùmetiam ad nos ipsos occendum excitarent, reliquos vero seculares presbyteros à prioribus opinione magnopere stractos, non solum in aliorum propositum, tanquam maximè execrandum & detestanum verbis ac scriptis suis liberè fuisse invectos, verùmetiam non abnuisse sanctè profiteri, semper paratissimos fore, qui rebellionis hujusmodi conjurationes ac tumultus omnes, vel imi prodere velint, armisq; propulsare.
units.tr: The Jesuits are bound most closely not only to the Pope but also to the King of Spain. The Jesuits are fomenters of rebellions and factions. Having been shaken off and cast aside, they have, with their minds most closely joined, now (if they could possibly do so) become more unbending and more pernicious than they ever were before. For they have broken out into such perversity and obstinacy that they have almost persuaded our subjects that they ought to take up arms against us and join their forces with whatever enemy the Pope may send to subjugate our realm under the pretext of restoring the Roman religion. Moreover, their arrogance is so shameless and so abandoned that they have not feared to meddle in all the affairs of the realm and, by their words and writings, to decide at their own pleasure concerning our Realm and Crown. And if any of them, perhaps, as a man of moderate temper, led by the dictates of his conscience, begins to acknowledge the evenhandedness of our government, he is judged especially worthy of being marked out for hostile hatred. Indeed, lest this wicked race of men be extinguished by the lapse of time, they practise a kind of monopoly over the young, catching up youths of the highest promise and sending them to foreign schools, so that our families are infected with their poison, and the seed and offspring of rebellion, hateful to us, is perpetually nourished. Furthermore, from the most bitter and savage quarrels which lately arose between the Jesuits and the secular priests who adhere to them, and also with other secular priests, various grounds of offence have emerged, which the men of each sect have conceived against us and against our realm. Namely, that all the Jesuits, with their conspiring secular priests, have directed all their thoughts to this: to stir up foreign princes not only to seize our kingdom but also to kill ourselves; while the remaining secular priests, greatly offended by the former opinion, have not only freely inveighed against it with words and writings as most execrable and detestable, but have also not refused to profess solemnly that they will always be most ready to betray, or with arms to repel, all such conspiracies and tumults of rebellion.

units.la: Quapropter tametsi pro ea opinione, quam de his concepimus, in discrimine aliquo igendi ab iis destinatum ex lege supplicium, propensiorem erga hos voluntatem nostram lumus ostendere: tamen hi quoque ita sunt in nos animati, itaque se gerunt, ut (quamvis natura nostra alioquin ad misericordiæ occasionem vel tenuissimam amplectendam omnissima semper fuerit) nunc expectatio clementiæ cum regiminis nostri dignitate, cum silitate subditorum, cum Regni securitate diutius consistere non possit. Cuivis enim infestum est nimis hos Iesuitarum factionibus, quàm vis plurimum adversantes, tamen eàdem animi obstinatione convenire. Namq; prætextu conscientiæ (illudendi genus perulosissimum) subditorum animos ad se pellicere conati sunt, & ad Papam, hostem nomine infestissimum pertrahere, ut hoc pacto partes adversariæ augeri & stabiliri, nostræ vero nvelli atq; labefactari possint: id quod cum Regiminis nostro perniciosum, tum ex legibus ne constitutæ Reipub. minimè ferendum est: Cum præsertim hic hostis more Principis seularis in aperta acie vexillü suum jam adversus nos extulit, atq; erexit, assiduè novastragemata & artes bellicas cotra nos instruens atq; adornans. Præterea satis assequi aut miri non possumus (nisi forte abusu lenitatis nostræ hoc contigit) quid tandem eos in eam imlit amentiam, ut subditis fere nostris omnibus, tam bonis, qui graváte id ferunt; quàm probis, qui id ardenter & sitienter exoptant, jam pene persuaserint, eo nos esse animo, ut luno in Regno religionis cultum duplicem facile admittere velimus. Novit autem Deus Max. qui cordis nostri recessus intimos perscrutatur, & cui soli hanc gratiam referi-, nos in istam sententiam nunquam descendisse, ne per somnium quidem, & ex iis qui bis adfuerunt, neminem, propositi huiusce vel tenuissimam persuasionem nobis innuisse; imos si obtineat, pax Ecclesiæ & status nostri dignitas labefactetur, necesse est.
units.tr: Wherefore, although, according to the opinion we have formed of these men, we are inclined to show a more favourable will towards them, since they have been destined for punishment by the law in some danger of being burned, nevertheless these men too are so disposed towards us and so conduct themselves that (although our nature has always been most inclined to embrace even the slightest occasion for mercy) the expectation of clemency cannot any longer stand together with the dignity of our government, with the safety of our subjects, and with the security of the realm. For it is too hostile to anyone that these men, although very much opposed to the Jesuit factions, nevertheless agree with them in the same obstinacy of mind. For under the pretext of conscience (a most dangerous kind of deceit) they have tried to draw the minds of our subjects to themselves, and to lead them to the Pope, the enemy most hostile by name, so that by this means the opposing party may be increased and established, while our own may be shaken and weakened. This is both ruinous to our government and, by the laws of the constituted commonwealth, not at all to be tolerated, especially since this enemy, after the manner of a secular prince, has now raised and set up his banner in open battle against us, constantly devising and preparing new stratagems and warlike arts against us. Moreover, we cannot sufficiently understand or wonder (unless perhaps this has happened through the abuse of our leniency) what at last has driven them into such madness that they have almost persuaded nearly all our subjects, both the good, who bear it grievously, and the upright, who ardently and thirstily desire it, that we are so minded as to be willing easily to admit a double worship of religion in the realm. But God Most High, who searches the innermost recesses of our heart, and to whom alone this grace is to be ascribed, knows that we never descended into that opinion, not even in a dream; and among those who have been present with us, no one has suggested to us even the slightest persuasion of this purpose. Indeed, if it were to prevail, the peace of the Church and the dignity of our state would of necessity be overthrown.

units.la: Deinde intelligimus, (ex quo etiam magis eminneat præceps eorum audacia) hanc eò-m de religionis suæ tolerantia spem, cum intolerabili licentia atque impudentia esse conistam. Nam vel in summa luce in publicum prodire cœperunt, incarceratos palam saare, & (non sine contemptu legum maximo) religionis suæ munia exequi & ritus ce-
units.tr: Furthermore, we understand (from which their headlong audacity may stand out even more clearly) that this hope of theirs of toleration for their religion is joined with intolerable licence and impudence. For they have now begun to come forward openly in public, to visit the imprisoned openly, and (not without the greatest contempt of the laws) to perform the offices of their religion and to celebrate the rites of their

units.la: Ee librare. His & alijs modis, nullo modo feredis, irritare nö definūt legū vigore, qui (propter rationes ja expositas) aliquādiu quasi cōsopitus jacuit. Cū potiūs, (si unquā) nunc maxime præscribere sibi modū debuissent, sedulòq; præcavere, ne clementiam tam singularem, quæ nunquam nisi necessario parere severitati potuit) fuatam insigni insolentia repellerent.
units.tr: E e 1. By these and other means, which cannot be borne in any way, they do not cease to provoke us, relying on the force of the laws, which (for the reasons already set out) has lain for some time as if lulled to sleep. Whereas they ought now, if ever, to have set themselves a limit and taken care to prevent their own insolence from repaying such singular clemency, which has never been able to yield to severity except of necessity.

units.la: Porrò hoc, quod ad ipsos homines ingratos nimiūm parūq; consideratos conivere quodā modo videbamur, aliud quoq; malū invexit: videlicet homines alij rebus novis proni, & opinionib. suis addicti nimis, eò prolapsi sunt temeritatis, ut lenitate nostra libellus suis publicis vehementius exagitet, nobisq; negligentiæ nota inurant, acsi ab ipsis solis religio fuste tata & propugnata esset. Hi, quod innocentia nostra traducentes, piorum animos offendūt (qui cum Pontificiæ sectæ inimicissimi, tum ipsor ūpetulcis ingenijs adversarij sunt) certe non debent ferre impune.
units.tr: Moreover, the fact that we seemed in some measure to connive at these men, who are too ungrateful and too thoughtless, has brought in another evil. Men too prone to novelties and too devoted to their own opinions have fallen so far into rashness that, relying on our leniency, they assail the public with their libels more fiercely, and brand us with the mark of negligence, as if the religion had been established and defended by them alone. These men, by slandering our innocence, offend the minds of the pious (who are the bitter enemies of the Papist sect, and also opponents of those rash wits). Certainly they ought not to go unpunished.

units.la: Quin etiam ut Regni nostri, (cuius administrationis ratio omnis Ecclesiastica & Politica Senatus, quem Parlamentum dicimus: Confultis & decretis comunibus sanciri & confirmari solet) scandalis, periculis incommodis omnibus necessario occurratur: ministri & officiarij nostri oes, quibus Reipub. cura jo credita est, admonedi sunt, quam nobis vehementer displicuerit, quod tantum de officij sui severitate remiserint, ut in apprehendendis Pontificijs Sacerdotibus, ex legib. sibi imperata diligentiam raro admodū præstiterint.
units.tr: Indeed, so that the scandals, dangers and inconveniences of our realm (whose whole ecclesiastical and civil administration is customarily sanctioned and confirmed by the common counsels and decrees of the senate which we call Parliament) may be necessarily met, all our ministers and officers, to whom the care of the commonwealth has been entrusted, must be warned how greatly it has displeased us that they have relaxed the strictness of their office so far that, in apprehending Papist priests, they have shown very little of the diligence the laws required of them.

units.la: Nos igitur hæc nostra monita atq; imperata publiè promulgari volumus: in quibus rogamus & jubemus Iesuitas & cū eis conjunctos & consociatos presbyteros seculares oes jam libertatem nactos ex Dominijs & Territorijs nostris, quāmprimū discedere necper importunā moram sua nos vehementius incedere velint, ut in ipsos ex rigore legis scelera vindicemus. Sacerdotes quoq; alios Iesuitarū impietatē nonnihil aversantes nunc in libertate constitutos ante primū die Ianuarij proxime subsequentis, Regnis nostris exulare mādamus. Illos tantum excipimus, qui ante die indictum, Consiliariorum nostrorū cuiquam aut Cambrienfi vel Eboracensi præsidi, aut Diæcesium Episcopis præsentes sese exhibuerint, & agnoscentes suum erga nos obsequium ad nostram se clementiam receperint: de quorum submissione intra dies 20. per præsides, &c. Episcopos ubi acceperimus, ita cum illis agituri sumus, ac pietas & æquitas ipsaposlula verit.
units.tr: We therefore wish these our admonitions and commands to be published openly. In them we ask and order that all Jesuits, and the secular priests joined and associated with them, who have now obtained liberty, depart from our dominions and territories as soon as possible, and that they do not, by unseasonable delay, provoke us to proceed more severely, so that we may avenge their crimes by the rigour of the law. We also command the other priests, who in some measure dislike the impiety of the Jesuits and are now at liberty, to go into exile from our kingdoms before the first day of January next following. We except only those who, before the appointed day, have presented themselves to one of our councillors, or to the president of Wales or of York, or to the bishops of the dioceses, and, acknowledging their obedience to us, have taken refuge in our clemency. Once we have received word through the presidents and bishops of their submission within twenty days, we shall deal with them as piety and equity themselves require.

units.la: Deinde Iesuitis & Sacerdotibus Pontificijs alijs omnibus tam secularib. quàm regularibus, sive in Regno, sive extra Regnum agentibus, interdicimus, ne quo vis prætextu in Regnum revertantur. Nisi Iesuitæ, & qui se illis addixerunt seculares Presbyteri ante triginta dies, reliqui vero seculares Sacerdotes à prioribus opinione divulsi, ante primum diem mensis Februarij, postquam hoc Edictum denunciatum est, portum aliquem maritimum petierint, navemq; conscenderint in regiones exteras traiecturi, tum illos illisq; subsidium ullum exhibentes, (ubi deprehenduntur) ministris nostris pro legum nostrarum summo jure pœnis afficiendos esse permittimus: idq; magistratibus omnibus, quibus Reipub. administratio demandata est, ex hoc nostro Mandato significamus.
units.tr: Next, we forbid Jesuits and all other Papist priests, both secular and regular, whether they are working within the realm or outside it, to return to the realm on any pretext whatever. Unless the Jesuits, and those secular priests who have attached themselves to them, have done so within thirty days, and the remaining secular priests, who have been separated in opinion from the former, have before the first day of February, after this Edict is proclaimed, made for some seaport and boarded a ship intending to cross to foreign lands, then we permit our ministers, by the supreme right of our laws, to punish those persons, and anyone giving them aid, wherever they are caught. We signify this by our present mandate to all magistrates to whom the administration of the commonwealth is entrusted.

units.la: Iesuitæ et Sacerdotes ex Anglia proscribuntur.
units.tr: Jesuits and priests are banished from England.

units.la: Quo etiam Regnum nostrum a huius pestis contagione facilius liberari possit: hoc edicto præsidibus nostris, Vicepræsidibus Comissarijs, Iusticiarijs, Prætoribus, Vicecomitibus, Baliuis, aliisq; cujusque ordinis Magistratibus omnibus severe præcipimus, ut in suo quisq; munere exquendo curā omnem & diligentiam adhibeant, loces omnes sedulò pervestigent, ac perscrutentur (quì vel ex opinione sua, vel per significationem aliorum suspicionem ullam afferat) & Iesuitas & secu-lares presbyteros omnes apprehendant, & nostris denique consiliarijs rationem reddant tandem, quam probè suo munere sint perfuncti, nec per negligentiam suam permittant, aut dum alios legum periculo liberare velint, ipsi involvantur.
units.tr: So that our realm may be more easily freed from the contagion of this plague, by this edict we strictly command our presidents, vice-presidents, commissioners, justices, praetors, sheriffs, bailiffs, and all magistrates of every rank, that each, in performing his office, apply all care and diligence, search out and examine every place, and seize all Jesuits and secular priests (whoever gives rise to any suspicion, either by his own opinion or by the information of others). Finally, they must render account to our councillors of how well they have discharged their duty, and not allow, through their negligence, or while wishing to free others from the peril of the law, themselves to become entangled in it.

units.la: In hoc Edicto Serenissima Regina de Iesuitis testatur primò, quod alienâ potestate, nempe Papæ & Hispaniæ Regis permoti, in Angliam ingressint, quo populum à veræ Religionis, adeoque fidelis erga Regīnam subiectionis studio abducerent. Secundò, cūm Don Giouan Regnum Hiberniæ occupare, seseque Regem ac Dominum illius declarare conatus esset, quòd Iesuitæ huius facinoris & molitionis suasores & quasi buccinatores fuerint nt, vel ipsis Hispanis testibus, in maximas tum angustias redactis, & infortunium suum deplorantibus. Regi enim Hispaniarum persuasisse Iesuitas, Anglicanas vires ita concisas, Hispanicas contra tantas, tamque firmatas esse, ut de victoria minime dubitandum sit. Tertio, Iesuitas ad hostium Reginae laudes praeclarandas, subditos Angliae in partes adversarias pertrahendos, & ad interitum Reginae totiusque regni machinandum, consensu maximo; vel intra regnum male conspirasse. Quarto, Iesuitas subditis Angliae iam fere persuasisse; ut arma contra Reginam suscipiant, & copias suas cum iis hostibus coniungant, quos apa ad Regnum hoc subiugandum misserit. Quinto, Iesuitas in omnibus Regni Anglicani negotiis se immiscuisse, publice quoque & privatim de Regno & Companiam Anglicana decrevisse. Sexto, Iesuitas quoddam quasi iuventutis monopolium instituisse, summae indolis iuuenes aucupantes, & ad exteras Scholas transmittentes, quo nobilissimae ipsorum familiae veneno Iesuitico inficiantur, & religionis tax perpetuo alatur.
