Septimo, Iesuitas omnes, cum aliquibus Secularium et Regularium, eo cogitationes suas omnes contulisse, ut principes exteros non modo ad occupandum Regnum Anglicanum, sed etiam ad Reginam ipsam occidendam excitarint. Octavo, Iesuitas subditos a Principum suorum amore & obedientia, ad Papam illorum hostem infensissimum seducere.
units.tr: In this edict the most serene Queen testifies concerning the Jesuits. First, that, moved by a foreign power, namely that of the Pope and the King of Spain, they entered England, to draw the people away from the true religion, and thus from the zeal of faithful subjection to the Queen. Second, when Don Juan tried to seize the kingdom of Ireland and proclaim himself its king and lord, the Jesuits were the instigators and, as it were, the trumpeters of this crime and enterprise, as even the Spaniards themselves bear witness, who were then reduced to the greatest straits and lamented their misfortune. For the Jesuits had persuaded the King of Spain that the English forces were so weakened and the Spanish so great and so firm that there was no room to doubt victory. Third, that the Jesuits, to magnify the praises of the Queen's enemies, to draw English subjects into the hostile party, and to plot the destruction of the Queen and of the whole realm, have conspired wickedly, with the greatest agreement, either within the realm. Fourth, that the Jesuits have now almost persuaded English subjects to take up arms against the Queen and to join their forces with those enemies whom the Pope has sent to subdue this realm. Fifth, that the Jesuits have meddled in all the affairs of the English realm, and have decided publicly and privately concerning the realm and the English Company. Sixth, that the Jesuits have established a kind of monopoly over youth, snatching up young men of the highest promise and sending them to foreign schools, so that the noblest families are infected with Jesuit poison and the religion is perpetually nourished. Seventh, that all the Jesuits, together with some secular and regular priests, have directed all their thoughts to this end: to stir up foreign princes not only to occupy the English kingdom but even to kill the Queen herself. Eighth, that the Jesuits seduce subjects from the love and obedience of their princes towards the Pope, their most bitter enemy.

units.la: Fuit igitur haec ratio omnium mitissima & iustissima prohibendi Iesuitas fibus & regno suo: cum nullus unquam Princeps exiterit, qui eos tolerarit, & on summo potius supplicio affecerit eos, qui intra ditionem suam legitimos reges abrogarent, aut subditos ab imperio eorum abstraherent, vel ad arma, arricidia & proditiones excitarent.
units.tr: This, therefore, was the mildest and most just of all plans for forbidding the Jesuits to enter his lands and kingdom. For no prince has ever existed who tolerated them, and rather than punish them with the utmost severity, who within his dominion would overthrow lawful kings, draw subjects away from their rule, or stir them up to arms, murders and treasons.

units.la: Sequente anno 1603. April. 4. die Serenissima Regina Angliae Elizabetha moritur. Hic verbis satis exprimi non potest, ut illa mendacijs obruerint & convi-jis lacerarint Iesuitae eorumque affectae laici; & Ecclesiastici in primis post & ante mortem eius. Appellarunt eam immitem, crudelem, humani sanguinis avidam, Christiani nominis hostem acerrimam & perfecutricem, lupam denique Anglicanam, & ut talis fuisse ab omnibus credatur, quantum ingenii viribus valent, etiam hodie annitentur. Texuerunt Catalogos eorum, qui toto regni eius tempore, quod longissimum fuit, vel ob proditiones & parricidia, vel ob nefas aliud legibus regni vetitum, supplicio affecti sunt: deinde istud esse Anglicanum martyrologium miseris populis, & rei veritate ignorantibus persuadere conantur.
units.tr: In the following year, 1603, on 4 April, the most serene Queen Elizabeth of England died. It cannot be expressed in words how the Jesuits and their lay adherents, and especially the clergy, before and after her death, have overwhelmed her with lies and torn her with reproaches. They have called her cruel, savage, greedy for human blood, the most bitter enemy and persecutor of the Christian name, in short the English she-wolf; and so that she may be believed by everyone to have been such, they still strive with all the power of their wits, even today. They have drawn up catalogues of those who, throughout her reign, which was the longest, were put to death either for treason and murder or for other crimes forbidden by the laws of the realm. Then they try to persuade wretched peoples, ignorant of the truth, that this is the English martyrology.

units.la: Videre est in Iesuitarum nonnullorum aliorumque libris de persecutione Anglicana; Pastiarum alios ferarum pellibus insutos a rabidis canibus & molosis dilaniari; alios ad equorum praesepia alligatos foeno ibi pascendos. Cernas; glires pelvisclusos Papistarum viscera exedentes. Omitto alias supplicior-um diras & horribiles species, in cerebris fingentium pingentiumque Iesuitarum & similium impie fictae natas, neque in Angliae regno unquam visas vel auditas. Si quae aut supplicia maxime sumpta sunt, pauciora tamen illa sunt per totum spatium regni Elisabethae, quod fuit annorum 5. supra 40. quam per 4. annos Reginae Mariae; de quibus inter illos altissimum est silentium. De sumptis autem supplicis, quam causam iustam habet conquerendi Iesuitae & alii: Licuit Rom. Pontifici Pio V. Reginam, in quam tamen nihil prorsus iuris vel potestatis habuit, diris devovere, es sibi morigeros Reges, Principes & populos in ipsius perniciem & universi regni ruinam excitare; Reginae vero & proceribus regni, pestem hanc & ruinam avertere & vim vi repellere non licebat. Ausi sunt Iesuitae, Cleri & Laici, doctissimi & peregrini seditiones in Angliae regno periculosissimas concitare, ad arricidia, caedes, omnis generis dolos, fraudes, cofilia sanguinolenta & nefaria scelera plurimos instigare & impellere, in qua necessaria Reginae & consiliariorum eius conspirare; & Regina Cofiliarijque eius de seditiosis illis, proditoribus, latronibus, ac arricidis nō supplicia & meritissimas poenas sumere audeat.
units.tr: One may see, in certain books of the Jesuits and others about the English persecution, some men sewn into the skins of beasts and torn apart by rabid dogs and mastiffs, and others tied to horses' mangers to be fed with hay there. You may see dormice shut in basins gnawing at the entrails of Papists. I omit the other dreadful and horrible kinds of torture, born in the brains of the impious inventors and painters of the Jesuits and their like, never seen or heard of in the realm of England. If any punishments have been inflicted at all, yet these are fewer over the whole span of Elizabeth's reign, which lasted forty-five years, than in the four years of Queen Mary's reign, about which they keep the deepest silence. But as for the punishments inflicted, what just cause the Jesuits and others have to complain! It was allowed to the Roman Pontiff Pius V to curse the Queen with dreadful curses, although he had no right or power whatever over her, and to stir up kings, princes and peoples obedient to him to her destruction and the ruin of the whole realm. Yet it was not permitted to the Queen and the nobles of the realm to avert this pestilence and ruin, and to repel force with force. The Jesuits, clergy and laymen, learned and foreign alike, have dared to stir up seditions most dangerous in the realm of England, and to incite and drive very many to assassinations, murders, every kind of trick and fraud, bloody counsels and nefarious crimes, in which they conspire against the necessary safety of the Queen and her councillors. Yet the Queen and her councillors dare not inflict punishments and most deserved penalties on those seditious, traitorous, thieving and murderous men.

units.la: E e 2
units.tr: E e 2

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: Of the Nefarious Deeds

units.la: Serenissimæ Reginæ Elisabethæ in Regno successit Serenissimus Iacobus 6. Scotiæ Rex. A primo autem eius in Angliam adventu non tres vel quatuor menses effluxerunt, in quibus non aliqua contra illum fabricata sit conspiratio vel proditio à Papistis; quos inter Iesuitæ primas semper tenuerunt. Scripsit etiam doctissimus Casaubonus ad Frontone Ducæum Iesuitam pag. 52. Vuatsonus & Clercum, Sacerdotes seculares, Regem Iacobum vix in Angliam ingressum, nondum certe coronatum anno 1603, machinatione clandestina, tollere de vivis aggressos esse: Et hanc quidem primam conspirationem in Regis perniciem, postquam in Angliam appulit in apertum & hominum cognitione venisse. Captos autem & tortura interrogatos, dixisse illos, saepeque & constanter affirmasse, se cum sua consilia Iesuitis in Anglia tum degentibus communicasse, petiisse ab iis, ut tam praeclari scilicet incepti participes esse vellent, hoc responsum tulisse; Non posse Iesuitas illis se adjungere, ut qui suam ipsi quoque parilem telam orsi, memorabilem in omne aevum techam pararent, tempore opportuno exitum habituram: pergerent modo illi in hoc suo instituto, & rem agerent strenue: quo responso nihil aliud quam coniurationem, quam pulverariam vocant, significarunt, de qua postea agetur; eoque haud obscure demonstrarunt, se eius mox post ingressum Regis Iacobi in Angliam consciós & coadiutores fuisse. Et omnino ita erat. Nam etsi anni demum 1605. mense Novemb. patefacta est coniuratio ista, prima tamen eius initia anno primo Regis Iacobi, & secundi principio iacta esse, ex Vuatsoni & Clerci presbyterorum testimonio liquido constat, tum vero multo magis ex iis quae infandae huius proditionis rei apud Iudices confessi sunt. Haec Casaubonus.
units.tr: King James VI of Scotland succeeded the most serene Queen Elizabeth in the kingdom. Not three or four months passed from his first arrival in England before some conspiracy or treason was contrived against him by the Papists, among whom the Jesuits always held the first place. The most learned Casaubon also wrote to the Jesuit Fronton du Duc, p. 52, that the secular priests Watson and Clarke, soon after King James had entered England and before he was crowned in 1603, set about removing him from the living by a secret plot; and that this was the first conspiracy against the King's life to come into the open and to the knowledge of men after he landed in England. When they were captured and questioned under torture, they said, and often and consistently affirmed, that they had shared their plans with the Jesuits then living in England, and had asked them whether they would be willing to take part in so splendid an enterprise. The answer they received was this: The Jesuits could not join them, since they too had begun a similar web of their own, which would have an outcome at a suitable time and would prepare a memorable snare for all ages; they should only persist in this their undertaking and carry it out vigorously. By this answer they signified nothing other than the conspiracy which they call the gunpowder plot, of which more will be said later, and so they showed clearly enough that they had been aware of it and had helped it along almost as soon as King James entered England. And indeed it was so. For although that conspiracy was not discovered until November 1605, its first beginnings were laid in the first year of King James's reign, and the start of his second, as is plainly established by the testimony of the priests Watson and Clarke, and even more so by what those who confessed to this unspeakable treason before the judges said. So far Casaubon.

units.la: Haud diu post Christophorus Vurigth ab Henrico Garneto, qui etiamperim cum ad rem acceleradam ad Crefuuellum Iesuitam literas dederat, itemque à Caesbeio & Treshamo ex parte Anglorum Romanae-Catholicorum submissus fuit in Hispaniam, tum ut Reginae Elizabethae mortem nuntiaret; tum ut negotium de Angliae invadenda & pensionibus submittendis urgeret. Uno vel altero mense post adventum Vurigth, in Hispaniam, eo etiam venit Guido Fauukius, qui 22. Iunii Bruxellis Brabantiae missus erat à Guilielmo Stanleio, Hugone Owen, qui se plurimis proditionibus multos iam annos contra Reginam immiscuerat, & Balduino Iesuitico in Belgio Legato ordinario, qui etiam Guidoni litteras ad Crefuuellum, ut rem studiose diligenterque curaret, perferendas dedit.
units.tr: Not long afterwards, Christopher Wright was sent into Spain by Henry Garnet, who had even written letters to the Jesuit Creswell to speed the business, and likewise by Cesbeius and Tresham on behalf of the English Roman Catholics. His purpose was both to announce the death of Queen Elizabeth and to press the project of invading England and sending in pensions. One or two months after Wright's arrival in Spain, Guy Fawkes also came there. He had been sent from Brussels in Brabant on 22 June by William Stanley and Hugh Owen, who had for many years already been mixed up in many treasons against the Queen, and by Baldwin, the ordinary Jesuit legate in Belgium, who also gave Guy letters to Creswell to be carried, so that he might attend to the matter eagerly and diligently.

units.la: Guuidoni Fauukes impositum erat à praedictis, priusquam Iacobus Rex vere de facie illis notus erat, ut Regi Hispaniarum significaret, Regem Angliae aperius cum Romanae-Catholicis acturum, & eandem viam Reginae Elizabethae ingressurum; nec non ut obsecraret Regem, copias in Angliam ad Milfordum portum submitteret, ubi Angli Romanae-Catholici praesto illis futuri sint, eodemque tempore cohortes, quae è Belgio Spinolae triremibus transvehendae essent, ubi possent commodissime terram conscenderent. Haec Christophorus Vurigth & Guido Fauukes Hispaniarum Regi seorsim expositerunt, Rex autem tunc illis respondit, Se post hac his similibus si postulatis eorum aures praebiturum, quod Legatum in Angliam ad Regem de pace tractandā mississet.
units.tr: Before King James was truly known to them by sight, the aforesaid men charged Guy Fawkes to tell the King of Spain that the King of England would more openly deal with the Roman Catholics and would enter upon the same course as Queen Elizabeth; and also to beg the King to send troops to Milford Haven into England, where the English Roman Catholics would be ready to receive them, and, at the same time, cohorts which were to be ferried from Belgium in Spinola's galleys, so that they might land at the most convenient place. Christopher Wright and Guy Fawkes set out these matters to the King of Spain separately. The King then answered them: that he would lend his ear to such requests as theirs in future, since he had sent an ambassador to the King of England to treat of peace.

units.la: Hispanica Iesuitarum auxilia contra Angliam.
units.tr: The Spanish aid of the Jesuits against England.

units.la: CONSILIVM ET FACINVS INAVDITVM DE PVLVERE FVLMINALI EXSTIRPANDO IN ANGLIA REGE, REGIA FAMILIA, PROCERIBVS ET PRAECIPVA NOBILITATE AN- GLICANA.
units.tr: A Plan and Unheard-of Deed for Blowing Up, with Gunpowder, the King, the Royal Family, the Nobles and the Principal English Nobility

units.la: NVM Hispaniarum Rex non amplius probaret consilium de copiis in AnglIam transmittendis, propter pacis inter utrumque Regem tractationem, propterea vi ac armis nihil ultra posset, ad occulta molimina protinus conserunt. Nam primo ut Mercurius Gallo-Belgicus refert tom. 5. lib. 1. pagina 4. mense Maio anni 1603. quinque ex Scotia oriundi in vincula Londini coniecti sunt, a Iesuitis, ut ferebatur, subornati, ut eo die quo coronationis solemnitas perageretur, excitato diversis in locis ingenti incendio, turbas Londini quam maximas darent, quibus quod insidiose decretum esset, in actum eo commodius perduceretur.
units.tr: Now, since the King of Spain no longer approved the plan of sending troops into England, because of the negotiations for peace between the two kings, and since he could accomplish nothing further by force and arms, they at once turned to secret schemes. For first, as the Mercurius Gallo-Belgicus reports (vol. 5, book 1, p. 4), in May of the year 1603 five men born in Scotland were thrown into prison at London, allegedly suborned by the Jesuits, so that on the day on which the solemnity of the coronation was to be celebrated, a huge fire would be started in various places and they would cause the greatest possible disorder in London, by which the plot that had been laid could more easily be carried into effect.

units.la: Secundo, consilia de pulvere fulminali agitarunt. Incuius sceleratissimi & a ultis seculis inaudити facinoris descriptione octo in primis considerabimus ordine: primo personas per quas; 2. in quas; 3. quo tempore; 4. quo loco; 5. quibus mediis; 6. quem ad finem inauditum hoc facinus tentatum sit; 7. occultam moliendi rationem; 8. admirabilem eiusdem detestationem.
units.tr: Second, they discussed plans involving gunpowder. In describing this most wicked deed, unheard of for many ages, we shall consider eight points in order: first, the persons by whom; second, against whom; third, at what time; fourth, at what place; fifth, by what means; sixth, to what end this unheard-of deed was attempted; seventh, the secret method of carrying it out; eighth, its remarkable detestability.

units.la: Personae delinquentes, & praecipui huius facinoris authores, fuerunt Laici nonnulli & Clerici. Laici fuerunt nobili genere orti & eximiis naturae dotibus praediti: Percius, Guilielmus Stanley, Guido Faunkes, Ioannes Talbot, Thomas Winter, Robertus Keies, & Catesbei famulus, & Franciscus Tresham. Percius ex familia Comitis Northumbriae fuit: Stanley & Talbot ex honoratissimis familiis: Thomas Vuinter Generosus, Robertus Vuinter armiger, Guido Faunkes Generosus, Ioannes & Christophorus Vurigth Generosi & Regis, ut ocant, Pensionarii.
units.tr: The guilty persons and the chief authors of this crime were some laymen and clergymen. The laymen were born of noble families and endowed with excellent natural gifts: Percy, William Stanley, Guy Fawkes, John Talbot, Thomas Winter, Robert Keyes, the servant of Catesby, and Francis Tresham. Percy was of the family of the Earl of Northumberland; Stanley and Talbot were from most honourable families; Thomas Winter, gentleman, Robert Winter, esquire, Guy Fawkes, gentleman, John and Christopher Wright, gentlemen, and, as they are called, pensioners of the King.

units.la: Ex indubitatae aut fidei Actis, quae de hac coniuratione sunt edita, potest intelligi, Robertum Catesbeium, Regis armigerum, & nobilem primarium, huius drama tis primum actorem fuisse, & statim, ut de Rege armis pellendo, & auxiliis Hispanicis spes esset amissa, nulla interiecta mora, a vi aperta ad dolos, & Sinonias res scelere contulisse. Cumque dies noctesque de aliquo inani facinore perpetrando cogitasset, tandem machinationem per pulverem tormentarium, ipsissimo haud dubie Satana, qui a principio homicida est, suggerente, idem excogitavit, aliisque dende, ut sese dabant opportunitates, horribile secretum indicavit, & inceptis sibi accivit. Et est certe admiratione dignissimum, inter homines aliquem reperiri fuisse, qui scelus adeo inhumanum adeo impium excogitaret; semel excogitatum approbaret, & ad facinus patrandum ita animo obstinato pergeret, ut ne tanto temporis intervallo quidem, morsus conscientiae ullus, aut poenitentia aliqua mentem subiret. Quid dico de poenitentia? Certum est, plerosque complicium ad suscipiendum scelus persuasione meriti esse impulsos. Itaque Ioannes Grant perduellis unus, quo die supplicium de ipso ad portam Occidentalem Ecclesiae Cathedralis S. Pauli Londini sumendum erat, monitus a Ministro verbi Dei, redire nunc altera ad se, & veniam delicti, sero poenitens a Deo peteret; respondit, Satis se acceptum habere, in suscepto negotio adeo nihil delicti fuisse, ut e contrario consideret generosi incepti id esse meritum, quod pro satisfactione omnium suorum in cetera vita peccatorum abunde sufficeret. Ex quo intelligitur, quam sint parricidae & sicarii isti Regibus & Principibus metuendi. Nam quis satis tutus ab iis esse potest, qui caedes infandas & detestanda parricidia dissidentium a se in Religionis causa, viam esse in coelos & sedes beatorum compendiariam autumant & sibi persuasissimum habent.
units.tr: From the trustworthy or credible accounts that have been published concerning this conspiracy, it can be understood that Robert Catesby, the King's esquire and a leading nobleman, was the first author of this drama, and that as soon as hope was lost of driving the King out by arms and of Spanish help, without any delay he turned the matter from open violence to deceit and Sinon-like tricks. And when he had pondered day and night on some empty crime to commit, at last, with Satan himself, who is from the beginning a murderer, undoubtedly suggesting it, he devised this scheme by means of gunpowder, and then, as opportunities offered themselves, he revealed the horrible secret to others and summoned them as partners in his undertakings. And it is certainly most worthy of wonder that there could be found among men someone who would devise a deed so inhuman and so impious; having devised it, would approve it, and would proceed to carry it out with such an obstinate mind that, not even in so long an interval of time, did any pang of conscience or any repentance enter his mind. Why do I speak of repentance? It is certain that most of the accomplices were driven to undertake the crime by the persuasion that it was meritorious. Thus John Grant, one of the traitors, on the day on which his execution was to be carried out at the west door of the Cathedral Church of St Paul at London, was admonished by a minister of the Word of God to come to himself again and, repenting too late, to seek pardon of his offence from God; he replied: that he considered himself well rewarded, since in the undertaking he had undertaken there was so little wrongdoing that, on the contrary, he judged it to be the merit of a noble enterprise, which would abundantly suffice as satisfaction for all his sins in the rest of his life. From this it is understood how dreadful these parricides and assassins are to kings and princes. For who can be safe enough from those who declare that the slaughter of unspeakable murders and the detestable parricides of those who dissent from them in the cause of religion is a short route to heaven and the seats of the blessed, and who hold this as most firmly persuaded?

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: Concerning the Nefarious Deeds

units.la: {a}Quod ad Clericos attinet, testatur Edmundus Coke Eques auratus, & Procurator in Anglia Regius Generalis in Actis Henrici Garneti pag. 20. se nullam unquam prolitionem meminisse in Anglia, cui non Sacerdos Romane Catholicus interfuerit: in hac vero, de qua agimus, Iesuitas plures non solum sese immiscuisse, sed etiam praefuisse dicit. Ex illis tres sunt Legati ordinarij; in Anglia Henricus Garnet, alias Vualley, Iesuitarum in illo regno Superior; in Hispania Gresuuellus; in Belgio Balduuinus; ut Romae Personius, praeter emissarios suos, quales fuerunt Gerardus, Ofvvaldus, Tesmond alias Greenuuelt Hamond, Haull, & alij ex Iesuitica societate. De quibus in Actione Henrici Garnetii iussu Magnae Britanniae Regis in lucem edita sic scribitur pag. 1. &
units.tr: As far as the clergy are concerned, Sir Edmund Coke, Knight of the Bath and the King's Attorney General in England, testifies in the Acts of Henry Garnet, p. 20, that he cannot recall any treason in England in which a Roman Catholic priest did not take part. In this one of which we are speaking, he says, not only did several Jesuits mix themselves in, but they even presided over it. Of these, three were ordinary legates: in England, Henry Garnet, alias Wally, Superior of the Jesuits in that kingdom; in Spain, Greenwell; in Belgium, Baldwin; and at Rome, Persons, besides his emissaries, such as Gerard, Oswald, Tesmond alias Greenwell, Hamond, Hall, and others of the Jesuit society. Concerning them, the Acts of Henry Garnet, published by order of the King of Great Britain, write thus at p. 1, and:

units.la: 2. Henricus Garnet Superior Iesuitica Societatis in Anglia; Ofwvaldus Tesmond & Iohannes Gerard Iesuita, Robertus Vuinter Armiger, Thomas Vuinter, &c. contra Regiam Majestatem convenerunt. Et Henricus Garnet, Ofuualdus Tesmond, Ioannes Gerard aliique Iesuitae malitiose, perfide & proditorie Thomae Vuintero, Guidoni Faunkes, Roberto Keies, &c. confirmarunt & persuaserunt, Serenissimum Regem Angliae Proceres & praesules, universamque Regni Angliae plebem, exceptis Papistis, esse haereticos omnesque haereticos anathematis vinculo esse innodatos & excommunicatos, nullumque posse regnare: sed licitum meritoriumque esse Regem & singulos in Anglia haereticos e medio tollere ad promovendam & propagandam fucatam illam & usurpatam Pontificis Rom. authoritatem & iurisdictionem, & ad superstitiosam illam Rom. religionem in Anglia restauranda. Cui proditoriae persuasioni Thomas Vuinter, Robertus Catesby, Guido Faunkes, Robertus Keyes, &c. perfide assensum praebuerunt. Et inde Henricus Garnet ille, Ofuualdus Tesmod, Ioannes Gerard & alij Iesuitae, Thomas Vuinter, Robertus Faunkes, &c. perfidiosissime consenserunt, & conspirarunt pulvere sulphureo, sive fulminali, quasi uno flatu erumpente Regem, &c. atrocissime, immanissime & perfidiosissime ex improviso in alium effla-re, membratim discerpere & funditus e medio tollere.
units.tr: 2. Henry Garnet, Superior of the Jesuit society in England; Oswald Tesmond and John Gerard, Jesuits; Robert Winter, Esquire; Thomas Winter, etc., met together against the royal majesty. And Henry Garnet, Oswald Tesmond, John Gerard and other Jesuits, maliciously, treacherously and perfidiously, confirmed and persuaded Thomas Winter, Guy Fawkes, Robert Keyes, etc., that the most serene King of England, the nobles and prelates, and the whole common people of the kingdom of England, except the Papists, are heretics, that all heretics are bound and excommunicated by the chain of anathema, and that no one can reign over them; but that it is lawful and meritorious for the King and for individuals to remove from the midst all the heretics in England, in order to promote and propagate that feigned and usurped authority and jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff, and to restore in England that superstitious Roman religion. Thomas Winter, Robert Catesby, Guy Fawkes, Robert Keyes, etc., treacherously gave their assent to this treasonous persuasion. And thereupon that Henry Garnet, Oswald Tesmond, John Gerard and the other Jesuits, together with Thomas Winter, Robert Fawkes, etc., most perfidiously consented and conspired to blow up the King, etc., most atrociously, most monstrously and most treacherously, by a sudden explosion of sulphurous or fulminating powder, as if by one blast, to tear him limb from limb and utterly remove him from the midst.

units.la: In Tortura Tortilegitur, Iesuitam Tesmundum Batesio cuidam persuasisse, in hac pulveraria coniuratione & facinore inaudito, nec periculum nec peccatum ullum subesse; rem licitam esse & magno bono futuram, animumque eius ad faciendum firmasse, & Eucharistiam insuper ei dedisse. Referturibidem, Iesuitam Gerardum uno eodemque tempore quinque simul viris, de conspiratorum numero, iuramentum taciturnitatis detulisse, quod per Sacram Trinitatem, perque, quod tum sumpturi erant Sacramentum, nec revelarent rem illam eorum tum fidei commendandam, nec nisi venia a reliquis data, umquam ab executione desisterent; & iuramentum post, data illis Eucharistia obsignasse. Iesuita Oldcornus seu Halus, detecta demum coniuratione, quasi bonum factum defendit, nec quia successu caruit, ideo non laudandum. De Garnetto suo loco dicemus. Hoc loco unum tantum de illo referam: Cum primum nunciaretur ei detectam esse coniurationem pulverariam & facinus inhumanissimum, At, at; dixisse illum aiunt, actum ergo de tota Societate nostra. Quae verba satis magno argumento sunt, Iesuitas in hoc nefario facinore vel consultores vel consentientes fuisse: sin minus, nullam certe trepidandi & timendi causam habuissent. Neque ipsi proditores vel in iudicio criminali, vel in ultimo supplicio negarunt, Iesuitas & consultores & consentientes fuisse. Greenuuellus etiam, alias Tesmundus, a quo rem totam, reliquas partes singulas rescivit Garnetus, & a quo omnia speciatim audivit, Iesuita fuit.
units.tr: In the torture, it is recorded, the Jesuit Tesmond persuaded a certain Bates that in this gunpowder conspiracy and unheard-of crime there was neither danger nor sin; that the deed was lawful and would bring great good; and he strengthened his resolve to do it, and moreover gave him the Eucharist. The same account says that the Jesuit Gerard, at one and the same time, administered to five men of the number of the conspirators an oath of secrecy, sworn by the Holy Trinity and by the Sacrament they were about to receive, that they would neither reveal that matter, which was to be entrusted to their faith, nor, unless pardon were granted by the rest, ever desist from carrying it out; and afterwards, having given them the Eucharist, he sealed the oath. The Jesuit Oldcorne, or Hall, when the conspiracy was at last discovered, defended it as a good deed, and said it was not to be disapproved merely because it had not succeeded. I shall speak of Garnet in his own place. For the present I will relate only one thing about him: when he was first told that the gunpowder conspiracy and that most inhuman crime had been detected, he is said to have cried, "Alas, alas, then our whole Society is undone." These words are a strong argument that the Jesuits were either counsellors or accomplices in this nefarious deed; otherwise they would certainly have had no cause to tremble and fear. Nor did the traitors themselves, either in the criminal court or at the final punishment, deny that the Jesuits were counsellors and accomplices. Greenwell also, otherwise called Tesmond, from whom Garnet learned the whole matter and each of the remaining parts, and from whom he heard everything in detail, was a Jesuit.

units.la: Et tamen M. Tortus scribit, in hoc coniurationis scelere, non ullum Iesuitam, vel consultorem, vel consentientem ullo modo fuisse. Tam manifestum hoc Tortis mendacium est, ut omnem omnino pudorem & conscientiam ipsum exuisse meritissime videri ac dici queat.
units.tr: And yet Mr. Tortus writes that in this crime of conspiracy no Jesuit, either as counsellor or as accomplice, was involved in any way. This lie of the Tortis is so manifest that he may most deservedly be said and thought to have stripped off all shame and conscience.

units.la: Hi Clerici
units.tr: These clerics:

units.la: {a} Clerici sanctissimi, hoc facinus...
units.tr: Most holy clerics, this deed...

units.la: Hi Clerici & Laici rem ipsam hoc modo aggrediuntur. Robertus Catesbeius, primarius in Anglia nobilis, accersitum ad se Thomam Vuinterū, quum sciret in Belgium eum iterū suscepturum, hortatur, ne curam religionis Pontificiae in patria restaurandae abijciat. Respondet ille, paratum & promptū se quidem esse cauiam Pontificiam etiam cum iactura vitae suae promovere; modum autem & viam qua id commode fieret, ignorare. Eam vero se scire Catesbeius respondit, Parlamenti nimirum domo, Regeque Regina cū liberis suis, cunctisque proceribus, primis Regni Comitiis in ea congregatis, pulveris tormentarij nitrati vi, ex fundamentis erutā & subversa. Exhorrescit primo Vuinterus ad mentionem huius tam horrendi facinoris: operam tamen suam in exequendo eo ipsi tandem pollicitus est, omni etiam vitae suae periculo neglecto. Convenit igitur inter eos, ut in Belgium profectus Thomas Vuinterus, aliquem inde secum in Angliam adduceret, cuius opera negotium hoc commode in actum perduceretur. Commorari ut e in Belgio quendam Guidonem Fauukes Catesbeius dicebat, quo magis quidē ad hanc rem perficiendam idoneus, inveniri non posset. Vuinterus in Belgium veniens, cum Ovveno quodā Iesuita de hoc suo proposito confert, qui confirmatum mirifice in Angliā redire iubet, promittens se Guidonem illum, hac de re bene informatū, breviterque eodē transmissurum. Nec morāilla, cū vix Obtēda affectus esset Vuinterus, ecce Iesuitae hortatu eode pervenit Guido ille, & in Angliam sine mora cum Vuintero traiecit. Dum abesset autem Vuinterus, communicat hoc suum consilium Catesbeius cum quibusdā aliis: itaque reverso iam Vintero, quinque sequentes, Rob. Catesbeius, Thomas Percius, Thomas Vuinter, Ioan. Vuright & Guido Faunkes ad S. Clementem congregati, iuramento praestito invicem se obstringunt, quod quorum conscij essent nihil effutire velent, ad Missam abeunt & Eucharistiam accipiunt, ministrantibus illam eis Iesuitis & in proposito eos confirmantibus.
units.tr: These clerics and laymen approached the matter itself in this way. Robert Catesby, the foremost nobleman in England, summoned Thomas Winter, who he knew would soon return to Belgium, and urged him not to abandon the cause of restoring the Papist religion in his country. Winter replied that he was indeed ready to advance the Papist cause, even at the cost of his life, but that he did not know the means and way by which this could be done conveniently. Catesby answered that he knew that way: namely, the House of Parliament, with the King, the Queen with their children, and all the nobles, gathered there at the first assembly of the realm, was to be blown up from its foundations by the force of nitrated gunpowder. Winter at first shrank back at the mention of so horrible a deed; yet at last he promised his services in carrying it out, disregarding every danger to his own life. It was therefore agreed between them that Thomas Winter, once he had gone to Belgium, should bring back someone from there to England, by whose work this business could be conveniently brought to completion. Catesby said that a certain Guy Fawkes was staying in Belgium, and that no one could be found more suitable for carrying this out. Winter, coming to Belgium, conferred about this plan with a certain Owen, a Jesuit, who wonderfully confirmed him and bade him return to England, promising that he would send that Guy, well informed on the matter, across immediately. And without delay, when Winter had scarcely reached Ostend, behold, at the Jesuit's urging, Guy himself arrived at the same place, and crossed with Winter into England without delay. While Winter was away, Catesby communicated this plan of his to certain others; so when Winter had now returned, five men, Robert Catesby, Thomas Percy, Thomas Winter, John Wright and Guy Fawkes, met together at St. Clement's, and by a mutual oath bound themselves that they would reveal nothing of what they knew; then they went to Mass and received the Eucharist, the Jesuits administering it to them and confirming them in their purpose.

units.la: Cum etiā animadvertisset Catesbeius famulū suū Thomā Bates curiosius observare, & quasi in suspicionē vocare quid dominus eius moliretur, in aedes suas apud Puddie uuharfe eum accersit, & Thomā Vuintero adstante interrogavit, quidnā ille suspicaretur de suis & sociorū conatib. cum iam pridē accurate illos observārit. Bates respondit, se suspicari illos aliquid magnū & periculi plenum, quicquid illud fit, machinari. Hinc iterū interrogarunt eum, quodnā esse opinaretur: respondit, se opinari eos aliquid periculosum de aedibus. Parlamentarijs motiuis, quia ad domum proximā conducendam ab illis missus fuerit. Tunc Batesiū diuisiurandum adegerunt, ut rem omne celaret. Cū iurāsset, rem omnē illi communicarunt: ad Eucharistiae etiā sumptionem eū hortati sunt, propter maiorem autionē & rei occultationē. Hinc Tesmondum Iesuitam, ut peccata ei confiteretur, accessit, & inter cōfitendū significat, rem admodū periculosam & maximī tormenti, qua Catesbeius & Vuinterus sibi communicarint, occultanda esse, sed vehementer dubitare, an licitū sit, ideoque Iesuita consuluit & rem omnē ei aperuit. Iesuita autē, qui ex coniuratis iam ante erat, illi persuasit, id licere maximē, eiusque nimīū ad facinus firmavit, iusitque ut quod dominus eius illi significarit, quam maxime occultaret. Adiunxit praeterea, in occultatione neque periculum, neque peccatum subesse, eumque absolvit: & Bates cū domino suo Catesbeio & Vuintero Eucharistiam sumpsit. Bockuuodus etiam, fide ad rem occultandam iureiurando praestita, cum ex Catesbeio cognovisset, machinationē illā ad regem ac regnum extinguendū pertinere, attonitus & stupore percussus, dixit, falsā cōscientiā tantum sanguinis innocentis effundi non posse. Catesbeius autē respondit, sibi a Iesuita Superiore Henr. Garneto plane persuasum esse, sine aliqua conscientiae offensa id fieri posse. Hamondus Iesuita quoque coniurationis socios oēs in aedibus Roberti Vuinteri absolvit die Iovis proxime post proditionem detectam, cum impiū parricidae arma induissent.
units.tr: Since Catesby had also noticed that his servant Thomas Bates was watching more closely and seemed to be becoming suspicious of what his master was plotting, he summoned him to his house at Puddle Wharf, and with Thomas Winter standing by, asked him what he suspected of the plans of himself and his associates, since he had been observing them carefully for some time. Bates replied that he suspected them of plotting something great and full of danger, whatever it might be. Then they asked him again what he thought it was; he answered that he supposed they were up to something dangerous concerning the Parliament buildings, because he had been sent by them to rent a neighbouring house. Then they made Bates swear an oath to conceal the whole matter. When he had sworn, they communicated the whole affair to him, and urged him to receive the Eucharist as well, for greater assurance and for keeping the matter hidden. Afterwards he went to the Jesuit Tesmond to confess his sins, and during confession he indicated that the matter which Catesby and Winter had communicated to him was very dangerous and of the greatest gravity, and had to be kept secret; but he was greatly doubtful whether it was lawful, and so he asked the Jesuit for advice and disclosed the whole matter to him. The Jesuit, who was already one of the conspirators, persuaded him that it was entirely lawful, and strengthened his resolve for the deed, and ordered that whatever his master had told him he should keep as hidden as possible. He added moreover that in concealing it there was neither danger nor sin, and absolved him; and Bates received the Eucharist together with his master Catesby and Winter. Bowes too, having sworn an oath to keep the matter secret, when he learned from Catesby that this plot pertained to the destruction of the king and kingdom, astonished and struck dumb, said, that so much innocent blood could not be shed with a clear conscience. Catesby, however, replied that he had been fully persuaded by the Jesuit Superior, Henry Garnet, that this could be done without any offence to conscience. The Jesuit Hamond also absolved all the conspirators in the house of Robert Winter on the Thursday immediately after the plot was detected, when they had put on the arms of the impious murderers.

units.la: Personæ contra quas hæc diabolica machinatio suscepta erat, flos totius regni fuerunt. Primaria fuit Rex ipse Angliæ, adeoque legitimus coniuratorum magnus stratus, ad quem diadema regium hæreditario iure pertinuit: deinde Regina, regia soboles mascula, quæ Anglici regni vnica spes, solatium, vita & anima est: quarto, prudentissimi Regis consiliarij, fidelissimi proceres, reverendi Præsules, grauissimi iudices, præcipui equestris dignitatis, generosi Comites, Cives & Parlamenti assessores: Vt si consilium & machinatio hæc illis ex animi sententia successisset, nullus in Anglia futurus fuisset Rex, nulla Regina, Princeps nullus, proles mascula regia nulla, Regni consiliarij nulli, Proceres nulli, nulli Episcopi, nulli iudices.
units.tr: The persons against whom this devilish plot was undertaken were the flower of the whole kingdom. First was the King of England himself, whom the conspirators would have struck down, and to whom the royal crown belonged by hereditary right. Next was the Queen, a royal male offspring, who is the sole hope, comfort, life and soul of the English kingdom. Fourthly came the wisest counsellors of the King, the most loyal nobles, the reverend bishops, the most serious judges, the chief men of the knightly order, the noble earls, the citizens and the members of Parliament. So if this plan and machination had succeeded as they wished, there would have been no King in England, no Queen, no prince, no male royal offspring, no counsellors of the realm, no nobles, no bishops, no judges.

units.la: Consilium autem hoc immanissimum initum est anno primo Iacobi Regis, adeoque illo tempore, quo insignem clementiam in exordio regni sui erga rebelles exercuit, & per integrum annum, quatuorque menses legibus multam inflictam ab illis nullam exigeret. Tantum etiam a severitate regia maiestas abfuit, ut præter indultam illam gratiam, omnes dignitate pariter & honore promoverit. Non tamen hoc pacto ad sanitatem revocati fuerunt, sed deteriores Iesuitarum adhortationibus ac stimulis evaserunt.
units.tr: This most monstrous plot was devised in the first year of King James, at the very time when, at the beginning of his reign, he showed remarkable clemency towards the rebels, and for a whole year and four months exacted none of the fines the laws imposed on them. His Majesty was so far from severity that, besides granting that pardon, he promoted all of them alike in rank and honour. Yet they were not brought back to soundness by this course; under the urging and goads of the Jesuits they became worse.

units.la: Locus autem huic facinori destinatus, sacræ Parlamenti ædes fuerunt, in quibus Senatus ex omnium totius regni hominum genere congregari debuit. Hunc locum propterea se huic facinori destinasse dixerunt, quod præteritis temporibus iniquæ leges in eo contra Romane-Catholicos latæ ac promulgatæ fuissent. Sed verissimam causam ex coniurationis fine intelligemus.
units.tr: The place chosen for this crime was the sacred house of Parliament, in which the assembly of men from every rank of the whole kingdom was to gather. They said they had chosen this place for the deed because in past times unjust laws had been passed and promulgated there against the Roman Catholics. But we shall understand the truest cause from the aim of the conspiracy.

units.la: Finis huius facinoris fuit, ut Rex, omnesque totius regni proceres, in hoc loco congregati, delerentur, & universus totius regni status funditus subverteretur.
units.tr: The aim of this crime was that the King and all the nobles of the kingdom, gathered in that place, should be destroyed, and the whole state of the realm utterly overthrown.

units.la: Sexto, progrediendi rationem in hoc scelere, & instrumenta quod attinet, Parlamenti congregatio ad Februar. 7. diem instituta erat: ut igitur tunc diabolica hæc machinatio in effectum perduceretur, Thomas Perceius domum Parlamenti ædibus contiguam certo pretio conducit, ut cuniculis sub fundamentis Parlamenti agendis, operam dare commodius possent. Sed & domum aliam pro tormentarij pulveris & lignorum, quibus ad hanc rem opus esset, comportatione conducunt, unde nocturno tempore transferre illa ad domum Parlamento proximam, commode possent. Domus hæc Lamberti cuiusdam erat, apud quem diverteret Catesbeius plerunque solebat, qui famulum etiam Lamberti Robertum Keest nomine, ut eo secretiora & tutiora essent omnia, in societatem sceleris pertraxit. Sub initium Decembris cum difficultatem cuniculos sub muro Parlamenti tres perticas crasso, agendi sentirent, seq; perficiendo operi non sufficere viderent, duos adhuc alios iuramento obstrictos, Christophorum Vurigth & Robertum Vuinterum sibi adiungunt. Pergunt ergo iam in suffodiendo muro strenuè, Guidone Faux in excubijs interea constituto, ut si forte accederent aliqui, certo signo cessandum a labore esse, eos monneret. Accidit autem ut dum in opere essent, strepitum quendam quasi carbonum, in cella subterranea proxima audirent. Ablegatus igitur eò Perceius, ut illis certo precio coëmptis, cellam negotio suo ad modum oportunam conducit, eamque cadis seu vasculis 36. tormentarij pulveris replet, vectes etiam ferreos, lapides & lignæ cadis superimponit, ad maiorem perniciem & vastitatem. Differtur interea publicis literis Parlamenti congregatio in mensem Octobrem, atque porro ad 15. Novemb. diem reiicitur. Proinde rebus omnibus iam constitutis & perfectis domum coniurati cescuntur igitur, Guido autem Faukes in Belgium ad tempus concedens, Guilielmo Stanleio & Oveno Iesuitæ, quid effecerint exponit: erat enim inter eos ita conuentum, ut quem fidum quisque nosset, eum hac de re edoceret.
units.tr: Sixthly, as regards the manner of proceeding in this wickedness and the instruments, the meeting of Parliament had been appointed for 7 February. So that this devilish machination might then be carried into effect, Thomas Percy rented for a set price a house adjoining the Parliament building, so that they might more conveniently be able to dig mines beneath the foundations of Parliament. They also rented another house for bringing in the gunpowder and the wood needed for the business, from which they could conveniently carry those things by night to the house next to Parliament. This house belonged to a certain Lambert, at whose place Catesby mostly lodged; and he also drew into the conspiracy Lambert's servant, Robert Keyes, so that everything might be more secret and safer. At the beginning of December, when they found it difficult to dig the mines under the wall of Parliament, which was three poles thick, and saw that they could not finish the work with what they had, they added two more men bound by oath, Christopher Wright and Robert Winter. So they now pressed on vigorously with breaking through the wall, while Guy Fawkes was posted on watch meanwhile, so that if anyone happened to approach, he might warn them by a certain signal to cease work. It happened, however, that while they were at work they heard a noise, as of coals being moved, in a vault next door. Percy was therefore sent there, and having bought the cellar for a set price, which suited his purpose, he filled it with thirty-six barrels or casks of gunpowder, and also laid iron bars, stones and wood on top of the casks, for greater destruction and devastation. Meanwhile the meeting of Parliament was put off by public letters until October, and then further deferred to 15 November. Therefore, with everything now arranged and completed, the conspirators dispersed. Guy Fawkes, however, withdrew to Belgium for a time and set out to Guillaume Stanley and the Jesuit Owen what they had accomplished; for it had been agreed among them that each should inform whichever trusted person he knew about the matter.

units.la: Ad consilij autem huius seu propositi truculentissimi occultationis his potissimum rationibus usi sunt. Primum, Catesbeius Marchioni Spinolae ut equitum turmae in Belgio praeesset, commendatus est, ut hoc praetextu sine omni suspicione coniuratos equis instrueret. Deinde, Iusiurandum omnes, tam pro taciturnitate, quam perseverantia & constantia in proditione praestanda iurarunt. Iuramenti autem forma haec erat: Iurabis per sacram Trinitatem, & per id quod jam sumpturus es sacramentum, nunquam vel directe vel indirecte, verbis aut circumstantijs istam rem revelare, uitae tuae iam commendandae fidei, neque ab exequutione huius destistere, donec reliqui tibi venia concedant. Iuramentum hoc Catesbeio, Percio, Vurighto & Thomae Vuintero uno eodemque tempore, per Gerardum alias Lec & Brokenominatum, Iesuitam, alioque tempore Batesio & reliquis per Greenvellum alias Ofvvaldum Tesmond Iesuitam datum est.
units.tr: For the concealment of this plan, or rather this most savage purpose, they used chiefly these means. First, Catesby was recommended to Marquis Spinola to command a troop of horsemen in Belgium, so that under this pretext he could equip the conspirators with horses without any suspicion. Next, all of them swore an oath, binding themselves to silence as well as to perseverance and constancy in carrying out the betrayal. The form of the oath was this: You shall swear by the holy Trinity, and by the sacrament you are about to receive, never to reveal this matter, either directly or indirectly, by words or by circumstances, pledging your life to faithfulness; nor shall you desist from carrying it out until the others grant you release. This oath was given to Catesby, Percy, Wright and Thomas Winter at one and the same time, through the Jesuit Gerard, alias Lee, and the man named Broke; and at another time to Bates and the rest, through Greenwell, alias Oswald Tesmond, a Jesuit.

units.la: Denique detestandum hoc facinus, ab uno coniurationis socio, qui invitus & iuramentum & sacramentum accepit, subobscuris literis ad Dominum de Monte-Aquila datis, detectum est: coniurati plerique comprehensi sunt & comeritas poenas luerunt. Haec cum ita sint, non iniuria Eduuardus Coke Eques auratus & Procurator Regius in Anglia hanc coniurationem appellat Iesuiticam, ut ad Iesuitas ex congruo & condigno spectantem: hi enim, ut intelligit Lector, architecti eius fuerunt, ut est videre in Actis Garneti pag. 66. In huiusmodi autem criminibus plus peccat Auctor quam Actor.
units.tr: Finally, this detestable crime was disclosed by one of the conspirators, who had received both the oath and the sacrament reluctantly, in a rather obscure letter sent to Lord Monteagle. Most of the conspirators were arrested and paid the penalties they deserved. Since this is so, Sir Edward Coke, Knight, and the King's Attorney in England, not without reason calls this conspiracy Jesuitical, as belonging to the Jesuits by due and proper right: for they, as the reader understands, were its architects; as may be seen in the Acts of Garnet, p. 66. In crimes of this kind, however, the author sins more than the doer.

units.la: Sed de hoc inaudito & horrendo facinore Rex ipse Britanniae maioris sic scripsit, & veritate eiusdem contra nefarias quorundam calumnias veritate regia his verbis asseruit: Horrenda illa & prodigiosa coniuratio (inquit Rex) quae per tormentarij pulveris impetu destinabatur, de cuius flagitij immanitate nulla unquam aetas consticet (quanquam illius mentio tam saepe repetita Parsonij animum perfodiat) non in me tantum, neque posteros inita, publicos etiam regni ordines evertere ac delere instituerat: nec alij tanti scelerisque auctores, qua Papistae aliquot, praepostero suae religionis sub vehendae zelo ad hanc immanitatem induci. Ex ijs nonnulli tanta pertinacia obstinaverat sceleris, ut nec in supremo vitae articulo detestaretur suum crimen, supremis verbis, & pene supervenientem morte praesentis, reos se ullius flagitij confiteri abnuerit, aut petere cogitati facinoris veniam, nisi prius Ecclesia hoc tanta coniurationis consilium sua sententia damnavisset. Nec multo post inou it, non paucos ex meorum subditorum numero, qui Romanae Religione profitentur, omnes conditiones & sexus, alios domi, alios foris, & apud gentes exteras, confusa & obscura significatione esse, magnum aliquid, quo Rom. Ecclesiae utilitas promoveretur, in id coeuntium ordinum empus comparari: quanquam illis, ne vulgata res secretum omnem panderet, destinata rei modus, et consiliorum ratio nequaquam proderetur. Sed & certae praetationum formulae concepta, a multis usurpata, quibus prosperos successus tanto & tam gravi negotio precabantur. Ipsi quoque coniurationis auctores, atque architecti in constantia sua pignus & silentij auctoramentum apius multorum Sacerdotum ministerio Eucharistia Sacramento supto, animos suos ad flagitium obfirmarunt. Quidam etiam ex Iesuitarum primarijs contagione tanti scelerisque infecti. Ex his aliquot matura ad exteras gentes fuga vim judiciorum eluserunt, intercepti aliquot, inter quos ille Garnetus & Ouldcor, & facinus confitentes capitis supplicio affecti sunt. Et paulo post: Iam vero ille alter qui Garneto hac pulveranam coniurationem aperuit, Greenuvel Iesuita est: sic Iesuita nefaria proditionis ordinem exposuit, nec ille, qui tantum scelus peruit, ullum conscientiae stimulum senserit, neque is cui patefactum est, ullam confitenti ob coitatum scelus paenitentiam indixit. Acutius palam fit, plures ex Iesuitis huius coniurationis conscios fuisse, Ouldcornius alter ille sulphureus martyr, cum in irritum cessisset e lachryma sua extracta coniuratio, concionem Catholicorum suorum habuit, ubi eos consolatus, ac etiam hortatus est, ne animos sinistro & infelici coniurationis eventu desponderent, aut de causa, quod parum prospere cecidisset, desperarent: saepe antea Sanctis ipsi modi consilibus fortunam defuisse, idque sancti Ludovici Regis exemplo, cum secunda in terram sanctam expeditione suscepta, morbo in itinere periisse, maximam exer-citus partem perijse esse absumptam; sed & parum feliciter priorem expeditionem cessisse, in qua à Soldano & Mahumetanis captus est. Eos itaque hortabatur, ne ab incepto desisterent: sperarent potius suis illis consiliis, quanquam hoc tempore deploratis, divinam alicuando opem nequaquam defuturam. Quod & Attorniatus Regius probat, qui in hac coniuratione testatur, Iesuitas, ut diximus, plures non solum se immiscuisse, sed etiam praefuisse: ex illis tres esse Legatos ordinarios; in Anglia Henr. Garnetum, alias V Vallay, Iesuitarum in eo regno Superiorem; in Hispania Cresswellum, in Belgio Balduinum & Romae Persomium, praeter emissarios suos, quorum sunt Gerardus, Oliualdus, Tesmund alias Greenuuell, Hamond, Haul, & e Societate Iesuitarum alij; ita ut Iesuitas huius nefandi sceleris Antesignanos & primarios autores non immerito nominet.
units.tr: Concerning this unheard-of and horrible crime, the King of Great Britain himself wrote thus, and by his royal truthfulness asserted its truth against the wicked calumnies of certain people, in these words: That horrible and prodigious conspiracy (says the King), which was aimed at blowing up with gunpowder, whose enormity no age will ever be silent about (although its mention, so often repeated, pierces the mind of Parsons), had resolved to overthrow and destroy not only me and my posterity, but also the public orders of the realm; nor were the authors of so great a wickedness only a few Papists, who were induced to such savagery under the perverted zeal of promoting their religion. Some of them were so obstinate in their crime that, even at the last moment of life, they did not detest their sin; with their final words, and almost with death coming upon them, they refused to confess themselves guilty of any crime, or to ask pardon for the plan they had devised, unless first the Church had condemned such a great conspiracy by its own judgement. And shortly afterwards he said: Not a few of my subjects who profess the Roman religion, of every condition and sex, some at home and some abroad and among foreign nations, were known in confused and obscure terms to be preparing a great thing, a time to gather the orders in which the advantage of the Roman Church might be promoted; although the manner of the thing and the reasoning of their plans were in no way revealed to them, lest a matter once divulged should lay open all its secrecy. Also, certain formulas of prayers were composed and used by many, by which they prayed for prosperous success in so great and grave an undertaking. The very authors and architects of the conspiracy, to confirm their constancy and as a pledge of silence, bound their minds to the crime by receiving the Eucharist sacrament from the ministry of many priests. Some also of the chief Jesuits were infected with the contagion of so great a wickedness. Of these, some by timely flight to foreign lands escaped the force of the courts; some were caught, among whom were that Garnet and Oldcorne, and they were put to death by the axe, confessing the deed. And a little later: Now, that other man who revealed this gunpowder conspiracy to Garnet is Greenwell the Jesuit: thus a Jesuit set out the order of the foul betrayal, and he who committed so great a crime felt no sting of conscience, nor did he to whom it was disclosed impose any penance on the confessed crime. It becomes clearer and clearer that several of the Jesuits were privy to this conspiracy. That other sulphurous martyr, Oldcorne, when the conspiracy extracted from his tears had come to nothing, gave a sermon to his Catholics, in which he consoled and also exhorted them not to lose heart at the sinister and unhappy outcome of the conspiracy, nor to despair of the cause because it had turned out not very favourably. He said that often before, fortune had failed holy men in such plans, and he pointed to the example of holy King Louis, who, when he had undertaken a second expedition to the Holy Land, died on the way of disease, and the greater part of his army perished and was consumed; and that the earlier expedition also ended unhappily, in which he was captured by the Sultan and the Mahometans. He therefore urged them not to abandon what they had begun: they should rather hope that divine help would not fail them at some time, despite those plans now given up for lost. The King's Attorney also confirms this, who in this conspiracy testifies that the Jesuits, as we have said, not only took part in great numbers but also presided over it. Of these, three were ordinary legates: in England, Henry Garnet, alias Vaux, superior of the Jesuits in that kingdom; in Spain, Creswell; in Belgium, Baldwin; and at Rome, Persons; besides their emissaries, among whom are Gerard, Oswald, Tesmond alias Greenwell, Hamond, Hall, and other members of the Society of Jesus. So he rightly names the Jesuits the standard-bearers and chief authors of this nefarious crime.

units.la: Ex his igitur omnibus intelligit universus orbis, proditiones, insidias, parricidia, & veneficia Iesuitica non a levi singulorum Iesuitarum provenire motu, sed illos ea, velut summa, generalia, indubitata, & immutabilia doctrinae suae principia, & praecepta constituta, suis monitis & adhortationibus, omnibus, qui ipsis aures praebent, pernicio sissime infundere, atque ita imprimere, donec eos deliberato, pervicaci, caeco & obstinato corde, in illis ad supremum vitae spiritum persequendis obfirmatos esse agnoscant.
units.tr: From all of this, then, the whole world understands that the treacheries, plots, murders of kings and poisonings of the Jesuits do not arise from the rash impulse of individual Jesuits; rather, they most perniciously instil these things, as the highest, general, unquestioned and unchangeable principles and precepts of their doctrine, by their admonitions and exhortations, into all who lend them their ears, and so impress them, until they recognise that those men have been hardened in pursuing these things to the last breath of life, with a deliberate, obstinate, blind and stubborn heart.

units.la: DE CONIVRATIONIBVS AC PRODITORIIS CONSILIIS HENRICI GARNETI IESVITAE AD- VERSVS REGIAM MAIESTATEM IN ANGLIA.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE CONSPIRACIES AND TREACHEROUS COUNSELS OF HENRY GARNET THE JESUIT AGAINST THE ROYAL MAJESTY IN ENGLAND.

units.la: Henricus Garnetus professione Iesuita, alias Vualleius, alias Darcius, alias Robertus, alias Farmerus, alias Philippus nominatus fuit, & haec nomina omnia ipsemet sibi effinxit, pro more & consuetudine Iesuitarum, qui se in omnes figuras transformare, & nomina sua subinde, ad decipiendos ac fallendos homines, mutare solent.
units.tr: Henry Garnet, a Jesuit by profession, was also called Walley, Darcy, Robert, Farmer and Philip. He invented all these names himself, following the custom and practice of the Jesuits, who are accustomed to transform themselves into every shape and to change their names from time to time in order to deceive and mislead men.

units.la: Patria fuit Anglus, genere clarus, in scholis institutus: postea sub Totteloo Typographo, iuris Municipalis praelo Corrector praefuit. Non paucis dotibus ornatus fuit, modo divina accessisset gratia; quae cum abesset, tanto nequior, quanto ornatior erat. Professione fuit Iesuita, & in Anglia Iesuiticae Societatis Superior; & quidem optimo iure: Omnes enim quotquot ante eum fuerunt conspiratione diabolica multis, quod aiunt, parasangis superavit. Iesuitarum Doctor, id est, in quinque D. magister excellentissimus: videlicet Dissimulando, Deponendo Reges, Disponendo regna, Deterrendo subditos ab officio, Destruendo denique omnia.
units.tr: He was English by birth, of distinguished family, and educated in the schools. Afterwards, under the printer Tottel, he served as corrector at the press of the municipal law. He was endowed with no small gifts, had divine grace been added; but since that grace was lacking, he was all the more wicked the more gifted he was. He was a Jesuit by profession and Superior of the Jesuit Society in England, and indeed by the best right: for he surpassed all who had been before him in diabolical conspiracy, as they say, by many parasangs. He was the Doctor of the Jesuits, that is, the most excellent master of the five D's: namely, Dissembling, Deposing kings, Disposing kingdoms, Deterring subjects from their duty, and finally Destroying everything.

units.la: De hoc Garneto referre quidem & scribere non pudet Andream Eudaemon Iohannem Cretensem in sua pro illo Apologia, eum nullius sceleris convictum, odio duntaxat religionis, aut Iesuitici nominis, fuisse damnatum & supplicio affectum: Tortus quoque scribit, Garnetum ipsum constanter affirmasse, non se, non ullum Iesuitam, vel consultorem vel consentientem ullo modo fuisse in hoc scelere. At vero ex universa narratione, quae actis publicis continetur, & ex Epistolis, quas de se & rebus suis in arce Londinensi scripsit plurimas, quaeque Elienfis Episcopus in Tortura sua Torti descripsit & publicavit, certo certius constat, Garnetum zeli praeposteri fervore, & caeco studio Romanae religionis promovendae accensum, ea gesisse, quae nemo vere Christianus & pius ab honesto viro, nedum Theologo expectaverit. Pulverariae coniurationis fuisse eum conscium, ne illi quidem negant, qui eum pro martyre haberi volunt. mt. Constat autem & sine ulla haesitatione affirmari potest, Garnetum sceleris istius non tantum conscium fuisse, verum etiam approbatorem, & genere quodam auctorem. Liquet enim, cum Catesbeius, Princeps proditorum, & doliptius primarius architectus, socios facinoris quaereret, eum in eas difficultas incidisse, quarum gratia adire ad Garneti oraculum oportuerit, ut rem eflicitam cunctis persuaderetur. Ipse quidem Catesbeius, pro ea consuetudie & familiaritate, quae illi cum Garneto intercedebat, non ignorans ad excluendum Regem Iacobum, Brevia duo ipsum Roma accepisse, ijs acquiescebat, hoc argumento utebatur, Quem voluit Papa aditu prohiberi, eum sine dubio vult dimissum deturbari. Sed cum non dubitaret Catesbeius, ad Regem deiciendum omnes sibi licitas esse fraudes ac dolos, quia tamen placitae machinationis ea ratio erat, ut Rex cum suis tolli aliter non posset, nisi ut multae Papistae simul perirent: super hoc dubio Catesbeius, ut & se & alios scrupulo molesto liberaret, non multo post, sub initium anni 1604. ut Acta testantur, Garnetum consuluit. Ex hoc colloquio & pluribus aliis Catesbei cum ipso, atque etiam ex Grenuelissaepe repetitis sermonibus, de quibus & Acta, & plurimae Garneti epistolae extant, luce clarius probatur, Garnetum Iesuitam coniurationis huius nefastae non minus conscium fuisse, quam alium quemvis complicum. Neque vero solum arcani conscius Garnetus fuit, sed etiam plerisque coniuratorum, ut Vuinters, Rookuuodo, & ipsi Faukio incendiario, audendi auctor extitit, cunctantibus et horrescentibus, priusquam probari rem tanto viro ex verbis Catesbei cognoscent, sicut fuse narratur actione in proditores priore. Iccirco ubi tempus excludendi dolum advenit, quum inter coniuratos convenisset, ut Conghtotiam omnes convenirent de rebus necessariis consultaturi, inter caeteros etiam Garnetus adfuit, omniaque ibi egit, quae a coniurationis conscio, suasore & upidissimo incensore agi par erat. Omitto alia indicia in actis & Tortura forti diligenter exposita, ut ne ipsi quidem hostes veritatis profesi id negare possint.
units.tr: Concerning this Garnet, Andreas Eudaemon-Joannes of Crete, in his Apology for him, does not blush to write that he, convicted of no crime, was condemned and put to death merely from hatred of his religion or of the Jesuit name. Tortus also writes that Garnet himself constantly affirmed that neither he nor any Jesuit, whether as counsellor or as consenting party, had in any way been involved in this crime. But from the whole account contained in the public records, and from the many letters which he wrote about himself and his affairs in the Tower of London, and which the Bishop of Ely described and published in his Tortura Torti, it is certain beyond doubt that Garnet, inflamed with the fervour of a perverse zeal and a blind eagerness to promote the Roman religion, did things which no truly Christian and pious man would expect from an honest man, let alone a theologian. Even those who wish him to be held a martyr do not deny that he knew of the gunpowder conspiracy. It is moreover established, and can be affirmed without any hesitation, that Garnet was not merely privy to this crime but also its approver and, in a certain sense, its author. For it is clear that when Catesby, the ringleader of the traitors and the chief architect of the plot, sought companions for the deed, he fell into difficulties, for the sake of which he had to go to Garnet's oracle so that the matter might be persuaded to all as feasible. Catesby himself, because of the custom and familiarity that existed between him and Garnet, knowing that two Briefs had been sent from Rome for the exclusion of King James, acquiesced in them, and used this argument: "Whom the Pope wills to be barred from access, he without doubt wills to be cast out once let go." But although Catesby did not doubt that all frauds and tricks were lawful for deposing the King, since the planned machination was such that the King could not be removed with his people unless many Papists perished at the same time, Catesby, to free both himself and others from this troublesome scruple, consulted Garnet not long afterwards, at the beginning of the year 1604, as the records attest. From this conversation and several others between Catesby and him, and also from the frequently repeated talks with Grenville, of which both the records and many letters of Garnet's survive, it is proved more clearly than light that Garnet the Jesuit was no less privy to this nefarious conspiracy than any other accomplice. Nor was Garnet merely a knower of the secret: he was also the author of daring to act for most of the conspirators, such as Winter, Rookwood and the incendiary Fawkes himself, who were hesitating and shrinking back, before they had come to know that the matter had been approved by so great a man through the words of Catesby, as is related at length in the earlier action against the traitors. Therefore, when the time for carrying out the treachery arrived, and the conspirators had agreed to meet together at Coughton to take counsel on the necessary matters, Garnet was present among the others, and did there all that a privy and approving accomplice and most eager instigator of the conspiracy ought to do. I omit the other proofs carefully set out in the records and in the strong Tortura, so that not even the enemies of truth themselves can deny them.

units.la: Vt autem adhuc minus de his dubitari posset, apertissimam ipsius Garnetii confessionem, ex literis eius propria manu scriptis Dominica Palmarum huc adcribam: quarum haec est inscriptio, Ad dilectissimos Patres & Fratres: His graviter ii succensentibus, quod proditione sibi innotuisse confessus esset, ita respondet: Nam quid facerem? Primo accusabant me reliqui omnes conjurati: Secundo, Catesbeius ipsius semper apud eos fuerat auctoritate mea, qua adduxit pene omnes, ut bene sentirent de negotio, quo factum, ut ad unum omnes me haberent pro reo. Tertio, duo quidam Corycaei nau-dierant me cum Oldcorno colloquentem, atque tota de re cum eo differentem, quid ad objecta singula responsurus essem. Quarto, literae etiam a me aurantiarum succo scriptae ad D. Annam Vaulx, nescio quomodo in illorum manus pervenerant, quibus sententiam mea non obscure confessus sum: Ingenue etiam fassus est, mortis sententiam justissime in se pronunciatam esse, quod, quae sibi COMPERTA fuissent, Regiae Majestati non aperuisset. Negat hoc Tortus; fatetur Garnetus: cui credimus?
units.tr: But so that there might be even less doubt about these matters, I shall here subjoin Garnet's own most manifest confession, from his letters written in his own hand on Palm Sunday. The heading of these is: To my most beloved Fathers and Brothers: When they were gravely incensed that he had confessed to having learned of the plot through betrayal, he replies as follows: For what was I to do? First, all the other conspirators accused me. Second, Catesby had always been among them through my authority, by which I had brought nearly all of them to think well of the business, so that they all held me guilty. Third, two certain Corycaeans had seen me conversing with Oldcorne and discussing with him the whole matter, and what I would answer to each objection. Fourth, letters written by me in orange juice to Mrs. Anne Vaux also somehow came into their hands, in which I openly confessed my opinion. He also freely confessed that the sentence of death had been most justly pronounced upon him, because he had not revealed to His Royal Majesty what had been DISCOVERED to him. Tortus denies this; Garnet confesses it. Whom shall we believe?

units.la: Grenuuellus quoque, cum detecta esset proditio, de Garneti consilio, in Vualia festinavit, ut quod occulte non poterant, aperta seditione efficerent: ad eamque rem Henlipae in aedibus Abingtoni, se a Provinciali Garneto missum, & hoc in mandatis habere palam contestatus est.
units.tr: Grenville too, when the treachery had been detected, hastened into Warwickshire on Garnet's counsel, so that what they could not do in secret they might accomplish by open rebellion. And he openly testified that he had been sent by the Provincial Garnet to Holbeach, to the house of Abington, and had this in his instructions.

units.la: Huc referri etiam debet manifestum testimonium Endaemon, Iohan. Cretensis, qui in Apologia pro Garneto scribit, Garnetum rogasse Deum, ut vel pestem hanc pulverariam averteret, vel si ita expediret, felicem funesto facinori exitum daret: monuisseque insuper omnes, qui ad solennes eius conciones Ecclesiasticas convenerant, ut bnixe Deum orent pro felici successu gravissimae cujusdam rei in causa Catholicorum & initium Comitiorum. Non probabat igitur factum Garnetus, hoc est, caede Regis,
units.tr: To this must also be referred the clear testimony of Eudaemon-Joannes of Crete, who writes in his Apology for Garnet: that Garnet asked God either to avert this gunpowder pestilence, or, if it were so expedient, to grant a happy outcome to the deadly deed; and moreover that he admonished all who had gathered at his solemn ecclesiastical sermons to pray earnestly to God for a fortunate success in a most serious matter for the cause of the Catholics and the beginning of the Parliament. Garnet therefore did not approve the deed, that is, the slaughter of the King,

units.la: Garnet confes-sio de seipso.
units.tr: Garnet's confession concerning himself.

units.la: Act. 19. &c. Acto in Scripta Ciaccio p. 1.
units.tr: Acts 19 etc. Acto in Scripta Ciaccio p. 1.

units.la: Ioan. Cretensis Iesuitae testimo-nium de Garneto. Regiæ familiæ, & procerum totius Angliæ; sed tamen amabat eventum, id ef gratum eifuturum erat, si caederentur & interirent omnes. Scilicet vere Catholica religio scelere tanto ut promoveatur opus habet. Pudeat Christianos tan manifestæ & proiectæ impietatis. Turcas non Catholicos decet hæc sententia. Sane ipse Garnetus cum postea a Magistratu interrogaretur; qua fronte ausu ausus esset ad precationem adeo detestandam ovibus sui gregis præire; facti pudendi infamiam quoquo modo a se amoliri conatus est: dixit enim, sed mentitus esse orationes illas fieri jussisse, non eo animo, ut ex sententia proditorum, sed potius, ut contra proditorum mentem res eveniret, utque eo pacto saluti Regis ac Regni consuleretur. Apologista hoc factum negat, & de re incomperta temere affirmans, ridicule si bi credi postulat: in Tortura autem Tortimendacij & falsitatis convincitur.
units.tr: Testimony of the Jesuit Joannes Cretensis concerning Garnet. He did not approve the deed, that is, the slaughter of the King, the royal family and the nobles of all England; yet he loved the outcome, which would be pleasing to him if all were slain and perished. Clearly the Catholic religion needs such a crime for its advancement. Christians should be ashamed of so manifest and abandoned impiety. This opinion befits Turks, not Catholics. Indeed, when Garnet was afterwards questioned by the magistrate as to what face he had had to lead the sheep of his flock in such a detestable prayer, he tried in every way to put away from himself the infamy of a shameful deed. For he said that he had ordered those prayers to be made, not with the intention that the traitors' purpose should be fulfilled, but rather that the outcome should be contrary to the traitors' mind, and that by this means the safety of the King and the kingdom should be looked after. The Apologist denies this fact, and rashly asserting something unknown, asks ridiculously to be believed; but under torture he is convicted of lying and falsehood.

units.la: Hoc igitur primum crimen Garneto obiectum fuit, quod malo consenserit, ut bonum, quod existimabat, eveniret, atque adeo totis viribus procurarit malum, quo maius aliud a condito mundo Sol non vidit. Garnetum igitur, & cæteram Iesuitarum & coniuratorum in Anglia colluviem, qui cædes tam atroce parabant, iustissimas Deo & hominibus pœnas pependisse, nemo inficiar potest.
units.tr: This, then, was the first crime laid against Garnet: that he consented to evil so that the good he thought of might come about, and thus with all his strength procured an evil greater than the sun has seen since the world was made. No one can deny that Garnet, and the rest of the Jesuit and conspirator rabble in England who prepared so atrocious a slaughter, paid the most just penalties to God and men.

units.la: Alterum crimen ei obiectum hoc fuit, quod amicos pariter & inimicos, fontes & insontes sine omni discrimine perdere voluit: quo nihil magis inhumanum aut belluinum est. Atqui Garnetus a Catesbeio consultus, esset ne hoc licitum, si alteri sine alteris exstingui non possent? semel ita respondit in privatis suis sedibus Licere, si tantum ex ea re boni proventurum esset, quantum aliquot insontium necem compensare posset. Iterum in campis suburbanis, quibus a palude nomen est, in hanc sententiam Catesbeio respondit: Et posse & licere, cum fontibus insontes ex sufflari, magnique adeo meriti rem fore, si id magno alicui bono Catholicis cederet. Constat de veritate huius responsionis, primo, ex Actione in proditores posteriore deinde ex Comitis Northamptoniæ, qui in præsentia Procerum Regni & ipsius Garneti hæc fuse narravit; quæ si dubia aut falsa fuit, cur tacuit Garnetus? Servantur autem duæ ipsius propria manu scriptæ epistolæ, quibus ea res omnis ingenue exponitur. Earum altera scripta est Pridie Non. Aprilis; altera
units.tr: The second charge brought against him was this: that he wished to destroy friends and enemies alike, the guilty and the innocent, without any distinction, than which nothing is more inhuman or brutal. Yet when Garnet was consulted by Catesby whether this would be lawful if one could not be destroyed without the others, he answered once, in his private lodgings, that it was lawful, if so much good would come from the thing as could make up for the killing of some innocent people. Again, in the suburban fields named after the marsh, he gave Catesby this answer: that it was both possible and lawful, since the innocent would be blown up with the guilty, and it would be a deed of great merit if it brought some great good to the Catholics. The truth of this answer is established, first, by the later Act against the traitors, and then by the Earl of Northampton, who related these matters at length in the presence of the peers of the realm and of Garnet himself. If the account were doubtful or false, why did Garnet keep silent? Moreover, two letters written in his own hand survive, in which the whole matter is openly set out. One was written on the day before the Nones of April; the other

units.la: 3. Idus mensis eiusdem. Hoc autem responso suo, eos animos Catesbeio Garne tus addidit, ut nihil amplius deliberaret unquam, sed ferretur post totus ad facinus. Quod si aliqui postea inhorruerunt ad scelus tantum, statim Catesbeio in promptu erat responsio: Confare sibi rem hanc licitam esse authoritate optimâ Garneti, cuius sibi vox esset pro oraculo: nec quisquam postea, nisi illius authoritate adductus, in sceleris tanti societatem adscitus est.
units.tr: on the third Ides of the same month. By this answer Garnet gave Catesby such courage that he never deliberated again, but was carried headlong into the deed. If some afterwards shrank from the crime, Catesby had a ready reply: that the matter was lawful on the best authority of Garnet, whose voice was to him as an oracle. Nor did anyone afterwards join this partnership in so great a crime except under his authority.

units.la: Similiter Garnetus Æquivocandi arte Serenissimum Regem, Illustrissimos Principes & prudentissimos Iudices nefarie decepit in Anglia; isque illusit turpissime. Nam toto iudicij sui tempore ex eius ore nulla unquam fuit prius expressa veritas, quam teneri se inevitabiliter indubitatæ fidei testibus, aut testimoniis cognosceret. Quoniam autem Rex Iacobus pro sua clementia quæstionem de eo per tormenta haberi vetuerat, ne semper lateret veritas, excogitatum est a viris prudentibus, ut Garneto & Oldcorno Iesuitis, qui in eadem Arcis parte vicinis cubiculis servabantur, sermones una ferendi potestas fieret, quos viri honesti, ad id ministerium electi, in proximo latentes, exciperent. Post hæc iussus Garnetus pro tribunali se sistere, & an ullum sibi cum Hallo sive Oldcorno fuisset colloquium interrogatus, petitione etiam adiecta, ut sine æquivocatione verum diceret, pertinacissime per animæ suæ salutem iurans, negavit, idque toties cum tantis tamque horrendis execrationibus repetiit, ut auditum animis gravem vulnus infligeret. Sunt hæc Comitis Salisburiensis verba, Garnetum de eo compellantis. Vt autem Halli confessione, & testimoniis eorum
units.tr: In the same way Garnet, by the art of equivocation, shamefully deceived the most serene King, the most illustrious princes and the most prudent judges in England, and he mocked them most disgracefully. For throughout the whole course of his examination, no truth was ever drawn from his mouth until he recognised that he was inevitably held by witnesses of unquestionable good faith or by testimonies. Since King James, out of his clemency, had forbidden that Garnet be examined under torture, lest the truth remain forever hidden, wise men devised a plan: the words of Garnet and of Oldcorne, the Jesuits, who were kept in adjoining rooms in the same part of the Tower, should be overheard. Honest men, chosen for this service, lay hidden nearby and caught what was said.
