After this, Garnet was ordered to present himself before the tribunal and was asked whether he had any conversation with Hall or with Oldcorne. With the added request that he speak the truth without equivocation, he swore most obstinately by the salvation of his soul that he had not. He repeated this so often, with such dreadful curses, that it inflicted a grave wound on the minds of those who heard him. These are the words of the Earl of Salisbury, addressing Garnet about it. But when, by Hall's confession and the testimonies of those who had overheard the conversations, he saw that he was caught on every side,

units.la: {a} Garnetus Æquivocandi arte deceptt Regem & Ordines regni. orum qui sermones exceperunt, irretitum undique se teneri animadvertit; udore suffusus miser senex, veniam delicti sui petijt sic, ut beneficio aequi‐ ocationis idsibi licere diceret. Nam cum aliquis, inquit, de crimine a magistra‐u interrogatur, is magistratui respondere, antequam testes producti fuerint, non tenetur: quia nemo tenetur seipsum prodere. Atque haec constans illius fuit sententia, in qua semper manssit, omnia pernegans, & facti rationem hanc postea afferens.
units.tr: {a} Garnet, by the art of equivocation, deceived the King and the orders of the realm. the wretched old man, suffused with shame, asked pardon for his offence, saying that by the benefit of equivocation this had been lawful for him. For when anyone, he said, is questioned about a crime by the magistrate, he is not bound to answer the magistrate before witnesses have been produced, because no one is bound to betray himself. This was his constant opinion, and he remained in it always, denying everything and afterwards giving this as the reason for his conduct.

units.la: Quadam etiam die magistratum accusare ausus est Garnetus, quod legitimis probationibus instructus, non esset veritus cum interrogare. Res sic se habet et ex scriniis publicis. Die 27. Aprilis interrogatus per presbyteratum suum, scelene fecisset, quando coram Magistratu negavit, manibus etiam appositis evangelij codici, se neque nuncium misisse, neque scripsisse ad Tesmundum sive Greenuuellum Iesuitam, ex quo una fuerant Cougthonae; cum sciret id falsum esse; Respondit: Nihil se fecisse non legitimum: sed magistratus rem illegitimam & nullam fecisse, qui de eiusmodi rebus se interrogarint per presbyteratum suum, quando ipsi literas a se scriptas haberent. Neque enim fuisse animum sibi eas denegare, siquidem civiliter in potestatem magistratus devenisse. Nunc quia crederet illas literas non esse interceptas, rem negasse, idque a se legitime fieri potuisse. En remnovam & novam iuram. Reus Garnetus magistratibus praescribit, quo pacto de sceleribus suis interrogari debeat: & si non pareatur a magistratu, cum eo gravissime expostulat. Satis hoc quidem pro imperio.
units.tr: One day Garnet even dared to accuse the magistrate, because, though he had been instructed by lawful proofs, the magistrate was not ashamed to question him. The matter stands thus according to the public records. On 27 April, Garnet was asked on his priestly oath whether he had committed a crime when he denied before the magistrate, laying his hand even on the book of the Gospels, that he had sent a messenger or written to Tesmond or Greenwell the Jesuit, through whom letters had gone to Coughton, though he knew this to be false. He answered: "I have done nothing unlawful; but the magistrate has done an unlawful and void thing, in questioning me on such matters on my priestly oath, when they themselves had letters written by me." For he had not intended to deny them, since they had come civilly into the power of the magistrate. But now, because he believed those letters had not been intercepted, he denied the matter, and he said he could lawfully do so. Behold a new and strange right! The accused Garnet prescribes to the magistrates how they ought to question him about his crimes, and if the magistrate does not comply, he complains most bitterly against him. That is quite enough of his arrogance.

units.la: Die etiam quadam Garnetus convictus, multa apud cognitores suae causae lentius est; reductus autem in Arcem, & postea ibidem interrogatus, ecquid ceniteret ipsum infamis artis, & an id serio licitum esse crederet? an pro tempore, necessitate premente, illa diceret? ipse manu sua responsi loco in charta haec scripsit, ex Anglico fideliter translata: Hoc ego cognosco esse consentiens opinioni meae omnium Scholasticorum. Et ratio eorum est, quod ubi de legitima aequivocatione agitur, primo qui per aequivocationem liberatur a mendacio, idem etiam per iusiurandum sine periurio potest confirmari, & per quem vis alium in eam rem usitatum modum: quamvis id erit per sumptionem Sacramenti, si iusta necessitas ita requirat. Heinricus Garnetus. Iuxta Garnetu igitur eiusque Socios, equivocandi disciplina, non hoc solum permitt hominibus, ut simplici affirmatione mentiantur, sed etiam ut fidei faciendae gratia nihil eorum praetermittant, quae inter mortales eo valere censentur. Turabunt igitur posthac, sacra Evangelia tangent, & quid vis facient; atque adeo opus sit, sumptione corporis Christi mendacia sua firmabunt.
units.tr: One day Garnet, when convicted, argued rather feebly before the examiners of his case. Brought back into the Tower and questioned there, he was asked whether he thought this infamous art itself was lawful, and whether he believed that in a time of pressing necessity such things might be said. In reply he wrote the following words on paper with his own hand, faithfully translated from English: I acknowledge that this agrees with the opinion of all the Schoolmen. Their reasoning is that, where lawful equivocation is concerned, first, whoever is freed from a lie by equivocation can also confirm the same by an oath without perjury, and by whatever other usual method you wish in that matter; although this will be by the taking of the Sacrament, if necessity so requires. Henry Garnet. According to Garnet and his fellows, then, the discipline of equivocation permits men not only to lie with a plain affirmation, but also, for the sake of gaining belief, to omit nothing of those things which among mortals are thought to have force. They will therefore swear, touch the holy Gospels and do whatever you like, and, if need be, will confirm their lies by receiving the body of Christ.

units.la: Garnetus etiam homo plurimorum nominum fuit. Appellatus enim fuit Garnetus, Vuallia, Darcia, Robertus Farmerius, Philippus, &c. Et hoc usitatu apud Iesuitas hodie, qui se in omnes formas transformare, & nomina sua subinde ad decipiendos ac falsedos homines mutare solent. Unde etiam scribit Edmundus Campianus in epistola ad Generalem Societatis Iesu anno 1583. Treviexcusa, pag. 23. & 24. in Anglia saepe se commutare nomina, & habitu dementissimo se. Vide eundem de persequutione Anglicana pag. 126, 212, 314, de mentitis nominibus pag. 130, mutatis vestibus. 126.
units.tr: Garnet was also a man of many names. He was called Garnet, Wall, Darcy, Robert Farmer, Philip, and so on. This is the practice among the Jesuits today, who are accustomed to transform themselves into every shape and to change their names from time to time in order to deceive and mislead men. Hence Edmund Campion also writes in a letter to the General of the Society of Jesus in 1583 (Treves edition, pp. 23 and 24) that in England they often change their names and dress in the most absurd fashion. See the same author on the English persecution, pp. 126, 212, 314; on false names, p. 130; on changed clothes, p. 126.

units.la: Nullum autem virum bonum tam multiplici falsorum nominum varietate ilutatum invenimus unquam, vel rarissime.
units.tr: We have never found, or only very rarely, a good man soiled by such a manifold variety of false names.

units.la: Septuagenarius quoque ad Regis mandatum una cum aliis conspirationis ociis & conscijs, tam Iesuitis, quam politicis, captus ad quaestionem sive tormentum adhibitus, cofessus est integros iam fere viginti duos annos, velut supremum Provincialem, Romani Pontificis nomine, Papistis, qui Papam eum Angliae nominaverunt, & tanto honore prosecuti sunt, ut pedes etiam eius osculerentur, praefuisse, omniumque, quae toto illo tempore, contra Reginam Elizabetham, & Regem Iacobum, Regnumq; hactenus susceptæ proditionis essent, conciium fuisse.
units.tr: A man of seventy also, by the King's command, was captured along with others who were accomplices and confidants of the conspiracy, both Jesuits and politicians. He was subjected to examination or torture, and confessed that for nearly twenty-two whole years he had presided, as supreme Provincial in the name of the Roman Pontiff, over the Papists, who called him the Pope of England and honoured him so greatly that they even kissed his feet. He confessed also that he had been privy to all the treason undertaken until then, throughout that whole period, against Queen Elizabeth, King James and the kingdom.

units.la: Itaq; ipso ad mortem condemnato, omnibus per Angliam Regi subditis, ne Pontificijs & Hispanis operam suam posthac offerrent, prohibitum est.
units.tr: Therefore, once he had been condemned to death, it was forbidden to all the King's subjects throughout England to offer their services henceforth to the Papists and the Spaniards.

units.la: Accidit autem, ut cum sententia in Garnetum pronunciaretur, Comes fanti Georgij magna cum pompa in Angliam adveniret, impetratáq; aquid Regem dicendi copia, Non potuisse, inquit, Regem Hispaniæ Dominum suum intermittere, quin peculiarem ad fratrem suum Britanniæ Regem Legatum mitteret, & ei ob singularem in tanto periculo liberationem gratulaturus, cum salus eius ipsi tantæ curæ sit, ut pro ea vota quotidie faciat, &c. Erat hoc quidem Regi gratum, verum cum idem Legatus non precibus solum apud Regem pro Garneto instaret, sed & triginta millia coronatorum summa eum redempturum esse profiteretur, animum Regis mirifice commovit. Itaq; licet Iesuita ille spe veniæ impetrandæ, res alias momenti manifestaret, tamen tertio die Maij Anno 1605. ad supplicij locum ductus est. Cum scalam innixa patibulo ascenderet, inter alia dixit: Me cum Dominus à Sanctiori consilio simulate egisse male me habet. Verum non putaram eos talia contra me indicia & argumenta habere, donec coram produxissent. Item: Faxit Deus ne gravius cum Catholicis meo nomine agatur, eosque adhortor, ne eiusmodi proditionibus, & rebellionibus contra Regem se immiscear; Simulque orare coepit, & crucem se signans dixit; In nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. Maria mater gratiæ, Maria mater misericordiæ, tu me à malo protege, & horam mortis suscipe, &c. Tunc scala submota suspendio vitam finivit.
units.tr: It happened, moreover, that while sentence was being pronounced against Garnet, the Count of San Giorgio arrived in England with great pomp, and, having obtained an opportunity to speak to the King, said: "The King of Spain, my lord, could not refrain from sending a special legate to his brother, the King of Britain, to congratulate him on his singular deliverance from so great a danger, since his safety is of such concern to him that he prays for it every day", and so on. This was indeed pleasing to the King, but when the same legate not only urged the King with entreaties on behalf of Garnet, but also declared that he would redeem him for the sum of thirty thousand crowns, it greatly moved the King's mind. Therefore, although that Jesuit, hoping to obtain pardon, disclosed other matters of importance, nevertheless on 3 May 1605 he was led to the place of execution. As he ascended the ladder set against the gallows, he said, among other things: "It grieves me that I acted feignedly before the Lord from the more holy council. But I did not think they had such evidence and proofs against me until they had produced them in court." Likewise: "God grant that Catholics not be treated more severely on my account, and I exhort them not to meddle in such treasons and rebellions against the King." He then began to pray, and, signing himself with the cross, said: "In the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Mary, mother of grace, Mary, mother of mercy, protect me from the evil one and receive me at the hour of death", and so on. Then the ladder was removed, and he ended his life by hanging.

units.la: Hæc omnia quæ hucusque de Garneto Iesuita recensuimus, superfuit autem alia plurima, etsi verissima sint, extant enim Acta, publica authoritate edita, ex quibus liquido & sine ullo dubio constat, Garnetum, non, ut quidam in vulgus imperitum sparserunt, proditionis aliquo saltem rumore aspersum fuisse; sed e contrario, ut etiam in Tortura Torti scribitur, veritatis voce, & vi tabularum, testium, probationum luce, soliditate, pondere convictum, ore proprio & manu propria confessum ea fuisse, & nemo mortalium effect, cui vel in animum veniret, inventum iri aliquem, qui hæc facinora defenderet: repertus tamen est, ut supra diximus, Iesuita Andreas Eudæmon Iohannes Cretensis Græcus, qui Apologiam pro Garneto scripsit, in qua vel novæ doctrinæ Iesuiticæ contra Reges & Principes immanitas caute dissimulatur, vel confessiones Garneti & cæterorum proditorum, impudentissime negantur, vel eorum molitiones seditiosas, consilia proditoria, aliaq; nefaria facinora extenuantur & excusantur.
units.tr: All these things which we have so far recounted about the Jesuit Garnet, and much else besides, though it is all most true, remain. For the public Acts, published by public authority, survive, and from them it is clear and beyond any doubt that Garnet was not, as some have spread among the ignorant populace, tainted even by some rumour of treason. On the contrary, as is also written in the Tortura Torti, he was convicted by the voice of truth and the force of the records, witnesses, proofs, their clarity, solidity and weight, and he confessed these things with his own mouth and hand. No mortal would have imagined that anyone would be found to defend these crimes. Yet, as we said above, a Jesuit was found: Andreas Eudaemon-Joannes, a Greek from Crete, who wrote an Apology for Garnet. In it either the savagery of the new Jesuit doctrine against kings and princes is cautiously concealed, or the confessions of Garnet and the other traitors are most shamelessly denied, or their seditious undertakings, treasonous plans and other nefarious crimes are minimised and excused.

units.la: Neque vero solum Garneti facinora & maleficia defendunt, excusant & extenuant Iesuitæ, sed eum insuper in numerum Deorum suorum retulerunt & tamquam martyrem colunt. Sitne autem martyr ipse an non censendus, ipsummet Garnetum arbitrum habemus, quo nemo lití huic terminandæ magis idoneus inveniri possit. Paucis diebus ante supplicium eius, venerunt in Arcem & cubiculum ipsius aliquot e præcipuis Theologis, una cum viro nobili Arcis præfecto: inter quos hi quoque erant, D. Iacobus Montacutus, Decanus tum Regij Sacelli, nunc Episcopus Bathoniensis & Vuellensis; D. Neilus Sacellanus tum Regius, Regiique Oratorij Clericus & Vuestmonasteriensis Decanus, nunc Episcopus Lichfeldensis; & Dns. Iohannes Queralus, Decanus æedis Paulinæ Londini. Hi cum Garneto multa cum essent locuti, forte evenit, ut unus illorum hanc quæstionem illi proponeret; Si post supplicium Ecclesia Romana Martyrem ipsum declararet, num factum illud laudaret, & verum Martyrem futurum se crederet? tum ille ex alto suspirium trahens. ahens, humeros adducens, Martyrem me? inquit; o qualem Martyrē? sed neque ecclesia hoc facit: & ego Deum oro, ne huius unquam illi in mente veniat. Etenim si pro religione Catholica morte obire, neque aliud, infelix, scivissem, praeter illa quae per viam confessionis scivi, poteram fortasse honore martyrij non indignus videri, & judicium Ecclesiae provocare. Nunc peccatum ego agnosco meum, & sententiam, quae adversus me pronunciata est, esse justissimam. Deinde iterum atque iterum suspiria ingeminans, & poenitentiae signa exhibens; Utinam, inquit, quae facta sunt, possem infecta reddere. Utinam quis alius mihi potius accidisset casus, qui ut nomine proditionis infamia deturparetur; quod nec peccatum, etsi gravissimum, per veram poenitentiam spero delendum, & Christum mei serturum. Ego certè si vel universum orbem terrarum in potestate mea haberem, universa lubens dare, ut a proditionis crimine, quod conscientiae meae impressum est, quodque in elogio denationis meae extabit, purus mori possem. Hanc historiam audivisse se scribit Canonus in epist. ad Frontem Ducaeum pag. 126. a Decano Paulino & duobus Episcopis supra nominatis, quos interfuisse huic Colloquio diximus. Quum igitur meritas se dare poenas non semel confessus sit Garnetus; quae insania, imo impietas est, pronunciari & haberi eum martyrem a Iesuitis, qui iustissima damnatum sententia agnovit?
units.tr: Nor do the Jesuits merely defend, excuse and minimise Garnet's crimes and misdeeds; they have moreover counted him among their gods and honour him as a martyr. Whether he is to be judged a martyr or not, we have Garnet himself as arbiter, and no one could be found more suitable to settle this dispute. A few days before his execution, some of the leading theologians came to the Tower, to his cell, together with a noble governor of the Tower. Among them were Dr James Montacute, then Dean of the Royal Chapel, now Bishop of Bath and Wells; Dr Neile, then Royal Chaplain and Clerk of the Royal Oratory and Dean of Westminster, now Bishop of Lichfield; and Dr John Overall, Dean of St Paul's in London. When they had talked with Garnet at length, it happened that one of them put this question to him: if after his execution the Roman Church were to declare him a martyr, would he approve of that deed and believe that he would be a true martyr? Then he, drawing a deep sigh and shrugging his shoulders, said: "A martyr, I? Oh, what sort of martyr? But the Church does not do this, and I pray God that it never comes into her mind. For if, unhappy man that I am, I had known nothing beyond what I learned through confession, and had died for the Catholic religion, I might perhaps have seemed not unworthy of the honour of martyrdom, and might have challenged the judgment of the Church. Now I acknowledge my sin, and I confess that the sentence pronounced against me is most just." Then, again and again sighing and showing signs of repentance, he said: "Would that I could undo what has been done! Would that some other misfortune had befallen me, one that did not disgrace me with the name of treason, a sin which, though most grievous, I hope can be wiped out by true repentance, and which Christ will bear with me. Certainly, if I had the whole world in my power, I would gladly give everything, so that I might die free of the crime of treason, which is stamped on my conscience and will stand in the record of my condemnation." Canonus writes in his letter to Front Ducaeus, p. 126, that he heard this account from the Dean of St Paul's and the two bishops named above, whom we said were present at this conversation. Since Garnet therefore confessed more than once that he was suffering a deserved punishment, what madness, or rather impiety, is it that the Jesuits pronounce and hold him a martyr, when he himself acknowledged the most just sentence against him?

units.la: Cum vero Rex proditionis & conspirationis eiusmodi pericula cavere in pos-rum modis omnibus adniteretur, 22. Febr. anno 1604. mandatum edidit, quo fuitas, cum sacrificulis & Romano-Catholicae religionis propagatoribus omnis, proscriptos, ante 19. diem Martij ex universo Angliae, Scotiae & Hiberniae regno discedere iussit, hac conditione & severitate, ut qui post diem nominatum comprehensi in regno fuerint, extemplo nullo ordine aut mora iudicij poenas dant. Indicitu etiam omnibus indigenis, ne hospitio, tecto, mensa, aut alia ope eos iuvent, ni eandem cum illis poenam incurrere velint.
units.tr: When the King, in every way, strove to guard against such dangers of treason and conspiracy in future, he issued on 22 February 1604 a mandate by which he ordered all Jesuits, priests and propagators of the Roman Catholic religion to be proscribed and to leave the whole kingdom of England, Scotland and Ireland before 19 March. This was on the condition and with the severity that those who were caught in the realm after the appointed day should be punished at once, without any order or delay of judgment. He also forbade all natives to help them with lodging, shelter, table or any other aid, unless they were willing to incur the same penalty.

units.la: Principio autem quantum laboris post politicae quidem gubernationis constitutionem, in formandis ac reparandis ceremonijs Ecclesiasticis, in Anglia haftenus receptis, fustinue-, exponit. Quae dum ita constituere, ut nemini pietatis amanti displicere posse consideret, animadvertisse se interim ait; universum illud religionis negotium non parum deformari ab illis, qui eius hostes sint acerrimi, nempe, a Iesuitis, sacrificulis, & id genus aliis, in qui ante suum adventum in regno isto fuerint, quam qui postmodum acceperunt; qui idem omnes iam religionis suae multo quam ante liberius in regno isto professionem faciunt, sive partim mutationis alicuius introducendae, de qua tamen nec ipse unquam cogitavit, nec suspicandi ansam ulli praebuerit, partim vero abusu generalis illius omnium deflorum remissionis, quae tempore coronationis suae consueto more facta fit, quam quidam fuitarum sub sigillo regio sibi comparaverint, sperantes se ea liberos fore ab omni judiciopericulo, & propterea eo confidentius celebrandis Missis & aliis officiis Ecclesiasticis vacantes, cum seductione subditorum ab obedientia sibi debita ad Romanae Ecclesiae venerationem. Cum igitur non minima Regij muneris & officij pars sit, attendere, ne subditi in religione, pietate & obedientia corrumpantur, obligatum se vel sua ipsius conscientia esse affirmat, advigilare sedulo, ne sui superstitiosi in religione opinionibus, quae non animabus tantum ipsorum officiant, sed & instrumentum sint, quo ab obedientia debita averuntur; fascinati pereant. Cum autem id alia ratione fieri non possit, quam ut corruptionis istius ministris obviam tempestive eatur, [qui quidem sint Sacerdotes & Clerici omnis generis, qui ab externa & in Angliae Regno prohibita potestate ordinationem suam ceperunt. Itaque decernere se, ut omnes Sacerdotes, sive regulares sint sive non, captivi & liberi, sive remissionis beneficium sub sigillo regio habeant sive non, tam qui ante suum adventum in Anglia fuerunt, quam qui post modo advenerunt, regno suo exeant; & captivi quidem primo quoque tempore navibus impositi dimittantur, cum exeffo mandato, nunquam sine permissione sua ad fines istos revertendi, sub poena editis nomine legibus definita. Reliqui vero Sacerdotes, Iesuitae & alij cujuscunque Ordinis sint, qui ordinationem & confirmationem suam ab aliena potestate habent, licbeneficio remissionis istius (quae quidem a legibus & judiciis publicis neminem Sacerdotabsolvit) gaudeant, ante 19. Martij diem ex Regnis suis omnibus discedant: addita hamanifesta interminatione, eos, qui post dictam diem in quibuscunque Regni sui partibus inventi, aut postmodo unquam reversi fuerint, judicio stare & poenam legibus persolvere debere sine ulla spe veniae aut remissionis consequenda. Mandat igitur omnibus Archiepisco- pis, Episcopis, Iudicibus, & aliis Iustitiae ministris, ut termino isto elapso, quam diligentisime in omnes, qui forte superfuerint, inquirant, & judicio eos sistant.
units.tr: First, he sets out how much labour he had undergone, after the establishment of civil government, in shaping and restoring the ecclesiastical ceremonies hitherto received in England. While arranging these so that he thought they could not displease anyone who loves piety, he says he noticed in the meantime that the whole business of religion was not a little disfigured by those who are its bitterest enemies, namely the Jesuits, priests and that kind of people, both those who were in this kingdom before his arrival and those who came afterwards. All of them now profess their religion in this kingdom much more openly than before. This happens partly through some change to be introduced, of which he himself never thought and never gave anyone cause to suspect, and partly through abuse of that general remission of all offences which is granted, in the customary manner, at the time of his coronation. Some of them have obtained this under the royal seal, hoping that it would make them free from all danger of judgment, and therefore they devote themselves more confidently to celebrating Masses and other ecclesiastical offices, seducing the subjects from the obedience due to him towards veneration of the Roman Church. Since it is not the least part of the royal office and duty to see that subjects are not corrupted in religion, piety and obedience, he affirms that he is bound, even by his own conscience, to watch carefully that his subjects do not perish, bewitched by superstitious opinions in religion. These opinions not only harm their souls but are also an instrument by which they are turned away from due obedience. Since this cannot be done in any other way than by opposing the ministers of this corruption in good time, [who are indeed priests and clergy of every kind who received their ordination from a foreign power, forbidden in the kingdom of England]. He therefore decrees that all priests, whether regular or not, captive or free, whether or not they hold the benefit of remission under the royal seal, both those who were in England before his arrival and those who came afterwards, must leave his kingdom. The captives shall be placed on ships and dismissed at the first opportunity, with a strict order never to return to those shores without his permission, under penalties defined by name in the laws. As for the remaining priests, Jesuits and others of whatever order, who have their ordination and confirmation from an alien power, they may enjoy the benefit of that remission (which indeed absolves no priest from the laws and public judgments), but they must leave all his kingdoms before 19 March. A plain threat is added: anyone found in any part of his kingdom after that day, or who shall return at any time afterwards, must stand trial and pay the penalty under the laws, with no hope of pardon or remission. He therefore orders all archbishops, bishops, judges and other ministers of justice, once that term has passed, to search as diligently as possible for all who may have remained, and to bring them to judgment.

units.la: Ne vero constitutio haec speciem alicuius rigoris habere videatur, adversus eos, qui pIesuitas & Sacerdotes isti in Regno suo fedu.. Catholicos se nominant, rationes huiussua proscriptionis affert; periculum illud inprimis exaggerans, in quo non ipse tantum sed & universum suum Regnum nuper fuerit, propter conspirationem, quae ab isto quidem hominum genere primum exorta fit: itaque ut, sicut supra quoq; diximus, eius modi periclum caveri in posterum eo melius & vitari possit, aliter quidem se facere non potuisse affirrit, quum alia quidem ratione illud avertere nullo modo potuerit; siquidem Iesuitae & Sacerdotes isti eius potestati se addictos agnoscant, qui dispensare sese posse in causa arctissmi, quod inter Regem & subditos exiit, foederis profitetur.
units.tr: Lest this constitution seem to have any appearance of severity, he gives the reasons for this proscription against those who, in his kingdom, call themselves Catholics, Jesuits and priests. He especially magnifies the danger in which not only he himself but his whole kingdom was recently placed, because of the conspiracy which first arose from that class of men. Therefore, as we also said above, so that such a danger may be guarded against and avoided more effectively in future, he affirms that he could not act otherwise, since he could in no way avert it by any other means. For these Jesuits and priests acknowledge themselves bound to that foreign power, which, he declares, can dispense even in a matter of the closest bond of covenant that exists between King and subjects.

units.la: Sub initium igitur Aprilis ex Anglia navis multis Iesuitis, Monachis, & al- liorum Ordinum clericis onerata, ad portum Vlissingensem in Selandia appuliAntverpiam inde petitura. Impetraverant illi, intercessione Legati Hispanici, a Rege Angliae, ut sibi per aliquot adhuc septimanas, post tempus praestitutum subsistere, & commorari in Regno Angliae liceret. Interea vero Legatus Regemmitionem aliquanto Iesuitis reddere studens, interrogat, quid causae Rex habuerit, quod tam asperam in Catholicos sententiam tulisset. Rex igitur, ut causam proscriptionis istius Legatus cognosceret, literas ei praelegi curavit, quibus de conspiratione Papistarum in Regis & Regni perniciem facta, prolixperscriptum fuerat: imprimis autem, quod Rege Reginaque cum universa familia eorum sublatis, universum Reipublicatum, mutatis praecipuis officijs, pervertere decrevisset. Auditis hisce literis Legatus obticuit, nihil amplius in causa eorum agere expetens.
units.tr: At the beginning of April, therefore, a ship from England, laden with many Jesuits, monks, and clergy of other orders, put in at the port of Vlissingen in Zeeland, intending to make for Antwerp from there. They had obtained, through the intercession of the Spanish ambassador, leave from the King of England to remain and stay in the Kingdom of England for some weeks more after the time appointed. Meanwhile, however, the ambassador, eager to make the King's proscription somewhat more palatable to the Jesuits, asked what reason the King had for pronouncing so harsh a sentence against the Catholics. So the King, in order that the ambassador might learn the cause of this proscription, had letters read aloud to him, which had been written at length about the conspiracy of the Papists against the King and the kingdom's destruction: above all, that, with the King and Queen and their whole family removed, they had decided to overturn the entire commonwealth, changing its principal offices. Having heard these letters, the ambassador fell silent, no longer wishing to press their cause.

units.la: Sub initium tamen mensis Iunij Anno 1606 nova iterum adversus Regem Angliae Iacobum detecta est conspiratio, quae in Flandria quidem initio coepisse ferebatur, Iesuitis & sacrificulis quibusdam authoribus, quorum suasu & hortatu sex primarij quidam viri, inito foedere, & Eucharistiae Sacramento accepto silentium & fidem sibi invicem promiserunt. Convenit autem inter eos de Rege vel in venatione glande plumbea transfigendo, vel alia quacunque ratione e medio tollendo, eumque in finem monilia quaedam & clenodia pulcherrima pretiosissimaque veneno ita infecta sibi comparârant, ut vel solo attactu letalia essent, eaque, si in venatione res non succesisset, Regi offerre & exhibere animus erat, ut illis acceptis necem evitare non posset. Haec conspiratione mirabiliter patefacta, Rex paulo post promulgato denuo edicto publico, omnes Iesuitas, Monachos & Romanae religionis ministros, propter conspirationum turbas continuas & machinationes perpetuas sub capitali supplicij poena, regno suo ante prima Augusti diem excedere iussit: hoc tamen benevolentiae ipsis exhibitum inpromittens, ut si se in portubus maris aperiant, navibus Anglicis quocunque cuperent deferantur. Edictum autem de verbo ad verbum sic habet.
units.tr: Nevertheless, at the beginning of June in the year 1606, a new conspiracy against King James of England was discovered, which was said to have begun in Flanders, with certain Jesuits and priests as its authors. At their urging and exhortation, six leading men, having entered into a covenant and received the Sacrament of the Eucharist, promised one another silence and loyalty. They agreed to remove the King, either by shooting him with a leaden bullet while hunting or by some other means whatever. To this end they had procured for themselves certain necklaces and very beautiful and precious jewels, infected with poison so that they would be deadly even by touch alone; and they intended to offer and present these to the King, in case the hunting attempt should fail, so that once he received them he could not escape death. When this conspiracy had been wonderfully brought to light, the King, a little later, having once more published a public edict, ordered all Jesuits, monks, and ministers of the Roman religion to leave his kingdom before the first day of August, under pain of capital punishment, because of the constant disturbances of conspiracies and their perpetual machinations. He nevertheless promised this kindness to them, that if they presented themselves at the seaports, they would be carried by English ships wherever they wished to go. The edict, however, reads word for word as follows.

units.la: EDICTVM
units.tr: EDICTVM

units.la: EDICTVM SERENISSIMI MAGNAE BRITANNIAE REGIS. IACOBI I. FIDEI DEFENSORIS, CONTRA PONTIFICIOS ANGLIÆ RECVSANTES, ET IESVITAS, SACRIFICVLOSQVE AD DIEM 2. Iunij M. DC. X. publicè promulgatum.
units.tr: THE MOST SERENE EDICT OF JAMES I, KING OF GREAT BRITAIN, DEFENDER OF THE FAITH, AGAINST THE PAPISTS, THE RECUSANTS OF ENGLAND, THE JESUITS AND THE PRIESTS, PUBLISHED ON 2 JUNE 1610

units.la: Qvanquam summa Regis pij & sapientis cura circa Religionis verè Catholicæ & Christianæ conservationem & amplificationem versari debeat, atque in hunc finem, sicuti una manu bonum eius semen spargere, sic altera malas herbas & hæreses, quæ inter Domini semina plerunque succrescunt, quantum fieri potest, evellere & extirpare oporteat: nihilominus tamen natura nostra ad clementiam perpetuò tam proclivis fuit, ac præsertim ab effusione sanguinis, in iis rebus, quæ conscientiam quocunque modo tangere possunt (quanquam nihil aliud quàm simulata & ficta in quibusdam conscientiis erat) ita semper alieni fuimus, ut, non obstante ea cura & zelo, quibus huius nostræ anquæ & verè Catholicæ Religionis, quam profitemur, conservationem & propagationem perpetuò prosecuti fuimus, dicta nobis innata clementia nos semper retinuerit, ne Legem illam quæ contra Sacrificulos & Recusantes lata fuit, quamquè pessimis suis facinoribus contra nos diversis vicibus perpetratis, perversisque & superbis actionibus illi iure eruerant; debitæ executioni mandari fecerimus.
units.tr: Although the king's supreme care, being pious and wise, ought to be devoted to the preservation and enlargement of the true Catholic and Christian religion, and for this purpose he ought, as far as possible, to sow the good seed with one hand and with the other to pull up and root out the bad weeds and heresies, which commonly spring up among the Lord's seed; nevertheless our nature has always been so inclined to clemency, and especially so averse to the shedding of blood in matters which touch the conscience in any way (although in some consciences there was nothing but pretence and feigning), that, notwithstanding that care and zeal with which we have always pursued the preservation and propagation of this our ancient and truly Catholic religion, which we profess, our innate clemency has always restrained us from having that law enacted against the priests and the recusants carried out, although they had by their very wicked crimes, committed against us on various occasions, and by their perverse and proud actions, forfeited the right to it.

units.la: Postquam verò pessimum hoc ipsorum institutum, principiò per immediatam Sacrificulorum proditionem, in ipso nostro in hoc regnum aditu, ac postea per horrendos istos cuniculos Sulphureos (quæ immanissima crudelitas oblivioni nunquam tradenda) manifestatum, cui deinde supervenit simul horribile & deplorandum illud facinus extra hoc Regnum designatum (Diabolicum & immanissimum nimirum parricidium illud in ultimo Galliarum Rege fratre nostro charissimo perpetratum) animos dilectissimorum subditorum nostrorum, quos domus & corpus Parmenti repræsentant, ita excitavit, ut utraque Domus nos humillimè rogaverint & obstatæ sint, ut in Papicolarum actiones & vestigia accuratius quàm antehac umquam inquisti essemus, & ut in hunc finem, optimas & salubérrimas huius Regni Leges contra ipsos, quidem majori ex parte ante nostrum in hoc Regnum ingressum, latas, quarumq; observationem in Inauguratione nostra juravimus, sine ulla ulteriori dilatione executioni mandare vellemus: justissimam certè causam habemus, ut juxta humillimas ipsorum petitiones, in posterum magis, quàm antehac umquam, sollicitisimus, dictasq; Leges nostras exectioni diligentius mandari faciamus.
units.tr: But since this most wicked design of theirs has now been made manifest, first by the open treachery of the priests at our very entry into this kingdom, and afterwards by those horrible sulphurous mines (a most savage cruelty never to be forgotten), and since there followed upon these that horrible and lamentable crime, plotted outside this kingdom (namely that diabolical and most savage parricide committed upon the late French king, our dearest brother), which so stirred the minds of our most beloved subjects, whom the houses and body of Parliament represent, that both Houses most humbly petitioned us and begged that we would inquire into the actions and footsteps of the followers of the Pope more carefully than ever before, and that to this end we would be pleased, without any further delay, to have executed those excellent and most salutary laws of this kingdom against them, which were for the most part enacted before our entry into this kingdom, and whose observance we swore at our inauguration: we certainly have a most just cause to be more solicitous than ever before in the future, in accordance with their most humble petitions, and to have the said laws of ours carried out more diligently.

units.la: In hoc etenim negotio conscientia nostra, respectu religionis, honor noster, respectu eius, quod nihil nisi Legum nostrarum executio petitur, securitas nostra (ac non solum nostra, verùm etiam totius posteritatis nostræ) respectu sanguinolentæ Pontificiorum doctrinæ, qui in Martyrum & Sanctorum referunt numeros eos, qui proprios suos Reges, Vnctos Dei, trucidant (sicuti nunc cum horrore execramur hanc ipsorum doctrinam toties effectui mandatam, & parricidialem hanc Theoriam & Praxin ita conjunctas videmus, ut facinorosi & maligni homines nullo medio melius, quàm per parricidium Regis cuiusquam, qui aut Hæreticus, ipsorum judicio, aut fautor Hæreticorum habetur, animam suam ab æterna damnatione se liberare posse putent) Hæ, quam, tres causæ, quæ conscientiam, honorem & securitatem nostram tangunt, atq; etiam populum nostrum permoverunt, providentiam in nobis Regiam & sollicitam, qua unusquisque. gnifq Rex pius, justus, & prudens, rebus ita contingentibus & sese habentibus, prædictas esse debet, necessario excitant.
units.tr: For in this matter our conscience, with respect to religion, our honour, with respect to the fact that nothing is sought but the execution of our laws, and our security (and not only ours but that of all our posterity), with respect to the bloody doctrine of the Papists, who count among the martyrs and saints those who slaughter their own kings, the anointed of God (just as we now curse with horror this doctrine of theirs, so often put into effect, and see this parricidal theory and practice so bound together that wicked and malicious men think that they can free their souls from eternal damnation by no means better than by the murder of any king whatever who is held, in their judgement, to be a heretic or a supporter of heretics), these three causes, which touch our conscience, honour and security, and which have also moved our people, necessarily stir up in us a royal and watchful providence, which every pious, just and prudent king ought to have, when matters stand and turn out thus.

units.la: Ac propterea cum certiores facti simus, quod hoc præcipue tempore major, quam antehac unquam, Recusantium numerus in hanc nostram urbem Londinensem venerint, licet per Leges Regni nostri certis limitibus circumscripti esse, & intra quinque illa milliaria pro habitatione ipsis designata, manere debebant: certo nobis constitutum est revocare, sicuti priorem omnem in hunc locum redeundi datam licentiam per præsens Edictum dictum revocamus. Et quanquam hoc tempore, quo Parlamentum haberi, & Inaugurationem filii nostri primogeniti institui debet, eos hic tolerare periculosum & periculosum est, quam & ob causam Parlamentum nostrum humillime requisivit, ut universi ad domicilia sua remitterentur, & urbs hæc ab illis, pro Inauguratione dicti nostri filii charissimi, vacuaretur: nihilominus tamen tantum consuetæ nostra bonitatis retinere constitutum nobis est non respiciendo ullas ipsorum vafras machinationes aut periculosas, quæ tempore hoc durante inde nobis, in recompensationem dictæ nostræ clementiæ, pro venire possent, ut, consideratis negotiis ipsorum gravioribus, privatum ipsorum statum attingentibus, quæ fortasse adhuc in proximo termino peragenda haberent, ipsis terminum usque ad ultimum Junij prolongare velimus: intra quod tempus ad domos suas, & ad ea loca, ad quæ per Leges remissi sunt, redeunto, nec unquam posthac ad hanc urbem nostram & Cameram Londinensem, vel ad Aulam nostram, nec ad Aulam dilectissimæ Reginæ nostræ conjugis, vel charissimi Principis nostri filij, quocumque loco sit, intra decimum ab hac urbe Londinensi milliarium, sine singulari veniæ impetratione, remeare præsumunto, cum Leges nostras contra transgressores quam strictissimè executioni mandare, & summum illum Authoritatis nostræ contemptum severissimè vindicare decretum sit. Et similiter, juxta dictam humillimam charissimorum subditorum nostrorum in Parlamento congregatorum petitionem, omnibus superioribus Magistratibus, in omnibus hujus Regni nostri partibus, strictissimè mandandum decrevimus, ut juxta Leges nostras, ab omnibus Papistis inobedientiæ convictis, omnia arma, pulveres tormentarios, & quæ eiusdem sunt generis, quæ quisquis sive in propria habet potestate, sive apud alium depositum fuerit, recipiant, & providean, ut bene custodiantur, & secundum leges deponantur, tantum ipsis pro necessaria domuum & sui defensione relinquentes, quantum per leges concessum est. Qua in re, cum Magistratus nostri hactenus nimis negligentes fuerint, ut expressum hoc nostrum mandatum vel neglectum, vel executioni non satis diligenter, ut decet, datum, deprehenderimus, per severissimas pœnas ipsis notum faciemus, quam gravi vel delictum fit, in Regijs nostris mandatis, præsertim in rebus talis momenti, negligentem esse.
units.tr: And therefore, since we have been informed that at this present time a greater number of recusants than ever before has come into this our city of London, although by the laws of our realm they are bound to be confined within certain limits, and were obliged to remain within those five miles designated for their residence: it has been firmly decided by us to revoke, as we now revoke by this present Edict, every licence previously granted to return to this place. And although at this time, when Parliament is to be held and the inauguration of our eldest son is to be arranged, it is dangerous and perilous to tolerate them here, which is also why our Parliament most humbly requested that all of them be sent back to their homes, and that this city be cleared of them for the inauguration of our said dearest son: nevertheless we have resolved to keep up our customary goodness, and, disregarding their crafty or dangerous schemes which might come upon us in this period in return for our said clemency, so that, having considered their more serious affairs which touch their private condition, which perhaps they still have to settle in the near term, we are willing to extend to them a term until the last day of June: within which time they are to return to their homes and to those places to which they have been sent back by the laws, and they are never again to presume to come back to this our city and Chamber of London, or to our Court, nor to the court of our most beloved queen, our consort, or of our dearest son, our Prince, wherever it may be, within ten miles of this city of London, without a special grant of pardon; since it has been decreed that our laws against transgressors are to be executed as strictly as possible, and that the supreme contempt of our authority is to be most severely punished. And likewise, in accordance with the said most humble petition of our dearest subjects gathered in Parliament, we have decided to order most strictly all the superior magistrates, in all parts of this our realm, that, in accordance with our laws, they are to receive from all Papists convicted of disobedience all arms, gunpowder, and things of that kind, which anyone has either in his own power or which has been deposited with another; and they are to provide that these are kept safely and laid down according to the laws, leaving to them only so much as the law allows for the necessary defence of their houses and persons. In this matter, since our magistrates have hitherto been too negligent, if we find that this our express command has been either neglected or not carried out with the care that is fitting, we shall make it known to them by the most severe penalties how serious an offence it is to be negligent in our royal commands, especially in matters of such importance.

units.la: Et quandoquidem Iesuitæ & Sacrificuli majori numero nunc, quam antehac unquam, tam per totum nostrum Regnum, quam in urbe nostra Londinensi, circumvagantur, non solum gregatim ad Domum nostram venientes, maximo cum Authoritatis & Legum nostrarum contemptu, verum etiam permixta sibi alium personarum particularium caterva, quæ postea quam carceribus detenta & per Leges nostras convicta, & nihilominus tamen (ex bonitate nostra) è Regno, sub hac conditione, ne umquam redirent, deducti fuerunt, in Regnum redire ausæ sunt, maximo cum summæ ergæ eos bonitatis & clementiæ nostræ contemptu, manus nostras ad justissimas pœnas provocantes: Nos ad tales abusus & confusiones in posterum prævenien-das, omnibus istis Legibus frena amplius non inhibere, sed easdem, ut ratas, prout decet, executioni contra eiusmodi transgressores mandare decrevimus. Et quoniam semper proni sumus ad severitatem aliqua clementiæ nostræ parte temperandam (non jam respicientes, quod statim in primo, ac posteà in quarto Regni huius nostri anno, per duo diversa clementissima Edicta omnibus Sacrificulis & Iesuitis certum diem præstituimus, ante quem ex nostris ditionibus discederent, gravissimis etiam pœnis, si in Regnum nostrum redire auderent, propositis) decrevimus, non ob-stante adate praecedentis nostrae gratiae contemptu, ad duas illas priores profectiones ipsis indi-ctas, etiam tertiam adjicere; ac propterea per praesens hoc Edictum declaramus & promulgamus, quod omnibus Iesuitis, Scholaribus, & caeteris cuiusque conditionis Sacrificulis in hoc Regno nunc agentibus, tam ijs, quos carceribus liberare voluerimus, quam ijs, qui nondum in vincula conjecti sunt, liberè & tutè ex Regno nostro discedere liceat, sic ut in hunc finem ad quemdam nostrum portum ante 4. Julij proxime venturi se conferant, ac ipsi primâ occasione in exteras Regiones traijciant.
units.tr: And since the Jesuits and priests now wander about in greater numbers than ever before, both throughout our whole realm and in our city of London, not only coming in crowds to our house, with the greatest contempt for our authority and our laws, but also, mingled with them, a crowd of other particular persons, who, after being held in prison and convicted under our laws, and nevertheless (by our goodness) sent out of the kingdom on this condition, that they should never return, have dared to come back into the kingdom, with the greatest contempt for that exceptional goodness and clemency of ours, thereby provoking our hands to the most just punishments: we, wishing to prevent such abuses and confusions in future, have decided no longer to restrain all these laws with a bridle, but to have them, as valid, as is fitting, executed against transgressors of this kind. And since we are always inclined to temper severity with some part of our clemency (not now taking into account that at the very beginning, and afterwards in the fourth year of our reign, by two different most merciful Edicts, we set a fixed day for all priests and Jesuits, before which they were to leave our dominions, with the most grievous penalties also proposed if they should dare to return to our kingdom), we have decided, notwithstanding the contempt of our previous grace, to add a third to those two earlier departures imposed on them; and therefore by this present Edict we declare and proclaim that for all Jesuits, scholars, and other priests of every rank now active in this kingdom, both those whom we are willing to free from prison and those who have not yet been thrown into chains, it shall be lawful to leave our kingdom freely and safely, provided that for this purpose they betake themselves to one of our ports before the fourth of July next, and that they cross over to foreign regions by the first opportunity.

units.la: Admonemus & certos facimus, dictos Iesuitas, Scholares, & cujuscunque generis Sacrificulos, juxta dictum nostrum placitum discedentes, ut & caeteros omnes, qui antehac per clementiam nostram eadem cum conditione libertati fuere restituti, quod, si quisquam ipsorum posthac in Regnum hoc nostrum reverti ausus fuerit, sanguis ipsorum super proprio ipsorum, atque etiam eorum, qui ipsos miserint, capite esse debeat, quandoquidem hoc facientes, non solum in poenas, quas leges nostrae ipsis minantur, verum etiam in eas, quas summus & superbus clementiae bonitatisque nostrae erga eos ostensae contemptus ipsis pariet, incurrent.
units.tr: We admonish and make certain that the said Jesuits, Scholars and Sacrificuli of every kind who depart in accordance with our decree, as well as all the others who previously were restored to liberty by our clemency on the same condition, shall understand this: if any of them shall afterwards dare to return to this our Realm, his blood shall be upon his own head, and also upon the head of those who sent him, since in doing so they will incur not only the penalties which our laws threaten against them, but also those which the arrogant and haughty contempt they show for the clemency and goodness we have extended to them will bring upon them.

units.la: Et in genere (ne quisquam ignorantiam legum nostrarum praetendere possit:) Universi Iesuitae & Sacrificuli, cujuscunque sint Ordinis, ipsorumque missores hoc Edicto admonentur, ut sibi caveant, supra quod per clementiam nostram ipsis indultum est, amplius aliquid a nobis petere, quo in Regnum hoc nostrum redire possint, propter pericula notissima, quae ab ipsis jure timentur, & sollicitudinem, quam pro bonis nostris subditis gerere decrevimus, quo a periculis corporis & animae, quae a Iesuitarum & caeterorum Sacrificulorum doctrina ijs immientiant, liberentur, cum horum in hoc Regno actiones & studia ad nullum alium scopum tendant, quam ut animos optimorum subditorum nostrorum a debita & Deo & nobis obedientia avertant.
units.tr: And in general (so that no one may plead ignorance of our laws), all Jesuits and Sacrificuli, of whatever Order, and those who send them, are admonished by this Edict to take care not to ask us for anything beyond what our clemency has granted them, namely permission to return to this our Realm. This is because of the well-known dangers which are rightly feared from them, and because of the concern we have resolved to show for our good subjects, that they may be freed from the dangers to body and soul which come upon them from the teaching of the Jesuits and other Sacrificuli, since the actions and studies of these men in this Realm aim at no other end than to turn the minds of our best subjects away from the obedience due to God and to us.

units.la: Et quia denique horror immanissimae Proditionis pulveraria animas Parlamenti nostri occupavit, & insuper, inter caetera, Iuramentum Fidelitatis nobis a subditis nostris praestandum tantopere a Papa & Asseclis ipsius oppugnatum fuit, ut ipsi calamum arriperent, & causae nostrae, quae Iuramentum illud spectat, defensionem suscipere cogeremur (quod quamvis Papae odiosissimum esset, summi tamen favoris & clementiae opus fuit erga tam multos nostros subditos, qui, licet superstitione Pontificia excaecati, animo tamen erant parato, ad obedientiam nobis praestandam; in quo etiam inter huius conditionis Papistas, & alterum illud pestiferum genus, qui supra dictas damnatas & maledictas doctrinas & artes commiscent, discrimen habitum fuit.)
units.tr: And finally, because the horror of the most monstrous Gunpowder Treason has taken hold of the souls of our Parliament, and because, among other things, the Oath of Allegiance to be sworn to us by our subjects has been so fiercely attacked by the Pope and his adherents that they took up their pens and we were compelled to undertake the defence of our cause, which concerns that Oath (which, although most hateful to the Pope, was nonetheless a work of the highest favour and clemency toward so many of our subjects who, though blinded by Papist superstition, were nevertheless of a mind prepared to render obedience to us; in this matter also a distinction was made between Papists of this kind and that other pestilential sort who mix in the aforesaid damnable and accursed doctrines and arts).

units.la: Nos considerantes, quod dictum Iuramentum divini vero & clementi inter duo ista Papistarum genera faciendo serviat, ut jam dictum est, non possumus quin omnium bonorum nostrorum subditorum saluti, & malignorum hominum detectioni peropportunum existimemus, ut in posterum in generali huius Juramenti apud omnes nostros subditos promotione, major quam antehac unquam cura adhibeatur.
units.tr: Considering that the said Oath serves, as has already been said, to divide these two kinds of Papists in a manner both divine and merciful, we cannot but judge it most opportune for the safety of all our good subjects and for the detection of wicked men that, in the future, greater care than ever before be taken in the general promotion of this Oath among all our subjects.

units.la: Ac propterea expressum nostrum Decretum est, omnibusque & singulis nostris Episcopis, Iudicibus Civilibus & Criminalibus, atque omnibus aliis nostris Ministris, quos hoc attinet, strictissime mandamus, ut illud ab omnibus illis personis, & in omnibus rebus, quibus leges fieri jubent, exigant, scientes, Leges ipsos hac auctoritate non ornasse, ut hoc pro libitu facere, & omittere pro beneplacito liceret; verum nos hoc, tamquam necessarium ac debitum officium ipsis mandatum & impositum, velut personis publicis, & a nobis pro maxime fidelibus habitis, pro bono & securitate nostra statuque nostri, ab ipsorum manibus postulaturos.
units.tr: Accordingly, it is our express decree, and we most strictly charge all and each of our Bishops, our Civil and Criminal Judges, and all other our Ministers whom this concerns, that they exact it from all those persons, and in all those matters, for which the laws order that it be required; knowing that the laws have not endowed them with this authority so that they might do it at their pleasure or omit it at their convenience. Rather, we shall require it from their hands as a necessary and due duty enjoined and imposed upon them, as upon public persons, and regarded by us as most faithful, for the good, the security and the state of ourselves.

units.la: Datum in Palatio nostro Whitehallij 2. Junij, Regni nostri Magnae Britanniae, Franciae & Hyberniae anno octavo.
units.tr: Given at our Palace of Whitehall, 2 June, in the eighth year of our reign over Great Britain, France and Ireland.

units.la: Deus custodiat Regem.
units.tr: God save the King.

units.la: Hanc Inquisitionem & proscriptionem Anglicanam in Proditores, veneficos, parricidas institutam, Gretscherus Iesuita contra Stenium cum Hispanica confert, Oceanum scilicet cum Limago nostro, & elephantum cum formica. Σύγκειται haec mirarer,
units.tr: This Anglican inquisition and proscription, instituted against traitors, poisoners and parricides, Gretser the Jesuit compares against Stenius with the Spanish one: the ocean, namely, with our Limagus, and the elephant with the ant. I would be amazed that such things are put together [Σύγκειται].

units.la: Calumniae de proscriptione Iesuitarum in Ang. nisi ex solo Gretschero frons Iesuitarum omnibus nota esset. Quis enim non ri[?] deat, vel potius exsecretur impudentiam eius, affirmantis nihil certius expectandum Papistis, quam carcerem, exilium, &, ut alius Iesuita loquitur, rotas, cataslas, catapultas, frixoria, pugillaria, manus ferreas, ollas aeneas, &c. similia tormenta, in illis Provinciis & civitatibus, quas solus Lutherus vel Calvinus occupat. Refutat fatis Iesuitas Ecclesiarum statVS, qui est in Germania, Gallia, Belgio & aliis in regnis. Ubi enim vel fando auditum est, a Lutheranis vel Calviniistis combustos heterodoxos? Vnum vel alterum nominant, qui capitis supplicio affecti sunt: sed causam, factscio, non exprimunt, ut ita eorum ignari, quae gesta sunt, Calvinianos esse crudeles statuant: multo minus aliquid addunt de rogis Hispanicis, lanienis Gallicis, supplicijs Belgicis, coniurationibus Britannicis, exiliis Carinthicis, turbis Polonicis, tumultibus Suecicis, & motibus Vngaricis.
units.tr: The slanders about the proscription of the Jesuits in England would not be known to everyone, except from Gretser alone and the brazenness of the Jesuits. For who would not laugh at, or rather execrate, his impudence in affirming that nothing more certain is to be expected by the Papists than prison, exile and, as another Jesuit puts it, wheels, racks, catapults, frying pans, thumbscrews, iron gloves, brazen pots and the like tortures, in those provinces and cities which only Luther or Calvin holds. He sufficiently refutes the Jesuits by the state of the Churches which exists in Germany, France, the Netherlands and other kingdoms. For where has it ever been heard, even by report, that heretics were burned by the Lutherans or the Calvinists? They name one or two who were put to death, but they do not state the cause of the matter, and thus, ignorant of what was done, they declare the Calvinists to be cruel. Much less do they add anything about the Spanish stakes, the French butcheries, the Belgian tortures, the British conspiracies, the Carinthian exiles, the Polish disturbances, the Swedish tumults and the Hungarian commotions.

units.la: Comprehensi sunt etiam Anno 1606. duo alij ex Iesuitis coniurationis huius conscij in Anglia, & ad Regem adducti: Ex eorum uno, Parcio nempe, Sociétatis in Anglia Provinciali, Rege praesente, quaesitum est primo, Possitne Pontifex Romanus excommunicare Iacobum praesentem Angliae Regem? qui respondit, omnes Catholicos fuisse hactenus & esse adhuc in illa sententia, licere summo Pontifici, tanquam summo Christi in terris Vicario, omnes Reges & Principes haereticos excommunicare. Instantibus vero Consiliariis, non esse hoc diiudicandum in recto responsum ad propositam quaestionem, respondendum enim esse praecise ad hoc; Vtrum Paulus V. Pontifex modo Romae residens, possit juste excommunicare Iacobum I. magnae Britanniae Regna hoc tempore gubernantem? ille, respondit se in genere ad propositam quaestionem ex mente omnium Catholicorum ait, velleque in responsione ista acquiescere, cum in individuo respondere aut deficere velle, quid Paulus V. Pontifex Max. in Iacobum I. possit, maioris esse authoritatis, maturioris consilij & superioris arbitrij, petit igitur sibi, quod salcem in alienam messem mittere nolit, ignosci. Quaesitum deinde ex illo est, An Angli omnes, qui Anglicanam confessionem sequuntur, sint haeretici? Respondit ille, Quicunque scientes volentes, ab Ecclesia Catholica Romana divortium faciunt, inque eo perseverant, sunt haeretici. Vrgebant illi, responsionem magis ad Anglos, eorumque religionem applicandam esse, at ille in hoc suo generali responso subsistit, ne in prima quidem quaestione laesae Maiestatis, in altera vero fractae seu perturbatae pacis publicae reus fieret. Quaesitum porro est, An proditio proxima, sua authoritate, consilio & praescitu facta esset? Ille negando respondit, & adiunxit simul, se detestari ex animo tam horrendos conatus contra magistratum legitimum conceptos, iudicareque autores non eo tantum, quod aliqui eorum iam sustinuissent, sed graviori etiam supplicio, (si tamen aliquid gravius excogitari posset) dignos esse. Postremo quaesitum ex eo fuit, An autor esset libelli cuiusdam, contra statum Regis & regni Anglicani conscripti? Respondit ille, autorem se non esse, vidisse tamen istum libellum, & in multis correxisse, cum quicquid in provincia illa a Societate conscriberetur, censurae uti suae subiciatur, necesse omnino esset. Hoc audito in carcerem uterque mandato Regis translati sunt.
units.tr: In the year 1606 two other Jesuits, privy to this conspiracy, were also arrested in England and brought before the King. Of one of them, Garnet, namely the Provincial of the Society in England, the following was asked in the King's presence, first: Can the Roman Pontiff excommunicate James, the present King of England? He answered that all Catholics had hitherto been and still were of the opinion that it is lawful for the supreme Pontiff, as the highest Vicar of Christ on earth, to excommunicate all heretical kings and princes. But when the Counsellors pressed him that this was not a direct answer to the question proposed, and that he must answer precisely to this: Can Paul V, the Pontiff Maximus now residing at Rome, justly excommunicate James I, who at this time governs the kingdoms of Great Britain? he replied that, speaking generally to the question proposed and in the mind of all Catholics, he was content to rest in this answer; but that to answer individually what Paul V, the supreme Pontiff, can do against James I, was a matter of greater authority, of more mature counsel and of higher judgment; he therefore asked that it be pardoned him that he was unwilling to put his sickle into another man's harvest. Next he was asked: Are all the English who follow the Anglican confession heretics? He answered: Whoever, knowingly and willingly, separates from the Roman Catholic Church and perseveres in that, is a heretic. They urged him that the answer should be applied rather to the English and their religion, but he persisted in this general answer, so that he might not be made guilty of treason in the first question, nor of breaking or disturbing the public peace in the second. Further, he was asked: Was the approaching treason undertaken by his own authority, counsel and foreknowledge? He answered in the negative, and added at the same time that he detested from his heart such horrendous attempts conceived against the lawful magistrate, and judged that their authors deserved not only what some of them had already suffered, but also a heavier punishment (if indeed anything heavier could be devised). Lastly, he was asked: Was he the author of a certain libel written against the state of the King and the English kingdom? He answered that he was not the author, but that he had seen this libel and corrected it in many places, since whatever was written in that province by the Society had of necessity to be submitted to his censorship. Having heard this, both were taken to prison by the King's command.

units.la: Anno etiam 1607. Iesuita quidam in quatuor partes dissectus est, quod in contumeliam & contemptum mandatorum Regiorum, Sacerdotes aliquos sui ordinis creare, in locis occultis conciones habere, & populum ita docere, quod Rex in Ecclesiam ius nullum habeat, Pontifex eius caput fit & subditi ad servandam Regi fidem non teneantur, ausus fuerit.
units.tr: In the year 1607 a certain Jesuit was quartered, because he had dared, in contempt and scorn of the King's commands, to create some priests of his Order, to hold sermons in secret places, and to teach the people that the King has no right over the Church, that the Pope is its head, and that subjects are not bound to keep faith with the King.

units.la: QVERELA ANGLICANI CLERI AD CLEMENTEM VIII. PONTIFICEM ROMANVM DE MVLTIS AC VARIIS Iesuitarum studijs, dolis, impost< ... > Transcription of the title block is partly illegible on the scan. IESVITARVM GESTA AD REGINAM ELISABETHAM SPECTANTIA.
units.tr: COMPLAINT OF THE ENGLISH CLERGY TO POPE CLEMENT VIII, THE ROMAN PONTIFF, CONCERNING THE MANY AND VARIOUS PURSUITS, DECEITS, AND IMPOSTURES OF THE JESUITS: THE DEEDS OF THE JESUITS RELATING TO QUEEN ELIZABETH.

units.la: ELisabetha in Anglia regnante, non modò neglecta fuerunt multa media ad regnum illud convertendum proposita, sed eorum loco propter libellos famosos quàm plurimos, timores annuos, menstruosque futuræ invasionis, aliasque molitiones frequentes à Iesuitis profectas, tam gravis tot annorum persequutio exstitata est, ut magnum Catholici nominis exterminandi periculum sæpe imminerēt. Et quamvis ad minuendam hæreticorum superbiam debita & proportionata media assumenda esse non inficiemur, multa tamen in materia, ut appellant, statūs omnibus Catholicis obiecta, se obtulerunt, quæ Sacerdotes cum sēbe Catholica graviter offenderent.
units.tr: Under Queen Elizabeth's reign, not only were many means of converting that kingdom neglected, but in their place such a severe persecution, lasting many years, arose, on account of very many defamatory libels, yearly and monthly fears of a future invasion, and other frequent schemes set on foot by the Jesuits, that the great danger of exterminating the Catholic name often hung over us. And although we do not deny that due and proportionate means ought to be used to curb the pride of heretics, many things were nevertheless put forward against all Catholics in the matter, as they call it, of state, which gravely offended the Priests along with the sound Catholic cause.

units.la: 1. Sacerdotes in Angliam missi, sub Alani auspiciis, ex institutione Pontificis probiti, materiæ statūs se immiscere, post aliquot annos, Iesuitas sub eadem conditione, in subsidium asciverunt. Eam tamen conditionem violabant, quàm cum Sacerdotibus, & cum illis, in quorum domibus excipiendi erant, pacti fuerant, quàm eorum Generalis inscriptis sub obedientia illis mandaverat: quam regulam suæ religionis fundamentale faciunt, scilicet querelis Dominorum temporalium se ingerant, ut ex libro Regularum impresso, utet, quàm ubique ab illis observari Franciscus Montanus in Apologia Iesuitarum profetur.
units.tr: 1. The Priests sent into England under Allen's auspices, who had been bound by the Pope's instruction not to meddle in affairs of state, after some years admitted the Jesuits to their aid on the same condition. Yet they violated that condition, which they had agreed upon with the Priests and with those in whose houses they were to be received, and which their General had enjoined on them in writing under obedience. They make this their fundamental rule: that they should thrust themselves into the complaints of temporal lords, as Francis Montanus declares in his Apology for the Jesuits, from the printed book of Rules, which he says is observed everywhere by them.

units.la: 2. Iesuitæ libellum supplicem ad Elisabetham, typis impressum, ediderunt. In eo illam Reginam omnibus regijs virtutibus ornatam, & totius illorum iustæ spei, post Deum, uchoram appellant. In eo profitentur, se ab Elisabethæ partibus futuros contra Pontificem Romanum, etiam pro causa religionis Catholicæ Angliam invasurum, nec aliter sentire quenquam Catholicum, nisi ignorantem aut scrupulosum. In eo etiam coram Deo & angelis protestantur, se immunes esse & fore ab omnibus contra Elisabetham molitionibus, propter quas tamen quàm plurimos ab Elisabetha morte affectos noverant: Quæ Iesuitarum purgatio tantum non erat Sacerdotum accusatio. In eo multas alias absurdissimas adulationes congerunt. Adulationes, reclamante etiam conscientia, effusitas appellare possumus, quo quam laudaverant vivam, vituperabant statim mortuam.
units.tr: 2. The Jesuits published a supplicating libel to Elizabeth, printed in type. In it they call that Queen, adorned with all royal virtues, the sole anchor of all their just hope, after God. In it they profess that they would side with Elizabeth against the Roman Pontiff, and that they would invade England even for the cause of the Catholic religion, and that no Catholic thinks otherwise unless he is ignorant or scrupulous. In it, too, they protest before God and the angels that they are and will be innocent of all plots against Elizabeth, although they knew that very many had been put to death by Elizabeth on account of such plots. This Jesuit purgation was scarcely anything other than an accusation of the Priests. In it they heap up many other most absurd flatteries. We may call these flatteries outpourings, which, even while conscience protested, they praised her while alive and at once reviled her when dead.

units.la: Robertus Persoñius pro more suo, librum de Conversionibus tribus Angliæ, ab alio quodam, nomine Harbsfildo, insignissimo Doctore compositum, suo nomine promulgavit. Præfigit Epistolas, unam vivæ Elisabethæ factam, in quà illam commendat; aliam mortuæ Elisabethæ factam, in quà illam condemnat: utraque jam in eodem volumine iuncta circumfertur.
units.tr: Robert Persons, true to his custom, published under his own name a book on the Three Conversions of England, composed by another man, named Harbsfield, a most distinguished Doctor. He prefixed two letters: one written to Elizabeth while alive, in which he commends her; another written after Elizabeth's death, in which he condemns her. Both are now circulated together in the same volume.

units.la: 3. Librum Titulorum ad regnum Angliæ pro Infanta Hispanica compositum, insinuatus, seditionisque plenissimum, ad augendam contra Sacerdotes suspicionem, sub nomine Sacerdotis secularis Dolmanni viri singularis meriti, promulgarunt.
units.tr: 3. They published under the name of the secular priest Dolman, a man of singular merit, a book of Titles to the kingdom of England composed for the Spanish Infanta; it was insinuated, and very full of sedition, and was meant to increase suspicion against the Priests.

units.la: 4. Assassinos ad occidendam Elisabetham subornatos, ex Hispania ad Sacerdotes quot in Anglia, quorum unus erat prefatus Dolmannus, quasi cadit complices, misent. Unde Sacerdotes illi, eorumque amici, nonnulli magnæ nobilitatis viri, in maximum periculum conjecti, sed propter perspectissimam eorum innocentiam mirabiliter liberati sunt.
units.tr: 4. They sent assassins, suborned to kill Elizabeth, from Spain to the Priests in England, of whom the aforesaid Dolman was one, as if they were their accomplices. Whence those Priests, and their friends, some men of great nobility, were thrown into the greatest danger, but were wondrously freed on account of their most clearly proven innocence.

units.la: 5. Sacerdotes illos, aliosque, quorum integritas, & in patriam debita affectio jam uterere cœpit, infamare non cessârunt, & magis quàm antea, tanquam nimium à magistratibus favorem ex necessaria innocentiae defensione consequutos. Sciebant ex illo favore Sacerdotibus impense plurima plurimis Catholicis bona obtingere. Sciebant ex eo favore honorem & incrementum religionis Catholicae provenire. Sed religionis & rebellionis perspecta differentia cum honore etiam Sacerdotum conjuncta, magno designationi bus Iesuitarum non potuit non esse praejudicio, qui librum de Reformatione Anglicana, tanquam extincto clero, aut mox extinguendo, conscripserant, in quo tanquam omnium Domini de dispositionibus Episcoporum & Episcopatuum, de redditibus omnibus Ecclesiasticis in massam redigendis & distribuendis, de proceribus in ordinem cogendis, de aliis Ordinibus religiosorum vix, aut ne vix quidem admittendis, de Provincialibus Iesuiticis loco Abbatum Benedictinorum creandis, de emolumentis ad summum Pontificem pertinentibus, ad quinquennium in usum Iesuitarum intervertendis, praeter multos alios articulos determinaverant.
units.tr: 5. They did not cease to defame those Priests, and others whose integrity and due affection toward their country had already begun to be apparent, and more than before, as though they had obtained too much favour from the magistrates through the necessary defence of their innocence. They knew that from that favour many good things came to very many Catholics, through the great benefit it bestowed on the Priests. They knew that from that favour the honour and growth of the Catholic religion came forth. But the clearly perceived difference between religion and rebellion, joined with the honour of the Priests, could not but be a great prejudice to the designs of the Jesuits, who had written a book on the English Reformation as though the clergy were extinct, or about to be extinguished. In it they had laid down, among many other articles, that they would be lords of all: over the arrangement of bishops and bishoprics; over gathering all ecclesiastical revenues into one mass and distributing them; over compelling the nobles into order; over admitting scarcely, or hardly at all, other orders of religious; over creating Jesuit provincials in place of the Benedictine abbots; and over diverting to the use of the Jesuits, for five years, the emoluments belonging to the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Nec horum memoria jam fuisset refricanda, si simul cum Elisabetha molimina Iesuitarum terminum suum habuissent. Iam vero quia perpetua eorum series, non minus contra Iacobum Angliae Regem, quam contra Elisabetham, & forte magis, persequutionis causam valde promoveat, ne omnibus crimine involutis seditionis, religio Catholica exosa fiat, cum multarum animarum detrimento, operae pretium est, ut Sacerdotum innocentia, moderni Regis Britanniae justae expectationi respondisse appareat, in iis praecipue rebus, quarum veritas apparere debet.
units.tr: Nor would the memory of these things need to be revived now, if the plots of the Jesuits had come to an end together with Elizabeth. But since their unbroken succession greatly promotes the cause of persecution, no less against James, King of England, than against Elizabeth, and perhaps more so, it is worth the effort, lest the Catholic religion become hateful, with harm to many souls, by all being implicated in the crime of sedition, to show that the innocence of the Priests has answered the just expectation of the present King of Britain, especially in those matters whose truth ought to become evident.

units.la: GESTA IESVITARVM AD IACOBVM RE- GEM BRITANNIAE MATREMQVE SPECTANTIA.
units.tr: THE DEEDS OF THE JESUITS CONCERNING KING JAMES OF BRITAIN AND HIS MOTHER.

units.la: AMultis annis sic constat, ut nulla tergiversatione celari possit, Iesuitas manibus pedibusque, ut aiunt, laborasse, ut apud Catholicos Anglos gratiam popularem aucuparentur, Sacerdotibus aversione conflata, & praecipue praetextu ad speciem pulchro, quod Sacerdotes Regis Scotiae, qui esset haereticus, favorent titulo; Iesuitae vero laborarent ad sceptrum Angliae evehere personam Catholicam, vel Hispanum, vel Hispanam, vel Parmensem, vel Sabaudum, vel quintam, vel sextam, vel nescio quotuplam personam (pro bono Societatis omni vento velificare decreverunt) sed semper Catholicam. Unde consequens erat necessario, ut Rex Scotiae tanquam persona inidonea, nihil in se regium habens (id quod sedulo factum est) traduceretur. Nec defuerunt molitiones Iesuitarum varias, ut Rex Scotiae Angliae regno privaretur: in quibus tamen omnibus dicunt, non defuisse eis summi Pontificis consensum.
units.tr: For many years it has been so well established, and no evasion can conceal it, that the Jesuits, as they say, laboured hand and foot to win popular favour among the English Catholics, stirring up hostility against the priests. They did this especially under the fair-seeming pretext that the priests favoured the title of the King of Scots, who was a heretic, whereas the Jesuits would work to raise to the sceptre of England a Catholic person: either a Spaniard, or a Spanish woman, or the Parmesan, or the Savoyard, or a fifth or sixth, or some further person whose number I do not know. They resolved to sail with every wind for the good of the Society, but always for a Catholic. Hence it necessarily followed that the King of Scots was to be disparaged as an unfit person with nothing kingly in him, and this was diligently done. Nor were the Jesuits' various schemes lacking to deprive the King of Scots of the kingdom of England. In all of these, however, they say, the consent of the supreme Pontiff was not lacking.

units.la: Liber Titulorum ab illis conscriptus est pro titulo Infantae Hispanicae ad Regnum Angliae contra titulum Regis Scotiae. Ad illum librum Titulorum additio postea divulgata est, in qua omnis melioris notae Catholici Angli afferuntur (sed salsissime) Scotico titulo refragati esse.
units.tr: A book of Titles was written by them in support of the title of the Infanta of Spain to the kingdom of England, against the title of the King of Scots. Later an addition to that book of Titles was published, in which all the Catholics of England of better standing are cited (very falsely) as having opposed the Scottish title.

units.la: Anno 1589. Cum Rex Hispaniae Philippus II. in Collegio Anglicano Vallisoleti exciperetur, moderantibus eam actionem quatuor Iesuitis, quorum unus erat Robertus Personius, Oratione publica unius Angli ex persona omnium, oblati sunt ei animi, vires, conatus, studia, vitae, mortesque non eorum solum, qui in Collegio erant, sed & parentum, amicorum, necessariorum & Catholicorum omnium in Anglia, ut patet ex libro ad rei memoriam ab illis impresso anno 1593.
units.tr: In 1589, when King Philip II of Spain was received at the English College at Valladolid, the proceedings being directed by four Jesuits, one of whom was Robert Persons, there were offered to him, in a public oration delivered by one Englishman on behalf of all, the minds, strength, efforts, studies, lives and deaths, not only of those who were in the College, but also of their parents, friends, relatives and all Catholics in England. This appears from a book they published in 1593 to record the matter.

units.la: In Collegijs Anglicanis Vallisoleti & Sivilia, inducti sunt Angli Iesuitarum fraudibus & minis, ut titulo Infantae ad regnum Anglicanum subscriberent, & in missionibus ad Angliam subscriptum titulum promoverent: quamvis nonnulli subscriptiones has alibi procuratas fuisse asserant.
units.tr: In the English Colleges at Valladolid and Seville, the Englishmen were induced, by Jesuit deceits and threats, to subscribe to the title of the Infanta to the English kingdom, and in the missions to England to promote the subscribed title, although some assert that these subscriptions were procured elsewhere.

units.la: Archiduci Alberto & Infantae intimarunt, totpro illis obsides esse, quot Angli in Seminario S. Audomari nutrirentur. Infantam Hispanicam, venientem in Belgium, deliberârunt titulo Reginæ Angliæ signire⁠_. Hoc cùm notum esset factum in Anglia, magna tumultuum Belgicorum oc- casio fuit.
units.tr: They gave notice to the Archduke Albert and the Infanta that there were as many hostages for them as there were Englishmen being nourished in the seminary of St Omer. They resolved to greet the Infanta of Spain, on her coming into Belgium, with the title of Queen of England. When this became known in England, it was a great occasion of Belgian tumults.
