units.la: Die Herren Evangelischen Ständt deß Königreichs Hungarn tragen in güter gedechtnus/ wie bald von den zeiten an als die Jesuiten bey Keyser Ferdinandi zeiten in das Königreich Böheimb eingeführt worden/ die selben viel vnd mancherley vnwillen mit ihren practicken gestifftet/ ja sie seind auch viel mehr darduch bewegt worden/ daß durch ihren rath vnd verursachung bey Keyser Rodolphi hochlöblicher gedechtnus zeiten/ der Türcken krieg casirt/ Sintemahl der Römische Bischoff/ welches den Herren Ständen deß Königreichs Hungern wol bewußt/ Keyser Rodolphen/ damit der Türcken krieg befriediget/ vnnd solche kriegsmacht auff die Kätzer/ welche bey solchem Türcken krieg in auffnemen geriet/ verwandt werden möchte/ sehr starck vermanet: So daß auch beschehen/ vnd der Türcken krieg/ welcher 16. jar continuë gewäret/ jedoch nicht mit geringem despect vnd verachtung der gantzen Christenheit/ am meisten aber deß Königreichs Hungarn/ vnd mit vnaußsprechlichem schaden/ in deme viel gewaltig: vnnd ansehenliche Personen schlechter ermordet/ auch vmb ihre güter gebracht/ verhöret worden. Dann was durch der Jesuiter practicken Keyser Rodolphi kriegsheer/ vber welches Georg Basta zum Obersten General verordnet/ vnnd der Belliosa ein außländer/ erstlich wider alle Ordnung vnd freyheit deß Königreichs Hungern in der Hauptstatt Cascha in Oberungern zu einem Hauptman angesetzt/ welcher die Kirchen vnnd Schulen hinweg genommen/ die Priester vnd Schulmeister zusambt den Studenten auß der Statt verjaget/ vnd ein blutvergiessen zwischen den Christen selbst in dem Königreich Hungern angerichtet/ das ist nunmehr der gantzen welt kundt vnd offenbar.
units.tr: The lords, the Evangelical Estates of the Kingdom of Hungary, keep in good remembrance how, from the time when the Jesuits were introduced into the Kingdom of Bohemia under Emperor Ferdinand, they stirred up much and varied displeasure by their practices. Moreover, they were especially moved by their counsel and urging, in the time of Emperor Rudolf of blessed memory, to bring the war against the Turks to an end. For the Roman bishop, as the lords Estates of the Kingdom of Hungary well know, strongly urged Emperor Rudolf to satisfy the Turkish war in this way and to turn that military force against the heretics, who were gaining ground during that war. This was done, and the Turkish war, which lasted sixteen years, was brought to an end. Yet it was waged with no small contempt and scorn for the whole of Christendom, and above all for the Kingdom of Hungary, and with inexpressible loss, in which many powerful and distinguished persons were wretchedly murdered and deprived of their goods. For through the practices of the Jesuits, the army of Emperor Rudolf, over which Georg Basta was appointed commander-in-chief and the foreigner Belliosa was first placed as captain in the chief town of Cascha in Upper Hungary, against all order and the liberty of the Kingdom of Hungary, took away the churches and schools, drove the priests and schoolmasters together with the students out of the town, and caused bloodshed among Christians themselves in the Kingdom of Hungary. This is now known and evident to the whole world.

units.la: Es hat sich aber bemeldte Jesuitische Secte/ welcher insonderheit vom Keyser Mathia grosser vnd übermässiger fortgang gestattet/ hieran nicht benügen lassen/ sondern sich in alle Politische händel eingetrungen/ vnd von vnsern aller geheimbsten rathschlägen deß Königreichs Hungarn wissenschafft gehabt/ vnd solches alles durch ihre practicken bey der Oberkeit/ in deme sie alle sachen ein andere außlegung ingedrehet/ zu nicht gemachet. Ja es hat sich auch diese Jesuitische Secte offentlich in den predigten/ daß die Kätzer aufgerieben vnd ermordet werden müssen/ hören und verlauten lassen/ vnd andere schwere/ zu dieses Königreichs vntergang/ gereiende bedrouwung zûthûn sich vnterfangen.
units.tr: But this Jesuit sect, to which in particular the excessive and immoderate growth was granted by Emperor Matthias, was not content with this. It thrust itself into all political affairs, and had knowledge of all our most secret counsels of the Kingdom of Hungary, and by its practices with the authorities it turned all these matters to nothing by twisting every affair into a different interpretation. Indeed, this Jesuit sect has also been heard and spoken of openly in its sermons, to the effect that the heretics must be wiped out and murdered, and it has undertaken to make other grave threats tending to the ruin of this kingdom.

units.la: Wann dann die H. Ständte deß Königreichs Hungern solche practikanten vnderlistige mörder der Könige vnd Potentaten/ zerstörer deß allgemeinen friedens/ verrâther der Provincien vnd Königreichen/ vnd der Christlichen jugendt mit jrer argen vnd bösen lehre/ verführer nit länger im Königreich dulden nach leiden kondten/ als seind dieselben der H. Ständte deß Königreichs Böheimb/ vnd auch deß Mar-graffthumbs Mähren/ vnser lieben Herren freünde vnd nachbarn exempel nach/ daß zu ewigen zeiten das Königreich Hungern meiden/ vnd darein nimmermehr vnder einer erdachten gestalt in ewigkeit wider kommen sollen/ proscribirt, vnd verwiesen worden. Wo fern aber einer vnder ihnen den Jesuiten nach dieser gethanen verweisung/ in dem Königreich Hungern innerthalb 4. tagen ertapt vnnd ergriffen wurde/ der sol ohne alle gnad am leben gestraffet werden. Und so jemand/ sich gleich wer er wolle/ einen auß der Jesuitischen Secte nachhausgang vier sagen/ in dem Königreich Hungern betretten wurde/ den selben kan er als einen aufrührer vnnd verrätber des Königreichs frey vnd füglich ermörden vnd vmbbringen/ vnd sol daran nichts verlieren.
units.tr: Since the lords, the Estates of the Kingdom of Hungary, could no longer tolerate or endure such plotters, crafty murderers of kings and potentates, destroyers of the general peace, betrayers of provinces and kingdoms, and seducers of Christian youth with their wicked and evil teaching, they have, following the example of our dear lords, friends and neighbours, the Estates of the Kingdom of Bohemia and also of the Margraviate of Moravia, proscribed and banished them, so that they shall avoid the Kingdom of Hungary for all time and never return into it for ever, under any invented guise. But if any one of them, after this banishment, is caught and seized within four days in the Kingdom of Hungary, he shall be punished with death without any mercy. And if anyone, whoever he may be, meets one of the Jesuit sect in the Kingdom of Hungary after this four-day period, he may freely and lawfully kill and destroy him as a rebel and traitor to the kingdom, and shall incur no penalty for doing so.

units.la: DE PRODITIONIBVS, TVRBIS, SEDITIO- NIBVS IN POLONIA A IESVITIS EXCITATIS.
units.tr: On the Treacheries, Disturbances and Seditions Stirred Up in Poland by the Jesuits

units.la: DE tumultibus in Polonia multi passim rumores audiri sunt. De Rege quidem eorum moderno Sigismundo omnes, qui eum propius nosse videntur, testantur, nihil illo mansuetius, nihil humanius, nitius & fingi posse. Harum tamen tam popularium naturae dotium usum & fructum Iesuitarum panurgia actum corrupit & intercepit, ut primum avitum eius & hereditarium regnum ab ipso prorsus abalienaverint: quod eorum instinctu haeresin, quam vocant, Lutheranam neglecta iurisiurandi praestiti religione prorsus exsitirpare voluit: Regnum vero Poloniae, quod ad eundem libera electione delatum fuit, odio mutuaq; diffidentia & perniciosa dissensione repletum ita turbarunt, ut & Rex & Regnum ex aequo variis, ac gravibus quidem periculis expositi fuerint.
units.tr: Many rumours of tumults in Poland have been heard everywhere. Concerning their present king, Sigismund, all who seem to know him well testify that nothing could be imagined gentler, more humane or more refined than he. Yet the Jesuits' trickery has corrupted and cut off the use and benefit of these popular qualities of his nature, so that they have entirely estranged him from his ancestral and hereditary kingdom. At their instigation he wished to root out completely the heresy they call Lutheran, disregarding the obligation of the oath he had sworn. As for the kingdom of Poland, which had been conferred on him by free election, they have so disturbed it, filled as it is with mutual hatred, distrust and pernicious dissension, that both king and kingdom have been equally exposed to various and serious dangers.

units.la: Refert Eques Polonus Papisticae religionis in Oratione sua, quam in frequenti procerum eius Regni Conventu habuit, quamq; paulo infra integram adscribemus, Cracoviam urbe celeberrima, domicilium atq; ornamentum totius Re-gni ita vexata fuisse a Iesuitis, ut plurimi viri boni, quantumvis Catholici, af-firmarint; se malle in sylvis inter feras vitā degere, quam in ista inhumanitate versari. Conspiratione enim facta, cuius Iesuitae authores atq; duces exti-terunt, magna vi atque impetu in eam domum irruerunt, quae unum in tota urbe monimentum antiquitatis extat, & Evangelicis concessa fuit, ex Regis & omnium proceram permissu & approbatione. Apparebant effusae aliquot diebus flammae, quae per multas urbis partes sparsae, toti urbi interitum minabantur. Audiebantur clamores praedas efferentium hominum, inter quos etiam versabantur Iesuitae attritis rusticorum vestibus induti, ne agnosci possent: totaq; urbs in summo periculo versata fuit, a quo ante Iesuitarum adventum tutissima fuit.
units.tr: A Polish knight of the Papist religion, in his speech delivered before a full assembly of the nobles of that kingdom (which we will quote in full a little further on), reports that Cracow, the most famous city, the home and ornament of the whole kingdom, was so harassed by the Jesuits that many good men, however Catholic, affirmed that they would rather live out their lives among the wild beasts in the woods than endure such inhumanity. For a conspiracy was made, of which the Jesuits were the authors and leaders, and with great force and violence they burst into that house, which is the only monument of antiquity in the whole city and had been granted to the Evangelicals with the permission and approval of the king and all the nobles. For several days flames were seen pouring out, spreading through many parts of the city and threatening its total destruction. Shouts of men carrying off plunder could be heard, and among them were Jesuits, dressed in worn-out peasant clothing so that they could not be recognised. The whole city was in the greatest danger, from which it had been most safe before the arrival of the Jesuits.

units.la: Posnaniae, quae civitas Poloniae insignis est, instinctu Iesuitarum, templum Augustanam confessionem profitentium, igne delere saepe antehac conati sunt, non successit tamen ipsis propositum, excubitoribus id facinus semper impedientibus. Anno autem 1606. Mayi die 13. Iesuitarum discipuli, trecenti fere numero, instinctu suorum superiorum & praeceptorum, inita cum aliis conspiratione, sub vespera impetum cum in templum illud fecissent, custodes quidem & excubitores in fugam facile coniecerunt, postmodo perfractis vi summa foribus subsellisq; templi in unum locum congestis, incendium excitarunt, quo totum illud aedificium in cineres brevi tempore versum est, furentibus nimirum tantopere Catholicis illis, ut extinguendo incendio operam dare cives non auderent. Ferventibus hisce turbis, quidam in Xenodochium irruerunt, aegrotos vi summa inde exturbarunt, fornacem, scamna, mensas, fenestras & alia dissiparunt, & perfregerunt, male affectorum suppellectilem abstulerunt partim, partim per plateas dissiminarunt, & ita se fe gesserunt, ut facinus nullu tam abominabile ipsis malus inspirare potuisse genius videretur, quin in actu illud statim producerent perficerentq;. Ad de igitur hac subversa et vastata, qui confessionem Augustanam profitebantur, in aperto postmodum & patenti campo convenire, sacraq; sua celebrare coacti sunt, cumq; nec ibi tutos se fe satis ab iniuria fore, ex minis atrocioribus colligerent, sclopis semper hastisq; & gladijs armati ad exercitia. ercitia concionum processerunt, rei totius serie VVarsoviam ad Ordines elatâ. Cæterum Iesuitæ, ut se aliquo modo purgarent, missis ad Regem legatis, non potuisse se discipulos suos in officio continere, qui religionis Catholicæ zelo accensi, templum illud dirutum modis omnibus voluisset, significarunt, petentes simul ut pro turbis maioribus vitandis reparatio templi inhibeatur, metuere enim se, illud quantumvis reparatum, flammas evitare vix posse. Cum igitur non in hac solum civitate, sed et alibi passim pro libitu omnia Iesuitas agere, nec esse qui in eos animadverteret nobilitas videret, ad Comitia VVarsoviæ paulo post celebrata comparere præcipui quique ex Poloniæ Prouinciis recusarunt, Lublini vel alibi de refrenanda hac contumacia deliberaturi.
units.tr: At Posen, which is a notable city of Poland, at the instigation of the Jesuits, they have often before this tried to destroy by fire the church of those professing the Augsburg Confession, but their purpose did not succeed, since the guards always prevented the deed. In the year 1606, on 13 May, however, the pupils of the Jesuits, nearly three hundred in number, at the instigation of their superiors and teachers, and having joined in conspiracy with others, made an assault on that church in the evening. The guards and watchmen they easily put to flight. Afterwards, having forced the doors and benches of the church with great violence and piled them into one place, they started a fire, by which that whole building was reduced to ashes in a short time, the Catholics there, of course, being so furious that the citizens did not dare to give help in putting out the fire. While these riots were raging, some of them burst into the hospital, violently drove the sick out of it, and smashed and broke the furnace, benches, tables, windows and other things. Partly they carried off the belongings of the afflicted, partly they scattered them through the streets. And they behaved in such a way that no crime so abominable would seem to be beyond what the wicked spirit could inspire them to, and they would carry it out at once. Then, after this church had been overthrown and laid waste, those who professed the Augsburg Confession were forced to gather in an open and exposed field and celebrate their worship there. And since they judged from the most savage threats that they would not be safe enough even there from injury, they went to their preaching exercises armed with muskets, spears and swords. The whole matter was carried to Warsaw and brought before the Estates. Meanwhile the Jesuits, to clear themselves in some way, sent envoys to the king, signifying that they could not keep their pupils in check, who, fired with zeal for the Catholic religion, had wished in every way to demolish that church. At the same time they asked that the repair of the church be forbidden, in order to avoid greater disturbances, for they feared that, however well it was repaired, it could hardly escape the flames. Since, therefore, the Jesuits were acting at will everywhere, not only in this city but also elsewhere, and the nobility saw that there was no one to call them to account, the chief men from the provinces of Poland refused to attend the assembly held at Warsaw shortly afterwards, intending to deliberate at Lublin or elsewhere on how to curb this insolence.

units.la: Thoruniæ, urbis Borussiæ ad Vistulæ fluvii situ, templis, ædificiis et emporio clarissimæ, Ordines cum Plebano quodam de possessione et iure Patronatus ecclesiæ ad S. Ioannem multis annis altercati sunt. Convenit autem tandem inter eos, ut Plebanus quidem solus in domo parochiali habitans, templum reficeret, ministeriumque Ecclesiæ per ministros suos more hactenus usitato constitueret, ius vero patronatus penes civitatem et ordines eius permaneret, in cuius rei confirmationem non solum literæ confectæ sunt, quas Episcopus quidem Culmensis, quemadmodum etiam Culmense Capitulum subscriptas sigillis suis obsignarunt, sed et diploma à Rege, Ordines quo debitum civitati ius patronatus de novo confirmatum est, obtinuerunt. Postquam igitur iam Plebanus Ecclesiæ domumque parochialem, certis tamen cum conditionibus, obtinuit, Episcopus statim Culmensis, contra conventionis literas, pro rio ausu, duos in aulam parochialem Iesuitas, alterum qui confessiones audiret, et alterum qui concionaretur in templo, introducere, Plebano ex domo illa emoto conatus est, Ordines vero hoc videntes, solenniter contra aliquoties protestari, Plebanum, uti memor contractus ab utraque parte initi, Iesuitas iterum revoveret, monuerunt, intercessione totius Regionis in Comitiis publicis adhibita. Cæterum monitionibus et intercessionibus illis non solum nihil proficere actenus potuerunt, sed et præter duos illos Iesuitas, subinde alii advenerunt, ut occupata aula parochiali, clam Ordinibus civitatis, privilegium tandem aliquod obtinere conati sunt, quo templo illo Iesuitarum ordini attributo, Plebanus quidem in Vicarium promoveretur, possessio vero Ecclesiæ una cum domo parochiali et schola Iesuitis relinqueretur, clavibus Ecclesiæ scholæque in manus eorum traditis et oblatis. Hoc facto Iesuitæ, auctoritate indies magis magisque numero viduarum et pupillorum domus emere, scholam aperire, et Collegium in civitate constituere amplius non dubitarunt, constituta peculiari iurisdictione, unde creberrimi per plateas et vicos civitatis tumultus, Iesuitis quidem ipsis multa insidiose molientibus, discipulis vero eorum omne petulantia exercentibus, ivesque iniuria et contumelia varia afficientibus, extiterunt. Ordines igitur civitatis ne iure suo per conniventiam sese ipsos privarent, consilium tandem cepe unt, quomodo excusso hoc iugo, molestis illis hospitibus cives suos liberaret. Missis igitur ad Plebanum aliquibus, eum de inito secum contractu admonentes, promiserunt, se secundum contractus illius tenorem in Ecclesia et aula parochiali eum quidem relicturos, Scholam etiam, quam tanquam propriam civitatis domum, precib. hactenus obtinuisset, impositurum etiam, donec bene de Republica promeriturus esset, ei relicturos, verum uti Iesuitas, tanquam huiusmodi hospites, qui et civitatem iure patronatus spoliare, et Plebanum ipsum possessione templi per insidias evacuare, molirentur, et in conturbationem status publici, collegium aliquod instituere scholamque aperire, pro sua authoritate auri essent, removeret domoque illis parochiali et Ecclesia interdiceret, vehementer postulârunt. Cum vero eo quidem die resolvere se Plebanus non posset, sed ad Episcopum negotium hoc relaturum se diceret, non expectandum diutius rati Ordines sequenti statim die quosdam, qui in integrum eum restituerent, ablegarunt, quod ipsum quidem fieri facili & lubenti animo passus est. Caeterum hoc facto expetierunt postmodum Ordines, ageret cum Iesuitis, ut sponte sua domo parochiali cederent, & a templo scholaque in posterum abstinerent, Ordines enim civitatis nolle eos tanquam turbatores publici Ecclesiae & civitatis iuris statusque diutius in parochiali aula ferre, urbe tamen ipsis interdictum nolle, donec quietos se fore, velut hospites deceret, intra suos terminos contenturi essent. Plebanus igitur mentem hanc & intentionem Ordinum Iesuitis expositit, qui scholam quidem claudere & collegio abstinere statim promiserunt, dummodo domum parochialem retinere & ministerium Ecclesiasticum peragere sibi permitteretur. Verum cum non contenti hac Iesuitarum resolutione Ordines urgerent Plebanum, ut tenore contractus observato, ad statum pristinum omnia revocaret, quo & ius patronatus civitati integrum, & decretum Regium fartum tectumque conservaretur, coacti sunt tandem Iesuitae, & clavium restitutionem Plebano facere, & ministerio docendi tam in Ecclesia quam in schola sese abdicare, atque ita tandem domo parochiali cedentes discipulis suis valedixerunt. Accidit autem porro ut orator quidam Regius ad civitatem in causa quadam ablegatus, Culminensem secum Episcopum adduceret, qui in aulam parochialem cum suis, quod hospitium a multis annis in urbem veniens habere solitus est, divertit. Iesuitae igitur hanc suis rebus occasionem commodam fore putantes, sequenti statim die Confessionariis operam dare & concionem iterum habere die Solis auspicati sunt. Ordines igitur hoc intellecto, ad Episcopum statim aliquos miserunt, qui eum rogarunt, ne post discessum suum Iesuitas eo loco relinqueret, addita denunciatione, si remanentibus ibi Iesuitis, contumeliae vel detrimenti aliquid a civibus inferatur, propriae uti id proterviae imputarent. At vero Episcopus neglectis hisce omnibus, non solum Iesuitas duos vel tres, post discessum suum, in domo parochiali reliquit, sed salvum conductum a Rege pro illis impetratum Senatui exhiberi curavit. Cum autem salvum conductum illum ad malam informationem impetratum esse, nemo dubitaret, Ordines statim contra protestati, scriptum publicum ad valvas templi, eius quidem sententiae, quod Regem melius informare, & de iure suo cedere ne latum quidem unguem cogitarent, affigi curarunt, ut ita nihil proficere machinationibus suis amplius valentes, domo parochiali cedere iterum necesse habuerint.
units.tr: At Thorn, a city of Prussia situated on the river Vistula, famous for its churches, buildings and trade, the estates had for many years disputed with a certain parish priest over the possession and right of patronage of the church of St John. Eventually it was agreed between them that the parish priest, living alone in the parish house, should repair the church and maintain the ministry of the church through his ministers in the manner used until then, while the right of patronage should remain with the city and its estates. To confirm this arrangement, not only was a document drawn up, which the bishop of Culm, as well as the chapter of Culm, signed and sealed with their seals, but the estates also obtained from the king a charter by which the right of patronage due to the city was newly confirmed. Therefore, when the parish priest had already obtained the church and the parish house, though under certain conditions, the bishop of Culm at once, contrary to the terms of the agreement and with a bold and shameless presumption, tried to introduce into the parish residence two Jesuits, one to hear confessions and the other to preach in the church, and to remove the parish priest from that house. The estates, seeing this, repeatedly protested solemnly against it, and warned that the parish priest, mindful of the contract made by both parties, should recall the Jesuits, with the support of the whole region brought to bear in the public assemblies. But by these warnings and interventions they not only achieved nothing up to that point, but besides those two Jesuits, others came in from time to time. Having occupied the parish residence, they then tried, secretly from the city's estates, to obtain some privilege by which, the church having been assigned to the Jesuit order, the parish priest would be promoted to vicar, and the possession of the church together with the parish house and the school would be left to the Jesuits, the keys of the church and school being handed over and delivered into their hands. After this was done, the Jesuits, with their authority growing more and more day by day, no longer hesitated to buy the houses of widows and orphans, to open a school and to establish a college in the city, with a special jurisdiction set up. Hence there arose very frequent tumults through the streets and lanes of the city, the Jesuits themselves plotting many treacheries secretly, while their pupils committed every kind of wantonness and inflicted various injuries and insults on the citizens. The estates of the city, therefore, so that they would not by their tolerance deprive themselves of their own rights, at last resolved how, by shaking off this yoke, they might free their citizens from those troublesome guests. So they sent some men to the parish priest, reminding him of the contract made with them, and promised that, according to the terms of that contract, they would leave him in the church and parish residence, and would also leave him the school, which he had obtained hitherto by prayer as a house of the city's own, to be governed by him until he should have deserved well of the commonwealth. But, as for the Jesuits, who, as guests of this kind, were attempting both to despoil the city of its right of patronage and to drive the parish priest himself out of possession of the church by plots, and who, by their own authority, were establishing a college and opening a school to the disturbance of the public order, they strongly demanded that he remove them and forbid them the parish house and the church. But since the parish priest could not decide on that day, and said he would refer the matter to the bishop, the estates, judging that they should wait no longer, sent some men on the very next day to restore him fully, which he allowed to be done with an easy and willing mind. However, after this had been done, the estates afterwards asked that he should act with the Jesuits, so that they would of their own accord give up the parish house and in future keep away from the church and school. For the city's estates were unwilling to tolerate them any longer, as disturbers of the public church and of the city's right and order, in the parish residence; yet they were unwilling to forbid them the city altogether, and would be content if, as guests should, they kept within their own bounds until they were quiet. The parish priest therefore explained this resolve and intention of the estates to the Jesuits, who immediately promised to close the school and abstain from the college, provided that they were allowed to keep the parish house and carry on the ecclesiastical ministry. But since the estates, not content with this resolution of the Jesuits, pressed the parish priest to restore everything to its former state, observing the terms of the contract, so that the right of patronage would remain whole for the city and the royal decree would be preserved intact and undamaged, the Jesuits were at last compelled both to restore the keys to the parish priest and to renounce the office of teaching both in the church and in the school. And so, at last giving up the parish house, they bade farewell to their pupils. It then happened that a certain royal envoy was sent to the city on some business and brought with him the bishop of Culm, who lodged in the parish residence with his people, as he had been accustomed to do for many years whenever he came to the city. The Jesuits, thinking this a convenient opportunity for their affairs, began the very next day to hear confessions and to preach again on Sunday. When the estates learned of this, they at once sent some men to the bishop to ask him not to leave the Jesuits in that place after his departure, adding a warning that if any insult or harm should be inflicted on the citizens because the Jesuits remained there, they would impute it to his own arrogance. But the bishop, disregarding all these things, not only left two or three Jesuits in the parish house after his departure, but also took care that a safe-conduct obtained for them from the king should be presented to the senate. Since no one doubted that this safe-conduct had been obtained through false information, the estates at once protested against it, and had a public document affixed to the doors of the church, to the effect that they would not even consider giving up their right by a hair's breadth, and that they would inform the king better. Thus, no longer able to achieve anything by their schemes, the Jesuits were once again obliged to give up the parish house.

units.la: CONSILIVM DATVM PROCERIBVS POLO- NIAE, DE RECVPERANDA, ET IN POSTERVM STABI- LIENDA PACE REGNI POLONIAE PER IESVITARVM EIECTIONEM.
units.tr: THE ADVICE GIVEN TO THE NOBLES OF POLAND, ON RECOVERING AND THEREAFTER ESTABLISHING THE PEACE OF THE KINGDOM OF POLAND BY THE EXPULSION OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: Quamvis tumultus in Polonia aliquo modo sedati a Rege fuissent, Iesuitarum irrequietis ingeniis, artibus ac studiis maxima ex parte excitati, Anno 1607. promissione & spe Nobilitati de Comitiis instituendis facta, quibus deliberatio de remedio malis huic tempestive adhibendo suscipereretur; Nobilitas tamen cum inani ac vana sese spe quasi lactari, & promissa Comitia de die in diem differri videret, magna copia denuo Anno eodem ad Proftovicum civitatem, quatuor millibus Cracovia distantem, ubi regia quaedam Curia est Conventibus Nobilium celebrandis iam olim destinata, confluxit, & novo Consilio instituto, quae malo huic medicina adhibenda potissimum esset, deliberare coepit. Inter varias autem consultationes scriptum quoddam Proceribus [illegible, ~10 letters] congre[?] ongregatis Polonica lingua exhibitum fuit, in quo auctor palam profitetur inter alia, Iesuitarum practicas & artes multivarias et cruentas, omnium in Polonia turbarum ac motuum causam primariam esse. Si morborum, inquit, in praefatione, publicorum regni nostri causae interius & foris diligentius perpendantur, primam erit, & omnium maxime principalem, Iesuitarum exquisitissimas artes, & astutissimam omnium sibi subiectorum ad conatus suos promovendos Dispositionem facile cordatus usq; deprehendet: adeo, ut quicquid usquam malorum in Repub. nostra praeteritis annis acciderit, magna ex parte solis illud Iesuiticis artibus imputandum veniat. Ad hoc utem demonstrandum, offendit primo, quam institutum Iesuiticum libertae Reipub. inimicum & adversum sit: Deinde quam periculose facta haec statum politicum non solum in Polonia, sed hinc inde per universam Europam turbarunt & labefactarunt. Ex quibus tandem colligit, pacem nec constitui nec stabilii posse in Polonia, quandiu Iesuitae in ea maneant, proindeque eos inde expellendos, nec amplius recipiendos; & quae in contrariam sententiam pro Iesuitis brjciuntur, refutari solide. Quia vero Consilium hoc seu Scriptum sublatum, ideoque in paucorum manibus versatur, totum adscribam in Lectoris gratiam, ut inde Iesuitarum artes, dolos, imposturas, fraudes, impudentiam, audaciam, studiaque denique omnia cognoscat & intellegat. Verba authoris haec sunt.
units.tr: Although the tumults in Poland had been somewhat quelled by the King, they were stirred up again for the most part by the restless minds, arts and schemes of the Jesuits. In 1607 a promise was made to the nobility that a Diet would be convened, at which deliberation on a remedy for these evils would be taken up in good time. But the nobility, seeing that they were being lulled, as it were, with an empty and vain hope, and that the promised Diet was being put off from day to day, came together again in great numbers in the same year at Proszowice, a town four miles from Kraków, where there is a royal court long ago designated for holding gatherings of the nobles. Once a new assembly had been set up, they began to deliberate on what remedy ought chiefly to be applied to this evil. Among the various discussions, a certain writing was presented to the nobles assembled there, written in the Polish language, in which the author openly declares, among other things, that the many and bloody practices and arts of the Jesuits are the chief cause of all the disturbances and upheavals in Poland. "If," he says in the preface, "the causes of the public ills of our kingdom are weighed more carefully, both at home and abroad, the first and most principal of all will be found to be the most exquisite arts of the Jesuits and their most cunning management of everyone subject to them in advancing their attempts; so that whatever evil has befallen our Commonwealth in past years will for the most part be attributed to the Jesuit arts alone. To demonstrate this, he first shows how hostile and adverse the Jesuit institute is to the liberty of the Commonwealth. Then he shows how dangerously these deeds have disturbed and weakened the political state, not only in Poland but here and there throughout all Europe. From these things he finally concludes that peace can neither be established nor made stable in Poland as long as the Jesuits remain in it; that they must therefore be expelled from there and not received again; and that what is put forward in favour of the Jesuits against this view must be soundly refuted." Since this counsel, or writing, has been suppressed and is therefore held in the hands of a few, I shall set out the whole of it for the reader's benefit, so that he may learn and understand the Jesuits' arts, tricks, impostures, frauds, shamelessness, audacity, and in short all their aims. The author's words are these.

units.la: Praesentes Polonici Regni turbae ex ejusdem generis morbo promanant, quo hactenus Occidentalis Europa periculose laborarit. Certum est, omnes Europae tumultus & inte stinas passiones ab hisce 40. & amplius annis per Executionem Concilij Tridentini excitatas esse, & ex eadem ortum traxisse. Si forte bellum Balthicum, quod inter Scardiae reges ante annos 36. gestum est, & nuperrimum Brunsuicensium tumultum excipias.
units.tr: The present troubles of the Polish kingdom spring from the same kind of disease by which Western Europe has hitherto suffered dangerously. It is certain that all the tumults and internal passions of Europe have been stirred up by the execution of the Council of Trent during these forty and more years, and have arisen from it; unless perhaps you exclude the Baltic war, which was waged between the kings of Scardia some thirty-six years ago, and the very recent tumult at Brunswick.

units.la: Haec inquam est illa praesentis seculi Pandora, ex cujus fatali pyxide omnes Europorum intestinae calamitates hactenus mihi scaturire videntur, ita tamen ut eas non tam ipsa Concilij executio, quam executionis modus pariat.
units.tr: This, I say, is that Pandora of the present age, from whose fatal box all the internal calamities of Europeans seem to me to have flowed up to now; yet these calamities are produced not so much by the execution of the Council itself as by the manner of its execution.

units.la: Hoc forte ulterius tibi vis declarari? Sic igitur habeto, Executionis modus in duabus accipiue rebus hactenus fuit repositus. Primum sedulo annixi sunt, quibus haec cura incubuit, ut illos Reges & familias, quorum in Europa hoc seculo praecipua est autoritas, cum invicem adunarent, & sic adunitos ad Concilij Tridentini executionem exstimularent. Et hinc est illa famata Catholicorum unio.
units.tr: Do you wish this to be explained to you further? Know, then, that the manner of execution has hitherto consisted of two things. First, those to whom this care has been entrusted have diligently laboured to bring together those kings and families who hold the chief authority in Europe in this age, and, once united, to spur them on to the execution of the Council of Trent. Hence came that famous Catholic union.

units.la: Deinde ut per certos & qualificatos homines impedimenta, quae vel in politiis, politiaeque formis & legibus, vel populorum moribus negocio huic obstarent, quasi e via removerentur.
units.tr: Second, by means of certain qualified men, the obstacles that stood in the way of this business, whether in the states, in the forms and laws of the states, or in the customs of the peoples, were removed, as it were, from the road.

units.la: Hac ratione praedicta Concilij executio fuit instituta, quantum nimirum ad gentilem conatum attinet: Opus profecto magnum & arduum, quod melioribus Mundi temporibus peculiari fortunae afflatu opus habuisset, quoque ipsius Alexandri M. victoriosum genium frangere & defatigare potuerit. Nunc autem pro ratione praesentis Europae tuus infinita conatui huic & longe robustissima impedimenta extra ordinem fuerunt objecta. Quibus tamen non obstantibus, res ab iis, quibus hoc per praedicti Concilij conclusionem mandatum erat, fortiter & ingenti nixu tentata fuit: sed eo hactenus eventu, ut mouina ista turbas quidem longe maximas & valde horribiles ubique gentium in vulgus pererint, ad exitum tamen nusquam perducti potuerint.
units.tr: By this method the aforesaid execution of the Council was instituted, so far as its worldly attempt is concerned. Certainly it was a great and arduous undertaking, which in better times of the world would have needed a special blast of fortune, and which could have crushed and worn out even the victorious genius of Alexander the Great. But now, given the state of present-day Europe, countless and far more powerful obstacles have been thrown in the way of this endeavour beyond the ordinary. Nevertheless, despite these, the matter was attempted boldly and with great effort by those to whom it had been committed by the conclusion of the said Council. But so far the outcome has been such that these movements have indeed brought very great and very dreadful disturbances among the common people everywhere in the world, yet they have never been carried through to their end.

units.la: Regum enim adunitio partim per connubia, partim per confoederationes, pacificanes & similia media tentari cepit & promoveri: In tanta tamen nationum regnorumque Europaeorum discrepantia fere consecutum est, ut pro ea quae sperabatur unione, infinitae autoritatibus difficultates, subiectis autem populis varia molestia emergerunt. Cum praesertim Reges ipsi, qui se interdum ad praedictam Executionem obtulerunt, negocium illud tam sincere nunquam tractarent, ut sub ejusdem praetextu non privata commoda quaeritarent. Sicuti non ita dudum in Gallijs licuit perspicere,
units.tr: For the uniting of kings began to be attempted and promoted partly by marriages, partly by confederations, peace treaties and similar means. Yet amid such great disagreement among the nations and kingdoms of Europe, it has come about that, instead of the union that was hoped for, countless difficulties arose for the authorities, and various troubles for the subject peoples. This was especially so because the kings themselves, who at times offered themselves to the aforesaid execution, never handled that business so sincerely as not to seek, under cover of it, their private advantages. As was not long ago possible to see in France,

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: On Nefarious Deeds

units.la: quando Philippus Hispanus partium Catholicorum (hunc enim cucullum factio illa induxit) patrocinium & defensionem vtilis est suscipere: Ibi inquam vel tandem apparuit, eum sub hoc obtentu Galliae regnum affectare. Cum enim animadverteret plerosque factionis illius proceres ab Imperio Hispanico abhorrere, oblitus personae, quam agendam susceperat, manus auxiliatrices retrahere coepit, ut qui videret, se ipse sua frustratum. Id quod Sixtus V. tempestive odoratus est, illudque egerrime tulit.
units.tr: When Philip of Spain undertook the patronage and defence of the Catholic party (for that faction had put this cowl on him), it finally became clear, I say, that under this pretext he was aiming at the kingdom of France. For when he noticed that most of the leaders of that faction shrank from Spanish rule, he forgot the part he had undertaken to play and began to withdraw the hands that were meant to help, like one who saw that he himself had been frustrated by his own schemes. Sixtus V sensed this in good time and took it very badly.

units.la: Talia autem plura exempla adduci possent ex iis etiam, quae nos aliquanto propius tangunt. Ex his ergo personatis & malefidis Regum molitionibus in unionis istius agro perpetuarum simultatum copiosissimam segetem adhuc succrescere videmus, per quas praedictae executionis negocium, per se haud facile turbatur, et Nationes ijs, de quibus dictum est, difficultatibus implicantur.
units.tr: Many more such examples could be cited from those that touch us somewhat more closely. From these masked and faithless schemes of kings we see a very abundant crop of lasting quarrels still springing up in the field of this union. Through them the business of the aforesaid execution is not easily disturbed in itself, and the nations are entangled in the difficulties described.

units.la: Idem fere in reliquorum impedimentorum remotione accidit. Cum enim Tridentina reformatio non solum diversus religionis sensus, per universam jam Europam latissime sparsus, sed etiam nationum, populorumque privilegia, libertates, leges & mores obstare, illa citra tumultum removeri quidem potuerunt.
units.tr: Almost the same happens in the removal of the other obstacles. For although the Tridentine reform could indeed be removed without tumult, there stood in its way not only the differing sense of religion, now spread very widely through all Europe, but also the privileges, liberties, laws and customs of nations and peoples.

units.la: Quae omnia tamen a praefervidis ingenijs, quibus haec Provincia non citra delectum demandata erat, non solum mota, sed acriter commota & vehementer perturbata esse constat. Hinc ergo turbae, hinc simultates, hinc odia, hinc diffidentia cum reliquis fatalibus Furijs, quibus nostro tempore status politicus infestatur, ceu ex Orco prorupernt. Id quod omnes Europae nationes, quae haec pestis pervasit, sonora voce profitentur: hanc & non aliam calamitatum suarum causam omnes, qui citra morbi affectionem judicant, summo consensu allegant.
units.tr: Yet it is well known that all these things were not only stirred but violently agitated and greatly disturbed by hot-headed minds, to whom this province was entrusted, and not without choice. Hence crowds, hence quarrels, hence hatreds, hence distrust, together with the other fatal Furies with which political life is afflicted in our time, have burst forth as if from Orcus. All the nations of Europe that this plague has overrun declare it with a loud voice: everyone who judges without being affected by the disease agrees unanimously that this, and no other, is the cause of their calamities.

units.la: Videamus nunc ergo num malorum nostrorum Polonicorum eadem ratio sit, & eidem generali causae adscribi queant. Id quod multis forte difficulter persuadebitur. Ego tamen illud constanter affero, & assertionis meae has probationes affero.
units.tr: Let us now see whether our Polish troubles have the same reason and can be ascribed to the same general cause. Perhaps many will find this hard to believe. Yet I steadily maintain it, and I offer these proofs of my assertion.

units.la: Certum est, Clerum Poloniae non minus hactenus laborare, ut Concilij Tridentini decreta intra regnum executioni mandentur, eorundemque observationi omnes subijciantur, quam in plerisque hactenus Occidentis partibus laboratum fuit.
units.tr: It is certain that the clergy of Poland has been labouring no less than most parts of the West have laboured hitherto to have the decrees of the Council of Trent carried into effect within the kingdom, and all people made subject to their observance.

units.la: In hunc enim & non alium finem mox post ingressum moderna Regiae Majestatis in regnum Synodus illa Petricoviensis celebrata fuit: quam ceu Filiam Poloniae Medea illa Tridentina peperit. Ex cujus vultu prudentiores jam tum secuturae in regno administrationis omen capiebant. Cujus etiam Decreta plerisque vel eo saltem nomine suspecta fuerunt, quod tanto studio occultata fuerunt & suppressa.
units.tr: For it was to this end, and to no other, that the Synod of Piotrków was held soon after His present Royal Majesty entered the kingdom. That Synod the Tridentine Medea bore as a daughter of Poland. From its countenance the more prudent already took an omen of the administration that would follow in the kingdom. Its decrees too were suspect to many, at least on this account, that they were so carefully hidden and suppressed.

units.la: Executio Concilii Tridentini quomodo in Polonia institua. Synodus Petricoviensis.
units.tr: How the execution of the Council of Trent was set up in Poland. The Synod of Piotrków.

units.la: Sed nec illud cuiquam dubium esse potest, ab his ipsis primo loco diligenter curatum fuisse, ut Reges Poloniae praedictae Unioni implicarent, eosdemque cum Domo praecipua Austriaca quam arctissime conjungerent. Ex qua nimirum conjunctione maximum ad praedictae Executionis promotionem emolumentum sperabatur: Ut quae ad subditos in utroque Regno magis perterrendos & in ordinem redigendos permultum factura videbatur, quantumvis consilijs illis longe aliud pallium obduceretur.
units.tr: But nor can anyone doubt that these very men first took care, with great diligence, to entangle the kings of Poland in the aforesaid union, and to bind them as closely as possible to the chief house of Austria. From this connection the greatest advantage for promoting the aforesaid execution was certainly hoped for, since it seemed likely to do much to terrify the subjects of both kingdoms and bring them into line, however much a quite different cloak might be thrown over these plans.

units.la: Suecia amissa.
units.tr: Sweden lost.

units.la: Harum vero rerum praxis post infelicem illam expeditionem in speciem quasi renovata fuit, ubi nonnullorum studia valde conspicua exiterunt. Eorum videlicet, quos praeterjam dictas causas Suecia amissae invidia urgebat, qua nempe ordinem suum premi sentiebant. Quipropterea omnem lapidem moverunt ut novis Regum amicitijs acceptri infortunij sensum nonnihil mitigarent.
units.tr: Indeed, after that unhappy expedition, the practice of these things was in appearance revived, and the zeal of some became very conspicuous: namely of those whom, besides the causes already mentioned, the envy of the loss of Sweden urged on, since they felt their own order was being pressed down. For this reason they moved every stone, so that by new friendships with the kings they might somewhat soften the sense of the misfortune they had suffered.

units.la: Austriacorum studia Polonis suspecta.
units.tr: The zeal of the Austrians suspected by the Poles.

units.la: Verum tamen ut inter vicina regna fere fieri consuevit, Austriacorum studia nostribus semper suspecta fuerunt, ideoque pro hac etiam vice ad Agentium illorum consilia promovenda tantum non contulerunt, quantum sperabatur fuerat. Cum praesertim praeteres vulgares illas Regum regnorumque vicinorum simultates & dissensiones, alia non pauca quotidie intra & extra regnum inciderent, quae hujusmodi conjunctionem Reipub. nostrae minus commodam, ipsis etiam Civibus formidabilem efficerent. Per ejus itaque attentationem nil amplius effectum fuit, quam ut inveteratae suspiciones periculosius recrudesce-rent.
units.tr: But, as usually happens between neighbouring kingdoms, the zeal of the Austrians was always suspect to ours. So on this occasion too they contributed hardly as much to advancing those agents' plans as had been hoped. Especially since, besides the common quarrels and disagreements between kings and neighbouring realms, many other matters arose daily within and outside the kingdom, which would make such a union less convenient for our commonwealth and even frightening to the citizens themselves. Thus nothing more was achieved by their attempt than that long-standing suspicions broke out again more dangerously.

units.la: Quod ipsum etsi iis, qui haec agitabant, non ignotum esset, se tamen adeo non passi sunt pediri, publicamque indignationem tam secure contempserunt, ut tanto potius confidentes in propositio perrexerint, illudque tandem per fas & nefas ad exitum conati sint percere.
units.tr: Although this was not unknown to those who were pushing these things, they did not allow themselves to be checked. They despised public indignation so confidently that, all the more assured in their proposal, they pressed on, and at last tried to bring it to an end by fair means or foul.

units.la: Hic ergo molitionum jam antea suspectarum tam importunus fervor, eum tandem en- tum sortitus est, ut offensa Nobilitate regnum factionibus mutuaque diffidentia imtum fit, & Rex ipsemet subditis, subditi vero Regi suspecti esse ceperint. Quam nos- tri oximam & compendiosissimam esse ad Reipub. dismembrationem & interitum viam. Et hac ratione prius illud Executionis Tridentinae turbataque Europa medium satis fer nos, ut opinor, efficaciter operatum est.
units.tr: So this rather importunate zeal for schemes already suspected finally reached such a pitch that, with the nobility offended, the kingdom became full of factions and mutual distrust, and the king himself began to be suspect to his subjects, and the subjects to the king. We find this to be a very short and direct road to the dismemberment and ruin of the commonwealth. And in this way, I think, that means of the Tridentine execution, together with the disturbance of Europe, has been effectively served first.

units.la: Ad alterum quod attinet, Popularium nempe obstaculorum remotionem, tu non gabis, opinor, In hoc regno maiora & robustiora eis objecta fuisse & adhuc obijci, quam ulla Europaea Natione. Concilium enim Tridentinum inter nos, ut quidem nunc res it, ad effectum, quem ipsi cupiunt perducî nullo modo potest, nisi aut Hispanica Inquisitio, aut quiddam quod Inquisitioni illi aequivaleat, in regnum introducatur. Per od nempe Polonia ad Hispanismi aliquam similaritatem redacta, praedicta Executioopportuna reddatur: Patria vero nostra ea corporum animorumque libertate hactenus tur, quale fortissimae nationes & generosissimus quisque sibi optare poterit. Quis ergo non det, quam duro collisu haec inter se committi oportuerit? Postquam inprimis libertas ilquatenus animum praecipue & conscientias concernit, non ita dudum per Confoederationem publicam denuo & quasi extra ordinem confirmata est?
units.tr: As to the other matter, namely the removal of popular obstacles, you are not unaware, I think, that in this kingdom greater and stronger obstacles have been placed in the way, and still are, than in any European nation. For the Council of Trent among us, as things now stand, can in no way be brought to the effect they desire, unless either the Spanish Inquisition, or something equivalent to it, is introduced into the kingdom. By that means Poland would be reduced to some likeness of Spain, and the aforesaid execution made convenient. Our country, however, has hitherto enjoyed that liberty of body and mind which the bravest nations and every most generous person could wish for. Who then would not see how harsh a clash it would be to set these against each other? Since liberty concerns above all the mind and conscience, was it not confirmed again, not so long ago, through a public confederation, and as it were outside the ordinary course?

units.la: Quamvis autem Hispanicam Inquisitionem nemo nobis hactenus aperte & exprofesconatus fit obtrudere, quod intelligerent, hoc citra periculum vix posse tentari: Via tamen ad hujusmodi aliquam imperiosam coercitionem variis artibus paulatim & quasi cuniculos parata est, sensimque muniri coepit. Eo nimirum adhibito artificio, quorum ra omnem mutationis sensum Tractitantes illi se consecuturos sperabant. Tam caute nen & circumspecte incedere non potuerunt, quodque agebant, tam probe nunquam posit dissimulari, ut rerum e diametro pugnantium tamque asperarum vel levis agitatio ingentem flammam vel tandem eliceret. De quo ipso, proh dolor, oculorum aspectus die testatur.
units.tr: Although no one has hitherto openly and boldly tried to force the Spanish Inquisition upon us, because they understood this could hardly be attempted without danger, the way to some such domineering coercion has been prepared little by little by various arts, as if by mines, and has begun to be fortified. They could not proceed so cautiously and circumspectly, nor could what they were doing be so well concealed, that a slight stirring of such opposed and harsh matters would not at last kindle a great flame. Of this very thing, alas, the sight of our eyes bears witness by day.

units.la: Haec a me omnia verissime dici ipsemet optime nosti, & fatebuntur hoc illi, qui rerum nostratium aliquam saltem noticiam habent, quique actiones nostras Comitiales ab quot annis vel e longe spectarunt. Nec diffitentur hoc ij, qui in partibus adhuc inter nos tenus haerent: ut & Concilium Tridentinum amplectantur, ejusque studiosae, per legitimi tamen media, executioni faveant.
units.tr: You yourself know best that all these things are told by me most truly, and those will admit it who have at least some knowledge of our affairs, and who for some years have watched our assembly proceedings even from afar. Nor do those deny it who still remain among us in the parties, namely that they embrace the Council of Trent and favour its zealous execution, though by lawful means.

units.la: Adhuc ergo perspicuum est, Reipub. nostrae mala non solum ex iisdem causis, quibus liquorum Europaeorum regnorum tumultus, sed etiam ex eodem operationis illorum do proficisci.
units.tr: It is therefore still plain that the ills of our commonwealth arise not only from the same causes as the disturbances of the European kingdoms, but also from the same working of those men.

units.la: In his igitur tollendis & amovendis opera nostra occupari debet, siquidem ordine prodere Matrij, nostrae cum aliqua spe salutis opem ferre voluerimus.
units.tr: In removing and driving out these, our effort must be employed, if we wish to bring help to our country in an orderly way and with some hope of safety.

units.la: Scio tamen quid tu hoc dicere possis & haud dubie dicturus sis, Me videlicet haec dis- ... endo, Morbum fere incurabilem ostendere, cum harum rerum studio, Concilii praesertim ... Executioni potissima pars Regni implicata sit, ut curatio ipso morbo difficili- & periculosior futura videatur.
units.tr: I know, however, what you may say to this, and undoubtedly will say: namely that by discussing these matters I show the disease to be almost incurable, since zeal for these things, especially for the execution of the Council, to which the chief part of the kingdom is committed, makes the cure seem more difficult and more dangerous than the disease itself.

units.la: Non est de nihilo quod dicis, novi, egomet multos prudentes Viros in eo tibi consenti- ... Exiistimo autem omnia opinione tua faciliora fore, si primum inter res ipsas earundem usum, deinde inter personas, a quibus illae tractantur, accurate distinguantur.
units.tr: It is not without reason that you say this. I myself know many prudent men who agree with you on this point. ... I think, however, that everything will appear easier than you suppose if we first distinguish carefully between the things themselves and their use, and then between the persons by whom those things are handled.

units.la: Adres quod attinet, nec Austriaca Familia, inter Europaeas haud dubie eminentissie, nec quorumcunque exterorum Regum & Principum cum nostris Regibus legitima & cera conjunctio per se vel Nos vel Rempub. nostram in minimo laedit, sed eidem potius fidio et ornamento futura esset, si a Tractitantibus illis adfinitas suspiciones non tam nse nostratibus occasiones praberentur.
units.tr: As for the Austrian family, which is undoubtedly among the most eminent in Europe, and as for the lawful and close alliance of any foreign kings and princes with our kings, such connections in themselves do no harm to us or to our commonwealth in the least. They would rather be a support and an ornament to it, if the negotiators did not give our countrymen grounds for suspicion of affinity.

units.la: Eadem fere ratio est Concilij Tridentini: Ab hujus enim executione nihil turbarum nobis esset metuendum, si modo ita instituueretur, ut intra legitimum docendi modum consisteret, missisque aliis parum convenientibus practicis eventus Deo committeretur. Non igitur res ipsa per se, sed earum abusus & perversus tractationis modus Rempub. laedunt, & has in praesentia difficultates nobis pariunt.
units.tr: The reasoning about the Council of Trent is almost the same. Nothing of disturbance need be feared from its execution, provided only that it were carried out so as to keep within the lawful manner of teaching, and that, with other poorly fitting practical measures set aside, the outcome were left to God. Therefore it is not the thing itself, but its abuse and its perverse manner of handling, that harms the commonwealth and creates the difficulties we now face.

units.la: Haec itaque in rebus diffidentia si observetur, inter ipsas etiam personas manifestam nobis discriminis rationem offendet: Ut nempe non omnes eos, qui praedictis rebus manum quocunque modo admovent, pro veris calamitatis nostrae autoribus habeamus, ut curationis, de qua dicturus sum, actum ad omnes & singulos extendi oporteat: sed eos tantum qui praedicti abusus praecipuam culpam sustinent.
units.tr: If this distinction between the things is observed, it will also show us a clear basis of discrimination among the persons themselves. We should not regard as the true authors of our calamity all who in any way lay hands on these matters, so that the cure I am about to describe must be extended to every individual. It should apply only to those who bear the chief blame for the abuses mentioned.

units.la: Si quaeris, quinam illi sint? Respondeo, si eorum, quos in hisce rebus periculosa experientia longo tempore eruditi, consentiens testimonium admitteretur. Si praeterea ipsam rerum evidentem inter nos experientiam in consilium adhibere volumus, Iesuitas & Institutum Iesuiticum pro iis nobis necessario esse habendos. Hi inquam, sicut in supradictorum consiliorum executoriali praxi primas sibi ubique arrogant: Ita alteram ejus, & quidem odiosissimam & nostrarum imprimis rerum rejectu perniciosissimam partem extra ordinem sibi suaque actualitati desumpserunt. In qua agitanda ita hactenus versantur, ut quod in hisce consiliis pessimum est, praecipue arripiant, arreptum peius efficiant, & vim eius malitiosam per subjectum Reipub. corpus quo jure quave injuria quasi transfadigere & per partes applicare conentur. Ut sic prorsus sentiam, si uni Iesuitae non essent, Nos aut turbas hujusmodi nullas habituros, aut si quae forte, ut ex consensu reliquarum partium Europaearum, obortae fuissent, eas multo facilius minorique periculo consopiri potuisse.
units.tr: If you ask who these are, I answer: if we admit the agreed testimony of those who have long been instructed by dangerous experience in these matters. And if we also wish to take into counsel the plain experience of things among ourselves, we must regard the Jesuits and the Jesuit Institute as necessarily those men. These men, I say, just as they claim the first place everywhere in the practical execution of the aforesaid councils, have likewise taken to themselves, beyond their proper role and for their own present advantage, the other part of it, the most hateful and the most ruinous to our affairs above all. In handling this part they have so far acted in such a way that they seize especially upon what is worst in these councils, make the seized matter even worse, and try, by right or by wrong, as it were to push its malicious force through the body of the commonwealth and apply it part by part. So much so that I am fully persuaded that if there were no Jesuits, we would have no disturbances of this kind; or, if any had arisen, as they would have done in agreement with the other parts of Europe, they could have been quelled far more easily and with less danger.

units.la: Hoc vero cum illud ipsum sit, de quo inter nos quam maxime controvertitur, judicij hujus rationes tibi aliquanto accuratius erunt demonstranda. Quod ita faciam ut tibi prius ad oculum demonstrem: Instituti Iesuitici, si per se consideretur, eam esse rationem, ut liberae Reipub. valde inimicum & adversum, Libertati vero Polonicae imprimis formidandum sit. Deinde vivis aliquot exemplis ostendam, quam periculose festa haec sint tum Politicum hinc inde per Europam turbarit. Tertio, objectiones nonnullas diluam, quae sententiae huic a contrarium sententibus fere opponuntur.
units.tr: Since this is precisely the point over which we are most hotly disputing among ourselves, the grounds for this judgment must be demonstrated to you rather more carefully. I shall do so in the following way, so that you may see it clearly before you. First, I shall show that the Jesuit Institute, considered in itself, is of such a kind that it is very hostile and adverse to a free commonwealth, and above all to be feared by Polish liberty. Second, I shall show by several living examples how dangerously these men have stirred up politics here and there throughout Europe. Third, I shall refute some objections which are commonly raised against this view by those who hold the contrary opinion.

units.la: Quae tria si a me demonstrata fuerint, quartum quod principaliter intendo, sua sponte sequetur: Is nempe qui Rempub. restitutam & salvam cupiunt, praecipue operam dandam esse, Ut Iesuitae & Iesuitismus extra regnum eliminentur, quo fit remotis hisce curationis interturbatoribus certa aliqua & firma pacis stabiliendae ratio iniri queat.
units.tr: If these three points are demonstrated by me, the fourth, which is my principal aim, will follow of its own accord: namely, that those who desire the commonwealth restored and safe should above all take care that the Jesuits and Jesuitism be eliminated from the kingdom. In this way, once these disturbers of the cure are removed, a certain and firm method of establishing peace can be undertaken.

units.la: Ad primum quod attinet, in eo tria consīdero: Ipsam Ordinis politiam: Finem ad quem tendit: Operationes sive praxin, per quas hunc finem conatur assequi.
units.tr: As for the first point, I consider three things in it: the constitution of the Order itself; the end toward which it tends; and its operations, or practice, by which it attempts to attain this end.

units.la: Politiam si penitius introspiciemus, fatendum nobis erit, eam in hoc genere accurate dispositam, firmissimam & ad res magnas gerendas aptissimam esse: Ut parti cuique applicaverit, permultum prodesse queat. Generalis dispositio pure Monarchica est, forma nimirum politia, ad movendum & agendum commodissima. Monarchicae dispositionis nervi in hisce rebus consistunt: Capite primum uno regitur, deinde hoc ipsum caput uni etiam loco, urbi nimirum Romae alligatum est, ubi perpetuo residere cogitur. Quae res festa huic inter alia hoc praestat, ut uno certo & uniformi aere perpetuo regatur, & vetegetur, Romani nempe confisitorij afflatu, prout nempe is ab iis, qui Romae omnia possunt, afficitur. Disciplina denique forma Instituti hoc longe artissima utitur, quia cives ejus ad caecam obedientiam (sic ipsimet loqui consueverunt) astringuntur, in tantum, ut minoribus in nulla Majorum vel absurdissima imperia inquirere liceat: nedum ut aliquis ea detrectare audeat. Quae obedientia in Orbem Europaeum hactenus optimes & plane desperatae audaciae sicarios progenuit: ideoque Ordo iste a nonnullis cum Assassinorum institustituto comparatur, quod in Asia olim à Saracenis contra Christianos fuit intro-ductum.
units.tr: If we look more deeply into the constitution, we must admit that in this kind it is carefully arranged, very firm, and best suited to carrying out great undertakings, so that it can be of great benefit when applied to any part. Its general arrangement is purely monarchical, which is indeed the form most convenient for moving and acting. The sinews of the monarchical arrangement consist in these things. First, it is ruled by one head; then this same head is bound to one place, namely the city of Rome, where it is compelled to reside permanently. Among other things, this arrangement brings the advantage that it is governed and animated by one fixed and uniform spirit, namely the breath of the Roman council, as it is inspired by those who hold all power in Rome. Finally, the form of the Institute uses a very strict discipline, because its members are bound to blind obedience (this is how they themselves customarily speak), to such an extent that the lesser members may not inquire into any command of their superiors, however absurd, much less dare to refuse it. This obedience has so far produced in the European world the best and utterly desperate assassins; for this reason the Order is compared by some with the institution of the Assassins, which was once introduced in Asia by the Saracens against the Christians.

units.la: Hæc ergo formam illam Monarchicam constituunt, constitutam firmissimè constringunt, ideoque faciunt ut actiones ejus efficacissimæ sint, & ceu cuneus quidam penetrent.
units.tr: These things, then, make up that monarchical form, bind it firmly once it is constituted, and therefore make its actions very effective, so that they penetrate like a kind of wedge.

units.la: Illa vero hanc compactionis soliditatem adjuvant, eandemque solidiorem efficiunt: quod primum communitatis hujus basis per fixam illam Generalis sedem Romana sedi consistorio, ut dictum est, quasi affigitur & implantatur. Deinde quod eandem Hispanico Imperio similiter inserunt, dum inter septem Generales, qui sibi huc usque, si recte memini, invicem successerunt, neminem elegerunt, qui non vel natione, vel ditione Hispanus esset, quæ res non caret mysterio. Tertiò quod ex tot diversis Clericorum ordinibus solæ Iesuitæ ab utriusque Fori ordinaria iurisdictione exempti sunt: Ut nullum prorsus in Nationibus nisi sui corporis Superiorem agnoscant, quiplerunque Italus aut Hispanus est. Ut sic Ordo Iesuiticus ab omni juris, coercitione solutus inter nos liberrimè refertur, suisque molitionibus secure incumbat. Quarto quod etiam in subdelegatis Imperiis hactenus diligenter cavent, ne in Nationibus Provincialibus unquam ex indigenis gant, sed vel Hispanis vel Italis dignitates illas conferunt, aut saltem ijs qui ex Anglia, Gallia, &c. propter facinora aliqua profugerunt, & propter nimium Hispaniæ studium ex prædictis Nationibus proscripti sunt. Seniores vero, Rectores & his similes inter sararissime ex Nobilium Ordine, sed ex plebe tantum adoptant. Quod cur fiat, conjectunon est difficilis: Generosa nempe nobilitatis pectora erga Patriam ita affecta non sunt, suis consiliis & practicis ea minus commoda & opportuna statuant. Interim his rebus, ut cum Iesuitismi venter nostras fere sit quem videlicet nostris opibus explere & suf-fercire cogimur: caput tamen Hispanico & Italico cerebro repletum habeat, ad cujus nemsensum reliquum corpus movetur.
units.tr: Other things, however, add to this solidity of the structure and make it still more solid. First, the fixed seat of the General in Rome, as has been said, is as it were fastened and planted in the Roman see and its consistory. Second, they likewise join the Order to the Spanish Empire, since among the seven Generals who, if I remember rightly, have succeeded one another up to now, they have chosen none who was not a Spaniard either by birth or by dominion; a fact that is not without mystery. Third, of so many different orders of clergy, the Jesuits alone are exempt from the ordinary jurisdiction of both forums, so that in the nations they acknowledge no superior except of their own body, who is for the most part an Italian or a Spaniard. Thus the Jesuit Order, freed from all restraint of law, is most freely carried among us and applies itself securely to its schemes. Fourth, they have also been careful until now in the subordinate provinces never to appoint natives to the provincial posts, but to confer those dignities either on Spaniards or Italians, or at least on men who have fled from England, France, and so on, on account of some crimes, and who have been banished from those nations because of their excessive devotion to Spain. Their elders, rectors, and such like they very rarely take from the order of the nobility, but adopt them only from the common people. The reason for this is not hard to guess: noble hearts so disposed toward their country do not judge those things to be sufficiently convenient and suitable for their counsels and practices. Meanwhile, in these matters, the belly of Jesuitism is, as it were, largely ours, which we are compelled to fill and supply with our own resources, while the head is filled with Spanish and Italian brains, at whose nod the rest of the body is moved.

units.la: Hæ igitur ad Monarchicum robur iterum per quam multum faciunt, incursus Iesui-ti impetum certissimè dirigunt, & sedæ huic ad consiliorum suorum executionem invium plane & penetrantem constantiam præbent.
units.tr: These things, therefore, contribute greatly once again to the strength of the monarchy: they direct the Jesuit's assault with great certainty, and they give that seat a constancy that is wholly unbending and penetrating for carrying out its designs.

units.la: Porro huic ipsi Imperij Iesuitici formæ per subordinatarum dignitatum distinctos adus variasque species egregiè contra omnes Monarchiæ incommoditates & vitia protectum est; Ut si ex humano sensu judicetur, ei neque à tyrannica oppressione, nec seditione dissolutione ullum periculum sit extimescendum. Quod ipsum etiam prædictæ Sodalitaad res gerendas miram corporis agilitatem conciliat.
units.tr: Moreover, this very form of the Jesuit empire, by its distinct grades and various kinds of subordinate dignities, has been admirably guarded against all the inconveniences and vices of monarchy; so that, judging by human reason, there is no danger to be feared from either tyrannical oppression or the dissolution of sedition. This same arrangement also gives the Sodality a remarkable agility of body for carrying out its undertakings.

units.la: Quarum rerum omnium illustre documentum nobis historia postremi motus Galliæ habet, ubi compertum est: In illa desperata totius Regni perturbatione, ex solo Iesuitarum Ordine Neminem, ac ne unum quidem Iesuiticum Individuum fuisse, qui Reipub. rtes secutus esset. Cum contra ex omnibus aliis Clericorum ordinibus permulti Regias eique publicæ partes fideliter tuerentur. Hispano autem hi ipsi Iesuitæ tam pertinaciter lhæserunt, itaque fervidè stiduerunt, ut factioni ejus pro anima aut potius pro corde fuent, de quo vulgo dicunt, quod in corporis humani structura sit primum vivens & ulti- um moriens. Prædicta sane factio prius opprimi non potuit aut eradicari, quàm Iesuitæ gno exigerentur. Quod fidele & perdurans robur Instituto huic in tam variegata homi-m colluvie nil aliud præstat, quàm ea quæ hactenus de Politiæ forma diximus.
units.tr: Of all these things the recent uprising in France gives us a clear proof. In that desperate upheaval of the whole kingdom it was found that from the Jesuit order alone not one single Jesuit had sided with the Republic, whereas from all the other orders of clergy many had faithfully upheld the royal and public cause. But these same Jesuits clung so stubbornly to Spain and burned so fervently for its cause that they were to that faction what the soul, or rather the heart, is to a body, which people say is the first part of the body's structure to live and the last to die. That faction could not be crushed or uprooted before the Jesuits were driven out. The steadfast and enduring strength that this Institute gives to such a varied mass of men is nothing other than what we have so far said about the form of its polity.

units.la: Num vero hæc talia sint, à quibus sibi Respub. Polona metuere debeat, tibi cogitanum relinquo. Ego interim Factionem Iesuiticam inter nos non aliter æstimo, quàm agin quendam & acutum gladium, cujus lamina quidem in vaginam Polonicam recondisit, sed ita ut capulum Romana Aula & Hispanus manibus teneant, & sic eum ad num suum vibrent. Id quod Instituti huius proprius finis aliquanto clarius docebit.
units.tr: Whether these are the kinds of things that the Polish Commonwealth ought to fear, I leave for you to consider. For my part, I judge the Jesuit faction among us to be nothing other than a sharp, double-edged sword. Its blade is indeed sheathed in the Polish scabbard, but in such a way that the Roman Court and the Spaniard hold the hilt in their hands and so brandish it at their pleasure. What the proper end of this Institute is will show this rather more clearly.

units.la: Hic autem & ipse quiddam singulare et ab omnibus aliis Monachorum ordinibus versum habet. Omnes enim aliorum Religiosorum Ordines in hunc finem ut plurimum venti & approbati sunt, & eo tendunt, ut popularis devotio per eos augeatur, Religio Romano Catholica magis splendeat & Ordinis spiritualium pomœria dilatentur, &c.
units.tr: This Order, however, has something singular about it and turned away from all the other monastic orders. For the other religious orders have for the most part been founded and approved for this purpose, and they aim at this: that popular devotion be increased through them, the Roman Catholic religion be more splendid, and the boundaries of the spiritual realm be extended, and so on.

units.la: Iesuitæ vero etsi hisce rebus & ipsi pro virili studeant, sui tamen principalis fini longè sublimiorem scopum sibi præfixum habent. Qui nempe est, ut Romana Ecclesia in Imperij Ecclesiastici collapsam auctoritatem, non solum recuperent, in quo studio reliquos clericos commilitones habent: sed ut subjectum præcipuè Europæ Orbem ita corrigant & reformEnt, ut hujusmodi insultus quos res Romana hactenus est perpessa, in longum præcaveant: sublatis & quasi obstructis omnibus occasionibus, per quas antehac Hæretici ad eandem oppugnandam aditus præbitus fuit.
units.tr: The Jesuits, although they too strive manfully in these matters, have set before themselves as their principal end a far loftier goal. Namely, that they may recover the authority of the Roman Church, which has collapsed from its ecclesiastical empire, and in this effort they have the rest of the clergy as fellow soldiers. But above all they wish to correct and reform the European world that is subject to them, so that they may guard against, for the long term, the kinds of assault that the Roman cause has hitherto suffered. All the occasions, through which heretics previously found access to attack it, are to be removed and, as it were, blocked up.

units.la: Quas occasiones norunt non aliunde denuo emersisse, quam ex subditorum in hisce septentrionalibus regnis, nimia, ut quidem Romæ semper visa est, libertate, illisque barbaris legibus, quibus hactenus ita firmatur ut Inquisitionis Hispanicæ intentatum jugum constanter repellat.
units.tr: They know that these occasions have emerged again from nowhere else than the excessive liberty of subjects in these northern kingdoms, which Rome has always thought excessive, and from those barbarous laws by which these kingdoms are so firmly held that they constantly repel the yoke of the Spanish Inquisition, which has been attempted against them.

units.la: Horum igitur remotio & annihilatio Iesuitis per quartum illud & festa huic proprium votum extra ordinem injuncta est. In hunc finem tot extraordinarijs privilegijs, bullis & Indultis instructi & muniti sunt, ut non solum agendi facultate reliquo clero universo præpolleant: sed jam ipsis Episcopis & superiorum Prælatorum ordini gravės & formidabiles esse incipiant. Nec ego dubito quin gens Iesuitica aliquando Romanæ Ecclesiæ horrendi schismatis occasionem præbitura sit. Interea in his ipsis rebus specifica differentia constitit Iesuitismi, per quam à reliquo clero discernitur, eiusdemque qualitas transcendit.
units.tr: Therefore the removal and annihilation of these things has been enjoined on the Jesuits beyond the ordinary course, by that fourth vow peculiar to their order. To this end they have been equipped and fortified with so many extraordinary privileges, bulls and indults that they not only excel the whole rest of the clergy in their power to act, but already begin to be grave and formidable even to the bishops and the order of the superior prelates. Nor do I doubt that the Jesuit people will one day give the Roman Church an occasion for a dreadful schism. Meanwhile, in these very matters there lies a specific difference of Jesuitism, by which it is distinguished from the rest of the clergy, and its character goes beyond theirs.

units.la: Cum vero hoc ipsi constanter negare consueverint, vivo illud exemplo tibi demonstrandum est. Inter Venetos & Pontificem hoc maximè tempore controversia intercedit super constitutionibus quibusdam, quarum renovandarum occasionem Magistratui Veneto præbuerunt Iesuitarum artes testamentariæ. Pontifex autem eas in fraudem Ecclesiæ factas conqueritur.
units.tr: Since they are accustomed to deny this constantly, it must be demonstrated to you by a living example. At this very time a controversy has arisen between the Venetians and the Pontiff over certain constitutions. The occasion for renewing them was given to the Venetian magistracy by the testamentary arts of the Jesuits. The Pontiff, however, complains that these were made to the defrauding of the Church.

units.la: Veneti hoc nomine à Pontifice compellati jure suo cedere nolunt, sed palam præfentur sibi in sua ditione supremam juris dictionem, & sic etiam legum ferendarum potestatem, non autem Pontifici competere, &c. Quo animadverso Pontifex Excommunicationis fulmine eos territat. Senatus hoc cognito Clerum suum convocat, jus Reipub. eidem exponit, Pontificiaque Excommunicationis iniquitatem demonstrat, eos deniq; pro auctoritate hortatur, ut curato officio Excommunicationem pro nulla habeant, &c. Quid fit? Antiquus clerus unanimi consensu Reipub. cuiusdam contra Pontificem probat & de fide sua prolixè pollicetur: Recentiores verò Religiosi, quorum nempe regulæ præsentis temporis conditioni accommodatæ sunt, Ducibus Iesuitis Reipub. cuiusdam damnant, stationem quam deserunt. Quamvis Iesuitæ Magistratus edicto nominatim expulsi, et in æternum relegati perhibeantur.
units.tr: Summoned by the Pontiff on this account, the Venetians are unwilling to yield their right, but openly maintain that supreme jurisdiction in their own dominion, and so also the power of making laws, belongs to them and not to the Pontiff, and so on. When the Pontiff noticed this, he terrified them with the thunderbolt of excommunication. The Senate, on learning of this, summoned its clergy, set out the right of the Commonwealth before them, demonstrated the iniquity of the papal excommunication, and finally exhorted them, by their authority, that having attended to their duty they should regard the excommunication as nothing, and so on. What happened? The old clergy, with unanimous consent, approved of the commonwealth of a certain republic against the Pontiff and pledged their loyalty at length. But the more recent religious, whose rules are adapted to the present state of affairs, under Jesuit leaders condemned that republic and deserted their post. Yet the Jesuits are said to have been expelled by name by the edict of the Magistrate and banished forever.

units.la: Hoc autem Iesuitæ non aliam ob causam fecerunt, quàm quòd viderent, sese stante & defensa Reipub. Venetæ libertate, stantibusq; legibus nec stare nec instituti sui finem obtinere posse. Quod ipsum sane discrimen illud, quod inter Iesuitas & quoscunque alios Clericos constituimus, satis evidenter probat & confirmat. Tu ergo nunc, mi Frater, cogita quid de Polonia nostra futurum sit, si inter nos omnia illa removeri debeant, ut profectò illa remota cupiunt, per quæ in finis ipsius adeptione impediuntur? Adhuc de Fine.
units.tr: The Jesuits did this for no other reason than that they saw that, while the liberty of the Venetian Republic stood and was defended, neither they nor their Institute's end could stand or be attained. This very distinction, which we draw between the Jesuits and all other clergy, sufficiently clearly proves and confirms it.
