Do you not usually attend sermons in which our most learned theologians assert, constantly and gravely, with that voice and bodily gesture, with that seriousness and steadfastness of most learned men, that the Jesuits are a plague which cannot be noticed until it has set the whole body of the commonwealth on fire; that their manners, gestures, dress, the shape of their eyes, and the moderation of their mouth and countenance are all designed to weaken and overthrow those institutions, well devised and established by our ancestors, which have been handed down to us, I say, all those things? Is this new, senators? Did the chief church of Lublin not resound with these voices and these outcries? Did the chief church of Cracow not fill and crowd with these Jesuit ornaments and testimonies, for the lasting memory of the place, the time, and the man? Was this not, I say, sung in those churches? Senators of your body are witnesses; men adorned with great authority, counsel, and prudence, and with the other ornaments of honour, talent, and industry, who affirm this. What shall I say of the illustrious Bishop of Cracow, whom I name out of respect and for his dignity? His age, prudence, authority, learning, humanity, judgement, steadfastness, and keenness of mind are such that you may admit his speech under oath. What, then, does he say? He has affirmed constantly and gravely, with a voice and countenance suited to the outrageousness of the matter, that this family of monks, newly invented not many years ago and adorned with the name of Jesus the Saviour, has been prepared to overthrow the doctrines of the Roman Church, to kindle the fires of sedition, and to overthrow the good customs of our commonwealth, customs established with the approval of all. John Zamoyski, Chancellor of the kingdom and supreme commander of the armies, whose prudence, skill in war, virtue, authority, good fortune, and courage every age will always admire, has affirmed truly and wisely, as he is often wont to say about everything, that these priests should be granted some place in the churches and on the pulpits, but that they should in no way be allowed to come from the monasteries and churches to conduct the affairs of the commonwealth. Why should I now produce Doctor Pico, a citizen of Cracow and a senator, whom we may truly call a most subtle philosopher and a most experienced physician, in whose life there stands an image of ancient virtue, and whose speech is a model of copious eloquence and wisdom? He certainly judges the Jesuits in such a way that he often affirms that our country has fared very badly in not having long ago cast them out. Why should I now bring before you the voices of individual men? Why should I bring forward the complaints of those widows who could not detect these saviours' arts until they noticed their houses stripped of all silver vessels and all golden ornaments, in which there was any workmanship or such singular value as could inflame their greed? O times, O manners! These things are now discussed in the forum, bandied about in the palaces, recited in all places, condemned in the churches, in view of the Trinity, before the image of Christ and of all the saints, men and women. These things are declaimed before the saints, and to stir up the saints, male and female, they are often and at length, vehemently and gravely, copiously and elegantly set out by those who preside over the religious orders of the saints, male and female. And are these things unknown to you? But they are most useful because of their schools. They have already opened many literary schools. There is a great rush of young people; a large part of the nobility, and that the chief part, wishes its sons to be educated by them, on account of the high esteem in which they stand for learning, faith, seriousness, and steadfastness, and because of their singular method of teaching. Added to this, although no rewards for their labours are offered, they nevertheless undertake and endure great labours. Alas, wretched me! Why am I, who have always praised you, forced to reprove you? Do you not see, do you not understand, senators, that all these things tend to disturb our peace? Do you not notice that very many schools have already been broken up by them? That one most famous school at Cracow, most splendidly furnished with most learned men in every kind of discipline, is now foul and squalid through neglect and retains none of its ancient ornaments? Before these Jesuit monks, Poland had men most learned, most vehement orators, most acute philosophers, most prudent jurists, and theologians most thoroughly equipped with every gravity, copiousness, and elegance of speech. Our country had schools from which, as from the Trojan horse, very many learned men came forth. The one Academy of Cracow counted four hundred young men of letters. From that school there came forth those men whose talent, prudence, and authority the present age still admires. It is now nearly twenty years since we have seen these Jesuits in our kingdom, who set up their schools in such a way that they wish to snatch away from all others every effort and the praise of diligence. Very often they put on plays of comedies and tragedies, furnished with every splendour, abundance, and elaboration; and in these shows they think the highest praise and usefulness is placed, and by this one art they draw many pupils to themselves. Yet among those most distinguished masters, and among the pupils, we see no one who could compete in any kind of learning with those old masters and teachers of our school. In that age we had Luke the preacher, whose power of speech was such that he could easily turn the minds of men to whatever side he wished. I believe you still remember that preacher whom our Poles called the Leopolitan: he was a man of such refinement and courtesy of manners that he always brought some new pleasure to the minds and ears of his hearers, and with such keenness of wit and such learning that by the subtlety of his speech he always made his hearers more learned. How much and how many praises are due to Cardinal Hosius, to Cromer, Bishop of Warmia, to Orichovius, to Fricius! Here a certain desire inflames me to speak somewhat more fully of these men. But I forbid that, by the recollection of their virtues and learning, your wounds, which our country received from the death of these men, be reopened. Those men were most splendid and most illustrious lights of the Roman Church. You have, I think, in your minds that famous volume of Fricius on the commonwealth. Many books of Cardinal Hosius and of Cromer survive; the speeches of Orichovius are still in the hands of many; and no age, I think, will be able to obscure their memory. Indeed, if I were able to enumerate and praise, as is only fair, the books of Bembo, Sadoleto, Contarini, Reginald Pole, and the other greatest men, the days would fail me sooner than my speech. What like these things do the Jesuits have? Some of their writings also come forth. Would that they had devoted to their tragedies, or rather their comedies, that labour which they undertook in writing those books! For those books have been so refuted and overthrown by the heretics that the whole of our Roman Church has received a glaring blow. Last year at Lublin they challenged the Antitrinitarians and Anabaptists to dispute; they were singing a triumph before the victory. In that disputation they achieved nothing beyond a certain overflowing volubility of words and tragic outcries, in which outcries all the Jesuit praises consist; and they obtained approval only from the common people, from old women, and from their own drinking companions. And although they ought to have conquered the Antitrinitarians by the force of reasons, they published that victory in written records before the contest had even taken place; and when that triumph before the victory had its outcome, the Arians were struck with threats, insults, terrors, and shouts, and one of their chief men, Niemojewski, even felt blows. We grieved, most distinguished senators, that the dignity of the Roman Church had been so mocked by these men that many of that party, most devoted to the Roman Church, now speak with doubtful and wavering minds. A little book by the Italian Possevino came out, like a torch to kindle a fire; if you had wished to follow its authority, would we not now see the commonwealth overthrown by domestic discord? What reasoning is this, senators? That a most learned man should not bring the weapons of his learning and the instruments of his doctrine to conquer his adversaries, but should run to barbarous cruelty and savagery! They wish to heal our country; this is a respectable pretext. But if the scalpel is applied to a healthy part of the body, if good men and men useful to the commonwealth are banished from it, this is not medicine but butchery. Why, then, is no council convened? Why is no public disputation arranged? Why are these torches applied to kindle a fire? It is no great undertaking for a learned man to defeat one who has not been trained in the knowledge of letters, especially when the goodness of his cause is added. Whoever runs to the sword, to fire, to water, to slaughter, to violence, let him confess that he is more able to cut a man's throat than to teach him; and that he has the mind of a butcher, of a barbarian and cruel robber, rather than the mind of a theologian."

units.la: Juventutem numerosam habent suis in scholis: quibus artibus eam colligant & retineant, metuo, ne fere admodum animad vertamus, et tum demum velimus huic malo remedium adhibere, cum jam non poterimus fi ad maturitatem pervenerit illa improbitas, cujus jam magna apparent et extant vestigia. Putatisne Senatores Amplissimi, disciplina Monachorum juventutem nobilium recte ad res bene gerendas erudiri posse? Utinam tandem aliquando perspicere possitis, Poloniam de statu optimo ad eas calamitates devolutam esse moribus Gallicis, Italicis, Hispanicis in patriam nostram receptis. Si majorum nostrorum tempora, quibus illae regiones non fuerunt cognitae, cum hoc nostro saeculo conferamus, quae summum dolorem atque metum nobis adferant, plurima occurrunt: quae fere aliquam mentem aliorum animum erigant, admodum pauca & exigua, vel potius nulla solatia veniunt in mentem. Quid igitur agimus Senatores? Volumusne scholas evertere? Ego vero hanc sententiam a vobis abesse cupio. Placet enim & utile est revocare veterem disciplinam, & patrium morem: praemia Magistris & Praeceptoribus proponi: eos gratitudinis & utilitatis spe, ad scholasticum laborem suscipiendum excitari. Novam istam, nostris majoribus incognitam, nobis ac juventuti nostrae inutilem, patriae perniciosam docendi rationem retineri non placet.
units.tr: They have a large crowd of young people in their schools. I fear that we are paying far too little attention to the methods by which they gather and keep them, and that we will want to apply a remedy to this evil only when that wickedness has grown to maturity, though its large traces are already visible. Do you think, most distinguished senators, that noble youths can be rightly trained for managing public affairs under the monastic discipline? I wish you could at last see that Poland has fallen from its excellent condition into those calamities, now that Gallic, Italian and Spanish customs have been received into our homeland. If we compare the times of our ancestors, when those regions were unknown to us, with this age of ours, which brings us the greatest grief and fear, many things come to mind that might lift the spirits of others, but very few and slight consolations, or rather none, come to mind. What then shall we do, senators? Do we want to overthrow the schools? I certainly wish that this opinion be far from you. For it pleases us and is useful to restore the old discipline and our national custom: that rewards be offered to the masters and teachers, and that they be stirred to take up their scholarly labour by the hope of gratitude and usefulness. We do not wish that this new method of teaching, unknown to our ancestors, useless to us and our youth, and harmful to the fatherland, be retained.

units.la: Sed Iesuitarum opera, studio & diligentia effectum est, ut Africa, Asia, America, Persia, Romana Ecclesia instituta & placita ampleatur. Quinam sunt illi viri? quae est ista pietas? quae vitae sanctimonia, ut tantum bonum orbi Christiano importaverint? Aspicite istos patres nostros Iesuitas, ut recte de illis Apostolis fratribus eorum positis judicare. Non enim, Senatores Amplissimi, simia simiam tam bene referi, neque ovum ovo, nec lac lacti tam simile est, quam Monachus Iesuita, Iesuita Monacho. Quid igitur ipsi habent? vel in pietate, vel in moribus, vel in eruditione, quo nostris antecellant?
units.tr: But by the work, zeal and diligence of the Jesuits it has been brought about that the institutions and doctrines of the Roman Church are spreading in Africa, Asia, America and Persia. Who are these men? What kind of piety is theirs? What holiness of life, that they could bring so great a good to the Christian world? Look at these fathers of ours, the Jesuits, so that you may judge rightly about those brothers of theirs, the Apostles. For, most distinguished senators, one ape does not resemble another ape so closely, nor one egg another egg, nor milk milk, as a Jesuit monk resembles a Jesuit, and a Jesuit a monk. What then do they have, either in piety, in morals or in learning, by which they surpass our men?

units.la: Si enim vultum ipsum ad decipiendos homines accommodatum: si os in illis latebrosum, Iesuiticis compositum: si oculos & totius corporis habitum, atque ipsam orationem adjuvandum & dissimulandum conformatam mutes atque adimas: nihil habebunt quod prae ceteris Monachis possint venditare, quibus se illi usque adeo anteferunt; ut quilibet Iesuita cum Iesu in coelo esse existimet, propterea quod sanctimoniam quandam possit simulare, & eam, quae intus inclusa est, impietatem bene dissimulet.
units.tr: For if you were to take away and strip from them the face fitted for deceiving men, the mouth hidden and shaped in the Jesuit manner, the eyes, the whole bearing of the body, and the very speech, all arranged and disguised for helping and concealing, they would have nothing that they could peddle beyond other monks, over whom they set themselves so far above; so that any Jesuit is thought by someone to be in heaven with Jesus, simply because he can feign a certain sanctity and cleverly conceal the impiety that is shut up within.

units.la: Jam ut totius corporis mutatum atque vestitum, ad colligendam hominum gratiam, mira quadam cura & sollicitudine moderantur: ita quoque in templis, non veterem illam a majoribus receptam & approbatam tam simplicem, & non multum exquisitam in Dei cultu; atque sanctorum consuetudinem retinent: sed superbas, stultas, atque impudicas mulieres imitantur, quae splendidius vestiri volunt, quam honestae matronae. Quo fit ut etiam oculos spectatorum in se convertant, & eorum cupiditatem inflamment. Quis autem est ab omni ratione ita alienus, ut non perspiciat illis illecebris, ipsis ornamentis, ipsoque subtili sane & suavi vocum, & tibiarum concentu, barbaram gentem, incultos atque horridos homines posse excitari? & ab illis sordibus & squalore, ad ipsum splendorem, & cultum, omnes humanos sensus converti? Hoc certe est homini a natura tributum, ut omnia jucunda sequatur. Iam legem non audivimus, legimus, didicimus: sed ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus (quemadmodum inquit summus ille orator) ut rem jucundam, aliquo sensu perceptam, homines magis amplectantur, quo magis etiam sensibus & cupiditatibus obediant. Currunt igitur mulierculae & juvenes in aedes Iesuiticas, sanctae Barbarae; sed graves viri & prudentes retinent veterem cultum Mariae, qui scilicet novitatis dulcedine non moventur.
units.tr: Just as they regulate the change and dress of their whole bodies with a wonderful care and anxiety, in order to win the favour of men, so too in their churches they do not keep that old worship, received and approved by our forefathers, so simple and not much elaborated in the worship of God, nor the customs of the saints. Instead they imitate proud, foolish and shameless women, who want to be dressed more splendidly than honest matrons. As a result they draw the eyes of spectators to themselves and inflame their desire. Who is so far removed from all reason that he does not see that by those enticements, by the very ornaments, and by the subtle, indeed sweet, harmony of voices and flutes, a barbarous people, uncultivated and rough men, can be stirred up, and that all human senses can be turned from that filth and squalor to the very splendour and finery? This is certainly a gift given by nature to man, that he follows all things that please him. Now we have not heard or read or learned the law, but have seized it, drawn it and pressed it from nature itself (as that great orator says), so that men embrace more eagerly a pleasing thing perceived by some sense, the more they yield to their senses and desires. So the little women and young men run to the Jesuit houses of St Barbara; but grave and prudent men keep the old worship of Mary, which of course is not moved by the sweetness of novelty.

units.la: Gratulor ergo, viri Amplissimi, Asiae, Africae, Americae, Persiae iam mentem, quae velint Catholicae Ecclesiae nomen suum dare, sed ut verum fit, quod Iesuitae referunt: sa enim multa ab illis jactari, jam nonnulli affirmant, & res ipsa loquitur: Sed quemadmodum lum dico, ut verum sit, ne tamen Iesuitæ servitutis jugum nobis imponant, magna cauadhibenda est. Ijsdem enim artibus & hoc religionis nomine, illas Provincias Hino Regi potentissimo subjecerunt, à quo illi emissi, ut exploratores eò consilia omnia ulerunt; ut primùm domestica dissidia excitarent, deinde Hispanicos exercitus regna convulsa, & dissidijs domesticis debilitata adducerent: Quod cum assequu- ntur, omnia cædibus & sanguine ita replent, ut non solùm consilij capiendi, sed etiam respirandi quidem spatium relinquant, illis, à quibus amanter & humaniter fuerant epti. Legimus in sacris libris, extitisse quosdam Gabaonitas astutissimos exploraes, qui simulatâ Legatione, exoletos saccos asinis impososuerunt, utreque vinarios obtos, laceros & resartos: calceamenta vetera & lacerata pedibus induxerunt: penuvetustis se texerunt, omnique in commeatum pane mucido sumpto, ad Iosuam se in cacontulerunt: eique & Israelitis nunciaverunt, se velle cum eis fœdus percutere. Iesæ Gabaonitæ sunt à Rege Hispaniæ Catholicissimo legati, pallio modestiæ contecti, ceis hypocrisfeos induti, simulatione paupertatis, modestiæ, pietatis, castitatis ornati: Iesu missos esse quasi ad novam aliquam salutem adferendam hominibus affirmant, se ilijs, laboribus, studijs literarum & pietatis, noctumis atque diurnis precationibus auftos esse offendunt. Metuendum autem nobis esse, ne quid Andria apportet mali, indicat miserabilis casus eorum hominum, qui sunt in Africa, Asia, Persia, Ame- a. Neque illarum regionum terminis hoc malum inclusum est: latius diducitur, & lies longius progreditur istud incendium. Nam etiam in Germania inferiori excitasam sunt ab istis Gabaonitis tanti motus, quibus multæ jam urbes & Provinciæ flo- tissimæ, quasi uno impetu prostratæ jacent. Non possum sine lachrymis Antverpiæ is potentissimæ & amplissimæ luctuosam & funestam direptionem commemorare, nulnque esse existimo hominem tam durum, quem non moveat tot hominum mors acerbisa & crudelissima, bonorum direptio ac venditio. Nolo autem vos ad summi istius dois societatem pertrahere. Eodem motu ab istis Iesuiticis Gabaonitis excitato, imfa est Anglia & Scotia: quæ regna cum antea externorum hostium impetum delerint, nunc domesticis dissidijs debilitata, & ad interitum jam inclinata sunt. Id ro totum acceptum referedum est istis sanctissimis Patribus Gabaonitis Iesuiticis. Hos stus, ista commoda illi depromunt ex illis suis sacculis obsoletis. Vita Reginæ Angliæ neno & insidijs sæpè appetita est. Scotiæ Regina crudelissimo & indignissimo mortis nere sublata est. Nullum locum nominare possum, Senatores Amplissimi, in quo isti Gaonitæ pedem posuerint; ut etiam non in eodem tristissima & luctuosissima exempla crulitatis reliquerint. Et accidit jam aliquoties, Deo ita permittente; ut ijsdem ruinis, arum authores extiterint, ipsi fuerint oppressi. Nam in Anglia multi isti Patres Gaonitici, ita, ut æquum fuit, supplicio affecti sunt; quos nostri Gabaonitæ in numerum lartyrum referunt. O præclaros Martyres, qui tantorum scelerum convicti fuerunt. Iulta prætereo, Senatores Amplissimi, quæ in Helvetia, quæ in Germania superioab istis Patribus sunt excitata. Currit enim magnis progressibus ista Iesuitarum pestis, omnes urbes, omnes Provincias, omnia regna obvia evertit & dissipat.
units.tr: I congratulate you, therefore, most distinguished senators, that the minds of Asia, Africa, America and Persia now wish to give their name to the Catholic Church; but I say this so that it may be true, as the Jesuits report. For many things are boasted of by them, as some now affirm, and the thing itself speaks. But, as I say, if it is true, we must still take great care lest the Jesuits impose on us the yoke of servitude. For by the same arts, and under this same name of religion, they subjected those provinces to the powerful King of Spain, from whom they were sent out as spies and carried all their plans there: so that first they might stir up domestic quarrels, and then bring in Spanish armies against kingdoms convulsed and weakened by internal discord. When they accomplish this, they fill everything with slaughter and blood, so that they leave no room, not only for taking counsel, but even for breathing, to those by whom they had been received kindly and humanely. We read in the sacred books that there were certain most crafty Gibeonite spies, who, under the pretence of an embassy, loaded worn-out sacks on their asses, wineskins torn and patched, and put on old and ragged shoes on their feet; they covered themselves with old clothes, took mouldy bread for provision, and went to Joshua in the camp, and announced to him and to the Israelites that they wished to make a covenant with them (Josh. 9). These Jesuit Gibeonites are sent as envoys by the most Catholic King of Spain, covered with the cloak of modesty, clothed in the garb of hypocrisy, adorned with the pretence of poverty, modesty, piety and chastity. They affirm that they have been sent by Jesus, as if to bring some new salvation to men; they show themselves worn out by labours, studies of letters and piety, and nocturnal and diurnal prayers. We must fear, however, lest some evil come upon us from these men, as the miserable fate of those men in Africa, Asia, Persia and America shows. Nor is this evil confined within the borders of those regions: this fire spreads more widely and advances farther. For even in Lower Germany such great disturbances have been stirred up by these Gibeonites, that many cities and most powerful provinces lie prostrate, as if struck down by a single blow. I cannot recall without tears the lamentable and deadly sack of the most powerful and most splendid Antwerp, and I think there is no man so hard that he is not moved by the bitter and most cruel death of so many people, and the plunder and sale of goods. But I do not wish to draw you into the fellowship of that most high... [sic]. By the same movement stirred up by these Jesuit Gibeonites, England and Scotland are also undone: these kingdoms, which before had repelled the attack of foreign enemies, are now weakened by domestic dissensions and already inclined to ruin. All this must be credited to those most holy Gibeonite Jesuit fathers. They bring out these advantages from their old sacks. The life of the Queen of England has often been sought by their plots and ambushes. The Queen of Scotland was taken away by a most cruel and most unworthy death. I cannot name any place, most distinguished senators, where these Gibeonites have set foot without also leaving the most sorrowful and lamentable examples of their cruelty. And it has already happened several times, God so permitting, that the authors of the same ruins were themselves overwhelmed by them. For in England many of those Gibeonitic fathers were, as was only fair, put to death; yet our Gibeonites count them among the martyrs. O splendid martyrs, who were convicted of such great crimes! I pass over, most distinguished senators, what has been stirred up by these fathers in Switzerland and in Upper Germany. For this Jesuit pestilence advances with great strides, and overturns and scatters every city, every province and every kingdom that lies in its way.

units.la: Ad ea mala, quæ jam nos tangunt, properat animus. Non ignoratis, quas turbas tulerit nobis in Livonia ista Gabaonitica & Iesuitica modestia: jam potentissima urbs Riga, ad portum posita ardebat eo incendio, quod fuit excitatum ab istis Gabaoni- tis. Abreptus fuit ijsdem procellis & fluctibus, Stephanus Rex fortissimus: qui nisi ad animi sui magnitudinem, consilium & moderationem adhibuisset, jam omnino & cum Riga cum Rege Suecia, aut certè Rege Daniæ bellum nobis fuisset susceptum. Urbem profectò totam Provinciam multis laboribus, magnis sumptibus, magno nostrorum hominum interitu, ad Regni nostri imperium jam diu aggregatam: multò majore cæde, aut maribus impensis atque sudoribus, nunc restituueremus. Tota Lithuania & Vilna urbs primaria nonne eodem spiritu Iesuitico & Gabaonitico est agitata? Nonne civium atque multorum nobilium fuit concursus ad praelium committendum? unde illae procellae perturbationum profectae sunt, nisi ab Iesuitis nostris iisdem Gabaonitis? potestisne dubitare viri Amplissimi, totam Lithuaniam ad interitum ab iisdem Gabaonitis ita impulsam fuisse, ut ja nunc tantummodo ruinas illius Provinciae aspicere potuissemus, nisi ad haec mala restinguenda Rex sapientissimus authoritatem suam contulisset. Coactus est ille fortissimus Imperator obsidionem & expugnationem urbis Plescoviana intermittere, ut istius tumultus a Iesuitis excitatis occurreret. O miseram patriam nostram, o deplorandam conditionem, qui istam pestem, & haec monstra in visceribus nostris alimus, & quicquid increpuerit, Iesuitas jam metuere cogimur: quos otium & cibus alienus ita feroces reddit, ut etiam authoritas & sapientia potentissimi Regis eos coercere non potuerit. Vidistis, Senatores Amplissimi, Cracoviam urbem celeberrimam, domicilium atque ornamentum totius Regni, fidem Majestatis Regiae, omnium ordinum Ecclesiasticorum, et secularium, ut vocant, receptaculum praecipuum regni praesidium, mercatorum & reliquae plebis emporium, matrem artium atque disciplinarum, ita vexatam esse ab istis Gabaonitis, ut plurimi boni viri, utiles cives patriae nostrae homines Catholici affirmant, se malle in sylvis, inter feras vitam degere, quam in ista immanitate versari. Conspiratione enim facta, cujus Iesuitae authores atque duces extiterunt, magna vi atque impetu in eam domum irruunt, quae una in tota urbe monumentum antiquitatis extat, Lutheranis concessa, Rege atque Senatoribus approbantibus. Apparebant effusae aliquot diebus flammae, quae per multas urbis partes fusae, toti urbi minabantur interitum. Audiebantur voces celeratorum hominum, praedas efferentium: inter quos, ut quidam affirmant, etiam versabantur isti Patres, non religiosi isto habitu induti, sed attritis rusticorum vestibus cooperti. Commodum illis fuit, & jucundum etiam, ut opinor, istam adorandam personam Iesuiticam ad aliquod tempus deponere. Tota urbs in summo periculo versabatur. Neque ego sum adeo amens, ut negem, istam vim ad alios quoque Magistros, & Professores, & totam Scholasticorum turbam pertinere: qua de re jam primarii Lutherani retulerunt ad Senatores. Verum si rem bene considerete, & istum Gabaonitticum & Iesuiticum spiritum cognoveritis, intelligetis ab hoc Iesuitico nomine haec fulmina profecta esse. Quis enim adeo rerum ignarus, ut nesciat talia perturbationis consilia, plena sceleris, a Hispanicis Iesuitis agitari, & nulla unquam ante adventum Iesuitarum talia pericula civibus nostris accidisse? Quid multis opus est? Sunt qui affirment, totum hoc quicquid est mali, Iesuitis tribuendum esse, quibus hoc propositum est, ut Evangelici cum Rectore atque Professoribus, & tota universitate Academica ignis collatis congrediantur, & Iesuitae habeant suavissimum spectaculum, atque in locum illius partis, quae fuerit fusa atque deleta, succedant, & amplissima spolia, eorum consiliorum praemia auferant.
units.tr: Our minds hurry on to the evils that already touch us. You are not unaware what disturbances this Gibeonite and Jesuit moderation has brought upon us in Livonia. Already the most powerful city of Riga, set by the harbour, was burning with the fire kindled by these Gibeonites. King Stephen, most brave, was swept away by the same storms and waves. Had he not applied the greatness of his spirit, his counsel and his moderation, war would have been undertaken against us by Riga together with the King of Sweden, or certainly the King of Denmark. We would now be restoring that city and the whole province, joined to the empire of our kingdom long ago, at great labour, great expense and the loss of many of our men, with far greater slaughter, or with greater expense and sweat. Was not the whole of Lithuania, and the chief city of Vilna, stirred by the same Jesuit and Gibeonite spirit? Did not citizens and many nobles gather to join battle? Whence did those storms of disorder arise, if not from our Jesuits, the same Gibeonites? Can you doubt, most distinguished sirs, that Lithuania was driven by these same Gibeonites so near to ruin that we would now see only the ruins of that province, had the most wise King not brought his authority to bear to quench these evils? That most brave Emperor was forced to break off the siege and storming of the city of Pskov, to meet the tumult stirred up by the Jesuits. O our wretched country! O deplorable condition, that we nourish this plague and these monsters in our bowels, and that, whenever anything stirs, we are forced to fear the Jesuits, whom leisure and another's bread make so fierce that not even the authority and wisdom of the most powerful King could restrain them. You have seen, most distinguished sirs, how the famous city of Kraków, the home and ornament of the whole kingdom, the trust of the royal majesty, the common refuge of all the ecclesiastical and so-called secular orders, the chief bulwark of the realm, the marketplace of merchants and the rest of the common people, the mother of the arts and disciplines, has been so harassed by these Gibeonites that many good men, useful citizens of our country and Catholics, declare that they would rather live out their lives in the woods among the wild beasts than dwell in such savagery. For, a conspiracy having been made, whose authors and leaders were the Jesuits, they burst with great force and violence into that house which alone in the whole city remains a monument of antiquity, granted to the Lutherans with the approval of the King and the Senators. For several days flames were visible, spreading through many parts of the city and threatening the whole city with destruction. The voices of criminals were heard, carrying off plunder; among them, as some affirm, those Fathers were also present, not clothed in their religious habit but covered in the worn clothes of peasants. It was convenient for them, and pleasant too, I think, to lay aside for a time that adorable Jesuit persona. The whole city was in the greatest danger. Nor am I so mad as to deny that this violence also reached other masters and professors, and the whole crowd of scholars; on this matter the leading Lutherans have already reported to the Senators. But if you consider the matter carefully, and recognise this Gibeonite and Jesuit spirit, you will understand that these thunderbolts came from this Jesuit name. For who is so ignorant of affairs as not to know that such plans of disorder, full of crime, are set in motion by the Spanish Jesuits, and that no such dangers ever befell our citizens before the arrival of the Jesuits? Why need there be more? There are those who maintain that all this evil, whatever it is, must be ascribed to the Jesuits, who have this purpose: that the Evangelicals should clash, with the rector, the professors and the whole academic body, in a fire of their own making, and that the Jesuits should have a most pleasant spectacle, and should step into the place of that part which has been overthrown and destroyed, and carry off the ample spoils as the reward of their plans.

units.la: Hic fortasse dicat aliquis Iesuita: Tu Lutheranae causae patrocinium suscipis. Ego vero Patres sancti Iesuitae, non meam nunc de Lutherana religione sententiam explico, sed quid metuendum sit a vobis Reipublicae nostrae offendo: & superius testatus sum me Catholicum esse. Neque vero is Ecclesiam Romanam oppugnat, neque haereticos defendit, qui libere, ad Reipublicae utilitates conservandas, ea, quae sentit, dicit. Quamobrem jam repeto id, quod saepius affirmavi, & magna voce proclamo, Tametsi Iesuitae professione Catholici sint, pestem tamen Reipublicae nostrae ab illis metuendam esse. Erant quoque majores nostri Catholici, & tamen arma contra illos Iesuitas Cruciferos sumpserant, & eos omni ratione persequendos esse exististimabant, summo Pontifice repugnante, & eius legatis resistentibus. Archiepiscopi nostri & Episcopi capitali odio ab illis dissidebant, & vi atque armis opprimendos esse statuebant. Vos ego appello Reverendissimi Domini Episcopi: non ignoro, quam observantia ac pietate summum Pontificem colatis: hortor tamen vos, ut tranquillitatem patriae nostrae vobis commendatam esse velitis. Exiguum enim admodum est discrimen inter Cruciferos & Iesuitas, inter crucem & Iesum, sed intra hujus disputationis nostrae limites oratio contineatur. Crux & Iesus eandem propemodum vim habent pietatis, modestiæ, religionis: Cruciferi crucis imagine erant insigniti: uitæ Iesu Salvatoris nomine sunt ornati. Quid modestius? quid magis pium & religiosum? In illis Cruciferis illo sæculo extitit, qui verecundi admodum, humani, humiles, abjecti, res Cruciferi apparebant. Ipsi quoq; Iesuitæ, omni virtutum genere sunt larvati: domi tantâ solicitudine & diligentiâ gestus suos conformant, ut nihil diversum in illis appareat huic personæ, quam sustinent: etiam capita eleganter & moderatè in unam partem inclinata habent, ut videantur Iesu similes esse, qui pendebat in Cruce. Cruces etiam pictas habent, etiam in valvis suorum collegiorum cruces pingunt. In ista tam pulcra herba latet antiquus ille serpens, inimicus & accusator fratrum, Diabolus, author idiorum, perturbationum, bellorum intestinorum, cædis & rapinarum.
units.tr: Here perhaps some Jesuit will say: "You take up the cause of the Lutherans." But I, holy Jesuit Fathers, am not now setting out my opinion of the Lutheran religion, but pointing out what must be feared from you by our commonwealth; and above I have declared that I am a Catholic. Nor does he attack the Roman Church or defend heretics who, freely and for the preservation of the public good, says what he thinks. Therefore I repeat now what I have affirmed more often, and proclaim with a loud voice: although the Jesuits are Catholic by profession, the plague to be feared from them by our commonwealth is real. Our ancestors too were Catholics, and yet they took up arms against those Jesuits, the Crosiers, and judged that they must be pursued by every means, even though the supreme Pontiff opposed this and his legates resisted. Our archbishops and bishops were divided from them by deadly hatred, and decided that they must be crushed by force and arms. I appeal to you, Most Reverend Lord Bishops: I am not unaware with what reverence and piety you honour the supreme Pontiff; yet I urge you to be willing to keep in view the tranquillity of our country, which is committed to you. For the difference between the Crosiers and the Jesuits is very small, the difference between the cross and Jesus; but let my speech be kept within the limits of this discussion. Cross and Jesus have almost the same force of piety, modesty and religion: the Crosiers were marked with the image of the cross; the Jesuits are adorned with the name of Jesus the Saviour. What is more modest? What is more pious and religious? In that century there existed among those Crosiers men who appeared very retiring, humane, humble, abject, truly Crosiers. The Jesuits themselves are masked with every kind of virtue: at home they shape their gestures with such care and diligence that nothing in them appears different from the persona they maintain; they even hold their heads elegantly and modestly inclined to one side, so that they seem like Jesus, who hung on the Cross. They have painted crosses too, and they paint crosses even on the doors of their colleges. In this so beautiful grass lies hidden that ancient serpent, the enemy and accuser of the brethren, the Devil, author of quarrels, disorders, civil wars, slaughter and plunder.

units.la: Dicite mihi S. Patres, pro vestra pietate, candore, modestia, humanitate, quamobrem apud istam hominum multitudinem, cujus benevolentiam ita vobis collegistis, ut etiam multæ mulierculæ, imò verò præclaræ mulieres, ornamenta aurea atq; argentea, quæ à matris suis amoris causa dantur, vobis libenter, furto propemodum ablata, tradant; & entius jam peccatorum suorum causa ad vos accedant propter vestram humanitatem: ite, quamobrem Hispanicam monarchiam in cœlum laudibus effertis? eam commendatis & exemplum illius monarchiæ tanquam ad imitandum proponitis? Non ignoratis, ut ortor, in Hispania cives non malos propter levissimam religionis suspicionem jactari connelijs, notari ignominiâ, exilio puniri, morte denique acerbissima multari. Extant, viclarissimi, istorum patrum hæc præclara facinora in tabulis depicta: fortasse propterea, ut illud exemplum Hispanicum vos imitari velitis. Sed non admodum commodè oculos nostros illâ imagine erudiunt, neque satis copiosè, quid ipsi faciunt, ostendunt. Non est his est malorum exitus, quem ostendunt illæ imagines; non his terminis istorum sanctorum patrum religio continetur. Nam ad turbandos sepultorum manes progreditur illorum destia & charitas: effodiuntur ossa, dissipantur cineres, & quem terminum, ut vitæ, ita feriarum natura constituit: ultra hunc terminum grassatur ista Iesuitica mansuetudo charitas. O miseram & lamentabilem illorum hominum conditionem. O Regem crudelem. O Regnum cito periturum. Cogitate etiam atque etiam, Senatores Amplissimi, num tanto furori locus in patria nostra concedi debeat, ut fratribus nostris, propter diversas in religione sententias, hoc modo, hac crudelitate & immanitate lucis hujus usura eripiatur: alij, quamvis sint Catholici, tamen propter opes, vel uxoris vel filiarum formam, in numerum hereticorum referantur, quia istorum sanctorum patrum cupiditatem, maritorum vel parentum vita impedit. Dicite igitur aliquando patres sancti, si idem in Polonia facere possis, quid sitis facturi? Etiá illud dicite, Si Hispanorum Rex patronus & propemodum Dei ordinis vestri, huc in Poloniâ, vel mari vel terrâ exercitus suos cupiat adducere, quid, quâ, sitis facturi patres S. Iesuitæ? Video enim vos tantis sumptibus tam firma palatia, æstidia, & propugnacula erigere, quos vos monasteria appellatis, quæ si vere, ut sunt, non nominari debeant, domicilia scelerum omnium atq; flagitiorum receptacula appellari possint. Ideo Posnaniæ arcem munitissimam summis præsidiis à vobis ædificatam esse: & cum in urbis mœnia contineatur, aditum ad urbe patefacere posset omnibus, cum quibus communis est vobis cupiditas. Regis palatium Posnaniense nulla parte cum isto vestro propugnaculo est conferendum. Iesus locum, in quo caput reponeret, non habuit: in campis, in montibus versari potius quam in urbe maluit. Iesuitæ in commodissimo urbium loco, ad milites depellendos, vel excipiendos, si velint urbem oppugnare, castra sua ædificant. Video Vrosláviæ, etiam Lublini, atque in aliis civitatibus eiusdem munitionis, firmamenti, intorum præsidiorum extructas arces, ut non scholasticos docere, aut mulierculârum pectora cognoscere, sed bellum gerere velle videantur. Respondete igitur patres sancti atque modesti, num etiam illos Hispanicos exercitus in ista palatia vestra sitis admissuri? lius nimirum Hispanorum Regis, cui vos divinos cultus tribuitis: præsertim si eò accedat Papæ authoritas: si quoque eòdem vires suas conferat, tota illa in flagitiis & sceribus exercitata juventus, illi scilicet vestri greges aleatorum, in quibus etiam adul-
units.tr: Tell me, holy Fathers, by your piety, candour, modesty and humanity: why, among that multitude of people whose goodwill you have so gathered to yourselves that many little women, indeed excellent women, hand over to you willingly, almost stolen, golden and silver ornaments given them by their mothers out of love; and whose sins they bring to you more readily now because of your humanity; tell me, why do you extol the Spanish monarchy to heaven with praises? Why do you commend it and set the example of that monarchy before us as something to imitate? You are not unaware, as I urge you to remember, that in Spain citizens who are not bad men are hurled into chains for the slightest suspicion of religion, branded with infamy, punished with exile, and finally tormented with the bitterest death. These famous deeds of your fathers, most illustrious men, are painted on tablets: perhaps it is for this reason, so that you may wish to imitate that Spanish example. But these images do not very conveniently instruct our eyes, nor do they show quite fully what they themselves do. The outcome of evils which those images show is not the end for them; the religion of those holy fathers is not confined within these limits. For their zeal and charity advance to disturbing the rest of the dead: bones are dug up, ashes scattered, and beyond that limit which nature has set for life, and likewise for holidays, this Jesuit gentleness and charity rages. O wretched and lamentable condition of those men! O cruel King! O kingdom soon to perish! Consider again and again, most distinguished Senators, whether room ought to be granted in our country for such fury, so that our brothers, because of differing opinions in religion, should be deprived of the use of this light in this way, by this cruelty and savagery; and others, although they are Catholics, should nevertheless be counted among the heretics because of their wealth, or the beauty of their wives or daughters, because the life of husbands or parents stands in the way of the greed of those holy fathers. Tell us then, holy Fathers, if you could do the same in Poland, what you would do. Tell us this also: if the King of Spain, patron and almost god of your order, should wish to bring his armies here to Poland, by sea or by land, what, and how, would you do, holy Jesuit Fathers? For I see you erecting, at such great expense, such firm palaces, citadels and bulwarks, which you call monasteries, and which, if they should not be called by that name as they really are, could well be called dens of all crimes and receptacles of every disgrace. Hence the most fortified citadel at Poznań, built by you with the highest garrisons, and since it is set within the city walls, could open access to the city for all those with whom you share the same desires. The royal palace at Poznań is in no way to be compared with that bulwark of yours. Jesus had no place to lay his head; he preferred to dwell in fields and mountains rather than in a city. The Jesuits build their camps in the most convenient place of the cities, to repel or receive soldiers, should they wish to attack the city. I see at Wrocław, and at Lublin too, and in other towns, citadels built with the same defences, strength and garrisons, so that they seem to want to wage war rather than to teach schoolboys or to know the hearts of women. Answer then, holy and modest Fathers: would you also admit those Spanish armies into your palaces? Those of the Spanish King, that is, to whom you give divine honours, especially if the authority of the Pope should be added to it, and if he should bring his own forces there too, and all that youth trained in crimes and wickedness, namely your flocks of gamblers, among whom are also the adul-

units.la: Iesuitarum Collegia sunt propugnacula. teri, impuri, atque omnes impudici versantur. Qui cum sint absque re, absque fede, ne spe, fine fortunis, per urbes pexo capillo, nitidi imberbes, aut etiam barbati, volutant: qui totam industriam suam in noclurnis insidiis expromunt. Expecto, quid situs re sponsuri. Moneo tamen vos S. Patres, ut existimetis istos homines non adeo stupidos esse, ut non intelligant, quo referantur omnia vestra consilia, quae jam ita in lucem producta sunt, ut omnibus appareant.
units.tr: The Jesuit colleges are strongholds. Adulterers, the impure, and all the shameless move about among them. Since they have no property, no faith, no hope, and no fortune, they wander through the cities with combed hair, sleek and smooth-faced, or even bearded, and they spend all their effort on nocturnal ambushes. I wait to see what they will answer. I warn you, holy Fathers, to consider that these men are not so stupid as to fail to understand where all your plans lead, plans which have now been brought into the light so plainly that everyone can see them.

units.la: Cogitate etiam atque etiam, Senatores Amplissimi, ne cum inter abjectissimos homines Iesuitarum fraudes sint detectae, vobis tantum consilium & prudentia defuisse videatur, ut non animad vertere potuistis, quam horrendum exitium vobis immineat. Quod enim eo turpius est, fi obliviscamini, quibus fluctibus jactata & quae naufragia fecerit nostra Respub. eo tempore, cum vi & armis Cruciferorum improbitas multis annis non potuit reprimi tanta contentione, tanta sanguinis profusione, multis annorum centuriis bellu gerebatur, ad illius temporis memoriam animus exhorrescat. Fuerunt enim omnes campi majorum vestrorum sanguine cooperti. Quis fuit illo seculo tanto ingenio, tanto acumine, tanta prudentia praeditus, ut perspicere potuerit, talem exitum, & tam tristem & luctuosum, ac toti orbi Christiano periculosum, atque multis Europae partibus perniciosum esse expectandum, atque metuendum ab illis Cruciferis? qui in loco sancto in urbe Hierosolyma, apud sepulchrum Domini vivebant, scilicet studio commemorandae mortis Christi erant illi loco ita affixi, ut totum vitae suae curriculum in eo consumere statuerent, & talem ordinem omnium actionum suarum ampletterentur, ut nemo dubitaret, illis hominibus nihil propositum fuisse, praeter ipsam pietatem. Habebant monasteria, certis fratrum atque fororum familiis, ut illi vocabant, distincta: ea disciplina, eujfmodi moribus informata, ut nihil reperirent homines, quod in illis reprehenderent. Quae autem laudarent, & quae admiratione digna judicarent, ea plurima, vel potius omnia extabant: quo fiebat, ut Principes certatim in eos beneficia conferrent. Sed quo tanta pietatis & religionis simulatio recidit, fero admodum majores vestri intellexerunt, et magno suo malo experti sunt, quid momenti habeat ad decipiendos homines simulata pietas. Vos autem, vos Senatores, qui in locum Principum Mazovia successistis, cito & minime cito memoriam illorum fluctuum deposuistis, quibus Provincia haec fuit jactata, excitata illa Cruciferorum tempestate: & his ad eundem scopulum delati estis, quasi confulto & meditate naufragium facere velitis.
units.tr: Consider again and again, most distinguished Senators, whether, now that the Jesuits' frauds have been exposed among the lowest of men, you will seem to have lacked so much counsel and prudence that you could not notice what dreadful ruin hangs over you. For it is all the more shameful if you forget what waves our Commonwealth was tossed by, and what shipwrecks it suffered, at the time when the wickedness of the Cross-bearers could not be checked for many years except by force and arms, with such great struggle and such a flood of blood. The mind shudders to recall that age, for all the fields of your ancestors were covered with their blood. Who in that century was endowed with such talent, such keenness, and such prudence that he could foresee that such an outcome, so sad and so grievous, and so dangerous to the whole Christian world and so destructive to many parts of Europe, was to be expected and feared from those Cross-bearers? They lived in the holy place, in the city of Jerusalem, at the sepulchre of the Lord, and they were so fixed to that place, evidently for the sake of commemorating the death of Christ, that they resolved to spend the whole course of their lives there and embraced such an order of all their actions that no one doubted these men had no aim except piety itself. They had monasteries divided into what they called families of brothers and sisters, governed by such a discipline and formed by such morals that people found nothing in them to blame. Indeed, there were very many, or rather all, the things that they would praise and judge worthy of admiration, and so princes competed to confer benefits upon them. But where such a pretence of piety and religion led, your ancestors learned only too well, and they found to their great cost what power simulated piety has for deceiving men. You, however, you Senators, who have succeeded the princes of Mazovia, have quickly, and not so quickly, put aside the memory of those waves by which this province was tossed when that storm of the Cross-bearers was stirred up. And you have been carried to the same rock, as if you wanted to make a shipwreck deliberately and by design.

units.la: Conferte enim Senatores Ampliff. Iesuitas cum Cruciferis, vos, inquam, primum in vestrum patrocinium Iesuitas recepistis. Recordamini Cruciferorum, quam ex remotis regionibus ad vos opprimendos praesidia habuerint, & simul ad istos vestros Patres, istos inquam vestros Gabaonitas, oculos convertite. Cogitate etiam atque etiam, ut ab omnibus rebus inopes & egeni fuerint, cum primum huc venissent iftinostri Gabaonitae. Iam vero quantas opes possideant, quibus artibus collectas, videtis. Si vero rem totam bene quemadmodum debetis, examinare vultis, cogitate etiam atque etiam, ut non admodum longo intervallo a nobis Hispanorum Rex fit remotus: a Dantifco sex dierum itinere abest Antverpia, quae urbs domicilium, & sedes potentiae Hifpanicae esse dicitur. Quid agimus? Senatores Amplissimi? quid agimus? Non nos commovent, neque commonent aliorum regnorum triftiffima exempla, quod tanto est magis admirandum, quia ad vestram prudentiam & rerum usum accessit etiam eruditio. Cur non evolvitis aliorum regnorum historias? Cato ille, cui omnium cofenfu locus inter sapientes primus conceditur, cum vellet Romanis ea pericula ante oculos ponere, quae illis imminebat a Carthaginenfib.ficus recetes, quae mari a veftorib.adferebatur, in Senatu adferebat cum hac oratione: Qua prope ia nostri inimici ad patria no ftra fui imperii terminos porrexerint, videtis Patres cofcripti: Istarum enim ficus succus ita integer in itinere retinetur, ut nulla in illis videatur esse facta mutatio, & quemadmodum istae uvae recentes sunt, dum adferuntur: ita quoque exercitus Carthaginenfium firmi & robusti, parati & erecti, non itineris molestia defessi possunt advolare. Recitavi Catonis verba, quibus animos suorum excitare voluit, vt de accommodata, ut opinor, nostro huic tempori: Quid enim est, Senatores Amplissimi ò minus idem de nobis aliquis Cato dicere posset? Afferuntur ad nos poma Hispanica, illua uissima & pulcherrima, maioribus nostris incognita, in quibus colorem, odorem, saporem, succum, si consideres, nunc primùm de arboribus decerpta esse videntur. Non ignoramus, quantum detrimentū morum & virtutis importent in patriam nostram illæ delicie Hispanicæ & Italicæ. Sunt multi viri primarij, qui intelligunt, magis ac magis hostibus stris in regnū nostrū aditū patefieri: & tamen non cogitamus, quibus artib. aliorū regna persa sint, ijsdem Reip.nostra adeo debilitata esse, ut ruere incipiat. Et in his nostris moribus et ruinis, vos Senatores Amplis. quibus cura Reip.tradita est, vos, inquâ, in utramque aurem dormitis. Aspicitis exploratores istos Gabaonitas, istos inquam Iesuitas exploratores Hispanicos, qui antea fuerant pallidi & squalidi, pannis & pulvere obsiti, nunc vero sunt nitidi & splendidi, potentes & gratiosi. Hos non videtis in regno nostro ita versari, ut pro suo arbitrio velint Regem eligere, & illius authoritatem totam & Majestatem ad libidinem suam convertere? Non videtis quid moliantur? Properavit ter in Sueciam plenis velis: eoq; omnium opinione celerius pervenit. Alter 6 o. milliaria ibus diebus Viennam Cifis pervolavit. O celeritatem incredibilem. O nuntium voluem. Quæ causa est tantæ celeritatis? Vobisne Patres Sancti Regni administrandi ra ita commissa est, ut si paululum remiseritis, periturum esse existimetis? quaspe ut re adductus & incitatus est unus vester Monachus primarius, vestrorū consiliorū morator, ac defensor, ut munus illud pacis constituendæ inter Stephanū Regē & Magnum ucem Moschovīæ susciperet? Quamobrem ista pacificatione sibi non tradita sumpsit? Tantùmne vobis authoritatis patres S. tribuitis? & tantum prudentiæ in vobis esse exi-stimatis, ut credatis, omnes conditiones pacis vos animadvertere & constituere posse, com-modas patriæ nostra: quam vis nesciatis, quib. de causis, quàm magnis atq; arduis tam longum, tam grave & periculosum bellum gereretur? Multorū vocibus, & diu usurpatū est proverbiū: Quicquid agit mundus, monachus vult esse secundus, quod tam pulchrè vobis suasistis; & vestro huic principi convenit, quàm etiam vobis conveniret Bernhardinorum e horribilis habitus, à quo vos ita abhorretis, ut etiam mentio illius sit vobis valdè molesta: fortassis propterea, ne eam, quam habetis gratiam amittatis? si hunc nitorem, & hanc egantiam, quæ vobis multorū hominū amore colligit, cucullo contegatis, atq; ita obscurá ddatis. Sed quæ est ista temeritas, inter tantos Principes & Monarchas authoritate suin ita interponere tanquam si antea nihil sapientiæ in omnib. Senatoribus fuisset? Iā verò jam fuerit studiosus pacis & gentis nostræ is vester Pater; libellus, quem postea edidit unde indicat, plenus contumeliarum et maledictorum. Hunc si exterarum nationum homines legerint, quibus nondum mores nostri sunt cogniti, existimabunt, in Polonia nullam pietatem, nullam rationem, nullam virtutem, nullum ordinem. Etiam reliqui Iesuitæ Monachi hujus ducis exemplum sequuntur. Emittunt subinde non solum illos suos juvenes ad omnia sua facinora exercitatos, verùm etiam & libellos, quibus calamitosam famam, inquam flammam & incendium, in nostræ Reip. cives viros bonos, volunt excitare. Hæc tam vis ita sint, tamen illi vivunt delicatè & suaviter, non solùm nullas pœnas suorum scinorum non metuunt, sed magnos etiam honores sibi deferri debere existimant. Magnici appellari cupiunt, atq; ad tanti nominis & dignitatis fidem confirmandam omnibus arbus multa prædia colligunt: vel potius ab ijs hominibus, qui fallacem spem precio emere on dubitant, oppida & prædia exigunt. Atq; hoc pacto nobilitatem, quæ est ornamentum pace, præsidium & robur in bello, quæ sanguinem suum pro patriæ salute effundit, in mares angustias redigūt. Sunt multi equites, viri fortissimi & costantissimi, singulari anii atq; consilij magnitudine præditi, quorū majores in bello fortissimè occubuerunt, patrionia sua pro patriæ salute effuderunt, ipsi quoq; magna vitæ suæ parte in aula Regum colcarunt, hi aliquot famulos quotidiani ministerij vix alere possunt. Isti verò patres Gatonitæ hoc assecuti sunt, pietate simulatâ, illo vultu et habitu ad decipiēdos homines comirato, ut multos non tantummodò Equites, sed etiā regni Senatores jam opibus superent, sq; non tantum contemnere, verum jam ad eādem quosdam, & animo & oculis suis & liillis designare incipiant.
units.tr: For compare, most distinguished Senators, the Jesuits with the Cross-bearers. You, I say, first received the Jesuits under your protection. Remember how many resources the Cross-bearers had from distant regions to oppress you, and at the same time turn your eyes to those Fathers of yours, those Gabaonites of ours, I say. Consider again and again how destitute and needy they were in every respect when those Gabaonites first came here. Now, indeed, you see what great wealth they possess and by what arts they have gathered it. But if you wish to examine the whole matter as thoroughly as you ought, consider again and again that the King of Spain is not very far from us: Antwerp, which is said to be the home and seat of Spanish power, is six days' journey from Danzig. What are we doing, most distinguished Senators? What are we doing? The most miserable examples of other kingdoms do not move us or warn us, which is all the more astonishing because learning has been added to your prudence and practical experience. Why do you not read through the histories of other kingdoms? That Cato, who by general agreement is granted first place among the wise, when he wished to set before the Romans the dangers that hung over them from the Carthaginians, brought in the Senate, in this speech, the figs that were brought by sea from your land: "You see, conscript Fathers, how near our enemies have come to the borders of our empire. For the juice of these figs is kept so intact on the journey that no change seems to have been made in them, and just as these grapes are fresh when they are brought in, so too the armies of the Carthaginians, firm and robust, ready and upright, can fly in, not worn down by the trouble of the journey." I have recited Cato's words, which he used to rouse the spirits of his people, and which, I think, fit our present time well. For what could some Cato not say about us, most distinguished Senators? Spanish apples are brought to us, very sweet and very beautiful, unknown to our ancestors, in which colour, scent, flavour, and juice, if you consider them, seem to have been picked from the trees only just now. We are not unaware how much harm to morals and virtue those Spanish and Italian delights bring into our country. There are many leading men who understand that more and more access to our kingdom is being opened to our enemies, and yet we do not consider by what arts other kingdoms have been ruined, which are the same arts by which our Commonwealth has been so weakened that it begins to collapse. And in these our morals and our ruins, you, most distinguished Senators, to whom the care of the Commonwealth has been entrusted, you, I say, sleep through both ears. You see those spies, those Gabaonites, I say, those Jesuits, Spanish spies, who before were pale and squalid, covered with rags and dust, but who now are sleek and splendid, powerful and favoured. Do you not see that they are active in our kingdom in such a way that they wish to choose the King at their own pleasure and turn all his authority and majesty to their own lust? Do you not see what they are plotting? One of them sped three times to Sweden under full sail, and reached it faster than anyone thought possible. Another flew 600 miles to Vienna in a few days. O incredible speed! O winged messenger! What is the reason for such speed? Is the government of the holy Kingdom entrusted to you in such a way that you think it would perish if you relaxed a little? Why else was your leading monk, the defender and delayer of your plans, moved and urged to take on the task of establishing peace between King Stephen and the Grand Duke of Muscovy? Why did he take up this peace-making without being given it? Do you, holy Fathers, attribute so much authority to yourselves, and think you have so much prudence that you believe you can see and set up all the terms of peace that are good for our country, although you do not know for what causes so long, so grave, and so dangerous a war is being waged? It has been said by many voices, and for a long time, the proverb: Whatever the world does, the monk wants to be second to it, which you have so nicely persuaded yourselves of, and which suits this prince of yours just as well as the dreadful habit of the Bernardines would suit you, from which you shrink so much that even the mention of it is very troubling to you. Perhaps that is so that you do not lose the favour you enjoy, if you cover this polish and this elegance, which gathers you the love of many men, with a hood and so hide it in obscurity. But what recklessness is this, to insert your authority among such great princes and monarchs, as if there had been no wisdom at all among the Senators before? Indeed, this Father of yours, who claims to be a zealous supporter of peace and of our nation, has since published a pamphlet full of insults and abuse. If men of foreign nations read it, who do not yet know our customs, they will think that in Poland there is no piety, no reason, no virtue, no order. The other Jesuit monks also follow the example of this leader. They send out from time to time not only those young men of theirs, trained for all their crimes, but also pamphlets, by which they wish to stir up a calamitous reputation, or rather a flame and a conflagration, against the citizens and good men of our Commonwealth. However much these things may be so, they still live delicately and pleasantly, and not only do they fear no punishment for their crimes, but they also think that great honours ought to be conferred on them. They desire to be called magnificent, and to keep up the reputation of so great a name and dignity they gather many estates by every means, or rather they extract towns and estates from those men who do not hesitate to buy a deceptive hope at a price. And in this way they reduce to narrow straits the nobility, which is the ornament of peace, the defence and strength in war, which pours out its blood for the safety of the fatherland. There are many knights, very brave and very steadfast men, endowed with singular courage and greatness of counsel, whose ancestors fell most bravely in war and poured out their blood for the safety of the fatherland, and who themselves spent a great part of their lives at the courts of kings, and who can scarcely support a few servants for their daily service. But those holy Gabaonites have achieved this, by pretended piety and by adorning themselves with that face and habit to deceive men, so that they already surpass many not only knights but also senators of the kingdom in wealth, and they have begun not only to despise them, but to mark some of them for the same fate with their minds, their eyes, and their lips.

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: Of the Nefarious Crimes

units.la: O tempora, o mores, o magnam iniquitatem hominum. Legibus cautum est, ne homo peregrinus ad aliquam dignitatem Regni conjunctâ, ne etiam homo plebejus aspirare velit. Vt legis istius authoritas contempta jaceat, quid multis opus est demonstrare? Istud enim multorum vocibus, imò verò multorum graui & acerbâ oratione reprehensum est? Istud in omnibus comitijs Regni, omnium prope Senatorum clamoribus notatum est: & tamen non animadvertimus, Iesuitas, homines obscuros, peregrinos, & plebejos, tanta bona regni inuadere? imò verò jam non pauci reperiuntur nobiles regni nostri, quise cum illis conjungunt, & sua nomina in illum ordinem Monachorum referunt, ad perpetuam familiæ suæ ignominiam malunt inter monachos, quàm inter nobiles patritios viuere. O casus hominum, o pectora caeca. Non videmus Senatores? Italos atq; Hispanos esse, quos illi jam generales Patres appellant: vere autem duces seditionum atq; conspirationum in patria nostra nominari possunt. Isti duces jam templa Cracouiæ occupauerunt. Sacerdotes, qui in istis templis sacris præerant, nostros præceptores, homines ætate & morbo confectos, sedibus suis eijciunt atq; exturbant. Apud Polokam villas Parochorum eripiunt, vel potius jam juris quadam simulatione eripuerunt. In multis regionibus Rutenia omnes illas partes opimas & fertiles, ubertate agrorum, varietate fructuum, magnitudine pastionis, & multitudine omnium rerum, quæ exportantur, præstantissimas inuadunt: suorum agrorum terminos in singulos menses extendunt: nobiles, & reliquos homines utiles Reip. exterminant, patrijs sedibus nudos prorsus eijciunt: multas viduas, præclaras fœminas eò deducunt, ut cogantur suis filijs bona erepta, illorum finibus adjungere: liberos suos spem parentum, memoriam nominis, subsidium generis, hæredes familiæ, designatos Reip. ciues, patrimonio priuare. O misera illorum filiorum conditione. In omnib. couiuijs disputatur quotidie, in comitijs, in omnium hominum nobilium concursu, vim dulcissimæ patriæ nostræ fieri. Testantur multi prudentes, & patriæ amantes viri, violari patriam, si illius bona in eos homines conferantur, quorum nulla in Remp. merita extent: qui tempore pacis & belli in Reip. salute defendenda & dignitate amplificanda, operam suam non collocant: qui non vitam suam pro patriæ salute effundunt. Quid verò Iesuitæ habent, quod nõ sit perniciosum nobis omnibus? Quid habent præter admirabilem pecuniæ magnitudinem, Hispanicis artibus, hoc est, fraude collectam? quā pecuniam, Senatores, ut videtis, ad agros amplificandos, ad palatia sua extruenda conferunt: reliquam ad nos oppugnandos & jugulandos conservant. Habent ubiq; animi relaxandi gratia, rura amœna, & suburbana, plura etiam prædia, neq; tamen ullum nisi præclarum & propinquum, domos refertas vasis Turcicis & Italicis. Quid præterea auri, quid argenti apud illos esse putatis? tantum scilicet, quantum è multis familijs coacervari religionis simulatione potuit. Familiam verò quantam & quàm variis cum artificijs habeat, quid ego dicam? ut enim omittam coquos, pistores & alias artes vulgares; videtis ut quotidiano cantu vocum & nervorum & tibiarum tota vicinitas personet illius urbis, quam semel occupaverunt, etiam ut homines Sacerdotes despiciant, ut neminem hominem præ se esse putent, ut se solos sanctos, solos doctos existiment. Quid futurum esse putatis, Senatores, si quis apertius hæc reprehendere velit? Si quò spectet isti tanti quotidiani sumptus & effusiones, multis rationibus demonstret? si quis etiam postulet, ut ea bona, quæ turpiter his lenocinijs suis occupauerunt, honestè dimittant? & istam colligendarum opum rationem, quam humanâ æquitate defendere non possunt, diuinâ religione tueri desinant? quos tumultus, quas perturbationes futuras esse existimatis? quem putatis ab hæreseos crimine liberum fore? nullum certè, nisi hunc, qui ad illorum nutum & voluntatem fit accommodatus futurus. Stephanus Rex adjuravit, se omni ratione pacem esse conservatum, inter eos, quorum in religione sunt discrepantes sententiæ. Quamobrem igitur homines novi & peregrini in regnum nostrum sunt recepti, qui dum seruant seminâ discordiarum, bellorum ciuilium, inter nos, & contra nos: ita viuunt, ut curiculam suâ curent, pecuniâ colligant, quicquid est pretiosi in alicujus Equitis domo, illud ad se pertrahant, in fraude & extraude viuant? Cur non retinetur authoritas Concilij illius amplissimi & sacratissimi Lateranensis, quod vetuit, ne in posterum nova aliqua Monachorum familia à quo instituatur? Intellexerunt homines illi sapientissimi, quòd quanta fiat accessio ad monachorum familias, tanta etiam detrahatur facultatibus nobilium, mercatorum, agricolarum, viduarum & reliquorum ordinum. Voluerunt igitur illi viri sancti orbi Christiano consulere, ne crescente numero monachorum, tanquam fundi calamitate, opprimantur boni & prudentes cives patriæ, & viduæ. Metuebant, ne eò res decideret, quod jam videmus, ut crescente malâ hac Iesuitarum tanquam viperarum progenie, augeantur illa mala, quæ metuenda sunt ab illis hominibus, qui in ocio & cibo alieno non possunt nisi ad perniciem patriæ vivere. Videtis enim Senatores, quid effecerint Cruciferi: videtis etiam quid faciant Iesuitæ.
units.tr: O the times, O the morals, O the great wickedness of men! The laws provide that a foreigner shall not aspire to any dignity of the Kingdom, and that not even a man of the common people shall desire it. What need is there to show at length that the authority of this law lies flouted? For has this not been condemned by the voices of many, indeed by the bitter and serious speeches of many? Has it not been noted at every assembly of the Kingdom, almost by the outcry of all the Senators? And yet do we not notice that the Jesuits, obscure men, foreigners and commoners, are seizing the great goods of the Kingdom? Indeed, not a few of the nobles of our Kingdom are already found joining themselves to them and entering their names in that order of monks, preferring, to the lasting disgrace of their families, to live among monks rather than among noble patricians. O the misfortune of men, O blinded hearts! Do we not see, Senators, that they are Italians and Spaniards, whom they now call "General Fathers," but who may truly be named the leaders of sedition and conspiracy in our country? These leaders have already occupied the churches of Cracow. The priests who presided over those churches as sacred ministers, our teachers, men worn out by age and sickness, they cast out and drive from their seats. At Polock they have snatched away the parsonages of the parish priests, or rather they have already snatched them away under some pretence of law. In many regions of Ruthenia they invade all those rich and fertile districts, most excellent for the richness of the fields, the variety of crops, the abundance of pasture and the multitude of all the goods that are exported. They extend the boundaries of their estates month by month. They drive out the nobles and the other men useful to the Commonwealth, and throw them out utterly bare from their ancestral seats. They lead many widows and distinguished women to such straits that they are compelled to add the goods taken from their sons to those men's estates. They deprive their children, the hope of their parents, the memory of the name, the support of the family, the heirs of the house, the future citizens of the Commonwealth, of their patrimony. O the wretched condition of those sons! At every drinking party, every day, in the assemblies, in the gathering of all the noble men, it is argued that violence is being done to our most sweet fatherland. Many prudent men and lovers of their country bear witness that the fatherland is violated if its goods are conferred on those men who have no merit toward the Commonwealth, who in time of peace and war do not devote their efforts to defending the safety and enlarging the dignity of the Commonwealth, who do not pour out their lives for the welfare of the country. And what do the Jesuits have that is not harmful to us all? What do they have, apart from an astonishing amount of money, gathered by Spanish arts, that is, by fraud? This money, Senators, as you see, they devote to enlarging their estates and building their palaces; the rest they keep in reserve for assaulting and throttling us. Everywhere they have pleasant country houses and suburban estates for the relaxation of their minds, and many farms too, yet none that is not splendid and close at hand; their houses are crammed with Turkish and Italian vessels. What other gold and silver do you think they have? Just as much, no doubt, as could be heaped together from many families under the pretence of religion. As for how large their household is and with what varied crafts it is furnished, what need I say? For to pass over the cooks, bakers and other common trades: you see how the whole neighbourhood of that city, which they have once occupied, resounds every day with the singing of voices, strings and flutes; they despise the priests so that they think no man is their equal, and they believe themselves alone holy and alone learned. What do you think will happen, Senators, if anyone wishes to criticise these things more openly? If he should demonstrate by many arguments where all these great daily expenses and profusions are tending? If he should even demand that they honourably give up those goods which they have shamefully seized by these enticements, and cease to defend by divine religion that method of gathering wealth which they cannot defend by human justice? What tumults, what disturbances do you think will follow? Whom do you think will be free of the charge of heresy? Certainly no one, except him who is going to be adapted to their nod and will. King Stephen swore that he would by every means preserve peace among those whose opinions in religion differ. Why then have men new and foreign been received into our kingdom, who, while they sow the seeds of discord and civil wars among us and against us, live in such a way that they look after their own careers, gather money, draw to themselves whatever is precious in any knight's house, and live in fraud and more than fraud? Why is the authority of that most ample and most sacred Council of the Lateran not upheld, which forbade that in future any new family of monks should be founded by anyone? Those most wise men understood that as the number of monastic families increases, so much is taken away from the resources of the nobles, merchants, farmers, widows and the other orders. Those holy men therefore wished to provide for the Christian world, so that, with the number of monks growing, the good and prudent citizens of the country and the widows should not be crushed as by a sort of collapse of the estate. They feared that matters would come to what we now see: that as this wicked brood of Jesuits, like a brood of vipers, grows, those evils increase which are to be feared from men who cannot live, in idleness and on other people's food, except to the ruin of the fatherland. For you see, Senators, what the Crosiers have done; you see also what the Jesuits are doing.

units.la: Sed quorsum hæc omnis spectat oratio, Senatores Amplissimi? quid enim facturus sit nmus Pontifex, nondum scimus, quem etiam hoc consilium cepisse ex multis intelleximus, ut ipsos Iesuitas ex hoc splendore, in aridioris & horridioris vitæ circulum reducat, ut omnibus sit perspicuum, illos esse Monachos. Hoc fortasse beatissimi patris consilium, ad ecclesiæ tranquillitatem habet aliquid momenti: sed metuo, ne parum admodum aut omnino nihil ad has perturbationes mitigandas, quæ sunt à Iesuitis excitatæ, conferat, & ista quoque incommoda atque detrimenta, quæ Reipublicæ allata sunt, compensanda.
units.tr: But to what end does this whole speech tend, most distinguished Senators? For we do not yet know what our most holy Pontiff will do, though we have learned from many sources that he has also resolved on this plan: to lead the Jesuits themselves down from this splendour into the round of a drier and rougher life, so that it may be plain to all that they are monks. This resolution of the most blessed Father may have some weight for the tranquillity of the Church; but I fear it will contribute very little, or nothing at all, to calming those disturbances which the Jesuits have stirred up, or to making up for the losses and injuries which have been inflicted on the Commonwealth.

units.la: Nam enim, ut est monachorum ingenium, pilum, non animum mutabunt. Quamobrem oportet nos semper esse excitatos, erectos, & propemodum animis ita armatos, ne blanda aut suplici oratione, aut etiam pietatis simulatione fallamur. Satis enim jam, satis oppressi sumus: multorum nobilium domus sunt eversæ, fortunæ vexatæ, dissipati agricolæ, raptatæ conjuges: multi nobiles, incredibili pietate & amore in patriam, magnis in angustiis versantur, & propemodum ad pedes istorum Iesuitarum abjecti sunt: multi subditi nobilium in Lithuania atque in Mazovia pertulerunt crudelitatem istorum Iesuitarum, pulsi sunt sedibus, patriis focis, distracti à suis: videre licet multos oculis lachrymantibus squalidos, sæpe etiam sordidatos & reos. Videtis quotidie magnam accessionem ad numerum Iesuitarum fieri. Videtis, multos ex Hispania atque Italia advolare. Animadvertitis, ut opinor, aliis Sacerdotibus iniquissimam vim fieri: viros senes Sacerdotes nostros ab istis Iesuitis miserè jactatos, & repudiatos, perterritos, & sedibus suis exturbatos esse. Hi, quem præter vos appellent, habent neminem. Vobis suas fortunas commendant. Vobis existimationem committunt ac spem vitæ reliquæ. Miserum est exturbari fortunis omnibus, miserius cum injuriis. Constituite etiam vobis ante oculos reliquorum minimum nobilium & agricolarum miseram senectutem, qui ita bonis spoliati sunt, ut videant Iesuitas in suis bonis paternis dominari, ipsi filios atque filias suas juvare non possint. Hi vos orant atque obsecrant judices, ut ad illorum dolorem sublevandum recordatione parentum vestrorum, & liberorum jucunditate commoveamini, & pietatisque iudulgentiæ vestræ serviatis. Omnes Ordines Regni vos orant atque obsecrant, Senatores Amplissimi ut patriæ salutem ante oculos vestros constituatis. Libertas enim nostra, quæ est commendata vobis: vita & fortuna omnium bonorum agitur, ita cupiditatem infinitam cum immani crudelitate intendunt isti Hispani atque Itali Iesuitæ: quorum potentiam cum immani cupiditate conjunctam, nisi represseritis, videte Senatores Amplissimi, ne hoc tempore, quo maximè Respubl. sapientiam, & authoritatem vestram requirit, patriæ, & vobis atque vestris omnibus, quibus omnia propemodum debetis, defuisse videamini.
units.tr: For, as is the nature of monks, they will change their hair, not their disposition. Therefore we must always be roused, alert, and almost so armed in mind that we are not deceived by a smooth or humble speech, or even by a pretence of piety. For we have already been oppressed enough, more than enough: the houses of many nobles have been overthrown, their fortunes harassed, their farmers scattered, their wives seized. Many nobles, with incredible devotion and love for their country, are in great distress, and have almost thrown themselves at the feet of these Jesuits. Many subjects of the nobles in Lithuania and in Masovia have endured the cruelty of these Jesuits; they have been driven from their seats, their ancestral hearths, separated from their own people. One may see many, with weeping eyes, squalid, often in mourning clothes and made defendants. Every day you see a great addition to the number of Jesuits. You see many flying in from Spain and Italy. You notice, I think, that most unjust violence is done to other priests: that our old priests have been wretchedly harassed, rejected, terrified by these Jesuits and driven from their seats. Those who call upon anyone but you have no one. They commit their fortunes to you. They entrust their reputation to you, and the hope of their remaining life. It is wretched to be driven out of all one's fortune, more wretched still with insults. Set before your eyes also the miserable old age of the lesser nobles and farmers, who have been so stripped of their goods that they see the Jesuits lording it over their paternal estates while they themselves cannot help their own sons and daughters. These men beg and beseech you, judges, that to relieve their grief you be moved by the memory of your own parents and by the joy of your children, and that you serve the leniency of your piety. All the Orders of the Kingdom beg and beseech you, most distinguished Senators, to set the safety of the fatherland before your eyes. For our liberty, which has been committed to you, and the life and fortune of all good men are at stake, since these Spanish and Italian Jesuits press forward with boundless greed and monstrous cruelty.
