units.la: ANNO 1611. cives Aquisgranenses inter alia multa Senatui querentes gravamina de Iesuitarum in urbem admissione, dixerunt eos contra decretum a Senatu anno millesimo quadringentesimo quinquagesimo sexto factum, quo cautum esset, ne privatae aedes bonis Ecclesiasticis impostérum accenserentur, aedes suas inscijs & invitis tribubus, acquisivisse, instituisseque periculosis San Mariae & aliis Societatibus, apud primarios quosque Senatores & alios, ut & ipsi in San Mariae Societatem admissi, certis diebus peccata sua confessuros se, & quicquid vel in Senatu vel alibi gestum nossent, manifestaturos obtinuisse, Insuper etiam ut nullae de rebus arduis consultationes ipsis inscijs instituantur, nullaque nisi ab ipsis profecta consilia approbentur, utque ingens ipsis pecuniae summa ex aerario publico inscijs civibus quotannis numeretur effecisse.
units.tr: In the year 1611 the citizens of Aachen, among many other grievances, complained to the Senate about the admission of the Jesuits into the city. They said that, contrary to a decree of the Senate made in the year 1456, by which it had been provided that private houses should not in future be annexed to ecclesiastical property, the Jesuits had bought their houses without the knowledge and against the will of the tribes, and had founded there, by dangerous means, a Sodality of Mary and other societies, among the chief senators and others; and that they had themselves been admitted into the Sodality of Mary, had secured that on fixed days they would confess their sins and make known whatever they had learned of what was done in the Senate or elsewhere. Moreover, they had brought it about that no serious consultations were held without their knowledge, that no counsels were approved unless they had originated with them, and that a huge sum of money was paid out each year from the public treasury without the knowledge of the citizens.

units.la: IESVITARVM CONATVS ET FACINORA IN VALESIA HELVETIORVM PRO- VINCIA
units.tr: THE ATTEMPTS AND CRIMES OF THE JESUITS IN THE SWISS PROVINCE OF VALAIS

units.la: DIximus supra, Iesuitas in Valesia Helvetiorum non ignobili provincia sedes etiam suas figere tentasse. Huic autem illorum conatui vehementer restitit, ob causas supra enumeratas, Bartholomaeus Alettus, Leucensis vir nobilis & magnae in hac Provincia authoritatis & existimationis. Hunc illi e medio tollere veneno, cum aliis artibus & medijs non possent, conati sunt. Facinus hoc illorum ipsiúsmet DN. Aletti verbis referam ex literis eius ad amicum suum C. V. scriptis. Ea autem sic habent. Anno 1611. Hat es sich zu getragen auff S. Johanns tag im Winter/ daß etliche Jesuiter von Sidero zu mir kommen sind am morgen in mein Hauß/ haben mich salutiert, und mir etliche scripta praesentiert, und zu handen gestellet/ welche ich von ihnen empfangen/ und in der Tischgehalten. Hinwider habich ihnen auch gewiesen einen Extract, so auß Petro Martyre copiert, nemblich de Poenitentia & vera confessione. Auff solches habe ich uns ein gut Morgenbrot zurüsten lassen/ zu welchem wir miteinander gesessen/ ein fröhlichen Trunck gethan/ und mit gütem willen widerum von einandern geschieden. Nachfolgendes Tags/ war Sambstag/ bin ich über die mir/ durch die Jesuiten gelieferte Scripta, als ich noch nüchter/ gesessen/ welche die Jesuiter de begangenen Mordts am König entschuldigen thun. Als ich nun diese Scripta nüchter gelesen/ ist mir ein böser Staub/ oder Geruch in meine Nasen kommen/ inmassen ich vermeinet/ es wolte mir meine Augen zum Kopff auß stoßen/ ja meinen Kopff gar zerbrechen. Vnnd dieweil ich hierumb einen starcken Argwohn wider die Jesuiten gefasset/ habich mich starck zu sternutieren oder neüßen beweget: Hierauf Carbobenedicten Wasser getruncken/ und folgend Venedischen Triacks genossen. Vnd als ich vermeinet/ alles böses entledigt seyn/ ist mir doch etwas im Hals und in der Kählen verblieben/ inmassen es mir den appetit hinweggenommen und mir vorab das Fleisch essen gar erleydet/ mit hin abgetorzet/ und zu letst gar in das Bethgeleget/ also daß jederman vermeinet/ ich wurde den Geist aufgeben müssen: Jedoch ist es von den Gnaden GOttes besser worden/ wiewol ich drei halb Jahr daran zu thûwen gehabt. Volgends hab ich gemelte Scripta einer gütigen üiten Freund zu lesen vergönnet / der meinung / solcher Staub oder Geruch were rauß gar verrochen oder verlohren / so ist doch gemeldtem Freundt auch widerfahren / daß er ab dem lesen dieser Schrifften acht Tag ist kranck gelegen / Er hat mir auch solches verweißlich vor zweyen Herren fürgeworffen / als ob ich das studio gethan habe/&c.
units.tr: I said above that the Jesuits also tried to set up their seats in Valais, a not unimportant province of the Swiss. The man who strongly resisted this attempt of theirs, for the reasons listed above, was Bartholomaeus Alettus, a nobleman of Leuk and a man of great authority and reputation in this province. They tried to remove him from the scene by poison, since they could not do so by other arts and means. I will relate this crime of theirs in the words of Herr Alet himself, from a letter he wrote to his friend C. V. It runs as follows. "In the year 1611 it happened on St John's day in winter that some Jesuits came to me from Sion, in the morning, into my house. They greeted me and presented me with some writings, which I received from them and put on the table. In return I showed them an extract copied from Peter Martyr, namely on repentance and true confession. Thereupon I had a good breakfast prepared for us, we sat down together, drank a cheerful draught, and parted again with goodwill. On the following day, which was Saturday, I sat down while still fasting to read the writings the Jesuits had delivered to me, which excuse the murder of the king that they had committed. Now as I read these writings fasting, a foul dust or smell came into my nose, so that I thought my eyes would be forced out of my head, and indeed my head would burst. And since I had a strong suspicion against the Jesuits because of this, I was moved to sneeze violently. Thereupon I drank carduus benedictus water and afterwards took Venice treacle. And when I thought I was rid of all the evil, something remained in my throat and gullet, so that it took away my appetite, and above all I could scarcely bear to eat meat; I wasted away, and at last I was put to bed altogether, so that everyone thought I would have to give up the ghost. Yet by the grace of God it became better, although I had to deal with it for two and a half years. Afterwards I allowed the said writings to be read by a kindly and honest friend, thinking that the dust or smell had quite evaporated or been lost; yet it happened to the said friend too that after reading these writings he lay ill for eight days. He has also reproached me with this, shamefully, before two gentlemen, as if I had done it on purpose, etc."

units.la: EPILOGVS LIBRI III. DE STVDIIS IESVITARVM ABSTRVSIORIBVS, DOLIS ETIAM, FRAV- DIBVS, IMPOSTVRIS ET CONSILIIS EORVMSAN- GVINARIIS, EX RECENSIONE IOHAN. CAM- BILTONI, GRAECENSIS OLIM IESVITAE.
units.tr: EPILOGUE OF BOOK III. ON THE MORE HIDDEN PURSUITS OF THE JESUITS, ALSO THEIR FRAUDS, DECEITS, IMPOSTURES AND MURDEROUS SCHEMES, FROM THE REVISION OF JOHANN CAMBILTON, ONCE A JESUIT OF GRAZ.

units.la: Quod Marcus Cato olim dixit: Mirum si Aruspex Aruspicem videns non rideat: idem quis non incommodè de Iesuitis pronunciet, Mirum si Iesuita Iesuitam intuens, risum cohibeat.
units.tr: As Marcus Cato once said: "It is a wonder if a haruspex, seeing a haruspex, does not laugh." Someone might not unfairly say the same of the Jesuits: it is a wonder if a Jesuit, looking at a Jesuit, can hold back his laughter.

units.la: Loquor autem non de simplicibus Iesuitis, quibus vel ob ingenij debilitatem, vel religionis opinionem, vel temporis brevitatem abstrusiores Iesuitarum technæ ignotæ sunt. Hi namq; tanta disciplinæ severitate coercentur, ut nemo illorum, nisi sagacissimus, rhodorari possit, quid monstri subsit. Sermo mihi est de ipsis Iesuitarchis, Regentibus, Patribus, Provincialibus, Generalibus. Quorum tota est cum omnium flagitiorum, tum maxime scortationum, proditionum, & Magicarum artium communio atq; societas: ut omnino mirum videri debeat, si quis alicui repente fiat obviam, statimq; quasi quoddam exemplar contueatur sui, non extemplo rideat effusissimè.
units.tr: I am not speaking of the ordinary Jesuits, to whom the more hidden arts of the Jesuits are unknown, whether through dullness of wit, a reputation for piety, or the shortness of their time in the order. For these are kept under such strict discipline that none of them, unless he is very shrewd, can make out what monstrosity lies beneath. My discourse concerns the Jesuit leaders themselves: the regents, the fathers, the provincials and the generals. Their whole fellowship and partnership is in every kind of crime, and above all in fornication, treachery and the magic arts. So it must truly seem strange if someone suddenly meets one of them, and, as if looking at a sort of image of himself, does not at once laugh heartily.

units.la: Placet ergo hoc loco nonnulla recensere, quæ maximam partem ipsemet vidi, partim à Iesuitis audivi, quos nominare possum, & certè nominabo, si contra hæc vel hisce ausint.
units.tr: I therefore think it fitting here to set out some things, most of which I saw myself and some of which I heard from Jesuits whom I can name, and indeed will name, if they dare to deny these things or to speak against them.

units.la: Omnia autem nunc breviter & rudi quadam delineatione: at suo tempore Deo volente fusius & prolixius, assignatis omnibus circumstantiis.
units.tr: For now I will give everything briefly and in a rough outline; but in due time, God willing, more fully and at greater length, with all the circumstances set out.

units.la: Principio, si ingrederis Collegium aliquod Iesuiticum, præcipuè in urbe aliqua ample & populosa constructum, At quid dico præcipuè? quum nullum sit Collegium in loco humili atq; obscuro. Si inquam tale aliquod Collegium ingrederis, jam primum ab ianitione, intuere diligenter Ianitorem, alterum Charontem, aut potiùs Cerberum. Is est senio confectus, aut si junior, certè exploratissimæ fidei & taciturnitatis. Dic si quisquam alius, omnia mysteria Iesuiticæ Cabalæ novit, apud hunc repositæ sunt omnis generis & status virilia & muliebria vestimenta. Hisce variis modis quam quisque personam agere se posse confidit, induti Iesuitæ, mirabiles exercent impostures. Nunc etiam militari habitu conspicui per plateas & compita vagantur, & in publicis lupanaribus fortantur & helluantur. Nunc civicam vestem induti, seq; Lutheranos aut Calvinistas profess, explorant in diversoriis, in foro, in tribubus, quid vulgò de se dicatur, quæ consilia volvantur & ineantur.
units.tr: First, if you enter some Jesuit college, especially one built in a large and populous city. But why do I say "especially"? There is no college in a humble and obscure place. If, I say, you enter such a college, first look carefully at the doorkeeper at the gate: he is a second Charon, or rather a Cerberus. He is worn out with age, or if he is younger, he is certainly of most tried faith and silence. Tell me, if anyone knows all the mysteries of the Jesuit Cabala, it is he: stored with him are male and female garments of every kind and rank. Dressed in these, the Jesuits, each trusting that he can play any part he likes, carry out wonderful impostures. Now they wander through the squares and crossroads, conspicuous in military dress, and they gorge and carouse in public brothels. Now, clad in civilian dress and professing themselves Lutherans or Calvinists, they spy in inns, in the marketplace and in the guilds on what is commonly said about them, and on what plans are being turned over and set in motion.

units.la: Nunc doctorio habitu clari, & annulis radiantes, & ex professo se Pontificios ferenres, ubi sciunt locupletiores è plebe, quibus sunt filij, eos tanquam aliud quid scisciturí adeunt, & in eorum familiaritatem se insinuant mirùs modis.
units.tr: Now they appear as famous doctors, glittering with rings, openly showing themselves as Papists. Wherever they know that there are wealthier common people with sons, they approach them as though seeking something else, and insinuate themselves into their friendship in wonderful ways.

units.la: Hortantur ad extremum, ut filios suos Iesuitarum disciplinæ committant. Nam & se adjunxerunt, ipsis Magistris usos, & non poenitendos fecisse progressus. Nunc nobilem induti, conducto foris vestredo, Principum aulas frequentant causâ officij. Nunc exulem præ se ferunt, sibique subveniri petunt, præsertim à Theologis Protestantibus & Calvinianis, ut explorent, quid contra se scriptitent. Et tales omnino puto fuisse eos, qui vos hactenus viri Reverendi, tam miserè deceperunt. Sed quo magis hujusmodi exploratores in posterum caveatis, dicam vobis posthac, quid consilij modò, modò inquam ceperint Iesuitæ.
units.tr: Finally they urge these people to entrust their sons to the Jesuit discipline. For they have also attached to themselves those who have used the masters themselves and have made no regrettable progress. Now, dressed as noblemen, with hired servants from abroad, they frequent the courts of princes on the pretext of duty. Now they put themselves forward as exiles and ask for help, especially from Protestant and Calvinist theologians, so that they may find out what is being written against them. And I think those were altogether the sort of spies who have so wretchedly deceived you until now, reverend gentlemen. But so that you may guard better against such spies in future, I will tell you hereafter what plans the Jesuits have now devised, and then again, I say, what they have devised.

units.la: Iam verò quorsum Muliebres illæ vestes? Audite. Nullus Terentianus Leno tam subducta ratione ad conciliandos meretricios amores fuit, quàm sùɑt hodie Iesuitæ. Ad præsertim is, quem dixi Ianitor. Nam quod alij in penetralibus & adytis templorum per auricularem confessionem, consequi nequeunt: Hic blanditijs & mirîs alleßamentis fàcile impetrat, maximè apud pauperiores viduas & mulierculas, quæ filias eò mittunt, acquirendæ causâ eleemosynæ. Et adde nomina in ix; ut Lotrix, Netrix. Has ubi in najjas attraxit impurißimus Ianitor, etsi illæ laceris & detritis squalent vestibus, tamen alijs quas habet in promptu, splendidè ipsas exornat, easque per varios anfractus & meatus ad Venerabiles Dominos Patres deducit. Ist hæc autem non fiunt interdiu, sed sub ferum crepusculum. Inde totam noctem helluationibus & tripudijs exigunt: Iunioribus hæc non admodum advertentibus. Habent enim ad hanc rem reducta, & concamerata, aut etiam subterranea loca, & laqueâria, ut illi, qui olim Romæ Veneri initiabantur. Quorum tam bellua fuit ad carnis lasciviam projectio, ut iram Deorum veritus Senatus, lupanar illud funditus everterit, sicut Livius testatur.
units.tr: But why those women's clothes? Listen. No Terentian pimp ever devised so cunning a way of winning over the loves of harlots as the Jesuits do today, especially that doorkeeper I mentioned. For what the others cannot obtain in the inner recesses and shrines of the churches through auricular confession, he easily gains by flattery and wonderful enticements, especially among poorer widows and humble women, who send their daughters there to obtain alms. Add to these names ending in -ix, such as Lotrix and Netrix. When the most impure doorkeeper has drawn these women into his snares, although they are squalid in torn and worn clothes, he splendidly dresses them in others he has ready to hand, and leads them through various winding passages and corridors to the Venerable Lord Fathers. These things are not done by day, but at the dim twilight. Then they spend the whole night in revelry and dancing, the younger ones not paying much attention. For they have for this purpose secluded, vaulted, and even underground rooms, and panelled chambers, like those who were once initiated into the rites of Venus at Rome. The beast's throwing open of his flesh to lust was such that the Senate, fearing the anger of the gods, utterly overthrew that brothel, as Livy testifies.

units.la: Hæc de Ianitore Iesuitico. Quibus & hoc addo, si qui forte talem & tantum apparatum vestimentorum conspiciunt, mirantur quid sibi velit, his respondetur, isthæc omnia comparari agendarum comœdiarum gratiâ. Sed hic est finis minus principalis.
units.tr: So much for the Jesuit doorkeeper. To this I add: if anyone happens to see such a great stock of clothing and wonders what it is for, the answer is that all of it is got ready for the sake of the comedies they act. But this is a less important purpose.

units.la: Iam porro templum ubi es ingressus, ne dubita, quin sub ferreo cœlo ambules, Mars ubi imminet cruentus, non Princeps ille pacis. Subter te luridum inferni barathrum & officina carnificum. Referam hic bona fide quæ ipse vidi. Pragæ supra templi laquearia, aliquot millia ferrearum cestuum & flagellorum invenies, ut Bohemis ferre mos est. Ad latera dispositâ sunt tormenta bellica, & musquettæ quàm plurimæ interpositis lanceis & bipennibus. In medio ubi coeunt arcus laquearium, prægrandium missilium lapidum aggeres conspicies quamplurimos. Similem apparatum deprehendes etiam Cracoviæ. De reliquis Collegijs non dubito. At in quem finem quæritis obsecro? Fateor & mihi rem admirabilem & prodigiosam visam. Sed res sic habet. Sciunt Iesuitæ, se in omnium proprium hominum etiam sanctorum Papistarum odio versari, propter res turbulenter & nefarias sefegestas. Neminem enim curant, ne confortes quidem Religionis, dummodo Pontifices gratificentur, etiam cum totius orbis confusione, & Patriæ proditione. Quia ergo in perpetuis animi consternationibus hærent, maturè cautum sibi volunt, eiusmodi apparatu bellico. Metuunt enim ut egomet ab ipsis aliquoties audivi, ne sibi accidat idem, quod Teplarijs, qui licet impensè Pontificij essent, tamen propter nimiam ambitionem & avaritiam intolerabiles effecti, de consensu omnium Christianorum Principum, & ipsius quoque Pontificis approbatione, uno prope momento per universum mundum, e medio sublati atque extincti fuerunt. Idem accidit & Pythagoricis Ethnicorum Iesuitis in Italia. Verùm in Templis potißimum repositæ sua volunt præsidia & arcana, idque propterea: Si enim exorto tumultu concursus fiat à Papistis, auxiliandi gratiâ, ut subito armari possint, sive diripiendi & prædandi causâ confluant alienæ religionis asseclæ, ut superne telis & lapidibus obrui queant. An verò non hoc est ex Domo orationis facere spelunçam latronum? Sed audite, quæ magis miremini & detestemini. Nam hæc sunt aurea & eburnea pro illis quæ sequuntur. Subter pavimentum Templi, Græcij & alibi, quæ cavernæ & carceres subterranei, ad quos superne descenditur per cochleas. Huc conferunt, ut Virgilianus ille Cacus, rapinas & thesauros suos, stipantque cavernis ingens argentum. Et sic noodò summo cum voluntatis consensu, sed etiam incredibili cum voluptate sunt pauperes, quamque paupertatem admirabili patientia [?]fulserunt, Involuntarios autem pauperes ut dignos tam beata cruce, diris devoventes. Divitias autem suas ita plerunque condunt, ut directè & perpendiculariter subjaceant Altari majori & eminentiori. Atque cum Missam cudunt, supra Marti & infra Mammonæ sacra faciunt. In carceribus ero subterraneis miram videas Bibliothecam: Funes, Fidiculas, gladios, secures, forcipes, cippos, numellas, scalas, quibus illigati miseri, artuatim distrahuntur, si in deveniunt in istorum Mezentiorum & Phalaridum manus. Non desunt tragicæ estes carnificum, pileus pyramidalis atris plumis ornatus, thorax fimbriatus & difformes, caligæ hydropicæ & follicantes, ad talos usque demissæ, ut vel intuenti horrorem inferant. In quem finem, malum, hæc officina parata est, à viris Religiosis, & mitissimi Salvatoris nostri æmulis? Audi. Istiusmodi instrumentis intelleētu discipulorum suorum captivum ducunt, sub obsequium Iesuiticum. Si quem enim non duraturum suspicantur in propositio, aut erupturum, & arcana Iesuitica proditurum metuunt: huncippo insufum, diuque fame et inedia maceratum, tandem exquisitissimis tormentis enecant. Nihil fis affingo, scribo quod res est.
units.tr: Further, when you have entered the church, do not doubt that you are walking under an iron sky, where bloody Mars looms, not that prince of peace. Beneath you lies the livid pit of hell and the workshop of the executioners. I will here relate in good faith what I myself saw. At Prague, above the church vaulting, you will find several thousand iron scourges and whips, as the Bohemians customarily use. Along the sides are arranged war engines and very many muskets, with pikes and battleaxes set between them. In the middle, where the arches of the vaulting meet, you will see very many heaps of huge missile stones. You will find a similar equipment at Cracow too. Of the other colleges I have no doubt. But to what end, I beg you? I admit this seemed to me a wonderful and monstrous thing as well. But the matter stands thus. The Jesuits know that they are hated by all men, even by the Papists' own saints, on account of their turbulent and wicked deeds. For they care for no one, not even fellow members of their religion, provided they please the Pontiffs, even at the cost of the confusion of the whole world and the betrayal of their country. Since therefore they are in constant disquiet of mind, they wish to take early precautions for themselves with such warlike equipment. For they fear, as I have often heard from them myself, that what happened to the monks of Tepl may happen to them too. Although these were very zealous Papists, nevertheless, made intolerable by excessive ambition and greed, they were, with the consent of all Christian princes and the approval of the Pontiff himself, removed from the midst and wiped out in almost a single moment throughout the whole world. The same happened to the Pythagorean Jesuits of the heathen in Italy. But they especially want their defences and secrets kept in the churches, and for this reason: if a tumult breaks out and a crowd of Papists gathers to help, so that they can arm at once, or if adherents of the other religion flock together to plunder and pillage, they can be pelted from above with missiles and stones. Is this not to make of a house of prayer a den of robbers? But hear what you will marvel at and detest even more. For these are golden and ivory things compared with what follows. Beneath the floor of the church, at Graz and elsewhere, there are caverns and underground prisons, into which one descends from above by spiral stairs. Here, like that Virgilian Cacus, they carry their plunder and treasures, and they pack great silver into the caves. And so they are poor not only with the greatest consent of their will, but also with incredible pleasure; and they have shone with admirable patience in their poverty, while they curse those who are poor against their will, as unworthy of so blessed a cross. They usually store their riches so that they lie directly and perpendicularly beneath the main and most prominent altar. And when they celebrate Mass, they perform sacred rites above to Mars and below to Mammon. In the underground prisons you may see a marvellous library: ropes, thumbscrews, swords, axes, pincers, stocks, nails, ladders, by which the wretched men who fall into the hands of these Mezentii and Phalarides are bound and torn limb from limb. There is no lack of the tragic outfits of executioners: a pointed cap adorned with black plumes, a fringed and misshapen breastplate, and dropsical, swollen boots reaching down to the ankles, enough to strike horror even into the onlooker. To what end, in heaven's name, has this workshop been prepared by religious men, rivals of our most gentle Saviour? Hear. With such instruments they lead the captive into Jesuit obedience by the understanding of their disciples. For if they suspect that someone will not hold out in the purpose, or will break away, and fear that he will betray the Jesuit secrets, they put him in the stocks, and, after he has been long worn down by hunger and starvation, at last they kill him with the most exquisite tortures. I invent nothing; I write what is the case.

units.la: Fuit Græcij ante biennium, Iacobus quidam Clusæus, præstantis ingenij adolescens: hunc virgis & lorîs ob rem leviculam, miserrime concisum, cum se profugitum, & quæ præterea in se flagitiosè commisissent, palam conquesturum affirmaret, ismodi carceri mancipârunt, ex quo postea nunquam emersisse visus. Nulli junior orum habitabamus, quin diris cruciatibus exspiraret. Hoc inauditæ Tyrannidis exemplum, o tempore consignatis omnibus circumstantijs, quod ipse miser Clusæus factunus erat, ego vulgabo. Quin & aliud huic non dissimile facinus, in Martinuquenda (cuius parentes minor adhuc vivunt Miltenbergæ aut Milbergæ) scelerato latrocinio à Fuldensib. Iesuitæ admissum, omnium hominum oculis subijciam. Et quot existimatis istiusmodi barathro deloratas & abfumtas fœminas? quot interemtos infantulos? quot luculenti & amplipatrimonij sublatos adolescentes? Ego quidem non existimo, sed hoc ipsum firmissimè statuo, quoties sub noctem auditi Novitijs nobis ejulatus, vagitus, suspiria & lamenta longè ferrima? gelidissimum exigente metu per corpus sudorem, & pilis horrore rigenes. Crediderunt simpliciores esse animas recens defunctorum. Ego credidi recens natorum & occisorum.
units.tr: Some two years ago at Graz there was a certain Jacob Clusaeus, a young man of outstanding talent. For some trivial fault he was cruelly beaten with rods and whips. When he declared that he would flee and would openly complain of the crimes they had committed against him, they consigned him to a prison of that kind, from which he was afterwards never seen to emerge. While we lived among the younger men, none of those confined there failed to die in dreadful torments. I will make public this example of unheard-of tyranny, with all the circumstances attested, as it befell that wretched Clusaeus himself. Moreover, I will set before the eyes of all men another deed not unlike this, a wicked robbery committed by the Jesuits of Fulda against a certain Martin, whose parents are still living in Miltenberg or Milberg. And how many women do you think were swallowed up and consumed by that pit? How many little children were killed? How many young men of bright prospects and ample inheritance were carried off? I for my part do not guess, but I firmly maintain this very thing: as often as, towards night, we heard from the novices' quarters wailing, crying, sighs and lamentations most dreadful, a cold sweat broke over my body from fear, and my hair stood on end with horror. Simpler folk believed they were the souls of the recently dead. I believed they were those of the recently born and slain.

units.la: Cæterum, nè quid Iesuitis ad extremam Diabolicam malitiam deest, solent illi nonnunquam in eiusmodi subterraneis locis diabolo jucundum præbere spectaculum, duni rrificas induti larvas, Novitijs ad hanc Tragœdiam evocatis, horrendo cum boatu occurrunt, exploraturi eorum constantiam & præsentiam animi. Nam qui fraëto & jeëto sunt corde, eos ceu degeneres, ad Magicarum artium penetralia non admittunt, sed ad inferiorum artium vestibula abijciunt. Audaciores diligenter notant, ferijs studijs reservant: sed res sæpenumero cadit infeliciter, ut Anno 1602. mensis Septembri Pragæ contigit, dum quinque Iesuitæ primarijs, sub Diabolicis larvis, juventuti obludentibus, immisceuit se sextus, & is quidem haud dubie verus Diabolus, qui num ex quinque fictis Diabolis, medium complexus sic præsit, ut triduo post moreretur. Factum id lippis & tonsoribus notum est Pragæ. Nec tamen tragico illo exitu deterriti, in crilego Magiæ studio obstinatè pergunt, Inter omnes autem Iesuitas, Magicarum artium peritia eminet Pere Cotton Gallus quem Rex ipse tanti facit, ut Regiæ mensæ admbeat, & familiares cum eo miscat sermones. De quo ipsi iactant Iesuitæ, quòd speculum habeat constellatum, quo quicquid Rex scire aveat, perspicuè ipsi repræsentet. Nec esse id tam abstrusum, aut geri & consultari in reliquorum Monarcharum intimis conclavibus, quod illius constellati, vel potius condiabolati speculi beneficio, non in lucem proferposset. Et qui dem hujus Iesuitæ Magi operâ, confisi sunt Iesuitæ, potentissimum quendam Imperij Principem, eumq; Evangelicum, in partes suas pertrahere, quandoquidem is Magico studio mirificè delectatus fuisse dicebatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anything be lacking to Jesuit diabolical malice, they sometimes, in such underground places, provide a delightful spectacle for the devil. Dressed in terrifying masks, they meet the novices summoned to this tragedy with a horrible roar, to test their steadfastness and presence of mind. Those who are feeble and timid of heart they do not admit to the inner sanctums of the magical arts, but cast off to the vestibules of the lesser arts. The bolder ones they note carefully and reserve for graver studies. But the matter often turns out unhappily, as happened at Prague in September 1602, when five Jesuits in the guise of chief devils were confronting the youth with diabolical masks, and a sixth joined them, who was undoubtedly a true devil. Seizing the middle one of the five feigned devils, he so crushed him that three days later he died. This is known at Prague to the bleary-eyed and to the barbers. Yet not deterred by that tragic outcome, they persist obstinately in the criminal study of magic. Among all the Jesuits, however, the skill in magical arts is pre-eminent in Père Cotton, the Frenchman, whom the king himself values so highly that he admits him to the royal table and mixes familiar conversation with him. Of him the Jesuits boast that he has a constellated mirror, in which whatever the king wishes to know is plainly presented to him. Nor is this so hidden, or transacted and deliberated in the innermost chambers of the other monarchs, that it could not be brought to light by the benefit of that constellated, or rather condiabolated, mirror. And indeed, trusting in the work of this Jesuit magician, the Jesuits were confident of drawing a certain most powerful prince of the Empire, and an Evangelical one, to their side, since he was said to be wonderfully delighted by the magical study.

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: ON THE WICKED DEEDS

units.la: Quos vero inter sese Novitios huic artificio perdiscendo deputárunt, ijs explican
units.tr: Those whom they assign as novices to learn this art thoroughly, they explain to them

units.la: nongentas illas propositiones, quas Mirandulanus ille Comes Romæ affixit. Item, Ioannis Trittemij librum de Secundeis. Item, Cornelij Agrippæ tractatum de occulta Philosophia. Item, Theophraftum de Constellatione, & sigillis Planetarum. Item, nescio cujus Abbatis Steganographiam. Item, artem Pauli ad conciliandas revelationes. Vbi Divum illum Paulum intelligunt, quem dicunt arte quadam Magica instructum, tantas percepisse divinitus revelationes. Eandemque calluisse dicunt & Ioannem, imo Christum ipsum omnibus numeris absolutissimum fuisse Magum, non dubitant. Vt egomet ab ipsis non fe-
units.tr: those nine hundred propositions which the Count of Mirandola posted at Rome. Likewise Johannes Trithemius's book on the Secundei. Likewise Cornelius Agrippa's treatise on occult philosophy. Likewise Theophrastus on constellations and the seals of the planets. Likewise the Steganographia of I know not what abbot. Likewise the art of Paul for reconciling revelations. There they understand the divine Paul, whom they say was equipped with a certain magical art and so received such great revelations from God. They also say that John was skilled in the same art, and they do not doubt that Christ himself was a Magus in every respect most accomplished. As I myself have heard from them more than once, and I can name from whom.

units.la: mel audivi, & nominare possum a quibus. Et haftenus de Templo Iesuitico, quibus addu-
units.tr: And so far concerning the Jesuit temple, to which they add

units.la: subterraneas illas latebras, & Cyrcea antra subesse plerumque choro, aut peristylio, non ubi populus consistit.
units.tr: that those subterranean hiding places and prison caves lie beneath, for the most part, the choir or the peristyle, not where the people stand.

units.la: Nunc ubi te contuleris ex templo in Musaeum (de triclinio enim, cubiculis & Area recreatoria) : Item de disciplina Novitiorum, qui jam fe votis astrinxerunt, & de convictu caeterorum discipulorum, qui Iesuitarum curae sunt commissi ; Item de Methodo & ordine studiorum, nihil nunc quidem dicam, sed in aliud tempus differam, & sunt pleraque aliunde nota) ubi inquam in Musaeum te contuleris, ad dextrum latus te converte ; videbis ibi leftiffimam & conquisitissimam Bibliothecam omnis generis auftorum, libri omnes in pelles aut membranas niditiffimas compacti, auro & argento radiant. Quorum usus est quotidianus, illi pulpitis dispositi in praelonga tabula & catenulis sunt alligati. Ad interiorem Bibliothecam solis ingredi licet Patribus, & libros inde mutuari quos volunt, Iunioribus prostant illi quotidiani, necfine venia Regentis e reliquis vel apicem excerpere licet.
units.tr: Now, when you have gone from the temple into the museum (I say nothing for now about the dining hall, the bedrooms and the recreation yard, but will defer them to another time, since most of these are known from elsewhere), when, I say, you have gone into the museum, turn to your right. There you will see a most choice and carefully chosen library of authors of every kind, all books bound in very neat leather or parchment, gleaming with gold and silver. Those in daily use are set out on reading desks along a long table and fastened with little chains. Only the Fathers may enter the inner library and borrow from it whatever books they wish. The younger men have only those daily books on offer, and not even a single title may be picked from the rest without the permission of the prefect.

units.la: Caeterum in hac Bibliotheca nulli sunt libri Haereticorum, sed probatiffimorum autorum & Catholici omnes. Indignos enim iudicant, ut inter reliquos locum aliquem obtineant, & forte metuunt, ne pestifera contagione caeteros inficiant. Quare ad sinistram intuere, ibi cernes miseros Haereticorum libros, in luftu & squalore constitutos, & quidem matris pellibus, atris membranis ligatos, & atro colore desuper tinctos omnes.
units.tr: Moreover, in this library there are no books of heretics at all, but only those of the most approved authors, and all are Catholic. For they judge heretical books unworthy of holding any place among the rest, and they fear perhaps that they might infect the others with their pestilent contagion. So when you look to the left you will see the wretched books of the heretics, set in mourning and squalor, bound in dark membranes and in the skins of mothers, and all coloured black over the top.

units.la: Ex his ne Patribus quidem eximere fas est, quos defiderant fine praefcitu Regentis. Iunioribus autem ne peter quidem licet, nisi carmine prius, aut alio scripto, hunc ipsum Auctorem cuius scripta cognoscere cupiunt, omni genere convitiorum prosciderint. Inter haec Bibliothecas medium occupat Musaeum, multis cellulis, caeruleo velo ab invicem separatis distinctum. Dextrum latus obsident Patres, sinistrum Iuniores, qui jam ordines aliquot susceperunt. Reliqui qui Novitij communibus convictoribus sunt immixti, ut ipsos obferyent, eifq; Iesuitici ordinis suavitatem & excellentiam continuis vicibus depraedicent, maxime locupletioribus & Haeredibus patrimoniorum suorum unicis.
units.tr: Of these, not even the Fathers may lawfully take out any, unless the prefect knows of it beforehand. The younger men may not even ask for one unless first, in a poem or some other writing, they have heaped every kind of abuse upon the very author whose works they wish to read. In the middle of this, between the libraries, lies the museum, divided into many small cells separated from one another by blue curtains. The Fathers occupy the right side, the younger men the left, those who have already taken some orders. The rest, who are novices, are mixed in with the common fellow-residents so that they may watch them and, in constant turns, extol to them the sweetness and excellence of the Jesuit order, especially to the wealthier ones and to those who are the sole heirs of their family estates.

units.la: De studiis Iesuitarum hic nihil subijciam.
units.tr: I shall say nothing here about the studies of the Jesuits.

units.la: Sed describam breviter Examen Provincialis, quod nusquam extare arbitror. Vnus quisque Provincialis ab ea Provincia, aut Regno potius, quod inspectioni & curae suae commissum habet, denominatur. Eius officium est, invisere collegia, eorumque supputare reditus & census, insuper annotare diligenter, quinam ex Magnatibus liberos in Collegijs erudiri curent, & quot illorum sint numero? Num quotannis aliqua fiat accessio discipulorum, & amplificatio fortunarum & opum? Num qui sint, & quot ex Lutheranis conversi? Si nulli, aut etiam facta aliqua Pontificiae Religionis imminutio, & jactura bonorum: exprobrat negligentiam & socordiam, mandatque feveriter, ut acceptum damnum resarciant. Quod fi egesserunt fe egregie, multos converterunt, multum comparaverunt & corraserunt, omni laude cumulat & caelo effert. Insuper sciscitatur, quaenam sint vicinorum Haereticorum de ipsis opinio, quaenam consilia Magnatum? quales habeant conventus, & quot & ubi? quid decernant, quid volutent? Item, an Haereticorum Principes crebrius sint domi, an alibi? ad quosnam profificantur frequentius? Quali quisque fit ingenio? quibus rebus ut plurimum delectetur? An curam aliquam suscipiat Reipub. n amore & studio aliquo teneatur Religionis? An potius vino, veneri & venatui indulgent? An quos habeat in aula Catholicos? Qui nam sint populares rumores de suis Principibus? Num Ecclesiae adversariorum ferveant? Num pastores Ecclesiarum sint viri docti & diligentes, an vero somnolenti & illiterati? Num Theologica facultas in via Academia Haereticorum floreat? Num crebriores habeant Theologi disputationes? & contra quos maxime? quos libros & de qua materia in lucem ediderint nuper? Ad haec & alia si responderet Regens & Reliqui patres appositè: mirificè praeclari industriam & vigilantiam. Sin minus, eosque adeo rerum istarum nescios deprehendit, acerbè vituperat. Quid agitis, inquit, vos somnolenti & desides? Cur perditum Romanam Ecclesiam? Quomodo summo Pontifici hanc inertiam vestram probabitis? Cur non insinuatis vos agendis rebus? Cur metuitis? cur non intrepidè rem aggredimini? Dudum haec gesta, dudum perfecta oportuit? Videte vigilantiam Haereticorum credibilem? Et vos sterteritis? His & similibus verbis ipsos increpat & exacuit. Tantum quaerit de discipulis, convictoribus, Novitiis & reliquis: Quot eorum sint numero, quantus cujusque profectus? ad quod quisque studium inclinet? num quis inter eos spinosior, scrupulosiorque? Talem enim à Theologico studio prorsus removendum existimant, nisi holasticis disputationibus probè exercitatum, & opinione Religionis imbutum. Quaerit deinde, num quem habeant in grege, qui pro amplificanda Romana Ecclesia, laudabili quo facinore se obstringere & vitam denique profundere non dubitet, siquidem necessitas aliquando flagitare videatur.
units.tr: But I shall briefly describe the Provincial's examination, which I think is nowhere else to be found. Each Provincial is named after the province, or rather the kingdom, which is entrusted to his oversight and care. His duty is to visit the colleges and to reckon up their revenues and incomes, and besides, to note carefully which of the magnates take care to have their children educated in the colleges, and how many of them there are. Is there some addition of pupils each year, and an increase of fortunes and wealth? How many, and how many of the Lutherans have been converted? If none, or if there has been some decline of the Papist religion and loss of goods, he rebukes the negligence and sloth and sternly orders them to make good the loss. But if they have acquitted themselves well, converted many, acquired and gained much, he heaps on every praise and raises them to the skies. Moreover, he enquires what the opinion of the neighbouring heretics about them is, what the plans of the magnates are, what assemblies they hold, how many and where, what they decree and what they mull over. Likewise, whether the heretical princes are more often at home or elsewhere, and to whom they travel most frequently. What is each one's disposition, and in what things does he for the most part take pleasure? Does he take any care for the commonwealth, or is he held by some love and zeal for religion? Or does he rather indulge in wine, love and hunting? Which Catholics does he have at court? What are the popular rumours about their princes? Do the enemies of the Church rage? Are the ministers of the churches men learned and diligent, or rather drowsy and unlettered? Does the theological faculty flourish in the heretics' academies? Do their theologians hold more frequent disputations, and against whom especially? Which books, and on what subject, have they lately published? To these and other questions, if the prefect and the rest of the fathers answer aptly, he praises their wonderful diligence and vigilance. But if not, and he finds them ignorant of these matters, he rebukes them bitterly. "What are you doing," he says, "you drowsy and idle men? Why are you ruining the Roman Church? How will you show this idleness of yours to the supreme Pontiff? Why do you not insinuate yourselves into affairs? Why are you afraid? Why do you not attack the matter fearlessly? This should have been done and finished long ago! See the credible vigilance of the heretics, and do you go on snoring?" With such words and similar ones he scolds and spurs them on. He enquires only about the pupils, fellow-residents, novices and the rest: how many of them there are, how much progress each has made, to what study each one inclines, and whether any among them is more prickly and scrupulous. For they judge such a one must be utterly removed from theological study, unless he has been thoroughly trained in scholastic disputations and imbued with the opinion of the Order. He then asks whether they have anyone in the flock who would not hesitate to bind himself to some praiseworthy deed for the enlargement of the Roman Church, and even to pour out his life, should necessity at some point seem to demand it.

units.la: Ad extremum omnia isthaec consignata Generali transmittit Romam, per quem immediatè significantur Pontifici. Atque sic per totum Christianum orbem nihil geritur ut consultatur, quod non per hos Imperij proditores Papae innotescat. Per Provincialem iam Iesuitae ab uno Collegio in aliud transferuntur, idque fere triennio quolibet.
units.tr: At the end, the Provincial sends all these things, sealed up, to the General at Rome, through whom they are directly reported to the Pontiff. And so throughout the whole Christian world nothing is done or planned that does not become known to the Pope through these traitors to the Empire. Through the Provincial the Jesuits are then moved from one college to another, roughly every three years.

units.la: Addam postremo corollarij loco miras Iesuitarum technas, quas nuper admodum communi consilio fabricatas, ad subvertendum Ecclesiae & Reipub. statum in Imperio Romano, in effectum traducere conati sunt, & conantur etiam nunc hodie. Etenim hic eorum unicus, quo pacto commissis inter se Imperij Principibus, & sublatis è medio praecipuis Ecclesiae doctoribus, Hispanicam Tyrannidem, & Primatum Pontificis in Germaniam subinferant. De qua ipsum Provincialem Dei Rie verba facientem commeminit. Consilia & machinae fere sunt eiusmodi, ut sequitur.
units.tr: Finally, by way of a corollary, I shall add the wonderful contrivances of the Jesuits, which they lately devised by common counsel to overthrow the state of Church and commonwealth in the Roman Empire, which they have tried to carry into effect and are still trying today. For this is their single device: how, by setting the princes of the Empire against one another and by removing the chief teachers of the Church from the middle, they may insinuate Spanish tyranny and the primacy of the Pontiff into Germany. The Provincial himself, Dei Rie, spoke of this, and he recalled it. The plans and machines are roughly of the following kind.

units.la: Principio videndum & elaborandum, quomodo Potentissimi Imperij Principes à invicem abalienentur. Hic finis est. Medium, ut abalienentur est ipsa Religionis inter ipsos diversitas. Caesar ita declaret, Religionis libertate locu non habere, nisi prius ablata ei stituantur, post Pataviensem transactionem. Hoc illi certò renuent & excutient. Mittit ergo Principes, & idem flagitet à civitatibus Imperij: illae aut obedient aut non obedient: Si prius, salva res est: si posterius, proscribat eas & vicinis Principibus, ut semper uni Calviniano, alteri Lutherano diripiendas tradat. Non enim putarunt Pontificij, tam prudentes fore Principes Protestantes in causa Tonna V Verdensi, quinse vel ad minimum Palatinus aut V Wirtenbergicus oppositurus esset Bavaro. Quo facto proscripti fuissent & ipsi, & omnis conscissa pacificandi ratio, non modò ex Pontificijs, sed etiam Calvinianis. Quia vero considerantes egerunt, quàm exiguum existimatum sit; Ad has se converterunt fraudes Iesuitae; Nam proscriptis una atque altera civitatibus Imperij, nullus sibi temperaturus est Principum, quin malit sibi potius, quàm alteri aemulo ex communi praeda consultum. Hoc in genere. In specie autem adnitendum esse, ut commissis inter se Saxonici Principibus, potentia eorum frangatur. Id autem fieri posse commodissimè.
units.tr: First, it must be seen to and worked at how the princes of the most powerful Empire may be estranged from one another. This is the aim. The means by which they may be estranged is the very diversity of religion among them. The Emperor so declares that there is no room for freedom of religion unless it has first been taken away from them, which was settled after the Passau treaty. They will certainly refuse this and shake it off. Therefore they send to the princes, and the same demand is made of the cities of the Empire. Those will either obey or not obey. If first, all is well; if the latter, let them proscribe those cities and hand them over to the neighbouring princes to be plundered, so that always one (a Calvinist) and another (a Lutheran) may get the spoil. For the Papists did not think the Protestant princes would be so wise as to oppose in the affair of Tonna of Verden, which the Palatine, or at least the Duke of Württemberg, would do against the Bavarian. By this act they, too, would have been proscribed, and every scheme for peace would be broken, not only by the Papists but also by the Calvinists. But since they considered carefully how little this was judged to be worth, the Jesuits turned to these other deceits. For once one or another city of the Empire has been proscribed, there will be no prince who will hold back, but each will rather prefer to look after himself from the common booty than to let a rival get it. This is the general plan. In particular, however, they must strive to ensure that the power of the Saxon princes, who are joined with one another, is broken. This can be done most conveniently as follows.

units.la: Primò, Si primatus Magdeburgicus, qui nunc vacat, Electori Coloniensi Bavaro deferatur administrandus, id neque Brandeburgicus, neque Saxo facilè concesserint.
units.tr: First, if the archbishopric of Magdeburg, which is now vacant, were conferred for administration upon the Bavarian Elector of Cologne, neither the Brandenburger nor the Saxon would easily concede it.

units.la: Secundò, Id si non succedat pro votis, aliquid causae obtendendum, quare videatur, aut videri saltem debeat ab Electorali dignitate removendus Saxo. Si enim
units.tr: Second, if this does not succeed as they wish, some pretext must be put forward for why the Saxon ought to be seen, or at least ought to be seen, to be removed from electoral dignity. For if…

units.la: DE NEFARIIS FACINORIBVS
units.tr: Concerning the Wicked Deeds

units.la: Imperij proceres VVenceslaum à Cæsareo culmine dejecerunt, quia ipsis videbatur ignavior: habere etiam posse Cæsarem justam causam, quare Saxonem emissum, quotidie ebrium ab Electorali dignitate removeat. Tradat igitur & restituat hanc dignitatem familiæ VVimariensi: & quia Principes illi adhuc minorennes, administrationem Electoratus committat Henrico Brunsvicensi Principi literato & vigilanti. Hæc res sine dubio incredibiles excitabit turbas per totam Saxoniam: Ita mutuis se conficient & attritent viribus, ut communi mox superveniente hosti resistere nequeant. Brandenburgicum & Pomeranos quod attinet, dandam operam, ut Affinis Cæsaris Rex Poloniæ cum patruo suo Rege Suecia Carolo, sic paciscatur, ut Prußiam communi tectioni subjiciant, & in capita dividant. Contra quod se Brandeburgicus totis viribus opponet. Hassiæ vero Landgravum adurgendum, ut cum patruo Ludovico dividat æquabiliter Hæreditatem, & Hersfeldensem administrationem resignet Episcopo Herbipolensi. Sin minus, ut proscribatur, & Ludovico ditiones ejus assignentur. VVirtenbergicum porro ducem & Electorem Palatinum, facile committi posse inter se, si ad restitutionem Cœnobiorum aliquot Dux adigatur, & si nolit proscribatur, assignatis Electori vicinis aliquot monasteriis, & inter ea, comprimis uno, quod pridem desiderare dicitur.
units.tr: The nobles of the Empire deposed Wenceslaus from the imperial throne, because he seemed to them too sluggish; and the Emperor might have a just reason for removing the Saxon, who is drunk every day, from the electoral dignity, once he had been released. Let him therefore hand over and restore this dignity to the House of Weimar; and since those princes are still minors, let him entrust the administration of the Electorate to Henry of Brunswick, a learned and watchful prince. This affair will without doubt stir up incredible disturbances throughout Saxony, so that they will wear themselves down and exhaust one another's strength, and be unable to resist the common enemy when he soon arrives. As for the Brandenburger and the Pomeranians, care must be taken that the Emperor's kinsman, the King of Poland, make an agreement with his uncle King Charles of Sweden, so that they subject Prussia to their joint protection and divide it into portions. The Brandenburger will oppose this with all his strength. As for the Landgrave of Hesse, he must be pressed to divide the inheritance evenly with his uncle Ludwig, and to resign the administration of Hersfeld to the Bishop of Würzburg; but if he will not, he is to be outlawed and his territories assigned to Ludwig. Further, the Duke of Württemberg and the Elector Palatine can easily be set against each other, if the Duke is compelled to restore some monasteries, and if he will not, he is to be outlawed, with some neighbouring monasteries assigned to the Elector, and among them especially one which he is said to have long desired.

units.la: Hæc sunt funesta consilia Iesuitarum, quæ ex ore ipsorum audivi, summo cum stupore & admiratione. Sunt quæ quam plurima alia, quæ non omnia mihi occurrunt: & in hunc finem spectat pax Belgica & Turcica. Sed DEVM credo sic rem direxisse in Ecclesiæ salutem, ut quas illi inimicitias inter Germaniæ proceres serere nituntur, eas jam conspiciant, flagrare inter Cæsarem & fratrem ejus Matthiam, Pontifici addictissimos & charissimos filios.
units.tr: These are the baneful counsels of the Jesuits, which I heard from their own mouths, with great astonishment and amazement. There are many others besides, which do not all occur to me now; and to this end the Belgian and Turkish peace tends. But I believe God has so directed the matter for the Church's good that the enmities which they strive to sow among the princes of Germany are now plainly seen to blaze between the Emperor and his brother Matthias, who are most devoted and dearest sons to the Pope.

units.la: Quin & hoc deliberatum & consultatum est à Iesuitis, ut emissis aliquot audacissimis finis sicariis, præcipue Evangelicæ & Calviniana Ecclesiæ Doctores, veneno tollant, tanta intoxicandi peritia instructis, ut patinas, saliva, malluvia, Lebetes, & quæ reliqua ad usum quotidianum destinata sunt, sic inficere valeant, ut licet decies extergantur, tamen atrocissimi & præsentissimi veneni vim retineant. Quapropter omnes pios & sinceros Ecclesiæ Antistites hortor, ut in posterum sibi caveri velint, nec cuiquam facile fidem adjungant, nisi prius probè exploraverint.
units.tr: Indeed, the Jesuits have also resolved and deliberated that, after sending out some most daring assassins, they should kill with poison the chief teachers of the Evangelical and Calvinist Church, being so skilled in poisoning that they could contaminate dishes, spittle, washing basins, kettles, and whatever else is intended for daily use, in such a way that, even if they are wiped clean ten times, they would still retain the force of the most atrocious and immediately active poison. Therefore I urge all pious and sincere bishops of the Church to take care for the future, and not to readily trust anyone unless they have first examined him thoroughly.

units.la: Hæc in mentem mihi nunquam venire potuissent, nunquam etiam venissent, nisi à primarijs Iesuiticæ colluvieı socijs hæc singula, & multò alia plura accepissem, quæ in Patriæ & Ecclesiæ salutem, in apricum producere debui, nunc quidem solum delineando, at suo tempore, Deo volente, omnibus coloribus & circumstantijs, loci, temporis & persorum exprimende.
units.tr: These things could never have come into my mind, nor would they ever have come to me, unless I had received these particulars, and many more besides, from the leading associates of the Jesuit rabble; which I ought to bring to light for the good of the Fatherland and the Church, now indeed only sketching them in outline, but at the proper time, God willing, setting them forth in every colour and circumstance of place, time and persons.

units.la: LIBRI TERTII FINIS.
units.tr: End of Book Three.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA IE- SVITARVM. Liber Quartus.
units.tr: BOOK FOUR ON THE DOCTRINE OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: In hoc Libro eam tantum DOCTRINAM IESVITARVM referam, quae ipsi & alij Pontifici parricidia Regum ac Principum: item, proditiones, seditiones, periuria, Ligas & coniurationes Subditorum adversus Reges, alios{q} legitimos & a Deo ordinatos Magistratus, Amphibologias quoque seu Aequivocationes, ac similia multa approbant, & horum scelerum patrocinium suscipiunt.
units.tr: In this book I shall report only that doctrine of the Jesuits which they themselves, and other Papists, approve: the parricides of kings and princes; likewise treasons, seditions, perjuries, leagues and conspiracies of subjects against kings and other lawful magistrates ordained by God; also equivocations or ambiguities, and many similar things, and which take up the defence of these crimes.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De parricidiis & abdicationibus Regum ac Principum, &c.
units.tr: On the murders and deposings of kings and princes, etc.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: PRIMO, docent, pro invalidis & plane nullis haberi debere Imperatorum, Regum, Principum, aliorumq; Ordinum Constitutiones, pacta, conventa, capitulationes, fraternitates, concessiones, quibus alia religio, quam moderna RomanoCatholica indulgetur: Etiamsi juramento confirmata, non autem a Romano Pontifice approbata sint.
units.tr: FIRST, they teach that the constitutions, pacts, agreements, capitulations, brotherhoods and concessions of emperors, kings, princes and other estates, by which a religion other than the modern Roman Catholic is tolerated, must be held invalid and altogether null, even if they have been confirmed by oath, provided they have not been approved by the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Iacobus Simancha Episcopus Pacensis de Cathol. Institut. c. 46. Vbi post- uam num. 25. dixit, Se Lutheranorum nomine etiam Sacramentarios intelligere, postea num. 52. docet; Ad haereticorum istorum (Lutheranorum) poenam & odium etiam pertinere, Quod fides illis data servanda non sit (ut in Concilio Constantiensi factum) non obstante juramento. Item: Cum haereticis nullum commercium, nec pacem ullam esse posse; ideoq; fidem illis datam, etiam juramento firmatam, nullo modo servandam esse. Sane (addit) id a nobis dictum; necesse est tamen incessabiliter iterari, & tamdiu non tacere, tamdiu pacis illud nomen obtenditur.
units.tr: James Simancas, Bishop of Badajoz, in De Catholicis Institutionibus, chapter 46. There, after saying at number 25 that by the name of Lutherans he understands also the Sacramentarians, he later teaches at number 52: "It is part of the punishment and hatred of these heretics (the Lutherans) that faith given to them need not be kept, as was done at the Council of Constance, notwithstanding an oath." Likewise: "There can be no dealings or peace of any kind with heretics; therefore the faith given to them, even if confirmed by oath, must in no way be kept. Indeed," he adds, "this has been said by us; yet it must be repeated without ceasing, and we must not keep silent for as long as the name of peace is put forward."

units.la: Cunradus Brunus qui etiam ex Schola Iesuitica emersit, de Haereticis lib. 3. cap. 15. ponit quaestionem de tali pace religionis, qualis est in Imperio ex conventionibus Anni 1552. & 1555. An rata sint & valeant pacta, conventiones, leges & rescripta, quibus haeretici pacem & securitatem impetrant, ut qui eos offenderit, fractae pacis teneatur? Item, Quibus permittitur, ut Ecclesias, Episcopos, Sacerdotes & clericos habeant, Ecclesias reformare, Ecclesiarum bona possidere, administrare & dispensare possint, utq; Ecclesiastica jurisdictio ipsos suspendatur? Et respondet, non valere; cum haereticis Catholico nullam pacem esse posse. Et esse conditionem iniquam & blasphemam, quà haereticis permittitur, ut dogmata sua doceant. Et in fine eius d. capit. Hodie nulla pax rata esse potest, quæ cum haereticis ea lege contrahitur, ut offendi non possint; Horrendam & abominandam esse pacem ea conditione initam, ut qui eos offenderint, fractæ pacis condemnentur. Econtra omnia divina & humana jura illos exstinctos velle.
units.tr: Conrad Brun, who also came out of the Jesuit school, in On Heretics, book 3, chapter 15, raises the question concerning such a peace of religion as exists in the Empire under the agreements of 1552 and 1555: whether the pacts, conventions, laws and rescripts by which heretics obtain peace and security are valid and binding, so that whoever offends them is held guilty of breaking the peace; and likewise, by which they are permitted to have churches, bishops, priests and clergy, to reform the churches, to possess, administer and dispense the goods of the churches, and to be exempt from ecclesiastical jurisdiction. He answers that they are not valid, since a Catholic can have no peace with heretics; and that the condition by which heretics are permitted to teach their doctrines is iniquitous and blasphemous. At the end of the same chapter he writes: "No peace can be held valid today which is concluded with heretics on the condition that they may not be offended. A peace entered into on the condition that whoever offends them be condemned for breaking the peace is dreadful and abominable. On the contrary, all divine and human laws wish them to be wiped out."

units.la: Petrus Ribadeneira Iesuita de Principe libro primo postquam capite 16. pagina 104. editionis Moguntinæ de Anno 1603. Protestantes Principes iniuriose rebelles & summe impios appellavit (ut & socius illius Iacobus Sylvanus alias Iacobus Keller Iesuita Ratisbonensis in nuper edita Philippica eosdem Principes Perduellium appellatione diffamare non erubuit) subiicit capite 17. & 18. Pacem hanc religionis, quam Politici nostri invexerant, quamque Germani Lutherana factionis affectae sunt amplexati, & in Belgio nonnulli sibi concedi postulant, non indulgendam neque ferendam. Idem affert etiam Andreas Erstenberger sive Franciscus Buchardus in Anatomia (laudata a Iesuita Ribadeneira) parte 3. capite 13. pag. 306.
units.tr: Peter Ribadeneira, a Jesuit, in On the Prince, book 1, after calling the Protestant princes unjustly rebellious and most impious, at chapter 16, page 104 of the Mainz edition of 1603 (as his fellow Jesuit James Sylvanus, also called James Keller of Regensburg, was not ashamed to brand the same princes with the name of traitors in his recently published Philippica), adds in chapters 17 and 18 that this peace of religion, which our politicians introduced, and which the Germans of the Lutheran faction have embraced, and which some in the Netherlands demand be granted to them, is not to be tolerated or endured. Andreas Erstenberger, or Franciscus Buchardus, says the same in his Anatomy (praised by the Jesuit Ribadeneira), part 3, chapter 13, page 306.

units.la: Martinus Becanus Iesuita Moguntinus in disputa. de Fide haereticis servanda, nuper Anno 1607. Moguntiae impressa c. 10. pag. 88. & seqq. asserit, Libertatem sive patientiam illam religionis, qua liberum permittitur, esse Catholicum, vel Lutheranum, vel Calvinistam, omnino esse illicitam, & divino praecepto repugnantem, nec aliter quam aliquo tempore, majoris damni vitandi causa, tolerari posse. Imo haec libertas potius (ait pagina 94.) à Catholicis omnibus modis, quantum commode fieri potest, impediri & profligari debet. Nullus sit istis ministeriorum locus: Sciant omnes, etiamsi quid speciali rescripto vel pacto ab hujusmodi hominum genere impetratum sit, non valere.
units.tr: Martin Becanus, a Jesuit of Mainz, in his disputation On the Keeping of Faith with Heretics, printed at Mainz in 1607, chapter 10, page 88 and following, asserts that that liberty or toleration of religion by which it is permitted freely to be a Catholic, or a Lutheran, or a Calvinist, is altogether unlawful and contrary to the divine precept, and can be tolerated only for a time, for the sake of avoiding a greater harm. Indeed, he says at page 94, this liberty ought rather to be hindered and crushed by all Catholics by every means that can conveniently be used. Let such people have no place in ministries. Let all know that, even if anything has been obtained from this kind of men by a special rescript or pact, it is not valid.

units.la: Sic Iulianus Cardinalis S. Angeli Ladislao Regi Hungariae & Poloniae post pacis conventionem cum Amurathe initam, & iuramento ad hostiam sacramentalem firmatam, persuasit fidei datae violationem; Inania, inquit Iulianus, fidei ac foederis nomina, & verba quaedam inconsulta, perjpem, metumque mutuo jactata esse, quae foederis nomen sanctitatemque non obtineant. Iuramentum interpositum, ceremoniam tantum temere jactatam fuisse. Eorundem Principum aliorum consensu bellum intermitti oportuisse, quorum ope, auspicijsque geri susceptum oportuit. Et nedum foedus cum hujusmodi hominum genere inire licuisse, sed & initum non tenere in jussu Pontificis maximi. Ac postquam de potestate Pontificis multa praemisisset, tandem subiecit; Pontificis maximi auctoritate se id foedus, qualecunque esset, rescindere & abrogare; Regemque & caeteros, quorum intererat, a juramento & responsione quam Turcis fecerant, absolvere. Philippus Callimachus Florentinus (qui Romano-Catholicae religionis fuit) historiarum de rebus gestis Ladislai Regis Vngariae, libro 3. Et Aeneas Sylvius (qui idem postea Papa Pius II.) epistola 81. Et notandum, Quod licet Iesuita Petrus Ribadeneira, De Principe libro secundo capite vigesimo decimo, hanc perfidiam improbet, & causam maximae cladis fuisse fateatur, illum tamen suppresisse, quod Cardinalis Iulianus auctor illius perfidiae & periurij fuit. Alter vero Iesuita Martinus Becanus in disputatione de Fide Haereticis servanda capite septimo pagina sexagesima sexta falso allegat, A nonnullis Principibus Christianis Ladislaum ad violandam fidem & bellum redintegrandum, sollicitatum fuisse.
units.tr: So also Julian, Cardinal of St Angelo, persuaded King Ladislaus of Hungary and Poland to violate the faith he had given, after a peace agreement had been made with Murad and confirmed by oath on the sacramental host. "The names of faith and covenant," says Julian, "are empty, and certain rash words, flung about through fear and mutual perjury, which cannot hold the name or sanctity of a covenant. The oath sworn was only a ceremony rashly uttered. The war, which had been undertaken with the help and under the auspices of other princes, ought to have been suspended with the consent of those same princes. Not only was it lawful to enter a covenant with this kind of men, but a covenant once entered need not be kept at the command of the supreme Pontiff." And after setting out much about the power of the Pontiff, he finally adds that by the authority of the supreme Pontiff he himself rescinds and abrogates that covenant, whatever it was, and absolves the king and the others concerned from the oath and the promise they had made to the Turks. Philip Callimachus of Florence (who was of the Roman Catholic religion), in his history of the deeds of King Ladislaus of Hungary, book 3; and Aeneas Silvius (who afterwards became Pope Pius II), in letter 81. It should be noted that although the Jesuit Peter Ribadeneira, in On the Prince, book 2, chapter 21, disapproves of this perfidy and admits it was the cause of the greatest disaster, he nevertheless passes over the fact that Cardinal Julian was the author of that perfidy and perjury. The other Jesuit, Martin Becanus, in his disputation On Keeping Faith with Heretics, chapter 7, page 66, falsely alleges that Ladislaus was urged to violate his faith and renew the war by some Christian princes.

units.la: Sic Iohannem Strigoniensem Archiepiscopum, & Iohannem Episcopum Quinque Eccles. Erga Matthiam Regem suum ingratissimos Friderico II Imperatori, authores consilij de violanda fide & iureiurando fuisse, tradit Ranzanus in Epitome rerum Hung. Ideoque Matthiam instructo exercitu Germaniam aniæ fines ingressum, quicquid locorum occurrit, diripuisse, vastasse, incendisse; Austriam denique, Stiriam, Charinthiam occupasse.
units.tr: So also Ranzanus, in his Epitome of Hungarian Affairs, reports that John, Archbishop of Esztergom, and John, Bishop of Pécs, most ungrateful towards their King Matthias, were the authors of the counsel to violate faith and oath towards the Emperor Frederick III. Therefore Matthias, with an army drawn up, entered the frontiers of Germany, plundered, laid waste and burned whatever places he came to; and finally occupied Austria, Styria and Carinthia.

units.la: At non tantum illis, quos hæreticos fingit Pontifex Rom. fidem ipsemet non servat, docetq; non servandam, sed & domesticis fidei suæ. Ne longe exempla petantur: Extant inter acta & recessus Imperij duo Maximiliani I. programmata, quibus conqueritur, Iulium II. Pontificem Rom. cum ipso Imperatore, nec non Regibus Galliarum & Arragoniæ de conjungendis armis contra Venetos pactum fuisse, nec cuiquam cum Venetis absq; communi consensu pacem inire liceret, donec sua prorsus accepissent. Sed Pontificem fidem violasse, cum Venetis ad partem transisse. Et hanc violationem insignem perfidiam & dolum vocat.
units.tr: But the Roman Pontiff does not keep faith only with those whom he pretends are heretics, and he teaches that it need not be kept; he does the same with his own people. Not to seek examples from afar: among the acts and recesses of the Empire there are two proclamations of Maximilian I, in which he complains that Julius II, the Roman Pontiff, had agreed with the Emperor himself, and also with the Kings of France and Aragon, to join arms against the Venetians; that no one was to make peace with the Venetians without common consent until they had received all their demands. But the Pontiff had violated the faith by going over to the other side with the Venetians. And he calls this violation a notable perfidy and deceit.

units.la: Recte itaque Senator Venetus Dominicus Trevisanus cum Leo X. a patione Cameracensi resiliret, & Venetis pactionem offerret, in Senatu dixit, ut apud Guicciardinum lib. 8. histor. Ital. pag. 264. Si in hoc Pontifice Sacerdotalis fides non constantior, quam fere semper in aliis fuerat, existeret; se minime cernere, quæ cautio haberi posset, Pontificem Arimino & Faventia adeptis, non etiam Cerviam & Ravennam repetiturum esse, ni data fide majorem rationem haberet, quam Ponticum mos esset; Qui ut hunc morem suum tueantur, legibus sanxerunt, Ecclesiam suorum institutum promissis & contrariis contravenire posse.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, when Leo X backed away from the Treaty of Cambrai and offered the Venetians a pact, the Venetian senator Domenico Trevisan said in the Senate, as reported by Guicciardini in book 8 of his History of Italy, page 264: "If in this Pontiff the priestly faith should prove no more constant than it has nearly always been in others, I cannot see what security could be had: that the Pontiff, having gained Rimini and Faenza, will not also seek back Cervia and Ravenna, unless he gave his faith and had a greater regard for it than is the custom of the Pontiffs. And to defend this custom of theirs, they have enacted by law that the Church may act contrary to its promises and undertakings made to its own institution."

units.la: Anno 1527. edita est Moguntiæ cum privilegio Cæs. pactio Caroli V. Imperatoris cum Clemente VII. contra Franciscum Regem Galliæ inita, cum Responso sive Querela eiusdem Imperatoris; Quod Clemens Papa fidem non servasset, sed ejus violationem prætextu ad pietatem composito tegere conatus fuisset. Ideoq; Carolum Imp. dixisse, vocem esse Iacobi, manus autem Esau. Et addidisse; Toties sine violatam fidem ruptaq;, sæpe dera. Item; Contra jus & æquitatem datam fidem, prælium juramentum violatu esse. Cum hujusmodi hominibus deinde tute contrahi non posse.
units.tr: In the year 1527 there was published at Mainz, with the imperial privilege, the pact of the Emperor Charles V with Clement VII, made against Francis, King of France, together with the response or complaint of the same Emperor: that Pope Clement had not kept faith, but had tried to cover its violation with a pretext devised for piety. Therefore the Emperor Charles said that the voice was the voice of Jacob, but the hands were the hands of Esau. And he added: so often has faith been violated and broken, and often deceived. Likewise: faith given, a treaty and an oath have been violated, contrary to law and equity. With such men one cannot then safely contract.

units.la: Hosius Cardinalis epistola 193. 202. 226. Henricum Poloniæ Regem hortatur, eum nullo modo debere fidem datam Evangelicis Polonis servare. Nunquam it, patiaris ulla te ratione ad ea, quæ promisisti, servanda teneri: quia Iuramentum non debet esse vinculum iniquitatis. Et hanc admonitionem postea ad Regem Poloniæ Stephanum Antonius Possevinus Iesuita repetit.
units.tr: Cardinal Hosius, in letters 193, 202 and 226, urges King Henry of Poland that he must in no way keep the faith given to the Evangelical Poles. "Never allow yourself, in any way, to be bound to keep what you have promised, because an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity." And afterwards Antonius Possevinus, a Jesuit, repeats this admonition to King Stephen of Poland.

units.la: Sententia ergo Iesuitarum aliorumq; Papistarum hæc est, Huiusmodi parificationes ex ipsorum parte non esse obligatorias, nisi cum authoritate & consensu Pontificis Rom. initæ sint, sed nullas & irritas esse. Sed etsi validæ essent, tamen ad Papæ nutum rescindi ac cassari, & iuramentum interpositum, Pontificis relaxari, imo & post periurium admissum absolutionem facile impetrari posse.
units.tr: The view therefore of the Jesuits and of other Papists is this: such agreements, so far as concerns their side, are not binding unless they were entered into with the authority and consent of the Roman Pontiff; otherwise they are null and void. But even if they were valid, they could nevertheless be rescinded and annulled at the Pope's nod, the oath sworn could be released by the Pontiff, and indeed, even after perjury has been committed, absolution could easily be obtained.

units.la: In eandem sententiam docent porro ex priore axiomate, Pacem religionis inter ordines Germanici Imperij conventam, uti per vim extortam, non esse obligatoriam, imo & ad tempus tantum concessam, dilationem, moratorium & tolerantiam fuisse. Nempe usq; ad Concilii Tridentini publicationem, quæ Anno 1564. secuta est.
units.tr: They teach to the same effect, further, from the earlier axiom, that the peace of religion agreed among the orders of the German Empire, since it was extorted by force, is not binding, and that it was granted only for a time, as a postponement, a moratorium and a toleration; namely, until the publication of the Council of Trent, which followed in the year 1564.

units.la: Iohannes Paulus VVindeck in deliberat. de hæresibus exstirpandis, impre-sa Coloniæ cum gratia et privilegio Cæs. Maiestatis A. 3. in responso ad 4. obiect. pag. 324. Quod hac pacis formula Cæsar Protestantibus cavit, summa necessitate adductus fecit: nam irruente tum in Austriam Turca, necesse erat, omnes undecunq; vires contrahere.
units.tr: Johannes Paulus Windeck, in his deliberation on the extirpation of heresies, printed at Cologne with the grace and privilege of His Imperial Majesty, in the year 1603, in his reply to the fourth objection, page 324: "Caesar granted the Protestants peace in this formula of the pact because he was compelled by the greatest necessity; for since the Turk was then invading Austria, it was necessary to gather forces from every quarter."

units.la: Ibidem VVindeck, Constat ex eo edicto, Cæsarem pacem Protestantibus tantum ad usque Concilii tempus, quo dissidium hoc sanari posset, concessisse. Idem pag. 326. ubi subjicit; Protestantibus tantum moratorium, dilationem, & tolerantiam concessisse usque ad iudicium Concilii Tridentini. Quamobrem mirari animum subit vecordiam sectariorum, qui pro religione tuenda toties Comitiorum decreta contra nos stultissime detonare & delaterare solent.
units.tr: Windeck, in the same place: "It is clear from that edict that Caesar granted the Protestants peace only until the time of the Council, by which this dissension might be healed." The same, page 326, where he adds: "The Protestants were granted only a moratorium, a postponement and a toleration, until the judgment of the Council of Trent." Wherefore one is moved to wonder at the madness of the sectaries, who, in defence of their religion, so often and most foolishly thunder and bawl against us with the decrees of the Diets.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: DE DOCTRINA

units.la: Idem VVindeck pag. 414. Quod nonnunquam Catholici cum Sectarijs transfegerunt, eo fine fecerunt, ut interea reliquis negotijs expediti, posteaunum hoc bellum contra Sectarios administrarent, omnemq; eius molem in ipsos converterent. Idem docet etiam Andreas Erstenberg alias Fr. Burckhardus de Anatomia lib. 3. cap. 13. pag. 305. & seq. Et Auffwecker der Geistlichen cap. 3. sol. 66. & 70.
units.tr: The same Windeck, page 414: What the Catholics have sometimes concluded with the Sectarians, they did with this aim: that, once free of their other business, they might afterwards wage this one war against the Sectarians and turn its whole weight against them. The same is taught also by Andreas Erstenberg, alias Fr. Burckhardus, in On Anatomy, book 3, chapter 13, page 305 and following. And in Auffwecker der Geistlichen, chapter 3, folios 66 and 70.

units.la: Melchior Cleselius quoq; quondam Archiepiscopus Viennensis, eiusdem farinæ censuram conscripsit anno 1606. ad Matthiam tunc Archiducem Austriæ directam.
units.tr: Melchior Cleselius, once Archbishop of Vienna, likewise wrote a censure of the same kind in 1606, addressed to Matthias, then Archduke of Austria.

units.la: Et Possevinus aliiq; Iesuitæ Henrico Gallo & Stephano Bathorio Poloniæ Regibus autores fuerunt, ut de hæreticis (Evangelicis) extirpandis serio cogitarent. Nullo enim modo fidem, Evangelicis Polonis datam, servandam esse: quia iuramentum non debeat esse vinculum iniquitatis.
units.tr: Possevinus and other Jesuits were the advisers of Henry, King of Poland and of France, and of Stephen Báthory, King of Poland, that they should seriously consider rooting out the heretics (the Evangelicals). For in no way, they said, was the faith given to the Evangelical Poles to be kept, since an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: SECUNDO, docent etiam, hoc tempore adlaborandum Pontificijs ubiq;, ut omnes hæreticos, inprimis Lutheranos & Calvinianos, illorumq; fautores, politicos illos Catholicos, qui potius pacem servare, quam auxilia ad hæreticorum oppressionem conferre malunt, igne, ferro, veneno, pulvere tormentario, bellis & aliis machinationibus opprimant. Nisi forte majus incommodum Pontificij metuant, si id jam tentent, tunc enim tempori serviendum: aliis contra sentientibus, non amplius temporisandum.
units.tr: SECONDLY, they also teach that at this time the Papists must labour everywhere to crush all heretics, above all the Lutherans and Calvinists, and their supporters, those politic Catholics who prefer to keep the peace rather than to lend aid for the oppression of heretics, with fire, sword, poison, gunpowder, wars and other machinations. Unless perhaps the Papists fear a greater inconvenience if they attempt it now; for then one must serve the time; but when others think otherwise, one must no longer delay.

units.la: Paulus Chirlandus de hæret. q. 3. num. 2. Simancha Instit. Catho. c. 46. num. 45. & seq. Actio Henrici Garneti Iesuitæ, per totum.
units.tr: Paulus Chirlandus, On Heresies, question 3, number 2. Simancha, Catholic Institutes, chapter 46, number 45 and following. The deed of Henry Garnet the Jesuit, throughout.

units.la: Iesuita Cresvvel sub nomine Andreæ Philopatris contra edictum Reginæ Angliæ fecit. 2. num. 157. Ubi tradit, Principem, qui à Catholica religione deflexit, excidere statim omni potestate, argumento ejus quod Paulus 1. Cor. 7. dicit; Si infidelis discedit, discedat; in huiusmodi enim casu non ligatur frater aut soror. Idem paulo post num. 160. Omnium Catholicorum sententiam esse, obligatos esse subditos ad Principes hæreticos depellendos, qui fidei Catholicæ injuriosi sunt, si modo vires ad hoc habeant idoneas. Et ibidem num. 162. Subditi huiusmodi Principes suos non tantum legitime possunt deturbare, sed etiam ad hoc præcepto divino, & conscientiæ vinculo arctissimo, ac extremo animarum suarum periculo tenentur. Idem in prædicto Resp. pag. 109. Si Imperator vel Rex hæreticum favore prosequatur, ipso facto regnum amittet.
units.tr: The Jesuit Creswell, under the name of Andreas Philopater, wrote against the edict of the Queen of England, section 2, number 157, where he teaches that a prince who has turned aside from the Catholic religion falls at once from all power, arguing from what Paul says in 1 Cor. 7: "If the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for in such a case the brother or sister is not bound." A little later, number 160: It is the opinion of all Catholics that subjects are obliged to depose heretical princes who injure the Catholic faith, provided they have adequate strength for it.
