And there, number 162: Such subjects not only may lawfully depose their princes, but are bound to do so by the divine precept, by the tightest bond of conscience, and at the extreme peril of their souls. Again, in the aforesaid Response, page 109: If an Emperor or King favours a heretic, he will by that very fact lose his kingdom.

units.la: Cardinalis Reginaldus Polus in Orat. ad Carolum V. Imperat. Relicta bello Turcico, contra hæreticos bellum movendum. His enim compositis (ait) minori negotio reliqua aggredi ac perficere poteris. A Turca minus periculi imminet.
units.tr: Cardinal Reginald Pole, in his oration to the Emperor Charles V: Leave the Turkish war aside and move war against the heretics. For once these are settled (he says) you will be able to attack and finish off the rest with less trouble. Less danger threatens from the Turk.

units.la: Cunradus Brunus de Hæret. lib. 3. c. ult.
units.tr: Conradus Brunus, On Heresies, book 3, last chapter.

units.la: Bulla Papalis, quam vocant Cœnæ Domini, sic habet: Excommunicamus & anathematizamus ex parte Dei & nostra quoscunq; Lutheranos & ipsorum receptatores aut fautores, & generaliter quoslibet illorum defensores.
units.tr: The papal bull which they call In Coena Domini says: We excommunicate and anathematize, on the part of God and on our own, all Lutherans and their harbourers or supporters, and generally any defenders of them whatsoever.

units.la: Stapletonus in Oratione contra Politicos Duacii habita, quæ primum in inferiori Germania typis vulgata est, tales Politicos Hæreticis & Turcis deteriores esse dicit, quia armis & bellis Catholicismum propagare recusant. Eos etiam ut novos Diagoras & Protagoras ex omnibus civitatibus pelli debere, ut veteres illos expulerunt Athenienses, propositá etiam mercede ei, qui illos interfceret. In edit. Bavarica quæ nuper Monachio prodijt, hæc inveniuntur pag. 15. & 24.
units.tr: Stapleton, in his oration against the Politicians, delivered at Douai, which was first printed in lower Germany, says that such Politicians are worse than heretics and Turks, because they refuse to spread Catholicism by arms and wars. They too, like the new Diagoras and Protagoras, ought to be driven out of all cities, as the Athenians drove out those old ones, with a reward offered to whoever should kill them. These things are found on pages 15 and 24 of the Bavarian edition which recently came out at Munich.

units.la: Baronius Cardinalis in Epistola contra Venetos; Duplex est, ait, Beate Petri ministerium, Pascere & Occidere, juxta illud, Pasce oves meas, & juxta illud, Occide ccide & manduca. Quando enim Pontifici negotium est cum refractarijs & adversanibus (Quales sunt Veneti) tum jubetur Petrus eos mactare et occidere, atq; in viscera sua condere. Idem in sua Paraenesi ad Venetos pag. 9. Restat pater (Papa) ut exratis in maleficos gladium Petri, quem ad hoc constituit super regna & gentes Christus.
units.tr: Cardinal Baronius, in his letter against the Venetians: The ministry of blessed Peter is twofold, he says, to feed and to kill, according to that, "Feed my sheep," and according to that, "Kill and eat." For when the Pope has business with the refractory and the opposed (such as the Venetians), then Peter is commanded to slaughter them and kill them, and plunge them into his own bowels. The same in his Exhortation to the Venetians, page 9: It remains, Father (Pope), that you turn the sword of Peter against evildoers, which Christ has appointed for this purpose over kingdoms and nations.

units.la: Rosephus Ste Vanus Valentinus, Doctor Theologus, in libro de osculantione pedum Romani Pontificis, ad Gregorium XIII. edito Coloniae, Anno 580. capite 4. pag. 33. Oportet, ait Paulus 1. Corinth. 15. Christum regnare, donec ponat inimicos sub pedibus ejus, &c. Cum hic locus Pauli Ecclesiae potestatem exprimat, metò reluctantes & contumaces hostes pedibus trahet, comminuet, proteret, atque sua potestate subditas nationes coercebit, donec veneraturi, pro ejus dominatione & dignitate, manus protendant, & vestigijs osculA jaciant. Quos omnes sua auctoritate confringit & onterit Ecclesia: quia primo praedicatori dictum est: Occide & manduca. Tunc malat Petrus, cum impiorum reprimit conatus, & colla furore turgentia pedibus contundit ac comprimit.
units.tr: Rosephus Stevanus Valentinus, Doctor of Theology, in his book on kissing the feet of the Roman Pontiff, addressed to Gregory XIII and published at Cologne in 1580, chapter 4, page 33: "It is necessary," says Paul in 1 Cor. 15, "that Christ reign until he has put his enemies under his feet," etc. Since this passage of Paul expresses the power of the Church, it will drag the stubborn and obstinate enemies by the feet, crush, grind down and trample them, and will restrain the nations subject to its power, until they, to venerate its dominion and dignity, stretch out their hands and press kisses to its footprints. The Church breaks and crushes all these by its authority, because it was said to the first preacher: "Kill and eat." Then Peter rages when he restrains the efforts of the impious, and crushes and presses down with his feet their necks swollen with fury.

units.la: Sic etiam Cardinalis maximus Polus Iesuitarum fautor, tuba seditionis lafsicum canens, ad arma Carolum V. vocat, hanc luem ab Ecclesia Christi aertat, malumq; domesticum congrua severitate rescindat, ne universum Christianae Reipub. corpus ad extremum infociatur. Gladium enim justitiae diviniis illi, ad Ecclesiae defensionem & vindictam malefactorum traditum esse. Acingatur itaq; subiungit, gladio suo super femur, potentissimus Imperator, haereticos & christiani nominis hostes perniciosissimos sub jugum mittat. Et utilem hanc fore sanguinis profusionem profitetur: Quid enim, ait, pestiferum membrum in corpore? Quid homo desperatus in Republica? Quid ursus in vinea? quid lupus in ovili? quid proditor in castris? quid seditiosus in civitate? &c. Item, Quid paras? quid cogitas? Innon, unde majus periculum Reipub. nostrae imminet, & tibi praesens jam malum, et novus hostis multo periculosior & infestior, quam prior Turca, jam urget: eo potius currum & arma te converterere oportet? Horum femen, seu Evangelium Turco deterius est, &c. Ad eundem fere modum Antonius Posseuinus scribit, in bellocui titulum fecit in Italica lingua Li Soldato Christiano: cum Papa Pius V. Coroloo 9. Gallorum Regi milites mitteret. Sic enim inter caetera: Nisi, insit, milites omnes Christianos seu Protestantes occidant, eos patriam, uxores, liberos, omnem substantiam, atque adeo etiam fidem & salutem amissuros: & vocat illos: qui verbum Dei tuentur, scelerados ministros, qui nihil aliud quaerant, quam corporis & animae proditionem.
units.tr: So also the most eminent Cardinal Pole, a favourer of the Jesuits, sounding the trumpet of sedition, calls Charles V to arms, so that he may turn away this plague from the Church of Christ and cut out the domestic evil with fitting severity, lest the whole body of the Christian Commonwealth be finally set on fire. For the sword of justice, he says, was divinely handed to him for the defence of the Church and the punishment of evildoers. Let the most powerful Emperor, he adds, gird his sword upon his thigh and put the heretics and the most pernicious enemies of the Christian name under the yoke. He declares that this outpouring of blood will be useful: "For what," he says, "is a pestilent limb in the body? What is a desperate man in the Commonwealth? What is a bear in the vineyard? What a wolf in the sheepfold? What a traitor in the camp? What a seditious man in the city?" etc. Likewise: "What are you preparing? What are you thinking? Do you not see from where a greater danger threatens our Commonwealth, and that a present evil is already upon you, and a new enemy, much more dangerous and hostile than the former Turk, is already pressing? To that rather you ought to turn your chariot and arms. The seed of these men, or the Gospel, is worse than the Turk," etc. Antonius Possevinus writes in much the same way in the war to which he gave the title Li Soldato Christiano in Italian, when Pope Pius V sent soldiers to Charles IX, King of the French. For among other things he says: Unless all the soldiers kill the Christians, or Protestants, they will lose their country, wives, children, all their substance, and indeed their faith and salvation. And he calls those who defend the word of God wicked ministers, who seek nothing but the betrayal of body and soul.

units.la: Hasenmullerus pag. 126. testatur, se audivisse Landspergae Georgium Saderum, Iesuitarum per Bavariam Provincialem, & Iacobum Crusium, Novitiorum Iesuiticorum Rectorem, aliosque saepe dicentes: Nulla nobis pax, nulla tuta rerum possessio erit in Germania: quandiu non curaverimus Augustanam Consessionem deleri, & Protestantes ejus defensores trucidari & comburi. Illud enim homium genus non alia ratione, quam ignis ardore emolliri & dissolvi poterit. Quibus subjunxit Pater Petrus Italus rerum Spiritualium Magister: Utinam, inquit, is- tius etiam esset animus & spiritus, qualem habuere ij, qui Evangelicos Gallia expulerunt. Nisi consimilis in Germanos instituatur laniena, nostra Societas inter ipsos tuta esse non poterit. Pater vero Iacobus Lutzius Landspergae concionator addebat: Quid est, quod nostri, Augusta, tanta severitate, jussu Pontificis Romani, novum Calendarium urgent? Si potius curarent, milites conscribi, Confessionistas trucidari, Lutherana praedicabilia Urbe ejici, Textorum domos & bona confiscari, tunc & Calenlarium tuto recipi, & nostri ibi quiete vivere possent. Pertinaces enim Lutherani, nonnisi morte emendantur. Haec & similia inter se agitabant Iesuitae.
units.tr: Hasenmüller, page 126, testifies that he heard at Landsberg Georg Sader, the Jesuit provincial in Bavaria, and Jacob Crusius, rector of the Jesuit novices, and others often saying: "There will be no peace for us in Germany, no safe possession of our property, as long as we do not take care that the Augsburg Confession is destroyed and its Protestant defenders are butchered and burned. For that kind of people can be softened and dissolved by no other means than the heat of fire." To these words Father Peter Italus, master of spiritual affairs, added: "Would that he had the spirit and mind of those who drove the Evangelicals out of France. Unless a similar slaughter is carried out against the Germans, our Society cannot be safe among them." Father Jacob Lutzius, preacher at Landsberg, added: "What is it that our men at Augsburg press so severely, by order of the Roman Pontiff, the new Calendar? If they rather took care to enlist soldiers, to butcher the Confessionists, to expel the Lutheran preachers from the city, and to confiscate the houses and goods of the weavers, then the Calendar too could safely be received, and our men could live there in peace. For stubborn Lutherans are amended only by death." These and similar things the Jesuits discussed among themselves.

units.la: Cum etiam ad Iesuitas Landspergenses per Noribergensem quendam hypocritam scriberetur, Illustrissimam Principem ac Dominam, D. Virsulam Dorotheam, &c. Illustris. Principis ac Domini, Domini Ludovici, Ducis VVirtenbergici, coniugem pientissimam defunctam esse; & spem etiam esse, ipsum quoque Principem ob nimium dolorem & luctum, quem ex coniugis carissimae morte conceperit, mox eam subsecuturum, Christophorus Zieglerus Stuttgardianus, ingratus ergà patriam cuculus, dicebat: Si hoc fieret, omnia nostra consilia & omnes vires conjungere vellemus, ut ditione ista, Dux Ferdinandus Oenipontanus potiretur. Quia autem id sine gladio & sanguine fieri non posset, sua fore esset, ut Clerici & Devoti, omnes Monachi & Canonici, & quicunque per vires possent, concurrerent, uno impetu Vuirtebergam invaderent, reficientes contrucidarent, & sic illorum Templa & Scholas nostri inhabitarent. Scio, inquit, alia ratione ipsos vinci, & ad obedientiam redigi non posse. Nam Vuirtebergenses in sua religione sunt rigidiores & pertinaciores, quam ut promissis, vel minis, vel muneribus, vel scriptis, vel consiliis ad Romanae Ecclesiae subjectionem & obsequium perrahi possint. Iacobus Crusius quoque, Rector Landpergensis, pro publica concione aliquoties dixit, Hasenmullero teste, Nonpotissimum ob hunc finem in Germaniam misi fumus, ut Doctores, Concionatores & Praeceptores in scholis & templis agamus; sed ut operam demus, ne Lutherani seu Evangelici protestantes majora incrementa sumant. Si id nostrates ab ortu Lutheri fecissent, jam Ecclesia Rom. in pace viveret. Verum causa nondum cetidimus; conjungamus mutuas opera, vires & arma, tunc facile poterimus illos exstirpare. Ad hunc finem nisi omnia nostra consilia & actiones direxerimus, periculum est, ne nobis idem quod intendimus, faciant, & in foveam, quam paramus haereticis, ipsi nostra negligentia incidamus.
units.tr: When it was also written to the Jesuits of Landsberg, through a certain hypocritical Nuremberg man, that the most pious consort of the most illustrious Princess and Lady, Lady Sybilla Dorothea, and of the illustrious Prince and Lord, Duke Ludwig of Württemberg, had died, and that there was even hope that the Prince himself would soon follow her because of the excessive grief and mourning he had conceived from the death of his dearest wife, Christoph Ziegler of Stuttgart, an ungrateful cuckoo towards his country, said: If this should happen, we would wish to join all our counsels and all our strength, so that the Duke Ferdinand of Innsbruck might gain possession of that dominion. But since this cannot be done without the sword and bloodshed, it will be for our side that the clergy and devotees, all the monks and canons, and whoever can by force, should gather, attack Württemberg with one onslaught, slaughter the rebuilt people, and so our men would occupy their churches and schools. I know, he said, that they cannot be conquered and brought to obedience by any other means. For the Württembergers are too stiff and obstinate in their religion to be drawn to the submission and obedience of the Roman Church by promises, threats, gifts, writings or advice. Jacob Crusius too, rector of Landsberg, said several times in a public sermon, as Hasenmüller testifies: It is not chiefly for this purpose that we have been sent into Germany, to act as teachers, preachers and tutors in the schools and churches; but that we should take care that the Lutherans or Evangelical Protestants do not gain greater growth. If our people had done this from the rise of Luther, the Roman Church would now be living in peace. But we have not yet cut off the cause; let us join our efforts, strength and arms, and then we will easily be able to root them out. Unless we direct all our counsels and actions to this end, there is danger that they may do to us what we intend, and that we ourselves, through our negligence, fall into the pit which we prepare for the heretics.

units.la: Franciscus Veronus Constantinus Iesuita Gallus, in Apologia sua Gallica pro Ioanne Castello Parisiensi, Henrici 4. Galliarum & Navarrae Regis parricida, contra Arrestum Parlamenti Parisiensis adversus eundem pronunciatum 29. Decemb. 1594. impressa Anno 1595. in quintae partis cap. 13. cum variis multisque locis per totam Apologiam, & verbis expressissimis ostendere adnixus est, Haeresin omni infidelitate deteriorem esse, tandem ad arma concitamat; ad Regem Henricum, tanquam haereticum & haereticorum fautorem, Hispanicarum gentium pio parente agmen ducente, communibus armis delendum. Verba eius fideliter ex Gallico Latina facta, sic habent: In eam, inquit, rem arma sunt justa, imo justiora, quam contra omnes alios infideles. (Loquitur de haereticorum exstirpatione) sicuti haeresis etiam peior est, omni infidelitate secundum verbum Dei, qui permittens populo suo inire pacem & foedus cum civitatibus Gentilium, longe ab illo disiunctis, sed minime cum propinquioribus: quas Deus citra illius exceptione sunctas extirpatas volebat, docet nos hanc Theologiam; cum infidelis, qui est propinquus, nihil aliud fit, quam, qui sub nomine Christiani seminant suas impietates & blasphemias, sicuti facit omnis haereticus (nominatim autem Iesuitae) sed si justum bellum contra haereticos, quanto justius contra caput haereticorum? (de Henrico quarto Galliarum Rege agit) etsi, inquit, justum est ad exstirpandas Reges haereticos, ex omnibus Regnis Christianis, quanto, inquit, justius ex regno Christianissimo? Hucusque Veronus.
units.tr: Franciscus Veronus, a Gallic Jesuit and Constantine, in his French Apology for Jean Châtel of Paris, the parricide of Henry IV, King of France and Navarre, printed in 1595 against the decree of the Parlement of Paris pronounced against the same man on 29 December 1594, in the thirteenth chapter of the fifth part, tries to show, with many places throughout the Apology and in the most express words, that heresy is worse than any unbelief, and at last rouses them to arms: King Henry, as a heretic and a patron of heretics, is to be destroyed by common arms, with the pious parent of the Spanish nations leading the army. His words, faithfully rendered from the French into Latin, run as follows: There are just arms against this, indeed more just than against all other unbelievers. (He speaks of the extermination of heretics.) Heresy is worse than any unbelief, according to the word of God, who, while permitting his people to enter into peace and covenant with the nations far away from them, but by no means with those nearer to them, whom God wished to be utterly destroyed without any exception, teaches us this theology. For the unbeliever who is near us does nothing else than sow his impieties and blasphemies under the name of Christian, as every heretic does (and the Jesuits by name). But if a war against heretics is just, how much more just is it against the head of the heretics? (He is speaking of Henry IV, King of France.) Even if, he says, it is just to root out heretical kings from all Christian kingdoms, how much more just is it, he says, from the most Christian kingdom? So far Veronus.

units.la: Ribadeneira libro 1. cap. 18. in Principe suo scribit etiam, Concilij Toletani decretum esse, Bellum gerendum adversus Haereticos: idque etiam Principibus & Magistratibus Catholicorum Romanis praeceptum, illosque ad hoc jurejurando adstringendos esse. Et eodem libro cap. 24. dicit, Explicari facile non posse, quanto odio Catholici in haereticos ferri debeant.
units.tr: Ribadeneira, in his Prince, book 1, chapter 18, also writes that it is a decree of the Council of Toledo that war is to be waged against heretics, and that this is also enjoined on the princes and magistrates of the Roman Catholics, who are to be bound to it by an oath. And in the same book, chapter 24, he says that it cannot easily be explained how great the hatred is with which Catholics ought to be moved against heretics.

units.la: Ioan. Paulus Vuindeck de exstirpendis haeref. Antidoto 10. p. 404. & Antidoto 11. p. 480. scribit, Lutheranos bellis persequendos, & non solum armis terrendos, sed etiam delendos, excindendos, tollendos, exstirpandos: Nec curandum si Catholici numero pauciores, cum multo pluribus haereticis confligere debeat. Et exemplis ostendere conatur parvam Papistarum manum, contra numerosissimum haereticorum exercitum saepe victricem exstitisse. Idem Vuindek ib. p. 412. & seqq. Ad Sectarios profligandos Catholicoum Princip. Liga & consociatio requiritur: & Iesuita Cresvvel p. 161. dicit, Ligam ne necessariam, & ex obligatione; V Vindeck pag. 244. Fœdus sive unionem in Gallia initā, & Anno 1587. publicatam, quam Sacram Ligam vocant, salutare consilium fuisse. II. Dein (pergit V Vindeck) nec negligenda est occasio, Quando videlicet Prote-stantes pecuniis exhausti sunt. Vt̄ facilius Catholici Sectarios opprimere possint, variis deductis causis & artibus alios ab aliis ut divellant, occasiones captandæ; Idq; à Carolo V. Imperat. observatum magno suo emolumento. Sed & externa auxilia Catholici sibi adjungant ad subjugandos Sectarios. Econtra ne hi exterorum suppetias sibi adscisçant, cavebut.
units.tr: John Paul Windeck, On the Extirpation of Heretics, Antidote 10, p. 404, and Antidote 11, p. 480, writes that the Lutherans are to be pursued with wars, and not only frightened with arms but also destroyed, cut down, removed and rooted out; nor is it to be a concern if the Catholics are fewer in number, since they must fight with a far greater number of heretics. He also tries to show by examples that a small band of Papists has often been victorious against the very numerous army of heretics. The same Windeck, ibid., p. 412 and following: For the overthrow of the sectaries a league and association of the Catholic princes is required. And the Jesuit Creswell, p. 161, says that a league is not unnecessary, and arises from obligation; Windeck, p. 244: the covenant or union entered into in France, and published in 1587, which they call the Holy League, was a salutary plan. II. Next (Windeck goes on), the opportunity is not to be neglected, namely when the Protestants are drained of money. So that Catholics may more easily be able to oppress the sectaries, they should seize opportunities, by various devices and arts, to set some apart from others; and this was observed by the Emperor Charles V to his great advantage. But the Catholics should also join foreign aids to themselves for subduing the sectaries. On the other hand, they should take care that these do not take foreign help for themselves.

units.la: Ex eadem hac Iesuitarū doctrina, & spectoris Pontificij scrinio manavit proletoria illa & inhumanis laniena Parisiensis contra pacificationem fide Regis firmatā, in qua supra 30000. innocentiū hominū omnis ordinis, Sexus, ætatis, inter paucos ies in domicilijs suis, vel ab ijsdem extracti fœdissime trucidati sunt: Quo spectaculo tunc tempore Iesuitæ oculos & animos suos recreárunt; Idq; Papa Rō. in suo patio, ut & suosmet, & Cardinalium oculos pascaret depingendū curavit. Iacobus Aug. Thuanus Præses Regius Historiarum sui temporis in historia Anni 1572.
units.tr: From this same doctrine of the Jesuits, and from the papers of the Papist writing-desk, came that notorious and inhuman butchery at Paris against the peace confirmed by the king's faith, in which more than 30,000 innocent people of every rank, sex and age were most foully slaughtered, after being dragged out of their houses or from them, while a few escaped. At that spectacle the Jesuits then refreshed their eyes and minds; and the Roman Pope, that his own and the cardinals' eyes might feast upon it, had it painted in his palace. Jacques-Auguste de Thou, royal president and historian of his own time, in his history of the year 1572.

units.la: Hinc etiā manárunt cōspiratio Guisianorū & sociorū anno 1587. in Gallia publicata, & quæ ea secuta sunt bella, & Regū ac Principū parricidia, ac à Iesuitis i tepōris magno zelo repetitus hæreticus Iohā. Parvi Parisiensis, damnatus iadum in Coitantiensi concilio, de necandis & loco movendis Regibus & Principibus, quos Theologi, viri scilicet eruditi & graves, pro tyrannis habent; de uibus exitant 6. Tomi Memor. Ligæ. Ideoq; Iohan. Mariana Iesuita Toletanus De Rege lib. 1. c. 6. id decretum Constantiense non probat; Quia non inveniat probat à Martino V. aut Eugenio Pontificibus, & quia tricipiti Pontificum dissidio consilium illud celebratum sit.
units.tr: From this also came the conspiracy of the Guises and their associates, published in France in 1587, and the wars that followed it, and the parricides of kings and princes; and the heretic Jean Petit of Paris, condemned long ago at the Council of Constance, was taken up with great zeal by the Jesuits of that time, on the killing and removal of kings and princes, whom theologians, that is learned and serious men, regard as tyrants; on this see the six volumes of the Memoirs of the League. Therefore Juan de Mariana, the Jesuit of Toledo, in On the King, book 1, chapter 6, does not approve that decree of Constance: because it is not found to have been approved by Popes Martin V or Eugene, and because that council was held in the threefold schism of the Popes.

units.la: Hinc etiam fluxit consilium illud & conatus invadendi, & subiugū Pontificis & Hispani mittendi Regnū Angliæ, ad quem perficiendum classis Hispanica anno 1588. iam fere ad litora & portus Anglicanos pervenerat; quo eventu, notū est, quod & ex 158. navibus optimē instructis vix 40. in Hispaniam redierunt. Et tetur Iesuita Cresvvel, alias Andreas Philopater, in Responso ad edictum Regis Angliæ pag. 139. Dei voluntate adversum illum belli successum evenisse: causas fuisse illius cladis, aeris inclementiam, incogniti maris inexperietiam, fortasis etiam nullorum hominum negligentiam vel infscitiam. Et forte Deum voluisse arborem Anniæ infructuosam adhuc dimittere ad tertium annum Evangelicum, ut videat, num ad fructum meliorem reducipossit, antequam succidatur.
units.tr: From this also flowed that plan and attempt to invade England, to subdue it and to send it under the Pope and the Spaniard, for the accomplishment of which the Spanish fleet had in 1588 already almost reached the English shores and harbours; and by that outcome, as is well known, of 158 well-equipped ships scarcely forty returned to Spain. And the Jesuit Creswell, otherwise Andreas Philopater, in his Answer to the Edict of the King of England, p. 139, testifies: That this war turned out badly by the will of God; that the causes of that disaster were the harshness of the air, inexperience with an unknown sea, and perhaps also the negligence or ignorance of some men. And perhaps God wished to let the unfruitful tree of Anna stand for a further third Gospel year, so that he might see whether it could be brought back to better fruit before it is cut down.

units.la: Et quia ab illo tepore usq; ad secundū Regis moderni annū Iesuitæ in Anglia peratos fructus colligere non potuerunt, sed eiusdem Dei Opt. Max. voluntate rohibiti sunt, conspirárunt tandē tres Iesuitæ Henricus Garnetus Provincialis Stvvaldus Tesmond & Iohan. Gerard, cum aliquot nobilibus suæ factionis hominibus ad perdendū & disploendum uno momento ipsum Regē & oēs regnī rdines in Comitijs Londinensib. suppositā & incensā pulveris tormentarij coia; ut apparet ex Actis publicis Henrici Garneti nuper Londini editis, & ex siusmet Regis Britanniarū edicto promulgato 15. Ian. Anno 1606. in quibus xpressum, tres ‹stos Iesuitas auctores & inventores illius proditoriæ machinaonis: Ite præcipuos practicantes sive machinatores fuisse. Præmonuerunt etiā imdudū Iesuitæ & publice contestati sunt, se ob huiusmodi detectas punitasq; prodiones à propositio suo non desituros; velim sciatis (aiunt Iesuita Campianus & eius soij in concertatione Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Anno 1583. Treverīs excusa pag. 22.) quod societatem nostram attinet, oēs nos, qui per totū orbem longè lateq; diffusi sumus, quorum continua succesio & magnus numerus, Sanctum Fœdus iniisse, nec quandiu vel unus norum supererit, studium & consilia nostra de salute vestra (hoc est, & religionis & regni vestri eversione) intermissuros. Iampridem inita ratio est, & inchoatum certamen nullis vis, nullus Anglorum impetus superabit.
units.tr: And because from that time until the second year of the present King the Jesuits in England could not gather the fruits they desired, but were prevented by the will of the same God, Best and Greatest, three Jesuits, Henry Garnet, Provincial, Oswald Tesmond and John Gerard, at last conspired, together with some nobles of their faction, to destroy and blow up in a single moment the King himself and all the orders of the realm assembled in Parliament at London, with gunpowder placed beneath and set alight; as appears from the public acts of Henry Garnet, lately published at London, and from the edict of the King of Britain himself, promulgated on 15 January 1606, in which it is expressly stated that these three Jesuits were the authors and inventors of that treacherous machination, and its chief practisers or contrivers. The Jesuits also long before forewarned and publicly declared that they would not desist from their purpose on account of such betrayals detected and punished; I would have you know (say the Jesuit Campian and his companions in the Challenge of the Catholic Church, printed at Trier in 1583, p. 22) that as far as our Society is concerned, all of us, who are spread far and wide throughout the whole world, whose continual succession and great number have entered into a holy covenant, will not cease, as long as even one of us survives, our zeal and counsels concerning your salvation (that is, the overthrow both of your religion and of your kingdom). The plan was long ago undertaken, and the struggle begun will be overcome by no force, no assault of the English.

units.la: Excipiunt tamen quidam Iesuitarum, si Pontificij metuerent ne conatus ipsorum irritus futurus esset. Hoc enim casu ad tempus aliquid indulgendum, & commodiorem opportunitatem expectandam.
units.tr: Some of the Jesuits make an exception: if the Papists fear that their attempts would come to nothing, then for this case something must be conceded for the time being, and a more convenient opportunity awaited.

units.la: Memor. Ligae Tom. 6. pag. 262. & seq. Iesuitae habent breve Apostolicum, in quo per dispensationem ipsis permittitur, ut Serviant tempori: Item, dissimulandum, & Regi obediendum ad tempus per dissimulationem.
units.tr: Memor. Ligae Tom. 6. pag. 262. & seq. The Jesuits have an apostolic breve, by which a dispensation permits them to serve the time: likewise, to dissemble, and to obey the king for a time by dissimulation.

units.la: Petrus Ribadeneira de Principe lib. 1. c. 26. pag. 178. Christiana prudentia docet, dissimulatione utendum, si magna pericula timentur.
units.tr: Petrus Ribadeneira, De Principe, lib. 1. c. 26. pag. 178. Christian prudence teaches that dissimulation is to be used if great dangers are feared.

units.la: Martinus Becanus Iesuita Magunt. de fide haeret. servan. cap. 16. pag. 89. Si Lutherana religio commode impediri & profligari non poterit, nisi cum majori damno Reipub. tunc aliquo tempore tolerari poterit. Et pag. 102: Magistratus Catholicus omnibus, omnibus modis impedire debet libertatem religionis Lutheranae; Si tamen id facere non poterit sine gravi incommodo boni publici, poterit eam tolerare ad evitandum majus malum.
units.tr: Martinus Becanus, Jesuit of Mainz, De fide haeretic. servanda, cap. 16. pag. 89. If the Lutheran religion cannot conveniently be hindered and overthrown except with greater loss to the commonwealth, then it may be tolerated for some time. And p. 102: A Catholic magistrate must hinder the liberty of the Lutheran religion in every way and by every means; but if he cannot do so without serious harm to the public good, he may tolerate it to avoid a greater evil.

units.la: Iohannes Paulus V Vindeck in delib. de haeret. extirp. pag. 333. Nihil, nihil in religionis negotiis oportet connivere aut indulgere; nisi ubi libertas publica authoritate, & validis viribus nititur.
units.tr: Iohannes Paulus V Vindeck, in Delib. de haeret. extirp. pag. 333. Nothing, nothing in matters of religion ought to be connived at or indulged, except where public liberty rests on authority and strong forces.

units.la: Andreas Philopater, alias Crefvvel Iesuita Ad edict. Reginae Angliae pag. 151. Si vires Catholici ad hoc habeant idoneas inquit.
units.tr: Andreas Philopater, otherwise Creswell, Jesuit, Ad edictum Reginae Angliae pag. 151. If Catholics have suitable forces for this, he says.

units.la: Sic Henricus Garnetus Iesuita Provincialis Angliae scripto testatus, & coram tribunali confessus est; Pium V. & Gregorium XIV. monitos, Quod ipsorum Bullae contra Reginam Elisabetham magnas calamitates Pontificijs conflarent, eosdem hac indulta venia demulserunt; Licere omnibus Catholicis, externam obedientiam praeferre ad vexationem redimendam, his tamen cautelis & cancellis circumscriptam, Primo, Rebus sic stantibus. Secundo, Donec publica Bullae executio fieri poterit. In actis Garneti, pag. 68.
units.tr: Henricus Garnetus, Provincial of the Jesuits in England, has testified in writing, and confessed before the tribunal, that Pius V and Gregory XIV, being warned that their bulls against Queen Elizabeth would bring great calamities upon the Papists, soothed them with this granted indulgence: that it is lawful for all Catholics to render outward obedience in order to buy off vexation, yet hemmed in by these cautions and limits: first, while things stand thus; second, until the public execution of the bull can be carried out. In the acts of Garnet, pag. 68.

units.la: Nonnulli vero Iesuitarum docent; Nimis tributum tempori; Nunc itaque omnes Lutheranos & Calvinianos passim exterminandos, opprimendos, funditus & radicitus delendos, ne ullum eiusmodi semen renascatur.
units.tr: Some of the Jesuits, however, teach: Too much has been yielded to the time. Now therefore all Lutherans and Calvinists must be everywhere exterminated, oppressed, and utterly destroyed root and branch, so that no seed of this kind may spring up again.

units.la: Crefvvel Iesuita in eod. lib. de quo supra, pag. 8. Satis jam cessatum est ab inno centum defensione, ad placandum hostem, si fieri potuisset; Satis datum tempori, satis, satis tributum [?]spei. Quid ni obsistamus tam sceleratae tyrannidi?
units.tr: Creswell, Jesuit, in the same book as above, pag. 8. Enough has now been held back from the defence of the innocent, to placate the enemy, if that could have been done; enough has been given to the time, enough, enough has been paid to [?]hope. Why should we not resist such wicked tyranny?

units.la: Petrus Ribadeneira De Principe, lib. 1. c. 15. pag. 90. & seqq. ubi politicam prudentiam illam Reginae Scotiae & Regum Galliae ac Consiliariorum graviter accusat; Qui putarunt, serviendum tempori, utilius que esse conniventia quadam & lenitate se servare, quam severa animadversione totum regnum evertere. Et pag. 94: addit, Nullum Regem, nullum Principem esse, cui haec politiae ratio potior visa est, qui non stultitiae & temeritatis gravissimas poenas dederit.
units.tr: Petrus Ribadeneira, De Principe, lib. 1. c. 15. pag. 90 et seqq., where he severely accuses the political prudence of the Queen of Scots and of the Kings of France and their counsellors: Those who thought that one must serve the time, and that it was more useful to preserve oneself by a certain connivance and leniency than to overthrow the whole kingdom by severe punishment. And at p. 94 he adds: There is no king, no prince, to whom this policy seemed preferable, who has not paid the gravest penalties for folly and rashness.

units.la: Sic Iesuita Ratisbonensis in publica concione, nuper prima Dominica post Adventum in praesentia Commissarij Caesareae Maiestatis habita, classicum hoc modo cecinit; Nunc tempus esse, haereticorum istorum, quos prius expresserat, oppressionem & deletionem maturare: Catholicis nec nervum pecuniam, nec militem, nec consilia deesse.
units.tr: So the Jesuit of Regensburg, in a public sermon lately preached on the first Sunday after Advent in the presence of the commissioner of His Caesarean Majesty, sounded the trumpet in this way: Now is the time to hasten the oppression and destruction of those heretics whom he had earlier named. Catholics lack neither the sinews of war, money, nor soldiers, nor plans.

units.la: Sic & in commonefactione ab Episcopis quibusdam Anno 1603. Ratisbonae exhibita Matthiae Archiduci Austriae; Non amplius temporisandum, sed vitam, sanguinem & omnes fortunas ad hoc exponendas, ut cogantur Imperij Ordines in ipsorum territorijs sita monasteria Abbatibus & Monachis restituere. Et in hunc finem Catholicorum majorem conjunctionem omnino necessariam esse; extrema omnia tentanda; animos non despondendos. Cum & parva Catholicorum manus (ait VVindeck in delib. de haeret. extirp. Antidoto 11. pag. 410.) saepe ingentes haereticorum copias trucidaverint & internecione deleverint. Ex eodem scrinio pectoris nuper sub dato 22. Octobris Anni 1667. prodijt epistola sive exhortatio Episcopalis ad aliquot Pontificiae religionis Praelatos, sic habet; Maximopere dolendum est, quod inter politicos nostros reperiantur, qui Caesarea Majestati, Electoribus & Principibus persuadere conantur, Ob horum temporum difficultatem aliquid connivendum & temporisandum esse. Id enim dum a politicis fit, Protestantes commoda sua in Rom. religionis detrimentum promovent.
units.tr: So also in an admonition presented at Regensburg in 1603 to Archduke Matthias of Austria by certain bishops: No longer is delay to be made, but life, blood and all fortunes are to be exposed to this end, so that the Estates of the Empire may be compelled to restore to the Abbots and monks the monasteries situated in their territories. And to this end a greater union of Catholics is altogether necessary; every extreme measure must be tried; spirits must not be despaired. For a small band of Catholics (says Windeck, in Delib. de haeret. extirp., Antidotum 11, pag. 410) has often slaughtered and wiped out huge hordes of heretics. From the same storehouse of the heart, lately dated 22 October 1667, there came forth an episcopal letter or exhortation to some prelates of the Papist religion, which says thus: It is most grievous that among our politicians there are some who try to persuade His Caesarean Majesty, the electors and the princes that, because of the difficulty of these times, something must be connived at and delayed. For while this is done by the politicians, the Protestants advance their own interests to the detriment of the Roman religion.

units.la: Haec quae hucusque sub numero primo & secundo capitis huius diximus, ea & in sequentibus etiam referemus, confirmat apertis verbis Thuanus lib. 47. p. 877. & seq. inquiens, Ratas novorum Theologorum, qui se Iesuitas appellent, esse sententias, pacem cum sectarijs (Evangelicis) nec fieri debere, nec coire posse: fide eis data neminem obligari: rem piam ac salutarem esse, in impuros homines manus violentas inijcere: Christianos omnes adversus pestem eam armari debere: ac praeter Decretu Synodi Constantiensis, de fide haereticis non servanda, depromere eos exempla ex sacris literis depropta, ijs, qui a Levitis & Mosis mandatu occisi sint: de ijs praeterea, qui vitulum aureum adorarunt; ac denique de Iehu, qui re alia simulata sacerdotes Baali inclusos interfecerit.
units.tr: Thuanus, lib. 47, p. 877 et seq., clearly confirms what we have said so far under the first and second numbers of this chapter, and what we shall also cite below, saying: the opinions of the new theologians who call themselves Jesuits are settled, namely that peace with the sectaries (Evangelicals) neither ought to be made nor can be made; that no one is bound by a pledge given to them; that it is a pious and salutary thing to lay violent hands on impure men; that all Christians must be armed against that pestilence; and that, besides the decree of the Council of Constance that faith is not to be kept with heretics, they draw examples from the sacred letters: from those who were slain by the Levites at the command of Moses; concerning those also who worshipped the golden calf; and finally concerning Jehu, who, under a pretended pretext, shut in and killed the priests of Baal.

units.la: Idem lib. 65. pag. 152. Cum, inquit, res in Senatu Sebastiani Regis Lusitaniae de bello in Africa contra Mauros gerendo agitaretur, ij qui Iesuitarum partes fovebant, ut Regem a periculoso consilio dimoverent, sic censebat: Principi Christiani nominis propagandi videri flagrati potius adversus sectarios (Evangelicos) quam eos, qui Christi nomen oninò nesciant, bellum suscipiendum esse: quippe cum plus periculi ab illis (Evangelicis) am ab his impendeat, & quo facilius sectarium malum inter Christianos serpit, eo majores odijs vere Christianos sectario veneno infectos detestari, vitare, atq; ad internecionem persequi, quam infideles Machometanos, debere.
units.tr: The same, lib. 65, p. 152. When, he says, the matter of waging war in Africa against the Moors was being debated in the senate of Sebastian, King of Portugal, those who favoured the Jesuits' side, in order to turn the king from a dangerous plan, gave this opinion: that a Christian prince, zealous for the propagation of the Christian name, ought rather to take up war against the sectaries (Evangelicals) than against those who are wholly ignorant of the name of Christ; since more danger hangs over him from the former than from the latter; and the more easily the sectarian evil creeps in among Christians, the more they ought to detest, avoid and pursue to destruction, as with a sectarian poison, those who are truly Christian and infected with it, than the infidel Mohammedans.

units.la: Rursus idem lib. 67. p. 190. scribit, Iesuitarum sententiam esse, bella, quae communi sensu Christianorum contra Mahometanos gerantur, utilius ad Dei gloriam contra sectarios (Evangelicos) qui inter nos sint, omissis Turcis verti debere. Vbi recte addit Thuanus: Hoc quam pie, & juxta mansuetudinem Christianam dicatur, ipsi, qui conscientias aliorum moderantur, conscientiam suam rogent.
units.tr: Again the same, lib. 67, p. 190, writes that it is the opinion of the Jesuits that the wars which are waged by the common sense of Christians against the Mahometans should, with the Turks set aside, be turned more usefully to the glory of God against the sectaries (Evangelicals) who are among us. Where Thuanus rightly adds: let those who regulate the consciences of others ask their own conscience how piously, and in accordance with Christian gentleness, this is said.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: TERTIO docent etiam, Quando subditi Romano-Catholici Imperatore, Rege, sive Principem suum pro tyranno habendum in Concilijs vel consentib. suis statuerint, tum illum abdicare, & seipsos omni obligationis nexu liberare posse. Si vero Comitia habere prohibeatur, tu cuiusvis subdito, moneat Iesuitarum, aut aliorum huiusmodi Theologorum usus sit consilio, perissum; imo laude dignum & meritorium futurum, huiusmodi Regem vel Principem occidere. Proinde recte fecisse monachum Iacobum Clementem, quod Henricum III. Regem Galliae cultro venenato interfecit; recte etiam illos, qui & illius successorem Henricum IV. interimat.
units.tr: Thirdly, they also teach that when the subjects of a Roman Catholic emperor, king or prince have decided in their councils or assemblies that their ruler is to be regarded as a tyrant, they may then depose him and free themselves from every bond of obligation. But if they are forbidden to hold assemblies, then it is no crime for any subject to kill such a king or prince on the advice of the Jesuits or other theologians of this kind; indeed, it would be a deed worthy of praise and merit. Accordingly, the monk Jacques Clément acted rightly in killing Henry III, king of France, with a poisoned knife, and those who later murdered his successor Henry IV acted rightly too.

units.la: Ioh. Mariana Iesuita Toletan. De Rege lib. 1. c. 6. in Mogunt. edit. p. 57. A populi sive subditis volentibus, Regem Principatu spoliari posse. Et ab omni memoria in magna ude fuisse, quicunque tyrannos opprimere aggressi sunt. Et ostendit rationem abdicandi eiusmodi Principem: Expedita & maxime tuta via est, inquit, si publici Conventus facultas detur, ut communi consensu statuatur, quid fixum ratumque esse debeat; Et si monitis rinceps non obediat, consilia explicanda, arma expediunda, pecunias in belli sumptus subditis imperandas, Principem etiam privata auctoritate ferro perimendum. Et p. 60. Si puici Conventus facultas sublata erit, tum etiam qui votis publicis favens Regem sive Principe perimere tentarit, haud quaqua iniq eum fecisse exististimabo. Ac nisi publica vox populi adsit, quae Regem pro tyranno habeat; adhibendos esse in consilium viros eruditos & graves; Subijcit Mariana; Præclare, præclare cum rebus humanis ageretur, si multi homines forti pectore inuenirentur, pro libertate patriæ vitæ contemptores & salutis: & dolet, quod plerosque incolumitatis cupiditas retineat, magnis sæpe conatibus aduersa.
units.tr: John Mariana, Jesuit of Toledo, On the King, book 1, chapter 6, Mainz edition, p. 57: a king can be stripped of his principate by the people or by the subjects, if they are willing. And from all memory, whoever has undertaken to oppress tyrants has been held in great esteem. He also sets out the method of deposing such a prince: "The easiest and surest way, if there is an opportunity for a public assembly, is that by common consent it be decided what ought to be settled and ratified; and if the prince does not obey the warnings, counsels are to be drawn up, arms made ready, money for the expenses of war to be exacted from the subjects, and the prince himself to be struck down with the sword, even by private authority." And at p. 60: "If the opportunity for a public assembly is taken away, then I will judge that whoever, favouring the public wishes, attempts to kill the king or prince has by no means acted unjustly. And unless there is a public voice of the people which holds the king to be a tyrant, learned and serious men should be called in as counsellors." Mariana adds: "Splendidly, splendidly would it go with human affairs if many men were found with a brave heart, despisers of life and safety for the liberty of their country; and it is a pity that most are held back by the desire for safety, which often thwarts great efforts."

units.la: Tales etiam libri à Iesuita Guignardo scripti Lutetiæ in Collegio Iesuitarum post tentatum à Casfello parricidium Henrici IV. Regis Galliæ inuenti sunt, ut ex actis Parlamenti Parisiensis referuntur in Memor. Ligæ Tom. 6. pag. 256. & sequent.
units.tr: Books of this kind, written by the Jesuit Guignard, were found in Paris in the Jesuit college after the attempted parricide of Henry IV of France by Châtel, as is reported from the acts of the Parlement of Paris in the Mémoires de la Ligue, vol. 6, pp. 256 and following.

units.la: Iesuita Crefvvel, alias Philopater, aduersus edicta Regináe pag. 145. Potestatem Regiam esse juris civilis, Ergo in arbitrio populi esse, Rex quis sit, an non.
units.tr: The Jesuit Crefwel, otherwise called Philopater, against the edicts of the Queen, p. 145: Royal power belongs to civil law; therefore it lies in the judgment of the people who the king is, or whether there is one at all.

units.la: Defensio Iesuitarum in Tom. 6. Memor. Ligæ pag. 281, ubi (ut & a Mariana De Rege pag. 59.) allegatur ad hoc exemplum Aiod. Iudic. 3. Adduntur etiam Pontificij Doctores, Cajet. Dom. Soto, Thom. Aquinas, Sylvester Futmus.
units.tr: The Jesuits' defence in vol. 6 of the Mémoires de la Ligue, p. 281, where (as also in Mariana, On the King, p. 59) Ehud from Judges 3 is cited as an example for this. The Papist teachers Cajetan, Dominic Soto, Thomas Aquinas and Sylvester Prierias are added as well.

units.la: Cardinalis Pelvaei consilium interceptum a Vivonaeo Marchione Pisanc Regis Gall. Legato in Hispania; Monendos Guisianarum partium Sacerdotes, ut dum peccata confitentes, & ad se accedentes consultores audirent, monerent illos, fauendum Lotharingis & Guisianis a Carolo Magno oriundis, a quibus sperandum Romanae religionis labefactentis restaurationem: Henricum Tertium Regno deiiciendum, In Vindic. sec. lib. pag. 13.
units.tr: The counsel of Cardinal Pellevé, intercepted by Vivonne, Marquis of Pisani, the French king's envoy in Spain: The priests of the Guise party are to be advised that, while hearing confessions and when consulted by those who come to them, they should admonish them to favour the Lorrainers and the Guisards, descended from Charlemagne, from whom the restoration of the crumbling Roman religion is to be hoped for; Henry III is to be cast down from the kingdom. In Vindiciae, second book, p. 13.

units.la: Totus Iesuitarum liber De abdicatione Henrici III. Regis Galliæ editus durante adhuc Iesuitarum rebellione anno 1591. Lugduni apud Iohannem Pillehotte, S. Ligæ seu Vnionis Gallicanæ Bibliopolam, ex præcepto Superiorum & cum insignibus Iesuitarum, hoc ipsum quoque docet. Accusatur in eo Henricus III. quod sit impius & impurus Tyrannus, & præclare actum iri, si is cum suis similibus Regibus & Principibus, interficeretur ab uno vel pluribus vasallis aut subditis, non expectata speciali aliqua excommunicatione vel mandato, & qui tale facinus patrent, eo ipso magnam gloriam & vitam æternam consequuturos, atque etiam Reipubl. commodum & utilitatem promoturos esse. Non desinemus etiam, inquit, auxilia & media quærere, quibus Rex ipse, cum omnibus ei adhærentibus, opprimi & interfici possit. Cumque editio libri ad finem perducta & simul Rex à Iacobo Clemente interfectus, Henricus Quartus autem in eius locum Rex creatus esset, in præfatione & fine libelli additum fuit, ut, nulla parricidij Henrici III. ratione habita, huiusmodi libelli, & doctrina hæc in vulgus spargantur, quo sciatur, iure & merito Henricum III. abdicatum & interfectum esse, indeque intelligatur, eius successorem quoque Henricum IV. eodem modo iuste abdicari, & opprimi posse: utque ei adhærentes exemplo Henrici III. monitis, sapere discant, ne in exitium præcipitentur, quod poit necem Henrici IV. ipsis paratum sit: tempus enim iam adesse, quo Regnum Galliæ de gente in Gentem (à Gallis ad Hispanos) transferendum sit.
units.tr: The whole Jesuit book On the Abdication of Henry III, King of France, published in 1591 at Lyon by Jean Pillehotte, bookseller of the Holy League or Gallican Union, while the Jesuit rebellion was still going on, by order of the superiors and bearing the Jesuits' insignia, teaches this same thing. In it Henry III is accused of being an impious and impure tyrant, and it is said that it would be splendidly done if he, together with his like kings and princes, were killed by one or more vassals or subjects, without waiting for any special excommunication or mandate; and that those who carry out such a deed will by that very fact win great glory and eternal life, and will also promote the good and advantage of the commonwealth. "We will not cease," it says, "to seek aids and means by which the king himself, together with all who cling to him, can be crushed and killed." And since the printing of the book was finished and at the same time the king had been killed by Jacques Clément, and Henry IV had been made king in his place, it was added in the preface and at the end of the booklet that, with no account taken of the parricide of Henry III, such booklets and this doctrine should be spread among the public, so that it may be known that Henry III was rightly and deservedly deposed and killed, and so that it may be understood that his successor Henry IV can likewise justly be deposed and crushed; and that his adherents, warned by the example of Henry III, may learn to be wise and not rush headlong to ruin, which is prepared for them after the death of Henry IV; for the time is now at hand when the kingdom of France is to be transferred from nation to nation (from the French to the Spanish).

units.la: Idem etiam docet liber sub nomine Francois de Verone Constantini in lucem editus, hoc titulo; Apologie pour Jean Chastell. Parisien. & pour les peres de la Societe de Jesus: id est, Apologia pro Ioanne Castellio & Iesuitis. Hunc libellum Iesuitae post eiectionem suam ex Gallia scripserunt & ediderunt in Belgio: in eo a principio ad finem usque discipuli sui Ioannis Castellij propositum, quo Henricum IV. perimere conatus est, tamquam heroicum & iustum, laudant & approbant; utramque Henrici III. parricidium, & Castellium merito in numerum Martyrum relatum fuisse affirmant.
units.tr: The same doctrine is taught by a book published under the name of Francois de Verone, Constantine, with this title: Apology for Jean Châtel, of Paris, and for the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits wrote and published this booklet in Belgium after their expulsion from France. Throughout, from beginning to end, they praise and approve the purpose of their disciple Jean Châtel, by which he tried to kill Henry IV, as heroic and just; and they affirm that both the parricide of Henry III and Châtel were rightly counted among the martyrs.

units.la: Eiusdem argumenti est quoque Iesuitae Reinaldi liber, de Iusta Reipub. Christianæ in Reges impios & hæreticos authoritate, iustissimaque Catholicorum confederatione, ad repellendum Henricum Navarræum a Regno; editus sub Guilelmi Rossæi nomine.
units.tr: Of the same kind is also the book of the Jesuit Reinaldus, On the Just Authority of the Christian Commonwealth against Impious and Heretical Kings, and on the Most Just Confederation of Catholics, written to repel Henry of Navarre from the kingdom; it was published under the name of Guillaume Rossée.

units.la: Post tentatum etiam à Castellio Henrici IV. parricidium, decrevit Parlamentum ... lamentum. entum Parisiensc, ut omnia in Collegio Iesuitarum diligenter investigaren- : & cognoverunt inquisitores, Castellij praeceptorem Ioannem Gueret Ietam, hoc ipsum discipulos suos publice ac privatim docuisse, ob eamque cauin perpetuo exilio multatus est. Eademque poena tum etiam affectus est aIesuita Alexander Haius ob similem culpam. Reperti quoque sunt libri Ieæ Guignardi, in quibus parricidium Henrici III. valde commendat, hortaęs subditos, ne Henricum IV. ferant, sed eodem modo eum interficiant. Doibidem, in lanicna Parisina anno 1572. peccatum esse a regis, quod non una in reliquis etiam Henricum Navarraeum iugulárint.
units.tr: After the attempted parricide of Henry IV by Châtel, the Parlement of Paris decreed that everything in the Jesuit college be carefully investigated; and the inquisitors found that Châtel's teacher, the Jesuit Jean Guéret, had taught this same thing to his pupils, both publicly and privately, and for this reason he was punished with perpetual exile. The same penalty was then also imposed on the Jesuit Alexander Hay for a similar fault. Books of the Jesuit Guignard were also found, in which he greatly commends the parricide of Henry III, urging subjects not to tolerate Henry IV but to kill him in the same way. Likewise, in the Paris massacre of 1572 it was a sin on the part of the kings that they did not also cut the throat of Henry of Navarre along with the rest.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: QVARTO docent, Si subditi Lutheranu sive Calvinianu habeant gemaut Principe, qui ipsos in haeresin inducere conetur (ut fit in Anglia) in illos subditos ab omni homagio & obligatione solutos esse: ipsisq; liberu permissum huiusmodi Regem vel Principe abdicare, exterminare & opprimere, licet nihil tale in prima Christi Ecclesia factum sit.
units.tr: Fourthly, they teach that if subjects have a Lutheran or Calvinist prince who tries to lead them into heresy (as happens in England), those subjects are freed from all homage and obligation, and it is lawful for them to depose, expel and crush such a king or prince, although nothing of the kind was done in the first Church of Christ.

units.la: Sic in actis Henrici Garneti Iesuitae pag. 68. An. 26. Regni Elisabethae venit Angliam Parri a Cardinali de Como persuasus, Reginam, ut ex Ecclesia eius m, occidere, & hoc iure optimo licere dicebat.
units.tr: Thus in the acts of the Jesuit Henry Garnet, p. 68: in the twenty-sixth year of Elizabeth's reign, Parry came to England, persuaded by the Cardinal of Como to kill the Queen, as being excommunicated from the Church, and he said that this was entirely lawful.

units.la: Sic dictus Henric. Garnet, Ofwvaldus Tesmond, Ioh. Gerard Iesuitae, cum acomplicibus nuper Anno 1605. in Anglia Regem & Ordines regni in Comipulvere tormentario displodere & perdere conspirarunt: ut ex actis HenriGarneti Londini a Regio Typographo editis apparet, ubi etiam pag. 66. dici- ; Hanc proditionem Iesuiticam proprie appellari, uti ad Iesuitas ex congruo & condispectantem. Hi enim architecti & machinatores exstiterunt; Et in huiusmodi minibus plus peccare auctorem, quam actorem. Idq; confirmatur edicto ReBritanniae publicato 15. Ian. Anno 3. Regis moderni.
units.tr: Thus the aforementioned Henry Garnet, Oswald Tesmond and John Gerard, Jesuits, together with their accomplices, lately in the year 1605 conspired in England to blow up and destroy the King and the estates of the realm with gunpowder, as appears from the acts of Henry Garnet published at London by the royal printer, where also on p. 66 it is said: This treason is properly called Jesuitical, as it is suitable and fitting for the Jesuits to be its authors. For they were the architects and contrivers of it, and in such crimes the instigator sins more than the agent. This is confirmed by the edict of the British realm published on 15 January in the third year of the present king.

units.la: Bellarminus de Rom. Pontifice lib. 5. cap. 7. pag. 1073. & Paulus V Vindeck Deliber. de Haeref. extirp. Antidoto 10. pag. 407. alias rationes habet, Tunc, multi fideles cum gentibus conversabantur, quibus Ecclesiae mansuetudinem commendi expediebat; Ideoq; Christiani suis infestissimis hostib. parcebant. Altera huius manfuetudinis causa; Quod metuebant Christiani Episcopi, ne morte haereticorum patientia Catholicorum obscuraretur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book 5, ch. 7, p. 1073, and Paul V (Vindeck, Deliberation on Extirpating Heresy, Antidote 10, p. 407), give other reasons: At that time many faithful lived among the Gentiles, to whom it was expedient to commend the gentleness of the Church; therefore Christians spared their most hostile enemies. Another cause of this gentleness was that the Christian bishops feared that by the death of heretics the patience of Catholics would be obscured.

units.la: Conradus Brunus de Haereticis lib. 3. cap. ult. num. 13. pag. 309. Non obstat quod Christus non coegit discipulos recedentes, ut redirent: nam tunc Ecclesia in novello germine pullulante, neque Christus, neque Apostoli omni potestate uti voluerunt; Quia nondum completa fuerat prophetia; Et adorabunt eum omnes Reges terrae; omnes gentes Psal. 71. Iam impleta est illa prophetia: merito igitur Ecclesia iam plenissima utitur potestate, ut etiam haereticos redire nolentes & invitos cogat. Iuxta illud Luc. 14. Compelle intrare.
units.tr: Conrad Bruno, On Heretics, book 3, last ch., num. 13, p. 309: It is no objection that Christ did not compel the departing disciples to return; for then the Church was a tender shoot just sprouting, and neither Christ nor the apostles wished to use all their power, because the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled: "And all kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations" (Ps. 71). That prophecy is now fulfilled; rightly therefore the Church now uses its full power, so that it may compel even heretics who are unwilling to return, and against their will. According to that saying in Luke 14: Compel them to come in.

units.la: Alanus in Apologia Stanleianae proditionis, quam etiam publicavit, hoc defendit, Quandoquidem Elizabetha Angliae Regina & haeretica excommunicata esset, quod non modo liceret jam ejus subditis, verum etiam conscientiae nexu tenerentur, nure eam omni quo possent praesidio, & sive exercitus, sive oppida, sive arces & propugna- cula ejus obtinerent, Regi Hispano tradere, ut Regina nihil amplius haberet proprium ut suum.
units.tr: Allen, in his Apology for the Stanley Treason, which he also published, defends this: Since Elizabeth, Queen of England, is a heretic and excommunicated, not only may her subjects now do so, but they are even bound in conscience to deprive her by every means they can, and to hand over to the Spanish King, whether her armies, towns, citadels or fortifications, so that the Queen may have nothing further that is her own.

units.la: Gretscherus contra Stenium sic argumentatur: Omnis ille, qui loquitur quae Deus in praecepit, jure interficitur. Omnis haereticus loquitur quae Deus no praecepit. Ergo. Vies quid maneat orthodoxos non loquentes quae Papa, Papistarū Deus, no praecepit. Vide Stenium in Apologia contra Gretscherū Triumphatum pag. 291. 292.
units.tr: Gretser argues against Stenius thus: Every man who speaks what God has not commanded is lawfully put to death. Every heretic speaks what God has not commanded. Therefore... See what then remains for orthodox men who do not speak what the Pope, the God of the Papists, has not commanded. See Stenius, in his Apology against the Triumph of Gretser, pp. 291, 292.

units.la: Vel si verum Deum intelligat, tum Iesuitae cum suis erutis haeretici & interfici[?] di, quia loquuntur ac docent, quae Deus nunquam praecepit.
units.tr: Or, if he understands the true God, then the Jesuits and their like are heretics and ought to be killed, because they speak and teach what God has never commanded.

units.la: Franciscus Suarez in Defensione fidei Catholicae adversus Anglicanae sectae errores, lib. 6. c. 4. n. 5. pag. 814. & seq. quaestione facta (Liceatne in defensionem propriae vitae Principem occidere) sic ait, Si defensio sit propriae vitae, quam Rex violenter auferre aggreditur, tum quidem ordinarie licebit subdito seipsum defendere, etiam inde mors. Principis sequatur, quia jus tuendae vitae est maximum, & tunc Princeps non est in necessitate, quae obligat subditum ad vitam pro illo perdendam, sed ipse voluntarie & inique in illo discrimine se constituit. Deinde pag. 815. num. 7. ostendit, Tyrannum in titulo, id est, eum, qui vi & injuste Regnum occupavit, posse a privato licite occidi.
units.tr: Francisco Suárez, in his Defence of the Catholic Faith against the Errors of the Anglican Sect, book 6, ch. 4, n. 5, p. 814 and following, raises the question whether it is lawful to kill a prince in defence of one's own life, and says: If the defence is of one's own life, which the king is violently attempting to take away, then indeed it will ordinarily be lawful for the subject to defend himself, even if the prince's death follows from it, because the right to protect one's life is the greatest, and the prince is not in that necessity which obliges the subject to lose his life for him, but he himself voluntarily and unjustly places himself in that danger. Then on p. 815, n. 7, he shows that a tyrant in title, that is, one who has seized the kingdom by force and unjustly, can lawfully be killed by a private person.

units.la: Tum pag. 817. num. 10. citat authores, qui aliter senserunt, & maxime D. Augustinum, qui absolute dicit, sine publica administratione non licere aliquem occidere & num. seq. adhunc modum respondet. Ad Augustinum (inquit) respondeo; Illum privatum hominem, qui hujusmodi tyrannum occidit, non id facere sine publica administratione, quia vel id facit authoritate Reipub. facile consentientis; vel facit authoritate Dei, qui per naturalem legem dedit unicuique potestatem defendendi se, & Remp. suam a vi tyranni, quam similis Tyrannus facit.
units.tr: Then on p. 817, n. 10, he cites authors who thought otherwise, and above all St Augustine, who says absolutely that no one may be killed without public authority, and in the following number he replies in this way: To Augustine (he says) I reply that the private man who kills such a tyrant does not do so without public authority, because he does it either by the authority of the commonwealth, which readily consents, or by the authority of God, who by natural law gave to each person the power of defending himself and his commonwealth from the violence of a tyrant, which a like tyrant exercises.

units.la: Eodem cap. pag. 818. n. 13. sic concludit, non per modum vindictae aut punitionis, sed licere privatae personae hunc tyrannum occidere, & addit, In hoc vero est magna differentia inter hunc & Regem pravum: Nam Rex licet tyrannice gubernet, quandiu non movet actualem bellum injustum contra Rempub. sibi subditam, non infert illi actualem vim & ideo respectu illius non habet locum defensio, neque ullus subditus potest hoc titulo illum aggredi aut bellum contra ipsum movere. At vero proprius tyrannus quamdiu Regnum injuste detinet, & per vim dominatur, semper actu infert vim Reipubl. & ita ipsa semper gerit cum illo actuale seu virtuale bellum, non vindicativum, ut sic dicam, sed defensivum. Et quandiu contrarium non declarat, semper censetur velle defendi a quolibet suorum civium, imo etiam a quolibet extraneo: Ideoque fi aliter defendi non potest, nisi interficiendo tyrannum, cuilibet de populo licet illum interficere. Unde etiam in rigore verum est id non fieri tunc authoritate privata, sed publica, vel potius regni volentis a quolibet civi tanquam a membro & organo suo defendi, vel Dei authoris naturae dantis cuicunque hominum potestatem defendendi innocentem. Unde etiam in hoc non est discrimen inter utrumque tyrannum. Neuter enim potest occidi authoritate privata, sed necessaria semper est potestas publica. Differentia vero est, quod haec potestas censetur commissa cuilibet particulari personae contra proprium tyrannum, non vero contra proprium Dominum propter discrimen declaratum.
units.tr: In the same chapter, p. 818, n. 13, he concludes thus: not by way of vengeance or punishment, but it is lawful for a private person to kill this tyrant, and he adds: There is, however, a great difference between this man and a wicked king. For a king, although he governs tyrannically, so long as he does not actually wage an unjust war against the commonwealth subject to him, does not inflict actual force upon it, and therefore with respect to him there is no place for defence, nor can any subject on this title attack him or make war against him. But a true tyrant, as long as he unjustly holds the kingdom and rules by force, always actually inflicts force on the commonwealth, and so the commonwealth always wages with him an actual or virtual war, not a war of vengeance, so to speak, but a defensive one. And as long as it does not declare otherwise, it is always presumed to wish to be defended by any of its citizens, indeed even by any foreigner; therefore, if it cannot be defended otherwise than by killing the tyrant, it is lawful for anyone of the people to kill him. Hence it is also true in strict sense that this is not done by private authority, but by public authority, or rather by the kingdom wishing to be defended by any citizen as by its own member and organ, or by God the author of nature, who gives to any man whatever the power of defending the innocent. Hence also in this there is no distinction between the two tyrants. For neither can be killed by private authority, but public power is always necessary. The difference, however, is that this power is considered to be committed to any private person against his own tyrant, but not against his own lord, on account of the distinction declared.

units.la: Inde Suarez num. 14. infert, Regem, postquam legitime depositus est, pro vero etiam proprio tyranno haberi, & consequenter non posse in illo subsistere assertionem, quae de legitimo Rege loquitur. Imo (inquit) si Rex talis post depositionem legitimam in sua pertinacia perseverans Regnum per vim retineat, incipit esse tyrannus in titulo: quia non est legitimus Rex, nec justo titulo regnum possidet. Declaratur hoc amplius in Rege haeretico. Nam statim per haeresim ipso facto privatur aliquo modo Dominio, & proprietate sui Regni, quia vel confiscatum manet, vel ad legitimum successorem Catholicum ipso jure transit: & nihilominus non potest statim regno privari, sed juste illud possidet & administrat donec per sententiam saltem declaratoriam criminis condemnetur: juxta c. cum sec. leges de Haer. in 6. At vero post sententiam latam omnino privatur regno, ita ut non possit juste titulo illud possidere. Ergo ex tunc poterit tanquam omnino Tyrannus tractari, & consequenter a quocunque privato poterit occidi.
units.tr: From this Suárez infers at n. 14: that the king, once he has been lawfully deposed, is to be regarded as a true and proper tyrant, and consequently the assertion that speaks of a lawful king cannot stand with regard to him. Indeed (he says) if such a king, persisting in his obstinacy after lawful deposition, holds the kingdom by force, he begins to be a tyrant in title, because he is not a lawful king nor holds the kingdom by a just title. This is made clearer in the case of a heretic king. For by heresy he is at once, by the very fact, deprived in some way of lordship and ownership of his kingdom, because it either remains confiscated or passes by law to a lawful Catholic successor; and yet he cannot immediately be stripped of the kingdom, but possesses and administers it justly until he is condemned by at least a declaratory sentence of the crime, according to c. cum sec. leges, De haereticis, in the sixth book. But after the sentence has been pronounced he is wholly deprived of the kingdom, so that he cannot justly hold it by any title. Therefore from that time he may be treated as a complete tyrant, and consequently may be killed by any private person.

units.la: A quo autem possit fieri talis sententia, tractat num. 15. pag. 819. & ait, Potestatem hanc deponendi Regem esse posse vel in ipsa Rep. vel in S. Pontifice, diversimodo tamen modo. Nam in Rep. (inquit) solum per modum defensionis necessariae ad conservationem suam. Ideoque si Rex legitimus tyrannice gubernet, & regno nullum aliud subditum... remedium adse defendendum nisi Regem expellere ac deponere, tum ex vi juris naturalis poterit Respublica tota publico & communi consilio Civitatum & Procerum, Regem deponere, tum ex vi juris naturalis, quo licet vim vi repellere, tum quia semper hic casus ad propriam Reipub. conservationem necessarius intelligitur exceptus in primo illo fœ-dere, quo Respub. potestatem suam in Regem transtulit, &c. At vero (inquit n. 16.) in S. Pontifice, est hæc potestas tanquam in superiori habente jurisdictionem ad corripiendum Reges etiam supremos tanquam sibi subditos. Unde si crimina sint in materia spirituali, ut est crimen hæresis, potest direcè illa punire in Regem, etiam usque ad depositionem à regno, si pertinacia Regis & providentia communis boni Ecclesiæ ita postulent. Si vero crimina sint in materia temporali: quatenus peccata sunt, etiam potest illa corripere per rectam potestatem; quatenus vero temporaliter nociva Reipublicæ Christianæ, indirectè saltem poterit ea punire, quatenus tyrannicum regimen temporalis Principis semper est saluti animarum perniciosum.
units.tr: Suárez then deals, at n. 15, p. 819, with by whom such a sentence can be given, and says: This power of deposing a king can be in the commonwealth itself or in the Supreme Pontiff, but in different ways. For in the commonwealth (he says) it exists only by way of the defence necessary for its own preservation. Therefore if a lawful king governs tyrannically, and the kingdom has no other remedy to defend itself than to expel and depose the king, then by force of natural law the whole commonwealth, by public and common counsel of the cities and nobles, may depose the king, by force of natural law, by which it is lawful to repel force with force, and because this case is always understood as excepted for the preservation of the commonwealth in that first covenant by which the commonwealth transferred its power to the king, etc. But in the Supreme Pontiff (he says at n. 16) this power is held as in a superior having jurisdiction to chastise even supreme kings as subject to himself. Hence if the crimes are in spiritual matters, as the crime of heresy is, he can directly punish the king with that punishment, even to deposition from the kingdom, if the king's obstinacy and the care for the common good of the Church so require. But if the crimes are in temporal matters, insofar as they are sins, he can also correct them by his proper power; insofar as they are temporally harmful to the Christian commonwealth, he can at least indirectly punish them, inasmuch as the tyrannical rule of a temporal prince is always destructive to the salvation of souls.

units.la: Posthæc, pagina 820. num. 17. & 18. sic ait Suarez: Unde in historiis legimus sæpe semper regna in hujusmodi casibus Pontifices consuluisse, vel etiam ab eo petivisse, ut Regem ineptum vel tyrannum deponeret, ut de Childerico Rege Galliæ tempore Zachariæ Papæ C. alius 15. q. 6.
units.tr: Afterwards, on page 820, numbers 17 and 18, Suarez says thus: "Whence we often read in histories that kingdoms in such cases consulted the Pontiffs, or even asked of him, that he should depose a King who was unfit or a tyrant, as concerning Childeric, King of France, in the time of Pope Zachary, C. alius 15, q. 6."

units.la: Et aliquanto post: Secundò pendet Regnum Christianum à Pontifice in hoc, ut sit Pontifex non solum consulere, aut consentire ut Regnum Regem sibi perniciosum denat, sed etiam præcipere & cogere, ut id faciat, quando saluti spirituali Regni, & præsertim ad vitandas hæreses vel schismata, necessarium esse judicaverit: quia tunc maximè habet locum usus potestatis indirectæ circa temporalia propter spiritualem fi-nem: & quia potest per se immediatè Regem deponere in tali casu: Ergo potest cogere regnum ut id exequatur, si necessarium sit: Alias esset eius potestas non solum inefficax, sed etiam insufficiens, &c.
units.tr: And somewhat later: "Secondly, the Christian kingdom depends on the Pontiff in this, that the Pontiff may not only advise or consent that the kingdom deprive a king who is harmful to it, but may also command and compel it to do so, when he has judged this necessary for the spiritual welfare of the kingdom, and especially for averting heresies or schisms: for then above all the exercise of the indirect power over temporal matters for a spiritual end has its place; and because he can himself directly depose the King in such a case, therefore he can compel the kingdom to carry this out, if it be necessary. Otherwise his power would be not only ineffective but also insufficient, etc."

units.la: Hoc ergo supposito fundamento dicendum est (inquit Suarez) post sententiam condenatoriam Regis de regni privatione latam per legitimam potestatem, vel (quod perinde est) post sententiam declaratoriam criminis habentis talem pœnam ipso jure impositam, posse quidem eum, qui sententiam tulit, vel cui ipse commiserit, Regem privare regno, etiam illum interficiendo, si aliter non potuerit, vel si justa sententia ad hanc etiam pœnam extendatur, &c. Deinde paulò post addit: Ita ergo quando Respub. justè potest regem deponere, tunc faciunt ministri eius Regem cogendo, vel interficiendo, si sit necessarium, quia jam non potestate privata, sed publica operantur. Sicque recè dixit Soto lib. 5. de instit. q. 1. art. 4. Licet Rex in solo Regimine tyrannus non possit à quolibet interfici, lata vero sententia ab ipsa (inquit) potest institui executionis minister. Eodemque modo, si Papa Regem depo-suit, ab illis tantum poterit expelli vel interfici, quibus ipse id commiserit. Quod si nulli executionem imperet, pertinebit ad legitimum in regno successorem, vel si nullus invectus fuerit, ad regnum ipsum spectabit. Quod quidem apertius etiam declaratur in pag. seq. n. ubi ita concludit: Ideo ut dicebam (inquit) solus legitimus successor ejus si Catholicus sit, habet tunc illam facultatem, vel si ipse negligat, vel nullus sit, communitas Regni illo jure successeret, dummodo sit Catholica. Ipsa vero petente auxilium ab aliis Principibus, illam præstare poterunt, ut per se constat. Si autem Pontifex (quod sæpius fecisse explis ostensum est in lib. 3.) aliis Regibus potestatem tribuat invadendi tale regnum, tum sè fieri potest, quia neque deest justa causa, nec potestas.
units.tr: With this foundation laid down, it must be said (says Suarez) that after a sentence of condemnation depriving the King of his kingdom, passed by lawful authority, or (which comes to the same thing) after a declaratory sentence of a crime carrying such a penalty imposed by law itself, the one who pronounced the sentence, or the one to whom he has committed it, may indeed deprive the King of the kingdom, even by killing him, if he cannot otherwise do so, or if the just sentence extends to this penalty as well, etc. Then a little later he adds: "So when the commonwealth can justly depose the king, then its ministers act by compelling him, or by killing him if this is necessary, because they now act not by private power but by public power. And so Soto rightly said, in book 5 of De iustitia et iure, question 1, article 4: 'Although a king who is a tyrant only in his rule cannot be killed by just anyone, once sentence has been pronounced, a minister of execution can be appointed by that sentence.' And in the same way, if the Pope has deposed a King, he may be expelled or killed only by those to whom he has himself committed this. But if he commands no one to carry out the execution, it will belong to the lawful successor in the kingdom, or if none has been installed, to the kingdom itself." This is declared still more plainly on the following page, number ..., where he concludes thus: "Therefore, as I was saying, the sole lawful successor, if he is Catholic, has that power then; or if he neglects it, or if there is none, the community of the kingdom would succeed by that right, provided it is Catholic. And if it asks for help from other princes, they may give it, as is clear of itself. But if the Pontiff (as has been shown at length in book 3 that he has often done) grants to other kings the power of invading such a kingdom, then this may be done, since there is neither lack of just cause nor of authority."

units.la: Ex eod. lib. 6. pag. 834. num. 22. Si Rex (inquit) per justam Papæ sententiam ipso facto depositus, eo ipso, qui antea erant illi subditi, desinunt esse subditi. Nam Rex ipse non esset Rex, nec superior, ideoque neque jam possent proprie dici proditiones, si quæ conjurationes contra ipsum fierent, neque cives tenerentur saltem titulo fidelitatis aut subjectionis ei revelare. Et num. seq. addit: Si post Regem depositum aliqui per privatas insidias, & acceptâ à legitimo judice potestate, illi mortem machinarentur, qui extra confessionem scitum esset conscius, obligari posset ex charitate eas detegere, ut malū proximi impediret, concurrentibus circumstantijs, quæ ad talem obligationem necessaria esse solent. Quando vero contra personam talis Regis juxta tenorem justæ sententiæ procederetur, non excedendo limites potestatis à legitimo judice concessæ, tunc cessaret omnis obligatio detegendi secretum, quia jam illæ non effent insidiæ iniquæ, sed effet justum bellum.
units.tr: From the same book 6, page 834, number 22: "If a King has been deposed by a just sentence of the Pope, by that very fact those who were previously his subjects cease to be subjects. For the King himself would no longer be King nor superior, and therefore neither could treasons properly be spoken of, if any conspiracies were made against him, nor would citizens be bound, at least by the title of fidelity or subjection, to reveal them to him." And the following number adds: "If after the deposed King some men were plotting his death by private snares, having received power from a lawful judge, and someone outside confession had knowledge of it, he could be bound out of charity to disclose it, so as to prevent his neighbour's harm, when the circumstances which are usually necessary for such an obligation concur. But when proceedings are taken against the person of such a King according to the tenor of a just sentence, not exceeding the limits of the power granted by the lawful judge, then every obligation to disclose the secret would cease, because those would no longer be wicked snares but a just war."

units.la: Eodem lib. 6. c. 844. n. 8.
