units.tr: a cruel mind to treachery.

units.la: Gallia & in media conscripto milite regnas,
units.tr: Gaul, you reign even in the midst of war, with your soldiers enrolled,

units.la: Diraq; fraterno nomine bella geris.
units.tr: and you wage dire wars under the name of brotherhood.

units.la: Nempe tua à bello cunctorum fonte malorum
units.tr: Indeed, from the source of all evils, your sect, which was born of war,

units.la: Secta fata est: bellu hinc nunc et adulta ferit.
units.tr: has grown up and now strikes with war.

units.la: Aspice Carrafam, placida qui tempora vita
units.tr: Look at Carafa, who spent his peaceful life

units.la: Impendit studijs, secta profana, tuis:
units.tr: on your studies, profane sect.

units.la: Mox septem impositas insedit collibus arces,
units.tr: Soon he settled the citadels set upon the seven hills,

units.la: Cornua terrificis intonuere minis.
units.tr: and the horns thundered with terrifying threats.

units.la: Tympanaq; Italiam confestim audita per omnem
units.tr: Drums, heard at once throughout all Italy,

units.la: Vrbis & ad portas Hannibal alter adest.
units.tr: and another Hannibal stands at the gates of the city.

units.la: Nosq; leves adeò, nos, credula pectora, Galli
units.tr: And us, so light, so credulous in heart, the French

units.la: Ad bellum infausta sollicitamur ave.
units.tr: stir up to war with an ill-omened bird.

units.la: Protinus induciæ violantur patre Quiritum
units.tr: Straightway the truce is broken at the instigation of the Roman father,

units.la: Auctore, & Martis nuncius urbe venit.
units.tr: and the messenger of Mars comes to the city.

units.la: Pignora jam belli rutilant, micat igneus ensis:
units.tr: Now the pledges of war gleam, the fiery sword flashes,

units.la: Livida adhuc stridens à Phlegethontis aqua.
units.tr: still hissing, livid, from the waters of Phlegethon.

units.la: Hæc infelicis Gallis primordia belli,
units.tr: These are the first beginnings of war, unhappy for the French,

units.la: Quod nos exitio nostraq; pæne dedit.
units.tr: which almost gave us over to destruction and ruin.

units.la: Hûc ergò huc animos, terræ qui sceptra tenetis:
units.tr: Turn your minds here, you who hold the sceptres of the earth:

units.la: Nunc velo moto cernere vera licet.
units.tr: now that the veil is drawn back, it is permitted to see the truth.

units.la: Causa hæc vestra agitur, nam credite, vestra potentia
units.tr: This cause is yours, for believe me, your power

units.la: In vita HENRICI vertitur ecce salus.
units.tr: lies, behold, in the life of Henry, and your safety with it.

units.la: Ille quidem petitur, sed per latus illius omnes,
units.tr: He indeed is the one aimed at, but through his side, believe me, you kings,

units.la: Credite, vos Reges, mens nisi læva, peti.
units.tr: all of you are attacked, unless your mind is perverse.

units.la: Nullus jam miseris toto patet orbe receptus,
units.tr: No refuge now lies open to the wretched anywhere in the whole world,

units.la: Præsentem ostentant obvia cuncta necem.
units.tr: and every object before them displays imminent death.

units.la: Nil secarum usquam est, stimulis furialibus actus
units.tr: Nowhere is there anything safe; driven by furious goads

units.la: Percussor, quo quò vertitis ora, latet.
units.tr: the assassin lurks, wherever you turn your faces.

units.la: Nam quibus ex cubijs Majestas Regia post hac,
units.tr: For from what chambers, after this, can royal majesty

units.la: Aut quo stipatu vivere tuta queat?
units.tr: or with what retinue can it live in safety?

units.la: Si pueri discunt his vitam odisse magistris,
units.tr: If boys learn from these masters to hate life,

units.la: Extrema & mortis temnere supplicia?
units.tr: and to despise even the extreme torments of death?

units.la: Si tormenta pati possunt, nilq; inde fateri,
units.tr: If they can endure torture and confess nothing,

units.la: Hacq; polum sperant scandere posse viâ?
units.tr: and hope to climb to heaven by this way?

units.la: In vitam alterius nil non permittitur illi,
units.tr: Against the life of another nothing is forbidden to him

units.la: Cui propria est odio negligitúrve salus?
units.tr: for whom his own safety is an object of hatred or is neglected?

units.la: Mentibus hinc teneris glisicit præposterus ardor,
units.tr: Hence a perverse ardour creeps into tender minds,

units.la: Et cacos juvenes in scelus omne rapit.
units.tr: and drags the blinded youths into every crime.

units.la: Heu sapimus sero, sapimus tamen, atq; potenti
units.tr: Alas, we grow wise too late, yet we grow wise, and it lies open that

units.la: Esse Deo curæ Gallica sceptra patet:
units.tr: the Gallic sceptre is a care to almighty God.

units.la: Qui nos admonitos, tacta tam leniter aure,
units.tr: He, who has touched our ears so gently, admonishing us,

units.la: De propria memores esse salute jubet.
units.tr: bids us remember our own salvation.

units.la: Vos Veneti vidit prudentia cana Senatus,
units.tr: The hoary prudence of the Venetian Senate saw you, saw you,

units.la: Vidit, & est nostris reddita cauta malis.
units.tr: and what was learned by caution has been returned to our misfortunes.

units.la: Dum timida secreta his credere mentis ephebos
units.tr: While it forbids the timid youths to entrust their secrets to these foxes,

units.la: Vulpibus, atq; animi pondere vota vetat:
units.tr: and their vows to the weight of their minds,

units.la: Dumq; sub his operam studijs navare magistris,
units.tr: and while it prevents them from devoting their effort to studies under these masters,

units.la: Et ferulæ prohibet suppositíssemanum.
units.tr: and from putting their hands under the cane.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: Concerning Doctrine

units.la: Vos quoq;, quos cœli rector diademate cinxit, Hoc sapere exemplo discite, noxa prope est: Nec temerè errones in regna admittite vestra, Hostis si quis erit, præbeat hospitium. Sentiet is præsto damnum, recteq; monenti Flebit, at heu sero, non habuisse fidem. Mitior infames exercuit ira volucres, Quas Phinei mensis incubuisse ferunt. Nempe per hos factum, divinæ ut vocis apud nos Esset ubiq; fames, esset ubiq; sitis. Quis Deus alipedes Arctoo ex axe gemellos Misit, & ætheria monstra fugavit ope? Fercula nunc nullo fœtentia sumere tactu, Nunc licet è puro fonte levare sitim. Reddita libertas nunc pristina, reddita regno Majestas: sacris nunc quoque constat honos. Dicere nunc verum licet, atque audire vicissim, In Dei templo nunc bona verba sonant: Nullaq; mendacì ponet jam præmia linguæ, Venalis ve animas stator Iherus emet. Turba inimica vale, non exarsisse furore Centauros tanto fabula prisca refert. Marte Pelethonijs ausos confligere iniquo Convivæ rapta conjuge Pirithoi: Quos prius Alcides casum indignatus amici Lernea fixos grandine strav it humi. Quid loquor? Alcidæ est inflicta injuria nostro, Nec tamen Alcidæ est ultio facta manu: Nempe quod hic Grajo generosior Hercule Gallus, Turba Ixionio pejor ut ista grege est: Quæ gremio sponsam conata revellere nostro Sacra inter mensæ bella cruenta movet, Monstrorum^q; dolo domitorem aggressa nefando Nunc passim nostro crimine monstra facit. Non mihi vaticino pectus quod turgeat æstro Glorior, aut intus numen habere puto: Sed si præsaga non me prudentia mentis Decipit, hæc alios deinde pericla manent. Tuq; adeò nostris nimis heu conterminus oris, Grande domi fratrum qui miser agmen alis: Si sapis à magno tibi missa hæc Rege putato Præsidia, haud arces vi subitura tuas: Sed quæ compedibus mentes animosq; tuorum, Et duris stringant nexibus ingenia. Mutatoq; procul coget abire solo. Cum volet ille per hos te finibus exiget hostes, Et nisi sponte feras, nigrum damnabit ad Orcum: Namq; etiam in Stygios jus habet ille lacus. Tu quoq; Vindelicos, qui, Gallica nomina, Bojos, Qui trans Danubium Norica Regna tenes.
units.tr: You too, whom the Ruler of heaven has crowned with a diadem, learn to be wise from this example: the harm is nearly at hand. Do not carelessly admit wandering teachers into your kingdoms; if any enemy should be offered hospitality, he will at once feel the damage. He will weep, but alas too late, that he did not heed the one who warned him rightly. A milder anger afflicted the foul birds, which they say settled on the table of Phineus. Through them it came about that among us the divine word was everywhere hungry and everywhere thirsty. What God sent the two winged twins from the Arctic pole, and put the heavenly monsters to flight by his power? Now we may take food that is no longer fouled by any touch, now we may lift our thirst from a pure spring. Our ancient liberty is restored now, and majesty is restored to the kingdom; now too the honour of sacred things stands firm. Now it is lawful to speak the truth and in turn to hear it; now good words sound in the temple of God. No more shall the reward of the lying tongue be paid, and no venal Iherus, the hireling bailiff, shall buy souls. Begone, hostile crowd; the old fable tells how the Centaurs were not so inflamed with fury. The guests of Pirithous, who dared to fight with unequal war at Pelethronium over the stolen bride, were struck down on the ground by Alcides, who first, indignant at his friend's wrong, pierced them with Lernaean hail. Why do I speak of this? A wrong has been done to our Hercules, yet no vengeance has been wrought by the hand of Hercules. For this Gaul is less noble than the Greek Hercules, and this crowd is worse than the Ixionian herd, which, trying to tear the bride from our bosom, stirs up bloody wars amid the sacred feast, and, having attacked the tamer of monsters with unspeakable treachery, now makes monsters everywhere by our fault. I do not boast that my breast swells with prophetic frenzy, or that I think a divinity dwells within me. But if my mind's foresight does not deceive me, other dangers still await. And you, alas, who are too close a neighbour to our borders, who with your wretched swarm of brothers flap great wings at home: if you are wise, consider these garrisons sent to you by a great King; they will not come to take your citadels by force, but to bind the minds and spirits of your people with fetters and hard knots, and they will compel you to leave your land and go elsewhere. When he wishes, he will drive you from your lands as enemies through these men, and unless you bear it willingly, he will condemn you to black Orcus; for he has right even over the Stygian lakes. You also, who hold the Vindelici, the Boii (who are called Gallic names), and the Norican realms beyond the Danube.

units.la: Quòq; juves Patres, vestem queis Fibula nestit, Effundis totas luxuriosus opes: Sumptibus immodicis acceptaque damna dolebit, Ingentem ingratam qui periere, nepos: Bello internecino cum dulcia patris avitæ Otiamutabit seditiosa cohors, Et tua regna dabit placito rapienda tyranno, Quippe sibi id proprio jure licere putat. Quin procul ad fuscos gens dira remittitur Indos! Illic mira canunt edere facta Patres. Illic religio per sola silentia crescit, Nec res verbo agitur, jussit ut ille, Dei. Consita sed grauis in sacra rosaria ramos Fundit, & in ramis multa sigilla gerit. His, quibus inter nos periit artibus, incipit illic Religio, in cunis mox peritura suis: Et noua cunēta placent, quoniam novis orbis & ille est, Ex prisca superest & pietate nihil. At procul Harpyiæ hinc, procul hinc Ixione nati Semiferi, gravidæ nubis inane genus Este novi procul hinc, hominum delicia, cultus, Et quæ sponte sibi numina quisq; facit. Gallia (nam decorat Gallos hac laude vetustas) Non alit in gremio talia monstra suo. Nos juvat antiquo vitam producere ritu, Nos juvat in prisca simplicitate mori.
units.tr: You also, who help the fathers whose clothing the brooch fastens, you lavish all your wealth in luxury. Your grandson will grieve at the immoderate expenses and at the losses he has received, he who has perished as a great and ungrateful heir. The seditious band will exchange your sweet ancestral Otium for a war of mutual slaughter, and it will give your kingdoms to be seized by a pleasing tyrant, since it thinks it may do so by its own right. Indeed, let that dreadful race be sent far away to the dark Indians! There the fathers sing that they perform wonderful deeds. There religion grows only through silence, and affairs are not conducted by the word, as God commanded. But the rose-garden planted there spreads heavy branches, and bears many images on its boughs. By those arts through which religion perished among us, it begins there, soon to perish in its own cradle. And all new things please, since that world too is new, and nothing of the old piety remains. But far from here, far from here, you Harpies, sons of Ixion, half-beast, empty race of the pregnant cloud! Be far from here, new things, delights of men, worship, and whatever gods each man makes for himself. France (for antiquity adorns the French with this praise) does not nourish such monsters in her bosom. It pleases us to lead our life in the ancient manner, it pleases us to die in ancient simplicity.

units.la: Claudius igitur de Aquaviva Præpositus Generalis Iesuitarum, cum hæc procurator adeum retulisset, simulq; intellexisset, Mariānæ librum in Gallia damnatum, hanc doctrinam haud obscure etiam improbavit, seriòne an dolo, & sucum faceret Regibus, alij iudicent: Respondit enim, Primum collaudare se idium, iudiciumq; Provinciæ; deinde ægerrimè tulisse, quòd libri si ante essi essent, quàm eius rei quicquam ad se deferretur. Cæterum, & ubi primum m accepisset, mandasse uti corrigerentur, & sedulo daturum operam, ne quid usmodi in posterum accideret. Neque eo contentus, decretum etiam addidit shemens & graue, ne quis posthac ex Iesuitis aut publicè quicquam scriberet, doceret: aut privatim consilium cuiquam daret, quod in Regum & Principum cædem, perniciemq; ulla ratione vergeret. Verba eius hæc sunt:
units.tr: Claudius Aquaviva, therefore, the General Prefect of the Jesuits, when his agent had reported these things to him, and at the same time had learned that Mariana's book had been condemned in France, did not hide his disapproval of this doctrine. Whether he did so in earnest or by guile, to put on a show before the kings, let others judge. For he replied that, first, he commended the zeal and judgement of the Province; then, that he had taken it very ill that the book had been published before anything about the matter had been reported to him. Moreover, as soon as he had received word, he had ordered that the book be corrected, and he would take care diligently that nothing of the kind happened in future. Not content with this, he also added a decree, severe and grave, that no one of the Jesuits should from now on publicly write or teach anything, or privately give advice to anyone, that tended in any way to the murder or destruction of kings and princes. His words are these:

units.la: QVANDOQVIDEM Societatis scriptoribus, ac Theologis, qui docent, cæteris omnibus operarijs haud satis est id solum prouidere, quod in aliorum scriptorum libris peritur, sed illud etiā apprimè considerandum, sintne opiniones validis nixæ fundamentis, tutæ, probatæ, scandalis, aut alijs incommodis minimè obnoxiæ: Ideò sane justissimas causas, quæ ad hoc consilij nos impellunt, præsenti decreto præcipimus in virtute sanctæ obedientiæ, sub pœna excommunicationis, & inhabilitatis ad quævis officia, suspensionis à diuinis & aliis arbitrio nostro reseruatis, ne quis deinceps nostræ Societatis Religiosus publicè, aut privatim prælegendo, seu consulendo, multò etiam minus libros conscribendo affirmare præsumat, licitum esse cuicunque personæ, quocunq; prætextu tyrannidis, Reges aut Principes occidere, seu mortem eis machinari. Ne videlicet isto prætextu ad perniciem Principum aperiatur via atque ad turbandam pacem, eorumque securitatem dubium vocandam, quos potius ex diuino mandato reuereri, ac obseruare oportear, nunquam personas sacras à Domino Deo pro felici populorum gubernatione in eo grad⁠u constitutas. Provinciales autem, qui aliquid horum resciverint, nec emendaverint, aut non prævenerint hujusmodi incommoda efficiendo, ut hoc decretum sanctè observetur, volumus eos non modò prædictas pœnas incurrere, sed etiam officio privari. Ut sic omnes intelligant, quis sit ea de re Societatis sensus, neque privati unius error suspectam reddat societatem universam, quum apud aquos rerum æstimatores certum sit, partis unius, aut membri culpam toti corpori reliquo attribui jure non debere. Volumus præterea, ut Provinciales de hoc accepto decreto certiores nos faciant, idemque per suam quisque Provinciam curent promulgandum, & in singulis domibus & collegiis referendum in libros ordinationum ad perpetuam eius memoriam.
units.tr: SINCE it is not enough for the writers and theologians of the Society, who teach, to take care only of what is found in the books of other writers, but it must also be considered most carefully whether opinions rest on firm foundations, are safe, approved, and not liable to scandals or other inconveniences: therefore, for the most just reasons that move us to this decision, we by the present decree command, in the virtue of holy obedience, under penalty of excommunication, and of disqualification from all offices, and of suspension from divine offices and from others reserved to our judgement, that no religious of our Society shall from now on presume to affirm, publicly or privately, whether in lecturing or in counselling, and much less in writing books, that it is lawful for any person, under any pretext of tyranny, to kill kings or princes, or to plot their death. Otherwise, under this pretext, a way would be opened to the destruction of princes and to the disturbance of peace, and their security would be made doubtful, whom we ought rather, by divine command, to revere and obey, since sacred persons, placed by the Lord God in such a rank for the happy government of peoples, must never be harmed. Moreover, we wish that the Provincials, who learn anything of these things and do not correct them, or do not forestall such inconveniences, should, so that this decree may be holily observed, incur not only the aforesaid penalties but also be deprived of their office. So that everyone may understand what the sentiment of the Society is on this matter, and so that the error of one private person may not make the whole Society suspect, since it is certain among fair judges of affairs that the fault of one part or member ought by right not to be attributed to the rest of the body. We wish furthermore that the Provincials inform us of this decree once received, and that each of them see to its publication throughout his own Province, and that it be entered in the books of ordinances in each house and college, for its perpetual memory.

units.la: Est & hoc superioribus addendum, quod tyrannis & excommunicatio non tollit iura politica & civilis societatis, quemadmodum nec ipsa infidelitas vel apostasia aperta à Deo tollit ea. Nam infidelis & apostata Imperator, qualis Iulianus olim, manet Imperator, & magistratus, & pro tali à Christianis agnitus est. Ergo falsa est Iesuitarum & Scholasticorum sententia, qui volunt, non esse parendum Principibus tyrannis & excommunicatis: & contrà sentire videtur Thomas Aquinas in 2. secundæ quæst. 10. Sigebertus etiam Monachus scribit in Odone pagina 101. hanc doctrinam & novam & hæretica esse, quæ iubet, ne hypocritis Principibus, id est, excommunicatis pareamus, quam Hildebrandus, qui & Gregorius 7. Papa primus promulgasse videtur, quum veteres Christiani Iuliano Apostatæ paruerint: Ambrosius Theodosio à se excommunicato: Apostoli etiam infidelibus & persequutoribus Ecclesiæ Principibus, qualis Nero, Domitianus, &c. paruerunt.
units.tr: This too must be added to what has been said above: tyranny and excommunication do not take away the political and civil rights of society, just as even unbelief or open apostasy from God does not take them away. For an unbelieving and apostate Emperor, such as Julian once was, remains Emperor and magistrate, and as such was acknowledged by Christians. Therefore the opinion of the Jesuits and the Schoolmen is false, who hold that tyrannical and excommunicated princes are not to be obeyed; and Thomas Aquinas seems to think otherwise, in the second part of the second part, question 10. Sigebert the Monk also writes, in his work on Odo, page 101, that this doctrine, which bids us not to obey hypocritical princes, that is, excommunicated ones, is both new and heretical; it seems that Hildebrand, who is also called Gregory VII, was the first Pope to promulgate it, whereas the early Christians obeyed the apostate Julian, and Ambrose obeyed Theodosius, although he had excommunicated him; and the Apostles too obeyed unbelieving princes who persecuted the Church, such as Nero, Domitian, and so on.

units.la: Anno etiam 1614. edita est in lucem cum Iesuita Sicario Apodixis, quâ multis gravissimis argumentis ac rationibus probatur, Non licitum esse Subdito maledicere Regi vel Principi suo: multoque minus personam eius adoriri, obtruncare & interficere. Ex multis pauca referam.
units.tr: In the year 1614 also, a work was published together with the Jesuit assassin, the Apodixis, in which it is proved by many most weighty arguments and reasons that it is not lawful for a subject to speak evil of his King or Prince, much less to attack, cut down, or kill his person. I will report a few of the many.

units.la: Quod ad Maledicentiam attinet ea in S. Scriptura expressè prohibetur. In Exodo dicitur, Deos ne exsecrator: & Principi in populo tuo ne maledicito. Hoc mandatum formidabilius reddiderunt horrendæ pœnæ, quas Deus ipse sumsit de iis, qui illud non observârunt. Exemplum habemus in Aarone & Maria, quum contra Mosem murmurâssent ob Æthiopissam fœminam. Hoc simplici murmure iritatus Deus ab iis abiit, & Maria leprosa facta est. Ex his colligitur, si lege Dei puniuntur, qui Principi suo maledicunt, quid iis fiet, qui Reges suos & Principes adoriuntur ac interficiunt. David etsi Saul esset tyrannus, iniuste eum persequeretur, & magnum Sacerdotum numerum crudelissimè interficeret; personam tamen eius adoriri noluit, quantumvis commoditate optimâ ad id instructus esset: imo servum, qui mortem eius acceleraverat, licet ab hero sollicitatus, e medio tollendum curavit. Excommunicantur etiam tales & Satanæ traduntur Conciliis aliquot, ut paulo ante indicavimus.
units.tr: As regards slander, Scripture expressly forbids it. In Exodus it says: "You shall not revile the gods, nor curse a ruler among your people." The horrible punishments that God himself inflicted on those who did not observe this command have made the commandment more formidable. We have an example in Aaron and Miriam, when they murmured against Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman. God was angered by this mere murmuring, withdrew from them, and Miriam became leprous. From this it is gathered that if those who curse their prince are punished by the law of God, what will become of those who attack and kill their kings and princes? David, although Saul was a tyrant, unjustly persecuted him and most cruelly slew a great number of priests, nevertheless refused to attack his person, however well he was placed for doing so by the best opportunity. Indeed, he took care to remove the servant who had hastened Saul's death, even though he had been solicited by his master. Such men are also excommunicated and delivered to Satan by several councils, as we indicated a little earlier.

units.la: MYSTERIVM IESVITARVM QVO INITIARE SOLENT EVM, QVEM AD PRINCIPIS alicujus parricidium induxerunt: ubi & de Meditationum eorum Camera: & Origine doctrinæ Iesuitarum de parricidijs.
units.tr: THE MYSTERY OF THE JESUITS, BY WHICH THEY USUALLY INITIATE THE MAN WHOM THEY HAVE LED TO THE MURDER OF SOME PRINCE: WHERE ALSO CONCERNING THEIR CHAMBER OF MEDITATIONS AND THE ORIGIN OF THE JESUITS' DOCTRINE ON PARRICIDE.

units.la: TEsuitæ cubilia habent mystica & exorcizata in quibus, quos ad facinus patrandum destinaverunt, benedicendi, sanctificandi, & in beatorum ac cœlitum ceteritatem adscribendi introducuntur. Exstat Processus integer Delphis apud Iohannem Andreæ bibliopolam excusus, quem quia non ingratum Lectori futurum confido, totum hoc loco adponendum censui. Habet autem in hunc modum. Is cui cædem Domini, aut Principis sui suscipiendam Iesuitæ persuaserunt, infelix homo in meditatorium seu oratorium secreto introduci solet. Ibi culter inteolo, involutus & eburnâ circumque circâ characteribus variegatâ cistulâ, in qua agno Dei inclusus profertur. Quem, dum e vagina educitur, aquæ benedictæ guttis stillatim irrorant, & globulos corallinos consecratos manubrio appendunt, indulgentiâ factâ, ut quot ictibus necandum Principem petitus esset, totidem animas ex purgatorio educeret. Tum cultrum parricidæ in manum præbent, hisce verbis commendantes: Electe fili Dei, accipe gladium Ephte, gladium Samsonis, gladium Davidis, quo Goliatho caput præcidit, gladium Gedeonis, gladium Iudithæ, gladium Maccabæorum, gladium Papæ Ulij secundi, quo se a principum manibus, plurimo civitatum sanguine fuso, liberavit. Vade & esto prudenter animosus. Deus brachium tuum confortet. Quo facto omnes in genua procidunt, & primarius ex eis talem recitat exorcismum. Adeste Cherubim, adeste Seraphim, vos Throni, vos potestates, adeste vos sancti angeli, & replete beatum hoc vas perpetuâ gloriâ, & quotidie illi offerte coronam B. Mariæ virginis SS. Patriarcharum & Martyrum. Non amplius nostri est, sed vestri consortij particeps. Et tu Deus, qui terribilis & vincibilis es, qui vel ei in meditatorio, ac oratorio suo, ut Tyrannû, ac Hæreticum extinguere, & coronam eius in Catholicum Regem conferre vellet, revelasti; cuius obora quæsumus huius, quem ad id opus consecravimus, membra: adauge ius vires, ut voluntatem suam perficere possit: da ei loricam divini potentem, quâ comprehendentium manus effugiat: da ei alas, quibus sancta eius memora Barbarorum proditorum conatus vitabunda evadant: effunde in eius animam lætificantes tuos radios, quibus corpus, omni metu depositò, in mediis periculis & cruciatibus gaudio & exsultatione perfusum anim etur. Hoc persecto exorcismo ducitur parricida ante altare, in cuius pinace depicta est historia Iacobi Clementis, Monachi Dominicani, cum imaginibus Angelorum eum protegentium ad cœlumq; ducentium. Hanc ei Iesuitæ ostendunt, & simul praesentant cœlestem coronam, dicentes, Domine, respice hic brachium tuum & exaudi ecurorem iustitiæ tuæ: Omnes sancti assurgant, & huic locum cedant. Quibus omnibus completis, quatuor tantùm Iesuitæ deputati sunt, qui soli cum parricida colloquantur. Hi inter sermones sæpe dicere solent, divinâ quandam in eo laritatem apparere, cuius radijs permoveantur ad manus eius & pedes oscuandos: nec amplius sibi eum hominem videri, sed iam in divis repositum. Sese etiam assimulant, quasi tantam ei gloriam ac beatitudinem, ad quam iam nunc provectus, sit invideant, ingemendo dicentes: Quod utinam Deus me tuo loco legisset, & hac ratione confirmasset, ut liberatus à pœnis purgatorij, rectâ via in paradisum perducerer. Quod si vero is, quem idoneum esse rentur parricidio perpetrando, tergiversetur & persuasionibus recalcitret, tum aut terriculamentis nocturnis, monstrorumque occurfaculis ad votum, quod eiusmodi concipiendum adigunt, aut per subornatas D. Mariæ virginis, vel Angelorum, vel aliorum cœlitum, nec non ipsius aliquando Ignatij ac sociorum eius personas ἀπὸ μηχανῆς apparenies ad facinus animant, & inducunt. Ita scelerati isti & parricidiales magistri, nunc formidine pœnæ, nunc adumbratæ virtutis amore incautos adolescentes miseris, & ô vindicandis exemplis circumscribunt, & in animæ pariter corporisq; discrimina præcipitant. Genus hominum in Oriente fuisse memorant, quos plerique Historicorum Assassinos, Pius Papa & Nicolaus Gillius Arsacidas, Nicetas Chasios nominarunt. Hi Mahumetanæ disciplinæ addicti novam sibi sectam instituerunt, cuius Præfecto Generali sedem Muletæ, qui locus sanctus habebatur ordinavere. Auctor sectæ ac princeps ALAODIM quidam fuisse perhibetur, miles veteranus, vulgò Senex de Montanis, à suis Pater & Propheta dictus. Iste sub se & Rectores alios habuit, qui Palatia munita, splendida, & admodum quàm elegantia amœna hortorum colebant. Ratio & disciplinæ institutum in tuenda absoluta Prophetæ ac Principis sui autoritate super universas gentes vertebatur. In eam rem ipsa Palatia sive Collegia instituta, ut studiosam iuventutem ad Mahumeti legem, Alcorano comprehensam, conformarent, & delectu ingeniorum habito, iuvenes audaciores ac ferociori animo præditos observarent, secernerent, segregarentque.
units.tr: The Jesuits have mystical, exorcised lairs in which those whom they have designated for carrying out the deed are introduced to be blessed, sanctified, and enrolled among the blessed and the heavenly host. A complete proceeding survives, printed at Delft by the bookseller Johannes Andreae. I trust it will not be unwelcome to the reader, so I have thought fit to append the whole of it here. It runs as follows. The unhappy man whom the Jesuits have persuaded to undertake the murder of his lord or prince is usually led secretly into a meditation room or oratory. There a knife is presented, wrapped in ivory and variegated all round with characters, in a small case in which the Lamb of God is enclosed. As it is drawn from its sheath they sprinkle it drop by drop with holy water, and they hang consecrated coral beads on the handle, with an indulgence granted that as many souls as there are blows aimed at the prince who is to be killed, so many shall be released from purgatory. Then they put the knife into the parricide's hand, commending him in these words: "Chosen son of God, take the sword of Jephthah, the sword of Samson, the sword of David with which he cut off the head of Goliath, the sword of Gideon, the sword of Judith, the sword of the Maccabees, the sword of Pope Julius II, with which he freed himself from the hands of princes, after much blood of cities had been shed. Go, and be wisely bold. May God strengthen your arm." When this is done, they all kneel, and the foremost of them recites an exorcism of this kind: "Come, Cherubim; come, Seraphim; you Thrones, you Powers, come, you holy angels, and fill this blessed vessel with perpetual glory, and offer him daily the crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary, of the holy Patriarchs and Martyrs. He is no longer ours but a sharer in your fellowship. And you, God, who are terrible and invincible, who wished to reveal to him in his meditation and oratory that the tyrant and heretic should be extinguished and his crown transferred to the Catholic King: we beseech you, strengthen the limbs of this man whom we have consecrated to this work, and increase his strength so that he may accomplish your will. Give him a breastplate of divine power, by which he may escape the hands of those who seize him. Give him wings, by which your holy servant may escape, avoiding the attempts of barbarous traitors. Pour your joyful rays into his soul, so that his body, with all fear laid aside, may be animated amid dangers and torments, bathed in joy and exultation." When this exorcism is finished, the parricide is led before the altar, on whose panel is painted the story of James Clement, the Dominican monk, with pictures of angels protecting him and carrying him up to heaven. The Jesuits show him this, and at the same time present the heavenly crown, saying: "Lord, look upon your arm here, and hear the avenger of your justice. Let all the saints rise and give place to this man." When all these things have been completed, only four Jesuits are appointed, and they alone converse with the parricide. In their talks they often say that a certain divine brightness appears in him, by whose rays they are moved to kiss his hands and feet, and that they no longer see him as a man but as already placed among the gods. They also pretend to envy him such great glory and blessedness, to which he is now advanced, and sighing, they say: "Would that God had chosen me in your place, and had so ordained it that, freed from the pains of purgatory, I might be led by the straight road into paradise." But if the man whom they judge fit to perpetrate the murder hesitates and kicks against their persuasions, then either by nocturnal terrors and apparitions of monsters they drive him to make the vow they demand, or else, through personages suborned to appear as the Blessed Virgin Mary, or the angels, or other heavenly beings, and even Ignatius himself and his companions, appearing as a deus ex machina [ἀπὸ μηχανῆς], they animate him and lead him to the deed. Thus these wicked and parricidal masters ensnare unwary young men, sometimes by fear of punishment, sometimes by love of a shadowy virtue, and by the lure of avenging examples, and cast them headlong into danger of soul and body alike. They record that there was once a race of men in the East whom most historians called Assassins; Pope Pius, Nicolas Gilles, and Nicetas Choniates called them Arsacides. Devoted to the Mahometan discipline, they established a new sect, and appointed as the seat of its Prefect General Muleta, which was regarded as a holy place. The author and prince of this sect is said to have been a certain Alaodim, a veteran soldier, commonly called the Old Man of the Mountains, and known to his followers as Father and Prophet. Under him he had other rectors, who tended fortified palaces, splendid and very elegant, pleasant with gardens. The aim and purpose of their discipline was to maintain the absolute authority of the Prophet and of their Prince over all nations. To this end the palaces, or colleges, were established, to mould studious youth to the law of Mahomet contained in the Alcoran; and, after a selection of talents, they watched over, separated and set apart young men endowed with bolder and fiercer spirits.

units.la: Dogmata nefariæ huius disciplinæ hæc cumprimis referuntur.
units.tr: The doctrines of this nefarious discipline are chiefly these:

units.la: 1. Mahumetum esse Dei Prophetam, reparatorem generis humani, bonorum ac malorum retributorem.
units.tr: (1) That Mahomet is the prophet of God, the restorer of the human race, and the rewarder of good and evil.

units.la: 2. Eius vicarium Prophetam, ac Principem Muletanum esse in terris constitutum super omnes gentes, unicum divini & humani iuris à Mahumeto tradidit interpretem.
units.tr: (2) That his vicar, the Prophet and Prince of Muleta, set up on earth over all nations, is the sole interpreter of divine and human law delivered by Mahomet.

units.la: 3. Ius fasq; esse Principes eius dicto non audientes occidere, vi, fraude, dolo, pro re nata & oblata occasione.
units.tr: (3) That it is right and lawful to kill, by force, fraud or guile, as occasion arises and offers, those princes who do not obey his word.

units.la: 4. Nec discipulos eius Principi alteri cuiquam obstrictos ac obnoxios esse, licet fidem simulatam sacramento iurárint.
units.tr: (4) That his disciples are not bound or obligated to any other prince, even if they have sworn a feigned allegiance by oath.

units.la: 5. Animam esse immortalem, eiq; post hanc vitam imminere præmia aut pœnas pro dictorum factorumq; commeritis.
units.tr: (5) That the soul is immortal, and that rewards or punishments await it after this life according to the merits of its words and deeds.

units.la: 6. Paradisum esse, hortum lacte & melle affluentem, & omni delitiarum ac voluptatum genere abundantem, in quo beatorum animæ præmia, quæ ad totius corporis voluptatem faciunt, pro virtute recipiant.
units.tr: (6) That there is a paradise, a garden flowing with milk and honey and abounding in every kind of delight and pleasure, where the souls of the blessed receive, as rewards for their virtue, pleasures that serve the enjoyment of the whole body.

units.la: 7. Primam ac summam virtutem Deóque omnium gratissimam esse obedientiam, eámve in eo consistere, ut Præpositos suos vereantur, ac observent, & in iussis eorum exsequendis promptos sese, paratos & alacres præstent, hoc est, ut Paulus ait, ut animi sui (scilicet Prophetæ) detestabile exequantur propositum.
units.tr: (7) That the first and highest virtue, and the one most pleasing to God, is obedience, and that this consists in reverencing and observing their superiors and in showing themselves prompt, ready and eager in carrying out their orders; that is, as Paul says, to carry out the detestable purpose of their mind (namely, the Prophet's).

units.la: 8. Qui pro legis Mahumetanæ æmulatione, aut bello occumbat, aut in cæde hostis comprehensus interficiatur, animam suam recta & cum ipso exhalitu ad gaudia illa Paradisiaca transmittere. Qui vero domi defides & lecto immorientes pereant, summis prius cruciatibus, per multa annorum curricula purgari, quàm ad Paradisum queant penetrare, ubi tamen nec solidis gaudiis & minus perfectis, quàm illi audaces bellatores, perfruituri sint.
units.tr: (8) That whoever perishes in battle, in zeal for the Mahometan law, or is killed by an enemy's blow after being seized, sends his soul straight away, with his last breath, to those Paradisiacal joys. But whoever dies at home, idle and on his bed, must first be purged through many courses of years by the most severe torments before he can enter paradise, where even then he will enjoy not solid joys, and those less perfect than those bold warriors.

units.la: 9. Qui autem Principem aliquem Legis adversarium interemerit, proximum à Mahumeto locum in Paradiso cum sanctis Prophetis adepturum esse.
units.tr: (9) That whoever kills some prince who is an adversary of the Law will obtain the place next to Mahomet in paradise, among the holy prophets.

units.la: 10. Denique esse in potestate Prophetæ, quem, uti dictum, Patrem sive semem indigetabant, sibi à Mahumeto data atque concessa, Paradisi gaudia distribuere, eorumque gustum aliquem, etiam in hoc corpore constitutis modo incomprehensibili exhibere.
units.tr: (10) Finally, that it lies in the power of the Prophet, whom they called Father or Old Man, as has been said, a power given and granted to him by Mahomet, to distribute the joys of paradise and to show a taste of them, in an incomprehensible manner, even to those still in this body.

units.la: Ad hæc pestifera, & horrenda dogmata in Scholis ac collegiis suis adolescentum animis ad audaciam iturìs viam faciebant, ut eos obsequentiores sibi redderent, & ad omne vitæ periculum intrepidos, quorum primarium Muletæ seminarium fuit. Hęc delecti iuvenes ad eam, quam dixi, institutionem docti & educti, potu soporifero hausto, in viridarium Palatio seu Collegio contiguum portabantur, ubi somno experrecti illarum voluptatum experimentum caperent. Rivuli varij, aqua, melle, vino & lacte fluentes, varia
units.tr: To these pestilent and horrible doctrines their schools and colleges opened the way to boldness in the minds of the young, so as to make them more compliant and fearless of every danger of life; the chief seminary of this was Muleta. Chosen youths, taught and trained in the instruction I have described, after drinking a sleeping potion, were carried into a garden adjoining the palace or college, where, roused from sleep, they might taste those pleasures. Various streams flowing with water, honey, wine and milk, and various

units.la: Dogmata Assa. aríæ Musicæ artis instrumenta, melodíæ, choreæ, tripudia, palæstræ, vestes præ‑ciosæ, & mirus apparatus omnium delectabilium rerum, quibus pro voto uebantur iuvenes intra viridarium positi, qui aliud nihil faciebant, quàm quod vitam beatam vivebant, tristitiæ nullum dantes locum. Præsto erant, & uellæ formosæ variarum libidinum spinthrices & pueri calamistrati ad nutum ministrantes.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Assassins: musical instruments, melodies, dances, wrestling grounds, costly garments, and a marvellous array of every delightful thing. The young men placed within the garden were supplied with all of these as they wished. They did nothing else but live a happy life, allowing no place for sadness. Beautiful young women, wanton in every kind of lust, were at hand, along with curled-haired boys who waited on their every nod.

units.la: Tanto gustu voluptatis imbibito, iterum in Soporem dati ad Collegium & habita a la sua reducebantur. Tunc illi redeuntes (verba sunt Pauli Veneti) & reminiscentes, ibus & quatis ad modicum tempus potiti fuissent gaudijs, supra modum dolebant, & tries efficiebantur, quòd delitijs illis perpetuò frui non concessum sit, mortem libenter subiri, modò hac vita tam modicè degustata, semper vivant. Tunc Tyrannus ille, qui Dei prophetam se esse mentiebatur, ajebat illis, si parati estis, ut promea obedientia mortem inepide, ubi illata fuerit, subeatis, participes vos pronuntio futuros illorum gaudiorum, ad horam vidistis. At miseri illi mortem lucrum putantes, nihil tam difficile ajunt, jungendum, quod pro illa beata vita consequenda non libenter subeant. Abutitur igitur rannus ille his præfractis hominibus ad innumera homicidia, quippe qui corporalem vim proflituentes, contemnebant etiam mortem ipsam, &c. Hæc Paulus: Cui Nicetas honiates cōsonans; Et ad eos missi, infit, quos eorum Principes occisos volunt, ut hostes & amici adeunt, & aut se habere, quod eis dicant, aut Legatos venire fingulantes, fæDominorum suorum adversarios pugionibus occidunt, nulla difficultatis & explorati pplicij ratione habitâ, etiamsi alterum non occiderint. Et pergit Paulus; Ut omnibus ominibus essent formidini, & nemo insaniæ illorum resistere auderet: Sicq; fiebat, ut mulregiones, & potentes viri Tyranno illi tributarij fierent: donec tandem à Tartaris feudopropheta ille oppressus & cum omnibus Assassinis suis exstinctus fuit circa Annum N. M. CCLXII.
units.tr: Having drunk so deeply of this taste of pleasure, they were again put to sleep and carried back to the college and to their former place. Then, on waking (these are the words of Paulus Venetus), and recalling the joys they had enjoyed for a short time, they grieved beyond measure and became sad, because it was not granted to them to enjoy those delights forever. They would gladly undergo death, provided that after this life, so briefly tasted, they might live forever. Then that tyrant, who lied that he was a prophet of God, said to them: "If you are ready, in obedience to me, to face death without fear when it is inflicted, I declare that you will be sharers in those joys which you saw for a time." But those wretches, thinking death a gain, say that nothing is so hard that they would not gladly undergo it to attain that blessed life. The tyrant therefore misused these reckless men for countless murders, since, devoting their bodily strength to this, they despised death itself, and so on. These are Paulus' words. Nicetas Choniates agrees with him: And when they are sent to those whom their princes want killed, they go as enemies and friends. Either they pretend to have something to tell them, or they pretend to come as envoys, and then they kill their lords' adversaries with daggers, taking no account of the difficulty or of the punishment they know awaits them, even if they do not kill the other man. Paulus goes on: So that they would be a terror to all men, and no one would dare to resist their madness. And so it came about that many regions and powerful men became tributaries of that tyrant, until at last that feudal prophet was overcome by the Tartars and destroyed, together with all his Assassins, around the year CCLXII.

units.la: Ad eundem prorsus modum Iesuitæ iuventutem in scholis & Collegijs suis formant, & erudiunt: propositaq; præstantissimi gaudij cœlestis mercede, & divinæ venerationis honore, ad quodvis parricidiale facinus perpetrandum inflammant & propellunt.
units.tr: In exactly the same way the Jesuits form and train young people in their schools and colleges. Holding out the reward of the most excellent heavenly joy and the honour of divine veneration, they inflame and drive them to commit any parricidal crime.

units.la: CAPVT II. DE AEQVIVOCATIONIBVS IESVITARVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. ON THE EQUIVOCATIONS OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Vndecimo docent Iesuitæ, Amphibologijs seu Æquivocationibus, mentiendi & pejerandi arte, hæreticos & quosvis alios decipere, allère & eludere permissum esse.
units.tr: In the eleventh place, the Jesuits teach that it is permitted to deceive, mislead and ensnare heretics and any others by the art of amphibologies or equivocations, and by the art of lying and perjury.

units.la: Docent etiam Iesuitæ, sibi aliisque Papistis, præsertim Clericis & Ecclesiasticis liberum permissumque esse, quando ab hæreticis magistratibus examinantur, æquivocationum deceptionibus, itemque mentitis nominibus, & vestibus uti, & veritatem supprimere, nimirum, ut commodius se insinuare, & conatus suos promovere possint. Hoc est, licere fini & aliis Pontificijs, non tantum simpliciter manifestam veritatem celare, ut denegare, sed pie & religiosè asserere, perque salutem æternam protestari, mò liquidò iurare, in illa quæ certissimè cognoscunt salsissima esse; retinendo tantum proprium quendam & reconditum animo sensum, quo à Patribus suis persuasi sunt, se tuto & iuste quæstionem quamvis eludere posse. Est hæc communis Iesuitarum omnium sententia, sed tamen cum exceptione quorundam. His artibus instituuntur à Iesuitis ij, quos ad Regum & Principum exitium incitant, ne facinoris conscios & participes prodant: utrem ipsam aperte negent, conditionem aliquam mente retineant. Atque hæc demum causa est, cur parricidæ tam constanti animo à Iudicibus interrogati, quibus socijs aut auctoribus scelus tantum aggressi sint, negant & peiërant, quòd Iesuitarum artibus inducti sibi persuadent, dum conditionem aliquam mente tegant, nullam in periurio noxam esse.
units.tr: The Jesuits also teach that it is free and permitted for themselves and other Papists, especially clergy and churchmen, when they are examined by heretical magistrates, to use the deceptions of equivocation, as well as false names and clothing, and to suppress the truth, so that they may insinuate themselves more conveniently and advance their undertakings. That is, it is lawful for the Papists not merely to conceal plain truth by simply denying it, but to assert the opposite piously and religiously, to protest it by their eternal salvation, indeed to swear outright to things which they know most certainly to be utterly false, retaining only a certain private and hidden sense in the mind. By this they have been persuaded by their fathers that they can safely and justly evade any question whatever. This is the common opinion of all the Jesuits, yet with an exception for certain ones. The Jesuits train by these arts those whom they incite to the destruction of kings and princes, so that they do not betray accomplices and participants in the crime. They openly deny the deed itself, while keeping some condition in mind. And this is finally the reason why regicides, questioned by judges with such steadfast spirit as to which accomplices or instigators they had in the crime, deny it and perjure themselves: led on by the arts of the Jesuits, they persuade themselves that, so long as they conceal some condition in their mind, there is no guilt in perjury.

units.la: Sic Toletus Iesuita & Cardinalis de Instruct. Sacerd. lib. 4. cap. 21. Si quis, inquit, à Superiore interrogetur juratus, tum si juste interrogetur, tenetur respondere absque æquivocatione. Si vero injuste, tum potest uti æquivocatione, & respondere non secundum judicis mentem, sed secundum propriam. Et si crimen omnino occultum est, de quo quis interrogatur, tum æquivocatione uti poterit, respondendo: Nescio: intelligendo tamen intra se, Ut dicam tibi: vel respondendo, Non feci; intelligendo intra se, Nunc non feci, vel quid simile. Et sic interrogatum: An ex tali civitate veniat (de qua nempe communis fama est, quòd peste infecta sit) ut ut sub juramento interrogatus sit, posse tamen respondere, Quòd non; licet inde veniat: quia nempe tacitum intellectum in sua mente habet, quòd civitas illa non sit infecta: aut quòd ipse non sit infectus, licet civitas infecta sit. Quia nempe non facit contra præcipuam intentionem custodum.
units.tr: Thus Toletus the Jesuit and Cardinal, in De Instructione Sacerdotum, book 4, chapter 21: If someone is questioned under oath by a superior, then if he is justly questioned, he is bound to answer without equivocation. But if unjustly, then he may use equivocation, and answer not according to the judge's mind but according to his own. And if the crime about which someone is questioned is wholly hidden, then he may use equivocation, answering: I do not know, understanding inwardly, "that I may tell you"; or answering, I did not do it, understanding inwardly, "Now I did not do it", or something similar. And when someone is asked under oath whether he comes from such a city (of which common report says it is infected with plague), he may nevertheless answer, No, although he comes from there: because he has in his own mind a tacit understanding that the city is not infected, or that he himself is not infected, although the city is infected. Because it does not work against the chief intention of the guardians.

units.la: Similia docet Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 3. Disput. 5. q. 13. De reo pun. 2. pag. 1350. & seqq. Quandocunque (ait) iniqua interrogatio fit, etiamsi juramentum ac cesse-rit, nullum tamen committetur perjurium, quamvis juramento affirmet alium aliquid sensum verum, alienum ab interrogatione: talis non mentitur, nec vane usurpat nomen Dei, si quidem ad se, vel sua tuendum, id facit.
units.tr: Gregorius de Valentia teaches similar things, vol. 3, disputation 5, question 13, On the punishment of the guilty, point 2, p. 1350 and following: Whenever (he says) an unjust question is put, even if an oath is taken, no perjury will nevertheless be committed, although by the oath he affirms some other true sense, foreign to the question. Such a person does not lie, nor vainly use the name of God, if indeed he does it to defend himself or his own.

units.la: Andræas quoq; Eudæmon Ioannes in Anticotoni confutatione docet, cum iudex rite, acservato iuris ordine rerum interroget, teneri quemcunq; sine tergiverfatione ulla ad mentem iudicis etiam cum capitis sui periculo respondere, quòd si vero Magistratus præter ius & fas, sine ullis indicijs ad quæstionem aliquem rapiat, tum tergiversationi locum esse. Verba eius hæc sunt: Cum qui nullis justis indicijs in jus vocatur, quia nemo tenetur seipsum Magistratui prodere, id quod lex ipsa naturæ satis docet: aperte & liberè sine omni tergiversatione negare potest, id cum jus gratia accersitur: quia semper clausula illa intelligitur, ita ut tenear dicere.
units.tr: Andreas Eudaemon-Joannes also teaches, in his refutation of Anticoton, that when a judge questions someone rightly and with the order of law preserved, that person is bound to answer without any evasion according to the judge's mind, even at risk to his life. But if a magistrate, beyond right and law, drags someone to questioning without any indications, then there is room for evasion. His words are these: When someone who is summoned to court without any just indications, since no one is bound to betray himself to the magistrate, which the law of nature itself teaches sufficiently, can deny openly and freely, without any evasion, that he has done it, when he is summoned by the court. For that clause is always understood: "so that I am bound to say".

units.la: Martinus Navarrus Azpilcueta in d. c. humanæ aures. 22. q. 5. pag. 348. post Angelum de Perufio & Ioan. ab Anagnia refert & probat: Aequivocationem S. Francisci, qui interrogatus à latronibus, homicidam (Iesuita Sylvanus in Philippic. sua pag. 5. pro homicida furem supponit) persequentibus, An illhac, ubi Franciscus erat, talis homicida transfijffet? immissis manibus intra manicas, respondet, Hac non transfijffe; subintelligendo tacitè contra communem intelligentiam: Non transfijffe per illas manicas. Et addit Azpilcueta: Hanc doctrinam de Aequivocationibus fundari in illo insigni facto magni illius Patriarchæ Francisci. Cui similis est illa, quæ habet Gloss. in c. Ne quis. c. 2. q. 2. si quis videlicet interrogetur, an hic vel illic fit, & respondeat non, sub intelligendo, ut hic comedat, quam folennem & receptam Azpilcueta dicit, & uti justam refponfionem laudat.
units.tr: Martinus Navarrus Azpilcueta, on the chapter "Humanae aures", 22 q.5, p. 348, after Angelus de Perusio and John of Anagni, reports and approves: The equivocation of St Francis, who, when questioned by robbers pursuing a murderer (the Jesuit Sylvanus, in his Philippic, p. 5, substitutes a thief for the murderer): "Did such a murderer pass through here, where Francis was?" with his hands thrust into his sleeves, he answers, "He did not pass through here", tacitly understanding, against the common meaning: "He did not pass through those sleeves". And Azpilcueta adds: This doctrine of equivocations is founded on that notable deed of the great Patriarch Francis. Similar to it is that which the Gloss has on the chapter "Ne quis", 2 q.2: namely, if someone is asked whether this or that person is here or there, and he answers no, understanding "that he may eat here". Azpilcueta calls this a solemn and accepted formula, and praises it as a just answer.

units.la: Ibidem Navarrus ex Thoma, quòd rerum interrogatus de crimine à judice non procedente juridice, non teneatur fateri veritatem, sed possit uti Aequivocatione, subintelligendo aliquid aliud, quàm verba sonant. Imò & qui respondet judici, sive superiori, vel sub juramento, potest uti Amphibologia, sive illa contingat ex diversa verbi significatione, sive ex diversa intentione interrogantis & respondentis, & licet falsum sit, secundum mentem interrogantis.
units.tr: In the same place Navarrus, following Thomas, says: that a man questioned about a crime by a judge who does not proceed judicially is not bound to confess the truth, but may use equivocation, understanding something other than what the words sound. Indeed, also one who answers a judge or superior, even under oath, may use amphibology, whether it arises from a different meaning of the word or from a different intention of the questioner and the answerer, even if it is false according to the mind of the questioner.

units.la: Iden
units.tr: The same.

units.la: Idem Navarrus pag. 351. Etiam magistratui, vel judici injustè interroganti vel uranti, non tenetur quis secundum suam intentionem respondere. Sic & testem instruit Navarrus ut dicat, Se nihil scire, subintelligendo intra se, Nihil, quod dicere teneatur. Idem etiam instruit litigantes, qui iubentur iurare de calumnia, verita⁠&c. Ut si non ordinatè, vel juste, à judice jubeantur, possint negare vel affirmare, secundum propriam mentem, non curando de illa quam judex habet. Et postalia pag. 352. n. 16. cer etiā, Licite posse aliquem occultare, Quod sit Catholicus. Rursus c. humanae auctoritatis 3. 22. q. 5. inquit: N. N. clàm, sine testibus absentibus, cuidam foeminae dixit, Accipe in uxorem meam: sed sine animo eam ducendi. Postea judici eum adjuranti, & interroganti, an ea verba dixisset? Respondit, se illa non dixisse; subintelligendo, in mente quo dilla non dixerit animo illam ducendi. Et addit Azpilicueta, hoc non esse mendacium, sed aequivocationem prudentem & honestam.
units.tr: The same Navarrus, p. 351: Even to a magistrate or judge who questions or urges unjustly, one is not bound to answer according to his intention. Thus Navarrus also instructs a witness to say that he knows nothing, understanding inwardly, "nothing that he is bound to tell". The same man also instructs litigants, who are ordered to swear about calumny and truth, so that if they are ordered by the judge not in order or not justly, they may deny or affirm according to their own mind, not caring about what the judge has in mind. And after other things, p. 352, n. 16, also: That one may lawfully conceal that he is a Catholic. Again, on the chapter "Humanae auctoritatis", 3, 22 q.5, he says: N.N. secretly, with no witnesses present, said to a certain woman, "Take me as your husband", but without intention of taking her. Afterwards, when a judge adjured him and asked whether he had said those words, he replied that he had not said them, understanding in his mind that he had not said them with the intention of taking her. And Azpilcueta adds that this is not a lie, but a prudent and honest equivocation.

units.la: Toletus ut supra, scribit, Quaerenti judici, fecistine illud? respondeat; intelligendo intra se; ut dicam tibi, vel hoc tempore, vel quid simile: Et si vir uxorem petat, an sit altera? illa potest dicere, non sum, quàm vis verum fuerit, intelligendo, ut tibi revelem. Qui cogitur jurare alteram in sponsam accepturum, intelligendo, si postea placuerit: & latronibus comprehensus juraverit, se postea daturum centum aureos, ut liberetur, & equivocè jurans, intra se dicens, si postea liberetur, tunc nō tenetur solvere: sic à custode inriosè detentus, ut dimittatur, jurans se redditurum postea, potest uti aequivocatione, & non tenetur reddere.
units.tr: Toletus, as above, writes: When the judge asks, "Did you do that?", let him answer, understanding inwardly, "that I may tell you", or "at this time", or something similar. And if a husband asks whether his wife is another's, she may say, "I am not", however true it may be, understanding, "that I may reveal it to you". One who is compelled to swear that he will take another as his bride may understand, "if it afterwards pleases me". And one seized by robbers who swears that he will afterwards give a hundred gold pieces in order to be freed, and swears equivocally, saying inwardly, "if I am afterwards freed, then I am not bound to pay", is not bound to pay. So too one unjustly detained by a guard, who swears that he will return something afterwards in order to be let go, may use equivocation and is not bound to return it.

units.la: Interrogatus alius, & jurejurando obstrictus, ut verum dicat, talémne viderit hodiè? ... c aequivocationis arte illud plane denegat, prudens licet, sciensq; illum viderit. Ille verò nc sensum sibi reservavit, Non vidi illum, scilicet, ut Magistratui hoc dicerem, vel non sione beatifica, vel non Venetijs, &c. illum vidi.
units.tr: Another person, questioned and bound by oath to tell the truth, whether he had seen such a man today ... by the art of equivocation flatly denies it, although he is prudent and knows that he saw him. But he reserved to himself this sense: "I did not see him", namely, so that I might say this to the magistrate, or "not in the beatific vision", or "not at Venice", and so on. "I saw him."

units.la: Francisco Treshamo in arce Londinensi morti proximo ut uxori ipsum in latium inviseret permissum est. Illa verò haud ignara maritum suum coniuctionis Hispanicae directe & verè Garnetum insimulasse, sed veritate ne mactus sine morsu conscientiae aliquid de Garneto detexisset, cùm iam extremos spiritus exhalaret, eò adegit, ut cùm ipse scribere non posset, famulum scribere iussit, quae ipse dictaret. In quo scripto seipsum iureiurando obstrinxit, atque in animae suae salutem testatus est, sedecim annis totis iam transactis Garnetum nè vidisse quidem, eamque ob causam, priorem suam confessionem irritam haberi obtestatur. Petit denique ut praesens ista retractatio pro vera habeatur. Cùm tamen Garnetus ipse confessus sit, se Hispanicae coniurationis conscium fuisse, sequecum Treshamo saepissimè proximis annis loquutum esse his rebus esse.
units.tr: Francis Tresham, close to death in the Tower of London, was permitted to be visited on his bed by his wife, who was well aware that her husband had directly and truly accused Garnet of the Spanish conspiracy. Yet, lest he should die without a pang of conscience, having disclosed something about Garnet by the truth, she brought it about, when he was already breathing his last, that since he could not write himself, he ordered a servant to write what he dictated. In this writing he bound himself by oath, and testified for the salvation of his soul that for sixteen full years he had not even seen Garnet, and on that account he entreats that his former confession be held void. Finally he asks that this present retraction be held as true. Yet Garnet himself has confessed that he was privy to the Spanish conspiracy, and that he had spoken very often with Tresham in the last years about these matters.

units.la: Interrogatus tandem pro tribunali Garnetus, quid de hac Treshami retractatione sentiret, Hoc unicum respondit, Ipsum aequivocare voluisse credo.
units.tr: Questioned at last before the tribunal, Garnet was asked what he thought of this retraction of Tresham's. He gave only this answer: "I believe he meant to equivocate."

units.la: Garnetus etiam de toto hoc argumento & natura aequivocationis quid sentiret explicare iussus, hoc 20. die Martii anni 1606. respondsum dedit. De aequivocatione ita censeo. In rebus moralibus & communi usu vitae, quando veritas inter amicos requiritur, uti aequivocatione haud licet: id enim societati hominum magno malo cederet. Quare huic remedio in istis nullus locus. Quoties verò de necessaria defensione agitur, deiuria aliqua evitanda, aut damno, aut de consequendo aliquo bono non parvi momenti sine ullo cujusquam periculo, tum licita est aequivocatio.
units.tr: Garnet was also ordered to explain his view of this whole question and the nature of equivocation, and on 20 March 1606 he gave the following answer. "On equivocation I hold as follows. In moral matters and in the common use of life, when the truth is required between friends, it is not at all lawful to use equivocation, for that would bring great harm to human society. Therefore there is no place for this remedy in such matters. But whenever there is question of necessary defence, of avoiding some injury, or of gaining some good of no small importance without danger to anyone, then equivocation is lawful."

units.la: Idem Garnetus quoq; has Iesuitarum fraudulentas aequivocationes, quum Londini pro tribunali staret, hoc mendacio defendere & excusare conatus est: Iesuitarum Ordo, inquit, mendacium quodcunque improbat, praesertim verò in causis fidei & religionis, cùm sit illud genus mendacij omnium perniciosissimum, & D. Augustino in Priscillianistas condemnatum. Imò verò quacunque in causa mentiri,
units.tr: When he stood before the tribunal in London, Garnet himself also tried to defend and excuse these fraudulent equivocations of the Jesuits by this lie: "The Order of Jesuits, he said, condemns every kind of lie, especially in matters of faith and religion, since that kind of lie is the most pernicious of all, and it was condemned by St Augustine in the case of the Priscillianists. Indeed, whatever the cause, they do not lie..."

units.la: In Actis Garnet pag. 96.
units.tr: In the Acts of Garnet, p. 96.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: ON DOCTRINE

units.la: & malum & peccatum est, ut cunque inter octo gradus, quos Augustinus facit, ille revera gradus infimus habeatur, ita mentiri, ut uni in commodum cedat, quod sine cujusvis sit incommodo. Illa igitur, quam nos defendimus Aequivocatio, legitimum quarundam propositionum usum defendit, mendacijs neutiquam patrocinatur. Fieri enim potest, ut quis ab homine, penes quem nulla sit inquirendi authoritas, interrogetur, aut de re aliqua examinetur, cuius cognitio ad interrogantem minime pertineat; verbi causa, Quid aliquis cogitet? Quo tempore igitur oportet veritatem dicere, aequivocare non licet, quod si fecus fit, licet, &c. Attornatus autem Generalis Angliae ad hoc sic respondit: Verum quidem est, specie tenus mendacium & perjurium condemnare videntur, quod si secus fecerint, ipsorum scelera essent in medio posita, omnibusque exosi essent. Verum quae con-demnant mendacia perjuriaque aperta sunt & hiantia: mendacia autem secreta, perjuria clancularia, falsa testimonia, quae maxime detestanda, quaeque neque defensionem, neque exemplum habent, approbare videntur. Quod si in alijs ut plurimum non probent, at in semetipsis & sui similibus, atq; conjurationum socijs, probant & defendunt; praesertim cum ad conatus suos perficiendos illis usui & administrculo esse possit.
units.tr: Such a lie is evil and sinful, however the lowest of the eight degrees that Augustine lists may be held to be lying so as to benefit one person without harm to anyone. That equivocation which we defend therefore upholds the lawful use of certain propositions; it by no means condones lies. For it can happen that someone is questioned by a man who has no authority to inquire, or is examined about some matter whose knowledge does not properly concern the questioner, for example, "What is someone thinking?" At the time when one ought to tell the truth, it is not lawful to equivocate; but if otherwise, it is lawful, etc. The Attorney General of England answered this as follows: It is true that they seem to condemn lying and perjury in appearance, but if they acted otherwise, their crimes would be laid open and they would be hateful to all. But the lies and perjuries they condemn are open and gaping; secret lies, hidden perjuries and false testimonies, which are most detestable and have neither defence nor precedent, they seem to approve. And if they do not approve these in others as a rule, yet they do approve and defend them in themselves and their like, and in the partners of their conspiracies, especially since these can serve them as a tool and aid in carrying out their attempts.

units.la: Haec quoque Garneti protestatio est contraria suo ipsius facto. Cum enim a magistratu interrogatus maxime, pernegassèt, se conscium machinationis cum pulvere tormentario fuisse, ac pro eius felici successu preces habuisse; mendacij deinde convictus respondit pag. 101. Se quidem de prospero magnae illius actionis eventu preces obtulisse; illud tamen eo animo sensuque fecisse, quod se veriores quasdam lege-stum subveritus fuisset. Rursus interrogatus a iudice; An Iesuitam Hallum, aliasve Oldcornum non convenisset, monitusque, ut sine aequivocatione in veritate responderet; pertinaciter & animae salutem testatus respondit, Se cum illo non fuisse: idque horrendis execrationibus repetijt. Postea vero quum Hallus contrarium fassus fuerat, in mendacio aperto deprehensus Garnetus, erubuit, & misericordiam imploravit, agnovitque se deliquisse, Nisi ipsum Aequivocatio tueretur. Hinc intellígit Lector mentitum fuisse Garnetum Aequivocationum Iesuiticarum defensione. Nam & interrogatus a delegatis Regijs, penes quos fuit interrogandi authoritas & potestas; & a iudice ipso monitus fuit ut sine aequivocatione & dolo aliquo responderet: & cognitio rei, de qua examinatus fuit, ad interrogantes maxime pertinuit, & tamen aequivocavit, id est, mentitus est.
units.tr: This protestation of Garnet is also contrary to his own deed. For when he was questioned by the magistrate, he flatly denied that he had known of the plot with gunpowder, or had offered prayers for its happy outcome. Then, convicted of lying, he replied at p. 101 that he had indeed offered prayers for the prosperous outcome of that great action, but he had done so with the intention and feeling that he feared certain more truthful things might come to light. Questioned again by the judge, whether he had not met the Jesuit Hall, or else Oldcorne, and warned to answer truthfully without equivocation, he swore steadfastly by the salvation of his soul that he had not been with him, and repeated this with dreadful curses. Afterwards, however, when Hall confessed the contrary, Garnet, caught in an open lie, blushed, begged for mercy, and acknowledged that he had done wrong, unless equivocation defended him. From this the reader understands that Garnet lied by relying on the defence of Jesuit equivocations. For he was questioned both by the royal delegates, who had the authority and power to question him, and was warned by the judge himself to answer without equivocation or any deceit; and the knowledge of the matter about which he was examined belonged chiefly to his questioners. Yet he equivocated, that is, he lied.

units.la: Eadem fraude illusit Garnetus Iesuita Illustrissimo Comiti Salisburgiensi, petenti, ut sine aequivocatione proferret, quid de excommunicatione Regis sentiret, dicens, Regem Iacobum nondum excommunicatum esse. Nam Iacobi Stuardum excommunicatum animo sentiebat. Vide eius acta pag. 107.
units.tr: Garnet the Jesuit mocked the most illustrious Earl of Salisbury with the same deceit. When the Earl asked him to state without equivocation what he thought about the excommunication of the King, Garnet said that King James had not yet been excommunicated, though in his mind he regarded James Stuart as excommunicated. See his proceedings, p. 107.

units.la: Eadem fraude utuntur Iesuitae, cum ipsi, vel eorum discipuli Reges & Principes Evangelicos, imo & Pontificios eorum fautores, & sedi Roman. minus obedientes, occidunt. Negat enim se Reges aut Principes occidisse. Quare? quia non ut Reges & Principes, sed ut haereticos, haereticorumque fautores & excommunicatos, atq; Tyrannos eos occidunt: Non enim in eodem subjecto esse posse, ait, Regnum, haeresin & tyrannidem.
units.tr: The Jesuits use the same deceit when they, or their disciples, kill Protestant kings and princes, and indeed even their Papist supporters and those less obedient to the Roman see. For they deny that they have killed kings or princes. Why? Because they kill them not as kings and princes, but as heretics, supporters of heretics, excommunicated persons and tyrants. For, he says, kingdom, heresy and tyranny cannot be in the same subject.

units.la: Hac arte Richeomus in sua Expostulatione Apologetica pro Iesuitarum Societate Henrico IV. Regi Galliae illusit, dum aequivocando impudenter affirmavit: Se nunquam audivisse, postremo defunctum Henricum Regem, a quoquam suorum hominum Tyrannum esse nominatum. Non enim postremo defunctum Henricum Regem, sed bene postremo occisum Henricum Valesium Henricum Tyrannum & quidem saepissime audivit nominari; quum hoc & pro concione ubique inter Ligistas, & quam plurimis libellis e ditis factitatum sit.
units.tr: By this art Richeome, in his Apologetic Expostulation on behalf of the Society of Jesus, mocked Henry IV, King of France, when he shamelessly affirmed by equivocation that he had never heard King Henry, lately deceased, named a tyrant by any of his men. For he had heard not that King Henry, lately deceased, but Henry of Valois, lately slain, very often named Henry the Tyrant; since this has been done everywhere in sermons among the Leaguers and in very many published pamphlets.

units.la: Simili aequivocandi arte utitur Tortuosus Bellarminus, dum negat Sixtum Quintum Papam imperasse eundem Henricum Regem interficere, ut est videre in Responsione ad Apologiam pro iuramento fidelitatis pag. 85. Non enim Papae imperant ant occidere Reges, sed Tyrannos tantū, id est, eos, qui dicto suo minus sunt obedientes. Hoc enim decretum Papae axioma indubitatum esse, ille ipse Torsus multis locis tradit. Constitutum etiam apud eosdem est, Omnes Reges ac Principes Evangelicos, imò & quosdam Pontificios, minus dicto Papae-rum patres, nec Reges & Principes, sed Tyrannos esse.
units.tr: Crafty Bellarmine uses a similar art of equivocation when he denies that Pope Sixtus V commanded the same King Henry to be killed, as can be seen in his Response to the Apology for the oath of fidelity, p. 85. For Popes do not command kings to be killed, but only tyrants, that is, those who are less obedient to their word. That same crooked Bellarmine teaches in many places that this decree of the Pope is an indubitable axiom. It is also established among the same men that all Protestant kings and princes, and indeed certain Papists, who are less obedient to the Pope's word, are not kings and princes but tyrants.

units.la: Docent praeterea Iesuitae, Quosvis non teneri privatis quoq; Catholicis admentem dare, sed æquivocare & interrogantes decipere posse. Navarrus ubi supra p. 351. Per hanc doctrinam, inquit, æquivocationis innumera mendacia & peccata evitari possunt, semper respondeatur cum aliqua subintellectione: ut si interrogemur, quo vadimus? quanta pecunia habemus? mutua damus? donamus? quid scripsimus? quid nobis ille vel ille dixit? omnibus illis absque peccato respondere non posse, subintelligenda aliqua. Vt si quis petenti librum, &c. respondeat, Non habeo; licet habeat, subintelligendo, Ita non habeo, tenear praestare, vel, ut tenear tibi dicere, dare, manifestare, &c.
units.tr: Moreover the Jesuits teach that not even private Catholics are bound to give an answer to everyone, but may equivocate and deceive those who question them. Navarrus, above cited, p. 351: By this doctrine of equivocation, he says, countless lies and sins can be avoided. One should always answer with some implied qualification, as when we are asked: Where are we going? How much money do we have? Do we lend? Do we give? What have we written? What did this or that man say to us? To all these questions one cannot answer without sin unless something is understood. As, if someone asked for a book answers, "I do not have it," although he has it, understanding, "Thus I do not have it, so that I am bound to hand it over," or "so that I am bound to tell you, give, reveal," etc.

units.la: Iesuita Iacobus Sylvanus, alias Keller, in Philippica contra Anonymum redicantem, pag. 5. ait: Æquivocatione uti licet, quando qui interrogat, non est superior, aut judex. Anne, ait, ego obligatus sum cuique ex rure vel plaustro roganti respondere mentem? quis me omnium debitorem fecit?
units.tr: The Jesuit James Sylvanus, otherwise Keller, in his Philippic against an anonymous opponent, p. 5, says: Equivocation may be used when the questioner is not a superior or a judge. Am I, he says, obliged to answer the thoughts of anyone who asks me from the countryside or from a cart? Who has made me a debtor to everyone?

units.la: Quod vero ad Æquivocationis huius originem & antiquitatem attinet, videlicet primo referri posse ad Priscillianistas haereticos, qui docuerunt, mendacia perjuria religionis suae causa gratia fieri bona conscientia posse, quod etiam Audiani ferunt: Unde illud est eorum, Iura, pejura, secretum prodere noli. Vide Hieron. in ep. ad Ctesiphont. de Pelag. Augustin. in Enchirid. & lib. de mendacio, Bernard. serm. 65. in Cantic. Sixtum Senensem lib. 3. Bibliothecae.
units.tr: As for the origin and antiquity of this equivocation, it may first be traced to the heretical Priscillianists, who taught that lies and perjuries for the sake of their religion can be done with a good conscience. The Audians also report this. Hence their saying: "Swear, forswear, but do not betray the secret." See Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon against Pelagius; Augustine in the Enchiridion and in the book on lying; Bernard, sermon 65 on the Song of Songs; and Sixtus of Siena, book 3 of his Bibliotheca.

units.la: Æquivocatio etiā talis Iesuitica ab Arrio haeretico usurpata fuit. Is enim cum Niceno Conc. damnatus esset, & a Constantino Imp. in exilium eiectus, ad illius petitionem, fide prius data se Niceno Concilio subscripturum, eodem Imperatore revocatus fuit. Ille vero domum reversus, suam ipsius opinionem ac sententiam in charta clam consignavit, eamque in sinu gestavit. Cum coram pectu Imperatoris Nicenam fidem sibi propositam videret, interrogatus, num Concilij Niceni decretis vere consentiat, & in futurum constanter adhaerevelit? Ille, manu ad sinum admota, ubi charta occultabatur, sine mora, alacri animo coram Imperatore subscripsit, cum tamen ea quae in Concilio Fide decisa erant, astute & aequivoce eluderet. Cogitavit enim apud se tacite aequivoce, se subscripturum isti fidei, quam in sinu gestavit, non ei quae sibi ab Imperatore propositae fuit.
units.tr: This Jesuitical equivocation was also used by the heretic Arius. For when he had been condemned by the Council of Nicaea and cast into exile by the Emperor Constantine, he was recalled by the same Emperor at his own petition, having first promised in good faith that he would subscribe to the Council of Nicaea. He, returning home, secretly wrote his own opinion and view on a paper and carried it in his bosom. When he saw the Nicene faith put before him in the presence of the Emperor, he was asked whether he truly agreed with the decrees of the Council of Nicaea and would constantly adhere to them in future. He, with his hand pressed to his breast where the paper was hidden, without delay and with a cheerful spirit subscribed before the Emperor, though he cunningly and equivocally evaded what had been decided as faith at the Council. For he had silently thought to himself, equivocally, that he would subscribe to that faith which he carried in his bosom, not to the one which had been put before him by the Emperor.

units.la: Nostra autem memoria Æquivocandi hanc scientiam ab inferis refuscitam, multos Iesuitarum magna cura & explicuisse & asseruisse ex iis testimoniis, quae paulo ante ex illorum scriptis adduximus, constat, ut non immerito authores & inventores eius esse vulgo dicantur. Praecipue autem eam exerciuerunt Angliae regni Iesuitae. Extant enim Iesuitae Personij Angli, qui Romae vixit ibique mortuus est, disputationes eius argumenti prolixae, in quibus æquivocandi, seu mentiendi & peierandi artem acriter defendere conatur: sunt tamen a Thoma Mortono solidissime confutatae. Liber quoque paulo ante mortem Elisabethae Reginae editus est hoc titulo, Æquivocationis tractatus a Garneto Iesuitarum in Anglia Provinciali & Blackwvello Angliae Archiepiscopo non solum visus, sed etiam approbatus. In principio autem Garnetus sua ipsius manu verbum hoc tituli Æquivocationis, delevit, & sic utavit, Tractatus contra æquivocationes & falsas dissimulationes, cum rem ipsam o virili tueatur. In fine etiam Blackwellus librum hunc approbavit & commendavit his verbis: Tractatus iste vere doctus & vere pius & Catholicus est.
units.tr: In our own memory it is well known that many Jesuits have, with great care, explained and asserted this science of equivocation, recalled from the dead, on the basis of those testimonies which we have just cited from their writings. So they are commonly, and not undeservedly, called its authors and inventors. The Jesuits of the English realm practised it especially. For there survive the lengthy disputations on this subject of the English Jesuit Persons, who lived and died at Rome, in which he strenuously tries to defend the art of equivocating, that is, of lying and forswearing. Yet they have been most solidly refuted by Thomas Morton. Also a book published shortly before the death of Queen Elizabeth, with the title A Treatise of Equivocation, was not only seen but also approved by Garnet, the Jesuit Provincial in England, and by Blackwell, Archbishop of England. At the beginning, however, Garnet with his own hand deleted the word Equivocation from the title and wrote instead A treatise against equivocations and false dissimulations, though he defended the thing itself manfully. At the end Blackwell also approved and commended the book in these words: This treatise is truly learned, truly pious and Catholic.

units.la: certè sacrarum Scripturarum, Patrum, Doctorum, Scholasticorum, Canonistarum, & primarum rationum prasfidijs plenissimè firmat æquitatem Æquivocationis; ideoque dignissimus qui typis propagetur ad consolationem afflictorum Catholicorum, & omnium piorum instructionem. Et tamen Apologista quidam in secunda Apologia sua negat ullum unquam eiusmodi Tractatum in rerum natura fuisse, & qui eius memoriam nerunt impostores vocat.
