Sunt autem in Anglia plurimi, qui partim viderunt legerúntque eum librum, partim etiam hodie eum servant: Si etiam Ar dreæ Eudæmoniohannis Apologiam c.2. inspexerit, levitatem & imprudentiam suam agnoscere cogetur Apologista ille.
units.tr: She most fully establishes the equity of equivocation by the support of the Holy Scriptures, the Fathers, the Doctors, the Schoolmen, the Canonists, and the strongest first principles; therefore it is most worthy to be published in print for the comfort of afflicted Catholics and the instruction of all the pious. And yet a certain Apologist, in his second Apology, denies that any such treatise ever existed in nature, and calls those who remember it impostors. There are, however, many in England who partly saw and read that book, and some even keep it to this day: if the Apologist also looks into chapter 2 of Andreas Eudaemonojohannes's Apology, he will be forced to acknowledge his own levity and imprudence.

units.la: In hoc Tractatu citatur ab authore Æquivocationis exemplum Coventriense, sermonibus multorum in Anglia iactatum, & sic narratur ac defenditur: Grassante in Anglia peste silentia, præsertim Londini, quidam inde Coventriam venit. Ad portam urbis occurrunt destinati à Magistratu, qui delato jurejurando eum interrogant, veniat nec ne Londino? Ille negat strenuè, & distis jurejurando fidem facit. Hic auctor libelli negat eum peccasse. Causam hanc affert: Principali, inquit, & finali propositæ quæstioni scopo; scilicet, an sic venerit ut civitati pestem adferret, respondedit, licet immediatus quæstionis sensus fuerit, scire utrum Londino profectus sit nec n... De hoc bona conscientia jurare ut posset, perfuasio præstitit, aut scientia certa, quam habuit, vel pestem jam non esse Londini, vel aerem non esse ibi infectum, neque præteeun tes inficere: vel se equo vehentem citato cursu absque noxa transfijfse. Hæc est decisio illius Tractatus auctoris: & ut illustret novam hanc doctrinam, admirabilem profert Theoriam, de differentia propositionis verbalis, & reservationissive retentionis mentalis: item de propositione scripta vel mixta, quæ partim vocis prolatione, partim silentio constat: quando animi sensum partim verbis exprimimus, partim silentio premimus & in mente reservamus.
units.tr: In this Treatise the author of equivocation cites the Coventry example, bandied about in the sermons of many in England, and it is related and defended thus: While plague was raging in England, especially in London, a certain man came from there to Coventry. At the city gate he is met by men appointed by the magistrate, who, having administered an oath, ask him whether he has come from London or not. He stoutly denies it, and by his oath gives assurance of what he says. The author of the booklet holds that he has not sinned. He gives this reason: "The principal and final aim of the question, namely whether he came in order to bring plague to the city, he answered; although the immediate sense of the question was to know whether he had set out from London or not..." For this he was able to swear with a good conscience, being persuaded, either by a certain knowledge he had, that the plague was no longer in London, or that the air there was not infected and would not infect passers-by, or that he had passed through riding a horse at full gallop without harm. This is the decision of that Treatise's author; and to illustrate this new doctrine he sets forth an admirable theory of the difference between a verbal proposition and a reservation, or mental retention; likewise of a written or mixed proposition, which consists partly of the utterance of words and partly of silence: when we express the sense of our mind partly in words, and partly suppress it in silence and keep it back in the mind.

units.la: Extat in eodem Tractatu aliud exemplum: Quidam post contractam sponsalper verba de praesenti mox ad alias nuptias convolans, fidem suam alteri sponsæ similiter verba de præsenti obligat. Vocatur in jus, & præstito jurejurando verum dicere jubetur: deinde interrogatus, an non priori sponsæ per verba de tempore præsenti sese obstrinxerit? negat ille & pernegat. Auctor dicti Tractatus negat in hoc peccatum esse, Nam judicis, inquit, quæstio eo tendebat, ut justumne esset prius matrimonium cognoscret: quum igitur reus id matrimonium pro irrito & illegitimo haberet, nullo conscientiæpericulo, jurare potest non fecisse quod fecerat, cum hac utique retentione mentali, Eo animout id esset legitimum matrimonium.
units.tr: There is another example in the same Treatise: a certain man, after contracting betrothal by words of the present tense, soon hurried off to other nuptials, and similarly bound his faith to another bride by words of the present tense. He is summoned to court, and, having taken an oath, is ordered to tell the truth; then, when asked whether he had not bound himself to his former bride by words of the present tense, he denies it and utterly denies it. The author of the said Treatise denies that this is a sin: "For the question of the judge, he says, aimed at this: whether that earlier marriage was just. Since therefore the accused held that marriage to be void and illegitimate, with no danger to his conscience he can swear that he did not do what he had done, namely with this mental reservation, that he meant it to be a lawful marriage."

units.la: Magni scilicet pretij hæc Æquivocationis doctrina est, quæ tam facile cmnia peccata & scelera excusare poterit. Illud quoque fateantur omnes necessarium est, per hanc novam doctrinam, ad omnia quamvis execranda piacula, lataspatefieri, non dico fenestram, sed ianuam & portam: ut merito facturi sint himines facinorosi, & ad omnem impietatem proiecti, si patronos & assertores Æquivocationis pro bene de se meritis habeant.
units.tr: Of great worth, no doubt, is this doctrine of equivocation, which can so easily excuse all sins and crimes. Everyone must also admit that through this new doctrine there is opened wide, for all however execrable atonements, not a window, I say, but a door and a gate; so that criminal men, and those thrown headlong into every impiety, will rightly act if they have the patrons and advocates of equivocation as men who deserve well of them.

units.la: Est & scitum eiusdem disciplinæ, ab auctore dicti Tractatus defensum, Licere criminis alicuius reo pejerare, & omnibus modis factum negare; si ab eo interrogetur, qui auctoritatem legitimam non habet; etiam apud legitimum judicem licere: non tamen in definitè, sed cum hac exceptione, Tantisper dum probationes deficiunt.
units.tr: There is also a rule of the same discipline, defended by the author of the said Treatise: that it is lawful for a person accused of some crime to commit perjury and deny the deed in every way, if he is questioned by one who has no lawful authority; and even before a lawful judge it is lawful, yet not absolutely, but with this exception: "for as long as the proofs are lacking."

units.la: Hæc omnia cum ita sint, Tamen æquivocationes has utilem artem & bonam prudentiam esse dicunt. Ideoque Navarrus sibi ipsi gratulatur, & iactat, se maximo cum primis Principi usum illius Apophthegmatis, qui nescit dissimulare nescit regnare commendâsse, & istam doctrinam Principi illi profuisse. Idem Navarrus in d. humanæ cap. 3 4. hanc simulandi & dissimulandi artem ex Thema prudentia ac virtutem appellavit, & qui ea utantur laudandos esse. Hanc Navarri doctrinam Gregorius 1. 3. tanquam sanctam, veram & inconcussam approbavit & commendavit. Et Gregorius de Valentia Iesuita Tom. 3. disput. 5. q. 1. 3. eam prudentem defensionem vocavit.
units.tr: Although all these things are so, yet they say that these equivocations are a useful art and good prudence. Therefore Navarrus congratulates himself and boasts that he especially commended to the prince the use of that saying, "he who does not know how to dissemble does not know how to reign," and that this doctrine benefited that prince. The same Navarrus, in the said chapter 34 of his Humanae, called this art of pretending and dissembling "prudence and virtue", and said that those who use it are to be praised. This doctrine of Navarrus Gregorius 1. 3. approved and commended as holy, true and unshaken. And Gregory of Valencia the Jesuit, Tom. 3. disput. 5. q. 1. 3., called it a prudent defence.

units.la: Convellitur autem haec mentiendi doctrina Iesuitarum, aperto Scripturae testimonio. Nam Hebr. c. 6. dicitur, Omnis controversiae finis jusjurandum est ad confirmationem adhibitum. Hoc autem verum non est, si Iesuitarum doctrina vera est: nam eorum juramento controversiae non finiuntur, nec res dubiae deciduntur, sed explexae magis redduntur. Et Ephes. 4. c. Depositio mendacio loquimini veritatem unusquisque proximo suo. Et Isa. 28. Posuimus fallaciam spem nostram, & in mendacio abscondimus nos, &c.
units.tr: This Jesuit doctrine of lying is overthrown by the plain testimony of Scripture. For Heb. 6 says, "An end of all controversy is the oath given for confirmation." But this is not true if the doctrine of the Jesuits is true: for by their oath controversies are not ended, nor are doubtful matters decided, but rather made more entangled. And Eph. 4: "Putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour." And Isa. 28: "We have made falsehood our hope, and in lies we have hidden ourselves," etc.

units.la: Longe etiam aliter de hoc mentiendi genere docuerunt Patres. Isidorus in Synonymis c. 1 o. Omne, inquit, genus mendacij summopere fuge: nec casu, nec studio loquaris falsum; nec ut praesites, mentiri studeas: nec qualibet fallacia vitam alicuius defendas. Cave mendacium in omnibus. Refertur etiam cap. Omne. causa 22. q. 2. Et Augustinus in lib. de Mendacio c. 6. Si quis, inquit, ad te confugiat, qui mendacio tuo possit a morte liberari, non es mentiturus. Os enim quod mentitur, occidit animam. Et mox: Cum ergo mentiendo vitae aeterna amittitur, nunquam pro cuiusquam vita temporali mendum est. 22. q. 2. c. omne. Cum Origenes ex sententia Platonis permitteret sapienti bono viro mendacium, modo salutare ejus esset, quorum gratia fieret; et Hieronymus non careret omnino suspicione Origenici dogmatis; (Nam hunc secutus sententiam in commentariis in Epist. ad Galat. scripserat, utrosque Petrum & Paulum, pro tempore simulatione usos: Petrum, quod se subduceret a mensa, supervenientibus Iudaeis; Paulum, quum illum in os acriter obiurgaret, ut per eam illos deterreret;) Augustinus in epist. ad Hieron. quae extat inter epist. Hieronymi tom. 3. p. 150. b. ipsum hac de re diligenter admonet, negatque hoc licere. Rursus Isidorus lib. 2. sentent. c. 31. Quacunque, inquit, arte verborum quisque iuret, Deus omnem, qui conscientiae testis est, ita hoc accipit, sicut ille, cui iuratur, intelligit. Dupliciter autem reus fit: quia & Dei nomen assumit, & proximum dolo capit. 2. q. 5. c. Quacunque. Ibid. c. Qui peierare, additur, Deus duplicitatis aspernator, simpliciter intentionem utriusque, interrogantis & respondentis considerat; verborum artem aspernatur & odit.
units.tr: The Fathers taught quite differently about this kind of lying. Isidore in his Synonyms, ch. 10: "Avoid every kind of lie most carefully: neither by chance nor by design speak what is false; nor strive to lie in order to please, nor defend anyone's life by any deceit. Beware of lying in all things." This is also cited in cap. Omne, causa 22, q. 2. And Augustine in his book On Lying, ch. 6: "If anyone should flee to you who could be freed from death by your lie, you are not to lie. For the mouth that lies kills the soul." And soon after: "Since therefore eternal life is lost by lying, one must never lie for anyone's temporal life." 22 q. 2 c. Omne. Although Origen, following the opinion of Plato, would allow a wise and good man a lie, provided it was salutary to those for whose sake it was told; and Jerome would not be entirely free from suspicion of the Origenist dogma (for following him he had written in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians that both Peter and Paul had used simulation for the occasion: Peter, in withdrawing from the table when Jews came in; Paul, when he sharply rebuked him to his face, so that by this he might deter them): Augustine, in his letter to Jerome, which is among Jerome's letters, vol. 3, p. 150 b, carefully admonishes him on this matter and denies that it is lawful. Again Isidore, Book 2 of the Sentences, ch. 31: "By whatever art of words anyone swears, God, who is witness of conscience, takes it as he to whom the oath is made understands it. And he becomes guilty in two ways: because he both takes the name of God and catches his neighbour by deceit." 2 q. 5 c. Quacunque. In the same place, in c. Qui peierare, it is added: "God, the despiser of duplicity, considers simply the intention of each, of the questioner and of the one who answers; he despises and hates the art of words."

units.la: Et quae non tantum certa verborum Iesuiticorum fides, sed quis certus adeo esse sensus, si verba extrinsecus prolata, liceat ad hunc modum intentionem non expressam, aut aequivocationibus eludere, etiam in sanctissima iuramenti religione. Hoc est enim mirum quod aiebat ille, Linguam juratam, mentem injuriatam habeo.
units.tr: And so there is not only no certain faith in Jesuit words, but what certain sense is there, if words spoken outwardly may in this way be eluded by equivocations and an unexpressed intention, even in the most holy religion of an oath? For that man's saying is remarkable: "I have a tongue that is sworn, a mind that is wronged."

units.la: Ideo ne Iesuitae quidem omnes & Pontificii hanc doctrinam probant. Nam Ioan. Maldonatus Iesuita Coment. in 24. c. Luc. n. 36. Quisquis, inquit, fingendo aliquid fallere conatur, etiamsi praeterea aliquid significare velit (id est, aequivocatione utens) haud dubie mentitur, alioqui nullum esset mendacium, quod non defendi possit.
units.tr: Therefore not even all the Jesuits and Papists approve this doctrine. For John Maldonatus the Jesuit, in his commentary on chapter 24 of Luke, n. 36: "Whoever tries to deceive by pretending something, even if he also wishes to signify something else (that is, using equivocation), undoubtedly lies; otherwise there would be no lie that could not be defended."

units.la: Sic etiam Sacerdotes Vuisbyeenses in epistola quam ad Generosum Papiam nuper scripserunt, Ars est, inquiunt, nostrorum Iesuitarum ut in juramentis Magistratus illudant. Cum a Magistratibus quaeritur, Esne Sacerdos? tum Sacerdoti, inquiunt, licebit respondere, Non sum, sed addita hac intentione, intus in animo conceptâ, non ore prolata, talis nimirum, qualem me esse cupitis, aut ut narrem vobis, aut aliquid simile.
units.tr: So too the priests of Wisbeach, in the letter which they lately wrote to the noble Generosus Papia: "It is an art of our Jesuits," they say, "to mock magistrates in oaths. When the magistrates ask, 'Are you a priest?', then the priest, they say, will be allowed to answer, 'I am not', but with this intention, conceived inwardly in the mind and not uttered by the mouth, namely such as you wish me to be, or in order that I may tell you, or something of the kind."

units.la: Etnici quoque damnarunt doctrinam hanc. Cicero enim lib. 3. Offic. Quod nquit, affirmate, quasi Deo teste, promiseris, id tenendum est. Et qui hoc sibi sumunt, Nullam esse fidem, quae infideli data sit; videant, ne quaeratur latebra perjurio.
units.tr: Heathens too condemned this doctrine. Cicero, in Book 3 of De Officiis, says: "What you have promised, having affirmed it as if God were witness, must be kept. And those who claim for themselves the principle that no faith is to be kept with an unbeliever should see that they are not seeking a hiding-place for perjury."

units.la: Homerus etiam, quem omnium aetatum sapientes demirati sunt, sub Achille lis persona gravissimé detestatur cura, qui aliud in mente celat, aliud lingua loquitur, inquiens:
units.tr: Homer too, whom the wise men of every age have admired, through the person of Achilles most strongly detests the man who hides one thing in his mind and speaks another with his tongue, saying:

units.la: Haud minus ille mihi exosus quàm janua Ditis,
units.tr: "No less hateful to me than the gate of Hades,"

units.la: Mens aliud cui tecta tegit quàm lingua loquatur.
units.tr: "Is the man who hides one thing in his mind and says another with his tongue."

units.la: Turcæ quoque hodie improbarent, satscio, si quis inter ipsos, talia mendacia, & mentiendi, magistratusq; decipiendi artes populo discendas proponeret, utlefuitæ faciunt.
units.tr: The Turks too would disapprove today, I am sure, if anyone among them proposed to the people that such lies, and the arts of lying and of deceiving magistrates, should be learned, as the Jesuits do.

units.la: Conantur quidem Iesuitæ hoc suum mendacij genus, & mentiendi artes defendere primo exemplis Patriarcharum: Vsi sunt, inquiunt, Abrahamus & Isaacus æquivocatione, quum negarunt Saram & Rebeccam suas uxores esse. Gen. 12. 20. & 26. Iacobus etiam Patri Iacobo dixit, aut simulavit Esauum se esse.
units.tr: The Jesuits indeed try to defend this kind of lying, and these arts of deception, first by the examples of the Patriarchs: "Abraham and Isaac," they say, "used equivocation when they denied that Sarah and Rebecca were their wives" (Gen. 12, 20 and 26). Jacob also said to his father Isaac that he was Esau, or pretended to be.

units.la: Respondet autem eis Augustin. contra Cresc. c. 9. & 15. Hæc, inquit, quando in Scripturis legimus, non ideo quia facta credimus, etiam facienda credamus: ne violemus præcepta, dum passim festamur exempla. Et constat, quod non omnia quæ à sanctis viris legimus facta, transferre debeamus in mores. Et cap. 21. Testimonia illa, quibus sanctos libros mendacijs suos Patronos adhibere moliuntur, partim non esse mendacia, partim etiam, quæ sunt, non imitanda esse, docet.
units.tr: Augustine, however, answers them in Contra Cresconium, chapters 9 and 15: "When we read these things in the Scriptures, we do not therefore believe that they are to be done merely because we believe they were done, lest we violate the precepts while we everywhere applaud the examples." And it is agreed that we ought not to carry over into our conduct everything that we read was done by holy men. And in chapter 21: "He teaches that those testimonies by which they labour to bring the holy books in as patrons of their lies are partly not lies at all, and partly, where they are lies, are not to be imitated."

units.la: Secundò, blasphemè dicunt, ipsum quoque Christum æquivocationibus usum esse, quum dixit Marci 13. De die illo & hora nemo scit, ne Angeli quidem qui in cælo sunt: nec ipse Filius, sed solus Pater. His verbis, aiunt, simulavit se nescire secundum humanam naturam novißimum diem: cùm tamen sciverit illum. Et Bellarminus lib. 4. de Christo, c. 1. Suarez tom. 1. in Thom. quæst. 10. artic. 1. disput. 11. Gregor. de Valent. tom. 4. disput. 1. q. 15. part. 1. & Armandus Iesuita in epist. ad Chamierum, dicunt, Errare omnes ferè huius temporis hæreticos, & protestantes præcipuos, sicut olim Agnoitas hæreticos, quia dicant, Christi animam humanam aliquid ignorâsse. Maldonatus autem in Matth. 24. c. ex Damasceno scribit, Agnoitas simpliciter Christo ignorantiam tribuisse. Et Alphons. de Castro adversus hæres. tit. Deus. indicat, Agnoitas ignorantiam simpliciter impegisse Deo ex his verbis, De die illo nemo scit. Idem Maldonatus scribit contra Bellarminum & socios, Athanasium, Ambrosium, Gregorium Nazianz. Theodoretum, Cyrillum, &c. aperte docuisse, Christum, quatenus hominem, diem judicij ignorâsse.
units.tr: Secondly, they blasphemously say that Christ himself also used equivocations, when he said in Mark 13: "Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son himself, but only the Father." "By these words," they say, "he pretended not to know the last day according to his human nature, although he did know it." And Bellarmine, Book 4 on Christ, chapter 1; Suárez, tome 1 on Thomas, question 10, article 1, disputation 11; Gregory of Valencia, tome 4, disputation 1, question 15, part 1; and Armandus the Jesuit in a letter to Chamier, say that almost all the heretics of this time, and the chief Protestants, err, just as the Agnoetae formerly did, because they say that the human soul of Christ was ignorant of something. Maldonatus, however, writes on Matthew 24, drawing on Damascene, that the Agnoetae simply ascribed ignorance to Christ. Alphonsus de Castro, against the heretics, under the title "God," indicates that the Agnoetae simply attributed ignorance to God from these words, "Of that day no one knows." The same Maldonatus writes against Bellarmine and his companions that Athanasius, Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzen, Theodoret, Cyril, and others plainly taught that Christ, as man, was ignorant of the day of judgment.

units.la: CAPVT III. MISCELLANEA DE IE- SVITIS EORVMQVE DOCTRINA.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS CONCERNING THE JESUITS AND THEIR TEACHING.

units.la: VT Iesuitæ quum aliis Doctoribus Pontificijs, tùm etiam in multis Sociis suis contradicant aliquot, saltem demonstrabo exemplis. Mendacia enim certius dignosci non possunt, nisi quando sibimetipsis contraria sunt: A Deo enim ita ordinatum est, ut impij semper seipsos confundant, & mendacia non consonent, sed contra semetipsa semper testentur.
units.tr: That the Jesuits contradict not only other Papist teachers but also several of their own fellows, I will show at least by examples. For lies can be detected most surely only when they contradict themselves. God has so ordained that the wicked always confound themselves, and their lies do not agree but always bear witness against themselves.

units.la: Bellarminus de Notis Ecclesiæ lib. 4. c. 9. Nunc scribit: Docuerunt Eunomiani, neminem peccata nocere, modo fidem habeat. Idem Protestantes.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in On the Notes of the Church, book 4, chapter 9, writes: Now the Eunomians taught that sins do no harm provided a man has faith. The Protestants teach the same.

units.la: Bellarminum autem Iesuitam haud obscurè mendacij insimulat Toletus Iesuita Coim. in Ioan. 13. Affirmavit, inquit, Eunomius, fide sufficere ad salutem, quàm vis mala opera adessent. Protestantes dicunt quidem ad salutem sufficere, negant tamen si demillam sine operibus esse posse. Agnoscit igitur Toletus, Eunomianos fidem mortuam, Protestantes vivam profiteri.
units.tr: Toletus, the Jesuit, in his commentary on John 13, plainly accuses Bellarmine, a fellow Jesuit, of falsehood: Eunomius, he says, affirmed that faith suffices for salvation, however many evil works are present. The Protestants indeed say that it suffices for salvation, yet they deny that faith can be without works. Toletus therefore acknowledges that the Eunomians profess a dead faith and the Protestants a living one.

units.la: Deiustificatione hominis coram Deo. Rursus Bellarminus lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 12. Nos, inquit, SOLA fide justifiri coram Deo, est opinio paradoxa. Et Maldonatus Comment. in Matth. 15. Hoc quod, omnium haereseum seminarium est: Et Feuardent. Com. in Iac. Iustitia fictitia imaginaria est.
units.tr: On the justification of man before God. Again, Bellarmine, in book 1 On Justification, chapter 12: That we are justified before God by faith alone is a paradoxical opinion. And Maldonatus, in his commentary on Matthew 15: This, which is the seminary of all heresies. And Feuardent, in his commentary on James: Fictitious righteousness is imaginary.

units.la: Contradicunt autem aliis Pontificijs doctissimis. Colonienses Canonici; quin etiam authores libelli oblati a Caesare Collocutoribus Protestantibus in Comitijs Ratisbon. dicunt: Tantum per imputationem justitiae Christi, quatenus fides ipsa apprehendit misericordiam atq; justitiam Christi, propter meritum Christi, nos justificari coram Deo. Praeterea Casiandrum, Stapulensem, Peraldum, Ferum & alios, qui huius sententiae fuerunt. Stapleton etiam lib. 7. de Iustificat. c. 9. (alioli, aiunt, aliqui (quos Vega lib. 15. de Iustificat. c. 26. pag. 712. viros doctos & sos vocat) tenebant, nullum alium esse iustitiae conservandae modum, quam si iustitia Christi nobis imputetur.
units.tr: Yet they also contradict other very learned Papists: the Cologne canons, and indeed the authors of the document that Caesar offered to the Protestant colloquists at the Diet of Regensburg, who say: Only through the imputation of Christ's righteousness, insofar as faith itself apprehends the mercy and righteousness of Christ, are we justified before God on account of Christ's merit. Besides these there are Cassander, Stapulensis, Peraldus, Ferus, and others who held this view. Stapleton too, in book 7 On Justification, chapter 9, says that some others (whom Vega, in book 15 On Justification, chapter 26, page 712, calls learned and sound men) held that there is no other way of preserving righteousness than that Christ's righteousness be imputed to us.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Notis Eccles. capit. 9. Calvini doctrinam, fidem vera, semel habitam, amisisse non posse, inter Ioviniani haereses numerat. Campianus contra Rat. 10. Nisi, inquit, Divi e coelo deturbentur, cadere ego nunquam potero. Calarinus quoque, ipso Bellarmino teste lib. 3. de Iustificat. c. 9. docuit ex his verbis, Fideles in perfuasione de sua salute non posse falli. Contradicit etiam Augustinus de Corrept. & Grat cap. 7. Horum fides, inquit, quae per dilectionem operatur, aut omnino non deficit, aut reparatur priusquam haec vita finiatur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 4 On the Notes of the Church, chapter 9, counts among the heresies of Jovinian: the doctrine of Calvin, that true faith once held cannot be lost. Campian, against the Ten Reasons: Unless the gods, he says, are cast down from heaven, I can never fall. Calarinus too, by Bellarmine's own testimony in book 3 On Justification, chapter 9, taught from these words: The faithful cannot err in their persuasion of their own salvation. Augustine also contradicts this, in On Correction and Grace, chapter 7: Their faith, which works through love, either does not fail at all or is restored before this life ends.

units.la: Azorius Iesuita Instit. lib. 9. capit. 7. Appellat, inquit, Calvinus imagines Sanctorum, idola, & simulachra, quasi a sacris auctoribus promiscue usurpentur, idolum vocant.
units.tr: Azorius the Jesuit, in Institutes, book 9, chapter 7: Calvin calls the images of the saints idols and simulacra, as though the sacred authors used these words indiscriminately.

units.la: Valentianus autem lib. 3. de Idol. capit. 8. ff. Quod autem hoc ipsum facit, quod damnat in Calvino Azorius. Idolum, inquit, Graece imaginem, sive simulacrum significat. Haec nomina usque adeo confundit Valentianus, ut non vereatur simulachrorum cultum in hunc modum ex Scripturis defendere. Innuit, inquit, Beatus Petrus aliquem esse simulachrorum & idolorum cultum licitum. Ibidem, Cardinalis etiam Platus lib. 1. de sacris & prophanis Imag. c. 3. Idolum, imaginem & simulachrum pro eodem accipi testatur. S. Hieronymus, inquit, scribit, ubi in sacris literis Idola positum est, Aquilam figuras vel imagines interpretatum esse. Et apud Ciceronem legimus, Imagines quae Idola nominantur. Et Plato, Idola vocamus Imagines, quae & in aquis, & in speculis sunt, & quae picta sunt, & quae typis seu figuris expressa, atque alia huiusmodi: Ita simulachri nomen quod Latine dicitur, pro eo acceperunt quod est idolum apud Graecos, cum in Latina interpretatione vbi dicitur in Psalmo: Simulachra gentium, argentum & aurum, Graece dicuntur eidola. Additibidem: Imaginis nomen, si vocis proprietatem inspiciamus, impia & diabolica forma convenit.
units.tr: Yet Valentianus, in book 3 On Idols, chapter 8 ff., does the very thing that Azorius condemns in Calvin: Idolum, he says, in Greek signifies an image or a statue. Valentianus so confounds these names that he does not hesitate to defend the worship of images from Scripture in this way: He hints, he says, that blessed Peter allowed some worship of images and idols. In the same place, Cardinal Plato, in book 1 On Sacred and Profane Images, chapter 3, also testifies: Idol, image and simulacrum are taken to mean the same thing. St Jerome, he says, writes that where idols is found in the sacred letters, Aquila translated it as figures or images. And in Cicero we read, Images which are called idols. And Plato: We call idols the images which appear in waters and in mirrors, and which are painted, and which are expressed by types or figures, and other things of this kind. Thus they took the word simulacrum, which in Latin is used for that which is idolum among the Greeks, since in the Latin translation, where it is said in the Psalm, the simulacra of the nations, silver and gold, they are called eidola [εἴδωλα] in Greek. He adds there: If we look at the proper meaning of the word image, it fits an impious and diabolical form.

units.la: Bellarminus de Ecclesia triumph. cap. 8. ff. Ergo inquit: Calvinus ait nefas esse Deo invisibili & incorporeo, imaginem corpoream & visibilem collocare: nos Catholici contra. Mox autem, quasi verborum suorum oblitus, dicit: Opinio illa Calvini, non licere pingere imaginem Dei in forma hominis, est etiam ALIQVOT Catholicorum, ut Abulensis Durandi, Perefij, qui dicunt, haec non recte fieri.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in On the Triumph of the Church, chapter 8 ff., says: Calvin says it is wrong to set up a corporeal and visible image of God, who is invisible and incorporeal; we Catholics say otherwise. Soon afterwards, however, as if he had forgotten his own words, he says: That opinion of Calvin, that it is not lawful to paint an image of God in the form of a man, is also held by some Catholics, such as Abulensis, Durandus and Perefius, who say that these things are not done rightly.

units.la: Bellarminus in Praefat. libri de Beat. Sanct. Quis, inquit, Catholicorum unquam divinum honorem imaginibus detulit? At hoc fieri in Papatu testatur Polydorus Vergilius de Invent. rer. capit. 13. Corn. Agrippa de Vanit. capit. 37. Georgius Cassander in Consult. art. 21. & Ioannes Gerson quaestione de neglig. Praelat. capit. 7. Sed quia hos fastidiunt, audiatur Bellarminus sibi ipsi contradicens: Nam lib. 2. de Eccles. triumph. capit. 21. in principio: Sit, inquit, haec nostra propositio: Imagines Christi & Sanctorum venerandae sunt, non solum per accidens, vel improprie verum etiam proprie: ita ut terminetur adoratio in Imagine, non solum ut vicem gerit exemplaris. Vasquez autem libro secundo de Adorat. disput. 8. capit. 3. & 8. Stultum hoc est, inquit, & superstitiosum: idque accurate probat. Docet ibidem, Veteres Scholasticos absolute dixisse, Imagines Christi esse colendas adoratione latriae. Eandemque opinionem fuisse Thomae. Azorius etiam Instit. lib. 9. cap. 6. f. Tota haec Constans, inquit, est Theologorum sententia, imaginem eodem honore & cultu coli, quo colitur id cujus est imago. Et Bellarm. lib. 2. de Imaginib. c. 22. ait: Quantum ad modum loquendi, praesertim in concione ad populum, non est dicendum, imagines ullas adorari debere latriâ, sed e contrario non debere sic adorari.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in the preface to the book On the Blessed Saints: Which of the Catholics has ever given divine honour to images? But that this happens in the Papacy is attested by Polydore Vergil, On the Discoveries of Things, chapter 13; Cornelius Agrippa, On the Vanity, chapter 37; Georgius Cassander, in Consultation, article 21; and John Gerson, in his question on the neglect of prelates, chapter 7. But since Bellarmine disdains these men, let him be heard contradicting himself. For in book 2 On the Triumph of the Church, chapter 21, at the beginning: Let this be our proposition: the images of Christ and of the Saints are to be venerated, not only by accident or improperly but also properly, so that the adoration terminates in the image itself, and not only insofar as it stands in for the exemplar. Vasquez, however, in book 2 On Adoration, disputation 8, chapters 3 and 8: This is foolish, he says, and superstitious, and he proves it carefully. He teaches there that the ancient Scholastics said without qualification that the images of Christ are to be worshipped with the worship of latria, and that Thomas held the same opinion. Azorius too, in Institutes, book 9, chapter 6 ff.: This whole is the constant opinion of the theologians, that an image is honoured with the same honour and worship with which that is honoured of which it is the image. And Bellarmine, in book 2 On Images, chapter 22, says: As to the manner of speaking, especially in sermons to the people, one should not say that any images ought to be adored with latria; on the contrary, they ought not to be so adored.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 2. de Monachis c. 15. Promissionem, inquit, in Baptismo non esse votum proprie ac vere dictum est communis Theologorum sententia, & quidem verissima. Azorius autem lib. 11. c. 14. f. Tertio quaeritur. Baptisma, inquit, esse votum proprie, ac vere dictum, veteres Theologi cum Magistro sentire videntur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 2 On Monks, chapter 15: That a promise made in baptism is not a vow properly and truly so called is the common opinion of the theologians, and indeed a most true one. Azorius, in book 11, chapter 14 ff.: The third question is raised: Baptism, he says, seems to be a vow properly and truly so called; the ancient theologians seem to agree with the Master.

units.la: Rursus Bellarminus ibid. cap. 16. Dico, inquit, votum, de re praecepta, non esse proprie votum, nisi quatenus res illa praecipitur, ut non praecepta. Contradicit autem Azorius Instit. lib. 11. cap. 14. f. Sexto quaeritur. Qui vovet, inquit, rem indifferentem, eius votum, ex communi omnium sententia est inane. Idem ibid. Nihil impedit, inquit, quo minus aliis se denuo voti religione obstringat, ad quod alioqui faciendum lege & praecepto compellitur. Deus enim nos sibi suis legibus devinxit, & nos ipsos ei parite voti nexu vinculo obligamus, & c.
units.tr: Again Bellarmine, ibid., chapter 16: I say, he says, that a vow concerning a commanded thing is not properly a vow, except insofar as that thing is commanded, not as commanded. Azorius, in Institutes, book 11, chapter 14, contradicts him: The sixth question is raised: he who vows an indifferent thing, his vow, by the common opinion of all, is void. The same author, in the same place: Nothing prevents, he says, someone from binding himself again by the bond of a vow to something which he is otherwise compelled to do by law and precept. For God has bound us to himself by his laws, and we ourselves bind ourselves to him by the bond of a vow, and so on.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 5. de Christo c. 9. in princip. & f. Haec. Conveniunt, inquit, inter se Theologi omnes, & uno consensu docent, Christum, praeter ea bona, quae suis laboribus peperit nobis, meruisse etiam sibi corporis gloriam, & nominis exaltationem, & omnia quae accepit post passionem.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 5 On Christ, chapter 9, at the beginning and in the passage beginning Haec: All theologians agree among themselves, and with one consent teach that Christ, besides those goods which he won for us by his labours, merited also for himself the glory of his body, the exaltation of his name, and all that he received after the passion.

units.la: Contra Vega in Opusc. de Meritis q. 6. Christus, inquit, totam suam gratiam, totamque gloriam essentialem SINE meritis habuit, in primo suo humanitatis instanti. Et Scotus dist. 18. Nec, nisi indirecte meruit gloriam corporis.
units.tr: Against this, Vega, in the Opuscula On Merits, question 6: Christ, he says, had his whole grace and his whole essential glory without merits, in the first instant of his humanity. And Scotus, distinction 18: Nor did he merit the glory of the body except indirectly.

units.la: Bellarminus citato loco sententiam suam defendere conatur ex Scriptura sacra. Hebr. 4. inquit, sic legitur: Videmus Iesum PROPTER passionem mortis gloria coronatum. Philip. 2. Humiliavit seipsum, factus obediens usque ad crucem. PROPTER quod exaltavit eum Deus, & dedit ei nomen super omne nomen, &c. Addit, Respondet Calvinus, has voces, QUA PROPTER & PRO TER, non causam exaltationis significare, sed consequentiam. Suarez autem dicit Tom. 1. in Thom. disput. 41. sect. 1. à Calvino hoc dici Haeretice. Et Iesuitae Anglo-Rhem. in Phil. 2. c. Scripturas impudenter detorquet.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in the place cited, tries to defend his opinion from Holy Scripture. He says that Hebrews 4 reads thus: "We see Jesus, crowned with glory on account of [propter] the suffering of death." Philippians 2: "He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto the cross. Wherefore [propter quod] God also exalted him and gave him a name above every name," etc. He adds that Calvin answers that these words, "for which cause" and "wherefore" [qua propter and pro ter], signify not the cause of the exaltation but its consequence. But Suárez says, in Tom. 1 on Thomas, disputation 41, section 1, that this is said by Calvin in a heretical manner. And the Anglo-Rhemish Jesuits, on Philippians 2 (chapter 'Scripturas'), shamelessly twist the Scriptures.

units.la: Contra vero Ribera Iesuita Com. in Heb. 1. capit. ad verba verf. 9. Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem, propterea unxit te Deus, &c. Sanctus, inquit, Thomas affirmat, cum dicitur, PROPTEREA, non meritum indicari, sed finem; ut sit sensus, Ad hoc te unxit Deus, ut habeas haec omnia, quod satis probabiliter dicitur. Suarez quo supra disput. 10. sect. 4. f. sed contra. Per unctionem, inquit, intelligunt multi Patres ipsam incarnationem, & unionem ad verbum, Augustinus, Anshelmus, Beda & Cyrillus Alexandrinus: atque ita particula PROPTER, non de causa meritoria, sed de finali intelligenda est. Et disput. 18. sect. 2. f. Dico primo, Athanasius, inquit, illum locum exponit de gratia animae habituali. Et disput. 40. sect. 2. f. Nihilominus. Communis, ait, est Theologorum sententia, Christum non meruisse gratiam animae habitualem, sed eam ab instantia incarnationis suae habuisse. Ergo contra Bellarminum ipsis Iesuitis testibus, vox PROPTEREA, non causam meritoriam, sed consequentiam finalem significat.
units.tr: On the contrary, Ribera the Jesuit, in his commentary on Hebrews 1, at the words of verse 9, "Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee," etc., says: St. Thomas affirms that when it is said "therefore" (propterea), not merit is indicated but the end, so that the sense is: God anointed you for this, that you should have all these things; which is said with considerable probability. Suárez, in the work cited above, disputation 10, section 4, near the end, but against this: many Fathers, he says, understand by the anointing the incarnation itself and the union with the Word, Augustine, Anselm, Bede and Cyril of Alexandria; and thus the particle "therefore" is to be understood not of a meritorious cause but of a final one. And in disputation 18, section 2, near the end: I say first, he says, that Athanasius explains that place of the habitual grace of the soul. And in disputation 40, section 2, near the end, "Nevertheless": it is, he says, the common opinion of the theologians that Christ did not merit habitual grace for the soul, but had it from the first instant of his incarnation. Therefore, against Bellarmine, with the Jesuits themselves as witnesses, the word "therefore" (propterea) signifies not a meritorious cause but a final consequence.

units.la: Greg. de Valentia Analys. lib. 8. c. 2. Papa, inquit, ut Papa, id est, quoad publicam personam, haereticus esse nequit. Bellarminus etiam lib. 4. de Pontifice Roman. c. 6.
units.tr: Gregory of Valencia, Analysis, book 8, chapter 2: "The Pope," he says, "as Pope, that is, as regards his public person, cannot be a heretic." Bellarmine too, book 4 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 6.

units.la: Probabile robabile, inquit, est, pieque credi potest, summum Pontificem, ut Pontificem, non solum errare non posse, sed etiam ut particularem personam hæreticum esse non posse, sed falsum aliquid contra fidem pertinaciter credendo. Papam etiam non posse ullo modo esse hæreticum, nec hæresin publicè docere, etiamsi solus rem aliquam definiat, Pigghius acerrimè defendit lib. 4. Ecclesiast. Hierarch. c. 8.
units.tr: It is probable, he says, and it can piously be believed, that the supreme Pontiff, as Pontiff, not only cannot err, but also cannot, as a particular person, be a heretic, though he may believe something false against the faith stubbornly. That the Pope cannot in any way be a heretic, nor publicly teach heresy, even if alone he defines some matter, Pighius defends most vigorously in book 4 of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 8.

units.la: Catharinus autem Com. in Galat. 2. c. Falsum, inquit, hoc est, etiamsi novitij Scriptores ausi sunt oppositum defendere. Præterea, Legimus multos Pontifices apostatâsse à fide: Honorium in Concilijs duobus, vel tribus Papam damnatum; Cœlestinum quoque & alios. Verba sunt Lyra, in Matt. 16. Cani in Loc. Theolog. lib. 6. c. 8. Alphonsi de Castro lib. 1. hæref. c. 2. p. 7. Pontificem etiam ut Pontificem, posse esse hæreticum, si absque generali concilio definiat, tuetur Nilus in lib. adversus primatum Papæ; Gerson & Alain in libris de potest. Ecclesiæ, & Adrianus 6. Papa in quæst. de Confirmatione: qui omnes non in Pontifice, sed in Ecclesia sive in Concilio generali tantùm, constituuntinfallibilitatem iudicij de rebus fidei. Et Bellarm. lib. 4. de Pontifice Rom. c. 2. inquit, Papam, ut Papam hæreticum esse posse Doctores Parisienses tenuerunt. Vide Vuitakerum de Pontifice Romano pag. 737. Hanovien. editionis, item pag. 769.
units.tr: Catharinus, however, in his commentary on Galatians 2 (chapter 'Falsum'), says: this is false, even though novice writers have dared to defend the opposite. Moreover, "We read that many Pontiffs have apostatized from the faith: Honorius, condemned as Pope in two or three councils; Celestine also, and others." These are the words of Lyra, on Matthew 16; of Cano, in Loci Theologici book 6, chapter 8; of Alfonso de Castro, book 1 Against Heresies, chapter 2, p. 7. That the Pontiff, even as Pontiff, can be a heretic, if he defines without a general council, is maintained by Nilus in his book against the primacy of the Pope; by Gerson and Alain in their books on the power of the Church; and by Adrian VI in his question on Confirmation. All of these place the infallibility of judgment in matters of faith not in the Pope but only in the Church or in a general council. And Bellarmine, book 4 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 2, says that the Parisian doctors held that the Pope, as Pope, can be a heretic. See Whitaker on the Roman Pontiff, p. 737 of the Hanau edition, and likewise p. 769.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 2. de Pontifice Rom. c. 26. Pontifex, inquit, Romanus non potest ullo Principe Christiano, sive seculari, sive Ecclesiastico judicari in terris, neque ab omnibus simul in Concilio congregatis.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 2 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 26: The Roman Pontiff, he says, cannot be judged on earth by any Christian prince, whether secular or ecclesiastical, nor by all together gathered in a council.

units.la: Iohannes Ferus autem in Act. 11. c. Cur cum incircumcisis comedisti, &c. Petrus, inquit, respondebat, & omnia narrabat. Potest igitur Ecclesia à Ministris non solùm exigere rationem, sed etiam deponere & repudiare potest. Impij autem nostri Pontifices, quasi Domini sint, non Ministri, ab Ecclesia quidem argui & in ordinem cogi nolunt. Sic refert Bellarminus lib. 4. de Rom. Pontifice c. 9. celebratum fuisse Concilium Sinuessanum anno Domini 295. in causa Pontificis Marcelli, ad eum deponendum, si hæreticus inveniretur: & Ecclesiam Rom. ex suspicione hæreseos Liberio Papæ anno Christi 351. Pontificatum abrogâsse; Constantinopolitanam quoque Synodum 6. & 7. deposuisse Iulium.
units.tr: John Ferus, however, on Acts 11 (chapter 'Why did you eat with the uncircumcised', etc.): Peter, he says, answered and related everything in order. The Church therefore can not only demand an account from its ministers, but can also depose and reject them. Our impious Pontiffs, however, as if they were lords and not ministers, are unwilling to be called to account and brought into order by the Church. So Bellarmine reports, book 4 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 9: that the Council of Sinuessa was held in the year of the Lord 295, in the case of Pope Marcellus, to depose him if he were found a heretic; and that the Roman Church, on suspicion of heresy, abrogated the pontificate of Pope Liberius in the year of Christ 351; and that the Sixth and Seventh Constantinopolitan Synods deposed Julius.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 5. de Rom. Pontifice c. 9. Non pugnat, inquit, cum verbo Dei, ut unus homo sit Princeps Ecclesiasticus & politicus simul, & ut possit unus homo regere sacerdotium & Principatum. Et mox: Etsi absolute forte præstaret, Pontifices tractare solum spiritualia, Reges temporalia, tamen propter malitiam temporis experientia clamat siliter temporales aliquos Principatus Pontifici donatos esse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 5 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 9: It is not contrary to the word of God, he says, that one man should be ecclesiastical and political prince at once, and that one man should be able to rule both priesthood and principality. And soon after: Although absolutely it might perhaps be better for Pontiffs to deal only with spiritual matters and kings with temporal ones, yet experience of the wickedness of the times cries out that some temporal principalities have been given to the Pontiff.

units.la: Contrà verò Episcop. Espensæus in 1. Tim. lib. 2. c. 9. Nos, inquit, proh dolor, pacificis in litigiosos degeneramus, eaque est hodierna Ecclesiæ praxis, ut quæri serìò possit, Theologùne, an Canonista sit ad Episcopum aptior? &c. Dicunt quidam, priscis quidem Episcopis Theologia magis convenijse, cujus gladio Catholicis contra hæreticos procedere mos fit. Hodiè verò contrà, jurisperitia magis congruere, quia plures accidunt quæstiones juris, quæ ad fidem spectantes. Sed longè aberrant; quia Episcopi nö minus hodiè quàm antea prædicare tenentur, quibus non minus nunc, quàm tunc in consecratione prædicandi officium imponitur: prædicationis autem materia est divina Scriptura, hanc igitur docere magis tenentur quàm Canones, quos nö immediatè Dñs, sed sancti Dei homines ediderunt. Et c. 10. Multi quidem tempus secu affert & immutat, utinam in melius. Et c. 11. Quàm non expediret hominibus Episcopos Cancellariatu fungi? Frăcifc. de Vičt. Relečt. 1. q. 1. Regimen, inquit, nimarũ est ars artiũ, ergo non potest unus & idem utrumq; munus implere, administrandi seculare & Ecclesiast. potestatem. Salmerò Iesuita tractatu 18. in parabola hominis divistis luc. 18. n. 1. Tempore, inquit, Augustini, ut ipse docet lib. de opere Monach. c. 29. Episcopi litibus Christianorum vacare solebant, non ita tamen litibus vacabant sicernendis, ut interim à prædicatione & Episcopi munere vacarent: Quod nunc Episcopi ausis incumbunt civilibus, consuetudine Ecclesiæ introductum est, &c.
units.tr: On the contrary, Bishop Espencaeus, on 1 Timothy, book 2, chapter 9: "We," alas, "have degenerated from peaceable men into litigious ones, and it is the present practice of the Church that one may seriously ask whether a theologian or a canonist is the more suitable for a bishop? etc." Some say that theology was more suited to the ancient bishops, by whose sword it was customary to proceed among Catholics against heretics; but today, on the contrary, jurisprudence is more fitting, because many questions of law arise which touch on faith. But they stray far; for bishops are bound to preach no less today than before, and the office of preaching is laid on them no less now than then at their consecration; the matter of preaching is divine Scripture, which they are therefore more bound to teach than the canons, which were published not immediately by the Lord but by holy men of God. And chapter 10: Time indeed brings many changes, would that they were for the better. And chapter 11: How would it not be inexpedient for men that bishops should hold the office of chancellor? Francisco de Vitoria, Relectio 1, question 1: "Government," he says, "is the art of arts; therefore one and the same person cannot fulfil both offices, that of administering secular and ecclesiastical power." Salmerón the Jesuit, tractate 18 on the parable of the man divided, Luke 18, number 1: In the time of Augustine, as he himself teaches in the book On the Work of Monks, chapter 29, bishops used to be occupied with the lawsuits of Christians; yet they were not so occupied with settling lawsuits as to be kept meanwhile from preaching and the office of bishop. That bishops now busy themselves with civil affairs has been introduced by custom of the Church, etc.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: On Doctrine

units.la: Papam esse Monarcham seu Dominum totius orbis Christiani negat Bellarminus lib. 5. de Pontif. Rom. c. 3. & dicit, Si res ita se haberet, deberet id constare ex Scripturis, aut saltem ex traditione Apostolica.
units.tr: Bellarmine denies that the Pope is the monarch or lord of the whole Christian world (On the Roman Pontiff, book 5, chapter 3). He says that if this were so, it would have to be established from Scripture, or at least from apostolic tradition.

units.la: Contrarium autem affirmat, Iesuita Alvarez, Hostiensis, Sylvester & alij multi, ut Bellarminus fatetur ibid. c. 1.
units.tr: The contrary is affirmed by the Jesuit Alvarez, Hostiensis, Sylvester and many others, as Bellarmine admits in the same place (chapter 1).

units.la: Malos & impios non esse quidem membra vera, nec simpliciter corporis Ecclesiae, sed tamen secundum quid & aequivoce; Ioannes de Turrecremata Cardinalis lib. 5. c. 57. probat ex Alexandro de Ales, Hugone & Thoma; idem etiam docent Petrus à Soto, Melchior Canus, & alij. Aliquid dicant, malos non esse membra vera, dicunt nihilominus vere esse in Ecclesia, sive in corpore Ecclesiae, & esse simpliciter fideles, seu Christianos. Neque enim, inquiunt, sola membra sunt in corpore, sed etiam humores, dentes, pili, & alia quae non sunt membra: neque fideles aut Christiani dicuntur tales à charitate, sed à fide, sive à fidei professione. Sic etiam docet Coste-rus Iesuita Apolog. part. 3. c. 12. s. Et Hugo. Vt flegma, inquit, pituita, sanies, saliva, sanguis abundans viventis hominis neque membra sunt, neque partes, & tamen non sunt extra corpus: Ita impij ad superfluos humores referuntur, qui suo tempore, ubi maturi fuerint, cum stercoribus egeruntur.
units.tr: Evil and impious men are indeed not true members, nor members simply of the body of the Church, but they are so in a certain respect and equivocally. John de Torquemada, the Cardinal, proves this in book 5, chapter 57, from Alexander of Hales, Hugh and Thomas. Peter de Soto, Melchior Cano and others teach the same. Although they say that evil men are not true members, they nevertheless say that such men truly are in the Church, or in the body of the Church, and are simply faithful, or Christians. For, they say, not only limbs are in the body, but also humours, teeth, hairs and other things that are not members; and men are not called faithful or Christians from charity, but from faith, that is, from profession of faith. The Jesuit Coster also teaches this, in his Apology, part 3, chapter 12, section 's'. Hugh says: as phlegm, pituita, pus, saliva and excess blood in a living man are neither members nor parts, and yet are not outside the body, so the wicked are classed with superfluous humours, which in due time, when they have ripened, are expelled along with the excrement.

units.la: Contrà vero Bellarminus libro tertio de militante Ecclesiae capit. 9. s. ad ultimum, Si ita est, inquit, sequitur, Pontificem malum non esse caput Ecclesiae: & alios Episcopos, si mali sint, non esse capita suarum Ecclesiarum. Caput enim non est humor, aut pilus, sed membrum, & quidem praecipuum: At hoc est contra Concilium Constantiense, in quo Sess. 15. damnatur error 22. Ioan. Huss, quo asserebat, Pastorem malum esse aequivoce Pastorem; & error 30. quo asseritur, Prælatum malum non esse Prælatum. Bellarminus igitur, ne cogatur fateri, Ecclesiam Romanam non habere caput, si malum Pontificem habet, ibidem docet, malos non esse membra VIVA corporis Ecclesiae. Sed non elabitur; nam hoc modo Ecclesia Rom. si habet malum Pontificem, ut perpetuò habet, caput non vivum habet.
units.tr: On the contrary, Bellarmine, in book 3 of On the Militant Church, chapter 9, near the end, says: If this is so, it follows that the Pope, if he is evil, is not the head of the Church; and other bishops, if they are evil, are not the heads of their churches. For the head is not a humour or a hair, but a member, and indeed the chief one. But this is contrary to the Council of Constance, in which, in session 15, error 22 of John Hus is condemned, the error by which he asserted that an evil minister is a minister only equivocally, and error 30, which asserts that an evil prelate is not a prelate. Bellarmine, therefore, so as not to be forced to admit that the Roman Church has no head if it has an evil Pope, teaches in the same place that evil men are not living members of the body of the Church. But he does not escape; for in this way the Roman Church, if it has an evil Pope, as it always does, has a head that is not alive.

units.la: Collegiū Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in Ephes. 5. Si, inquiunt, Protestantes ullum in fide Theologiae sensum haberent, nunquam diceret Ecclesiam posse à fide deficere, id est, à Christi sponso divortium pati. Bellarm. vero lib. 3. de Milit. Eccles. c. 3. Notandum est, inquit, multos ex nostris tempus terere, dum probant absolute Ecclesiam non posse à fide deficere: nam Protestantes id concedunt, sed dicunt, id intelligi de Ecclesia invisibili. Ita Bellarminus Stapletonus igitur & Valetianus Iesuita operam multam luduntque, qui hoc etiam prolixè satis stre-nueque probare conantur.
units.tr: The English College at Rheims, in its Annotations on Ephesians 5, says: If the Protestants had any sense of theology, they would never say that the Church can fall from the faith, that is, suffer divorce from Christ her spouse. But Bellarmine, in book 3 of On the Militant Church, chapter 3, writes: It must be noted that many of our people waste their time proving absolutely that the Church cannot fall from the faith; for the Protestants concede this, but they say it is to be understood of the invisible Church. So Bellarmine, Stapleton and the Jesuit Valentia spend much labour in vain, and they strive to prove this at great length and with great vigour.

units.la: Bellarmin. lib. 3. c. 24. de Pontif. Rom. sic scribit: Si Pontifices non concionantur, tamen multos alios Pastorales actus exercent, ligant, solvunt, controversias judicant, Episcopos creant, & quod per se concionando non faciunt, faciunt per alios.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 3, chapter 24, of On the Roman Pontiff, writes thus: If the Popes do not preach, they nevertheless perform many other pastoral acts: they bind and loose, they judge controversies, they create bishops; and what they do not do by preaching themselves, they do through others.

units.la: Contrà Maldonatus Summula q. 16. art. 3. 5. 6. Notarunt, inquit, Hieron. in c. 4. ad Ephes. & Aug. epist. 57. propterea Paulu non distinxisse Pastores & Doct. quia omnis Pastor debet docere: & nomen Pastoris significat actionem personalem, sicut nomen Medici. Itaque sicut nemo potest per alium curare, ita nemo potest suas oves per alium pascere. Nec quic-quam valet responsio communis: Satis esse per Vicarium laborare, quia secundum eandem regulam satis esset manducare per Vicarium; quia scriptum est, Qui non laborat, non manducet. De di-vino jure multa sunt testimonia in sacris literis, ut n. 12. Excubate in custodia Tabernaculi. Nemo autem potest excubare, nisi praesens. Christus etiam describit nobis Pastorem notis suis inter alias, ut oves suas cognoscat, & illæ audiant vocem illius. At nec ille eas cognoscere, nisi praesens, nec illæ, nisi praesentem, audire possunt. Valentianus Iesuita quoque Tom. 4. disput. 19. q. 1. punct. 3. Christus, inquit, Dominus Matth. 28. Apostolis & eorum successoribus Episcopis mandat, Ite, & docete. Paulus 1. Cor. 1. Misit me Dominus Evangelizare, non baptizare, id est, praecipue me misit ad praedicandum, non autem ad administranda Sacramenta.
units.tr: Against this, Maldonatus, in his Summula, question 16, articles 3, 5 and 6, says: Jerome on Ephesians 4 and Augustine in letter 57 have noted that Paul did not therefore distinguish ministers and teachers, because every minister must teach. The name minister signifies personal action, just as the name physician does. Therefore, just as no one can care for a patient through another, so no one can feed his sheep through another. Nor is the common reply of any value, that it is enough to labour through a vicar; for by the same rule it would be enough to eat through a vicar, since it is written, He who does not work shall not eat. There are many testimonies on divine right in the sacred letters, as in n. 12: Keep watch in the guard of the Tabernacle. But no one can keep watch unless he is present. Christ also describes the shepherd to us by his marks, among others, that he knows his sheep and they hear his voice. But neither can he know them unless he is present, nor can they hear him unless he is present. The Jesuit Valentia also, in Tome 4, disputation 19, question 1, point 3, says: Christ the Lord, in Matthew 28, commands the Apostles and their successors the bishops, Go and teach. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 1: The Lord sent me to evangelize, not to baptize; that is, he sent me chiefly to preach, not to administer the sacraments.

units.la: Bellarminus lib.4. c.8. de Notis Ecclesiæ inquit: Successione in Rom. Eccleab Apostolis deducta usq; ad nos, veteres tanquam argumento evidentissimo usi sunt ad eram Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 4, chapter 8, of On the Notes of the Church, says: The succession in the Roman Church, traced from the Apostles down to us, the ancients used as the most evident argument for the true Church.

units.la: Stapletonus autem lib.13. de doct. princip. ca. 6. Personalem inquit, successionem nihil moramur, modo doctrinam nostram consentientem Scripturis ostendere possimus. Bellarminus quoq; lib. de Eccles. milit. c.8. Successio vera non est, quam hæresis interrumpit.
units.tr: Stapleton, however, in book 13, chapter 6, of On the Principal Doctrine, says: We are not concerned with personal succession, provided we can show that our doctrine agrees with the Scriptures. Bellarmine too, in On the Militant Church, chapter 8, says: That is not a true succession which heresy interrupts.

units.la: Bellarm. lib.5. c.1. & 6. de Pontifice Rom. dicit, Papam non habere summam aliquam potestatem temporalem jure divino, nec posse ullo modo imperare (temporaliter) principibus secularibus, nedum eos regno & principatu privare, etiamsi illi privari aliquo modo mereantur, sed tamen habere eum hanc potestatem indirecte in ordine ad bonum spirituale. Et hoc modo potest Reges deponere, regna transferre, & uni auferre, alteri conferre, inquam summus Pontifex spiritualis. Et hæc est hodie lesuitarum omnium novissima & pestilentissima sententia.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 5, chapters 1 and 6, of On the Roman Pontiff, says that the Pope does not have any supreme temporal power by divine right, nor can he in any way command secular princes in temporal matters, much less deprive them of kingdom and principality, even if they somehow deserve to be deprived. But he does have this power indirectly, in relation to the spiritual good. And in this way he can depose kings, transfer kingdoms, take away from one and confer on another, I mean the supreme spiritual Pontiff. And this is today the newest and most pestilential opinion of all the Jesuits.

units.la: Tolosanus autem lib.26. de Repub. c.7. ƒ 10. A Christo, inquit, passo per intervallum ducentorum annorum, nusquam legitur Christianos contra Imperatores, jam sævientes in eos, et plurimos necantes, & contra Rempub. esse quidquam molitos. Bellarm. lib. de Rom. Pontif. c.7. ƒ. Quod si: hoc factum dicit, quia defuerint vires temporales Christianis. Respondet vero Tolosanus, etiam cum Christiani pares viribus & numero fuerint, sese tamen eis non opposuisse: imo duxisse in hoc religionem suam anteferri omnibus, seq; ab eo Christianos appellari, cujus sit hoc piissimum dogma, ut magistratibus pareant. Espenseus Episcopus Com. in Titum 3. digress. 10. Apostolus, inquit, docet, redentes omnes mundi potestatibus debere esse subjectos. Sed turbulenti quidam, mota inter regnum et Sacerdotium controversia, mirum est, quot, quantasq; turbas dederint. Torante hanc Camerinam annorum centuriis Chrysostomus nihil tale unquam futurum suspicans, ex Apostolo (omnis anima potestatibus subjecta sit) Omnis, inquit, sive Apostolus, sive Propheta, sive Evangelista, sive Episcopus subjectus sit. Sequuntur Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Oecumenius, & Græci omnes. Idem Gregorius M. ingenuè agnoscebat, Nam epist.42. inquit, Imperatoribus concenceffum esse Sacerdotibus dominari. Et Bernardus ad Archiepisc. Senonensem idem colligit: Si omnis anima, inquit, tum vestra, quis vos excipit ex universitate? si quis tentat excipere, tentat decipere.
units.tr: Tolosanus, however, in book 26, chapter 7, section 10, of On the Commonwealth, says: From the passion of Christ, for a space of two hundred years, it is nowhere read that the Christians, although the emperors were then raging against them and putting very many to death, attempted anything against the commonwealth. Bellarmine, in On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 7, section: But if he says this was done because the Christians lacked temporal strength. Tolosanus replies: even when the Christians were equal in strength and number, they did not set themselves against the emperors; indeed they judged in this that their religion was to be preferred above all, and that they were called Christians after him whose most pious doctrine it is that men should obey the magistrates. Espenseus, bishop, in his commentary on Titus 3, digression 10, says: The Apostle teaches that all men ought to be subject to the powers of the world. But certain turbulent men, once the controversy between kingdom and priesthood had been stirred up, have caused amazing turmoil, many and great. For many centuries, Chrysostom, suspecting that nothing of the kind would ever happen, took from the Apostle (let every soul be subject to the powers) the words: Every one, he says, whether Apostle, or Prophet, or Evangelist, or Bishop, is subject. Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius and all the Greeks follow him. Gregory the Great frankly acknowledged the same, for in letter 42 he says that it has been conceded to emperors to rule over priests. Bernard draws the same conclusion in his letter to the Archbishop of Sens: If every soul, he says, then yours too; who excepts you from the universal rule? If anyone tries to except you, he tries to deceive.

units.la: Pontifices quoq; ipsi in suis decretis fatentur, se Imperatoribus subiectos esse. Iurfus idem Espenseus Com. in Timoth. lib. 2. digress. & pag. 275. Gregorius 7. inquit, Pontifex, cui nomen erat Hildebrandus, exemplo suo NOVO, & omnis bibliotheca veteris invento novello schismate regnum & sacerdotium scindens, primus Sacerdotem lancem contra Imperij diadema elevans, se, suoq; exemplo Pontifices alios contra principes & excommunicatos, gladio accinxit, belloq;, qua hæreditario, insurrexit, ut justa prophetiam Mich. 2. Dentibus mordentes pacem prædicarent. Utinam Petrum in feiendo imitati, Petrum in recondendo gladio imitarentur.
units.tr: The Pontiffs themselves also confess in their decrees that they are subject to the emperors. Again Espenseus, in his commentary on 1 Timothy, book 2, digression, and page 275: Gregory VII, the Pontiff whose name was Hildebrand, by his new example, and with a novel schism unknown to the whole old library, dividing kingdom from priesthood, was the first to raise the priestly dish against the imperial diadem. He girded himself and other Pontiffs with the sword against princes and the excommunicated, and rose up in war as if by hereditary right, so that, in accordance with the prophecy of Micah 2, they might bite with their teeth and proclaim peace. Would that they had imitated Peter in striking, and imitated Peter in sheathing the sword.

units.la: Otto Frisingensis quoque in suo Chron. lib.6. c.35. Lego, inquit, ac relego Regum & Imperatorum res gestas, & nusquam invenio quenquam eorum, ante hunc Henricum Imperatorem, quem Hildebrandus deposuit, à summo Pontifice regno privatum.
units.tr: Otto of Freising also, in his Chronicle, book 6, chapter 35: "I read and re-read the deeds of kings and emperors, and nowhere do I find anyone, before this Emperor Henry whom Hildebrand deposed, stripped of his kingdom by the Supreme Pontiff."

units.la: Bellarminus scribit lib.1. de Ecclesia triumphante, Invocationem Sanctorum & defunctorum universa antiquitas docuit. Et lib.1. de Beat. Sanct. c.20. ƒ Argumentum sextum. Dicunt Protestantes, inquit, nullum extare in Scripturis exemplum, nullum præceptum, nullam promissionem de Invocatione Sanctorum. Nos vero exemplis roboravimus Invocationem Sanctorum ex utroq; Testamento.
units.tr: Bellarmine writes in book 1 of De Ecclesia triumphante: "The whole of antiquity taught the invocation of the saints and the dead." And in book 1 of De beatorum sanctorum ch. 20, the sixth argument: "The Protestants say," he says, "that there is no example, no precept and no promise in Scripture concerning the invocation of the saints. But we have confirmed the invocation of the saints by examples from both Testaments."

units.la: Contra vero Bellarm. ibid. c.6. scribit, Sanctos veteris Testamenti invocare potulus non solebat, Et Eckius in Enchirid. sub finem loci de venerat. Sanct. Nec hoc licuit, inquit, in primordio Ecclesiæ in Novo Test. ne Gentiles recens conversi, se iterum idololatriam inducipaterentur. Salmeron etiam in 1. Timoth. 2. disput. 8. ƒ. uldocet, Non esse expressum in novo Testamento de Invocatione Sanctorum: quia durum esset id Iudaeis praecipere: Gentibus vero periculosum.
units.tr: On the contrary, Bellarmine in the same place, ch. 6, writes: "The saints of the Old Testament were not accustomed to be invoked." And Eck in the Enchiridion, near the end of the section on the veneration of the saints: "Nor was this permitted," he says, "in the early Church, in the New Testament, lest the newly converted Gentiles should be led back into idolatry." Salmeron also, on 1 Timothy 2, disputation 8, teaches that there is nothing expressed in the New Testament about the invocation of the saints, because it would be hard to command this to the Jews and dangerous for the Gentiles.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 2. de Purgatorio, Orationem, inquit, pro defunctis omnis antiquitas probavit: Ibid. c. 15. Suffragia vivorum prosunt defunctis, qui sunt in Purgatorio.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 2 De Purgatorio: "All antiquity," he says, "approved prayer for the dead." Likewise, ch. 15: "The intercessions of the living profit the dead who are in Purgatory."

units.la: Georgius Cassander vero in Consult. artic. de Missa, Usque ad hodiernum diem, inquit, nusquam in Ecclesia statutum fuit, quomodo nostrae preces defunctorum animis prodesse possint: sed fuisse merum testimonium charitatis nostrae erga defunctos, et articuli immortalitatis animae, et corporum resurrectionis futurae. Huius etiam luculentum testimonium esse potest illud Augustini Confess. lib. 9. c. 13. orantis pro matre sua defunctae: Credo, inquit, quod jam feceris quae rogo, sed voluntaria oris mei approba Domine.
units.tr: Georg Cassander, however, in his Consultatio on the article concerning the Mass, says: "Up to the present day it has nowhere been laid down in the Church how our prayers could benefit the souls of the dead; rather, they were a mere witness of our love towards the departed, and of the article on the immortality of the soul and the future resurrection of the body." A clear testimony to this may also be that saying of Augustine, Confessions, book 9, ch. 13, praying for his deceased mother: "I believe, Lord, that you have already done what I ask; accept the willing offerings of my mouth."

units.la: Lyrinensis inquit, Catholicus est, qui verae fidei non praeponit cujusquam authoritatem. Contra Bellarm. lib. 3. de Eccles. Milit. c. 2. Nostra, Catholicus est, ait, qui est uni pastori Papae subditus.
units.tr: Vincent of Lérins says: "He is Catholic who does not put the authority of anyone above the true faith." Against this, Bellarmine, De Ecclesia militante, book 3, ch. 2: "Our Catholic," he says, "is one who is subject to the one shepherd, the Pope."

units.la: Bellarminus libro 3. de Rom. Pontifice dicit: Roma non erit Sedes Antichristi.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 3 De Romano Pontifice, says: "Rome will not be the seat of Antichrist."

units.la: Ribera Iesuita vero Comment. in Apocal. 14. inquit, Roma dicitur Babylon, quia ad finem seculi futura est officina omnis idololatriae. Adhuc clarius Collegium Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in Apocal. 175. Roma, inquit, erit sedes Antichristi. Et Vega Iesuita in Apoc. 18. Com. 1. 4. Illud etiam nobis dicendum videtur ex Aretha, Primasio, Ansberto, Hannono, Ambrosio, et aliis hoc loco Idololatriam urbis Romanae signisicari, defecturamque esse Romam a fide: atque adeo futuram esse habitationem daemoniorum, et omnis spiritus immundi, obflagitia, et idololatriam, quae tunc temporis in Romana civitate, Romanoque imperio late grassabitur.
units.tr: The Jesuit Ribera, however, in his commentary on Apocalypse 14, says that Rome is called Babylon because at the end of the age it will be the workshop of all idolatry. Even more clearly, the Anglo-Rhemish college, in its Annotations on Apocalypse 175, says: "Rome will be the seat of Antichrist." And the Jesuit Vega, on Apocalypse 18, commentary 1, section 4, writes: "It also seems to us that we must say, following Arethas, Primasius, Ansbert, Hannon, Ambrose and others, that in this place the idolatry of the city of Rome is signified, and that Rome will fall away from the faith; and so it will become a habitation of demons and of every unclean spirit, on account of crimes and idolatry, which will then spread widely through the Roman city and the Roman empire."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Christo c. 7. dicit: Est sententia Calvini, Christum pertulisse poenas animarum damnatarum, &c. Idem de Calvino scribit Georg. de Valent. Tom. 4. in Thom. disp. q. 4. punct. 3. Quintó certum.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 4 De Christo, ch. 7, says: "It is the opinion of Calvin that Christ endured the punishments of the damned souls, etc." Georg of Valencia writes the same about Calvin, vol. 4 on Thomas, disputation 4, question 4, point 3, "Fifthly, it is certain."

units.la: Contra Colleg. Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in Matth. 17. 47. Calvinus dicit, Christum has tam diras poenas tantum in cruce pertulisse. Non igitur in inferno, ut Bellarminus ait et Valentianus.
units.tr: Against the Anglo-Rhemish college, notes on Matthew 17:47: "Calvin says that Christ endured these terrible punishments only on the cross. Therefore not in hell, as Bellarmine and Valencia say."

units.la: Deinde quod affingunt Bellarminus, Valentianus et alii Iesuitae Calvino, in eoque damnant, illorum ipsorum magistri docent: Nam, ut Bellarminus refert libro 4. de Christo c. 19. Dubium. Aquinas dicit, Christum voluisse in inferno esse, ut poenas nostras in se suscipieret. Et Medina dicit, ut testatur Suarez in Thom. parte 3. q. 52. art. 8. disp. 43. 1. aliquos catholicorum sensisse, Christum passum esse aliquas extrinsecas poenas damnatorum in inferno, non tamen eo modo, quo damnati.
units.tr: Moreover, what Bellarmine, Valencia and the other Jesuits attribute to Calvin, and for which they condemn him, their own masters teach. For, as Bellarmine reports in book 4 De Christo, ch. 19, under the heading "Doubt": Aquinas says that Christ willed to be in hell so that he might take our punishments upon himself. And Medina says, as Suárez testifies on Thomas, part 3, question 52, article 8, disputation 43, section 1, that some Catholics have held that Christ suffered certain external punishments of the damned in hell, yet not in the same way as the damned.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Christo cap. 15. in princip. In hoc dicit, Opinio catholica haec est, Christum vere, secundum essentiam in inferno fuisse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 4 De Christo, ch. 15, at the beginning: In this matter, he says, "the Catholic opinion is this: that Christ truly, according to his essence, was in hell."

units.la: Durandus contra in 3. d. 22. q. 3. docet, Christi animam descendisse ad inferos, non secundum essentiam, sed per efficaciam: et existimavit, non credendum esse necessario, Christi animam reipsa secundum essentia descendisse ad inferos. Hanc sententiam Bellarminus in Durando tanquam erroneam, in Calvino autem ut haereticam damnat. Fevardentius etiam in Theomach. lib. 7. c. 1. scribit: Non descendit Christi anima ad inferos damnatorum, sed ad locum, qui est sinus Abrahae, vel communiter limbus patrum dicitur.
units.tr: Durandus, on the other hand, in book 3, distinction 22, question 3, teaches that the soul of Christ descended into the underworld not according to his essence, but through its efficacy; and he thought it not necessary to believe that the soul of Christ actually descended into the underworld according to its essence. Bellarmine condemns this opinion in Durandus as erroneous, but in Calvin as heretical. Fevardentius also, in Theomachia, book 7, ch. 1, writes: "The soul of Christ did not descend into the place of the damned, but into the place which is called the bosom of Abraham, or commonly the limbo of the fathers."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Christo c. 16. dicit, Christus descendit ad inferos, ut inde animas defunctorum Patriarcharum sub veteri Testamento fidelium, ex limbo, seu carcere infernis educeret, ubi ante ejus adventum continebantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 4 De Christo, ch. 16, says: Christ descended into hell so that from there he might lead out the souls of the deceased patriarchs, the faithful under the Old Testament, from the limbo or prison of the underworld, where they had been held before his coming.

units.la: Gregorius Valentianus autem Tomo 4. in Thom. disput. 1. q. 19. punct. 4. Secundo sequitur, et disp. 6. q. 11. punct. 1. Ratio. Omnes Christus similiter redemit, sive ante Christi adventum, sive post vixerunt, qui aliquando futuri erant: quamobrem Apoc. 13. dicitur Agnus occisus ab origine mundi.
units.tr: Gregory of Valencia, however, in vol. 4 on Thomas, disputation 1, question 19, point 4: "Secondly it follows," and disputation 6, question 11, point 1: "The reason is this: Christ redeemed all alike, whether they lived before Christ's coming or after it, who were to exist at some time; wherefore in Revelation 13 the Lamb is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world."

units.la: Bellarminus dicit lib.1.de Sanct.beat.c.4. Calvinistæ nolunt S. Martyres è mundo proficiscentes: rectâ ad Deum ire, sed ad infernum, aut alium locum extra cœlum.
units.tr: Bellarmine says, book 1 De sanctorum beatitudine, ch. 4: "The Calvinists are unwilling that the holy martyrs, when departing from the world, go straight to God, but rather to hell, or to some other place outside heaven."

units.la: Contra Valentianus libro de purgat.c.8.& Iesuitæ AngloRhemen. in Apostal.annot.c.14.15. Obijciunt nobis, inquiunt, protestantes loca Scripturarum & Patrum, in quibus duplex status eorum, qui moriuntur, significatur. Impiorum in supplicium æternum, Iustorum in vitam æternam; & deinde huiusmodi Scripturarum testimonia referunt & urgent, quibus determinatè significari videtur, eos, qui ex vita discedunt, in statu gratiæ statim recipi ad beatitudinem. Denique obijciunt ex Augustino, nullum locum medium esse post hanc vitam, præter regnum cœlorum, & infernum damnatorum.
units.tr: Against Valencia, book De purgatorio, ch. 8, and the Anglo-Rhemish Jesuits in their notes on Apocalypse, ch. 14–15: "The Protestants object to us," they say, "passages of Scripture and of the Fathers, in which the twofold state of those who die is signified: of the impious to eternal punishment, of the just to eternal life." And then they cite and press such testimonies of Scripture, by which it seems plainly to be indicated that those who depart from this life are at once received into blessedness, being in a state of grace. Lastly, they object from Augustine that there is no intermediate place after this life, apart from the kingdom of heaven and the hell of the damned.

units.la: Bellarminus libro 3.de pœnit.c.1.scribit, Audianos hæreticos docuisse, Confessionem auricularem non esse necessariam; idem etiam Lutheranos docere, Et mox. Quam robabimus de jure divino esse antiquissimam, & à Christo salubriter institutam.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 3 De paenitentia, ch. 1, writes: "The heretical Audians taught that auricular confession is not necessary; the Lutherans also teach the same." And soon after: "Which we shall prove to be of divine right, most ancient, and wholesomely instituted by Christ."

units.la: Maldonatus autem de Sum.q.18.art.4.scribit, Sunt etiam inter Catholicos, qui putant, nullum esse præceptum divinum de Confessione; ut omnes decretorum interpretes, & inter Scholasticos Scotus. Erasmus in Epist.de amabili Ecclesiæ Concord. Nonnulum, inquit, persuasum est hominibus horum temporum sacramentalem Confessionem fuisse à Christo ipso institutam. Glossator apud Gratian.de pœnitent. ist.5.c.In pœnitentia. Melius, inquit, dicitur, ab Ecclesiæ traditione, quam novi Testamenti authoritate institutam fuisse, quæ non est apud Græcos necessaria, ad quos non mavit. Gratianus ipse ibidem plures, inquit, Religiosi etiam Confessionem secretam non necessariam esse censuerunt, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & alij patres. B.Rhenanus in Argumento ad Tertulliani lib.1.de pœnit. Publica, inquit, exomologesis ustfuit antiqui multis seculis priusquam ista secreta nasceretur, de nua Tertullianus nihil habet, quæ penitus id temporis ignorabatur. Eandem, ut Valentianus referr lib.2.de Missa c.4. Panormitanus & Gerson non necessariam esse consenderunt. Maldonatus etiam Iesuita in Summula q.20.art.1. Confessio, inquit, ingo tempore in Ecclesia prisca est olim facta publica.
units.tr: Maldonatus, however, on the Summa, question 18, article 4, writes: "There are also among Catholics some who think there is no divine precept concerning confession, as all the interpreters of the decrees, and among the Schoolmen Scotus." Erasmus, in his letter on the lovable concord of the Church: "It has been persuaded to some men of our times," he says, "that sacramental confession was instituted by Christ himself." The Glossator, cited in Gratian, De paenitentia, dist. 5, ch. "In paenitentia": "It is better said," he says, "that it was instituted by the tradition of the Church rather than by the authority of the New Testament; it is not necessary among the Greeks, to whom it has not come." Gratian himself, in the same place: "Several religious men," he says, "have also judged that secret confession is not necessary: Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact and other fathers." B.
