Rhenanus, in the argument to Tertullian's book 1 De paenitentia: "Public exomologesis," he says, "was in use for many centuries before that secret confession was born," of which Tertullian says nothing, since at that time it was entirely unknown. The same, as Valencia reports, book 2 De Missa, ch. 4: Panormitanus and Gerson "judged it not necessary." Maldonatus the Jesuit also, in the Summula, question 20, article 1: "Confession," he says, "in the early Church was once made publicly."

units.la: Bellarminus in præfatione ad lib.de Eccles triumph. & lib.1.c.16.§.quinto.ibi sic scribit: Papistæ, inquit Lutherus, B. Mariam Deum constituunt, omnipotentiam ei tribuunt, omnes se ad eam conferunt, & plus gratiæ ab ea expectant quam à Christo Iesu. Horrenda est hæc eius impostura. Quis Catholicorum unquam uni Deo B.Mariam æquavit?
units.tr: Bellarmine, in the preface to De Ecclesia triumphante, and book 1, ch. 16, section 5, there writes thus: "The Papists," says Luther, "make the Blessed Mary God, they attribute omnipotence to her, they all betake themselves to her and expect more grace from her than from Christ Jesus. This is a horrible imposture of theirs." Which of the Catholics ever equated the Blessed Mary with the one God?

units.la: Negat his verbis Iesuita hanc idololatriam á Papistis admitti; quod tamen multi eorum ultro fatentur, multi etiam scriptis suis Bellarminum mendacij concincunt, Espenseus Episcopus Pontificius Commin 2.Tim.3.c. Multi sunt, inquit, qui non minus fidunt ac tribuunt Diuis, quam Deo: quia hunc quam illos minus placabilem putant & exorabilem. Cassander in Consult.art.21. Eo ventum est, inquit, ut Christus etiâ jam in cœlo regnans Matri subiciatur. Quinimò multi Pontificiorum Iesuitarum in scriptis à se editis B.Mariâ Salvatori Iesu Christo nomine, authoritate, gratiâ, dignitatéq; non adæquant modo, sed interdum etiam anteponunt.
units.tr: The Jesuit denies in these words that the Papists admit this idolatry. Yet many of them freely confess it, and many in their writings echo Bellarmine's lie. Espencaeus, the Papist bishop, in his commentary on 2 Timothy 3: There are many, he says, who trust in and ascribe no less to the saints than to God, because they think the saints are less easily appeased and less easily moved to pity than God. Cassander in Consultation, article 21: It has come to this, he says, that Christ, even though he already reigns in heaven, is made subject to his Mother. Indeed, many Jesuit Papists in the books they have published do not merely equal the Blessed Virgin Mary to our Saviour Jesus Christ in name, authority, grace and dignity, but sometimes even put her above him.

units.la: Vega Iesuita Comment. in Apocal. 12.sect.1.num.9. de nomine eius sic scribit: Tetragrammaton (quod est Deo proprium apud Hebræos; ut Sixtus Senensis in Bibliot. gca refert) est nomen sacerrimæ virginis: nec hoc solum, sed etiam suo modo inaffabile, non solum hominibus, verum & ipsis angelis. Et Sect.2.num.6. Item Sect.20: Nec prætermittendum est, inquit, illud doctissimi Idiotæ encomium: Dedit tibi Maria tota Trinitas nomen, quod, post nomen filij tui, est supra omne nomen: ut in nomine tuo flectatur omne genu, cœlestium, terrestrium & infernorum, nomen tantæ virtutis, ut ad ejus invocationem cœlum rideat, infernus conturbetur, est illa spiraculum hominis, quia sublato ejus patrocinio, peccator vivere diutius non poterit.
units.tr: The Jesuit Vega, in his Commentary on Revelation 12, section 1, number 9, writes thus of her name: The Tetragrammaton (which is proper to God among the Hebrews, as Sixtus of Siena reports in his Bibliotheca sancta) is the name of the most holy Virgin. Nor is this all: in its own way it is also unspeakable, not only to men but even to the angels. And in section 2, number 6; likewise section 20: Nor must we pass over that encomium of the most learned Idiota: "The whole Trinity has given you a name which, after the name of your Son, is above every name, so that at your name every knee should bow, of heaven, of earth and of the underworld; a name of such power that at its invocation heaven laughs, hell is thrown into confusion; she is the breath of man, for if her patronage were taken away, the sinner could not live any longer."

units.la: Quod ad gratiam & authoritatem B. Mariæ attinet Cassander in Consult. art. 21, sic scribit: Non defuerunt viri celebres, qui dixerunt, Deum regni sui (quod ex justitia & misericordia constat) dimidium hoc est, misericordiam, in Mariam translulisse. Holcotus Theol. Com. in lib. Sap. lect. 36. edit. vet. Si quis, inquit, a filio, quiad dexteram patris sedet, terreatur, quia judex est, matrem adeat, quia medicina est. Etiuxta quosdam rituales libros sic canitur: Iube filio, felix puerpera, Iure matris impera Redemptori.
units.tr: As for the grace and authority of the Blessed Virgin, Cassander writes thus in Consultation, article 21: There have not been lacking celebrated men who have said that God transferred to Mary half of his kingdom, that is, mercy, the other half, justice and righteousness, being kept for himself. Holcot, in his Commentary on the Book of Wisdom, lecture 36, old edition: If anyone is frightened of the Son, who sits at the right hand of the Father, because he is judge, let him go to the Mother, because she is medicine. And according to certain ritual books it is sung thus: Command your Son, O happy mother, rule over the Redeemer by a mother's right.

units.la: Vega in Apocal. 12. sect. 2. num. 3. de authoritate B. Mariae sic scribit: Merito virgo DOMINA dicta est, cujus typus eam ob causam fuit Sarah: quae cum antea diceretur Sarai, id est, Domina & Princeps mea, postea, Deo jubente, dicta est Sarah; quod nomen sonat Principem sive Dominam absolute: est enim virgo Domina per excellentiam, & Princeps omnium creaturarum, ut egregie expendit Arnoldus Carn. sic scribens: Maria lingua Syriaca Domina dicitur, Christus Dominus; & licet ipsa se profiteatur Christi ancillam, hoc servitium genus omni regno sublimius esse intelligit: Constituta quippe est super omnem creaturam, & quicunque Jesu curvat genu, Matri quoque pronus supplicat: & filii gloria cum Matre non tam COMMUNEM judico quam EANDEM. Oforius Homil. tom. 4. Conc. de Devotione Mariae inquit: Sine Maria decrevit Deus nihil dare, Caput est Christus, Maria collum: quia omnis influxus a capite per collum derivatur. Turfellinus Iesuita in Praefat. histor. Lauretanae scribit: Ut omnes intelligant, se, quicquid ab aeterno illo augusto bonorum omnium fonte in terras profluat, sumere per Mariam.
units.tr: Vega, in Revelation 12, section 2, number 3, writes thus of the authority of the Blessed Virgin: She is rightly called Lady, and the type of her was Sarah for this reason: she who was formerly called Sarai, that is, "my lady and my princess," was afterwards, at God's command, called Sarah, a name which means princess or lady in an absolute sense. For the Virgin is Lady par excellence and Princess of all creatures, as Arnoldus Carnotensis rightly explains, writing thus: Mary is called Lady in the Syriac tongue, Christ is Lord; and although she herself professes herself Christ's handmaid, she understands that this kind of service is higher than every kingdom. For she has been set above every creature, and whoever bends the knee to Jesus also bows down in supplication to the Mother; and I judge the glory of the Son to be not so much common with the Mother as the same. Oforius, Homily, vol. 4 of the Councils, on the devotion to Mary, says: Without Mary God has decreed to give nothing. Christ is the head, Mary the neck, because every influence flows from the head through the neck. Turfellinus, the Jesuit, in the preface to his history of Loreto, writes: So that all may understand that whatever flows from that eternal and august fountain of all good things onto the earth, they receive through Mary.

units.la: De Merito B. Mariae
units.tr: On the Merit of the Blessed Virgin

units.la: Delrius Iesuita Comment. in Cant. cap. 1. sect. 2. sic scribit: Obedientia Mariae similis facta est obedientiae Christi, magna ergo in hoc laus Mariae, magna ejus gloria, quod imitatio ejus gloriae EX AEQUO VATUR obedientiae Christi, quam imitatur illa.
units.tr: Delrio the Jesuit, in his Commentary on the Song of Songs, chapter 1, section 2, writes thus: The obedience of Mary has been made like the obedience of Christ; great, therefore, is the praise of Mary, great her glory, in that her imitation of his glory is EQUAL to the obedience of Christ, which she imitates.

units.la: De Majestate B. Mariae
units.tr: On the Majesty of the Blessed Virgin

units.la: De majestate eius Turfellinus in Epist. dedic. hist. Lauretanae haec scribit: Matrem suam praepotens ille Deus divinae majestatis potestatisque SOCIAM, quatenus licuit, adscivit. Item: Huic olim coelestium mortalium-que principatum detulit: ad hujus arbitrium, quoad hominum tutela postulat, terras, mare, coelum, naturamque totam moderatur: haec annuente, & per hanc divinos thesauros mortalibus, & coelestia dona largitur. Oforius Iesuita tom. 3. Conc. in assumpt. S. Bartholom. quid ergo? Dubitant, inquit, aliqui, an Maria adeo bona mater Christi dici debeat, ac bonus est aeternus pater. Item: Certe diversa est admodum generatio, quia diversa natura, hac in re excedit aeternus Pater matrem Mariam. At vero si duntaxat filium ab utroque genitum attendamus, in nihilo Pater excedit matrem, idem enim filius est ab utroque genitus, & hac ratione mater adeo bona Maria est, ac aeternus pater. Idem tom. 5. Dominic. 4. Epiph.
units.tr: Turfellinus, in the dedicatory epistle of his history of Loreto, writes these words about her majesty: That all-powerful God has taken his own Mother as a PARTNER in his divine majesty and power, so far as was lawful. Again: To her he once committed the rule over heavenly and mortal beings; at her decision, so far as the protection of men requires, he governs lands, sea, heaven and all nature; at her nod, and through her, he bestows divine treasures and heavenly gifts on mortals. Oforius the Jesuit, vol. 3 of the Councils, on the Assumption of St Bartholomew: What then? Some doubt, he says, whether Mary ought to be called as good a mother of Christ as the eternal Father is a good father. Again: Certainly the generation is very different, because the nature is different; in this respect the eternal Father surpasses the mother Mary. But if we consider only the Son begotten by each, the Father surpasses the mother in nothing, for it is the same Son who is begotten by both; and on this reasoning Mary is as good a mother as the eternal Father is a father. The same, vol. 5, Dominic. 4 Epiph.

units.la: Voluit autem: sic scribit: Cui igitur B. Mariam comparabimus? Non Evae, quia &c. non Sarae, quia &c. nec Rachel, nec Heslerae, nec Lunae; nec Soli: cui igitur? PLANE DEO, bona omnia continenti.
units.tr: Elsewhere he writes thus: To whom then shall we compare the Blessed Virgin Mary? Not to Eve, because etc.; not to Sarah, because etc.; nor to Rachel, nor to Hesler, nor to the moon, nor to the sun: to whom then? Clearly to God, who contains all good things.

units.la: De libro Arbitrio
units.tr: On Free Will

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 6. de libero arbitrio c. 12. reprehendit Calvinum, quod dicit, Chrysostomum in hac quaestione repudiandum esse. Et lib. 5. c. 26. itemque Canisius in Praefat. ad librum Vegae, exagitant illud, quod Calvinus dixit: Visus est mihi Chrysostomus nimius in liberi arbitrii viribus praedicandis: similiter Campianus Petrum Martyrem, qui dixit, Chrysostomum liberi arbitrii immodicum assertorem fuisse. Canisius dicit, Calvinus hic suam infscitiam prodit: & Campianus, Isti haeretici nihil non immodicum videtur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 6 of On Free Will, chapter 12, rebukes Calvin for saying that Chrysostom must be rejected on this question. In book 5, chapter 26, and likewise Canisius in the preface to his book on Vega, they attack Calvin's remark: "Chrysostom seemed to me too extravagant in praising the powers of free will." Similarly Campian rebukes Peter Martyr, who said that Chrysostom was too immoderate a champion of free will. Canisius says, "Calvin here betrays his ignorance"; and Campian says, "To these heretics nothing seems immoderate."

units.la: Contra vero Sixtus Senensis in Bibliotheca lib. 5. in praefat. Chrysostomus, inquit, imperu dicendi cum Manichaeis, qui Fati necessitatem defendebant, Naturae viriplus aequo attollit. Maldonatus Com. in Ioan. c. 6. scribit, Etiam Theophylactus, Euthymius, Arnobius ita loquuntur, ac si homo, antequam per gratiam ad gratiam trahatur, possit gratiam mereri. Et Tolletus Com. in Ioan. 6 c. Chrysostomi, inquit doctrina haec est; hominem per liberum arbitrium seipsum dignum facere gratia: eadem est doctrina Cyrilli: nec istorum tantum, sed aliorum Doctorum, maxime Graecorum. Maldonatus onatus autem dicto loco inquit: Haec doctrina eorum nimis affinis est Pelagianorum errori: caveat Lector, si Chrysostomum in hunc locum legat, ne in Pelagianorum haeresin incidat. Et Toletus Iesuita Com. in Ioan. 6. Augustinus, inquit, multo aliter quam illi. Docet enim a Deo nobis dari non modo gratiam, ut credere possimus, verum etiam ut velimus: In hoc igitur praedicti Doctores non probantur. Idem Com. in Rom. 9. Annot. 9. Eorum inquam doctrinam in hac parte non probo. Et Pererius Iesuita in Rom. 9. num. 33. Profecto, inquit, illa doctrina contraria videtur iis, quae in hoc loco disputat Apostolus. Sententia Augustini est doctrinae Pauli convenientior.
units.tr: On the other side, Sixtus of Siena, in the Bibliotheca, book 5, in the preface, says: "Chrysostom, in his eagerness to argue against the Manichaeans, who defended the necessity of fate, raises the powers of nature higher than is right." Maldonatus, in his commentary on John 6, writes: "Theophylact, Euthymius and Arnobius also speak as if a man, before he is drawn by grace to grace, could merit grace." And Tolet, in his commentary on John 6, says: "This is the teaching of Chrysostom, that a man makes himself worthy of grace through free will; the same is the teaching of Cyril, and not of these alone but of other teachers, especially the Greeks." Maldonatus, however, says of the same passage: "This teaching is too closely akin to the error of the Pelagians; let the reader beware, if he reads Chrysostom on this passage, lest he fall into the heresy of the Pelagians." And Tolet the Jesuit, in his commentary on John 6: "Augustine," he says, "teaches far differently from those men. For he teaches that God gives us not only grace that we may be able to believe, but also that we may be willing. In this respect, therefore, the aforesaid teachers are not approved." The same author, on Romans 9, annotation 9: "I, I say, do not approve their teaching on this point." And Pererius the Jesuit, on Romans 9, number 33: "Surely," he says, "that teaching seems contrary to what the Apostle argues in this place. The opinion of Augustine agrees better with the teaching of Paul."

units.la: Bellarminus scribit: Docet Calvinus filium subjectum Patri ratione divinitatis, et ista veteres omnes contrarium docent, ipse ait omnes errasse.
units.tr: Bellarmine writes: "Calvin teaches that the Son is subject to the Father in respect of his divinity, and yet all the ancients teach the contrary; he himself says that they all erred."

units.la: Toletus autem et Maldonatus inquiunt: Quidam censent, Patrem majorem esse filio ratione divinitatis, non quoad substantiam naturae, sed respectu originis, quia filius Patre; quam expositionem Doctores illustres sequuntur, inter quos Athanasius, &c. ubi plurosundecim refert nominatim.
units.tr: Tolet and Maldonatus, however, say: "Some hold that the Father is greater than the Son in respect of his divinity, not as to the substance of the nature, but with respect to origin, because the Son is from the Father." This explanation is followed by distinguished teachers, among whom are Athanasius, etc., where he lists by name more than eleven.

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 4. de Christo c. 11. in princip. Luc. 16. inquit, Dives in inferno cum esset, vidit a longe animam Lazari in sinu Abrahae, et audivit inter loca ipsorum magnum chasma seu hiatum esse interiectum. Animae piorum in hoc sinu Abrahae fuerunt. Staplesius in Prompt. in feria 5. hebdom. 2. et Costerus in Enchirid. c. 12. Probo, inquit, contra impiu Calvinum, Sinum Abrahae non in coelo, sed in loco subterraneo et inferis esse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 4 On Christ, chapter 11, at the beginning, on Luke 16, says: "The rich man, when he was in hell, saw from afar the soul of Lazarus in Abraham's bosom, and heard that a great chasm or gulf lay fixed between their places. The souls of the pious were in this bosom of Abraham." Staplesius, in the Promptuarium, on the Thursday of the second week, and Costerus, in the Enchiridion, chapter 12, say: "I prove, against the impious Calvin, that the bosom of Abraham is not in heaven but in a subterranean place, in the underworld."

units.la: Contra vero Maldonat. Com. in Luc. 16. c. Haec, inquit, pars de Epulone non historica, sed parabola videtur: quia qui in inferno sunt, nondum corporibus punmuntur; at hic fit mentio Epulonis et linguae. Ubi sinus Abrahae esset Augustinus prudenter dubitat: et ex eo quod dicitur magnum chasma, valde suspicor, per sinum Abrahae summum coelum designari.
units.tr: On the other side, Maldonatus, in his commentary on Luke 16, says: "This part about the rich man seems not to be history but a parable, because those who are in hell are not yet punished in their bodies; yet here mention is made of the rich man's tongue. Augustine prudently doubts where the bosom of Abraham is; and from the fact that it is called a great chasm, I strongly suspect that by the bosom of Abraham the highest heaven is meant."

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 3. de Pontifice Rom. c. 23. Alterum est, scribit, Opera, quatenus ex gratia, et adiutorio divino proficiscuntur, divina esse opera, et suo modo mereri, hoc est, imetrare peccatorum remissionem. Ibid. Postremum scribit, Operibus, quae a justificatis jam homine fiunt, meritum a Papistis tribui.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 3 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 23: "The first point," he writes, "is that works, insofar as they proceed from grace and divine help, are divine works, and in their own way merit, that is, obtain the remission of sins." Also, in the same place: "Lastly, he writes that the Papists attribute merit to works which are done by a man already justified."

units.la: Vega autem in Opusc. de Meritis q. 4. pag. 782. sic scribit: Thomas Vualensis haec scribit: Ille est senior Theologus, fidelior Catholicus, et sacris Scripturis consentiens, qui merita simpliciter abnegat, et cum modificatione Apostoli et Scripturarum agnoscit, quod simpliciter nemo meretur regnum coelorum, sed ex gratia Dei, et voluntate largitoris. Loquitur Vualdensis, inquit Vega, de operibus justificatorum.
units.tr: Vega, however, in the treatise On Merits, question 4, page 782, writes thus: "Thomas Waldensis writes this: he is the older theologian, the more faithful Catholic, and in agreement with the holy Scriptures, who simply denies merits, and, with the qualification of the Apostle and the Scriptures, acknowledges that no one simply merits the kingdom of heaven, but (receives it) from the grace of God and the will of the giver." Waldensis, says Vega, is speaking of the works of the justified.

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 1. c. 8. de Clericis docet, Caelibatum perpetuum, ex institutione Apostolorum, omnibus Clericis et verbi ministris necessario servandum esse: functionem enim illorum cum usu conjugii plane pugnare sive ante, sive post ordinationem id contrahant.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1 On Clerics, chapter 8, teaches: "Perpetual celibacy, by the institution of the Apostles, must necessarily be kept by all clerics and ministers of the Word; for their office plainly conflicts with the use of marriage, whether they contract it before or after ordination."

units.la: Idem ibid. c. 23. docet, Digamos, qui successive duas vel plures uxores habuerint, eam Apostolica constitutione ab Ecclesiasticis officiis arcendos esse.
units.tr: The same author, in the same place, chapter 23, teaches: "Digamists, who have had two or more wives in succession, are to be excluded from ecclesiastical offices by apostolic constitution."

units.la: Costerus in Enchirid. c. de Caelibatu propos. 9. dicit, Sacerdos, si fornicetur, aut mi concubinam foveat, tametsi gravi sacrilegio se obstringat, gravius tamen peccat, si contrahat matrimonium.
units.tr: Costerus, in the Enchiridion, chapter on celibacy, proposition 9, says: "A priest, if he commits fornication or keeps a concubine, though he binds himself by grave sacrilege, nevertheless sins more gravely if he contracts marriage."

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 1. de Clericis c. 19. haec habet: Votum caelibatus annexum est Ordinis jure antiquissimo, ita ut nec uxores ducere, nec ductis uti liceat: Ethoc quidem jure vino, ut Ioannes Maior refert distinct. 24. Calsander in Consult. art. 23. sic scribit: Theologus quidam (intelligit Turrianum Iesuitam lib. 2. de dogmaticis chasteribus, ut est in margine apud Calsandrum) caelibatum sacris ordinibus adjunctum esse contendit, nec esse in potestate Ecclesiae, ut conjugii usum magis, quam latrocinii, Sacerdotibus permittat. Eadem est sententia Medinae. Clichtoneus etiam lib. de Continentia cap. 4. docet, de jure divino esse, ut qui est sacris ordinibus initiatus, non possit uxorem ducere, neque in hoc ullam dispensationem cadere posse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1 On Clerics, chapter 19, has this: "The vow of celibacy is attached to the order by a most ancient right, so that it is lawful neither to take wives nor to use those taken." And this right, as John Major reports, distinction 24, is indeed very ancient. Calsander, in his Consultation, article 23, writes thus: "A certain theologian (he means Turrian the Jesuit, book 2 On Dogmatic Chastities, as is noted in the margin by Calsander) contends that celibacy is joined to the holy orders, and that it is not in the power of the Church to permit priests the use of marriage any more than of robbery." Medina holds the same opinion. Clichtoneus also, in book On Continence, chapter 4, teaches: "It is by divine right that one who has been initiated into the holy orders cannot take a wife, and no dispensation in this matter can fall (to him)."

units.la: Aquinas autem 2. 2. q. 88. art. 1. Usus, inquit, conjugalis interdicitur Sacerdotibus tantum jure humano, ac proinde dispensabile est. Idem docet Caietanus in Opusc. tract.27.tom.1.& Socus lib.7.de Iustit.q.6.art.2. Bellarm. etiam docet & probat lib.1.de Cleric.c.18. non iure divino, sed humano duntaxat prohibitum esse conjugium Sacerdotibus, & proinde in hoc dispensari posse. Concilium etiam Tridentinum legem Ecclesiasticam hanc prohibitionem vocat.
units.tr: Aquinas, however, 2.2, question 88, article 1: "The use of marriage," he says, "is forbidden to priests only by human right, and therefore it is dispensable." Caietan teaches the same in the Opuscula, treatise 27, volume 1, and Soto, book 7 On Justice, question 6, article 2. Bellarmine also teaches and proves, book 1 On Clerics, chapter 18, that marriage is forbidden to priests not by divine right but by human right only, and therefore a dispensation can be granted in this matter. The Council of Trent also calls this prohibition an ecclesiastical law.

units.la: Bellarminus ut supra c.19.probat. , Coelibatum jure humano quidem, sed tamen Apostolico sacris ordinibus annexum esse. Et Valentianus Iesuita lib. de Coelib. c.3. dicit, Lege plane Apostolica hoc factum.
units.tr: Bellarmine, as above, chapter 19, proves that celibacy is attached to the holy orders by human right indeed, but yet by apostolic (authority). And Valentian the Jesuit, book On Celibacy, chapter 3, says: "This was done clearly by an apostolic law."

units.la: Cofterus autem in Enchir. tract.de Coelibatu, Antiquissimis, inquit, Ecclesiae temporibus viventibus adhuc Apostolis, & post Apostolos aliquot adhuc annos, admissi adhuc fuerunt ad sacros ordines viri conjugati, non quidem promiscue, sed electi, qui unicam tantum duxissent uxorem, eamque virginem. Episcopus Espenseus Com. in Tit. c.1. Multis, inquit, annorum centuriis post Apostolos Ecclesia Primitiva, defectu coelibum Sacerdotes habuit maritos.
units.tr: Costerus, however, in the Enchiridion, treatise on celibacy, says: "In the most ancient times of the Church, while the Apostles were still living, and for some years after the Apostles, married men were still admitted to the holy orders; not indeed indiscriminately, but those chosen, who had taken only one wife, and she a virgin." Bishop Espenseus, in his commentary on Titus, chapter 1: "For many centuries after the Apostles, the primitive Church, through lack of celibate priests, had married priests."

units.la: Addit autem Valentianus quo supra, Maritos illos Sacerdotes non usos esse concubitu matrimonij post ordinationem.
units.tr: Valentian, in the place cited above, adds further that those married priests did not use the intercourse of marriage after their ordination.

units.la: Et Cofterus quo supra, Nunquam, ait, licuit Sacerdoti iam sacris Ordinibus initiato uxorem ducere; neque ullus est antiquorum Patrum qui aliter scripsisse vel sensisse legitur. Bellarminus quoque ut supra, Nullum, inquit, probati viri exemplum proferre possunt.
units.tr: And Costerus, in the place cited above: "It was never lawful," he says, "for a priest already initiated into the holy orders to take a wife; nor is it read that any of the ancient Fathers wrote or thought otherwise." Bellarmine likewise, as above: "They can produce no example from a approved man."

units.la: Licuisse autem maritis uti uxoribus suis, quas ante ordinationem duxerant; licuisse item Sacerdotibus etiam post ordinationem uxores ducere, probatur Pontificiorum testimoniis. Georgius Caffander quo supra, De maritis ad Ecclesiae ministerium eligendis non tantopere quidam reluctantur, cum ea res exemplum habeat prisca Ecclesiae, & ab Orientalibus omnibus Ecclesiis hucusque servetur, cum res in plerisque ita comparata sint, ut conjugum piarum consortio, non modo ad functiones Ecclesiasticas non impediantur, sed etiam ad earum procurationem adjuvent, ut quemadmodum de patre suo Gregorio, & matre Nomina Gregorius Nazianzenus testatur. De Hilario Episcopo sic cecinit Mantuanus, Non nocuit tibi progenies, non obstitit uxor Legitimo conjuncta thoro, &c. Idem de Nazianzeno: Praesule patre satus; nam tunc id jura sinebant Pastorale pedum gessit post funera patris. Paulo post: Non horruit illa Tempestate Deus thalamos, cunabula, tedas, Concludit: Tutius esse volunt, qua lex divina sinebat, Ipse via, veterumque sequi vestigia patrum.
units.tr: That it was lawful for husbands to use the wives they had married before ordination, and likewise that it was lawful for priests to take wives even after ordination, is proved by the testimonies of the Papists. Georgius Cassander, in the work cited above: "On choosing married men for the ministry of the Church, some do not struggle so greatly, since the matter has the example of the early Church, and is still observed by all the Eastern churches to this day; since such things are so arranged in most cases that the fellowship of pious spouses not only does not hinder them from ecclesiastical functions, but even helps them in carrying them out; just as Gregory Nazianzen bears witness concerning his father Gregory, and his mother Nonna." Of Bishop Hilary, Mantuan sang thus: "Your offspring did not harm you, nor did a wife joined in lawful marriage stand in your way, etc." Of Nazianzen, the same: "Begotten while his father was bishop, for then the laws allowed it; he bore the pastoral staff after his father's funeral." A little later: "In that age God did not shrink from bridal chambers, cradles, torches." He concludes: "They wish it to be safer to follow the way which divine law allowed, and the footsteps of the ancient Fathers."

units.la: Aeneas Sylvius de Gestis Concilij Basil. Fuerunt, inquit, ex nostris Pontificibus aliqui in matrimonio. Gratianus dist.26. Can. Sors. Copula, inquit; Sacerdotalis nec legali, nec Evangelica, nec Apostolica authoritate prohibetur. Idem dist.28.c.de Syracus. loquens de Pelagij Pontificis decreto, Ecce, inquit, hac authoritate electus in Episcopum non prohibetur habere uxorem & filios. Dist.56.can. Cenoman. Sacerdotibus, inquit, ante prohibitionem ubique licita erant, & in Orientali Ecclesia usque hodie licere probatur. Leo Papa epistola 87. Is, inquit, Episcopus ordinetur, quem unius uxoris virum esse constiterit. Paulo post: Ut virginem uxorem accipiat, & alterius thorum nesciat conjugis, quae futura est uxor Pontificis. Cajetanus libro 1. Opusc. tract. 17. teste Valentiano tom.4. disp.9.q.3. Licuit, inquit, in Ecclesia orientali matrimonium post ordinationem contrahere. Caffander art.23. Matrimonij, inquit, contractio post ordinationem solo statuto prohibita fuit, & exempla prisca extant, quae testantur hujusmodi statuta non tam auxie observata fuisse, quin ob Ecclesiae necessitatem aliquando relaxata fuerint. Epiphanius ait etiam, suo tempore (anno 390.) quibusdam in locis presbyteros matrimonio uti, et liberos gignere, quamvis id fiat contra Canones Ecclesiasticos. Balsamon etiam in Can. Apost. 5. testatur, Antiquam Synodum quae fuit in Trullo, licuisse Episcopis habere uxores, etiam post Episcopatum palam. lem dignitatem, quemadmodum qui post matrimonium ordinentur Sacerdotes.
units.tr: Aeneas Sylvius, in his account of the Council of Basel: "Some of our Popes, he says, were married." Gratian, Dist. 26, Can. Sors: "Sacerdotal copulation is forbidden by neither the law, nor the Gospel, nor apostolic authority." The same, Dist. 28, c. de Syracusa, speaking of the decree of Pope Pelagius: "Behold, he says, by this authority a man elected bishop is not forbidden to have a wife and children." Dist. 56, Can. Cenomanensis: "Before the prohibition, he says, priests everywhere were permitted to marry, and it is shown that this is still allowed today in the Eastern Church." Pope Leo, Epistle 87: "He is to be ordained bishop who is shown to be the husband of one wife." A little later: "that he may take a virgin as his wife, and not know the bed of another spouse, since she is to be the wife of a Pontiff." Cajetan, Opuscula, book 1, tract 17, as cited by Valentia, vol. 4, disp. 9, q. 3: "In the Eastern Church it was lawful to contract marriage after ordination." Cassander, art. 23: "The contracting of marriage after ordination was forbidden by statute alone, and there are ancient examples which show that such statutes were not so strictly observed but that they were sometimes relaxed for the needs of the Church." Epiphanius also says that in his own time (in the year 390) in some places priests used marriage and begat children, although this was done against the ecclesiastical canons. Balsamon, too, on Apostolic Canon 5, testifies that the older Synod held in Trullo allowed bishops to have wives, even openly after their episcopate, and likewise those who were ordained after marriage.

units.la: Georgius de Valencia de numero Sacram. c. 7. pag. 543. probare vult Matrimonium esse Sacramentum proprie dictum ex c. 5. Ephes. Matrimonium, inuit, esse signum rei sacrae, & proinde mysterium quoddam & Sacramentum, probamus ex c. 5. epistola ad Ephes. Sacramentum hoc magnum est: ego dico de Christo & Ecclesia.
units.tr: Georgius de Valencia, De numero sacramentorum, c. 7, p. 543, wants to prove that marriage is a sacrament properly so called from Ephesians 5: "Marriage, he says, is a sign of a sacred thing, and therefore a certain mystery and sacrament; we prove this from Ephesians 5: This is a great sacrament: I speak of Christ and the Church."

units.la: Contra vero Perերius Iesuita Comment. in Gen. 2. c. evincit, mysterium hoc & sacramentum non debere proprie ad novam legem restringi, quia allegoria Apostolica maxime de matrimonio Adami & Evae, non etiam de aliorum coniugiis instituatur: inquit enim, Quemadmodum, ut Scholastici definiunt, ex Adami dormientis latere formata est Eva: ita ex latere Christi morientis profluxit sanguis & aqua, unde condita est Ecclesia. Ideo voluit Deus mulierem ex viro etiam propter figuram. Etenim coniunctio Adami & Evae continebat Sacramentum illud magnum, de quo Paulus dicit Ephes. 5. Ego dico de Christo & Ecclesia.
units.tr: On the other hand, the Jesuit Pererius, in his commentary on Genesis 2, argues that this mystery and sacrament ought not to be strictly restricted to the new law, because the apostolic allegory concerns chiefly the marriage of Adam and Eve, and not the marriages of others. For he says: "As the Schoolmen define, Eve was formed from the side of Adam while he slept, so from the side of Christ dying flowed blood and water, from which the Church was founded. Therefore God willed that the woman be made from the man, also for the sake of a figure." For the union of Adam and Eve contained that great sacrament of which Paul speaks in Ephesians 5: "I speak of Christ and the Church."

units.la: Concilium Tridentinum Sess. 14. de Vnctione extrema sic decrevit: Si quis dixerit, Extremam unctionem non esse proprie Sacramentum, tum a Christo institutum, & a Iacobo promulgatum, anathema sit. Suarez Iesuita tom. 4. disp. 39. sect. 1. num. 1. & sect. 2. num. 2. Dicendum est, inquit, Extremam unctionem esse Sacramentum a Christo institutum immediate, unumque ex septem novae legis, Assertio est de fide.
units.tr: The Council of Trent, Session 14, on Extreme Unction, decreed as follows: If anyone shall say that Extreme Unction is not properly a sacrament, instituted by Christ and promulgated by James, let him be anathema. The Jesuit Suarez, vol. 4, disp. 39, sect. 1, num. 1, and sect. 2, num. 2: It must be said, he says, that Extreme Unction is a sacrament immediately instituted by Christ, and one of the seven of the new law; the assertion is of faith.

units.la: Idem tamen ibidem, Inter Catholicos, inquit, nonnulli negarunt Christum Dominum instituisse hoc Sacramentum: ex quo consequebatur, non esse verum Sacramentum.
units.tr: Yet the same author, in the same place: Among Catholics, he says, some have denied that Christ the Lord instituted this sacrament; from which it followed that it was not a true sacrament.

units.la: Maldonatus Iesuita Comment. in Marcum, Lutherus, inquit, & Calvinus docent in loco Marci 6. (ungebant multos oleo & sanabantur) non agi de Sacramento extremae unctionis; quo nunc Ecclesia utitur; neque ut jam oleum ad sanandos animos adhibitum fuisse. Vbi ergo est si sic non est?
units.tr: The Jesuit Maldonatus, in his commentary on Mark: Luther and Calvin teach, he says, on the passage in Mark 6 (they anointed many with oil and they were healed), that it is not about the sacrament of extreme unction, which the Church now uses; nor about oil already used to heal souls. Where then is it, if it is not so?

units.la: Bellarminus autem lib. 1. de Vnctione extrema c. 3. & Suarez tom. 4. disp. 39. sect. 1. num. 4. ita fere: Illud oleum apud Mar. 6. non erat hoc Sacramentum extremae unctionis: quia Apostoli utebantur illa unctione SOLVM, aut praecipue ad curationem morbi corporalis. Et Cajetanus in Comment. Iacob. 5. c. Ex hoc loco, nec ex verbis, nec ex affectibus colligitur extrema unctio, sed unctio illa miraculosa, quam Christus instituerat sanandis aegrotis in initio Evangelij. Nam textus promittit alleviationem infirmi, & de remissione peccatorum non nisi conditionaliter loquitur. At unctio extrema, non nisi in extremo mortis articulo, adhibetur, & directe rendit ad remissionem peccatorum. Illa multos presbyteros vexabat, quod ea ab extrema unctione aliena. Sequitur enim in textu (confitemini invicem) at quod in extrema unctione fit, non fit invicem, sed tantum a Sacerdotibus. Et Maldonatus quo supra, Idem, inquit, quod Calvinus, nonnulli (mitto vetustiores, quos probibet reverentia nominare) nuper Catholici docuerunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine, however, in book 1, On Extreme Unction, c. 3, and Suarez, vol. 4, disp. 39, sect. 1, num. 4, say roughly this: That oil in Mark 6 was not this sacrament of extreme unction, because the Apostles used that anointing ALONE, or chiefly, for the healing of bodily sickness. And Cajetan, in his commentary on James 5: From this passage, neither from the words nor from the circumstances, is extreme unction gathered, but that miraculous anointing which Christ had instituted for healing the sick at the beginning of the Gospel. For the text promises the relief of the sick, and speaks of the remission of sins only conditionally. But extreme unction is applied only at the very point of death, and is directly aimed at the remission of sins. That anointing was used by many elders, which is foreign to extreme unction. For the text continues (confess your sins to one another), but what is done in extreme unction is not done to one another, but only by priests. And Maldonatus, in the work cited above: The same, he says, as Calvin; some recent Catholics (I pass over the older ones, whom reverence forbids me to name) have taught it.

units.la: Bellarm. de Pontifice Rom. Pontifex, inquit, Rom. in omnes Pastores potestatem supremam habet.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff: The Roman Pontiff, he says, has supreme power over all ministers.

units.la: Cusanus autem Cardinalis lib. 2. de Concord. Eccles. c. 13. & 14. Quia, inquit, ab illa potestate ligandi & solvendi, quae est immediate a Christo, est divinae juris dictionis potestas, patet omnes Episcopos, & forte etiam omnes presbyteros, aequalis potestatis, quo ad juris dictionem, esse. Et Marsilius tom. 2. c. 16. Vsque ad tempora Constantini nemo Episcoporum in alios juris dictionem exercuit.
units.tr: But Cardinal Cusanus, book 2, On the Concord of the Church, c. 13 and 14: Since, he says, from that power of binding and loosing, which is immediately from Christ, there is the power of divine jurisdiction, it is clear that all bishops, and perhaps all elders, are of equal power as regards jurisdiction. And Marsilius, vol. 2, c. 16: Up to the time of Constantine, no bishop exercised jurisdiction over others.

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 2. de Rom. Pontifice, & lib. de Notis Ecclesiae c. 10. Ad potestatem Papae, inquit, omnes veteres Patres confugiebant.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, and book On the Marks of the Church, c. 10: All the ancient Fathers, he says, had recourse to the power of the Pope.

units.la: Cusanus autem quo supra c. 17. Ex Epistola Augustini, inquit, ad Gloriam, & ex antiquorum Pontificum Confessionibus contrarium ostenditur. Et Marsilius quo supra c. 16. Non aliter, inquit, Romanam sedem in dubijs consuluerunt, quam sicut Episcopus Aurelianensis olim, Universitatem Parisiensem, cui tamen non erat aliqua juris dictione subjectus. jeĉa. Æneas Sylvius de Concilio Basil. Ante Concilium, inquit, Nicænum non magnus ad Ecclesiam Rom. respectus habebatur. In tomis Concil. quoq; legitur, Ius appellationis Concilij Africani Patres Rom. Pontifici denegâsse.
units.tr: Cusanus, however, in the work cited above, c. 17: From the Epistle of Augustine to Gloria, and from the confessions of the ancient Pontiffs, the contrary is shown. And Marsilius, in the work cited above, c. 16: They consulted the Roman see on doubtful matters no differently than the Bishop of Orléans once consulted the University of Paris, although he was not subject to it in any jurisdiction. Likewise Aeneas Sylvius, on the Council of Basel: Before the Council of Nicaea, he says, no great regard was had for the Roman Church. It is also read in the volumes of the Councils that the Fathers of the African Council denied the Roman Pontiff the right of appeal.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 1. c. 13. de Conciliis, Est, inquit proprium Pontificis munus Concilium generale convocare; & hoc est Christi nomine congregari. Canus in Locis Theol. Sine Pontificis Romani consensu, Concilium non est, sed conciliabulum.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1, c. 13, On Councils: It is the proper office of the Pontiff, he says, to convoke a general council; and this is to gather in the name of Christ. Canus, in Loci theologici: Without the consent of the Roman Pontiff, there is no council, but a conventicle.

units.la: Cusanus autem lib. 2. de Concord. Eccles. c. 25. Ex illo tempore, inquit, quo Imperatores Christiani esse cœperunt, ex illorum nutu pendere visa sunt negotia Ecclesiæ, atque adeo maxima Concilia ex eorum sententia convocabantur, ut ex Eusebio, Socrate, Sozomeno, Nicephoro patet. Rursus: Octo prima Concilia generalia ab Imperatoribus erant colleċta, & Pontifex Rom. ad instar aliorum Patriarcharum divales sacras jussiones pro veniendo aut mittendo ad Concilia, recepit. Canus in Locis Theol. lib. 5. c. 3. Concilium, inquit, Constantiense & Milevitanum à nullo Rom. Pontifice congregata erant, & tamen illud Martinus & Cælestinus, hoc Innocentius approbant. Franciscus de Vict. Relect. 4. Prop. 23. Posse quoque, inquit, congregari Concilium contra voluntatem Papæ expresse tenet Cardinalis Turrecremata, & Sylvester, & est vera sententia.
units.tr: Cusanus, however, book 2, On the Concord of the Church, c. 25: From the time when Christian emperors began to exist, the affairs of the Church seemed to depend on their will, and so the greatest councils were convoked by their decision, as is clear from Eusebius, Socrates, Sozomen and Nicephorus. Again: The first eight general councils were gathered by the emperors, and the Roman Pontiff, like the other patriarchs, received their sacred commands to come to or to send to the councils. Canus, in Loci theologici, book 5, c. 3: The Council of Constance and the Council of Milevis, he says, were convoked by no Roman Pontiff, and yet Martin and Celestine approved the one, Innocent the other. Francisco de Vitoria, Relectio 4, prop. 23: That a council may also be convoked against the will of the Pope is expressly held by Cardinal Turrecremata and Sylvester, and it is the true opinion.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 1, c. 4. dicit, Concilium legitimum non est, in quo non præsidet Pontifex, aut alius ejus nomine.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1, c. 4, says: A council is not lawful in which the Pontiff, or another in his name, does not preside.

units.la: Capite autem 5. Bellarminus, In secundo, inquit, Concilio generali non omnino interfuit Pontifex, nec per se, nec per alium. Et Card. Turrecremata lib. 3. de Eccles. c. 11. In Octo, inquit, Conciliis prioribus Papa nullus præfuit. Et Bellarm. lib. 5. de Concil. c. 19. In nullis, ait, Conciliis Orientalibus interfuit Papa. Et lib. 2. de Rom. Pontif. c. 17. In Chalcedonensi ne per legatos quidem.
units.tr: In chapter 5, however, Bellarmine: The Pontiff, he says, was not at all present at the second general council, neither in person nor through another. And Cardinal Turrecremata, book 3, On the Church, c. 11: In the eight earlier councils, he says, no pope presided. And Bellarmine, book 5, On Councils, c. 19: The Pope, he says, was present at none of the Eastern councils. And book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, c. 17: Not even through legates at Chalcedon.

units.la: Bellarminus & Stapleton us de Concil. dicunt, In Conciliis soli Episcopi vocem decisivam habent.
units.tr: Bellarmine and Stapleton, in their books on the Council, say that in councils only the bishops have a decisive vote.

units.la: Card. Arelat. vero, ut refert Æneas Sylvius de gestis Concilij Basil. Quid prohibet, inquit, exemplum Apostolicum imitari? In Concilio Nicæno 1. Athanasius, vel solus argumentationes Arianorum disturbabat, et in Constantiensi Concilio vidi presbyteros ad decisionem rerum admitti arduarum: idem observari in Pisano & Lateranensi nemini dubium est. Espensæus Com. in Tim. Ut, inquit, soli Episcopi Iudices sint, factum est postremis seculis. Et Card. Turrecrem. In præteritis, ait, temporibus aliter factitatum vidimus.
units.tr: The Cardinal of Arles, however, as Aeneas Sylvius reports in his account of the Council of Basel, says: "What forbids us to imitate the apostolic example? At the first Council of Nicaea, Athanasius alone, or nearly alone, refuted the arguments of the Arians. At the Council of Constance I saw presbyters admitted to the decision of difficult matters. That the same practice was followed at Pisa and at the Lateran, no one doubts." Espencaeus, in his commentary on Timothy: "That bishops alone should be judges was a practice of the last ages." And Cardinal Turrecremata: "In earlier times we have seen it done otherwise."

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 2. de Concil. c. 17. Pontifex, inquit, Est absolute supra Concilium. Et Valentianus Analys. 8. c. 7. Qui, inquit, contrarium sentiunt, pugnant revera cum primatu Pontificis. Et Index Expurg. pag. 165. Hoc, ait, minime tolerandum censuimus.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 2 on the Council, chapter 17: "The Pope is absolutely above the Council." And Valentianus, in his Analysis, book 8, chapter 7: "Those who think otherwise really fight against the primacy of the Pope." And the Index Expurgatorius, page 165: "We have judged that this must by no means be tolerated."

units.la: Cardinalis Cusanus vero de Concord. Cath. lib. 2. c. 17. 18. & 28. Papa, inquit, non esse supra Ecclesiam ex Augustino, Cypriano & Gregorio Papa; etiam ex Ambrosio et Confessione Pontificum constat. Et Bellarm. lib. 2. de Concil. c. 14. Papam, inquit, esse infra Concilium, Cardinalis Cameracensis, Almain, Gerson, Nicol. Campanus, Panormitanus Cardinalis, Florentinus & Patres Concilij Basil. censuerunt: Et, inquit, Æneas Sylvius de Gest. Concilij Basil. qui Papæ authoritatem authoritati Concilij anteponeret, hæreticum esse statuerunt. Item, Tempore antiquorum Conciliorum Pontifices Conciliorum acta, tanquam divina oracula observabant, & Papa Damasus negabat sui muneris esse in causis à Concilio definitis manum suam apponere. Franciscus de Vict. Relect. 4. Si bene, inquit, revolvantur historiæ tempora antiquorum Conciliorum, reperiemus Pontifices similes fuisse Conciliorum Patribus, nec præsumpsisse decreta Conciliorum tam facile dispensare, sed tanquam divina oracula observare. Iam vero nec mala nostra, nec remedia ferre possumus.
units.tr: Cardinal Cusanus, however, in On the Catholic Concord, book 2, chapters 17, 18 and 28: "That the Pope is not above the Church is clear from Augustine, from Cyprian and from Pope Gregory; it is also clear from Ambrose and from the confession of the Pontiffs." And Bellarmine, book 2 on the Council, chapter 14: "The Cardinal of Cambrai, Almain, Gerson, Nicolaus Panormitanus, the Cardinal, the Florentines and the Fathers of the Council of Basel have held that the Pope is below the Council. And," he says, "Aeneas Sylvius, in his account of the Council of Basel, records that they declared it heretical to set the authority of the Pope above the authority of the Council." Likewise: "In the time of the ancient Councils the Pontiffs observed the acts of the Councils as divine oracles," and "Pope Damasus denied that it was his office to set his hand to matters decided by a Council." Francisco de Victoria, Relection 4: "If we carefully review the history of the ancient Councils, we shall find the Pontiffs were like the Fathers of the Councils, and did not presume to set aside the decrees of the Councils so easily, but observed them as divine oracles. Yet now we can bring neither our evils nor their remedies."

units.la: Omnium Pontificum decreta, etiam in omnibus dogmatibus, inter se conveniunt, licet edita sint à diversis hominibus, diversis temporibus: quod est apertum signum unius et ejusdem Spiritus sancti, hac Ecclesiam gubernantis: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Eccles. Milit. c. 10. Iam ex hoc.
units.tr: The decrees of all the Pontiffs, even on all doctrines, agree with one another, although they were issued by different men at different times. This is the plain sign of one and the same Holy Spirit governing this Church. Bellarmine, book 4 on the Church Militant, chapter 10: "Now from this..."

units.la: Contra Erasmus Annot. in 1. Cor. 7. Ut taceam Formosum, inquit, nonne Papa Ioannes 22. & Nicolaus decretis toti inter se pugnant, idq; in his quae videntur ad fidei negotium pertinere? Innocentius 3. & Coelestinus prorsus pugnantia de Matrimonio dederunt: quorum hic Decret. 4. Tit. de Divortijs alteri parti jus facit iterandi matrimonium, si pars altera fuerit in haeresin prolapsa: Innocentius autem negat, non dissimulans quendam praedecessorem suum aliter statuisse, indicans Coelestinum, ut glossema aderit. Pelagius Papa constituerat, ut Subdiaconi ab uxoribus suis abstinerent, quas ante ordinationem legitime duxerant, ut est videre dist. 51. c. Ante triennium. Id vero decretum, tanquam iniquum, & Evangelio repugnans, Gregorius I. abrogavit.
units.tr: On the other side, Erasmus, in his Annotations on 1 Corinthians 7: "To say nothing of Formosus, do not Popes John XXII and Nicholas contradict each other in their decrees, and that on matters which seem to pertain to the business of faith? Innocent III and Celestine gave utterly contradictory rulings on marriage. Of these, the former, in Decretals book 4, title On Divorces, gives the other party the right to marry again if the other party has fallen into heresy; but Innocent denies it, not concealing that a certain predecessor of his had decided otherwise, and he indicates Celestine, as the gloss will show. Pope Pelagius had ordained that subdeacons should abstain from their wives, whom they had lawfully taken before ordination, as can be seen in Distinction 51, the chapter Ante triennium. But Gregory I abrogated that decree as unjust and contrary to the Gospel."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 1 de Verbo Dei c. 1o. Omnes, inquit, protestantes sex illos libros, quos Apocryphos vocant, ut Thobia, Iudith, Sapientiae, Ecclesiastici & Machabaeorum negant pro Scripturis Canonicis habendos esse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1 on the Word of God, chapter 10: "All Protestants deny that those six books which they call Apocryphal, such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus and the Maccabees, are to be held as canonical Scripture."

units.la: Bellarminus tamen eodem loco & Pererius lib. 16. Com. in Danielem, pag. 41. Catholici, inquiunt, multi libros hos apocryphos esse censuerunt.
units.tr: Yet Bellarmine in the same place, and Pererius in his commentary on Daniel, book 16, page 41: "Many Catholics, they say, have judged these apocryphal books to be such."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 2. de Verbo Dei c. 10. Protestantes, inquit, regant vulgatam Latinam translationem habendam esse pro authentica. Ibid. c. 2. Igitur omnes omnia ad fontem Graecum & Hebraeum examinari volunt. Ibid. c. 10. multis contendit, vulgatam Latinam versionem in omnibus lectionibus & disputationibus pro authentica habendam esse: ita ut nemini liceat ab ea, quam vis sanctissimae causae praetextu, provocare.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 2 on the Word of God, chapter 10: "Protestants, he says, want the Latin Vulgate translation to be held as authentic." The same, chapter 2: "Therefore all men want everything to be examined against the Greek and Hebrew source." The same, chapter 10, he argues at length that "the Latin Vulgate version is to be held as authentic in all readings and disputations, so that no one may appeal from it to the original, under whatever pretext of most holy cause."

units.la: Maldonatus autem Iesuita Comment. in Matth. Existimo, inquit, Latinam nostram vulgatam esse in hoc loco ex Graecis corrigendam. Cajetanus, Est, inquit, vulgata multis viris conspurcata. Franciscus Lucae in Annot. ad Biblia, Ridiculum est, ait, hoc quorundam responsum, vulgatam Latinam authenticam esse, nec esse ex Hebraeis & Graecis corrigendam.
units.tr: But Maldonatus the Jesuit, in his commentary on Matthew: "I think that our Latin Vulgate in this place is to be corrected from the Greek." Cajetan: "The Vulgate has been defiled by many men." Francis Lucas, in his Annotations on the Bible: "That answer of some men is ridiculous, that the Latin Vulgate is authentic and is not to be corrected from the Hebrew and Greek."

units.la: Bellarminus libro quarto c. 3. Docent, inquit, protestantes, omnes omnia ad salutem necessaria in Scripturis expresse contineri. Costerus in Enchirid. pag. 45. affirmat, sacras literas non omnia continere religionis mysteria explicite; &c. Et pag. 48. In membranis, inquit, tam veteris quam novi Testamenti multa desiderantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 4, chapter 3: "The Protestants teach that all things necessary to salvation are expressly contained in the Scriptures." Costerus in his Enchiridion, page 45, affirms that the sacred letters do not explicitly contain all the mysteries of religion; and on page 48: "In the manuscripts, he says, both of the Old and of the New Testament, many things are missing."

units.la: Idem tamen Costerus ibid. c. 1. Non, inquit, inficiamur praecipua illa fidei dogmata ad salutem omnibus necessaria perspicue satis comprehendi in Scripturis. Ederus in Decon. bibl. lib. 1. pag. 44. Quaecunque non sunt necessaria, ea consulto sunt omissa; quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, ea pro culdubio praescripta sunt omnia. Stapletonus praefat. in Evang. Scriptura sufficit ad vitam, quae unica vitae aeternae regula est: caetera, quibus non adlucet verbum Dei, tam non sunt necessaria, quam superflua. Rursus ibid. Vinam redeundi forma a primaeva peteretur Ecclesia, quae tot Martyres Christo consecravit, quae nullam regulam praeter Evangelium novit, nullum sicopum praeter Christum, nullum cultum, praeterquam Trino Deo impendit. Alphonsus lib. de Haeresi. tit. Scriptura, inquit, est mystica turris David, ex qua omnis armatura fortium & catholicorum virorum pendet: ideo haeretici conantur sacra Scripturae detrahere.
units.tr: The same Costerus, in the same place, chapter 1: "We do not deny that those chief doctrines of faith which are necessary to salvation for all are comprehended in the Scriptures clearly enough." Ederus, in his Deconstruction of the Bible, book 1, page 44: "Whatever is not necessary has deliberately been omitted; whatever is necessary to salvation has without doubt been prescribed in full." Stapleton, in his preface to the Gospel: "Scripture suffices for life, which is the only rule of eternal life. Other things, in which the word of God does not shine, are no more necessary than they are superfluous." Again, in the same place: "Would that the form of returning were sought from the primitive Church, which consecrated so many martyrs to Christ, which knew no rule but the Gospel, no leader but Christ, and offered no worship except to the Triune God." Alphonsus, in his book on heresy: "Scripture, he says, is the mystical tower of David, from which hang all the armour of brave and Catholic men; therefore heretics try to take away the sacred Scripture."

units.la: Iacobus Gretserus contra Sim. Stenium, Non injuria, inquit, prohibetur & arcetur populus a lectione Scripturae: quid enim rudi vulgo cum Scriptura? Et Hosius de Verbo Dei, Laicis, inquit, lectionem Scripturarum permittere, est Sanctum dare canibus, & margaritas ante porcos proicere.
units.tr: Jacob Gretser, against Simon Stenius: "The people are not without reason forbidden and kept away from reading Scripture; for what has the rude crowd to do with Scripture?" And Hosius, on the Word of God: "To allow laymen to read the Scriptures is to give what is holy to dogs and to cast pearls before swine."

units.la: Espencaeus Episcopus autem Com. in Tit. c. 2. & 2. Tim. c. 5. Aliqui, inquit, existimant Scripturas difficiliores esse, quam ut debeant laicorum manibus conteri: sed aliter visum est Patribus veteris & novi Testamenti.
units.tr: Espencaeus, the bishop, however, in his commentary on Titus chapter 2 and 2 Timothy chapter 5: "Some think the Scriptures are too difficult to be worn in the hands of laymen; but the Fathers of the Old and New Testament have judged otherwise."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 1. de Purgatorio. c. 6. Purgatorium, inquit, esse, Patres Graeci & Latini asseruerunt. Lindanus Panopl. lib. 4. pag. 314. Purgatorium, inquit, esse, veteres Patres uno ore statuunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine, book 1 on Purgatory, chapter 6: "The Greek and Latin Fathers have asserted that there is a Purgatory." Lindanus, Panoply, book 4, page 314: "The ancient Fathers affirm with one voice that there is a Purgatory."

units.la: Roffensis Episcopus autem artic. 18. contra Lutherum, Legat, inquit, qui vellit Graecorum Patrum Commentarios, & nullam, quantum opinor, aut rarissimam Purgatarij mentionem inveniet: sed neque Latini simul omnes hujus rei veritatem conceperunt: neque tam necessaria fuit primitivæ Ecclesiæ purgatorij fides, atque nunc est; ex qua pendet omnis Indulgentiarum existimatio: his enim, si nullum fuerit Purgatorium, nihil indigebimus. Contemplantes igitur aliquandiu Purgatorium incognitum fuisse, deinde quibusdam pedetentim, partim ex revelationibus, partim ex Scripturis creditum fuisse, & tam sero cognitum & receptum Ecclesiæ universæ, &c.
units.tr: The Bishop of Rochester, however, in article 18 against Luther: "Let whoever wishes read the commentaries of the Greek Fathers, and he will find, I suppose, no mention of Purgatory, or only the rarest. Nor did all the Latins at once grasp the truth of this matter; nor was faith in Purgatory as necessary to the primitive Church as it is now, on which the whole estimation of indulgences depends; for if there were no Purgatory, we should need nothing of them. Considering, then, that for some time Purgatory was unknown, and afterwards was gradually believed by some, partly from revelations, partly from Scripture, and was so late known and received by the whole Church, etc."

units.la: Costerus in Enchirid. de Imag. Quod ad inquit: Quod ad veterem Ecclesiam pertinet, certum est imagines Christi & Sanctorum non sine cultu & veneratione in usu fuisse.
units.tr: Costerus, in his Enchiridion, on images: "As far as the ancient Church is concerned, it is certain that images of Christ and of the saints were in use, not without cult and veneration."

units.la: Cassander vero in Consult. art. 21. de Imaginibus, Certum est, inquit, initio prædicati Evangelij, & aliquanto tempore post; Imaginum usum non fuisse, ut ex Clemente Alexandrino & Arnobio patet. Erasmus in Catech. lib. 2. Vsq; ad tempora Hieronymi, inquit, probatæ religionis viri fuerunt, qui nullam faciebant imaginem, ne ipsius quidem Christi. Rursus Cassander quo supra: Quæ fuerit, inquit, Romanæ Ecclesiæ tempore Gregorij mens, ex ejus scriptis colligitur, haberi nimirum pictura, non ut colerentur, sed ut per eas imperiti rerum gestarum admonerentur. Agrippa de Vanitate Scientiarum c. 57. Judæi, inquit, qui erant Dei populus, nihil magis horrebant, inquit, Iosephus, quam simulachra. Ipsi Ethnici cum ad Christi religionem converti erant, in Ecclesiam nostram simulachra, & multas steriles ceremonias introducebant; quarum omnino nihil est apud primos illos, & vere Christianos. Et Polydorus Virgil. lib. 6. Invent. c. 13. Omnes, inquit, veteres Patres, teste Hieronymo, simulachrorum cultum damnabant.
units.tr: Cassander, however, in his Consultation, article 21, on images: "It is certain that at the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, and for some time after, the use of images did not exist, as is clear from Clement of Alexandria and Arnobius. Erasmus, in his Catechism, book 2: Right up to the times of Jerome there were men of approved religion who made no image, not even of Christ himself." Again Cassander, as above: "What the mind of the Roman Church was in the time of Gregory is gathered from his writings: namely, that pictures were kept, not that they should be worshipped, but that through them the unlearned might be reminded of the things done." Agrippa, On the Vanity of the Sciences, chapter 57: "The Jews, who were the people of God, dreaded nothing more, says Josephus, than images. The Gentiles themselves, when they were converted to the religion of Christ, introduced into our Church images and many barren ceremonies, of which there is absolutely nothing among those first and truly Christian people." And Polydore Vergil, book 6 of On Discoveries, chapter 13: "All the ancient Fathers, as Jerome testifies, condemned the worship of images."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Verbo Dei c. 3. Aqua, inquit, lustralis, qua populo benedicimus, merito dicitur Apostolica traditio.
units.tr: Bellarmine, Book 4 of On the Word of God, ch. 3: "Lustral water, which we bless for the people, is rightly called an apostolic tradition."

units.la: Franciscus de Vict. autem Relect. 11. q. 1. inquit, Est tantum ex jure positivo. Et Platina in Vita Alex. 1. Alexander 1. inquit, instituit, ut aquam, quam Sanctam appellamus, interpositis sacris orationibus, sale admixto, in templis atq; cubiculis adfugandos dæmones retinerent.
units.tr: Francisco de Victoria, however, in Relectio 11, q. 1, says: "It rests only on positive law." And Platina, in the Life of Alexander I, says: "Alexander I instituted that water, which we call holy, with sacred prayers said over it and salt mixed in, should be kept in churches and bedchambers to drive away demons."

units.la: Anglo-Rhemense Collegium Iesuit. in 1 Cor. 14. pag. 462. inquit. Populus Christianus antiquæ suæ consuetudini parere debet, & Latinis precibus uti, potius quam vulgaribus. Ambrof. Compsa, ut refert Sixtus Senensis, Doctrina, inquit, Lutheri, quæ linguam cognitam in precibus exigit, diaboli calliditatem sapit.
units.tr: The English-Rheims college of Jesuits, on 1 Corinthians 14, p. 462, says: "The Christian people ought to obey its ancient custom and use Latin prayers rather than the vernacular." Ambrosius Compsa, as Sixtus of Siena reports, said: "The doctrine of Luther, which requires prayers in a language the people understand, savours of the devil's cunning."

units.la: Bellarminus vero lib. 2. de Verbo Dei c. 16. Tempore, inquit, Apostolorum omnes Christiani simul psallebant in divinis officijs, & preces intelligebant. Lyranus in 1. Cor. 14. Omnia, inquit, in Ecclesia primitiva lingua vulgari fiebant. Et Bellarminus, quo supra. Idem etiam Longo, inquit, tempore post in Occidente & in Oriente, ut ex Chrysostomo & Cypriano constat, populus in divinis respondebat, Amen. Et Erasmus 1 Cor. 14. Hac in re, ait, mirum est quomodo mutata est, Ecclesiæ consuetudo. Ergo, inquit Defensor libelli contra Calvinum, optandum esset, ut juxta Apostolorum mandatum, & prisicum Ecclesiæ morem in lingua vulgari preces peragerentur. Et Vitalianus Papa circa annos Domini 666. primus iuxta Platinam, omnia Latino sermone in Ecclesia fieri mandavit.
units.tr: Bellarmine, however, in Book 2 of On the Word of God, ch. 16, says: "In the time of the Apostles all Christians sang together in the divine offices and understood the prayers." Lyra, on 1 Corinthians 14, says: "In the primitive Church everything was done in the common tongue." Bellarmine, cited above, also says: "Later, for a long time afterwards, in both the West and the East, as is clear from Chrysostom and Cyprian, the people answered 'Amen' in the divine services." Erasmus, on 1 Corinthians 14, says: "It is remarkable how the custom of the Church has changed in this matter." Therefore, says the defender of the little book against Calvin, it would be desirable that, according to the command of the Apostles and the ancient custom of the Church, the prayers be said in the vernacular. And Pope Vitalian, around the year of the Lord 666, was the first, according to Platina, to order that everything in the Church be done in the Latin language.

units.la: Suarez Iesuita in Thomam part. 3. q. 27. art. 1. & 2. Est hoc, inquit, privilegium B. Virginis speciale, in prima sua conceptione immunem a peccato fuisse. Antiqui Patres pauca de hoc privilegio loquuti sunt, tum quia spiritus sanctus Ecclesiam paulatim instruit, tum etiam quia illi in aliis gravioribus mysterijs explicandis distinebantur. Postquam vero ante 500. annos veritas hæc cœpit clarius doceri, ita incendit fidelium animos, crevitq; paulatim ejus fides, ut jam fere omnium consensu recepta sit, & præsertim ab hinc ducentis annis Ecclesiastici Doctores omnes, & universa Academia huic sententiæ scripserint, &c.
units.tr: Suárez the Jesuit, on Thomas, part 3, q. 27, arts. 1 and 2, says: "It is a special privilege of the Blessed Virgin that she was free from sin in her first conception. The ancient Fathers spoke little of this privilege, partly because the Holy Spirit instructs the Church gradually, and partly because they were occupied in explaining other, weightier mysteries. But after about five hundred years ago this truth began to be taught more clearly, it so kindled the hearts of the faithful, and its belief grew gradually, so that it has now been received almost by universal consent; and especially for the last two hundred years all the ecclesiastical teachers, and the whole university, have written in support of this opinion, etc."

units.la: Melchior Canus autē in Loc. Theol. lib. 7. c. 1. B. Virginem, inquit, fuisse à peccatis liberam, e sacris literis, juxta germanum litera sensum, nusquā habetur: quin imo lex generalis in iis traditur, qui ex Adæ carnali propagatione creatos, sine ulla exceptione comprehenditur. Nec vero dici potest Apostolorum tempore in Ecclesiam defecisse; nam constat prisfcos Scriptores non id a majoribus suis accepisse. Imo sancti omnes, qui in hujus rei memoriam inciderunt, uno ore asseverarunt, B. Virginem in peccato Originali conceptam fuisse.
units.tr: Melchior Cano, however, in Loci Theologici, Book 7, ch. 1, says: "That the Blessed Virgin was free from sins is nowhere found in Holy Scripture according to the plain sense of the letter. Indeed, the general rule is laid down for those who are created by carnal propagation from Adam, and it covers them without any exception." Nor can it be said that this teaching failed in the Church in the time of the Apostles, for it is certain that the earliest writers did not receive it from their elders. Rather, all the saints who have touched on this matter have declared with one voice that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in original sin. ...

units.la: Collegium Iesuiticum Anglo-Rhenan. Annot. in Act. 1. 24. B. Mariæ, inquit, corpus assumptum fuisse in cœlum ex antiqua historia verissimum esse constat.
units.tr: The Jesuit college of Anglo-Rhenish, in its notes on Acts 1:24, says: "That the body of Blessed Mary was taken up into heaven is quite certain from ancient history."

units.la: Sixtus Senensis autem in Bibliotheca lib. 2. Tit. Mariæ translatio. Nihil, ait, hujusmodi (inquit Augustinus) invenitur apud Latinos Patres. Est hoc apocryphum dogma, inquit Hieronymus, & illam historiam Beda refellit, ut Evangelistæ contradicentem.
units.tr: Sixtus of Siena, however, in Bibliotheca, Book 2, under the title "The translation of Mary," says: "Nothing of this kind (says Augustine) is found among the Latin Fathers. This is an apocryphal dogma, says Jerome, and Bede refutes that story as contradicting the Evangelist."

units.la: Bellarm lib 1 de Pontifice Rom. c. 23. dicit, Nisi Petrus alios Apostolos vel per se, vel per alios Episcopos ordinasset, nulla ratio est, cur Romam Ecclesiarum omnium Matrem esse dicamus.
units.tr: Bellarmine, Book 1 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 23, says: "Unless Peter ordained the other Apostles, either himself or through other bishops, there is no reason why we should call Rome the mother of all churches."

units.la: Franciscus autem de Vict. Relect. 2. q. 2. Utrum, inquit, Petrus eos ordinasset, est incertum. Greg. de Valent. Iesuita lib. 7 Analys. c. 2. pag. 52. Sententia, inquit, quæ negat Petrum alios ordinasse, magis est communis. Idem lib. 2 de Eucharist. pag. 2. Apostoli, inquit, à Christo Iesu in tempore Cœnæ Sacerdotalem potestatem acceperunt. (Ex iis talis Syllogismus formari potest: Si Petrus non alios Apostolos & Episcopos ordinavit, tum Romana Ecclesia reliquarum dici non debet Mater. Major hæc est Bellarm. Sequitur Minor Francisci de Vict. & Valentiæ: Secundum communem sententiam Petrus non ordinavit Apostolos & Episcopos. Ergo Rom. Ecclesia Matris prærogativam non habet.)
units.tr: Francisco de Victoria, however, in Relectio 2, q. 2, says: "Whether Peter ordained them is uncertain." Gregory of Valencia, the Jesuit, in Analysis, Book 7, ch. 2, p. 52, says: "The opinion which denies that Peter ordained the others is more common." The same, in Book 2 On the Eucharist, p. 2, says: "The Apostles received priestly power from Christ Jesus at the time of the Supper." (From these a syllogism can be formed: If Peter did not ordain the other Apostles and bishops, then the Roman Church ought not to be called the mother of the rest. The major premise is Bellarmine's. The minor follows from Francisco de Victoria and Valencia: according to the common opinion Peter did not ordain Apostles and bishops. Therefore the Roman Church does not have the prerogative of motherhood.)

units.la: Bellarm. lib. 4 de Ecclesia milit. c. 2. Sectarij, inquit, nostri temporis docent homines justificari sola fide speciali, qua quisque certo credit, se propter Christum coram Deo esse justum: quod cum quolibet paradoxo comparari potest. Et lib. 3. de Iustific. c. 1, & 2. Nos inquit, tantum certitudinem conjecturalem defendimus.
units.tr: Bellarmine, Book 4 On the Church Militant, ch. 2, says: "Our sectaries of this time teach that men are justified by a special faith alone, by which each one firmly believes that for Christ's sake he is righteous before God; this can be compared with any paradox." And in Book 3 On Justification, chs. 1 and 2: "We, he says, defend only a conjectural certainty."

units.la: Bellarm. vero ibid. c. 2. Aliqui, ait, Catholici docent quidem eam certitudinem, quæ nullam habeat de sua salute formidinem. Pererius Iesuita Com. ad Rom 8 num. 27. Certitudinem, inquit, Catholici eam docent, cui subesse falsum non possit. Vega lib 3 de Incertitudine Orat. c 36 Quidam, inquit, Catholicus tanto affectu fidem conjecturalem oppugnabat, ut eam Lutherana opinione deteriorem diceret, quia, inquit, cum Lutherani multum fidei tribuant, hæc opinio derogat. Ibid. c. 36. Guillandus certitudinem Gratiæ defendit prorsus ut Lutherani. Ibid c. 7. Talem certitudinem consequentem fidem, multi Catholici ante decretum Concilij Tridentini probabilem esse censebant, & eam pluribus argumentis suadere conabantur. Pererius Iesuita Com ad Rom. c. 8 num. 27. Catharinus, inquit, inter Theologos hujus temporis minime incelebris, docuit, certitudinem fidei, qua certo statuunt sibi peccata esse remissa: refert etiam Vega lib. 9. de Iustific. c. 46. Idem Catharinus, teste Bellarmino libro 3. de Iustific. Universi, inquit, patres hanc certitudinem contestantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine, however, in the same place, ch. 2, says: "Some Catholics do teach that certainty which has no fear for its own salvation." Pererius the Jesuit, Commentary on Romans 8, no. 27, says: "Catholics teach a certainty to which falsehood cannot attach." Vega, Book 3 On the Uncertainty of Prayer, ch. 36: "A certain Catholic attacked conjectural faith with such zeal that he said it was worse than the Lutheran opinion, because, he says, while the Lutherans attribute much to faith, this opinion detracts from it." Ibid., ch. 36: "Guillandus defends a certainty of grace exactly as the Lutherans do." Ibid., ch. 7: "Many Catholics before the decree of the Council of Trent thought such a certainty, which follows faith, was probable, and tried to persuade people of it by many arguments." Pererius the Jesuit, Commentary on Romans 8, no. 27: "Catharinus, who is by no means unknown among the theologians of this time, taught a certainty of faith by which they firmly determine that their sins have been forgiven." Vega also reports this in Book 9 On Justification, ch. 46. The same Catharinus, according to Bellarmine in Book 3 On Justification, says: "All the Fathers bear witness to this certainty."

units.la: Gregorius de Valentia Iesuita in lib. de Prædest. c. 8. f. Et præterea. Reprobationis, inquit, certitudinem Wiclefus & Calvinus explicare non possunt, qui sine præscientia peccatorum Deum reprobare hominem asserunt.
units.tr: Gregory of Valencia, the Jesuit, in his book On Predestination, ch. 8, letter f, "And besides": "Wycliffe and Calvin cannot explain the certainty of reprobation, since they assert that God reprobates a man without foreknowledge of his sins."

units.la: Pererius autem Iesuita Com. ad Rom. 9. c. num. 31. Deum, inquit, aliquos reprobare, & excludere à vita æterna, non quidem propter eorum prævisa opera, sed quia ipse non vult dare illis vitam æternam, est Augustini sententia. Est etiam hæc sententia Thomæ, quam alij quoque complures Theologi consequuntur. Ibidem Pererius num. 60. Si, inquit, Deus hominem in puris naturalibus, sine peccato consideratum, reprobaret, nolens illi dare vitam æternam, non faceret illi injuriam.
units.tr: Pererius the Jesuit, however, Commentary on Romans 9, ch. [?], no. 31, says: "That God reprobates some and excludes them from eternal life, not indeed on account of works he foresaw in them, but because he does not wish to give them eternal life, is the opinion of Augustine." This is also the opinion of Thomas, which many other theologians follow. In the same place, Pererius, no. 60, says: "If God were to reprobate a man considered in pure nature, without sin, unwilling to give him eternal life, he would not be doing him any injustice."

units.la: Gentiles, inquit Maldonatus Iesuita. Com. in Matth. 11. 21. Poterant servata lege naturæ, omnium Confessione salvi esse, Lex autem naturæ satis illis erat ab ipsa natura prædicata.
units.tr: "The Gentiles," says Maldonado the Jesuit, Commentary on Matthew 11:21, "could, by keeping the law of nature, be saved, as all admit; and the law of nature was sufficient for them, as nature itself proclaimed it."

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: DE DOCTRINA

units.la: Accßa autem Iesuita lib. 5. de procuranda Indorum salute c. 3. Vix, inquit, fatis mirari possum, quid Præceptoribus quibusdam Scholasticis nostri seculi in mentem venerit, ut nunc quoque temporis, post tamdiu revelatum Christum, sine Christi notitia salutem cuiquam æternam contingere posse confirment: indigna Theologo sententia, quæ (ut liberè & verè dicam) nihil in sacris literis, nihil in sanctis Patribus firmitudinis habet, tantum humana quadam suspicione introducta, propter infinitam eorum multitudinem, qui in hoc nostro orbe tam longa ætate Evangelij luce caruere, quibus aditus in cœlum omnis præcludi videtur, si ad salutem fuerit Christi notitia necessaria. Rigidum est, inquiunt, & à Deo, qui omnes vult salvos fieri, charitate alienum, ut ea exigat, quæ nec ipse dat, nec homines per se præstare possunt. Unde concludunt, sine fide per naturalem tantum cognitionem ipsos salutem consequi posse. Quorum sententia, tametsi ipsi Catholici sint, est aperte hæretica, ut nihil magis repugnet fidei; quasi verò fides ab Apostolis necessaria definiatur ad percipienda ea quæ à creatura cognosci possunt, & non potius ad ea quæ in cor hominis non ascenderunt, nobis verò revelavit Deus per Spiritum; revocat nos illud, quòd ad Patrem nemo venit nisi per Christum; nullam aliam viam qua eatur; nullum aliud ostium quo introretur ad vitam. Ac re quidem vera, si potest sine Christi notitia salus esse, aut justitia, ergo gratis Christus prædicatur, frustra Apostoli mittuntur in orbem; tam expressè docet hoc Apostolus ad Rom. 10. Finis legis est Christus ad salutem omni credenti. Non hic agitur utrum durum & severum sit hoc, an benignum & liberale, sed utrum verum nec ne. Augustinus docet, nemini ex ijs, qui ex Gentibus ante tempus Evangelij servati sunt, Christi salutem contigisse, absque revelatione unius Mediatoris Dei & hominum Iesu Christi. Toletus Iesuita quoque Comment. ad Rom. Hoc, inquit, non est catholicum assertum.
units.tr: Acosta the Jesuit, in his book on promoting the salvation of the Indians, chapter 3, says: "I can scarcely wonder what has come into the minds of certain scholastic teachers of our age, that even now, after Christ has been revealed for so long, they affirm that eternal salvation can come to anyone without knowledge of Christ: an opinion unworthy of a theologian, which (to speak freely and truly) has no firmness in the Holy Scriptures or in the holy Fathers, and has been introduced only by a certain human suspicion, on account of the infinite multitude of those who in this our world, for so long an age, have lacked the light of the Gospel, for whom every way into heaven seems to be shut off, if knowledge of Christ is necessary for salvation. It is harsh, they say, and foreign to the charity of God, who wishes all to be saved, to demand what neither he himself gives nor men can supply by themselves." From this they conclude that men can obtain salvation without faith, through natural knowledge alone. "Their opinion, although they are themselves Catholics, is plainly heretical, so that nothing is more opposed to the faith; as if faith were defined by the Apostles as necessary for grasping those things which can be known by a creature, and not rather for those things which have not ascended into the heart of man, but which God has revealed to us through the Spirit; it recalls us to the words that no one comes to the Father except through Christ; there is no other way by which one goes, no other door by which one enters into life. And indeed, in truth, if salvation or righteousness can be had without knowledge of Christ, then Christ is preached in vain, and the Apostles are sent into the world to no purpose; the Apostle teaches this as plainly as possible in Romans 10: Christ is the end of the law for salvation to everyone who believes. The question here is not whether this is harsh and severe or kind and generous, but whether it is true or not." Augustine teaches that none of those among the Gentiles who were saved before the time of the Gospel attained the salvation of Christ, apart from revelation of the one Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ. Toletus the Jesuit also, in his Commentary on Romans, says: "This is not a Catholic assertion."

units.la: Toletus Iesuita lib. 1. Instruct. Sacerd. c. 55. Si, inquit, conferretur Ordo etiam ante usum rationis, Ordo teneret, & character imprimeretur: etiam presbyteratum posse conferri infantibus nondum rationis usum habentibus, est communis doctrina Theologorum & Canonistarum. Si ad annum discretionis, nimirum septennium, puer suscepit ordines, & tunc erat voti capax, nec contradixit voto continentiæ, ordo tenet. Francíscus de Victoria Relect. 2. Nullus, inquit, alius de numero Christianorum, præter fœminas, divino jure excluditur à potestate Ecclesiastica, sive Ordinis, sive Juris dictionis, non puer, non amens; quia potest pervenire ad eum statum, ut commodè exerceat; nec video, cur non puer possit in Episcopum consecrari.
units.tr: Toletus the Jesuit, in book 1 of the Instruction of Priests, chapter 55: "If Holy Orders were conferred even before the use of reason, the Order would hold and the character would be imprinted: that the priesthood can be conferred on infants who do not yet have the use of reason is the common doctrine of theologians and canonists. If a boy at the age of discretion, that is, seven years, receives orders, and at that time was capable of a vow, and did not contradict the vow of continence, the order holds."
