Francisco de Victoria, Relection 2: "No one else of the number of Christians, except women, is excluded by divine law from ecclesiastical power, whether of Order or of jurisdiction: not a boy, not a madman; because he can come to that state that he may exercise it fittingly; nor do I see why a boy could not be consecrated as bishop."

units.la: Episcopus Espenfæus autem Comment. in 1. Tim. 4. digref. libro 2. c. 12. In Concilijs, inquit, cautum est, ne quis ad Ministerium neophytus ordinetur: Et Salmeron Iesuita Tract. 201. in Parab. A promovendis, inquit, pueris maximè abstinere debent Ecclesiarum rectores: nam pueri nesciunt regere seipsos, nedum alios: nec fatis est dicere, quòd est nobilis & illustris familiæ, quia propter Ecclesiam est Minister, non propter Ministrum Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Bishop Espenseus, however, in his Commentary on 1 Timothy 4, digression in book 2, chapter 12: "In the Councils it is provided that no neophyte be ordained to the ministry." And Salmeron the Jesuit, Tractate 201 on the Parables: "Rectors of churches ought especially to abstain from promoting boys: for boys do not know how to rule themselves, much less others; nor is it enough to say that he is of noble and illustrious family, because a minister is for the sake of the Church, not the Church for the sake of the minister."

units.la: Collegium Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in Lucam 12. Idiota, inquit, Catholicus cùm pro tribunali sæculari steterit, de causa fidei examinandus, etsi tantum responderit se esse virum Catholicum, & Ecclesiam, quam profitetur, posse fidei rationem reddere, nec quicquam præter hæc aliud responderit, satis viri Catholici munere faciet.
units.tr: The Anglo-Rhemish College, Annotations on Luke 12: "When a Catholic layman has stood before a secular tribunal to be examined on a matter of faith, even if he has answered only that he is a Catholic man, and that the Church which he professes is able to give an account of the faith, and has answered nothing else besides these things, he will have done enough to fulfil the office of a Catholic man."

units.la: Espenfæus autem Comment. in 2. Tim. 3. An sufficit, inquit, decantata hodie per Catholicos Carbonarij fides? Is interrogatus quid crederet, respondit, se credere quod Ecclesia credit.
units.tr: Espenseus, however, in his Commentary on 2 Timothy 3: "Is the faith of the Carbonari, much sung today by the Catholics, sufficient? When he was asked what he believed, he answered that he believed what the Church believes."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. de Verbo Dei, c. 16. Precibus, inquit, ignotis Ecclesia utijure potest. Ad ædificationem inquit Collegium Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in 1. Cor. 14. pag. 461. non minus, ad devotionem sæpe magis valent quam cognita. Cosferus inquit, Consolationem plurimum adjuvant. Aquinas autem Com. in 1. Cor. 14. Quantum, inquit, ad fructum devotionis pertinet, qui non in speciali intelligit quae orat. Et Caietan. Com. in 1. Cor. c. 14. Melius est, orare in mente distincte intelligere ea quae orat, quam confuse. Lyranus in eum locum. Quid proficit, inquit, populus non intelligens ea quae orat?
units.tr: Bellarmine, in the book on the Word of God, chapter 16: "The Church can rightly use prayers in an unknown tongue." "For edification," says the Anglo-Rhemish College, Annotations on 1 Corinthians 14, page 461, "they are often no less, and for devotion often more, effective than those that are understood. Cosferus," it says, "greatly helps consolation." Aquinas, however, in his Commentary on 1 Corinthians 14: "As far as the fruit of devotion is concerned, it pertains to one who does not understand in particular what he prays." And Cajetan, Commentary on 1 Corinthians chapter 14: "It is better to pray in the mind, understanding distinctly what one prays, than confusedly." Lyra on that place: "What profit does the people derive, not understanding what they pray?"

units.la: Toletus Iesuita lib. 4. Instructi. c. 24. Homo tenetur sub mortali peccato ad sanctificandum festum: sed non tenetur ad bene sanctificandum. Et c. 25. Licet interfacere audito Sacro prius, & venari; licet fundere super lites propter pecuniam: licet carnes vendere, animalia occidere ad victum, propter pecuniam: licet in solennitatibus construere loca pro spectaculis, quando non possunt fieri nisi in festo: denique Pontificis aut Episcopi licentia licet in festo operari.
units.tr: Toletus the Jesuit, in book 4 of the Instruction, chapter 24: "A man is bound under mortal sin to sanctify the feast, but he is not bound to sanctify it well." And chapter 25: "It is permitted to go to hunt after hearing Mass first; it is permitted to pour out lawsuits for money; it is permitted to sell meat and to kill animals for food, for money; it is permitted on solemn days to build places for spectacles, when they cannot be held except on a feast; finally, with the permission of the Pope or a bishop, it is permitted to work on a feast."

units.la: Catechismus autem Tridentinus Conc. Hoc praecepto, inquit, prohibemur, ut quaecunque divinum cultum impedire possunt, omnino vitemus: facile enim perspici potest, omne servilis operis genus prohiberi.
units.tr: The Tridentine Catechism, however, on the Council: "By this precept we are forbidden to avoid altogether whatever can hinder divine worship: for it can easily be seen that every kind of servile work is forbidden."

units.la: Cosferus in Apolog. par. 3. c. 9. Haec est, inquit, perpetua nota Ecclesiae, nullum sequlum, nulla aetas hominum miraculis caruit. Bellarm. lib. 4. de Ecclesia mil. c. 14. Undecimo saeculo. Nunc, inquit, nostram Ecclesiam demonstrabimus esse Dei veram Ecclesiam ex miraculis, quae singulis aetatibus plurima & testatissima fuerunt, usque ad hoc ultimum saeculum, in quo, &c.
units.tr: Cosferus, in the Apology, part 3, chapter 9: "This is the perpetual mark of the Church: no age, no period of men has been without miracles." Bellarmine, book 4 on the Church Militant, chapter 14, on the eleventh century: "Now we shall demonstrate that our Church is the true Church of God from the miracles which in every age have been very many and most attested, down to this last age, in which, etc."

units.la: Espensaeus Episcopus autem Com. in 2. Tim. 3. ex Aug. de civit. Dei lib. 22. c. 8. Ubi, inquit, nullus est infidelis, faciendorum miraculorum nulla est necessitas. Et Stella Com. in Luc. c. 11. Crede, inquit. Evangelio, quod fuit miraculis confirmatum. Sed dices, nonne rationi consentaneum est, ut nunc quoque fides confirmetur miraculis? Non: nam nunc quoque damnum potius afferrent, quam commodum, etiamsi in principio nascentis Ecclesiae fuerint necessaria. Puer enim, cum ambulare nequit, adjuvatur veiculo, quod homini adulto est impedimento. Et Gregorius Magnus homil. 29. in Evang. Numquid, inquit, fratres mei, quia ista signa non facitis, non creditis? sed haec necessaria in exordio Ecclesiae fuerunt, ut multitudo ad fidem crescere: quia & nos, cum robusta plantamus, tamdiu eis aquam infundimus, quousque ea in terra coaluisse videatur; & si semel radicem fixerint, irrigatio cessabit.
units.tr: Bishop Espenseus, however, in his Commentary on 2 Timothy 3, from Augustine, City of God book 22, chapter 8: "Where there is no unbeliever, there is no necessity for working miracles." And Stella, Commentary on Luke chapter 11: "Believe," he says, "the Gospel, which was confirmed by miracles. But you will say, is it not reasonable that now also faith should be confirmed by miracles? No: for now they would bring harm rather than advantage, even if they were necessary at the beginning of the nascent Church. For a boy, when he cannot yet walk, is helped by a carriage, which is a hindrance to a grown man." And Gregory the Great, Homily 29 on the Gospels: "Do you suppose, my brothers, that because you do not work these signs, you do not believe? But these were necessary at the beginning of the Church, so that the multitude might grow into the faith; for we too, when we plant young trees, pour water on them for as long as it seems they have taken hold in the ground; and once they have fixed their root, the watering ceases."

units.la: Acosta de procuranda Indorum salute libro secundo, capite nono. In hoc, inquit, signorum argumento explicando Chrysostomus mirifice versatur. Si enim miracula in initio Evangelicae praedicationis facta creduntur, certum est, inquit, doctrinam, cui confirmandae adhibebantur, divinam esse professam. Sin autem veritati historiae jam minus Gentilis credat, at longe omnibus signis majus est, homines illos paucos, ignobiles, illiteratos, omnibus mortalibus visos, toti orbi persuasisse? Non ergo fides jam satis firmata, miraculis novis indiget confirmari, quin potius utilius esse asserit, signa nunc carere, quoniam majoris meriti sit sine illis credere. Episcopus Roffensis de Captivit. Babylon. c. 16. part. 4. Promisit, inquit, Christus, ut discipuli daemonia ejicerent, quam promissionem nullum his diebus effectum sortiri dilucide cernimus. Nemo enim est qui nunc corporaliter daemonia ejicit, ut morbos sanat, & tamen minime ambigimus, quin plurimi sint, qui fidem eandem, & aequae magnam cum prisci fidelibus habeant, nec tamen inanis illa promissio fuit, quam noluit efficaciam habere perpetuam, sed pro tempore nascentis, & adolescentis Ecclesiae. Augustinus de Civit. Dei libro 22. cap. 8. Miracula, inquit, necessaria erant ut crederet mundus: sed nunc qui quaerit miraculum, postquam mundus credidit, maximum est ipse prodigium.
units.tr: Acosta, On Promoting the Salvation of the Indians, book 2, chapter 9: "In explaining this argument from signs Chrysostom is wonderfully engaged. For if the miracles done at the beginning of the Gospel preaching are believed, it is certain, he says, that the doctrine which they were used to confirm is divine, as it professes to be. But if the Gentile now believes less in the truth of the history, yet is it not far greater than all signs that those few, lowly, unlettered men persuaded the whole world, seen by all mortals? Therefore the faith, now already sufficiently firmed, does not need to be confirmed by new miracles; rather he asserts that it is more useful that signs now be lacking, since it is of greater merit to believe without them." Bishop of Rochester, On the Babylonish Captivity, chapter 16, part 4: "Christ promised that the disciples would cast out demons, a promise which we clearly see has in these days no effect. For there is no one who now corporeally casts out demons, as he heals diseases; and yet we do not doubt in the least that there are very many who have the same faith, and equally great, with the faithful of old; nor was that empty promise one which he did not wish to have a perpetual efficacy, but one for the time of the nascent and growing Church." Augustine, City of God, book 22, chapter 8: "Miracles were necessary so that the world might believe; but now he who seeks a miracle, after the world has believed, is himself the greatest prodigy."

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Ecclesia milit. cap. 14. Verum, inquit, miraculum sufficiens est testimonium verae Ecclesiae, ex quo fundamento probamus eam esse apud nos.
units.tr: Bellarminus, book 4 of On the Militant Church, chapter 14: Indeed, he says, a miracle is a sufficient testimony of the true Church, and on this foundation we prove that she is among us.

units.la: Maldonatus autem Com. in Matth. c. 7. Chrysostomus, inquit, Hieronymus, Eusebius, Theophylactus, probant exemplis, etiam per alios, quam Catholicos, vera miracula fieri. Et hoc ipso loco Matthaei septimo. Multi dicent in illo die, in nomine tuo
units.tr: Maldonatus, however, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 7: Chrysostom, he says, Jerome, Eusebius and Theophylact prove by examples, including those from people other than Catholics, that true miracles are performed. And this same passage, Matthew 7: "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name cast out demons

units.la: {§} De sanctificatione diei festi. ciecimus, &c. Facile colligitur, falsos illos Prophetas, de quib. Christus loquitur, vera miracula fecisse, vere prophetasse, vere daemonia ejecisse: nec enim respondet Christus mentiri eos: sed, se eos, quamvis ista fecerint, non nosse; nec magnum est, si monuerit nos, ne falsa miracula facientibus non crederemus; sed magnum et admirabile est omnino, quod monet ne falsis Prophetis credamus, vera etiam miracula facientibus. Nullum ergo, dicet aliquis, ad probandam veram doctrinam argumentum hinc sumi potest? Non sequitur omnino, Nullum; sed non necessarium sumi potest. Scimus enim Christum ad confirmandam doctrinam suam, potestatem faciendi miracula Apostolis suis tradidisse: scimus vi miraculorum totum pene orbem ad fidem fuisse pertractum; quod qui negant, ut dicit Augustinus, maius ipsi miraculum, miracula tollendo faciunt. Incredibilius enim tot Philosophos, tot sapientes viros, tam paucis Apostolis, tam imperitis, tamque incredibilia humanae rationi praedicantibus, sine ullis miraculis credidisse, quae illa ipsa miracula, quae ab illis facta narratur. Probabile igitur fidei argumentum est, quod ex miraculis sumitur, quia per fidem saepe sine fide raro fieri solent. Nec necessario demonstrant Ecclesiam, nisi ubi potestas miracula faciendi ordinaria contingit. Bellarminus asserit, verum miraculum esse sufficiens testimonium Ecclesiae; Maldonatus Iesuita ex Scripturis et Patribus contrarium demonstrat. Hieronymus in Comment. ad Galat. libr. 3. Observandum est, inquit, quod operari virtutes dicuntur ii, qui non tenent Evangelii veritatem. Hoc dico adversum haereticos, qui probationem esse fidei suae in eo, si signum aliquod fecerint, arbitrantur. Augustinus contra Epist. Fund. cap. 4. Quod si talia in Catholica Ecclesia fiunt, non ideo ipsa manifestatur Catholica, quia haec in ea fiant, sed ideo approbanda sunt, quia in Catholica fiant. Chrysostomus homil. 49. in Matth. Miraculorum, inquit, operatio magis apud eos invenitur qui sunt falsi Christiani. Tertul. praescript. cap. 44. Quae si hoc non fit scriptum, venturos esse qui maximas virtutes edent ad corrumpendam veritatem. Augustinus libro quo supra c. 16. Dominus igitur, inquit, adversus hos Mirabilarios cautos nos fecit, dicendo, Cavete. Et Theodoret. in Deut. 13. Instruimur non credere, quando, qui talia edit, contraria pietati docet.
units.tr: {§} On the sanctification of the festival day: "...have cast out demons, etc." It is easily gathered that those false prophets of whom Christ speaks did perform true miracles, truly prophesied and truly cast out demons. For Christ does not answer that they lied, but that, although they did these things, he did not know them. Nor is it a great thing if he warned us not to believe those who work false miracles. But it is truly great and wonderful that he warns us not to believe false prophets even when they perform true miracles. Will someone say, then, that no argument for proving true doctrine can be drawn from this? It does not follow at all that none can be drawn; but it cannot be drawn as a necessary one. For we know that Christ gave his Apostles the power of working miracles to confirm their teaching; we know that by the power of miracles almost the whole world was brought to the faith. Those who deny this, as Augustine says, make a greater miracle of it by removing the miracles. For it is more incredible that so many philosophers and so many wise men believed, without any miracles, a few Apostles, so unlearned, preaching things so incredible to human reason, than that they believed the miracles which are related as performed by them. Therefore the argument for faith drawn from miracles is probable, because faith is often produced by miracles, but rarely without faith. Nor do they necessarily demonstrate the Church, except where the ordinary power of working miracles is present. Bellarminus asserts that a true miracle is a sufficient testimony of the Church; the Jesuit Maldonatus, from the Scriptures and the Fathers, demonstrates the opposite. Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, book 3: It must be observed, he says, that those are said to work miracles who do not hold the truth of the Gospel. I say this against the heretics, who think that their faith is proved by this, if they have done some sign. Augustine, against the Letter of Fundamentum, chapter 4: But if such things happen in the Catholic Church, the Church is not shown to be Catholic because these things happen in her, but these things are to be approved because they happen in the Catholic Church. Chrysostom, homily 49 on Matthew: The working of miracles, he says, is found more among those who are false Christians. Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics, chapter 44: Unless this had been written, that there would come those who perform great virtues to corrupt the truth. Augustine, in the work cited above, chapter 16: The Lord, therefore, he says, has made us wary of these wonder-workers, by saying, "Beware." And Theodoret on Deuteronomy 13: We are taught not to believe when one who performs such things teaches what is contrary to piety.

units.la: Collegium Anglo-Rhem. in Annot. ad Apocal. 17. 9. Protestantes, inquit, extrema malitia excaecati adversus Rom. Ecclesiam usque adeo insaniunt, ut septem montes literaliter interpretentur, ut inde simplicibus persuadeant, Romam esse sedem Antichristi; cum tamen Angelus ipsum exponat verf. 7. septem montes idem esse quod septem capita, et septem Reges. Bellarminus etiam lib. 3. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 13. Nunc respondeo, inquit, cum aliis, per Meretricem, quae sedet super septem montes, non intelligi Romam, sed universam diaboli civitatem, quae vocatur saepe Babylon, et opponitur civitati Dei quae dicitur Hierusalem. Per septem montes intelligi universitatem superborum, et praecipue Regum terrae.
units.tr: The Anglo-Rhemish College, in its Annotations on Revelation 17:9: The Protestants, he says, blinded by extreme malice, rage so far against the Roman Church that they interpret the seven mountains literally, in order to persuade simple people that Rome is the seat of Antichrist; whereas the angel himself explains in verse 7 that the seven mountains are the same as the seven heads and the seven kings. Bellarminus also, book 3 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 13: Now I answer, he says, with others, that by the Harlot who sits on seven mountains is not meant Rome, but the whole city of the devil, which is often called Babylon and is opposed to the city of God, which is called Jerusalem. By the seven mountains is meant the whole company of the proud, and especially the kings of the earth.

units.la: Ribera autem in Apocal. 14. num. 30. Babylonem, inquit, esse Romam, ex textu confirmatur, quia nulli alii convenire potest, quod dicitur septem capita, septem montes sunt: Constat autem Romam super septem montes fundatam esse; de quibus Vergil. Aeneid. 6. Vega quoque cap. 13. sect. 2. Apostolus, inquit, eam (Romam) significat, ut manifestum est ex cap. 17. et 18.
units.tr: Ribera, however, on Revelation 14, number 30: That Babylon is Rome, he says, is confirmed from the text, because what is said of the seven heads, the seven mountains, can apply to no other city. It is certain, however, that Rome was founded upon seven mountains, which Virgil speaks of in the Aeneid, book 6. Vega too, chapter 13, section 2: The Apostle, he says, means by it Rome, as is clear from chapters 17 and 18.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 3. de Pontifice Rom. cap. 13. Denique. Loquitur, inquit, Iohannes de Roma, quae ebria erat sanguine Martyrum, quod certe non habebat locum, nisi in ea Roma, quae, regnantibus Nerone et Domitiano, martyres trucidabat. Collegium Anglo-Rhem. Annot. in Apocal. 17. 5. Patres, inquit, per Babylonem Romam partim terrenam interpretantur, sed ut erat cum jam scripserat Ioannes, et cum Paganis Christianos persequebantur: tantum igitur de Rom. dictum est, ut erat sedes Imperii, quod nunc ad Cathedram Petri accommodare summa est impudentia.
units.tr: Bellarminus, book 3 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 13: Finally. John speaks, he says, of Rome, which was drunk with the blood of the martyrs. This certainly could have no place except in that Rome which, under Nero and Domitian, put the martyrs to death. The Anglo-Rhemish College, Annotations on Revelation 17:5: The Fathers, he says, interpret Babylon partly as earthly Rome, but as it was when John had already written, and when the Christians were being persecuted by the pagans. So what is said of Rome applies only as it was the seat of the empire; to apply it now to the Chair of Peter is the height of impudence.

units.la: Ribera autem Iesuita in Apocal. c. 14. Num. 13. scribit: Cecidit Babylon, id est, ceteritum pro futuro; & nu ydan, urbs illa magna egregie in Romam convenit. Et n. 9.54.53.56. Roma, inquit, in fine seculi futura est Babylon. Ibidem: Divinare me cet quispiam: sed hunc ego oro ut praejudicii deponat, rem totam maturo iudicio examinet, necplus mihi credat, quam ratio aut veritas permiserit. Erat mater abominationum, im saevient Nerone, una die Petrum & Paulum occiderat. Et cap. decimo septimo, stendam tibi damnationem meretricis magnae: Haec, inquit, qui legit, de illis dicta tet, qui Ioannis tempore vixerunt: & est quidem verum hoc, sed de illis quoque cuntur, qui extremo mundi tempore vivent: ubi dicitur, Cum meretrice fornicabun-tur. Et Vega Iesuita cap. 17. Coment. 2. sect. 2. & 3. & cap. 18. Com. 1. sect. 4. Ioannes, inquit, non loquitur de impiorum multitudine sub typo mulieris & Babylonis, quia impeculiaribus suis signis distinguit, ut c. 17. & 18. manifestum est. Appellatur enim Babylon magna illa civitas, & mentio fit septem montium: deinde eversio eius praedicitur. Mercatores, qui in impiorum multitudine comprehenduntur, lugebunt propter tormenta eius; quod necesse est ad extrema tempora ante mundi finem referre. Quare expositionem communem deserere cogimur, & aliam cogitare textui magis congruentem; nimirum urbem Romam intelligi, non solum eam, quae erat tempore Iohannis, sed quae futura est tempore Antichristi, ut ex sequenti capite constat. Rursus ad haec verba, exite ex illa; Cum, inquit, acceptum est fidelibus, ut ex illa exeant, ne simul in eius calamitate involvantur; proba ostenditur, non de Roma illa antiqua, cum nulli adhuc fideles erat, sed de illa quae flobit in extremo mundi tempore.
units.tr: Ribera the Jesuit, however, on Revelation 14, number 13, writes: "Babylon has fallen," that is, the past for the future; and that great city fits Rome admirably. And at numbers 53, 54, 56: Rome, he says, will be Babylon at the end of the age. In the same place: Someone may say I am guessing; but I beg such a person to put aside prejudice, to examine the whole matter with mature judgment, and not to believe me more than reason and truth allow. She was the mother of abominations; when Nero was raging, on one day she had killed Peter and Paul. And on chapter 17: I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot. Whoever reads this, he says, will find these things were said of those who lived in John's time; and this is indeed true, but it is also said of those who will live at the last time of the world, where it is said, "They will commit fornication with the harlot." And the Jesuit Vega, on chapter 17, commentary 2, sections 2 and 3, and on chapter 18, commentary 1, section 4: John, he says, does not speak of the multitude of the impious under the type of a woman and Babylon, because he distinguishes them by his own particular signs, as is clear from chapters 17 and 18. For that great city is called Babylon, and mention is made of the seven mountains; then its overthrow is foretold. The merchants, who are included in the multitude of the impious, will mourn over her torments; which must be referred to the last times, before the end of the world. Therefore we are forced to abandon the common interpretation and to think of another more congruent with the text, namely that the city of Rome is meant, not only the one which existed in John's time, but the one which will exist in the time of Antichrist, as is clear from the following chapter. Again, on these words, "Come out of her": When it is said to the faithful, he says, that they should come out of her, lest they be involved together in her calamity, it is shown that this does not concern that ancient Rome, since there were as yet no faithful in it, but the one which will flourish at the last time of the world.

units.la: Costerus in Apolog. part. 3. cap. 2. pag. 39. Erras, inquit, haeretice: Antichristus neque de Ecclesia futurus est, neque in Ecclesia, neque in templis nostris, ut Patres docent, ex tribu Dan oriundus sedebit Hierosolymis. Bellarminus lib. 3. de Pontif. Rom. 13. f. At nihilominus Antichristi, inquit, sedem fore Hierusalem, non Romam, vera sima est sententia.
units.tr: Costerus in his Apology, part 3, chapter 2, page 39: You are wrong, heretic: Antichrist will be neither from the Church, nor in the Church, nor in our temples; as the Fathers teach, he will sit at Jerusalem, born of the tribe of Dan. Bellarminus, book 3 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 13: Nevertheless, he says, that the seat of Antichrist will be Jerusalem, not Rome, is the true opinion.

units.la: Collegium Anglo-Rhem. autem in Apocal. 17. Roma, inquit, ante finem mundi futura est sedes Antichristi. Ribera in Apocal. 14. Officina, inquit, est omnis idolatriae. Vega in Apocal. 18. Coment. 1. f. 4. Habitatio, inquit, erit daemoniorum, & fide Christi defectura.
units.tr: The Anglo-Rhemish College, however, on Revelation 17: Rome, he says, before the end of the world will be the seat of Antichrist. Ribera, on Revelation 14: She is the workshop of all idolatry. Vega, on Revelation 18, commentary 1, page 4: She will be the habitation of demons, and will fail in the faith of Christ.

units.la: Ad dictum Augustini: Ego Evangelio non crederem, nisi, &c. lib. contra Epistolam fundamenti c. 5. Stapletonus lib. 2. de auctoritate Script. c. Respondet, inquit, Protestantes, hoc Augustinum dixisse, cum adhuc erat Manichaeus, nimirum eum Ecclesiae authoritate tunc fuisse commotum, ut Evangelio crederet, ut esset Catholicus. At tamen eidem Augustino jam facto Catholico, ut Scripturis non crederet, ut potius Ecclesiam desereret, quam Evangelio non crederet: ergo majoris apud Augustinum momenti esse Scripturarum quam Ecclesiae authoritatem. Falsum autem omnino: nam sensus Quod ad me attinet; nisi me jam Catholicae Ecclesiae authoritas commoveret, nec nunc quidem Evangelio crederem. Itaque frigida est omnino isthaec Protestantium solutio, qui hunc sensum ponunt de praeterito, Ego nunc non essem Christianus, nisi me commovissent suis persuasionibus Christiani, quia de praesenti omnino agit Augustinus. Ioco etiam respondent Iesuitae Posnanienses, Costerus, Turrianus, Valentia us, Gretserus & alii.
units.tr: On the saying of Augustine: I would not believe the Gospel, unless, etc., from the book against the Letter of Fundamentum, chapter 5. Stapleton, book 2 On the Authority of Scripture, chapter: He replies to the Protestants, he says, that Augustine said this when he was still a Manichaean, namely that he was then moved by the authority of the Church to believe the Gospel, so that he might be a Catholic. But yet the same Augustine, now made a Catholic, would not believe the Scriptures, but would rather desert the Church than not believe the Gospel. Therefore the authority of the Scriptures was of greater weight with Augustine than the authority of the Church. This is altogether false, however: for the sense is: As far as I am concerned, if the authority of the Catholic Church had not already moved me, I would not now believe the Gospel either. Therefore that Protestant solution is altogether cold, which takes this sense as referring to the past: "I would not now be a Christian, unless Christians had moved me by their persuasions," since Augustine is speaking altogether of the present. The Jesuits of Posen, Costerus, Turrianus, Valentia, Gretser and others also answer this with jokes.

units.la: Melchior Canus autem in Loc. Theol. lib. 2. cap. 8. Augustino, inquit, negotium erat cum Manichaeis, qui absque controversia suo cuidam Evangelio credi volebant. Roit Augustinus, ecquid facturi sint, si in hominem incidant, qui ne quidem Evangelio credunt, quo genere persuasionis sint eum in suam sententiam adducturi? Certe se affirmat, non liter potuisse (praeterito tempore) adduci quam Ecclesiae authoritate victum. Non ita docet, in Ecclesiae authoritate fundatam esse Evangelii fidem. Agit enim Augustinus, quomodo infideles ad credendum adducantur. Et Driedo de variis dogmat. lib. 4. c. 4.
units.tr: Melchior Canus, however, in Loc. Theol. lib. 2. cap. 8.: Augustine, he says, had to deal with the Manichaeans, who without any dispute wanted to be believed on the strength of their own Gospel. Augustine asks what they would do if they fell in with a man who does not even believe the Gospel, and by what kind of persuasion they would bring him to their opinion. Certainly he affirms that he could not have been brought otherwise (in the past tense) than overcome by the authority of the Church. He does not teach that the faith in the Gospel is founded on the authority of the Church. For Augustine is dealing with how unbelievers are brought to believe. And Driedo, de variis dogmat. lib. 4. c. 4.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: Of Doctrine

units.la: Loquitur, inquit, Augustinus de Ecclesia illa, quae fuit ab initio fidei Christianae: (Ergo non de sola Romana, sed etiam de primitiva. Gerson de vita animae, Augustinus inquit, Ecclesiam ibi sumit pro Ecclesia primitiva fidelium, qui Christum viderunt, & audierunt, & eius testes exstiterunt.
units.tr: He speaks, they say, of that Church which existed from the beginning of the Christian faith. (Therefore not of the Roman Church alone, but also of the primitive one.) Gerson, in his work on the life of the soul: Augustine, he says, there takes "the Church" to mean the primitive Church of believers, who saw Christ, heard him, and were his witnesses.

units.la: MVLTI IESVITARVM SIBIIPSIS IN SCRIPTIS SVIS SAEPE CONTRA- DICVNT
units.tr: MANY JESUITS OFTEN CONTRADICT THEMSELVES IN THEIR OWN WRITINGS

units.la: Costerus in Enchiridio pag. 45. docet, Non omnia, quae ad fidem pertinent, explicite sacris literis expressa esse, quae non obid datae sint, ut formulam exactam fidei prae scribant. pag. 49. autem contradicit, Praecipua illa fidei capita, quae omnibus Christianis cognitu necessaria sint, perspicue solis Apostolicis literis comprehensa esse.
units.tr: Costerus, in his Enchiridion, p. 45, teaches that not everything that pertains to faith is expressly set down in the sacred letters, since they were not given in order to prescribe an exact formula of faith. But on p. 49 he contradicts this, holding that the chief articles of faith, which all Christians must know, are plainly contained in the Apostolic writings alone.

units.la: Item pag. 44. vocavit sacram Scripturam membranam & chartaceam, ac literam mortuam: Pag. 47. sic autem extollit, ut nullum iota, apicem nullum in illis agnoscat, cui non inest suum pondus & efficacitas: unde tanquam divina eloquia, mentem hominis, admirabili dulcedine & suavitate afficiant.
units.tr: Likewise, on p. 44 he called Holy Scripture parchment and paper, and a dead letter. Yet on p. 47 he exalts it so highly that he acknowledges no iota or tittle in it that does not have its own weight and efficacy, so that, as divine utterances, they move the mind of man with wonderful sweetness and delight.

units.la: Bellarminus in libris de iustificatione affirmat, quod propter incertitudinem propriae Iustitiae, & periculum inanis gloriae, tutissimum sit fiduciam totam in sola Dei misericordia & benignitate reponere. Haec autem eius assertio e regione contraria est toti tractationi, & quinque illorum de Iustificatione librorum instituto: in quibus tamen libris recitata verba reperiuntur.
units.tr: In his books on justification, Bellarmine asserts that, because of the uncertainty of one's own righteousness and the danger of vainglory, it is safest to place all trust solely in the mercy and kindness of God. But this assertion of his is directly opposed to the whole treatment and purpose of those five books on justification, although the words quoted are found in those very books.

units.la: Costerus in Enchiridio pag. 260. sic scribit: Nulla omnino creaturae opera, nullae poenitentiae, nullae martyria, nullae poenae, nulla virtus potest mereri cuiquam peccatori, remissionem peccatorum suorum. Peccatum enim, quod ex infinita Majestate Dei offensi infinitam malitiam contraxit; non nisi per infinitum meritum potest deleri, quod infinitum meritum in solis Christi operibus & perpessionibus ob infinitam divinae personae dignitatem cernitur; non autem in ulla actione aut merito creaturae. Quod hic soli Christo tribuit Iesuita, omnibus creaturis exclusis, nobis quoque nostrisque operibus eorumque merito paulo ante tribuerat. Sic enim pag. 259. Utitur quoque Deum instrumentis, quae ad efficientem causam aliquo modo revocantur, sicut etiam merita, ut aliquid concedatur vel fiat promeremur. In his manifestissima contradictio est: nulla merita, excepto Christi merito, iustificant: Et, quaedam merita, quibus aliquid promeremur, iustificant.
units.tr: Costerus, in his Enchiridion, p. 260, writes thus: "No works of any creature, no penances, no martyrdoms, no punishments, no virtue can merit for any sinner the forgiveness of his sins. For sin, which by offending the infinite Majesty of God has contracted an infinite malice, can be blotted out only by an infinite merit; and such infinite merit is found only in the works and sufferings of Christ, because of the infinite dignity of the divine person, and not in any action or merit of a creature." Here the Jesuit ascribes this to Christ alone, excluding all creatures; yet a little before he had ascribed it to us and our works and their merit. For on p. 259 he says: "We also use as instruments those things which are in some way reduced to the efficient cause, just as merits too, so that we merit something to be granted or done." In these statements there is a plain contradiction: no merits, apart from the merit of Christ, justify; and certain merits, by which we merit something, do justify.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Sanctorum beat. cap. 2. & 20. sic scribit. Hunc errorem Calvinus pertinaciter defendit; negans animas Sanctorum recta ad Deum ire, sed ad inferos, vel alium locum extra coelum.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 4 of On the Blessedness of the Saints, chapters 2 and 20, writes thus: "Calvin stubbornly defends this error, denying that the souls of the saints go straight to God, but say that they go to hell or to some other place outside heaven."

units.la: Contra vero Bellarminus lib. 4. de Christo cap. 18. Tertio Calvinus, inquit: Locat Calvinus Sanctorum animas in coelo etiam ante Christi adventum. Si ante Christi adventum, etiam ante Christi resurrectionem: Si in coelo, ergo non extra coelum. Si locat Sanctorum animas in coelo, ergo non spe, sed re ipsa.
units.tr: On the contrary, Bellarmine in book 4 of On Christ, chapter 18: "Thirdly, Calvin, he says, places the souls of the saints in heaven even before the coming of Christ. If before the coming of Christ, then also before Christ's resurrection; if in heaven, then not outside heaven; if he places the souls of the saints in heaven, then it is so not in hope but in fact."

units.la: Bellarminus in toto libro primo de Pontifice Rom. pro Petri primatu acriter pugnat, eumque omnibus defendere modis conatur.
units.tr: In the whole first book On the Roman Pontiff, Bellarmine fights fiercely for the primacy of Peter, and strives to defend it by every means.

units.la: Capite 9. autem col. 638. apertissime dicit; Summam potestatem omnibus Apostolis libertatemque datam esse. Hoc vero cum unius Principatu pugnat. Si enim omnes Apostoli summa potestate erant praepositi; nihil Petrus supra reliquos Apostolos habere potuit, nisi summo superius forsan aliquid fuerit: Et summum non est, supra quod positum quicquam erit. Et in summa aequalitate primatus nullus cogitari potest. Respondet eodem loco Bellarminus, Summam hanc potestatem datam esse Petro & ordinario Pastori, aliis vero Apostolis ut delegatis: Atque hac nova distinctione fretus, & summos omnes Apostolos fuisse; & Petrum tamen aliquid iquid superius reliquis habuisse affirmat: sed & hoc aperte pugnat cum eo, quod omnib. data esse summam potestatem dixit: estque in hoc responso manifesta contradictio. Nam si inter Apostolos summa potestas fuit, non igitur Petri delegati reliqui fuerunt: quia potestas delegati non potest esse tanta per omnia, quanta eius qui delegavit. Bellarm. autem fecit potestatem omnibus parem, id est, summam: at delegata potestas summa nunquam est.
units.tr: But in chapter 9, at col. 638, he says most openly that supreme power and liberty were given to all the Apostles. This, however, is inconsistent with the principate of one man. For if all the Apostles were set over with supreme power, Peter could have had nothing above the rest of the Apostles, unless perhaps something higher than the supreme; and nothing that is placed above the supreme can exist. Nor can any primacy be conceived in perfect equality. In the same place Bellarmine replies that this supreme power was given to Peter and to the ordinary pastor, but to the other Apostles as delegates; and relying on this new distinction, he asserts both that all the Apostles were supreme and that Peter nevertheless had something above the rest. But this too clearly conflicts with what he said, that supreme power was given to all; and in this reply there is a manifest contradiction. For if supreme power belonged to the Apostles, then the rest were not delegates of Peter, since the power of a delegate cannot be in every respect as great as that of the one who delegates. Yet Bellarmine makes the power equal for all, that is, supreme; but delegated power is never supreme.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 4. de Pontifice Romano capit. 2. in explicando statu quaestionis huius, duo esse dicit, in quibus non haeretici modo, sed & Catholici omnes conveniant, Primum, posse Pontificem, etiam ut Pontificem, & cum suo coetu filiariorum, vel cum Generali concilio errare in controversijs fidei particularibus, & ex informatione testimoniisque hominum praecipue pendent. Secundum, Papam posse, ut privatum Doctorem, errare, etiam in quaestionibus juris universalibus, in fidei, quam morum. Hoc vero Bellarminus eodem libro cap. 6. tolli, propositione 4. quaefic habet: Probabile est, pieque credi posse, summum Pontificem, non solum Pontificem errare non posse, sed etiam ut particularem personam haereticum esse non posse, falsum aliquid contra fidem pertinaciter credendo.
units.tr: In book 4 of On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 2, in explaining the state of this question, Bellarmine says there are two points on which not only heretics but all Catholics agree: "First, that the Pope, even as Pope, and together with his college of cardinals, or with a general council, can err in particular controversies of faith, depending chiefly on the information and testimony of men. Second, that the Pope, as a private teacher, can err, even in universal questions of law, of faith as well as of morals." But Bellarmine, in the same book, chapter 6, proposition 4, removes this, where he states: "It is probable, and it can piously be believed, that the supreme Pontiff not only cannot err as Pontiff, but cannot even be a heretic as a particular person, by pertinaciously believing something false against the faith."

units.la: Talis est Bellarminus in aliis quoque doctrinae capitibus. Nam de Amissione gratiae & statu peccati lib. secundo, cap. 13. dicit: Deus non inclinat hominem ad malum, neque physice, neque moraliter. Mox autem sui oblitus contrarium affirmat ibidem paulo post inquiens: Deus inclinat quidem ad malum, non physice, sed tamen moraliter.
units.tr: Bellarmine is like this in other heads of doctrine too. For in book 2 of On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, chapter 13, he says: "God does not incline man to evil, neither physically nor morally." Then, forgetting himself, he soon afterwards asserts the contrary, saying a little later in the same place: "God indeed inclines to evil, not physically, but nevertheless morally."

units.la: In lib. 1. de Clericis c. 14. inquit, Episcopos Apostolis succedere, Presbyteros autem discipulis. Contrarium autem affirmat lib. 4. de Pontif. Rom. c. 25. dicens, Episcopi non proprie succedunt Apostolis.
units.tr: In book 1 On the Clergy, chapter 14, he says: "Bishops succeed the Apostles, and presbyters succeed the disciples." But in book 4 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 25, he asserts the contrary, saying: "Bishops do not properly succeed the Apostles."

units.la: Lib. 1. de Pontif. c. 12. inquit: Judas non credidit. Contradicit autem de Iustificatione lib. 3. c. 14. inquiens: Judas justus fuit, & certe bonus.
units.tr: Book 1 On the Pope, chapter 12, says: "Judas did not believe." But in On Justification, book 3, chapter 14, he contradicts this, saying: "Judas was righteous, and certainly good."

units.la: Alio in loco dicit: Observatio Legis substantiam operis requirit, ut sic praeceptum servetur, ut peccatum non committatur, & non fiat homo reus ob praeceptum non impletum: Gratia & libero arbitrio libro 5. capit. 5. Contra vero ibid. capit. 9. Sciendum, ait, non esse omnino idem, facere bonum morale, & observare praeceptum secundum substantiam operis: potest enim servari praeceptum secundum substantiam operis, etiam in peccato.
units.tr: In another place he says: "Observance of the Law requires the substance of the work, so that the precept is kept in such a way that sin is not committed, and a man does not become guilty for a precept not fulfilled." (On Grace and Free Will, book 5, chapter 5.) On the contrary, in the same book, chapter 9: "It must be known," he says, "that it is not altogether the same thing to do a moral good and to observe a precept according to the substance of the work; for a precept can be observed according to the substance of the work even in sin."

units.la: De Pontifice Romano lib. 4. capit. 3. dicit, Petrus non amisit eam fidem, qua creditur ad justitiam: De Iustificatione autem libro 3. capit. 14. ait, Petri peccatum fuit lethale.
units.tr: In On the Roman Pontiff, book 4, chapter 3, he says: "Peter did not lose that faith by which one believes unto righteousness." But in On Justification, book 3, chapter 14, he says: "Peter's sin was mortal."

units.la: De Rom. Pontifice lib. 3. c. 14. Antichristus, inquit, Magus futurus est, & more Magorum Magorum occulte diabolum ipsum adoraturus. At contra ex sententia Hippolyti & Cyrilli, & c. 12. eiusdem libri, Abhorrebit, inquit, ab idololatria, execrabitur & pugnabit idola, deinde templum denuo aedificabit.
units.tr: In On the Roman Pontiff, book 3, chapter 14: "Antichrist, he says, will be a magician, and in the manner of magicians he will secretly worship the devil himself." But on the contrary, according to the judgment of Hippolytus and Cyril, and in chapter 12 of the same book: "He will abhor idolatry, will execrate and fight against idols, and then will build the temple anew."

units.la: Rursus Bellarminus de Missa libro primo, capit. 27. Verbis consecrationis & solennis oblatio celebratur. Contra de Missa libro 2. capit. 11. Sacrificij oblatio magis in re, quam in verbis consistit, & illa actio, qua corpus Domini super altare ponitur, vera & realis oblatio est.
units.tr: Again, Bellarmine in On the Mass, book 1, chapter 27: "The sacrifice of oblation is celebrated by the words of consecration and the solemn offering." On the contrary, in On the Mass, book 2, chapter 11: "The offering of the sacrifice consists more in the thing than in the words, and that action by which the body of the Lord is placed upon the altar is a true and real oblation."

units.la: In lib. de Christi anima 4. cap. 5. ait, Mundi finis non potest sciri. Contra, de Pontif. lib. 3. c. 17. Post Antichristi mortem non futuri sunt nisi 45. dies usque ad finem mundi.
units.tr: In On the Soul of Christ, book 4, chapter 5, he says: "The end of the world cannot be known." On the contrary, in On the Pope, book 3, chapter 17: "After the death of Antichrist there will remain only forty-five days until the end of the world."

units.la: Libro 3. de Pontifice Romano cap. 13. Decem Reges comburent purpuream meretricem. Contra ibidem, Antichristus Romam odio habebit, & pugnabit contra eam, & comburet.
units.tr: In On the Roman Pontiff, book 3, chapter 13: "Ten kings will burn the purple harlot." On the contrary, in the same place: "Antichrist will hate Rome, will fight against her, and will burn her."

units.la: · De Pontifice Romano lib. 2. capit. 31. Duobus modis intelligi potest nomen universalis Episcopi: uno modo, ut ille qui dicitur universalis, intelligatur esse solus Episcopus omnium urbium Christianarum, ita ut ceteri non sint Episcopi, sed Vicarij tantum illius, qui dicitur Universalis Episcopus: quo sensu Papa NON est Universalis Episcopus. Contrà de Pont. Rom. lib. 4. c. 24. Omnis ordinaria jurisdictio Episcoporum descendit immediatè à Papa, & est in eo, & ab eo in alios derivatur.
units.tr: In On the Roman Pontiff, book 2, chapter 31: "The name of universal bishop can be understood in two ways: in one way, so that he who is called universal is understood to be the sole bishop of all Christian cities, so that the rest are not bishops but only his vicars; in which sense the Pope is NOT universal bishop." On the contrary, in On the Roman Pontiff, book 4, chapter 24: "All ordinary jurisdiction of bishops descends immediately from the Pope, and is in him, and is derived from him to the others."

units.la: Et quod peculiariter ad Bellarminum, eiusque consuetudinem attinet, hoc in lectione scriptorum eius, cum multis aliis observavi, eum, quotiescunque graviori aliquâ objectione premitur, quæ ipsum vellicet & pungat, nihil moratur, nec meminisse, utrum argumenti solutio, doctrinæ suæ alibi traditæ sit contraria, dummodo ei pro tempore inserviat, & effugio esse possit, quo præsentem procellam declinet.
units.tr: And as for Bellarmine in particular and his habit, I have observed this in reading his writings, along with many others: whenever he is pressed by some weightier objection that galls and stings him, he takes no trouble, nor does he remember whether his solution to the argument contradicts the doctrine he has taught elsewhere, provided it serves him for the moment and can be a way of escape by which he may dodge the present storm.

units.la: DE CALVMNIIS IESVITARVM, SEV INSONTIVM MALITIOSA AC MENDA- CI INFAMATIONE.
units.tr: On the Calumnies of the Jesuits, or the Malicious and Lying Defamation of the Innocent.

units.la: IN bello civili ultimo Regni Galliæ, Iesuitæ sparserunt rumorem, Huguenottos, quos sic in Gallia vocant, in necem Caroli IX. Regis, duorum eius fratrum ac Reginæ matris conspirâsse, & hanc veri simam lanienæ Parisiensis anno 1572. occasione & causam fuisse: maluisse enim eos prævenire quàm prævenīri. Sic enim Crefuuellus in suo Philopatre contra Edictum Elisabethæ Reginæ, pag. 119. Regina, inquit, Angliæ conscia fuit illius conjurationis, quæ anno 72. in nuptijs Regis Navarrei executioni mandari debebat: de qua scribit Genebrardus his verbis: Regis Navarræ nuptias excepit dies Bartholomæanus, ob quandam in Catholicos Principes conjurationem.
units.tr: In the last civil war in the kingdom of France, the Jesuits spread the rumour that the Huguenots, as they are called in France, had conspired against the life of King Charles IX, his two brothers, and the queen mother, and that this was the occasion and cause of the truly savage slaughter at Paris in 1572, because they preferred to strike first rather than be struck. Thus Crefuellus, in his Philopater, against the edict of Queen Elizabeth, p. 119: "The Queen of England," he says, "was privy to that conspiracy which was to be carried out in the year 72 at the wedding of the King of Navarre. Of this Genebrardus writes in these words: 'The wedding of the King of Navarre was followed by St Bartholomew's Day, because of a certain conspiracy against the Catholic princes.'"

units.la: Franciscus Costerus Iesuita, de eodem in Sica Tragica capit. 7. pag. 60. sic scribit: Anno 72. Catholici multos in Gallia Calvinistas, jussu Regis, quos ille cognoverat de sua caterorumque Catholicorum cædè cogitâsse, idque certo die, quam præfinierat, necarunt. Idem Costerus in Sica cap. 11. pag. 107. Conscivit Rex, inquit, Anno 1572. conscelerato consilio conclusum fuisse ab Huguenotis, ut conditio die, tempore quarundam nuptiarum, se cum tota progenie, omnibus Catholicis, interneccione confatali delerent. Huic Calvinianorum horrendo sceleri, & Regis Christianissimi, patriæque parricidio, obviam itum est: & qui ferrum alteri acuerant, suis illud jugulis excepere. Hæc sunt testatissima, & in luce omnium gentium.
units.tr: Francisco Costerus, a Jesuit, writes on the same matter in his Sica Tragica, chap. 7, p. 60: "In the year 72 the Catholics in France, by the king's command, killed many Calvinists whom he knew to have plotted the slaughter of himself and the other Catholics, and this on the day he had appointed." The same Costerus, in the Sica, chap. 11, p. 107: "The king learned," he says, "that in the year 1572 the Huguenots had concluded by a criminal plot that on a certain day, at the time of a certain wedding, they would destroy with fatal slaughter both himself and his whole family, and all the Catholics. Against this horrible crime of the Calvinists, and this parricide of the most Christian king and of his country, they were forestalled; and those who had sharpened the sword for others received it at their own throats. These things are most fully attested and known to all nations."

units.la: Causa autem lanienæ huius omnibus tam nota est, ut omnes Pontificios tam de fidelibus Gallis, præter solos Iesuitas, scribere, hactenus puduerit. Ribadeneira certè, etsi lib. 1. de Principe cap. 27. multa mendaciter scripserit de infinitis ab Huguenotis vitæ Catholicorum structis, huius tamen coniurationis nec uno quidem verbo meminit. Et Iacobus Aug. Thuanus in sua Historia, Tomo 2. part. 2. pag. 842. præsertim pag. 846. aliam, & quidem veram huius inauditæ lanienæ causam commemorat, videlicet, Ut sub specie arctioris amicitiæ, & quidem nuptiarum Huguenoti Lutetiam, tanquam aves in cafes pelliierentur & simul omnes opprimerentur.
units.tr: The cause of this slaughter is so well known to all that the Papists, apart from the Jesuits alone, have hitherto been ashamed to write about it among the faithful of France. Ribadeneira, indeed, although in book 1, On the Prince, chap. 27, he wrote many lies about the countless plots of the Huguenots against the lives of Catholics, yet does not mention this conspiracy even in a single word. And James Augustus Thuanus, in his History, vol. 2, part 2, p. 842, and especially p. 846, records another and indeed the true cause of this unheard-of slaughter, namely, "that under the guise of a closer friendship, and indeed of a marriage, the Huguenots might be enticed to Paris like birds into snares, and all be destroyed together."

units.la: Cum etiam Iesuitæ intelligerent, se sub Regina Elizabetha, suamque doctrinam de Regicidijs, omnibus bonis in Anglia exosos esse, Apologiam ediderunt, in qua inter alia probare conantur, Regicidium & Regnicidium non a sua doctrina placitisque promanare, sed figmentum & technam solummodo esse pōlitiæ nostræ; ut sic Papismus contemptui & despicatui foret. Hoc etiam testantur Acta Henrici Garneti & Sociorum eius pag. 64. Supra etiam indicavimus quibus quantisq; medacijs & calumnijs Serenissi‑ am Angliae Reginam obruerint & lacerarint Iesuitae.
units.tr: Since the Jesuits also understood that under Queen Elizabeth they and their doctrine of regicide were hated by all good people in England, they published an apology, in which among other things they try to prove that regicide and the murder of kings do not spring from their doctrine and opinions, but are merely the invention and trickery of our polemic, so that Popery might be held in contempt and scorn. The Acts of Henry Garnet and his Associates, p. 64, also bears witness to this. Above we have also shown with how many and how great lies and calumnies the Jesuits have overwhelmed and torn apart the most serene Queen of England.

units.la: Fulminalis quoq; pulveris molitiones contra Regem Angliae & regiam stir‑ em, regnicq; totius proceres, Iesuitae Coloniefes a Calvinianis, nec ab ullo Ca‑ tolico excogitatas esse, impudentissime calumniati sunt.
units.tr: The Jesuits of Cologne have also most shamelessly slandered the Calvinists, and not any Catholic, by alleging that the plots of gunpowder against the King of England, the royal house, and all the nobles of the kingdom were devised by them.

units.la: Anno 1597. rumorem sparserum Iesuitae, qui fere per totam Europam per‑sit, de Clarissimi viri Theodori Bezae, Pastoris Genevensis Ecclesiae, morte, & constanter affirmarunt, quod paulo ante mortem omnem doctrinam suam re‑ tarit, & confessus sit, se Romanae Ecclesiae doctrinam pro vera agnoscere, que in ea mori velle. Auctor huius commenti ferebatur Clemens Puteanus, Iesuita Parisiensis. Mendacium autem illud impudentissimum Pastores Ge‑nevenses refutarunt, editis nomine suo publicis duobus scriptis, altero Latine (cui Beza Redivivus nomen fecerunt) altero Gallice. Beza quoque ipse Epistola ad Guilielmum Stuckium Theologum Tigurinum vanitatem ill‑ am redarguit.
units.tr: In the year 1597 the Jesuits spread a rumour, which ran through almost the whole of Europe, about the death of the most illustrious man Theodore Beza, minister of the church of Geneva, and they steadfastly affirmed that shortly before his death he recanted all his doctrine, and confessed that he acknowledged the doctrine of the Roman Church as true, and wished to die in it. The author of this fiction was said to be Clement Puteanus, a Jesuit of Paris. The ministers of Geneva refuted that most shameless lie, publishing in their own name two public writings, one in Latin (which they called Beza Redivivus) and one in French. Beza himself also, in a letter to Wilhelm Stuck, a theologian of Zurich, refuted that falsehood.

units.la: Anno Domini 1605. editae sunt Theses a Iesuitis Monasteriensibus hoc ti‑tulo: Credo Calvinisequarum, plenae prodigiosarum Calumniarum ac menda‑ciorum de Calvinianis. Thesi octava hoc Corollarium plane blasphemum & ad‑horrendum afferunt: Articulum primum Calviniani symboli hunc esse: Credo in diabolum, Carnificem, Orcipotentem, Corruptorem coeli & terrae. Ibidem asse‑runt, Calvinianos simpliciter & generatim docere, Non patientia & permissione, sed po‑tentia & operatione Dei, peccata fieri.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 1605 theses were published by the Jesuits of Münster under this title: Credo Calvinisequarum, full of monstrous calumnies and lies about the Calvinists. In the eighth thesis they add this corollary, plainly blasphemous and horrible: that the first article of the Calvinist creed is this: "I believe in the devil, the Hangman, the Omnipotent Corrupter of heaven and earth." In the same place they assert that "the Calvinists teach simply and generally that sins are done not by the patience and permission of God, but by the power and operation of God."

units.la: Thesi 9. dicunt, Calvinianos prohibere caput aperire; aut genua flectere ad mentionem Domini Iesu, adeoq; honorem etiam politicum ei derogare.
units.tr: In the ninth thesis they say that "the Calvinists forbid uncovering the head or bending the knee at the mention of the Lord Jesus, and so detract from him even political honour."

units.la: Thesi 14. dicunt, Calvinigenas in Anglia, &c. negare Christum verum esse Deum: sed tantum nudum hominem & Philosophum, datum humano generi, ut sit rectum vivendi templum.
units.tr: In the fourteenth thesis they say that "the Calvinists in England, etc., deny that Christ is true God, but hold him to be only a bare man and philosopher, given to the human race so that he might be a right temple of living."

units.la: Thesi 15. afferunt, Calvinianos docere, Christum natum ex Maria non Virgine.
units.tr: In the fifteenth thesis they allege that "the Calvinists teach that Christ was born of Mary, not a virgin."

units.la: Thesi 17. aiunt, Turcas de tertio articulo Fidei Christianae, multo sanius sentire quam Calvinistas.
units.tr: In the seventeenth thesis they say that "the Turks think much more soundly than the Calvinists about the third article of the Christian faith."

units.la: Iesuitae Coloniensis in Censura sua pagina 176. audacter affirmant, pri‑vatim ac publice coram populo, Evangelicos Doctores sua doctrina frena ad omnem impietatem laxare, & facultatem flagitiosis hominibus facere, quaevis etiam scelera (quo ures in suam sententiam pertrahant) committendi. Ad hanc calumniam dico, quod Cicero pro Cluentio dixit, Magnum & impudens est hoc mendacium. Quam serio ea‑dem in nostris Ecclesijs surgeantur ad vere bona opera quotidianae conciones, co‑am toto mundo testantur.
units.tr: The Jesuit of Cologne, in his Censure, page 176, boldly affirms that both privately and publicly before the people, "the Evangelical teachers by their doctrine loosen the reins to all impiety, and give wicked men the liberty to commit any crimes whatever, so that they may draw others into their opinion." To this calumny I say what Cicero said in defence of Cluentius: "This is a great and shameless lie." How earnestly the daily sermons in our churches urge the truly good works, the whole world bears witness.

units.la: Thomas Bozius Eugubinus lib. 12. de signis Eccles. cap. 12. per summam ca‑lumniam Evangelicis Doctoribus bonarum artium ignorantiam objicere au‑ent; alij dicunt, non esse inter Praedicantes, qui solida imbuti sint artium & scien‑tiarum doctrina, ut eos apud Principes, nobiles & ignobiles in contemptu addu‑cant: E contra solis Iesuitis attribuunt literarum cognitionem, linguarum multiplicium studia humaniorum disciplinarum profesionem, & Schola‑rum frequentiam.
units.tr: Thomas Bozius of Gubbio, in book 12 of On the Signs of the Church, chap. 12, dares with the greatest calumny to charge the Evangelical teachers with ignorance of the liberal arts. Others say that among the preachers there is none imbued with a solid doctrine of the arts and sciences, so that they may bring them into contempt with princes, nobles and commoners alike. On the contrary, they attribute knowledge of letters, the study of many languages, the pursuit of the humane disciplines, and a crowd of scholars to the Jesuits alone.

units.la: Imo criminati sunt & calumnijs obruerunt suae quoque religionis socios Doctores, utpote quorum doctrina venalis esset, quorum Scholae nulli nisi mercede paterent, & interdum doctrina peregrina personarent. Mirum quantum haec criminatio & calumnia valuerit, quantasque Papae & Iesuitis uti‑litatem attulerit.
units.tr: Indeed they have accused and overwhelmed with calumnies even the teachers of their own religion, as if their doctrine were for sale, their schools open to none except for pay, and as if they sometimes sounded of foreign doctrine. It is remarkable how much this accusation and calumny has prevailed, and how much advantage it has brought to the Pope and the Jesuits.

units.la: Et ut summatim dicam, Iesuitae in suis scriptis & concionibus nihil fere aliud Sf agunt, quàm ut omnis generis calumniis & crassimis mendacijs Evangelicos praegravent, cosque haereticos, seditionis, rebellionis, conspirationis, & aliorum nefariorum scelerum insimulent, sicq; illos, ut Pharisaei Christum, in odium magistratuum adducant.
units.tr: And, to sum up briefly, the Jesuits in their writings and sermons scarcely do anything else than overwhelm the Evangelicals with every kind of calumny and the crassest lies, accuse them of heresy, sedition, rebellion, conspiracy, and other wicked crimes, and so, like the Pharisees with Christ, bring them into hatred with the magistrates.

units.la: IESVITAE MVLTA IN EVANGELICIS R- EPREHENDVNT, QVAE IPSIMET FACIVNT ET IN PRINCIPIBVS CATHOLICIS LAVDANT.
units.tr: THE JESUITS REPROACH EVANGELICALS FOR MANY THINGS THAT THEY THEMSELVES DO AND PRAISE IN CATHOLIC PRINCES.

units.la: CRefuuelus in suo Philopatre contra Edictum Elizabethae Reginae Angliae pag. 74. scribit, Iniquissimam esse regulam, quae in Anglia vivendi locum Iesuitis negat: cum tamen ipsis sub Turcis, sub Mauris, sub Persis, sub AEthiopibus vivendi locum permittatur. Et in Apologia Alani contra duo Edicta Elizabethae Reginae pag. 21. & 22. In Regnis inquiunt, & Provincijs Turco Persaque subiectis, Catholici liberè suâ religione uti permittuntur. Sed & in Germania, Helvetia, Suecia, Polonia, Boemia nullus Catholicorum compellitur ad alterius religionis professionem, at solis Catholicis in Anglia negatur religionis libertas. Dicas autem Alane, quae liberas Evangelicis in Stiria, Carinthia, Carniola, aliisque Provincijs & urbibus concedatur, in quibus Iesuitae dominantur. Nulla prorsus, sed in exilium crudelissimè pelluntur. Et hoc aeterno encomio dignum esse dicit, Iacobus Sylvanus in sua Philippica. Item, Secessistis à nobis in fide: & cur non etiam à nobis abiretis in terras AEthiopum Sole calentes? Ribadeneira quoque de Rege lib. 1. c. 18. pag. 117. Principibus, ait, & magistratibus sub gravi poena praeceptum esse in Concilio Lateranensi sub Innocentio III. Ut finibus suis haereticos exturbarent: idque iurejurando facturos se promitterent. Sic etiam olim in Hispania lege cautum fuisse, Symmancha dicit de Catholic. Institut. c. 46. n. 55.
units.tr: Crefuuelus, in his Philopater against the Edict of Queen Elizabeth of England, p. 74, writes: It is a most unjust rule that denies the Jesuits a place to live in England, when yet they are permitted a place to live under the Turks, under the Moors, under the Persians, under the Ethiopians. And in Alan's Apology against the two Edicts of Queen Elizabeth, pp. 21 and 22: In the kingdoms and provinces subject to the Turk and the Persian, Catholics are freely permitted to use their religion. But also in Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Poland and Bohemia no Catholic is compelled to profess another religion, whereas only in England is freedom of religion denied to Catholics alone. But you may say, Alan, what freedom is granted to Evangelicals in Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and other provinces and cities where the Jesuits hold sway? None at all; they are cruelly driven into exile. And this, he says, is worthy of eternal praise, according to Jacobus Sylvanus in his Philippic. Likewise: you have departed from us in faith; so why do you not also depart from us into the lands of the Ethiopians, scorched by the sun? Ribadeneira too, in his De Rege, book 1, ch. 18, p. 117: Princes and magistrates, he says, were commanded under severe penalty by the Lateran Council under Innocent III to drive heretics out of their lands, and to promise under oath that they would do so. Symmancha says that in the same way it was formerly provided by law in Spain, in De Catholica Institutione, ch. 46, n. 55.

units.la: IESVITAE TEMPORIBVS SESE AC- COMMODANT. <bl>Hencken den Mantel nach dem Wind.</bl>
units.tr: THE JESUITS ADAPT THEMSELVES TO THE TIMES. Hang the cloak according to the wind.

units.la: POssumus hoc loco commodissime uti verbis Costeri Iesuitae ex Sica Tragica capite ultimo, pagina centesima decima, & dicere: Ita norunt Iesuitae vela obliqua in ventos, & undecunque se prosper aliquis flatus ostenderit, captare vento Euros, vel Zephyros. Nam facile opinabantur haec verba iam in Gallia non placere. Et Ribadeneira de Principe lib. 1. c. 26. pag. 178. Christiana, ait, prudentia docet Dissimulatione utendum, quando magna pericula timentur: Qui tamen antea pag. 90. politicam illam prudentiam Reginae Scotiae & Regum Galliae accusavit; quod putarunt, serviendum tempori, utilius que esse nonnunquam quadam & lenitate servare, quam severa animadversione totum regnum evertere. Et pag. 94. addit: Nullum Regem, nullum Principem esse cui haec politicae ratio potior visa, qui non stultitiae & temeritatis gravissimas poenas dederit:
units.tr: We may most conveniently use the words of the Jesuit Coster from his Sica Tragica, last chapter, p. 110, and say: Thus the Jesuits know how to set their sails obliquely to the winds, and wherever any favourable breeze shows itself, to catch the east or the west wind. For they easily supposed these words would no longer please in France. And Ribadeneira, De Principe, book 1, ch. 26, p. 178: Christian prudence, he says, teaches that dissimulation must be used when great dangers are feared. Yet earlier, at p. 90, he had accused that political prudence of the Queen of Scots and the Kings of France, who thought that one must serve the times, and that it is sometimes more useful to preserve order by a certain gentleness than to overturn the whole kingdom by severe punishment. And at p. 94 he adds: There is no king, no prince, to whom this political reasoning has seemed more advantageous, who has not paid the gravest penalties for folly and rashness.

units.la: In actis Henrici Garneti & Sociorum pag. 68. haec leguntur. Cum viderent Pontificij, hanc calamitatem (nempe poenalia Reginae Edicta) sibi à Bulla Pij V. conflatam, hac indulta venia demulserunt eos Pius V. & Gregorius XIII. licere omnibus Catholicis, EXTERNAM erga Reginam obedientiam praestare, ad redimenda vexationem: his tamen CAUTELIS & Cancellis circumscriptam; 1. Rebus sic stantibus; 2. dum nec publica Bullae executio fieri posset. Omnia haec scripto testatus est Iesuita Garnetus, & nunc etiam pro tribunali confessus est.
units.tr: In the Acts of Henry Garnet and his Companions, p. 68, the following is read: When the Papists saw that this calamity (namely the penal Edicts of the Queen) had been brought upon them by the Bull of Pius V, Pius V and Gregory XIII soothed them with this granted indulgence: that all Catholics may render EXTERNAL obedience to the Queen, in order to redeem themselves from vexation; yet this is hemmed in by these CAUTIONS and barriers: 1. with things standing thus; 2. while the public execution of the Bull could not take place. The Jesuit Garnet has testified all this in writing, and now also confessed it before the tribunal.

units.la: In extract. Parlamenti Parisiensis Tomo sexto Memorial. Ligae haec vera exstant: Les Iesuites avoyent vnbref de sa saincteté, qui les dispensoit d'obeir, ... d'obei obeit an temps. Id est, Iesuitae habebant Papales literas & dispensationes, quibus se tempori adcommodare possent. Rursus in eodem Extractu pagina 52. Alexander Haius Iesuita aliquot in seigne publiquement, qu'il falloit dissimulet & obeir au Roy pour vn temps par feintise disant fort souvent ces mots, Iesuita est omnis homo.
units.tr: In the extract of the Parliament of Paris, in the sixth volume of the Memorial of the League, these true words are found: The Jesuits had a brief from His Holiness, which dispensed them from obeying ... to obey the time. That is, the Jesuits had papal letters and dispensations by which they could accommodate themselves to the times. Again in the same extract, p. 52: Alexander Haius, a Jesuit, in some sermon publicly taught that one must dissemble and, by pretence, obey the King for a time, often saying these words: Every man is a Jesuit.

units.la: Alexander Haius Iesuita publice, & saepe docuit, ad tempus externe aliud simulandum, quam intus in corde sentias: & sic ad tempus simulandum, ac si Regi obedire velis. Saepe etiam dicere solebat; Iesuita est omnis homo. Iesuitam instar Protei se omnes figuras transformare posse.
units.tr: Alexander Haius, a Jesuit, taught publicly and often that one must feign outwardly something other than what one feels inwardly in the heart, and so pretend for a time as if one wished to obey the King. He also used often to say: Every man is a Jesuit. That the Jesuit can transform himself into all shapes, like Proteus.

units.la: Similiter Iesuitae in Anglia docent, subdole agere & loqui licere. In Anglia no vox, non religio, non internus de Deo, rebusq; divinis sensus Catholicis liber & integer relinquitur (ut scribitur in Epistola Iesuitica in lib. de Concertat. Ecclesiae) loquendum tibi est cum alijs, affirmandum juramento, quod caeteri affirmant, etiamsi animo longe iter opineris, etiamsi in conscientia plane contrarium senseris.
units.tr: Likewise the Jesuits in England teach that it is permitted to act and speak deceitfully. In England no voice, no religion, no inward sense of God and of divine things is left free and whole to Catholics (as is written in a Jesuit letter in the book on the Dispute of the Church): you must speak with the others, you must affirm with an oath what the others affirm, even if you think quite otherwise in your mind, even if you have plainly felt the opposite in your conscience.

units.la: Ante annos non ita multos Iesuitae Duacenses in Belgio statuerunt, Pium õ meritorium esse, haereticis se in speciem adjungere, haereses profiteri, sacris eorum omnibus communicare, atq; adeo nihil non agere, dummodo id studio promovendae rei Catholicae fiat, ut testatur Daniel Plancius Belga in disp. cum Iesuita Antverpiensi De haereticis non servanda, pag. 23.
units.tr: Not many years ago the Jesuits of Douai in Belgium decided that it is pious and meritorious to join heretics in outward appearance, to profess their heresies, to take part in all their sacred rites, and indeed to do anything at all, provided it is done with zeal for promoting the Catholic cause, as the Belgian Daniel Plancius testifies in his disputation with an Antwerp Jesuit, On Faith Not to Be Kept with Heretics, p. 23.

units.la: IESVITAE MVLTA A SE ET ALIIS PON- TIFICIIS FACTA, DICTA ET SCRIPTA IMPV- DENTER NEGANT.
units.tr: The Jesuits rashly deny many things done, said and written by themselves and by other Pontiffs.

units.la: Pichaeomus Iesuita in sua Expostulatione Apologetica pro Societate Iesu anno 1603 edita, Nunquam, ait, ego audivi, posteremo defunctum Henricum a quoquam nostrorum hominum Tyrannum esse nominatum, & tamen cum illis familiarius aliquanto fuisset, quam ille (adversarius) versatus. Negat hoc quoque Iacobus Sylvanus, alias Keller, in sua Philippica contra Admonitionem adversus Reges ac Principes de nefariis & exitialibus Papae & Iesuitarum conatibus & practicis.
units.tr: Pichaeomus the Jesuit, in his Apologetic Expostulation for the Society of Jesus, published in 1603, says: "I have never heard it said by any of our people that Henry, who died recently, was a tyrant, and yet they had been on rather more familiar terms with him than his adversary was." Jacobus Sylvanus, also called Keller, denies this too, in his Philippic against the Admonition to Kings and Princes concerning the wicked and deadly attempts and practices of the Pope and the Jesuits.

units.la: Negat idem Sylvanus ibidem, Iesuitas docere, Eodem modo reliquos etiam Principes & Reges, si a Theologis, viris eruditis & gravibus pro tyrannis habeantur, interfici posse: ideoque recte fecisse Iacobum Clementem Monachum, quod Henricum III. Regem Galliae interfecerit: Recte etiam facturum, qui illius successorem Henricum IV. oppresserit.
units.tr: The same Sylvanus denies, in the same place, that the Jesuits teach: In the same way, other princes and kings too may be killed if theologians, learned and serious men, regard them as tyrants; and therefore Jacob Clement the monk did right in killing Henry III, King of France. He will also do right who has overthrown Henry IV, his successor.

units.la: Negat idem, Iesuitas docere, Tyrannos (excommunicatos & Evangelicos) venenis a subditis vel ministris necari posse.
units.tr: The same man denies that the Jesuits teach: Tyrants (excommunicated and evangelical) may be put to death with poison by their subjects or ministers.

units.la: Iohannes Mariana autem in lib. 1. de Regis institut. c. 6. hanc quaestionem tractans, An Tyrannum opprimere fas sit? affirmantem sententiam probat, & inter alia meminit Henrici III. Regis, ut Tyranni, & merito propterea occisi. Quod utique invenitur, si eum non pro Tyranno habuisset. Ibidem etiam causas indicat, cur illum pro Tyranno habuerint: videlicet, propter impios illius ius.
units.tr: But John Mariana, treating this question in book 1 of On the Institution of a King, chapter 6, Whether it is lawful to crush a tyrant?, supports the affirmative view, and among other things mentions King Henry III as a tyrant, and therefore rightly killed. This is certainly what one finds, if he did not regard him as a tyrant. In the same place he also gives the reasons why they regarded him as a tyrant: namely, his impious laws.

units.la: Addidit ibidem Mariana, Iacobum Clementem praemeditate & de consilio Theologorum hoc facinus perpetrasse, qui eum docuerint, in eoque confirmarint, talem Regem, veluti Tyrannum, iuste occidi posse. Cognito, inquit, a Theologis, quos erat sciscitatus, Tyrannum jure interficiposse, &c.
units.tr: Mariana adds in the same place that Jacob Clement committed this crime deliberately and on the advice of theologians, who had taught him and confirmed him in the view that such a king, as a tyrant, may justly be killed. Having learned, he says, from the theologians whom he had consulted, that a tyrant may lawfully be killed, etc.

units.la: Sed & Petrus Ribadeneira de Principe libro primo, capit. 15. quaest. 91. ait; Quod Henricus Tertius ex pernicioso humanae prudentiae consilio, & nefaria Politicorum calliditate, Henricum Guisiae Ducem, & Ludovicum Cardinalem eius fratrem fortissimos Principes, in Blesensibus Comitiis crudeliter sustulerit: sed necdum decurso anno, aequissimus sceleris vindex, Deus, a caedis authore meritissimas poenas exegerit. Haec certe est luculenta & viva Tyranni descriptio.
units.tr: But Peter Ribadeneira too, in book 1 of On the Prince, chapter 15, question 91, says: That Henry III, out of the pernicious counsel of human prudence and the wicked cunning of the Politiques, cruelly put to death at the Estates of Blois the most valiant princes Henry, Duke of Guise, and his brother Cardinal Louis; but before the year was out, God, the most just avenger of the crime, exacted most deserved punishment from the author of the murder. This is certainly a clear and vivid description of a tyrant.

units.la: In libris etiam Parisiis in Iesuitarum Collegio repertis, & a Ioanne Guignardo Iesuita scriptis, inter multa alia quoque docet, Permissum esse Reges ac Principes occidere. Disertis etiam verbis Henricum III. TYRANNVM nominat.
units.tr: In books also found in the Jesuit college at Paris, and written by the Jesuit John Guignard, he teaches, among many other things, that it is permitted to kill kings and princes. He also explicitly names Henry III a TYRANT.

units.la: In libro quoque toto de Henrici III. abdicatione: Rex ille dicitur fuisse crudelissimus tyrannus; in primis lib. 2. per aliquot capita nominatur perjurus, parricida, assassinus, homicida & quidem Ecclesiasticarum personarum: haereticus & haereticorum amicus & fautor, Schismaticus, Simoniacus, sacrilegus, nigromanticus, &c. Proinde permissum fuisse subditis eius, atque alijs ipsum occidere. Gratulantur etiam sibi Iesuitae tam in procemio, quam lib. 4. c. 23. de nece & interitu eius. Ecce, inquiunt, dum feri-mus, dum variis distractus in concione, in concilio & militiae negotijs, opus, ut licet, maturamus: dum capta Pontisara, occupatoque Clodealdi poto, staret ad ponte omnibus suis copijs auctus Hannibal, & positis secundo ab urbe miliari castris, urbem ac regnum terribus replevisset, atque conspecta urbe, caedes, incendia ac sanguinem spirans, in eam iamiam, ut sibi videbatur, devoraturus TYRANNVS infremeret; mirabilis & simul terribilis dies prima Augusti nuncius venit, Henricu in medio exercitu, gregarij cuiusdam & contempti fraterculi manu esse interfectum, uti Eglonem Moabitam ab Aiod. Et consilium ille prius die, quam in castra abierat, nonnullis revelaverat: idque incredibili bonorum omnium gaudio & exultatione factum est.
units.tr: In the whole of the book on the abdication of Henry III, that king is called a most cruel tyrant. Above all, in book 2, over several chapters, he is called a perjurer, a parricide, an assassin, a murderer, and indeed of ecclesiastical persons; a heretic and a friend and patron of heretics; a schismatic, a simoniac, a sacrilegious man, a necromancer, and so on. Therefore, they say, his subjects and others were permitted to kill him. The Jesuits also congratulate themselves, both in the preface and in book 4, chapter 23, on his death and destruction. "Behold," they say, "while we strike, while we are pulled in various directions by preaching, by councils and by military business, we hasten the work as far as we may; while Pontoise was taken and Saint-Cloud occupied, and Hannibal stood at the bridge, augmented with all his forces, and having pitched camp a mile from the city, had filled the city and the kingdom with terror, and, the city having come into view, the TYRANT, breathing slaughter, fire and blood, roared as if about to devour it at once, a marvellous and at the same time terrible day, the first of August, brought the news that Henry had been killed in the middle of his army by the hand of a certain common and contemptible little friar, just as Ehud killed Eglon the Moabite. He had revealed the plan to some people the day before he left for the camp; and this was done to the incredible joy and exultation of all good men."

units.la: Et subjiciunt: Nihil jam ut fit, quod Iudithae Holofernem, & Davidis Goliathum obtruncantis, & Samsonis in maxilla asini mille viros interficientis, historias admiremur. Dextera Domini fecit virtutem: Dextera Domini exaltavit nos, &c. A Domino factum est illud, & est mirabile in oculis nostris. Discite ergo, qui alterius Henrici anathematis reliquias sectamini, discite, quid sit illud: Maledictus qui confidit in homine. Ut quid enim anathema alterum sectantes, hoc terribili edocti exemplo, in voluntarium excidium ruitis? Et relapsum haereticum, tot sceleribus ac crudelitatibus insignem sustinetis? Et strictum in vos gladium, qui terribiliter caput vestrum demessuit, non timetis?
units.tr: And they add: "Now, as it happens, we no longer need to marvel at the stories of Judith beheading Holofernes, of David slaying Goliath, or of Samson killing a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted us, etc. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes. Learn then, you who follow the remnants of the other Henry's anathema, learn what that means: Cursed is the man who trusts in man. For why, you who follow another anathema, taught by this terrible example, do you rush into voluntary destruction? Why do you tolerate a relapsed heretic, notable for so many crimes and cruelties? And do you not fear the sword drawn against you, which has terribly cut off your head?"

units.la: Sic & in Praefatione eiusdem libri: Non enim, aiunt, id agimus tandem, ut Henricum Tertium abdicemus; quod factum nuper & probatum divinitus, etiam gratulamur. Sed omnino, ut impios & TYRANNOS a nobis excludamus; ut Gallorum, imo omnium animos ad pestem hanc excitiendam excitemus: Ut in prototypo nequitiae Henrico, quid in Principe execrari, quid fugere oporteat, doceamus.
