Proinde, ut, cum haec communis alterius Henrici, pariter impij, haeretici, relapsi, TYRANNI, sacrilegi, impuri, incestuosi, homicidae atque excommunicati, & ut nunc audimus, etiam hypocritae, causa sit: proterea fiat, ut, cum de priore juste abdicato dixerimus, de hoc quoque excludendo ac perdendo dixisse videri cupiamus. Nam hic operis huius fructus erit: qui utinam non tantum esset, atque in eo statur res foret, ut, extincto etiam posteriore Herico, hoc confectum negotium laudare tantum, non etiam futurum iudere oporteret. Sed quia id nobis ab omnipotente Deo postulandum est, ut, qui nobis priora ocia fecit, miseratus aliquando ab altero quoque, nec minus impuro, eripiat. Interim dum gratiam hanc expectamus, admoneamus certe non cessemus; ut, quia Deus facientes juvat, omnes omnium vires in exequendum istud caput, eiusque assertores colligantur. Denique omni ratione fiat, ut anathemata ista e medio nostri, imo Ecclesiae universae abigantur. Quod si, miserante Deo, factum aliquando erit, tum nos praeclarum, non operis huius tantum, sed vitae etiam ac mortis fructum videbimur consecuti. Item, Ut, quod factum a nobis est in eijciendo Henrico, id, si quid tale occurrerit, Optimi quique aemulentur, utque Henricones illi, qui id factum, improbarunt non desinunt, imo ultionem mu-tir re non verentur, confusi & elingues reddantur, si quid frontis habent, tacere impellantur: utque etiam alter Henricus tollatur, & sic Ecclesiae hostes penitus conterantur, regnum a gente in gentem (e Gallia in Hispaniam) transferatur, & utilis Rector in tempore suscitetur.
units.tr: So also in the preface of the same book: "For we do not aim, in the end, merely to depose Henry III, which was done recently and divinely approved, and we rejoice in it. Rather, we aim altogether to exclude impious men and TYRANTS from ourselves, and to rouse the minds of the French, indeed of all men, to drive out this plague; so that, in the archetype of wickedness, Henry, we may teach what to execrate in a prince and what to flee. Therefore, since this other Henry, equally impious, heretical, relapsed, a TYRANT, sacrilegious, impure, incestuous, a murderer and excommunicated, and, as we now hear, also a hypocrite, is the cause, let it come about that, since we have spoken about the former, justly deposed, we should also be seen to have spoken about excluding and destroying this one. For this will be the fruit of this work. Would that it were only so, and that the matter stood so that, once the latter Henry too was extinguished, we ought not only to praise this finished business but also to judge it as still to come! But since this must be asked of almighty God, that he who gave us the former leisure may at some time, taking pity on us, rescue us also from the other, no less impure. Meanwhile, while we await this grace, let us certainly not cease to urge: since God helps those who act, let all the strength of everyone be gathered to carry out this task and to support its advocates. Finally, let it be done by every means that these anathemas be driven out from our midst, indeed from the whole Church. If this is ever accomplished, by God's mercy, then we shall seem to have obtained a splendid fruit, not only of this work but of life and death as well." Likewise: "That what was done by us in driving out Henry should, if anything of the kind occurs, be imitated by all the best men; and that those Henricians who disapprove of that deed, and do not cease, indeed do not shrink from threatening vengeance, should be made confused and speechless, and be compelled to be silent, if they have any shame; and that the other Henry too should be removed, and so the enemies of the Church be utterly crushed, and the kingdom be transferred from nation to nation (from France to Spain), and a useful ruler be raised up in due time."

units.la: Becanus Iesuita Moguntiensis contra Christianum Batavum negat cum socio suo, Romano-Catholicos docere, & in tribus Concilijs, Lateranensi sub Julio II. & Leone X. celebrato, Tridentino item & Constantiensi decretum esse, Haereticis fidem non esse servandam.
units.tr: Becanus the Jesuit of Mainz, against the Dutch Christian, denies, together with his fellow Jesuit, that Roman Catholics teach that faith is not to be kept with heretics, and that in three councils, the Lateran council celebrated under Julius II and Leo X, likewise the Council of Trent and the Council of Constance, a decree was issued that faith is not to be kept with heretics.

units.la: Iacobus Simancha autem Episcopus Pacensis in Institutione sua Catholica tit. 46. articul. 52. haec scribit: Ad haereticorum poenam & odium pertinet, QVOD IDES ILLIS DATA SERVANDA NON sit, ut in Concilio Constantiensi factum, non obstante juramento. Et mox rationem addit: Si enim, inquit, tyrannis, piratis, & caeteris praedonibus fides servanda non sit, qui corpus occidunt, longe magis haereticis pertinacibus qui occidunt animas. Rursus: Cum haereticis, ait, nullum commercium, nulla Pax Catholicis esse debet. Quamobrem fides illis data, etiam juramento firmata, contra publicum bonum, contra salutem animarum, contra jura divina & humana, nullo modo servanda est. Allegat etiam ibidem huius sententiae suae stipulatores, Marium Salmonium, leg. 2. §. de exact. de origine iuris. Melchium & alios, ne solus sic sentire videatur. Citat etiam Thomam secunda secundae quaest. 70. art. 1. ubi vult, Haereticum indocilem prodendum esse judicibus, non obstante fide & juramento.
units.tr: But Jacobus Simancha, Bishop of Pasencia, in his Catholic Institution, title 46, article 52, writes this: It belongs to the punishment and hatred of heretics that the faith given to them is not to be kept, as was done at the Council of Constance, notwithstanding an oath. And he soon adds the reason: For if, he says, faith is not to be kept with tyrants, pirates and other robbers, who kill the body, much less with obstinate heretics, who kill souls. Again: With heretics, he says, there should be no commerce and no peace for Catholics. Therefore the faith given to them, even when confirmed by oath, is in no way to be kept, when it is against the public good, against the salvation of souls, and against divine and human law. He also cites in the same place, as sponsors of this opinion of his, Marius Salmonius, law 2, §. de exact., On the origin of law, Melchior and others, lest he seem to be alone in thinking so. He also cites Thomas, Secunda Secundae, question 70, article 1, where he holds that an unteachable heretic is to be handed over to the judges, notwithstanding faith and oath.

units.la: Simanchae assentit etiam Crefuuel Iesuita in suo Philopatre pagina centesima nona. Quemcunque, inquit, Principem Christianum, si a Religione Catholica manifesto deflexerit & alios avocare voluerit, excidere statim omni potestate ac dignitate, ex ipsa vi juris tum humani tum divini, hacque ante dictam sententiam supremi Patroris ac judicis contra ipsum prolatam, & subditos quoscunque liberos esse ab omni juramenti obligatione, quod de obedientia, tamquam Principi legitimo, praestitissent, posse et debere, si vires habeant, istiusmodi hominem, tamquam Apostatam, ac Christi Domini desertorem, & Reipublicae suae inimicum & hostem, ex hominum Christianorum dominatu eijcere, ne alios inficiat, vel suo exemplo & imperio a fide avertat. Atque haec certa, definita, & indubitata virorum doctissimorum (Iesuitarum) est sententia. Et tamen adhuc negare audent, se & alios Pontificios docere, Fidem haereticis servandam non esse.
units.tr: Crefuuel, a Jesuit, also agrees with Simancas in his Philopater, page 109: Any Christian prince whatsoever, if he manifestly falls away from the Catholic religion and seeks to draw others away, immediately loses all power and dignity by the very force of law, both human and divine, and, once the sentence of the supreme Father and judge has been pronounced against him, all his subjects are free from every bond of the oath by which they swore obedience to him as a lawful prince, and they can and should, if they have the strength, drive such a man out of the rule of Christian men, as an apostate, a deserter of Christ the Lord, an enemy and foe of his own commonwealth, so that he may not infect others or turn them from the faith by his example and command. This, says he, is the certain, settled and indubitable opinion of the most learned men (the Jesuits). Yet they still dare to deny that they and the other Papists teach that faith is not to be kept with heretics.

units.la: Hoc etiam generale Papistarum dogma esse, Tortuosus Bellarminus in Respositione ad Apologiam pro iuramento fidelitatis his verbis testatur: Iam supra, inquit, docuimus, supremum universae Ecclesiae Rectorem id juris habere, ut Princeps ab Ecclesiae unitate per haeresin vel schisma deficiat, possit eum excommunicare, vel excommunicatum declarare, ET SVBDITOS EIVS a FIDE ET OBEDIENTIA LIBERARE. Neque hanc esse novam doctrinam, sed in Concilio LATERANENSI omnium maximo & celeberrimo approbatam, atque sub Christiani populi per multa secula receptam. Qui enim non timent occidere, quid timebunt jurejurando religionem violare? Et adhuc audent negare ie hoc docere.
units.tr: That this is also the general dogma of the Papists, the crafty Bellarmine bears witness in his reply to the Apology concerning the oath of allegiance, in these words: Above, he says, we have taught that the supreme ruler of the whole Church has the right, if a prince falls away from the unity of the Church through heresy or schism, to excommunicate him or declare him excommunicated, and TO FREE HIS SUBJECTS from FAITH AND OBEDIENCE. And this, he says, is not a new doctrine, but was approved at the Lateran Council, the greatest and most famous of all, and has been received among the Christian people for many centuries. For those who do not fear to kill, what will they fear in violating religion by an oath? And still they dare to deny that they teach this.

units.la: Hosius quoque Cardinalis Epistola centesima nonagesima tertia, & ducentesima secunda, & ducentesima vigesima. Henricum Poloniae Regem monet, eum nullo modo debere fidem datam Evangelicis Polonis servare. Nunquam, ait, patiaris ulla ratione ad ea quae promisisti, praestanda teneri: Quia juramentum non debet esse vinculum iniquitatis. Idem repetit Stephano Regi Antonius Possevinus Iesuita.
units.tr: Cardinal Hosius likewise, in his letters 193, 202 and 220, warns King Henry of Poland that he must in no way keep the faith given to the Evangelical Poles. Never, he says, allow yourself to be bound by any reason to perform what you have promised, because an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity. Antonius Possevinus, a Jesuit, repeats the same to King Stephen.

units.la: Molanus item libro tertio, capit. 27. objecti. 1. & 6: expresse docet, Regulam
units.tr: Molanus likewise, in book three, chapter 27, objections 1 and 6, expressly teaches that the rule

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: CONCERNING THE DOCTRINE

units.la: Pontificijs generalem esse, Fidē hæreticis vel non danda vel non esse servandam; si illis data fit super libero Religionis suæ exercitio: & in specie de Fœderatis Belgis, quos dum Hispaniæ Regi vim intulisse tradit, Merentur, inquit, ut eis promissum non servetur. Et cap.7. lib.4. addit: Nam quotquot contra Catholicam Majestatem Philippi arma in Belgio sumunt, quia potius rebelles, quam hostes dicendi sunt, ut sitate prædones dicuntur: atque si illis aliquid promissum sit, claram & indubitatam esse resolutionem, ijs nihil debeni.
units.tr: It is the general doctrine of the Papists that faith is either not to be given to heretics, or is not to be kept, if it was given to them concerning the free exercise of their religion. And specifically concerning the united Belgians, whom, as he reports, they have done violence to the King of Spain, deserve, he says, that the promise made to them should not be kept. And in chapter 7 of book 4 he adds: For however many take up arms in Belgium against the Catholic majesty of Philip, since they are to be called rebels rather than enemies, just as they are called robbers rather than soldiers, and if anything has been promised to them, it is a clear and indubitable resolution that they are owed nothing.

units.la: Bellarminus libro quarto de Pontifice Romano c. 10. scribit; Calvinum impudenter mentiri, quod scribat libro quarto Instit. c. 12. & 24. Siricium in epistola ad Hispanos conjugium Sacerdotum vocasse immunditiem & pollutionem. Legatur autem epistola illa. Prohibet in ea presbyteris matrimonium, quia Dominus præcepit, Sancti estote, quia & ego sanctus sum. Si recte disputet Siricius, certe etiam coniugium verum & legitimum impurum est; & non presbyteris tantum, sed omnibus etiam hominibus illicitum: hoc enim Deus non a solis Levitis, sed a cuncto populo exigit, ut sancti sint, quemadmodum & ipse sanctus est. Siricius igitur existimavit, Coniugium in se immundum esse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book four of On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 10, writes that Calvin lies shamelessly when he writes, in book four of the Institutes, chapters 12 and 24, that Siricius, in his letter to the Spaniards, called the marriage of priests uncleanness and pollution. But let that letter be read. In it he forbids marriage to the elders, because the Lord commanded, Be holy, for I am holy. If Siricius reasons rightly, then certainly even lawful and true marriage is unclean, and illicit not only for elders but for all men. For God requires holiness not only of the Levites but of the whole people, as he himself is holy. Siricius therefore judged that marriage is in itself unclean.

units.la: Eodem loco negat Bellarminus Liberium Papam fuisse Arianum & Arij doctrinæ subscripsisse: affirmat autem Athanasius in Epistola ad solitvit agentes. Negat etiam Felicem Arianum fuisse: affirmat Hieronymus in Catal. in Acacio, ubi ait, Acacij opera Felicem Arianum Romæ Episcopum constitutum esse. Negat Coelestinum Papam Nestorianum fuisse; affirmat Laurent. Valla in libro de Donat. Constantini. Negat Vigilium fuisse Monophysitam; & Epistolam Liberati, in qua hoc diserte affirmatur, ab hæreticis vel corruptam, vel totam confictam & scriptam fuisse: sed non probat. Negat capite undecimo Honorium Papam hæreticum fuisse; At sunt duæ Epistolæ Honorij in Synodo 6. Actio 12. & 13. in quibus doctrinam Sergij Principis Monothelitarum approbavit. In eadem Synodo Actio decima tertia Honorius nominatim damnatur, & eius Epistolæ comburendæ iudicantur, & hæc damnatio repetitur in omnibus actionibus sequentibus plus quam viginti. In Synodo septima etiam damnatur Honorius tanquam Monothelita. In Synodo 8. generali Actio septima afferitur; Honorium fuisse a Synodo 8. generali Actio 7. asseritur; Honorium fuisse a Synodo 6. post mortem damnatum. Agatho Papa in Epistola ad Constantinum Imperatorem, quæ habetur Act. 4. Synodi 6. anathema dicit Honorio tanquam Monothelitæ: idem etiam facit Leo 2. in Epistola ad eundem Imperatorem, quæ habetur in Synodo 6. in fine. His accedunt authores plurimi tam Græci quam Latini. Nilus Archiepiscopus Thessalonicensis in libro de primatu Papæ; Tharasius Episcopus Constantinop. in Epistola ad Patriarchas quæ extat in Synodo 7. Actione tertia; Theodorus Episcopus Hierosol. in Epistola Synodica, quæ ibidem habetur: Epiphanius Diaconus Catholicus in disputatione cum Gregorio hæretico, quæ extat in Synodo 7. Actione sexta. Item, Psellus in carmine de septem Synodis; Beda de sex ætatibus in vita Constantini quarti. Imper. & Liber Pontificalis in Vita Leonis 2. His addendi sunt Melchior Canus libro sexto Comment. c. ult. Sanderus libro septimo de visib. Monarch. Alphonsus de Castro libro quarto de hæret. pun. Torrensis de 6. 7. & 8. Synod. Hardingus contra Iuellum, Genebrardus in Chron. in Honorio I. qui omnes hæreticum eum fuisse testantur: solus Bellarminus cum paucis negat. Et quamvis fateatur lib. 4. de Pontifice, c. 14. Ioannem 22. Papam revera sensisse, animas non visuras Deum, nisi post resurrectionem demum, hoc tamen peccatum quantum potest extenuat & excusat: ut impudentissimum Cofterum Iesuitam esse oporteat, qui in suo Enchiridi aperte asserit, in tanto Pontificum numero, qui ui Beato Petro successerunt, neunum quidem inventum esse, qui haeresin docuerit, aut in errorem lapsus sit.
units.tr: In the same place Bellarmine denies that Pope Liberius was an Arian or subscribed to the doctrine of Arius; but Athanasius affirms it in his letter to those who were living in solitude. He also denies that Felix was an Arian; but Jerome affirms it in the Catalogue, under Acacius, where he says that through the work of Acacius Felix was made bishop of Rome as an Arian. He denies that Pope Coelestine was a Nestorian; Laurentius Valla affirms it in his book on the Donation of Constantine. He denies that Vigilius was a Monophysite, and that the letter of Liberatus, in which this is plainly asserted, was either corrupted by heretics or wholly invented and written by them; but he does not prove it. He denies in chapter eleven that Pope Honorius was a heretic; yet there are two letters of Honorius, in the Sixth Synod, Actions 12 and 13, in which he approved the doctrine of Sergius, the prince of the Monothelites. In the same Synod, Action 13, Honorius is named and condemned, and his letters are judged to be burned, and this condemnation is repeated in more than twenty subsequent actions. In the Seventh Synod too Honorius is condemned as a Monothelite. In the Eighth General Synod, Action 7, it is asserted that Honorius was condemned after his death by the Sixth Synod. Pope Agatho, in his letter to the Emperor Constantine, which is in Action 4 of the Sixth Synod, pronounces an anathema on Honorius as a Monothelite; Leo II does the same in his letter to the same Emperor, which is found at the end of the Sixth Synod. To these are added very many authors, Greek as well as Latin: Nilus, Archbishop of Thessalonica, in his book on the primacy of the Pope; Tarasius, Bishop of Constantinople, in his letter to the Patriarchs, which is in the Seventh Synod, Action 3; Theodore, Bishop of Jerusalem, in the Synodal Letter found there; Epiphanius, the Catholic deacon, in his disputation with the heretic Gregory, which is in the Seventh Synod, Action 6. Also Psellus in his poem on the seven Synods, and Bede in On the Six Ages, in the life of the Emperor Constantine IV, and the Liber Pontificalis in the life of Leo II. To these should be added Melchior Cano in book six of his Commentaries, chapter last; Sanders in book seven of On the Visible Monarchy; Alfonso de Castro in book four of On Heresies; Torrensis on the sixth, seventh and eighth Synods; Harding against Jewel; and Genebrard in his Chronicle, under Honorius I. All of these testify that he was a heretic; only Bellarmine, with a few others, denies it. And although he admits, in book 4 of On the Pope, chapter 14, that John XXII really held that souls would not see God until after the resurrection, he nonetheless minimises and excuses this error as far as he can. So the Jesuit Coster must be most shameless, for in his Enchiridion he plainly asserts that among so great a number of Popes who succeeded blessed Peter, not one is found who taught heresy or fell into error.

units.la: Amphitheatrum Honoris Anno 1606. excusum, Clari Bonarscij nomine, cuius proprium nomen Carolus Scribanius erat, antehac Antverpiani Collegij Rectoris, Cotton Iesuita dixit, neque quaquam a suae Societatis hominibus emanasse, sed Geneuae, ad conflandum Iesuitis odium, fictum ab haereticis fuisse: qui tamen postea, longe aliter, quid sentiret expressit, laudato Scribanij opere, & distributis multis exemplaribus.
units.tr: Cotton, a Jesuit, said that the Amphitheatrum Honoris, printed in 1606 under the name of Clarus Bonarscius, whose real name was Carolus Scribanius, formerly Rector of the Antwerp college, did not come from members of his Society at all, but was made up by heretics at Geneva to stir up hatred against the Jesuits. Yet he later declared quite otherwise what he thought, praising Scribanius's work and distributing many copies of it.

units.la: Negare quoque audent Iesuitae tam imprudenter, quam confidenter, corrasis & oblectis ad hoc undique argumentis, Historiam de Ioh. Papissa Romana eiusque puerperio, de cuius tamen veritate a plerisque per 800. iam fere annos, in ipsomet Pontificio regno, nunquam dubitatum aut disputatum est. Nunc demum in dubium vocatur a Pontificiis adulatoribus, inprimis Bellarmino & Baronio, qui hanc historiam fabulam esse contendunt: eoque plerosque, integros, gravesque scriptores, in quorum consentientium monumentis expressa & contestata legitur, vanitatis & medacij non minus arroganter, quae in vereundae, arguunt: idque non adferendae veritatis causa, quae ubicunque eis adversatur, adulterant & supprimunt; sed ut probrosam hanc puerperij Papalis labem diluant, hoc cum primis tempore plurimum iactatam in despectum & ignominiam Hierarchiae Romanae, cuius fundamentum in perpetua inde usque a Petro successione (si modo Petrus unquam Romae fuit) situm praedicant: quam catenam ab hac muliere interruptam dolenter ferunt, & omnibus modis sepultam esse cupiunt. Ranolphus autem Flaviacensis Monachus Benedictinus, hanc historiam Pontificalis puerperij primus commemoravit: & ab aliis propter deformitatem facti omissam aperte taxus est. Vixit iuxta Trithemium anno 930. ut Papa e hoc puerperium ab iis accipere potuerit, qui illud viderunt. Hunc sequutus est Marianus Scotus. Anno Domini, inquit 854. anno Lotharij 14. successit Leoni Iohanna mulier. Natus fuit Anno 1028. ut hanc historiam vel ex seniorum relatione, vel ex superiorum scriptorum relictis monumentis cognitam habuerit. Tertius est testis veritatis huius historiae Sigebertus Gallus Gemblacensis abbas. Fama est, inquit, Iohannem foeminam fuisse, & uni soli familiari cognitam, qui hunc eam complexus est: Gravida facta peperit Papa existens. Quare eam inter Pontifices non numerant quidam, Graue de eo extat iudicium apud Trithemium in libro de Script. Eccles.
units.tr: The Jesuits also dare to deny, as rashly as they do confidently, the story of Pope Joan of Rome and her childbirth, though they have gathered and brought together arguments from every quarter for this purpose. Yet for nearly 800 years now, in the very kingdom of the Papacy, its truth has never been doubted or disputed by most people. Only now is it called into question by Papist flatterers, above all by Bellarmine and Baronius, who contend that this history is a fable; and with it they accuse very many entire, serious writers, in whose records this matter is expressed and attested, of vanity and lying, no less arrogantly than shamelessly. And they do this not for the sake of bringing forward the truth, which they distort and suppress wherever it stands against them, but in order to wash away this disgraceful stain of the Papal childbed, which was much bandied about, above all at that time, to the disparagement and shame of the Roman hierarchy, whose foundation they proclaim to lie in an unbroken succession from Peter (if indeed Peter was ever at Rome). They grieve that this chain was broken by this woman and wish it buried by every means. Ranulf of Chester, however, a Benedictine monk of Flaviacum, was the first to mention this history of the Papal childbed, and was openly censured by others because of the foulness of the deed. He lived, according to Trithemius, in the year 930, so that he could have received this childbed from those who saw it. Marianus Scotus followed him: In the year of the Lord 854, in the fourteenth year of Lothar, Joan, a woman, succeeded Leo. He was born in 1028, so he may have known this history either from the report of the elders or from the surviving records of earlier writers. The third witness to the truth of this history is Sigebert of Gembloux, abbot: There is a report, he says, that John was a woman, known only to one familiar who had intercourse with her; having become pregnant, she gave birth while being Pope. For this reason some do not count her among the Popes. There is a grave judgment on him in Trithemius, in his book on ecclesiastical writers.

units.la: Superstunt alia quoque de eod. facto ac sceleris testimonia. 1. Primus est Martini Poloni. Is inquit, Ioan. 8. foemina fuit, & in Papatu a familiari suo impraegnatur. Verum tempus partus ignorans, qui de S. Petro in Lateranu tenderet, angustiata partu inter Colosseum & S. Clement. Ecclesia peperit, & postea mortua ibidem, ut dicitur, sepulta fuit. Et propterea, quod Deus Papa semper eandem viam obliquat, creditur omnino a quibusdam quod ob detestationem facti hoc fiat. Nec ideo in Catalogo sanctorum Pontificum ponitur, tam propter mulieebrem sexum, quam propter deformitatem facti.
units.tr: There are yet other testimonies to this deed and crime. 1. The first is that of Martin of Poland. He says: Joan. 8. was a woman, and in the papacy she was made pregnant by a familiar of her own. But not knowing the time of the birth, as she was going from St Peter's to the Lateran, she was overtaken by labour between the Colosseum and the church of St Clement, gave birth there, and afterwards died and was buried on the spot, as it is said. And for this reason, because God always turns the Pope aside along the same path, it is believed by some altogether that this happens on account of the detestation of the deed. Nor is she therefore placed in the catalogue of holy popes, both on account of her female sex and on account of the deformity of the deed.

units.la: 2. Alterum testimonium est Francisci Petrarchae, qui Martini Poloni coaetaneus fuit. Is eadem quae Martinus commemorat in suo Chronico Italice conscripto, & Florentiae excuso anno 1478. Iohannes, inquit, Anglicus non ponitur in Catalogo Paparum, quia foemina fuit.
units.tr: 2. The second testimony is that of Francesco Petrarch, who was a contemporary of Martin of Poland. In his Chronicle, written in Italian and printed at Florence in 1478, he records the same things as Martin. John, he says, the Englishman is not placed in the catalogue of popes, because she was a woman.

units.la: 3. Tertium est Iohannis Bocatij, qui intimus Petrarchae fuit. Is libro de claris mulieribus capite 99 graphice probrosum illud Pontificis puerperium descripsit, ita ut etiam effigiem parientis, & obstetricantes Cardinales & Episcopos exhibeat.
units.tr: 3. The third is that of Giovanni Boccaccio, who was an intimate friend of Petrarch. In his book On Famous Women, chapter 99, he described that shameful childbirth of the pope in such vivid detail that he even portrays the figure of the woman in labour, and the cardinals and bishops attending as midwives.

units.la: His testibus accedunt alij pietate, doctrina & fide dignissimi. 1. Otto Episcopus Frisingensis, qui ante annos 400. claruit: 2. Annales Augustani antiqui: 3. Vuilhelmus Occamus c. 124. operis 90. dierum: 4. Raphael Volateranus in Comsuis Iulio II. dicatis: 5. Platina, qui fuit Sixto IV. à Secretis: 6. Sabellicus Ennead. 9. lib. 1. Iacobus Philippus Bergomensis: 7. Trithemius in Chronicis: 8. Iohannes Stella: 9. Nauclerus: 10. Albertus Krantzius: 11. Fasciculus temporum, Coelius Rhodiginus, ac plures alij. Horum tantorum virorum testimonio & affirmationi plus credendum est, quam Iesuitarum negationi, qui id solum dicunt, quod Pontificis sui maiestatem & authoritatem stabiliat, contrarium simpliciter vel negant, vel saltem eludunt.
units.tr: Besides these witnesses, there are others most worthy of trust for their piety, learning and faithfulness: (1) Otto, Bishop of Freising, who flourished about 400 years ago; (2) the ancient Augsburg Annals; (3) William of Ockham, in chapter 124 of his work of 90 days; (4) Raphael Volaterranus, in his Commentaries dedicated to Julius II; (5) Platina, who was secretary to Sixtus IV; (6) Sabellicus, Ennead 9, book 1; (7) Jacobus Philippus of Bergamo; (8) Trithemius, in his Chronicles; (9) Giovanni Stella; (10) Nauclerus; (11) Albert Krantz, the Fasciculus temporum, Coelius Rhodiginus, and many others. More credit is to be given to the testimony and assertion of these so great men than to the denial of the Jesuits, who say only what supports the majesty and authority of their Pontiff, and either flatly deny the contrary or at least evade it.

units.la: Refutarunt etiam solidissime Iesuitarum mendacia & exceptiones, quibus hanc historiam suspectam & falsam esse probare volunt, & veritatem eius asseruerunt, Vuitakerus in suo libro de Pontifice Rom. pag. 719. & 720. Deinde Franciscus Junius in Animadversionibus ad Controversiam 3. generalem Bellarmini de Pontifice Rom. lib. 3. c. 24. pag. 439. & seqq. Imprimis autem Conradus Deckherus Praeceptor in Sapientia Heydelbergen. in libro de Papa Romano & Papatu Romana.
units.tr: Moreover, the lies and exceptions by which the Jesuits seek to prove this history suspect and false have been most thoroughly refuted, and its truth affirmed, by Whitaker in his book on the Roman Pontiff, pp. 719 and 720; then by Franciscus Junius in his Animadversions on Bellarmine's third general controversy concerning the Roman Pontiff, book 3, chapter 24, p. 439 and following; and above all by Conrad Dieckmann, teacher in Wisdom at Heidelberg, in his book on the Roman Pope and the Roman papacy.

units.la: Negant insuper Iesuitae Coniurationi pulverariae in Anglia, qua maius authorribilius scelus post homines natos nunquam suscepetum fuit, quenquam Iesuitarum immixtum, vel eius conscium et participem fuisse. Facit hoc Andreas Eudaemono Iohannes Cretensis in sua Apologia pro Henrico Garnetto: & addit, cum nullius scelerts convictum, odio duntaxat religionis, aut Iesuitici nominis damnatum fuisse.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Jesuits deny that any of the Jesuits was involved in or privy to the Gunpowder Plot in England, the most dreadful crime ever undertaken since men were born. Andreas Eudaemono Iohannes Cretensis does this in his Apology for Henry Garnet, and adds that he was convicted of no crime, and was condemned only out of hatred of religion, or of the Jesuit name.

units.la: At vero coniurationis istius negotio, minimum 4. Iesuitas intervenisse supra indicavimus. Illorum 4. nomina haec sunt: Henricus Garnettus in Angliae regno ab annis 19. Provincialis: Hallus qui & Oldcornus: Ofvvaldus Telmend sive Grenvvellius: & Iohannes Gerardus. Ac caeteri quidem, ut supra quoque pluribus indicavimus, pro sua quisque viribus, singula, quae res aut tempus postulare viderentur, exsequentes, negotium per patres curarunt: Henricus Garnettus autem, ut qui inter Pontificios Anglos dignitate, authoritate, & longo tractandarum rerum usu supra alios emineret, de universo negotio cum unico fere Catisbeio solitus fuit communicare, caeterorum omnium conscientiam sollicite reflugiens, ut ex Epistolis ipsius, propria manu scriptis, & a multis lectis apparet. Ad hunc in rebus dubiis, ceu ad oraculum Catisbeius doli totius architectus, ventitans, aut Grenvvellium suo nomine missitans, oracula petebat. Ex Colloquiis etiam, & pluribus aliis Catisbeij cum illo, quam ex Grenvvelli saepe repetitis sermonibus, de quibus & plurimae Garnetti Epistolae testatur, luce clarius probari poterit, hunc Iesuitam coniurationis nefariae non minus conscium fuisse, quam alium quemvis complicum. Neque vero arcani solum conscius Garnettus fuit, sed pleriisque coniuratorum, & Vuintero, Rookuodo, & ipsi Fauxio incendiario, qua fuit authoritate, audendi auctor extitit, cunctantibus & horrescentibus priusquam probari rem tanto viro ex verbis Catisbeij cognoscent. Sed de his satis supra, quo Lectorem remittimus.
units.tr: Yet in truth, as we indicated above, at least four Jesuits took part in the business of that conspiracy. The names of these four are: Henry Garnet, Provincial in the kingdom of England for nineteen years; Hall, who was also called Oldcorne; Oswald Tesmond, otherwise Greenwell; and John Gerard. The others, as we have also indicated above in several places, each carried out, according to his own abilities, whatever matters or occasions seemed to require, and handled the business through their fathers. But Henry Garnet, as one who surpassed the other English Papists in dignity, authority and long experience in managing affairs, was accustomed to discuss the whole business with almost only Catesby, anxiously shunning the awareness of all the others, as appears from his Letters, written in his own hand and read by many. Catesby, the architect of the whole fraud, came often to him in doubtful matters, as to an oracle, or sent Greenwell in his name to seek answers. From his conversations with Catesby, and from many other things, and from the words of Greenwell often repeated, of which many letters of Garnet also bear witness, it can be proved clearer than light that this Jesuit was no less aware of the wicked conspiracy than any other accomplice. Nor was Garnet merely privy to the secret; he also, by his authority, became the author of the daring deed to several of the conspirators, and to Wintour, Rookwood, and Fawkes the incendiary himself, who hesitated and shrank back until they learned from Catesby's words that the matter had been approved by so great a man. But of these things enough has been said above, to which we refer the reader.

units.la: CAVSAE PPIMARIAE PARRICIDIORVM, ALIORVM, QVE NEFARIORVM FACINORVM &c. IESVITARVM.
units.tr: THE PRINCIPAL CAUSES OF THE PARRICIDES, AND OTHER WICKED AND NEFARIOUS DEEDS, OF THE JESUITS, &c.

units.la: Causa parricidiorum, proditionum, aliorumque nefandissimorum facinorum Iesuitarum non postrema est Caeca illorum quam sic ipsimet vocant, obedientia, quam Superioribus vovent, de qua sic scribitur in Constitutionibus eorum part. 3. §. 1. Ut sancta obedientia tum in executione, tum in voluntate, tum in intellectu sit nobis semper ex omni parte perfecta: cum magna celeritate, spirituali gaudio & perseverantia, quidquid nobis injunctum fuerit, obeundo, OMNIA justa esse nobis persuadendo, omnem sententiam ac judicium nostrum caeca quadam obedientia abnegando. Et id quidem in omnibus quæ à superiore disponuntur, ubi definiri non possit aliquod peculiari genus intercedere. Et sibi quisque persuadeat, quod qui sub obedientia viviunt, se ferri regi à divina providentia per Superiores suos, vivere debent perinde ac si cadaver essent, quod quoquo versus se ferri, & quacunque ratione tractari se sinit: vel similiter atque baculus, qui ubicunque & quacunque in re velit eo uti, qui eum in manu tenet, ei inserit. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: One of the chief causes of the parricides, treasons and other most abominable deeds of the Jesuits is that blind obedience which they call their own and which they vow to their Superiors. Their Constitutions speak of it thus, part 3, §1: That holy obedience, whether in execution, in will, or in understanding, may always be perfect in us in every respect: carrying out whatever is enjoined upon us with great speed, spiritual joy and perseverance, persuading ourselves that ALL things are just, and denying every opinion and judgement of our own by a certain blind obedience. And this holds indeed for all things which are ordered by a superior, unless some particular kind of exception can be defined. Let each one persuade himself that those who live under obedience should allow themselves to be carried and directed by divine providence through their Superiors, and should live as if they were a corpse, which lets itself be moved in any direction and handled in any way; or like a staff, which the one who holds it in his hand uses wherever and for whatever purpose he wishes. Thus far the Constitutions.

units.la: Ubi animadvertendum, etiamsi iuxta literam ab obedientia ista cæcaid, quod absque peccato fieri non posit, aliquatenus excipi videatur, Iesuitis tamen in mandata Superiorum inquirendi eaque penitus scrutandi potestatem ademptam, sicque teneri eos pro iustis ac legitimis agnoscere omnia sibi iniuncta; Omnia videlicet iusta esse sibi persuadendo, non secus ac si Christus ipse præcepisset, à quibus etiam tractari se permittere debeant, ac si cadaver aliquod aut baculus senis essent; ita ut nulla vel temporis, vel rationis, vel sensus etiam communis aut externi ratio habeatur; nimirum, ut obedientia sit in cæcitate sua omnimode perfecta; secundum voluntatem Ignatii, de quo Maffæus in eius vita lib. 3. c. 7. testatur; Quum in Societate nostra virtutem hanc cæteris virtutibus anteferret, tum nihil huic laudi tam contrarium dicebat esse, quam in Superiorum iussis & imperiis examinando, moram, vel potius arrogantiam, negabatque obedientis nomine dignum esse oportere, qui legitimo Superiori non cum voluntate iudicium quoque submitteret. Et hoc: Ad sapientem hanc sanctamque stultitiam cæcæ obedientiæ, suos, ut essent ad subita & fortia promptiores, interdum etiam fictis in rebus erudiebat. Hinc ergo fit, ut nihil tam nefarium, seditiosum, inhonestum & horrendum inferioribus iniungant Superiores, quod illi detrectare audeant.
units.tr: Here it must be noted that, although according to the letter this obedience seems to be somewhat excepted from blind obedience, which cannot be done without sin, the Jesuits are nonetheless deprived of any power to inquire into the commands of their Superiors or to examine them thoroughly, and so they are bound to acknowledge as just and lawful everything enjoined on them, persuading themselves that all things are just; and they must allow themselves to be handled as if they were some corpse or an old man's staff. In this way no consideration of time, reason, or even common sense or outward judgement is taken into account. Clearly obedience is thus made perfect in its blindness in every way; this is according to the will of Ignatius, of whom Maffei, in his life, book 3, chapter 7, testifies: since he placed this virtue above all others in our Society, he said that nothing was so contrary to this praise as to examine the orders and commands of Superiors, which he called delay or rather arrogance; and he denied that anyone deserved the name of obedient unless he submitted not only his will but also his judgement to a lawful Superior. And he also says: by this wise and holy folly of blind obedience he trained his men, so that they might be readier for sudden and bold actions, sometimes even in matters that were feigned. Hence it follows that Superiors enjoin upon their inferiors nothing so wicked, seditious, dishonourable and horrible that they would dare to refuse it.

units.la: Altera causa est, quod se Regibus, Principibus aliisque Magistratibus politicis nullo prorsus fidelitatis sacramento, sed soli Papæ, supremo suo Induperatori obstrictos esse putant Iesuitæ, & propterea se in illos nullum læsæ Maiestatis crimen committere posse, etiamsi pro nutu ac libitu Papæ in illos insurgant. Cum autem origo, patria, incolatus, & ipse delicti locus, Iesuitas legibus regni & Reip. in quibus sunt, adstringat hoc ipso, quod Regibus & Principib. fidelitatem iurare recusant, fidè quidè, si fides dicenda est, Antichristo integram servat; sed cæcâ sua perfidia duplex rebellionis crimen incurrunt, omittendo id, ad quod origo & patria eos adstringit, et recusando id quod omnis magistratus iure ab ipsis poscit ac debet postulare. Non enim eb hoc minus Regibus & Magistratibus politicis obedientia civili parere debet, quod singulari voto Papæ obstricti sunt, sed eo ipso magis se Principibus suis perfidos & rebelles ostendunt: Nam illis non propter metum tantum, sed etiam propter conscientiam parendum est: Nec contraria sunt Deo obedire & Magistratui; sed sunt subordinata: neque Deo plene obtemperat, qui Magistratui debitam obedientiam negat. Cum itaque non ipsis tantum armis rebellio committatur, sed & perversa animi destinatione, qualicunque voluntatis significatione patefacta, malo consilio atque inobedientia: usurpata hæc ipsorum exemtio & immunitas rebellio est, nec magis ea à crimine læsæ Maiestatis Iesuitas liberari debere, ratio & disciplina publica dictat, etiamsi universalis esset, quam libertates legitimæ eximunt civitates eas, quæ vel ex privilegio, vel ex longa patientia exemtionem ab Imperatoribus recognoscunt, quæ nihilominus legitimi Regis mandatis rebellando læsæ Maiestatis crimen incurrere iurisperiti tradunt. Quis enim unquam audivit libertatis et exemtionis iure contineri impunitatem commissorum criminum? cum libertas sit facultas agendi quod velis, nisi iure aut vi prohibearis? An non intolerandâ insolentiam ipsi Iesuitæ, si modo ipsis aliquid mentis et iuris reliquum est, iudicarent, si quis ita argumentaretur: Verbi divini authoritas est super omnem humanam authoritatem : Ergo eiusdem Ministri super omnes Reges & Principes esse debent; Et Regibus ac Principibus nullum in eos ius est. Sed hinc Principes Christiani facile intelligunt, Antichristum Rom. non alio consilio Iesuitas tam liberalibus exemptionis privilegiis munire voluisse, quam ut impune per eos, velut excaecatos, omnia in alienis imperiis agere, turbare, rapere, Reges, Principes & Ordines ad nutum suum occidere possit.
units.tr: The second cause is that the Jesuits think they are bound by no oath of fidelity at all to kings, princes and other political magistrates, but only to the Pope, their supreme emperor; and therefore they believe they cannot commit any crime of treason against those rulers, even if at the nod and pleasure of the Pope they rise up against them. But since their origin, country, residence, and the very place of their offence bind the Jesuits to the laws of the kingdom and commonwealth in which they are, by the very fact that they refuse to swear fidelity to kings and princes, they keep faith, if faith is to be called faith, with Antichrist alone; but by their blind perfidy they incur a double crime of rebellion: by omitting what their origin and country bind them to, and by refusing what every magistrate may and ought rightly to demand from them. For it is not on that account the less true that they must render civil obedience to kings and political magistrates, because they are bound by a special vow to the Pope; rather, by that very fact they show themselves all the more faithless and rebellious towards their princes. For obedience is owed to them not only from fear but also from conscience; nor is it contrary to obey God and the magistrate, for they are subordinate; nor does he fully obey God who denies the due obedience to the magistrate. Since rebellion is committed not only with weapons, but also by a perverse intention of mind, made clear by some expression of will, by evil counsel and by disobedience, this claimed exemption and immunity of theirs is itself rebellion; and public reason and order dictate that the Jesuits should be no more freed from the crime of treason by it, even if it were universal, than cities are freed by the legitimate liberties which they hold, whether by privilege or by long-standing indulgence, and which they have acknowledged as exemption from the Emperors. Yet jurists teach that, by rebelling against the commands of a lawful king, such cities incur the crime of treason all the same. For who has ever heard that impunity for crimes committed is contained in the right of liberty and exemption? Since liberty is the power to do what you wish, unless you are prevented by right or by force. Would not the Jesuits themselves judge it intolerable insolence, if they still had any sense or right left in them, if someone argued thus: the authority of the divine Word is above every human authority; therefore its ministers ought to be above all kings and princes; and kings and princes have no right over them. But from this Christian princes easily understand that the Roman Antichrist had no other purpose in fortifying the Jesuits with such generous privileges of exemption than that he might, through them as through men blinded, do everything with impunity in foreign realms, disturb and plunder, and be able to put to death kings, princes and estates at his nod.

units.la: Tertia causa est, quod sentiunt, Reges & Principes, qui vel a Papa, vel a viris eruditis & gravibus, Iesuitis scilicet, vel communi populi opinione haeretici habentur, eo ipso neque Imperii, neque Regni, neque Principatus, neque alicuius civilis dignitatis capaces, sed diros tyrannos, & regio nomine indignos esse; atque ideo subditis omni obedientiae vinculo solutis, ipsos interficere atque e medio tollere licere: imo parricidia talium meritoria esse.
units.tr: The third cause is that they hold that kings and princes who are regarded as heretics, either by the Pope or by learned and serious men, that is, the Jesuits, or by the common opinion of the people, are by that very fact incapable of empire, kingdom, principality or any civil dignity, and are fearful tyrants unworthy of the royal name; and therefore, since their subjects are released from every bond of obedience, it is lawful for them to kill such rulers and remove them from the scene; indeed, the parricides of such men are meritorious.

units.la: Hic vero aliquis mihi objicere posset: Quicquid est in Iesuitis mali, vel nefariorum facinorum & scelerum, studiose conquisivisti, dissimulatis interim virtutibus, & ingenii dotibus, quibus isti homines excellunt. Non nego, non inficior. Sed, ut venena non dantur, nisi melle circumlita; sic & vitia non decipere possunt, nisi sub specie & pallio virtutum. Proinde nihil aliud est eruditio & doctrina Iesuitarum, quam mel, sub cuius dulcedine pestilentissimum virus occultant. Est enim haec non scripta, sed nata lex, quam non audivimus, legimus, didicimus, sed ex natura arripuimus, haurimus, expressimus, ut eos favore complectamur, qui modestia, humanitate, pietate & literis aliis praestant. Hoc, inquam, omnibus hominibus, qui non plane monstrosi & barbari sunt, a natura tributum est: nec ignorat id Satanas: mittit igitur istos angelos suos in omnes orbis partes, pallio humanitatis & modestiae contectos: calceis hypocriseos indutos: simulatione castitatis, & pietatis circumvestitos: inprimis vero pileo doctrinae & eruditionis mirifice exornatos. Sed nos fugere debemus pestem hanc: sub illa enim tam pulchra & elegante veste venenum latet, quavis peste pestilentius.
units.tr: Here someone might object to me: whatever evil or wicked deeds and crimes there are in the Jesuits, you have eagerly sought out, while passing over their virtues and the gifts of mind in which these men excel. I do not deny it, I do not disown it. But just as poisons are not given unless smeared with honey, so vices cannot deceive unless under the appearance and cloak of virtues. Therefore the learning and erudition of the Jesuits is nothing other than honey, under whose sweetness they hide the most pestilent poison. For this is not a written law but a born one, which we have not heard, read or learned, but have snatched, drawn and absorbed from nature itself, so that we embrace with favour those who excel in modesty, courtesy, piety and other literary gifts. This, I say, has been granted by nature to all men who are not utterly monstrous and barbarous; and Satan does not fail to know it. Therefore he sends his angels into every part of the world, covered with the cloak of courtesy and modesty, shod with the shoes of hypocrisy, clothed in the pretence of chastity and piety, and above all wonderfully adorned with the cap of teaching and learning. But we must flee this plague; for poison lies hidden under that so fair and elegant garment, more pestilent than any plague.

units.la: Deinde hoc quoque fuco sese defendere conantur, parricidia, caedes, proditiones, veneficia & similia nefanda facinora, a paucis sui Ordinis patrata, non toti Ordini imputanda esse.
units.tr: Next they also try to defend themselves with this pretence: that parricides, murders, treasons, poisonings and similar wicked deeds, committed by a few of their Order, should not be imputed to the whole Order.

units.la: Respondeo; Iesuiticarum Constitutionum apertissimis testimoniis, & communibus scriptis eorum offendi & probari potest; haec non unius alicuius Iesuitae opinionem aut facinus esse; sed communi ipsorum consilio & perpetuo proposito, velut principia quaedam & praecipua ad institutum Monarchiae Pontificis Romani promovendum praecepta adinventa, praemiaque ad animos hominum in eiusmodi scelera excitanda & exsequenda instigandos per Iesuitas constituta esse: Deinde, Iesuitas omnes ac singulos factis suis atrocissimis, ubi & quocunque tempore id Papae acceptum fore viri graves & eruditi existimant, illeque id vel solo nutu indicet, caeca obedientia quam promptissime comprobare paratos fuisse; & etiam nunc esse. Notum enim est, singulis Iesuitis motu animi proprio aliquid tentare sub poena inobedientiae prohibitum esse. Sic enim habet Constitutio eorum part. 9. c. 2. §. 1. Vnusquisque plenam in his ac liberam sui dispositionem Superiori, qui eum Christi loco dirigit, relinquat. Sed clarius hoc docetur Constitutione tertia capite trigesimo primo libro tertio de Vita Ignatii Loyolae, cuius haec sunt verba: Et ne quis utatur zelo, sed non secundum scientiam, proprii cujusque gradus indicium, & munerum fortitio & distributio tota sit in potestate Generalis aut praelati, qui quocunque tempore eligetur per nos, aut per ipsos, quos cum hac potestate substituimus. Deinde, cum inter Papam, velut caput universale, Generalem Ordinis; & ipsos Iesuitas æque arcta sit coniunctio; qualis inter caput & cætera membra est, absurdissimum foret, adscribere aliquid dexterae, quod à mente & intellectu primum suum motum habere negare vellemus. Hoc etiam expresse Regulæ Unionis & Conformationis mutuæ probant, quum nulli eorum vel scripto, vel verbo, vel facto quid in publicum proferre liceat, quod non ante legitime approbatum fuerit. An ergo Regum parricidia, regnorum eversiones, & si quid grave is & magis heroicum, ut ipsi appellant, reperiri possit, unius præpositro intempestivo iudicio permisseritis? Minime. Sic enim Constitutio eorum habet part. 3. c. 1. § 11. Idem sapiamus, idem quoad ejus fieri potest, dicamus omnes, juxta Apostolum. Doctrinae igitur differentes non admittantur, nec verbo in concionibus vel lectionibus publicis, nec scriptis libris, qui quidem edi non potuerunt in lucem sine approbatione & consensu Præpositi Generalis, imo & iudiciorum de rebus agendis diversitas, quae natter solet esse discordiae, & inimica unionis voluntatum, quantum fieri potest, evitari debet. Unio vero & conformitas mutua diligentissime curanda est, nec quae ei adversantur, permittenda, &c. Hinc vident Reges & Principes, veneficia, parricidia & incendia Iesuitarum non à propriis singulorum motibus, ut delicta malefactorum procedere, sicut isti hoc fraudium & scelerum suorum imperitis persuadere conantur; sed ab unanimi totius progeniei suae decreto & ab ipsius Superioris voluntate ac iudicio, cui motus animi proprios & cogitationes aperire debent; sic ut unius criminis omnes rei sint. Pontifex autem, velut caput omnium, præcipue. Sicuti etiam Bullam de Cœna Domini & Pontificum Brevia pro basi tuarum actionum omnium sumunt cooperantes in Spiritu. Nisi forte Regnum & Principum parricidia, Regnorumque & Rerumpublicarum eversiones, more suo, inter peccatula referre velint, quæ cuiusque arbitrio ac voluntati relicta sint. Hoc etiam factis suis & scriptis probant luculenter, ut suo loco pluribus indicatur. Neque furor hic tantum Iesuitas Gallos invasit, sed omnes eos quoque qui proditionum & rebellionum monita ex Iesuitica disciplina hauserunt, sive Iesuitæ, clerici, vel laici sint.
units.tr: I answer: from the most open testimonies of the Jesuit Constitutions and from their common writings it can be shown and proved that these are not the opinion or deed of any single Jesuit; rather, that by their common counsel and perpetual purpose, certain principal precepts, devised as foundations for advancing the monarchy of the Roman Pontiff, and rewards for stirring up and urging men's minds towards such crimes and their execution, have been established through the Jesuits. Further, that all and each of the Jesuits have been and still are prepared to confirm by blind obedience, as promptly as possible, their most atrocious deeds, whenever and at whatever time wise and learned men think they will be acceptable to the Pope, and he signifies this by a mere nod. For it is well known that it is forbidden to every Jesuit, under penalty of disobedience, to attempt anything on his own initiative. Thus their Constitution, part 9, chapter 2, §1, says: Let each one leave his whole and free disposition in these matters to the Superior, who directs him in the place of Christ. But this is taught more clearly by the Constitution in the third book of the Life of Ignatius Loyola, chapter thirty-one, whose words are these: And lest anyone use zeal, but not according to knowledge, the indication of each one's grade and the lot and distribution of offices shall be wholly in the power of the General or prelate, who shall be chosen at any time by us, or by those whom we substitute with this power. Further, since the bond between the Pope, as the universal head, and the General of the Order, and the Jesuits themselves, is as close as that between the head and the other members, it would be most absurd to attribute to the right hand something which we would deny has its first movement from the mind and understanding. The Rules of Union and of mutual conformity prove this expressly too, since no one is allowed to bring forward anything in public, whether in writing, word or deed, which has not first been lawfully approved. Would you then have entrusted the parricides of kings, the overthrow of kingdoms, and whatever else might be found grave and more heroic, as they call it, to the untimely judgement of one Superior? By no means. For their Constitution says, part 3, chapter 1, §11: Let us all think the same, and, as far as possible, say the same, according to the Apostle. Therefore differing doctrines are not to be admitted, neither in word in sermons or public lectures, nor in books written, which indeed cannot be brought to light without the approval and consent of the Father General; indeed, diversity of judgements about matters to be done, which is wont to be the source of discord and the enemy of union of wills, must as far as possible be avoided. Mutual union and conformity must be most diligently cultivated, and things opposed to it must not be permitted, etc. Hence kings and princes see that the poisonings, parricides and arsons of the Jesuits do not proceed from the individual impulses of each, like the crimes of wrongdoers, as these men try to persuade the inexperienced of their frauds and crimes; but from the unanimous decree of their whole brotherhood and from the will and judgement of its Superior, to whom they must disclose their personal impulses and thoughts; so that all are guilty of one crime. And the Pontiff, as head of all, especially so. Just as they also take the Bull of the Lord's Supper and the Pontifical Briefs as the basis of all their actions, cooperating in the Spirit. Unless perhaps they wish, in their usual way, to count the parricides of kings and princes, and the overthrow of kingdoms and commonwealths, among trifling sins, which are left to each one's judgement and will. They also prove this clearly by their deeds and writings, as will be shown in more detail in its place. Nor has this madness seized only the French Jesuits; it has also seized all those who have drawn the counsels of treason and rebellion from Jesuit discipline, whether they are Jesuits, clergy or laymen.

units.la: Campianus Iesuita in sua Epistola ad Consiliarios Reginæ Angliæ, Tre viris Anno 1583. excusa pag. 22. rotunde fatetur, Iesuitas OMNES in universo terrarum orbe fœdus, ad Reges hæreticos quovis modo tollendos iam pridem iniisse. Quod, inquit, ad Societatem nostram attinet, velim scias, OMNES nos, qui sumus de Societate Iesu, per totum terrarum orbem longe lateque diffusi, sanctum fœdus iniisse, vestras machinas facile superaturos, neque unquam desperaturos, quamdiu vel unus quispiam e nobis supererit. Et Philopater Cresuel monet, ita informandos quoscunque Catholicos, ut oblata cædis occasione, nullo impedimento se dimoveri patiantur.
units.tr: Campian the Jesuit, in his Letter to the Counsellors of the Queen of England, printed at Tre (Trier? — no: printed 1583), page 22, plainly admits that ALL the Jesuits throughout the whole world had long since entered into a covenant to remove heretical kings by whatever means. "As for our Society," he says, "I would have you know that ALL of us who belong to the Society of Jesus, spread far and wide throughout the whole world, have entered into a holy covenant: that we will easily overcome your machinations, and will never despair, as long as even one of us remains alive." And Philopater Cresuel advises that all Catholics be so instructed that, when an opportunity for slaughter is offered, they do not allow themselves to be deterred by any hindrance.

units.la: DE TYRANNIDE IESVITARVM ERGA EOS QVI à SOCIETATE EORVM DEFICIVNT.
units.tr: ON THE TYRANNY OF THE JESUITS TOWARDS THOSE WHO DEFECT FROM THEIR SOCIETY.

units.la: Apostatas factos & Ordinem Iesuitarum deserentes, in quocunque habitu contigerit inveniri, solent excommunicare, capere, retrahere, incarcerare, & si opus sit, auxilio brachii invocato, libere & licite invadere, captivos ducere, & pro arbitrio tractare. Talem tyrannidem & insidias Viennae exercuerunt Iesuitae in Kratzerum, qui ex Societate eorum egressus est; sed miranda ope iterum salvus sanguinariis illorum manus effugit. Cum etiam Hafenmullerus Ordinem eorum dilleruisset, omnibus modis insidias illi struxerunt, sed Dei auxilio in equentium manus quoque effugit. Et si qui fugam vel meditari fallem deprehenduntur, vel incarcerantur, vel igni, vel aquâ, vel fune, vel veneno tolluntur.
units.tr: Those who have become apostates and desert the Order of the Jesuits, wherever they happen to be found and in whatever dress, are customarily excommunicated, seized, dragged back, imprisoned, and, if need be, with the help of the secular arm invoked, freely and lawfully attacked, taken captive, and treated at will. The Jesuits at Vienna practised this sort of tyranny and these plots against Kratzer, who had left their Society; but by a wonderful help he again escaped the bloody hands of those men. When Hafenmüller had also renounced their Order, they laid snares for him in every way, but by the help of God he escaped the hands of his pursuers as well. And if anyone is caught even contemplating flight, he is either imprisoned, or removed by fire, water, rope, or poison.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA IESVITOGRAPHIA, IN QVA RHYTHMIS OMNIA FERE, QVAE HVCVSQVE DE IESVITIS DIXIMVS, COMPREHENDVNTVR.
units.tr: ON THE DOCTRINE OF JESUITOGRAPHY, IN WHICH ALMOST ALL THE THINGS WE HAVE HITHERTO SAID ABOUT THE JESUITS ARE COMPRISED IN RHYTHMS.

units.la: O Pulentas Civitates, Vbi sunt commoditates, Semper quaerunt isti patres. Claras aedes, bonum vinum, Bonum panem, bonum linum, Et pallium tempestivum. Indiae Galli, Capones, Turdi, lepores, pavones, Sunt horum patrum buccones. Pingui carne vitulina, Non bovina, sed ovina, Horum plena est coquina. Ambiunt ubique primum, Non admittunt peregrinum, Nec surgunt ad matutinum. Vivunt una lovialesDies agunt feriales. Quot optarent esse tales?In singulos speculantur, Et ubique perscrutantur, Quid vel agant vel loquantur. Confessores curiosi,Praedicatores verbosi, Et doctores fastuosi. Solliciti de gloriaSemper, & de pecunia, Et augenda familia. Sui summi laudatores, Aliorum despectores, Et omnium sunt Censores. Ex cohorte iuventutisIllos agunt blandimentis, In hos saeviunt tormentis. Qui nobiles, qui formosi, Divites, ingeniosi, Sunt Iesuitis pretiosi. Istos sibi praedestinantIn illos flagris ferinamExercent carnificinam. Si successio speratur, Haec societas laetatur, Et qui finquit, praedicatur. Si cui caligant oculi, Circumstant ripam lectuli
units.tr: O wealthy cities, where the comforts are, these fathers always go looking. Bright houses, good wine, good bread, good linen, and a cloak for the season. Indian fowl, capons, thrushes, hares, peacocks are the gullets of these fathers. Their kitchen is full of fat veal, not beef but mutton. Everywhere they court first, they admit no stranger, and they do not rise for matins. They live together in jovial fashion and spend their days as holidays. How many would wish to be such? They spy on each individual and pry everywhere into what he does or says. Curious confessors, verbose preachers, and haughty teachers. Always anxious for glory, and for money, and for enlarging the family. Praisers of themselves, despisers of others, and censors of all. From the cohort of youth they lure them with flattery; on these they rage with torments. Those who are noble, handsome, rich, or clever are precious to the Jesuits. These they predestine for themselves; on those they inflict butchery with the whip. If a succession is hoped for, this society rejoices, and the one who dies is praised. If someone's eyes grow dim, they gather round the edge of his bed.

units.la: Animam sunt habituri, Illi bonis potituri. Ad illos institutio Spectat vel substitutio, Vel delegata portio. Nam semper ob causam piam, Ad augendam familiam Detrahunt Falcidiam. O vulpinam sanctitatem! Praedicando charitatem Subducunt haereditatem. Sunt audaces ad petendū, Prompti sunt ad capiendum, Habiles ad succedendum Norunt blanda cantilena Cum doctrina Christiana, Allicere aliena. Heus tu bone confitere, Sed o nostri miserere, Si salutem vis habere. Nil habemus ut videtis, Date nobis quae habetis, Centuplum accipietis. Si quem contigit donasse. Redi saepe, semper race, Absolvo te, vade in pace. Hi periti mendicantes, Sunt quasi nil habentes, Et omnia possidentes. Eminent inter clericos, Imperant inter laicos, Excellunt inter aulicos. Heu quot ex istis patribus Spretis spiritualibus, Incumbunt saecularibus! Martem norunt animare, Et tumultus suscitare, Inter Reges, & sedare. In occulto multa tractant: Quae vel ipsum Papam celant Quid non istae vulpes tentant Multa mere ridicula, Nobis velut oracula Sua iactant miracula. Versipelles, gloriosi Victores, seditiosi
units.tr: They are going to have his soul and will take hold of his goods. To them belong the institution, or the substitution, or the delegated portion. For always, for a pious cause, to increase the family, they cut off the Falcidian portion. O foxy sanctity! Preaching charity, they remove the inheritance. They are bold in seeking, prompt in taking, skilled in succeeding. They know how, with a smooth song and Christian doctrine, to entice others' goods. "Hey you, good man, confess, but have mercy on us, if you wish to have salvation. We have nothing, as you see; give us what you have, and you will receive a hundredfold. If anyone has given, come back often, always again; I absolve you, go in peace." These skilled beggars are as if having nothing, and yet they possess everything. They stand out among the clergy, rule among the laity, and excel among courtiers. Alas, how many of these fathers, having spurned spiritual things, devote themselves to worldly ones! They know how to stir up war and raise tumults among kings, and how to calm them. In secret they manage much, which they hide even from the Pope himself. What do these foxes not attempt? Many utterly ridiculous things, and, like oracles to us, they boast of their miracles. Turncoats, boasters, victors, seditious men...

units.la: Iesuitae, daemon, angeli. Hi, vel ille morituri
units.tr: Jesuits, demons, angels. These, whether living or dying...

units.la: Sunt isti religiosi. Si illos petunt potentes,Et opibus affluentes,Sedes habent diligentes. Si quid quaerant carcerati, Et omnibus spoliati,Dicunt, sumus occupati. Non haec IESVS vos docuit, Cuius nomen si placuit,Cur & vitam non induit? Inter greges afflictorumPrimus egit ille Chorum,Turbam vitans superborum. At Iesuitae non hos greges,Sed solos sectantur Reges,Obsis & facturi leges. IESVS peram & sacculumDuxit esse ridiculumVelle ferre Apostolum.At hi quamvis in MammonamDe cathedra multa tonant,Semper ipsis aera sonant. Domus, agros, uniones,Aureorum millnionesHabent isti sancti patres,
units.tr: They are religious men. If powerful men seek them out, and those abounding in wealth, they have their diligent seats. If prisoners seek anything, or those despoiled of everything, they say, "We are occupied." Did Jesus not teach you this? If his name has pleased you, why did he not also put on such a life? Among the flocks of the afflicted, he first led the chorus, avoiding the crowd of the proud. But the Jesuits do not pursue these flocks; they pursue only kings, intending to make laws for them. Jesus thought it ridiculous to carry a wallet and purse; the Apostle did not wish to bear them. Yet these men, although they thunder from the chair against Mammon, always have the bronze ringing for them. Houses, fields, pearls, millions of gold coins: these holy fathers have.

units.la: IN OFFICINA
units.tr: IN THE WORKSHOP

units.la: Iesuitica
units.tr: Jesuitical

units.la: Euge praeco quin exclamas?Quis quis mores novos amas,Quisque in aula vis amari,Et a vulgo collaudari? Si magistros quaeris doctos,Et praestantes probe coctos,Ex Ignatii culina,In hac nostra Officina. Quaeris merum Ostentatorem,Et nugarum venditorem;Vin' tu doctum sycophantam,Et peritum Halophantam; Vin' tu suavem palpatorem,Adulicumque assentatorem? En tibi hunc nostrum Cottonem:Eget vel si vis Lenonem. Vis virum tibi gloriosum?Animisque superciliosum;Hat est si habes Bellarminum, Ipsi mavis Possevinum; Idem Delrio hoc praestabit,Et Gretzerus pulcre dabit, Cum hoc fastu dignitatis Iunge votum paupertatis, Et decus humilitatis. Habent opes Venetorum, Habent fastum Hispanorum, Imperium Romanorum. Tanquam sancti adorantur, Tanquam Reges dominantur, Tanquam fures deprædantur. Dominantur temporale, Dominantur spiritale, Dominantur omnia male. Hos igitur Iesuitas, Nebulones, Hypocritas Fuge, si cœlica quæras. Vita namque Christiana Abhorret ab hac doctrina Tanquam ficta & insana. Ergo Vos qui cum Iesuitis Non ite cum Iesuitis.
units.tr: Well done, herald! Why do you not cry out? Who is it, whoever you are, that loves new manners, and who wants to be loved at court and praised by the common crowd? If you seek learned masters, and men well and thoroughly cooked, come from Ignatius's kitchen, into this workshop of ours. Do you seek a sheer show-off and seller of trifles? Or do you want a learned sycophant and a skilled trickster? Do you want a smooth flatterer and a fawning toady? Here is our Cotton for you; or, if you like, a pimp. Do you want a man of glory for yourself, proud in spirit? If you have Bellarmine, you would rather have Possevinus. Delrio will provide the same, and Gretser will supply it finely. Join to this pride of dignity the vow of poverty and the honour of humility. They have the wealth of the Venetians, the pomp of the Spaniards, and the empire of the Romans. They are worshipped as saints, they rule as kings, and they plunder as thieves. They rule over temporal things and over spiritual things; they rule over everything, and badly. So flee these Jesuits, these scoundrels, these hypocrites, if you seek heavenly things. For the Christian life shrinks from this doctrine as false and mad. Therefore you who go with the Jesuits, do not go with the Jesuits.

units.la: ICINAM
units.tr: WORKSHOP

units.la: icam. Nec quisquam nostrum his sudabit. Vin' tu doctus prædicari, Et Centones concinnare Ex alienis tam latenter, Ut de cuncti admirentur? Tunc imitare Maldonatum, Vel quemvis illâ stirpe natum. Carpe viros, carpe mores, Quorum tu decerpis flores. Vin' virum loquentissimum, Mendacem mendacissimum, Os maledicentissimum; Et detractorem pessimum, Qui ampullata verba fundat Et scelerum theatrum condat, Omnes bonos denigrando Omnes pessimos laudando: Cloacam convitiorum, Baratrum mendaciorum: En furiosus & insanus, Solus dabit hæc Scribanus. Si nova quæris ex Inferno, Tt
units.tr: Nor will any of us sweat over these things. Do you want to be a learned man, to be publicised, and to stitch together patchwork from other men's writings so artfully that everyone marvels at you? Then imitate Maldonatus, or anyone born of that stock. Pluck at men, pluck at their manners, from whom you pick the flowers. Do you want the most eloquent of men, the most lying of liars, with the most slanderous mouth, and the worst defamer, who pours out bombastic words and builds a theatre of crimes, blackening all good men and praising all the worst? A sewer of insults, a pit of lies: behold a raving and insane man, and Scribanus alone will supply these. If you seek news from hell, (…)

units.la: Non opus est nunc averno, Nam quivis DæmoniacusCottoni est vatidicus. Tu qui adís officinamAudi nostram disciplinam: Si piget multum laborareCum velís laute víctitare, Confer te ad nostras caulas, Faxo spernas Regum aulas. Nos nihil vile obsonamus: Austerum vinum non potamus, Non libet nobis mendicare, Nudisq; plantis oberrare, Nec nos duriter cubamus, Plumam mollem nos amamus: Odimus mendicitatem, Dum crepamus paupertatem. Pauperes quidem nos amamus, Sed perraró hos visitamus: Divitum lectis assidemus, Vbi est, unde quid speremus: Dum narrant quantum peccaverint, Nos quærímus quid legaverint: Scribe fili nos hæredes, Lega fundum, dona ædes, Nos pro te supplicabimusEt requiem cantabimus. Semper cura est de culina, Hæc est nostra disciplina, Quid tu qui hic substitisti, An quod quæris invenisti? Dic in aurem, si profariTimes, noli me celare; Doceri vis æquivocare, Absq; culpa peierare, Vis mentiendo non mentiri, Et in arte hac erudiri: Lege nostros Aphorismos, Et contortos syllogismos. Novi: quæris percussorem, Vel murorum suffossorem, Qui nôrit sicam intentare, Vel venenum temperare: Intra nostrum penetrale, Quamvis nil hic prostet tale, Producet tamen noster penus, Omne sicariorum genus. Non nos ipsi hoc præstamus, Assassinos subornamus, Magnis promissis oneratos, Atque ad quidvis animatos. Præcipui nostri RectoresHuius sunt artis Professores.
units.tr: There is no need now for the lower world, for any demoniac is a prophet for Cotton. You who enter our workshop, hear our discipline: if it grieves you to labour much while you want to live in luxury, betake yourself to our folds, and I shall make you scorn the courts of kings. We buy nothing cheap: we do not drink sour wine, we do not care to beg and wander with bare feet, nor do we lie down hard; we love a soft feather bed. We hate beggary, while we bewail poverty. We indeed love the poor, but we very rarely visit them. We sit beside the beds of the rich, where there is something from which we may hope for something. While they recount how much they have sinned, we seek what they have bequeathed. "Write us down as heirs, my son; leave an estate, give houses." We will pray for you and sing a requiem. The concern is always for the kitchen; this is our discipline. What about you, who have stopped here: have you found what you were looking for? Tell me in my ear, if you are afraid to speak; do not hide it from me. Do you want to be taught to equivocate, to commit perjury without guilt, to lie without seeming to lie, and to be trained in this art? Read our Aphorisms and our twisted syllogisms. I know: you are looking for an assassin, or a digger under the walls, one who knows how to aim a dagger or mix poison. Within our inner sanctum, though nothing of that sort is on display here, our store will still produce every kind of murderer. We do not ourselves perform these deeds; we suborn assassins, loaded with great promises and spurred on to anything. Our leading Rectors are the professors of this art.

units.la: Hi submittunt proditores, Hi subornant percussores, Excitant seditiones, Nutriunt rebelliones.
units.tr: They send out traitors, they suborn murderers, they stir up sedition, they foster rebellions.

units.la: Modo iubeat RomanusVel sic postulet Hispanus; Servit his, cor, sermo, manus.
units.tr: If the Roman orders it, or if the Spaniard so demands, heart, tongue and hand serve them.

units.la: Omnis iam terra nostris scatetQua fidelis Orbis patet, Vbiq; aut iam succrevimus, Aut iam sementem sevimus.
units.tr: Now every land swarms with our men, wherever the faithful world extends; and everywhere we have either already grown up, or already sown the seed.

units.la: Hispania nobis genetrix, Italia nobis obstetrixGallia nobis mammam dedit, Atq; hucusq; victum praebet.
units.tr: Spain is our mother, Italy our midwife; Gaul has given us her breast, and up to now provides our food.

units.la: Hinc Germania late patens, Et Polonia fructu scatens, Noster fundus, noster penus, Hic augescit nostrum genus.
units.tr: Hence Germany, spreading far and wide, and Poland, teeming with fruit: our estate, our store; here our race increases.

units.la: Hæc alte præco gloriatur. Hos qui profectus admiratur, Is certe vetus dictum nescit, Quod mala herba cito crescit.
units.tr: The herald boasts loudly of these things. Whoever marvels at these advances surely does not know the old saying, that bad weeds grow quickly.

units.la: Sed iam accurrunt mercatores, Nondum spernuntur mali mores, Sceleri dum cedunt honores, Nunquam deerunt hic emtores.
units.tr: But now the merchants come running; the bad morals are not yet despised; as long as honours yield to crime, there will never be lack of buyers here.

units.la: ALIVD.
units.tr: ANOTHER.

units.la: Veni Rythme mi dilecte, Surge versus nunc neglecte, Quondam lepos antiquorum, Pange labes seductorum.
units.tr: Come, my dear Rhyme, rise up, you Verse now neglected, once the charm of the ancients; sing the stain of the seduced.

units.la: Fratres carpe Iesuitas, Et perversos hypocritas, Qui pastore gloriantur, Cuius gregem populantur.Sancto gaudentes nomine, Sed cuius carent omine, Non sunt Christi satellites, Sed Antichristi velites:
units.tr: Brethren, attack the Jesuits and the perverse hypocrites, who boast of the Shepherd whose flock they plunder. Rejoicing in a holy name but lacking its sign, they are not the attendants of Christ but the skirmishers of Antichrist.

units.la: Ævi nostri Legulei, Renascentes Pharizæi, Quæ perversa sunt probantes,Et quæ recta sugillantes.
units.tr: Lawyers of our age, reborn Pharisees, approving what is perverse and censuring what is right.

units.la: Christi legem ore sonant,Iesu fidem verbis tonant, Sed dictis facta dissonant, Nec sunt quod esse simulant. Iesus dabat cunctis pacem, edhi subdunt bellis facem, Hi principum sicarij, rbisq; incendiarij. Iesus regna stabilivit, egi Regis obedivit, Cæsari tributum pendit, um quid iuris sit ostendit. Hi regnorum proditores, tq; legum fraudatores, Reges volunt iugulare, sic plebem subiugare. Sentit magnus Rex Francorum tum sepło labiorum; Præsens læthum vix evasit, quod hic sacer ordo suasit. Rex Anglorum est documento, um Magnatum Parlamento. Vnoq; ictu destinati eci, Rex, Regina, Nati. Horum grex hoc adornarat, Garnetus comprobarat, Cum Gerardo, cum Greenvvello, cum perfido Cresvvello, Omnes falli proditores, liferorum seductores Qui quod pijs præparârunt se & suos derivarunt. Dum Romano famulantur, Hispanis adulantur. Nil nisi lites quærunt e bellis bella serunt. Testis bellum Hungarorum, estis lites Polonorum Et Ruffotum dira pestis argus nostris dictis testis. Nam cur aulas frequentatis, ures principum captatis,
units.tr: They sound Christ's law with their mouths and thunder his faith with their words, but their deeds clash with their speech, and they are not what they pretend to be. Jesus gave peace to all, but these men kindle the torch of war; they are the assassins of princes and the incendiaries of cities. Jesus established kingdoms; he obeyed the king, paid tribute to Caesar, and showed what is right. These men are betrayers of kingdoms and defrauders of laws; they want to cut the throats of kings and so bring the people under their yoke. The great King of the French felt it from their lips; present, he barely escaped the death which this holy order urged. The King of the English is an example, along with the Parliament of the nobles. With one blow they were destined to kill the King, the Queen and their children. Their flock had devised this, and Garnet approved it, together with Gerard, with Greenwell, and with the treacherous Creswell. All were traitors, seducers of the young, who turned upon themselves and their own what they had prepared for the godly. While they serve Rome, they flatter Spain. They seek nothing but quarrels, and from wars they sow more wars. Witness the war of the Hungarians, you are witnesses to the strife of the Poles, and the dire plague of the Ruthenians; let these be a proof of our words. For why do you frequent the courts and seek to catch the ears of princes?

units.la: SUPPLICATIONES
units.tr: SUPPLICATIONES

units.la: D PAVLVM V. PONTIFICEM
units.tr: To Pope Paul V

units.la: torem Aug. Reges Franciæ & Hispaniæ pro Reformatione, seu tione ad primum nis Iesu
units.tr: ...the Emperor Augustus; the Kings of France and Spain, for the Reformation, or ... to the first ... of Jesus

units.la: IAM omnia quæ ab initio huius Trium Vimus, cum ita se habeant, ut hab Nisi ut dolos necteretis, Et secreta proderetis? Iesus docet ignorantes, Et attollit laborantes; Ignorantes isti incantant, Laborantesæ̨ supplantant. Ignoranti nugas vendunt, Imprudenti rete tendunt, Tam nummorum appetentes, Quam salutis negligentes. Hinc moribundos fascinant Et cor aegrorum lancinant, Non ut ferant levamentum, Sed ut auferant argentum. Sic professi paupertatem, Et crepantes egestatem, Arcas suas implevere Opibus, quas corrasere. Iesus non vult superbire Suos nec faštu prurire, Sed suadens humilitatem Omnes docet lenitatem. Quid istis arrogantius? Quid istis petulantius? Dum detrectant alienis, Sua laudant buccis plenis. Bonosæ̨ calumniantur, Dum de bonis mutuantur, Neve advertant hi qui legunt, Probris sua furta tegunt. Gratis legunt, gratis docent, Aurum legunt, viro nocent: Cum promittant cuncta gratis Nulla merces ipsis satis. Vt a luce lucus dictus, Et ut homo est, homo pictus: Sic a Iesu, Iesuita, Quem, si sapis, semper vita.
units.tr: Now we have seen all that has happened since the beginning of this ... Since things stand as they do, did you not weave deceits and betray secrets? Jesus teaches the ignorant and lifts up the labouring; these men charm the ignorant and trip up the labouring. They sell trifles to the ignorant and spread nets for the imprudent, so eager for money, so careless of salvation. Hence they bewitch the dying and tear the hearts of the sick, not to bring relief but to carry off silver. So they profess poverty and bewail their want, yet they have filled their coffers with the wealth they scraped together. Jesus does not want his people to be proud or to itch with pride, but by urging humility he teaches gentleness to all. What is more arrogant than these? What more insolent? While they disparage others, they praise themselves with full cheeks. They slander good men while borrowing from their goods; lest those who read should notice, they cover their thefts with insults. They read for free, they teach for free, yet they read gold and harm the man: though they promise everything for nothing, no reward is enough for them. As lucus is named from lux, and a man is a painted figure, so from Jesus comes Jesuit, whom, if you are wise, is life for ever.

units.la: THEOPHILI EVGENII
units.tr: Theophilus Eugenius

units.la: ROM. ITEMQVE AD IMPERA- TORES, Albaniae, omnesque Principes Christianos ... redintegratione & restaura- tione ... institutum Ordinem Iesuitarum.
units.tr: To the Roman Emperors, the Albanians, and all Christian Princes ... concerning the renewal and restoration ... of the Order of Jesuits instituted.
