units.la: Tractatus Iesuitici hucusque commemorarent certissime, non immerito Theophi-
units.tr: Treatises of the Jesuits, which up to now they would most certainly have commemorated, not undeservedly Theophi-

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: Concerning Doctrine

units.la: lus Eugenius quidam in sua PROTOCATASTASI vehementer queritur, hanc praesentem Societatem, ut hodie se habet, a prima sua institutione in peius subinde ruisse, & in aliam prorsus declinasse: utque reformetur & in pristinum statum reducatur supplicitèr petit. Respublica, inquit, Romana a Cosulibus ad Decemviros, rursus a Decemviris ad Consules redijt; ab uno Dynastia Athenienses excusserunt jugum, ut sibi jui rursus praeessent. Hunc recursum praesens Societas Iesuitarum exquirit, quousque (inclamant Patres) exulem patiemur sacram Themidem? quousque a nobis peregrinabitur prima Societas? verine sumus an affecti Iesuitae? si veri, cur primis dissimiles sumus? una erat prima Societas, unis votis, una solennitate, una prosessione, nunc duplex: illi profitentur se professos, & eminent; isti diffitentur, & subjacent: illi solennes sunt religiosi, isti simplices. Duces sunt illi, & regunt: Coadjutores sunt isti, & serviunt: illi coluntur ut domini, isti despiciuntur ut subditi; habentur illi in Collegijs ut Senatores, isti ut plebei; illis obligatur, ac debet seipsam, Societas; isti seipsos obligant Societati, nec tamen illis obligatur Societas, nihil promittit: suaviter illi monentur ut socij, si quid peccent, severe dimittuntur isti, ut ascripti clientes, si quid aberrent; splendide illi in congregationibus vivunt, & lautis excipiuntur mensis, parce isti, in collegijs, & communibus pascuntur cibis: comoda ferunt illi viatica, dum peregre mittuntur, equis et rhedis feruntur, isti subsidiaria pecuniola, & aere leves, ire jubentur, sarcinulis onusti, & pedites itinera carpunt: si quid facile ac molle est, hoc illis molitur, ac mollitur, isti si quid durum ac difficile, cudendum ac tundendum imponitur. Ubi prima Societas? in qua eodem omnes religionis gradu ac voto, Professi, mirifica ac singulari charitate intenti, tunc se beatos putabant, cum suis fratribus pauperiores, ac dejectiores essent, cum durioribus clavis in cruce confixi, cum sitim, frigus, inediam, nuditatem, ad fratres redimendos perferrent? Abijstis in caelum Ignatij, Xaverij, qui vestris corporibus infensi, aspera quaeque patiebamini ut fratribus vestris, commodo effetis. Alijs praecipiebatis temporata, ac non difficilia, vobis importuna, ac vix ferenda tenebatis, nunquam hilares, nusquam contenti, nisi in laboribus supra modum, semper orantes, semper attenti, ne vestri fratres supra modum urgerentur. Quis nunc in Societate tutus? si superiore adversum habueris? quis tranquillus degere potest, si tempestates excitet Rector? quis recta ire si cornu ferit, non habet collegam superior, abrogata est Collateralis potestas, qui sevientem poterat coercere, suffragiis vis omnis adempta, omnis potestas, in Dynastia superiorum includitur, nihil consultores ratum faciunt, verbo ac mente superioris stant & cadunt omnia. Si vafer sit superior, quem non deludet? si praeceps, quem non offendet? si tectus, cui non cavendus? si levis, quem non avertet? nullus excandescat, nemini convitium faciat, justis ac bonis sua sit laus, virtutem amplector & suspicio, vitijs securim injicio. Quis superiores aliquos nesciat, hac summa potestate abuti posse? cur tot querelae emergerent? cur tot supplices libelli? cur tam crebrae vituperationes? cur tam multorum hominum frementibus iris e Societate abacti? quos tamen omnes Ordines amant, & optimi quique in caelum laudibus vehunt: cur tot accusationes? Si non jam alii quid rei tenerentur, si modestiae fines nulli transilijssent? Quid audentes facit? impunitas. Quid praepotentes? Dictatura. quid securos? caeterorum infirmitas. quid fortes? impe rium, quid inclementes? pertinacia; quid imperterritos? enervata suffragia. Nihil in prima Societate simile visum est, cum suffragijs cohiberentur superiores, nihil incompositum, aut iniquum Patres animadverterint. Si quid imminueret periculi, conspirantibus animis e vestigio propellebant: si quem vexatum conspiceret, non sinebant extrema pati, ereptum molestijs paci restituebant suae, & religioni servabant, aequa justitiae lance ponderabant omnia, nulli, si non propria stultitia procrearet, malum accersebatur. Haec inter privatos parietes.
units.tr: Theophilus Eugenius, in his PROTOCATASTASIS, complains bitterly that this present Society, as it now stands, has from its first institution steadily declined for the worse and turned altogether aside into something else, and he humbly petitions that it be reformed and restored to its former state. The Roman republic, he says, passed from consuls to decemvirs, and again from decemvirs back to consuls; the Athenians shook off the yoke of a single dynast so that they might once more be ruled by their own laws. The present Society of Jesuits seeks this same return. How long, the Fathers cry out, shall we suffer holy Themis to be exiled? How long shall the first Society be a stranger among us? Are we truly Jesuits, or are we only counterfeits? If we are genuine, why are we so unlike the first? The first Society was one: one vow, one solemnity, one profession. Now it is double. The one sort profess themselves professed and stand out; the other disclaim it and are subordinate. The one sort are solemn religious, the other simple. The one sort are leaders and rule; the other are coadjutors and serve. The one sort are honoured as lords, the other despised as subjects. In the colleges the one sort are regarded as senators, the other as commoners. The Society binds itself to the one sort, and they owe it their whole selves; the others bind themselves to the Society, yet the Society is not bound to them and promises them nothing. The one sort are gently admonished as companions if they err; the others are severely dismissed, like hired clients, if they go astray. The one sort live splendidly in their residences and are welcomed at well-stocked tables; the others are fed sparingly in the colleges and common refectories. The one sort are given comfortable travelling allowances when they are sent abroad and are carried on horses and in carriages; the others, given a small sum for their expenses and light of money, are ordered to go on their way, loaded with little baggage, and make their journeys on foot. If anything is easy and soft, it is devised for the one sort and they are softened by it; if anything is hard and difficult, it is laid upon the others to be hammered and beaten. Where is the first Society? In it all professed members, of the same religious rank and vow, given over to a wonderful and singular charity, thought themselves blessed when they were poorer and more abject than their brothers, when they were nailed to the cross with harsher nails, when they endured thirst, cold, hunger and nakedness to redeem their brothers. You have departed to heaven, Ignatius and Xavier, who, hostile to your own bodies, bore every harsh thing for the sake of your brothers and were content with little. You prescribed what was moderate and not difficult for others, while you regarded what was burdensome to yourselves and scarcely bearable as your own lot; you were never cheerful, never content, except in labours beyond measure, always praying, always watchful lest your brothers be pressed beyond measure. Who now is safe in the Society if he has offended his superior? Who can live in quiet if the Rector stirs up storms? Who can walk straight if the superior strikes with his horn? The superior has no colleague; the collateral authority has been abolished, the power that could restrain a raging superior has been taken away, all the force of votes has been stripped off, and all power is enclosed within the will of the superiors. Consultors make nothing binding; everything stands or falls by the word and mind of the superior. If the superior is crafty, whom will he not deceive? If headlong, whom will he not offend? If secretive, whom should one not beware of? If fickle, whom will he not turn away? Let no one grow angry, let no one reproach anyone; let praise be given to the just and good, I embrace virtue and esteem it, I lay the axe to vices. Who does not know that some superiors can abuse this supreme power? Why did so many complaints arise? Why so many humble petitions? Why such frequent reproaches? Why were so many men, raging with anger, driven out of the Society, men whom all Orders nevertheless love, and whom all the best people raise to heaven with praise? Why so many accusations? Would not others already have been held to account for something, if they had not overstepped the bounds of moderation? What does impunity make the bold do? What does dictatorship make the overbearing do? What does the weakness of others make the secure do? What does imperium make the strong do? What does obstinacy make the harsh do? What does the enfeebling of votes make the fearless do? Nothing like this was seen in the first Society, when superiors were restrained by votes, and the Fathers noticed nothing disorderly or unjust. If any danger threatened, with minds united they drove it off at once; if they saw anyone harassed, they did not allow him to suffer extremes, but rescued him from troubles and restored him to his own peace and kept him in his religious life; they weighed everything on the even scale of justice, and no evil was brought upon anyone except that which his own folly produced. These things happened within private walls.

units.la: Quid si externa referam? si ausim compellare Xaverium ut sanctitate sua pudorem injiciat? nihil de paupertate, nihil de laboribus, nihil de manfuetu[?] dine, nihil de religioso in socios amore, nihil de visceribus charitatis, quae omnia in illo commendatissima erant. Sed audiant, quis erga Episcopos fuerit, nonne ut Subditus obsequebatur? nonne prehensabat genua, nonne singulari cum modestia facultatem poscebat praedicandi verbum Dei? nonne socijs hoc praescribebat, ut Episcoporum dicto audientes essent, ut nihil nisi probantib. ac benedicentib. illis aggrederetur, cum omni hominum genere simplices ac sinceri viveret? summos & imos, aeque, tenues, divites, nobiles ac ignobiles, pari charitatis lege, ad viam salutis, ad regnum Dei adhortarentur? Nunc vero quis Episcopis honor redditur a Iesuitis? urgent summum Pontificem, ut ab eorum ditione vindicentur, jura nova extorquent, quibus, ajunt, se sine Episcoporum approbatione ac benedictione concendere pulpita, conciones habere, suscipere poenitentes ad absolutionem peccatorum, ampla cum legatione ac potestate solvenda ab Episcopis crimina dissolvunt, Pontificium exercent poenitentiae tribunal. Clemens VIII. providentissimus Pontifex, hoc satis intelexit, cum societati prohibuit in Italia, ut ne ulli ex socijs confessiones exciperent, sine suorum Episcoporum facultate, nulli de casibus ab Episcopo reservatis absolverent, nulli per Episcopum excommunicatos Ecclesiae communioni redderent. Privilegia vel revocavit, vel diminuit. Quomodo subsunt Episcopis? quos ut patres ac judices suos recusant? quibus occludunt januas, si mores explorare, si domesticae disciplinae ordinem introspicere, si monere velint, si emendare, si ad suam aedem pro majori cultu divini numinis advocent, si uti illis ad divina ministeria cogirent; Novit illustris admodum ac reverendus Episcopus Carpentoratensis, Caponius, Florentinus quoties appellaverit suos Iesuitas, ut cum novos Sacerdotes consecraret, aut sollemnioribus festis sacrum faceret, sibi praesentes habitu clericali assisterent, quoties id se non posse objecerint, petenti nuncium remiserint.
units.tr: What if I relate external matters? What if I dared to call upon Xavier, so that his holiness might put them to shame? Nothing about his poverty, nothing about his labours, nothing about his meekness, nothing about his religious love for his companions, nothing about the bowels of charity, all of which were most commendable in him. But let them listen to how he behaved towards the bishops. Did he not obey them as a subject? Did he not embrace their knees? Did he not, with singular humility, ask for permission to preach the word of God? Did he not prescribe to his companions that they should obey the bishops' word, and that they should undertake nothing except with the bishops' approval and blessing? Did he not live among all kinds of people in simplicity and sincerity, exhorting high and low alike, the lowly and the rich, the noble and the ignoble, by the same law of charity, to the way of salvation and the kingdom of God? But now what honour is shown to the bishops by the Jesuits? They press the supreme Pontiff to free them from the bishops' authority; they extort new rights by which, they say, they may mount pulpits, preach sermons, and receive penitents for the absolution of sins without the approval and blessing of the bishops. With a wide commission and power to absolve, they loosen crimes that ought to be loosed by bishops, and they set up a papal tribunal of penance. Clement VIII, the most provident Pontiff, understood this well enough when he forbade the Society in Italy that any of its members should hear confessions without the permission of their own bishops, or absolve in cases reserved to the bishop, or restore to the communion of the Church those excommunicated by a bishop. He either revoked or diminished their privileges. How do they submit to the bishops, whom they refuse to acknowledge as their fathers and judges? They shut the doors against them, if they wish to examine their morals, to look into the order of domestic discipline, to admonish, to correct, or to summon them to their church for greater worship of the divine majesty, or to use them for the divine ministries. The most illustrious and reverend Bishop of Carpentras, Caponius of Florence, knows how often he called upon his Jesuits to stand present in clerical dress when he consecrated new priests or celebrated the mass on more solemn feasts, and how often they objected that they could not, and sent back a messenger to him when he asked.

units.la: Sicut prima Societas unam charitatem, unam professionem, unam vitae sanctitatem, ita unam Ecclesiae sanctae consuetudinem, unam Episcoporum observantiam, unam cum omnibus religiosis unitatem ac conjunctionem, jus unum religionis amplectebatur. Quis non clamet Iesuitis? induimini Christum, sicut induerunt patres vestri, vivite recti ac boni, eundem famite spiritum. Concionamini, gratissimum est, quis non vos admonet? consolaminii poenitentes, quis non laudet? adolescentes instituitis, sanctè & egregiè factum: haereticos confunditis? pergite, vincetis, Deus pugnabit praelia vestra. Sed quis domesticae vestrae ambitionis consilia probet: quam ut fulciretis Coadjutorium Sacerdotum gradum, praeter Ignatij mentem compositis, quos vestrae Societatis levis armatura milites, & quasi velites, facile sacramento exolvendos de industria facitis, ut per illorum tenuitatem, abjectionem, conditionem denique instabilem professionem erigatis? Cur vestram Societatem comminuitis? cur tot indoctis vel imperitis obscuram redditis? cur Ecclesiae Dei hujusmodi religiosos paratis, quos vestrae professionis indignos judicatis? Cur non omnes vestros Sacerdotes, ut poteritis, ut commodissimum ac facillimum vobis sit, ad unam professionem, iisdem armis, eadem virtute, eadem Scientia vià instituitis? dornatis? cur Pij V. de hac re decretum extinxistis? cur primorum patrum vestrorum exemplum contemnitis? qui ut omnium animos religioni connecterent, eadem studia, eadem amoris ac professionis vincula, proponebant, qui nullum ferre poterant, quem non donum ac factum ad hanc unam votorum solennitatem comprobassent. Hinc ardor omnium communis, unum opus, una contentio, ut Christo frugem aliquam facerent, ut Ecclesiae non infructuose operarentur. Nemo se ipsum, nemo professionem illam vestram dissimulatione, contentione, & mirificis illis artibus venabatur. Non hoc erat adhuc territorium, quo integrae virtutis, & eruditionis religiosi, non juste à Superioribus deiiciuntur, si quid miserabile persuaserit invidia, vel impos mentis alicujus exarserit impotentia. Quid tam invisum in prima Societate, quam supremus ipse paucorum dominatus? qui ad dignitates provecti, cum ex voluntatis suae ductu omnia meditentur, & faciant, eos tantum promoveant, qui ad ipsorum mores sese totos componunt, qui ne transversum quidem unguem à nutu discedere, qui placere, qui capiti pulvinum subijcere, qui cubicula quasi beatas sedes invisere, qui omnia clientium officia noverint exhibere? quid minus religiosum? quam velle coli? quid tam factum ad fastum, quam encomia, acraomata, libenter audire, sui observantes extollere, honores honoribus remunerari? odia malefactis explere? ultione delectari? Quid aliud videre licet in aula Principum? quas alias artes didicerunt ij, de quibus Christus ait, Qui in domibus Regum sunt? Resumite suffragia, unus regat Senatus religiosus, non unus, sed unitas Patrum, non una, sed unanimis voluntas? plus vident oculi, quam oculus, plures manus fortiores: Spiritualis ista tam absoluta potestas in sola fede Apostolica & Ecclesia a Deo constituta est. Nihil moveret Rector, nihil tentaret ab aequitate dissentaneum, nihil quod grave esset, sociis imponeret, si sociorum expectarentur suffragia. Si superiorum electio ab his votis penderet, frigerent aulicae ista affectationes, contemnerentur inania illa obsequia, aliusomnis, & industria vilibus tantum animis insisterent. Multi ex fortunatis illis superioribus, quos potentiorum favor unus erexit, quos artes suae, ad celsos gradus extulerunt, jacerent in pulvere, imis subsellis subsiderent, vix aditum ad infima munia reperirent. Sua illi decoquerent iras, non impellerent tam crebris molestiis obsistentes adversus cupiditates suas, religiosos, continerent se, ne Patrum suffragijs fraudi, poenas in propria capita contorquerent. Quod bonum orbi? nonne illucebit pulcherrimus ille dies? quo renascentem primam Societatem intueri licebit? quo Patres antiquiores sibi reddi praeteritos annos gratulabuntur? Decernat Pontifex, procurent Episcopi, suis in Regnis imperent Reges, Respublicae statuant, inferatur Societati primus Societatis spiritus, firmitas religiosis reddatur, solenni professione: modestia, suffragiorum authoritate; justitia, plurium & optimatum gubernatione: Charitas, una votorum, studiosorum ac consiliorum communicatione. Non est antiquanda Societas, sed renovanda, non fulmine percutienda, sed sua luce illustranda: quis obductam caligine hanc lucem velit? quis obtectum & oppressum amplissimum ordinem? Nullus condemnet Theophilum, si hoc peroptet, vel D. Bernardum infestetur; qui suae familiae religiosos & externos Epistolis & adhortationibus severa reprehensione plenis commonefacit. D. Bernardum dilaceret ille, qui summo Pontifici Eugenio non parcit, qui vitia aperit, ut avellantur, pericula designat, ut evitentur, nec tamen existimavit, se ulla infamia vel suos religiosos, vel curiam Romanam aspergeret. D. Gregorium Nazianzenum discerpat ille, qui Episcopos ferme religiosos omnes, et ex coenobijs ad Episcopatus abstractos justissimis aculeis pungit, ut sentiant: armata oratione huc illuc versat, ut ad se redeat, ut perversis moribus renuncient. Ne dentem infigas, quisquis eris in Palamedem Ulysses: Certe si verus Iesuita, si Loyolaeus, vera, sana, at utilia proponenti nunquam succensebis, nec alios, quam dissimiles Beatis Ignatio et Xavereo vita ac moribus homines verberari censebis.
units.tr: Just as the first Society embraced one charity, one profession, one holiness of life, so too it embraced one custom of the holy Church, one observance toward the bishops, one unity and fellowship with all the religious orders, and one law of religion. Who would not cry out to the Jesuits: "Put on Christ, as your fathers put him on; live uprightly and well; drink in the same spirit." You preach, which is most welcome; who does not urge you on? You console the penitent; who does not praise you? You teach the young; it is a holy and excellent work. You confound the heretics? Press on, you will conquer, God will fight your battles. But who could approve the schemes of your domestic ambition, which you have devised, contrary to Ignatius's intention, to secure the rank of coadjutor priests? These are the light-armed soldiers and, as it were, skirmishers of your Society, whom you deliberately make easy to release from their vows, so that by means of their meagreness, their abjection, and finally their unstable profession, you may raise yourselves up. Why do you break up your Society? Why do you make it obscure by admitting so many untaught and unskilled men? Why do you train up such religious for the Church of God, whom you yourselves judge unworthy of your profession? Why do you not form all your priests, as far as you can, so that it may be most convenient and easiest for you, in one profession, with the same weapons, the same virtue, and the same learning? Why have you suppressed the decree of Pius V on this matter? Why do you despise the example of your first fathers, who, in order to bind the minds of all to religion, set before them the same zeal, the same bonds of love and profession, and who would admit no one whom they had not first tested as fit for this one solemnity of vows? Hence came the common ardour of all, one work, one striving, so that they might bear some fruit for Christ and labour not fruitlessly for the Church. No one hunted after himself or that profession of yours by dissimulation, contention, and those wonderful arts. This was not yet a territory where religious of upright virtue and learning were not justly thrown down by their superiors, if envy had persuaded some wretched charge or the frenzy of some unbalanced mind had flared up. What was so hateful in the first Society as the supreme domination of a few? Once they have been raised to dignities, they plan and do everything at the bidding of their own will, and they promote only those who shape themselves wholly to their manners, who will not depart a finger's breadth from their nod, who please them, who place a cushion under their head, who visit their bedchambers as if they were blessed seats, and who know how to render every service of clients. What is less religious? What is more suited to pride than to wish to be worshipped, to listen gladly to eulogies and acclamations, to exalt those who observe them, to repay honours with honours, to fulfil hatreds with wrongdoing, and to delight in revenge? What else can one see in the courts of princes? What other arts have those learned who are described by Christ as "those who are in kings' houses"? Take back your votes! Let a religious senate rule, not one man, but the unity of the Fathers, not a single, but a unanimous will! The eyes see more than one eye, and more hands are stronger. That absolute power, such as this, rests only on the Apostolic faith and on the Church constituted by God. A rector would not undertake anything, would not attempt anything at odds with fairness, would not impose anything grievous on his companions, if the votes of the companions were awaited. If the choice of superiors depended on such votes, those courtly affectations would cool, those empty obsequies would be despised, and the other arts and diligence would cling only to base spirits. Many of those fortunate superiors, whom the favour of the powerful alone raised up, whom their own schemes lifted to lofty grades, would lie in the dust, would sink to the lowest benches, and would scarcely find access to the humblest offices. They would boil away their own anger, and they would not, by so many vexations, resist their own desires against religious; they would restrain themselves, lest they twist punishments back upon their own heads through a fraud practised on the votes of the Fathers. What good would come to the world? Would not that most beautiful day dawn, on which it will be possible to behold the first Society being reborn? On which the older Fathers will rejoice that their bygone years have been restored to them? Let the Pope decree it, let the bishops take care of it, let kings command in their kingdoms, let commonwealths ordain it: let the first spirit of the Society be brought back into it; let firmness be restored to the religious through solemn profession, modesty through the authority of votes, justice through the government of the many and the best, and charity through the common sharing of vows, zeal, and counsels. The Society is not to be abolished but renewed; it is not to be struck down with a thunderbolt but illumined by its own light. Who would wish this light covered over with darkness? Who would wish that most ample order to be concealed and crushed? No one would condemn Theophilus if he should desire this, or would harass Saint Bernard, who, by letters and exhortations full of stern rebuke, admonishes the religious and outsiders of his own family. Let him tear Saint Bernard to pieces who does not spare Pope Eugene, who lays bare the vices so that they may be torn away, and points out the dangers so that they may be avoided, and yet did not think that he would splash any infamy either on his own religious or on the Roman curia. Let him tear Saint Gregory Nazianzen to pieces who, with the most just stings, pricks almost all the religious bishops who have been drawn from the monasteries to episcopates, so that they may feel it; with armed speech he turns them this way and that, so that they may come back to themselves and renounce their perverse manners. Do not sink your tooth into Palamedes, whoever you are, Ulysses: certainly, if you are a true Jesuit, a Loyolan, you will never be angry at one who proposes things that are true, sound, and useful, nor will you think that men who differ in life and manners from the Blessed Ignatius and Xavier are being beaten by anyone else.

units.la: PRÆSENTIS ORDINIS IESVITARVM GRADVS ET IVRA, ET EIVSDEM AD PRIMVM INSTITV- TVM REFORMATIO AC REDVCTIO PETITVR.
units.tr: The Present Order of the Jesuits: Its Grades and Rights, and a Call for Its Reform and Restoration to the Original Institute

units.la: Non omnes eodem jure potiuntur, qui in hac Societate sunt, non eodem titulo Religiosi. Alij Scholastici, alij Sacerdotes Coadjutores spirituales nuncupati, alij Coadjutores Laici, alij Professi sunt. Haec est Scholasticorum sors. Post duos novitiatus annos, tribus Paupertatis, Castitatis, et Obedientiae votis obstringuntur, quae simplicia secundum Societatis constitutiones emittuntur: haec vota deviñtos tenent, quamdiu Societati placet. Scholasticos suos Societas, si velit, dimittet, et non ob grandes causas? quartum insuper addit votum scholasticus, nempe se ingressurum in Societatem, esto enim, per biennium in novitiatu fuerit, nondum tamen de Societate est, in quam se pollicetur ingressurum, quam vis parentibus valedixerit, Clericali Iesuitarum habitu vestitus inter ipsos degat, doceat, concionetur, nondum tamen ingressus est Societatem, cui se mancipavit, & in quam admissum se iri sperat. Nihil enim illi aliud praeter spem, fiducia, ac securitas nulla, si recusat Societas. d nutum Scholastici obedire debent, non utuntur quidem bonis suis, suaque re paterna, mini tamen sunt patrimonij sui, & jus in illud integrum retinent, (adhuc enim periculum curfumstudiorum tenent) in quo si quid adversum incidat, repelli possunt a Societate, & ad suos dimitti. Probantur in hoc gradu diutissimè: & ad arbitrium superioris eriguntur, vel jacent, non est Sacerdotium huius exercitationis meta, sed probationis dicium: quicquid laboret, valeatve Scholasticus, nullum suffragij jus habet, nisi Regr constitutus, sive literas humaniores, sive Philosophiam, sive Theologiam docuerit, ens & nulla impensi laboris habita ratione amandari potest. De illo gradu tenetur ad aum progredi, si eum Generalis admittere velit. Toto quo sunt Scholastici tempore, nō dent se Societatis Patres, sed Societatis devotos, atq; obligatos profiteri, vicesimū tricesiue numerent licet a prima admissione vertente annum, adhuc quasi in praetexta sunt, & ita per Superiores dimissione, seculares esse possunt. Ne miremur deinceps, tam multorū eocietate exitum: hac enim lege admittuntur, ut à Societate dimitti possint, & ad saeculam vitam reduci sive invitì, sive volentes: nec curae est Societati, quid inde conquestionis clamet familia, nec interest, quod inde in multos gravis offensio incurrat. Sic enim praeSocietas suis, sicut clientibus domini, quos, cum videtur, à se repellunt: ita suos tum scholasticos, tum Coadjutores Societas reijcit. Vbi satis emeriti sunt, & laboribus fracti scholastici, vel fiunt Coadjutores spirituales, vel Professi.
units.tr: Not all who belong to this Society enjoy the same rights, nor do they all hold the same religious title. Some are called Scholastics, some Priests who are Spiritual Coadjutors, some Lay Coadjutors, and some Professed. Such is the lot of the Scholastics. After two years of novitiate they are bound by the three simple vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, which are taken according to the Society's constitutions. These vows hold them bound as long as the Society wishes. The Society may dismiss its Scholastics whenever it likes, and not always for grave reasons. Besides this, the Scholastic takes a fourth vow, namely that he will enter the Society. For although he has spent two years in the novitiate, he is not yet a member of the Society he promises to enter. Though he has bid farewell to his parents and lives among the Jesuits dressed in the clerical habit, teaching and preaching, he has not yet entered the Society to which he has pledged himself and into which he hopes to be admitted. He has nothing but hope and confidence, and no security at all, if the Society refuses him. Scholastics must obey at the nod of their superiors. They do not indeed use their own goods or their paternal inheritance, yet they remain the owners of their patrimony and keep full right to it, since they are still in the course of their studies. If something adverse befalls them there, they may be cast out by the Society and sent back to their families. They are tested in this grade for a very long time, and they are raised up or left lying according to the judgement of the superior. Priesthood is not the goal of this training but the decision on their probation. Whatever a Scholastic may suffer or be capable of, he has no right to a vote unless he has been appointed a teacher by the Rector, whether he has taught the humanities, philosophy or theology. He may be dismissed without any regard for the labour he has expended. He is bound to advance from this grade to the next if the General is willing to admit him. During the whole time they are Scholastics, they must not profess themselves Fathers of the Society but devoted and obliged servants of it. Even if they have reached twenty or thirty years from their first admission, they are still, as it were, in the praetexta, and so, by the decision of the superiors, they may become secular again. We should not wonder, then, at the great number who leave the Society. They are admitted on this condition: that they may be dismissed from the Society and returned to secular life, whether they are unwilling or willing. The Society does not care what complaints their families raise, nor does it matter that great offence arises from this for many. For just as patrons cast off their clients when it suits them, so the Society rejects its Scholastics and Coadjutors. When the Scholastics are sufficiently worn out and broken by their labours, they become either Spiritual Coadjutors or Professed.

units.la: Ecce tibi, Coadjutoris spiritualis jura: Coadjutor spiritualis declaratur non aptus, & habilis ad Generalis & Provincialis dignitatem, nulli congregationi, nisi alio titulo inresse potest. Tria vovet, Paupertatis, Castitatis, & Obedientiae vota simplicia, quibus ocietati se totum tradit, non tamē pacificitur cū illo Societas quidquā, sed jus integrū sibi servat, sicut in Scholasticorum votis, ut si ipsa velit, absolvere possit à votis, & ad saecularem statum remittere: ne obulum quidem pro remuneratione operae impensae, aut pro a-mentis, dimissis Sacerdotibus tenetur subministrare: statutum est enim Sacerdotes huiusodi institutos esse ad titulū paupertatis, nō professae quidem, neq; stabilis, sed quam facilicet rvare cogetur, & servant, si dimissi nihil patrmonij vel subsidij aliunde suppetat: si diites fundos habeant & aes aliquod, à paupertate exempti sunt. Novae & insolitae, in Sardotum ordinatione non ab Episcopis, nō à Consilijs, aut Pontificibus receptus Paupertatis titulus. Sic figitur Coadjutor spiritualis: cui dulce sit oportet, aliorum servire volunti: & omnia perferre: ne si jus suum prosequatur, vel extra Societatem abire compellatur, vel se in difficile, ac fastidijs implicatissimum vitae genus demergat. Hic Sacerdos Societatis Coadjutor non est religionis socius, nisi adscititius, (si à Iulio summo Pontifice excripta discrimina retinenda sunt.)
units.tr: Here, then, are the rights of the Spiritual Coadjutor. The Spiritual Coadjutor is declared not apt or suitable for the dignity of General or Provincial, and he can hold no office in any congregation except under another title. He takes the three simple vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, by which he surrenders himself entirely to the Society. Yet the Society does not enter into any binding agreement with him, but keeps its full right over him, just as with the Scholastics' vows: if it wishes, it may absolve him from his vows and send him back to the secular state. He is not even obliged to pay a penny for the labour he has expended, or for his expenses, when Priests are dismissed. For it is established that Priests of this kind are instituted under a title of poverty, not indeed a professed or fixed poverty, but one which they will be forced to keep and do keep, since, once dismissed, they have no patrimony or support from elsewhere. If they have rich estates and some money, they are exempt from poverty. The title of poverty is new and unusual in the ordination of priests; it was not received from the Bishops, nor from the Councils, nor from the Popes. Thus the Spiritual Coadjutor is held fast. He must be one who is glad to serve the wishes of others and to bear everything, lest, if he pursues his right, he be compelled to leave the Society, or plunge himself into a difficult and most wearisome manner of life. Here the Priest-Coadjutor of the Society is not a companion of the religious order, except as an adjunct (if the distinctions set out by Pope Julius are to be retained).

units.la: Vltimò, Professi creantur, qui solemnia non simplicia (debet hoc animadversum es-e maximum discrimen legenti.) Paupertatis, Castitatis, & obedientiae vota emittunt: um quartum addunt obedientiae praestandae summo Pontifici, ad missiones. Hi Professi Societati se sese obligant, & quia solenibus votis, & non simplicibus se sese obligant, haec vicissim ota recipit Societas, & contractu mutuo se sese Professis suis obstringit. Non possunt illi ad saecularem vitam remitti, firmo & constanti sunt in statu, nec nisi ex privilegio Gregorij XIII. in alium ordinem religiosum à Generali summa cum difficultate, aut certe volentes expelli possunt. Societatem illi administrant: soli Generalis, ac Provincialis munus obeunt. Ius habent suffragij ferendi tum in Generali, tum in Provinciali congregatione, sunt & alij Professi, quos trium votorum appellant, secuti quidem sui statūs, & à dimissione exempti, sed suffragiorum inanes, & à primis dignitatibus exclusi.
units.tr: Lastly, the Professed are created: those who take solemn, not simple, vows. (The reader should note this as a very great distinction.) They take the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and they add a fourth, the vow of obedience to be rendered to the Supreme Pontiff in regard to the missions. These Professed bind themselves to the Society, and because they bind themselves by solemn and not simple vows, the Society in turn receives these vows and binds itself to its Professed by a mutual contract. They cannot be sent back to secular life; they are firm and constant in their state, and they cannot be expelled to another religious order by the General, except under a privilege of Gregory XIII, and then only with great difficulty, or certainly only if they are willing. They alone administer the Society; only they discharge the office of General and Provincial. They have the right to vote both in the General Congregation and in the Provincial Congregation. There are also other Professed, whom they call of the three vows. They are indeed kept in their status and exempt from dismissal, but they are empty of votes and excluded from the highest dignities.

units.la: Haec coniuctus ratio. Scholasticis, & Sacerdotib. Coadjutoribus protrita, ac vilia quae servantur: Professis praestantioria ac selectiora: Professis redduntur obsequia, aliis mantantur imperia: Professis, qui ex instituto pauperiores, & dejectiores esse deberent, lucidiora & sublimiora concediuntur: aliis, quibus obligatio minor, nec tam multa vota, graviora onera, molestiores curae, & obscurae imperantur.
units.tr: This is the whole arrangement. For Scholastics and Priest-Coadjutors there are the worn-out and cheap conditions that are kept; for the Professed, the more excellent and select. The Professed receive services, while others are given commands. To the Professed, who by their institute ought to be poorer and more humble, brighter and more exalted privileges are granted, while to others, who have a lighter obligation, not so many vows, heavier burdens, more troublesome cares and obscure tasks are imposed.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: DE DOCTRINA

units.la: Non sic factum in prima Societate, quam restituendam affero, in qua, ut Ribadeneira refert in vita Ignatij lib. 2. cap. 13. & professio una fancita est, & suffragiorum vigebat authoritas, & duobus tantum gradibus, Scholasticorum ac Professorum tota Societas comprehendebatur. Scholastici, ut tyrones, toto studiorum tempore probari debebant. Societatis tantum alumni, & candidati habebantur. Professi & probati, pari lege, & eadem conditione cum caeteris Ordinibus religiosis Ordini suo vacabant, ac divino cultui in perpetuum inserviebant. Nulla Coadjutorum Sacerdotum instabili forte praescriptio & nullus de illorum ascriptitia, & rejectitia conditione sermo: Quae Episcopis gravis familijs dura ac non ferenda, ipsi Societati, quae tam multis imperitis, & rudibus sua profes-sione indignis impletur, nec utilis, nec necessaria est. Inferam hic authenticum primae Societatis Iesu institutum, ipso decem Primorum Patrum stylo expressum, & Paulo III summo Pontifici anno 1540. propositum.
units.tr: It was not so in the first Society, which I propose to restore, in which, as Ribadeneira relates in the Life of Ignatius, book 2, chapter 13, a single profession was enacted and the authority of votes prevailed, and the whole Society was comprehended under only two grades, Scholastics and Professed. Scholastics, like novices, had to be proved throughout the whole time of their studies. They were regarded only as alumni and candidates of the Society. The Professed and the approved, under the same law and the same condition as the other religious orders, devoted themselves to their Order and served divine worship in perpetuity. There was no talk of any unstable prescription for the Coadjutor priests, nor of their being enrolled as bondsmen and cast off at will: conditions burdensome and unbearable to bishops and families, and neither useful nor necessary to the Society itself, which is filled with so many inexperienced and rude men unworthy of its profession. I shall insert here the authentic institute of the first Society of Jesus, expressed in the very style of the ten first Fathers, and presented to Pope Paul III in the year 1540.

units.la: PAVLI III. PRIMA PRIMI INSTITVT- I SOCIETATIS IESV APPROBATIO CVM RESTRI- CTIONE NVMERI AD PERSONAS 60. DVNTAXAT, ANNO 1540.
units.tr: Approval of the First Institute of the Society of Jesus by Paul III, with the Number Restricted to Sixty Persons Only, in the Year 1540

units.la: Paulus Episcopus servus servorum Dei, ad perpetuam rei memoriam. Regimini Militantis Ecclesiae, meritis licet imparibus, disponente Domino praesidentes, & animarum salutem pro ut ex debito pastoralis officij tenemur, & solicitus studijs exquirentes fideles quoslibet, qui vota sua in id exponunt, Apostolici favoris gratia confovemus, aliaque desuper disponimus, pro ut temporum, & locorum qualitate pensata, id in Domino conspicimus salubriter expedire. Nuper siquidem accepimus, quod dilecti filij, Ignatius de Loyola, & Petrus Faber, ac Jacobus Laynez, nec non Claudius Jajus, & Pafchafius Broet, ac Franciscus Xavier, nec non Alphonsus Salmeron, & Simon Rodericus, ac Joannes Coduri, & Nicolaus de Bobadilla, Presbyteri Pompilonen Gebennen. Segunti-n. Toletan. Visen. Ebredunen. & Palentin. civitatum, & dioec. respectivè, in artibus Magistri, in Universitate Parisiensi graduati, & in Theologicis studijs per plures annos exercitati, Spiritu sancto, ut pie creditur, afflati, jam dudum e diversis mundi regionibus discedentes, in unum convenerunt, & socij effecti, abdicatis hujus saeculi illecebris, eorum vitam perpetuo Domini nostri Iesu Christi, atque nostro & aliorum successorum nostrorum Romanorum Pontificum servitio dedicarunt, & jam quam pluribus annis laudabiliter in vinea Domini se exercuerunt: Verbum Dei praevia sufficienti licentia publice praedicando, fideles privatim ad bene beateque vivendum exhortando, & ad pias meditationes excitando, hospitalibus inserviendo, pueros, & personas rudes ea, quae ad Christianam hominum institutionem sunt necessaria, & docendo, & demum omnia charitatis officia, & quae ad animarum consolationem faciunt ubique terrarum, ubi peregrinati sunt, multa cum laude obeundo. Cumque ad hanc almam urbem se contulerint, & in charitatis vinculo perfistentes ad perficiendam & conservandam eorum Societatis in Christo unionem, quandam vivendi formulam, juxta ea, quae ad propositum sibi finem conducere ut sic didicerunt, Evangelicis consilijs, & canonicis Patrum sanctionibus conformem ediderint, factum est, ut ipsorum sociorum vitae institutum, sub dicta formula comprehensum, non solum a multis probis viris, & Deum zelantibus laudetur, verum etiam a quibusdam ita approbetur, ut illud etiam sequi velint. Formulae autem praedictae tenor sequitur, & est talis.
units.tr: Paul, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter. We who, though unequal to the task, by the Lord's appointment preside over the government of the Church Militant, and who are bound by the duty of our pastoral office to care for the salvation of souls, and who with anxious diligence seek out whatever faithful persons present their wishes to this end, grant them the favour of Apostolic goodwill, and make other provisions for them, as we judge, having weighed the nature of the times and places, that this is salutary and expedient in the Lord. For we have recently learned that our beloved sons Ignatius de Loyola, Peter Faber, James Laynez, Claude Jay, Paschasius Broët, Francis Xavier, Alphonsus Salmeron, Simon Rodriguez, John Codure and Nicholas de Bobadilla, priests of the cities and dioceses of Pamplona, Geneva, Sigüenza, Toledo, Viseu, Embrun and Palencia respectively, graduates in arts as Masters in the University of Paris, and practised for many years in theological studies, having been moved, as we piously believe, by the Holy Spirit, and having long since departed from the various regions of the world, have come together into one body, and, being made companions, have renounced the allurements of this age and dedicated their life to the perpetual service of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of ourselves and our other successors, the Roman Pontiffs; and for many years now they have laboured praiseworthily in the Lord's vineyard, preaching the Word of God publicly with proper licence, exhorting the faithful in private to live well and blessedly, stirring them to pious meditation, serving in hospitals, teaching children and unlearned persons the things necessary for the Christian instruction of men, and finally performing, with much praise, all the offices of charity and whatever serves the consolation of souls wherever they have travelled. And when they came to this kindly city, and, persisting in the bond of charity in order to bring about and preserve the union of their Society in Christ, they published a certain formula of life, in conformity with the Evangelical counsels and the canonical sanctions of the Fathers, as they had learned to be suited to the end they had set before themselves, it has come about that the institute of life of these companions, comprised under the said formula, is not only praised by many upright men and zealots for God, but is also approved by some to such a degree that they wish to follow it as well. The tenor of the aforesaid formula follows, and it is as follows.

units.la: Quicunque in Societate nostra, quam Iesu nomine insigniri cupimus, vult sub cruce vexillo Deo militare, & soli Domino, atque Romano Pontifici eius in terris Vicario servire, post solemne perpetuae castitatis votum, proponat sibi in animo, se partem esse Societatis, ad hoc potissimum institutae, ut ad profectum animarum in vita, & doctrina Christiana, ad fidei propagationem per publicas praedicationes, vel verbi Dei ministerium, spirituilia exercitia, & charitatis opera, & nominatim per puerorum ac rudium in Christianismo institutionem, ac Christi fidelium, in confessionibus audiendis, spiritualem consolationem praecipue intendat: curetq; primo Deum, deinde hujus sui instituti ratione, quae via quaedam est ad illum, semper ante oculos habere, & finem hunc sibi a Deo propositum totis viribus assequi, unusquisq; tamen secundum gratiam sibi a spiritu sancto subministratam, & vocationis suae proprium gradum, ne quis forte zelo utatur, sed non secundum scientiam. Cujus proprij cujusque gradus judicium, & officiorum discretio ac distributio tota fit in manu Praepositi seu Praelati, per nos eligendi, ut congruus ordo servetur, in omni bene constituta communitate necessarius. Qui quidem Praepositus de consilio consociorum, Constitutiones ad constructionem hujus propositi nobis finis conducentes in consilio condendi auctoritatem habeat, majori suffragiorum parte semper statuendi jus habente. Concilium vero intelligatur esse in rebus quidem gravioribus, ac perpetuis, major pars totius Societatis, quae a Praeposito commode convocari poterit: in levioribus tamen, & temporaneis, omnes illi, quos in loco, ubi Praepositus noster residebit, praesentes esse contigerit. Iubendi autem jus totum penes Praepositum erit. Sciant omnes socij, & non solum in primis professionis suae foribus, sed quo ad vixerint, quotidie animo volvant, Societatem hanc universam, & singulos sub sanctissimi Domini nostri Papae, & aliorum Romanorum Pontificum successorum eius fideli obedientia DEO militare. Et quamvis Evangelio doceamur, & fide orthodoxa cognoscamus, ac firmiter profiteamur, omnes Christi fideles Romano Pontifici, tanquam capiti ac IESV CHRISTI Vicario subesse: ad maiorem tamen nostrae Societatis humilitatem ac perfectam uniuscuiusque mortificationem, & voluntatum nostrarum abnegationem summopere conducere judicavimus, singulos nos, ultra illud commune vinculum, speciali voto astringi, ita, ut quicquid modernus, & alij Romani Pontifices, pro tempore existentes jusserint, ad profectum animarum, & fidei propagationem pertinens, & ad quascunque Provincias nos mittere voluerit, sine ulla tergiversatione, aut excusatione illico, quantum in nobis fuerit, exequi teneamur, sive miserit nos ad Turcas, sive ad quoscunque alios infideles, etiam in partibus, quas Indias vocant, existentes: sive ad quoscunque haereticos, seu schismaticos, seu etiam ad quosvis fideles. Quamobrem qui ad nos accessuri sunt, & antequam huic oneri humeros suppondant, diu multumque meditentur, ac tantum pecuniae spiritualis in bonis habeant, ut turrim hanc juxta consilium Dominicum possint consummare: hoc est, an Spiritus sanctus, qui illos impellit, tantum illis gratiae polliceatur, ut hujus vocationis pondus, illo adjuvante, se laturos sperent: & postquam Domino inspirante, huic Iesu Christi militiae nomen dederint, die noctuque succincti lumbos, & ad tam grandis debiti solutionem prompti esse debebunt. Ne qua autem possint esse inter nos missionum, ac Provinciarum hujusmodi, aut ambitio vel detractatio; profiteantur singuli, se nunquam directe aut indirecte de hujusmodi missionibus quidquam cum Romano Pontifice curaturos; sed omnem hanc curam Deo, & ipsi Pontifici tanquam eius Vicario, & Societatis Praeposito dimissuros. Qui quidem Praepositus, sicut ceteri, etiam profiteatur, se nihil de semetipsius missione in alterutram partem, nisi de Societatis consilio, cum dicto Pontifice esse curaturum. Voveant singuli, se in omnibus, quae ad Regulae huius nostrae observationem faciunt, obedientes fore Societatis Praeposito. Ille autem jubeat ea, quae ad constructionem propositi sibi a Deo, & a Societate finis cognoverit esse opportuna. In praelatione autem sua, benignitatis, ac mansuetudinis, charitatisque Christi, Petri Pauliique formulae semper sit memor: & tamipse, quam Consilium ad normam hanc assidue spectent; & nominatim commendatam habeant institutionem puerorum, ac rudium in Christiana doctrina decem praeceptorum, atq; aliorum similium rudimentorum, quaecunq; secundum circumstantias personarum, locorum, ac temporum, illis congrua videbuntur. Est enim maxime necessarium, circa providentiam huius rei diligenter Praepositum, & Consilium inVigilare; cum & in proximis aedificium fidei sine fundamento non possit con-surgere, & in nostris periculum sit, ne, ut quisque erit doctior, ita Provinciam hanc, tanquam primo aspectu minus speciosam, forsitan detrectare conetur: cum tamen re vera nulla sit fructuosior, vel proximis ad aedificationem, vel nostris ad charitatis, & humilitatis simul officia exercenda. Subditi vero tum propter ingentes Ordinis utilitates, tum propter nunquam satis laudatum humilitatis assiduum exercitium, Praepposito in omnibus ad institutum Societatis pertinentibus parere semper tenentur, & in illo Christum, veluti praesentem agnoscant, & quantum decet, venerentur. Cum autem experti fuerimus, jucundiorem, puriorem, & ad proximi aedificationem aptiorem esse vitam ab omni avaritiae contagione quam remotissimam, & Evangelicae paupertati quam simillimam; cumque sciamus, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum servis suis regnum Dei solum inquirentibus necessaria ad victum, & vestitum esse subministraturum; voveant singuli, & universi perpetuam paupertatem, declarantes, quod non solum privatim, sed neque etiam communiter possint pro Societatis sustentatione, aut usu, ad bona aliqua stabilia, aut ad proventus, seu introitus aliquos, jus aliquod civile acquirere: sed sint contenti, usum tantum rerum sibi donatarum ad necessaria sibi comparanda recipere.
units.tr: Whoever wishes in our Society, which we desire to be marked with the name of Jesus, to serve God as a soldier under the banner of the cross, and to serve the Lord alone and the Roman Pontiff, His Vicar on earth, after the solemn vow of perpetual chastity, let him propose to himself in his mind that he is a member of the Society, instituted chiefly for this purpose: that he should aim, above all, at the advancement of souls in Christian life and doctrine, at the propagation of the faith through public preaching or the ministry of the Word of God, through spiritual exercises and works of charity, and especially through the instruction of children and unlearned persons in Christianity, and through hearing confessions and giving spiritual consolation to Christ's faithful; and let him take care always to keep before his eyes, first God, and then the purpose of this his institute, which is a certain way to Him, and let him pursue with all his strength the end set before him by God; yet each one according to the grace given him by the Holy Spirit and the particular degree of his calling, lest anyone perhaps use zeal without knowledge. The judgment of each one's particular degree, and the discretion and distribution of offices, rest entirely in the hand of the Provost or Prelate, to be elected by us, so that a fitting order may be kept, which is necessary in every well-constituted community. This Provost, with the counsel of the companions, shall have authority to frame Constitutions conducive to the furtherance of this purpose of ours, and always the right to decide by the greater part of the votes. A council, moreover, is to be understood as follows: in weightier and perpetual matters, the greater part of the whole Society, which the Provost can conveniently summon; but in lesser and temporary matters, all those whom it happens to be present in the place where our Provost resides. The whole right of command shall rest with the Provost. Let all the companions know, and not only at the threshold of their profession but as long as they live let them daily ponder in their minds, that this whole Society and each of its members serve God under the faithful obedience of our most holy Lord the Pope and of his successors, the other Roman Pontiffs. And although we are taught by the Gospel, and know and firmly profess by the orthodox faith, that all Christ's faithful are subject to the Roman Pontiff as head and Vicar of Jesus Christ, nevertheless, for the greater humility of our Society and the perfect mortification of each one and the denial of our wills, we have judged it highly conducive that we each be bound, beyond that common bond, by a special vow, so that whatever the present and other Roman Pontiffs in their time shall command for the advancement of souls and the propagation of the faith, and whenever he wishes to send us into any provinces, we are bound to carry out at once, as far as lies in us, without any evasion or excuse, whether he sends us to the Turks or to any other infidels, even those living in the regions called the Indies, or to any heretics or schismatics, or even to any faithful. Therefore, those who are to come to us, before they put their shoulders to this burden, should deliberate long and much, and should have such a store of spiritual wealth that they can complete this tower according to the Lord's counsel: that is, whether the Holy Spirit, who impels them, promises them so much grace that they may hope, with His help, to bear the weight of this calling. And after, by the Lord's inspiration, they have given their name to this militia of Jesus Christ, they shall have to be girded day and night in their loins and ready for the discharge of so great a debt. Lest there be any ambition or disparagement among us concerning such missions and provinces, let each one profess that he will never, directly or indirectly, take any care with the Roman Pontiff concerning such missions, but will leave all this care to God and to the Pontiff himself as His Vicar, and to the Provost of the Society. The Provost himself, like the others, shall also profess that he will take no care of his own mission in either direction except with the counsel of the Society and with the said Pontiff. Let each one vow that he will be obedient to the Provost of the Society in all things pertaining to the observance of this our Rule. He, for his part, shall command what he has recognised to be opportune for the furtherance of the purpose and end set before the Society by God. In his governing, let him always be mindful of the formula of Peter and Paul, of kindness, gentleness and the charity of Christ; and let him and the Council keep these norms constantly in view; and let them especially commend the instruction of children and the unlearned in the Christian doctrine of the Ten Commandments, and of other similar rudiments, in whatever ways seem fitting to them according to the circumstances of persons, places and times. For it is most necessary that the Provost and the Council watch carefully over the provision of this matter, since the building of faith cannot rise among neighbours without a foundation, and among our own members there is a danger that, the more learned each one is, the more he may try to shun this work, as though it were less showy at first sight, when in truth there is nothing more fruitful, either for building up the neighbour or for exercising at once the duties of charity and humility among our own. The subjects, moreover, both on account of the great usefulness of the Order and on account of the constant exercise of humility, which can never be praised enough, are always bound to obey the Provost in all matters pertaining to the institute of the Society, and to recognise and reverence Christ in him, as present, as far as is fitting. Since we have found by experience that a life free from every contagion of avarice, as far removed as possible, and as closely resembling Evangelical poverty, is more pleasant, purer, and better suited to the edification of the neighbour; and since we know that our Lord Jesus Christ will supply necessities of food and clothing to His servants who seek the kingdom of God alone, let each one and all vow perpetual poverty, declaring that they may acquire no civil right to any stable goods or revenues or incomes, either privately or even in common, for the support or use of the Society; but that they be content to receive only the use of the things given to them for procuring what they need.

units.la: Possint tamen habere in Universitatibus Collegium, seu Collegia habentia redditus, census, seu possessiones, usibus, & necessariis studentium applicandas: retenta penes Praepositum, & Societatem omnimoda gubernatione, seu superintendentia super dicta Collegia, & praedictos studentes, quoad gubernatoris, seu gubernatorum, ac studentium electionem, ac eorundem admissionem, emissionem, receptionem, exclusionem, statutorum ordinationem, circa studentium instructionem, erudificationem, aedificationem, ac correctionem: victus, vestitusque eis ministrandi modum, atque aliam omnimodam gubernationem, regimen, ac curam; sic tamen, ut neque studentes ditiis[?] bonis abuti, neque Societas in proprios usus convertere possit, sed studentium necessitati subvenire. Qui quidem post cognitum in spiritu & literis eorum profectum, & post sufficientem probationem, in Societatem nostram admitti possint, socij omnes quicunque in sacris fuerint, quamvis beneficia Ecclesiastica, aut eorum redditus non habeant, teneantur tamen singuli privatim, ac particulariter, & non communiter, ad dicendum officium secundum Ecclesiae ritum.
units.tr: They may, however, have in the universities a college, or colleges, holding revenues, rents or possessions to be applied to the uses and needs of the students, the Provost and the Society retaining complete governance and oversight over these colleges and the said students: in the choice of the governor or governors and of the students, their admission, dismissal, reception and exclusion, the drawing up of statutes, the instruction, education, formation and correction of the students, the manner of supplying them with food and clothing, and all other government, rule and care. Yet the students may not abuse the richer goods, nor may the Society turn them to its own uses; they are to meet the students' need. After the students have shown progress in spirit and learning, and after sufficient testing, they may be admitted into our Society. All the members who have been ordained, even if they have no ecclesiastical benefices or revenues from them, are nevertheless bound each individually and particularly, not jointly, to say the office according to the rite of the Church.

units.la: Haec sunt, quae sub praefati Domini nostri Pauli, & sedis Apostolicae beneplacito, de nostra professione, typo quodam explicare potuimus. Quod nunc fecimus, ut summatim scriptione hac informaremus tum illos, qui nos de nostro vitae instituto interrogant, tum etiam posteros nostros, si quos, Deo volente, imitatores unquam habebimus hujus viae, quam cum multas magnasque habere annexas difficultates fuerimus experti, opportunum judicavimus etiam statuere: ne quis in hac Societate recipiatur, nisi diu ac diligentissime fuerit probatus; cumque prudens in Christo, & vel doctrina, seu vitae Christianae puritate apparuerit conspicuus; tunc demum admittatur ad Iesu Christi militiam, qui tenuibus coeptis nostris favere dignetur ad gloriam Dei Patris, cui soli sit semper decus, & honor in saecula, Amen.
units.tr: These are the things which, under the good pleasure of our lord Pope Paul and of the Apostolic See, we have been able to set out in outline concerning our profession. We have now done so in order to inform, in this brief writing, both those who ask us about our way of life and also our successors, should God will that there ever be imitators of this path, which we have found to have many great difficulties attached, and which we judged it right to lay down: that no one is to be received into this Society unless he has been tested long and very carefully; and when he has appeared prudent in Christ, and outstanding either in doctrine or in the purity of the Christian life, only then is he to be admitted into the warfare of Jesus Christ, who may deign to favour our humble beginnings, to the glory of God the Father, to whom alone be honour and glory forever, Amen.

units.la: Cum autem nil in praemiis reperiatur, quod pium non sit, aut sanctum; Nos, ut iidem Socij, qui nobis super hoc humillime supplicari fecerunt, in eorum pio vivendi proposito, eo promptiores existant, quo se majori sedis Apostolicae gratia completi cognoscunt, & praemissa per nos approbari viderint, praemissa omnia, & singula tamquam ad spiritualem profectum eorundem Sociorum, & reliqui Christiani gregis opportuna, Apostolica authoritate, tenore praesentium ex certa scientia approbamus, confirmamus, & benedicimus: ac perpetuae firmitatis munimine roboramus, ipsosque socios sub nostra, & hujus sanctae sedis Apostolicae protectione suscipimus: Eis nihilominus concedentes, quod particulares inter eos Constitutiones, quas ad Societatis hujusmodi finem, & Iesu Christi Domini nostri gloriam, ac proximi utilitatem conformes esse judicaverint, condere liberè, & licitè valeant. Non obstantibus Generalis Concilij, & felicis recordationis Gregorij Papae X. praedecessoris nostri, ac quibusvis aliis constitutionibus, & ordinationibus Apostolicis, caeterisque contrariis quibuscunque. Volumus autem, quod in Societate huiusmodi, neque ad umerum sexaginta personarum, Normulam vivendi eiusmodi profiteri cupientium, & on ultra admitti, & Societati præfatæ aggregari duntaxat valeant. NVLLI ergo oninò hominum liceat, hanc paginam nostræ approbationis, confirmationis, benedictionis, ɔborationis, susceptionis, concessionis & voluntatis infringere, velei ausu temerario conraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare præsumpserit, indignationem omnipotentis Dei, &c. Datum Rom. apud S. Marc. Anno 1540. 5. Cal. Octob. Pontificatus nostri anno 6.
units.tr: Since nothing is found in these rules that is not pious or holy, we, so that the same Fellows, who have most humbly petitioned us about this, may be the more ready in their pious purpose of living, the more they know themselves to be endowed with the greater favour of the Apostolic See, and see the aforesaid rules approved by us, approve, confirm and bless all the aforesaid rules and each of them, as opportune for the spiritual progress of these same Fellows and of the rest of the Christian flock, by Apostolic authority and from certain knowledge, by the tenor of these present letters. We strengthen them with the safeguard of perpetual firmness, and we take these Fellows under our protection and that of this holy Apostolic See. We also grant to them that they may freely and lawfully draw up particular constitutions among themselves, which they judge to be in harmony with the end of such a Society, the glory of Jesus Christ our Lord, and the benefit of the neighbour. Notwithstanding the General Council, and of our predecessor of happy memory Pope Gregory X, and any other Apostolic constitutions and ordinances, and whatever else is contrary. We will, moreover, that in this Society there be no more than sixty persons who wish to profess this form of living, and that they may be admitted and aggregated to the aforesaid Society only in this number. Therefore let it in no way be lawful for anyone to infringe or to contravene rashly this page of our approval, confirmation, blessing, corroboration, reception, concession and will. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God, etc. Given at Rome, at St Mark's, in the year 1540, on the 5th day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

units.la: Inhis principiis (inquit Theophilus Eugenius) animad vertere licet, quàm sinceri fueint 10 primi illi Patres, qui suis professis, Christum unum & pauperpatatem eius, ut certū itæ religiosæ signum tradiderunt. Hic gubernationem antiquam & optimam commedari ides, quâ de majoris partis sententia definiri ac fulciri omnia debebant. Ius religionis unū, ɔlenni professione sacrum, probationem Scholasticorum egregiam: qui diu in Collegijs pieɪte & literis exercebātur, donec eum doctrinæ, ac præsertim austerę & pauperis vitæ spiitū concepissent, ut solo Christo contenti, sine pecunijs, sine viatico, quæ cunq; itinera, etiam d infensas Christo, infestafq; Provincias capesserent; nullos reditus, nullū æs annuū pofderent, ut sic expediti, atq; omni mundi sarcina spoliati, quo mundo abjectiores, ita Christo hariores viverent. Nihil in hoc instituto, de amplissimis fundis, quibus nunc comodissime r lautissimè professi in Collegijs utuntur & summo jure potiuntur. Nihil de excelso illo rincipatu Monarchiæ, tum Generalis, tum aliorum superiorum Societatis: nullū, de ruibus doctrinâ Christianâ imbuendis mandatum, quod in speciem tantum ac raptim professi aciunt, quibus præsenti corruptelâ, hoc præsertim infixum, ut de sublimi loco dicere, & in obiliori circulo versari possint. Absens primorum Patrum Societatis Iesu paupertas reonenda est, & despicientia rerum hujus sæculi, non ultra despicienda, sed recipienda: sima lex, & novis artibus minimè versatilis vita repetenda.
units.tr: From these principles (says Theophilus Eugenius) one may see how sincere those first Fathers were, who handed down to their professed members Christ alone and his poverty as the certain sign of the religious life. Here one may commend the ancient and best government, by which all things were to be decided and upheld by the opinion of the greater part. The right of the religious life is one, sacred by solemn profession, and the testing of the Scholastics was outstanding: they were trained for a long time in the colleges in piety and learning, until they had grasped the spirit of doctrine, and especially of a austere and poor life, so that, content with Christ alone, without money, without travelling provisions, they undertook whatever journeys, even into provinces hostile to Christ, and possessed no revenues and no yearly income, so that, thus unencumbered and stripped of every burden of the world, they lived as much more despised by the world as they were more dear to Christ. Nothing in this rule concerns the very ample estates, which the professed now most conveniently and sumptuously use in the colleges and enjoy with the highest right. Nothing concerns that lofty princely rule of the Monarchy, both of the General and of the other superiors of the Society; nor is there any command to imbue people with Christian doctrine, which the professed perform only in outward show and in haste, while by present corruption this has been fixed especially in them, that they may speak from a lofty place and live in a more respectable circle. The poverty of the first Fathers of the Society of Jesus is to be restored, and the contempt of the things of this age is not to be despised any further but embraced; the simple law and a life not at all given to new arts is to be sought again.

units.la: SANCTISSIMO D. N. D. PAVLO QVINTO SVMMO ECCLESIÆ Dei Pontifici.
units.tr: TO OUR MOST HOLY LORD, POPE PAUL V, SUPREME BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF GOD.

units.la: Theophilus Eugenius pro redintegratione ordinis Iesuitarum.
units.tr: Theophilus Eugenius, for the restoration of the Order of the Jesuits.

units.la: BENè, unus ex Christianissimis Galliæ Regibus, de sancti Ludovici semine & genere, sacrorum te summum Antistitem, & universum Ecclesiæ patrem appellavit. Non minus pie ac verè serenissima illa Angliæ Regina, te Petri collegam, legatum Dei, judicem orbis Christiani salutavit. Excelsa tamen ista, & super omnes elata dignitas, omnibus te, servis Christi, jure paternæ sollicitudinis, & Apostolicæ administrationis, obligatum facit. Nō adimit curas, sed adijcit Petri principatus. Quidam ex vatibus, ait, sapiens sapientiâ profitetur ac proloquitur: vertam ego in præstantius elogium, summus Pontifex de summæ potestatis folio, veritatis oracula reddit, nulli justam opem flagitanti denegat. Multorum ego nomine, tenuitatis licet meæ conscius, ad hanc sedem Themidis, & justitiæ, ad hanc aram fiduciæ, ad hoc commune solatium bonorum omnium confugio. Non est nostræ causæ leve argumentum. Aggrediar illud, et proponam tibi, Maxime Pontifex, cum Religiosi ac viri graves quam plurimi pervelint expositum, & declaratum esse.
units.tr: Rightly did one of the most Christian Kings of France, of the seed and stock of St Louis, call you the supreme Bishop of sacred things and the universal father of the Church. No less devoutly and truly did that most serene Queen of England greet you as the colleague of Peter, the legate of God, and the judge of the Christian world. Yet this lofty dignity, raised above all others, binds you, by the right of a father's care and of apostolic administration, to all of us who are servants of Christ. It takes away no cares; rather, it adds to them, as the primacy of Peter did. One of the poets, a wise man, declares and utters wisdom; I shall turn his words into a more excellent praise: the Supreme Pontiff, from the throne of supreme power, gives forth the oracles of truth and denies just help to no one who asks for it. In the name of many, though conscious of my own humble station, I take refuge at this seat of Themis and of justice, at this altar of trust, at this common comfort of all good men. Our cause is no slight matter. I shall take it up and set it before you, Most Holy Pontiff, since many religious men and grave men have very much wished it to be laid out and explained.

units.la: Societatem Iesu, ordinem ab antecessoribus tuis approbatum, & auctum, periclitari dicimus, si non adsis, non hoc ab externo conflictu, sed ab intestinis malis creatur periculum. Periculosa sunt illa vulnera, quæ sub ossibus luridam cogunt saniem, nec ulla se aperiente cicatrice sub oculum veniunt: perniciosius & intimius ulcerant, quò interior plaga.
units.tr: We say that the Society of Jesus, an order approved and enlarged by your predecessors, is in danger, and if you do not help it, the danger does not arise from outside conflict but from internal evils. Those wounds are dangerous which force foul matter beneath the bones and do not come to the surface under any opening scar: they ulcerate more harmfully and more deeply, the more hidden the wound is.

units.la: Antiquum est Pontificibus Romanis, favere Societati, Pius IV. majori præ cæteris amore prosequendos ajebat, Societatis Iesu Religiosos, ob præstantiores abipsis Ecclesiæ Dei fructus allatos. Paulus III. pium & sanctum institutum vocavit, non patietur sanctitas vestra deficere, & collabi, sultam & sublatam à Pontificibus Societatem.
units.tr: It has long been the custom of the Roman Pontiffs to favour the Society. Pius IV used to say that the religious of the Society of Jesus ought to be cherished with greater love than others, on account of the more outstanding fruits which they had brought to the Church of God. Paul III called it a pious and holy institute; your Holiness will not allow the Society, approved and raised up by the Pontiffs, to fail and fall.

units.la: Non est deliberatius ullum consilium, quàm primæ Societatis constitutio: hoc est, quod redintegrari cupiunt omnes Societatis Patres, qui primis primorum Patrum suorum viftigijs insistunt. Convenerant Romam Patres socij Beati Patris Ignatij Anno 1538. Deum appellant per tres menses effusa in preces mente, tum haec decernunt. Societatem sub uno Generali perpetuo constituendam, emittendum votum expressum obedientiae summo Pontifici, ut sacrae fidei causa, parati sint Socij, ad nutum summi Pontificis, quasvis obire regiones, nullum abnuere pro animarum salute, laborem: Ijs, qui profitentur, imbuendos esse catechesi Christianapueros, unam quatuor votorum professionem, potestatem omnem in majori suffragiorum numero stabiliendam. Qui probarentur ad Societatem, Xenodochijs, pijs itineribus, & secretis meditationibus exercendos. Tum exscripta est haec formula, & summo Pontifici Paulo III. oblata. Probat institutum, non plures tamen ad illud admittendos edidit, quam sexaginta. Nondum Sacerdotum Coadjutorum est ulla mentio: tum permittente Paulo crescit Societas, admittuntur permulti ad Professionem unam: nihil sanctius, nihil religiosius, mens omnibus una. Paulo post occurrit, Sacerdotes aliquos Coadjutores Professis jungendos esse, qui absolvi possent a votis, & a Societate repelli: difficile est hoc impetrare: non audit libenter Paulus III. tamen quinque annis circiter ab institutione Societatis, anno videlicet 1546. concedit, ut 2o. duntaxat Sacerdotes Coadjutores ascribantur. Animad vertebat optimus Pontifex, religiosorum Ordi-num astimator, & judex æquissimus, dissestum iri Societatis spiritum, si votorum illa varietas passim liceret, latere sub illa novitate aliquid, quod postmodum experientia detexit: Stetit primum Societas sine ulla Coadjutorum accessione, & juris incrementis late provesta est, vigebat sine ullo decreto, quod, ut ipsorum linguâ utar, essentiale postea visum est: Integra erat, nec tamen illa Coadjutorum ascititia supplementa noverat. Appendix iste Coadjutorum ad Societatem alligatus, Julio III. annuente persistit anno 1550. tum sub Pio V. anno 1576. & Gregorio XIII. 1584. constitutiones augentur, & illud præsertim de Coadjutoribus nova editione, & novo jure concessum est. Ut nova placet, & quæ ad dignitatem tuendam sunt accommodata: gratissimum est Professis, super Coadjutores eminere, & ne molestum sit illis subesse, dulci deliniunt hanc conditionis abjestionem convictu ac familiaritate.
units.tr: No plan was ever more deliberate than the original constitution of the Society. This is what all the Fathers of the Society desire to restore, those who follow in the footsteps of their first Fathers. The fellow Fathers of Blessed Father Ignatius had gathered at Rome in the year 1538. They spent three months pouring out prayers to God, and then they decreed these things: that the Society should be established under one perpetual General; that an express vow of obedience should be made to the supreme Pontiff, so that, for the cause of the sacred faith, the members should be ready, at the nod of the supreme Pontiff, to go to whatever regions he chose, and to refuse no labour for the salvation of souls; that those who professed should be instructed in Christian catechesis; that there should be one profession of four vows; that all authority should be established by the greater number of votes. Those who were found fit for the Society were to be exercised in hospices, in pious journeys and in private meditations. Then this formula was copied out and offered to the supreme Pontiff Paul III. He approved the institute, but he allowed no more than sixty to be admitted to it. There was as yet no mention of coadjutor priests. Then, with Paul's permission, the Society grew, and very many were admitted to the one profession; nothing was holier, nothing more religious, and all had one mind. Soon afterwards it occurred to some that priests should be joined to the professed as coadjutors, who might be absolved from the vows and dismissed from the Society. This was hard to obtain; Paul III did not readily listen to it. Yet about five years after the institution of the Society, namely in the year 1546, he granted that only two priests should be enrolled as coadjutors. The excellent Pontiff, a great esteemer of religious orders and a most fair judge, noticed that the spirit of the Society would be broken if such variety of vows were allowed everywhere, and that something lay hidden under that novelty which experience later revealed. The Society first stood without any accession of coadjutors, and spread far by the increase of its rights; it flourished without any decree, which, to use their own language, was later judged essential. It was whole, and yet it did not know those supplementary coadjutors added from outside. This appendix of coadjutors attached to the Society persisted with the consent of Julius III in the year 1550; then under Pius V in 1576 and Gregory XIII in 1584 the constitutions were enlarged, and especially in regard to the coadjutors a new edition and a new law were granted. As they like new things, and things suited to preserving their dignity, it is very pleasing to the professed to stand above the coadjutors, and so that it may not be irksome for these to be under them, they soothe this lowering of status with sweet companionship and familiarity.

units.la: Professis Professi succedunt, Coadjutores Coadjutoribus, sed ubique datur progenies vitiosior, isti de iniqua sua sorte queruntur, illi de sua retinenda, plus æquo sunt solliciti. Professi Coadjutores suos Sacerdotes ut clientes habere volunt. Coadjutores vero Profes-sos, ut fratres. Sed cum apud Professos omnis sit potestas, ijdem evincunt facile, & sub jugum Coadjutores mittunt, relegant ad vilísima quæque, a gubernatione amovent, in modum Plebejorum & rejectorum hominum tradant, dimissionem comminantur, omnii suffragiorum jure interdicunt. Coadjutores vociferantur, non debere fratres dominari in clero, vim istam esse, quæ diuturna esse non potest, primæ Societatis consuetudinem repetendam, una professione, æquali omnes firmitate in uno ordine fulciendos, adolescentibus evellendum ambitionis aculeum, non decere ex Apostoli verbis dominationem in Clero, proscribi oportere aliquorum decemviratus, qui strenuos, quos suis vitijs obstare viderint, ad expulsionem deijciunt: Ut paria sunt religionis onera, etsi dispares, pro diversis meritis, sint honores, vitæ tamen religiosæ statum, eadem Professione ac solennitate votorum fir-mandum esse. Quid vetat Beatissime Pontifex jure Societatis antiquo, Societatis Sacerdotes ad unam professionem admitti? Quæ Societas, in qua dissociantur vota? discre-pant status? diversa est religio? Quomodo unus ordo, una religio, in qua alij perpetuo ac solenni voto constant, alij nonnisi ad voluntatem præsixo, & ad arbitrium aliorum persistunt? Quomodo non duplex religionis ordo, ubi duplex votorum conditio? Religiosi sunt Coadjutores, sed dimittendi ad saeculum, si Societati videbitur. Religiosi sunt professi, sed a religione nunquam absolvendi: Secura in Professis vita, in Coadjutoribus anceps, & plena periculis: Hinc ingemuit & indoluit aliquando Clemens VIII. Pontifex maximus, cum audivisset, eos, qui ad Professionem Societatis provesti essent, non aliter efferri, quàm sie Coadjutorum servitute erepti essent.
