Si una religio, cur non una firmitas? si una omnium pietas, cur non una religionis in omnes charitas? cur alios ut filios adoptat, alios ut mancipes, & assectlas frænat?
units.tr: Professed succeed the professed, and coadjutors succeed coadjutors, but everywhere a more faulty progeny is born. The latter complain of their unfair lot, the former are over-anxious about keeping theirs. The professed want their coadjutor priests to be as clients; the coadjutors want the professed to be as brothers. But since all power lies with the professed, they easily prove the point and bring the coadjutors under the yoke: they relegate them to the lowest tasks, remove them from government, hand them over like plebeians and rejected men, threaten dismissal, and deprive them of the right to vote. The coadjutors cry out that brothers ought not to lord it over the clergy; that this domination cannot last long; that the custom of the first Society must be restored, that all should be supported in one order by one profession and equal firmness; that the sting of ambition must be torn out of young men; that it is not fitting, in the words of the Apostle, to lord it over the clergy; that the decemvirate of some men must be banned, which casts down the vigorous and those whom they see standing in the way of their vices, for expulsion. Since the burdens of religion are equal, even if honours differ according to different merits, the state of religious life ought to be confirmed by the same profession and solemnity of vows. Most Blessed Pontiff, what forbids that, by the ancient law of the Society, all the Society's priests should be admitted to one profession? What society is it in which the vows are divided? Where the status differs? Where the religion is diverse? How can there be one order and one religion in which some persist by a perpetual and solemn vow, and others only at the will of a fixed term and at the discretion of others? How is it not a double order of religion, where the condition of vows is double? The coadjutors are religious, but they may be dismissed to the world if the Society thinks fit; the professed are religious, but are never to be absolved from religion. The life of the professed is secure, that of the coadjutors uncertain and full of dangers. Hence Clement VIII, the supreme Pontiff, once groaned and grieved, when he heard that those who had advanced to the profession of the Society were carried out in no other way than as men rescued from the servitude of coadjutors. If there is one religion, why not one firmness? If the piety of all is one, why not one charity of religion towards all? Why does it adopt some as sons, and hold others in check as servants and followers?

units.la: Consules ordini, Beatissime Pontifex, si jubeas, restaurato primo Societatis jure Sacerdotes omnes Societatis, ad professionem quatuor votorum admitti, nullum in Coadjutorem spiritualem cooptari, ut ad unam pietatem, & consentiens virtutis studium animos omnium una professio accendat. Superstes florebit simplicitas, frigescet ambitio, tranquillè tractabunt litterarum studia Scholastici Societatis, cùm tranquillum sibi spatium ætatis cursum, non minùs virtuti, quàm doctrinæ se dedent, valedicent versutijs, & superiorum benevolentiam sinceritate non prosequutione sibi conciliabunt: non assuescent prehensationibus, & blanditijs, quæ omnem prorsus religionis spiritum extinguunt: non adulationi servient, non illi observantiæ dabunt operam, quâ Professionem potius, quàm pietatem colunt. Satis acres sunt ad litterarum studia stimuli, subeunda doctorum hominum judicia, excellentibus tantùm ingenijs patens palæstra honoris litterarij, laureæ, sedræ, & alia eruditionis ornamenta, Minervæ tholo suspensa, suum ad gloriam ignem satis suscitabunt. Virtutem verò advocabit, & religionem aspirabit Professio. Liberè & vere dicam, non ut Societati labem aspergam, aut ullius nomen proscissum velim, sed ut consulas Ordini Max. Pontifex, quem si non consentanei mores exceperint, in suum sponte exibit exitium.
units.tr: Consult the order, Most Blessed Pontiff, if you so command: with the first law of the Society restored, let all the Society's priests be admitted to the profession of four vows, and let no spiritual coadjutor be co-opted, so that one profession may kindle the minds of all to one piety and to a harmonious zeal for virtue. Simplicity will flourish again, ambition will grow cold, the scholastics of the Society will pursue their studies of letters in tranquillity, since they will devote the peaceful course of their age no less to virtue than to learning, will bid farewell to cunning, and will win the goodwill of their superiors by sincerity rather than by pursuit. They will not grow used to fawning and flattery, which utterly extinguish all the spirit of religion; they will not serve adulation, nor give their effort to that show of deference by which they cultivate the profession rather than piety. The goads to the study of letters are sharp enough: the judgements of learned men must be undergone, and the arena of literary honour lies open only to outstanding talents, with laurel, chair and other ornaments of learning hung on the dome of Minerva; these will kindle fire enough for their glory. But the profession will summon virtue and inspire religion. I will speak freely and truly, not to cast a stain on the Society or to wish any man's name torn, but so that you may consult the Supreme Order, Most Holy Pontiff; if its manners do not agree with it, it will of its own accord go out to its own ruin.

units.la: Duo sunt, quæ vi aperta in hunc Ordinem sese ingerunt: Ambitionis ardor, fastus, & astus, religiosæ simplicitatis fatum: quæ non sine acerbo luctu sentiunt inviti antiquiores & sinceriores Patres. Professorum potestas, immunitas, dignitas, ambitioni fomitem suggerit: Coadjutorum Patrum tenuitas, repulsa, abiectio, Professorum fastui obstetricantur, astum in nefastam simplicitatis lumini, lucem educunt. Professi Patres regunt ad arbitrium; hinc oboriuntur offuciæ: cæteros attollunt, vel deprimunt, ut collibitum fuerit: audax penes illos fandi fuclamandiq; libertas, suppetit illis aurata rerum omnium provisio, eunt & redeunt itinera, equo, pecunia, & multo apparatu ommuniti. Sed quid peccant, per medias telas soluti erumpunt, opipara illis in congregationibus, magno sumptu, mensa paratur: egeant omnes, vexentur imperijs, versentur in omne latus, convicijs exagitentur, pœnis comminuantur: suum si regnum teneat Professus, non est qui judicium ferat, felici loco stant omnia. Hæc videre possunt optimi religiosi, nec tamen pro religiosæ vitæ incolumitate vindicare possunt.
units.tr: There are two things that force themselves upon this Order in plain view: the fire of ambition, with pride and craft, which is the ruin of religious simplicity. The older and more sincere Fathers, though unwillingly, feel this with bitter grief. The power, exemption and dignity of the Professed supply fuel to ambition. The poverty, rejection and abjection of the Coadjutor Fathers serve the pride of the Professed, and they bring forth craft, a light of cunning, against the light of unlearned simplicity. The Professed Fathers rule at their own pleasure, and from this arise deceits. They raise up or cast down others as they please. They have a bold freedom of speech and of thundering, and they have a golden supply of all things. They go and come on journeys equipped with horses, money and a great retinue. But if they sin, they break free through the middle of the nets. Lavish banquets are prepared for them in their gatherings at great expense. Everyone else is in want, is harassed by commands, is hunted on every side, is worn down by abuse and punishments. If the Professed holds his own kingdom, there is no one to pass judgment, and everything stands in a happy position. The best religious can see these things, yet they cannot defend them for the safety of the religious life.

units.la: Tunc Beatissime Ignatie sperâsti huius notæ Professos? extincti sunt excellentes illi minùs virtutis genere Professi, nunc ad ambitionem pietas conversa: debent in domibus Professis arctissimam degere paupertatem, ac victum emendicare, contrà, delibant optima quæque in Collegijs, usu possident exquisita, vestiuntur commodiùs, habitant laxiùs, utuntur fratribus ut pedisequis, silent rarius, liberius loquuntur. Quàm conferti ad vestram Sanctitatem accurrunt, ut sine viatico, sola Christi opefulti, vel ad infideeles, vel ad hæreticos mittantur!? Scholasticos plures solent ad Indias dimittere, suo non obligatos voto, ipsi sponsionis rei, & quarto constricti voto, sospites se servant in paratioribus locis, & cùm duriora & asperiora inferioribus prædicent, meliora & molliora sibi eliguntur. Hæ cum prima B. Ignatij professione longè disconvenit vita, jam tamen Professus usitata, & Scholasticis inspem propositâ.
units.tr: Did you then, most blessed Ignatius, hope for Professed Fathers of this kind? Those excellent Professed, who were less eminent in virtue, have died out. Now piety has been turned to ambition. They ought to live in the Professed houses in the strictest poverty and beg their food. On the contrary, they skim off all the best things in the Colleges, possess exquisite goods, dress more comfortably, live more loosely, use the brothers as servants, keep silence less often and speak more freely. How crowded they rush to your Holiness, to be sent without provision, relying only on the help of Christ, either to the unbelievers or to the heretics! They often send the Scholastics to the Indies. They are not bound by their own vow, but they themselves are bound by the matter of the promise and by the fourth vow. They keep themselves safe in the more comfortable places, and while they preach the harder and rougher things to their inferiors, they choose the better and softer things for themselves. This life differs widely from the first profession of Blessed Ignatius, yet it is now customary for the Professed and is set before the Scholastics as a hope.

units.la: Ecce Ambitionis artes: Professi sunt in apice splendidioris, & facilioris vitæ. Hic Scholastico corum scopus, ne hoc excidant honore, magistris assentantur, suis superioribus blanditur, dant auribus quod placet, dicunt referuntque quod arrideat, modestiores ex suis socijs, absimiles sibi, ab astuta illa consuetudine aversos, ad Coadjutores mandant. Vbi religiosus convictus? quæ Christianæ vitæ perfectio? Artifices sæcu-
units.tr: See the arts of ambition! The Professed are at the summit of a more splendid and easier life. This is the goal of the Scholastics: so that they do not lose this honour, they flatter their masters and fawn upon their superiors. They lend their ears to whatever pleases, they say and repeat whatever pleases, and they send the more modest of their companions, who are unlike them and who shrink from that crafty custom, off to the Coadjutors. Where is religious fellowship? Where is the perfection of the Christian life? The craftsmen of the worldly-

units.la: Vu laris prudentiæ nec dissimulationis expertes evadunt religiosi alumni. Profesionem spirant, & sperant, ut suos superent fratres: videt patricios ad dignitates Profesione sibi viam fecisse: hæc attingenda est meta. Cum involarunt in arcem, præsunt Coadjutoribus Sacerdotibus eosque despiciunt, hujusmodi professi Rectores pleŧunt inclementer, pertinaci probro fodiunt, nullas constantiæ dant inducias, quibus gradibus ascendit ambitio, ijsdem religiosa simplicitas demittitur, nihil prodest ad firmum & clarum Societatis statum obtinendum, pudentis ac sinceri animi moderatio: advocanda est industria, occultis nitendum est machinis, versuta solum emergunt ingenia: qui vaferrimus est hic digito significatur, conijciuntur in illum ora & oculi, committuntur illi Collegia, si quæ sunt res cum illustribus viris, ipsius consilio componuntur, laudatur quidem sed absens, & exul a Societate candida simplicitas, ne manum quidem ad illum verterint, qui nesciat simulare expressum; per hanc morum corruptelam quis illuceat virtutis dies? ubi vinculum? quod conjunctos religiosa necessitudine animos, devinciat & cum nullus adsit expressus dictis & factis candor? Nihil in hominum cœtu mutua illa, quæ inter Societates intercedit, confidentia dulcius, nihil beatius, nullum gratius solatium ore fideli, & consentienti pectore: si cura, & sollicitudo ambitionis se interserit, acescunt hæc omnia, sapit fucus: est qui pigmentis bona decoloret sua, & malit imagine sinceritatis illudere quam vera virtute ambire. Defertur religiosus habitus, ferpit sæcularis animus, immittit se blandus, & cum externa disciplina consuescit, in aula, in cameris, in scholis, in porticu, in impluvio, in Aede, in suggestu, nusquam non adest prudentiæ perversæ genius, inepta gloriolæ præstigijs, piæ simplicitatis egentes, & ad astutiam verbi faciles irretit. Hinc illæ totius orbis querelæ, astutos esse Iesuitas, non esse rudes versutiæ secularis. Hinc exigua dictis fides, suspiciones artificiorum satis firmæ, alienatio optimatum a Societate: subdividunt de fidelitate respublicæ, Senatus regij de factione nimia conqueruntur, multa graviter incusant, scripta cautius interpretantur, & notant. Socios calliditatis potius tentandæ, quam eruditionis aut salutis accipiendæ studio explorant.
units.tr: wise prudence, and not strangers to dissimulation, are what the religious pupils become. They breathe and hope for profession, so that they may surpass their brothers. They see that men of noble birth have made a way to dignities by means of profession, and this is the goal to be reached. When they have flown into the citadel, they preside over the Coadjutors, priests though they are, and despise them. Such Professed Rectors rule harshly, they stab with stubborn reproach, and they grant no truce to constancy. By the same steps by which ambition climbs, religious simplicity is cast down. The moderation of a modest and sincere mind avails nothing for securing a firm and clear state for the Society. Industry must be summoned, one must strive with hidden machines, and only crafty talents rise to the top. The most cunning man is pointed at with a finger. Eyes and mouths are turned upon him. The Colleges are entrusted to him. If there are any dealings with distinguished men, they are arranged on his advice. Candid simplicity is praised, but only in absence, and it is an exile from the Society. They would not even raise a hand against the man who does not know how to feign what is plain. Through this corruption of morals, what dawn of virtue can shine? Where is the bond which should bind together minds joined by religious fellowship, when there is no open candour in words and deeds? Nothing in a gathering of men is sweeter than that mutual confidence which exists between companies. Nothing is more blessed, and no comfort is more pleasing, than a faithful mouth and a heart in agreement. But if the care and anxiety of ambition intrudes, all these things turn sour, and the drone tastes of its own dye. There is one who discolours his goods with paints, and prefers to deceive by the image of sincerity than to strive for by true virtue. The religious habit is put on, and a worldly mind creeps in. It enters flatteringly, and grows accustomed to outward discipline. In the court, in the chambers, in the schools, in the portico, in the courtyard, in the church, on the pulpit, everywhere is present the spirit of perverse prudence. It ensnares those who are easy to lead into cunning words, those who are open to the empty illusions of a little glory and lack pious simplicity. Hence come those complaints throughout the whole world that the Jesuits are crafty and are not unskilled in worldly cunning. Hence come little faith in their words, quite firm suspicions of their artifices, and the alienation of the nobles from the Society. Men doubt their loyalty to the commonwealth. Royal senates complain of excessive partisanship, gravely accuse them of many things, interpret their writings more cautiously and mark them. They test their companions for the purpose of trying their cunning, rather than of receiving learning or salvation.

units.la: Perperam illa præclara munia, si evellitur ex animis hominum, sanctitatis opinio, si minus simplex, & a sæculo parum remota Societas habeatur.
units.tr: Those distinguished offices are wrongly held if the opinion of holiness is torn from men's minds, if the Society is regarded as less simple and not far removed from the world.

units.la: Nollem propterea Selectis viris, qui in Societate sunt, injuriam fieri, admiratus sum sapientiam & prudentiam Claudij Aquavivæ Generalis, Mutij Vitellescchi astientis comitatem, Fabij de Fabijs pietatem, Iustiniani Genuensis doctrinam & integritatem, ut ne quam plurimos alios citem, quorum nomina in diversis Provincijs illustria sunt, & ob clarissimas virtutes celebrata: sed ea vestræ Sanctitati redhibeo reconcinnanda, quæ multorum vel vitio, vel incuria pessundata sunt, & afflicta. Religiosæ modestiæ placida demissio dimissa est? revocetur. Squallet ignara fraudis simplicitas? suo nitori restituatur. Insidiantur angues gemini, ambitio & versutia? suffocentur.
units.tr: I would not wish that any injustice be done to the select men who are in the Society. I have admired the wisdom and prudence of Claudio Acquaviva, the General; the courtesy of Muzio Vitelleschi, the assistant; the piety of Fabio de Fabiis; the learning and integrity of Giustiniani of Genoa; not to mention very many others whose names are illustrious in various provinces and celebrated for their most distinguished virtues. But I am restoring to your Holiness those things that need to be set right, which have been ruined and afflicted through the fault or carelessness of many. The gentle humility of religious modesty has been dismissed: let it be recalled. Sincere simplicity, ignorant of deceit, lies in squalor: let it be restored to its former brightness. Two snakes lie in ambush, ambition and cunning: let them be stifled.

units.la: Postulant præterea sinceri Patres Societatis, ut innovetur statutum decem Patrum, quo res omnes ex majori suffragiorum pondere, ac numero, & non ex unius definitione concludi debebant. Quæ ad institutionem animæ spectant, ad morum examen, ad fidei stabilitatem, solus Pontifex Rom. etiam de fede motu proprio constituit, & dicta Rom. Pontificis Spiritus sancti afflatu inspirata, secure pronunciantur. Illi non caligo potest, non nubes eripere lucem, immotum est divinæ pollicitationis decretum, hæresis ineluctabile fatum, Petri fidem deficere nunquam. Non habes Collegam Beatiss. Pater, & in Ecclesia Dei præsente, semper & custodiente divino spiritu, a recta sapientia dimoveri non potes. Hanc possidesque potestatem, figendi refigendique motu proprio quod suggesserit in Ecclesia Deus. Non est in religiosorum superioribus similis authoritas: praecipere debent statuta, quae non sit illis suorum rejectis suffragijs, pro arbitrio quae visa fuerint, imperare. Stent pluribus & melioribus sententijs, ne Rectores ac superiores Societatis in suo ordine parem cum vestra Sanctitate, sibi potestatem vindicent: non est illis major promissa coelitus gratia, quam Ecclesiae Episcopis, nihil tamen Episcopi, ac diaecetae in Synodis sine suorum suffragijs determnunt, cur se subducent a communi jure, qui ad errorem proclives, ut caeteri, in eandem jactisunt humanae infirmitatis aleam? cur in suis Collegijs affectent eam authoritatem, quam Romae & in universa Ecclesia summus Pontifex detinet? Vidi deceptos hoc errore Rectores aliquot, qui etsi Clemens Octavus sanxerit, ne quis Societatis, Sedem Apostolicam petens, per superiores a cepto deturbaretur, tamen suos Romam petentes, ut summo Pontifici multa detegerent, injusto anathemate afflixerunt, (non enim ligare poterant) & impatientes appellationis ad sanctam sedem diris devoverunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, the sincere Fathers of the Society ask that the statute of the Ten Fathers be renewed, by which all matters ought to be decided by the greater weight and number of votes, and not by the definition of one man. Matters that concern the formation of the soul, the examination of morals, and the stability of the faith, the Roman Pontiff alone establishes even concerning faith, on his own initiative. The words of the Roman Pontiff, inspired by the breath of the Holy Spirit, are pronounced with confidence. No darkness can take away his light, no cloud can obscure it. The decree of divine promise is immovable, the fate of heresy is inescapable, and the faith of Peter never fails. Most blessed Father, you have no colleague, and while God is present in the Church and the divine Spirit always guards it, you cannot be moved from right wisdom. You possess this power, to fix and unfix on your own initiative whatever God has suggested in the Church. The superiors of the religious have no such authority. They ought to prescribe statutes, but they may not command whatever seems fit to them at their own discretion, with their subjects' votes set aside. Let them stand by the greater and better opinions. Let the Rectors and superiors of the Society not claim for themselves power in their own order equal to your Holiness. They have no greater grace promised from heaven than the bishops of the Church. Yet bishops and dioceses do not decide anything in synods without the votes of their members. Why should those withdraw from the common law who, being prone to error like the rest, have been thrown into the same gamble of human weakness? Why in their own Colleges do they aspire to that authority which the supreme Pontiff holds at Rome and in the whole Church? I have seen several Rectors deceived by this error. Although Clement VIII has decreed that no member of the Society who seeks the Apostolic See should be thrown off his course by his superiors, yet they, when their subjects went to Rome to disclose many things to the supreme Pontiff, afflicted them with an unjust anathema (for they could not bind them), and, impatient of appeal to the Holy See, they cursed them with dire imprecations.

units.la: Hoc mihi semper suspectum fuit, atque esse debuit, religiosos, qui se gloriantur summo Pontifici servire, & vivere, Pontificis tamen judicio nolle se sistere, ne de suis negotijs ac rebus certior fiat summus Pontifex pertimescere. Technas moliri omnes, ne consilius sit gubernationis, ducere criminii, si quis Pontifici castiganda proponat, proscindere verbis, aspergere dedecore, quem viderunt apud Pontificem esse, & sanctae sedis Apostolicae, & Ecclesiae, ut par est, magis, quam suae dominationis, amare. Nec vir ipsi Societatis Superiores, ne plus aequo potentes, ex primae Societatis decreto, sui vandis suffragijs alligentur, nihil innovent, aut mandent, refragante Sacerdotum Collegio: nullus excepto Generali proposito, ultra triennium superior perstitit. Non praeter illos, quem vel congregatio, vel Collegiorum Professi non elegerint, nullus ad congregationem Generalem vel Provincialem proficiscatur, quem non statuerint Collegiorum Sacerdotes.
units.tr: This has always seemed suspicious to me, and it ought to be so: religious who boast that they serve and live for the supreme Pontiff, yet are unwilling to submit themselves to the Pontiff's judgment, fear lest the supreme Pontiff be informed of their affairs and dealings. They devise every trick so that the fault of government is not discussed. They make it a crime if anyone proposes something to be corrected to the Pontiff. They tear him apart with words and smear him with disgrace, a man whom they have seen to love the Pontiff, and the Holy Apostolic See and the Church, more than their own dominion, as is right. Nor let the superiors of the Society themselves, lest they become more powerful than is fair, be bound by their own votes, contrary to the first decree of the Society. Let them not change or command anything against the opposition of the college of priests. No superior has remained beyond three years, except the General by proposal. Let no one go to the General or Provincial congregation unless he has been chosen by the congregation, or by the professed of the Colleges, and unless he has been approved by the priests of the Colleges.

units.la: Nec vestrae Sanctitati satis unquam cautum sit: inquirat de illis, audiat, probet, quid rerum agant, num ut superiorum jus augeant, de vestra potestate aliquid detrahant: num putent, vestrae Sanctitatis esse, religiosorum querelas rescire, leges ac disciplinam omnem ponderare: Subodoratus enim sum nescio quid, secularem nimirum appellabant Pontificem aliqui: Ignatios vitae religiosae Cardinales: eosdem esse saeculares, ac de obedientia religiosa, de mente, de consuetudine, de administratione sententiam ferre non posse. Objupui, nec nisi offensis auribus recessi, multa volutans animo, & hoc praesertim, praesentes vestrae Sanctitatis oculos, quasi de speculata prospicere debere, quo tam multae immunitates, tam magnae facultates hujusmodi religiosos efferre possint.
units.tr: Your Holiness can never be careful enough. Let her inquire into these men, hear them, and test what they are doing: whether they are enlarging the authority of their superiors, whether they are taking something away from your power, and whether they think it is for your Holiness to learn of the complaints of the religious and to weigh all their laws and discipline. For I have caught a whiff of something. Some men have been calling the Pontiff a secular, and the Ignatian cardinals of religious life have claimed that the same men are secular and cannot pass judgment on religious obedience, on the spirit, on custom, or on administration. I was astonished, and I withdrew only with offended ears, turning many thoughts over in my mind. Above all, I thought that your Holiness ought to look out, as from a watchtower, with your own eyes, to see how such religious could have won so many immunities and so great powers.

units.la: Superest, ut inane otium, quod in aula multis hominibus Societate, pernitiosum est, utilia ac religioso otio hauriatur. Superfluis excursionibus erecti, ac laeti vagantur ex illis plurimi: volitant per urbes, & ne sellis suis immorentur, occupationes externas quaerunt, alienis distinentur negotijs; solemni tandem choro poterunt contineri. Si decantent officium, Beatissime Pater, si concentum amet coelestem, si rebus divinis adsint, si hoc genere religiosae servitutis non eximantur, si die ac nocte bonas horas psalmodiae impendant, otium futile, serijs impedimentis trudent, non salutationibus crebris, non protractis sermonibus sese effundent, non de Principibus, non de Praelatis curiosus inquirent. Rixae, dissensiones, admurmurationes, risus, de coetu Societatis disijcientur, cotentiones, quae religiosos animos decent, cavillationes, (quod decurtatae simplicitatis ludibrium?) & alia noxae amovebuntur. Si divino huic officio assuefacient adolescentes Societatis saecularia fastidient colloquia, non tenebuntur illa urbanitate saeculari, ad quam se instituere solent; syncerio res & puriores gemitus Christo suo dabunt, non se vertent in illam verborum dissimulationem, ac varietatem, senes felicem obitum meditabuntur, habebunt in quo desertam senectutem consolentur, taedium cubiculi jucundissima divini cantus vicissitudine traducent in tranquillissimum otium: pax vigebit summa in Collegijs, non observabunt saeculares, Societatis religiosos, tam familiares & vagos: & ideo diligent magis. Sedisti omnibus reclamabunt aliqui. Qui? Maxime Pontifex? Quinam obsistent? qui professionem illam unam condemnabunt? qui debilitare suffragiorum vim? qui psalmodiae obstrepere poterunt? illi, quos professio, at non religiosa perfectio delectat, qui soli decernere, qui studeant vivere liberi ab omni religiosa observantia. Quinam insurgent? illi, qui decem primorum Patrum institutionem sepultam esse cupiunt, qui nolunt in primam pietatem recurrere, quos pudet et taedet multos habere pares, multos professionis suae Socios, qui se examinari, facta sua in judicium vocari, qui se ad obedientiae ordinem redigi pertimescunt. Romae numerantur ferme quingenti: si libere loqui possent, nec impedirent pauci philautiae et honoris sui tenaces, primos decem primorum Patrum mores reposcerent, Professionem unicam, jus commune suffragiorum repeterent, et solemnem celebrarent chorum in locum illius, quam retinent molestissimae, optimis quibusque pomeridianae et vespertinae recreationis: quam parum abest, quin jam congregationis statuto sustulerint.
units.tr: It remains that the empty leisure which is pernicious to many men of the Society at court be replaced by useful and religious leisure. Many of them, lifted up by superfluous excursions and in high spirits, wander about. They flit through the cities, and so as not to linger in their chairs they seek outside occupations and are distracted by other people's business. Only in the solemn choir can they at last be contained. If they chanted the Office, Most Blessed Father, if they loved heavenly harmony, if they attended to divine things, if they were not freed from this kind of religious service, and if they spent good hours of the day and night on psalmody, they would thrust out idle leisure with serious occupations. They would not pour themselves out in frequent greetings or long conversations, and they would not busily inquire about princes or prelates. Quarrels, dissensions, grumblings, laughter, and the chatter that befits a company of the Society would be cast out, along with contentions which suit religious minds, cavils (what mockery of a cut-down simplicity?), and other harms. If they accustomed the young men of the Society to this divine office, they would come to loathe worldly conversations, and they would no longer be held by that secular urbanity for which they are usually trained. They would offer their Christ sincere and purer groans, and they would not turn to that dissembling and changeable way of speaking. Old men would meditate on a happy death, and they would have something to console a forsaken old age. They would turn the weariness of the bedchamber, by the most delightful alternation of divine song, into the most tranquil leisure. Supreme peace would flourish in the colleges. They would not be watched by secular men, the religious of the Society being so familiar and wandering. And so they would be loved more. Some will object from every seat. Who? Most Holy Pontiff? Who will resist? Those who would condemn that single profession? Those who would weaken the force of the votes? Those who could disturb the psalmody? Those who delight in the profession but not in religious perfection, who want to decide matters alone and who strive to live free of all religious observance. Who will rise up? Those who want the institution of the first ten Fathers to lie buried, who are unwilling to return to the early piety, who are ashamed and weary of having many equals, many companions in their profession, who fear being examined, having their deeds called into judgment, and being brought back under the discipline of obedience. About five hundred are counted at Rome. If they could speak freely, and if a few who cling tenaciously to self-love and their own honour did not hinder them, they would demand back the manners of the first ten Fathers, the single profession, and the common right of voting. They would celebrate the solemn choir in place of that most troublesome recreation of the afternoon and evening, which most of the best men keep. How little is lacking for them to have already abolished it by a decree of the congregation!

units.la: Hanc repetunt primae Societatis redintegrationem selectissimi e Societate Religiosi. Vestrae Sanctitati gratias agent immortales, si ambitionem, ac versutias excedere jubeat, aurea sibi gratulabuntur vestro Pontificatu redijisse pietatem, suo aequitatem sejuram loco, reperta primae Societatis fundamenta, statum erectum. Potuit a Professis indifferentium Ordo, a Beato Ignatio institutus, abrogari, expunctus est collateralis a Collegiis, quem B. Ignatius ad temperandam Rectorum potestatem, Rectoribus opposuerat, Collateralis Patris ipsius consortium Rectores, ut potestati suae adversum extinxerunt: cur non ab iis pari ratione Coadjutorum inutilis gradus auferetur? Cur non a vestra Sanctitate (cum soli caenodoxiae, et propriae amantes dignitatis hoc facere recusent) Sacerdotum Coadjutorum gradus obliterabitur? Plures et meliores erunt in Societate viri, si omnes prosessione digni esse debebunt: Confessarios et Coadjutores Societas habebit praestantiores. Quid mirum si examinari volunt Episcopi Jesuitas, ne indigni confessiones audiant? nimirum Coadjutores Sacerdotes ad id muneris dantur, quibus interdictum est studere, qui repulsi sunt a scientiis, vel quod genere viles essent (quod heu inter religiosos discrimen?) vel quod ad mensae ministerium magis apti. Quis non juste dicat, conqueri Episcopos, dum Sacerdotes eos sibi consecrandos vident, quos nec patrimonii, nec beneficii, nec Professionis titulus, de certis alimentis securos facit? quos hodie religiosos, cras seculares esse posse norunt, si Superiores velint? quos mediocriter literis tinctos, Philosophiae ac Theologiae rudes, ad gubernandas tamen conscientias deputinari sciunt? Quod si sint Coadjutores aliqui Sacerdotes, qui virtute, scientia, eloquentia non solum adaequent Professos, sed superent, (non incredibile certe facinus, sed exemplis clarum) quis non videt, diversam illam distributionem, ex aliquorum sensu, ac voluntate, ut ambitioni suae velificentur, obfirmatis animis retineri? Quis non hanc manifestam dissensionis, ac divisionis sementem, ac segetem putet? Qui Sacerdotio dignus esse poterit, Professione sui ordinis (quae est religionis et sanctitatis solenne pignus) indignus esse non debet. Urgent Episcopi, ne Sacerdotes vitae ac firmitatis suae incertos, ne parum ad Societatis munera dignos instituant. Patres Societatis eximii, quorum haec dictata scripsi, pro Christi amore, pro Societatis nomine, et redintegratione vehementer expostulant. Reges et Principes peroptant, ne dimissos et afflictos tam saepe religiosos in suis Provinciis habeant: indigenae, ac cives percupiunt, ne de Societatis Religiosis subdividant, ne coguntur per contestari, sitne Coadjutor, an Professus ille Sacerdos: videlicet doctus, an indoctus, servus an liber, aliquis aut nihil, stabilis religiosus, an ad Superioris duntaxat nutum. Religiosae annuunt omnes familiae, quae sanctorum Patrum institutis, et religiosae antiquitati Societatem adaptatam gratulabuntur.
units.tr: The most select religious of the Society seek this restoration of the early Society. Immortal thanks will be given to your Holiness if you command them to put aside ambition and cunning. They will rejoice that under your pontificate piety has returned, that equity has been restored to its place, and that the foundations of the first Society have been found and its condition raised up again. The order of the indifferents, instituted by Blessed Ignatius, could be abrogated by the Professed. The collateral was struck out of the colleges, the office which Blessed Ignatius had set over against the Rectors to temper their power. The Rectors, to oppose their own power, extinguished the companionship of the Father's own collateral. Why should the useless grade of coadjutors not be removed by them in like manner? Why should the grade of priest-coadjutors not be blotted out by your Holiness, since only those who love vainglory and their own dignity refuse to do this? The Society will have more and better men if all must be worthy of profession. The Society will have more excellent confessors and coadjutors. What wonder is it if bishops wish to examine the Jesuits, lest they hear confessions unworthily? Priest-coadjutors are indeed given to that office, men who are forbidden to study, who have been rejected by the sciences, either because of their lowly birth (alas, what distinction among religious?) or because they are better suited to serving at table. Who would not justly say that bishops complain when they see priests being given to them for consecration, men whom neither a patrimony, nor a benefice, nor the title of profession makes secure of a fixed livelihood? Men whom they know may be religious today and secular tomorrow, if the superiors so wish? Men whom they know to be only moderately learned, unskilled in philosophy and theology, and yet appointed to govern consciences? But if some priest-coadjutors equal the Professed in virtue, learning, and eloquence, and even surpass them (certainly no incredible deed, but one made clear by examples), who does not see that this different distribution is retained with minds fixed hard, according to the feeling and will of some men, so that they may spread their sails to their ambition? Who would not think this the manifest seed and crop of dissension and division? Whoever may be worthy of the priesthood should not be unworthy of the profession of his order, which is the solemn pledge of religion and holiness. The bishops press that priests, uncertain of their own life and stability, should not be appointed who are scarcely worthy of the offices of the Society. The distinguished Fathers of the Society, for whose sake I have written these things, earnestly demand this for the love of Christ, for the name of the Society, and for its restoration. Kings and princes earnestly wish not to have in their provinces the religious of the Society so often dismissed and afflicted. The natives and citizens greatly desire that they not be forced to question each religious of the Society, to ask whether this priest is a coadjutor or a professed man: that is, whether he is learned or unlearned, a slave or free, someone or nobody, a stable religious or one who depends only on the nod of his superior. All religious families agree, and will rejoice that the Society has been adapted to the institutes of the holy Fathers and to religious antiquity.

units.la: IMPERATORI AVGVSTO, FRANCIAE REGI CHRISTIANISSIMO, HISPANIAE REGI CA- THOLICO, OMNIBVSQVE PRINCIPI- BVS CHRISTIANIS. PRO REFORMATIONE ORDINIS IESVITARUM, Theophilus Eugenius.
units.tr: To the August Emperor, the Most Christian King of France, the Catholic King of Spain, and all Christian princes. For the Reform of the Order of the Jesuits, by Theophilus Eugenius.

units.la: CAESAR, Reges Augusti, manu, consilio, armis invicti, favete, & estote boni. Non ullus coram Agamemnone Achivorum Principe, nisi sit prorsus amens, nemo vana & inepta dixerit, sed apud vos delectui & rerum & verborum excogitatus sit oportet. Quis accessum speret, qui non sit mente digna? quem non absoluta prudentia efformarit? nec levia, nec nimia referam, sed quae ab ornatissimis & sapientissimis de Societatis IESV ordine amplissimo didici, & quae de conscia rerum experientia accepi. Xaverius Navarraeus Societatis IESV vir religiosissimus, ultra Calpen, & non jam amplius ultimam Thulem, praeter Herculis columnas, fidem apud ignotas & exteras regiones propagavit. Unus ex illorum decem primorum Patrum Societatis IESV, Collegio sanctiones cum Beato Patre Ignatio Loyola, & aliis decem, ad religiosum convictum exactas & breves dederat, quas approbaverat sanctus Pontifex, laudabant Episcopi, convenientes & accommodatas sanctorum Patrum institutis asserebant. Postea adjunxit Beatus Ignatius aliqua, quae posteri in detrimentum Ordinis trahunt. Privilegia & nova jura a sancta sede obtinuerunt, quibus non sine totius orbis querimonijs, praeter summi Pontificis mentem utuntur, ut volunt. Ne averti mores a Beato Ignatio, ne aliena ab illustri Xaverio vita, ne in Societatem se nova Societas inijciat, ad initia redeundum, hauriendi sunt fontes. Vestri quotquot sunt in orbe subditi Christiani; ac praesertim Patres Societatis, cum ij, qui adhuc in Societate vivunt, tum ij, quos atrox superiorum quorundam animus e Societate migrare compulit, vestris omnes advolvuntur genibus, ut vere Christiano & justo edicto tot selectos religiosos ab importuna vexatione liberos faciatis, arreptam illam superiorum, atque inusitatam potestatem temperetis ac lenibus vestris Imperijs moderemini. Quid tam insolens? quid tam durum ac dirum, quam tot insignes religiosos, quibus hic ardor erat, ut in votis perfisterent, e Societate evulsos? eosque etsi non alienum a Christo, alium tamen ab instituto propositio ducere spiritum? quid tam ferreum? quid tam inhumanum? quam a Sacerdotum religiosorum coetu abactos optimos viros, inhospitis & immitibus linguis proscindi? filios de matris uberibus violenta dejectione ad solum allidi? Quid ita a Societate abhorret, cujus omnes socij dicuntur, quam ista, non ex primorum Patrum Societatis instituto, non ex Beati Patris Ignatij studio, indueta conditionis dissimilitudo? vitae disparitas, religiosae vocationis incertitudo, morum discrepantia, disciplinae discrimen, onerum & laborum fors disjunctissima? Si qui recurrere audent ad sanctum Pontificem, & quae animadvertunt proponere decreverint, inconstantiae & levitatis notantur, in desertionis & Apostasiae crimen ac suspicionem pertrahuntur, tam assiduis & acerbis molestijs premuntur, ut etiam opprimantur. Unde haec malorum Ilias? quae parte certe fatalis illa Monarchia transcendit muros, qua certe dejecta strues, qua plena Professis potestas, ac libertas patet. Rogitabunt quis sim, ut ille Homericus, patria mihi omne solum, in quo Justitia & pietas sedent: Ego Theophilus vester, qui quod olim Athenienses magno Pompeio, ita hac schedula, quid petant, quid obtestentur a vobis, optimi religiosi, manifestum facio. Non sum vs, qui quaeram, quid Tyridatem terreat, paci studeo, & musis meis, nec tamen quasi qui ad Lucrinum conchas, ita tempus eludo.
units.tr: Caesar, august kings, invincible in hand, counsel and arms, show your favour and be kind. No one should speak before Agamemnon, prince of the Achaeans, unless he is utterly out of his mind; no one should say vain or foolish things. Before you, both matter and words must be carefully chosen. Who can hope for an audience if he is not worthy of the mind, or if absolute wisdom has not shaped him? I will not recount trivial or excessive matters, but what I have learned from the most distinguished and wisest men of the illustrious Order of the Society of Jesus, and what I have received from experience of the facts that I share. Xavier of Navarre, a most devout member of the Society of Jesus, spread the faith beyond Calpe, and no longer only to the farthest Thule beyond the Pillars of Hercules, among unknown and foreign regions. He was one of the first ten Fathers of the Society of Jesus, who together with Blessed Father Ignatius Loyola and ten others drew up and handed to the College short and precise rules for religious life. The holy Pontiff approved them, the bishops praised them, and they declared them suited and in keeping with the institutes of the holy Fathers. Afterwards Blessed Ignatius added some provisions which later members have turned to the Order's harm. They obtained from the Holy See privileges and new rights, which they use, not without complaints from the whole world and contrary to the mind of the supreme Pontiff, as they please. So that the Society's character may not turn away from Blessed Ignatius, and its life may not become alien to the illustrious Xavier, and so that a new Society does not thrust itself into the Society, we must return to the beginnings and draw from the sources. All of you who are Christian subjects in the world, and especially the Fathers of the Society, both those who still live in the Society and those whom the cruel spirit of certain superiors has compelled to leave it, all fall at your feet, so that by a truly Christian and just edict you may free so many chosen members from unbearable harassment, restrain that unusual power which the superiors have seized, and govern it with your gentle rule. What is more insolent? What is more hard and dreadful than that so many distinguished religious, whose zeal was such that they persevered in their vows, should be torn from the Society; and that, although they are not hostile to Christ, the proposition should nonetheless lead them to a spirit different from the Institute? What is more iron-hearted? What is more inhuman than that the best men, driven from the company of religious priests, should be torn apart by inhospitable and merciless tongues; that sons should be violently dragged from their mothers' breasts and dashed to the ground? Why does a condition so unlike the Society, of which all are said to be companions, shock us, one not derived from the Institute of the first Fathers of the Society, nor from the zeal of Blessed Father Ignatius: the disparity of condition, the difference of life, the uncertainty of religious vocation, the discrepancy of manners, the distinction of discipline, the most disjointed lot of burdens and labours? If any dare to appeal to the holy Pontiff, and resolve to set out what they have observed, they are branded with inconstancy and levity, dragged into suspicion of the crime of desertion and apostasy, and so harassed by such constant and bitter vexations that they are even crushed. Whence this Iliad of evils? It surely comes from that fatal monarchy which has crossed the walls, where, once that is overthrown, the structure falls, and where power and liberty lie open, full, for the professed. They will ask who I am, like that Homeric figure: every land is my fatherland in which justice and piety dwell. I am Theophilus, your servant, who, as the Athenians once did with great Pompey, so by this little writing I make plain to you, best of religious men, what they seek and what they beseech from you. I am not one who asks what frightens Tyridates; I devote myself to peace and to my Muses, yet I do not waste my time like one who plays with oysters at Lucrinus.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA
units.tr: DE DOCTRINA

units.la: Catholicis Regibus, patriæ & amicis meis servio, & fidem servo, patriæ obsequor, cuius querelas expono, amicis adsum, quibus hanc operam præsto. Regem justam exposcimus. Ordinem Iesuitarum restitui in primogenium vigorem; quid æquius? jus abrogari, quo abuntur in suam perniciem Religiosi, quid justius? religiosos cum religiosis convenire, quid congruentius? communi lege obstringi, quid cautius? charitatis necessitudinem servare, quid mansuetius? Deo & religionis cultui vacare, quid salubrius? Quinque primis annis, cum sub decem primorum Patrum legibus viguit Societas, unica Patrum tenebatur Professio, omnes eodem religionis jure potiebantur, ijsdem quoque votis solennibus sese Deo consecrabant, non erat novus Coadjutorum Sacerdotum gradus, qui cum solennibus votis astricti non sint, e Societate cum videbitur dimitti possunt, quidquid in ea tempora, etiam si triginta annis perstiterint. Non erat hæc religiosorum Sacerdotum forma, quorum status ex mero superiorum arbitrio pendet, non illa Malea, non Syrtis periculosus scopulus, non hoc votorum discrimen: ex quo magna est in Societate perturbatio, quæ in prima eiusdem institutione inaudita erat, cum secundum jura solita religionum, una duntaxat Professio colebatur. Præfigatur iterum justitiæ & pacis regula, unius Professionis vinculo: nemo queretur de perpetua vitæ suæ inconstantia, nemo vicissitudinem rerum pertimescet.
units.tr: We serve the Catholic kings, my country and my friends, and we keep faith. We obey our country, whose complaints we set out; we stand by our friends, to whom we offer this work. We demand that the king restore the Order of the Jesuits to its original vigour. What is fairer? Let the law be repealed by which religious men are abusing it to their own ruin. What is more just? Let religious men live together with religious men. What is more fitting? Let them be bound by a common law. What is more prudent? Let them keep the bond of charity. What is gentler? Let them be free for God and the worship of religion. What is more wholesome? In the first five years, while the Society flourished under the laws of the first ten Fathers, one profession alone was required of all of them. All enjoyed the same right of religion, and they consecrated themselves to God by the same solemn vows. There was no new grade of coadjutor priests, who, since they are not bound by solemn vows, may be dismissed from the Society whenever it seems good, however many years, even thirty, they have remained in it. That was not the form of the religious priests, whose status depends entirely on the arbitrary will of their superiors. It was not that Malea, not that dangerous reef of the Syrtes, not this peril of vows, from which great disorder has arisen in the Society, a disorder unheard of in its first institution, when, according to the customary laws of religious orders, only a single profession was observed. Let the rule of justice and peace be set up again, under the bond of one profession. Let no one complain of the perpetual uncertainty of his life, and let no one fear the changing of circumstances.

units.la: Sperabunt Scholastici post aliquos annos Professione statuta, certum a religione amoris fideique pignus, non alienas vestigabunt artes, unicam virtutem colent, ut Religiosa professione & solennitate non sint indigni. Qui dimittentur, mature exibunt, nulla solenni obligatione constricti, & eo probationis tempore, quo quidem secundum Beati Patris Ignatij institutum, etsi devincti simplicibus votis, non debent tamen aliud testari, quam se Candidatos esse Societatis, & in eam ingredi velle. Desinent tum a nobilibus, tum plebeis familijs frequentes querelæ, quæ hoc obtrudunt Societati, liberis & adolescentibus suis uti quamdiu placet, & tum, ubi avertit sententiam Superior aliquis infestus, torqueri suos miris modis, confulto duris Imperijs onerari, & nulla habita ratione contemptæ pridem pristinæ fortunæ, rejectæ rei familiaris & desertæ domus, de Societate hostili animo deturbari. Qui erunt adhuc Scholastici, vel perficient se & proficient, vel si deficere malint, & apostasione abhorreant, non invitis & sine parentum offensione ad sua revertentur antequam ad Sacerdotium pervenerint: stabilienda est altera, quæ erat in prima gubernatione ex primorum Patrum statuto moderatio, videlicet ut suffragijs jus suum reddatur.
units.tr: The scholastics will hope that after some years a profession will be fixed, a sure pledge of love and faith from the religious life. They will not hunt after other arts, but will cultivate the one virtue, so that they may not be unworthy of religious profession and solemnity. Those who are dismissed will leave early, bound by no solemn obligation. And during that time of probation, in which, according to the institute of the blessed Father Ignatius, even though they are bound by simple vows, they ought to declare nothing more than that they are candidates of the Society and wish to enter it, the frequent complaints of noble and plebeian families will cease. These complain that the Society claims the right to use their children and young men as long as it pleases, and that whenever some hostile superior turns his mind against them, they are tormented in strange ways, deliberately burdened with harsh commands, and, with no regard for their former fortune, their neglected family property, and the house they have abandoned, are driven out of the Society with hostile intent. Those who are still scholastics, whether they perfect and advance themselves, or if they prefer to fail and shrink from apostasy, shall return to their own homes, not against their will and without offence to their parents, before they reach the priesthood. The other moderation must be established, which was in the first government by the statute of the first Fathers: namely, that their right be restored to them in the votes.

units.la: Rector, Provincialis, Generalis in suos subditos omnem potestatem exercent, suis sententijs, quæ occurrunt, omnia definiunt, aliquotum audiunt sensa & monita, sed tamen ipsi soli quasi Dynastæ & Monarchæ, authoritate summa, & arbitrio suo constituunt. Cur antiquiores in Collegijs de sententia rogabuntur? Cur ad suffragia ferenda vocabuntur, si vnico Rectoris suffragio, velint, nolint, stare oporteat? Si quod velit Rector, idaperiet ac significabit, quod reticere voluerit, occultum silentio teget, nec mandabit effectui, nisi quod ipse apud se defixerit? Si quem ex suis ille pollens Rector odio ac male volentia infestetur, quis temperet homini? Si fallere velit, & prævaricari, quis deteget dolos? Si res Collegij dissipet, quis convincet criminis? Si plura in suos usus sibi arroget, quis commonefaciat liberè? Si a lege aberret, quis exolutum omni lege reprehendet? Si quid in Ecclesiam, si quid in Principem ausit, quis velit hunc hominem judicare, quem intelligit si infestum habeat, gravia & acerba quæque sibi perferenda? Quam multi ex Societate Davidicum illud non sine lachrymis repetunt, impositi homines super capita nostra. Qui sunt isti homines? infirmi ut homines propriis dediti commodis; non ut illi Stoici ad laborum perpessionem fortes ac duri, sed inclinantes quo præponderant sensus, & ad facilioris vitæ usum ac fruitionem non indociles: qui homines? deteriores an meliores Paulo Apostolo? Credo non meliores; qui collultantem adversus carnem spiritum experiuntur, qui qui timere debent, ne fiant reprobi. Cur ijs omnis in religiosos potestas? cur res collegij omnes, sacras ac profanas ex propria sententia statuent? Patrum sequuntur vel respuent, prout viderint, definitiones? Quis dicet incolumem diu Societatem, si tantum Rectores expatiari, si nullis finibus imperia sua coercere, si nullis metis obedientiae jura velint terminare? Propterea S. Pontificem urgere solent, ut hujusmodi principatum authoritate Apostolica communiat, ne si consensus Principum, ac populorum expectetur, tanta, tamque absoluta dominatio excindatur. Sed neque hoc tantum extorquent, verum si quos excelsi animi id aegre ferre senserint, auferre habent, consilijs suis abigunt, immoderatae severitatis tormento exagitant, quasi noxia capita, huc illucque distijcint, Romana professione interdicunt, non expedire, aiunt, nec tutum esse sancto Pontifici ad haec detegenda se sistere.
units.tr: The rector, the provincial and the general exercise every power over their subjects. They settle all matters by their own judgments as they arise. They hear some opinions and admonitions, but they alone, as if they were dynasts and monarchs, decide by supreme authority and their own will. Why will the older men in the colleges be asked for their opinion? Why will they be called to give their votes, if they must abide, whether they wish it or not, by the single vote of the rector? If the rector wishes something, he will reveal and announce it; what he has wished to keep silent, he will hide in silence, and he will carry out nothing except what he himself has resolved in his own mind. If that powerful rector should attack someone of his own people with hatred and ill will, who can restrain the man? If he wishes to deceive and to prevaricate, who will detect his tricks? If he squanders the goods of the college, who will convict him of the crime? If he claims more for his own uses, who will freely admonish him? If he strays from the law, who will rebuke a man who has been released from every law? If he dares anything against the Church or against the Prince, who would want to judge this man, when he knows that if he holds him in enmity, every harsh and bitter thing must be endured by himself? How many of the Society repeat with tears that saying of David: "You have set men over our heads." Who are these men? Weak, as men are, given over to their own advantages; not strong and hard for the endurance of labours, like those Stoics, but inclining wherever their senses weigh them down, and not unskilled at using and enjoying an easier life. What kind of men are they? Are they worse or better than the Apostle Paul? I believe not better, who experience the spirit struggling against the flesh, who ought to fear lest they become reprobate. Why is all power over religious men given to them? Why do they decide all the affairs of the college, sacred and profane, by their own opinion? Do they follow or reject the definitions of the Fathers, as they see fit? Who will say that the Society will remain safe for long, if the rectors are allowed to range freely, if they are willing to restrain their commands within no limits, if they wish to bound the laws of obedience by no boundaries? For this reason they are accustomed to urge the Holy Pontiff to fortify such a principate with apostolic authority, lest, if the consent of princes and peoples were awaited, so great and so absolute a domination should be overthrown. But they do not stop at extorting this. If they perceive that any men of lofty spirit take this badly, they have the means to remove them: they drive them away from their counsels, harass them with the torment of immoderate severity, and, as if they were guilty heads, scatter them hither and thither, and forbid them the Roman profession, saying that it is not expedient, nor safe for the Holy Pontiff, to submit himself to hearing these things revealed.

units.la: Refcire potuistis Augustissimi Principes, quis fuerit animus illorum Rectorum, qui Religiosum optimum de palatio Regis Hispaniae, ipso Rege nesciente, abripere moliebantur: Hinc illae ad Clementem octavum querelae, qui Patrem Claudium Aquavivam Generalem in Hispaniam ire iussit, ne Regibus suis auferretur Cliens, nulla integerrimo Patrifieret injuria. Si notae, si calculi parum vim haberent, si vigerent suffragia, non efferrentur ad hos animos, non hoc tenerent, non hos fluctus immiti suo tridente commoverent, non tot Religiosos ad scopulos impellerent, e quibus non nisi facto naufragio confractas tabulas, ac vix haerentes educere potuissent.
units.tr: Most august princes, you may have learned what was the purpose of those rectors who were planning to snatch the best religious man from the palace of the King of Spain, without the King himself knowing it. Hence those complaints to Clement VIII, who ordered Father Claudius Aquaviva, the General, to go to Spain, so that the most upright Father would not be taken from his kings as their client, and no injury would be done to him. If notes and votes had little force, if suffrages prevailed, these men would not be raised to such spirits, they would not keep to this course, they would not stir these waves with their cruel trident, they would not drive so many religious men onto the rocks, from which they could scarcely bring back the broken planks, with the ship wrecked, except after a shipwreck.

units.la: Queruntur denique viri Nobilissimi, Religiosos, quibus nulla saecularis cura incumbere deberet, sollicitos tamen esse de gubernatione Principum, de statu: falcem immittere in alienam segetem, humana tractare, cum divina deberent; certius ea cognoscere, quae in aedibus Regijs dicta vel facta sunt, quam quae in suis Collegijs sub umbra litteraria: paratiores viderint audiant Romanusne superbas invidae Carthaginis everterit arces, quam quid ad promovendam fidem Episcopi, sui vel alij religiosi excogitent, aut agrediantur: non convenire Patres Societatis ad publica pietatis munia, ad indictas supplicationes non adesse; quamvis nec Coenobitae sint, nec Monachi, nec solitudinis cultores, imo ne religiosi quidem professi; nisi admodum pauci: percurrere tamen vicos, obire civitates, obambulare in compitis, spectatores esse religiosae Pompae, cujus actores esse respuunt in communi sanctitatis theatro, cujus cultum, ut suis moribus abstmiem, exercere incommodum sibi esse existimant. Quod tam praesens consilium ad inanes illas curas exinaniendas? quae tam utilis & religiosa cura? illa nimirum, quam Basilius, Ambrosius, Gregorius Magnus, & multis retro seculis Patres viris religiosis antiquam & solennem esse voluerunt: decantandae destinatis horis sanctae Psalmodiae consuetudo, continua in divina Hierurgia, & ministerijs sacris occupatio. Si choro detinentur Iesuitae, puderet otiari, cum id muneris praestandum esset; nec tam multi patres a litterarum studijs, & ab omni Collegiorum cura reiecti familiares congressus quaererent, quibus extrudant tempus, et cubiculi mora se redimant: haberent, unde divini spiritus sofatium perfentirent, publicum illud Dei cum hominibus colloquium, ut fatigationis & laboris omnis levamen, felices experirentur, & tam secura ac pura cum Deo conversatione recreati, nihil de saecularium societate, convictu, de aucupandis sermonibus cogitarent.
units.tr: Finally, the most noble men complain that religious men, to whom no worldly care ought to belong, are nonetheless anxious about the government of princes and about the state. They put the sickle into another's harvest, they handle human matters when they ought to handle divine ones; they know more certainly what has been said or done in royal houses than what is done in their own colleges under the literary shade. Let them consider whether the Roman people overthrew the proud citadels of envious Carthage more readily than the bishops, or their own or other religious men, devise or undertake anything to advance the faith. The Fathers of the Society, they say, do not assemble for the public duties of piety, and do not attend the appointed supplications, even though they are neither cenobites, nor monks, nor cultivators of solitude, not even professed religious, except very few of them. Yet they run through the streets, visit the cities, stroll about the crossroads, and are spectators of the religious procession, whose actors they refuse to be in the common theatre of holiness, and they think it an inconvenience to them to practise its worship, lest they should abstain from their own customs. What is so useful and so religious a care for emptying out those idle cares? Surely it is that which Basil, Ambrose, Gregory the Great, and the Fathers in many earlier centuries wished to be ancient and solemn for religious men: the custom of singing the holy psalmody at appointed hours, and constant occupation in divine worship and sacred ministries. If the Jesuits were kept at the choir, they would be ashamed to be idle, since that duty was to be performed. Nor would so many Fathers, cast out from literary studies and from all care of the colleges, seek familiar gatherings by which they might pass their time and redeem the delay of the chamber. They would have the means from which to find the comfort of the divine Spirit, to experience that public conversation of God with men as a relief from all weariness and labour, and, refreshed by such a secure and pure converse with God, they would think nothing of the company of worldly people, of their dinners, or of hunting for their conversation.

units.la: Haec tria sunt, Principes, quae pro Societatis restauratione necessaria suaserunt mihi ipsi religiosi patres Societatis, ut proponerem, ne quis quasi ex pseudothyro egressam orationem meam contumeliose objiciat: Nullus est, si sana mentis, qui pulcherrimum istum & utilissimum ordinem deturbari velit, sed imprudens & indignus sit ille arbiter, qui negat ad primam frugem revocari debere, pacis ac virtutis leges ijs repetendas abnuat; qui primae regulae usu ac fructu spoliati, non sine ingenti maestitia testantur, penè se alios a primis suis Patribus ac degeneres exijsse. Una & aequali omnium professione (Augustissimi) ut jura communia sanciunt, & primi Societatis patres voluerunt, pacem, aequalitatem, sinceritatem ordini restituite, suffragiorum vi ac potestate dignitate, libertatem, ac
units.tr: These three things, Princes, are what the religious fathers of the Society themselves urged me to set out for its restoration, so that no one may spitefully object to my speech as though it had slipped out from behind a door. No one of sound mind wishes this most beautiful and most useful order to be overthrown. But that judge is unwise and unworthy who denies that the Society must be called back to its first fruit, or refuses to have the laws of peace and virtue restored to it. Those who have been deprived of the use and benefit of the original rule testify, not without great sorrow, that they have almost become degenerate children of their first fathers. By one and the same profession, most august princes, as the common laws decree and as the first fathers of the Society wished, restore to the order peace, equality and sincerity, the power and weight of votes, dignity, liberty, and

units.la: DE DOCTRINA res Societatis servate, Decantatione psalmodiæ, religionem, pietatem ac sanctitatem Societatis tueamini. CASPARI HAYVODI ANGLICI IE- SVITÆ SVPPLICATIO PRO EIVSDEM ORDI- NIS REFORMATIONE.
units.tr: On the Doctrine: keep the affairs of the Society, the chanting of the psalms; defend the religion, piety and holiness of the Society. The Supplication of Caspar Hayvodus, an English Jesuit, for the Reformation of the Same Order.

units.la: CAspar quoque Hayvodus Anglus, & Iesuitarum Anglorum tum in Anglia, tum extra ob animi dotes, & natalium honestatem celebratissimus ante aliquot annos Neapoli dicitur mortem obiisse. Is postquam in Societate Iesu annos triginta unum egisset, & eiusdem Societatis per annos viginti tres professus esset, & per tantum temporis suorum Iesuitarum mores, & procedendi modum, ut ipse ait, in omnibus fere Christiani orbis regionibus expertus esset, iam senex, totius Provinciæ Neapolitanæ professus (uno excepto) omnium antiquissimus esset, zelo ductus Societatis suæ ad patrem Claudium Aquavivam Præpositum generalem scripsit petens, ut ipsum iuberet Romam venire. Habere enim se multa, quæ illi coram ediceret in bonum Societatis, cuius infirmitatibus mederi cupiebat, antequam aliquis Societatis vel adversarius, vel Apostata eius defectus publicaret.
units.tr: Caspar Hayvodus, an Englishman, was also a Jesuit, highly celebrated among the English Jesuits both in England and abroad for his gifts of mind and the honourable standing of his birth. He is said to have died at Naples some years ago. After he had spent thirty-one years in the Society of Jesus and had been professed in it for twenty-three years, he had, as he himself says, experienced the conduct and methods of procedure of his fellow Jesuits in almost all the regions of the Christian world over so long a time. Now old, and the most senior of all the professed members of the Neapolitan Province except one, he was moved by zeal for his Society and wrote to Father Claudius Aquaviva, the Father General, asking that he be ordered to come to Rome. He had many things, he said, which he wished to set out to him in person for the good of the Society, whose weaknesses he desired to remedy before any adversary of the Society, or any apostate, made its defects public.

units.la: Ne vero pater Generalis rem levem, aut negligendam hanc illius petitionem existimaret, argumenta eorum, quæ compluria coram dicenda habuit, ad hæc quæ sequuntur, capita revocavit, & Romam ad Patrem Generalem misit anno 1590.
units.tr: So that the Father General should not think this request a trivial or negligible matter, he summarised the points of the many things he had intended to say in person under the following heads, and sent them to the Father General at Rome in 1590.

units.la: 1. Dicta, & facta publice circa primatum summi pontif. fidem sedis Apostolicæ, & potestatem illius.
units.tr: 1. The things said and done publicly concerning the primacy of the supreme pontiff, the faith of the Apostolic See, and its power.

units.la: 2. De modo procedendi superiorum in Societate in gravissimis Christi causis, in quibus mori tenebantur potius quam sic prodere veritatem.
units.tr: 2. The manner in which the superiors in the Society proceed in the most serious causes of Christ, in which they ought rather to die than thus betray the truth.

units.la: 3. Concernit admiranda in administrando Sacramento Pœnitentiæ, & varias superiorum ordinationes in eadem materia.
units.tr: 3. Concerning the admirable things in the administration of the Sacrament of Penance, and the various directives of the superiors on the same matter.

units.la: 4. De periculosis dogmatibus & doctrinis inauditis, quas (licet multa eiusmodi intelligat) tamen nunquam tales audivit Reverentia vestra.
units.tr: 4. Concerning dangerous doctrines and unheard-of teachings, which (though he understands many things of this kind) your Reverence has never heard such things.

units.la: 5. Aperientur multa, eaque periculosiora, & contradictoria nostrorum in dictis & factis circa negotia maxima Christi & Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 5. Many things will be disclosed, and those more dangerous, and the contradictory sayings and doings of our men concerning the greatest affairs of Christ and the Church.

units.la: 6. Continet stupenda de Societate in dictis & factis tum Superiorum, tum aliorum, ad exaltationem Societatis nostræ.
units.tr: 6. It contains astonishing things about the Society, in the words and deeds both of the superiors and of others, for the exaltation of our Society.

units.la: 7. Concernit varia negotia circa iustitiam & iniustitiam.
units.tr: 7. It concerns various matters touching justice and injustice.

units.la: 8. Quod multis in locis despolijs Amalech, & Iericho forte nostris adhæserunt (nesciente vestra Paternitate) ut metuendum sit, ne tangatur anathemate.
units.tr: 8. In many places our men have clung to the spoils of Amalek and Jericho, perhaps (your Paternity being unaware), so that it is to be feared they have been touched by the anathema.

units.la: 9. De mala fide Superiorum Societatis, tum in mandandis suis subditis, tum in relationibus ad Provinciales, & Provincialium ad Patrem Generalem, & litteris intercipiendis.
units.tr: 9. Concerning the bad faith of the superiors of the Society, both in their instructions to their subjects and in their reports to the provincials, and of the provincials to the Father General, and in the interception of letters.

units.la: 10. Concernit quasdam evasiones, quibus se defendunt in tenebris, ne inlucem veniant, & illis remedium afferatur.
units.tr: 10. It concerns certain evasions by which they defend themselves in darkness, so that they do not come into the light, and a remedy for these.

units.la: 11. De falsitatibus, signis & miraculis, narrationibus & mirandis, quibus non solum apud nostros, sed etiam apud exteros Societatis dignitatem extollunt, de quibus necesse est, ut veritas manifestetur, aliter metuendum est, ne veniat exitium Societatis.
units.tr: 11. Concerning falsehoods, signs and miracles, and wonderful narratives, by which they extol the dignity of the Society not only among our own people but also among outsiders. Of these it is necessary that the truth be made plain; otherwise it is to be feared that the ruin of the Society will come.

units.la: Hisce & huiusmodi litteris ad Patrem Generalem semel atque iterum scriptis P. Caspar nihil responsi ab illo habere potuit, nisi molles & frigidas quasdam ain excusationes, scilicet, ob adventantes ad Congregationem Generalem intantem Procuratores tantas esse angustias domus & camerarum parvitatem, ut locus non esset P. Caspar recipiendo.
units.tr: Although Father Caspar wrote these and similar letters to the Father General once and again, he could get nothing from him in reply except some soft and lukewarm excuses: namely, that because the procurators coming to the General Congregation were so many, the house and its rooms were so cramped that there was no place for Father Caspar to be received.

units.la: Ea tempestate D. Ludovicus Adoenus Anglus piae memoriae Episcopus Cafanensis in Curia Rom. sanctiss. D. Nostri assistens regularium omnium vilitatio-ni & reformationi praefuit, cui P. Caspar notus a multis annis, & carus fuit; quapropter P. Caspar cernens se zelumque suum a P. Generali suo contemtum esse, ad Episcopum Cafanensem tamquam regularium reformatorem, & Pontificis regularium causis assistentem scripsit, & exemplar suarum litterarum ad Patrem Generalem una cum Patris Generalis ad illum responso mittens, ut Pontifici rem totam insinuaret, & si videretur, se Romam vocari uraret ad reddendam summo Pontifici de his omnibus rationem, sed in hac re & secreto, & festinatione opus esse, periculum enim esse maximum, ne Patres Iesuitae, qui tantum pollent, & omnia scrutantur in Curia Romana, rem comertam summi Pontificis iussum anticipent, & se longius aliquo ablegent, ut in conspectum Pontificis unquam venire illi impossibile sit.
units.tr: At that time Lewis Adoenus, an Englishman of pious memory, Bishop of Cassano, who was attending upon our most holy Lord in the Roman Curia, presided over the visitation and reformation of all the regular orders. Father Caspar had been known to him and dear to him for many years. Therefore Father Caspar, perceiving that he and his zeal were despised by his own General, wrote to the Bishop of Cassano as reformer of the regulars and as one assisting the Pope in matters concerning the regular orders. He sent a copy of his letters together with the Father General's reply to them, so that the whole matter might be laid before the Pontiff; and, if it seemed good, that he might urge that he himself be summoned to Rome to render an account to the supreme Pontiff of all these things. But in this matter, he said, secrecy and haste were needed, for there was the greatest danger that the Fathers the Jesuits, who are very powerful and pry into everything in the Roman Curia, might anticipate the matter, which had come to the notice of the supreme Pontiff, and send him some distance away, so that it would be impossible for him ever to come into the sight of the Pontiff.

units.la: Interea temporis P. Caspar nactus hominem C. P. Iosephum a Costa Hispanum Iesuitam, qui plurimum pollebat apud Nuncium in Urbe Catholicum, ad Pontificem scripsit litteras, quae summam rerum continebant, quas D. Nuncius in Urbe Catholicus summo Pontifici porrexit, is autem fuit Dux de essa.
units.tr: Meanwhile Father Caspar found a man, Joseph a Costa, a Spanish Jesuit who had great influence with the Catholic Nuncio in the City, and wrote a letter to the Pontiff containing the substance of the matter. The Catholic Nuncio in the City handed it to the supreme Pontiff; and this man was the Duke of Essa.

units.la: Pontifex & verbis Episcopi Cafanensis monitus, & ipsius P. Caspari litteris excitatus, rem putat non esse neglígendam. Antequam tamen P. Casparum Romam venire iuberet, mandat Nuncio suo Neapoli agenti, ut P. Casparum Ioyvodum Iesuitam ad se accersitum audiret. Nuncius hominem accersit, mandata summi Pontificis exponit, his de rebus differentem & pluries, & singulis vicibus per aliquot horas audit. Quid Iesuitae? illico suspicantur, illico rem sublent. Quid multa? effectum est Neapoli, ut D. Nuncius Apostolicus perterriret P. Casparum deferret, Romae vero ut Pontifex persuasus, hunc P. Casparum insanire, & ab illo Romam vocando desisteret.
units.tr: The Pontiff, warned both by the words of the Bishop of Cassano and roused by the letters of Father Caspar himself, judged that the matter should not be neglected. Before he ordered Father Caspar to come to Rome, however, he instructed his Nuncio, who was at Naples, to summon Father Caspar Hayvodus, the Jesuit, to him and hear him. The Nuncio summoned the man, set out the commands of the supreme Pontiff, and heard him speaking on these matters many times, each time for some hours. What then did the Jesuits do? At once they suspected, and at once they undermined the matter. To make a long story short: at Naples the Apostolic Nuncio was made to frighten Father Caspar and to put him down, while at Rome the Pontiff was persuaded that this Father Caspar was insane, and gave up calling him to Rome.

units.la: Pater Casparus cernens, se quidem a Domino Nuncio Apostolico & delictum, & sanctissimum hac falsa suggestione delusum, scripsit ad Episcopum Cafanensem, se quidem aequissimo animo ferre, quod zelus suus pro Domino Dei non successerit, sufficere enim sibi, quod functus sit, quod potuit, officio viri bene cupientis Societati suae & Ecclesiae Catholicae, reliquum quod est, se Deo committere, demirari tamen se tam ineptam stropham, qua Patres sui per sanctissimum Dominum deluserant: nam inquit, si me stultum sanctissimi Dominum nostrum alloqui sivissent, Pontifex sapientissimus me despientem esse in primo congressu statim deprehendisset & reiecisset cum magno Patrum nostrorum honore, & conscientiae testimonio: constitisset enim illos ficin-tes esse, ut neminem invenirent reprehensorem nisi unum insanum. Haec P. Caspar in litteris suis ad Episcopum Cafanensem.
units.tr: Father Caspar, seeing that he had been both wronged by the Apostolic Lord Nuncio and deluded by this false suggestion of the most holy man, wrote to the Bishop of Cassano that he bore it with the most equable mind that his zeal for the Lord God had not succeeded; for it was enough for him that he had done what he could in the office of a man who wished well to his Society and to the Catholic Church, and that the rest he committed to God. Yet he marvelled at so inept a trick by which his Fathers had deluded the most holy Lord. For, he said, if they had allowed me, a fool, to address our most holy Lord, the wisest Pontiff would at once have detected in the first meeting that I was raving, and would have rejected me, with great honour to our Fathers and with a testimony of conscience; for they would have been shown to be pretenders, since they could find no one to reprove them except a madman. Such is what Father Caspar wrote in his letters to the Bishop of Cassano.

units.la: DE DOCTRINA IESVITARVM. APPENDIX.
units.tr: APPENDIX TO THE DOCTRINE OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: PAgina 134. facì ëb. sequentia sunt addenda: paulò post hoc Decretum in Comitiis Vratislaviæ a Protestantibus Silesiæ Ordinibus habitis Decretum inter alia quoq; de Iesuitis Provincia tota profligandis factum est, Iohanne Christiano Duce Lignitzensi programma eiusmodi publicante. Non dubitare, inquit, quin Principes & Ordines utriusque superioris & inferioris Silesiæ Augustanam Confessionem amplectentes omnes, in recenti adhuc memoria habeant, quid ante hæc tempora, maximè vero 12. Martij anno 1596. supplicando à Cæsare petierint, ut nimirum pestilens illa Iesuitarum secta, ob perniciosa consilia & machinationes varias ad statum omnem politicum quietum turbandum ab ipsis directas regionibus istis suis excluderetur, addita malorum omnium, quæ à Secta ista, nisi ei mature occurreretur, expectanda patriæ & posteritati essent, prolixa demonstratione. Etsi vero Deo mentem Cæsaris mirabiliter tum gubernante, regiones istæ à Iesuitarum accessu liberatæ & prohibitæ fuerint, ipsam tamen experientiam jam testari, & deplorandum potius quam probandum esse, quid in vicino & confæderato Bohemiæ Regno ab ipsis factum hactenus fuerit, eundem enim jam effectum fructumque, quem pleraque in orbe Christiano Regna alia, turbas nimirum & confusiones maximas experiri. Quod igitur à Bohemis & confæderatis Provinciis factum, dum decreverint, ut communi consensu simul omnes ex regionibus suis proscriberentur, idem & sibi faciendum Principes & Ordines Silesiæ Protestantes, justissimis de causis censuisse, cum dubitandum non sit id daturos operam Iesuitas, ut quemadmodum ad alia antehac regna, sic ad suas quoq; Regiones aditum sibi per insidias patefaciant, nec defuturos cogitent, qui locum ipsis in ditionibus suis permittant. Ne igitur hoc fiat, Iesuitis quidem ne quis Regionem istam ingrediatur sub capitis pœna, aliis vero ne locum ipsis permittant sub dignitatis et honorum omnium amissione severissime mandare. Hoc suum decretum pacis amantes Catholicos statuos finistre acceptu-ros non putare, quin potius statuere, intellecturos eos facile, medium hoc esse ad pacem & concordiam inter eos & Protestantes Augustanæ Confessionis Ordines conservandam unicum & verissimum, si ab irrequietis istis & maleferiatis hominibus, qui ipsum humanæ Societatis vinculum, quod in data fide, & pactorum observantia consistit, pervertere conantur, liberi & immunes esse possint. Si vero aliter facere non posse, quam ut bro pace, & tranquillitate conservanda, decretum hoc, experientibus ita Principibus Statibusque Protestantibus aliis publici juris faciat. Omnes igitur & singulos monere, ut decretum hoc strictissime observent, nec quicquam vel contra faciant, vel contra fieri quacunque ratione permittant.
units.tr: Page 134, the following must be added. Shortly after this decree, at the Diet of Breslau held by the Protestant Estates of Silesia, a decree was made, among other things, concerning the total expulsion of the Jesuits from the province, John Christian, Duke of Liegnitz, publishing a notice of this kind. He does not doubt, he says, that all the Princes and Estates of both Upper and Lower Silesia who embrace the Augsburg Confession still keep in fresh memory what they earlier petitioned of the Emperor, especially on 12 March in the year 1596: that this pestilent sect of the Jesuits, on account of their pernicious counsels and various machinations directed by them to disturb the whole political peace, should be shut out of their regions, with a lengthy demonstration added of all the evils to be expected from this sect by the country and by posterity unless it were promptly countered. And although, at that time, God wonderfully governed the mind of the Emperor, and these regions were freed and barred from the admission of the Jesuits, experience itself now bears witness, and it is to be lamented rather than approved, what has so far been done by them in the neighbouring and allied Kingdom of Bohemia; for they are now experiencing the same effect and fruit that most other kingdoms of the Christian world have experienced, namely very great disturbances and confusions. Therefore, since the Bohemians and the allied provinces have resolved that all of them be banished together from their regions by common consent, the Protestant Princes and Estates of Silesia have judged, for most just reasons, that the same should be done by themselves; for there is no doubt that the Jesuits will take pains, by plots, to open for themselves access to their regions just as they have done before to other kingdoms, nor will there be lacking those who think they should be allowed a place in their dominions. Lest this happen, they strictly order that no one enter this region under pain of death for the Jesuits, and that others not permit them a place under pain of severe loss of all dignities and honours. They do not think that Catholics who love peace will take this their decree badly; rather, they judge that such Catholics will easily understand that this is the one and only true means of preserving peace and concord between them and the Estates of the Augsburg Confession, if they can be free and exempt from these restless and mischievous men, who strive to pervert the very bond of human society, which consists in good faith and the observance of agreements. But if they cannot act otherwise than by making this decree known publicly to other Princes and Estates, for the sake of preserving peace and tranquillity, let them do so. Therefore they admonish all and each to observe this decree most strictly, and neither to act against it nor to permit anything to be done against it by any means whatever.

units.tr: Page 113, back side, lines 7 and 8, let these be corrected. For "exsequutionum," read "exsecutionem"; for "teδnis," read "technis"; for "animus," read "artibus." The remaining errors, if any, the kind reader will easily correct.
